cards.standardTitle: Key literary elements add layers of meaning
cards.excerpt: OEDIPUS. Stern-visaged queens, since coming to this land First in your sanctuary I bent the knee, Frown not on me or Phoebus, who, when erst He told me all my miseries to come, Spake of this respite after many years, Some haven in a far-off land, a rest Vouchsafed at last by dread divinities. “There,” said he, “shalt thou round thy weary life, A blessing to the land wherein thou dwell’st, But to the land that cast thee forth, a curse.” And of my weird he promised signs should come, Earthquake, or thunderclap, or lightning flash. And now I recognize as yours the sign That led my wanderings to this your grove; Else had I never lighted on you first, A wineless man on your seat of native rock. O goddesses, fulfill Apollo’s word, Grant me some consummation of my life, If haply I appear not all too vile, A thrall to sorrow worse than any slave. Hear, gentle daughters of primeval Night, Hear, namesake of great Pallas; Athens, first Of cities, pity this dishonored shade, The ghost of him who once was Oedipus.
cards.whyThisWorks: Oedipus's speech reveals his character through a combination of humble supplication, self-deprecation ('all too vile, / A thrall to sorrow worse than any slave'), and appeal to divine prophecy, showing how a broken man still claims prophetic significance—a rich tension that rewards analysis of characterization.
cards.skillStrategy: When a character speaks, notice what they say about themselves and what they ask for—the gap between how they describe themselves and what they believe they deserve reveals who they truly are.
evidencePoints: If haply I appear not all too vile, / A thrall to sorrow worse than any slave.
The ghost of him who once was Oedipus.
cards.question: In his speech, Oedipus refers to himself as 'A thrall to sorrow worse than any slave' and then as 'The ghost of him who once was Oedipus.' What do these self-descriptions reveal about his character?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Oedipus is consumed by bitterness toward the gods who cursed him and refuses to accept their authority over his fate.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Oedipus presents himself as utterly degraded and nearly erased, yet he still appeals to divine prophecy as proof that his suffering carries a larger purpose.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Oedipus acknowledges his past crimes and seeks to warn Athens that sheltering him will bring the same destruction he brought to Thebes.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Oedipus uses humble language only to flatter the goddesses, while his true confidence in his own greatness remains unchanged from his days as king.

cards.standardTitle: Theme development across a literary text
cards.excerpt:
ISMENE. Bethink thee, sister, of our father’s fate, Abhorred, dishonored, self-convinced of sin, Blinded, himself his executioner. Think of his mother-wife (ill sorted names) Done by a noose herself had twined to death And last, our hapless brethren in one day, Both in a mutual destiny involved, Self-slaughtered, both the slayer and the slain. Bethink thee, sister, we are left alone; Shall we not perish wretchedest of all, If in defiance of the law we cross A monarch’s will?—weak women, think of that, Not framed by nature to contend with men. Remember this too that the stronger rules; We must obey his orders, these or worse. Therefore I plead compulsion and entreat The dead to pardon. I perforce obey The powers that be. ’Tis foolishness, I ween, To overstep in aught the golden mean.

ANTIGONE. I urge no more; nay, wert thou willing still, I would not welcome such a fellowship. Go thine own way; myself will bury him. How sweet to die in such employ, to rest,— Sister and brother linked in love’s embrace— A sinless sinner, banned awhile on earth, But by the dead commended; and with them I shall abide for ever. As for thee, Scorn, if thou wilt, the eternal laws of Heaven.
cards.whyThisWorks: The excerpt contrasts Ismene's submission to mortal authority with Antigone's willingness to die for divine law, giving students two competing value systems from which to identify which details actually develop the theme of moral duty versus self-preservation rather than merely referencing the family's tragic history.
cards.skillStrategy: Ask yourself: does this detail show the theme being tested, or does it just describe what happened in the story? Only choose the detail that proves the theme is growing.
evidencePoints: Scorn, if thou wilt, the eternal laws of Heaven.
How sweet to die in such employ, to rest,— / Sister and brother linked in love's embrace— / A sinless sinner, banned awhile on earth, / But by the dead commended
cards.question: The exchange between Ismene and Antigone develops the theme that devotion to divine or moral law outweighs the fear of death or punishment. Which detail from the excerpt most directly develops this theme?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Ismene recounts that their father was 'self-convinced of sin' and became 'himself his executioner,' showing the family has already suffered from defying fate.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Antigone calls death 'sweet' in the act of burying her brother and declares she will be 'by the dead commended,' framing sacrifice as honorable fulfillment of a higher duty.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Ismene reminds Antigone that they are 'weak women, not framed by nature to contend with men,' establishing that gender limits their choices.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Ismene notes that both brothers were 'self-slaughtered, both the slayer and the slain,' confirming the family's history of mutual destruction.

cards.standardTitle: Text structure and feature purpose
cards.excerpt:
THESEUS. I know that none Shall hale thee hence in my despite. Such threats Vented in anger oft, are blusterers, An idle breath, forgot when sense returns. And for thy foemen, though their words were brave, Boasting to bring thee back, they are like to find The seas between us wide and hard to sail. Such my firm purpose, but in any case Take heart, since Phoebus sent thee here. My name, Though I be distant, warrants thee from harm.

CHORUS. (Str. 1) Thou hast come to a steed-famed land for rest, O stranger worn with toil, To a land of all lands the goodliest Colonus’ glistening soil. ’Tis the haunt of the clear-voiced nightingale, Who hid in her bower, among The wine-dark ivy that wreathes the vale, Trilleth her ceaseless song; And she loves, where the clustering berries nod O’er a sunless, windless glade, The spot by no mortal footstep trod, The pleasance kept for the Bacchic god, Where he holds each night his revels wild With the nymphs who fostered the lusty child.
cards.whyThisWorks: The two sections perform distinct structural jobs—Theseus's speech delivers a personal pledge of military protection against named enemies, while the Chorus's ode pivots to lyrical celebration of Colonus's sacred natural landscape—giving students a clear contrast to analyze for paragraph/section purpose.
cards.skillStrategy: Ask yourself what each section is doing: is it arguing, promising, describing, warning, or celebrating? Then match each section's job to the specific words the author chose.
evidencePoints: My name, Though I be distant, warrants thee from harm.
Thou hast come to a steed-famed land for rest, O stranger worn with toil, To a land of all lands the goodliest Colonus' glistening soil.
cards.question: Theseus ends his speech by pledging, 'My name, Though I be distant, warrants thee from harm,' focusing on protection from enemies. The Chorus then opens its ode: 'Thou hast come to a steed-famed land for rest, O stranger worn with toil, To a land of all lands the goodliest Colonus' glistening soil.' What is the primary job of the Chorus's ode section compared to Theseus's speech section?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The Chorus's ode extends Theseus's argument against the stranger's enemies by describing the 'wide and hard to sail' seas and the military strength behind Colonus's 'steed-famed' reputation as reasons the enemies cannot reach him.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The Chorus's ode shifts from Theseus's personal pledge of protection against enemies to celebrating the sacred natural beauty of Colonus—its nightingale, 'wine-dark ivy,' and Bacchic groves—as the stranger's place of rest.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The Chorus's ode contradicts Theseus's welcome by warning the stranger that the grove 'by no mortal footstep trod' and its connection to the Bacchic god make Colonus a forbidden and dangerous place for him.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The Chorus's ode repeats Theseus's promise of safety by directly addressing the stranger's enemies and reminding them that the 'sunless, windless glade' and 'clustering berries' of Colonus will conceal him from pursuit.

cards.standardTitle: Key literary elements add layers of meaning
cards.excerpt: CREON. O cease, you vex me with your babblement; I am like to think you dote in your old age. Is it not arrant folly to pretend That gods would have a thought for this dead man? Did they forsooth award him special grace, And as some benefactor bury him, Who came to fire their hallowed sanctuaries, To sack their shrines, to desolate their land, And scout their ordinances? Or perchance The gods bestow their favors on the bad. No! no! I have long noted malcontents Who wagged their heads, and kicked against the yoke, Misliking these my orders, and my rule. ’Tis they, I warrant, who suborned my guards By bribes. Of evils current upon earth The worst is money. Money ’tis that sacks Cities, and drives men forth from hearth and home; Warps and seduces native innocence, And breeds a habit of dishonesty. But they who sold themselves shall find their greed Out-shot the mark, and rue it soon or late. Yea, as I still revere the dread of Zeus, By Zeus I swear, except ye find and bring Before my presence here the very man Who carried out this lawless burial, Death for your punishment shall not suffice. Hanged on a cross, alive ye first shall make Confession of this outrage. This will teach you What practices are like to serve your turn. There are some villainies that bring no gain. For by dishonesty the few may thrive, The many come to ruin and disgrace.
cards.whyThisWorks: Creon's escalating threats, sweeping condemnation of money, and invocation of Zeus reveal a ruler whose paranoia and self-righteousness define his character and foreshadow his tragic downfall.
cards.skillStrategy: When a character speaks, notice what they assume, accuse, and threaten — those choices reveal who they really are beneath the surface.
evidencePoints: I have long noted malcontents / Who wagged their heads, and kicked against the yoke, / Misliking these my orders, and my rule.
Hanged on a cross, alive ye first shall make / Confession of this outrage.
cards.question: In his speech, Creon immediately assumes that his guards were bribed by political enemies and threatens them with death by crucifixion. What do these actions reveal about Creon's character?

choices.label: A
choices.text: He is a deeply religious ruler whose primary concern is honoring Zeus above all other obligations.

choices.label: B
choices.text: He is a paranoid and authoritarian leader who interprets any challenge to his rule as personal betrayal deserving extreme punishment.

choices.label: C
choices.text: He is a just ruler who carefully weighs evidence before deciding how to punish those who disobey his laws.

choices.label: D
choices.text: He is a pragmatic leader whose anger is directed at the corrupting power of money rather than at the guards themselves.

cards.standardTitle: Text structure and feature purpose
cards.excerpt:
POLYNEICES. Ah me, my sisters, shall I first lament My own afflictions, or my aged sire’s, Whom here I find a castaway, with you, In a strange land, an ancient beggar clad In antic tatters, marring all his frame, While o’er the sightless orbs his unkept locks Float in the breeze; and, as it were to match, He bears a wallet against hunger’s pinch. All this too late I learn, wretch that I am, Alas! I own it, and am proved most vile In my neglect of thee: I scorn myself. But as almighty Zeus in all he doth Hath Mercy for co-partner of this throne, Let Mercy, father, also sit enthroned In thy heart likewise. For transgressions past May be amended, cannot be made worse.

Why silent? Father, speak, nor turn away, Hast thou no word, wilt thou dismiss me then In mute disdain, nor tell me why thou art wrath? O ye his daughters, sisters mine, do ye This sullen, obstinate silence try to move. Let him not spurn, without a single word Of answer, me the suppliant of the god.
cards.whyThisWorks: The two paragraphs have distinct jobs—the first builds a mercy appeal through vivid description of Oedipus's suffering, while the second pivots to demanding a verbal response—making this excerpt ideal for teaching how paragraph sections serve different structural purposes within a speech.
cards.skillStrategy: Ask yourself: what task is each paragraph doing for the speaker's argument—is it building a case, shifting focus, or doing something else entirely?
evidencePoints: Father, speak, nor turn away
This sullen, obstinate silence try to move
cards.question: In the first paragraph, Polyneices builds his appeal by describing Oedipus as a 'castaway' in 'antic tatters' and asking that Mercy 'sit enthroned / In thy heart likewise.' What is the primary job of the second paragraph in relation to the first paragraph?

choices.label: A
choices.text: It deepens the mercy appeal by returning to the image of Oedipus as a 'castaway' and adding new details about his suffering to strengthen the case for forgiveness.

choices.label: B
choices.text: It shifts from making the mercy appeal to pressing urgently for a spoken reply, commanding 'Father, speak, nor turn away' and enlisting his sisters to break Oedipus's 'sullen, obstinate silence.'

choices.label: C
choices.text: It replaces the appeal to Mercy with a new argument grounded in sacred duty, reframing Oedipus's silence as a wrong against 'me the suppliant of the god' and making divine obligation the paragraph's central focus.

choices.label: D
choices.text: It closes Polyneices' speech by accepting Oedipus's 'mute disdain' as a final answer and withdrawing the request that Mercy 'sit enthroned' in his father's heart.

cards.standardTitle: Key literary elements add layers of meaning
cards.excerpt: ANTIGONE. What but the thought of our two brothers dead, The one by Creon graced with funeral rites, The other disappointed? Eteocles He hath consigned to earth (as fame reports) With obsequies that use and wont ordain, So gracing him among the dead below. But Polyneices, a dishonored corse, (So by report the royal edict runs) No man may bury him or make lament— Must leave him tombless and unwept, a feast For kites to scent afar and swoop upon. Such is the edict (if report speak true) Of Creon, our most noble Creon, aimed At thee and me, aye me too; and anon He will be here to promulgate, for such As have not heard, his mandate; ’tis in sooth No passing humor, for the edict says Whoe’er transgresses shall be stoned to death. So stands it with us; now ’tis thine to show If thou art worthy of thy blood or base.
cards.whyThisWorks: Antigone's closing challenge—'now 'tis thine to show / If thou art worthy of thy blood or base'—reveals her as someone who frames defiance of Creon's edict as a matter of family honor and moral courage, allowing students to analyze how her speech characterizes her values and her relationship with her sister.
cards.skillStrategy: When a character speaks directly to another, pay attention to the words they choose and the challenge they issue—those choices reveal what the character believes and what kind of person they are.
evidencePoints: 'now 'tis thine to show / If thou art worthy of thy blood or base'
'our most noble Creon'—said of the man who issued the edict
cards.question: Read Antigone's closing words: 'now 'tis thine to show / If thou art worthy of thy blood or base.' What do these words reveal about Antigone's character?

choices.label: A
choices.text: She is frightened by Creon's edict and is asking her sister to help her escape punishment.

choices.label: B
choices.text: She measures loyalty to family above obedience to the state, and she pressures her sister to prove the same courage.

choices.label: C
choices.text: She believes her sister is already planning to defy Creon and is simply confirming that plan.

choices.label: D
choices.text: She is indifferent to Polyneices' burial and is only concerned with whether her sister will support her politically.

cards.standardTitle: Key literary elements add layers of meaning
cards.excerpt: CREON. Not deeming this city void of men Or counsel, son of Aegeus, as thou say’st I did what I have done; rather I thought Your people were not like to set such store by kin of mine and keep them ’gainst my will. Nor would they harbor, so I stood assured, A godless parricide, a reprobate Convicted of incestuous marriage ties. For on her native hill of Ares here (I knew your far-famed Areopagus) Sits Justice, and permits not vagrant folk To stay within your borders. In that faith I hunted down my quarry; and e’en then I had refrained but for the curses dire Wherewith he banned my kinsfolk and myself: Such wrong, methought, had warrant for my act. Anger has no old age but only death; The dead alone can feel no touch of spite. So thou must work thy will; my cause is just But weak without allies; yet will I try, Old as I am, to answer deeds with deeds.
cards.whyThisWorks: Creon's speech reveals his character through self-justifying reasoning, his invocation of divine justice, and his defiant closing threat, showing how his pride and anger define him even when he acknowledges weakness.
cards.skillStrategy: When a character speaks to defend himself, ask what his word choices and logic reveal about his values and flaws—not just what he says, but what it shows about who he is.
evidencePoints: Anger has no old age but only death; The dead alone can feel no touch of spite.
So thou must work thy will; my cause is just But weak without allies; yet will I try, Old as I am, to answer deeds with deeds.
cards.question: Read the following lines from Creon's speech: 'Anger has no old age but only death; The dead alone can feel no touch of spite. So thou must work thy will; my cause is just / But weak without allies; yet will I try, / Old as I am, to answer deeds with deeds.' What do these lines reveal about Creon's character?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Creon admits his actions were wrong and asks for forgiveness, showing he has grown humble through conflict.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Creon acknowledges his disadvantaged position yet refuses to back down, revealing that his pride and anger override his awareness of his own weakness.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Creon warns his opponent that the gods will punish anyone who acts against justice, showing his deep religious devotion.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Creon reveals that he acted out of grief rather than anger, showing that his emotions have softened as he has grown older.

cards.excerpt:
ISMENE. Bethink thee, sister, of our father’s fate, Abhorred, dishonored, self-convinced of sin, Blinded, himself his executioner. Think of his mother-wife (ill sorted names) Done by a noose herself had twined to death And last, our hapless brethren in one day, Both in a mutual destiny involved, Self-slaughtered, both the slayer and the slain. Bethink thee, sister, we are left alone; Shall we not perish wretchedest of all, If in defiance of the law we cross A monarch’s will?—weak women, think of that, Not framed by nature to contend with men. cards.whyThisWorks: Antigone's speech functions as a direct structural counter to Ismene's speech, shifting from submission and fear to defiant acceptance of death, making the paragraph's job identifiable through contrasting claims and evidence.
cards.skillStrategy: Ask yourself: what does this paragraph do in relation to what came before—does it extend, contradict, qualify, or redirect the argument?
evidencePoints: I would not welcome such a fellowship
How sweet to die in such employ…A sinless sinner, banned awhile on earth, / But by the dead commended
cards.question: Ismene closes her speech by calling defiance 'foolishness' and declaring 'I perforce obey / The powers that be.' What is the structural job of Antigone's speech that immediately follows?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Antigone's speech extends Ismene's argument by conceding that 'the stronger rules' and that their shared suffering—their father's fate and their brothers' deaths—makes open defiance too dangerous for either sister.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Antigone's speech directly counters Ismene's case for submission by rejecting her help—'I would not welcome such a fellowship'—and reframing burial as honorable: dying is 'sweet,' she is a 'sinless sinner,' and she will be 'by the dead commended.'

choices.label: C
choices.text: Antigone's speech qualifies Ismene's position by accepting that 'weak women' cannot contend with Creon alone, but arguing that the dead—their 'hapless brethren'—deserve private mourning rather than public burial.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Antigone's speech redirects Ismene's catalog of family suffering toward a shared plan, urging Ismene to reconsider her refusal before Antigone acts and both sisters risk perishing 'wretchedest of all.'

cards.standardTitle: Key literary elements add layers of meaning
cards.excerpt: ANTIGONE. Yea, for these laws were not ordained of Zeus, And she who sits enthroned with gods below, Justice, enacted not these human laws. Nor did I deem that thou, a mortal man, Could’st by a breath annul and override The immutable unwritten laws of Heaven. They were not born today nor yesterday; They die not; and none knoweth whence they sprang. I was not like, who feared no mortal’s frown, To disobey these laws and so provoke The wrath of Heaven. I knew that I must die, E’en hadst thou not proclaimed it; and if death Is thereby hastened, I shall count it gain. For death is gain to him whose life, like mine, Is full of misery. Thus my lot appears Not sad, but blissful; for had I endured To leave my mother’s son unburied there, I should have grieved with reason, but not now. And if in this thou judgest me a fool, Methinks the judge of folly’s not acquit.
cards.whyThisWorks: Antigone's declaration that she 'feared no mortal's frown' and counts death a 'gain' rather than a punishment reveals her as someone whose moral courage is rooted in divine law over human authority, adding meaning to her defiance as principled rather than reckless.
cards.skillStrategy: When a character speaks about why they acted, look for the values or beliefs behind their words — those reveal who they truly are and what the author wants you to understand about them.
evidencePoints: I was not like, who feared no mortal's frown, / To disobey these laws and so provoke / The wrath of Heaven.
For death is gain to him whose life, like mine, / Is full of misery.
cards.question: When Antigone declares 'I was not like, who feared no mortal's frown' and calls death a 'gain,' what do these words reveal about her character?

choices.label: A
choices.text: She is reckless and has not considered the consequences of defying Creon's decree.

choices.label: B
choices.text: She is guided by a moral conviction so absolute that neither Creon's authority nor the threat of death can override it.

choices.label: C
choices.text: She resents her miserable life and welcomes death primarily as an escape from personal suffering.

choices.label: D
choices.text: She believes Creon is foolish and is more concerned with insulting him than with defending divine law.

cards.standardTitle: Text structure and feature purpose
cards.excerpt: GUARD. I cannot tell, for there was ne’er a trace Of pick or mattock—hard unbroken ground, Without a scratch or rut of chariot wheels, No sign that human hands had been at work. When the first sentry of the morning watch Gave the alarm, we all were terror-stricken. The corpse had vanished, not interred in earth, But strewn with dust, as if by one who sought To avert the curse that haunts the unburied dead: Of hound or ravening jackal, not a sign. Thereat arose an angry war of words; Guard railed at guard and blows were like to end it, For none was there to part us, each in turn Suspected, but the guilt brought home to none, From lack of evidence. We challenged each The ordeal, or to handle red-hot iron, Or pass through fire, affirming on our oath Our innocence—we neither did the deed Ourselves, nor know who did or compassed it. Our quest was at a standstill, when one spake And bowed us all to earth like quivering reeds, For there was no gainsaying him nor way To escape perdition: _Ye_are_bound_to_tell_ _The_King,_ye_cannot_hide_it; so he spake. And he convinced us all; so lots were cast, And I, unlucky scapegoat, drew the prize. So here I am unwilling and withal Unwelcome; no man cares to hear ill news.
cards.whyThisWorks: The Guard's speech moves through a clear internal structure—establishing the mysterious crime scene, then shifting to describe the guards' chaotic conflict and failed investigation, then concluding with how the Guard was compelled to deliver the news—giving students a rich single-paragraph example of a section that extends and then resolves a central problem.
cards.skillStrategy: Ask yourself: what job does this section do—does it introduce a new idea, extend a problem already raised, or shift to show how that problem gets resolved?
evidencePoints: Our quest was at a standstill, when one spake / And bowed us all to earth like quivering reeds
And he convinced us all; so lots were cast, / And I, unlucky scapegoat, drew the prize.
cards.question: The Guard's speech moves from describing the crime scene to recounting the guards' argument and finally to explaining how he came to stand before Creon. What is the primary job of the final section of the speech, beginning with 'Our quest was at a standstill'?

choices.label: A
choices.text: It introduces the idea that the guards are collectively guilty of failing to protect the corpse from burial.

choices.label: B
choices.text: It resolves the deadlock among the guards by showing how one voice compelled them to act and how chance forced the Guard to deliver the news.

choices.label: C
choices.text: It contrasts the Guard's courage with the cowardice of the other sentries who refused to come forward.

choices.label: D
choices.text: It extends the description of the crime scene by adding new evidence about who performed the burial rites.

cards.question: Read the following lines from Theseus's speech: 'My name, Though I be distant, warrants thee from harm.' What does this statement reveal about Theseus's character?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Theseus is uncertain about his ability to protect the stranger and relies on the god Phoebus to provide safety in his absence.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Theseus is so confident in his authority and reputation that he believes his name alone is enough to shield the stranger from danger even when he is not present.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Theseus is dismissing the stranger's fears as exaggerated, suggesting that the enemies who threatened him are not truly dangerous.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Theseus is warning the stranger that his protection is temporary and that the stranger must eventually face his enemies on his own.

cards.standardTitle: Theme development across a literary text
cards.excerpt: ANTIGONE. Yea, for these laws were not ordained of Zeus, And she who sits enthroned with gods below, Justice, enacted not these human laws. I knew that I must die, E’en hadst thou not proclaimed it; and if death Is thereby hastened, I shall count it gain. For death is gain to him whose life, like mine, Is full of misery. cards.whyThisWorks: Antigone's speech directly contrasts divine, unwritten law with human decree, and her willingness to die rather than violate those laws provides clear, quotable evidence that develops the theme that divine law supersedes human authority—while other true details (her grief, her family loyalty) relate only to the topic without advancing that theme.
cards.skillStrategy: Ask yourself: does this detail show WHY the theme is true, or does it just describe what is happening in the story?
evidencePoints: these laws were not ordained of Zeus, And she who sits enthroned with gods below, Justice, enacted not these human laws
I knew that I must die, E'en hadst thou not proclaimed it; and if death Is thereby hastened, I shall count it gain
cards.question: Which detail from Antigone's speech most directly develops the theme that divine law holds greater authority than any human decree?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Antigone states that leaving her brother unburied would have caused her genuine grief, showing how deeply she loves her family.

choices.label: B

cards.standardTitle: Text structure and feature purpose
cards.excerpt: CREON. O cease, you vex me with your babblement; I am like to think you dote in your old age. Is it not arrant folly to pretend That gods would have a thought for this dead man? Did they forsooth award him special grace, And as some benefactor bury him, Who came to fire their hallowed sanctuaries, To sack their shrines, to desolate their land, And scout their ordinances? Or perchance The gods bestow their favors on the bad. No! no! I have long noted malcontents Who wagged their heads, and kicked against the yoke, Misliking these my orders, and my rule. ’Tis they, I warrant, who suborned my guards By bribes. Of evils current upon earth The worst is money. Money ’tis that sacks Cities, and drives men forth from hearth and home; Warps and seduces native innocence, And breeds a habit of dishonesty. But they who sold themselves shall find their greed Out-shot the mark, and rue it soon or late. Yea, as I still revere the dread of Zeus, By Zeus I swear, except ye find and bring Before my presence here the very man Who carried out this lawless burial, Death for your punishment shall not suffice. Hanged on a cross, alive ye first shall make Confession of this outrage. This will teach you What practices are like to serve your turn. There are some villainies that bring no gain. For by dishonesty the few may thrive, The many come to ruin and disgrace.
cards.whyThisWorks: Creon's speech moves through a clear internal structure: it opens by dismissing the Guard's implied divine explanation, then shifts to accuse bribed malcontents, then concludes with a sworn death threat—making the paragraph's job traceable as one that extends Creon's authority by layering accusation, moral argument, and punishment into a single escalating declaration.
cards.skillStrategy: Ask yourself: what work is this paragraph doing—is it introducing a new idea, contrasting two positions, extending a claim with evidence, or shifting the focus entirely? Then find the exact words that signal that move.
evidencePoints: 'Tis they, I warrant, who suborned my guards / By bribes.
By Zeus I swear, except ye find and bring / Before my presence here the very man / Who carried out this lawless burial, / Death for your punishment shall not suffice.
cards.question: In this speech, Creon begins by rejecting the idea that the gods honored Polynices, then pivots to accuse bribed conspirators, and ends with a sworn death threat. What is the primary job of the paragraph as a whole?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The paragraph introduces Creon's uncertainty about who buried Polynices and invites the Guard to offer evidence.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The paragraph extends Creon's claim to absolute authority by layering a dismissal of divine interference, an accusation of corruption, and an escalating punishment into one unbroken assertion of power.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The paragraph contrasts Creon's respect for Zeus with his contempt for the gods' supposed protection of Polynices, showing that Creon is internally conflicted.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The paragraph concludes the conflict by revealing that Creon already knows the identity of the person who buried Polynices and is demanding a confession.

cards.standardTitle: Central idea and supporting evidence
cards.excerpt:
THESEUS. Oft had I heard of thee in times gone by— The bloody mutilation of thine eyes— And therefore know thee, son of Laius. All that I lately gathered on the way Made my conjecture doubly sure; and now Thy garb and that marred visage prove to me That thou art he. So pitying thine estate, Most ill-starred Oedipus, I fain would know What is the suit ye urge on me and Athens, Thou and the helpless maiden at thy side. Declare it; dire indeed must be the tale Whereat _I_ should recoil. I too was reared, Like thee, in exile, and in foreign lands Wrestled with many perils, no man more. Wherefore no alien in adversity Shall seek in vain my succor, nor shalt thou; I know myself a mortal, and my share In what the morrow brings no more than thine.

OEDIPUS. Theseus, thy words so apt, so generous So comfortable, need no long reply Both who I am and of what lineage sprung, And from what land I came, thou hast declared. So without prologue I may utter now My brief petition, and the tale is told.
cards.whyThisWorks: Theseus's speech contains a clear central idea—that shared suffering creates a moral obligation to help others—supported by specific references to his own exile and Oedipus's misfortune, giving students a rich passage to distinguish central idea from topic or isolated detail.
cards.skillStrategy: Ask yourself what the speaker most wants the listener to understand about why he is acting, then check that your answer covers the whole speech, not just one line.
evidencePoints: I too was reared, Like thee, in exile, and in foreign lands Wrestled with many perils, no man more.
Wherefore no alien in adversity Shall seek in vain my succor, nor shalt thou; I know myself a mortal, and my share In what the morrow brings no more than thine.

choices.label: B

cards.standardTitle: Key literary elements add layers of meaning
cards.excerpt:
POLYNEICES. Ah me, my sisters, shall I first lament My own afflictions, or my aged sire’s, Whom here I find a castaway, with you, In a strange land, an ancient beggar clad In antic tatters, marring all his frame, While o’er the sightless orbs his unkept locks Float in the breeze; and, as it were to match, He bears a wallet against hunger’s pinch. All this too late I learn, wretch that I am, Alas! I own it, and am proved most vile In my neglect of thee: I scorn myself. But as almighty Zeus in all he doth Hath Mercy for co-partner of this throne, Let Mercy, father, also sit enthroned In thy heart likewise. For transgressions past May be amended, cannot be made worse.

Why silent? Father, speak, nor turn away, Hast thou no word, wilt thou dismiss me then In mute disdain, nor tell me why thou art wrath? O ye his daughters, sisters mine, do ye This sullen, obstinate silence try to move. Let him not spurn, without a single word Of answer, me the suppliant of the god.
cards.whyThisWorks: Polyneices' speech moves from self-condemnation ('I am proved most vile / In my neglect of thee') directly into a mercy appeal and a logical argument that 'transgressions past / May be amended,' revealing how his characterization as a self-serving petitioner adds meaning to the scene.
cards.skillStrategy: Track what a character says about himself and then notice what he immediately asks for — the gap between the two reveals his true motivation.
evidencePoints: I am proved most vile / In my neglect of thee: I scorn myself
transgressions past / May be amended, cannot be made worse
cards.question: In his speech, Polyneices declares 'I am proved most vile / In my neglect of thee: I scorn myself,' then immediately argues that 'transgressions past / May be amended, cannot be made worse' and calls on his father to let Mercy 'sit enthroned / In thy heart.' What does this sequence reveal about Polyneices' character?

choices.label: A
choices.text: His admission that he is 'most vile' shows he has fully accepted blame for his neglect and expects nothing from his father in return.

choices.label: B
choices.text: His self-condemnation quickly becomes a tool for persuasion, as his confession of neglect leads directly into an argument for mercy and an appeal for his father's support.

choices.label: C
choices.text: His reference to Zeus and Mercy as co-partners on a throne shows he trusts divine authority more than his father's judgment and appeals to religion rather than family loyalty.

choices.label: D
choices.text: His detailed description of his father's 'unkept locks,' 'sightless orbs,' and 'antic tatters' shows he is more troubled by his father's appearance than by the harm his neglect caused.

cards.standardTitle: Text structure and feature purpose
cards.excerpt: CREON. Burghers, my noble friends, ye take alarm At my approach (I read it in your eyes), Fear nothing and refrain from angry words. I come with no ill purpose; I am old, And know the city whither I am come, Without a peer amongst the powers of Greece. It was by reason of my years that I Was chosen to persuade your guest and bring Him back to Thebes; not the delegate Of one man, but commissioned by the State, Since of all Thebans I have most bewailed, Being his kinsman, his most grievous woes. O listen to me, luckless Oedipus, Come home! The whole Cadmeian people claim With right to have thee back, I most of all, For most of all (else were I vile indeed) I mourn for thy misfortunes, seeing thee An aged outcast, wandering on and on, A beggar with one handmaid for thy stay. Ah! who had e’er imagined she could fall To such a depth of misery as this, To tend in penury thy stricken frame, A virgin ripe for wedlock, but unwed, A prey for any wanton ravisher? Seems it not cruel this reproach I cast On thee and on myself and all the race? Aye, but an open shame cannot be hid. Hide it, O hide it, Oedipus, thou canst. O, by our fathers’ gods, consent I pray; Come back to Thebes, come to thy father’s home, Bid Athens, as is meet, a fond farewell; Thebes thy old foster-mother claims thee first.
cards.whyThisWorks: Creon's speech moves through a clear rhetorical arc—establishing his authority, expressing pity, and then issuing a direct appeal—giving students a rich single-paragraph structure to analyze in terms of how each section advances his persuasive purpose.
cards.skillStrategy: Ask yourself: what job is this paragraph doing at each moment—is it building credibility, shifting to emotion, or driving toward a conclusion?
evidencePoints: It was by reason of my years that I / Was chosen to persuade your guest and bring / Him back to Thebes; not the delegate / Of one man, but commissioned by the State
O, by our fathers' gods, consent I pray; / Come back to Thebes, come to thy father's home

What shift occurs between these two moments in the speech?

choices.label: B

cards.standardTitle: Key literary elements add layers of meaning
cards.excerpt: GUARD. I cannot tell, for there was ne’er a trace Of pick or mattock—hard unbroken ground, Without a scratch or rut of chariot wheels, No sign that human hands had been at work. When the first sentry of the morning watch Gave the alarm, we all were terror-stricken. The corpse had vanished, not interred in earth, But strewn with dust, as if by one who sought To avert the curse that haunts the unburied dead: Of hound or ravening jackal, not a sign. Thereat arose an angry war of words; Guard railed at guard and blows were like to end it, For none was there to part us, each in turn Suspected, but the guilt brought home to none, From lack of evidence. We challenged each The ordeal, or to handle red-hot iron, Or pass through fire, affirming on our oath Our innocence—we neither did the deed Ourselves, nor know who did or compassed it. Our quest was at a standstill, when one spake And bowed us all to earth like quivering reeds, For there was no gainsaying him nor way To escape perdition: _Ye_are_bound_to_tell_ _The_King,_ye_cannot_hide_it; so he spake. And he convinced us all; so lots were cast, And I, unlucky scapegoat, drew the prize. So here I am unwilling and withal Unwelcome; no man cares to hear ill news.
cards.whyThisWorks: The Guard's self-described reluctance, his admission that he drew the short lot, and his closing remark that 'no man cares to hear ill news' reveal a character defined by fear and self-interest rather than duty, adding meaning to the theme of moral cowardice under authoritarian pressure.
cards.skillStrategy: When analyzing characterization, look at what a character says about himself and why he acts—his words and motivations expose his deeper values or fears.
evidencePoints: So here I am unwilling and withal / Unwelcome
I, unlucky scapegoat, drew the prize
cards.question: The Guard describes himself as an 'unlucky scapegoat' who arrives 'unwilling and withal / Unwelcome.' What does this self-characterization reveal about him?

choices.label: A
choices.text: He is a loyal soldier who volunteered to deliver the news because he believed it was his duty to the king.

choices.label: B
choices.text: He is driven primarily by self-preservation, having come forward only because chance forced him and not out of any sense of obligation or courage.

choices.label: C
choices.text: He is an honest man who suspects one of the other guards committed the crime and wants to expose the guilty party.

choices.label: D
choices.text: He is indifferent to the king's reaction because he knows the evidence will prove all the guards innocent.

cards.standardTitle: Text structure and feature purpose
cards.excerpt: GUARD. It happened thus. No sooner had we come, Driven from thy presence by those awful threats, Than straight we swept away all trace of dust, And bared the clammy body. Then we sat High on the ridge to windward of the stench, While each man kept he fellow alert and rated Roundly the sluggard if he chanced to nap. So all night long we watched, until the sun Stood high in heaven, and his blazing beams Smote us. A sudden whirlwind then upraised A cloud of dust that blotted out the sky, And swept the plain, and stripped the woodlands bare, And shook the firmament. We closed our eyes And waited till the heaven-sent plague should pass. At last it ceased, and lo! there stood this maid. A piercing cry she uttered, sad and shrill, As when the mother bird beholds her nest Robbed of its nestlings; even so the maid Wailed as she saw the body stripped and bare, And cursed the ruffians who had done this deed. Anon she gathered handfuls of dry dust, Then, holding high a well-wrought brazen urn, Thrice on the dead she poured a lustral stream. We at the sight swooped down on her and seized Our quarry. Undismayed she stood, and when We taxed her with the former crime and this, She disowned nothing. I was glad—and grieved; For ’tis most sweet to ’scape oneself scot-free, And yet to bring disaster to a friend Is grievous. Take it all in all, I deem A man’s first duty is to serve himself.
cards.whyThisWorks: The Guard's speech moves through a clear narrative arc—setting the scene, describing the discovery of Antigone, and then pivoting to a personal moral reflection—making the closing lines ('I was glad—and grieved…A man's first duty is to serve himself') a distinct concluding shift that students can identify and explain as a tonal and thematic turn away from the action.
cards.skillStrategy: Ask yourself: does this section keep building the same idea, or does it change direction and land on a new point? Track the moment the speaker stops reporting events and starts reflecting on himself.
evidencePoints: I was glad—and grieved; For 'tis most sweet to 'scape oneself scot-free, And yet to bring disaster to a friend Is grievous.
Take it all in all, I deem A man's first duty is to serve himself.
cards.question: The Guard's speech shifts in purpose when he says, 'I was glad—and grieved.' What is the primary job of the lines from that moment through the end of the speech?

choices.label: A

choices.label: B
choices.text: The lines shift from reporting the event to revealing the Guard's conflicted self-interest, concluding his speech with a personal moral claim rather than further action.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The lines contrast the Guard's loyalty to Creon with Antigone's defiance, proving that the Guard acted out of duty rather than personal gain.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The lines introduce a new conflict between the guards themselves by suggesting one of them felt sympathy for Antigone and nearly let her escape.

choices.label: A
choices.text: Creon is genuinely grief-stricken over Oedipus's suffering and speaks only out of kinship loyalty, as shown by his mourning Oedipus's misfortunes.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Creon presents himself as a selfless public servant while using emotional pressure and appeals to shame to manipulate Oedipus into returning, suggesting his concern is political rather than personal.

cards.standardTitle: Theme development across a literary text
cards.excerpt:
OEDIPUS. God speed thee! and as meed for bringing them May Providence deal with thee kindlier Than it has dealt with me! O children mine, Where are ye? Let me clasp you with these hands, A brother’s hands, a father’s; hands that made Lack-luster sockets of his once bright eyes; Hands of a man who blindly, recklessly, Became your sire by her from whom he sprang. Though I cannot behold you, I must weep In thinking of the evil days to come, The slights and wrongs that men will put upon you. Where’er ye go to feast or festival, No merrymaking will it prove for you, But oft abashed in tears ye will return. And when ye come to marriageable years, Where’s the bold wooers who will jeopardize To take unto himself such disrepute As to my children’s children still must cling, For what of infamy is lacking here? “Their father slew his father, sowed the seed Where he himself was gendered, and begat These maidens at the source wherefrom he sprang.” Such are the gibes that men will cast at you. Who then will wed you? None, I ween, but ye Must pine, poor maids, in single barrenness. O Prince, Menoeceus’ son, to thee, I turn, With the it rests to father them, for we Their natural parents, both of us, are lost. O leave them not to wander poor, unwed, Thy kin, nor let them share my low estate. O pity them so young, and but for thee All destitute. Thy hand upon it, Prince. To you, my children I had much to say, Were ye but ripe to hear. Let this suffice: Pray ye may find some home and live content, And may your lot prove happier than your sire’s.

CREON. Thou hast had enough of weeping; pass within.
cards.whyThisWorks: Oedipus's speech layers specific consequences—social rejection, unwed futures, inherited shame—that develop the theme that the sins of parents condemn their innocent children, forcing students to distinguish true-but-topical details from details that actually build that theme.
cards.skillStrategy: Ask yourself: does this detail show HOW the theme is proven, or does it just mention something that happened in the story?
evidencePoints: Who then will wed you? None, I ween, but ye Must pine, poor maids, in single barrenness.
Their father slew his father, sowed the seed Where he himself was gendered, and begat These maidens at the source wherefrom he sprang.
cards.question: Which detail from Oedipus's speech most directly develops the theme that innocent children suffer the consequences of their parents' sins?

choices.label: A

choices.label: B

cards.standardTitle: Key literary elements add layers of meaning
cards.excerpt: CREON. Well, let her know the stubbornest of wills Are soonest bended, as the hardest iron, O’er-heated in the fire to brittleness, Flies soonest into fragments, shivered through. A snaffle curbs the fieriest steed, and he Who in subjection lives must needs be meek. But this proud girl, in insolence well-schooled, First overstepped the established law, and then— A second and worse act of insolence— She boasts and glories in her wickedness. Now if she thus can flout authority Unpunished, I am woman, she the man. But though she be my sister’s child or nearer Of kin than all who worship at my hearth, Nor she nor yet her sister shall escape The utmost penalty, for both I hold, As arch-conspirators, of equal guilt. Bring forth the older; even now I saw her Within the palace, frenzied and distraught. The workings of the mind discover oft Dark deeds in darkness schemed, before the act. More hateful still the miscreant who seeks When caught, to make a virtue of a crime.
cards.whyThisWorks: Creon's speech reveals his authoritarian character through his extended metaphors, his gendered insult, and his declaration that even family ties will not spare Antigone—each detail layering meaning about his rigid need for control and his view of defiance as a personal threat.
cards.skillStrategy: When a character speaks, ask what his words reveal about his values and fears, not just what he says on the surface.
evidencePoints: Now if she thus can flout authority Unpunished, I am woman, she the man.
But though she be my sister's child or nearer Of kin than all who worship at my hearth, Nor she nor yet her sister shall escape The utmost penalty
cards.question: Read the following lines from Creon's speech: 'Now if she thus can flout authority / Unpunished, I am woman, she the man. / But though she be my sister's child or nearer / Of kin than all who worship at my hearth, / Nor she nor yet her sister shall escape / The utmost penalty.' What do these lines reveal about Creon's character?

choices.label: C

choices.label: D
choices.text: Creon's mention of his hearth and family shows that he is torn between his public duty and his private affection for Antigone, suggesting he may eventually relent.

cards.standardTitle: Key literary elements add layers of meaning
cards.excerpt: ANTIGONE. O heed me, father, though I am young in years. Let the prince have his will and pay withal What in his eyes is service to the god; For our sake also let our brother come. If what he urges tend not to thy good He cannot surely wrest perforce thy will. To hear him then, what harm? By open words A scheme of villainy is soon bewrayed. Thou art his father, therefore canst not pay In kind a son’s most impious outrages. O listen to him; other men like thee Have thankless children and are choleric, But yielding to persuasion’s gentle spell They let their savage mood be exorcised. Look thou to the past, forget the present, think On all the woe thy sire and mother brought thee; Thence wilt thou draw this lesson without fail, Of evil passion evil is the end. Thou hast, alas, to prick thy memory, Stern monitors, these ever-sightless orbs. O yield to us; just suitors should not need To be importunate, nor he that takes A favor lack the grace to make return.
cards.whyThisWorks: Antigone's speech reveals her character through a blend of reasoned argument, emotional appeal, and self-awareness of her youth, showing students how speech and rhetorical strategy together characterize a figure as both wise and diplomatically bold.
cards.skillStrategy: When a character speaks, ask what their word choices and arguments reveal about who they are — not just what they want, but how they think and feel.
evidencePoints: O heed me, father, though I am young in years.

cards.question: In her speech, Antigone acknowledges 'I am young in years' before urging her father to hear her brother. What does this acknowledgment, combined with her appeal to her father's own painful past, reveal about her character?

choices.label: A
choices.text: She is uncertain whether her brother deserves to be heard and relies on her father's judgment to decide the matter.

choices.label: B
choices.text: She is shrewd enough to disarm her father's resistance by admitting her inexperience while using his own suffering as proof that unchecked anger leads to ruin.

choices.label: C
choices.text: She is primarily motivated by obedience to the gods and shows little concern for her father's emotional state.

choices.label: D
choices.text: She distrusts her brother's intentions and warns her father that the visit may be a scheme of villainy in disguise.

cards.standardTitle: Key literary elements add layers of meaning
cards.excerpt:
CREON. What is this? Thy words inspire a dread presentiment.

TEIRESIAS. The divination of my arts shall tell. Sitting upon my throne of augury, As is my wont, where every fowl of heaven Find harborage, upon mine ears was borne A jargon strange of twitterings, hoots, and screams; So knew I that each bird at the other tare With bloody talons, for the whirr of wings Could signify naught else. Perturbed in soul, I straight essayed the sacrifice by fire On blazing altars, but the God of Fire Came not in flame, and from the thigh bones dripped And sputtered in the ashes a foul ooze; Gall-bladders cracked and spurted up: the fat Melted and fell and left the thigh bones bare. Such are the signs, taught by this lad, I read— As I guide others, so the boy guides me— The frustrate signs of oracles grown dumb. O King, thy willful temper ails the State, For all our shrines and altars are profaned By what has filled the maw of dogs and crows, The flesh of Oedipus’ unburied son. Therefore the angry gods abominate Our litanies and our burnt offerings; Therefore no birds trill out a happy note, Gorged with the carnival of human gore. O ponder this, my son. To err is common To all men, but the man who having erred Hugs not his errors, but repents and seeks The cure, is not a wastrel nor unwise. No fool, the saw goes, like the obstinate fool. Let death disarm thy vengeance. O forbear To vex the dead. What glory wilt thou win By slaying twice the slain? I mean thee well; Counsel’s most welcome if I promise gain.
cards.whyThisWorks: Teiresias's detailed recounting of failed omens and his direct rebuke of Creon reveal him as a morally authoritative figure whose speech exposes Creon's fatal pride and its consequences for the state.
cards.skillStrategy: When a character speaks at length, ask what their words reveal about both themselves and the person they are addressing — the contrast between the two characters often carries the deeper meaning.
evidencePoints: O King, thy willful temper ails the State, For all our shrines and altars are profaned
To err is common To all men, but the man who having erred Hugs not his errors, but repents and seeks The cure, is not a wastrel nor unwise.
cards.question: In his speech, Teiresias moves from describing failed omens to delivering a direct moral warning to Creon. What does this progression reveal about Teiresias as a character?

choices.label: A
choices.text: He is primarily concerned with demonstrating the accuracy of his prophetic methods to earn Creon's trust before making any demands.

choices.label: B
choices.text: He positions himself as a figure of moral authority whose role extends beyond reading signs to confronting a ruler whose pride is destroying the order of the state.

choices.label: C
choices.text: He reveals his own uncertainty about the gods' will by admitting that the omens are too confused for him to interpret with confidence.

choices.label: D
choices.text: He shows that his loyalty to Oedipus's family drives him to oppose Creon regardless of what the divine signs actually indicate.

cards.standardTitle: Text structure and feature purpose
cards.excerpt: CREON. Not deeming this city void of men Or counsel, son of Aegeus, as thou say’st I did what I have done; rather I thought Your people were not like to set such store by kin of mine and keep them ’gainst my will. Nor would they harbor, so I stood assured, A godless parricide, a reprobate Convicted of incestuous marriage ties. For on her native hill of Ares here (I knew your far-famed Areopagus) Sits Justice, and permits not vagrant folk To stay within your borders. In that faith I hunted down my quarry; and e’en then I had refrained but for the curses dire Wherewith he banned my kinsfolk and myself: Such wrong, methought, had warrant for my act. Anger has no old age but only death; The dead alone can feel no touch of spite. So thou must work thy will; my cause is just But weak without allies; yet will I try, Old as I am, to answer deeds with deeds.
cards.whyThisWorks: Creon's speech moves through a clear structural arc—justifying his past actions, then shifting to acknowledge his weakened position and vow to fight anyway—giving students a concrete paragraph whose closing lines ('my cause is just / But weak without allies; yet will I try') mark a distinct shift from defense to defiant resolve.
cards.skillStrategy: Track what the paragraph is doing at each moment: ask yourself whether the speaker is explaining, defending, shifting tone, or wrapping up an argument.
evidencePoints: Anger has no old age but only death; / The dead alone can feel no touch of spite.
my cause is just / But weak without allies; yet will I try, / Old as I am, to answer deeds with deeds.
cards.question: In Creon's speech, the lines 'my cause is just / But weak without allies; yet will I try, / Old as I am, to answer deeds with deeds' serve what purpose within the speech as a whole?

choices.label: A
choices.text: They continue Creon's earlier argument that Athens had no right to shelter his kinsmen, reinforcing his legal justification.

choices.label: B
choices.text: They shift the speech from Creon's defense of his past actions to a declaration that he will resist Theseus despite being at a disadvantage.

choices.label: C
choices.text: They introduce a new claim that Creon's anger toward his kinsmen has finally faded with age, softening his earlier hostility.

choices.label: D
choices.text: They conclude the speech by conceding that Theseus was correct and that Creon's original seizure of his kinsmen was unjust.

cards.standardTitle: Central idea and supporting evidence
cards.excerpt: GUARD. It happened thus. No sooner had we come, Driven from thy presence by those awful threats, Than straight we swept away all trace of dust, And bared the clammy body. Then we sat High on the ridge to windward of the stench, While each man kept he fellow alert and rated Roundly the sluggard if he chanced to nap. So all night long we watched, until the sun Stood high in heaven, and his blazing beams Smote us. A sudden whirlwind then upraised A cloud of dust that blotted out the sky, And swept the plain, and stripped the woodlands bare, And shook the firmament. We closed our eyes And waited till the heaven-sent plague should pass. At last it ceased, and lo! there stood this maid. A piercing cry she uttered, sad and shrill, As when the mother bird beholds her nest Robbed of its nestlings; even so the maid Wailed as she saw the body stripped and bare, And cursed the ruffians who had done this deed. Anon she gathered handfuls of dry dust, Then, holding high a well-wrought brazen urn, Thrice on the dead she poured a lustral stream. We at the sight swooped down on her and seized Our quarry. Undismayed she stood, and when We taxed her with the former crime and this, She disowned nothing. I was glad—and grieved; For ’tis most sweet to ’scape oneself scot-free, And yet to bring disaster to a friend Is grievous. Take it all in all, I deem A man’s first duty is to serve himself.
cards.whyThisWorks: The Guard's closing lines—'I was glad—and grieved' and 'a man's first duty is to serve himself'—state an explicit claim that students must distinguish from surrounding details about the whirlwind, Antigone's actions, and the guards' night watch.
cards.skillStrategy: Ask yourself: what does the speaker say this whole experience ultimately proves or means? That stated conclusion is the central idea, not the events that led to it.
evidencePoints: I was glad—and grieved; For 'tis most sweet to 'scape oneself scot-free, And yet to bring disaster to a friend Is grievous.
Take it all in all, I deem A man's first duty is to serve himself.
cards.question: At the end of his speech, the Guard states, 'Take it all in all, I deem / A man's first duty is to serve himself.' What central idea does this conclusion express about the experience the Guard has just described?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Enduring a night of hardship and a blinding whirlwind proves that soldiers must remain loyal to their commanders above all else.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Escaping punishment by capturing Antigone brought the Guard relief, but harming her revealed that personal survival comes at a painful moral cost.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Antigone's courage in standing undismayed after her capture shows that devotion to the dead is a higher duty than obedience to the state.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The guards' careful watch through the night demonstrates that disciplined soldiers will always succeed in catching those who break the law.

cards.standardTitle: Key literary elements add layers of meaning
cards.excerpt:
OEDIPUS. God speed thee! and as meed for bringing them May Providence deal with thee kindlier Than it has dealt with me! O children mine, Where are ye? Let me clasp you with these hands, A brother’s hands, a father’s; hands that made Lack-luster sockets of his once bright eyes; Hands of a man who blindly, recklessly, Became your sire by her from whom he sprang. Though I cannot behold you, I must weep In thinking of the evil days to come, The slights and wrongs that men will put upon you. Where’er ye go to feast or festival, No merrymaking will it prove for you, But oft abashed in tears ye will return. And when ye come to marriageable years, Where’s the bold wooers who will jeopardize To take unto himself such disrepute As to my children’s children still must cling, For what of infamy is lacking here? “Their father slew his father, sowed the seed Where he himself was gendered, and begat These maidens at the source wherefrom he sprang.” Such are the gibes that men will cast at you. Who then will wed you? None, I ween, but ye Must pine, poor maids, in single barrenness. O Prince, Menoeceus’ son, to thee, I turn, With the it rests to father them, for we Their natural parents, both of us, are lost. O leave them not to wander poor, unwed, Thy kin, nor let them share my low estate. O pity them so young, and but for thee All destitute. Thy hand upon it, Prince. To you, my children I had much to say, Were ye but ripe to hear. Let this suffice: Pray ye may find some home and live content, And may your lot prove happier than your sire’s.

CREON. Thou hast had enough of weeping; pass within.
cards.whyThisWorks: Oedipus's extended plea to Creon—begging him to protect his daughters while simultaneously cataloguing the shame his own actions have cursed them with—reveals a character torn between self-condemnation and fierce paternal love, layering tragic irony and meaning onto every word.
cards.skillStrategy: When a character speaks, ask what their words reveal about who they are inside—look for contradictions, emotions, or admissions that show more than the surface meaning.
evidencePoints: Hands of a man who blindly, recklessly, / Became your sire by her from whom he sprang.
O Prince, Menoeceus' son, to thee, I turn, / With the it rests to father them, for we / Their natural parents, both of us, are lost.
cards.question: In his speech, Oedipus calls his own hands 'hands that made / Lack-luster sockets of his once bright eyes' and then immediately reaches out to embrace his daughters. What does this combination of self-accusation and physical tenderness reveal about Oedipus as a character?

choices.label: A
choices.text: He is so consumed by guilt over his past crimes that he has become emotionally detached from his daughters and speaks to them only out of obligation.

choices.label: B
choices.text: He holds himself fully responsible for the ruin he has brought on his family, yet his love for his daughters drives him to act on their behalf even as he condemns himself.

choices.label: C
choices.text: He blames the gods for his blindness and uses his daughters' suffering as evidence that divine punishment has been unjust.

choices.label: D
choices.text: He recognizes that his daughters will suffer but believes Creon's protection will erase the shame attached to their family name.

cards.standardTitle: Theme development across a literary text
cards.excerpt:
ANTIGONE. O grave, O bridal bower, O prison house Hewn from the rock, my everlasting home, Whither I go to join the mighty host Of kinsfolk, Persephassa’s guests long dead, The last of all, of all more miserable, I pass, my destined span of years cut short. And yet good hope is mine that I shall find A welcome from my sire, a welcome too, From thee, my mother, and my brother dear; From with these hands, I laved and decked your limbs In death, and poured libations on your grave. And last, my Polyneices, unto thee I paid due rites, and this my recompense! Yet am I justified in wisdom’s eyes. For even had it been some child of mine, Or husband mouldering in death’s decay, I had not wrought this deed despite the State. What is the law I call in aid? ’Tis thus I argue. Had it been a husband dead I might have wed another, and have borne Another child, to take the dead child’s place. But, now my sire and mother both are dead, No second brother can be born for me. Thus by the law of conscience I was led To honor thee, dear brother, and was judged By Creon guilty of a heinous crime. And now he drags me like a criminal, A bride unwed, amerced of marriage-song And marriage-bed and joys of motherhood, By friends deserted to a living grave. What ordinance of heaven have I transgressed? Hereafter can I look to any god For succor, call on any man for help? Alas, my piety is impious deemed. Well, if such justice is approved of heaven, I shall be taught by suffering my sin; But if the sin is theirs, O may they suffer No worse ills than the wrongs they do to me.

CHORUS. The same ungovernable will Drives like a gale the maiden still.

CREON. Therefore, my guards who let her stay Shall smart full sore for their delay.
cards.whyThisWorks: Antigone's speech contains both true-but-topical details (her grief, her isolation) and details that actively develop the theme that conscience-driven loyalty to family can demand a price greater than life itself, making it ideal for teaching students to distinguish theme-developing evidence from mere topic-matching details.
cards.skillStrategy: Ask yourself: does this detail show WHY the theme is true, or does it just remind me what the passage is about?
evidencePoints: Thus by the law of conscience I was led / To honor thee, dear brother, and was judged / By Creon guilty of a heinous crime.
Alas, my piety is impious deemed.
cards.question: One theme of this passage is that acting according to personal conscience can lead to punishment by those in power. Which detail from Antigone's speech most directly develops this theme?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Antigone describes the grave as her 'everlasting home' and mourns that her 'destined span of years' has been cut short, showing she is aware she will die young.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Antigone declares she was 'led by the law of conscience' to honor Polyneices, yet Creon judged this act 'a heinous crime,' showing that following her moral duty directly results in her condemnation.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Antigone recalls that she 'laved and decked' the limbs of her dead family members and 'poured libations' on their graves, demonstrating her devotion to burial rituals.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Antigone laments that she is 'amerced of marriage-song and marriage-bed,' revealing that she will never experience the joys of marriage or motherhood.

cards.standardTitle: Text structure and feature purpose
cards.excerpt: Antigone, daughter of Oedipus, the late king of Thebes, in defiance of Creon who rules in his stead, resolves to bury her brother Polyneices, slain in his attack on Thebes. She is caught in the act by Creon’s watchmen and brought before the king. She justifies her action, asserting that she was bound to obey the eternal laws of right and wrong in spite of any human ordinance. Creon, unrelenting, condemns her to be immured in a rock-hewn chamber. His son Haemon, to whom Antigone is betrothed, pleads in vain for her life and threatens to die with her. Warned by the seer Teiresias Creon repents him and hurries to release Antigone from her rocky prison. But he is too late: he finds lying side by side Antigone who had hanged herself and Haemon who also has perished by his own hand. Returning to the palace he sees within the dead body of his queen who on learning of her son’s death has stabbed herself to the heart.
cards.whyThisWorks: The single paragraph functions as a prologue that introduces characters, establishes the central conflict, and traces the chain of consequences through to the final deaths, making its structural job as an introduction clearly demonstrable from specific textual moments.
cards.skillStrategy: Ask yourself: what work is this paragraph doing — is it setting up new information, shifting direction, or wrapping something up? Then point to specific words that prove your answer.
evidencePoints: Antigone, daughter of Oedipus, the late king of Thebes, in defiance of Creon who rules in his stead, resolves to bury her brother Polyneices
Returning to the palace he sees within the dead body of his queen who on learning of her son's death has stabbed herself to the heart.
cards.question: The paragraph opens by naming 'Antigone, daughter of Oedipus' and her defiance of Creon, then moves through her capture, Creon's condemnation, Haemon's plea, and the three deaths. What is the job of this sequence of events within the paragraph?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The sequence shifts the reader's sympathy toward Antigone by dwelling on Creon's cruelty and showing that every character who opposes him suffers.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The sequence introduces the central conflict between Antigone and Creon, the key figures involved, and the chain of tragic outcomes that results from that conflict.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The sequence concludes an argument by proving that Creon's refusal to release Antigone was the single cause of every death mentioned in the paragraph.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The sequence contrasts Antigone's courage with Creon's weakness by showing that she acts decisively while he repents only after Teiresias warns him.

cards.standardTitle: Central idea and supporting evidence
cards.excerpt: ANTIGONE. What but the thought of our two brothers dead, The one by Creon graced with funeral rites, The other disappointed? Eteocles He hath consigned to earth (as fame reports) With obsequies that use and wont ordain, So gracing him among the dead below. But Polyneices, a dishonored corse, (So by report the royal edict runs) No man may bury him or make lament— Must leave him tombless and unwept, a feast For kites to scent afar and swoop upon. Such is the edict (if report speak true) Of Creon, our most noble Creon, aimed At thee and me, aye me too; and anon He will be here to promulgate, for such As have not heard, his mandate; ’tis in sooth No passing humor, for the edict says Whoe’er transgresses shall be stoned to death. So stands it with us; now ’tis thine to show If thou art worthy of thy blood or base.
cards.whyThisWorks: Antigone's speech moves from describing the unequal treatment of her brothers to announcing a death penalty for disobedience, requiring students to synthesize details into a central idea rather than selecting an isolated fact.
cards.skillStrategy: Ask yourself: what is the speaker's main point after all the details are combined — not just one fact she mentions, but the idea that holds the whole speech together.
evidencePoints: Such is the edict...aimed / At thee and me, aye me too
now 'tis thine to show / If thou art worthy of thy blood or base
cards.question: Antigone ends her speech with the words 'now 'tis thine to show / If thou art worthy of thy blood or base.' Considering this conclusion alongside the details about Creon's edict and the punishment of death for disobedience, which statement most accurately expresses the central idea of Antigone's entire speech?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Creon has treated Eteocles honorably in death, and Antigone wants her sister to understand why Polyneices deserved the same treatment.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Creon's edict condemning Polyneices to lie unburied — and threatening death to anyone who defies it — places Antigone and her sister before a life-or-death test of loyalty to their family.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Creon will soon arrive to announce his decree, and Antigone is warning her sister so they can escape before he does.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Polyneices was left unburied and unmourned because he was an enemy of Creon, and Antigone believes this punishment was unjust.

cards.standardTitle: Key literary elements add layers of meaning
cards.excerpt:
CHORUS. (Str. 1) Sunbeam, of all that ever dawn upon Our seven-gated Thebes the brightest ray, O eye of golden day, How fair thy light o’er Dirce’s fountain shone, Speeding upon their headlong homeward course, Far quicker than they came, the Argive force; Putting to flight The argent shields, the host with scutcheons white. Against our land the proud invader came To vindicate fell Polyneices’ claim. Like to an eagle swooping low, On pinions white as new fall’n snow. With clanging scream, a horsetail plume his crest, The aspiring lord of Argos onward pressed.

(Ant. 1) Hovering around our city walls he waits, His spearmen raven at our seven gates. But ere a torch our crown of towers could burn, Ere they had tasted of our blood, they turn Forced by the Dragon; in their rear The din of Ares panic-struck they hear. For Zeus who hates the braggart’s boast Beheld that gold-bespangled host; As at the goal the paean they upraise, He struck them with his forked lightning blaze.

(Str. 2) To earthy from earth rebounding, down he crashed; The fire-brand from his impious hand was dashed, As like a Bacchic reveler on he came, Outbreathing hate and flame, And tottered. Elsewhere in the field, Here, there, great Area like a war-horse wheeled; Beneath his car down thrust Our foemen bit the dust.

Seven captains at our seven gates Thundered; for each a champion waits, Each left behind his armor bright, Trophy for Zeus who turns the fight; Save two alone, that ill-starred pair One mother to one father bare, Who lance in rest, one ’gainst the other Drave, and both perished, brother slain by brother.
cards.whyThisWorks: The Chorus's characterization of Zeus as one who 'hates the braggart's boast' and strikes the Argives precisely as they sing their victory paean reveals that divine justice—not military power—governs the outcome, adding a moral layer to what could otherwise be a straightforward battle narrative.
cards.skillStrategy: When analyzing characterization, look for specific words the author uses to describe a character's traits and ask how those traits shape the meaning of events in the passage.
evidencePoints: Zeus who hates the braggart's boast
As at the goal the paean they upraise, He struck them with his forked lightning blaze
cards.question: The Chorus describes Zeus as one who 'hates the braggart's boast' and strikes the Argive host with lightning 'as at the goal the paean they upraise'—at the exact moment they sing their victory song. How does this characterization of Zeus add meaning to the Chorus's account of the battle?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Zeus is portrayed as a guardian of Thebes's seven gates whose lightning is timed to prevent the city from burning, suggesting his concern is with protecting physical structures rather than punishing the Argives' pride.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Zeus is characterized as an enforcer of moral order who punishes the Argives at the peak of their arrogance, establishing that boastful pride—not military strength—determines the army's downfall.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Zeus is depicted as responding to the ritual of the paean itself, implying that singing a victory song before the battle ends is a tactical error that draws divine punishment regardless of any moral failing.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Zeus is shown targeting the 'gold-bespangled host' because of their visible wealth and gleaming armor, suggesting the gods punish displays of prosperity rather than the attitude of pride behind them.

cards.standardTitle: Theme development across a literary text
cards.excerpt:
THESEUS. What means this?

OEDIPUS. Thou hast heard my tale of wrongs.

THESEUS. Ho! hasten to the altars, one of you. Command my liegemen leave the sacrifice And hurry, foot and horse, with rein unchecked, To where the paths that packmen use diverge, Lest the two maidens slip away, and I Become a mockery to this my guest, As one despoiled by force. Quick, as I bid. As for this stranger, had I let my rage, Justly provoked, have play, he had not ’scaped Scathless and uncorrected at my hands. But now the laws to which himself appealed, These and none others shall adjudicate. Thou shalt not quit this land, till thou hast fetched The maidens and produced them in my sight. Thou hast offended both against myself And thine own race and country. Having come Unto a State that champions right and asks For every action warranty of law, Thou hast set aside the custom of the land, And like some freebooter art carrying off What plunder pleases thee, as if forsooth Thou thoughtest this a city without men, Or manned by slaves, and me a thing of naught. Yet not from Thebes this villainy was learnt; Thebes is not wont to breed unrighteous sons, Nor would she praise thee, if she learnt that thou Wert robbing me—aye and the gods to boot, Haling by force their suppliants, poor maids. Were I on Theban soil, to prosecute The justest claim imaginable, I Would never wrest by violence my own Without sanction of your State or King; I should behave as fits an outlander Living amongst a foreign folk, but thou Shamest a city that deserves it not, Even thine own, and plentitude of years Have made of thee an old man and a fool. Therefore again I charge thee as before, See that the maidens are restored at once, Unless thou would’st continue here by force And not by choice a sojourner; so much I tell thee home and what I say, I mean.
cards.whyThisWorks: Theseus's speech contrasts lawful conduct with Creon's violent seizure of the maidens, giving students multiple details to evaluate—some merely topical (the maidens are taken) and some genuinely thematic (law as the measure of justice and civilization).
cards.skillStrategy: Ask yourself: does this detail show HOW the theme is built, or does it just describe what happened in the scene?
evidencePoints: Unto a State that champions right and asks / For every action warranty of law
Were I on Theban soil, to prosecute / The justest claim imaginable, I / Would never wrest by violence my own / Without sanction of your State or King
cards.question: Which detail from Theseus's speech most directly develops the theme that true justice requires submission to law rather than the exercise of personal power?

choices.label: A
