choices.text: Theseus orders his men to ride to where the packmen's paths diverge so the maidens cannot escape, showing his authority over the land.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Theseus declares that even if he had the justest claim on Theban soil, he would never seize what was his without sanction of the State or King, holding law above personal right.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Theseus tells Creon that Thebes is not accustomed to breeding unrighteous sons, suggesting Creon's behavior dishonors his own city.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Theseus warns Creon that his many years have made him an old man and a fool, indicating that age has clouded Creon's judgment.

cards.standardTitle: Text structure and feature purpose
cards.excerpt: CREON. Well, let her know the stubbornest of wills Are soonest bended, as the hardest iron, O’er-heated in the fire to brittleness, Flies soonest into fragments, shivered through. A snaffle curbs the fieriest steed, and he Who in subjection lives must needs be meek. But this proud girl, in insolence well-schooled, First overstepped the established law, and then— A second and worse act of insolence— She boasts and glories in her wickedness. Now if she thus can flout authority Unpunished, I am woman, she the man. But though she be my sister’s child or nearer Of kin than all who worship at my hearth, Nor she nor yet her sister shall escape The utmost penalty, for both I hold, As arch-conspirators, of equal guilt. Bring forth the older; even now I saw her Within the palace, frenzied and distraught. The workings of the mind discover oft Dark deeds in darkness schemed, before the act. More hateful still the miscreant who seeks When caught, to make a virtue of a crime.
cards.whyThisWorks: Creon's speech opens with two analogies—overheated iron and a bridled horse—that establish a governing principle before he applies it to Antigone's specific acts, making the paragraph's internal structure a clear example of how an opening section sets up a claim that the rest of the paragraph supports.
cards.skillStrategy: Ask yourself: what job does this section do for the rest of the paragraph—does it introduce a principle, provide evidence, concede a point, or deliver a verdict?
evidencePoints: the hardest iron, O'er-heated in the fire to brittleness, Flies soonest into fragments, shivered through
First overstepped the established law, and then— A second and worse act of insolence— She boasts and glories in her wickedness
cards.question: In Creon's speech, the opening lines compare stubborn things to iron that 'Flies soonest into fragments' and a fierce horse curbed by 'a snaffle.' What is the job of these opening lines within the paragraph?

choices.label: A
choices.text: They describe the physical struggle Creon used to bring Antigone before him, connecting to his later statement that he saw her 'frenzied and distraught' inside the palace.

choices.label: B
choices.text: They establish a general principle that stubborn things must yield to force, which Creon then applies directly to Antigone, who 'overstepped the established law' and 'boasts and glories in her wickedness.'

choices.label: C
choices.text: They acknowledge that Antigone's resistance is understandable before Creon shifts to condemning her for committing 'a second and worse act of insolence.'

choices.label: D
choices.text: They announce Creon's final verdict that both sisters are 'arch-conspirators of equal guilt' who must face 'the utmost penalty.'

cards.standardTitle: Central idea and supporting evidence
cards.excerpt: ANTIGONE. Yea, for these laws were not ordained of Zeus, And she who sits enthroned with gods below, Justice, enacted not these human laws. Nor did I deem that thou, a mortal man, Could’st by a breath annul and override The immutable unwritten laws of Heaven. They were not born today nor yesterday; They die not; and none knoweth whence they sprang. I was not like, who feared no mortal’s frown, To disobey these laws and so provoke The wrath of Heaven. I knew that I must die, E’en hadst thou not proclaimed it; and if death Is thereby hastened, I shall count it gain. For death is gain to him whose life, like mine, Is full of misery. Thus my lot appears Not sad, but blissful; for had I endured To leave my mother’s son unburied there, I should have grieved with reason, but not now. And if in this thou judgest me a fool, Methinks the judge of folly’s not acquit.
cards.whyThisWorks: Antigone's speech explicitly contrasts 'immutable unwritten laws of Heaven' with 'human laws,' giving students a concrete textual anchor to distinguish the central idea from isolated details like her acceptance of death or her accusation of Creon.
cards.skillStrategy: When a character makes a direct contrast in their speech, ask what that contrast is really arguing — that argument is usually the central idea, not the details around it.
evidencePoints: The immutable unwritten laws of Heaven. They were not born today nor yesterday; They die not
Nor did I deem that thou, a mortal man, Could'st by a breath annul and override / The immutable unwritten laws of Heaven.
cards.question: In this speech, Antigone draws a direct contrast between 'human laws' and 'the immutable unwritten laws of Heaven.' What central idea does this contrast express?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Antigone argues that because she will die regardless of Creon's decree, his punishment is meaningless and she has nothing to lose by defying him.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Antigone argues that divine, unwritten laws carry an authority no mortal ruler can cancel, and that obeying those laws made her defiance of Creon's decree not only justified but necessary.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Antigone argues that Zeus and Justice personally issued commands to her, so her actions were a direct response to specific divine instructions rather than her own judgment.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Antigone argues that Creon's decree was foolish from the start and that his poor judgment will eventually be exposed and condemned by those around him.

cards.standardTitle: Key literary elements add layers of meaning
cards.excerpt:
ANTIGONE. (Ant. 1) Nay, but the piteous tale I’ve heard men tell Of Tantalus’ doomed child, Chained upon Siphylus’ high rocky fell, That clung like ivy wild, Drenched by the pelting rain and whirling snow, Left there to pine, While on her frozen breast the tears aye flow— Her fate is mine.

CHORUS. She was sprung of gods, divine, Mortals we of mortal line. Like renown with gods to gain Recompenses all thy pain. Take this solace to thy tomb Hers in life and death thy doom.

ANTIGONE. (Str. 2) Alack, alack! Ye mock me. Is it meet Thus to insult me living, to my face? Cease, by our country’s altars I entreat, Ye lordly rulers of a lordly race. O fount of Dirce, wood-embowered plain Where Theban chariots to victory speed, Mark ye the cruel laws that now have wrought my bane, The friends who show no pity in my need! Was ever fate like mine? O monstrous doom, Within a rock-built prison sepulchered, To fade and wither in a living tomb, And alien midst the living and the dead.

CHORUS. (Str. 3) In thy boldness over-rash Madly thou thy foot didst dash ’Gainst high Justice’ altar stair. Thou a father’s guild dost bear.

ANTIGONE. (Ant. 2) At this thou touchest my most poignant pain, My ill-starred father’s piteous disgrace, The taint of blood, the hereditary stain, That clings to all of Labdacus’ famed race. Woe worth the monstrous marriage-bed where lay A mother with the son her womb had borne, Therein I was conceived, woe worth the day, Fruit of incestuous sheets, a maid forlorn, And now I pass, accursed and unwed, To meet them as an alien there below; And thee, O brother, in marriage ill-bestead, ’Twas thy dead hand that dealt me this death-blow.
cards.whyThisWorks: Antigone's shift from comparing herself to a goddess-born figure (Niobe) to crying out 'Ye mock me' and then cataloguing her family's cursed bloodline reveals how her speech and emotional reactions characterize her as both self-aware of her doom and bitterly isolated, adding meaning to her tragic identity.
cards.skillStrategy: When a character's words shift suddenly in tone or target, ask what that shift reveals about who they are and what they believe about themselves.
evidencePoints: Alack, alack! Ye mock me. Is it meet / Thus to insult me living, to my face?
At this thou touchest my most poignant pain, / My ill-starred father's piteous disgrace, / The taint of blood, the hereditary stain, / That clings to all of Labdacus' famed race.
cards.question: In Antigone's second speech (Str. 2), she cries out 'Ye mock me. Is it meet / Thus to insult me living, to my face?' and then in her final speech (Ant. 2) she shifts to describing 'my ill-starred father's piteous disgrace' and 'the hereditary stain.' What do these two moments together reveal about Antigone's character?

choices.label: A
choices.text: She blames the Chorus entirely for her death sentence and refuses to accept any connection to her family's past crimes.

choices.label: B
choices.text: She feels both wounded by others' indifference to her suffering and burdened by a cursed identity she cannot escape, showing that her anguish is both personal and inherited.

choices.label: C
choices.text: She compares herself to Niobe to claim divine status and uses her family's history to argue that she deserves to be freed from punishment.

choices.label: D
choices.text: She grows increasingly calm as she accepts that her family's sins, not Creon's decree, are the true cause of her fate.

cards.standardTitle: Text structure and feature purpose
cards.excerpt: OEDIPUS. Dear son of Aegeus, to the gods alone Is given immunity from eld and death; But nothing else escapes all-ruinous time. Earth’s might decays, the might of men decays, Honor grows cold, dishonor flourishes, There is no constancy ’twixt friend and friend, Or city and city; be it soon or late, Sweet turns to bitter, hate once more to love. If now ’tis sunshine betwixt Thebes and thee And not a cloud, Time in his endless course Gives birth to endless days and nights, wherein The merest nothing shall suffice to cut With serried spears your bonds of amity. Then shall my slumbering and buried corpse In its cold grave drink their warm life-blood up, If Zeus be Zeus and Phoebus still speak true. No more: ’tis ill to tear aside the veil Of mysteries; let me cease as I began: Enough if thou wilt keep thy plighted troth, Then shall thou ne’er complain that Oedipus Proved an unprofitable and thankless guest, Except the gods themselves shall play me false.
cards.whyThisWorks: Oedipus's speech moves through three distinct structural jobs—universal claim, time-based warning, and personal conditional pledge—giving students a clear model for analyzing how a paragraph's sections build on each other.
cards.skillStrategy: Ask yourself what job each section of the paragraph does: does it introduce a claim, develop it, complicate it, or resolve it?
evidencePoints: Then shall my slumbering and buried corpse / In its cold grave drink their warm life-blood up
If Zeus be Zeus and Phoebus still speak true
cards.question: In this speech, Oedipus opens with a universal claim—'Earth's might decays, the might of men decays'—and then warns that Time will cut 'with serried spears your bonds of amity.' What is the structural job of the lines 'Then shall my slumbering and buried corpse / In its cold grave drink their warm life-blood up, / If Zeus be Zeus and Phoebus still speak true'?

choices.label: A
choices.text: They restate the opening claim that 'Earth's might decays' by using Oedipus's corpse as a second example of universal decay, adding no new condition or consequence beyond what the first lines already established.

choices.label: B
choices.text: They shift from the general warning that Time will cut 'bonds of amity' to a personal conditional pledge: Oedipus's buried corpse will exact vengeance on Thebes, but only 'if Zeus be Zeus and Phoebus still speak true,' making his own fate the consequence of the warning.

choices.label: C
choices.text: They resolve the tension created by the warning about 'serried spears' by confirming that Zeus and Phoebus will permanently protect the friendship between Athens and Thebes, canceling the threat Time poses to their 'bonds of amity.'

choices.label: D
choices.text: They contradict the earlier warning that 'sweet turns to bitter' by showing that Oedipus's corpse will prevent conflict between the two cities regardless of whether Aegeus keeps his 'plighted troth,' removing the conditional nature of the pledge.

cards.standardTitle: Central idea and supporting evidence
cards.excerpt: CREON. Well, let her know the stubbornest of wills Are soonest bended, as the hardest iron, O’er-heated in the fire to brittleness, Flies soonest into fragments, shivered through. A snaffle curbs the fieriest steed, and he Who in subjection lives must needs be meek. But this proud girl, in insolence well-schooled, First overstepped the established law, and then— A second and worse act of insolence— She boasts and glories in her wickedness. Now if she thus can flout authority Unpunished, I am woman, she the man. But though she be my sister’s child or nearer Of kin than all who worship at my hearth, Nor she nor yet her sister shall escape The utmost penalty, for both I hold, As arch-conspirators, of equal guilt. Bring forth the older; even now I saw her Within the palace, frenzied and distraught. The workings of the mind discover oft Dark deeds in darkness schemed, before the act. More hateful still the miscreant who seeks When caught, to make a virtue of a crime.
cards.whyThisWorks: Creon's speech layers multiple analogies and declarations, requiring students to distinguish the controlling claim—that defiance of authority must be punished without exception—from supporting comparisons and isolated details.
cards.skillStrategy: Ask yourself: what one idea do ALL the details in this passage point back to? That is the central idea, not a single example or comparison.
evidencePoints: Now if she thus can flout authority Unpunished, I am woman, she the man.
Nor she nor yet her sister shall escape The utmost penalty, for both I hold, As arch-conspirators, of equal guilt.
cards.question: Creon declares, 'Now if she thus can flout authority / Unpunished, I am woman, she the man,' and then states that neither Antigone nor her sister 'shall escape / The utmost penalty.' What central idea do these two moments together express?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Creon's greatest concern in this speech is proving that Ismene is equally guilty of plotting against him.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Creon insists that any act of defiance against his rule must be met with full punishment, no matter who the offender is.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Creon uses the image of brittle iron and a bridled horse to warn Antigone that pride always leads to personal destruction.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Creon argues that Antigone's real crime is boasting about what she did rather than the act of breaking the law itself.

cards.standardTitle: Key literary elements add layers of meaning
cards.excerpt:
CHORUS. (Str. 1) O when the flying foe, Turning at last to bay, Soon will give blow for blow, Might I behold the fray; Hear the loud battle roar Swell, on the Pythian shore, Or by the torch-lit bay, Where the dread Queen and Maid Cherish the mystic rites, Rites they to none betray, Ere on his lips is laid Secrecy’s golden key By their own acolytes, Priestly Eumolpidae.

There I might chance behold Theseus our captain bold Meet with the robber band, Ere they have fled the land, Rescue by might and main Maidens, the captives twain.

(Ant. 1) Haply on swiftest steed, Or in the flying car, Now they approach the glen, West of white Oea’s scaur. They will be vanquished: Dread are our warriors, dread Theseus our chieftain’s men. Flashes each bridle bright, Charges each gallant knight, All that our Queen adore, Pallas their patron, or Him whose wide floods enring Earth, the great Ocean-king Whom Rhea bore.

(Str. 2) Fight they or now prepare To fight? a vision rare Tells me that soon again I shall behold the twain Maidens so ill bestead, By their kin buffeted. Today, today Zeus worketh some great thing This day shall victory bring. O for the wings, the wings of a dove, To be borne with the speed of the gale, Up and still upwards to sail And gaze on the fray from the clouds above. (Ant. 2) All-seeing Zeus, O lord of heaven, To our guardian host be given Might triumphant to surprise Flying foes and win their prize. Hear us, Zeus, and hear us, child Of Zeus, Athene undefiled, Hear, Apollo, hunter, hear, Huntress, sister of Apollo, Who the dappled swift-foot deer O’er the wooded glade dost follow; Help with your two-fold power Athens in danger’s hour! O wayfarer, thou wilt not have to tax The friends who watch for thee with false presage, For lo, an escort with the maids draws near. [Enter ANTIGONE and ISMENE with THESEUS]

OEDIPUS. Where, where? what sayest thou?
cards.whyThisWorks: The Chorus's urgent, prayer-filled speech—invoking gods, imagining flight, and crying 'Today, today Zeus worketh some great thing'—reveals collective anxiety and devotion that characterizes the community's relationship to Oedipus and his daughters, adding meaning to the rescue's emotional stakes.
cards.skillStrategy: When a character or group speaks with strong emotion or makes repeated appeals, ask yourself what those words reveal about who they are and what they value.
evidencePoints: O for the wings, the wings of a dove, To be borne with the speed of the gale, Up and still upwards to sail And gaze on the fray from the clouds above.
Today, today Zeus worketh some great thing / This day shall victory bring.
cards.question: In the second strophe, the Chorus cries, 'O for the wings, the wings of a dove, / To be borne with the speed of the gale' and then declares, 'Today, today Zeus worketh some great thing.' What do these lines reveal about the Chorus as a character?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The Chorus is confident in Theseus's military skill and feels no real concern about the outcome of the battle.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The Chorus is gripped by helpless longing and desperate hope, revealing a community that can only watch and pray while the fate of the maidens hangs in the balance.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The Chorus doubts that the gods will intervene and wishes it could fight alongside Theseus instead of relying on divine aid.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The Chorus is angry at Oedipus for placing his daughters in danger and calls on Zeus to punish those responsible.

cards.standardTitle: Theme development across a literary text
cards.excerpt:
POLYNEICES. Ah me, my sisters, shall I first lament My own afflictions, or my aged sire’s, Whom here I find a castaway, with you, In a strange land, an ancient beggar clad In antic tatters, marring all his frame, While o’er the sightless orbs his unkept locks Float in the breeze; and, as it were to match, He bears a wallet against hunger’s pinch. All this too late I learn, wretch that I am, Alas! I own it, and am proved most vile In my neglect of thee: I scorn myself. But as almighty Zeus in all he doth Hath Mercy for co-partner of this throne, Let Mercy, father, also sit enthroned In thy heart likewise. For transgressions past May be amended, cannot be made worse.

Why silent? Father, speak, nor turn away, Hast thou no word, wilt thou dismiss me then In mute disdain, nor tell me why thou art wrath? O ye his daughters, sisters mine, do ye This sullen, obstinate silence try to move. Let him not spurn, without a single word Of answer, me the suppliant of the god.
cards.whyThisWorks: Polyneices both confesses guilt ('I am proved most vile / In my neglect of thee') and immediately pivots to argue that 'transgressions past / May be amended,' giving students a clear test case for distinguishing details that develop the theme of redemption through acknowledgment from true-but-topical details about poverty or divine mercy.
cards.skillStrategy: Ask yourself: does this detail show the theme being built, or does it just describe what is happening in the scene?
evidencePoints: I am proved most vile / In my neglect of thee: I scorn myself.
For transgressions past / May be amended, cannot be made worse.
cards.question: Polyneices says, 'I am proved most vile / In my neglect of thee: I scorn myself,' and then immediately argues, 'transgressions past / May be amended, cannot be made worse.' Which statement best explains how these two lines together develop the theme that genuine self-reproach opens the door to repair?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Polyneices describes Oedipus dressed in 'antic tatters' with 'unkept locks' to show how badly his father has suffered, which proves that neglect has real consequences.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Polyneices first names his own guilt without excuse, then uses that admission as the foundation for claiming that past wrongs can still be corrected, making self-reproach the necessary condition for the possibility of redemption.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Polyneices invokes Zeus and Mercy as divine co-partners to argue that mercy is a cosmic principle, which shows that forgiveness belongs to the gods rather than to human choice.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Polyneices asks his sisters to break Oedipus's 'sullen, obstinate silence,' revealing that he depends on others to earn forgiveness rather than seeking it through his own words.

cards.standardTitle: Text structure and feature purpose
cards.excerpt: JOCASTA. Then thou mayest ease thy conscience on that score. Listen and I’ll convince thee that no man Hath scot or lot in the prophetic art. Here is the proof in brief. An oracle Once came to Laius (I will not say ’Twas from the Delphic god himself, but from His ministers) declaring he was doomed To perish by the hand of his own son, A child that should be born to him by me. Now Laius—so at least report affirmed— Was murdered on a day by highwaymen, No natives, at a spot where three roads meet. As for the child, it was but three days old, When Laius, its ankles pierced and pinned Together, gave it to be cast away By others on the trackless mountain side. So then Apollo brought it not to pass The child should be his father’s murderer, Or the dread terror find accomplishment, And Laius be slain by his own son. Such was the prophet’s horoscope. O king, Regard it not. Whate’er the god deems fit To search, himself unaided will reveal.
cards.whyThisWorks: Jocasta's speech opens with an explicit claim ('no man hath scot or lot in the prophetic art') and then immediately marshals the story of Laius's oracle as proof, making the paragraph's job—proving a stated claim—directly traceable to exact words.
cards.skillStrategy: Find the paragraph's opening claim, then ask what the rest of the paragraph does to that claim—does it prove it, contrast it, extend it, or shift away from it?
evidencePoints: Listen and I'll convince thee that no man Hath scot or lot in the prophetic art. Here is the proof in brief.
So then Apollo brought it not to pass The child should be his father's murderer… Such was the prophet's horoscope. O king, Regard it not.
cards.question: Jocasta opens by saying, 'Listen and I'll convince thee that no man Hath scot or lot in the prophetic art. Here is the proof in brief.' What job does the rest of her speech perform in relation to that opening statement?

choices.label: A
choices.text: It shifts away from the claim about prophecy and instead focuses on Jocasta's personal grief over the infant whose ankles were pierced and cast onto the mountain.

choices.label: B
choices.text: It proves the opening claim by recounting how the oracle foretelling that Laius would be killed by his own son failed to come true.

choices.label: C
choices.text: It contrasts the failed oracle of Laius with a second, successful prophecy in order to show that some predictions do come true.

choices.label: D
choices.text: It introduces the character of Laius for the first time so that Oedipus can understand who Laius was before Jocasta makes any argument about prophecy.

cards.standardTitle: Central idea and supporting evidence
cards.excerpt: JOCASTA. Then thou mayest ease thy conscience on that score. Listen and I’ll convince thee that no man Hath scot or lot in the prophetic art. Here is the proof in brief. An oracle Once came to Laius (I will not say ’Twas from the Delphic god himself, but from His ministers) declaring he was doomed To perish by the hand of his own son, A child that should be born to him by me. Now Laius—so at least report affirmed— Was murdered on a day by highwaymen, No natives, at a spot where three roads meet. As for the child, it was but three days old, When Laius, its ankles pierced and pinned Together, gave it to be cast away By others on the trackless mountain side. So then Apollo brought it not to pass The child should be his father’s murderer, Or the dread terror find accomplishment, And Laius be slain by his own son. Such was the prophet’s horoscope. O king, Regard it not. Whate’er the god deems fit To search, himself unaided will reveal.
cards.whyThisWorks: Jocasta explicitly states her purpose—'I'll convince thee that no man hath scot or lot in the prophetic art'—and then marshals the story of Laius's unfulfilled oracle as her proof, giving students a clear central claim to identify against plausible distractors drawn from supporting details.
cards.skillStrategy: Find the sentence where the speaker announces what she is trying to prove, then check which answer choice matches that announced claim rather than one of the details she uses to support it.
evidencePoints: Listen and I'll convince thee that no man Hath scot or lot in the prophetic art.
So then Apollo brought it not to pass / The child should be his father's murderer... Such was the prophet's horoscope. O king, Regard it not.
cards.question: Jocasta opens her speech by saying, 'I'll convince thee that no man hath scot or lot in the prophetic art,' and closes by saying, 'Regard it not.' Which statement expresses the central idea that these lines frame?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Laius was killed by foreign highwaymen at a crossroads, which shows that fate operates in ways no oracle can predict.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Because the oracle about Laius and his son went unfulfilled, prophecy has no reliable claim on human affairs and should be dismissed.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The oracle came from Apollo's ministers rather than from Apollo himself, so its authority was never legitimate to begin with.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Laius's choice to abandon his infant son on a mountainside was the decision that ultimately prevented the prophecy from coming true.

cards.standardTitle: Key literary elements add layers of meaning
cards.excerpt:
THESEUS. What means this?

OEDIPUS. Thou hast heard my tale of wrongs.

THESEUS. Ho! hasten to the altars, one of you. Command my liegemen leave the sacrifice And hurry, foot and horse, with rein unchecked, To where the paths that packmen use diverge, Lest the two maidens slip away, and I Become a mockery to this my guest, As one despoiled by force. Quick, as I bid. As for this stranger, had I let my rage, Justly provoked, have play, he had not ’scaped Scathless and uncorrected at my hands. But now the laws to which himself appealed, These and none others shall adjudicate. Thou shalt not quit this land, till thou hast fetched The maidens and produced them in my sight. Thou hast offended both against myself And thine own race and country. Having come Unto a State that champions right and asks For every action warranty of law, Thou hast set aside the custom of the land, And like some freebooter art carrying off What plunder pleases thee, as if forsooth Thou thoughtest this a city without men, Or manned by slaves, and me a thing of naught. Yet not from Thebes this villainy was learnt; Thebes is not wont to breed unrighteous sons, Nor would she praise thee, if she learnt that thou Wert robbing me—aye and the gods to boot, Haling by force their suppliants, poor maids. Were I on Theban soil, to prosecute The justest claim imaginable, I Would never wrest by violence my own Without sanction of your State or King; I should behave as fits an outlander Living amongst a foreign folk, but thou Shamest a city that deserves it not, Even thine own, and plentitude of years Have made of thee an old man and a fool. Therefore again I charge thee as before, See that the maidens are restored at once, Unless thou would’st continue here by force And not by choice a sojourner; so much I tell thee home and what I say, I mean.
cards.whyThisWorks: Theseus's decision to restrain his personal rage and instead invoke the law to force Creon to return the maidens dramatizes the conflict between raw power and civic justice, adding a thematic layer about what distinguishes a just ruler from a tyrant.
cards.skillStrategy: When a character makes a deliberate decision in the middle of a conflict, ask what that choice reveals about a larger idea the author wants you to understand.
evidencePoints: had I let my rage, / Justly provoked, have play, he had not 'scaped / Scathless and uncorrected at my hands. / But now the laws to which himself appealed, / These and none others shall adjudicate.
Thou hast set aside the custom of the land, / And like some freebooter art carrying off / What plunder pleases thee
cards.question: Theseus admits his rage is 'justly provoked' yet chooses to let the law 'adjudicate' rather than punish Creon himself. What deeper meaning does this decision add to the conflict between Theseus and Creon?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Theseus's restraint shows he fears Creon's power and avoids direct confrontation to protect his own city from retaliation.

choices.label: B
choices.text: By choosing law over personal vengeance, Theseus demonstrates that true authority is defined by submission to civic order rather than by the force of individual will—the very principle Creon violated.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Theseus's decision to invoke the law reveals that he doubts his own soldiers can recover the maidens and needs a legal pretext to buy time.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Theseus suppresses his anger only because Oedipus is a guest, and the conflict ultimately centers on the obligations of hospitality rather than on justice.

cards.standardTitle: Theme development across a literary text
cards.excerpt:
POLYNEICES. Ah me, my sisters, shall I first lament My own afflictions, or my aged sire’s, Whom here I find a castaway, with you, In a strange land, an ancient beggar clad In antic tatters, marring all his frame, While o’er the sightless orbs his unkept locks Float in the breeze; and, as it were to match, He bears a wallet against hunger’s pinch. All this too late I learn, wretch that I am, Alas! I own it, and am proved most vile In my neglect of thee: I scorn myself. But as almighty Zeus in all he doth Hath Mercy for co-partner of this throne, Let Mercy, father, also sit enthroned In thy heart likewise. For transgressions past May be amended, cannot be made worse.

Why silent? Father, speak, nor turn away, Hast thou no word, wilt thou dismiss me then In mute disdain, nor tell me why thou art wrath? O ye his daughters, sisters mine, do ye This sullen, obstinate silence try to move. Let him not spurn, without a single word Of answer, me the suppliant of the god.
cards.whyThisWorks: Polyneices's self-condemnation ('I am proved most vile / In my neglect of thee') followed immediately by his appeal for mercy ('Let Mercy, father, also sit enthroned / In thy heart likewise') and Oedipus's unbroken silence together dramatize the theme that confession alone cannot restore a relationship—the wronged party must choose to grant mercy.
cards.skillStrategy: Track what a character admits and what he asks for next, then notice how the other character responds—that gap between confession, plea, and silence is where the theme lives.
evidencePoints: I own it, and am proved most vile / In my neglect of thee: I scorn myself.
Let Mercy, father, also sit enthroned / In thy heart likewise. For transgressions past / May be amended, cannot be made worse.
cards.question: Polyneices first declares, 'I own it, and am proved most vile / In my neglect of thee: I scorn myself,' and then immediately pleads, 'Let Mercy, father, also sit enthroned / In thy heart likewise.' Oedipus responds only with 'sullen, obstinate silence.' What theme do these two moments develop together?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A son who openly confesses neglect and begs forgiveness will eventually persuade even a deeply wounded father to speak.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Admitting guilt and pleading for mercy cannot repair a broken relationship unless the person who was wronged chooses to grant it.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Children who abandon aging parents in poverty lose the right to ask for anything in return, making reconciliation impossible.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Invoking the mercy of Zeus gives a wrongdoer the moral authority to demand that a parent set aside anger and respond.

cards.standardTitle: Text structure and feature purpose
cards.excerpt: OEDIPUS. Out on the twain! The thoughts and actions all Are framed and modeled on Egyptian ways. For there the men sit at the loom indoors While the wives slave abroad for daily bread. So you, my children—those whom I behooved To bear the burden, stay at home like girls, While in their stead my daughters moil and drudge, Lightening their father’s misery. The one Since first she grew from girlish feebleness To womanhood has been the old man’s guide And shared my weary wandering, roaming oft Hungry and footsore through wild forest ways, In drenching rains and under scorching suns, Careless herself of home and ease, if so Her sire might have her tender ministry. And thou, my child, whilom thou wentest forth, Eluding the Cadmeians’ vigilance, To bring thy father all the oracles Concerning Oedipus, and didst make thyself My faithful lieger, when they banished me. And now what mission summons thee from home, What news, Ismene, hast thou for thy father? This much I know, thou com’st not empty-handed, Without a warning of some new alarm.
cards.whyThisWorks: The paragraph moves from Egyptian comparison to daughters' past sacrifices and then pivots in the final two sentences to direct questions about Ismene's current visit, giving students a clear structural shift to analyze for section job.
cards.skillStrategy: Ask yourself: what work does this section do differently from the sentences before it—does it introduce, develop, shift, or conclude the paragraph's main idea?
evidencePoints: And now what mission summons thee from home, / What news, Ismene, hast thou for thy father?
This much I know, thou com'st not empty-handed, / Without a warning of some new alarm.
cards.question: In Oedipus's speech, the paragraph opens with a comparison to Egyptian customs and then recounts how his daughters—not his sons—have served him faithfully. What is the structural job of the final two sentences, beginning with 'And now what mission summons thee from home'?

choices.label: A
choices.text: They extend the praise of Ismene's past loyalty by adding a new example of her roaming 'hungry and footsore through wild forest ways' alongside her sister.

choices.label: B
choices.text: They shift the paragraph's focus from recounting his daughters' past devotion to pressing Ismene for the purpose and news behind her present arrival.

choices.label: C
choices.text: They return to the Egyptian comparison from the opening to explain why his sons, who 'stay at home like girls,' are still unwilling to help him.

choices.label: D
choices.text: They conclude the paragraph by summarizing both daughters' sacrifices equally, treating Ismene's past missions and her sister's wandering as the same kind of service.

cards.standardTitle: Central idea and supporting evidence
cards.excerpt: ANTIGONE. O heed me, father, though I am young in years. Let the prince have his will and pay withal What in his eyes is service to the god; For our sake also let our brother come. If what he urges tend not to thy good He cannot surely wrest perforce thy will. To hear him then, what harm? By open words A scheme of villainy is soon bewrayed. Thou art his father, therefore canst not pay In kind a son’s most impious outrages. O listen to him; other men like thee Have thankless children and are choleric, But yielding to persuasion’s gentle spell They let their savage mood be exorcised. Look thou to the past, forget the present, think On all the woe thy sire and mother brought thee; Thence wilt thou draw this lesson without fail, Of evil passion evil is the end. Thou hast, alas, to prick thy memory, Stern monitors, these ever-sightless orbs. O yield to us; just suitors should not need To be importunate, nor he that takes A favor lack the grace to make return.
cards.whyThisWorks: Antigone's speech builds a sustained argument that Oedipus should allow Polynices to speak, using multiple lines of reasoning—harm in listening is minimal, past suffering should teach patience, and a father owes a son a hearing—which requires students to synthesize across the paragraph rather than latch onto a single detail or topic word.
cards.skillStrategy: Ask yourself: what is the speaker trying to convince the listener of across the whole passage, not just in one line?
evidencePoints: To hear him then, what harm? By open words A scheme of villainy is soon bewrayed.
Look thou to the past, forget the present, think On all the woe thy sire and mother brought thee; Thence wilt thou draw this lesson without fail, Of evil passion evil is the end.
cards.question: Which statement best expresses the central idea of Antigone's speech to her father?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Oedipus has suffered so greatly from his own parents that he has lost the ability to feel compassion for anyone.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Oedipus should grant Polynices an audience because the risk of listening is small, past suffering should counsel patience over anger, and a father owes a son that much grace.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Polynices is acting in service to the gods, so refusing to hear him would be an act of impiety that Oedipus cannot afford.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Antigone believes that Polynices has a scheme of villainy that will be exposed the moment he is allowed to speak openly.

cards.standardTitle: Rhetorical appeals and author purpose
cards.excerpt:
THESEUS. I know that none Shall hale thee hence in my despite. Such threats Vented in anger oft, are blusterers, An idle breath, forgot when sense returns. And for thy foemen, though their words were brave, Boasting to bring thee back, they are like to find The seas between us wide and hard to sail. Such my firm purpose, but in any case Take heart, since Phoebus sent thee here. My name, Though I be distant, warrants thee from harm.

CHORUS. (Str. 1) Thou hast come to a steed-famed land for rest, O stranger worn with toil, To a land of all lands the goodliest Colonus’ glistening soil. ’Tis the haunt of the clear-voiced nightingale, Who hid in her bower, among The wine-dark ivy that wreathes the vale, Trilleth her ceaseless song; And she loves, where the clustering berries nod O’er a sunless, windless glade, The spot by no mortal footstep trod, The pleasance kept for the Bacchic god, Where he holds each night his revels wild With the nymphs who fostered the lusty child.
cards.whyThisWorks: Theseus uses a direct appeal to ethos by invoking his own name and authority as a guarantee of Oedipus's safety, while the Chorus shifts to pathos through lyrical imagery of Colonus, allowing students to judge which appeal is more appropriate for each speaker's purpose and audience.
cards.skillStrategy: Ask yourself: who is speaking, what do they want the listener to feel or believe, and why would that particular appeal work better than another for that moment?
evidencePoints: My name, Though I be distant, warrants thee from harm.
Thou hast come to a steed-famed land for rest, O stranger worn with toil, To a land of all lands the goodliest
cards.question: In his speech, Theseus tells Oedipus, 'My name, Though I be distant, warrants thee from harm.' Why is this appeal appropriate for Theseus's purpose in this moment?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Theseus appeals to Oedipus's emotions by describing the beauty of Colonus so that Oedipus will feel welcome and forget his fear of enemies.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Theseus appeals to his own authority and reputation as ruler so that Oedipus, who fears being seized by enemies, will trust that the promise of protection carries real power.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Theseus appeals to divine will by reminding Oedipus that Phoebus sent him here, making the gods, rather than Theseus himself, responsible for Oedipus's safety.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Theseus appeals to logic by explaining that the wide seas make it physically impossible for any enemy to reach Oedipus, so no further protection is actually needed.

cards.standardTitle: Key literary elements add layers of meaning
cards.excerpt:
POLYNEICES. Ah me, my sisters, shall I first lament My own afflictions, or my aged sire’s, Whom here I find a castaway, with you, In a strange land, an ancient beggar clad In antic tatters, marring all his frame, While o’er the sightless orbs his unkept locks Float in the breeze; and, as it were to match, He bears a wallet against hunger’s pinch. All this too late I learn, wretch that I am, Alas! I own it, and am proved most vile In my neglect of thee: I scorn myself. But as almighty Zeus in all he doth Hath Mercy for co-partner of this throne, Let Mercy, father, also sit enthroned In thy heart likewise. For transgressions past May be amended, cannot be made worse.

Why silent? Father, speak, nor turn away, Hast thou no word, wilt thou dismiss me then In mute disdain, nor tell me why thou art wrath? O ye his daughters, sisters mine, do ye This sullen, obstinate silence try to move. Let him not spurn, without a single word Of answer, me the suppliant of the god.
cards.whyThisWorks: Polyneices' self-serving confession ('All this too late I learn') paired with Oedipus's wordless rejection shows students how conflict between a plea and silence can reveal that remorse driven by need carries no restorative power.
cards.skillStrategy: Ask yourself what the conflict reveals about a character's true motives, then use the text's exact words to support your interpretation.
evidencePoints: All this too late I learn, wretch that I am, Alas! I own it, and am proved most vile In my neglect of thee
Hast thou no word, wilt thou dismiss me then In mute disdain, nor tell me why thou art wrath?
cards.question: Polyneices admits 'All this too late I learn' and begs Oedipus to speak, yet Oedipus answers only with silence. What meaning does this conflict add to the scene?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Oedipus's silence shows he has forgiven Polyneices inwardly but is too proud to say so, suggesting reconciliation is still possible.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Polyneices confesses his neglect only when he needs Oedipus's help, and Oedipus's silence suggests that remorse offered out of self-interest cannot undo past wrongs.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Oedipus's silence reveals he is too consumed by grief over his 'antic tatters' and blindness to hear Polyneices' appeal at all.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Polyneices' appeal to Zeus and Mercy shows his faith is sincere, but Oedipus's silence suggests he no longer believes in divine justice.

cards.standardTitle: Theme development across a literary text
cards.excerpt:
THESEUS. Oft had I heard of thee in times gone by— The bloody mutilation of thine eyes— And therefore know thee, son of Laius. All that I lately gathered on the way Made my conjecture doubly sure; and now Thy garb and that marred visage prove to me That thou art he. So pitying thine estate, Most ill-starred Oedipus, I fain would know What is the suit ye urge on me and Athens, Thou and the helpless maiden at thy side. Declare it; dire indeed must be the tale Whereat _I_ should recoil. I too was reared, Like thee, in exile, and in foreign lands Wrestled with many perils, no man more. Wherefore no alien in adversity Shall seek in vain my succor, nor shalt thou; I know myself a mortal, and my share In what the morrow brings no more than thine.

OEDIPUS. Theseus, thy words so apt, so generous So comfortable, need no long reply Both who I am and of what lineage sprung, And from what land I came, thou hast declared. So without prologue I may utter now My brief petition, and the tale is told.
cards.whyThisWorks: Theseus's confession of his own exile and peril directly mirrors Oedipus's suffering, and Oedipus's reply that Theseus's words need 'no long reply' shows how shared hardship collapses the distance between strangers—making this exchange a clear passage moment through which the theme of suffering fostering compassion is developed.
cards.skillStrategy: When tracking theme through moments, find the exact words a character uses to connect their experience to another's, then notice how the second character's response confirms that connection.
evidencePoints: I too was reared, Like thee, in exile, and in foreign lands / Wrestled with many perils, no man more.
Theseus, thy words so apt, so generous / So comfortable, need no long reply.
cards.question: When Theseus says 'I too was reared, Like thee, in exile, and in foreign lands / Wrestled with many perils, no man more,' and Oedipus replies that Theseus's words are 'so apt, so generous / So comfortable' that they 'need no long reply,' what theme do these two moments develop together?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A ruler earns loyalty by publicly recounting his past hardships before granting any petition from a foreign exile.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Shared experience of suffering creates genuine compassion between people, making lengthy explanation unnecessary when one sufferer recognizes another.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Theseus agrees to hear Oedipus's petition only because Oedipus's 'marred visage' provides visible proof of his identity, not because of any shared hardship.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Oedipus's brief reply shows that exiles distrust even generous rulers and prefer to withhold the full story of their suffering until safety is guaranteed.

cards.standardTitle: Text structure and feature purpose
cards.excerpt: OEDIPUS. I pray thee do not wonder if the sight Of children, given o’er for lost, has made My converse somewhat long and tedious. Full well I know the joy I have of them Is due to thee, to thee and no man else; Thou wast their sole deliverer, none else. The gods deal with thee after my desire, With thee and with this land! for fear of heaven I found above all peoples most with you, And righteousness and lips that cannot lie. I speak in gratitude of what I know, For all I have I owe to thee alone. Give me thy hand, O Prince, that I may touch it, And if thou wilt permit me, kiss thy cheek. What say I? Can I wish that thou should’st touch One fallen like me to utter wretchedness, Corrupt and tainted with a thousand ills? Oh no, I would not let thee if thou would’st. They only who have known calamity Can share it. Let me greet thee where thou art, And still befriend me as thou hast till now.
cards.whyThisWorks: The paragraph visibly shifts mid-speech from Oedipus expressing deep gratitude and reaching toward physical connection to pulling back in shame over his own corruption, making the paragraph's internal turn a clear teaching moment for the 'shifts' function of a section.
cards.skillStrategy: Ask yourself: does this paragraph stay on one idea the whole time, or does it start in one emotional direction and then turn — and what does that turn reveal about the speaker?
evidencePoints: Give me thy hand, O Prince, that I may touch it, / And if thou wilt permit me, kiss thy cheek.
Oh no, I would not let thee if thou would'st. / They only who have known calamity / Can share it.
cards.question: Within this speech, Oedipus moves from expressing gratitude and reaching toward physical connection to withdrawing that request. What is the primary function of this shift in the paragraph?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Oedipus concludes his speech by summarizing all the ways Theseus has helped him and his children, leaving the audience with a complete picture of their bond.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Oedipus introduces deep gratitude and then turns sharply inward, revealing that his sense of his own corruption prevents him from accepting the very closeness he desires.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Oedipus extends his earlier praise of Theseus by adding a new reason — that Theseus alone understands suffering — to explain why physical contact between them would be appropriate.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Oedipus contrasts his own wretchedness with Theseus's righteousness in order to argue that Theseus should step back and allow Oedipus to greet him from a distance out of respect.

cards.standardTitle: Central idea and supporting evidence
cards.excerpt: OEDIPUS. Stern-visaged queens, since coming to this land First in your sanctuary I bent the knee, Frown not on me or Phoebus, who, when erst He told me all my miseries to come, Spake of this respite after many years, Some haven in a far-off land, a rest Vouchsafed at last by dread divinities. “There,” said he, “shalt thou round thy weary life, A blessing to the land wherein thou dwell’st, But to the land that cast thee forth, a curse.” And of my weird he promised signs should come, Earthquake, or thunderclap, or lightning flash. And now I recognize as yours the sign That led my wanderings to this your grove; Else had I never lighted on you first, A wineless man on your seat of native rock. O goddesses, fulfill Apollo’s word, Grant me some consummation of my life, If haply I appear not all too vile, A thrall to sorrow worse than any slave. Hear, gentle daughters of primeval Night, Hear, namesake of great Pallas; Athens, first Of cities, pity this dishonored shade, The ghost of him who once was Oedipus.
cards.whyThisWorks: Oedipus's speech builds toward a single plea—'fulfill Apollo's word' and 'grant me some consummation of my life'—giving students a clear textual anchor to distinguish the central idea from supporting details like the signs or the curse.
cards.skillStrategy: Find the sentence where the speaker states what he most wants or needs; that moment usually carries the central idea, while surrounding details exist only to support it.
evidencePoints: O goddesses, fulfill Apollo's word, Grant me some consummation of my life
Hear, gentle daughters of primeval Night… pity this dishonored shade, The ghost of him who once was Oedipus.
cards.question: In this speech, Oedipus moves from recounting Apollo's prophecy to making a direct plea: 'O goddesses, fulfill Apollo's word, Grant me some consummation of my life.' What central idea does this plea, together with the rest of the speech, express?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Apollo's prophecy was unreliable, so Oedipus must personally persuade the goddesses to end his suffering rather than trust divine promises.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Oedipus, worn down by dishonor and suffering, calls on the goddesses to honor the divine promise that his long wandering will finally reach a peaceful end.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The signs of earthquake, thunderclap, and lightning that led Oedipus to the grove are the most important part of Apollo's message to him.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Oedipus's chief concern is warning Athens that the land which exiled him will suffer a curse, and he asks the goddesses to carry out that punishment.

cards.standardTitle: Rhetorical appeals and author purpose
cards.excerpt:
THESEUS. I know that none Shall hale thee hence in my despite. Such threats Vented in anger oft, are blusterers, An idle breath, forgot when sense returns. And for thy foemen, though their words were brave, Boasting to bring thee back, they are like to find The seas between us wide and hard to sail. Such my firm purpose, but in any case Take heart, since Phoebus sent thee here. My name, Though I be distant, warrants thee from harm.

CHORUS. (Str. 1) Thou hast come to a steed-famed land for rest, O stranger worn with toil, To a land of all lands the goodliest Colonus’ glistening soil. ’Tis the haunt of the clear-voiced nightingale, Who hid in her bower, among The wine-dark ivy that wreathes the vale, Trilleth her ceaseless song; And she loves, where the clustering berries nod O’er a sunless, windless glade, The spot by no mortal footstep trod, The pleasance kept for the Bacchic god, Where he holds each night his revels wild With the nymphs who fostered the lusty child.
cards.whyThisWorks: The Chorus's extended metaphor of Colonus as a sacred, untouched haven—'a spot by no mortal footstep trod'—works alongside the nightingale and Bacchic imagery to persuade the audience that Oedipus has arrived in a divinely protected place, making the figurative language directly tied to an explanatory and persuasive purpose.
cards.skillStrategy: When you spot figurative language, ask yourself: what idea is the author trying to make you believe or understand, and how does this image push you toward that belief?
evidencePoints: 'The spot by no mortal footstep trod, The pleasance kept for the Bacchic god'
'The seas between us wide and hard to sail'
cards.question: In Theseus's speech, he describes his enemies as likely to find 'the seas between us wide and hard to sail.' How does this figurative language support Theseus's purpose in speaking to Oedipus?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The image of wide seas shows that Theseus is uncertain whether he can protect Oedipus, since the distance between them creates real danger.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The image of wide, hard-to-sail seas exaggerates the obstacles facing Oedipus's enemies to persuade Oedipus that he is beyond their reach and can feel safe.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The image of the seas reflects Theseus's anger at his enemies and shifts the focus of his speech away from Oedipus's protection toward his own military power.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The image of the seas reminds Oedipus that he traveled a long distance to reach Colonus, reinforcing how exhausted and vulnerable he is as a stranger.

cards.standardTitle: Key literary elements add layers of meaning
cards.excerpt:
ISMENE. Bethink thee, sister, of our father’s fate, Abhorred, dishonored, self-convinced of sin, Blinded, himself his executioner. Think of his mother-wife (ill sorted names) Done by a noose herself had twined to death And last, our hapless brethren in one day, Both in a mutual destiny involved, Self-slaughtered, both the slayer and the slain. Bethink thee, sister, we are left alone; Shall we not perish wretchedest of all, If in defiance of the law we cross A monarch’s will?—weak women, think of that, Not framed by nature to contend with men. Remember this too that the stronger rules; We must obey his orders, these or worse. Therefore I plead compulsion and entreat The dead to pardon. I perforce obey The powers that be. ’Tis foolishness, I ween, To overstep in aught the golden mean.

ANTIGONE. I urge no more; nay, wert thou willing still, I would not welcome such a fellowship. Go thine own way; myself will bury him. How sweet to die in such employ, to rest,— Sister and brother linked in love’s embrace— A sinless sinner, banned awhile on earth, But by the dead commended; and with them I shall abide for ever. As for thee, Scorn, if thou wilt, the eternal laws of Heaven.
cards.whyThisWorks: The sisters' opposing responses to the same family tragedy—Ismene citing weakness and law, Antigone calling death 'sweet'—show how conflict between characters reveals competing values and deepens thematic meaning.
cards.skillStrategy: When two characters clash over a decision, ask what each character's choice reveals about what they believe matters most in life.
evidencePoints: How sweet to die in such employ
We must obey his orders, these or worse
cards.question: Ismene argues 'We must obey his orders, these or worse,' while Antigone replies 'How sweet to die in such employ.' What meaning does this conflict add to the scene?

choices.label: A
choices.text: It shows that Antigone is driven by grief over her father and brothers rather than by any belief in divine law.

choices.label: B
choices.text: It reveals that the sisters hold opposing definitions of duty—Ismene prizes survival under the king's law, while Antigone prizes loyalty to the dead above her own life.

choices.label: C
choices.text: It suggests Antigone agrees with Ismene's reasoning but rejects her out of personal pride and a wish to act alone.

choices.label: D
choices.text: It demonstrates that both sisters ultimately share the same values but differ only in how much courage each possesses.

cards.whyThisWorks: Ismene's catalog of family suffering followed by her plea for submission, contrasted with Antigone's embrace of death as honorable duty, gives students two distinct story moments that together develop the theme that loyalty to divine law demands personal sacrifice even when human authority threatens destruction.
cards.skillStrategy: When tracking theme, notice how two different characters' responses to the same crisis each add a new layer to the same central idea rather than repeating it.
evidencePoints: I perforce obey / The powers that be. 'Tis foolishness, I ween, / To overstep in aught the golden mean.
How sweet to die in such employ, to rest,— / Sister and brother linked in love's embrace— / A sinless sinner, banned awhile on earth, / But by the dead commended
cards.question: Both Ismene's speech and Antigone's reply contribute to a theme about the conflict between human law and personal duty. How do these two moments work together to develop that theme?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Ismene's recounting of their family's ruin shows that defying authority always leads to catastrophe, and Antigone's willingness to die confirms that their family is cursed beyond saving.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Ismene's surrender to the king's power out of fear of destruction establishes the cost of obedience to human law, while Antigone's acceptance of death as honorable service to the dead reveals that following divine duty requires sacrificing one's life.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Ismene's appeal to their shared weakness as women introduces the theme that women cannot challenge men, and Antigone's defiance develops the idea that exceptional individuals can overcome that limitation.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Ismene's list of family tragedies and Antigone's vow to bury their brother both show that grief drives people to reckless choices, suggesting the theme that sorrow destroys rational judgment.

O yield to us; just suitors should not need To be importunate, nor he that takes A favor lack the grace to make return.
cards.whyThisWorks: Antigone's speech demonstrates a clear paragraph job of building a persuasive case through layered appeals—logical ('To hear him then, what harm?'), historical ('Look thou to the past'), and emotional ('these ever-sightless orbs')—giving students a rich example of how a single paragraph can extend and prove an argument.
cards.skillStrategy: Ask yourself: does this paragraph start something new, push an idea further, or wrap something up? Then find the exact words that show that job.
evidencePoints: To hear him then, what harm? By open words A scheme of villainy is soon bewrayed.
Look thou to the past, forget the present, think On all the woe thy sire and mother brought thee; Thence wilt thou draw this lesson without fail, Of evil passion evil is the end.
cards.question: Antigone asks her father, 'To hear him then, what harm?' and then adds 'Look thou to the past, forget the present.' What job do these two moves together perform in her speech?

choices.label: A
choices.text: They introduce Polynices to Oedipus for the first time, establishing who is asking for the meeting and why he cannot come himself.

choices.label: B
choices.text: They extend her argument by first removing her father's fear of risk and then supplying a historical lesson to reinforce why he should agree.

choices.label: C
choices.text: They shift her argument away from Polynices entirely, redirecting her father's attention toward the suffering caused by his own parents rather than his son.

choices.label: D
choices.text: They conclude her appeal by summarizing the two conditions Oedipus has already accepted before granting Polynices an audience.

cards.standardTitle: Central idea and supporting evidence
cards.excerpt:
CREON. Be sure thou wilt not traffic on my wits.

TEIRESIAS. Know then for sure, the coursers of the sun Not many times shall run their race, before Thou shalt have given the fruit of thine own loins In quittance of thy murder, life for life; For that thou hast entombed a living soul, And sent below a denizen of earth, And wronged the nether gods by leaving here A corpse unlaved, unwept, unsepulchered. Herein thou hast no part, nor e’en the gods In heaven; and thou usurp’st a power not thine. For this the avenging spirits of Heaven and Hell Who dog the steps of sin are on thy trail: What these have suffered thou shalt suffer too. And now, consider whether bought by gold I prophesy. For, yet a little while, And sound of lamentation shall be heard, Of men and women through thy desolate halls; And all thy neighbor States are leagues to avenge Their mangled warriors who have found a grave I’ the maw of wolf or hound, or winged bird That flying homewards taints their city’s air. These are the shafts, that like a bowman I Provoked to anger, loosen at thy breast, Unerring, and their smart thou shalt not shun. Boy, lead me home, that he may vent his spleen On younger men, and learn to curb his tongue With gentler manners than his present mood. [Exit TEIRESIAS]

CHORUS. My liege, that man hath gone, foretelling woe. And, O believe me, since these grizzled locks Were like the raven, never have I known The prophet’s warning to the State to fail.
cards.whyThisWorks: Teiresias's speech builds a cumulative case—entombing the living, leaving the dead unburied, defying the gods—that culminates in the Chorus confirming his prophecies never fail, giving students a clear central idea to distinguish from isolated details.
cards.skillStrategy: Ask yourself what the whole passage adds up to, not just what one character says or does in a single moment.
evidencePoints: For this the avenging spirits of Heaven and Hell / Who dog the steps of sin are on thy trail: / What these have suffered thou shalt suffer too.
never have I known / The prophet's warning to the State to fail.
cards.question: Teiresias tells Creon, 'What these have suffered thou shalt suffer too,' and the Chorus adds that the prophet's warning has 'never' failed. What central idea do these two moments together express about Creon's situation?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Creon's neighboring states have already formed alliances and will soon attack him in battle to avenge their unburied warriors.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Creon's violations of divine law—entombing the living and leaving the dead unburied—will bring certain suffering upon him, as a prophet whose warnings never fail has declared.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Teiresias is primarily concerned with defending his reputation against Creon's accusation that he accepted gold in exchange for his prophecy.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The Chorus warns Creon that Teiresias has grown too old and angry to be trusted, and that his prophecies no longer apply to the State.

cards.standardTitle: Rhetorical appeals and author purpose
cards.excerpt: CREON. Burghers, my noble friends, ye take alarm At my approach (I read it in your eyes), Fear nothing and refrain from angry words. I come with no ill purpose; I am old, And know the city whither I am come, Without a peer amongst the powers of Greece. It was by reason of my years that I Was chosen to persuade your guest and bring Him back to Thebes; not the delegate Of one man, but commissioned by the State, Since of all Thebans I have most bewailed, Being his kinsman, his most grievous woes. O listen to me, luckless Oedipus, Come home! The whole Cadmeian people claim With right to have thee back, I most of all, For most of all (else were I vile indeed) I mourn for thy misfortunes, seeing thee An aged outcast, wandering on and on, A beggar with one handmaid for thy stay. Ah! who had e’er imagined she could fall To such a depth of misery as this, To tend in penury thy stricken frame, A virgin ripe for wedlock, but unwed, A prey for any wanton ravisher? Seems it not cruel this reproach I cast On thee and on myself and all the race? Aye, but an open shame cannot be hid. Hide it, O hide it, Oedipus, thou canst. O, by our fathers’ gods, consent I pray; Come back to Thebes, come to thy father’s home, Bid Athens, as is meet, a fond farewell; Thebes thy old foster-mother claims thee first.
cards.whyThisWorks: Creon's speech pairs a threatening image of vulnerability ('A prey for any wanton ravisher') with a nurturing metaphor ('Thebes thy old foster-mother claims thee first') to manipulate Oedipus through both fear and emotional longing, making this a rich example of figurative language serving a persuasive purpose.
cards.skillStrategy: When analyzing figurative language for purpose, ask what emotion each image is designed to trigger in the audience and how those emotions work together to push the listener toward the speaker's goal.
evidencePoints: A prey for any wanton ravisher
Thebes thy old foster-mother claims thee first
cards.question: In his speech, Creon describes Oedipus's daughter as 'A prey for any wanton ravisher' and calls Thebes 'thy old foster-mother.' How do these two figurative phrases work together to advance Creon's persuasive purpose of convincing Oedipus to return to Thebes?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The first phrase expresses Creon's sincere outrage at Athens for failing to protect Oedipus's daughter, while the second phrase reminds Oedipus that Thebes has always been governed by just laws that would keep his family safe.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The first phrase stirs guilt and fear by casting Oedipus's daughter as dangerously unprotected, while the second frames Thebes as a nurturing homeland, together pressuring Oedipus through both shame and the promise of belonging.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Both phrases appeal to Oedipus's civic pride by reminding him that the Cadmeian people have suffered without his leadership and that Thebes needs a ruler, not a wandering outcast, to restore its former greatness.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The first phrase highlights how deeply Oedipus has fallen from his former royal status, and the second phrase contrasts Athens as a foreign city with Thebes as his true home, making both phrases a logical argument about political obligation rather than an emotional appeal.

cards.standardTitle: Key literary elements add layers of meaning
cards.excerpt: ANTIGONE. What but the thought of our two brothers dead, The one by Creon graced with funeral rites, The other disappointed? Eteocles He hath consigned to earth (as fame reports) With obsequies that use and wont ordain, So gracing him among the dead below. But Polyneices, a dishonored corse, (So by report the royal edict runs) No man may bury him or make lament— Must leave him tombless and unwept, a feast For kites to scent afar and swoop upon. Such is the edict (if report speak true) Of Creon, our most noble Creon, aimed At thee and me, aye me too; and anon He will be here to promulgate, for such As have not heard, his mandate; ’tis in sooth No passing humor, for the edict says Whoe’er transgresses shall be stoned to death. So stands it with us; now ’tis thine to show If thou art worthy of thy blood or base.
cards.whyThisWorks: The excerpt places Antigone between two explicit consequences—leaving Polyneices 'tombless and unwept, a feast for kites' versus being 'stoned to death' for defying Creon—making the conflict between civic law and sacred duty the engine of the passage's meaning.
cards.skillStrategy: When a character faces two opposing forces with named consequences, ask what each side demands and what the character stands to lose either way—that tension is where the conflict adds meaning.
evidencePoints: tombless and unwept, a feast for kites to scent afar and swoop upon
whoe'er transgresses shall be stoned to death
cards.question: Antigone describes Polyneices as left 'tombless and unwept, a feast for kites to scent afar and swoop upon' under Creon's edict, while warning that 'whoe'er transgresses shall be stoned to death.' How does this specific conflict between the edict's punishment and the duty owed to the dead add meaning to the passage?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The contrast between Polyneices left as 'a feast for kites' and Eteocles given proper 'obsequies' shows that Antigone's concern is purely personal grief over a favored brother, so the conflict amounts to a family rivalry rather than a clash between political authority and sacred obligation.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The edict forces Antigone to choose between leaving her brother 'tombless and unwept' in obedience to Creon or honoring the dead at the cost of being 'stoned to death,' revealing that state power can demand a betrayal of what is owed to the dead.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Because Creon must still come 'to promulgate' the mandate 'for such as have not heard,' the edict is not yet fully binding, which means the threat of being 'stoned to death' carries no real weight and the conflict poses no genuine danger to Antigone.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Antigone's closing challenge—'now 'tis thine to show if thou art worthy of thy blood or base'—resolves the conflict by transferring all moral responsibility to her sister, indicating that Antigone herself has already decided to accept Creon's edict rather than risk being 'stoned to death.'

cards.standardTitle: Theme development across a literary text
cards.excerpt: GUARD. I cannot tell, for there was ne’er a trace Of pick or mattock—hard unbroken ground, Without a scratch or rut of chariot wheels, No sign that human hands had been at work. When the first sentry of the morning watch Gave the alarm, we all were terror-stricken. The corpse had vanished, not interred in earth, But strewn with dust, as if by one who sought To avert the curse that haunts the unburied dead: Of hound or ravening jackal, not a sign. Thereat arose an angry war of words; Guard railed at guard and blows were like to end it, For none was there to part us, each in turn Suspected, but the guilt brought home to none, From lack of evidence. We challenged each The ordeal, or to handle red-hot iron, Or pass through fire, affirming on our oath Our innocence—we neither did the deed Ourselves, nor know who did or compassed it. Our quest was at a standstill, when one spake And bowed us all to earth like quivering reeds, For there was no gainsaying him nor way To escape perdition: _Ye_are_bound_to_tell_ _The_King,_ye_cannot_hide_it; so he spake. And he convinced us all; so lots were cast, And I, unlucky scapegoat, drew the prize. So here I am unwilling and withal Unwelcome; no man cares to hear ill news.
cards.whyThisWorks: The Guard's account of guards turning on each other under suspicion and then the lone Guard arriving 'unwilling' before Creon as an 'unlucky scapegoat' provides two concrete passage moments that together develop the theme that authoritarian power compels people to act against their own interests and will.
cards.skillStrategy: To find theme developed through moments, identify two specific events in the passage and ask what idea about human experience both events point toward.
evidencePoints: Guard railed at guard and blows were like to end it, For none was there to part us, each in turn Suspected, but the guilt brought home to none
So here I am unwilling and withal Unwelcome; no man cares to hear ill news
cards.question: In the Guard's speech, the guards 'railed at' one another and nearly came to blows when no one could prove guilt, and after lots were cast the Guard arrives before Creon calling himself an 'unlucky scapegoat' who is 'unwilling' and 'unwelcome.' What theme do these two moments develop together?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The guards' inability to find 'a trace of pick or mattock' or chariot ruts proves that a divine force acted, so no human soldier could be held responsible for reporting the burial.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Fear of Creon's authority forces people to act against their own will—driving the guards to turn on each other to escape blame and then compelling one unwilling man to deliver dreaded news under threat of 'perdition.'

choices.label: C
choices.text: Loyalty among soldiers collapses entirely when a crime goes unsolved, since the guards could neither identify the guilty party nor willingly agree on who should face the king.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The guards' railing at one another and the Guard's reluctant arrival both show that soldiers are cowards who prioritize self-preservation over their duty to investigate who strewed dust on the corpse.

cards.standardTitle: Text structure and feature purpose
cards.excerpt: OEDIPUS. Stern-visaged queens, since coming to this land First in your sanctuary I bent the knee, Frown not on me or Phoebus, who, when erst He told me all my miseries to come, Spake of this respite after many years, Some haven in a far-off land, a rest Vouchsafed at last by dread divinities. “There,” said he, “shalt thou round thy weary life, A blessing to the land wherein thou dwell’st, But to the land that cast thee forth, a curse.” And of my weird he promised signs should come, Earthquake, or thunderclap, or lightning flash. And now I recognize as yours the sign That led my wanderings to this your grove; Else had I never lighted on you first, A wineless man on your seat of native rock. O goddesses, fulfill Apollo’s word, Grant me some consummation of my life, If haply I appear not all too vile, A thrall to sorrow worse than any slave. Hear, gentle daughters of primeval Night, Hear, namesake of great Pallas; Athens, first Of cities, pity this dishonored shade, The ghost of him who once was Oedipus.
cards.whyThisWorks: Oedipus's speech moves in a clear three-part structure—recalling Apollo's prophecy, recognizing the grove as the promised sign, then issuing his plea—so students can identify exactly what job the recognition moment performs in connecting the prophecy to the petition.
cards.skillStrategy: To find a paragraph section's job, ask what it connects: does it introduce, bridge, or conclude the paragraph's central idea?
evidencePoints: And now I recognize as yours the sign / That led my wanderings to this your grove
O goddesses, fulfill Apollo's word
cards.question: In his speech, Oedipus first recalls Apollo's promise of 'some haven in a far-off land' and then states, 'And now I recognize as yours the sign / That led my wanderings to this your grove.' What is the structural job of this recognition moment within the paragraph?

choices.label: A
choices.text: It introduces a new conflict by suggesting the grove may not be the promised haven, because Apollo also warned that Oedipus would be 'a curse' to 'the land that cast thee forth,' leaving his welcome uncertain.

choices.label: B
choices.text: It serves as the turning point that links Apollo's earlier prophecy to Oedipus's closing petition, giving him the evidence that this grove is the promised place and justifying his appeal, 'O goddesses, fulfill Apollo's word.'

choices.label: C
choices.text: It shifts the paragraph's focus from the prophecy to Oedipus's past suffering, explaining why he calls himself 'a thrall to sorrow worse than any slave' and why he was cast out of his homeland.

choices.label: D
choices.text: It marks the moment Oedipus stops addressing the Furies entirely and redirects his appeal to Athens—'first of cities'—naming the city rather than the goddesses as the source of his promised rest.

cards.standardTitle: Central idea and supporting evidence
cards.excerpt:
CREON. What is this? Thy words inspire a dread presentiment.

TEIRESIAS. The divination of my arts shall tell. Sitting upon my throne of augury, As is my wont, where every fowl of heaven Find harborage, upon mine ears was borne A jargon strange of twitterings, hoots, and screams; So knew I that each bird at the other tare With bloody talons, for the whirr of wings Could signify naught else. Perturbed in soul, I straight essayed the sacrifice by fire On blazing altars, but the God of Fire Came not in flame, and from the thigh bones dripped And sputtered in the ashes a foul ooze; Gall-bladders cracked and spurted up: the fat Melted and fell and left the thigh bones bare. Such are the signs, taught by this lad, I read— As I guide others, so the boy guides me— The frustrate signs of oracles grown dumb. O King, thy willful temper ails the State, For all our shrines and altars are profaned By what has filled the maw of dogs and crows, The flesh of Oedipus’ unburied son. Therefore the angry gods abominate Our litanies and our burnt offerings; Therefore no birds trill out a happy note, Gorged with the carnival of human gore. O ponder this, my son. To err is common To all men, but the man who having erred Hugs not his errors, but repents and seeks The cure, is not a wastrel nor unwise. No fool, the saw goes, like the obstinate fool. Let death disarm thy vengeance. O forbear To vex the dead. What glory wilt thou win By slaying twice the slain? I mean thee well; Counsel’s most welcome if I promise gain.
cards.whyThisWorks: Teiresias's speech moves from ominous omens to a direct moral argument—that Creon's stubborn refusal to bury Polynices has angered the gods and that wise men correct their errors—giving students a clear central idea to distinguish from the surrounding details about birds and sacrifices.
cards.skillStrategy: Ask yourself what the speaker most wants the listener to understand by the end; that overarching message is the central idea, not any single sign or event described along the way.
evidencePoints: thy willful temper ails the State, For all our shrines and altars are profaned By what has filled the maw of dogs and crows, The flesh of Oedipus' unburied son.
the man who having erred Hugs not his errors, but repents and seeks The cure, is not a wastrel nor unwise.
cards.question: Which statement best expresses the central idea of Teiresias's speech to Creon?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The gods communicate their will through the behavior of birds and the results of fire sacrifices, which only trained seers can interpret.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Creon's refusal to bury Polynices has brought divine punishment upon Thebes, and a truly wise ruler admits his error and changes course before the damage grows worse.

choices.label: C
