choices.text: Teiresias depends on a young guide to read omens, which shows that even the most experienced prophet can lose his powers over time.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Punishing an enemy after death by leaving the body unburied is a common practice among kings, but it carries serious risks for the kingdom.

cards.standardTitle: Rhetorical appeals and author purpose
cards.excerpt:
THESEUS. I know that none Shall hale thee hence in my despite. Such threats Vented in anger oft, are blusterers, An idle breath, forgot when sense returns. And for thy foemen, though their words were brave, Boasting to bring thee back, they are like to find The seas between us wide and hard to sail. Such my firm purpose, but in any case Take heart, since Phoebus sent thee here. My name, Though I be distant, warrants thee from harm.

CHORUS. (Str. 1) Thou hast come to a steed-famed land for rest, O stranger worn with toil, To a land of all lands the goodliest Colonus’ glistening soil. ’Tis the haunt of the clear-voiced nightingale, Who hid in her bower, among The wine-dark ivy that wreathes the vale, Trilleth her ceaseless song; And she loves, where the clustering berries nod O’er a sunless, windless glade, The spot by no mortal footstep trod, The pleasance kept for the Bacchic god, Where he holds each night his revels wild With the nymphs who fostered the lusty child.
cards.whyThisWorks: Theseus's speech blends logos (logical reasoning about the difficulty enemies will face crossing the seas) with ethos (his personal authority and name as a guarantee of protection), giving students a clear contrast of two distinct rhetorical appeals within a single short passage.
cards.skillStrategy: Ask yourself: is the speaker giving reasons and evidence (logos), using their own reputation or authority (ethos), or stirring feelings (pathos)? Then match the specific words to the appeal.
evidencePoints: they are like to find / The seas between us wide and hard to sail
My name, / Though I be distant, warrants thee from harm
cards.question: In Theseus's speech, he tells Oedipus that his enemies 'are like to find / The seas between us wide and hard to sail' and then adds that his 'name… warrants thee from harm.' Which statement best explains how these two moments work together as rhetorical appeals?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Both statements appeal to emotion by making Oedipus feel the fear of being surrounded by enemies on all sides.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The first statement uses logic by pointing to a physical obstacle that will stop enemies, while the second uses Theseus's personal authority as a guarantee of safety.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The first statement appeals to Theseus's credibility as a ruler, and the second appeals to Oedipus's emotions by reminding him he is far from home.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Both statements rely on the divine authority of Phoebus, since Theseus credits the god's guidance as the true reason enemies cannot reach Oedipus.

cards.standardTitle: Key literary elements add layers of meaning
cards.excerpt: Antigone, daughter of Oedipus, the late king of Thebes, in defiance of Creon who rules in his stead, resolves to bury her brother Polyneices, slain in his attack on Thebes. She is caught in the act by Creon’s watchmen and brought before the king. She justifies her action, asserting that she was bound to obey the eternal laws of right and wrong in spite of any human ordinance. Creon, unrelenting, condemns her to be immured in a rock-hewn chamber. His son Haemon, to whom Antigone is betrothed, pleads in vain for her life and threatens to die with her. Warned by the seer Teiresias Creon repents him and hurries to release Antigone from her rocky prison. But he is too late: he finds lying side by side Antigone who had hanged herself and Haemon who also has perished by his own hand. Returning to the palace he sees within the dead body of his queen who on learning of her son’s death has stabbed herself to the heart.
cards.whyThisWorks: The excerpt's compressed plot—Creon condemning Antigone to the rock-hewn chamber, repenting only after Teiresias's warning, and arriving 'too late' to find three deaths—directly illustrates how the conflict between royal authority and Antigone's defiance generates irreversible, cascading consequences that add meaning to the tragedy.
cards.skillStrategy: When a plot sequence shows a character acting too late to undo harm, ask what that timing reveals about the conflict's deeper meaning—specifically what the delay says about the forces driving the story.
evidencePoints: Creon repents him and hurries to release Antigone from her rocky prison. But he is too late
he finds lying side by side Antigone who had hanged herself and Haemon who also has perished by his own hand
cards.question: The excerpt states that after Teiresias's warning 'Creon repents him and hurries to release Antigone from her rocky prison,' yet 'he is too late'—finding Antigone hanged, Haemon dead beside her, and his queen stabbed upon learning of her son's death. What meaning does the phrase 'too late' add to the conflict between Creon's condemnation of Antigone and Antigone's defiance of his authority?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The phrase 'too late' shifts blame entirely to Teiresias's delayed warning, suggesting that if the seer had spoken sooner, Creon's condemnation of Antigone to the rock-hewn chamber would have caused no lasting harm to Haemon or the queen.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The phrase 'too late' shows that Creon's condemnation of Antigone to the rock-hewn chamber set in motion a chain of deaths—Antigone's, Haemon's, and the queen's—that even his eventual repentance could not reverse, meaning inflexible authority destroys what it cannot control.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The phrase 'too late' suggests that Antigone's choice to hang herself rather than wait in the rock-hewn chamber is the primary cause of Haemon's death and the queen's suicide, making Antigone's own defiance more destructive than Creon's condemnation.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The phrase 'too late' reveals that Creon's authority was never truly absolute, because his willingness to release Antigone after Teiresias's warning proves the conflict between royal law and Antigone's defiance had already been resolved before the three deaths occurred.

cards.standardTitle: Theme development across a literary text
cards.excerpt: CREON. Well, let her know the stubbornest of wills Are soonest bended, as the hardest iron, O’er-heated in the fire to brittleness, Flies soonest into fragments, shivered through. A snaffle curbs the fieriest steed, and he Who in subjection lives must needs be meek. But this proud girl, in insolence well-schooled, First overstepped the established law, and then— A second and worse act of insolence— She boasts and glories in her wickedness. Now if she thus can flout authority Unpunished, I am woman, she the man. But though she be my sister’s child or nearer Of kin than all who worship at my hearth, Nor she nor yet her sister shall escape The utmost penalty, for both I hold, As arch-conspirators, of equal guilt. Bring forth the older; even now I saw her Within the palace, frenzied and distraught. The workings of the mind discover oft Dark deeds in darkness schemed, before the act. More hateful still the miscreant who seeks When caught, to make a virtue of a crime.
cards.whyThisWorks: Creon's speech contains two distinct moments—his metaphor of iron breaking under heat and his condemnation of Antigone's double act of insolence—that together develop the theme that unchecked pride and defiance of authority lead to destruction, requiring students to track how both moments build the same message rather than isolating one.
cards.skillStrategy: Find two separate moments in the passage and ask what idea they both point toward—that shared idea is the theme being developed.
evidencePoints: the hardest iron, O'er-heated in the fire to brittleness, Flies soonest into fragments, shivered through
First overstepped the established law, and then— A second and worse act of insolence— She boasts and glories in her wickedness
cards.question: Read the two moments in Creon's speech: his description of iron that 'O'er-heated in the fire to brittleness, / Flies soonest into fragments,' and his account of Antigone who 'First overstepped the established law' and then 'boasts and glories in her wickedness.' How do these two moments work together to develop a theme?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Both moments show that Creon is a fair ruler who applies the same standard of justice to family members and strangers alike.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Both moments develop the idea that those who refuse to bend their pride invite their own ruin—the iron shatters precisely because it will not yield, just as Antigone's defiance compounds into a destruction she cannot escape.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The iron metaphor shows Creon's admiration for strength, while Antigone's double offense shows his personal anger at being humiliated, making the two moments contrast rather than reinforce each other.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Both moments reveal that written law is always superior to personal loyalty, since Creon condemns the iron for being too rigid and condemns Antigone for placing family above the state.

cards.standardTitle: Text structure and feature purpose
cards.excerpt: ISMENE. The toil and trouble, father, that I bore To find thy lodging-place and how thou faredst, I spare thee; surely ’twere a double pain To suffer, first in act and then in telling; ’Tis the misfortune of thine ill-starred sons I come to tell thee. At the first they willed To leave the throne to Creon, minded well Thus to remove the inveterate curse of old, A canker that infected all thy race. But now some god and an infatuate soul Have stirred betwixt them a mad rivalry To grasp at sovereignty and kingly power. Today the hot-branded youth, the younger born, Is keeping Polyneices from the throne, His elder, and has thrust him from the land. The banished brother (so all Thebes reports) Fled to the vale of Argos, and by help Of new alliance there and friends in arms, Swears he will stablish Argos straight as lord Of the Cadmeian land, or, if he fail, Exalt the victor to the stars of heaven. This is no empty tale, but deadly truth, My father; and how long thy agony, Ere the gods pity thee, I cannot tell.
cards.whyThisWorks: Ismene's speech has a clear two-part structure—a brief dismissal of her own hardships followed by a detailed political report—making it an ideal model for analyzing how a paragraph section fulfills a specific informational job within a larger text.
cards.skillStrategy: Ask yourself: what task does this section of the speech accomplish that the rest of the speech does not? Look for the moment the speaker shifts focus and identify what new information or purpose that shift introduces.
evidencePoints: 'Tis the misfortune of thine ill-starred sons I come to tell thee
This is no empty tale, but deadly truth, My father
cards.question: After Ismene announces, ''Tis the misfortune of thine ill-starred sons I come to tell thee,' what is the primary job of the lines that follow in this section of her speech?

choices.label: A
choices.text: To describe the personal hardships Ismene endured finding Oedipus, establishing that her loyalty to her father exceeds that of either of his sons.

choices.label: B
choices.text: To report that Eteocles has seized the throne and driven Polyneices into exile, where Polyneices now threatens to conquer Thebes with Argive armies—what Ismene calls 'deadly truth.'

choices.label: C
choices.text: To explain that the brothers' original plan to give the throne to Creon successfully removed 'the inveterate curse of old' and brought lasting peace to Oedipus's family.

choices.label: D
choices.text: To confirm that Polyneices has already defeated Eteocles in battle and used the armies of Argos to 'exalt the victor to the stars of heaven.'

cards.standardTitle: Central idea and supporting evidence
cards.excerpt:
OEDIPUS. God speed thee! and as meed for bringing them May Providence deal with thee kindlier Than it has dealt with me! O children mine, Where are ye? Let me clasp you with these hands, A brother’s hands, a father’s; hands that made Lack-luster sockets of his once bright eyes; Hands of a man who blindly, recklessly, Became your sire by her from whom he sprang. Though I cannot behold you, I must weep In thinking of the evil days to come, The slights and wrongs that men will put upon you. Where’er ye go to feast or festival, No merrymaking will it prove for you, But oft abashed in tears ye will return. And when ye come to marriageable years, Where’s the bold wooers who will jeopardize To take unto himself such disrepute As to my children’s children still must cling, For what of infamy is lacking here? “Their father slew his father, sowed the seed Where he himself was gendered, and begat These maidens at the source wherefrom he sprang.” Such are the gibes that men will cast at you. Who then will wed you? None, I ween, but ye Must pine, poor maids, in single barrenness. O Prince, Menoeceus’ son, to thee, I turn, With the it rests to father them, for we Their natural parents, both of us, are lost. O leave them not to wander poor, unwed, Thy kin, nor let them share my low estate. O pity them so young, and but for thee All destitute. Thy hand upon it, Prince. To you, my children I had much to say, Were ye but ripe to hear. Let this suffice: Pray ye may find some home and live content, And may your lot prove happier than your sire’s.

CREON. Thou hast had enough of weeping; pass within.
cards.whyThisWorks: Oedipus's speech moves from lamenting his daughters' bleak marriage prospects to begging Creon to protect them, giving students a clear central idea to distinguish from isolated details like his blindness or his crimes.
cards.skillStrategy: Ask yourself what the speaker keeps returning to across the whole passage — not just one line — and state that repeated concern in plain language.
evidencePoints: Where's the bold wooers who will jeopardize / To take unto himself such disrepute / As to my children's children still must cling
O leave them not to wander poor, unwed, / Thy kin, nor let them share my low estate
cards.question: In his speech, Oedipus moves from warning 'Where's the bold wooers who will jeopardize / To take unto himself such disrepute' to pleading with Creon, 'O leave them not to wander poor, unwed.' What central idea do these two moments together express?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Oedipus believes his past crimes against his father are the direct cause of his own blindness and suffering.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The shame of Oedipus's sins will deny his daughters marriage and security, leaving them dependent on Creon's protection.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Creon bears personal responsibility for the misfortunes that have fallen on Oedipus's entire family.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Oedipus's daughters are too young to understand the gravity of the social disgrace their family name carries.

cards.standardTitle: Key literary elements add layers of meaning
cards.excerpt: CREON. O cease, you vex me with your babblement; I am like to think you dote in your old age. Is it not arrant folly to pretend That gods would have a thought for this dead man? Did they forsooth award him special grace, And as some benefactor bury him, Who came to fire their hallowed sanctuaries, To sack their shrines, to desolate their land, And scout their ordinances? Or perchance The gods bestow their favors on the bad. No! no! I have long noted malcontents Who wagged their heads, and kicked against the yoke, Misliking these my orders, and my rule. ’Tis they, I warrant, who suborned my guards By bribes. Of evils current upon earth The worst is money. Money ’tis that sacks Cities, and drives men forth from hearth and home; Warps and seduces native innocence, And breeds a habit of dishonesty. But they who sold themselves shall find their greed Out-shot the mark, and rue it soon or late. Yea, as I still revere the dread of Zeus, By Zeus I swear, except ye find and bring Before my presence here the very man Who carried out this lawless burial, Death for your punishment shall not suffice. Hanged on a cross, alive ye first shall make Confession of this outrage. This will teach you What practices are like to serve your turn. There are some villainies that bring no gain. For by dishonesty the few may thrive, The many come to ruin and disgrace.
cards.whyThisWorks: Creon's escalating threats—from death to crucifixion—alongside his dismissal of divine authority reveal how the conflict between human law and divine order drives the plot toward tragic excess.
cards.skillStrategy: When a character's punishment goes beyond what the crime demands, ask what that escalation reveals about the deeper conflict driving the plot.
evidencePoints: Hanged on a cross, alive ye first shall make Confession of this outrage.
Did they forsooth award him special grace… Who came to fire their hallowed sanctuaries
cards.question: Creon dismisses the gods' possible role in the burial—'Did they forsooth award him special grace'—then threatens to crucify the guards alive rather than simply execute them. What does this escalation reveal about the central conflict?

choices.label: A
choices.text: It shows that Creon's real struggle is financial: he believes bribery, not divine defiance, caused the burial, so his cruelty is meant to recover lost money.

choices.label: B
choices.text: It shows that by rejecting divine authority and demanding total obedience, Creon's human law has become so absolute that it produces cruelty rather than justice.

choices.label: C
choices.text: It shows that Creon trusts Zeus to punish the guilty and uses the crucifixion threat only to mirror the divine justice he believes is already at work.

choices.label: D
choices.text: It shows that Creon fears personal betrayal by the guards themselves, making the conflict one of loyalty to him rather than defiance of his political decrees.

cards.standardTitle: Theme development across a literary text
cards.excerpt: OEDIPUS. Out on the twain! The thoughts and actions all Are framed and modeled on Egyptian ways. For there the men sit at the loom indoors While the wives slave abroad for daily bread. So you, my children—those whom I behooved To bear the burden, stay at home like girls, While in their stead my daughters moil and drudge, Lightening their father’s misery. The one Since first she grew from girlish feebleness To womanhood has been the old man’s guide And shared my weary wandering, roaming oft Hungry and footsore through wild forest ways, In drenching rains and under scorching suns, Careless herself of home and ease, if so Her sire might have her tender ministry. And thou, my child, whilom thou wentest forth, Eluding the Cadmeians’ vigilance, To bring thy father all the oracles Concerning Oedipus, and didst make thyself My faithful lieger, when they banished me. And now what mission summons thee from home, What news, Ismene, hast thou for thy father? This much I know, thou com’st not empty-handed, Without a warning of some new alarm.
cards.whyThisWorks: Oedipus's contrasting descriptions of his daughters' sacrifices—Antigone's years of 'hungry and footsore' wandering and Ismene's secret mission past the Cadmeians—provide two concrete passage moments that together build the theme of loyalty expressed through personal sacrifice.
cards.skillStrategy: When a character describes two separate actions by different people, ask what those actions have in common and what idea about life that shared pattern suggests.
evidencePoints: Hungry and footsore through wild forest ways, / In drenching rains and under scorching suns, / Careless herself of home and ease
thou wentest forth, / Eluding the Cadmeians' vigilance, / To bring thy father all the oracles
cards.question: Oedipus describes Antigone as wandering 'hungry and footsore through wild forest ways' and Ismene as 'eluding the Cadmeians' vigilance' to deliver oracles to him. What theme do these two specific moments develop together?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Daughters who endure physical hardship outdoors are more trustworthy than sons who remain comfortable at home.

choices.label: B
choices.text: True loyalty shows itself through personal sacrifice and risk—enduring hunger and danger—on behalf of someone powerless to help himself.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Exile destroys a family's unity, and only the daughters' return can repair the damage caused by Oedipus's banishment.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Women are forced into roles of service because men, like Oedipus's sons, abandon their responsibilities without consequence.

cards.standardTitle: Text structure and feature purpose
cards.excerpt:
CREON. Be sure thou wilt not traffic on my wits.

TEIRESIAS. Know then for sure, the coursers of the sun Not many times shall run their race, before Thou shalt have given the fruit of thine own loins In quittance of thy murder, life for life; For that thou hast entombed a living soul, And sent below a denizen of earth, And wronged the nether gods by leaving here A corpse unlaved, unwept, unsepulchered. Herein thou hast no part, nor e’en the gods In heaven; and thou usurp’st a power not thine. For this the avenging spirits of Heaven and Hell Who dog the steps of sin are on thy trail: What these have suffered thou shalt suffer too. And now, consider whether bought by gold I prophesy. For, yet a little while, And sound of lamentation shall be heard, Of men and women through thy desolate halls; And all thy neighbor States are leagues to avenge Their mangled warriors who have found a grave I’ the maw of wolf or hound, or winged bird That flying homewards taints their city’s air. These are the shafts, that like a bowman I Provoked to anger, loosen at thy breast, Unerring, and their smart thou shalt not shun. Boy, lead me home, that he may vent his spleen On younger men, and learn to curb his tongue With gentler manners than his present mood. [Exit TEIRESIAS]

CHORUS. My liege, that man hath gone, foretelling woe. And, O believe me, since these grizzled locks Were like the raven, never have I known The prophet’s warning to the State to fail.
cards.whyThisWorks: The Chorus's closing speech functions as a distinct section that validates Teiresias's prophecy and shifts the dramatic weight from confrontation to impending doom, giving students a clear example of a paragraph that confirms and extends a prior idea rather than introducing or contrasting one.
cards.skillStrategy: Ask yourself: does this paragraph start something new, push back on what came before, or build on and confirm it? Then find the exact words that show which job it is doing.
evidencePoints: that man hath gone, foretelling woe
never have I known / The prophet's warning to the State to fail
cards.question: What is the primary job of the Chorus's speech that begins 'My liege, that man hath gone, foretelling woe'?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The Chorus introduces a new concern about Creon's treatment of the neighboring states whose warriors were left unburied.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The Chorus confirms the authority of Teiresias's warning by drawing on its own long experience of the prophet's accuracy.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The Chorus contrasts its own hopeful view of Creon's future with the grim fate Teiresias has just predicted.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The Chorus shifts the focus away from Teiresias's prophecy and urges Creon to seek counsel from younger advisors.

cards.standardTitle: Central idea and supporting evidence
cards.excerpt:
OEDIPUS. O what avails renown or fair repute? Are they not vanity? For, look you, now Athens is held of States the most devout, Athens alone gives hospitality And shelters the vexed stranger, so men say. Have I found so? I whom ye dislodged First from my seat of rock and now would drive Forth from your land, dreading my name alone; For me you surely dread not, nor my deeds, Deeds of a man more sinned against than sinning, As I might well convince you, were it meet To tell my mother’s story and my sire’s, The cause of this your fear. Yet am I then A villain born because in self-defense, Striken, I struck the striker back again? E’en had I known, no villainy ’twould prove: But all unwitting whither I went, I went— To ruin; my destroyers knew it well, Wherefore, I pray you, sirs, in Heaven’s name, Even as ye bade me quit my seat, defend me. O pay not a lip service to the gods And wrong them of their dues. Bethink ye well, The eye of Heaven beholds the just of men, And the unjust, nor ever in this world Has one sole godless sinner found escape. Stand then on Heaven’s side and never blot Athens’ fair scutcheon by abetting wrong. I came to you a suppliant, and you pledged Your honor; O preserve me to the end, O let not this marred visage do me wrong! A holy and god-fearing man is here Whose coming purports comfort for your folk. And when your chief arrives, whoe’er he be, Then shall ye have my story and know all. Meanwhile I pray you do me no despite.

CHORUS. The plea thou urgest, needs must give us pause, Set forth in weighty argument, but we Must leave the issue with the ruling powers.
cards.whyThisWorks: Oedipus's speech builds a layered argument—invoking Athens's reputation, his own innocence, divine justice, and a prior pledge—that requires students to distinguish the central claim from supporting details or isolated moments.
cards.skillStrategy: Ask yourself: what is the one idea that every part of the speech is working to prove? That is the central idea, not a single detail or the topic alone.
evidencePoints: I came to you a suppliant, and you pledged / Your honor; O preserve me to the end
Deeds of a man more sinned against than sinning
cards.question: Oedipus opens by asking, 'O what avails renown or fair repute? Are they not vanity?' and closes by reminding the Chorus, 'I came to you a suppliant, and you pledged / Your honor; O preserve me to the end.' What central idea do these two moments, taken together, develop across his entire speech?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Athens has earned its reputation as the most devout city in Greece, and Oedipus is grateful for the welcome he has received there.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Because Oedipus acted without knowledge and suffered wrongs he did not cause, Athens must back its praised reputation with real action by honoring its pledge to protect him.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The gods punish every sinner without exception, so the Chorus members personally risk divine punishment if they remain near Oedipus.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Oedipus refuses to share the full story of his parents until the city's chief ruler arrives, making any judgment about his guilt premature.

cards.standardTitle: Key literary elements add layers of meaning
cards.excerpt: ANTIGONE. Yea, for these laws were not ordained of Zeus, And she who sits enthroned with gods below, Justice, enacted not these human laws. Nor did I deem that thou, a mortal man, Could’st by a breath annul and override The immutable unwritten laws of Heaven. They were not born today nor yesterday; They die not; and none knoweth whence they sprang. I was not like, who feared no mortal’s frown, To disobey these laws and so provoke The wrath of Heaven. I knew that I must die, E’en hadst thou not proclaimed it; and if death Is thereby hastened, I shall count it gain. For death is gain to him whose life, like mine, Is full of misery. Thus my lot appears Not sad, but blissful; for had I endured To leave my mother’s son unburied there, I should have grieved with reason, but not now. And if in this thou judgest me a fool, Methinks the judge of folly’s not acquit.
cards.whyThisWorks: Antigone's declaration that death is 'gain' rather than punishment directly deepens the conflict between divine and human law, showing how the plot consequence of her execution exposes the limits of Creon's mortal authority.
cards.skillStrategy: When a character reframes a punishment as a reward, ask what that reversal reveals about the central conflict and what the author wants you to understand about power.
evidencePoints: if death / Is thereby hastened, I shall count it gain
I was not like, who feared no mortal's frown, / To disobey these laws and so provoke / The wrath of Heaven
cards.question: Antigone says 'if death / Is thereby hastened, I shall count it gain' after invoking 'the immutable unwritten laws of Heaven.' What meaning does this reframing of death as gain add to the conflict between divine and human law?

choices.label: A
choices.text: It shows Antigone has grown indifferent to life because years of misery have made her reckless rather than principled.

choices.label: B
choices.text: It reveals that Creon's decree holds no real power over Antigone, since her loyalty to divine law makes his mortal punishment meaningless.

choices.label: C
choices.text: It suggests Antigone regrets burying her brother and sees death as the deserved consequence of defying Creon's authority.

choices.label: D
choices.text: It implies Antigone expects the gods to intervene and prevent her death once Creon hears her argument about Heaven's laws.

cards.standardTitle: Theme development across a literary text
cards.excerpt: CREON. O cease, you vex me with your babblement; I am like to think you dote in your old age. Is it not arrant folly to pretend That gods would have a thought for this dead man? Did they forsooth award him special grace, And as some benefactor bury him, Who came to fire their hallowed sanctuaries, To sack their shrines, to desolate their land, And scout their ordinances? Or perchance The gods bestow their favors on the bad. No! no! I have long noted malcontents Who wagged their heads, and kicked against the yoke, Misliking these my orders, and my rule. ’Tis they, I warrant, who suborned my guards By bribes. Of evils current upon earth The worst is money. Money ’tis that sacks Cities, and drives men forth from hearth and home; Warps and seduces native innocence, And breeds a habit of dishonesty. But they who sold themselves shall find their greed Out-shot the mark, and rue it soon or late. Yea, as I still revere the dread of Zeus, By Zeus I swear, except ye find and bring Before my presence here the very man Who carried out this lawless burial, Death for your punishment shall not suffice. Hanged on a cross, alive ye first shall make Confession of this outrage. This will teach you What practices are like to serve your turn. There are some villainies that bring no gain. For by dishonesty the few may thrive, The many come to ruin and disgrace.
cards.whyThisWorks: Creon's speech contains two distinct moments—his dismissal of divine authority over Polynices and his tirade against bribery—that together develop the theme that unchecked power corrupts a leader's judgment, allowing students to track theme across multiple story moments rather than a single detail.
cards.skillStrategy: Find two separate moments in the passage where the character's words or actions point to the same big idea, then ask what message both moments share.
evidencePoints: Did they forsooth award him special grace, And as some benefactor bury him, Who came to fire their hallowed sanctuaries
Of evils current upon earth The worst is money. Money 'tis that sacks Cities, and drives men forth from hearth and home
cards.question: Read the two moments in Creon's speech: first, when he dismisses the idea that the gods would honor Polynices, and second, when he declares that money is 'the worst of evils' and blames bribery for the burial. What theme do both moments develop together?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Religious devotion is the only reliable guide for a ruler, and Creon's rejection of divine will proves he has already lost his kingdom.

choices.label: B
choices.text: A leader who trusts only his own authority—dismissing both divine judgment and the loyalty of his guards—shows how absolute power distorts a ruler's reasoning.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Greed is the root cause of all political collapse, and Creon's speech exists mainly to warn citizens against accepting bribes from enemies of the state.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The gods ultimately control human affairs, and Creon's oath by Zeus at the end of the speech signals that he has finally recognized his own limits.

cards.standardTitle: Text structure and feature purpose
cards.excerpt:
CREON. Yea, for thyself wouldst credit now his word.

OEDIPUS. Aye, and on thee in all humility I lay this charge: let her who lies within Receive such burial as thou shalt ordain; Such rites ’tis thine, as brother, to perform. But for myself, O never let my Thebes, The city of my sires, be doomed to bear The burden of my presence while I live. No, let me be a dweller on the hills, On yonder mount Cithaeron, famed as mine, My tomb predestined for me by my sire And mother, while they lived, that I may die Slain as they sought to slay me, when alive. This much I know full surely, nor disease Shall end my days, nor any common chance; For I had ne’er been snatched from death, unless I was predestined to some awful doom. So be it. I reck not how Fate deals with me But my unhappy children—for my sons Be not concerned, O Creon, they are men, And for themselves, where’er they be, can fend. But for my daughters twain, poor innocent maids, Who ever sat beside me at the board Sharing my viands, drinking of my cup, For them, I pray thee, care, and, if thou willst, O might I feel their touch and make my moan. Hear me, O prince, my noble-hearted prince! Could I but blindly touch them with my hands I’d think they still were mine, as when I saw. [ANTIGONE and ISMENE are led in.] What say I? can it be my pretty ones Whose sobs I hear? Has Creon pitied me And sent me my two darlings? Can this be?
cards.whyThisWorks: Oedipus's speech has a clear two-part structure—resignation about his own fate followed by an urgent plea for his daughters—making 'So be it. I reck not how Fate deals with me' a pivot sentence that students can identify as closing one section and opening another.
cards.skillStrategy: To find a paragraph or sentence's job, ask what it closes and what it opens—look for a shift in topic, tone, or audience address right after the sentence.
evidencePoints: So be it. I reck not how Fate deals with me

But my unhappy children—for my sons / Be not concerned, O Creon, they are men, / And for themselves, where'er they be, can fend. / But for my daughters twain, poor innocent maids, / Who ever sat beside me at the board
cards.question: Read the following lines from Oedipus's speech: 'So be it. I reck not how Fate deals with me / But my unhappy children—for my sons / Be not concerned, O Creon, they are men.' What is the structural job of the sentence 'So be it. I reck not how Fate deals with me' within this section of the speech?

choices.label: A
choices.text: It returns to Oedipus's opening request that Creon perform burial rites for 'her who lies within,' signaling that the burial topic is fully resolved before the speech continues.

choices.label: B
choices.text: It closes Oedipus's acceptance of his predestined doom on 'yonder mount Cithaeron' and pivots to an urgent new plea that Creon care for 'my daughters twain, poor innocent maids, / Who ever sat beside me at the board.'

choices.label: C
choices.text: It introduces Oedipus's argument that Fate, not Creon, is equally responsible for protecting both his sons and 'my daughters twain' after Oedipus is exiled from Thebes.

choices.label: D
choices.text: It extends Oedipus's prediction about dying on 'yonder mount Cithaeron' by linking his predestined doom directly to the suffering his daughters will face once he is gone.

cards.standardTitle: Central idea and supporting evidence
cards.excerpt:
CHORUS. (Str. 1) Sunbeam, of all that ever dawn upon Our seven-gated Thebes the brightest ray, O eye of golden day, How fair thy light o’er Dirce’s fountain shone, Speeding upon their headlong homeward course, Far quicker than they came, the Argive force; Putting to flight The argent shields, the host with scutcheons white. Against our land the proud invader came To vindicate fell Polyneices’ claim. Like to an eagle swooping low, On pinions white as new fall’n snow. With clanging scream, a horsetail plume his crest, The aspiring lord of Argos onward pressed.

(Ant. 1) Hovering around our city walls he waits, His spearmen raven at our seven gates. But ere a torch our crown of towers could burn, Ere they had tasted of our blood, they turn Forced by the Dragon; in their rear The din of Ares panic-struck they hear. For Zeus who hates the braggart’s boast Beheld that gold-bespangled host; As at the goal the paean they upraise, He struck them with his forked lightning blaze.

(Str. 2) To earthy from earth rebounding, down he crashed; The fire-brand from his impious hand was dashed, As like a Bacchic reveler on he came, Outbreathing hate and flame, And tottered. Elsewhere in the field, Here, there, great Area like a war-horse wheeled; Beneath his car down thrust Our foemen bit the dust.

Seven captains at our seven gates Thundered; for each a champion waits, Each left behind his armor bright, Trophy for Zeus who turns the fight; Save two alone, that ill-starred pair One mother to one father bare, Who lance in rest, one ’gainst the other Drave, and both perished, brother slain by brother.
cards.whyThisWorks: The ode moves from Thebes's near-destruction by the Argive eagle to Zeus's lightning strike and finally to the brothers killing each other, giving students a full arc from which to distinguish central idea from isolated detail or topic.
cards.skillStrategy: Ask yourself what the entire passage keeps returning to — not just one image or event, but the idea that ties the eagle, the lightning, and the brothers together.
evidencePoints: For Zeus who hates the braggart's boast / Beheld that gold-bespangled host; / As at the goal the paean they upraise, / He struck them with his forked lightning blaze.
Who lance in rest, one 'gainst the other / Drave, and both perished, brother slain by brother.
cards.question: The Chorus describes Zeus striking the Argive host with lightning and then ends with 'both perished, brother slain by brother.' What central idea do these two moments together develop across the ode?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The Argive army's eagle-like assault on Thebes's seven gates was the greatest military threat the city had ever faced.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Thebes repelled the Argive invasion with divine help, but the war's origin in brotherly rivalry ended in mutual destruction, leaving the victory incomplete.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Zeus punishes every army that attacks a city, ensuring that no invader can ever succeed against a people who remain faithful to the gods.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Each of the seven Argive captains was defeated at one of Thebes's seven gates, and their abandoned armor became trophies dedicated to Zeus.

cards.standardTitle: Key literary elements add layers of meaning
cards.excerpt: CREON. Not deeming this city void of men Or counsel, son of Aegeus, as thou say’st I did what I have done; rather I thought Your people were not like to set such store by kin of mine and keep them ’gainst my will. Nor would they harbor, so I stood assured, A godless parricide, a reprobate Convicted of incestuous marriage ties. For on her native hill of Ares here (I knew your far-famed Areopagus) Sits Justice, and permits not vagrant folk To stay within your borders. In that faith I hunted down my quarry; and e’en then I had refrained but for the curses dire Wherewith he banned my kinsfolk and myself: Such wrong, methought, had warrant for my act. Anger has no old age but only death; The dead alone can feel no touch of spite. So thou must work thy will; my cause is just But weak without allies; yet will I try, Old as I am, to answer deeds with deeds.
cards.whyThisWorks: Creon's shift from citing Athenian Justice and legal warrant to confessing 'Anger has no old age but only death' exposes the gap between his stated justifications and his true motivation, showing students how plot conflict gains deeper meaning when a character's own words undercut his claims.
cards.skillStrategy: When a character gives a reason for his actions and then immediately says something that contradicts it, ask yourself which statement reveals the real motivation—that gap is where the conflict's deeper meaning lives.
evidencePoints: I had refrained but for the curses dire / Wherewith he banned my kinsfolk and myself
Anger has no old age but only death
cards.question: Creon argues that Athenian Justice 'permits not vagrant folk / To stay within your borders' and that Oedipus's curses gave him 'warrant for my act,' yet he immediately follows those legal justifications with 'Anger has no old age but only death.' What meaning does this sequence add to the conflict in the passage?

choices.label: A
choices.text: It shows that Creon's appeal to the Areopagus and Athenian Justice is the true foundation of his pursuit, and his statement about anger is simply a warning to Aegeus that the conflict will outlast both men.

choices.label: B
choices.text: It reveals that Creon's legal reasoning is a rationalization, because his own admission that anger 'has no old age but only death' exposes personal rage—not justice—as the real force driving his hunt for his quarry, suggesting that unchecked anger corrupts even a self-proclaimed just cause.

choices.label: C
choices.text: It demonstrates that the curses Oedipus directed at Creon's kinsfolk gave Creon a legitimate warrant under Athenian custom, so his anger and his appeal to Justice are fully consistent and do not create any meaningful tension.

choices.label: D
choices.text: It suggests that because Creon admits his cause is 'weak without allies,' he invokes the language of anger strategically to win Aegeus's sympathy, making the conflict a matter of political calculation rather than genuine personal feeling.

cards.standardTitle: Theme development across a literary text
cards.excerpt: CREON. Burghers, my noble friends, ye take alarm At my approach (I read it in your eyes), Fear nothing and refrain from angry words. I come with no ill purpose; I am old, And know the city whither I am come, Without a peer amongst the powers of Greece. It was by reason of my years that I Was chosen to persuade your guest and bring Him back to Thebes; not the delegate Of one man, but commissioned by the State, Since of all Thebans I have most bewailed, Being his kinsman, his most grievous woes. O listen to me, luckless Oedipus, Come home! The whole Cadmeian people claim With right to have thee back, I most of all, For most of all (else were I vile indeed) I mourn for thy misfortunes, seeing thee An aged outcast, wandering on and on, A beggar with one handmaid for thy stay. Ah! who had e’er imagined she could fall To such a depth of misery as this, To tend in penury thy stricken frame, A virgin ripe for wedlock, but unwed, A prey for any wanton ravisher? Seems it not cruel this reproach I cast On thee and on myself and all the race? Aye, but an open shame cannot be hid. Hide it, O hide it, Oedipus, thou canst. O, by our fathers’ gods, consent I pray; Come back to Thebes, come to thy father’s home, Bid Athens, as is meet, a fond farewell; Thebes thy old foster-mother claims thee first.
cards.whyThisWorks: Creon's speech layers civic authority ('commissioned by the State') with emotional manipulation (pity for Antigone's vulnerability) to pressure Oedipus, giving students two concrete moments through which to trace how the theme of power exploiting duty and emotion is built across the passage.
cards.skillStrategy: When tracking theme development, identify two or more specific moments in the text and ask what idea both moments point toward together—not just what each moment means on its own.
evidencePoints: not the delegate / Of one man, but commissioned by the State
A virgin ripe for wedlock, but unwed, / A prey for any wanton ravisher
cards.question: Creon claims he comes 'not the delegate / Of one man, but commissioned by the State,' and then warns that Antigone is 'A virgin ripe for wedlock, but unwed, / A prey for any wanton ravisher.' How do these two specific moments work together to develop a theme in the passage?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Both moments reveal Creon's sincere loyalty: invoking the State's commission shows his civic devotion, and mourning Antigone's danger shows his family love, developing a theme that a true leader must balance public duty with personal sacrifice.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Both moments show Creon using collective authority and pity for Antigone's suffering as instruments of pressure on Oedipus, developing a theme that those in power exploit appeals to duty and emotion to compel others into compliance.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The first moment establishes Thebes's legal claim on Oedipus, while the second focuses entirely on Antigone's personal hardship, so the two moments develop separate themes—one about civic obligation and one about the cost of exile—rather than a single shared idea.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Both moments show that Oedipus's continued absence harms Thebes and Antigone equally, developing a theme that an outcast's refusal to return home inevitably destroys the people who depend on him most.

cards.standardTitle: Text structure and feature purpose
cards.excerpt:
CREON. What is this? Thy words inspire a dread presentiment.

TEIRESIAS. The divination of my arts shall tell. Sitting upon my throne of augury, As is my wont, where every fowl of heaven Find harborage, upon mine ears was borne A jargon strange of twitterings, hoots, and screams; So knew I that each bird at the other tare With bloody talons, for the whirr of wings Could signify naught else. Perturbed in soul, I straight essayed the sacrifice by fire On blazing altars, but the God of Fire Came not in flame, and from the thigh bones dripped And sputtered in the ashes a foul ooze; Gall-bladders cracked and spurted up: the fat Melted and fell and left the thigh bones bare. Such are the signs, taught by this lad, I read— As I guide others, so the boy guides me— The frustrate signs of oracles grown dumb. O King, thy willful temper ails the State, For all our shrines and altars are profaned By what has filled the maw of dogs and crows, The flesh of Oedipus’ unburied son. Therefore the angry gods abominate Our litanies and our burnt offerings; Therefore no birds trill out a happy note, Gorged with the carnival of human gore. O ponder this, my son. To err is common To all men, but the man who having erred Hugs not his errors, but repents and seeks The cure, is not a wastrel nor unwise. No fool, the saw goes, like the obstinate fool. Let death disarm thy vengeance. O forbear To vex the dead. What glory wilt thou win By slaying twice the slain? I mean thee well; Counsel’s most welcome if I promise gain.
cards.whyThisWorks: Teiresias's speech has a clear two-part structure—evidence of failed omens followed by direct moral counsel—making it ideal for teaching how a paragraph section shifts its job from supporting a claim to urging action.
cards.skillStrategy: Ask yourself: what is this section doing that the previous section was not doing? Look for a signal word or shift in focus to identify the new job.
evidencePoints: O ponder this, my son. To err is common / To all men, but the man who having erred / Hugs not his errors, but repents and seeks / The cure, is not a wastrel nor unwise.
Such are the signs, taught by this lad, I read— / The frustrate signs of oracles grown dumb. / O King, thy willful temper ails the State, / For all our shrines and altars are profaned
cards.question: Teiresias's speech shifts at the line 'O ponder this, my son.' What job does this second section perform that the first section—describing the failed fire sacrifice and silent birds—does not?

choices.label: A
choices.text: It adds a final failed omen to the list, describing how the birds fell silent after the altar fire went out.

choices.label: B
choices.text: It moves from presenting evidence of divine anger—the failed sacrifice and silent birds—to urging Creon to repent and reverse his decision before the harm becomes permanent.

choices.label: C
choices.text: It shifts from describing omens to accusing Creon of personally setting fire to the altars and driving away the gods.

choices.label: D
choices.text: It restates the omen evidence from the first section and repeats that the gods are angry, reinforcing the same point without adding new purpose.

cards.standardTitle: Central idea and supporting evidence
cards.excerpt:
CHORUS. (Str. 1) Like to thee that maiden bright, Danae, in her brass-bound tower, Once exchanged the glad sunlight For a cell, her bridal bower. And yet she sprang of royal line, My child, like thine, And nursed the seed By her conceived Of Zeus descending in a golden shower. Strange are the ways of Fate, her power Nor wealth, nor arms withstand, nor tower; Nor brass-prowed ships, that breast the sea From Fate can flee.

(Ant. 1) Thus Dryas’ child, the rash Edonian King, For words of high disdain Did Bacchus to a rocky dungeon bring, To cool the madness of a fevered brain. His frenzy passed, He learnt at last ’Twas madness gibes against a god to fling. For once he fain had quenched the Maenad’s fire; And of the tuneful Nine provoked the ire.

(Str. 2) By the Iron Rocks that guard the double main, On Bosporus’ lone strand, Where stretcheth Salmydessus’ plain In the wild Thracian land, There on his borders Ares witnessed The vengeance by a jealous step-dame ta’en The gore that trickled from a spindle red, The sightless orbits of her step-sons twain.

(Ant. 2) Wasting away they mourned their piteous doom, The blasted issue of their mother’s womb. But she her lineage could trace To great Erecththeus’ race; Daughter of Boreas in her sire’s vast caves Reared, where the tempest raves, Swift as his horses o’er the hills she sped; A child of gods; yet she, my child, like thee, By Destiny That knows not death nor age—she too was vanquished. [Enter TEIRESIAS and BOY]

TEIRESIAS. Princes of Thebes, two wayfarers as one, Having betwixt us eyes for one, we are here. The blind man cannot move without a guide.
cards.whyThisWorks: The Chorus explicitly states 'Nor wealth, nor arms withstand, nor tower; / Nor brass-prowed ships, that breast the sea / From Fate can flee' and then closes with 'a child of gods' being 'vanquished' by 'Destiny That knows not death nor age,' giving students a clear central claim supported by three mythological examples that they must synthesize.
cards.skillStrategy: Identify the claim the speaker states directly, then check whether the examples in the passage all point back to that same idea.
evidencePoints: Nor wealth, nor arms withstand, nor tower; / Nor brass-prowed ships, that breast the sea / From Fate can flee
A child of gods; yet she, my child, like thee, / By Destiny That knows not death nor age—she too was vanquished
cards.question: The Chorus declares 'Nor wealth, nor arms withstand, nor tower; / Nor brass-prowed ships, that breast the sea / From Fate can flee,' and ends by noting that even 'a child of gods' was 'vanquished' by 'Destiny That knows not death nor age.' What central idea do these direct statements develop through the examples of Danae, the Edonian King, and the blinded step-sons?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Royal bloodlines offer partial protection from Fate, since Danae 'sprang of royal line' and survived her imprisonment, and the step-sons' mother traced her descent to 'great Erechtheus' race' and avoided punishment herself.

choices.label: B
choices.text: No one—whether imprisoned like Danae, maddened like the Edonian King who mocked Bacchus and 'the tuneful Nine,' blinded like the step-sons, or born of gods like the daughter of Boreas—can escape the force of Fate.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The gods punish only those who speak with 'high disdain' against divine authority, as shown by the Edonian King whose 'frenzy' came from provoking Bacchus, while Danae and the step-sons suffer for unrelated reasons.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Suffering falls most heavily on those of noble birth, since Danae 'sprang of royal line,' the step-sons' mother descended from Boreas, and their anguish is described as 'the blasted issue of their mother's womb.'

cards.standardTitle: Rhetoric and reader effect
cards.excerpt:
THESEUS. I know that none Shall hale thee hence in my despite. Such threats Vented in anger oft, are blusterers, An idle breath, forgot when sense returns. And for thy foemen, though their words were brave, Boasting to bring thee back, they are like to find The seas between us wide and hard to sail. Such my firm purpose, but in any case Take heart, since Phoebus sent thee here. My name, Though I be distant, warrants thee from harm.

CHORUS. (Str. 1) Thou hast come to a steed-famed land for rest, O stranger worn with toil, To a land of all lands the goodliest Colonus’ glistening soil. ’Tis the haunt of the clear-voiced nightingale, Who hid in her bower, among The wine-dark ivy that wreathes the vale, Trilleth her ceaseless song; And she loves, where the clustering berries nod O’er a sunless, windless glade, The spot by no mortal footstep trod, The pleasance kept for the Bacchic god, Where he holds each night his revels wild With the nymphs who fostered the lusty child.
cards.whyThisWorks: Theseus's closing declaration—'My name, Though I be distant, warrants thee from harm'—demonstrates how a speaker uses personal authority as a rhetorical guarantee, directly connecting his rhetoric to the purpose of establishing credible sanctuary for the stranger.
cards.skillStrategy: When analyzing rhetoric, ask what specific claim the speaker makes and how that claim is designed to achieve a particular effect on the listener—here, reassurance and trust.
evidencePoints: My name, Though I be distant, warrants thee from harm
Phoebus sent thee here
cards.question: In his speech, Theseus first credits Phoebus—'since Phoebus sent thee here'—and then closes with 'My name, Though I be distant, warrants thee from harm.' How does this shift from divine authority to personal authority serve Theseus's rhetorical purpose?

choices.label: A
choices.text: It shows that Theseus doubts the god Phoebus and must replace divine protection with his own military force against the 'foemen' he mentions.

choices.label: B
choices.text: It builds the stranger's confidence by first grounding the offer of safety in divine will and then reinforcing it with Theseus's own reputation, making the promise of sanctuary credible even in his absence.

choices.label: C
choices.text: It warns the stranger that Phoebus's protection is temporary and that only Theseus's physical presence can prevent the 'foemen' from bringing him back.

choices.label: D
choices.text: It shifts blame onto the gods so that Theseus is not personally responsible if the 'threats vented in anger' by his enemies prove stronger than his own name.

cards.standardTitle: Key literary elements add layers of meaning
cards.excerpt: OEDIPUS. Dear son of Aegeus, to the gods alone Is given immunity from eld and death; But nothing else escapes all-ruinous time. Earth’s might decays, the might of men decays, Honor grows cold, dishonor flourishes, There is no constancy ’twixt friend and friend, Or city and city; be it soon or late, Sweet turns to bitter, hate once more to love. If now ’tis sunshine betwixt Thebes and thee And not a cloud, Time in his endless course Gives birth to endless days and nights, wherein The merest nothing shall suffice to cut With serried spears your bonds of amity. Then shall my slumbering and buried corpse In its cold grave drink their warm life-blood up, If Zeus be Zeus and Phoebus still speak true. No more: ’tis ill to tear aside the veil Of mysteries; let me cease as I began: Enough if thou wilt keep thy plighted troth, Then shall thou ne’er complain that Oedipus Proved an unprofitable and thankless guest, Except the gods themselves shall play me false.
cards.whyThisWorks: Oedipus's prophecy that his buried corpse will 'drink their warm life-blood up' when Thebes and Athens eventually turn against each other transforms his death from a personal ending into a future weapon, adding a layer of meaning about how the powerless can still hold power over the living.
cards.skillStrategy: When a character makes a prediction or decision tied to their fate, ask what that moment reveals beyond the surface event — what deeper truth about power, time, or human nature does it expose?
evidencePoints: Then shall my slumbering and buried corpse / In its cold grave drink their warm life-blood up
Time in his endless course / Gives birth to endless days and nights, wherein / The merest nothing shall suffice to cut / With serried spears your bonds of amity
cards.question: Oedipus tells Aegeus that his buried corpse will 'drink their warm life-blood up' when Thebes eventually turns against Athens. What deeper meaning does this moment add to Oedipus's death?

choices.label: A
choices.text: His death signals that the alliance between Thebes and Athens is already broken, making his burial site irrelevant to future conflicts.

choices.label: B
choices.text: His death becomes a source of hidden power rather than a final defeat, suggesting that even the most dishonored and exiled figure can shape the fate of kingdoms from beyond the grave.

choices.label: C
choices.text: His death confirms that the gods have abandoned him, since he must rely on Zeus and Phoebus to fulfill promises he cannot keep himself.

choices.label: D
choices.text: His death warns Aegeus that loyalty between cities is impossible, so Athens should not trust any alliance, including the one Oedipus is offering.

cards.standardTitle: Theme development across a literary text
cards.excerpt: GUARD. It happened thus. No sooner had we come, Driven from thy presence by those awful threats, Than straight we swept away all trace of dust, And bared the clammy body. Then we sat High on the ridge to windward of the stench, While each man kept he fellow alert and rated Roundly the sluggard if he chanced to nap. So all night long we watched, until the sun Stood high in heaven, and his blazing beams Smote us. A sudden whirlwind then upraised A cloud of dust that blotted out the sky, And swept the plain, and stripped the woodlands bare, And shook the firmament. We closed our eyes And waited till the heaven-sent plague should pass. At last it ceased, and lo! there stood this maid. A piercing cry she uttered, sad and shrill, As when the mother bird beholds her nest Robbed of its nestlings; even so the maid Wailed as she saw the body stripped and bare, And cursed the ruffians who had done this deed. Anon she gathered handfuls of dry dust, Then, holding high a well-wrought brazen urn, Thrice on the dead she poured a lustral stream. We at the sight swooped down on her and seized Our quarry. Undismayed she stood, and when We taxed her with the former crime and this, She disowned nothing. I was glad—and grieved; For ’tis most sweet to ’scape oneself scot-free, And yet to bring disaster to a friend Is grievous. Take it all in all, I deem A man’s first duty is to serve himself.
cards.whyThisWorks: The Guard's closing declaration 'A man's first duty is to serve himself' directly contrasts with Antigone's act of returning to the body and disowning nothing, giving students two clear passage moments through which to trace a theme about duty and self-preservation.
cards.skillStrategy: When tracking theme, find two moments that pull in opposite directions and ask what idea the tension between them reveals.
evidencePoints: She disowned nothing.
A man's first duty is to serve himself.
cards.question: Antigone 'disowned nothing' when seized, while the Guard concludes 'A man's first duty is to serve himself.' How do these two moments work together to develop a theme?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Both moments show that obeying authority leads to safety, since the Guard followed orders and Antigone was punished for defying them.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Antigone's fearless admission and the Guard's self-serving relief together develop the idea that personal duty and self-preservation demand opposite choices.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Both moments suggest that grief drives people to reckless action, since Antigone wailed over the body and the Guard felt distress at capturing her.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The Guard's all-night vigil and Antigone's return show that determined individuals will succeed no matter what obstacles they face.

cards.standardTitle: Text structure and feature purpose
cards.excerpt:
OEDIPUS. God speed thee! and as meed for bringing them May Providence deal with thee kindlier Than it has dealt with me! O children mine, Where are ye? Let me clasp you with these hands, A brother’s hands, a father’s; hands that made Lack-luster sockets of his once bright eyes; Hands of a man who blindly, recklessly, Became your sire by her from whom he sprang. Though I cannot behold you, I must weep In thinking of the evil days to come, The slights and wrongs that men will put upon you. Where’er ye go to feast or festival, No merrymaking will it prove for you, But oft abashed in tears ye will return. And when ye come to marriageable years, Where’s the bold wooers who will jeopardize To take unto himself such disrepute As to my children’s children still must cling, For what of infamy is lacking here? “Their father slew his father, sowed the seed Where he himself was gendered, and begat These maidens at the source wherefrom he sprang.” Such are the gibes that men will cast at you. Who then will wed you? None, I ween, but ye Must pine, poor maids, in single barrenness. O Prince, Menoeceus’ son, to thee, I turn, With the it rests to father them, for we Their natural parents, both of us, are lost. O leave them not to wander poor, unwed, Thy kin, nor let them share my low estate. O pity them so young, and but for thee All destitute. Thy hand upon it, Prince. To you, my children I had much to say, Were ye but ripe to hear. Let this suffice: Pray ye may find some home and live content, And may your lot prove happier than your sire’s.

CREON. Thou hast had enough of weeping; pass within.
cards.whyThisWorks: Creon's single closing line performs a clear structural function—cutting off Oedipus's extended emotional appeal and direct plea to 'father them'—making it an ideal item for analyzing how a brief section closes or redirects a longer one.
cards.skillStrategy: Ask yourself: what work does this paragraph or line do compared to what came before it—does it extend, resolve, redirect, or shut down the previous section?
evidencePoints: Thy hand upon it, Prince
Thou hast had enough of weeping; pass within
cards.question: Oedipus's speech ends with a direct plea to Creon—'O leave them not to wander poor, unwed' and 'Thy hand upon it, Prince'—asking him to care for his daughters. What is the structural job of Creon's single-line reply, 'Thou hast had enough of weeping; pass within,' in relation to Oedipus's speech?

choices.label: A
choices.text: It signals Creon's acceptance of the plea—'Thy hand upon it, Prince'—by directing Oedipus inside as a gesture of welcome, resolving the daughters' uncertain future on a hopeful note.

choices.label: B
choices.text: It abruptly closes Oedipus's prolonged lament and direct plea—'Thy hand upon it, Prince'—with a terse command that ends the exchange without granting or denying the request, leaving the daughters' fate unresolved.

choices.label: C
choices.text: It shifts the section's focus away from the daughters' future back to Oedipus's past crimes—'blindly, recklessly, became your sire by her from whom he sprang'—by signaling that his guilt disqualifies the appeal.

choices.label: D
choices.text: It extends Oedipus's warning that his daughters will face 'slights and wrongs' by offering Creon's dismissal as the first concrete example of the public scorn Oedipus predicted they would suffer.

cards.standardTitle: Central idea and supporting evidence
cards.excerpt:
CHORUS. Why, Oedipus, why stung with passionate grief Hath the queen thus departed? Much I fear From this dead calm will burst a storm of woes.

OEDIPUS. Let the storm burst, my fixed resolve still holds, To learn my lineage, be it ne’er so low. It may be she with all a woman’s pride Thinks scorn of my base parentage. But I Who rank myself as Fortune’s favorite child, The giver of good gifts, shall not be shamed. She is my mother and the changing moons My brethren, and with them I wax and wane. Thus sprung why should I fear to trace my birth? Nothing can make me other than I am.

CHORUS. (Str.) If my soul prophetic err not, if my wisdom aught avail, Thee, Cithaeron, I shall hail, As the nurse and foster-mother of our Oedipus shall greet Ere tomorrow’s full moon rises, and exalt thee as is meet. Dance and song shall hymn thy praises, lover of our royal race. Phoebus, may my words find grace!

(Ant.) Child, who bare thee, nymph or goddess? sure thy sure was more than man, Haply the hill-roamer Pan. Of did Loxias beget thee, for he haunts the upland wold; Or Cyllene’s lord, or Bacchus, dweller on the hilltops cold? Did some Heliconian Oread give him thee, a new-born joy? Nymphs with whom he love to toy?

OEDIPUS. Elders, if I, who never yet before Have met the man, may make a guess, methinks I see the herdsman who we long have sought; His time-worn aspect matches with the years Of yonder aged messenger; besides I seem to recognize the men who bring him As servants of my own. But you, perchance, Having in past days known or seen the herd, May better by sure knowledge my surmise.
cards.whyThisWorks: Oedipus's back-to-back declarations—'Let the storm burst, my fixed resolve still holds' and 'Nothing can make me other than I am'—give students a clear, textually grounded central idea about unwavering self-determination to identify and support with evidence.
cards.skillStrategy: To find the central idea, look for the claim a character repeats or reinforces across multiple statements, then ask what those statements have in common about who the character is or what the character believes.
evidencePoints: Let the storm burst, my fixed resolve still holds, To learn my lineage, be it ne'er so low.
Nothing can make me other than I am.
cards.question: In his speech, Oedipus declares 'Let the storm burst, my fixed resolve still holds, To learn my lineage, be it ne'er so low' and then concludes 'Nothing can make me other than I am.' What central idea about Oedipus do these two statements together establish?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Oedipus fears that the queen's silent departure proves his parentage is so shameful that his identity as 'Fortune's favorite child' will be permanently destroyed.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Oedipus is unyielding in his determination to uncover the truth of his birth, confident that even humble or disgraceful origins cannot alter who he is.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Oedipus draws his confidence mainly from the Chorus's suggestion that he was fathered by a god such as Pan or Loxias, rather than from any personal inner resolve.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Oedipus's resolve to learn his lineage weakens once he spots the herdsman, revealing that his earlier declarations were empty boasts rather than genuine conviction.

cards.standardTitle: Rhetoric and reader effect
cards.excerpt: CREON. Burghers, my noble friends, ye take alarm At my approach (I read it in your eyes), Fear nothing and refrain from angry words. I come with no ill purpose; I am old, And know the city whither I am come, Without a peer amongst the powers of Greece. It was by reason of my years that I Was chosen to persuade your guest and bring Him back to Thebes; not the delegate Of one man, but commissioned by the State, Since of all Thebans I have most bewailed, Being his kinsman, his most grievous woes. O listen to me, luckless Oedipus, Come home! The whole Cadmeian people claim With right to have thee back, I most of all, For most of all (else were I vile indeed) I mourn for thy misfortunes, seeing thee An aged outcast, wandering on and on, A beggar with one handmaid for thy stay. Ah! who had e’er imagined she could fall To such a depth of misery as this, To tend in penury thy stricken frame, A virgin ripe for wedlock, but unwed, A prey for any wanton ravisher? Seems it not cruel this reproach I cast On thee and on myself and all the race? Aye, but an open shame cannot be hid. Hide it, O hide it, Oedipus, thou canst. O, by our fathers’ gods, consent I pray; Come back to Thebes, come to thy father’s home, Bid Athens, as is meet, a fond farewell; Thebes thy old foster-mother claims thee first.
cards.whyThisWorks: Creon's speech layers appeals to pity, kinship, and shame in a deliberate sequence that reveals his purpose is to manipulate Oedipus into returning to Thebes, giving students a clear opportunity to connect specific rhetorical moves to that persuasive goal rather than simply naming the devices.
cards.skillStrategy: Ask yourself: why does the author have this character make this specific move right here — what is the speaker trying to get the audience to do or feel, and how does the move serve that goal?
evidencePoints: Ah! who had e'er imagined she could fall / To such a depth of misery as this, / To tend in penury thy stricken frame, / A virgin ripe for wedlock, but unwed, / A prey for any wanton ravisher?
not the delegate / Of one man, but commissioned by the State, / Since of all Thebans I have most bewailed, / Being his kinsman, his most grievous woes.
cards.question: In his speech, Creon describes Antigone as 'A virgin ripe for wedlock, but unwed, / A prey for any wanton ravisher.' What is Creon's purpose in dwelling on Antigone's vulnerability at this moment in his argument?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Creon expresses genuine grief over Antigone's suffering to show that he, as Oedipus's kinsman, has personally mourned the family's misfortunes more than anyone else in Thebes.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Creon amplifies Oedipus's guilt and fear as a father in order to pressure him emotionally into agreeing to return to Thebes, where Creon claims protection and belonging await.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Creon warns the Athenian citizens that harboring Oedipus endangers Antigone, implying that Athens bears responsibility for whatever harm befalls her while she remains there.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Creon acknowledges the open shame the family has suffered so that Oedipus will feel free to speak honestly about his past crimes before the assembled Athenian elders.

cards.standardTitle: Key literary elements add layers of meaning
cards.excerpt:
CREON. Yea, for thyself wouldst credit now his word.

OEDIPUS. Aye, and on thee in all humility I lay this charge: let her who lies within Receive such burial as thou shalt ordain; Such rites ’tis thine, as brother, to perform. But for myself, O never let my Thebes, The city of my sires, be doomed to bear The burden of my presence while I live. No, let me be a dweller on the hills, On yonder mount Cithaeron, famed as mine, My tomb predestined for me by my sire And mother, while they lived, that I may die Slain as they sought to slay me, when alive. This much I know full surely, nor disease Shall end my days, nor any common chance; For I had ne’er been snatched from death, unless I was predestined to some awful doom. So be it. I reck not how Fate deals with me But my unhappy children—for my sons Be not concerned, O Creon, they are men, And for themselves, where’er they be, can fend. But for my daughters twain, poor innocent maids, Who ever sat beside me at the board Sharing my viands, drinking of my cup, For them, I pray thee, care, and, if thou willst, O might I feel their touch and make my moan. Hear me, O prince, my noble-hearted prince! Could I but blindly touch them with my hands I’d think they still were mine, as when I saw. [ANTIGONE and ISMENE are led in.] What say I? can it be my pretty ones Whose sobs I hear? Has Creon pitied me And sent me my two darlings? Can this be?
cards.whyThisWorks: Oedipus's insistence on Cithaeron as his 'predestined tomb' — the very mountain where his parents tried to kill him — layers the external conflict of exile onto the deeper thematic conflict between human agency and fate, directly illustrating how plot choices add meaning.
cards.skillStrategy: When a character's choice in the plot connects to a larger force like fate or prophecy, ask what that choice reveals about the story's central conflict and what it means beyond the surface action.
evidencePoints: yonder mount Cithaeron, famed as mine, / My tomb predestined for me by my sire / And mother, while they lived, that I may die / Slain as they sought to slay me, when alive
I had ne'er been snatched from death, unless / I was predestined to some awful doom
cards.question: Oedipus demands exile on 'yonder mount Cithaeron,' calling it the tomb 'predestined for me by my sire / And mother' who 'sought to slay me, when alive,' and concludes he 'had ne'er been snatched from death, unless / I was predestined to some awful doom.' What does Oedipus's insistence on Cithaeron as his exile destination reveal about the central conflict in this passage?

choices.label: A
choices.text: By naming Cithaeron as his exile destination, Oedipus reveals that his true conflict is with Creon, whom he blames for Antigone's death, and that choosing the mountain is a strategy to pressure Creon into caring for his daughters rather than an acceptance of predestined doom.

choices.label: B
choices.text: By choosing the mountain where his parents 'sought to slay me, when alive' and calling it his 'predestined tomb,' Oedipus reveals that fate has governed his life from birth to its end, making his exile the fulfillment of a doom set in motion before he could act against it.

choices.label: C
choices.text: By selecting Cithaeron rather than remaining in Thebes, Oedipus signals that he has forgiven his parents for trying to kill him and wishes to honor their memory, shifting the conflict away from predestined doom and toward personal reconciliation with his family's past.

choices.label: D
choices.text: By requesting exile on Cithaeron, Oedipus shows that his primary conflict is protecting his 'poor innocent maids' Antigone and Ismene, since removing himself from Thebes spares them public shame rather than fulfilling the doom his parents set in motion at his birth.

cards.standardTitle: Theme development across a literary text
cards.excerpt:
CREON. Be sure thou wilt not traffic on my wits.

TEIRESIAS. Know then for sure, the coursers of the sun Not many times shall run their race, before Thou shalt have given the fruit of thine own loins In quittance of thy murder, life for life; For that thou hast entombed a living soul, And sent below a denizen of earth, And wronged the nether gods by leaving here A corpse unlaved, unwept, unsepulchered. Herein thou hast no part, nor e’en the gods In heaven; and thou usurp’st a power not thine. For this the avenging spirits of Heaven and Hell Who dog the steps of sin are on thy trail: What these have suffered thou shalt suffer too. And now, consider whether bought by gold I prophesy. For, yet a little while, And sound of lamentation shall be heard, Of men and women through thy desolate halls; And all thy neighbor States are leagues to avenge Their mangled warriors who have found a grave I’ the maw of wolf or hound, or winged bird That flying homewards taints their city’s air. These are the shafts, that like a bowman I Provoked to anger, loosen at thy breast, Unerring, and their smart thou shalt not shun. Boy, lead me home, that he may vent his spleen On younger men, and learn to curb his tongue With gentler manners than his present mood. [Exit TEIRESIAS]

CHORUS. My liege, that man hath gone, foretelling woe. And, O believe me, since these grizzled locks Were like the raven, never have I known The prophet’s warning to the State to fail.
cards.whyThisWorks: Teiresias's prophecy of personal loss ('fruit of thine own loins / In quittance of thy murder') paired with the Chorus's confirmation that prophetic warnings 'never have I known…to fail' creates a two-moment structure that concretely develops the theme that defying divine law leads to unavoidable personal destruction.
cards.skillStrategy: When tracking theme development, identify two or more specific moments in the text and ask what idea they build together—look for how a warning and its confirmation, or an action and its consequence, point to the same central message.
evidencePoints: thou shalt have given the fruit of thine own loins / In quittance of thy murder, life for life
never have I known / The prophet's warning to the State to fail
cards.question: Teiresias tells Creon 'thou shalt have given the fruit of thine own loins / In quittance of thy murder, life for life,' citing Creon's act of entombing 'a living soul' and leaving a 'corpse unlaved, unwept, unsepulchered.' The Chorus then declares, 'never have I known / The prophet's warning to the State to fail.' How do these two moments work together to develop a theme?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Teiresias's charge that Creon 'usurp'st a power not thine' establishes that rulers must obey elders, and the Chorus confirms this by praising Teiresias's long record of advising the state.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Teiresias's prophecy that Creon will lose a child as payment for entombing a living soul and dishonoring the dead, combined with the Chorus's reminder that such prophecies never fail, develops the theme that defying divine law brings unavoidable personal destruction.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Teiresias's warning that 'neighbor States are leagues to avenge their mangled warriors' establishes a theme about political betrayal, and the Chorus reinforces this by mourning the collapse of Creon's alliances with those states.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Teiresias's parting command that Creon 'learn to curb his tongue / With gentler manners' establishes that pride destroys communication, and the Chorus develops this by urging Creon to seek a more trustworthy counselor.

cards.standardTitle: Text structure and feature purpose
cards.excerpt:
OEDIPUS. O what avails renown or fair repute? Are they not vanity? For, look you, now Athens is held of States the most devout, Athens alone gives hospitality And shelters the vexed stranger, so men say. Have I found so? I whom ye dislodged First from my seat of rock and now would drive Forth from your land, dreading my name alone; For me you surely dread not, nor my deeds, Deeds of a man more sinned against than sinning, As I might well convince you, were it meet To tell my mother’s story and my sire’s, The cause of this your fear. Yet am I then A villain born because in self-defense, Striken, I struck the striker back again? E’en had I known, no villainy ’twould prove: But all unwitting whither I went, I went— To ruin; my destroyers knew it well, Wherefore, I pray you, sirs, in Heaven’s name, Even as ye bade me quit my seat, defend me. O pay not a lip service to the gods And wrong them of their dues.
