Bethink ye well, The eye of Heaven beholds the just of men, And the unjust, nor ever in this world Has one sole godless sinner found escape. Stand then on Heaven’s side and never blot Athens’ fair scutcheon by abetting wrong. I came to you a suppliant, and you pledged Your honor; O preserve me to the end, O let not this marred visage do me wrong! A holy and god-fearing man is here Whose coming purports comfort for your folk. And when your chief arrives, whoe’er he be, Then shall ye have my story and know all. Meanwhile I pray you do me no despite.

CHORUS. The plea thou urgest, needs must give us pause, Set forth in weighty argument, but we Must leave the issue with the ruling powers.
cards.whyThisWorks: The Chorus's three-line reply directly follows Oedipus's extended plea, making it a clear structural pivot that acknowledges his argument while deferring resolution—an ideal model for teaching how a section's closing paragraph can suspend rather than settle a conflict.
cards.skillStrategy: Ask yourself: what job does this paragraph do in the section—does it resolve the conflict, introduce a new one, or hold the tension in place by shifting responsibility to someone else?
evidencePoints: The plea thou urgest, needs must give us pause, / Set forth in weighty argument
but we / Must leave the issue with the ruling powers
cards.question: Oedipus closes his speech by calling himself 'a holy and god-fearing man whose coming purports comfort for your folk' and demanding 'O preserve me to the end.' What is the structural job of the Chorus's reply—'The plea thou urgest, needs must give us pause, / Set forth in weighty argument, but we / Must leave the issue with the ruling powers'—within this section?

choices.label: A
choices.text: It rejects Oedipus's appeal by disputing his claim to be 'a man more sinned against than sinning' and insists he prove his innocence before Athens honors its pledge to shelter 'the vexed stranger.'

choices.label: B
choices.text: It acknowledges that Oedipus's argument is 'weighty' enough to 'give us pause' but transfers the final decision to 'the ruling powers,' leaving his demand for protection unresolved at the section's close.

choices.label: C
choices.text: It confirms that Athens has already fulfilled its duty as 'the most devout' state by sheltering 'the vexed stranger' and assures Oedipus that 'the ruling powers' will grant full protection without further deliberation.

choices.label: D
choices.text: It accepts Oedipus's self-description as 'a holy and god-fearing man' as sufficient grounds for immediate shelter and resolves the tension his speech introduced by granting the defense he demands.

cards.standardTitle: Central idea and supporting evidence
cards.excerpt:
CHORUS. (Str. 1) Races of mortal man Whose life is but a span, I count ye but the shadow of a shade! For he who most doth know Of bliss, hath but the show; A moment, and the visions pale and fade. Thy fall, O Oedipus, thy piteous fall Warns me none born of women blest to call.

(Ant. 1) For he of marksmen best, O Zeus, outshot the rest, And won the prize supreme of wealth and power. By him the vulture maid Was quelled, her witchery laid; He rose our savior and the land’s strong tower. We hailed thee king and from that day adored Of mighty Thebes the universal lord.

(Str. 2) O heavy hand of fate! Who now more desolate, Whose tale more sad than thine, whose lot more dire? O Oedipus, discrowned head, Thy cradle was thy marriage bed; One harborage sufficed for son and sire. How could the soil thy father eared so long Endure to bear in silence such a wrong?

(Ant. 2) All-seeing Time hath caught Guilt, and to justice brought The son and sire commingled in one bed. O child of Laius’ ill-starred race Would I had ne’er beheld thy face; I raise for thee a dirge as o’er the dead. Yet, sooth to say, through thee I drew new breath, And now through thee I feel a second death. [Enter SECOND MESSENGER.]

SECOND MESSENGER. Most grave and reverend senators of Thebes, What Deeds ye soon must hear, what sights behold How will ye mourn, if, true-born patriots, Ye reverence still the race of Labdacus! Not Ister nor all Phasis’ flood, I ween, Could wash away the blood-stains from this house, The ills it shrouds or soon will bring to light, Ills wrought of malice, not unwittingly. The worst to bear are self-inflicted wounds.
cards.whyThisWorks: The Chorus's repeated laments about Oedipus's fall from greatness to ruin, combined with the Second Messenger's warning about self-inflicted wounds, give students a clear central idea to articulate beyond mere topic or isolated detail.
cards.skillStrategy: Ask yourself: what point is the passage making about its subject — not just who or what it is about, but what it is saying about that subject?
evidencePoints: Thy fall, O Oedipus, thy piteous fall / Warns me none born of women blest to call.
The worst to bear are self-inflicted wounds.
cards.question: Which statement best expresses the central idea developed across the Chorus's odes and the Second Messenger's speech?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Oedipus was once celebrated as Thebes's greatest king because he defeated the Sphinx and brought the city peace.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Even the most celebrated human life can collapse into ruin, and the suffering that follows is made worse when it results from one's own actions.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The gods, particularly Zeus, are ultimately responsible for the downfall of Oedipus and the misery of the Theban people.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Time reveals all hidden guilt, and the house of Laius has been cursed since long before Oedipus was born.

cards.standardTitle: Rhetoric and reader effect
cards.excerpt:
THESEUS. I know that none Shall hale thee hence in my despite. Such threats Vented in anger oft, are blusterers, An idle breath, forgot when sense returns. And for thy foemen, though their words were brave, Boasting to bring thee back, they are like to find The seas between us wide and hard to sail. Such my firm purpose, but in any case Take heart, since Phoebus sent thee here. My name, Though I be distant, warrants thee from harm.

CHORUS. (Str. 1) Thou hast come to a steed-famed land for rest, O stranger worn with toil, To a land of all lands the goodliest Colonus’ glistening soil. ’Tis the haunt of the clear-voiced nightingale, Who hid in her bower, among The wine-dark ivy that wreathes the vale, Trilleth her ceaseless song; And she loves, where the clustering berries nod O’er a sunless, windless glade, The spot by no mortal footstep trod, The pleasance kept for the Bacchic god, Where he holds each night his revels wild With the nymphs who fostered the lusty child.
cards.whyThisWorks: The Chorus's ode layers vivid figurative language—'wine-dark ivy,' 'clear-voiced nightingale,' 'sunless, windless glade'—to create a sacred, otherworldly atmosphere that contrasts sharply with Theseus's political reassurances, giving students a clear opportunity to analyze how figurative language shapes the reader's emotional experience of Colonus.
cards.skillStrategy: When you spot figurative language, ask yourself: what feeling does this create in me, and why did the writer choose these images instead of plain description?
evidencePoints: 'Tis the haunt of the clear-voiced nightingale, / Who hid in her bower, among / The wine-dark ivy that wreathes the vale, / Trilleth her ceaseless song
The spot by no mortal footstep trod, / The pleasance kept for the Bacchic god
cards.question: In the Chorus's ode, the phrases 'wine-dark ivy that wreathes the vale' and 'The spot by no mortal footstep trod' are examples of figurative language. How do these images affect the reader's understanding of Colonus?

choices.label: A
choices.text: They warn the reader that Colonus is a dangerous place where mortals are forbidden to enter and will face punishment from the gods.

choices.label: B
choices.text: They present Colonus as a place of divine beauty untouched by ordinary human life, making it feel like a sacred refuge rather than a common city.

choices.label: C
choices.text: They suggest that Colonus is an isolated and gloomy land where the stranger will feel more trapped than protected.

choices.label: D
choices.text: They emphasize that Colonus is famous only for its horses and its soil, reinforcing Theseus's promise of military protection.

cards.standardTitle: Key literary elements add layers of meaning
cards.excerpt:
CREON. What is this? Thy words inspire a dread presentiment.

TEIRESIAS. The divination of my arts shall tell. Sitting upon my throne of augury, As is my wont, where every fowl of heaven Find harborage, upon mine ears was borne A jargon strange of twitterings, hoots, and screams; So knew I that each bird at the other tare With bloody talons, for the whirr of wings Could signify naught else. Perturbed in soul, I straight essayed the sacrifice by fire On blazing altars, but the God of Fire Came not in flame, and from the thigh bones dripped And sputtered in the ashes a foul ooze; Gall-bladders cracked and spurted up: the fat Melted and fell and left the thigh bones bare. Such are the signs, taught by this lad, I read— As I guide others, so the boy guides me— The frustrate signs of oracles grown dumb. O King, thy willful temper ails the State, For all our shrines and altars are profaned By what has filled the maw of dogs and crows, The flesh of Oedipus’ unburied son. Therefore the angry gods abominate Our litanies and our burnt offerings; Therefore no birds trill out a happy note, Gorged with the carnival of human gore. O ponder this, my son. To err is common To all men, but the man who having erred Hugs not his errors, but repents and seeks The cure, is not a wastrel nor unwise. No fool, the saw goes, like the obstinate fool. Let death disarm thy vengeance. O forbear To vex the dead. What glory wilt thou win By slaying twice the slain? I mean thee well; Counsel’s most welcome if I promise gain.
cards.whyThisWorks: Teiresias's failed omens and direct accusation that Creon's refusal to bury Polynices has 'profaned' the altars function as a plot reversal that deepens the conflict's meaning: Creon's political decree has now corrupted the divine order itself, raising the stakes from a personal power struggle to a cosmic crisis.
cards.skillStrategy: When a character delivers news that changes what another character—and the reader—understands about the consequences of a decision, ask what deeper truth that moment reveals about the conflict.
evidencePoints: thy willful temper ails the State, For all our shrines and altars are profaned By what has filled the maw of dogs and crows, The flesh of Oedipus' unburied son.
Therefore the angry gods abominate Our litanies and our burnt offerings; Therefore no birds trill out a happy note, Gorged with the carnival of human gore.
cards.question: Teiresias reveals that the sacrificial fires have failed and the gods now 'abominate' Thebes's offerings. What does this moment in the plot add to the meaning of Creon's conflict?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Creon's refusal to bury Polynices is shown to be a private family matter that has no real effect on the city's political stability.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Creon's single political decision has expanded into a divine catastrophe, revealing that defying the gods' laws carries consequences that no human authority can contain.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Teiresias's failed omens prove that his prophetic powers have weakened with age, making his warning to Creon unreliable and easy to dismiss.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The corrupted sacrifices show that the citizens of Thebes, not Creon, are responsible for angering the gods by allowing Polynices to remain unburied.

cards.standardTitle: Theme development across a literary text
cards.excerpt: ANTIGONE. What but the thought of our two brothers dead, The one by Creon graced with funeral rites, The other disappointed? Eteocles He hath consigned to earth (as fame reports) With obsequies that use and wont ordain, So gracing him among the dead below. But Polyneices, a dishonored corse, (So by report the royal edict runs) No man may bury him or make lament— Must leave him tombless and unwept, a feast For kites to scent afar and swoop upon. Such is the edict (if report speak true) Of Creon, our most noble Creon, aimed At thee and me, aye me too; and anon He will be here to promulgate, for such As have not heard, his mandate; ’tis in sooth No passing humor, for the edict says Whoe’er transgresses shall be stoned to death. So stands it with us; now ’tis thine to show If thou art worthy of thy blood or base.
cards.whyThisWorks: Antigone's side-by-side description of Eteocles receiving proper burial 'among the dead below' versus Polyneices left 'tombless and unwept, a feast for kites'—capped by the death penalty for any who disobey—creates a concrete moment that directly develops the theme of impossible conflict between civic law and personal duty.
cards.skillStrategy: When tracking theme, find the moment where two opposing forces collide and ask what truth about human experience that collision reveals.
evidencePoints: tombless and unwept, a feast for kites to scent afar and swoop upon
Whoe'er transgresses shall be stoned to death
cards.question: Antigone describes Eteocles as honored 'among the dead below' with full burial rites, while Polyneices is left 'tombless and unwept, a feast for kites'—and then states that anyone who defies Creon's edict 'shall be stoned to death.' How does this contrast, backed by the threat of execution, develop a theme in the passage?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The contrast between Eteocles' honored burial and Polyneices left 'a feast for kites' develops the theme that a ruler's authority is always just, and Antigone recounts the difference to show she accepts Creon's judgment as the rightful law of the city.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The gap between Eteocles receiving proper burial rites and Polyneices being left 'tombless and unwept'—enforced by death for any who disobey—develops the theme that state power can force individuals into an impossible conflict between family duty and the law.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Creon's decision to honor Eteocles while threatening death for anyone who buries Polyneices develops the theme that rulers who reward loyalty will always maintain stable authority, and Antigone's closing challenge to her sister signals her willingness to submit.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Leaving Polyneices 'tombless and unwept' while granting Eteocles full funeral rites develops the theme that public spectacle is the most effective tool of leadership, and Antigone presents Creon's edict as a reasonable exercise of royal power.

cards.standardTitle: Text structure and feature purpose
cards.excerpt:
CHORUS. (Str. 1) Sunbeam, of all that ever dawn upon Our seven-gated Thebes the brightest ray, O eye of golden day, How fair thy light o’er Dirce’s fountain shone, Speeding upon their headlong homeward course, Far quicker than they came, the Argive force; Putting to flight The argent shields, the host with scutcheons white. Against our land the proud invader came To vindicate fell Polyneices’ claim. Like to an eagle swooping low, On pinions white as new fall’n snow. With clanging scream, a horsetail plume his crest, The aspiring lord of Argos onward pressed.

(Ant. 1) Hovering around our city walls he waits, His spearmen raven at our seven gates. But ere a torch our crown of towers could burn, Ere they had tasted of our blood, they turn Forced by the Dragon; in their rear The din of Ares panic-struck they hear. For Zeus who hates the braggart’s boast Beheld that gold-bespangled host; As at the goal the paean they upraise, He struck them with his forked lightning blaze.

(Str. 2) To earthy from earth rebounding, down he crashed; The fire-brand from his impious hand was dashed, As like a Bacchic reveler on he came, Outbreathing hate and flame, And tottered. Elsewhere in the field, Here, there, great Area like a war-horse wheeled; Beneath his car down thrust Our foemen bit the dust.

Seven captains at our seven gates Thundered; for each a champion waits, Each left behind his armor bright, Trophy for Zeus who turns the fight; Save two alone, that ill-starred pair One mother to one father bare, Who lance in rest, one ’gainst the other Drave, and both perished, brother slain by brother.
cards.whyThisWorks: The final stanza of (Str. 2) shifts from the Chorus's celebration of Thebes's collective victory to the tragic fate of Eteocles and Polyneices, introducing the fratricidal conflict that will drive the rest of the play—making it a clear structural pivot students can analyze.
cards.skillStrategy: Ask yourself: does this paragraph continue the same idea as what came before, or does it introduce something new or contrasting? Look for a change in subject, tone, or focus.
evidencePoints: Seven captains at our seven gates / Thundered; for each a champion waits
Save two alone, that ill-starred pair / One mother to one father bare, / Who lance in rest, one 'gainst the other / Drave, and both perished, brother slain by brother.
cards.question: In (Str. 2), the final lines beginning with 'Seven captains at our seven gates' shift the focus of the Chorus's account. What is the primary job of these closing lines within the stanza?

choices.label: A
choices.text: They extend the celebration of Zeus's power by listing additional gods who aided Thebes in battle.

choices.label: B
choices.text: They contrast the broader Theban victory with the singular tragedy of two brothers who destroyed each other, introducing the conflict at the heart of the play.

choices.label: C
choices.text: They conclude the ode by confirming that all seven Argive captains were defeated and Thebes suffered no losses.

choices.label: D
choices.text: They prove that the Argive army was disorganized by showing that its commanders fought among themselves rather than against Thebes.

cards.standardTitle: Central idea and supporting evidence
cards.excerpt:
ANTIGONE. O grave, O bridal bower, O prison house Hewn from the rock, my everlasting home, Whither I go to join the mighty host Of kinsfolk, Persephassa’s guests long dead, The last of all, of all more miserable, I pass, my destined span of years cut short. And yet good hope is mine that I shall find A welcome from my sire, a welcome too, From thee, my mother, and my brother dear; From with these hands, I laved and decked your limbs In death, and poured libations on your grave. And last, my Polyneices, unto thee I paid due rites, and this my recompense! Yet am I justified in wisdom’s eyes. For even had it been some child of mine, Or husband mouldering in death’s decay, I had not wrought this deed despite the State. What is the law I call in aid? ’Tis thus I argue. Had it been a husband dead I might have wed another, and have borne Another child, to take the dead child’s place. But, now my sire and mother both are dead, No second brother can be born for me. Thus by the law of conscience I was led To honor thee, dear brother, and was judged By Creon guilty of a heinous crime. And now he drags me like a criminal, A bride unwed, amerced of marriage-song And marriage-bed and joys of motherhood, By friends deserted to a living grave. What ordinance of heaven have I transgressed? Hereafter can I look to any god For succor, call on any man for help? Alas, my piety is impious deemed. Well, if such justice is approved of heaven, I shall be taught by suffering my sin; But if the sin is theirs, O may they suffer No worse ills than the wrongs they do to me.

CHORUS. The same ungovernable will Drives like a gale the maiden still.

CREON. Therefore, my guards who let her stay Shall smart full sore for their delay.
cards.whyThisWorks: Antigone's speech contains a clearly stated argument—'Thus by the law of conscience I was led / To honor thee, dear brother'—that students must distinguish from surrounding grief and isolated details to identify the central idea.
cards.skillStrategy: Ask yourself: what is the speaker's main argument across the whole speech, not just one emotional moment or single detail?
evidencePoints: Thus by the law of conscience I was led To honor thee, dear brother, and was judged By Creon guilty of a heinous crime.
Yet am I justified in wisdom's eyes.
cards.question: In her speech, Antigone states, 'Thus by the law of conscience I was led / To honor thee, dear brother.' Which statement most accurately expresses the central idea that this line supports throughout her entire speech?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Antigone's deepest regret is that Creon has denied her the joys of marriage and motherhood, leaving her to die as 'a bride unwed.'

choices.label: B
choices.text: Antigone maintains that her conscience-driven duty to bury her brother was morally justified, even though Creon has condemned her as a criminal for defying the state.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Antigone believes the gods have abandoned her and that divine punishment will eventually fall on Creon for the wrongs he has done to her.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Antigone argues that a brother's death demands burial rites because, unlike a husband or child, a dead brother can never be replaced by another.

cards.standardTitle: Rhetoric and reader effect
cards.excerpt:
POLYNEICES. Ah me, my sisters, shall I first lament My own afflictions, or my aged sire’s, Whom here I find a castaway, with you, In a strange land, an ancient beggar clad In antic tatters, marring all his frame, While o’er the sightless orbs his unkept locks Float in the breeze; and, as it were to match, He bears a wallet against hunger’s pinch. All this too late I learn, wretch that I am, Alas! I own it, and am proved most vile In my neglect of thee: I scorn myself. But as almighty Zeus in all he doth Hath Mercy for co-partner of this throne, Let Mercy, father, also sit enthroned In thy heart likewise. For transgressions past May be amended, cannot be made worse.

Why silent? Father, speak, nor turn away, Hast thou no word, wilt thou dismiss me then In mute disdain, nor tell me why thou art wrath? O ye his daughters, sisters mine, do ye This sullen, obstinate silence try to move. Let him not spurn, without a single word Of answer, me the suppliant of the god.
cards.whyThisWorks: Polyneices' repeated rhetorical questions—'Father, speak,' 'Hast thou no word,' 'wilt thou dismiss me then'—create mounting desperation that students can analyze for emotional effect on the reader.
cards.skillStrategy: When you spot a rhetorical question, ask yourself: what feeling does the speaker want to stir, and how does repeating that move change the intensity for the reader?
evidencePoints: Why silent? Father, speak, nor turn away, Hast thou no word, wilt thou dismiss me then / In mute disdain, nor tell me why thou art wrath?
Let him not spurn, without a single word / Of answer, me the suppliant of the god.
cards.question: Read the lines from the second paragraph: 'Why silent? Father, speak, nor turn away, / Hast thou no word, wilt thou dismiss me then / In mute disdain, nor tell me why thou art wrath?' How does Polyneices' use of repeated rhetorical questions affect the reader?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The rapid questions suggest that Polyneices is confident his father will eventually forgive him, making the reader feel reassured about their reunion.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The accumulation of unanswered questions builds a sense of Polyneices' growing desperation, making the reader feel the weight of his father's crushing silence.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The questions shift blame onto Oedipus for refusing to speak, causing the reader to view Oedipus as the more guilty figure in their conflict.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The questions slow the scene's pace so the reader can reflect on Polyneices' earlier admission that he neglected his father.

cards.standardTitle: Key literary elements add layers of meaning
cards.excerpt:
OEDIPUS. O what avails renown or fair repute? Are they not vanity? For, look you, now Athens is held of States the most devout, Athens alone gives hospitality And shelters the vexed stranger, so men say. Have I found so? I whom ye dislodged First from my seat of rock and now would drive Forth from your land, dreading my name alone; For me you surely dread not, nor my deeds, Deeds of a man more sinned against than sinning, As I might well convince you, were it meet To tell my mother’s story and my sire’s, The cause of this your fear. Yet am I then A villain born because in self-defense, Striken, I struck the striker back again? E’en had I known, no villainy ’twould prove: But all unwitting whither I went, I went— To ruin; my destroyers knew it well, Wherefore, I pray you, sirs, in Heaven’s name, Even as ye bade me quit my seat, defend me. O pay not a lip service to the gods And wrong them of their dues. Bethink ye well, The eye of Heaven beholds the just of men, And the unjust, nor ever in this world Has one sole godless sinner found escape. Stand then on Heaven’s side and never blot Athens’ fair scutcheon by abetting wrong. I came to you a suppliant, and you pledged Your honor; O preserve me to the end, O let not this marred visage do me wrong! A holy and god-fearing man is here Whose coming purports comfort for your folk. And when your chief arrives, whoe’er he be, Then shall ye have my story and know all. Meanwhile I pray you do me no despite.

CHORUS. The plea thou urgest, needs must give us pause, Set forth in weighty argument, but we Must leave the issue with the ruling powers.
cards.whyThisWorks: Oedipus's conflict between his cursed reputation and his claim of unwitting innocence drives the plot and raises the deeper question of whether guilt requires intent, illustrating how conflict adds layers of meaning.
cards.skillStrategy: When a character's conflict involves a gap between reputation and self-defense, ask what larger question about justice or responsibility that gap forces the reader to consider.
evidencePoints: a man more sinned against than sinning
all unwitting whither I went, I went
cards.question: Oedipus claims he is 'more sinned against than sinning' and acted 'all unwitting.' How does the conflict between his cursed reputation and this claim of innocence add meaning to the passage?

choices.label: A
choices.text: It shows that Oedipus blames Athens for his suffering, making his appeal to the city's 'fair repute' an act of flattery rather than genuine belief.

choices.label: B
choices.text: It raises the question of whether guilt requires conscious choice, suggesting divine justice must weigh intent rather than reputation alone.

choices.label: C
choices.text: It reveals that Oedipus has accepted his fate and no longer disputes the gods, relying solely on the Chorus to protect him.

choices.label: D
choices.text: It demonstrates that Athens has broken its pledge of hospitality, and Oedipus's argument is mainly a criticism of the city's hypocrisy.

cards.standardTitle: Theme development across a literary text
cards.excerpt: ANTIGONE. Yea, for these laws were not ordained of Zeus, And she who sits enthroned with gods below, Justice, enacted not these human laws. Nor did I deem that thou, a mortal man, Could’st by a breath annul and override The immutable unwritten laws of Heaven. They were not born today nor yesterday; They die not; and none knoweth whence they sprang. I was not like, who feared no mortal’s frown, To disobey these laws and so provoke The wrath of Heaven. I knew that I must die, E’en hadst thou not proclaimed it; and if death Is thereby hastened, I shall count it gain. For death is gain to him whose life, like mine, Is full of misery. Thus my lot appears Not sad, but blissful; for had I endured To leave my mother’s son unburied there, I should have grieved with reason, but not now. And if in this thou judgest me a fool, Methinks the judge of folly’s not acquit.
cards.whyThisWorks: Antigone's speech pairs her defiance of Creon's 'human laws' with her acceptance of death as 'gain,' giving students a clear two-moment structure through which to trace how divine-law loyalty over mortal authority emerges as the passage's central theme.
cards.skillStrategy: Identify two specific moments in the passage, explain what each one shows about a character's belief or value, and then state how those two moments together point to one larger idea the author is developing.
evidencePoints: The immutable unwritten laws of Heaven. They were not born today nor yesterday; They die not
death is gain to him whose life, like mine, / Is full of misery
cards.question: Antigone declares that Creon, 'a mortal man,' cannot 'annul and override / The immutable unwritten laws of Heaven,' and she later calls death 'gain' because her life 'is full of misery.' How do these two specific moments work together to develop a theme in the passage?

choices.label: A
choices.text: They show that Antigone's real motivation is personal grief over her unburied brother, and her appeal to laws that 'die not' is only a public excuse she uses to make that private grief seem principled to Creon.

choices.label: B
choices.text: They develop the idea that loyalty to eternal divine law outweighs any mortal authority, so the death Creon threatens becomes, in Antigone's own words, a 'gain' rather than a punishment that defeats her purpose.

choices.label: C
choices.text: They suggest that Antigone welcomes death mainly to escape a miserable life, and her claim about laws that 'were not born today nor yesterday' is a rhetorical strategy to disguise that private wish as a stand against Creon.

choices.label: D
choices.text: They reveal that Antigone sees death as the unavoidable consequence of any defiance, and her reference to Heaven's 'immutable unwritten laws' shows she privately accepted Creon's proclamation as legitimate even while choosing to break it.

cards.standardTitle: Text structure and feature purpose
cards.excerpt:
CREON. She shall be taken to some desert place By man untrod, and in a rock-hewn cave, With food no more than to avoid the taint That homicide might bring on all the State, Buried alive. There let her call in aid The King of Death, the one god she reveres, Or learn too late a lesson learnt at last: ’Tis labor lost, to reverence the dead.

CHORUS. (Str.) Love resistless in fight, all yield at a glance of thine eye, Love who pillowed all night on a maiden’s cheek dost lie, Over the upland holds. Shall mortals not yield to thee?

(Ant). Mad are thy subjects all, and even the wisest heart Straight to folly will fall, at a touch of thy poisoned dart. Thou didst kindle the strife, this feud of kinsman with kin, By the eyes of a winsome wife, and the yearning her heart to win. For as her consort still, enthroned with Justice above, Thou bendest man to thy will, O all invincible Love.

Lo I myself am borne aside, From Justice, as I view this bride. (O sight an eye in tears to drown) Antigone, so young, so fair, Thus hurried down Death’s bower with the dead to share.

ANTIGONE. (Str. 1) Friends, countrymen, my last farewell I make; My journey’s done. One last fond, lingering, longing look I take At the bright sun. For Death who puts to sleep both young and old Hales my young life, And beckons me to Acheron’s dark fold, An unwed wife. No youths have sung the marriage song for me, My bridal bed No maids have strewn with flowers from the lea, ’Tis Death I wed.
cards.whyThisWorks: The Chorus section moves from praising Love as 'resistless in fight' to admitting it bends even 'the wisest heart' toward folly, then pivots to direct grief over Antigone being 'hurried down Death's bower,' showing students how a section can shift focus and build toward sympathy.
cards.skillStrategy: Ask yourself: what does this section open with, what does it shift to, and what feeling does it leave the reader with—that sequence reveals the section's job.
evidencePoints: Thou didst kindle the strife, this feud of kinsman with kin
Lo I myself am borne aside, From Justice, as I view this bride. (O sight an eye in tears to drown) Antigone, so young, so fair, Thus hurried down Death's bower with the dead to share.
cards.question: In the Chorus section that begins 'Love resistless in fight' and ends 'Thus hurried down Death's bower with the dead to share,' what is the job of this section in relation to Creon's decree and Antigone's fate?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The section reinforces Creon's decree by arguing that Love itself caused Antigone's crime, making her punishment just and her fate deserved.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The section first frames Love as an unstoppable force that 'kindled the strife' between kin, then turns that idea into open grief for Antigone, who is 'so young, so fair' and 'hurried down Death's bower.'

choices.label: C
choices.text: The section resolves the conflict between Creon and Antigone by showing that Love, 'enthroned with Justice above,' ultimately sides with Creon's authority over the State.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The section shifts focus entirely away from Antigone by using the praise of Love as 'all invincible' to introduce a new conflict among the other characters in the play.

cards.standardTitle: Central idea and supporting evidence
cards.excerpt:
OEDIPUS. They knew it, yet the ignoble greed of rule Outweighed all longing for their sire’s return.

ISMENE. Grievous thy words, yet I must own them true.

OEDIPUS. Then may the gods ne’er quench their fatal feud, And mine be the arbitrament of the fight, For which they now are arming, spear to spear; That neither he who holds the scepter now May keep this throne, nor he who fled the realm Return again. _They_ never raised a hand, When I their sire was thrust from hearth and home, When I was banned and banished, what recked they? Say you ’twas done at my desire, a grace Which the state, yielding to my wish, allowed? Not so; for, mark you, on that very day When in the tempest of my soul I craved Death, even death by stoning, none appeared To further that wild longing, but anon, When time had numbed my anguish and I felt My wrath had all outrun those errors past, Then, then it was the city went about By force to oust me, respited for years; And then my sons, who should as sons have helped, Did nothing: and, one little word from them Was all I needed, and they spoke no word, But let me wander on for evermore, A banished man, a beggar. These two maids Their sisters, girls, gave all their sex could give, Food and safe harborage and filial care; While their two brethren sacrificed their sire For lust of power and sceptred sovereignty. No! me they ne’er shall win for an ally, Nor will this Theban kingship bring them gain; That know I from this maiden’s oracles, And those old prophecies concerning me, Which Phoebus now at length has brought to pass. Come Creon then, come all the mightiest In Thebes to seek me; for if ye my friends, Championed by those dread Powers indigenous, Espouse my cause; then for the State ye gain A great deliverer, for my foemen bane.
cards.whyThisWorks: Oedipus's speech explicitly contrasts his sons' 'lust of power and sceptred sovereignty' with his daughters' 'filial care,' giving students a clear central claim supported by specific textual evidence to identify.
cards.skillStrategy: Find the claim the speaker keeps returning to—look for repeated contrasts or accusations—then check which answer choice is supported by the most details in the speech.
evidencePoints: their two brethren sacrificed their sire For lust of power and sceptred sovereignty
These two maids Their sisters, girls, gave all their sex could give, Food and safe harborage and filial care
cards.question: Oedipus states that his sons 'sacrificed their sire / For lust of power and sceptred sovereignty' while his daughters gave 'Food and safe harborage and filial care.' Which statement best expresses the central idea that these contrasting details develop throughout his speech?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Oedipus argues that the city of Thebes wrongfully banished him by force after he had already accepted his exile, making the state—not his sons—responsible for his suffering.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Oedipus argues that his sons abandoned him for the sake of power while his daughters proved their loyalty through genuine care, and therefore his sons will never have him as an ally.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Oedipus warns that the gods will settle the feud between his two sons, and that neither son deserves the throne because both have sinned against divine law.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Oedipus reveals that the prophecies of Phoebus have finally come true, and that Creon's arrival in Thebes will determine which of his sons gains the scepter.

cards.standardTitle: Rhetoric and reader effect
cards.excerpt:
THESEUS. Oft had I heard of thee in times gone by— The bloody mutilation of thine eyes— And therefore know thee, son of Laius. All that I lately gathered on the way Made my conjecture doubly sure; and now Thy garb and that marred visage prove to me That thou art he. So pitying thine estate, Most ill-starred Oedipus, I fain would know What is the suit ye urge on me and Athens, Thou and the helpless maiden at thy side. Declare it; dire indeed must be the tale Whereat _I_ should recoil. I too was reared, Like thee, in exile, and in foreign lands Wrestled with many perils, no man more. Wherefore no alien in adversity Shall seek in vain my succor, nor shalt thou; I know myself a mortal, and my share In what the morrow brings no more than thine.

OEDIPUS. Theseus, thy words so apt, so generous So comfortable, need no long reply Both who I am and of what lineage sprung, And from what land I came, thou hast declared. So without prologue I may utter now My brief petition, and the tale is told.
cards.whyThisWorks: Theseus's speech uses personal analogy ('I too was reared, Like thee, in exile') and contrast between his power and Oedipus's suffering to build an emotional appeal that establishes shared humanity, giving students a clear rhetorical device with a traceable effect on the reader.
cards.skillStrategy: When you spot a comparison or parallel structure in a speech, ask yourself: what feeling or belief does the speaker want the audience to accept because of that comparison?
evidencePoints: I too was reared, Like thee, in exile, and in foreign lands Wrestled with many perils, no man more.
Wherefore no alien in adversity Shall seek in vain my succor, nor shalt thou; I know myself a mortal, and my share In what the morrow brings no more than thine.
cards.question: In Theseus's speech, he states, 'I too was reared, Like thee, in exile, and in foreign lands / Wrestled with many perils, no man more.' How does this analogy affect the reader?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The comparison reveals that Theseus is boasting about surviving greater hardships than Oedipus, making him appear arrogant rather than sympathetic.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The comparison between Theseus's own exile and Oedipus's suffering establishes Theseus as a credible protector, making his promise of aid feel earned rather than merely charitable.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The comparison shifts the reader's focus away from Oedipus's petition entirely, centering the scene on Theseus's personal history instead.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The comparison signals that Theseus doubts Oedipus's identity and is stalling before deciding whether to grant him an audience.

cards.standardTitle: Key literary elements add layers of meaning
cards.excerpt:
CHORUS. (Str. 1) O when the flying foe, Turning at last to bay, Soon will give blow for blow, Might I behold the fray; Hear the loud battle roar Swell, on the Pythian shore, Or by the torch-lit bay, Where the dread Queen and Maid Cherish the mystic rites, Rites they to none betray, Ere on his lips is laid Secrecy’s golden key By their own acolytes, Priestly Eumolpidae.

There I might chance behold Theseus our captain bold Meet with the robber band, Ere they have fled the land, Rescue by might and main Maidens, the captives twain.

(Ant. 1) Haply on swiftest steed, Or in the flying car, Now they approach the glen, West of white Oea’s scaur. They will be vanquished: Dread are our warriors, dread Theseus our chieftain’s men. Flashes each bridle bright, Charges each gallant knight, All that our Queen adore, Pallas their patron, or Him whose wide floods enring Earth, the great Ocean-king Whom Rhea bore.

(Str. 2) Fight they or now prepare To fight? a vision rare Tells me that soon again I shall behold the twain Maidens so ill bestead, By their kin buffeted. Today, today Zeus worketh some great thing This day shall victory bring. O for the wings, the wings of a dove, To be borne with the speed of the gale, Up and still upwards to sail And gaze on the fray from the clouds above. (Ant. 2) All-seeing Zeus, O lord of heaven, To our guardian host be given Might triumphant to surprise Flying foes and win their prize. Hear us, Zeus, and hear us, child Of Zeus, Athene undefiled, Hear, Apollo, hunter, hear, Huntress, sister of Apollo, Who the dappled swift-foot deer O’er the wooded glade dost follow; Help with your two-fold power Athens in danger’s hour! O wayfarer, thou wilt not have to tax The friends who watch for thee with false presage, For lo, an escort with the maids draws near. [Enter ANTIGONE and ISMENE with THESEUS]

OEDIPUS. Where, where? what sayest thou?
cards.whyThisWorks: The Chorus's escalating prayers to Zeus, Athene, and Apollo—immediately answered by the stage direction '[Enter ANTIGONE and ISMENE with THESEUS]'—demonstrate how the plot's resolution layers divine justice onto the physical conflict between captivity and freedom.
cards.skillStrategy: When a conflict resolves at the exact moment characters invoke a cause or force, ask what meaning that timing adds beyond the surface event.
evidencePoints: All-seeing Zeus, O lord of heaven, / To our guardian host be given / Might triumphant to surprise / Flying foes and win their prize
[Enter ANTIGONE and ISMENE with THESEUS]
cards.question: The Chorus invokes 'All-seeing Zeus, O lord of heaven, / To our guardian host be given / Might triumphant to surprise / Flying foes and win their prize,' and the very next line is the stage direction '[Enter ANTIGONE and ISMENE with THESEUS].' How does this immediate plot resolution deepen the meaning of the conflict between the captive maidens and their abductors?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The instant arrival of Theseus with the maidens shows that human military skill alone resolved the conflict, because Theseus had already defeated the robber band before the Chorus began praying to Zeus, Athene, and Apollo.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The rescue arriving at the exact moment the Chorus invokes Zeus, Athene, and Apollo suggests that divine justice answers those who suffer unjustly, giving the conflict between captivity and freedom a meaning beyond physical rescue.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The entrance of Antigone and Ismene reveals that the Chorus's fear was exaggerated from the start, because the maidens were never truly in danger and the conflict was less serious than the prayers to Zeus and Athene implied.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The stage direction shifts the conflict entirely to Oedipus, whose cry 'Where, where? what sayest thou?' becomes the central dramatic tension, making the Chorus's prayers to Zeus and Apollo irrelevant to the scene's meaning.

cards.standardTitle: Theme development across a literary text
cards.excerpt: CREON. Not deeming this city void of men Or counsel, son of Aegeus, as thou say’st I did what I have done; rather I thought Your people were not like to set such store by kin of mine and keep them ’gainst my will. Nor would they harbor, so I stood assured, A godless parricide, a reprobate Convicted of incestuous marriage ties. For on her native hill of Ares here (I knew your far-famed Areopagus) Sits Justice, and permits not vagrant folk To stay within your borders. In that faith I hunted down my quarry; and e’en then I had refrained but for the curses dire Wherewith he banned my kinsfolk and myself: Such wrong, methought, had warrant for my act. Anger has no old age but only death; The dead alone can feel no touch of spite. So thou must work thy will; my cause is just But weak without allies; yet will I try, Old as I am, to answer deeds with deeds.
cards.whyThisWorks: Creon's speech contains two distinct moments—his calculated decision to seize his quarry based on legal reasoning and his admission that anger, not law, ultimately drove him—allowing students to track how both moments together develop the theme that unchecked anger corrupts justice.
cards.skillStrategy: Find two separate moments in the passage and ask what idea they both point to together, rather than letting one moment stand alone as the whole message.
evidencePoints: I hunted down my quarry; and e'en then I had refrained but for the curses dire Wherewith he banned my kinsfolk and myself
Anger has no old age but only death; The dead alone can feel no touch of spite.
cards.question: Read the two moments in Creon's speech: first, his claim that he acted within legal reasoning when he 'hunted down my quarry,' and second, his admission that 'Anger has no old age but only death.' Together, how do these two moments develop a theme in the passage?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Creon's reference to the Areopagus and his claim that 'my cause is just' show that he believes Athenian law fully supports his actions, developing a theme that legal institutions always protect the righteous.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Creon first frames his pursuit as lawful and reasoned, then reveals that personal anger over 'curses dire' was the true force behind it, together developing the theme that anger undermines the justice a person claims to uphold.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Creon's acknowledgment that his cause is 'weak without allies' and his vow to 'answer deeds with deeds' show that political isolation drives his choices, developing a theme that power depends entirely on forming alliances.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Creon's description of his quarry as 'a godless parricide' and 'a reprobate' develops the theme that criminals who violate family bonds deserve to be exiled from any city that values justice.

cards.standardTitle: Text structure and feature purpose
cards.excerpt:
By Nysa’s bastion ivy-clad, By shores with clustered vineyards glad, There to thee the hymn rings out, And through our streets we Thebans shout, All hall to thee Evoe, Evoe!

(Str. 2) Oh, as thou lov’st this city best of all, To thee, and to thy Mother levin-stricken, In our dire need we call; Thou see’st with what a plague our townsfolk sicken. Thy ready help we crave, Whether adown Parnassian heights descending, Or o’er the roaring straits thy swift was wending, Save us, O save!

(Ant. 2) Brightest of all the orbs that breathe forth light, Authentic son of Zeus, immortal king, Leader of all the voices of the night, Come, and thy train of Thyiads with thee bring, Thy maddened rout Who dance before thee all night long, and shout, Thy handmaids we, Evoe, Evoe!

[Enter MESSENGER]

MESSENGER. Attend all ye who dwell beside the halls Of Cadmus and Amphion. No man’s life As of one tenor would I praise or blame, For Fortune with a constant ebb and rise Casts down and raises high and low alike, And none can read a mortal’s horoscope. Take Creon; he, methought, if any man, Was enviable. He had saved this land Of Cadmus from our enemies and attained A monarch’s powers and ruled the state supreme, While a right noble issue crowned his bliss. Now all is gone and wasted, for a life Without life’s joys I count a living death. You’ll tell me he has ample store of wealth, The pomp and circumstance of kings; but if These give no pleasure, all the rest I count The shadow of a shade, nor would I weigh His wealth and power ’gainst a dram of joy.
cards.whyThisWorks: The Messenger's opening speech functions as a structural shift that moves the drama from the chorus's hymn of divine appeal to a philosophical reflection on fortune and Creon's fall, giving students a clear paragraph-job contrast to analyze.
cards.skillStrategy: Ask yourself: does this section start something new, push an idea further, or turn the drama in a different direction — then find the exact words that signal that move.
evidencePoints: No man's life / As of one tenor would I praise or blame, / For Fortune with a constant ebb and rise / Casts down and raises high and low alike
Take Creon; he, methought, if any man, / Was enviable. He had saved this land… Now all is gone and wasted
cards.question: The Messenger's speech that begins 'No man's life / As of one tenor would I praise or blame' serves what purpose in relation to the choral hymn that precedes it?

choices.label: A
choices.text: It extends the chorus's prayer by naming Creon as the mortal leader the gods must protect from the plague.

choices.label: B
choices.text: It shifts the drama away from divine appeal toward a human meditation on how fortune has reversed Creon's greatness.

choices.label: C
choices.text: It concludes the hymn's argument by confirming that Dionysus answered the Thebans' call for salvation.

choices.label: D
choices.text: It contrasts two equally powerful rulers — Creon and Amphion — to prove that no king can hold power permanently.

cards.standardTitle: Central idea and supporting evidence
cards.excerpt:
THESEUS. What means this?

OEDIPUS. Thou hast heard my tale of wrongs.

THESEUS. Ho! hasten to the altars, one of you. Command my liegemen leave the sacrifice And hurry, foot and horse, with rein unchecked, To where the paths that packmen use diverge, Lest the two maidens slip away, and I Become a mockery to this my guest, As one despoiled by force. Quick, as I bid. As for this stranger, had I let my rage, Justly provoked, have play, he had not ’scaped Scathless and uncorrected at my hands. But now the laws to which himself appealed, These and none others shall adjudicate. Thou shalt not quit this land, till thou hast fetched The maidens and produced them in my sight. Thou hast offended both against myself And thine own race and country. Having come Unto a State that champions right and asks For every action warranty of law, Thou hast set aside the custom of the land, And like some freebooter art carrying off What plunder pleases thee, as if forsooth Thou thoughtest this a city without men, Or manned by slaves, and me a thing of naught. Yet not from Thebes this villainy was learnt; Thebes is not wont to breed unrighteous sons, Nor would she praise thee, if she learnt that thou Wert robbing me—aye and the gods to boot, Haling by force their suppliants, poor maids. Were I on Theban soil, to prosecute The justest claim imaginable, I Would never wrest by violence my own Without sanction of your State or King; I should behave as fits an outlander Living amongst a foreign folk, but thou Shamest a city that deserves it not, Even thine own, and plentitude of years Have made of thee an old man and a fool. Therefore again I charge thee as before, See that the maidens are restored at once, Unless thou would’st continue here by force And not by choice a sojourner; so much I tell thee home and what I say, I mean.
cards.whyThisWorks: Theseus's speech builds a sustained argument that Creon violated the rule of law by seizing suppliants through force rather than legal process, giving students a clear central idea to distinguish from isolated details like the maidens' capture or Creon's age.
cards.skillStrategy: Ask yourself what the speaker is arguing throughout the whole passage, not just what happens in one moment or what topic comes up.
evidencePoints: Thou hast set aside the custom of the land, And like some freebooter art carrying off What plunder pleases thee
But now the laws to which himself appealed, These and none others shall adjudicate.
cards.question: Which statement best expresses the central idea of Theseus's speech to Creon?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Creon has dishonored Thebes by traveling to a foreign land and interfering in its religious ceremonies.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Creon acted as a lawless aggressor by seizing the maidens through force rather than through the legal process that any just state demands.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Theseus is angry that Creon has made him look weak in front of his own people by taking the maidens without warning.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Old age has made Creon foolish, and he can no longer be trusted to govern or make sound decisions for his city.

cards.standardTitle: Rhetoric and reader effect
cards.excerpt:
ISMENE. Bethink thee, sister, of our father’s fate, Abhorred, dishonored, self-convinced of sin, Blinded, himself his executioner. Think of his mother-wife (ill sorted names) Done by a noose herself had twined to death And last, our hapless brethren in one day, Both in a mutual destiny involved, Self-slaughtered, both the slayer and the slain. Bethink thee, sister, we are left alone; Shall we not perish wretchedest of all, If in defiance of the law we cross A monarch’s will?—weak women, think of that, Not framed by nature to contend with men. Remember this too that the stronger rules; We must obey his orders, these or worse. Therefore I plead compulsion and entreat The dead to pardon. I perforce obey The powers that be. ’Tis foolishness, I ween, To overstep in aught the golden mean.

ANTIGONE. I urge no more; nay, wert thou willing still, I would not welcome such a fellowship. Go thine own way; myself will bury him. How sweet to die in such employ, to rest,— Sister and brother linked in love’s embrace— A sinless sinner, banned awhile on earth, But by the dead commended; and with them I shall abide for ever. As for thee, Scorn, if thou wilt, the eternal laws of Heaven.
cards.whyThisWorks: Antigone's oxymoron 'A sinless sinner' and her contrast between earthly banishment and eternal commendation by the dead illustrate how figurative and contrasting language shapes the reader's perception of her moral courage versus Ismene's fearful compliance.
cards.skillStrategy: When you spot a contradiction packed into a single phrase or a sharp contrast between two ideas, ask yourself what feeling or belief the author wants you to walk away with.
evidencePoints: A sinless sinner, banned awhile on earth, But by the dead commended
Scorn, if thou wilt, the eternal laws of Heaven.
cards.question: Read Antigone's lines: 'A sinless sinner, banned awhile on earth, / But by the dead commended.' How does this oxymoron affect the reader's understanding of Antigone's position?

choices.label: A
choices.text: It shows that Antigone admits she has broken the law and accepts that she deserves punishment from Creon.

choices.label: B
choices.text: It frames Antigone's defiance as morally righteous by placing divine approval above earthly condemnation, making her sacrifice appear noble rather than reckless.

choices.label: C
choices.text: It reveals that Antigone is confused about whether her action is right or wrong, mirroring Ismene's own uncertainty about defying Creon.

choices.label: D
choices.text: It suggests that Antigone believes the dead will literally rise to defend her against Creon's punishment.

cards.standardTitle: Key literary elements add layers of meaning
cards.excerpt: ISMENE. The toil and trouble, father, that I bore To find thy lodging-place and how thou faredst, I spare thee; surely ’twere a double pain To suffer, first in act and then in telling; ’Tis the misfortune of thine ill-starred sons I come to tell thee. At the first they willed To leave the throne to Creon, minded well Thus to remove the inveterate curse of old, A canker that infected all thy race. But now some god and an infatuate soul Have stirred betwixt them a mad rivalry To grasp at sovereignty and kingly power. Today the hot-branded youth, the younger born, Is keeping Polyneices from the throne, His elder, and has thrust him from the land. The banished brother (so all Thebes reports) Fled to the vale of Argos, and by help Of new alliance there and friends in arms, Swears he will stablish Argos straight as lord Of the Cadmeian land, or, if he fail, Exalt the victor to the stars of heaven. This is no empty tale, but deadly truth, My father; and how long thy agony, Ere the gods pity thee, I cannot tell.
cards.whyThisWorks: Ismene's report of the brothers' failed plan to end the curse by yielding to Creon, immediately undone by 'some god and an infatuate soul,' dramatizes how the inherited curse overrides human agency, deepening the play's central conflict and adding meaning to Oedipus's ongoing suffering.
cards.skillStrategy: When a character's deliberate plan collapses into chaos, ask what that reversal reveals about the larger forces—fate, curse, or divine will—controlling the story's conflict.
evidencePoints: they willed To leave the throne to Creon, minded well Thus to remove the inveterate curse of old
some god and an infatuate soul Have stirred betwixt them a mad rivalry To grasp at sovereignty and kingly power
cards.question: Ismene tells Oedipus that his sons first 'willed to leave the throne to Creon…to remove the inveterate curse of old,' but then 'some god and an infatuate soul have stirred betwixt them a mad rivalry.' What meaning does this reversal—from a reasoned plan to divinely driven rivalry—add to the conflict Ismene describes?

choices.label: A
choices.text: It reveals that Creon secretly engineered the brothers' rivalry after receiving the throne, making him the true source of the 'inveterate curse' that has infected Oedipus's race.

choices.label: B
choices.text: It suggests the family curse cannot be escaped through deliberate choice alone, because even a reasoned plan to remove it is overturned by divine and infatuate force, leaving Oedipus's agony without a foreseeable end.

choices.label: C
choices.text: It establishes Polyneices as the more honorable brother because he honored the original agreement to yield power before Eteocles 'thrust him from the land' and drove him into exile in Argos.

choices.label: D
choices.text: It shows that Ismene holds both brothers entirely blameless, attributing the conflict solely to the gods and presenting their desire for 'sovereignty and kingly power' as something forced upon them against their will.

cards.standardTitle: Theme development across a literary text
cards.excerpt: Antigone, daughter of Oedipus, the late king of Thebes, in defiance of Creon who rules in his stead, resolves to bury her brother Polyneices, slain in his attack on Thebes. She is caught in the act by Creon’s watchmen and brought before the king. She justifies her action, asserting that she was bound to obey the eternal laws of right and wrong in spite of any human ordinance. Creon, unrelenting, condemns her to be immured in a rock-hewn chamber. His son Haemon, to whom Antigone is betrothed, pleads in vain for her life and threatens to die with her. Warned by the seer Teiresias Creon repents him and hurries to release Antigone from her rocky prison. But he is too late: he finds lying side by side Antigone who had hanged herself and Haemon who also has perished by his own hand. Returning to the palace he sees within the dead body of his queen who on learning of her son’s death has stabbed herself to the heart.
cards.whyThisWorks: The excerpt pairs Antigone's declaration that she obeyed 'eternal laws of right and wrong in spite of any human ordinance' with Creon's too-late repentance, showing how two contrasting moments together build the theme that defying moral law in favor of human authority produces irreversible tragedy.
cards.skillStrategy: To find theme developed through moments, identify what each key moment reveals about a character's choice or belief, then ask what idea both moments together prove about life.
evidencePoints: asserting that she was bound to obey the eternal laws of right and wrong in spite of any human ordinance
hurries to release Antigone from her rocky prison. But he is too late
cards.question: Antigone declares she was 'bound to obey the eternal laws of right and wrong in spite of any human ordinance,' yet Creon condemns her anyway; later, Creon 'hurries to release Antigone from her rocky prison. But he is too late.' How do these two moments work together to develop a theme?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Both moments highlight Antigone's willingness to die for her brother Polyneices, developing the theme that family loyalty is the highest form of devotion.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Both moments show that when Creon's human authority overrides Antigone's 'eternal laws of right and wrong,' the resulting deaths of Antigone, Haemon, and the queen cannot be undone, developing the theme that defying moral law leads to irreversible loss.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The first moment shows Antigone's defiance of Creon's rule, and the second shows Creon's change of heart, together developing the theme that rulers who listen to warnings will ultimately save those they have wronged.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Both moments focus on Creon's decisions as king, developing the theme that a ruler's inconsistency—first condemning Antigone, then rushing to free her—is the true cause of suffering in Thebes.

cards.standardTitle: Text structure and feature purpose
cards.excerpt:
CHORUS. (Str. 1) Like to thee that maiden bright, Danae, in her brass-bound tower, Once exchanged the glad sunlight For a cell, her bridal bower. And yet she sprang of royal line, My child, like thine, And nursed the seed By her conceived Of Zeus descending in a golden shower. Strange are the ways of Fate, her power Nor wealth, nor arms withstand, nor tower; Nor brass-prowed ships, that breast the sea From Fate can flee.

(Ant. 1) Thus Dryas’ child, the rash Edonian King, For words of high disdain Did Bacchus to a rocky dungeon bring, To cool the madness of a fevered brain. His frenzy passed, He learnt at last ’Twas madness gibes against a god to fling. For once he fain had quenched the Maenad’s fire; And of the tuneful Nine provoked the ire.

(Str. 2) By the Iron Rocks that guard the double main, On Bosporus’ lone strand, Where stretcheth Salmydessus’ plain In the wild Thracian land, There on his borders Ares witnessed The vengeance by a jealous step-dame ta’en The gore that trickled from a spindle red, The sightless orbits of her step-sons twain.

(Ant. 2) Wasting away they mourned their piteous doom, The blasted issue of their mother’s womb. But she her lineage could trace To great Erecththeus’ race; Daughter of Boreas in her sire’s vast caves Reared, where the tempest raves, Swift as his horses o’er the hills she sped; A child of gods; yet she, my child, like thee, By Destiny That knows not death nor age—she too was vanquished. [Enter TEIRESIAS and BOY]

TEIRESIAS. Princes of Thebes, two wayfarers as one, Having betwixt us eyes for one, we are here. The blind man cannot move without a guide.
cards.whyThisWorks: The final stanza (Ant. 2) concludes the Chorus's series of mythological examples by returning directly to Antigone's situation, making its paragraph job—to conclude and apply the pattern of Fate's inescapable power—clearly identifiable through the phrase 'yet she, my child, like thee, / By Destiny…she too was vanquished.'
cards.skillStrategy: Ask yourself: does this paragraph start something new, add another example, or wrap up and connect back to the main idea? Look for signal words and direct references to the central subject.
evidencePoints: yet she, my child, like thee, / By Destiny / That knows not death nor age—she too was vanquished.
Strange are the ways of Fate, her power / Nor wealth, nor arms withstand, nor tower
cards.question: What is the primary job of the final stanza (Ant. 2), beginning 'Wasting away they mourned their piteous doom'?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The stanza introduces a new argument that noble birth protects certain figures from the cruelty of Fate.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The stanza concludes the Chorus's series of mythological examples by applying their shared lesson—that Destiny defeats even those of divine lineage—directly to Antigone's fate.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The stanza contrasts the suffering of the step-sons with Antigone's suffering to suggest that her punishment is less severe than theirs.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The stanza shifts the Chorus's focus away from Fate toward praising the heroic ancestry of Boreas's daughter as a model Antigone should follow.

cards.standardTitle: Central idea and supporting evidence
cards.excerpt:
CHORUS. (Str. 1) O when the flying foe, Turning at last to bay, Soon will give blow for blow, Might I behold the fray; Hear the loud battle roar Swell, on the Pythian shore, Or by the torch-lit bay, Where the dread Queen and Maid Cherish the mystic rites, Rites they to none betray, Ere on his lips is laid Secrecy’s golden key By their own acolytes, Priestly Eumolpidae.

There I might chance behold Theseus our captain bold Meet with the robber band, Ere they have fled the land, Rescue by might and main Maidens, the captives twain.

(Ant. 1) Haply on swiftest steed, Or in the flying car, Now they approach the glen, West of white Oea’s scaur. They will be vanquished: Dread are our warriors, dread Theseus our chieftain’s men. Flashes each bridle bright, Charges each gallant knight, All that our Queen adore, Pallas their patron, or Him whose wide floods enring Earth, the great Ocean-king Whom Rhea bore.

(Str. 2) Fight they or now prepare To fight? a vision rare Tells me that soon again I shall behold the twain Maidens so ill bestead, By their kin buffeted. Today, today Zeus worketh some great thing This day shall victory bring. O for the wings, the wings of a dove, To be borne with the speed of the gale, Up and still upwards to sail And gaze on the fray from the clouds above. (Ant. 2) All-seeing Zeus, O lord of heaven, To our guardian host be given Might triumphant to surprise Flying foes and win their prize. Hear us, Zeus, and hear us, child Of Zeus, Athene undefiled, Hear, Apollo, hunter, hear, Huntress, sister of Apollo, Who the dappled swift-foot deer O’er the wooded glade dost follow; Help with your two-fold power Athens in danger’s hour! O wayfarer, thou wilt not have to tax The friends who watch for thee with false presage, For lo, an escort with the maids draws near. [Enter ANTIGONE and ISMENE with THESEUS]

OEDIPUS. Where, where? what sayest thou?
cards.whyThisWorks: The Chorus's escalating prayers to Zeus, Athene, and Apollo culminating in the stage direction '[Enter ANTIGONE and ISMENE with THESEUS]' give students a clear structural moment to identify how the central idea—that divine-aided human action rescues the vulnerable—is built and confirmed across the ode.
cards.skillStrategy: To find the central idea, track what the Chorus repeatedly asks for and then check whether the passage's ending moment answers or denies that request.
evidencePoints: Today, today Zeus worketh some great thing / This day shall victory bring
[Enter ANTIGONE and ISMENE with THESEUS]
cards.question: The Chorus declares 'Today, today Zeus worketh some great thing / This day shall victory bring' and then calls on Zeus, Athene, and Apollo to 'Help with your two-fold power / Athens in danger's hour.' The ode ends with the stage direction '[Enter ANTIGONE and ISMENE with THESEUS].' Which central idea do the Chorus's prayers and this entrance together express?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The Chorus's repeated references to sacred sites—the Pythian shore, the torch-lit bay, and white Oea's scaur—show that Athens's holy geography, not divine intervention, is the true source of the city's power.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The Chorus's urgent prayers to Zeus, Athene, and Apollo for the defeat of the enemy and the rescue of the captive maidens are answered when Theseus enters with Antigone and Ismene, confirming that divine-aided human action protects the vulnerable.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The Chorus praises Theseus's personal courage—charging on horseback near white Oea's scaur with 'each gallant knight'—making the invocations of Zeus and Athene ceremonial gestures rather than the true cause of victory.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Oedipus's closing cry 'Where, where? what sayest thou?' shifts the passage's focus away from the Chorus's prayers, making his private anguish over his daughters' captivity the dominant and unresolved concern.

cards.standardTitle: Rhetoric and reader effect
cards.excerpt: GUARD. I cannot tell, for there was ne’er a trace Of pick or mattock—hard unbroken ground, Without a scratch or rut of chariot wheels, No sign that human hands had been at work. When the first sentry of the morning watch Gave the alarm, we all were terror-stricken. The corpse had vanished, not interred in earth, But strewn with dust, as if by one who sought To avert the curse that haunts the unburied dead: Of hound or ravening jackal, not a sign. Thereat arose an angry war of words; Guard railed at guard and blows were like to end it, For none was there to part us, each in turn Suspected, but the guilt brought home to none, From lack of evidence. We challenged each The ordeal, or to handle red-hot iron, Or pass through fire, affirming on our oath Our innocence—we neither did the deed Ourselves, nor know who did or compassed it. Our quest was at a standstill, when one spake And bowed us all to earth like quivering reeds, For there was no gainsaying him nor way To escape perdition: _Ye_are_bound_to_tell_ _The_King,_ye_cannot_hide_it; so he spake. And he convinced us all; so lots were cast, And I, unlucky scapegoat, drew the prize. So here I am unwilling and withal Unwelcome; no man cares to hear ill news.
cards.whyThisWorks: The simile 'bowed us all to earth like quivering reeds' captures the guards' collective collapse under the weight of an inescapable command, giving students a concrete rhetorical device to analyze for its emotional and persuasive effect on the reader.
cards.skillStrategy: When analyzing a simile, ask what the comparison reveals about a character's emotional state and how that feeling is transferred to the reader.
evidencePoints: bowed us all to earth like quivering reeds
there was no gainsaying him nor way / To escape perdition
cards.question: In the lines 'one spake / And bowed us all to earth like quivering reeds, / For there was no gainsaying him nor way / To escape perdition,' what effect does the simile 'like quivering reeds' have on the reader's understanding of the guards' situation?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The simile suggests the guards are physically worn down from standing watch all night, making the reader sympathize with the exhausting demands of their duty.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The simile conveys that the guards were instantly and completely overwhelmed by the speaker's words, making the reader feel the full weight of their helplessness and dread at facing the king.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The simile shows that the guards respect the speaker's authority and willingly submit to his command, suggesting there is no real conflict among them about reporting to the king.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The simile emphasizes that the guards are naturally timid and therefore unreliable, causing the reader to doubt the accuracy of the guard's account of the unburied corpse.

cards.standardTitle: Key literary elements add layers of meaning
cards.excerpt:
CHORUS. (Str. 1) Sunbeam, of all that ever dawn upon Our seven-gated Thebes the brightest ray, O eye of golden day, How fair thy light o’er Dirce’s fountain shone, Speeding upon their headlong homeward course, Far quicker than they came, the Argive force; Putting to flight The argent shields, the host with scutcheons white. Against our land the proud invader came To vindicate fell Polyneices’ claim. Like to an eagle swooping low, On pinions white as new fall’n snow. With clanging scream, a horsetail plume his crest, The aspiring lord of Argos onward pressed.

(Ant. 1) Hovering around our city walls he waits, His spearmen raven at our seven gates. But ere a torch our crown of towers could burn, Ere they had tasted of our blood, they turn Forced by the Dragon; in their rear The din of Ares panic-struck they hear. For Zeus who hates the braggart’s boast Beheld that gold-bespangled host; As at the goal the paean they upraise, He struck them with his forked lightning blaze.

(Str. 2) To earthy from earth rebounding, down he crashed; The fire-brand from his impious hand was dashed, As like a Bacchic reveler on he came, Outbreathing hate and flame, And tottered. Elsewhere in the field, Here, there, great Area like a war-horse wheeled; Beneath his car down thrust Our foemen bit the dust.

Seven captains at our seven gates Thundered; for each a champion waits, Each left behind his armor bright, Trophy for Zeus who turns the fight; Save two alone, that ill-starred pair One mother to one father bare, Who lance in rest, one ’gainst the other Drave, and both perished, brother slain by brother.
cards.whyThisWorks: The mutual death of Eteocles and Polyneices—'brother slain by brother'—functions as a consequence of civil conflict that deepens the meaning of the ode by showing that the war's true destruction falls not on foreign enemies but within Thebes's own royal family, setting the tragic stakes for Antigone.
cards.skillStrategy: When a conflict ends in a consequence, ask what that outcome reveals about a larger truth the author wants you to understand beyond the surface event.
evidencePoints: Who lance in rest, one 'gainst the other Drave, and both perished, brother slain by brother.
Seven captains at our seven gates Thundered; for each a champion waits, Each left behind his armor bright, Trophy for Zeus who turns the fight
cards.question: The Chorus describes how Thebes repelled the Argive army and Zeus struck down the invaders, yet the ode ends with the detail that two brothers 'both perished, brother slain by brother.' What deeper meaning does this consequence add to the ode's account of Thebes's victory?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The brothers' deaths prove that Zeus punishes all warriors equally, whether foreign or Theban, making the victory feel divinely ordained and complete.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The brothers' mutual destruction reveals that the war's gravest wound is not the foreign invasion but the self-inflicted ruin within Thebes's own ruling family, undercutting the triumph the Chorus has been celebrating.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The detail that both brothers died fighting each other shows that the Argive army was ultimately more powerful than the Chorus admits, since Theban leaders fell alongside the enemy.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The brothers' deaths at the seven gates demonstrate that every captain on both sides was killed, suggesting the battle was evenly matched despite Thebes's eventual survival.

cards.standardTitle: Theme development across a literary text
cards.excerpt: OEDIPUS. Dear son of Aegeus, to the gods alone Is given immunity from eld and death; But nothing else escapes all-ruinous time. Earth’s might decays, the might of men decays, Honor grows cold, dishonor flourishes, There is no constancy ’twixt friend and friend, Or city and city; be it soon or late, Sweet turns to bitter, hate once more to love. If now ’tis sunshine betwixt Thebes and thee And not a cloud, Time in his endless course Gives birth to endless days and nights, wherein The merest nothing shall suffice to cut With serried spears your bonds of amity. Then shall my slumbering and buried corpse In its cold grave drink their warm life-blood up, If Zeus be Zeus and Phoebus still speak true. No more: ’tis ill to tear aside the veil Of mysteries; let me cease as I began: Enough if thou wilt keep thy plighted troth, Then shall thou ne’er complain that Oedipus Proved an unprofitable and thankless guest, Except the gods themselves shall play me false.
cards.whyThisWorks: Oedipus develops the theme that time destroys all earthly bonds and power through two distinct moments: his abstract declaration that 'Earth's might decays, the might of men decays' and his concrete prophecy that future days will 'cut with serried spears your bonds of amity,' requiring students to track how both moments build the same theme rather than treating either alone as the full message.
cards.skillStrategy: Find two separate moments in the passage that point to the same big idea, then ask yourself what message both moments share together.
evidencePoints: Earth's might decays, the might of men decays, Honor grows cold, dishonor flourishes
Time in his endless course Gives birth to endless days and nights, wherein The merest nothing shall suffice to cut With serried spears your bonds of amity
cards.question: Read the two moments from Oedipus's speech: 'Earth's might decays, the might of men decays, Honor grows cold, dishonor flourishes' and 'Time in his endless course Gives birth to endless days and nights, wherein The merest nothing shall suffice to cut With serried spears your bonds of amity.' How do these two moments work together to develop a theme?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The first moment warns that individual men lose honor, while the second moment shows that only political alliances between cities are permanent, suggesting that personal virtue outlasts political bonds.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The first moment establishes that time erodes all earthly power and virtue, and the second moment extends that idea to show that even the current friendship between Thebes and Athens will eventually be destroyed by time's passage, together building the theme that nothing human endures.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The first moment reveals that Oedipus is bitter about his own suffering, and the second moment reveals that he wants revenge on Thebes, together showing that personal grievance drives his prophecy more than any universal truth about time.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The first moment describes the decay of the natural world, while the second moment promises that Oedipus's buried corpse will restore what time has destroyed, together suggesting that death can reverse the damage caused by time.

cards.standardTitle: Text structure and feature purpose
cards.excerpt:
CHORUS. Why, Oedipus, why stung with passionate grief Hath the queen thus departed? Much I fear From this dead calm will burst a storm of woes.

OEDIPUS. Let the storm burst, my fixed resolve still holds, To learn my lineage, be it ne’er so low. It may be she with all a woman’s pride Thinks scorn of my base parentage. But I Who rank myself as Fortune’s favorite child, The giver of good gifts, shall not be shamed. She is my mother and the changing moons My brethren, and with them I wax and wane. Thus sprung why should I fear to trace my birth? Nothing can make me other than I am.

CHORUS. (Str.) If my soul prophetic err not, if my wisdom aught avail, Thee, Cithaeron, I shall hail, As the nurse and foster-mother of our Oedipus shall greet Ere tomorrow’s full moon rises, and exalt thee as is meet. Dance and song shall hymn thy praises, lover of our royal race. Phoebus, may my words find grace!

(Ant.) Child, who bare thee, nymph or goddess? sure thy sure was more than man, Haply the hill-roamer Pan.
