Of did Loxias beget thee, for he haunts the upland wold; Or Cyllene’s lord, or Bacchus, dweller on the hilltops cold? Did some Heliconian Oread give him thee, a new-born joy? Nymphs with whom he love to toy?

OEDIPUS. Elders, if I, who never yet before Have met the man, may make a guess, methinks I see the herdsman who we long have sought; His time-worn aspect matches with the years Of yonder aged messenger; besides I seem to recognize the men who bring him As servants of my own. But you, perchance, Having in past days known or seen the herd, May better by sure knowledge my surmise.
cards.whyThisWorks: Oedipus's final speech functions as a transitional paragraph that shifts from his defiant self-declaration to a practical, investigative focus on identifying the herdsman, giving students a clear structural pivot to analyze.
cards.skillStrategy: Ask yourself: does this paragraph continue the same idea, or does it change direction—and what signal words or content show that shift?
evidencePoints: Elders, if I, who never yet before Have met the man, may make a guess, methinks I see the herdsman who we long have sought
But you, perchance, Having in past days known or seen the herd, May better by sure knowledge my surmise.
cards.question: In the final paragraph, Oedipus shifts away from the Chorus's speculation about his divine origins. What is the primary job of this paragraph in the passage?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Oedipus continues defending his claim that Fortune is his true mother by pointing to the herdsman as proof of his noble birth.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Oedipus moves the action forward by redirecting attention from mythic speculation to the concrete task of identifying the herdsman who holds the truth about his origins.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Oedipus concludes the scene by accepting the Chorus's suggestion that a god or nymph was his true parent.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Oedipus contrasts his own certainty about his identity with the Elders' ignorance, proving that he alone can solve the mystery.

cards.standardTitle: Central idea and supporting evidence
cards.excerpt:
THESEUS. I know that none Shall hale thee hence in my despite. Such threats Vented in anger oft, are blusterers, An idle breath, forgot when sense returns. And for thy foemen, though their words were brave, Boasting to bring thee back, they are like to find The seas between us wide and hard to sail. Such my firm purpose, but in any case Take heart, since Phoebus sent thee here. My name, Though I be distant, warrants thee from harm.

CHORUS. (Str. 1) Thou hast come to a steed-famed land for rest, O stranger worn with toil, To a land of all lands the goodliest Colonus’ glistening soil. ’Tis the haunt of the clear-voiced nightingale, Who hid in her bower, among The wine-dark ivy that wreathes the vale, Trilleth her ceaseless song; And she loves, where the clustering berries nod O’er a sunless, windless glade, The spot by no mortal footstep trod, The pleasance kept for the Bacchic god, Where he holds each night his revels wild With the nymphs who fostered the lusty child.
cards.whyThisWorks: The two passages present distinct but complementary central ideas—Theseus's pledge of protection and the Chorus's celebration of Colonus as a sacred refuge—requiring students to synthesize rather than simply identify a topic or isolated detail.
cards.skillStrategy: Ask yourself what the passage as a whole is saying, not just what one character mentions or what one image describes.
evidencePoints: My name, Though I be distant, warrants thee from harm.
Thou hast come to a steed-famed land for rest, O stranger worn with toil, To a land of all lands the goodliest
cards.question: Both Theseus's speech and the Chorus's ode work together to develop which central idea?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Colonus is a dangerous place where enemies will pursue the stranger despite Theseus's warnings.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The weary stranger has arrived in a place where both human authority and sacred nature offer him safety and welcome.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Phoebus alone is responsible for guiding the stranger to Colonus, making Theseus's protection unnecessary.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The beauty of Colonus, with its nightingales and ivy, is more important than any promise a mortal king can make.

cards.standardTitle: Rhetoric and reader effect
cards.excerpt: CREON. O cease, you vex me with your babblement; I am like to think you dote in your old age. Is it not arrant folly to pretend That gods would have a thought for this dead man? Did they forsooth award him special grace, And as some benefactor bury him, Who came to fire their hallowed sanctuaries, To sack their shrines, to desolate their land, And scout their ordinances? Or perchance The gods bestow their favors on the bad. No! no! I have long noted malcontents Who wagged their heads, and kicked against the yoke, Misliking these my orders, and my rule. ’Tis they, I warrant, who suborned my guards By bribes. Of evils current upon earth The worst is money. Money ’tis that sacks Cities, and drives men forth from hearth and home; Warps and seduces native innocence, And breeds a habit of dishonesty. But they who sold themselves shall find their greed Out-shot the mark, and rue it soon or late. Yea, as I still revere the dread of Zeus, By Zeus I swear, except ye find and bring Before my presence here the very man Who carried out this lawless burial, Death for your punishment shall not suffice. Hanged on a cross, alive ye first shall make Confession of this outrage. This will teach you What practices are like to serve your turn. There are some villainies that bring no gain. For by dishonesty the few may thrive, The many come to ruin and disgrace.
cards.whyThisWorks: Creon's speech contains a striking anaphora and accumulation around money — 'Money 'tis that sacks / Cities, and drives men forth from hearth and home; / Warps and seduces native innocence, / And breeds a habit of dishonesty' — which allows students to analyze how repetition and figurative language build Creon's self-justifying rage and reveal his character.
cards.skillStrategy: When you spot repeated sentence structures or a word hammered again and again, ask yourself: what feeling or idea is the speaker forcing the reader to accept, and why does that repetition matter here?
evidencePoints: Money 'tis that sacks Cities, and drives men forth from hearth and home; Warps and seduces native innocence, And breeds a habit of dishonesty.
No! no! I have long noted malcontents / Who wagged their heads, and kicked against the yoke
cards.question: Read the following lines from Creon's speech: 'Money 'tis that sacks / Cities, and drives men forth from hearth and home; / Warps and seduces native innocence, / And breeds a habit of dishonesty.' How does the repetition of money's destructive actions affect the reader's understanding of Creon?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The accumulation of money's crimes makes Creon appear sympathetic, since the reader sees he is a victim of the same corruption he condemns in his guards.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The relentless piling of offenses — sacking cities, driving out families, warping innocence, breeding dishonesty — reveals that Creon is deflecting blame onto greed rather than examining his own harsh authority.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The repeated actions attributed to money show that Creon is primarily concerned with protecting the city's economy from outside threats rather than punishing the burial.

choices.label: D
choices.text: By cataloguing money's evils, Creon persuades the reader that his guards are certainly guilty, making his threat of crucifixion feel justified and proportionate.

cards.standardTitle: Key literary elements add layers of meaning
cards.excerpt:
By Nysa’s bastion ivy-clad, By shores with clustered vineyards glad, There to thee the hymn rings out, And through our streets we Thebans shout, All hall to thee Evoe, Evoe!

(Str. 2) Oh, as thou lov’st this city best of all, To thee, and to thy Mother levin-stricken, In our dire need we call; Thou see’st with what a plague our townsfolk sicken. Thy ready help we crave, Whether adown Parnassian heights descending, Or o’er the roaring straits thy swift was wending, Save us, O save!

(Ant. 2) Brightest of all the orbs that breathe forth light, Authentic son of Zeus, immortal king, Leader of all the voices of the night, Come, and thy train of Thyiads with thee bring, Thy maddened rout Who dance before thee all night long, and shout, Thy handmaids we, Evoe, Evoe!

[Enter MESSENGER]

MESSENGER. Attend all ye who dwell beside the halls Of Cadmus and Amphion. No man’s life As of one tenor would I praise or blame, For Fortune with a constant ebb and rise Casts down and raises high and low alike, And none can read a mortal’s horoscope. Take Creon; he, methought, if any man, Was enviable. He had saved this land Of Cadmus from our enemies and attained A monarch’s powers and ruled the state supreme, While a right noble issue crowned his bliss. Now all is gone and wasted, for a life Without life’s joys I count a living death. You’ll tell me he has ample store of wealth, The pomp and circumstance of kings; but if These give no pleasure, all the rest I count The shadow of a shade, nor would I weigh His wealth and power ’gainst a dram of joy.
cards.whyThisWorks: The Messenger's account of Creon's reversal—from a man who 'saved this land' and 'ruled the state supreme' to one whose 'all is gone and wasted'—directly illustrates how a consequence adds a deeper layer of meaning about the relationship between power and genuine happiness.
cards.skillStrategy: When a character's situation dramatically reverses, ask what the reversal reveals about a larger truth the author wants readers to understand beyond the plot event itself.
evidencePoints: He had saved this land Of Cadmus from our enemies and attained A monarch's powers and ruled the state supreme
Now all is gone and wasted, for a life Without life's joys I count a living death
cards.question: The Messenger describes Creon as once 'enviable' because he 'saved this land' and 'ruled the state supreme,' then declares 'Now all is gone and wasted.' What deeper meaning does this reversal add to the play?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Creon's fall proves that rulers who gain power through military victory will always lose it to a stronger enemy in the end.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Creon's collapse from supreme power to ruin suggests that political authority and wealth are hollow without joy, making his earlier choices the true source of his destruction.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The Messenger's speech shows that Fortune randomly destroys good and bad rulers alike, so Creon's suffering carries no special moral significance.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Creon's downfall reveals that the citizens of Thebes were never truly loyal to him, since the Messenger speaks of his ruin without expressing grief.

cards.standardTitle: Key literary elements add layers of meaning
cards.excerpt:
CHORUS. (Str. 1) Like to thee that maiden bright, Danae, in her brass-bound tower, Once exchanged the glad sunlight For a cell, her bridal bower. And yet she sprang of royal line, My child, like thine, And nursed the seed By her conceived Of Zeus descending in a golden shower. Strange are the ways of Fate, her power Nor wealth, nor arms withstand, nor tower; Nor brass-prowed ships, that breast the sea From Fate can flee.

(Ant. 1) Thus Dryas’ child, the rash Edonian King, For words of high disdain Did Bacchus to a rocky dungeon bring, To cool the madness of a fevered brain. His frenzy passed, He learnt at last ’Twas madness gibes against a god to fling. For once he fain had quenched the Maenad’s fire; And of the tuneful Nine provoked the ire.

(Str. 2) By the Iron Rocks that guard the double main, On Bosporus’ lone strand, Where stretcheth Salmydessus’ plain In the wild Thracian land, There on his borders Ares witnessed The vengeance by a jealous step-dame ta’en The gore that trickled from a spindle red, The sightless orbits of her step-sons twain.

(Ant. 2) Wasting away they mourned their piteous doom, The blasted issue of their mother’s womb. But she her lineage could trace To great Erecththeus’ race; Daughter of Boreas in her sire’s vast caves Reared, where the tempest raves, Swift as his horses o’er the hills she sped; A child of gods; yet she, my child, like thee, By Destiny That knows not death nor age—she too was vanquished. [Enter TEIRESIAS and BOY]

TEIRESIAS. Princes of Thebes, two wayfarers as one, Having betwixt us eyes for one, we are here. The blind man cannot move without a guide.
cards.whyThisWorks: The Chorus's catalog of mythological figures—Danae, Lycurgus, and the blinded stepsons—each imprisoned or destroyed by Fate, functions as a structural parallel that deepens the meaning of Antigone's conflict by showing her suffering as part of an inescapable, universal pattern rather than a personal injustice.
cards.skillStrategy: When a chorus or narrator references other characters' fates alongside the protagonist's, ask what pattern those examples create and what that pattern reveals about the central conflict's deeper meaning.
evidencePoints: Strange are the ways of Fate, her power / Nor wealth, nor arms withstand, nor tower
yet she, my child, like thee, / By Destiny / That knows not death nor age—she too was vanquished
cards.question: The Chorus describes Danae imprisoned in a brass-bound tower, Lycurgus punished in a rocky dungeon, and a princess of divine lineage ultimately 'vanquished' by Destiny. What deeper meaning does this pattern of events add to Antigone's conflict?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The examples show that only those of royal or divine birth suffer unjust punishment, suggesting Antigone's noble lineage is the true cause of her downfall.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The repeated fates of figures who were powerful, royal, or even god-born yet still destroyed by Destiny suggest that Antigone's conflict with Creon is not merely a political struggle but a collision with an inescapable force that no human authority can override.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The Chorus presents these figures to warn Creon that the gods will punish him specifically for imprisoning Antigone, just as Bacchus punished Lycurgus for his rash words.

choices.label: D
choices.text: By recalling Danae and the blinded stepsons, the Chorus implies that Antigone brought her suffering on herself through pride, mirroring Lycurgus whose 'frenzy' caused his own imprisonment.

cards.standardTitle: Key literary elements add layers of meaning
cards.excerpt:
ANTIGONE. (Ant. 1) Nay, but the piteous tale I’ve heard men tell Of Tantalus’ doomed child, Chained upon Siphylus’ high rocky fell, That clung like ivy wild, Drenched by the pelting rain and whirling snow, Left there to pine, While on her frozen breast the tears aye flow— Her fate is mine.

CHORUS. She was sprung of gods, divine, Mortals we of mortal line. Like renown with gods to gain Recompenses all thy pain. Take this solace to thy tomb Hers in life and death thy doom.

ANTIGONE. (Str. 2) Alack, alack! Ye mock me. Is it meet Thus to insult me living, to my face? Cease, by our country’s altars I entreat, Ye lordly rulers of a lordly race. O fount of Dirce, wood-embowered plain Where Theban chariots to victory speed, Mark ye the cruel laws that now have wrought my bane, The friends who show no pity in my need! Was ever fate like mine? O monstrous doom, Within a rock-built prison sepulchered, To fade and wither in a living tomb, And alien midst the living and the dead.

CHORUS. (Str. 3) In thy boldness over-rash Madly thou thy foot didst dash ’Gainst high Justice’ altar stair. Thou a father’s guild dost bear.

ANTIGONE. (Ant. 2) At this thou touchest my most poignant pain, My ill-starred father’s piteous disgrace, The taint of blood, the hereditary stain, That clings to all of Labdacus’ famed race. Woe worth the monstrous marriage-bed where lay A mother with the son her womb had borne, Therein I was conceived, woe worth the day, Fruit of incestuous sheets, a maid forlorn, And now I pass, accursed and unwed, To meet them as an alien there below; And thee, O brother, in marriage ill-bestead, ’Twas thy dead hand that dealt me this death-blow.
cards.whyThisWorks: Antigone's revelation that her brother's 'ill-bestead' marriage ultimately caused her death sentence shows how a prior family conflict becomes the consequence that seals her fate, adding the deeper meaning that inherited sin destroys the innocent.
cards.skillStrategy: When a character names a past event as the cause of their current suffering, ask what that connection reveals about the story's deeper message.
evidencePoints: And thee, O brother, in marriage ill-bestead, / 'Twas thy dead hand that dealt me this death-blow.
The taint of blood, the hereditary stain, / That clings to all of Labdacus' famed race.
cards.question: In her final speech, Antigone declares that her brother's 'ill-bestead' marriage dealt her 'this death-blow.' What deeper meaning does this moment add to the scene?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Antigone blames her brother personally for betraying her, suggesting that family loyalty is the play's central value.

choices.label: B
choices.text: By tracing her execution back through her brother's doomed marriage and her family's hereditary stain, Antigone reveals that the innocent suffer the consequences of sins they did not commit, making her death a punishment for her lineage rather than solely her own choice.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Antigone's reference to her brother shows she regrets burying him, implying that her act of defiance was a mistake she now wishes she could undo.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The Chorus's warning that Antigone bears 'a father's guilt' is confirmed when she admits her brother caused her death, showing that she accepts full responsibility for her own fate.

cards.standardTitle: Key literary elements add layers of meaning
cards.excerpt:
ANTIGONE. O grave, O bridal bower, O prison house Hewn from the rock, my everlasting home, Whither I go to join the mighty host Of kinsfolk, Persephassa’s guests long dead, The last of all, of all more miserable, I pass, my destined span of years cut short. And yet good hope is mine that I shall find A welcome from my sire, a welcome too, From thee, my mother, and my brother dear; From with these hands, I laved and decked your limbs In death, and poured libations on your grave. And last, my Polyneices, unto thee I paid due rites, and this my recompense! Yet am I justified in wisdom’s eyes. For even had it been some child of mine, Or husband mouldering in death’s decay, I had not wrought this deed despite the State. What is the law I call in aid? ’Tis thus I argue. Had it been a husband dead I might have wed another, and have borne Another child, to take the dead child’s place. But, now my sire and mother both are dead, No second brother can be born for me. Thus by the law of conscience I was led To honor thee, dear brother, and was judged By Creon guilty of a heinous crime. And now he drags me like a criminal, A bride unwed, amerced of marriage-song And marriage-bed and joys of motherhood, By friends deserted to a living grave. What ordinance of heaven have I transgressed? Hereafter can I look to any god For succor, call on any man for help? Alas, my piety is impious deemed. Well, if such justice is approved of heaven, I shall be taught by suffering my sin; But if the sin is theirs, O may they suffer No worse ills than the wrongs they do to me.

CHORUS. The same ungovernable will Drives like a gale the maiden still.

CREON. Therefore, my guards who let her stay Shall smart full sore for their delay.
cards.whyThisWorks: Antigone's reasoning that a brother is irreplaceable while a husband or child could be replaced is a pivotal decision that reveals the deeper conflict between personal loyalty and civic law, showing how a single choice carries layers of moral and political meaning.
cards.skillStrategy: When a character explains why they made a choice, ask what that reasoning reveals about the larger conflict or theme—not just what happened, but what it means.
evidencePoints: Had it been a husband dead I might have wed another, and have borne / Another child, to take the dead child's place.
Thus by the law of conscience I was led / To honor thee, dear brother, and was judged / By Creon guilty of a heinous crime.
cards.question: Antigone argues that a husband or child could be replaced, but a second brother could never be born to her. What does this reasoning add to the meaning of her conflict with Creon?

choices.label: A
choices.text: It shows that Antigone values her brother more than she values her own life, suggesting she has always been reckless with personal safety.

choices.label: B
choices.text: It reveals that Antigone's defiance of Creon's law is rooted in an irreplaceable bond that no civic authority can override, deepening the conflict between personal conscience and state power.

choices.label: C
choices.text: It demonstrates that Antigone regrets never marrying, and her grief over lost motherhood is the true source of her anger toward Creon.

choices.label: D
choices.text: It proves that Antigone believes Creon's law is unjust in all cases, not only in her brother's burial, and that she would defy any state decree.

cards.excerpt:
CHORUS. (Str. 1) Races of mortal man Whose life is but a span, I count ye but the shadow of a shade! For he who most doth know Of bliss, hath but the show; A moment, and the visions pale and fade. Thy fall, O Oedipus, thy piteous fall Warns me none born of women blest to call.

(Ant. 1) For he of marksmen best, O Zeus, outshot the rest, And won the prize supreme of wealth and power. By him the vulture maid Was quelled, her witchery laid; He rose our savior and the land’s strong tower. We hailed thee king and from that day adored Of mighty Thebes the universal lord.

(Str. 2) O heavy hand of fate! Who now more desolate, Whose tale more sad than thine, whose lot more dire? O Oedipus, discrowned head, Thy cradle was thy marriage bed; One harborage sufficed for son and sire. How could the soil thy father eared so long Endure to bear in silence such a wrong?

(Ant. 2) All-seeing Time hath caught Guilt, and to justice brought The son and sire commingled in one bed. O child of Laius’ ill-starred race Would I had ne’er beheld thy face; I raise for thee a dirge as o’er the dead. Yet, sooth to say, through thee I drew new breath, And now through thee I feel a second death. [Enter SECOND MESSENGER.]

SECOND MESSENGER. Most grave and reverend senators of Thebes, What Deeds ye soon must hear, what sights behold How will ye mourn, if, true-born patriots, Ye reverence still the race of Labdacus! Not Ister nor all Phasis’ flood, I ween, Could wash away the blood-stains from this house, The ills it shrouds or soon will bring to light, Ills wrought of malice, not unwittingly. The worst to bear are self-inflicted wounds.
cards.whyThisWorks: The Second Messenger's announcement that 'the worst to bear are self-inflicted wounds' arrives immediately after the Chorus mourns Oedipus's fall, creating a reversal that deepens the tragedy by shifting blame from fate to human agency.
cards.skillStrategy: When a character makes a statement or an event occurs at a turning point, ask yourself: what does this moment reveal about a larger truth the author wants readers to understand?
evidencePoints: The worst to bear are self-inflicted wounds.
Thy fall, O Oedipus, thy piteous fall / Warns me none born of women blest to call.
cards.question: The Chorus spends three stanzas attributing Oedipus's ruin to fate and 'All-seeing Time,' yet the Second Messenger closes the scene by declaring, 'The worst to bear are self-inflicted wounds.' What deeper meaning does this contrast add to the passage?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The contrast shows that the Second Messenger disagrees with the Chorus about whether Oedipus was ever a worthy king, suggesting his reign was fraudulent from the start.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The contrast reveals that suffering rooted in one's own choices carries a heavier burden than suffering imposed by outside forces, deepening the tragedy beyond simple misfortune.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The contrast demonstrates that the Chorus is unreliable because its praise of Oedipus as 'our savior and the land's strong tower' is immediately proven false by the Messenger's arrival.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The contrast emphasizes that Thebes will recover from Oedipus's fall because the Messenger's words reassure the senators that the bloodstains can eventually be washed away.

cards.standardTitle: Key literary elements add layers of meaning
cards.excerpt:
OEDIPUS. They knew it, yet the ignoble greed of rule Outweighed all longing for their sire’s return.

ISMENE. Grievous thy words, yet I must own them true.

OEDIPUS. Then may the gods ne’er quench their fatal feud, And mine be the arbitrament of the fight, For which they now are arming, spear to spear; That neither he who holds the scepter now May keep this throne, nor he who fled the realm Return again. _They_ never raised a hand, When I their sire was thrust from hearth and home, When I was banned and banished, what recked they? Say you ’twas done at my desire, a grace Which the state, yielding to my wish, allowed? Not so; for, mark you, on that very day When in the tempest of my soul I craved Death, even death by stoning, none appeared To further that wild longing, but anon, When time had numbed my anguish and I felt My wrath had all outrun those errors past, Then, then it was the city went about By force to oust me, respited for years; And then my sons, who should as sons have helped, Did nothing: and, one little word from them Was all I needed, and they spoke no word, But let me wander on for evermore, A banished man, a beggar. These two maids Their sisters, girls, gave all their sex could give, Food and safe harborage and filial care; While their two brethren sacrificed their sire For lust of power and sceptred sovereignty. No! me they ne’er shall win for an ally, Nor will this Theban kingship bring them gain; That know I from this maiden’s oracles, And those old prophecies concerning me, Which Phoebus now at length has brought to pass. Come Creon then, come all the mightiest In Thebes to seek me; for if ye my friends, Championed by those dread Powers indigenous, Espouse my cause; then for the State ye gain A great deliverer, for my foemen bane.
cards.whyThisWorks: Oedipus's curse on his sons—rooted in their silence during his banishment—reveals how a past conflict of abandonment directly shapes the present political struggle, adding the deeper meaning that power corrupts filial loyalty.
cards.skillStrategy: When a character makes a decision or curse based on a past conflict, ask what that moment reveals about a larger theme—here, what the sons' silence says about ambition versus duty.
evidencePoints: my sons, who should as sons have helped, Did nothing: and, one little word from them Was all I needed, and they spoke no word, But let me wander on for evermore, A banished man, a beggar.
Then may the gods ne'er quench their fatal feud, And mine be the arbitrament of the fight
cards.question: Oedipus reveals that his sons said nothing when he needed only 'one little word' to prevent his permanent exile, and he now curses them to destroy each other in battle. What deeper meaning does this conflict between Oedipus and his sons add to the passage?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The conflict shows that Oedipus is too consumed by self-pity to recognize that his sons were powerless to override the city's decision to banish him.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The sons' silence in the face of their father's suffering exposes how the desire for political power can hollow out even the most fundamental human obligations, making their coming destruction a consequence of their own moral failure.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The conflict between Oedipus and his sons demonstrates that prophecy, not personal choice, controls every character's fate, so the sons' silence was inevitable rather than a moral failing.

choices.label: D
choices.text: By contrasting the sons' inaction with the city's decision to banish Oedipus, the passage suggests that civic law is always a more powerful force than family loyalty.

cards.excerpt:
THESEUS. I know that none Shall hale thee hence in my despite. Such threats Vented in anger oft, are blusterers, An idle breath, forgot when sense returns. And for thy foemen, though their words were brave, Boasting to bring thee back, they are like to find The seas between us wide and hard to sail. Such my firm purpose, but in any case Take heart, since Phoebus sent thee here. My name, Though I be distant, warrants thee from harm.

CHORUS. (Str. 1) Thou hast come to a steed-famed land for rest, O stranger worn with toil, To a land of all lands the goodliest Colonus’ glistening soil. ’Tis the haunt of the clear-voiced nightingale, Who hid in her bower, among The wine-dark ivy that wreathes the vale, Trilleth her ceaseless song; And she loves, where the clustering berries nod O’er a sunless, windless glade, The spot by no mortal footstep trod, The pleasance kept for the Bacchic god, Where he holds each night his revels wild With the nymphs who fostered the lusty child.
cards.whyThisWorks: Theseus's decision to grant Oedipus protection despite threats from enemies creates a conflict between sanctuary and danger that deepens the theme of justice and refuge for the suffering outsider.
cards.skillStrategy: When a character makes a decision under pressure, ask what that choice reveals about the story's deeper meaning beyond the surface action.
evidencePoints: I know that none Shall hale thee hence in my despite.
Such my firm purpose, but in any case Take heart, since Phoebus sent thee here. My name, Though I be distant, warrants thee from harm.
cards.question: Theseus declares that no one shall remove Oedipus by force and that his name alone will protect the stranger even in his absence. How does this decision deepen the meaning of the conflict surrounding Oedipus?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Theseus's promise reveals that he underestimates the enemies who have threatened to bring Oedipus back, suggesting his confidence will lead to his own downfall.

choices.label: B
choices.text: By pledging protection to a hunted outcast on the grounds that a god directed him there, Theseus transforms Oedipus's conflict from a personal crisis into a question of whether divine will and human justice can shield the powerless from political force.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Theseus's declaration that the seas between Colonus and his enemies are wide and hard to sail shows that geography, not moral authority, is the true source of Oedipus's safety.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The Chorus's praise of Colonus as a sacred, untouched land directly causes Theseus to offer protection, meaning the setting resolves the conflict rather than the king's own judgment.

cards.standardTitle: Key literary elements add layers of meaning
cards.excerpt:
THESEUS. Oft had I heard of thee in times gone by— The bloody mutilation of thine eyes— And therefore know thee, son of Laius. All that I lately gathered on the way Made my conjecture doubly sure; and now Thy garb and that marred visage prove to me That thou art he. So pitying thine estate, Most ill-starred Oedipus, I fain would know What is the suit ye urge on me and Athens, Thou and the helpless maiden at thy side. Declare it; dire indeed must be the tale Whereat _I_ should recoil. I too was reared, Like thee, in exile, and in foreign lands Wrestled with many perils, no man more. Wherefore no alien in adversity Shall seek in vain my succor, nor shalt thou; I know myself a mortal, and my share In what the morrow brings no more than thine.

OEDIPUS. Theseus, thy words so apt, so generous So comfortable, need no long reply Both who I am and of what lineage sprung, And from what land I came, thou hast declared. So without prologue I may utter now My brief petition, and the tale is told.
cards.whyThisWorks: Theseus's revelation that he too was 'reared in exile' and 'wrestled with many perils' is a pivotal moment that transforms a simple request for help into a deeper conflict about shared human suffering and the moral obligation of the powerful to aid the vulnerable.
cards.skillStrategy: When a character makes a decision or reveals something unexpected, ask yourself: what does this moment say about a bigger idea in the story beyond just what is happening on the surface?
evidencePoints: I too was reared, Like thee, in exile, and in foreign lands Wrestled with many perils, no man more.
Wherefore no alien in adversity Shall seek in vain my succor, nor shalt thou; I know myself a mortal, and my share In what the morrow brings no more than thine.
cards.question: Theseus reveals that he was 'reared in exile' and 'wrestled with many perils' before pledging his aid to Oedipus. What deeper meaning does this disclosure add to the conflict between Oedipus's helplessness and Theseus's power?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Theseus's past suffering proves he is the most qualified ruler in Athens, which is why Oedipus trusts him immediately without offering a long explanation.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Theseus's shared experience of exile and hardship suggests that compassion and obligation to others arise not from rank or strength but from recognizing one's own vulnerability in another person's suffering.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Theseus's admission of past exile reveals that he and Oedipus are social equals, so Oedipus feels no need to explain his lineage or justify his petition to Athens.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Theseus's reference to his own perils signals that he doubts Oedipus's story and needs the details of Oedipus's suffering confirmed before he will offer any real protection.

cards.standardTitle: Key literary elements add layers of meaning
cards.excerpt: GUARD. I cannot tell, for there was ne’er a trace Of pick or mattock—hard unbroken ground, Without a scratch or rut of chariot wheels, No sign that human hands had been at work. When the first sentry of the morning watch Gave the alarm, we all were terror-stricken. The corpse had vanished, not interred in earth, But strewn with dust, as if by one who sought To avert the curse that haunts the unburied dead: Of hound or ravening jackal, not a sign. Thereat arose an angry war of words; Guard railed at guard and blows were like to end it, For none was there to part us, each in turn Suspected, but the guilt brought home to none, From lack of evidence. We challenged each The ordeal, or to handle red-hot iron, Or pass through fire, affirming on our oath Our innocence—we neither did the deed Ourselves, nor know who did or compassed it. Our quest was at a standstill, when one spake And bowed us all to earth like quivering reeds, For there was no gainsaying him nor way To escape perdition: _Ye_are_bound_to_tell_ _The_King,_ye_cannot_hide_it; so he spake. And he convinced us all; so lots were cast, And I, unlucky scapegoat, drew the prize. So here I am unwilling and withal Unwelcome; no man cares to hear ill news.
cards.whyThisWorks: The Guard's forced march to deliver unwanted news—captured in 'I, unlucky scapegoat, drew the prize' and 'no man cares to hear ill news'—dramatizes how Creon's power turns innocent bystanders into unwilling victims, giving the conflict between duty and self-preservation a deeper political meaning.
cards.skillStrategy: When a character describes a decision or event using emotionally loaded words, ask what that language reveals about the larger forces controlling the character's life.
evidencePoints: I, unlucky scapegoat, drew the prize
no man cares to hear ill news
cards.question: The Guard calls himself an 'unlucky scapegoat' who 'drew the prize' and ends by saying 'no man cares to hear ill news.' What deeper meaning does this moment in the passage add?

choices.label: A

choices.label: B
choices.text: The Guard's bitter description of himself as a 'scapegoat' who 'drew the prize' reveals that Creon's authority forces innocent, powerless men to suffer consequences for events they neither caused nor could prevent.

choices.label: C

choices.label: D

cards.standardTitle: Key literary elements add layers of meaning
cards.excerpt: CREON. Burghers, my noble friends, ye take alarm At my approach (I read it in your eyes), Fear nothing and refrain from angry words. I come with no ill purpose; I am old, And know the city whither I am come, Without a peer amongst the powers of Greece. It was by reason of my years that I Was chosen to persuade your guest and bring Him back to Thebes; not the delegate Of one man, but commissioned by the State, Since of all Thebans I have most bewailed, Being his kinsman, his most grievous woes. O listen to me, luckless Oedipus, Come home! The whole Cadmeian people claim With right to have thee back, I most of all, For most of all (else were I vile indeed) I mourn for thy misfortunes, seeing thee An aged outcast, wandering on and on, A beggar with one handmaid for thy stay. Ah! who had e’er imagined she could fall To such a depth of misery as this, To tend in penury thy stricken frame, A virgin ripe for wedlock, but unwed, A prey for any wanton ravisher? Seems it not cruel this reproach I cast On thee and on myself and all the race? Aye, but an open shame cannot be hid. Hide it, O hide it, Oedipus, thou canst. O, by our fathers’ gods, consent I pray; Come back to Thebes, come to thy father’s home, Bid Athens, as is meet, a fond farewell; Thebes thy old foster-mother claims thee first.
cards.whyThisWorks: Creon's calculated appeal to Oedipus—invoking family shame, Antigone's vulnerability, and civic duty—reveals the conflict between manipulation and genuine loyalty, adding meaning about how power exploits suffering.
cards.skillStrategy: When a character makes a persuasive move in a conflict, ask what that character stands to gain and what the appeal reveals about the deeper struggle for control.
evidencePoints: Ah! who had e'er imagined she could fall To such a depth of misery as this, To tend in penury thy stricken frame, A virgin ripe for wedlock, but unwed, A prey for any wanton ravisher?
Hide it, O hide it, Oedipus, thou canst. O, by our fathers' gods, consent I pray; Come back to Thebes, come to thy father's home
cards.question: Creon appeals to Oedipus by describing Antigone as 'a virgin ripe for wedlock, but unwed, a prey for any wanton ravisher.' How does Creon's use of Antigone's vulnerability in this conflict add a deeper layer of meaning to the scene?

choices.label: B
choices.text: Creon weaponizes Antigone's exposed condition to pressure Oedipus emotionally, revealing that his appeal to family loyalty is actually a tool of political manipulation rather than sincere compassion.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Creon's description of Antigone's suffering shifts the conflict away from Oedipus entirely, making Antigone the central figure whose fate the audience should focus on.

cards.standardTitle: Key literary elements add layers of meaning
cards.excerpt: GUARD. It happened thus. No sooner had we come, Driven from thy presence by those awful threats, Than straight we swept away all trace of dust, And bared the clammy body. Then we sat High on the ridge to windward of the stench, While each man kept he fellow alert and rated Roundly the sluggard if he chanced to nap. So all night long we watched, until the sun Stood high in heaven, and his blazing beams Smote us. A sudden whirlwind then upraised A cloud of dust that blotted out the sky, And swept the plain, and stripped the woodlands bare, And shook the firmament. We closed our eyes And waited till the heaven-sent plague should pass. At last it ceased, and lo! there stood this maid. A piercing cry she uttered, sad and shrill, As when the mother bird beholds her nest Robbed of its nestlings; even so the maid Wailed as she saw the body stripped and bare, And cursed the ruffians who had done this deed. Anon she gathered handfuls of dry dust, Then, holding high a well-wrought brazen urn, Thrice on the dead she poured a lustral stream. We at the sight swooped down on her and seized Our quarry. Undismayed she stood, and when We taxed her with the former crime and this, She disowned nothing. I was glad—and grieved; For ’tis most sweet to ’scape oneself scot-free, And yet to bring disaster to a friend Is grievous. Take it all in all, I deem A man’s first duty is to serve himself.
cards.whyThisWorks: Antigone's decision to return to the body and perform burial rites despite the guards' presence—and her calm refusal to deny the act—creates a conflict between personal loyalty and civic law that deepens the play's central meaning about duty, defiance, and moral courage.
cards.skillStrategy: When a character makes a decision or takes an action that leads to conflict, ask yourself what that choice reveals about what the author wants you to understand beyond the surface event.
evidencePoints: She disowned nothing.

cards.question: The Guard describes Antigone returning to the body, performing burial rites, and then standing 'undismayed' when seized. What deeper meaning does this sequence of events add to the passage?

choices.label: B

cards.standardTitle: Key literary elements add layers of meaning
cards.excerpt: CREON. Well, let her know the stubbornest of wills Are soonest bended, as the hardest iron, O’er-heated in the fire to brittleness, Flies soonest into fragments, shivered through. A snaffle curbs the fieriest steed, and he Who in subjection lives must needs be meek. But this proud girl, in insolence well-schooled, First overstepped the established law, and then— A second and worse act of insolence— She boasts and glories in her wickedness. Now if she thus can flout authority Unpunished, I am woman, she the man. But though she be my sister’s child or nearer Of kin than all who worship at my hearth, Nor she nor yet her sister shall escape The utmost penalty, for both I hold, As arch-conspirators, of equal guilt. Bring forth the older; even now I saw her Within the palace, frenzied and distraught. The workings of the mind discover oft Dark deeds in darkness schemed, before the act. More hateful still the miscreant who seeks When caught, to make a virtue of a crime.
cards.whyThisWorks: Creon's decision to punish Antigone despite her family ties—and his framing of her defiance as a threat to his authority as a man—reveals how the conflict between personal loyalty and political power carries a deeper meaning about gender, pride, and tyranny.
cards.skillStrategy: When a character makes a decision under pressure, ask what that choice reveals about the deeper conflict driving the story—look for what the character values most and what that costs them.
evidencePoints: But though she be my sister's child or nearer / Of kin than all who worship at my hearth, / Nor she nor yet her sister shall escape / The utmost penalty
Now if she thus can flout authority / Unpunished, I am woman, she the man.
cards.question: Creon declares that Antigone and her sister must face 'the utmost penalty' even though Antigone is his own kin. What deeper meaning does this decision add to the conflict in the passage?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Creon's willingness to punish his own family shows that he is motivated primarily by grief over the breakdown of order in Thebes after the recent war.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Creon's refusal to spare Antigone despite their family bond reveals that his need to preserve male authority and political power outweighs every personal loyalty, exposing how pride drives him toward a destructive extreme.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Creon's decision to punish both sisters equally suggests that he genuinely believes Ismene participated in the burial and is acting on careful, impartial evidence rather than wounded pride.

choices.label: D
choices.text: By condemning Antigone in front of his court, Creon demonstrates that public spectacle is the most effective tool a ruler has for discouraging future acts of rebellion among citizens.

cards.standardTitle: Key literary elements add layers of meaning
cards.excerpt: OEDIPUS. I pray thee do not wonder if the sight Of children, given o’er for lost, has made My converse somewhat long and tedious. Full well I know the joy I have of them Is due to thee, to thee and no man else; Thou wast their sole deliverer, none else. The gods deal with thee after my desire, With thee and with this land! for fear of heaven I found above all peoples most with you, And righteousness and lips that cannot lie. I speak in gratitude of what I know, For all I have I owe to thee alone. Give me thy hand, O Prince, that I may touch it, And if thou wilt permit me, kiss thy cheek. What say I? Can I wish that thou should’st touch One fallen like me to utter wretchedness, Corrupt and tainted with a thousand ills? Oh no, I would not let thee if thou would’st. They only who have known calamity Can share it. Let me greet thee where thou art, And still befriend me as thou hast till now.
cards.whyThisWorks: Oedipus's decision to withdraw his hand before Theseus can take it—because he considers himself 'Corrupt and tainted with a thousand ills'—dramatizes the conflict between his gratitude and his shame, adding a layer of meaning about how suffering isolates even those who are most loved.
cards.skillStrategy: When a character makes a decision or stops an action mid-moment, ask what that reversal reveals about the deeper conflict driving the scene.
evidencePoints: Can I wish that thou should'st touch / One fallen like me to utter wretchedness, / Corrupt and tainted with a thousand ills?
They only who have known calamity / Can share it.
cards.question: Oedipus reaches out for Theseus's hand, then immediately pulls back, saying, 'Can I wish that thou should'st touch / One fallen like me to utter wretchedness, / Corrupt and tainted with a thousand ills?' What deeper meaning does this reversal add to the scene?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Oedipus doubts Theseus's sincerity and fears that the prince's friendship is motivated by political obligation rather than genuine care.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Even in a moment of profound gratitude, Oedipus's shame over his own ruin prevents him from fully accepting human connection, showing that his suffering has become a barrier he cannot cross.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Oedipus withdraws his hand to demonstrate that he values Theseus's righteousness too highly to risk contaminating it with any gesture of familiarity.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Oedipus's hesitation reveals that he believes the gods have already punished Theseus for helping him and that further contact would bring additional divine wrath.

cards.standardTitle: Key literary elements add layers of meaning
cards.excerpt: ANTIGONE. O heed me, father, though I am young in years. Let the prince have his will and pay withal What in his eyes is service to the god; For our sake also let our brother come. If what he urges tend not to thy good He cannot surely wrest perforce thy will. To hear him then, what harm? By open words A scheme of villainy is soon bewrayed. Thou art his father, therefore canst not pay In kind a son’s most impious outrages. O listen to him; other men like thee Have thankless children and are choleric, But yielding to persuasion’s gentle spell They let their savage mood be exorcised. Look thou to the past, forget the present, think On all the woe thy sire and mother brought thee; Thence wilt thou draw this lesson without fail, Of evil passion evil is the end. Thou hast, alas, to prick thy memory, Stern monitors, these ever-sightless orbs. O yield to us; just suitors should not need To be importunate, nor he that takes A favor lack the grace to make return.
cards.whyThisWorks: Antigone's appeal to Oedipus—urging him to remember his own parents' suffering as a reason to forgive his son—creates a conflict between a father's wounded pride and a daughter's plea for mercy, deepening the theme that unresolved bitterness perpetuates cycles of suffering.
cards.skillStrategy: When a character makes a decision or plea in a conflict, ask what deeper idea about human nature or fate the author is exploring through that moment.
evidencePoints: Look thou to the past, forget the present, think / On all the woe thy sire and mother brought thee; / Thence wilt thou draw this lesson without fail, / Of evil passion evil is the end.
Thou hast, alas, to prick thy memory, / Stern monitors, these ever-sightless orbs.
cards.question: Antigone urges Oedipus to remember 'all the woe thy sire and mother brought thee' and warns that 'of evil passion evil is the end.' What deeper meaning does this moment in the conflict between Oedipus and his son add to the speech?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Antigone's reminder that Oedipus was once wronged by his own parents shows she believes Polynices deserves punishment equal to what Oedipus suffered.

choices.label: B
choices.text: By pointing to Oedipus's own history of familial suffering, Antigone suggests that refusing to break the cycle of bitterness will only extend the destruction that has already consumed their family.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Antigone's appeal to Oedipus's blindness as a 'stern monitor' reveals that she believes his physical suffering has already taught him to forgive, making her argument unnecessary.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Antigone's reference to past woe demonstrates that she is more concerned with honoring the gods than with reconciling her father and brother.

cards.standardTitle: Key literary elements add layers of meaning
cards.excerpt:
CREON. Be sure thou wilt not traffic on my wits.

TEIRESIAS. Know then for sure, the coursers of the sun Not many times shall run their race, before Thou shalt have given the fruit of thine own loins In quittance of thy murder, life for life; For that thou hast entombed a living soul, And sent below a denizen of earth, And wronged the nether gods by leaving here A corpse unlaved, unwept, unsepulchered. Herein thou hast no part, nor e’en the gods In heaven; and thou usurp’st a power not thine. For this the avenging spirits of Heaven and Hell Who dog the steps of sin are on thy trail: What these have suffered thou shalt suffer too. And now, consider whether bought by gold I prophesy. For, yet a little while, And sound of lamentation shall be heard, Of men and women through thy desolate halls; And all thy neighbor States are leagues to avenge Their mangled warriors who have found a grave I’ the maw of wolf or hound, or winged bird That flying homewards taints their city’s air. These are the shafts, that like a bowman I Provoked to anger, loosen at thy breast, Unerring, and their smart thou shalt not shun. Boy, lead me home, that he may vent his spleen On younger men, and learn to curb his tongue With gentler manners than his present mood. [Exit TEIRESIAS]

CHORUS. My liege, that man hath gone, foretelling woe. And, O believe me, since these grizzled locks Were like the raven, never have I known The prophet’s warning to the State to fail.
cards.whyThisWorks: Teiresias's prophecy functions as a reversal moment that reframes Creon's earlier decisions—entombing Antigone and leaving Polynices unburied—as acts of cosmic wrongdoing with fatal consequences, adding the deeper meaning that political authority cannot override divine law.
cards.skillStrategy: When a character delivers a prophecy or warning that directly responds to a prior decision, ask what that conflict reveals about the story's deeper message.
evidencePoints: For that thou hast entombed a living soul, And sent below a denizen of earth, And wronged the nether gods by leaving here A corpse unlaved, unwept, unsepulchered.
the coursers of the sun Not many times shall run their race, before Thou shalt have given the fruit of thine own loins In quittance of thy murder, life for life
cards.question: Teiresias tells Creon that he will lose 'the fruit of thine own loins' as 'quittance of thy murder, life for life.' How does this consequence deepen the meaning of Creon's earlier decisions?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Creon's punishment reveals that the gods are indifferent to human suffering and only intervene when a ruler becomes too powerful.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The promise of personal loss shows that Creon's political authority cannot shield him from divine justice, suggesting that no ruler stands above the laws of the gods.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The prophecy proves that Teiresias has always been Creon's enemy and has manipulated events to bring about his downfall.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Creon's coming grief demonstrates that his greatest error was refusing to listen to the Chorus rather than defying the burial rites.

cards.standardTitle: Key literary elements add layers of meaning
cards.excerpt:
OEDIPUS. God speed thee! and as meed for bringing them May Providence deal with thee kindlier Than it has dealt with me! O children mine, Where are ye? Let me clasp you with these hands, A brother’s hands, a father’s; hands that made Lack-luster sockets of his once bright eyes; Hands of a man who blindly, recklessly, Became your sire by her from whom he sprang. Though I cannot behold you, I must weep In thinking of the evil days to come, The slights and wrongs that men will put upon you. Where’er ye go to feast or festival, No merrymaking will it prove for you, But oft abashed in tears ye will return. And when ye come to marriageable years, Where’s the bold wooers who will jeopardize To take unto himself such disrepute As to my children’s children still must cling, For what of infamy is lacking here? “Their father slew his father, sowed the seed Where he himself was gendered, and begat These maidens at the source wherefrom he sprang.” Such are the gibes that men will cast at you. Who then will wed you? None, I ween, but ye Must pine, poor maids, in single barrenness. O Prince, Menoeceus’ son, to thee, I turn, With the it rests to father them, for we Their natural parents, both of us, are lost. O leave them not to wander poor, unwed, Thy kin, nor let them share my low estate. O pity them so young, and but for thee All destitute. Thy hand upon it, Prince. To you, my children I had much to say, Were ye but ripe to hear. Let this suffice: Pray ye may find some home and live content, And may your lot prove happier than your sire’s.

CREON. Thou hast had enough of weeping; pass within.
cards.whyThisWorks: Oedipus's act of pleading with Creon to care for his daughters—a direct consequence of his own catastrophic choices—layers the conflict between personal guilt and parental love onto the broader theme of inherited shame and fate.
cards.skillStrategy: When a character makes a desperate plea or decision, ask what that moment reveals about the deeper consequences of earlier events in the story.
evidencePoints: Hands of a man who blindly, recklessly, / Became your sire by her from whom he sprang.
O Prince, Menoeceus' son, to thee, I turn, / With the it rests to father them, for we / Their natural parents, both of us, are lost.
cards.question: Oedipus begs Creon to care for his daughters because 'we / Their natural parents, both of us, are lost.' What does this moment of desperation add to the meaning of the passage?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Oedipus's plea shows that he blames Creon for the suffering his daughters will face, suggesting that political power is the true source of the family's ruin.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Oedipus's plea reveals that his crimes have stripped him of the ability to protect his own children, so the consequences of his actions extend beyond himself and fall upon the innocent.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Oedipus's plea demonstrates that he has fully accepted his fate and feels no grief over his daughters' futures, only a calm desire to arrange their care before he departs.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Oedipus's plea suggests that his daughters are strong enough to survive without help, and he asks Creon only as a formality to honor the customs of his society.

cards.standardTitle: Key literary elements add layers of meaning
cards.excerpt: JOCASTA. Then thou mayest ease thy conscience on that score. Listen and I’ll convince thee that no man Hath scot or lot in the prophetic art. Here is the proof in brief. An oracle Once came to Laius (I will not say ’Twas from the Delphic god himself, but from His ministers) declaring he was doomed To perish by the hand of his own son, A child that should be born to him by me. Now Laius—so at least report affirmed— Was murdered on a day by highwaymen, No natives, at a spot where three roads meet. As for the child, it was but three days old, When Laius, its ankles pierced and pinned Together, gave it to be cast away By others on the trackless mountain side. So then Apollo brought it not to pass The child should be his father’s murderer, Or the dread terror find accomplishment, And Laius be slain by his own son. Such was the prophet’s horoscope. O king, Regard it not. Whate’er the god deems fit To search, himself unaided will reveal.
cards.whyThisWorks: Jocasta's retelling of the oracle and the infant's abandonment creates dramatic irony—her attempt to dismiss prophecy as meaningless actually reveals the very chain of events that will prove the prophecy true, adding a layer of meaning about human blindness to fate.
cards.skillStrategy: When a character makes a decision or shares a past event, ask yourself: does this moment reveal something deeper about fate, blindness, or consequence that the character cannot see?
evidencePoints: Laius—so at least report affirmed—Was murdered on a day by highwaymen, No natives, at a spot where three roads meet.
So then Apollo brought it not to pass The child should be his father's murderer
cards.question: Jocasta describes Laius being 'murdered on a day by highwaymen, No natives, at a spot where three roads meet' as evidence that prophecy is powerless. How does this detail add a deeper layer of meaning to the scene?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The detail confirms that Laius died at the hands of strangers, which fully supports Jocasta's argument that the oracle about her son was never fulfilled.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The detail Jocasta offers as proof against prophecy is the very clue that points toward its fulfillment, revealing that her confidence in disproving fate actually deepens the audience's sense of her blindness.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The detail shifts the conflict away from Oedipus and toward the unknown highwaymen, suggesting that human violence, not divine will, drives the tragedy.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The detail about the crossroads shows that Jocasta distrusts the Delphic god directly and only accepts prophecies delivered by his ministers.

cards.standardTitle: Key literary elements add layers of meaning
cards.excerpt: OEDIPUS. Stern-visaged queens, since coming to this land First in your sanctuary I bent the knee, Frown not on me or Phoebus, who, when erst He told me all my miseries to come, Spake of this respite after many years, Some haven in a far-off land, a rest Vouchsafed at last by dread divinities. “There,” said he, “shalt thou round thy weary life, A blessing to the land wherein thou dwell’st, But to the land that cast thee forth, a curse.” And of my weird he promised signs should come, Earthquake, or thunderclap, or lightning flash. And now I recognize as yours the sign That led my wanderings to this your grove; Else had I never lighted on you first, A wineless man on your seat of native rock. O goddesses, fulfill Apollo’s word, Grant me some consummation of my life, If haply I appear not all too vile, A thrall to sorrow worse than any slave. Hear, gentle daughters of primeval Night, Hear, namesake of great Pallas; Athens, first Of cities, pity this dishonored shade, The ghost of him who once was Oedipus.
cards.whyThisWorks: Oedipus's arrival at the sacred grove fulfills Apollo's prophesied sign, turning a moment of wandering into a destined reversal that deepens the theme of suffering transformed into unexpected blessing.
cards.skillStrategy: When a character reaches a turning point, ask what the event reveals about the larger meaning of their struggle — not just what happens, but what it means for who they are.
evidencePoints: Some haven in a far-off land, a rest / Vouchsafed at last by dread divinities
And now I recognize as yours the sign / That led my wanderings to this your grove
cards.question: Oedipus describes recognizing 'the sign / That led my wanderings to this your grove.' How does this moment of recognition add a deeper layer of meaning to his conflict?

choices.label: A
choices.text: It reveals that Oedipus has been deliberately searching for the grove, suggesting he has always controlled his own fate despite his suffering.

choices.label: B
choices.text: It marks the point where years of exile and suffering converge with divine prophecy, suggesting that Oedipus's long torment was always moving toward a destined purpose rather than meaningless wandering.

choices.label: C
choices.text: It shows that Oedipus doubts Apollo's earlier prophecy, since he only recognizes the sign after arriving by accident rather than by divine guidance.

choices.label: D
choices.text: It demonstrates that Oedipus has finally escaped the curse placed on him, because reaching the grove means the goddesses have already forgiven his past crimes.

cards.standardTitle: Key literary elements add layers of meaning
cards.excerpt:
CHORUS. Why, Oedipus, why stung with passionate grief Hath the queen thus departed? Much I fear From this dead calm will burst a storm of woes.

OEDIPUS. Let the storm burst, my fixed resolve still holds, To learn my lineage, be it ne’er so low. It may be she with all a woman’s pride Thinks scorn of my base parentage. But I Who rank myself as Fortune’s favorite child, The giver of good gifts, shall not be shamed. She is my mother and the changing moons My brethren, and with them I wax and wane. Thus sprung why should I fear to trace my birth? Nothing can make me other than I am.

CHORUS. (Str.) If my soul prophetic err not, if my wisdom aught avail, Thee, Cithaeron, I shall hail, As the nurse and foster-mother of our Oedipus shall greet Ere tomorrow’s full moon rises, and exalt thee as is meet. Dance and song shall hymn thy praises, lover of our royal race. Phoebus, may my words find grace!

(Ant.) Child, who bare thee, nymph or goddess? sure thy sure was more than man, Haply the hill-roamer Pan. Of did Loxias beget thee, for he haunts the upland wold; Or Cyllene’s lord, or Bacchus, dweller on the hilltops cold? Did some Heliconian Oread give him thee, a new-born joy? Nymphs with whom he love to toy?

OEDIPUS. Elders, if I, who never yet before Have met the man, may make a guess, methinks I see the herdsman who we long have sought; His time-worn aspect matches with the years Of yonder aged messenger; besides I seem to recognize the men who bring him As servants of my own. But you, perchance, Having in past days known or seen the herd, May better by sure knowledge my surmise.
cards.whyThisWorks: Oedipus's defiant decision to pursue his lineage despite Jocasta's anguished departure is a pivotal plot moment that deepens the tragedy's central irony: his relentless drive for truth accelerates his own destruction.
cards.skillStrategy: When a character makes a decision in the face of a warning, ask what that choice reveals about theme and what consequences it sets in motion.
evidencePoints: Let the storm burst, my fixed resolve still holds, To learn my lineage, be it ne'er so low.
Nothing can make me other than I am.
cards.question: After the Chorus warns that 'a storm of woes' may follow Jocasta's departure, Oedipus declares, 'Let the storm burst, my fixed resolve still holds.' What deeper meaning does this decision add to the play?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Oedipus's confidence that Fortune favors him shows he has correctly reasoned that his origins are noble, making his search for the truth a justified and ultimately harmless act.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Oedipus's refusal to heed the warning and his insistence that 'nothing can make me other than I am' reveal that the very pride driving him toward self-knowledge is the force that will bring about his ruin.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Oedipus dismisses Jocasta's reaction as wounded pride over his low birth, which shows that his conflict with her is rooted in a class dispute rather than in any deeper threat to his identity.

choices.label: D
choices.text: By welcoming the storm, Oedipus demonstrates that he trusts the Chorus's prophetic wisdom and believes their hymn to Cithaeron confirms his divine parentage.

cards.standardTitle: Key literary elements add layers of meaning
cards.excerpt: CHORUS. (Str.) Who craves excess of days, Scorning the common span Of life, I judge that man A giddy wight who walks in folly’s ways. For the long years heap up a grievous load, Scant pleasures, heavier pains, Till not one joy remains For him who lingers on life’s weary road And come it slow or fast, One doom of fate Doth all await, For dance and marriage bell, The dirge and funeral knell. Death the deliverer freeth all at last. (Ant.) Not to be born at all Is best, far best that can befall, Next best, when born, with least delay To trace the backward way. For when youth passes with its giddy train, Troubles on troubles follow, toils on toils, Pain, pain for ever pain; And none escapes life’s coils. Envy, sedition, strife, Carnage and war, make up the tale of life. Last comes the worst and most abhorred stage Of unregarded age, Joyless, companionless and slow, Of woes the crowning woe.
cards.whyThisWorks: The Chorus's ode presents the conflict between the human desire to live long and the suffering that accumulates with age, culminating in the reversal that 'not to be born at all / Is best,' which adds a layer of meaning about the futility of clinging to life—directly relevant to Antigone's impending death.
cards.skillStrategy: When a character or chorus describes a conflict or reversal, ask yourself what deeper truth about human experience that tension reveals beyond the surface situation.
evidencePoints: Not to be born at all / Is best, far best that can befall
For the long years heap up a grievous load, / Scant pleasures, heavier pains, / Till not one joy remains
cards.question: The Chorus declares that 'Not to be born at all / Is best, far best that can befall.' How does this reversal of the common human desire to live long add a deeper layer of meaning to the ode?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The reversal shows that the Chorus admires those who die young in battle, suggesting that war is the most honorable path a person can take.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The reversal reframes existence itself as a burden, suggesting that the suffering woven into every stage of life—youth, age, and death—makes living a punishment rather than a gift.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The reversal reveals that the Chorus believes only the gods are capable of true happiness, while mortals are condemned to envy the divine.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The reversal indicates that the Chorus is urging the audience to accept death calmly, because death arrives the same way for everyone regardless of how they lived.

cards.standardTitle: Key literary elements add layers of meaning
cards.excerpt:
CREON. She shall be taken to some desert place By man untrod, and in a rock-hewn cave, With food no more than to avoid the taint That homicide might bring on all the State, Buried alive. There let her call in aid The King of Death, the one god she reveres, Or learn too late a lesson learnt at last: ’Tis labor lost, to reverence the dead.

CHORUS. (Str.) Love resistless in fight, all yield at a glance of thine eye, Love who pillowed all night on a maiden’s cheek dost lie, Over the upland holds. Shall mortals not yield to thee?

(Ant). Mad are thy subjects all, and even the wisest heart Straight to folly will fall, at a touch of thy poisoned dart. Thou didst kindle the strife, this feud of kinsman with kin, By the eyes of a winsome wife, and the yearning her heart to win. For as her consort still, enthroned with Justice above, Thou bendest man to thy will, O all invincible Love.

Lo I myself am borne aside, From Justice, as I view this bride. (O sight an eye in tears to drown) Antigone, so young, so fair, Thus hurried down Death’s bower with the dead to share.

ANTIGONE. (Str. 1) Friends, countrymen, my last farewell I make; My journey’s done. One last fond, lingering, longing look I take At the bright sun. For Death who puts to sleep both young and old Hales my young life, And beckons me to Acheron’s dark fold, An unwed wife. No youths have sung the marriage song for me, My bridal bed No maids have strewn with flowers from the lea, ’Tis Death I wed.
cards.whyThisWorks: Creon's decision to bury Antigone alive rather than execute her directly creates a cruel irony that deepens the conflict between divine law and state power, while Antigone's lament reframes her punishment as a forced 'marriage to Death,' adding a layer of meaning about sacrifice and lost youth.
cards.skillStrategy: When a character's punishment or decision produces an unexpected consequence or irony, ask what deeper idea about justice, power, or human experience that moment reveals.
evidencePoints: Buried alive. There let her call in aid / The King of Death, the one god she reveres
No youths have sung the marriage song for me, / My bridal bed / No maids have strewn with flowers from the lea, / 'Tis Death I wed.
cards.question: Creon orders Antigone to be 'Buried alive' in a cave rather than killed outright, and Antigone responds by describing herself as an 'unwed wife' who weds Death. What deeper meaning does this conflict and its consequence add to the passage?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Creon's sentence reveals that he respects religious custom enough to avoid directly shedding Antigone's blood, showing his underlying piety toward the gods.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Creon's attempt to punish Antigone without technically killing her backfires in meaning: by burying her alive, he delivers her to the very god she honored, making his cruelty a fulfillment of her devotion rather than a defeat of it.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Antigone's description of herself as an unwed wife shows she regrets her choice to defy Creon and wishes she had lived a normal life instead of dying for her brother.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The Chorus's reference to Love kindling 'strife' and 'feud of kinsman with kin' suggests that Antigone's punishment is caused by a romantic rivalry between her and another character.

cards.standardTitle: Key literary elements add layers of meaning
cards.excerpt: ANTIGONE. What but the thought of our two brothers dead, The one by Creon graced with funeral rites, The other disappointed? Eteocles He hath consigned to earth (as fame reports) With obsequies that use and wont ordain, So gracing him among the dead below. But Polyneices, a dishonored corse, (So by report the royal edict runs) No man may bury him or make lament— Must leave him tombless and unwept, a feast For kites to scent afar and swoop upon. Such is the edict (if report speak true) Of Creon, our most noble Creon, aimed At thee and me, aye me too; and anon He will be here to promulgate, for such As have not heard, his mandate; ’tis in sooth No passing humor, for the edict says Whoe’er transgresses shall be stoned to death. So stands it with us; now ’tis thine to show If thou art worthy of thy blood or base.
cards.whyThisWorks: Antigone's first-person perspective frames Creon's edict not as law but as a personal threat aimed at her and Ismene, shaping the reader's sympathy and sense of injustice in ways a neutral narrator would not.
cards.skillStrategy: Ask yourself: because THIS character is speaking, what emotions and judgments color the information, and how would the meaning shift if someone else told it?
evidencePoints: Such is the edict (if report speak true) / Of Creon, our most noble Creon, aimed / At thee and me, aye me too
now 'tis thine to show / If thou art worthy of thy blood or base
cards.question: Antigone refers to Creon as 'our most noble Creon' while describing his order to leave Polyneices unburied and to stone anyone who disobeys. How does Antigone's point of view shape the meaning of this phrase?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The phrase shows that Antigone genuinely respects Creon's authority and believes his edict is just, even though it grieves her.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The phrase is bitterly sarcastic, and because Antigone is the one directly threatened by the edict, her contempt for Creon colors the entire account of his decree as an act of cruelty rather than governance.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The phrase signals that Antigone is uncertain whether the edict is real, since she repeatedly qualifies it with 'if report speak true' and 'by report.'

choices.label: D
choices.text: The phrase reflects the community's shared admiration for Creon, suggesting that Antigone is isolated in her grief over Polyneices.

cards.standardTitle: Key literary elements add layers of meaning
cards.excerpt:
THESEUS. I know that none Shall hale thee hence in my despite. Such threats Vented in anger oft, are blusterers, An idle breath, forgot when sense returns. And for thy foemen, though their words were brave, Boasting to bring thee back, they are like to find The seas between us wide and hard to sail. Such my firm purpose, but in any case Take heart, since Phoebus sent thee here. My name, Though I be distant, warrants thee from harm.

CHORUS. (Str. 1) Thou hast come to a steed-famed land for rest, O stranger worn with toil, To a land of all lands the goodliest Colonus’ glistening soil. ’Tis the haunt of the clear-voiced nightingale, Who hid in her bower, among The wine-dark ivy that wreathes the vale, Trilleth her ceaseless song; And she loves, where the clustering berries nod O’er a sunless, windless glade, The spot by no mortal footstep trod, The pleasance kept for the Bacchic god, Where he holds each night his revels wild With the nymphs who fostered the lusty child.
cards.whyThisWorks: The excerpt contrasts two distinct speakers—Theseus offering direct, protective reassurance and the Chorus painting a lyrical, almost mythic portrait of Colonus—showing students how point of view shapes tone and the reader's emotional experience of the same moment.
cards.skillStrategy: Ask yourself: who is speaking, what do they want the listener to feel, and how does that purpose change the tone of the words?
evidencePoints: Take heart, since Phoebus sent thee here. My name, Though I be distant, warrants thee from harm.
Thou hast come to a steed-famed land for rest, O stranger worn with toil, To a land of all lands the goodliest Colonus' glistening soil.
cards.question: Theseus speaks directly to the stranger, while the Chorus addresses him in song. How does this difference in point of view affect the tone of each passage?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Theseus creates a tone of reverence by invoking the gods, while the Chorus creates a tone of warning by describing a land untouched by mortals.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Theseus creates a tone of firm, personal reassurance by pledging his name as protection, while the Chorus creates a tone of lyrical wonder by celebrating Colonus as a sacred, beautiful refuge.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Theseus creates a tone of anger by threatening the stranger's enemies, while the Chorus creates a tone of sorrow by mourning the stranger's long toil.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Theseus creates a tone of uncertainty by admitting he may be distant, while the Chorus creates a tone of urgency by urging the stranger to rest immediately.

cards.standardTitle: Key literary elements add layers of meaning
cards.excerpt:
POLYNEICES. Ah me, my sisters, shall I first lament My own afflictions, or my aged sire’s, Whom here I find a castaway, with you, In a strange land, an ancient beggar clad In antic tatters, marring all his frame, While o’er the sightless orbs his unkept locks Float in the breeze; and, as it were to match, He bears a wallet against hunger’s pinch. All this too late I learn, wretch that I am, Alas! I own it, and am proved most vile In my neglect of thee: I scorn myself. But as almighty Zeus in all he doth Hath Mercy for co-partner of this throne, Let Mercy, father, also sit enthroned In thy heart likewise. For transgressions past May be amended, cannot be made worse.

Why silent? Father, speak, nor turn away, Hast thou no word, wilt thou dismiss me then In mute disdain, nor tell me why thou art wrath? O ye his daughters, sisters mine, do ye This sullen, obstinate silence try to move. Let him not spurn, without a single word Of answer, me the suppliant of the god.
cards.whyThisWorks: Polyneices speaks directly to his father and sisters, and his first-person perspective reveals his self-serving guilt and desperation, shaping the reader's understanding of his character and the tense, pleading tone of the scene.
cards.skillStrategy: Ask yourself: whose eyes and voice are we experiencing this moment through, and how does that shape what we feel or believe about what is happening?
evidencePoints: I own it, and am proved most vile / In my neglect of thee: I scorn myself.
Hast thou no word, wilt thou dismiss me then / In mute disdain, nor tell me why thou art wrath?
cards.question: Polyneices narrates this scene from his own perspective, confessing neglect and begging for a response. How does this first-person point of view shape the reader's understanding of the moment?

choices.label: A
choices.text: It causes the reader to trust Polyneices completely, since his open confession of neglect proves he has genuinely changed and deserves his father's forgiveness.

choices.label: B
choices.text: It filters the scene through Polyneices' self-interest, so his expressions of guilt and appeals to mercy feel calculated rather than purely sincere, creating an uneasy, pleading tone.

choices.label: C
choices.text: It shifts the reader's sympathy entirely to Oedipus, whose silence is presented as the emotional center of the scene because Polyneices never describes his own feelings.

choices.label: D
choices.text: It presents Polyneices as a detached observer of his father's suffering, keeping the tone calm and measured throughout the speech.

cards.standardTitle: Key literary elements add layers of meaning
cards.excerpt:
THESEUS. Oft had I heard of thee in times gone by— The bloody mutilation of thine eyes— And therefore know thee, son of Laius. All that I lately gathered on the way Made my conjecture doubly sure; and now Thy garb and that marred visage prove to me That thou art he. So pitying thine estate, Most ill-starred Oedipus, I fain would know What is the suit ye urge on me and Athens, Thou and the helpless maiden at thy side. Declare it; dire indeed must be the tale Whereat _I_ should recoil. I too was reared, Like thee, in exile, and in foreign lands Wrestled with many perils, no man more.
