Wherefore no alien in adversity Shall seek in vain my succor, nor shalt thou; I know myself a mortal, and my share In what the morrow brings no more than thine.

OEDIPUS. Theseus, thy words so apt, so generous So comfortable, need no long reply Both who I am and of what lineage sprung, And from what land I came, thou hast declared. So without prologue I may utter now My brief petition, and the tale is told.
cards.whyThisWorks: Theseus speaks in first person about his own exile and suffering before hearing Oedipus's petition, and this self-disclosure shapes the tone of the scene from one of supplication to one of mutual recognition, showing students how a speaker's revealed perspective transforms the emotional meaning of an exchange.
cards.skillStrategy: Ask yourself: what does the speaker reveal about themselves, and how does that personal disclosure change the way you understand the moment and the relationship between characters?
evidencePoints: I too was reared, Like thee, in exile, and in foreign lands Wrestled with many perils, no man more.
I know myself a mortal, and my share In what the morrow brings no more than thine.
cards.question: When Theseus says 'I too was reared, Like thee, in exile' and 'I know myself a mortal, and my share / In what the morrow brings no more than thine,' how does his point of view shape the meaning of this moment?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Theseus reveals his own suffering to warn Oedipus that Athens cannot offer permanent protection, creating a tone of cautious doubt about whether the petition will succeed.

choices.label: B
choices.text: By positioning himself as someone who has also endured exile and uncertainty, Theseus transforms the encounter from a powerful king judging a helpless outcast into a meeting between two men who share the same mortal vulnerability, making his offer of aid feel earned rather than charitable.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Theseus speaks from his own experience of exile primarily to establish his authority over Oedipus, signaling that he alone has the wisdom to decide whether the petition deserves a hearing.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Theseus mentions his past hardships to shift attention away from Oedipus's suffering, suggesting that his own story is more important than the petition Oedipus has come to make.

cards.standardTitle: Key literary elements add layers of meaning
cards.excerpt:
ISMENE. Bethink thee, sister, of our father’s fate, Abhorred, dishonored, self-convinced of sin, Blinded, himself his executioner. Think of his mother-wife (ill sorted names) Done by a noose herself had twined to death And last, our hapless brethren in one day, Both in a mutual destiny involved, Self-slaughtered, both the slayer and the slain. Bethink thee, sister, we are left alone; Shall we not perish wretchedest of all, If in defiance of the law we cross A monarch’s will?—weak women, think of that, Not framed by nature to contend with men. Remember this too that the stronger rules; We must obey his orders, these or worse. Therefore I plead compulsion and entreat The dead to pardon. I perforce obey The powers that be. ’Tis foolishness, I ween, To overstep in aught the golden mean.

ANTIGONE. I urge no more; nay, wert thou willing still, I would not welcome such a fellowship. Go thine own way; myself will bury him. How sweet to die in such employ, to rest,— Sister and brother linked in love’s embrace— A sinless sinner, banned awhile on earth, But by the dead commended; and with them I shall abide for ever. As for thee, Scorn, if thou wilt, the eternal laws of Heaven.
cards.whyThisWorks: The two-speaker structure lets students directly compare how Ismene's fearful, self-preserving perspective and Antigone's defiant, death-embracing perspective shape entirely different tones and meanings around the same act of burying their brother.
cards.skillStrategy: Ask yourself: whose eyes or voice am I seeing this moment through, and how does that person's position change what the moment feels like or means?
evidencePoints: 'weak women, think of that, / Not framed by nature to contend with men. Remember this too that the stronger rules; / We must obey his orders'
'How sweet to die in such employ, to rest,— / Sister and brother linked in love's embrace— / A sinless sinner, banned awhile on earth, / But by the dead commended'
cards.question: How does Antigone's point of view in her speech differ from Ismene's, and what does that difference reveal about the meaning of burying their brother?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Antigone, like Ismene, acknowledges the danger of defying Creon, but she believes the family has already suffered enough punishment to justify one final act of rebellion.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Antigone frames burying her brother as a sacred, even joyful duty that honors eternal law, while Ismene frames the same act as a reckless defiance of power that weak women cannot survive—making the burial mean sacrifice and love to one sister and certain destruction to the other.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Antigone speaks from a position of political authority that Ismene lacks, so her willingness to bury their brother reflects confidence in Creon's eventual mercy rather than a disregard for his law.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Ismene's focus on their father's fate shows she cares more about family honor than Antigone does, while Antigone's eagerness to die suggests she has given up hope for the family's future entirely.

cards.standardTitle: Key literary elements add layers of meaning
cards.excerpt:
CREON. She shall be taken to some desert place By man untrod, and in a rock-hewn cave, With food no more than to avoid the taint That homicide might bring on all the State, Buried alive. There let her call in aid The King of Death, the one god she reveres, Or learn too late a lesson learnt at last: ’Tis labor lost, to reverence the dead.

CHORUS. (Str.) Love resistless in fight, all yield at a glance of thine eye, Love who pillowed all night on a maiden’s cheek dost lie, Over the upland holds. Shall mortals not yield to thee?

(Ant). Mad are thy subjects all, and even the wisest heart Straight to folly will fall, at a touch of thy poisoned dart. Thou didst kindle the strife, this feud of kinsman with kin, By the eyes of a winsome wife, and the yearning her heart to win. For as her consort still, enthroned with Justice above, Thou bendest man to thy will, O all invincible Love.

Lo I myself am borne aside, From Justice, as I view this bride. (O sight an eye in tears to drown) Antigone, so young, so fair, Thus hurried down Death’s bower with the dead to share.

ANTIGONE. (Str. 1) Friends, countrymen, my last farewell I make; My journey’s done. One last fond, lingering, longing look I take At the bright sun. For Death who puts to sleep both young and old Hales my young life, And beckons me to Acheron’s dark fold, An unwed wife. No youths have sung the marriage song for me, My bridal bed No maids have strewn with flowers from the lea, ’Tis Death I wed.
cards.whyThisWorks: The excerpt shifts among three distinct voices—Creon's cold decree, the Chorus's torn sympathy, and Antigone's first-person lament—allowing students to see how each perspective shapes the emotional weight and meaning of her death sentence differently.
cards.skillStrategy: Ask yourself: whose eyes am I seeing this moment through, and how does that change what I feel or understand about what is happening?
evidencePoints: 'Tis labor lost, to reverence the dead.
Lo I myself am borne aside, From Justice, as I view this bride.
cards.question: The Chorus says, 'Lo I myself am borne aside, / From Justice, as I view this bride.' How does this moment of the Chorus speaking in first person shape the reader's understanding of Antigone's fate?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The Chorus confirms that Creon's punishment is legally justified, reinforcing the idea that Antigone broke the law and must face consequences.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The Chorus admitting it is pulled away from Justice by the sight of Antigone reveals that even those who uphold order feel her punishment is morally wrong, deepening the tragedy of her condemnation.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The Chorus speaking personally shows that it has abandoned its role as a neutral observer and now fully supports Antigone's rebellion against Creon.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The Chorus expressing emotion signals that Love, described earlier in the ode, has corrupted its judgment in the same way it corrupted Creon's decision to punish Antigone.

cards.standardTitle: Key literary elements add layers of meaning
cards.excerpt: GUARD. I cannot tell, for there was ne’er a trace Of pick or mattock—hard unbroken ground, Without a scratch or rut of chariot wheels, No sign that human hands had been at work. When the first sentry of the morning watch Gave the alarm, we all were terror-stricken. The corpse had vanished, not interred in earth, But strewn with dust, as if by one who sought To avert the curse that haunts the unburied dead: Of hound or ravening jackal, not a sign. Thereat arose an angry war of words; Guard railed at guard and blows were like to end it, For none was there to part us, each in turn Suspected, but the guilt brought home to none, From lack of evidence. We challenged each The ordeal, or to handle red-hot iron, Or pass through fire, affirming on our oath Our innocence—we neither did the deed Ourselves, nor know who did or compassed it. Our quest was at a standstill, when one spake And bowed us all to earth like quivering reeds, For there was no gainsaying him nor way To escape perdition: _Ye_are_bound_to_tell_ _The_King,_ye_cannot_hide_it; so he spake. And he convinced us all; so lots were cast, And I, unlucky scapegoat, drew the prize. So here I am unwilling and withal Unwelcome; no man cares to hear ill news.
cards.whyThisWorks: The Guard's first-person narration of drawing the lot and arriving 'unwilling' and 'unwelcome' reveals a self-serving, fearful perspective that shapes the reader's understanding of how ordinary soldiers experience royal authority—adding irony and tension absent from an omniscient or royal viewpoint.
cards.skillStrategy: Ask yourself: because THIS character is telling the story, what do I feel or understand that I would NOT feel or understand if someone else were speaking?
evidencePoints: I, unlucky scapegoat, drew the prize. So here I am unwilling and withal Unwelcome
no man cares to hear ill news
cards.question: The Guard narrates the events leading to his arrival before the King, describing himself as an 'unlucky scapegoat' who is 'unwilling' and 'unwelcome.' How does the Guard's point of view shape the reader's understanding of this moment?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The Guard's account establishes that the soldiers deliberately concealed the burial from the King, making them collectively guilty of defying royal authority.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The Guard's self-described reluctance and fear reveal that delivering bad news to a powerful ruler is experienced as a punishment in itself, creating sympathy for those caught between duty and danger.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The Guard's detailed description of the undisturbed ground proves that a god, not a human, performed the burial, which is the central meaning the Guard intends to convey.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The Guard's narration shows that he personally suspects one of the other sentries committed the burial but withholds that accusation to protect himself from blame.

cards.standardTitle: Key literary elements add layers of meaning
cards.excerpt: CREON. O cease, you vex me with your babblement; I am like to think you dote in your old age. Is it not arrant folly to pretend That gods would have a thought for this dead man? Did they forsooth award him special grace, And as some benefactor bury him, Who came to fire their hallowed sanctuaries, To sack their shrines, to desolate their land, And scout their ordinances? Or perchance The gods bestow their favors on the bad. No! no! I have long noted malcontents Who wagged their heads, and kicked against the yoke, Misliking these my orders, and my rule. ’Tis they, I warrant, who suborned my guards By bribes. Of evils current upon earth The worst is money. Money ’tis that sacks Cities, and drives men forth from hearth and home; Warps and seduces native innocence, And breeds a habit of dishonesty. But they who sold themselves shall find their greed Out-shot the mark, and rue it soon or late. Yea, as I still revere the dread of Zeus, By Zeus I swear, except ye find and bring Before my presence here the very man Who carried out this lawless burial, Death for your punishment shall not suffice. Hanged on a cross, alive ye first shall make Confession of this outrage. This will teach you What practices are like to serve your turn. There are some villainies that bring no gain. For by dishonesty the few may thrive, The many come to ruin and disgrace.
cards.whyThisWorks: Creon's first-person tirade filters every event—the burial, the guards, even the gods—through his obsession with political power and personal authority, making his point of view the lens that shapes how the reader understands the burial as a threat to his rule rather than a sacred act.
cards.skillStrategy: Ask yourself: whose eyes am I seeing this moment through, and how does that perspective change what the event means?
evidencePoints: I have long noted malcontents / Who wagged their heads, and kicked against the yoke, / Misliking these my orders, and my rule.
By Zeus I swear, except ye find and bring / Before my presence here the very man / Who carried out this lawless burial, / Death for your punishment shall not suffice.
cards.question: How does Creon's point of view shape the meaning of the burial when he declares, 'I have long noted malcontents / Who wagged their heads, and kicked against the yoke, / Misliking these my orders, and my rule'?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Creon frames the burial as a religious dispute, suggesting he is troubled by the possibility that the gods may have commanded it against his wishes.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Creon reframes the burial as an act of political rebellion against his personal authority, turning a question of divine law into evidence of a conspiracy to undermine his rule.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Creon reveals that he views the burial as a minor provocation that he is willing to forgive if the guards identify the person responsible.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Creon acknowledges that ordinary citizens acted out of genuine grief for the dead man, which is why he focuses his anger on the guards rather than the public.

cards.standardTitle: Key literary elements add layers of meaning
cards.excerpt: CREON. Burghers, my noble friends, ye take alarm At my approach (I read it in your eyes), Fear nothing and refrain from angry words. I come with no ill purpose; I am old, And know the city whither I am come, Without a peer amongst the powers of Greece. It was by reason of my years that I Was chosen to persuade your guest and bring Him back to Thebes; not the delegate Of one man, but commissioned by the State, Since of all Thebans I have most bewailed, Being his kinsman, his most grievous woes. O listen to me, luckless Oedipus, Come home! The whole Cadmeian people claim With right to have thee back, I most of all, For most of all (else were I vile indeed) I mourn for thy misfortunes, seeing thee An aged outcast, wandering on and on, A beggar with one handmaid for thy stay. Ah! who had e’er imagined she could fall To such a depth of misery as this, To tend in penury thy stricken frame, A virgin ripe for wedlock, but unwed, A prey for any wanton ravisher? Seems it not cruel this reproach I cast On thee and on myself and all the race? Aye, but an open shame cannot be hid. Hide it, O hide it, Oedipus, thou canst. O, by our fathers’ gods, consent I pray; Come back to Thebes, come to thy father’s home, Bid Athens, as is meet, a fond farewell; Thebes thy old foster-mother claims thee first.
cards.whyThisWorks: Creon speaks in first person directly to Oedipus, and his self-presentation as a grieving kinsman acting on behalf of all Thebes shapes the reader's understanding of his motives as potentially manipulative rather than genuinely compassionate.
cards.skillStrategy: Ask yourself: who is speaking, what do they want, and how does their perspective color what they say — then consider what the reader notices that the speaker may be hiding.
evidencePoints: not the delegate / Of one man, but commissioned by the State
O, by our fathers' gods, consent I pray; / Come back to Thebes, come to thy father's home
cards.question: Creon speaks directly to Oedipus in the first person throughout this passage. How does this point of view shape the reader's understanding of Creon's appeal?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Because Creon speaks as a fellow sufferer who has personally experienced exile, the reader trusts that his grief for Oedipus is genuine and his request is purely selfless.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Because Creon controls what he reveals about his own motives, the reader can see the gap between his claims of personal mourning and his repeated appeals to state authority, suggesting his compassion may be a persuasive strategy rather than sincere feeling.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Because Creon speaks on behalf of all Thebans, the reader understands that his individual feelings are unimportant and that the speech is purely a political announcement with no emotional dimension.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Because Creon addresses Oedipus's daughter directly when he calls her 'a virgin ripe for wedlock, but unwed,' the reader sees that Creon's true concern is for her welfare rather than for Oedipus himself.

cards.standardTitle: Key literary elements add layers of meaning
cards.excerpt: GUARD. It happened thus. No sooner had we come, Driven from thy presence by those awful threats, Than straight we swept away all trace of dust, And bared the clammy body. Then we sat High on the ridge to windward of the stench, While each man kept he fellow alert and rated Roundly the sluggard if he chanced to nap. So all night long we watched, until the sun Stood high in heaven, and his blazing beams Smote us. A sudden whirlwind then upraised A cloud of dust that blotted out the sky, And swept the plain, and stripped the woodlands bare, And shook the firmament. We closed our eyes And waited till the heaven-sent plague should pass. At last it ceased, and lo! there stood this maid. A piercing cry she uttered, sad and shrill, As when the mother bird beholds her nest Robbed of its nestlings; even so the maid Wailed as she saw the body stripped and bare, And cursed the ruffians who had done this deed. Anon she gathered handfuls of dry dust, Then, holding high a well-wrought brazen urn, Thrice on the dead she poured a lustral stream. We at the sight swooped down on her and seized Our quarry. Undismayed she stood, and when We taxed her with the former crime and this, She disowned nothing. I was glad—and grieved; For ’tis most sweet to ’scape oneself scot-free, And yet to bring disaster to a friend Is grievous. Take it all in all, I deem A man’s first duty is to serve himself.
cards.whyThisWorks: The Guard's first-person narration of Antigone's capture is filtered through his self-interested perspective, culminating in his admission 'I was glad—and grieved' and 'A man's first duty is to serve himself,' which reveals how point of view shapes the reader's understanding of both the Guard's moral character and Antigone's defiance.
cards.skillStrategy: Ask yourself: whose eyes and voice are telling this moment, and what does that narrator's attitude reveal about the events and the people involved?
evidencePoints: I was glad—and grieved; For 'tis most sweet to 'scape oneself scot-free, And yet to bring disaster to a friend Is grievous.
A man's first duty is to serve himself.
cards.question: The Guard concludes his account by saying, 'I was glad—and grieved' and 'A man's first duty is to serve himself.' How does the Guard's point of view shape the reader's understanding of Antigone's capture?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The Guard's self-congratulatory tone suggests he views Antigone as a dangerous criminal whose arrest was a heroic act, making the reader sympathize with Creon's authority.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The Guard's conflicted admission of personal relief over loyalty reveals a self-serving moral code, which contrasts with Antigone's unwavering defiance and deepens the reader's sense of her courage.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The Guard's detailed account of the whirlwind and dust storm shifts the reader's focus to the gods' role in the capture, suggesting divine forces, not the Guard, are responsible for Antigone's fate.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The Guard's neutral, factual reporting of events allows the reader to judge Antigone's guilt objectively without being influenced by the narrator's personal feelings.

cards.standardTitle: Key literary elements add layers of meaning
cards.excerpt: ANTIGONE. Yea, for these laws were not ordained of Zeus, And she who sits enthroned with gods below, Justice, enacted not these human laws. Nor did I deem that thou, a mortal man, Could’st by a breath annul and override The immutable unwritten laws of Heaven. They were not born today nor yesterday; They die not; and none knoweth whence they sprang. I was not like, who feared no mortal’s frown, To disobey these laws and so provoke The wrath of Heaven. I knew that I must die, E’en hadst thou not proclaimed it; and if death Is thereby hastened, I shall count it gain. For death is gain to him whose life, like mine, Is full of misery. Thus my lot appears Not sad, but blissful; for had I endured To leave my mother’s son unburied there, I should have grieved with reason, but not now. And if in this thou judgest me a fool, Methinks the judge of folly’s not acquit.
cards.whyThisWorks: Antigone speaks in first person directly to Creon, and her point of view—rooted in divine law over human authority—shapes the defiant, unrepentant tone and forces readers to weigh her moral reasoning against Creon's decree.
cards.skillStrategy: Ask yourself: because THIS character is speaking, what do I understand about the situation, the tone, and the stakes that I would NOT understand if someone else were telling it?
evidencePoints: Nor did I deem that thou, a mortal man, Could'st by a breath annul and override The immutable unwritten laws of Heaven.
I knew that I must die, E'en hadst thou not proclaimed it; and if death Is thereby hastened, I shall count it gain.
cards.question: Antigone speaks these lines directly to Creon in the first person. How does her point of view shape the meaning of her defense?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Because Antigone addresses Creon personally, the speech reveals her fear of punishment and her hope that he will reverse his decree before she is executed.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Because Antigone speaks as the one who acted and will suffer the consequences, her point of view frames death as a willing sacrifice rather than a defeat, making her defiance feel morally certain rather than reckless.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Because Antigone narrates events after they have already occurred, her point of view creates a reflective, sorrowful tone that suggests she regrets challenging Creon's authority.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Because Antigone speaks only about divine law and never mentions her brother by name, her point of view distances readers from her personal grief and makes her argument feel abstract.

cards.standardTitle: Key literary elements add layers of meaning
cards.excerpt: CHORUS. (Str.) Who craves excess of days, Scorning the common span Of life, I judge that man A giddy wight who walks in folly’s ways. For the long years heap up a grievous load, Scant pleasures, heavier pains, Till not one joy remains For him who lingers on life’s weary road And come it slow or fast, One doom of fate Doth all await, For dance and marriage bell, The dirge and funeral knell. Death the deliverer freeth all at last. (Ant.) Not to be born at all Is best, far best that can befall, Next best, when born, with least delay To trace the backward way. For when youth passes with its giddy train, Troubles on troubles follow, toils on toils, Pain, pain for ever pain; And none escapes life’s coils. Envy, sedition, strife, Carnage and war, make up the tale of life. Last comes the worst and most abhorred stage Of unregarded age, Joyless, companionless and slow, Of woes the crowning woe.
cards.whyThisWorks: The Chorus speaks as a collective, communal voice rather than an individual, which shapes the ode's meaning as universal moral judgment rather than personal grief, creating a tone of solemn, impersonal authority about the burden of long life.
cards.skillStrategy: Ask yourself: who is speaking, and how does that 'who' change what the words mean and how they feel?
evidencePoints: Who craves excess of days, Scorning the common span Of life, I judge that man A giddy wight who walks in folly's ways.
Not to be born at all Is best, far best that can befall, Next best, when born, with least delay To trace the backward way.
cards.question: The Chorus, rather than a single character, delivers the judgment that 'Not to be born at all / Is best, far best that can befall.' How does this collective point of view shape the meaning of that claim?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The Chorus speaks from personal suffering, so the claim reflects one character's private despair over a specific loss in the play.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Because the Chorus voices the shared wisdom of the community rather than one person's grief, the claim carries the weight of universal truth about human existence, not individual complaint.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The Chorus addresses only the young characters in the play, so the claim is a warning directed at a specific audience within the drama rather than a broad statement about life.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The Chorus is uncertain about its own beliefs, so the claim that not being born is best comes across as a tentative question rather than a confident judgment.

cards.standardTitle: Key literary elements add layers of meaning
cards.excerpt: CREON. Not deeming this city void of men Or counsel, son of Aegeus, as thou say’st I did what I have done; rather I thought Your people were not like to set such store by kin of mine and keep them ’gainst my will. Nor would they harbor, so I stood assured, A godless parricide, a reprobate Convicted of incestuous marriage ties. For on her native hill of Ares here (I knew your far-famed Areopagus) Sits Justice, and permits not vagrant folk To stay within your borders. In that faith I hunted down my quarry; and e’en then I had refrained but for the curses dire Wherewith he banned my kinsfolk and myself: Such wrong, methought, had warrant for my act. Anger has no old age but only death; The dead alone can feel no touch of spite. So thou must work thy will; my cause is just But weak without allies; yet will I try, Old as I am, to answer deeds with deeds.
cards.whyThisWorks: Creon's first-person self-justification reveals how his defensive, self-righteous point of view shapes the tone as calculating and unapologetic, allowing readers to judge the gap between his stated reasoning and his aggressive actions.
cards.skillStrategy: Ask yourself: whose voice controls this moment, and what does that speaker's word choice reveal about how they see themselves versus how the reader sees them?
evidencePoints: I hunted down my quarry; and e'en then I had refrained but for the curses dire
Anger has no old age but only death; The dead alone can feel no touch of spite.
cards.question: Creon speaks this passage in his own defense before Aegeus. How does Creon's first-person point of view shape the reader's understanding of his character?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Creon's direct address to Aegeus shows that he is genuinely remorseful for hunting down his quarry and wishes to make amends before it is too late.

choices.label: B
choices.text: By framing every action as a reasoned response to insult or law, Creon reveals a self-justifying perspective that exposes his pride and aggression even as he claims his cause is just.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Creon's point of view presents Aegeus as an unreliable judge whose city has failed to uphold the same standards of justice that Creon himself follows.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Speaking in first person allows Creon to distance himself from the curses and wrongdoing, shifting all blame onto his kinsfolk so the reader sympathizes with him.

cards.standardTitle: Key literary elements add layers of meaning
cards.excerpt: CREON. Well, let her know the stubbornest of wills Are soonest bended, as the hardest iron, O’er-heated in the fire to brittleness, Flies soonest into fragments, shivered through. A snaffle curbs the fieriest steed, and he Who in subjection lives must needs be meek. But this proud girl, in insolence well-schooled, First overstepped the established law, and then— A second and worse act of insolence— She boasts and glories in her wickedness. Now if she thus can flout authority Unpunished, I am woman, she the man. But though she be my sister’s child or nearer Of kin than all who worship at my hearth, Nor she nor yet her sister shall escape The utmost penalty, for both I hold, As arch-conspirators, of equal guilt. Bring forth the older; even now I saw her Within the palace, frenzied and distraught. The workings of the mind discover oft Dark deeds in darkness schemed, before the act. More hateful still the miscreant who seeks When caught, to make a virtue of a crime.
cards.whyThisWorks: Creon's first-person speech reveals his authoritarian point of view through self-justifying metaphors and gendered logic, showing how his perspective shapes the reader's understanding of his character as rigid and threatened rather than righteous.
cards.skillStrategy: Ask yourself: whose voice controls this moment, and what does that speaker's word choice reveal about how they see themselves and others?
evidencePoints: Now if she thus can flout authority Unpunished, I am woman, she the man.
More hateful still the miscreant who seeks When caught, to make a virtue of a crime.
cards.question: Creon declares, 'Now if she thus can flout authority / Unpunished, I am woman, she the man.' What does this moment in Creon's point of view reveal about the meaning of his conflict with Antigone?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Creon acknowledges that Antigone's courage deserves respect, even as he prepares to punish her.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Creon frames the conflict as a threat to his identity and power, revealing that his drive to punish Antigone is rooted in personal pride rather than purely in law.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Creon believes Antigone's sister is the more dangerous conspirator and uses this statement to shift blame away from Antigone.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Creon expresses uncertainty about whether Antigone actually broke the law, suggesting he may reconsider her punishment.

cards.standardTitle: Key literary elements add layers of meaning
cards.excerpt: OEDIPUS. Dear son of Aegeus, to the gods alone Is given immunity from eld and death; But nothing else escapes all-ruinous time. Earth’s might decays, the might of men decays, Honor grows cold, dishonor flourishes, There is no constancy ’twixt friend and friend, Or city and city; be it soon or late, Sweet turns to bitter, hate once more to love. If now ’tis sunshine betwixt Thebes and thee And not a cloud, Time in his endless course Gives birth to endless days and nights, wherein The merest nothing shall suffice to cut With serried spears your bonds of amity. Then shall my slumbering and buried corpse In its cold grave drink their warm life-blood up, If Zeus be Zeus and Phoebus still speak true. No more: ’tis ill to tear aside the veil Of mysteries; let me cease as I began: Enough if thou wilt keep thy plighted troth, Then shall thou ne’er complain that Oedipus Proved an unprofitable and thankless guest, Except the gods themselves shall play me false.
cards.whyThisWorks: Oedipus speaks in first person as a dying, prophetic figure, and his point of view—shaped by suffering, divine knowledge, and imminent death—transforms what could be political advice into a haunting warning about time, betrayal, and fate, giving the speech a tone of dark authority no outside narrator could achieve.
cards.skillStrategy: Ask yourself: because THIS character is speaking from THIS position, what do I understand or feel that I wouldn't if someone else told me the same information?
evidencePoints: Then shall my slumbering and buried corpse / In its cold grave drink their warm life-blood up
If Zeus be Zeus and Phoebus still speak true
cards.question: Oedipus delivers this speech directly to the son of Aegeus rather than having a messenger or narrator relay his warning. How does Oedipus's first-person point of view shape the meaning of his prophecy about Thebes?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Because Oedipus speaks as an outsider with no personal stake in Thebes, his warning about future betrayal sounds impartial and therefore more politically reliable.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Because Oedipus speaks as a dying man invoking his own buried corpse and the gods who have guided his suffering, his warning carries the weight of personal sacrifice and divine authority, making the threat of future bloodshed feel inevitable rather than merely possible.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Because Oedipus speaks directly to the son of Aegeus, the audience understands that the two men share equal power, so the speech reads as a negotiation between equals rather than a prophecy.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Because Oedipus refuses to reveal the full mystery behind his words, his point of view creates confusion that prevents the reader from understanding whether his warning about Thebes is genuine or a deception.

cards.standardTitle: Key literary elements add layers of meaning
cards.excerpt: JOCASTA. Then thou mayest ease thy conscience on that score. Listen and I’ll convince thee that no man Hath scot or lot in the prophetic art. Here is the proof in brief. An oracle Once came to Laius (I will not say ’Twas from the Delphic god himself, but from His ministers) declaring he was doomed To perish by the hand of his own son, A child that should be born to him by me. Now Laius—so at least report affirmed— Was murdered on a day by highwaymen, No natives, at a spot where three roads meet. As for the child, it was but three days old, When Laius, its ankles pierced and pinned Together, gave it to be cast away By others on the trackless mountain side. So then Apollo brought it not to pass The child should be his father’s murderer, Or the dread terror find accomplishment, And Laius be slain by his own son. Such was the prophet’s horoscope. O king, Regard it not. Whate’er the god deems fit To search, himself unaided will reveal.
cards.whyThisWorks: Jocasta's first-person retelling of the oracle and Laius's death creates dramatic irony—she dismisses prophecy as false while unknowingly confirming every detail that proves it true, making point of view central to meaning and tragic tension.
cards.skillStrategy: Ask yourself: what does the speaker believe, and what does the audience already know that the speaker does not? That gap is where point of view shapes meaning.
evidencePoints: I'll convince thee that no man Hath scot or lot in the prophetic art
So then Apollo brought it not to pass / The child should be his father's murderer
cards.question: Jocasta tells Oedipus the story of the oracle and Laius's death from her own point of view in order to reassure him. How does her role as the speaker shape the meaning of this moment for the audience?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Because Jocasta witnessed Laius's murder directly, her firsthand account makes the oracle seem genuinely disproven, and the audience accepts her conclusion that prophecy holds no power.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Because Jocasta believes she is disproving the oracle, she unknowingly recites every detail—the crossroads, the infant's pierced ankles, the son—that the audience recognizes as confirmation of the prophecy, creating dread beneath her confidence.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Because Jocasta speaks as a queen addressing her husband, her authoritative tone signals to the audience that her political judgment about prophecy should be trusted over religious tradition.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Because Jocasta distances herself from the oracle by noting it came from Apollo's ministers rather than the god himself, the audience understands the prophecy was never legitimate and shares her relief.

cards.standardTitle: Key literary elements add layers of meaning
cards.excerpt: OEDIPUS. Out on the twain! The thoughts and actions all Are framed and modeled on Egyptian ways. For there the men sit at the loom indoors While the wives slave abroad for daily bread. So you, my children—those whom I behooved To bear the burden, stay at home like girls, While in their stead my daughters moil and drudge, Lightening their father’s misery. The one Since first she grew from girlish feebleness To womanhood has been the old man’s guide And shared my weary wandering, roaming oft Hungry and footsore through wild forest ways, In drenching rains and under scorching suns, Careless herself of home and ease, if so Her sire might have her tender ministry. And thou, my child, whilom thou wentest forth, Eluding the Cadmeians’ vigilance, To bring thy father all the oracles Concerning Oedipus, and didst make thyself My faithful lieger, when they banished me. And now what mission summons thee from home, What news, Ismene, hast thou for thy father? This much I know, thou com’st not empty-handed, Without a warning of some new alarm.
cards.whyThisWorks: Oedipus speaks in first person as a blind, exiled father, and his point of view shapes the reader's understanding of his daughters' sacrifices as deeply personal debts rather than neutral facts, creating a tone of guilt-laden gratitude.
cards.skillStrategy: Ask yourself: because THIS character is speaking, what emotions and judgments color the information, and how would the meaning shift if someone else told it?
evidencePoints: those whom I behooved / To bear the burden, stay at home like girls
Lightening their father's misery
cards.question: Oedipus narrates his daughters' sacrifices directly to them in lines such as 'those whom I behooved / To bear the burden, stay at home like girls' and 'Lightening their father's misery.' How does Oedipus's point of view as the speaker shape the meaning of these details?

choices.label: A
choices.text: His perspective presents his sons' absence as understandable, suggesting he holds no real resentment toward them for staying home.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Because Oedipus speaks as the suffering father who owes his survival to his daughters, his account frames their hardships as personal debts he carries, filling the description of their loyalty with shame and gratitude rather than simple praise.

choices.label: C
choices.text: His role as an exiled king gives the speech an authoritative, detached tone, allowing him to judge his children's behavior without emotional involvement.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Speaking directly to Ismene causes Oedipus to focus only on her recent journey, leaving his older daughter's years of service unacknowledged and emotionally neutral.

cards.standardTitle: Key literary elements add layers of meaning
cards.excerpt: OEDIPUS. I pray thee do not wonder if the sight Of children, given o’er for lost, has made My converse somewhat long and tedious. Full well I know the joy I have of them Is due to thee, to thee and no man else; Thou wast their sole deliverer, none else. The gods deal with thee after my desire, With thee and with this land! for fear of heaven I found above all peoples most with you, And righteousness and lips that cannot lie. I speak in gratitude of what I know, For all I have I owe to thee alone. Give me thy hand, O Prince, that I may touch it, And if thou wilt permit me, kiss thy cheek. What say I? Can I wish that thou should’st touch One fallen like me to utter wretchedness, Corrupt and tainted with a thousand ills? Oh no, I would not let thee if thou would’st. They only who have known calamity Can share it. Let me greet thee where thou art, And still befriend me as thou hast till now.
cards.whyThisWorks: Oedipus speaks in first person about his own degradation, and his self-interruption—'What say I? Can I wish that thou should'st touch / One fallen like me to utter wretchedness'—reveals how his point of view as a shamed, suffering man shapes the tone of humility and self-loathing that a third-person narrator could not convey with the same immediacy.
cards.skillStrategy: Ask yourself: because THIS character is speaking, what do I feel or understand that I would not if someone else described the same moment from the outside?
evidencePoints: What say I? Can I wish that thou should'st touch / One fallen like me to utter wretchedness, / Corrupt and tainted with a thousand ills?
They only who have known calamity / Can share it.
cards.question: Read the lines: 'What say I? Can I wish that thou should'st touch / One fallen like me to utter wretchedness, / Corrupt and tainted with a thousand ills?' How does Oedipus's first-person point of view in this moment shape the reader's understanding of his condition?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Oedipus's self-address shows he is angry at the prince for offering sympathy, making the tone hostile and suspicious.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Oedipus's self-interruption reveals his inner conflict between gratitude and shame, creating a tone of painful self-awareness that makes his suffering feel immediate and personal rather than distant.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Oedipus speaks directly to the reader to explain that physical contact between royals was forbidden by Greek custom, adding historical context to the scene.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Oedipus questions the prince's sincerity, suggesting through his point of view that the prince's offer of friendship is merely a political gesture.

cards.standardTitle: Key literary elements add layers of meaning
cards.excerpt: ANTIGONE. O heed me, father, though I am young in years. Let the prince have his will and pay withal What in his eyes is service to the god; For our sake also let our brother come. If what he urges tend not to thy good He cannot surely wrest perforce thy will. To hear him then, what harm? By open words A scheme of villainy is soon bewrayed. Thou art his father, therefore canst not pay In kind a son’s most impious outrages. O listen to him; other men like thee Have thankless children and are choleric, But yielding to persuasion’s gentle spell They let their savage mood be exorcised. Look thou to the past, forget the present, think On all the woe thy sire and mother brought thee; Thence wilt thou draw this lesson without fail, Of evil passion evil is the end. Thou hast, alas, to prick thy memory, Stern monitors, these ever-sightless orbs. O yield to us; just suitors should not need To be importunate, nor he that takes A favor lack the grace to make return.
cards.whyThisWorks: Antigone speaks directly to her blind father Oedipus, and her youthful, pleading perspective shapes the tone as urgent yet tender, revealing how a daughter's point of view frames a family conflict as a matter of mercy rather than justice.
cards.skillStrategy: Ask yourself: who is speaking, what is their relationship to the situation, and how does their position change the way the moment feels or what it means?
evidencePoints: O heed me, father, though I am young in years.
Look thou to the past, forget the present, think / On all the woe thy sire and mother brought thee
cards.question: Antigone opens her speech by saying, 'O heed me, father, though I am young in years.' How does her position as a young daughter speaking to her father shape the meaning of her argument throughout the speech?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Her youth positions her as naive, so her appeal to Oedipus to forgive his son reads as misguided and ultimately undermines her credibility with the audience.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Because she speaks as a devoted child who acknowledges her own youth, her appeal carries a tone of humble urgency that frames the conflict as a family wound requiring compassion rather than punishment.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Her role as a daughter rather than a political figure means her speech focuses entirely on the gods' demands, removing any personal emotion from her argument.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Speaking as the younger sibling, she sides openly with her brother against Oedipus, creating a tone of defiance that signals she expects her father to refuse.

cards.standardTitle: Key literary elements add layers of meaning
cards.excerpt: OEDIPUS. Stern-visaged queens, since coming to this land First in your sanctuary I bent the knee, Frown not on me or Phoebus, who, when erst He told me all my miseries to come, Spake of this respite after many years, Some haven in a far-off land, a rest Vouchsafed at last by dread divinities. “There,” said he, “shalt thou round thy weary life, A blessing to the land wherein thou dwell’st, But to the land that cast thee forth, a curse.” And of my weird he promised signs should come, Earthquake, or thunderclap, or lightning flash. And now I recognize as yours the sign That led my wanderings to this your grove; Else had I never lighted on you first, A wineless man on your seat of native rock. O goddesses, fulfill Apollo’s word, Grant me some consummation of my life, If haply I appear not all too vile, A thrall to sorrow worse than any slave. Hear, gentle daughters of primeval Night, Hear, namesake of great Pallas; Athens, first Of cities, pity this dishonored shade, The ghost of him who once was Oedipus.
cards.whyThisWorks: Oedipus speaks in first person directly to the Furies, which forces readers to experience his suffering, humility, and desperate hope from inside his perspective, shaping the tone as both pitiable and spiritually charged.
cards.skillStrategy: Ask yourself: because THIS character is speaking, what do I feel and understand that I would not feel or understand if someone else described the same moment?
evidencePoints: The ghost of him who once was Oedipus.
Grant me some consummation of my life, If haply I appear not all too vile, A thrall to sorrow worse than any slave.
cards.question: Oedipus speaks this prayer in the first person, addressing the goddesses directly. How does this point of view shape the reader's understanding of his situation?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The first-person address allows Oedipus to boast about the prophecy Apollo gave him, making him appear confident that the goddesses will grant his request.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Because Oedipus speaks for himself, readers feel the full weight of his degradation and longing—he describes himself as less than a slave and as a ghost of his former self, creating a tone of desperate humility rather than heroic pride.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The first-person voice distances readers from Oedipus by focusing on divine prophecy rather than his personal suffering, making the passage feel more like a religious ritual than an emotional appeal.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Oedipus speaking directly to the goddesses reveals that he blames Apollo for his misfortunes, shifting the tone toward anger and resentment rather than sorrow.

cards.standardTitle: Paraphrase grade-level text
cards.excerpt:
CHORUS. (Str. 1) Sunbeam, of all that ever dawn upon Our seven-gated Thebes the brightest ray, O eye of golden day, How fair thy light o’er Dirce’s fountain shone, Speeding upon their headlong homeward course, Far quicker than they came, the Argive force; Putting to flight The argent shields, the host with scutcheons white. Against our land the proud invader came To vindicate fell Polyneices’ claim. Like to an eagle swooping low, On pinions white as new fall’n snow. With clanging scream, a horsetail plume his crest, The aspiring lord of Argos onward pressed.

(Ant. 1) Hovering around our city walls he waits, His spearmen raven at our seven gates. But ere a torch our crown of towers could burn, Ere they had tasted of our blood, they turn Forced by the Dragon; in their rear The din of Ares panic-struck they hear. For Zeus who hates the braggart’s boast Beheld that gold-bespangled host; As at the goal the paean they upraise, He struck them with his forked lightning blaze.

(Str. 2) To earthy from earth rebounding, down he crashed; The fire-brand from his impious hand was dashed, As like a Bacchic reveler on he came, Outbreathing hate and flame, And tottered. Elsewhere in the field, Here, there, great Area like a war-horse wheeled; Beneath his car down thrust Our foemen bit the dust.

Seven captains at our seven gates Thundered; for each a champion waits, Each left behind his armor bright, Trophy for Zeus who turns the fight; Save two alone, that ill-starred pair One mother to one father bare, Who lance in rest, one ’gainst the other Drave, and both perished, brother slain by brother.
cards.whyThisWorks: The Chorus makes a precise causal claim about Zeus's motivation and action in two lines, giving students a short, complete statement to paraphrase accurately while distractors can distort the cause, the target, or the outcome.
cards.skillStrategy: When paraphrasing a claim, keep the who, why, and what happened all intact — changing any one of those parts distorts the meaning.
evidencePoints: For Zeus who hates the braggart's boast / Beheld that gold-bespangled host
As at the goal the paean they upraise, / He struck them with his forked lightning blaze.
cards.question: Read these lines from the Chorus: 'For Zeus who hates the braggart's boast / Beheld that gold-bespangled host; / As at the goal the paean they upraise, / He struck them with his forked lightning blaze.' Which restatement most accurately preserves the meaning of this claim?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Zeus watched the Argive army march toward Thebes and struck them with lightning before they could reach the city's gates, because he favored the Theban people.

choices.label: B
choices.text: At the very moment the Argive soldiers were singing in celebration of a victory they had not yet won, Zeus — who despises arrogant boasting — struck them down with lightning.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Zeus punished the Argive army with lightning after they had already burned Thebes, because their destruction of the city offended the gods.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Zeus struck the Argive army with lightning to reward Thebes for the bravery its soldiers showed in defending the seven gates against the invaders.

cards.standardTitle: Key literary elements add layers of meaning
cards.excerpt:
Turnus takes advantage of Aeneas’s absence, fires some of his ships (which are transformed into sea nymphs,) and assaults his camp. The Trojans, reduced to the last extremities, send Ninus and Euryalus to recall Aeneas; which furnishes the poet with that admirable episode of their friendship, generosity, and the conclusion of their adventure.

While these affairs in distant places pass’d, The various Iris Juno sends with haste, To find bold Turnus, who, with anxious thought, The secret shade of his great grandsire sought. Retir’d alone she found the daring man, And op’d her rosy lips, and thus began: “What none of all the gods could grant thy vows, That, Turnus, this auspicious day bestows. Aeneas, gone to seek th’ Arcadian prince, Has left the Trojan camp without defence; And, short of succours there, employs his pains In parts remote to raise the Tuscan swains. Now snatch an hour that favours thy designs; Unite thy forces, and attack their lines.” This said, on equal wings she pois’d her weight, And form’d a radiant rainbow in her flight.
cards.whyThisWorks: Iris's speech to Turnus reveals his character through her manipulation of his ambition—she frames Aeneas's absence as a gift no god could grant, exposing Turnus as a man driven by opportunism and pride rather than honor.
cards.skillStrategy: When a character is addressed or described in a specific way, ask what that language reveals about who they are and what they value.
evidencePoints: What none of all the gods could grant thy vows, That, Turnus, this auspicious day bestows.
Retir'd alone she found the daring man
cards.question: Iris tells Turnus that 'What none of all the gods could grant thy vows, That, Turnus, this auspicious day bestows.' What does this appeal reveal about Turnus's character?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Turnus is a deeply religious man who has spent years praying to the gods for divine intervention in battle.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Turnus is driven by an intense desire for victory over Aeneas, making him vulnerable to flattery that frames opportunity as destiny.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Turnus is cautious and reluctant to act, so Iris must convince him that the gods have already decided the outcome of the battle.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Turnus distrusts the gods and requires proof of their favor before committing his forces to an attack on the Trojan camp.

cards.standardTitle: Key literary elements add layers of meaning
cards.excerpt:
Thus Turnus rav’d, and various fates revolv’d: The choice was doubtful, but the death resolv’d. And now the sword, and now the sea took place, That to revenge, and this to purge disgrace. Sometimes he thought to swim the stormy main, By stretch of arms the distant shore to gain. Thrice he the sword assay’d, and thrice the flood; But Juno, mov’d with pity, both withstood. And thrice repress’d his rage; strong gales supplied, And push’d the vessel o’er the swelling tide. At length she lands him on his native shores, And to his father’s longing arms restores.

Meantime, by Jove’s impulse, Mezentius arm’d, Succeeding Turnus, with his ardour warm’d His fainting friends, reproach’d their shameful flight, Repell’d the victors, and renew’d the fight. Against their king the Tuscan troops conspire; Such is their hate, and such their fierce desire Of wish’d revenge: on him, and him alone, All hands employ’d, and all their darts are thrown. He, like a solid rock by seas inclos’d, To raging winds and roaring waves oppos’d, From his proud summit looking down, disdains Their empty menace, and unmov’d remains.
cards.whyThisWorks: The simile comparing Mezentius to 'a solid rock by seas inclos'd' directly characterizes him as immovable and contemptuous under pressure, while his actions—rallying fleeing troops and renewing the fight—reveal a defiant, commanding nature that contrasts sharply with Turnus's wavering indecision, giving students two clear characterization moments to analyze for meaning.
cards.skillStrategy: When a character is compared to something in nature or described through their actions under pressure, ask what that comparison or action reveals about who they are and what the author wants you to think about them.
evidencePoints: He, like a solid rock by seas inclos'd, / To raging winds and roaring waves oppos'd, / From his proud summit looking down, disdains / Their empty menace, and unmov'd remains.
Mezentius arm'd, / Succeeding Turnus, with his ardour warm'd / His fainting friends, reproach'd their shameful flight, / Repell'd the victors, and renew'd the fight.
cards.question: Read the lines describing Mezentius: 'He, like a solid rock by seas inclos'd, / To raging winds and roaring waves oppos'd, / From his proud summit looking down, disdains / Their empty menace, and unmov'd remains.' What does this description reveal about Mezentius as a character?

choices.label: A
choices.text: He is isolated from his allies and has been abandoned on the battlefield, leaving him no choice but to stand his ground.

choices.label: B
choices.text: He faces overwhelming opposition with contempt and absolute resolve, suggesting a nature defined by unyielding pride rather than fear.

choices.label: C
choices.text: He is physically powerful enough to defeat the Tuscan troops on his own, which is why they resort to throwing darts at him from a distance.

choices.label: D
choices.text: He is indifferent to the battle around him because he has already accepted that he will lose, much as Turnus accepted his own fate earlier.

cards.standardTitle: Key literary elements add layers of meaning
cards.excerpt:
The Trojan chiefs behold, with rage and grief, Their slaughter’d friends, and hasten their relief. Bold Mnestheus rallies first the broken train, Whom brave Seresthus and his troop sustain. To save the living, and revenge the dead, Against one warrior’s arms all Troy they led. “O, void of sense and courage!” Mnestheus cried, “Where can you hope your coward heads to hide? Ah! where beyond these rampires can you run? One man, and in your camp inclos’d, you shun! Shall then a single sword such slaughter boast, And pass unpunish’d from a num’rous host? Forsaking honour, and renouncing fame, Your gods, your country, and your king you shame!” This just reproach their virtue does excite: They stand, they join, they thicken to the fight.

Now Turnus doubts, and yet disdains to yield, But with slow paces measures back the field, And inches to the walls, where Tiber’s tide, Washing the camp, defends the weaker side. The more he loses, they advance the more, And tread in ev’ry step he trod before. They shout: they bear him back; and, whom by might They cannot conquer, they oppress with weight.
cards.whyThisWorks: Mnestheus's speech directly shames the retreating Trojans by naming what they are abandoning—honor, fame, gods, country, and king—and the immediate result ('They stand, they join, they thicken to the fight') shows how his words function as a catalyst, revealing him as a leader whose moral authority carries more force than physical strength.
cards.skillStrategy: When a character speaks, ask what the speech reveals about who that character is and what effect it has on others—that effect is part of the meaning.
evidencePoints: "Forsaking honour, and renouncing fame, / Your gods, your country, and your king you shame!"
"This just reproach their virtue does excite: / They stand, they join, they thicken to the fight."
cards.question: Read the lines: "Forsaking honour, and renouncing fame, / Your gods, your country, and your king you shame!" followed by "This just reproach their virtue does excite: / They stand, they join, they thicken to the fight." How does this characterization of Mnestheus develop his role in the passage?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Mnestheus exposes his own fear of Turnus by urging the Trojans to retreat behind the camp's walls rather than face open battle.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Mnestheus functions as a moral authority whose appeal to shame and collective duty transforms a broken, fleeing force into a unified fighting force.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Mnestheus reveals his arrogance by taking sole credit for the Trojan resistance, overshadowing the contributions of Seresthus and his troop.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Mnestheus shows that the Trojans were already prepared to fight and needed only a signal, not genuine encouragement, to rejoin the battle.

cards.standardTitle: Key literary elements add layers of meaning
cards.excerpt:
Then Dares, Butes, Sybaris he slew, Whom o’er his neck his flound’ring courser threw. As when loud Boreas, with his blust’ring train, Stoops from above, incumbent on the main; Where’er he flies, he drives the rack before, And rolls the billows on th’ Aegaean shore: So, where resistless Turnus takes his course, The scatter’d squadrons bend before his force; His crest of horses’ hair is blown behind By adverse air, and rustles in the wind.

This haughty Phegeus saw with high disdain, And, as the chariot roll’d along the plain, Light from the ground he leapt, and seiz’d the rein. Thus hung in air, he still retain’d his hold, The coursers frighted, and their course controll’d. The lance of Turnus reach’d him as he hung, And pierc’d his plated arms, but pass’d along, And only raz’d the skin. He turn’d, and held Against his threat’ning foe his ample shield; Then call’d for aid: but, while he cried in vain, The chariot bore him backward on the plain. He lies revers’d; the victor king descends, And strikes so justly where his helmet ends, He lops the head. The Latian fields are drunk With streams that issue from the bleeding trunk.
cards.whyThisWorks: Phegeus's bold leap onto Turnus's chariot followed by his desperate cry for aid reveals a character whose courage collapses into helplessness, showing how a sequence of actions can expose the gap between a warrior's ambition and his fate.
cards.skillStrategy: Track what a character does AND what happens next — the contrast between a bold action and its outcome often reveals deeper meaning about who that character really is.
evidencePoints: Light from the ground he leapt, and seiz'd the rein.
Then call'd for aid: but, while he cried in vain, The chariot bore him backward on the plain.
cards.question: Read the following lines from the second paragraph: 'Light from the ground he leapt, and seiz'd the rein' and 'Then call'd for aid: but, while he cried in vain.' What do Phegeus's actions in these two moments reveal about his character?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Phegeus is a coward who attacks Turnus only because he believes Turnus is already weakened from earlier battles.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Phegeus possesses genuine courage, but his daring act of seizing the reins ultimately cannot save him, exposing the futility of individual bravery against an unstoppable force.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Phegeus acts out of loyalty to his fallen comrades Dares, Butes, and Sybaris, making his death a deliberate sacrifice rather than a defeat.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Phegeus's leap onto the chariot shows reckless pride rather than courage, and his call for aid proves he never intended to fight Turnus alone.

cards.standardTitle: Key literary elements add layers of meaning
cards.excerpt: Soothing his courage with a gentle stroke, The steed seem’d sensible, while thus he spoke: “O Rhoebus, we have liv’d too long for me— If life and long were terms that could agree! This day thou either shalt bring back the head And bloody trophies of the Trojan dead; This day thou either shalt revenge my woe, For murder’d Lausus, on his cruel foe; Or, if inexorable fate deny Our conquest, with thy conquer’d master die: For, after such a lord, I rest secure, Thou wilt no foreign reins, or Trojan load endure.” He said; and straight th’ officious courser kneels, To take his wonted weight. His hands he fills With pointed jav’lins; on his head he lac’d His glitt’ring helm, which terribly was grac’d With waving horsehair, nodding from afar; Then spurr’d his thund’ring steed amidst the war. Love, anguish, wrath, and grief, to madness wrought, Despair, and secret shame, and conscious thought Of inborn worth, his lab’ring soul oppress’d, Roll’d in his eyes, and rag’d within his breast. Then loud he call’d Aeneas thrice by name: The loud repeated voice to glad Aeneas came. “Great Jove,” he said, “and the far-shooting god, Inspire thy mind to make thy challenge good!” He spoke no more; but hasten’d, void of fear, And threaten’d with his long protended spear.
cards.whyThisWorks: Mezentius's speech to his horse Rhoebus—offering the horse a binary fate of victory or shared death—combined with the narrator's catalog of emotions ('Love, anguish, wrath, and grief, to madness wrought') reveals a character driven by grief and honor rather than rational strategy, showing how speech and description together deepen characterization.
cards.skillStrategy: When a character speaks or acts, ask what that moment reveals about who they are inside—look for the emotion or value driving the behavior, not just the behavior itself.
evidencePoints: Or, if inexorable fate deny / Our conquest, with thy conquer'd master die
Love, anguish, wrath, and grief, to madness wrought, / Despair, and secret shame, and conscious thought / Of inborn worth, his lab'ring soul oppress'd
cards.question: In the excerpt, Mezentius tells his horse Rhoebus, 'Or, if inexorable fate deny / Our conquest, with thy conquer'd master die.' What does this declaration, combined with the narrator's description of his 'lab'ring soul,' reveal about Mezentius as a character?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Mezentius is a calculating character who weighs the odds before calling Aeneas, showing strategy matters more than grief.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Mezentius is consumed by grief and wounded pride, so victory over Aeneas or death beside Rhoebus both seem acceptable to him.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Mezentius is mainly motivated by loyalty to the Trojan dead, so he asks Rhoebus to carry him safely out of battle.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Mezentius speaks to Rhoebus to calm the horse's fear before battle, showing that his concern for the animal outweighs his desire for personal revenge against Aeneas.

cards.standardTitle: Key literary elements add layers of meaning
cards.excerpt:
Within the space, an olive tree had stood, A sacred shade, a venerable wood, For vows to Faunus paid, the Latins’ guardian god. Here hung the vests, and tablets were engrav’d, Of sinking mariners from shipwreck sav’d. With heedless hands the Trojans fell’d the tree, To make the ground enclos’d for combat free. Deep in the root, whether by fate, or chance, Or erring haste, the Trojan drove his lance; Then stoop’d, and tugg’d with force immense, to free Th’ incumber’d spear from the tenacious tree; That, whom his fainting limbs pursued in vain, His flying weapon might from far attain.

Confus’d with fear, bereft of human aid, Then Turnus to the gods, and first to Faunus pray’d: “O Faunus, pity! and thou Mother Earth, Where I thy foster son receiv’d my birth, Hold fast the steel! If my religious hand Your plant has honour’d, which your foes profan’d, Propitious hear my pious pray’r!” He said, Nor with successless vows invok’d their aid. Th’ incumbent hero wrench’d, and pull’d, and strain’d; But still the stubborn earth the steel detain’d. Juturna took her time; and, while in vain He strove, assum’d Meticus’ form again, And, in that imitated shape, restor’d To the despairing prince his Daunian sword. The Queen of Love, who, with disdain and grief, Saw the bold nymph afford this prompt relief, T’ assert her offspring with a greater deed, From the tough root the ling’ring weapon freed.
cards.whyThisWorks: Turnus's desperate prayer to Faunus—acknowledging the Trojans' desecration of the sacred tree while claiming his own piety—reveals his character as a man who appeals to divine justice when human strength fails, adding meaning to his doomed struggle.
cards.skillStrategy: When a character speaks or acts under pressure, ask what that moment exposes about who they are and what they value.
evidencePoints: Confus'd with fear, bereft of human aid, Then Turnus to the gods, and first to Faunus pray'd
If my religious hand Your plant has honour'd, which your foes profan'd, Propitious hear my pious pray'r!
cards.question: In the second paragraph, Turnus prays to Faunus, saying his hand 'honour'd' the sacred plant 'which your foes profan'd.' What does this prayer reveal about Turnus's character?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Turnus is confident in his own physical strength and calls on the gods only as a formality before freeing the spear himself.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Turnus claims moral superiority over his enemies to justify divine help, revealing that he sees his survival as righteous and deserved.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Turnus blames the Trojans for the loss of his sword and prays to Faunus to punish them for cutting down the sacred tree.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Turnus's prayer shows that he has accepted defeat and is asking the gods for a peaceful end to the battle rather than continued fighting.

cards.standardTitle: Key literary elements add layers of meaning
cards.excerpt:
He said; and, pressing onward thro’ the crew, Pois’d in his lifted arm, his lance he threw. The winged weapon, whistling in the wind, Came driving on, nor miss’d the mark design’d. At once the cornel rattled in the skies; At once tumultuous shouts and clamours rise. Nine brothers in a goodly band there stood, Born of Arcadian mix’d with Tuscan blood, Gylippus’ sons: the fatal jav’lin flew, Aim’d at the midmost of the friendly crew. A passage thro’ the jointed arms it found, Just where the belt was to the body bound, And struck the gentle youth extended on the ground. Then, fir’d with pious rage, the gen’rous train Run madly forward to revenge the slain. And some with eager haste their jav’lins throw; And some with sword in hand assault the foe.

The wish’d insult the Latine troops embrace, And meet their ardour in the middle space. The Trojans, Tuscans, and Arcadian line, With equal courage obviate their design. Peace leaves the violated fields, and hate Both armies urges to their mutual fate. With impious haste their altars are o’erturn’d, The sacrifice half-broil’d, and half-unburn’d. Thick storms of steel from either army fly, And clouds of clashing darts obscure the sky; Brands from the fire are missive weapons made, With chargers, bowls, and all the priestly trade. Latinus, frighted, hastens from the fray, And bears his unregarded gods away. These on their horses vault; those yoke the car; The rest, with swords on high, run headlong to the war.
cards.whyThisWorks: The phrase 'fir'd with pious rage' applied to the 'gen'rous train' directly characterizes the Trojans' response to the slain youth, revealing how grief and loyalty transform into violent action and adding moral complexity to the outbreak of war.
cards.skillStrategy: When a character or group acts, look for the specific words the author uses to describe their motivation — those words reveal what the author wants you to understand about who they are.
evidencePoints: Then, fir'd with pious rage, the gen'rous train / Run madly forward to revenge the slain.
struck the gentle youth extended on the ground
cards.question: In the first paragraph, the narrator describes the companions as 'fir'd with pious rage' after the youth is struck down. What does this characterization reveal about the companions and the meaning of their actions?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Their rage is reckless and selfish, showing that they care more about personal glory than about the fallen youth.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Their fury is rooted in loyalty and duty, suggesting that their rush to violence is portrayed as morally justified grief rather than mere aggression.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Their anger is directed at Latinus, revealing that they blame him personally for ordering the attack on the youth.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Their response shows cowardice, because they throw javelins from a distance rather than engaging the enemy directly with swords.

cards.standardTitle: Key literary elements add layers of meaning
cards.excerpt: The pious prince was seiz’d with sudden fear; Mute was his tongue, and upright stood his hair. Revolving in his mind the stern command, He longs to fly, and loathes the charming land. What should he say? or how should he begin? What course, alas! remains to steer between Th’ offended lover and the pow’rful queen? This way and that he turns his anxious mind, And all expedients tries, and none can find. Fix’d on the deed, but doubtful of the means, After long thought, to this advice he leans: Three chiefs he calls, commands them to repair The fleet, and ship their men with silent care; Some plausible pretence he bids them find, To colour what in secret he design’d. Himself, meantime, the softest hours would choose, Before the love-sick lady heard the news; And move her tender mind, by slow degrees, To suffer what the sov’reign pow’r decrees: Jove will inspire him, when, and what to say. They hear with pleasure, and with haste obey.
cards.whyThisWorks: Aeneas's decision to secretly prepare his fleet while planning to gently break the news to Dido—rather than confronting her directly—reveals his conflicted nature as a man torn between divine duty and personal loyalty, making his characterization rich with moral complexity.
cards.skillStrategy: When a character chooses a roundabout or secretive action instead of a direct one, ask yourself what that choice reveals about who they are and what they value.
evidencePoints: Some plausible pretence he bids them find, / To colour what in secret he design'd.
And move her tender mind, by slow degrees, / To suffer what the sov'reign pow'r decrees
cards.question: In the excerpt, Aeneas orders his men to prepare the fleet in secret and plans to break the news to Dido gradually rather than telling her the truth directly. What does this behavior reveal about his character?

choices.label: A
choices.text: He is indifferent to Dido's feelings and focuses entirely on obeying Jupiter's command without hesitation.

choices.label: B
choices.text: He is caught between his sense of duty and his concern for Dido, choosing deception and delay as a way to manage both obligations at once.

choices.label: C
choices.text: He doubts whether Jupiter's command is truly meant for him and stalls in hopes that the gods will change their decree.

choices.label: D
choices.text: He fears his own men will refuse to leave Carthage, so he hides his plans to prevent a rebellion within the fleet.

cards.standardTitle: Key literary elements add layers of meaning
cards.excerpt: Turnus a while stood mute, with glad surprise, And on the fierce Virago fix’d his eyes; Then thus return’d: “O grace of Italy, With what becoming thanks can I reply? Not only words lie lab’ring in my breast, But thought itself is by thy praise oppress’d. Yet rob me not of all; but let me join My toils, my hazard, and my fame, with thine. The Trojan, not in stratagem unskill’d, Sends his light horse before to scour the field: Himself, thro’ steep ascents and thorny brakes, A larger compass to the city takes. This news my scouts confirm, and I prepare To foil his cunning, and his force to dare; With chosen foot his passage to forelay, And place an ambush in the winding way. Thou, with thy Volscians, face the Tuscan horse; The brave Messapus shall thy troops enforce With those of Tibur, and the Latian band, Subjected all to thy supreme command.” This said, he warns Messapus to the war, Then ev’ry chief exhorts with equal care. All thus encourag’d, his own troops he joins, And hastes to prosecute his deep designs.
cards.whyThisWorks: Turnus's shift from speechless admiration to confident tactical command—assigning roles, setting ambushes, and personally joining his troops—reveals a leader whose pride and military shrewdness define his character and drive the conflict forward.
cards.skillStrategy: When a character moves from one emotional state to action, ask what that shift tells you about who they are and what they value.
evidencePoints: Turnus a while stood mute, with glad surprise
With chosen foot his passage to forelay, And place an ambush in the winding way
cards.question: Read the following passage moment: 'Turnus a while stood mute, with glad surprise' and then consider how Turnus behaves for the rest of the excerpt. What does this shift from silence to detailed military planning reveal about Turnus's character?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Turnus is so overwhelmed by the Virago's praise that he loses confidence in his own judgment and defers all military decisions to Messapus.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Turnus's momentary speechlessness gives way to sharp tactical thinking and decisive command, showing that beneath his emotional response lies a calculating and ambitious warrior.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Turnus is primarily motivated by gratitude toward the Virago, and his military orders are meant to honor her rather than to defeat the Trojans.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Turnus's silence reveals that he distrusts the Virago's praise and is secretly planning to act without her knowledge.

cards.standardTitle: Key literary elements add layers of meaning
cards.excerpt: Now, where Messapus quarter’d, they arrive. The fires were fainting there, and just alive; The warrior-horses, tied in order, fed. Nisus observ’d the discipline, and said: “Our eager thirst of blood may both betray; And see the scatter’d streaks of dawning day, Foe to nocturnal thefts. No more, my friend; Here let our glutted execution end. A lane thro’ slaughter’d bodies we have made.” The bold Euryalus, tho’ loth, obey’d. Of arms, and arras, and of plate, they find A precious load; but these they leave behind. Yet, fond of gaudy spoils, the boy would stay To make the rich caparison his prey, Which on the steed of conquer’d Rhamnes lay. Nor did his eyes less longingly behold The girdle-belt, with nails of burnish’d gold. This present Caedicus the rich bestow’d On Remulus, when friendship first they vow’d, And, absent, join’d in hospitable ties: He, dying, to his heir bequeath’d the prize; Till, by the conqu’ring Ardean troops oppress’d, He fell; and they the glorious gift possess’d. These glitt’ring spoils (now made the victor’s gain) He to his body suits, but suits in vain: Messapus’ helm he finds among the rest, And laces on, and wears the waving crest. Proud of their conquest, prouder of their prey, They leave the camp, and take the ready way.
cards.whyThisWorks: Euryalus's decision to linger for glittering spoils despite Nisus's warning directly characterizes him as impulsive and dangerously vain, adding tragic irony and foreshadowing to the scene.
cards.skillStrategy: When a character acts against advice or better judgment, ask what that choice reveals about who they are and what consequences it might bring.
evidencePoints: fond of gaudy spoils, the boy would stay / To make the rich caparison his prey
Proud of their conquest, prouder of their prey, / They leave the camp, and take the ready way.
cards.question: Nisus warns that dawning light is 'Foe to nocturnal thefts' and urges an end to their raid, yet Euryalus lingers to collect armor and a plumed helmet. What does Euryalus's behavior in this moment reveal about his character?

choices.label: A
choices.text: He is calculating and patient, waiting for the right moment to secure supplies that will help both warriors survive the journey ahead.

choices.label: B
choices.text: He is driven by vanity and youthful recklessness, allowing the lure of shining prizes to override the caution that could protect his life.

choices.label: C
choices.text: He disobeys Nisus to prove his own leadership, showing that he no longer trusts the older warrior's judgment in dangerous situations.

choices.label: D
choices.text: He is motivated by loyalty to fallen comrades, collecting the armor of Rhamnes and Remulus as a tribute to those who died in battle.

cards.standardTitle: Key literary elements add layers of meaning
