choices.text: Aeneas hews through enemy fighters to reach Turnus after learning that his friends stand on the brink of ruin without his help.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Sad spectators, rather than uncertain rumor, bring Aeneas the news of Pallas's death on the battlefield.

cards.standardTitle: Epic poetry: characters, structures, and themes
cards.excerpt:
Messapus, eager to confound the peace, Spurr’d his hot courser thro’ the fighting press, At King Aulestes, by his purple known A Tuscan prince, and by his regal crown; And, with a shock encount’ring, bore him down. Backward he fell; and, as his fate design’d, The ruins of an altar were behind: There, pitching on his shoulders and his head, Amid the scatt’ring fires he lay supinely spread. The beamy spear, descending from above, His cuirass pierc’d, and thro’ his body drove. Then, with a scornful smile, the victor cries: “The gods have found a fitter sacrifice.” Greedy of spoils, th’ Italians strip the dead Of his rich armour, and uncrown his head.

Priest Corynaeus, arm’d his better hand, From his own altar, with a blazing brand; And, as Ebusus with a thund’ring pace Advanc’d to battle, dash’d it on his face: His bristly beard shines out with sudden fires; The crackling crop a noisome scent expires. Following the blow, he seiz’d his curling crown With his left hand; his other cast him down. The prostrate body with his knees he press’d, And plung’d his holy poniard in his breast.
cards.whyThisWorks: Messapus's taunt 'The gods have found a fitter sacrifice' frames Aulestes's death as divinely ordained, showing how supernatural will shapes the action and reinforces a theme of fate overriding human agency.
cards.skillStrategy: When a character invokes the gods to explain an event, ask yourself: does this suggest the gods are directing the outcome, and how does that change what the moment means?
evidencePoints: as his fate design'd, / The ruins of an altar were behind
The gods have found a fitter sacrifice.
cards.question: In the first paragraph, Messapus declares, 'The gods have found a fitter sacrifice.' How does this moment of divine framing shape the meaning of Aulestes's death?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Messapus claims personal credit for defeating Aulestes, presenting the kill as proof of his own superior skill in battle.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Aulestes's fall onto the altar ruins is recast as a divinely arranged sacrifice, suggesting that fate, not mere combat, determined his end.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The taunt reveals that Messapus is a priest who believes every enemy slain in war must be formally offered to the gods.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The remark shows that the Italians strip the dead out of religious duty, honoring the gods by taking Aulestes's armor and crown.

cards.standardTitle: Text structure and feature purpose
cards.excerpt:
Turnus two brothers from the Lycian shore, And from Apollo’s fane to battle sent, O’erthrew; nor Phoebus could their fate prevent. Peaceful Menoetes after these he kill’d, Who long had shunn’d the dangers of the field: On Lerna’s lake a silent life he led, And with his nets and angle earn’d his bread; Nor pompous cares, nor palaces, he knew, But wisely from th’ infectious world withdrew: Poor was his house; his father’s painful hand Discharg’d his rent, and plow’d another’s land.

As flames among the lofty woods are thrown On diff’rent sides, and both by winds are blown; The laurels crackle in the sputt’ring fire; The frighted sylvans from their shades retire: Or as two neighb’ring torrents fall from high; Rapid they run; the foamy waters fry; They roll to sea with unresisted force, And down the rocks precipitate their course: Not with less rage the rival heroes take Their diff’rent ways, nor less destruction make. With spears afar, with swords at hand, they strike; And zeal of slaughter fires their souls alike. Like them, their dauntless men maintain the field; And hearts are pierc’d, unknowing how to yield: They blow for blow return, and wound for wound; And heaps of bodies raise the level ground.
cards.whyThisWorks: The two paragraphs offer a clear structural contrast: the first establishes individual deaths including a peaceful man's biography, while the second pivots to extended similes of fire and torrents to amplify collective battlefield destruction, giving students a concrete example of a paragraph that extends and intensifies a prior idea.
cards.skillStrategy: Ask yourself: does this paragraph start something new, push the previous idea further, or wrap it up? Look for signal words, new images, or repeated ideas that show the relationship.
evidencePoints: As flames among the lofty woods are thrown / On diff'rent sides, and both by winds are blown
Not with less rage the rival heroes take / Their diff'rent ways, nor less destruction make
cards.question: The second paragraph opens with the simile 'As flames among the lofty woods are thrown / On diff'rent sides, and both by winds are blown' and closes with 'heaps of bodies raise the level ground.' What is the job of this paragraph in relation to the killing described in the first paragraph?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The second paragraph shifts focus away from Turnus entirely, introducing a new set of unnamed warriors whose fate contrasts with Menoetes' peaceful life.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The second paragraph extends the destruction established in the first by layering fire and torrent similes onto the battle, building the violence from individual deaths to a scene of mass slaughter.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The second paragraph concludes the conflict by showing that both sides have exhausted themselves, with 'heaps of bodies' signaling the battle's end.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The second paragraph contrasts the rage of the rival heroes with the quiet, withdrawn life of Menoetes described in the first paragraph, arguing that peaceful men are superior to warriors.

cards.standardTitle: Central idea and supporting evidence
cards.excerpt:
The pious Trojan then his jav’lin sent; The shield gave way; thro’ treble plates it went Of solid brass, of linen trebly roll’d, And three bull hides which round the buckler fold. All these it pass’d, resistless in the course, Transpierc’d his thigh, and spent its dying force. The gaping wound gush’d out a crimson flood. The Trojan, glad with sight of hostile blood, His falchion drew, to closer fight address’d, And with new force his fainting foe oppress’d.

His father’s peril Lausus view’d with grief; He sigh’d, he wept, he ran to his relief. And here, heroic youth, ’tis here I must To thy immortal memory be just, And sing an act so noble and so new, Posterity will scarce believe ’tis true. Pain’d with his wound, and useless for the fight, The father sought to save himself by flight: Encumber’d, slow he dragg’d the spear along, Which pierc’d his thigh, and in his buckler hung. The pious youth, resolv’d on death, below The lifted sword springs forth to face the foe; Protects his parent, and prevents the blow. Shouts of applause ran ringing thro’ the field, To see the son the vanquish’d father shield. All, fir’d with gen’rous indignation, strive, And with a storm of darts to distance drive The Trojan chief, who, held at bay from far, On his Vulcanian orb sustain’d the war.
cards.whyThisWorks: The narrator explicitly interrupts the battle narrative to announce he must honor Lausus's act as 'so noble and so new / Posterity will scarce believe 'tis true,' giving students a clear authorial signal to identify the central idea rather than a topic or isolated detail.
cards.skillStrategy: When a narrator pauses the action to make a direct claim about what matters most, that claim is your guide to the central idea of the passage.
evidencePoints: heroic youth, 'tis here I must / To thy immortal memory be just, / And sing an act so noble and so new, / Posterity will scarce believe 'tis true
The pious youth, resolv'd on death, below / The lifted sword springs forth to face the foe; / Protects his parent, and prevents the blow.
cards.question: The narrator interrupts the battle to declare he must honor Lausus's 'immortal memory' for 'an act so noble and so new.' What central idea do both paragraphs develop through this claim and the events surrounding it?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Aeneas's wound of Mezentius is the turning point of the battle, proving that even the most heavily armored warrior can be defeated by a skilled opponent.

choices.label: B
choices.text: A son's choice to step in front of a raised sword to shield his wounded father is an act of devotion so remarkable that it demands to be preserved in memory.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The soldiers on the field are driven by indignation at the sight of an unfair fight, and their loyalty to their own side determines the outcome of the battle.

choices.label: D
choices.text: War forces fathers and sons into impossible situations, and neither Mezentius nor Lausus is able to escape the suffering that combat brings to both of them.

cards.standardTitle: Rhetorical appeals and author purpose
cards.excerpt: He said, and rose; as holy zeal inspires, He rakes hot embers, and renews the fires; His country gods and Vesta then adores With cakes and incense, and their aid implores. Next, for his friends and royal host he sent, Reveal’d his vision, and the gods’ intent, With his own purpose. All, without delay, The will of Jove, and his desires obey. They list with women each degenerate name, Who dares not hazard life for future fame. These they cashier: the brave remaining few, Oars, banks, and cables, half consum’d, renew. The prince designs a city with the plow; The lots their sev’ral tenements allow. This part is nam’d from Ilium, that from Troy, And the new king ascends the throne with joy; A chosen senate from the people draws; Appoints the judges, and ordains the laws. Then, on the top of Eryx, they begin A rising temple to the Paphian queen. Anchises, last, is honour’d as a god; A priest is added, annual gifts bestow’d, And groves are planted round his blest abode. Nine days they pass in feasts, their temples crown’d; And fumes of incense in the fanes abound. Then from the south arose a gentle breeze That curl’d the smoothness of the glassy seas; The rising winds a ruffling gale afford, And call the merry mariners aboard.
cards.whyThisWorks: Virgil's closing personification of the wind as something that 'call[s] the merry mariners aboard,' paired with the image of a 'gentle breeze' that 'curl'd the smoothness of the glassy seas,' gives teachers a clear, passage-specific moment to teach how figurative language signals divine favor and authorial purpose.
cards.skillStrategy: When you spot figurative language near the end of a passage, ask what feeling or idea the author is reinforcing—then check how that figure connects to the events just described.
evidencePoints: a gentle breeze / That curl'd the smoothness of the glassy seas
The rising winds a ruffling gale afford, / And call the merry mariners aboard
cards.question: In the closing lines, Virgil personifies the wind as something that 'call[s] the merry mariners aboard' and pairs it with 'a gentle breeze / That curl'd the smoothness of the glassy seas.' What purpose do these two figurative details serve together, coming directly after nine days of feasts, the founding of the city, and the honors given to Anchises?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The wind 'calling' the mariners suggests the sailors are reluctant to leave after nine days of feasting, while the 'glassy seas' warn of dangerous calm before an approaching storm that will punish the community's pride.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The personification of the wind as an inviting voice, paired with the serene image of 'the glassy seas,' presents the departure as peaceful and divinely sanctioned, suggesting the gods have rewarded the community's rituals, city-founding, and honors to Anchises.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The shift from 'a gentle breeze' to 'rising winds' uses contrast to foreshadow hardship ahead, and the 'glassy seas' ironically highlight the fragility of the joy surrounding the new city's founding and the laws Aeneas ordained.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The 'glassy seas' and the wind 'calling' the mariners emphasize the sailors' eagerness to escape the new city, implying that the nine days of feasts and the senate Aeneas appointed were unwelcome obligations rather than genuine celebrations.

cards.standardTitle: Key literary elements add layers of meaning
cards.excerpt: To these the hero thus his thoughts explain’d, In words which gen’ral approbation gain’d: “One common largess is for all design’d, The vanquish’d and the victor shall be join’d, Two darts of polish’d steel and Gnosian wood, A silver-studded ax alike bestow’d. The foremost three have olive wreaths decreed: The first of these obtains a stately steed, Adorn’d with trappings; and the next in fame, The quiver of an Amazonian dame, With feather’d Thracian arrows well supplied: A golden belt shall gird his manly side, Which with a sparkling diamond shall be tied. The third this Grecian helmet shall content.” He said. To their appointed base they went; With beating hearts th’ expected sign receive, And, starting all at once, the barrier leave. Spread out, as on the winged winds, they flew, And seiz’d the distant goal with greedy view. Shot from the crowd, swift Nisus all o’erpass’d; Nor storms, nor thunder, equal half his haste. The next, but tho’ the next, yet far disjoin’d, Came Salius, and Euryalus behind; Then Helymus, whom young Diores plied, Step after step, and almost side by side, His shoulders pressing; and, in longer space, Had won, or left at least a dubious race.
cards.whyThisWorks: Aeneas's speech distributing equal prizes to both victors and the vanquished, combined with the vivid physical description of Nisus surging ahead 'as on the winged winds,' allows students to analyze how a character's words and actions together reveal his values of fairness and heroic generosity.
cards.skillStrategy: When a character speaks and then acts, ask yourself: what do the words reveal about who this person is, and does the action that follows confirm or complicate that?
evidencePoints: One common largess is for all design'd, The vanquish'd and the victor shall be join'd
Shot from the crowd, swift Nisus all o'erpass'd; Nor storms, nor thunder, equal half his haste.
cards.question: In the excerpt, Aeneas declares, 'One common largess is for all design'd, / The vanquish'd and the victor shall be join'd.' What does this speech reveal about Aeneas's character?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Aeneas is indifferent to the outcome of the race, since he distributes identical prizes to every competitor regardless of their placement.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Aeneas values the honor and unity of his people above individual triumph, ensuring that even those who lose the race are recognized and rewarded.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Aeneas doubts the skill of his competitors and offers prizes to the defeated runners because he expects the race to end without a clear winner.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Aeneas is primarily concerned with displaying his own wealth, using the elaborate prizes—steeds, quivers, and golden belts—to impress the crowd rather than reward effort.

cards.standardTitle: Theme development across a literary text
cards.excerpt:
Then Dares, Butes, Sybaris he slew, Whom o’er his neck his flound’ring courser threw. As when loud Boreas, with his blust’ring train, Stoops from above, incumbent on the main; Where’er he flies, he drives the rack before, And rolls the billows on th’ Aegaean shore: So, where resistless Turnus takes his course, The scatter’d squadrons bend before his force; His crest of horses’ hair is blown behind By adverse air, and rustles in the wind.

This haughty Phegeus saw with high disdain, And, as the chariot roll’d along the plain, Light from the ground he leapt, and seiz’d the rein. Thus hung in air, he still retain’d his hold, The coursers frighted, and their course controll’d. The lance of Turnus reach’d him as he hung, And pierc’d his plated arms, but pass’d along, And only raz’d the skin. He turn’d, and held Against his threat’ning foe his ample shield; Then call’d for aid: but, while he cried in vain, The chariot bore him backward on the plain. He lies revers’d; the victor king descends, And strikes so justly where his helmet ends, He lops the head. The Latian fields are drunk With streams that issue from the bleeding trunk.
cards.whyThisWorks: Phegeus's sequence of brave actions—leaping, seizing the reins, holding his shield—followed by his beheading directly evidences the theme that individual courage cannot overcome an unstoppable superior force.
cards.skillStrategy: Find the moment where a character's brave effort still ends in defeat, and ask what that outcome reveals about the text's central theme.
evidencePoints: Light from the ground he leapt, and seiz'd the rein
He lops the head.
cards.question: Phegeus leaps from the ground, seizes the reins, and holds his shield against Turnus—yet the passage ends with 'He lops the head.' Which detail most directly supports the theme that courage cannot overcome a superior force?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Phegeus calls for aid while hanging from the chariot, showing that teamwork, not individual bravery, determines survival in battle.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Phegeus leaps, seizes the reins, and holds his shield, yet the chariot drags him backward and Turnus beheads him, showing bravery cannot change the outcome.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Turnus's lance pierces Phegeus's plated arms but only grazes the skin, showing that Phegeus's armor gives him a meaningful advantage in the fight.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Phegeus holds his ample shield against Turnus, showing that a soldier's best defense is to protect himself rather than attack.

cards.standardTitle: Epic poetry: characters, structures, and themes
cards.excerpt:
A thousand various thoughts his soul confound; He star’d about, nor aid nor issue found; His own men stop the pass, and his own walls surround. Once more he pauses, and looks out again, And seeks the goddess charioteer in vain. Trembling he views the thund’ring chief advance, And brandishing aloft the deadly lance: Amaz’d he cow’rs beneath his conqu’ring foe, Forgets to ward, and waits the coming blow. Astonish’d while he stands, and fix’d with fear, Aim’d at his shield he sees th’ impending spear.

The hero measur’d first, with narrow view, The destin’d mark; and, rising as he threw, With its full swing the fatal weapon flew. Not with less rage the rattling thunder falls, Or stones from batt’ring-engines break the walls: Swift as a whirlwind, from an arm so strong, The lance drove on, and bore the death along. Naught could his sev’nfold shield the prince avail, Nor aught, beneath his arms, the coat of mail: It pierc’d thro’ all, and with a grisly wound Transfix’d his thigh, and doubled him to ground. With groans the Latins rend the vaulted sky: Woods, hills, and valleys, to the voice reply.
cards.whyThisWorks: The excerpt depicts Aeneas as a divinely empowered instrument of fate—his lance is described as 'fatal' and 'destin'd,' and his throw is compared to thunder, signaling that supernatural force, not mere human skill, drives the killing blow and fulfills the epic's larger theme of fated Roman destiny.
cards.skillStrategy: When identifying divine intervention in epic poetry, look for words like 'destin'd' or 'fatal' that signal a god or fate is directing the action, then ask how that force changes what a character can or cannot do.
evidencePoints: The hero measur'd first, with narrow view, / The destin'd mark
Not with less rage the rattling thunder falls
cards.question: In the second paragraph, the narrator describes Aeneas's lance as aimed at 'the destin'd mark' and compares its force to 'rattling thunder.' How do these details shape the theme of the passage?

choices.label: A
choices.text: They emphasize Aeneas's years of military training, suggesting that human discipline alone determines the outcome of the duel.

choices.label: B
choices.text: They present the killing blow as fated and divinely sanctioned, suggesting that supernatural forces—not individual choice—decide the duel's outcome.

choices.label: C
choices.text: They highlight Turnus's failure to use his shield properly, placing the blame for his defeat entirely on his own cowardice in the first paragraph.

choices.label: D
choices.text: They show that Aeneas acts out of personal rage toward Turnus, making revenge rather than fate the central force driving the action.

cards.standardTitle: Text structure and feature purpose
cards.excerpt:
What should he do! Nor arts nor arms avail; And various cares in vain his mind assail. The great Messapus, thund’ring thro’ the field, In his left hand two pointed jav’lins held: Encount’ring on the prince, one dart he drew, And with unerring aim and utmost vigour threw. Aeneas saw it come, and, stooping low Beneath his buckler, shunn’d the threat’ning blow. The weapon hiss’d above his head, and tore The waving plume which on his helm he wore. Forced by this hostile act, and fir’d with spite, That flying Turnus still declin’d the fight, The Prince, whose piety had long repell’d His inborn ardour, now invades the field; Invokes the pow’rs of violated peace, Their rites and injur’d altars to redress; Then, to his rage abandoning the rein, With blood and slaughter’d bodies fills the plain.

What god can tell, what numbers can display, The various labours of that fatal day; What chiefs and champions fell on either side, In combat slain, or by what deaths they died; Whom Turnus, whom the Trojan hero kill’d; Who shar’d the fame and fortune of the field! Jove, could’st thou view, and not avert thy sight, Two jarring nations join’d in cruel fight, Whom leagues of lasting love so shortly shall unite!
cards.whyThisWorks: The two paragraphs have clearly distinct jobs—the first narrates Aeneas's transformation from restrained warrior to rage-driven fighter, while the second steps back from the action to lament the unknowable scale of the carnage—making the structural shift between them a strong test of paragraph-job analysis.
cards.skillStrategy: Ask yourself: does this paragraph push the story forward, or does it pause the story to reflect, question, or comment on what just happened?
evidencePoints: With blood and slaughter'd bodies fills the plain.
What god can tell, what numbers can display, / The various labours of that fatal day
cards.question: The first paragraph ends with the line 'With blood and slaughter'd bodies fills the plain.' The second paragraph then opens with 'What god can tell, what numbers can display, / The various labours of that fatal day.' What is the job of the second paragraph in relation to the first?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The second paragraph extends the first by cataloguing the specific warriors Aeneas and Turnus each kill during the battle.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The second paragraph shifts away from the narrative of Aeneas's rage to a mournful reflection on the unknowable scale of the slaughter and the tragedy of two nations that will one day be united.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The second paragraph contrasts Turnus's battlefield deeds with Aeneas's, reversing the focus on Aeneas established at the close of the first paragraph.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The second paragraph concludes the episode by confirming that Aeneas's decision to abandon piety was the turning point that determined the battle's outcome.

cards.standardTitle: Central idea and supporting evidence
cards.excerpt:
Now with full force his spear young Pallas threw, And, having thrown, his shining falchion drew The steel just graz’d along the shoulder joint, And mark’d it slightly with the glancing point, Fierce Turnus first to nearer distance drew, And pois’d his pointed spear, before he threw: Then, as the winged weapon whizz’d along, “See now,” said he, “whose arm is better strung.” The spear kept on the fatal course, unstay’d By plates of ir’n, which o’er the shield were laid: Thro’ folded brass and tough bull hides it pass’d, His corslet pierc’d, and reach’d his heart at last. In vain the youth tugs at the broken wood; The soul comes issuing with the vital blood: He falls; his arms upon his body sound; And with his bloody teeth he bites the ground.

Turnus bestrode the corpse: “Arcadians, hear,” Said he; “my message to your master bear: Such as the sire deserv’d, the son I send; It costs him dear to be the Phrygians’ friend. The lifeless body, tell him, I bestow, Unask’d, to rest his wand’ring ghost below.” He said, and trampled down with all the force Of his left foot, and spurn’d the wretched corse; Then snatch’d the shining belt, with gold inlaid; The belt Eurytion’s artful hands had made, Where fifty fatal brides, express’d to sight, All in the compass of one mournful night, Depriv’d their bridegrooms of returning light.
cards.whyThisWorks: The excerpt contrasts Pallas's failed attack with Turnus's lethal spear throw, his taunting speech over the corpse, and his act of stripping the belt, giving students concrete textual moments to distinguish a central idea from isolated details or topics.
cards.skillStrategy: Ask yourself what the two paragraphs together are really saying about war or the characters—not just what happens, but what point the events add up to.
evidencePoints: "See now," said he, "whose arm is better strung."
He said, and trampled down with all the force / Of his left foot, and spurn'd the wretched corse; / Then snatch'd the shining belt
cards.question: After Turnus kills Pallas, he taunts the Arcadians with the words "Such as the sire deserv'd, the son I send," then tramples the body and strips the belt. What central idea do these actions together develop across both paragraphs?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Pallas's courage in attacking Turnus first, even though outmatched, earns him a warrior's respect on the battlefield.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Turnus uses his victory over Pallas not only to destroy an enemy but to humiliate and send a threatening message, showing war as an exercise of brutal, dominating power.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The belt stolen from Pallas, decorated with the story of fifty murdered bridegrooms, is the most important object in the passage because it foreshadows future tragedy.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The alliance between the Arcadians and the Phrygians is the source of Pallas's death, and Turnus blames Evander for placing his son in danger.

cards.standardTitle: Rhetorical appeals and author purpose
cards.excerpt:
Aeneas erects a trophy of the spoils of Mezentius, grants a truce for burying the dead, and sends home the body of Pallas with great solemnity. Latinus calls a council, to propose offers of peace to Aeneas; which occasions great animosity betwixt Turnus and Drances. In the mean time there is a sharp engagement of the horse; wherein Camilla signalizes herself, is killed, and the Latine troops are entirely defeated.

Scarce had the rosy Morning rais’d her head Above the waves, and left her wat’ry bed; The pious chief, whom double cares attend For his unburied soldiers and his friend, Yet first to Heav’n perform’d a victor’s vows: He bar’d an ancient oak of all her boughs; Then on a rising ground the trunk he plac’d, Which with the spoils of his dead foe he grac’d. The coat of arms by proud Mezentius worn, Now on a naked snag in triumph borne, Was hung on high, and glitter’d from afar, A trophy sacred to the God of War. Above his arms, fix’d on the leafless wood, Appear’d his plumy crest, besmear’d with blood: His brazen buckler on the left was seen; Truncheons of shiver’d lances hung between; And on the right was placed his corslet, bor’d; And to the neck was tied his unavailing sword.
cards.whyThisWorks: The passage's vivid description of Aeneas arranging Mezentius's blood-smeared crest, gleaming armor, and shattered lances on a trophy tree appeals to readers' emotions through sensory imagery, making it a clear example of pathos used to honor the fallen and glorify Aeneas's piety.
cards.skillStrategy: Ask yourself: Is the author trying to prove something with facts (logos), build trust through expertise (ethos), or stir feelings through vivid images and emotional moments (pathos)?
evidencePoints: His plumy crest, besmear'd with blood
The coat of arms by proud Mezentius worn, Now on a naked snag in triumph borne, Was hung on high, and glitter'd from afar
cards.question: In the second paragraph, Virgil describes Mezentius's 'plumy crest, besmear'd with blood' and his 'shiver'd lances' displayed on the trophy tree. Which rhetorical appeal does this description primarily represent, and how does it serve Virgil's purpose?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Ethos, because Virgil establishes Aeneas as a credible military commander by cataloguing each piece of enemy armor with precise detail.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Pathos, because the blood-stained crest and broken lances create a vivid, emotionally charged image meant to stir feelings of awe at Aeneas's victory and reverence for the ritual honoring the dead.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Logos, because the ordered list of Mezentius's armor pieces—buckler, corslet, sword, and crest—provides a logical, step-by-step account of how a Roman trophy was constructed.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Pathos, because Virgil mourns Mezentius as a sympathetic figure by emphasizing how his proud armor is now stripped away and left to decay on a bare tree.

cards.standardTitle: Key literary elements add layers of meaning
cards.excerpt: Her sister hears; and, furious with despair, She beats her breast, and rends her yellow hair, And, calling on Eliza’s name aloud, Runs breathless to the place, and breaks the crowd. “Was all that pomp of woe for this prepar’d; These fires, this fun’ral pile, these altars rear’d? Was all this train of plots contriv’d,” said she, “All only to deceive unhappy me? Which is the worst? Didst thou in death pretend To scorn thy sister, or delude thy friend? Thy summon’d sister, and thy friend, had come; One sword had serv’d us both, one common tomb: Was I to raise the pile, the pow’rs invoke, Not to be present at the fatal stroke? At once thou hast destroy’d thyself and me, Thy town, thy senate, and thy colony! Bring water; bathe the wound; while I in death Lay close my lips to hers, and catch the flying breath.” This said, she mounts the pile with eager haste, And in her arms the gasping queen embrac’d; Her temples chaf’d; and her own garments tore, To stanch the streaming blood, and cleanse the gore. Thrice Dido tried to raise her drooping head, And, fainting thrice, fell grov’ling on the bed; Thrice op’d her heavy eyes, and sought the light, But, having found it, sicken’d at the sight, And clos’d her lids at last in endless night.
cards.whyThisWorks: Anna's frantic speech and physical actions—tearing her hair, mounting the funeral pile, pressing her lips to Dido's—reveal a character consumed by grief and loyalty, showing students how action and speech together deepen meaning about sisterly devotion and tragic loss.
cards.skillStrategy: When a character speaks and acts at the same time, ask yourself what those combined choices reveal about who that character is and what the moment means.
evidencePoints: She beats her breast, and rends her yellow hair
Bring water; bathe the wound; while I in death / Lay close my lips to hers, and catch the flying breath.
cards.question: Read the following lines from the excerpt: 'Bring water; bathe the wound; while I in death / Lay close my lips to hers, and catch the flying breath.' What do Anna's words and the actions that follow—mounting the pile and embracing the dying queen—reveal about her character?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Anna is overwhelmed by guilt because she helped Dido build the funeral pile, and her commands show she blames herself for engineering the deception.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Anna's desperate commands and physical closeness to the dying Dido reveal a devotion so fierce that she refuses to accept separation even at the moment of death.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Anna's frantic orders reveal that she is a practical leader who takes charge in a crisis, shifting the focus of the scene from grief to organized rescue.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Anna's words show that she is angry at Dido for dying without warning her, and her actions on the pile are meant to express that anger rather than affection.

cards.standardTitle: Theme development across a literary text
cards.excerpt:
By Caedicus, Alcathous was slain; Sacrator laid Hydaspes on the plain; Orses the strong to greater strength must yield; He, with Parthenius, were by Rapo kill’d. Then brave Messapus Ericetes slew, Who from Lycaon’s blood his lineage drew. But from his headstrong horse his fate he found, Who threw his master, as he made a bound: The chief, alighting, stuck him to the ground; Then Clonius, hand to hand, on foot assails: The Trojan sinks, and Neptune’s son prevails. Agis the Lycian, stepping forth with pride, To single fight the boldest foe defied; Whom Tuscan Valerus by force o’ercame, And not belied his mighty father’s fame. Salius to death the great Antronius sent: But the same fate the victor underwent, Slain by Nealces’ hand, well-skill’d to throw The flying dart, and draw the far-deceiving bow.

Thus equal deaths are dealt with equal chance; By turns they quit their ground, by turns advance: Victors and vanquish’d, in the various field, Nor wholly overcome, nor wholly yield. The gods from heav’n survey the fatal strife, And mourn the miseries of human life. Above the rest, two goddesses appear Concern’d for each: here Venus, Juno there. Amidst the crowd, infernal Ate shakes Her scourge aloft, and crest of hissing snakes.
cards.whyThisWorks: The second paragraph explicitly states the theme of war's indiscriminate equality ('equal deaths are dealt with equal chance'), and the first paragraph provides multiple specific examples of reversals—most powerfully Salius killing Antronius only to be killed himself—that prove this theme through concrete evidence.
cards.skillStrategy: To find evidence that proves a theme, look for specific moments in the text where characters' actions or fates directly illustrate the theme statement the author makes.
evidencePoints: Thus equal deaths are dealt with equal chance; / By turns they quit their ground, by turns advance
Salius to death the great Antronius sent: / But the same fate the victor underwent, / Slain by Nealces' hand
cards.question: The narrator concludes, 'Thus equal deaths are dealt with equal chance; / By turns they quit their ground, by turns advance.' Which detail from the first paragraph most directly provides evidence that proves this theme about war?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Agis the Lycian steps forward 'with pride' to challenge 'the boldest foe' to single combat, showing that individual warriors seek personal glory rather than fighting as part of a larger army.

choices.label: B
choices.text: 'Salius to death the great Antronius sent: / But the same fate the victor underwent, / Slain by Nealces' hand,' showing that victory in one moment offers no protection from death in the next.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Valerus defeats Agis the Lycian and 'not belied his mighty father's fame,' showing that a warrior's inherited reputation determines the outcome of single combat.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Messapus kills Ericetes, 'who from Lycaon's blood his lineage drew,' showing that warriors of noble ancestry are more likely to fall in battle than those of common birth.

cards.standardTitle: Epic poetry: characters, structures, and themes
cards.excerpt:
Turnus two brothers from the Lycian shore, And from Apollo’s fane to battle sent, O’erthrew; nor Phoebus could their fate prevent. Peaceful Menoetes after these he kill’d, Who long had shunn’d the dangers of the field: On Lerna’s lake a silent life he led, And with his nets and angle earn’d his bread; Nor pompous cares, nor palaces, he knew, But wisely from th’ infectious world withdrew: Poor was his house; his father’s painful hand Discharg’d his rent, and plow’d another’s land.

As flames among the lofty woods are thrown On diff’rent sides, and both by winds are blown; The laurels crackle in the sputt’ring fire; The frighted sylvans from their shades retire: Or as two neighb’ring torrents fall from high; Rapid they run; the foamy waters fry; They roll to sea with unresisted force, And down the rocks precipitate their course: Not with less rage the rival heroes take Their diff’rent ways, nor less destruction make. With spears afar, with swords at hand, they strike; And zeal of slaughter fires their souls alike. Like them, their dauntless men maintain the field; And hearts are pierc’d, unknowing how to yield: They blow for blow return, and wound for wound; And heaps of bodies raise the level ground.
cards.whyThisWorks: The phrase 'nor Phoebus could their fate prevent' directly illustrates divine intervention's limits in epic poetry, showing that destiny supersedes a god's power even over warriors sent from his own temple.
cards.skillStrategy: When analyzing divine intervention in epic poetry, look for moments where a god's power is tested or overruled, and ask what that reveals about fate versus divine will.
evidencePoints: nor Phoebus could their fate prevent
from Apollo's fane to battle sent
cards.question: In the first paragraph, the brothers are sent 'from Apollo's fane to battle' yet 'nor Phoebus could their fate prevent.' What does this contrast reveal about divine power in the excerpt?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Apollo abandons the brothers because they left his temple without permission.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Even warriors sent from Apollo's own temple die, showing fate overpowers divine protection.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Phoebus grants Turnus extra strength to defeat the brothers from the Lycian shore.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The brothers' deaths prove that Apollo never intended to protect warriors in battle.

cards.standardTitle: Text structure and feature purpose
cards.excerpt:
Beneath his feet fell haughty Hebrus dead, Then Latagus, and Palmus as he fled. At Latagus a weighty stone he flung: His face was flatted, and his helmet rung. But Palmus from behind receives his wound; Hamstring’d he falls, and grovels on the ground: His crest and armour, from his body torn, Thy shoulders, Lausus, and thy head adorn. Evas and Mimas, both of Troy, he slew. Mimas his birth from fair Theano drew, Born on that fatal night, when, big with fire, The queen produc’d young Paris to his sire: But Paris in the Phrygian fields was slain, Unthinking Mimas on the Latian plain.

And, as a savage boar, on mountains bred, With forest mast and fatt’ning marshes fed, When once he sees himself in toils inclos’d, By huntsmen and their eager hounds oppos’d, He whets his tusks, and turns, and dares the war; Th’ invaders dart their jav’lins from afar: All keep aloof, and safely shout around; But none presumes to give a nearer wound: He frets and froths, erects his bristled hide, And shakes a grove of lances from his side: Not otherwise the troops, with hate inspir’d, And just revenge against the tyrant fir’d, Their darts with clamour at a distance drive, And only keep the languish’d war alive.
cards.whyThisWorks: The two paragraphs move from cataloguing named deaths to a sustained simile comparing the warrior to a cornered boar, giving students a clear structural shift to identify and explain.
cards.skillStrategy: Ask yourself: does this paragraph continue the same idea, or does it change direction—and what signal word or image marks that change?
evidencePoints: Beneath his feet fell haughty Hebrus dead, Then Latagus, and Palmus as he fled.
And, as a savage boar, on mountains bred... Not otherwise the troops, with hate inspir'd, And just revenge against the tyrant fir'd, Their darts with clamour at a distance drive
cards.question: The first paragraph names warriors—Hebrus, Latagus, Palmus, Evas, and Mimas—who fall in combat. What is the job of the second paragraph, which opens 'And, as a savage boar, on mountains bred'?

choices.label: A
choices.text: It extends the catalogue of the fallen by naming additional warriors who die in the same manner as Hebrus and Latagus.

choices.label: B
choices.text: It shifts from recording individual deaths to explaining, through the cornered-boar comparison, why the surrounding troops 'only keep the languish'd war alive' by attacking from a distance rather than closing in.

choices.label: C
choices.text: It concludes the battle by showing that the troops' javelins finally overwhelm the warrior the way hunters overwhelm the boar in the simile.

choices.label: D
choices.text: It contrasts the bravery of Lausus, who wears the slain Palmus's crest, with the cowardice of the troops who throw javelins from afar.

cards.standardTitle: Central idea and supporting evidence
cards.excerpt: Aeneas, setting sail from Afric, is driven by a storm on the coast of Sicily, where he is hospitably received by his friend Acestes, king of part of the island, and born of Trojan parentage. He applies himself to celebrate the memory of his father with divine honours, and accordingly institues funeral games, and appoints prizes for those who should conquer in them. While the ceremonies are performing, Juno sends Iris to persuade the Trojan woman to burn the ships, who, upon her instigation, set fire to them: which burned four, and would have consumed the rest, had not Jupiter, by a miraculous shower extinguished it. Upon this, Aeneas, by the advice of one of his generals, and a vision of his father, builds a city for the women, old men, and others, who were either unfit for war, or weary of the voyage, and sails for Italy. Venus procures of Neptune a safe voyage for him and all his men, excepting only his pilot Palinurus, who was unfortunately lost.
cards.whyThisWorks: The excerpt traces Aeneas through four sequential challenges—honoring his father, surviving the fire that 'burned four' ships, resettling those 'unfit for war, or weary of the voyage,' and sailing under Venus's protection—making it ideal for students to synthesize events into a central idea about persistent, goal-directed leadership.
cards.skillStrategy: To find the central idea, ask what single claim connects every major event in the passage, then check that your answer is supported by at least two specific details from the text.
evidencePoints: burned four, and would have consumed the rest, had not Jupiter, by a miraculous shower extinguished it
builds a city for the women, old men, and others, who were either unfit for war, or weary of the voyage, and sails for Italy
cards.question: The excerpt shows Aeneas instituting funeral games to honor his father, regrouping after a fire that 'burned four' ships, building a city for those 'unfit for war, or weary of the voyage,' and finally sailing for Italy under Venus's protection. Which statement best identifies the central idea that all four of these events together convey?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Juno's decision to send Iris to incite the Trojan women is the passage's turning point because losing four ships forces Aeneas to permanently divide his people and arrive in Italy with a weakened force.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Aeneas steadily advances toward Italy by responding to each obstacle in turn—honoring his father, recovering after the fire that 'burned four' ships, resettling those 'unfit for war, or weary of the voyage,' and accepting Venus's protection for the final voyage.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Divine intervention controls every outcome in the passage, since Jupiter extinguishes the fire and Venus secures Neptune's protection, leaving Aeneas himself—despite instituting the funeral games and building a new city—with little real agency over the journey.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The funeral games Aeneas institutes to honor his father are the passage's most important event because they unite the Trojans before Juno's interference and the burning of four ships threaten to end the voyage entirely.

cards.standardTitle: Key literary elements add layers of meaning
cards.excerpt: To whom Mezentius thus: “Thy vaunts are vain. My Lausus lies extended on the plain: He’s lost! thy conquest is already won; The wretched sire is murder’d in the son. Nor fate I fear, but all the gods defy. Forbear thy threats: my bus’ness is to die; But first receive this parting legacy.” He said; and straight a whirling dart he sent; Another after, and another went. Round in a spacious ring he rides the field, And vainly plies th’ impenetrable shield. Thrice rode he round; and thrice Aeneas wheel’d, Turn’d as he turn’d: the golden orb withstood The strokes, and bore about an iron wood. Impatient of delay, and weary grown, Still to defend, and to defend alone, To wrench the darts which in his buckler light, Urg’d and o’er-labour’d in unequal fight; At length resolv’d, he throws with all his force Full at the temples of the warrior horse. Just where the stroke was aim’d, th’ unerring spear Made way, and stood transfix’d thro’ either ear. Seiz’d with unwonted pain, surpris’d with fright, The wounded steed curvets, and, rais’d upright, Lights on his feet before; his hoofs behind Spring up in air aloft, and lash the wind. Down comes the rider headlong from his height: His horse came after with unwieldy weight, And, flound’ring forward, pitching on his head, His lord’s encumber’d shoulder overlaid.
cards.whyThisWorks: Mezentius's declaration 'Nor fate I fear, but all the gods defy' followed by his reckless, exhausting assault on Aeneas reveals a character defined by defiant pride and grief-driven recklessness, showing how speech and action together deepen meaning about a father's despair.
cards.skillStrategy: When a character speaks and then acts, ask yourself: do the actions match the words, and what does that combination reveal about who this person truly is?
evidencePoints: Nor fate I fear, but all the gods defy. Forbear thy threats: my bus'ness is to die
Impatient of delay, and weary grown, Still to defend, and to defend alone, To wrench the darts which in his buckler light, Urg'd and o'er-labour'd in unequal fight
cards.question: Read the following lines from the excerpt: 'Nor fate I fear, but all the gods defy. Forbear thy threats: my bus'ness is to die.' How do Mezentius's words here, combined with his actions in the battle that follows, reveal his character?

choices.label: A
choices.text: His declaration that he does not fear fate shows he is a skilled and confident warrior who believes his combat experience will carry him to victory over Aeneas.

choices.label: B
choices.text: His words announce a death-seeking resolve born from grief over Lausus, and his exhausting, futile assault confirms he is fighting not to win but to die defiantly alongside his son's memory.

choices.label: C
choices.text: His challenge to the gods and his relentless circling of the field show that he is motivated primarily by anger at Aeneas personally rather than by sorrow over his son's death.

choices.label: D
choices.text: His speech reveals a warrior who has accepted defeat calmly, and his continued fighting is simply an obligation of honor rather than an expression of grief or despair.

cards.standardTitle: Theme development across a literary text
cards.excerpt:
What should he do! Nor arts nor arms avail; And various cares in vain his mind assail. The great Messapus, thund’ring thro’ the field, In his left hand two pointed jav’lins held: Encount’ring on the prince, one dart he drew, And with unerring aim and utmost vigour threw. Aeneas saw it come, and, stooping low Beneath his buckler, shunn’d the threat’ning blow. The weapon hiss’d above his head, and tore The waving plume which on his helm he wore. Forced by this hostile act, and fir’d with spite, That flying Turnus still declin’d the fight, The Prince, whose piety had long repell’d His inborn ardour, now invades the field; Invokes the pow’rs of violated peace, Their rites and injur’d altars to redress; Then, to his rage abandoning the rein, With blood and slaughter’d bodies fills the plain.

What god can tell, what numbers can display, The various labours of that fatal day; What chiefs and champions fell on either side, In combat slain, or by what deaths they died; Whom Turnus, whom the Trojan hero kill’d; Who shar’d the fame and fortune of the field! Jove, could’st thou view, and not avert thy sight, Two jarring nations join’d in cruel fight, Whom leagues of lasting love so shortly shall unite!
cards.whyThisWorks: The excerpt explicitly contrasts Aeneas's 'piety' restraining his 'inborn ardour' with his eventual unleashing of 'blood and slaughter'd bodies,' and then closes with Jove watching nations fight that are 'shortly' fated to unite—giving students a true-detail distractor (the javelin near-miss) to reject and a theme-developing detail (the piety/rage collapse plus Jove's ironic witness) to select.
cards.skillStrategy: Ask yourself: does this detail show how the theme grows, or does it just describe something that happened in the story?
evidencePoints: The Prince, whose piety had long repell'd / His inborn ardour, now invades the field
Jove, could'st thou view, and not avert thy sight, / Two jarring nations join'd in cruel fight, / Whom leagues of lasting love so shortly shall unite!
cards.question: The narrator states that Aeneas's 'piety had long repell'd his inborn ardour' before he finally 'abandoning the rein' fills the plain 'with blood and slaughter'd bodies.' Which detail from the passage most directly develops the theme that war's destruction is made more tragic by the duty and destiny that bind those who wage it?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Messapus throws a javelin with 'unerring aim and utmost vigour,' and the weapon tears the plume from Aeneas's helmet, showing that Aeneas faces real physical danger on the battlefield.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Aeneas's long-suppressed 'piety' finally breaks under provocation, unleashing slaughter, while Jove watches the same nations 'join'd in cruel fight' that are fated to unite in 'leagues of lasting love' very soon.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Turnus repeatedly declines direct combat with Aeneas, which provokes Aeneas's spite and draws him back into the wider battle he had been restraining himself from joining.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The narrator asks what 'god can tell' or 'what numbers can display' the losses of that day, indicating that the casualties on both sides were too great to count or name.

cards.standardTitle: Epic poetry: characters, structures, and themes
cards.excerpt:
What should he do! Nor arts nor arms avail; And various cares in vain his mind assail. The great Messapus, thund’ring thro’ the field, In his left hand two pointed jav’lins held: Encount’ring on the prince, one dart he drew, And with unerring aim and utmost vigour threw. Aeneas saw it come, and, stooping low Beneath his buckler, shunn’d the threat’ning blow. The weapon hiss’d above his head, and tore The waving plume which on his helm he wore. Forced by this hostile act, and fir’d with spite, That flying Turnus still declin’d the fight, The Prince, whose piety had long repell’d His inborn ardour, now invades the field; Invokes the pow’rs of violated peace, Their rites and injur’d altars to redress; Then, to his rage abandoning the rein, With blood and slaughter’d bodies fills the plain.

What god can tell, what numbers can display, The various labours of that fatal day; What chiefs and champions fell on either side, In combat slain, or by what deaths they died; Whom Turnus, whom the Trojan hero kill’d; Who shar’d the fame and fortune of the field! Jove, could’st thou view, and not avert thy sight, Two jarring nations join’d in cruel fight, Whom leagues of lasting love so shortly shall unite!
cards.whyThisWorks: The excerpt shows Aeneas explicitly invoking divine powers to justify entering battle, and closes with a direct address to Jove questioning his inaction, making divine intervention central to both the action and the moral weight of the scene.
cards.skillStrategy: When identifying divine intervention, look for moments where a character calls on a god or a god is blamed for allowing events—then ask how that supernatural force drives what happens next or what the poem seems to argue.
evidencePoints: The Prince, whose piety had long repell'd / His inborn ardour, now invades the field; / Invokes the pow'rs of violated peace, / Their rites and injur'd altars to redress
Jove, could'st thou view, and not avert thy sight, / Two jarring nations join'd in cruel fight, / Whom leagues of lasting love so shortly shall unite!
cards.question: In the excerpt, Aeneas 'Invokes the pow'rs of violated peace' before entering battle, and the narrator then addresses Jove directly. How do these two moments of divine appeal work together to shape the theme of the passage?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Aeneas's prayer proves the gods have already chosen him as the victor, and the address to Jove confirms that divine favor guarantees his survival on the battlefield.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Aeneas's invocation frames his violence as divinely sanctioned rather than purely personal, and the address to Jove raises the tragic question of why the gods permit destruction between peoples destined for unity.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Aeneas's invocation shows he has abandoned all piety in favor of rage, and the address to Jove suggests the gods have permanently withdrawn from human affairs.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Aeneas's prayer to the gods replaces his need for military skill, and the address to Jove implies that the outcome of the battle has already been decided by fate alone.

cards.standardTitle: Text structure and feature purpose
cards.excerpt: Then Aruns, doom’d to death, his arts assay’d, To murder, unespied, the Volscian maid: This way and that his winding course he bends, And, whereso’er she turns, her steps attends. When she retires victorious from the chase, He wheels about with care, and shifts his place; When, rushing on, she seeks her foes in fight, He keeps aloof, but keeps her still in sight: He threats, and trembles, trying ev’ry way, Unseen to kill, and safely to betray. Chloreus, the priest of Cybele, from far, Glitt’ring in Phrygian arms amidst the war, Was by the virgin view’d. The steed he press’d Was proud with trappings, and his brawny chest With scales of gilded brass was cover’d o’er; A robe of Tyrian dye the rider wore. With deadly wounds he gall’d the distant foe; Gnossian his shafts, and Lycian was his bow: A golden helm his front and head surrounds A gilded quiver from his shoulder sounds. Gold, weav’d with linen, on his thighs he wore, With flowers of needlework distinguish’d o’er, With golden buckles bound, and gather’d up before. Him the fierce maid beheld with ardent eyes, Fond and ambitious of so rich a prize, Or that the temple might his trophies hold, Or else to shine herself in Trojan gold. Blind in her haste, she chases him alone. And seeks his life, regardless of her own.
cards.whyThisWorks: The excerpt's two-part structure—Aruns's patient, hidden stalking followed by Camilla's impulsive chase of Chloreus—lets students identify how the Chloreus section shifts the paragraph's job from showing an external threat to revealing Camilla's self-destructive flaw.
cards.skillStrategy: Ask yourself: what was the paragraph doing before this section, and what does it start doing here? The shift in subject and action signals a new job.
evidencePoints: Unseen to kill, and safely to betray
Blind in her haste, she chases him alone. And seeks his life, regardless of her own.
cards.question: The opening lines show Aruns scheming to kill Camilla while staying 'unseen.' What is the job of the section beginning 'Chloreus, the priest of Cybele, from far'?

choices.label: A
choices.text: It reveals that Aruns uses Chloreus as a deliberate decoy to draw Camilla away from her allies.

choices.label: B
choices.text: It shifts focus to Camilla's own fatal flaw—her greed for Chloreus's gold makes her chase him alone, 'regardless of her own' life.

choices.label: C
choices.text: It shows that Chloreus's glittering armor and Phrygian weapons make him a greater battlefield threat than Aruns.

choices.label: D
choices.text: It contrasts Chloreus's open fighting with Aruns's hiding, showing Camilla correctly abandons the lesser enemy.

cards.standardTitle: Central idea and supporting evidence
cards.excerpt: The clowns, a boist’rous, rude, ungovern’d crew, With furious haste to the loud summons flew. The pow’rs of Troy, then issuing on the plain, With fresh recruits their youthful chief sustain: Not theirs a raw and unexperienc’d train, But a firm body of embattled men. At first, while fortune favour’d neither side, The fight with clubs and burning brands was tried; But now, both parties reinforc’d, the fields Are bright with flaming swords and brazen shields. A shining harvest either host displays, And shoots against the sun with equal rays. Thus, when a black-brow’d gust begins to rise, White foam at first on the curl’d ocean fries; Then roars the main, the billows mount the skies; Till, by the fury of the storm full blown, The muddy bottom o’er the clouds is thrown. First Almon falls, old Tyrrheus’ eldest care, Pierc’d with an arrow from the distant war: Fix’d in his throat the flying weapon stood, And stopp’d his breath, and drank his vital blood Huge heaps of slain around the body rise: Among the rest, the rich Galesus lies; A good old man, while peace he preach’d in vain, Amidst the madness of th’ unruly train: Five herds, five bleating flocks, his pastures fill’d; His lands a hundred yoke of oxen till’d.
cards.whyThisWorks: The excerpt traces a clear escalation from crude brawl to armed slaughter to the death of a peacemaker, giving students concrete textual evidence to identify the central idea that unchecked violence consumes even those who oppose it.
cards.skillStrategy: Track how the passage moves from its opening scene to its closing image, then ask what idea all three stages share rather than focusing on just one detail.
evidencePoints: A good old man, while peace he preach'd in vain, Amidst the madness of th' unruly train
the fight with clubs and burning brands was tried; But now, both parties reinforc'd, the fields Are bright with flaming swords and brazen shields
cards.question: The conflict opens as 'the fight with clubs and burning brands was tried,' then escalates to 'flaming swords and brazen shields,' and closes with Galesus, who 'preach'd in vain' for peace, lying among 'huge heaps of slain.' What central idea does this three-stage progression develop?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The Trojan forces, described as 'a firm body of embattled men,' steadily gain the upper hand over the 'boist'rous, rude, ungovern'd crew,' showing that discipline determines the outcome of battle.

choices.label: B
choices.text: A brawl fought with crude weapons grows into full-scale slaughter that kills even Galesus, the wealthy peacemaker who 'preach'd in vain amidst the madness,' showing that unchecked violence destroys those who oppose it as readily as those who fuel it.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Galesus is the passage's most important figure because his wealth—'five herds, five bleating flocks' and 'a hundred yoke of oxen'—represents the prosperity that war erases, making his death the passage's sole central point.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The ocean simile, in which 'the billows mount the skies' and 'the muddy bottom o'er the clouds is thrown,' is the passage's central claim, arguing that the violence is a natural force beyond any human control or responsibility.

cards.standardTitle: Key literary elements add layers of meaning
cards.excerpt: But Salius enters, and, exclaiming loud For justice, deafens and disturbs the crowd; Urges his cause may in the court be heard; And pleads the prize is wrongfully conferr’d. But favour for Euryalus appears; His blooming beauty, with his tender tears, Had brib’d the judges for the promis’d prize. Besides, Diores fills the court with cries, Who vainly reaches at the last reward, If the first palm on Salius be conferr’d. Then thus the prince: “Let no disputes arise: Where fortune plac’d it, I award the prize. But fortune’s errors give me leave to mend, At least to pity my deserving friend.” He said, and, from among the spoils, he draws (Pond’rous with shaggy mane and golden paws) A lion’s hide: to Salius this he gives. Nisus with envy sees the gift, and grieves. “If such rewards to vanquish’d men are due.” He said, “and falling is to rise by you, What prize may Nisus from your bounty claim, Who merited the first rewards and fame? In falling, both an equal fortune tried; Would fortune for my fall so well provide!” With this he pointed to his face, and show’d His hand and all his habit smear’d with blood. Th’ indulgent father of the people smil’d, And caus’d to be produc’d an ample shield, Of wondrous art, by Didymaon wrought, Long since from Neptune’s bars in triumph brought. This giv’n to Nisus, he divides the rest, And equal justice in his gifts express’d.
cards.whyThisWorks: Aeneas's decision to award Salius a lion's hide and then smile at Nisus's bold complaint—giving him an even grander shield—reveals a ruler whose fairness and generosity define his character and reinforce the epic's theme of just leadership.
cards.skillStrategy: When a character acts or speaks in a key moment, ask what that action or speech shows about who they are and what the author wants readers to understand about them.
evidencePoints: Then thus the prince: 'Let no disputes arise: Where fortune plac'd it, I award the prize. But fortune's errors give me leave to mend, At least to pity my deserving friend.'
Th' indulgent father of the people smil'd, And caus'd to be produc'd an ample shield... This giv'n to Nisus, he divides the rest, And equal justice in his gifts express'd.
cards.question: Read the following lines: "Th' indulgent father of the people smil'd, And caus'd to be produc'd an ample shield... And equal justice in his gifts express'd." What do Aeneas's smile and his decision to give Nisus the shield reveal about his character?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Aeneas is easily manipulated by emotional appeals, showing that his rulings are inconsistent and driven by whoever complains most loudly.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Aeneas combines mercy with a sense of fairness, showing that a just leader can acknowledge misfortune and still honor those who truly deserved recognition.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Aeneas favors Nisus over Salius because Nisus's bloodied appearance proves he suffered more than any other competitor in the race.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Aeneas gives away prizes freely to end the argument quickly, revealing that he values peace among the crowd more than rewarding actual merit.

cards.standardTitle: Theme development across a literary text
cards.excerpt:
At this the lovely nymph, with grief oppress’d, Thrice tore her hair, and beat her comely breast. To whom Saturnia thus: “Thy tears are late: Haste, snatch him, if he can be snatch’d from fate: New tumults kindle; violate the truce: Who knows what changeful fortune may produce? ’Tis not a crime t’ attempt what I decree; Or, if it were, discharge the crime on me.” She said, and, sailing on the winged wind, Left the sad nymph suspended in her mind.

And now in pomp the peaceful kings appear: Four steeds the chariot of Latinus bear; Twelve golden beams around his temples play, To mark his lineage from the God of Day. Two snowy coursers Turnus’ chariot yoke, And in his hand two massy spears he shook: Then issued from the camp, in arms divine, Aeneas, author of the Roman line; And by his side Ascanius took his place, The second hope of Rome’s immortal race. Adorn’d in white, a rev’rend priest appears, And off’rings to the flaming altars bears; A porket, and a lamb that never suffer’d shears. Then to the rising sun he turns his eyes, And strews the beasts, design’d for sacrifice, With salt and meal: with like officious care He marks their foreheads, and he clips their hair. Betwixt their horns the purple wine he sheds; With the same gen’rous juice the flame he feeds.
cards.whyThisWorks: The excerpt contrasts Saturnia's command to 'violate the truce' with the mortals' elaborate peace ritual, giving students a true-but-off-topic detail (the priest's ceremony) to reject and a theme-developing detail (Saturnia's divine interference) to select.
cards.skillStrategy: Ask yourself: does this detail show the theme in action, or does it just describe what is happening in the scene without connecting to the theme?
evidencePoints: 'Tis not a crime t' attempt what I decree; Or, if it were, discharge the crime on me.'
Then issued from the camp, in arms divine, Aeneas, author of the Roman line; And by his side Ascanius took his place, The second hope of Rome's immortal race.
cards.question: The excerpt develops a theme about divine power undermining the fragile peace that mortals struggle to maintain. Saturnia tells the nymph, ''Tis not a crime t' attempt what I decree; Or, if it were, discharge the crime on me.' Which other detail from the excerpt most directly develops this same theme?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The priest strews the sacrificial animals with salt and meal, clips their hair, and pours purple wine between their horns, showing the careful ritual mortals perform to honor the gods before battle.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Aeneas is called 'author of the Roman line' and Ascanius 'the second hope of Rome's immortal race,' revealing that the mortal peace ceremony carries the entire future of Rome — a future a god is already plotting to destroy.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Latinus arrives with twelve golden beams around his temples to mark his lineage from the God of Day, showing that mortal kings claim divine ancestry to justify their authority.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Turnus shakes two massy spears from his chariot, signaling that he is a warrior who distrusts the truce and is ready to resume fighting at any moment.

cards.standardTitle: Epic poetry: characters, structures, and themes
cards.excerpt:
Within the space, an olive tree had stood, A sacred shade, a venerable wood, For vows to Faunus paid, the Latins’ guardian god. Here hung the vests, and tablets were engrav’d, Of sinking mariners from shipwreck sav’d. With heedless hands the Trojans fell’d the tree, To make the ground enclos’d for combat free. Deep in the root, whether by fate, or chance, Or erring haste, the Trojan drove his lance; Then stoop’d, and tugg’d with force immense, to free Th’ incumber’d spear from the tenacious tree; That, whom his fainting limbs pursued in vain, His flying weapon might from far attain.

Confus’d with fear, bereft of human aid, Then Turnus to the gods, and first to Faunus pray’d: “O Faunus, pity! and thou Mother Earth, Where I thy foster son receiv’d my birth, Hold fast the steel! If my religious hand Your plant has honour’d, which your foes profan’d, Propitious hear my pious pray’r!” He said, Nor with successless vows invok’d their aid. Th’ incumbent hero wrench’d, and pull’d, and strain’d; But still the stubborn earth the steel detain’d. Juturna took her time; and, while in vain He strove, assum’d Meticus’ form again, And, in that imitated shape, restor’d To the despairing prince his Daunian sword. The Queen of Love, who, with disdain and grief, Saw the bold nymph afford this prompt relief, T’ assert her offspring with a greater deed, From the tough root the ling’ring weapon freed.
cards.whyThisWorks: The excerpt shows two competing divine interventions—Faunus holding Aeneas's spear in response to Turnus's prayer and Juturna restoring Turnus's sword, then Venus freeing the spear—making the subskill of divine intervention shaping action directly traceable to specific lines.
cards.skillStrategy: When identifying divine intervention, find the exact moment a god or supernatural force changes what a character can or cannot do, then ask what would have happened without that force.
evidencePoints: Nor with successless vows invok'd their aid. Th' incumbent hero wrench'd, and pull'd, and strain'd; But still the stubborn earth the steel detain'd.
The Queen of Love…T' assert her offspring with a greater deed, From the tough root the ling'ring weapon freed.
cards.question: After Turnus prays to Faunus and the earth holds Aeneas's spear fast, Venus intervenes to free it. What does this sequence of opposing divine actions reveal about the forces controlling the duel?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Faunus's power over the earth proves stronger than Venus's, so Aeneas's eventual success depends entirely on Juturna's decision to restore Turnus's sword rather than on any goddess's help.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The gods intervene on opposite sides—Faunus trapping the spear for Turnus and Venus freeing it for Aeneas—so neither warrior's strength alone determines the duel's progress; supernatural forces keep the outcome in balance.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Turnus's prayer to Faunus succeeds permanently, and Venus frees the spear only because she is punishing Turnus for the Trojans' earlier desecration of Faunus's sacred olive tree.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Juturna's act of restoring Turnus's sword is the decisive intervention, and both Faunus and Venus act merely to delay the combat rather than to favor either warrior.

cards.standardTitle: Text structure and feature purpose
cards.excerpt:
The pious Trojan then his jav’lin sent; The shield gave way; thro’ treble plates it went Of solid brass, of linen trebly roll’d, And three bull hides which round the buckler fold. All these it pass’d, resistless in the course, Transpierc’d his thigh, and spent its dying force. The gaping wound gush’d out a crimson flood. The Trojan, glad with sight of hostile blood, His falchion drew, to closer fight address’d, And with new force his fainting foe oppress’d.

His father’s peril Lausus view’d with grief; He sigh’d, he wept, he ran to his relief. And here, heroic youth, ’tis here I must To thy immortal memory be just, And sing an act so noble and so new, Posterity will scarce believe ’tis true. Pain’d with his wound, and useless for the fight, The father sought to save himself by flight: Encumber’d, slow he dragg’d the spear along, Which pierc’d his thigh, and in his buckler hung. The pious youth, resolv’d on death, below The lifted sword springs forth to face the foe; Protects his parent, and prevents the blow. Shouts of applause ran ringing thro’ the field, To see the son the vanquish’d father shield. All, fir’d with gen’rous indignation, strive, And with a storm of darts to distance drive The Trojan chief, who, held at bay from far, On his Vulcanian orb sustain’d the war.
cards.whyThisWorks: The second paragraph clearly shifts from narrating Aeneas's battlefield dominance to introducing Lausus's heroic intervention, allowing students to identify how a new paragraph can signal a tonal and thematic pivot while extending the conflict.
cards.skillStrategy: Ask yourself: does this paragraph continue what came before, or does it introduce a new character, idea, or emotional direction that changes the focus?
evidencePoints: His father's peril Lausus view'd with grief; He sigh'd, he wept, he ran to his relief.
And here, heroic youth, 'tis here I must / To thy immortal memory be just, / And sing an act so noble and so new
cards.question: What is the primary job of the second paragraph, beginning with 'His father's peril Lausus view'd with grief'?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The paragraph concludes the battle by showing that Aeneas has defeated Mezentius and the fighting is over.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The paragraph shifts focus from Aeneas's victory over Mezentius to Lausus's act of self-sacrifice, introducing a new heroic figure and a contrasting emotional tone.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The paragraph extends the description of Mezentius's wound by providing additional details about how deeply the javelin pierced his thigh.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The paragraph proves that Aeneas is the superior warrior by showing that even Lausus's intervention cannot stop the Trojan chief from winning the fight.

cards.standardTitle: Central idea and supporting evidence
cards.excerpt: Then Nisus thus: “Alas! thy tender years Would minister new matter to my fears. So may the gods, who view this friendly strife, Restore me to thy lov’d embrace with life, Condemn’d to pay my vows, (as sure I trust,) This thy request is cruel and unjust. But if some chance—as many chances are, And doubtful hazards, in the deeds of war— If one should reach my head, there let it fall, And spare thy life; I would not perish all. Thy bloomy youth deserves a longer date: Live thou to mourn thy love’s unhappy fate; To bear my mangled body from the foe, Or buy it back, and fun’ral rites bestow. Or, if hard fortune shall those dues deny, Thou canst at least an empty tomb supply. O let not me the widow’s tears renew! Nor let a mother’s curse my name pursue: Thy pious parent, who, for love of thee, Forsook the coasts of friendly Sicily, Her age committing to the seas and wind, When ev’ry weary matron stay’d behind.” To this, Euryalus: “You plead in vain, And but protract the cause you cannot gain. No more delays, but haste!” With that, he wakes The nodding watch; each to his office takes. The guard reliev’d, the gen’rous couple went To find the council at the royal tent.
cards.whyThisWorks: Nisus's speech layers multiple specific reasons—youth, grief, a mother's sacrifice—all converging on the central idea that Euryalus should stay behind, giving students rich evidence to distinguish the overarching claim from supporting details.
cards.skillStrategy: Ask yourself what one idea all the details in the speech are working together to prove, rather than focusing on just one detail like burial or the mother.
evidencePoints: Thy bloomy youth deserves a longer date: Live thou to mourn thy love's unhappy fate
O let not me the widow's tears renew! Nor let a mother's curse my name pursue
cards.question: Nisus tells Euryalus, 'Thy bloomy youth deserves a longer date,' and warns against a 'mother's curse' pursuing his name. What central idea do these details, along with the rest of Nisus's speech, work together to express?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Nisus argues that the mission is so deadly that both soldiers should wait for better odds before attempting it together.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Nisus urges Euryalus to stay behind because his youth is too valuable to sacrifice and his death would bring devastating grief to those who love him.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Nisus is chiefly concerned that without Euryalus present, his own body will go unburied and his memory will be dishonored after battle.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Nisus reminds Euryalus that his mother gave up the safety of Sicily for him, so loyalty to her must take priority over loyalty to Nisus.

cards.standardTitle: Key literary elements add layers of meaning
cards.excerpt: While thus in talk the flying hours they pass, The sun had finish’d more than half his race: And they, perhaps, in words and tears had spent The little time of stay which Heav’n had lent; But thus the Sibyl chides their long delay: “Night rushes down, and headlong drives the day: ’Tis here, in different paths, the way divides; The right to Pluto’s golden palace guides; The left to that unhappy region tends, Which to the depth of Tartarus descends; The seat of night profound, and punish’d fiends.” Then thus Deiphobus: “O sacred maid, Forbear to chide, and be your will obey’d! Lo! to the secret shadows I retire, To pay my penance till my years expire. Proceed, auspicious prince, with glory crown’d, And born to better fates than I have found.” He said; and, while he said, his steps he turn’d To secret shadows, and in silence mourn’d.
cards.whyThisWorks: Deiphobus's final speech and silent departure reveal a character defined by resigned acceptance of punishment, contrasting with Aeneas's destined glory and adding meaning about fate, guilt, and the cost of war.
cards.skillStrategy: When a character speaks and then acts, ask yourself: what do the words AND the action together reveal about who this person is and what they represent?
evidencePoints: Lo! to the secret shadows I retire, To pay my penance till my years expire.
He said; and, while he said, his steps he turn'd To secret shadows, and in silence mourn'd.
cards.question: In the final lines, Deiphobus says 'Lo! to the secret shadows I retire, / To pay my penance till my years expire' and then 'turn'd / To secret shadows, and in silence mourn'd.' What does this combination of speech and action reveal about Deiphobus as a character?

choices.label: A
choices.text: He resents Aeneas's fortune and withdraws in bitterness, unable to accept that his suffering is deserved.

choices.label: B
choices.text: He has fully accepted his fate as just punishment, departing without protest or appeal, which marks him as a figure of sorrowful resignation rather than defiance.

choices.label: C
choices.text: He obeys the Sibyl's command out of fear, showing that supernatural authority controls every soul in the underworld.

choices.label: D
choices.text: He turns away quickly because he is ashamed to be seen by Aeneas, suggesting their friendship ended in betrayal before his death.

cards.standardTitle: Epic poetry: characters, structures, and themes
cards.excerpt:
Thus having said, the hero bound his brows With leafy branches, then perform’d his vows; Adoring first the genius of the place, Then Earth, the mother of the heav’nly race, The nymphs, and native godheads yet unknown, And Night, and all the stars that gild her sable throne, And ancient Cybel, and Idaean Jove, And last his sire below, and mother queen above. Then heav’n’s high monarch thunder’d thrice aloud, And thrice he shook aloft a golden cloud. Soon thro’ the joyful camp a rumour flew, The time was come their city to renew. Then ev’ry brow with cheerful green is crown’d, The feasts are doubled, and the bowls go round.

When next the rosy morn disclos’d the day, The scouts to sev’ral parts divide their way, To learn the natives’ names, their towns explore, The coasts and trendings of the crooked shore: Here Tiber flows, and here Numicus stands; Here warlike Latins hold the happy lands. The pious chief, who sought by peaceful ways To found his empire, and his town to raise, A hundred youths from all his train selects, And to the Latian court their course directs, (The spacious palace where their prince resides,) And all their heads with wreaths of olive hides. They go commission’d to require a peace, And carry presents to procure access. Thus while they speed their pace, the prince designs His new-elected seat, and draws the lines. The Trojans round the place a rampire cast, And palisades about the trenches plac’d.
