cards.whyThisWorks: Jupiter's triple thunderclap and the shaking of the golden cloud function as direct divine intervention that transforms the mood of the camp and authorizes Aeneas's mission to found a new city, making the supernatural force the pivot point of the entire passage.
cards.skillStrategy: When a god acts in an epic, ask what changes because of that action — the change reveals how divine intervention shapes the plot or theme.
evidencePoints: Then heav'n's high monarch thunder'd thrice aloud, And thrice he shook aloft a golden cloud.
Soon thro' the joyful camp a rumour flew, The time was come their city to renew.
cards.question: In the first paragraph, Jupiter thunders three times and shakes a golden cloud. How does this divine act shape the action that follows in both paragraphs?

choices.label: A
choices.text: It warns Aeneas that the Latins are hostile, so he sends scouts to gather information before risking an attack.

choices.label: B
choices.text: It signals divine approval of Aeneas's mission, transforming the camp's mood and setting the founding of the city and the embassy to the Latins into motion.

choices.label: C
choices.text: It fulfills the prayers Aeneas offered to Night and the stars, confirming that those lesser deities have already blessed the Trojans' voyage.

choices.label: D
choices.text: It frightens the Trojan soldiers into action, forcing Aeneas to restore order by selecting a hundred youths and sending them on a peaceful mission.

cards.standardTitle: Text structure and feature purpose
cards.excerpt:
At this the lovely nymph, with grief oppress’d, Thrice tore her hair, and beat her comely breast. To whom Saturnia thus: “Thy tears are late: Haste, snatch him, if he can be snatch’d from fate: New tumults kindle; violate the truce: Who knows what changeful fortune may produce? ’Tis not a crime t’ attempt what I decree; Or, if it were, discharge the crime on me.” She said, and, sailing on the winged wind, Left the sad nymph suspended in her mind.

And now in pomp the peaceful kings appear: Four steeds the chariot of Latinus bear; Twelve golden beams around his temples play, To mark his lineage from the God of Day. Two snowy coursers Turnus’ chariot yoke, And in his hand two massy spears he shook: Then issued from the camp, in arms divine, Aeneas, author of the Roman line; And by his side Ascanius took his place, The second hope of Rome’s immortal race. Adorn’d in white, a rev’rend priest appears, And off’rings to the flaming altars bears; A porket, and a lamb that never suffer’d shears. Then to the rising sun he turns his eyes, And strews the beasts, design’d for sacrifice, With salt and meal: with like officious care He marks their foreheads, and he clips their hair. Betwixt their horns the purple wine he sheds; With the same gen’rous juice the flame he feeds.
cards.whyThisWorks: The two paragraphs offer a clear structural contrast: the first ends with Juturna 'suspended in her mind' after a tense divine command, while the second opens with 'the peaceful kings appear' and details the public truce ceremony, giving students a concrete moment to identify a scene shift.
cards.skillStrategy: Ask yourself: does this paragraph continue the same scene and idea, or does it move to a new place, time, or focus? Look for signal words and changes in who or what is described.
evidencePoints: Left the sad nymph suspended in her mind.
And now in pomp the peaceful kings appear
cards.question: The first paragraph ends with Juturna left 'suspended in her mind.' What is the job of the second paragraph, which opens with 'And now in pomp the peaceful kings appear'?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The second paragraph extends the tension of the first by showing Juturna acting on Saturnia's command to 'kindle new tumults' among the assembled kings and priests.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The second paragraph shifts the scene from the private, unresolved divine exchange to the formal, public ceremony in which Latinus, Turnus, Aeneas, and a priest prepare the truce ritual.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The second paragraph contrasts Aeneas's role as 'author of the Roman line' with Juturna's grief in order to prove that mortal glory outweighs divine sorrow.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The second paragraph concludes the conflict introduced in the first paragraph by confirming that Saturnia's plan to violate the truce has already succeeded before the ceremony begins.

cards.standardTitle: Central idea and supporting evidence
cards.excerpt: But Salius enters, and, exclaiming loud For justice, deafens and disturbs the crowd; Urges his cause may in the court be heard; And pleads the prize is wrongfully conferr’d. But favour for Euryalus appears; His blooming beauty, with his tender tears, Had brib’d the judges for the promis’d prize. Besides, Diores fills the court with cries, Who vainly reaches at the last reward, If the first palm on Salius be conferr’d. Then thus the prince: “Let no disputes arise: Where fortune plac’d it, I award the prize. But fortune’s errors give me leave to mend, At least to pity my deserving friend.” He said, and, from among the spoils, he draws (Pond’rous with shaggy mane and golden paws) A lion’s hide: to Salius this he gives. Nisus with envy sees the gift, and grieves. “If such rewards to vanquish’d men are due.” He said, “and falling is to rise by you, What prize may Nisus from your bounty claim, Who merited the first rewards and fame? In falling, both an equal fortune tried; Would fortune for my fall so well provide!” With this he pointed to his face, and show’d His hand and all his habit smear’d with blood. Th’ indulgent father of the people smil’d, And caus’d to be produc’d an ample shield, Of wondrous art, by Didymaon wrought, Long since from Neptune’s bars in triumph brought. This giv’n to Nisus, he divides the rest, And equal justice in his gifts express’d.
cards.whyThisWorks: The prince's declaration 'But fortune's errors give me leave to mend' followed by his gifts to both Salius and Nisus gives students a concrete textual moment to identify the central idea about just leadership correcting chance's unfair outcomes.
cards.skillStrategy: When identifying the central idea, find the claim a character makes and then trace how the actions that follow either support or complicate that claim.
evidencePoints: But fortune's errors give me leave to mend, At least to pity my deserving friend.
equal justice in his gifts express'd
cards.question: After the prince states 'But fortune's errors give me leave to mend,' he awards a lion's hide to Salius and an elaborate shield to Nisus. What central idea do these specific words and actions together express?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The bribery of judges by Euryalus's 'blooming beauty' and 'tender tears' makes any fair outcome in the competition impossible, even for a prince.

choices.label: B
choices.text: A just ruler uses his own authority to correct the unfair outcomes of chance and recognize those who truly deserved reward, as shown when the prince gives gifts to both Salius and Nisus.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Nisus's complaint that he 'merited the first rewards and fame' reveals that personal ambition, not a desire for justice, is what motivates competitors to challenge the prince's decisions.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Because Diores 'fills the court with cries' and Salius demands his case 'be heard,' the passage shows that public pressure, not a ruler's judgment, ultimately determines who receives prizes.

cards.standardTitle: Key literary elements add layers of meaning
cards.excerpt: Thus far the sacred sports they celebrate: But Fortune soon resum’d her ancient hate; For, while they pay the dead his annual dues, Those envied rites Saturnian Juno views; And sends the goddess of the various bow, To try new methods of revenge below; Supplies the winds to wing her airy way, Where in the port secure the navy lay. Swiftly fair Iris down her arch descends, And, undiscern’d, her fatal voyage ends. She saw the gath’ring crowd; and, gliding thence, The desert shore, and fleet without defence. The Trojan matrons, on the sands alone, With sighs and tears Anchises’ death bemoan; Then, turning to the sea their weeping eyes, Their pity to themselves renews their cries. “Alas!” said one, “what oceans yet remain For us to sail! what labours to sustain!” All take the word, and, with a gen’ral groan, Implore the gods for peace, and places of their own.
cards.whyThisWorks: The Trojan matrons' collective grief—sighing over Anchises' death, lamenting 'what oceans yet remain,' and imploring the gods for peace—characterizes them as emotionally exhausted and vulnerable, which directly enables Juno's plot through Iris to exploit their weakness, layering meaning onto Juno's scheming.
cards.skillStrategy: When analyzing characterization, ask how a character's specific words or actions reveal a trait that drives or is shaped by the plot—then trace how that trait adds a deeper layer of meaning to the scene.
evidencePoints: "Alas!" said one, "what oceans yet remain / For us to sail! what labours to sustain!"
Implore the gods for peace, and places of their own.
cards.question: In the excerpt, the Trojan matrons cry out "what oceans yet remain / For us to sail! what labours to sustain!" and collectively "implore the gods for peace, and places of their own." How does this characterization of the matrons add meaning to Juno's decision to send Iris to them?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Their open longing for peace reveals that they have already rejected Aeneas's leadership, making Iris's mission unnecessary because the women will act on their own.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Their exhaustion and desperate longing for rest, expressed in their cries and prayers, reveal a vulnerability that makes them ideal targets for the revenge Juno directs Iris to carry out.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Their grief over Anchises and prayers to the gods show that divine intervention has already answered their pleas, which is why Juno must act quickly before the Trojans gain strength.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Their weeping over Anchises' death characterizes them as loyal only to the dead, suggesting they are indifferent to the fleet's fate and therefore unimportant to Juno's scheme.

cards.standardTitle: Theme development across a literary text
cards.excerpt:
Within the space, an olive tree had stood, A sacred shade, a venerable wood, For vows to Faunus paid, the Latins’ guardian god. Here hung the vests, and tablets were engrav’d, Of sinking mariners from shipwreck sav’d. With heedless hands the Trojans fell’d the tree, To make the ground enclos’d for combat free. Deep in the root, whether by fate, or chance, Or erring haste, the Trojan drove his lance; Then stoop’d, and tugg’d with force immense, to free Th’ incumber’d spear from the tenacious tree; That, whom his fainting limbs pursued in vain, His flying weapon might from far attain.

Confus’d with fear, bereft of human aid, Then Turnus to the gods, and first to Faunus pray’d: “O Faunus, pity! and thou Mother Earth, Where I thy foster son receiv’d my birth, Hold fast the steel! If my religious hand Your plant has honour’d, which your foes profan’d, Propitious hear my pious pray’r!” He said, Nor with successless vows invok’d their aid. Th’ incumbent hero wrench’d, and pull’d, and strain’d; But still the stubborn earth the steel detain’d. Juturna took her time; and, while in vain He strove, assum’d Meticus’ form again, And, in that imitated shape, restor’d To the despairing prince his Daunian sword. The Queen of Love, who, with disdain and grief, Saw the bold nymph afford this prompt relief, T’ assert her offspring with a greater deed, From the tough root the ling’ring weapon freed.
cards.whyThisWorks: The excerpt contrasts the Trojans' desecration of Faunus's sacred tree with Turnus's reverent prayer to that same god, allowing students to distinguish details that develop a theme about divine favor and piety from true-but-thematically-irrelevant details about the battle setting.
cards.skillStrategy: Ask yourself: does this detail show how the theme is built, or does it just describe what happened in the scene?
evidencePoints: With heedless hands the Trojans fell'd the tree, To make the ground enclos'd for combat free.
O Faunus, pity! and thou Mother Earth… If my religious hand Your plant has honour'd, which your foes profan'd, Propitious hear my pious pray'r!
cards.question: Which detail from the excerpt most directly develops the theme that reverence toward the divine is rewarded while disregard for it brings consequence?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Juturna disguises herself as Meticus and returns Turnus's Daunian sword, showing that human allies can intervene in battle when a warrior is in danger.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The Trojans cut down Faunus's sacred tree 'with heedless hands,' while Turnus prays to that same god by honoring his plant—and the earth holds the Trojan spear fast in answer to Turnus's prayer.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Mariners' votive tablets and garments hung on the olive tree, showing that the site near the combat ground had long been a place of worship for the Latin people.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The Queen of Love ultimately frees the Trojan's spear from the root, demonstrating that the gods on both sides of the conflict are equally willing to intervene for their chosen warriors.

cards.standardTitle: Epic poetry: characters, structures, and themes
cards.excerpt:
He said; and, pressing onward thro’ the crew, Pois’d in his lifted arm, his lance he threw. The winged weapon, whistling in the wind, Came driving on, nor miss’d the mark design’d. At once the cornel rattled in the skies; At once tumultuous shouts and clamours rise. Nine brothers in a goodly band there stood, Born of Arcadian mix’d with Tuscan blood, Gylippus’ sons: the fatal jav’lin flew, Aim’d at the midmost of the friendly crew. A passage thro’ the jointed arms it found, Just where the belt was to the body bound, And struck the gentle youth extended on the ground. Then, fir’d with pious rage, the gen’rous train Run madly forward to revenge the slain. And some with eager haste their jav’lins throw; And some with sword in hand assault the foe.

The wish’d insult the Latine troops embrace, And meet their ardour in the middle space. The Trojans, Tuscans, and Arcadian line, With equal courage obviate their design. Peace leaves the violated fields, and hate Both armies urges to their mutual fate. With impious haste their altars are o’erturn’d, The sacrifice half-broil’d, and half-unburn’d. Thick storms of steel from either army fly, And clouds of clashing darts obscure the sky; Brands from the fire are missive weapons made, With chargers, bowls, and all the priestly trade. Latinus, frighted, hastens from the fray, And bears his unregarded gods away. These on their horses vault; those yoke the car; The rest, with swords on high, run headlong to the war.
cards.whyThisWorks: The fatal javelin striking 'the gentle youth' mid-ceremony is a classic epic divine-intervention turning point where a single violent act collapses sacred order into total war, directly illustrating how structure and theme interact in epic poetry.
cards.skillStrategy: When analyzing epic structure, trace how one specific action—like the javelin throw—triggers a chain of consequences that shifts the poem's tone, setting, and theme from order to chaos.
evidencePoints: struck the gentle youth extended on the ground
Peace leaves the violated fields, and hate / Both armies urges to their mutual fate
cards.question: In the excerpt, the fatal javelin 'struck the gentle youth extended on the ground' during what appears to be a peace ceremony. How does this single strike function as a structural turning point in the passage, and what evidence from the text supports that reading?

choices.label: A
choices.text: It identifies the javelin's thrower as the decisive aggressor, prompting the nine sons of Gylippus to challenge him in single combat while Latinus attempts to restore the sacrifice at the altars.

choices.label: B
choices.text: It collapses the peace ritual into uncontrolled war: the nine brothers rush to 'revenge the slain,' the altars are overturned, sacrifices are left 'half-broil'd, and half-unburn'd,' and 'hate both armies urges to their mutual fate.'

choices.label: C
choices.text: It causes Latinus to rally both armies around the overturned altars, directing them to use 'chargers, bowls, and all the priestly trade' as weapons in a coordinated defense of the sacred space.

choices.label: D
choices.text: It exposes a hidden betrayal, since the nine sons of Gylippus—born of 'Arcadian mix'd with Tuscan blood'—abandon the Trojans and follow Latinus as he 'bears his unregarded gods away' from the field.

cards.standardTitle: Text structure and feature purpose
cards.excerpt:
Now with full force his spear young Pallas threw, And, having thrown, his shining falchion drew The steel just graz’d along the shoulder joint, And mark’d it slightly with the glancing point, Fierce Turnus first to nearer distance drew, And pois’d his pointed spear, before he threw: Then, as the winged weapon whizz’d along, “See now,” said he, “whose arm is better strung.” The spear kept on the fatal course, unstay’d By plates of ir’n, which o’er the shield were laid: Thro’ folded brass and tough bull hides it pass’d, His corslet pierc’d, and reach’d his heart at last. In vain the youth tugs at the broken wood; The soul comes issuing with the vital blood: He falls; his arms upon his body sound; And with his bloody teeth he bites the ground.

Turnus bestrode the corpse: “Arcadians, hear,” Said he; “my message to your master bear: Such as the sire deserv’d, the son I send; It costs him dear to be the Phrygians’ friend. The lifeless body, tell him, I bestow, Unask’d, to rest his wand’ring ghost below.” He said, and trampled down with all the force Of his left foot, and spurn’d the wretched corse; Then snatch’d the shining belt, with gold inlaid; The belt Eurytion’s artful hands had made, Where fifty fatal brides, express’d to sight, All in the compass of one mournful night, Depriv’d their bridegrooms of returning light.
cards.whyThisWorks: The two paragraphs have distinct jobs—the first narrates the fatal combat between Turnus and Pallas, while the second shifts to Turnus's triumphant speech and desecration of the corpse, allowing students to identify how the second paragraph extends and shifts the meaning of the first.
cards.skillStrategy: Ask yourself what new work the second paragraph is doing that the first paragraph did not already do—does it repeat, contrast, extend, or shift the focus?
evidencePoints: He falls; his arms upon his body sound; And with his bloody teeth he bites the ground.
Turnus bestrode the corpse: 'Arcadians, hear,' Said he; 'my message to your master bear'
cards.question: The first paragraph ends with Pallas falling in battle. What is the primary job of the second paragraph in relation to the first?

choices.label: A
choices.text: It returns to the moment of the spear throw to clarify how Turnus defeated Pallas in combat.

choices.label: B
choices.text: It shifts from the act of killing to Turnus's public humiliation of the fallen Pallas and his seizure of the belt as a trophy.

choices.label: C
choices.text: It introduces Eurytion as a new character whose craftsmanship becomes the central focus of the passage.

choices.label: D
choices.text: It contrasts Turnus's cowardice with the bravery Pallas showed during the fight described in the first paragraph.

cards.standardTitle: Central idea and supporting evidence
cards.excerpt: Amidst the loud applauses of the shore, Gyas outstripp’d the rest, and sprung before: Cloanthus, better mann’d, pursued him fast, But his o’er-masted galley check’d his haste. The Centaur and the Dolphin brush the brine With equal oars, advancing in a line; And now the mighty Centaur seems to lead, And now the speedy Dolphin gets ahead; Now board to board the rival vessels row, The billows lave the skies, and ocean groans below. They reach’d the mark; proud Gyas and his train In triumph rode, the victors of the main; But, steering round, he charg’d his pilot stand More close to shore, and skim along the sand. “Let others bear to sea!” Menoetes heard; But secret shelves too cautiously he fear’d, And, fearing, sought the deep; and still aloof he steer’d. With louder cries the captain call’d again: “Bear to the rocky shore, and shun the main.” He spoke, and, speaking, at his stern he saw The bold Cloanthus near the shelvings draw. Betwixt the mark and him the Scylla stood, And in a closer compass plow’d the flood. He pass’d the mark; and, wheeling, got before: Gyas blasphem’d the gods, devoutly swore, Cried out for anger, and his hair he tore. Mindless of others’ lives (so high was grown His rising rage) and careless of his own, The trembling dotard to the deck he drew; Then hoisted up, and overboard he threw: This done, he seiz’d the helm; his fellows cheer’d, Turn’d short upon the shelfs, and madly steer’d.
cards.whyThisWorks: The excerpt shows Gyas throwing his pilot overboard in a rage after losing the lead, giving students a concrete passage moment to anchor the central idea rather than a vague topic.
cards.skillStrategy: Ask yourself what the whole passage is really saying about a character or situation, not just what happens in one moment — then check that your answer covers the full excerpt, not just one detail.
evidencePoints: Mindless of others' lives (so high was grown / His rising rage) and careless of his own, / The trembling dotard to the deck he drew; / Then hoisted up, and overboard he threw
Gyas blasphem'd the gods, devoutly swore, / Cried out for anger, and his hair he tore.
cards.question: After Cloanthus passes Gyas at the mark, the narrator describes Gyas as 'Mindless of others' lives' and shows him throwing his pilot overboard. What central idea does this moment, along with the events leading to it, develop throughout the passage?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Menoetes's fear of hidden rocks is the true cause of Gyas losing the race, making Gyas's punishment of him justified.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Gyas's inability to control his anger leads him to violent, reckless decisions that endanger his crew and cost him the race.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The race between the Centaur and the Dolphin proves that a ship's speed matters more than its captain's judgment.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Cloanthus wins the race because he is a more experienced sailor who knows how to navigate close to the rocky shore.

cards.standardTitle: Key literary elements add layers of meaning
cards.excerpt: The prince then call’d Achates, to supply The spears that knew the way to victory— “Those fatal weapons, which, inur’d to blood, In Grecian bodies under Ilium stood: Not one of those my hand shall toss in vain Against our foes, on this contended plain.” He said; then seiz’d a mighty spear, and threw; Which, wing’d with fate, thro’ Maeon’s buckler flew, Pierc’d all the brazen plates, and reach’d his heart: He stagger’d with intolerable smart. Alcanor saw; and reach’d, but reach’d in vain, His helping hand, his brother to sustain. A second spear, which kept the former course, From the same hand, and sent with equal force, His right arm pierc’d, and holding on, bereft His use of both, and pinion’d down his left. Then Numitor from his dead brother drew Th’ ill-omen’d spear, and at the Trojan threw: Preventing fate directs the lance awry, Which, glancing, only mark’d Achates’ thigh.
cards.whyThisWorks: Aeneas's deliberate speech about the spears 'inur'd to blood' in Greek bodies, followed immediately by his precise, lethal throws, reveals a warrior defined by purposeful vengeance and controlled fury, showing how action and speech together characterize him.
cards.skillStrategy: When a character speaks a promise and then immediately acts on it, ask what that combination reveals about who they are and what they value.
evidencePoints: Not one of those my hand shall toss in vain / Against our foes, on this contended plain.
He said; then seiz'd a mighty spear, and threw; / Which, wing'd with fate, thro' Maeon's buckler flew
cards.question: Read the following lines from the excerpt: 'Not one of those my hand shall toss in vain / Against our foes, on this contended plain. / He said; then seiz'd a mighty spear, and threw.' What do Aeneas's words followed immediately by his action reveal about his character?

choices.label: A
choices.text: He is reckless in battle, throwing spears without considering the consequences for those around him, as shown when Achates is grazed by a redirected lance.

choices.label: B
choices.text: He is a warrior of absolute resolve whose vow of deadly precision is instantly fulfilled, showing that his words and deeds are one and the same.

choices.label: C
choices.text: He relies on the gods to guide his spears rather than his own skill, since the narrator credits fate rather than Aeneas with the kills.

choices.label: D
choices.text: He is driven primarily by grief for fallen comrades, calling for the spears as a way to honor those who died under Ilium rather than to win the battle.

cards.standardTitle: Theme development across a literary text
cards.excerpt:
Thus having said, the hero bound his brows With leafy branches, then perform’d his vows; Adoring first the genius of the place, Then Earth, the mother of the heav’nly race, The nymphs, and native godheads yet unknown, And Night, and all the stars that gild her sable throne, And ancient Cybel, and Idaean Jove, And last his sire below, and mother queen above. Then heav’n’s high monarch thunder’d thrice aloud, And thrice he shook aloft a golden cloud. Soon thro’ the joyful camp a rumour flew, The time was come their city to renew. Then ev’ry brow with cheerful green is crown’d, The feasts are doubled, and the bowls go round.

When next the rosy morn disclos’d the day, The scouts to sev’ral parts divide their way, To learn the natives’ names, their towns explore, The coasts and trendings of the crooked shore: Here Tiber flows, and here Numicus stands; Here warlike Latins hold the happy lands. The pious chief, who sought by peaceful ways To found his empire, and his town to raise, A hundred youths from all his train selects, And to the Latian court their course directs, (The spacious palace where their prince resides,) And all their heads with wreaths of olive hides. They go commission’d to require a peace, And carry presents to procure access. Thus while they speed their pace, the prince designs His new-elected seat, and draws the lines. The Trojans round the place a rampire cast, And palisades about the trenches plac’d.
cards.whyThisWorks: The excerpt pairs Aeneas's ritual prayers and olive-branch embassy with his simultaneous military fortification, giving students two categories of detail—those that develop the theme of reverence-plus-deliberate-action and those that are merely true topic details about celebration or divine signs.
cards.skillStrategy: Ask yourself: does this detail show the theme being built, or does it just describe something that happened in the same story?
evidencePoints: The pious chief, who sought by peaceful ways / To found his empire, and his town to raise
The Trojans round the place a rampire cast, / And palisades about the trenches plac'd.
cards.question: The narrator calls Aeneas 'the pious chief, who sought by peaceful ways / To found his empire, and his town to raise.' Which other detail from the excerpt most directly develops the theme that building a lasting civilization demands both sacred duty and practical preparation?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Heaven's monarch 'thunder'd thrice aloud' and 'thrice he shook aloft a golden cloud,' signaling that the gods have approved the Trojans' mission.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Aeneas sends a hundred olive-crowned envoys to seek peace with the Latins while at the same time drawing the lines of his new settlement and ordering trenches and palisades to be built.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Scouts divide into several parties to learn the natives' names, explore their towns, and map 'the coasts and trendings of the crooked shore.'

choices.label: D
choices.text: 'Ev'ry brow with cheerful green is crown'd, / The feasts are doubled, and the bowls go round,' showing the Trojans celebrate the news that their city will be renewed.

cards.standardTitle: Epic poetry: characters, structures, and themes
cards.excerpt: Then Nisus thus: “Alas! thy tender years Would minister new matter to my fears. So may the gods, who view this friendly strife, Restore me to thy lov’d embrace with life, Condemn’d to pay my vows, (as sure I trust,) This thy request is cruel and unjust. But if some chance—as many chances are, And doubtful hazards, in the deeds of war— If one should reach my head, there let it fall, And spare thy life; I would not perish all. Thy bloomy youth deserves a longer date: Live thou to mourn thy love’s unhappy fate; To bear my mangled body from the foe, Or buy it back, and fun’ral rites bestow. Or, if hard fortune shall those dues deny, Thou canst at least an empty tomb supply. O let not me the widow’s tears renew! Nor let a mother’s curse my name pursue: Thy pious parent, who, for love of thee, Forsook the coasts of friendly Sicily, Her age committing to the seas and wind, When ev’ry weary matron stay’d behind.” To this, Euryalus: “You plead in vain, And but protract the cause you cannot gain. No more delays, but haste!” With that, he wakes The nodding watch; each to his office takes. The guard reliev’d, the gen’rous couple went To find the council at the royal tent.
cards.whyThisWorks: Nisus's oath 'So may the gods, who view this friendly strife, / Restore me to thy lov'd embrace with life' is a classic epic divine-intervention appeal in which a mortal calls on the gods as guarantors of a personal vow, directly illustrating how divine witness shapes heroic argument and character motivation in The Aeneid.
cards.skillStrategy: When you see a character call on the gods in an epic, ask what the character wants the gods to do and how that divine appeal supports or weakens the character's argument to another person.
evidencePoints: So may the gods, who view this friendly strife, / Restore me to thy lov'd embrace with life, / Condemn'd to pay my vows
Thy bloomy youth deserves a longer date: / Live thou to mourn thy love's unhappy fate
cards.question: Nisus invokes the gods with the words 'So may the gods, who view this friendly strife, / Restore me to thy lov'd embrace with life, / Condemn'd to pay my vows.' How does this appeal to the gods function within Nisus's larger argument that Euryalus, whose 'bloomy youth deserves a longer date,' should stay behind?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Nisus calls on the gods as enforcers of punishment, implying that Euryalus will suffer a divine curse like the 'mother's curse' Nisus fears for his own name if Euryalus disobeys and joins the mission.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Nisus invokes the gods as guarantors of his own safe return, using that assurance to strengthen his plea that Euryalus, whose 'bloomy youth deserves a longer date,' need not risk death alongside him.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Nisus appeals to the gods to confirm that his vows bind him alone to the mission, arguing that because Euryalus has made no such vow, his insistence on joining is 'cruel and unjust' in the gods' eyes.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Nisus summons the gods as witnesses to the sacrifice of Euryalus's mother, who 'forsook the coasts of friendly Sicily,' making her devotion the divine reason the gods themselves require Euryalus to survive.

cards.standardTitle: Text structure and feature purpose
cards.excerpt:
Now had they reach’d the hills, and storm’d the seat Of salvage beasts, in dens, their last retreat. The cry pursues the mountain goats: they bound From rock to rock, and keep the craggy ground; Quite otherwise the stags, a trembling train, In herds unsingled, scour the dusty plain, And a long chase in open view maintain. The glad Ascanius, as his courser guides, Spurs thro’ the vale, and these and those outrides. His horse’s flanks and sides are forc’d to feel The clanking lash, and goring of the steel. Impatiently he views the feeble prey, Wishing some nobler beast to cross his way, And rather would the tusky boar attend, Or see the tawny lion downward bend.

Meantime, the gath’ring clouds obscure the skies: From pole to pole the forky lightning flies; The rattling thunders roll; and Juno pours A wintry deluge down, and sounding show’rs. The company, dispers’d, to converts ride, And seek the homely cots, or mountain’s hollow side. The rapid rains, descending from the hills, To rolling torrents raise the creeping rills. The queen and prince, as love or fortune guides, One common cavern in her bosom hides. Then first the trembling earth the signal gave, And flashing fires enlighten all the cave; Hell from below, and Juno from above, And howling nymphs, were conscious of their love. From this ill-omen’d hour in time arose Debate and death, and all succeeding woes.
cards.whyThisWorks: The second paragraph performs a clear structural shift from the active hunt scene to a storm-driven turning point, allowing students to identify how a paragraph can pivot the narrative and introduce consequences.
cards.skillStrategy: Ask yourself: does this paragraph continue what came before, or does it change the direction, mood, or focus of the passage — and what signal words or events mark that change?
evidencePoints: Meantime, the gath'ring clouds obscure the skies
From this ill-omen'd hour in time arose / Debate and death, and all succeeding woes.
cards.question: What is the primary job of the second paragraph, beginning with 'Meantime, the gath'ring clouds obscure the skies'?

choices.label: A
choices.text: It extends the hunting scene by describing how the storm forces Ascanius to abandon his pursuit of nobler prey.

choices.label: B
choices.text: It shifts the passage from a scene of active pursuit to a fateful moment that the narrator identifies as the origin of future suffering.

choices.label: C
choices.text: It contrasts Juno's power over the weather with Ascanius's earlier display of skill and ambition on horseback.

choices.label: D
choices.text: It concludes the hunt by proving that the queen and prince were always destined to seek shelter together in the cave.

cards.standardTitle: Central idea and supporting evidence
cards.excerpt: The rosy morn was risen from the main, And horns and hounds awake the princely train: They issue early thro’ the city gate, Where the more wakeful huntsmen ready wait, With nets, and toils, and darts, beside the force Of Spartan dogs, and swift Massylian horse. The Tyrian peers and officers of state For the slow queen in antechambers wait; Her lofty courser, in the court below, Who his majestic rider seems to know, Proud of his purple trappings, paws the ground, And champs the golden bit, and spreads the foam around. The queen at length appears; on either hand The brawny guards in martial order stand. A flow’r’d simar with golden fringe she wore, And at her back a golden quiver bore; Her flowing hair a golden caul restrains, A golden clasp the Tyrian robe sustains. Then young Ascanius, with a sprightly grace, Leads on the Trojan youth to view the chase. But far above the rest in beauty shines The great Aeneas, the troop he joins; Like fair Apollo, when he leaves the frost Of wint’ry Xanthus, and the Lycian coast, When to his native Delos he resorts, Ordains the dances, and renews the sports; Where painted Scythians, mix’d with Cretan bands, Before the joyful altars join their hands: Himself, on Cynthus walking, sees below The merry madness of the sacred show. Green wreaths of bays his length of hair inclose; A golden fillet binds his awful brows; His quiver sounds: not less the prince is seen In manly presence, or in lofty mien.
cards.whyThisWorks: The excerpt builds a detailed royal procession scene but culminates in the extended Apollo simile comparing Aeneas to a god, requiring students to distinguish the central idea from the topic (a hunt) and isolated details (the queen's gold, Ascanius leading youth).
cards.skillStrategy: Ask yourself: what point does the whole passage keep building toward, not just what happens at the start or in one line?
evidencePoints: But far above the rest in beauty shines / The great Aeneas, the troop he joins
Not less the prince is seen / In manly presence, or in lofty mien
cards.question: The passage opens with the queen's golden attire and proud horse, then shifts to the line 'But far above the rest in beauty shines / The great Aeneas.' What central idea does this shift reveal about the entire scene?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The elaborate preparations of the Tyrian court — the nets, hounds, Spartan dogs, and Massylian horses — show that the royal hunt is the most important event described.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Despite the grandeur of the queen and her court, the scene ultimately exists to establish Aeneas as a figure of surpassing, almost divine, beauty and commanding presence.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The queen's golden caul, golden quiver, and golden clasp mark her as the dominant figure whose splendor no one in the hunting party can rival.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Young Ascanius leading the Trojan youth to the chase signals that the passage centers on the next generation of Trojans joining Tyrian society.

cards.standardTitle: Key literary elements add layers of meaning
cards.excerpt: The Trojan prince beheld him from afar, And dauntless undertook the doubtful war. Collected in his strength, and like a rock, Pois’d on his base, Mezentius stood the shock. He stood, and, measuring first with careful eyes The space his spear could reach, aloud he cries: “My strong right hand, and sword, assist my stroke! (Those only gods Mezentius will invoke.) His armour, from the Trojan pirate torn, By my triumphant Lausus shall be worn.” He said; and with his utmost force he threw The massy spear, which, hissing as it flew, Reach’d the celestial shield, that stopp’d the course; But, glancing thence, the yet unbroken force Took a new bent obliquely, and betwixt The side and bowels fam’d Anthores fix’d. Anthores had from Argos travel’d far, Alcides’ friend, and brother of the war; Till, tir’d with toils, fair Italy he chose, And in Evander’s palace sought repose. Now, falling by another’s wound, his eyes He cast to heav’n, on Argos thinks, and dies.
cards.whyThisWorks: Mezentius's speech invoking only his 'strong right hand and sword' as his gods—while dismissing divine aid—reveals his arrogant self-reliance and adds meaning to his character as a warrior who trusts mortal strength over divine favor.
cards.skillStrategy: When a character speaks or acts in a distinctive way, ask what that choice reveals about who they are and what the author wants you to understand about them.
evidencePoints: 'My strong right hand, and sword, assist my stroke! (Those only gods Mezentius will invoke.)'
'Collected in his strength, and like a rock, / Pois'd on his base, Mezentius stood the shock.'
cards.question: When Mezentius declares 'My strong right hand, and sword, assist my stroke! (Those only gods Mezentius will invoke.),' what does this speech reveal about his character?

choices.label: A
choices.text: He is a pious warrior who honors traditional gods before every battle, showing his respect for divine authority.

choices.label: B
choices.text: He rejects divine assistance and places absolute faith in his own physical power, revealing a pride that sets him apart from warriors who seek the gods' favor.

choices.label: C
choices.text: He is desperate and frightened by the Trojan prince, so he calls on his sword as a last resort when no gods will answer him.

choices.label: D
choices.text: He invokes his weapons to honor his son Lausus, showing that his true motivation in battle is fatherly devotion rather than personal glory.

cards.standardTitle: Theme development across a literary text
cards.excerpt:
The herald summons all, and then proclaims Cloanthus conqu’ror of the naval games. The prince with laurel crowns the victor’s head, And three fat steers are to his vessel led, The ship’s reward; with gen’rous wine beside, And sums of silver, which the crew divide. The leaders are distinguish’d from the rest; The victor honour’d with a nobler vest, Where gold and purple strive in equal rows, And needlework its happy cost bestows. There Ganymede is wrought with living art, Chasing thro’ Ida’s groves the trembling hart: Breathless he seems, yet eager to pursue; When from aloft descends, in open view, The bird of Jove, and, sousing on his prey, With crooked talons bears the boy away. In vain, with lifted hands and gazing eyes, His guards behold him soaring thro’ the skies, And dogs pursue his flight with imitated cries.

Mnestheus the second victor was declar’d; And, summon’d there, the second prize he shar’d. A coat of mail, brave Demoleus bore, More brave Aeneas from his shoulders tore, In single combat on the Trojan shore: This was ordain’d for Mnestheus to possess; In war for his defence, for ornament in peace. Rich was the gift, and glorious to behold, But yet so pond’rous with its plates of gold, That scarce two servants could the weight sustain; Yet, loaded thus, Demoleus o’er the plain Pursued and lightly seiz’d the Trojan train. The third, succeeding to the last reward, Two goodly bowls of massy silver shar’d, With figures prominent, and richly wrought, And two brass caldrons from Dodona brought.
cards.whyThisWorks: The Ganymede embroidery and the paradox of Demoleus's armor both offer concrete textual moments where true-but-topic-only details (prizes awarded, combat history) must be distinguished from details that actually develop the theme of mortal glory constrained by greater forces.
cards.skillStrategy: Ask yourself: does this detail show the theme in action, or does it just describe what happened in the scene without connecting to a larger idea?
evidencePoints: In vain, with lifted hands and gazing eyes, His guards behold him soaring thro' the skies
Yet, loaded thus, Demoleus o'er the plain Pursued and lightly seiz'd the Trojan train
cards.question: The narrator describes the embroidered scene on Cloanthus's vest: Ganymede chases a hart through Ida's groves, but Jove's eagle seizes him and carries him skyward while 'In vain, with lifted hands and gazing eyes, His guards behold him soaring thro' the skies.' Which statement best explains how this specific moment develops a theme in the passage?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The scene records that Ganymede was hunting in Ida's groves, establishing the setting of the myth depicted on the prize garment.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The guards' helpless upward gaze as Ganymede is taken beyond their reach illustrates that mortal effort and protection are powerless against the will of divine forces.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The detail that Ganymede appears breathless yet eager shows that the pursuit of glory requires great physical effort and personal sacrifice.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The needlework's depiction of Jove's eagle demonstrates the high artistic skill of the craftsmen who created the victor's prize garment.

cards.standardTitle: Epic poetry: characters, structures, and themes
cards.excerpt: He said, and rose; as holy zeal inspires, He rakes hot embers, and renews the fires; His country gods and Vesta then adores With cakes and incense, and their aid implores. Next, for his friends and royal host he sent, Reveal’d his vision, and the gods’ intent, With his own purpose. All, without delay, The will of Jove, and his desires obey. They list with women each degenerate name, Who dares not hazard life for future fame. These they cashier: the brave remaining few, Oars, banks, and cables, half consum’d, renew. The prince designs a city with the plow; The lots their sev’ral tenements allow. This part is nam’d from Ilium, that from Troy, And the new king ascends the throne with joy; A chosen senate from the people draws; Appoints the judges, and ordains the laws. Then, on the top of Eryx, they begin A rising temple to the Paphian queen. Anchises, last, is honour’d as a god; A priest is added, annual gifts bestow’d, And groves are planted round his blest abode. Nine days they pass in feasts, their temples crown’d; And fumes of incense in the fanes abound. Then from the south arose a gentle breeze That curl’d the smoothness of the glassy seas; The rising winds a ruffling gale afford, And call the merry mariners aboard.
cards.whyThisWorks: The excerpt shows two distinct moments of divine intervention—Jove's vision compelling the companions to renew the fleet and found a city, and the southern breeze calling the mariners back to sea—allowing students to analyze how gods drive epic action at both a communal and a transitional level.
cards.skillStrategy: When analyzing divine intervention in epic poetry, identify what each god-sent sign causes characters to do next and how that action moves the story's plot forward.
evidencePoints: All, without delay, The will of Jove, and his desires obey.
Then from the south arose a gentle breeze That curl'd the smoothness of the glassy seas…And call the merry mariners aboard.
cards.question: In the excerpt, 'the will of Jove' moves the companions to act immediately after the vision is revealed, and later 'from the south arose a gentle breeze…And call the merry mariners aboard.' How do these two specific acts of divine intervention serve different functions in advancing the epic's action?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Jove's will directs the companions to honor Anchises as a god and plant groves around his abode, while the southern breeze signals that the nine days of feasting are complete and no further voyage is necessary.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Jove's will drives the companions to renew the fleet, cashier the unworthy, and found a new city, while the southern breeze then summons the mariners aboard, signaling the gods' approval of their departure.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Jove's will instructs the companions to build a permanent settlement on Eryx and raise a temple to the Paphian queen as their sole purpose, while the southern breeze arrives to warn the cashiered 'degenerate' men that they will be left behind.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Jove's will causes the companions to appoint judges and ordain laws as their primary duty, while the southern breeze serves as a divine punishment sent against those who refused to 'hazard life for future fame.'

cards.standardTitle: Text structure and feature purpose
cards.excerpt:
Within the space, an olive tree had stood, A sacred shade, a venerable wood, For vows to Faunus paid, the Latins’ guardian god. Here hung the vests, and tablets were engrav’d, Of sinking mariners from shipwreck sav’d. With heedless hands the Trojans fell’d the tree, To make the ground enclos’d for combat free. Deep in the root, whether by fate, or chance, Or erring haste, the Trojan drove his lance; Then stoop’d, and tugg’d with force immense, to free Th’ incumber’d spear from the tenacious tree; That, whom his fainting limbs pursued in vain, His flying weapon might from far attain.

Confus’d with fear, bereft of human aid, Then Turnus to the gods, and first to Faunus pray’d: “O Faunus, pity! and thou Mother Earth, Where I thy foster son receiv’d my birth, Hold fast the steel! If my religious hand Your plant has honour’d, which your foes profan’d, Propitious hear my pious pray’r!” He said, Nor with successless vows invok’d their aid. Th’ incumbent hero wrench’d, and pull’d, and strain’d; But still the stubborn earth the steel detain’d. Juturna took her time; and, while in vain He strove, assum’d Meticus’ form again, And, in that imitated shape, restor’d To the despairing prince his Daunian sword. The Queen of Love, who, with disdain and grief, Saw the bold nymph afford this prompt relief, T’ assert her offspring with a greater deed, From the tough root the ling’ring weapon freed.
cards.whyThisWorks: The second paragraph's job is clearly distinguishable from the first: it shifts from Aeneas's physical struggle at the tree to a chain of divine interventions—Faunus holding the lance, Juturna restoring Turnus's sword, and Venus freeing the lance for Aeneas—that rebalance the fight, making it an ideal paragraph-job item.
cards.skillStrategy: Ask yourself: what new work does this paragraph do that the previous one did not—does it introduce a new character, shift the conflict, or resolve something left unfinished?
evidencePoints: Juturna took her time; and, while in vain / He strove, assum'd Meticus' form again, / And, in that imitated shape, restor'd / To the despairing prince his Daunian sword.
The Queen of Love…T' assert her offspring with a greater deed, / From the tough root the ling'ring weapon freed.
cards.question: The first paragraph focuses on Aeneas driving his lance into the sacred tree root and struggling to pull it free while Turnus flees. What is the structural job of the second paragraph in the passage?

choices.label: A
choices.text: It continues Aeneas's physical struggle at the tree root and shows that his repeated pulling finally frees the lance on its own, with the line 'the stubborn earth the steel detain'd' marking the moment the earth releases its grip without any god acting.

choices.label: B
choices.text: It shifts focus to Turnus's desperate prayer—'O Faunus, pity!'—and then traces a sequence of divine interventions: Earth holding the lance fast, Juturna restoring 'his Daunian sword' in Meticus's disguise, and Venus freeing the lance for Aeneas, rearming both fighters and resetting the conflict.

choices.label: C
choices.text: It returns to the sacred olive tree to explain why Faunus answers Turnus's prayer, elaborating on how the 'vests, and tablets' of shipwrecked mariners made the tree holy and why the Trojans' act of felling it earns divine punishment.

choices.label: D
choices.text: It establishes Turnus as the episode's central figure by tracing his history as Faunus's 'foster son' and his bond with Juturna before either divine figure acts, making his prayer the paragraph's main structural purpose.

cards.standardTitle: Central idea and supporting evidence
cards.excerpt: Then old Evander, with a close embrace, Strain’d his departing friend; and tears o’erflow his face. “Would Heav’n,” said he, “my strength and youth recall, Such as I was beneath Praeneste’s wall; Then when I made the foremost foes retire, And set whole heaps of conquer’d shields on fire; When Herilus in single fight I slew, Whom with three lives Feronia did endue; And thrice I sent him to the Stygian shore, Till the last ebbing soul return’d no more— Such if I stood renew’d, not these alarms, Nor death, should rend me from my Pallas’ arms; Nor proud Mezentius, thus unpunish’d, boast His rapes and murders on the Tuscan coast. Ye gods, and mighty Jove, in pity bring Relief, and hear a father and a king! If fate and you reserve these eyes, to see My son return with peace and victory; If the lov’d boy shall bless his father’s sight; If we shall meet again with more delight; Then draw my life in length; let me sustain, In hopes of his embrace, the worst of pain. But if your hard decrees—which, O! I dread— Have doom’d to death his undeserving head; This, O this very moment, let me die! While hopes and fears in equal balance lie; While, yet possess’d of all his youthful charms, I strain him close within these aged arms; Before that fatal news my soul shall wound!” He said, and, swooning, sunk upon the ground. His servants bore him off, and softly laid His languish’d limbs upon his homely bed.
cards.whyThisWorks: Evander's speech moves from nostalgic boasting to a desperate prayer, requiring students to distinguish the central idea from isolated details like his past victories or his physical collapse.
cards.skillStrategy: Ask yourself: what is the speaker's main point across the whole speech, not just one moment or detail?
evidencePoints: If fate and you reserve these eyes, to see / My son return with peace and victory
But if your hard decrees—which, O! I dread— / Have doom'd to death his undeserving head; / This, O this very moment, let me die!
cards.question: In his speech, Evander recalls his past battles and then addresses the gods with two opposite requests: 'If fate and you reserve these eyes, to see / My son return' and 'This, O this very moment, let me die!' What central idea do these two requests together express?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Evander's memories of defeating Herilus and burning enemy shields prove he was once powerful enough to protect Pallas without divine help.

choices.label: B
choices.text: A father's love for his son is so consuming that he asks the gods for life only if Pallas survives, and for immediate death if Pallas does not.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Evander blames Mezentius's unpunished crimes on the Tuscan coast for forcing Pallas into a battle the young man cannot survive.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Old age has left Evander so helpless that he collapses and must be carried to bed, unable to act on any of his wishes.

cards.standardTitle: Key literary elements add layers of meaning
cards.excerpt: He said, and, rising from his homely throne, The solemn rites of Hercules begun, And on his altars wak’d the sleeping fires; Then cheerful to his household gods retires; There offers chosen sheep. Th’ Arcadian king And Trojan youth the same oblations bring. Next, of his men and ships he makes review; Draws out the best and ablest of the crew. Down with the falling stream the refuse run, To raise with joyful news his drooping son. Steeds are prepar’d to mount the Trojan band, Who wait their leader to the Tyrrhene land. A sprightly courser, fairer than the rest, The king himself presents his royal guest: A lion’s hide his back and limbs infold, Precious with studded work, and paws of gold. Fame thro’ the little city spreads aloud Th’ intended march, amid the fearful crowd: The matrons beat their breasts, dissolve in tears, And double their devotion in their fears. The war at hand appears with more affright, And rises ev’ry moment to the sight.
cards.whyThisWorks: The Arcadian king's actions—rising from his 'homely throne,' performing sacred rites, personally selecting the best soldiers, and gifting Aeneas a prized courser adorned with gold—reveal a ruler defined by both humble piety and generous, decisive leadership, giving students concrete character actions to analyze for deeper meaning.
cards.skillStrategy: When a character performs a series of actions, ask what those actions together reveal about who that character is and what the author wants readers to understand about them.
evidencePoints: rising from his homely throne
A sprightly courser, fairer than the rest, / The king himself presents his royal guest: / A lion's hide his back and limbs infold, / Precious with studded work, and paws of gold.
cards.question: Read the following lines from the excerpt: 'rising from his homely throne' and 'The king himself presents his royal guest: / A lion's hide his back and limbs infold, / Precious with studded work, and paws of gold.' What do these two details together reveal about the Arcadian king's character?

choices.label: A
choices.text: He is a ruler who values outward displays of wealth above all else, as shown by the elaborate golden gift he chooses for Aeneas.

choices.label: B
choices.text: He is a leader who combines personal humility with generous, honorable action, living simply yet giving his finest possessions to support a worthy cause.

choices.label: C
choices.text: He is an indecisive king who relies on ceremony and gift-giving to avoid making difficult military choices himself.

choices.label: D
choices.text: He is a ruler whose modest lifestyle reflects his kingdom's poverty, making his gift to Aeneas a sacrifice that weakens his own people.

cards.standardTitle: Theme development across a literary text
cards.excerpt:
Now, Erato, thy poet’s mind inspire, And fill his soul with thy celestial fire! Relate what Latium was; her ancient kings; Declare the past and present state of things, When first the Trojan fleet Ausonia sought, And how the rivals lov’d, and how they fought. These are my theme, and how the war began, And how concluded by the godlike man: For I shall sing of battles, blood, and rage, Which princes and their people did engage; And haughty souls, that, mov’d with mutual hate, In fighting fields pursued and found their fate; That rous’d the Tyrrhene realm with loud alarms, And peaceful Italy involv’d in arms. A larger scene of action is display’d; And, rising hence, a greater work is weigh’d.

Latinus, old and mild, had long possess’d The Latin scepter, and his people blest: His father Faunus; a Laurentian dame His mother; fair Marica was her name. But Faunus came from Picus: Picus drew His birth from Saturn, if records be true. Thus King Latinus, in the third degree, Had Saturn author of his family. But this old peaceful prince, as Heav’n decreed, Was blest with no male issue to succeed: His sons in blooming youth were snatch’d by fate; One only daughter heir’d the royal state. Fir’d with her love, and with ambition led, The neighb’ring princes court her nuptial bed. Among the crowd, but far above the rest, Young Turnus to the beauteous maid address’d. Turnus, for high descent and graceful mien, Was first, and favour’d by the Latian queen; With him she strove to join Lavinia’s hand, But dire portents the purpos’d match withstand.
cards.whyThisWorks: The excerpt contrasts peaceful Latinus's blessed but heirless reign with the arrival of rival suitors and 'dire portents,' giving students true-but-topic-only details to reject while identifying details that actually build the theme that fate and divine will override human ambition and peaceful order.
cards.skillStrategy: Ask yourself: does this detail show the theme being developed, or does it just describe what is happening in the story without connecting to a larger idea?
evidencePoints: But this old peaceful prince, as Heav'n decreed, Was blest with no male issue to succeed
But dire portents the purpos'd match withstand
cards.question: Which detail from the excerpt best develops the theme that divine forces override human plans and desires?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Latinus is described as 'old and mild' and has ruled the Latin people for a long time, establishing him as a respected and experienced king.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Although Turnus is favored by the Latian queen and courts Lavinia, 'dire portents' block the match, showing that supernatural signs override even royal approval and human desire.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Turnus is described as first among the suitors 'for high descent and graceful mien,' which shows that he is the most qualified candidate for Lavinia's hand.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Latinus traces his ancestry back through Picus and Faunus to Saturn, establishing that the royal family has an ancient and distinguished lineage.

cards.standardTitle: Epic poetry: characters, structures, and themes
cards.excerpt: To whom Mezentius thus: “Thy vaunts are vain. My Lausus lies extended on the plain: He’s lost! thy conquest is already won; The wretched sire is murder’d in the son. Nor fate I fear, but all the gods defy. Forbear thy threats: my bus’ness is to die; But first receive this parting legacy.” He said; and straight a whirling dart he sent; Another after, and another went. Round in a spacious ring he rides the field, And vainly plies th’ impenetrable shield. Thrice rode he round; and thrice Aeneas wheel’d, Turn’d as he turn’d: the golden orb withstood The strokes, and bore about an iron wood. Impatient of delay, and weary grown, Still to defend, and to defend alone, To wrench the darts which in his buckler light, Urg’d and o’er-labour’d in unequal fight; At length resolv’d, he throws with all his force Full at the temples of the warrior horse. Just where the stroke was aim’d, th’ unerring spear Made way, and stood transfix’d thro’ either ear. Seiz’d with unwonted pain, surpris’d with fright, The wounded steed curvets, and, rais’d upright, Lights on his feet before; his hoofs behind Spring up in air aloft, and lash the wind. Down comes the rider headlong from his height: His horse came after with unwieldy weight, And, flound’ring forward, pitching on his head, His lord’s encumber’d shoulder overlaid.
cards.whyThisWorks: Aeneas's divinely forged shield—described as an 'impenetrable shield' and 'golden orb' that 'bore about an iron wood'—directly illustrates divine intervention by making Mezentius's vow to 'defy all the gods' physically impossible to fulfill, showing how divine protection shapes both the battle's action and its thematic outcome.
cards.skillStrategy: When analyzing divine intervention in epic poetry, identify the exact moment a divine object or force changes what a character can or cannot do, then connect that moment to what the poem says about fate or the gods.
evidencePoints: the golden orb withstood / The strokes, and bore about an iron wood
Nor fate I fear, but all the gods defy
cards.question: Mezentius declares 'all the gods defy' before hurling dart after dart at Aeneas, yet the 'golden orb withstood / The strokes, and bore about an iron wood.' How does the shield's divine protection in this moment develop the theme of mortal defiance against fate?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The shield proves so heavy that Aeneas grows 'weary' and 'o'er-labour'd,' showing that divine gifts burden their bearer as much as they protect him, and that Mezentius's defiance nearly succeeds despite the gods' favor.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The shield makes every dart Mezentius throws futile—forcing him into helpless circling while Aeneas ultimately kills his horse instead—showing that Mezentius's vow to 'defy all the gods' cannot overcome the divine protection working against him.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The shield reveals that Mezentius is a poor fighter whose darts were never truly dangerous, so his boast about defying the gods is empty from the start and his defeat comes from inferior skill rather than any divine force.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The shield creates a lasting stalemate in which neither warrior can gain the upper hand, suggesting that divine intervention prevents a decisive outcome and leaves Mezentius's challenge to fate permanently unresolved.

cards.standardTitle: Text structure and feature purpose
cards.excerpt:
Ilioneus, as bold Lucetius came To force the gate, and feed the kindling flame, Roll’d down the fragment of a rock so right, It crush’d him double underneath the weight. Two more young Liger and Asylas slew: To bend the bow young Liger better knew; Asylas best the pointed jav’lin threw. Brave Caeneus laid Ortygius on the plain; The victor Caeneus was by Turnus slain. By the same hand, Clonius and Itys fall, Sagar, and Ida, standing on the wall. From Capys’ arms his fate Privernus found: Hurt by Themilla first—but slight the wound— His shield thrown by, to mitigate the smart, He clapp’d his hand upon the wounded part: The second shaft came swift and unespied, And pierc’d his hand, and nail’d it to his side, Transfix’d his breathing lungs and beating heart: The soul came issuing out, and hiss’d against the dart.

The son of Arcens shone amid the rest, In glitt’ring armour and a purple vest, (Fair was his face, his eyes inspiring love,) Bred by his father in the Martian grove, Where the fat altars of Palicus flame, And send in arms to purchase early fame. Him when he spied from far, the Tuscan king Laid by the lance, and took him to the sling, Thrice whirl’d the thong around his head, and threw: The heated lead half melted as it flew; It pierc’d his hollow temples and his brain; The youth came tumbling down, and spurn’d the plain.
cards.whyThisWorks: The two paragraphs serve distinct structural jobs—the first catalogs multiple warriors falling in rapid succession, while the second slows to focus on a single soldier's death in vivid detail, giving students a clear contrast in paragraph function to analyze.
cards.skillStrategy: Ask yourself what job each paragraph is doing: is it listing, zooming in, shifting focus, or wrapping up an idea?
evidencePoints: Ilioneus, as bold Lucetius came… Roll'd down the fragment of a rock… Two more young Liger and Asylas slew… Brave Caeneus laid Ortygius on the plain
The son of Arcens shone amid the rest… Him when he spied from far, the Tuscan king Laid by the lance… The youth came tumbling down, and spurn'd the plain.
cards.question: What is the primary job of the second paragraph compared to the first paragraph?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The second paragraph introduces the battle for the first time by naming the opposing sides and their leaders.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The second paragraph shifts from cataloging many deaths rapidly to dwelling on a single warrior's fate in close detail.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The second paragraph concludes the battle by showing that Turnus has defeated every enemy fighter on the field.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The second paragraph contrasts the cowardice of the son of Arcens with the bravery of the warriors named in the first paragraph.

cards.standardTitle: Central idea and supporting evidence
cards.excerpt: This lucky moment the sly traitor chose: Then, starting from his ambush, up he rose, And threw, but first to Heav’n address’d his vows: “O patron of Socrates’ high abodes, Phoebus, the ruling pow’r among the gods, Whom first we serve, whole woods of unctuous pine Are fell’d for thee, and to thy glory shine; By thee protected with our naked soles, Thro’ flames unsing’d we march, and tread the kindled coals Give me, propitious pow’r, to wash away The stains of this dishonourable day: Nor spoils, nor triumph, from the fact I claim, But with my future actions trust my fame. Let me, by stealth, this female plague o’ercome, And from the field return inglorious home.” Apollo heard, and, granting half his pray’r, Shuffled in winds the rest, and toss’d in empty air. He gives the death desir’d; his safe return By southern tempests to the seas is borne.
cards.whyThisWorks: The excerpt contrasts the warrior's prayer for a secret, shameful victory with Apollo's partial fulfillment—granting death but scattering the plea for safe return—giving students a clear central idea to distinguish from isolated details or topic labels.
cards.skillStrategy: Ask yourself what the whole passage is really saying about the warrior's prayer and Apollo's response together, not just what happens in one moment.
evidencePoints: Let me, by stealth, this female plague o'ercome, And from the field return inglorious home.
Apollo heard, and, granting half his pray'r, Shuffled in winds the rest, and toss'd in empty air.
cards.question: The warrior prays to Apollo to 'by stealth, this female plague o'ercome' and return 'inglorious home,' yet Apollo 'granting half his pray'r, Shuffled in winds the rest.' What central idea do these two moments together express?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A warrior's devotion to Apollo, shown by felling 'whole woods of unctuous pine' and marching through fire, earns him complete divine protection in battle.

choices.label: B
choices.text: A warrior who seeks a hidden, shameful victory receives only partial divine aid—his enemy's death is granted, but his safe return is left to destructive chance.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Apollo punishes the warrior for requesting an inglorious act by refusing to grant any part of the prayer and sending southern tempests as a sign of divine anger.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The warrior's ambush from hiding is the defining event, proving that surprise attacks succeed even without the gods' help.

cards.standardTitle: Rhetoric and reader effect
cards.excerpt: He said, and rose; as holy zeal inspires, He rakes hot embers, and renews the fires; His country gods and Vesta then adores With cakes and incense, and their aid implores. Next, for his friends and royal host he sent, Reveal’d his vision, and the gods’ intent, With his own purpose. All, without delay, The will of Jove, and his desires obey. They list with women each degenerate name, Who dares not hazard life for future fame. These they cashier: the brave remaining few, Oars, banks, and cables, half consum’d, renew. The prince designs a city with the plow; The lots their sev’ral tenements allow. This part is nam’d from Ilium, that from Troy, And the new king ascends the throne with joy; A chosen senate from the people draws; Appoints the judges, and ordains the laws. Then, on the top of Eryx, they begin A rising temple to the Paphian queen. Anchises, last, is honour’d as a god; A priest is added, annual gifts bestow’d, And groves are planted round his blest abode. Nine days they pass in feasts, their temples crown’d; And fumes of incense in the fanes abound. Then from the south arose a gentle breeze That curl’d the smoothness of the glassy seas; The rising winds a ruffling gale afford, And call the merry mariners aboard.
cards.whyThisWorks: The excerpt moves from 'holy zeal inspires' and 'adores with cakes and incense' directly into 'designs a city with the plow,' 'appoints the judges, and ordains the laws,' allowing students to trace how Virgil links divine sanction to civic authority as a unified rhetorical purpose.
cards.skillStrategy: Find the exact moment where the author shifts or connects two actions, then ask: why does the author put these together — what is he trying to make the reader believe?
evidencePoints: as holy zeal inspires, He rakes hot embers, and renews the fires; His country gods and Vesta then adores With cakes and incense, and their aid implores
The prince designs a city with the plow…Appoints the judges, and ordains the laws
cards.question: In the excerpt, Virgil places the line 'as holy zeal inspires, He rakes hot embers, and renews the fires' immediately before describing how Aeneas 'designs a city with the plow' and 'appoints the judges, and ordains the laws.' What purpose does this placement serve?

choices.label: A
choices.text: To show that Aeneas delays practical leadership until religious duties are fully completed, suggesting ceremony must always precede action.

choices.label: B
choices.text: To present Aeneas's religious devotion and civic founding as a single continuous act, so that his authority as a lawgiver appears rooted in divine approval.

choices.label: C
choices.text: To contrast Aeneas's personal piety with the indifference of his followers, who obey only because Jove commands them rather than out of shared belief.

choices.label: D
choices.text: To suggest that the laws Aeneas ordains are temporary measures, less important than the religious rituals that give the new city its true identity.

cards.standardTitle: Key literary elements add layers of meaning
cards.excerpt: Then thus the young Euryalus replied: “Whatever fortune, good or bad, betide, The same shall be my age, as now my youth; No time shall find me wanting to my truth. This only from your goodness let me gain (And, this ungranted, all rewards are vain) Of Priam’s royal race my mother came— And sure the best that ever bore the name— Whom neither Troy nor Sicily could hold From me departing, but, o’erspent and old, My fate she follow’d. Ignorant of this (Whatever) danger, neither parting kiss, Nor pious blessing taken, her I leave, And in this only act of all my life deceive. By this right hand and conscious night I swear, My soul so sad a farewell could not bear. Be you her comfort; fill my vacant place (Permit me to presume so great a grace) Support her age, forsaken and distress’d. That hope alone will fortify my breast Against the worst of fortunes, and of fears.” He said. The mov’d assistants melt in tears.
cards.whyThisWorks: Euryalus's confession that he left without a 'parting kiss' or 'pious blessing' and his plea that Nisus 'support her age, forsaken and distress'd' reveal that filial devotion, not just bravery, drives his character.
cards.skillStrategy: When a character confesses a fault and makes a request in the same speech, ask what that combination shows about what he truly values.
evidencePoints: Neither parting kiss, / Nor pious blessing taken, her I leave, and in this only act of all my life deceive.
That hope alone will fortify my breast / Against the worst of fortunes, and of fears.
cards.question: Euryalus admits he left without a 'parting kiss' or 'pious blessing' and then says 'that hope alone will fortify my breast.' What do these two moments together reveal about his character?

choices.label: A
choices.text: He uses his mother's situation to win the sympathy of the assembled men rather than out of genuine guilt.

choices.label: B
choices.text: His courage depends on knowing his mother is cared for, showing that filial devotion and bravery are inseparable in him.

choices.label: C
choices.text: He regrets joining the mission and raises his mother's welfare as a reason to abandon the plan.

choices.label: D
choices.text: He feels little guilt about deceiving his mother and mentions her only to arrange a practical matter before leaving.

cards.standardTitle: Theme development across a literary text
cards.excerpt:
Thus Turnus rav’d, and various fates revolv’d: The choice was doubtful, but the death resolv’d. And now the sword, and now the sea took place, That to revenge, and this to purge disgrace. Sometimes he thought to swim the stormy main, By stretch of arms the distant shore to gain. Thrice he the sword assay’d, and thrice the flood; But Juno, mov’d with pity, both withstood. And thrice repress’d his rage; strong gales supplied, And push’d the vessel o’er the swelling tide. At length she lands him on his native shores, And to his father’s longing arms restores.

Meantime, by Jove’s impulse, Mezentius arm’d, Succeeding Turnus, with his ardour warm’d His fainting friends, reproach’d their shameful flight, Repell’d the victors, and renew’d the fight. Against their king the Tuscan troops conspire; Such is their hate, and such their fierce desire Of wish’d revenge: on him, and him alone, All hands employ’d, and all their darts are thrown. He, like a solid rock by seas inclos’d, To raging winds and roaring waves oppos’d, From his proud summit looking down, disdains Their empty menace, and unmov’d remains.
cards.whyThisWorks: Both paragraphs show different characters—Turnus restrained by Juno and Mezentius standing firm against the Tuscan troops—each illustrating how individuals endure overwhelming force, giving students two distinct moments to trace the same theme of resilience under pressure.
cards.skillStrategy: Look at what each character faces and how they respond, then ask what idea both moments are building together.
evidencePoints: Thrice he the sword assay'd, and thrice the flood; But Juno, mov'd with pity, both withstood.
He, like a solid rock by seas inclos'd, To raging winds and roaring waves oppos'd, From his proud summit looking down, disdains Their empty menace, and unmov'd remains.
cards.question: Both paragraphs develop a theme about how individuals respond to overwhelming opposition. Which statement best identifies the theme developed through Turnus's repeated attempts and Mezentius's defiance against the Tuscan troops?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Divine intervention determines every outcome, since Juno stops Turnus and Jove drives Mezentius into battle, leaving human will powerless.

choices.label: B
choices.text: When faced with forces that could destroy them, individuals find ways to endure—Turnus through divine protection and Mezentius through unyielding resolve.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Revenge is the central motivation for all characters, as Turnus seeks to avenge his disgrace and the Tuscan troops seek revenge against Mezentius.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Loyalty to one's homeland is what sustains warriors in crisis, shown when Turnus is returned to his native shores and Mezentius fights for his fainting friends.

cards.standardTitle: Epic poetry: characters, structures, and themes
cards.excerpt: With anxious pleasure when Juturna view’d Th’ increasing fright of the mad multitude, When their short sighs and thick’ning sobs she heard, And found their ready minds for change prepar’d; Dissembling her immortal form, she took Camertus’ mien, his habit, and his look; A chief of ancient blood; in arms well known Was his great sire, and he his greater son. His shape assum’d, amid the ranks she ran, And humoring their first motions, thus began: “For shame, Rutulians, can you bear the sight Of one expos’d for all, in single fight? Can we, before the face of heav’n, confess Our courage colder, or our numbers less? View all the Trojan host, th’ Arcadian band, And Tuscan army; count ’em as they stand: Undaunted to the battle if we go, Scarce ev’ry second man will share a foe. Turnus, ’tis true, in this unequal strife, Shall lose, with honour, his devoted life, Or change it rather for immortal fame, Succeeding to the gods, from whence he came: But you, a servile and inglorious band, For foreign lords shall sow your native land, Those fruitful fields your fighting fathers gain’d, Which have so long their lazy sons sustain’d.” With words like these, she carried her design: A rising murmur runs along the line. Then ev’n the city troops, and Latians, tir’d With tedious war, seem with new souls inspir’d: Their champion’s fate with pity they lament, And of the league, so lately sworn, repent.
cards.whyThisWorks: Juturna's disguise as Camertus and her inflammatory speech directly demonstrate how divine intervention—hidden from mortals—overturns a sworn truce and reignites war, making this a clear teaching moment for the subskill of divine intervention in epic poetry.
cards.skillStrategy: When analyzing divine intervention in an epic, trace exactly what the god does in disguise, what words they use, and what changes in the mortals' behavior by the end of the passage.
evidencePoints: Dissembling her immortal form, she took Camertus' mien, his habit, and his look
even the city troops, and Latians, tir'd with tedious war, seem with new souls inspir'd… and of the league, so lately sworn, repent
cards.question: Juturna 'dissembling her immortal form' takes the shape of Camertus and calls the Rutulians 'a servile and inglorious band' who will 'sow your native land' for foreign masters. By the final lines, even soldiers 'tir'd with tedious war' are 'inspir'd with new souls' and 'repent' of 'the league, so lately sworn.' What does this sequence reveal about divine intervention in the epic?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Her arithmetic that 'scarce ev'ry second man will share a foe' convinces the soldiers the odds favor them, so they calmly hold their positions and leave 'the league, so lately sworn' undisturbed, showing divine speech can steady mortal resolve.

choices.label: B
choices.text: By hiding her immortal identity and shaming the troops as 'servile and inglorious,' Juturna stirs even the war-weary city troops to feel 'new souls inspir'd,' lament Turnus's fate, and repent of 'the league, so lately sworn,' showing that a disguised god's words can secretly overturn a sworn truce.

choices.label: C
