choices.text: Her promise that Turnus will gain 'immortal fame' by losing honorably persuades the soldiers to accept the outcome of single combat and honor 'the league, so lately sworn,' showing that divine speech here reinforces rather than disrupts the truce.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Her reminder that 'fighting fathers' won the 'fruitful fields' redirects the soldiers' anger specifically toward the Arcadian and Tuscan forces she names, leaving 'the league, so lately sworn' intact and Turnus's fate unlamented.

cards.standardTitle: Text structure and feature purpose
cards.excerpt:
Thus having said, the hero bound his brows With leafy branches, then perform’d his vows; Adoring first the genius of the place, Then Earth, the mother of the heav’nly race, The nymphs, and native godheads yet unknown, And Night, and all the stars that gild her sable throne, And ancient Cybel, and Idaean Jove, And last his sire below, and mother queen above. Then heav’n’s high monarch thunder’d thrice aloud, And thrice he shook aloft a golden cloud. Soon thro’ the joyful camp a rumour flew, The time was come their city to renew. Then ev’ry brow with cheerful green is crown’d, The feasts are doubled, and the bowls go round.

When next the rosy morn disclos’d the day, The scouts to sev’ral parts divide their way, To learn the natives’ names, their towns explore, The coasts and trendings of the crooked shore: Here Tiber flows, and here Numicus stands; Here warlike Latins hold the happy lands. The pious chief, who sought by peaceful ways To found his empire, and his town to raise, A hundred youths from all his train selects, And to the Latian court their course directs, (The spacious palace where their prince resides,) And all their heads with wreaths of olive hides. They go commission’d to require a peace, And carry presents to procure access. Thus while they speed their pace, the prince designs His new-elected seat, and draws the lines. The Trojans round the place a rampire cast, And palisades about the trenches plac’d.
cards.whyThisWorks: The two paragraphs offer a clear structural contrast: the first centers on Aeneas's religious rites and Jupiter's thunderous confirmation, while the second opens with 'When next the rosy morn disclos'd the day' and pivots to scouts, diplomats, and fortification—giving students a concrete textual moment to anchor the paragraph's job.
cards.skillStrategy: Find the sentence or phrase that signals a new direction, then ask what the paragraph is doing differently from the one before it.
evidencePoints: When next the rosy morn disclos'd the day, / The scouts to sev'ral parts divide their way
Then heav'n's high monarch thunder'd thrice aloud, / And thrice he shook aloft a golden cloud. / Soon thro' the joyful camp a rumour flew, / The time was come their city to renew.
cards.question: The second paragraph opens with the line 'When next the rosy morn disclos'd the day.' What job does this opening line perform in relation to the first paragraph's ending, where 'the feasts are doubled, and the bowls go round'?

choices.label: A
choices.text: It extends the celebration from the first paragraph by showing that the feasting and rejoicing continue into the following morning.

choices.label: B
choices.text: It shifts from the night of divine confirmation and communal feasting to the next morning's outward actions—scouting, diplomacy, and building fortifications.

choices.label: C
choices.text: It contrasts Aeneas's peaceful diplomatic mission with the violent military response the Latian prince launches against the Trojans.

choices.label: D
choices.text: It concludes the episode by returning to the religious theme of the first paragraph, showing that Aeneas's prayers have been fully answered.

cards.standardTitle: Central idea and supporting evidence
cards.excerpt: But, in the palace of the king, appears A scene more solemn, and a pomp of tears. Maids, matrons, widows, mix their common moans; Orphans their sires, and sires lament their sons. All in that universal sorrow share, And curse the cause of this unhappy war: A broken league, a bride unjustly sought, A crown usurp’d, which with their blood is bought! These are the crimes with which they load the name Of Turnus, and on him alone exclaim: “Let him who lords it o’er th’ Ausonian land Engage the Trojan hero hand to hand: His is the gain; our lot is but to serve; ’Tis just, the sway he seeks, he should deserve.” This Drances aggravates; and adds, with spite: “His foe expects, and dares him to the fight.” Nor Turnus wants a party, to support His cause and credit in the Latian court. His former acts secure his present fame, And the queen shades him with her mighty name.
cards.whyThisWorks: The excerpt presents two competing forces—the people's public condemnation of Turnus for 'a crown usurp'd, which with their blood is bought' and the countervailing protection of 'his former acts' and the queen's name—allowing students to identify the central idea that Turnus remains politically shielded despite widespread blame.
cards.skillStrategy: To find the central idea, look for the tension the passage keeps returning to and ask what single claim all the details—grief, accusation, and protection—add up to together.
evidencePoints: his former acts secure his present fame, and the queen shades him with her mighty name
a crown usurp'd, which with their blood is bought
cards.question: The crowd charges Turnus with 'a crown usurp'd, which with their blood is bought' and demands single combat, yet the passage closes by stating 'his former acts secure his present fame' and 'the queen shades him with her mighty name.' What central idea do these contrasting details develop?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The grief of 'maids, matrons, widows' and 'orphans their sires' has grown so overwhelming that it has erased whatever protection Turnus once received from his past reputation and the queen's support.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Although the people publicly blame Turnus for 'a crown usurp'd, which with their blood is bought' and demand he prove himself in single combat, his past reputation and the queen's backing continue to shield him from those accusations.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Drances is the most powerful voice in the Latian court because his charge that 'his foe expects, and dares him to the fight' does more to threaten Turnus's standing than either the crowd's grief or the queen's protection.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The passage centers on 'a broken league' and 'a bride unjustly sought' as the root cause of the people's suffering, suggesting that correcting those original wrongs matters more to the Latian court than Turnus's current political standing.

cards.standardTitle: Rhetoric and reader effect
cards.excerpt:
At this the lovely nymph, with grief oppress’d, Thrice tore her hair, and beat her comely breast. To whom Saturnia thus: “Thy tears are late: Haste, snatch him, if he can be snatch’d from fate: New tumults kindle; violate the truce: Who knows what changeful fortune may produce? ’Tis not a crime t’ attempt what I decree; Or, if it were, discharge the crime on me.” She said, and, sailing on the winged wind, Left the sad nymph suspended in her mind.

And now in pomp the peaceful kings appear: Four steeds the chariot of Latinus bear; Twelve golden beams around his temples play, To mark his lineage from the God of Day. Two snowy coursers Turnus’ chariot yoke, And in his hand two massy spears he shook: Then issued from the camp, in arms divine, Aeneas, author of the Roman line; And by his side Ascanius took his place, The second hope of Rome’s immortal race. Adorn’d in white, a rev’rend priest appears, And off’rings to the flaming altars bears; A porket, and a lamb that never suffer’d shears. Then to the rising sun he turns his eyes, And strews the beasts, design’d for sacrifice, With salt and meal: with like officious care He marks their foreheads, and he clips their hair. Betwixt their horns the purple wine he sheds; With the same gen’rous juice the flame he feeds.
cards.whyThisWorks: The second paragraph's elaborate ceremonial imagery—golden beams, snowy coursers, salt and meal, purple wine—functions rhetorically to build solemnity and legitimacy around the truce ritual, allowing students to connect the descriptive accumulation to Virgil's purpose of heightening the tragedy of what Saturnia has already plotted to destroy.
cards.skillStrategy: Ask yourself: why does the author include this specific detail here—what effect is it meant to have on the reader given what came just before?
evidencePoints: Twelve golden beams around his temples play, / To mark his lineage from the God of Day.
'Tis not a crime t' attempt what I decree; / Or, if it were, discharge the crime on me.'
cards.question: In the first paragraph, Saturnia tells the nymph, "'Tis not a crime t' attempt what I decree; / Or, if it were, discharge the crime on me." Then the second paragraph describes the kings and Aeneas arriving in solemn ceremony with golden beams, white-robed priests, and ritual offerings. What is Virgil's purpose in placing these two moments together?

choices.label: A
choices.text: To show that the gods and mortals share equal power over the outcome of the truce, since both Saturnia's command and the priests' rituals carry divine authority.

choices.label: B
choices.text: To deepen the sense of impending betrayal by showing the sacred ceremony the mortals believe will bring peace while the reader already knows a goddess has ordered it violated.

choices.label: C
choices.text: To contrast Latinus's divine lineage with Aeneas's mortal origins, suggesting that the truce is doomed because the two sides are unequal in status.

choices.label: D
choices.text: To reassure the reader that the elaborate ritual offerings will succeed in overriding Saturnia's scheme, since the gods of Day and the flaming altars outrank her authority.

cards.standardTitle: Key literary elements add layers of meaning
cards.excerpt: She wrench’d the jav’lin with her dying hands, But wedg’d within her breast the weapon stands; The wood she draws, the steely point remains; She staggers in her seat with agonizing pains: (A gath’ring mist o’erclouds her cheerful eyes, And from her cheeks the rosy colour flies:) Then turns to her, whom of her female train She trusted most, and thus she speaks with pain: “Acca, ’tis past! he swims before my sight, Inexorable Death; and claims his right. Bear my last words to Turnus; fly with speed, And bid him timely to my charge succeed, Repel the Trojans, and the town relieve: Farewell! and in this kiss my parting breath receive.” She said, and, sliding, sunk upon the plain: Dying, her open’d hand forsakes the rein; Short, and more short, she pants; by slow degrees Her mind the passage from her body frees. She drops her sword; she nods her plumy crest, Her drooping head declining on her breast: In the last sigh her struggling soul expires, And, murm’ring with disdain, to Stygian sounds retires.
cards.whyThisWorks: Camilla's dying speech to Acca—commanding Turnus to 'repel the Trojans' while she physically collapses—shows how action and speech together reveal a warrior identity that persists even through death.
cards.skillStrategy: When a character speaks or acts at a key moment, ask what that choice shows about who they are—look at what they say, what they do, and what they do NOT say.
evidencePoints: Bear my last words to Turnus; fly with speed, And bid him timely to my charge succeed, Repel the Trojans, and the town relieve
She said, and, sliding, sunk upon the plain: Dying, her open'd hand forsakes the rein
cards.question: In the excerpt, Camilla's final spoken words are a command—'Bear my last words to Turnus; fly with speed, And bid him timely to my charge succeed, Repel the Trojans, and the town relieve'—followed immediately by her physical collapse. What does this sequence reveal about Camilla's character?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Camilla's command to Acca shows she fears Turnus will abandon the battle without her direct instruction, revealing her distrust of his leadership.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Camilla's last words are military orders rather than expressions of personal grief, revealing that her identity as a warrior-commander remains intact even as her body fails.

choices.label: C
choices.text: By sending a message to Turnus, Camilla reveals she regrets entering the battle and wants Turnus to correct the mistakes that led to her death.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Camilla's final command to Acca reveals that she values her friendship with Acca above all else, choosing to spend her last breath ensuring Acca has a purpose after her death.

cards.standardTitle: Theme development across a literary text
cards.excerpt:
The Trojans, from above, their foes beheld, And with arm’d legions all the rampires fill’d. Seiz’d with affright, their gates they first explore; Join works to works with bridges, tow’r to tow’r: Thus all things needful for defence abound. Mnestheus and brave Seresthus walk the round, Commission’d by their absent prince to share The common danger, and divide the care. The soldiers draw their lots, and, as they fall, By turns relieve each other on the wall.

Nigh where the foes their utmost guards advance, To watch the gate was warlike Nisus’ chance. His father Hyrtacus of noble blood; His mother was a huntress of the wood, And sent him to the wars. Well could he bear His lance in fight, and dart the flying spear, But better skill’d unerring shafts to send. Beside him stood Euryalus, his friend: Euryalus, than whom the Trojan host No fairer face, or sweeter air, could boast. Scarce had the down to shade his cheeks begun. One was their care, and their delight was one: One common hazard in the war they shar’d, And now were both by choice upon the guard.
cards.whyThisWorks: Two distinct moments—the Trojans organizing collective defense on the walls and Nisus and Euryalus voluntarily sharing guard duty—both develop the theme that loyalty and unity sustain people in the face of danger, requiring students to track how separate story moments build the same idea.
cards.skillStrategy: Find two separate moments in the passage and ask what idea they both point to—that shared idea is the theme.
evidencePoints: One was their care, and their delight was one: / One common hazard in the war they shar'd, / And now were both by choice upon the guard.
Mnestheus and brave Seresthus walk the round, / Commission'd by their absent prince to share / The common danger, and divide the care.
cards.question: Both the description of Mnestheus and Seresthus dividing the care of the walls and the description of Nisus and Euryalus standing guard together develop which theme?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Individual warriors who seek glory in battle are the ones who ultimately protect their people from destruction.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Shared loyalty and mutual commitment are what hold a community together when it faces danger.

choices.label: C
choices.text: A soldier's noble birth and skill with weapons determine how much responsibility he is given in war.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Youth and inexperience make soldiers reckless, forcing older commanders to take control of the defense.

cards.standardTitle: Epic poetry: characters, structures, and themes
cards.excerpt: But old Anchises, in a flow’ry vale, Review’d his muster’d race, and took the tale: Those happy spirits, which, ordain’d by fate, For future beings and new bodies wait. With studious thought observ’d th’ illustrious throng, In nature’s order as they pass’d along: Their names, their fates, their conduct, and their care, In peaceful senates and successful war. He, when Aeneas on the plain appears, Meets him with open arms, and falling tears. “Welcome,” he said, “the gods’ undoubted race! O long expected to my dear embrace! Once more ’tis giv’n me to behold your face! The love and pious duty which you pay Have pass’d the perils of so hard a way. ’Tis true, computing times, I now believ’d The happy day approach’d; nor are my hopes deceiv’d. What length of lands, what oceans have you pass’d; What storms sustain’d, and on what shores been cast? How have I fear’d your fate! but fear’d it most, When love assail’d you, on the Libyan coast.” To this, the filial duty thus replies: “Your sacred ghost before my sleeping eyes Appear’d, and often urg’d this painful enterprise. After long tossing on the Tyrrhene sea, My navy rides at anchor in the bay. But reach your hand, O parent shade, nor shun The dear embraces of your longing son!” He said; and falling tears his face bedew: Then thrice around his neck his arms he threw; And thrice the flitting shadow slipp’d away, Like winds, or empty dreams that fly the day.
cards.whyThisWorks: Aeneas's direct speech—'Your sacred ghost before my sleeping eyes / Appear'd, and often urg'd this painful enterprise'—explicitly names a dream visitation by a divine/supernatural figure (Anchises' shade) as the motivating force behind the hero's quest, making this a clear example of divine intervention shaping epic action.
cards.skillStrategy: When identifying divine intervention in epic poetry, look for moments where a god, ghost, or supernatural figure appears to a hero and directly causes or compels a specific action—then trace how that moment drives the plot forward.
evidencePoints: Your sacred ghost before my sleeping eyes / Appear'd, and often urg'd this painful enterprise.
thrice the flitting shadow slipp'd away, / Like winds, or empty dreams that fly the day.
cards.question: Aeneas tells his father, 'Your sacred ghost before my sleeping eyes / Appear'd, and often urg'd this painful enterprise.' How does this moment of divine intervention function in the epic?

choices.label: A
choices.text: It shows that Anchises' ghost appeared once to warn Aeneas away from the Libyan coast, where Anchises feared love would permanently end the voyage.

choices.label: B
choices.text: It reveals that Anchises' ghost repeatedly visited Aeneas in dreams and urged him onward, making the supernatural visitation the driving force behind Aeneas's perseverance through the 'painful enterprise.'

choices.label: C
choices.text: It explains that the ghost guided Aeneas's navy safely into the bay after the crossing of the Tyrrhene sea, fulfilling the practical purpose of the supernatural visit.

choices.label: D
choices.text: It indicates that the ghost appeared in the flowery vale to review the 'muster'd race' of future souls and share their names and fates with Aeneas before the reunion.

cards.standardTitle: Text structure and feature purpose
cards.excerpt:
He said; and, pressing onward thro’ the crew, Pois’d in his lifted arm, his lance he threw. The winged weapon, whistling in the wind, Came driving on, nor miss’d the mark design’d. At once the cornel rattled in the skies; At once tumultuous shouts and clamours rise. Nine brothers in a goodly band there stood, Born of Arcadian mix’d with Tuscan blood, Gylippus’ sons: the fatal jav’lin flew, Aim’d at the midmost of the friendly crew. A passage thro’ the jointed arms it found, Just where the belt was to the body bound, And struck the gentle youth extended on the ground. Then, fir’d with pious rage, the gen’rous train Run madly forward to revenge the slain. And some with eager haste their jav’lins throw; And some with sword in hand assault the foe.

The wish’d insult the Latine troops embrace, And meet their ardour in the middle space. The Trojans, Tuscans, and Arcadian line, With equal courage obviate their design. Peace leaves the violated fields, and hate Both armies urges to their mutual fate. With impious haste their altars are o’erturn’d, The sacrifice half-broil’d, and half-unburn’d. Thick storms of steel from either army fly, And clouds of clashing darts obscure the sky; Brands from the fire are missive weapons made, With chargers, bowls, and all the priestly trade. Latinus, frighted, hastens from the fray, And bears his unregarded gods away. These on their horses vault; those yoke the car; The rest, with swords on high, run headlong to the war.
cards.whyThisWorks: The two paragraphs move from a single javelin throw and its immediate revenge to a full multi-army breakdown of peace, giving students a clear contrast in scope to analyze as a structural shift.
cards.skillStrategy: Ask yourself: what idea does the first paragraph end on, and does the second paragraph continue, contrast, or expand that idea using new details?
evidencePoints: Then, fir'd with pious rage, the gen'rous train / Run madly forward to revenge the slain.
Peace leaves the violated fields, and hate / Both armies urges to their mutual fate.
cards.question: The first paragraph ends with 'the gen'rous train / Run madly forward to revenge the slain.' What is the job of the second paragraph in relation to that moment?

choices.label: A
choices.text: It concludes the revenge of the gen'rous train by showing that their charge successfully defeats the Latine troops and ends the fighting.

choices.label: B
choices.text: It extends the revenge of the gen'rous train into a total collapse of peace, showing that 'hate / Both armies urges to their mutual fate' as all sides join the chaos.

choices.label: C
choices.text: It contrasts the courage of the gen'rous train with the cowardice of the Trojans and Tuscans, who are shown fleeing rather than fighting.

choices.label: D
choices.text: It introduces the conflict between the Trojans and the Latins for the first time, providing background that explains why the gen'rous train sought revenge.

cards.standardTitle: Central idea and supporting evidence
cards.excerpt: The pious prince was seiz’d with sudden fear; Mute was his tongue, and upright stood his hair. Revolving in his mind the stern command, He longs to fly, and loathes the charming land. What should he say? or how should he begin? What course, alas! remains to steer between Th’ offended lover and the pow’rful queen? This way and that he turns his anxious mind, And all expedients tries, and none can find. Fix’d on the deed, but doubtful of the means, After long thought, to this advice he leans: Three chiefs he calls, commands them to repair The fleet, and ship their men with silent care; Some plausible pretence he bids them find, To colour what in secret he design’d. Himself, meantime, the softest hours would choose, Before the love-sick lady heard the news; And move her tender mind, by slow degrees, To suffer what the sov’reign pow’r decrees: Jove will inspire him, when, and what to say. They hear with pleasure, and with haste obey.
cards.whyThisWorks: The excerpt shows Aeneas caught between divine duty and love for Dido, making students distinguish the central idea (conflicted secret planning) from isolated details like the chiefs' obedience or Aeneas's fear.
cards.skillStrategy: Ask yourself: what is the whole paragraph mostly about — not just one moment or one character's action, but the main tension or idea the narrator keeps returning to?
evidencePoints: Fix'd on the deed, but doubtful of the means
And move her tender mind, by slow degrees, / To suffer what the sov'reign pow'r decrees
cards.question: The narrator describes Aeneas as 'Fix'd on the deed, but doubtful of the means' and then details his secret preparations and plan to break the news gently to Dido. What central idea does this sequence of events develop?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Aeneas is so overwhelmed by fear — 'Mute was his tongue, and upright stood his hair' — that he cannot commit to any plan of action.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Although Aeneas is resolved to obey the divine command to leave, he carefully schemes to manage his departure in a way that shields Dido from immediate pain.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The three chiefs Aeneas summons are the true decision-makers, since they carry out the preparations while Aeneas remains paralyzed by indecision.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Jove's power over Aeneas is so total that Aeneas plays no active role in planning his departure, waiting entirely for divine inspiration before acting.

cards.standardTitle: Rhetoric and reader effect
cards.excerpt:
Turnus takes advantage of Aeneas’s absence, fires some of his ships (which are transformed into sea nymphs,) and assaults his camp. The Trojans, reduced to the last extremities, send Ninus and Euryalus to recall Aeneas; which furnishes the poet with that admirable episode of their friendship, generosity, and the conclusion of their adventure.

While these affairs in distant places pass’d, The various Iris Juno sends with haste, To find bold Turnus, who, with anxious thought, The secret shade of his great grandsire sought. Retir’d alone she found the daring man, And op’d her rosy lips, and thus began: “What none of all the gods could grant thy vows, That, Turnus, this auspicious day bestows. Aeneas, gone to seek th’ Arcadian prince, Has left the Trojan camp without defence; And, short of succours there, employs his pains In parts remote to raise the Tuscan swains. Now snatch an hour that favours thy designs; Unite thy forces, and attack their lines.” This said, on equal wings she pois’d her weight, And form’d a radiant rainbow in her flight.
cards.whyThisWorks: Iris's speech to Turnus uses a series of urgent imperatives ('snatch an hour,' 'Unite thy forces,' 'attack their lines') alongside contrast between Aeneas's absence and the Trojans' vulnerability, creating a rhetorical effect of manufactured urgency that manipulates Turnus into action.
cards.skillStrategy: When you spot repeated commands or a sharp contrast in a speech, ask yourself: how does this pattern push the listener—and the reader—to feel or act a certain way?
evidencePoints: Now snatch an hour that favours thy designs; Unite thy forces, and attack their lines.
Aeneas, gone to seek th' Arcadian prince, Has left the Trojan camp without defence
cards.question: Read the lines from Iris's speech to Turnus: 'Now snatch an hour that favours thy designs; / Unite thy forces, and attack their lines.' How does the repetition of commands in these lines affect the reader?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The commands reveal that Turnus is already planning an attack and needs no persuasion from Iris.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The rapid succession of commands creates a sense of urgency that makes the reader feel the pressure Iris is placing on Turnus to act immediately before the opportunity disappears.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The commands show that Iris doubts Turnus's courage and is scolding him for hesitating too long in the secret shade.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The commands slow the pace of the passage, giving the reader time to consider whether Turnus should trust a messenger sent by Juno.

cards.standardTitle: Paraphrase grade-level text
cards.excerpt:
As, compass’d with a wood of spears around, The lordly lion still maintains his ground; Grins horrible, retires, and turns again; Threats his distended paws, and shakes his mane; He loses while in vain he presses on, Nor will his courage let him dare to run: So Turnus fares, and, unresolved of flight, Moves tardy back, and just recedes from fight. Yet twice, enrag’d, the combat he renews, Twice breaks, and twice his broken foes pursues. But now they swarm, and, with fresh troops supplied, Come rolling on, and rush from ev’ry side: Nor Juno, who sustain’d his arms before, Dares with new strength suffice th’ exhausted store; For Jove, with sour commands, sent Iris down, To force th’ invader from the frighted town.

With labour spent, no longer can he wield The heavy falchion, or sustain the shield, O’erwhelm’d with darts, which from afar they fling: The weapons round his hollow temples ring; His golden helm gives way, with stony blows Batter’d, and flat, and beaten to his brows. His crest is rash’d away; his ample shield Is falsified, and round with jav’lins fill’d.
cards.whyThisWorks: The sentence 'He loses while in vain he presses on, / Nor will his courage let him dare to run' uses inverted syntax and compressed logic that requires students to untangle two competing ideas—futile aggression and pride-driven paralysis—making it ideal for chunking complex syntax.
cards.skillStrategy: Break the sentence into two parts: what the lion/Turnus is doing, and what is stopping him from doing the opposite—then restate each part in plain language before combining them.
evidencePoints: He loses while in vain he presses on
Nor will his courage let him dare to run
cards.question: Read the following lines from the excerpt: 'He loses while in vain he presses on, / Nor will his courage let him dare to run.' Which restatement most accurately captures the meaning of both lines?

choices.label: A
choices.text: He keeps attacking and eventually wins, because his courage drives him forward without hesitation.

choices.label: B
choices.text: His attacks accomplish nothing, yet his pride prevents him from retreating.

choices.label: C
choices.text: He presses forward recklessly and loses all courage when he realizes he cannot win.

choices.label: D
choices.text: He chooses to run rather than fight on, because continuing the battle would cost him too much.

cards.standardTitle: Paraphrase grade-level text
cards.excerpt:
Thus Turnus rav’d, and various fates revolv’d: The choice was doubtful, but the death resolv’d. And now the sword, and now the sea took place, That to revenge, and this to purge disgrace. Sometimes he thought to swim the stormy main, By stretch of arms the distant shore to gain. Thrice he the sword assay’d, and thrice the flood; But Juno, mov’d with pity, both withstood. And thrice repress’d his rage; strong gales supplied, And push’d the vessel o’er the swelling tide. At length she lands him on his native shores, And to his father’s longing arms restores.

Meantime, by Jove’s impulse, Mezentius arm’d, Succeeding Turnus, with his ardour warm’d His fainting friends, reproach’d their shameful flight, Repell’d the victors, and renew’d the fight. Against their king the Tuscan troops conspire; Such is their hate, and such their fierce desire Of wish’d revenge: on him, and him alone, All hands employ’d, and all their darts are thrown. He, like a solid rock by seas inclos’d, To raging winds and roaring waves oppos’d, From his proud summit looking down, disdains Their empty menace, and unmov’d remains.
cards.whyThisWorks: The simile 'He, like a solid rock by seas inclos'd, / To raging winds and roaring waves oppos'd, / From his proud summit looking down, disdains / Their empty menace, and unmov'd remains' is a single inverted, multi-clause sentence that requires students to untangle the subject, comparison, and predicate to restate its meaning accurately.
cards.skillStrategy: When a sentence stretches across several lines with comparisons and inverted word order, identify who is being described, what they are compared to, and what action or quality is stated at the end.
evidencePoints: He, like a solid rock by seas inclos'd, / To raging winds and roaring waves oppos'd, / From his proud summit looking down, disdains / Their empty menace, and unmov'd remains.
Against their king the Tuscan troops conspire; / Such is their hate, and such their fierce desire / Of wish'd revenge: on him, and him alone, / All hands employ'd, and all their darts are thrown.
cards.question: Read the following lines from the passage: 'He, like a solid rock by seas inclos'd, / To raging winds and roaring waves oppos'd, / From his proud summit looking down, disdains / Their empty menace, and unmov'd remains.' Which of the following most accurately restates the meaning of these lines?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Mezentius is overwhelmed by the Tuscan troops surrounding him, and he retreats to higher ground to escape their attacks.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Mezentius stands firm against the threats of his enemies, unmoved by their assault, just as a rock surrounded by sea resists wind and waves.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Mezentius looks down from a cliff and mocks the Tuscan troops below, then escapes across the sea before they can reach him.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Mezentius is compared to a rock because he has grown cold and indifferent to his allies, refusing to fight alongside them any longer.

cards.standardTitle: Paraphrase grade-level text
cards.excerpt:
A thousand various thoughts his soul confound; He star’d about, nor aid nor issue found; His own men stop the pass, and his own walls surround. Once more he pauses, and looks out again, And seeks the goddess charioteer in vain. Trembling he views the thund’ring chief advance, And brandishing aloft the deadly lance: Amaz’d he cow’rs beneath his conqu’ring foe, Forgets to ward, and waits the coming blow. Astonish’d while he stands, and fix’d with fear, Aim’d at his shield he sees th’ impending spear.

The hero measur’d first, with narrow view, The destin’d mark; and, rising as he threw, With its full swing the fatal weapon flew. Not with less rage the rattling thunder falls, Or stones from batt’ring-engines break the walls: Swift as a whirlwind, from an arm so strong, The lance drove on, and bore the death along. Naught could his sev’nfold shield the prince avail, Nor aught, beneath his arms, the coat of mail: It pierc’d thro’ all, and with a grisly wound Transfix’d his thigh, and doubled him to ground. With groans the Latins rend the vaulted sky: Woods, hills, and valleys, to the voice reply.
cards.whyThisWorks: The sentence 'Not with less rage the rattling thunder falls, / Or stones from batt'ring-engines break the walls' uses inverted syntax and compressed comparison that requires students to untangle the structure to grasp that the lance's force equals the fury of thunder and siege weapons.
cards.skillStrategy: When a sentence feels backwards or packed with comparisons, reorder the parts in your head—identify what is being compared to what—then restate the full meaning in plain language.

cards.standardTitle: Key literary elements add layers of meaning
cards.excerpt:
She crept out along the swaying oak limb at last, and took the daring step across into the old pine-tree. The way was harder than she thought; she must reach far and hold fast, the sharp dry twigs caught and held her and scratched her like angry talons, the pitch made her thin little fingers clumsy and stiff as she went round and round the tree’s great stem, higher and higher upward. The sparrows and robins in the woods below were beginning to wake and twitter to the dawn, yet it seemed much lighter there aloft in the pine-tree, and the child knew that she must hurry if her project were to be of any use.

The tree seemed to lengthen itself out as she went up, and to reach farther and farther upward. It was like a great main-mast to the voyaging earth; it must truly have been amazed that morning through all its ponderous frame as it felt this determined spark of human spirit creeping and climbing from higher branch to branch. Who knows how steadily the least twigs held themselves to advantage this light, weak creature on her way! The old pine must have loved his new dependent. More than all the hawks, and bats, and moths, and even the sweet-voiced thrushes, was the brave, beating heart of the solitary gray-eyed child. And the tree stood still and held away the winds that June morning while the dawn grew bright in the east.
cards.whyThisWorks: Jewett's personification of the pine tree responding to Sylvia's climb—holding twigs steady, loving her, shielding her from wind—works alongside the physical details of her struggle to reveal that her determined spirit earns a kind of sacred partnership with nature, deepening her characterization beyond simple bravery.
cards.skillStrategy: When a character's actions are described alongside how the world responds to them, ask what that response reveals about who the character is and what she means.
evidencePoints: it must truly have been amazed that morning through all its ponderous frame as it felt this determined spark of human spirit creeping and climbing from higher branch to branch
The old pine must have loved his new dependent. More than all the hawks, and bats, and moths, and even the sweet-voiced thrushes, was the brave, beating heart of the solitary gray-eyed child.

cards.standardTitle: Key literary elements add layers of meaning
cards.excerpt: The next day the young sportsman hovered about the woods, and Sylvia kept him company, having lost her first fear of the friendly lad, who proved to be most kind and sympathetic. He told her many things about the birds and what they knew and where they lived and what they did with themselves. And he gave her a jack-knife, which she thought as great a treasure as if she were a desert-islander. All day long he did not once make her troubled or afraid except when he brought down some unsuspecting singing creature from its bough. Sylvia would have liked him vastly better without his gun; she could not understand why he killed the very birds he seemed to like so much. But as the day waned, Sylvia still watched the young man with loving admiration. She had never seen anybody so charming and delightful; the woman’s heart, asleep in the child, was vaguely thrilled by a dream of love. Some premonition of that great power stirred and swayed these young foresters who traversed the solemn woodlands with soft-footed silent care. They stopped to listen to a bird’s song; they pressed forward again eagerly, parting the branches,—speaking to each other rarely and in whispers; the young man going first and Sylvia following, fascinated, a few steps behind, with her gray eyes dark with excitement.
cards.whyThisWorks: Sylvia's internal conflict—admiring the sportsman while being troubled by his killing of birds—reveals her deep connection to nature and foreshadows the moral tension that defines her character throughout the story.
cards.skillStrategy: When a character feels two opposite things at once, ask what that tension reveals about who they are and what they value.
evidencePoints: Sylvia would have liked him vastly better without his gun; she could not understand why he killed the very birds he seemed to like so much.

choices.label: B

cards.standardTitle: Narrator perspective, irony, and satire
cards.excerpt:
It was a surprise to find so clean and comfortable a little dwelling in this New England wilderness. The young man had known the horrors of its most primitive housekeeping, and the dreary squalor of that level of society which does not rebel at the companionship of hens. This was the best thrift of an old-fashioned farmstead, though on such a small scale that it seemed like a hermitage. He listened eagerly to the old woman’s quaint talk, he watched Sylvia’s pale face and shining gray eyes with ever growing enthusiasm, and insisted that this was the best supper he had eaten for a month; then, afterward, the new-made friends sat down in the doorway together while the moon came up.

Soon it would be berry-time, and Sylvia was a great help at picking. The cow was a good milker, though a plaguy thing to keep track of, the hostess gossiped frankly, adding presently that she had buried four children, so that Sylvia’s mother, and a son (who might be dead) in California were all the children she had left. “Dan, my boy, was a great hand to go gunning,” she explained sadly. “I never wanted for pa’tridges or gray squer’ls while he was to home. He’s been a great wand’rer, I expect, and he’s no hand to write letters. There, I don’t blame him, I’d ha’ seen the world myself if it had been so I could.
cards.whyThisWorks: The grandmother's fond, forgiving tone toward Dan—who has abandoned his family and never writes—directly contradicts what her words reveal about his neglect, creating situational and verbal irony through the contrast between her excuses and his actual behavior.
cards.skillStrategy: When a character's words seem to excuse or praise someone, ask whether the details they share actually reveal the opposite—that contrast is where irony lives.
evidencePoints: "He's been a great wand'rer, I expect, and he's no hand to write letters. There, I don't blame him"
"I never wanted for pa'tridges or gray squer'ls while he was to home."
cards.question: Read the grandmother's words about her son Dan: "He's been a great wand'rer, I expect, and he's no hand to write letters. There, I don't blame him, I'd ha' seen the world myself if it had been so I could." What contrast in this passage creates irony?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The grandmother praises Dan for providing game birds and squirrels, yet the hunter visiting her home is a stranger, suggesting Dan has been replaced.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The grandmother warmly defends Dan and says she does not blame him, yet her own words reveal he has abandoned the family, never writes, and may be dead.

choices.label: C

choices.label: D

cards.standardTitle: Key literary elements add layers of meaning
cards.excerpt: All night the door of the little house stood open, and the whippoorwills came and sang upon the very step. The young sportsman and his old hostess were sound asleep, but Sylvia’s great design kept her broad awake and watching. She forgot to think of sleep. The short summer night seemed as long as the winter darkness, and at last when the whippoorwills ceased, and she was afraid the morning would after all come too soon, she stole out of the house and followed the pasture path through the woods, hastening toward the open ground beyond, listening with a sense of comfort and companionship to the drowsy twitter of a half-awakened bird, whose perch she had jarred in passing. Alas, if the great wave of human interest which flooded for the first time this dull little life should sweep away the satisfactions of an existence heart to heart with nature and the dumb life of the forest!
cards.whyThisWorks: Sylvia's sleepless vigilance and secret predawn departure—contrasted with the sleeping sportsman and hostess—reveal her deep, instinctive bond with nature and the internal conflict between that bond and the 'great wave of human interest' the stranger has stirred in her.
cards.skillStrategy: When a character acts differently from everyone else in a scene, ask what that contrast reveals about who she is and what she values.
evidencePoints: She forgot to think of sleep.
listening with a sense of comfort and companionship to the drowsy twitter of a half-awakened bird

cards.standardTitle: Key literary elements add layers of meaning
cards.excerpt: Half a mile from home, at the farther edge of the woods, where the land was highest, a great pine-tree stood, the last of its generation. Whether it was left for a boundary mark, or for what reason, no one could say; the woodchoppers who had felled its mates were dead and gone long ago, and a whole forest of sturdy trees, pines and oaks and maples, had grown again. But the stately head of this old pine towered above them all and made a landmark for sea and shore miles and miles away. Sylvia knew it well. She had always believed that whoever climbed to the top of it could see the ocean; and the little girl had often laid her hand on the great rough trunk and looked up wistfully at those dark boughs that the wind always stirred, no matter how hot and still the air might be below. Now she thought of the tree with a new excitement, for why, if one climbed it at break of day, could not one see all the world, and easily discover whence the white heron flew, and mark the place, and find the hidden nest?
cards.whyThisWorks: Sylvia's physical gesture of laying her hand on the trunk and looking up 'wistfully,' combined with her sudden shift to purposeful excitement about climbing, reveals her as a child caught between passive longing and active determination, adding meaning to her relationship with the natural world.
cards.skillStrategy: When a character's action or thought shifts within a passage, ask what that shift reveals about who the character is becoming or what she values.

cards.standardTitle: Theme development across a literary text
cards.excerpt:
No, she must keep silence! What is it that suddenly forbids her and makes her dumb? Has she been nine years growing, and now, when the great world for the first time puts out a hand to her, must she thrust it aside for a bird’s sake? The murmur of the pine’s green branches is in her ears, she remembers how the white heron came flying through the golden air and how they watched the sea and the morning together, and Sylvia cannot speak; she cannot tell the heron’s secret and give its life away.

Dear loyalty, that suffered a sharp pang as the guest went away disappointed later in the day, that could have served and followed him and loved him as a dog loves! Many a night Sylvia heard the echo of his whistle haunting the pasture path as she came home with the loitering cow. She forgot even her sorrow at the sharp report of his gun and the piteous sight of thrushes and sparrows dropping silent to the ground, their songs hushed and their pretty feathers stained and wet with blood. Were the birds better friends than their hunter might have been,—who can tell? Whatever treasures were lost to her, woodlands and summer-time, remember! Bring your gifts and graces and tell your secrets to this lonely country child!
cards.whyThisWorks: The excerpt contrasts Sylvia's temptation to betray the heron for human connection against her ultimate silence, forcing students to distinguish details that develop the theme of loyalty to nature over personal desire from true-but-thematically-irrelevant details about the hunter.

cards.standardTitle: Narrator perspective, irony, and satire
cards.excerpt: There was the huge tree asleep yet in the paling moonlight, and small and hopeful Sylvia began with utmost bravery to mount to the top of it, with tingling, eager blood coursing the channels of her whole frame, with her bare feet and fingers, that pinched and held like bird’s claws to the monstrous ladder reaching up, up, almost to the sky itself. First she must mount the white oak tree that grew alongside, where she was almost lost among the dark branches and the green leaves heavy and wet with dew; a bird fluttered off its nest, and a red squirrel ran to and fro and scolded pettishly at the harmless housebreaker. Sylvia felt her way easily. She had often climbed there, and knew that higher still one of the oak’s upper branches chafed against the pine trunk, just where its lower boughs were set close together. There, when she made the dangerous pass from one tree to the other, the great enterprise would really begin.
cards.whyThisWorks: The narrator calls Sylvia a 'harmless housebreaker,' a phrase that contradicts itself and creates verbal irony by labeling an innocent child with a criminal term, giving students a precise, textual moment of irony through reversal.
cards.skillStrategy: When you spot a word or phrase that seems to contradict what you know about a character or situation, ask yourself what the contrast reveals—that gap between expectation and reality is where irony lives.
evidencePoints: a red squirrel ran to and fro and scolded pettishly at the harmless housebreaker
small and hopeful Sylvia began with utmost bravery to mount to the top of it
cards.question: Read this phrase from the passage: 'a red squirrel ran to and fro and scolded pettishly at the harmless housebreaker.' What makes this phrase ironic?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The squirrel's scolding suggests that Sylvia is genuinely threatening the forest animals, which contradicts the narrator's earlier praise of her bravery.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The word 'housebreaker' implies criminal trespass, yet 'harmless' and the context of a child climbing a familiar tree reveal that no real wrongdoing is taking place, making the label a contradiction.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Calling Sylvia a 'housebreaker' shows that the narrator disapproves of her decision to climb the tree and wants readers to see her as reckless.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The squirrel's reaction mirrors Sylvia's own fear, so the phrase reinforces that both creatures are equally startled by the dangerous climb.

cards.standardTitle: Key literary elements add layers of meaning
cards.excerpt:
Sylvia’s heart gave a wild beat; she knew that strange white bird, and had once stolen softly near where it stood in some bright green swamp grass, away over at the other side of the woods. There was an open place where the sunshine always seemed strangely yellow and hot, where tall, nodding rushes grew, and her grandmother had warned her that she might sink in the soft black mud underneath and never be heard of more. Not far beyond were the salt marshes and beyond those was the sea, the sea which Sylvia wondered and dreamed about, but never had looked upon, though its great voice could often be heard above the noise of the woods on stormy nights.

“I can’t think of anything I should like so much as to find that heron’s nest,” the handsome stranger was saying. “I would give ten dollars to anybody who could show it to me,” he added desperately, “and I mean to spend my whole vacation hunting for it if need be. Perhaps it was only migrating, or had been chased out of its own region by some bird of prey.”

Mrs. Tilley gave amazed attention to all this, but Sylvia still watched the toad, not divining, as she might have done at some calmer time, that the creature wished to get to its hole under the doorstep, and was much hindered by the unusual spectators at that hour of the evening. No amount of thought, that night, could decide how many wished-for treasures the ten dollars, so lightly spoken of, would buy.
cards.whyThisWorks: Sylvia's silent fixation on the toad while the stranger speaks, followed by her nighttime calculation of what ten dollars would buy, reveals an inner conflict between her natural world and material longing that deepens her characterization.
cards.skillStrategy: When a character's outward action contrasts with their inner thoughts, ask what that gap reveals about who they really are.
evidencePoints: Sylvia still watched the toad, not divining...that the creature wished to get to its hole under the doorstep
No amount of thought, that night, could decide how many wished-for treasures the ten dollars, so lightly spoken of, would buy
cards.question: In the third paragraph, Sylvia watches the toad while the stranger speaks, yet that night she cannot stop thinking about the ten dollars. What does this contrast reveal about her character?

choices.label: A
choices.text: She is too distracted by the toad to hear the stranger's offer at all.

choices.label: B
choices.text: She appears detached in the moment, but the offer quietly consumes her, showing a longing beneath her quiet exterior.

choices.label: C
choices.text: She deliberately ignores the stranger to show she will not betray the heron's location.

choices.label: D
choices.text: She is indifferent to money because the natural world around her holds her complete attention.

cards.standardTitle: Narrator perspective, irony, and satire
cards.excerpt: Half a mile from home, at the farther edge of the woods, where the land was highest, a great pine-tree stood, the last of its generation. Whether it was left for a boundary mark, or for what reason, no one could say; the woodchoppers who had felled its mates were dead and gone long ago, and a whole forest of sturdy trees, pines and oaks and maples, had grown again. But the stately head of this old pine towered above them all and made a landmark for sea and shore miles and miles away. Sylvia knew it well. She had always believed that whoever climbed to the top of it could see the ocean; and the little girl had often laid her hand on the great rough trunk and looked up wistfully at those dark boughs that the wind always stirred, no matter how hot and still the air might be below. Now she thought of the tree with a new excitement, for why, if one climbed it at break of day, could not one see all the world, and easily discover whence the white heron flew, and mark the place, and find the hidden nest?
cards.whyThisWorks: The pine tree's identity as 'the last of its generation'—a lone survivor of the woodchoppers' destruction—makes it deeply ironic that Sylvia plans to climb it to expose the white heron's hidden nest to a hunter, turning a symbol of refuge and survival into an instrument of another creature's destruction.
cards.skillStrategy: When looking for irony, find a detail the author emphasizes as meaningful, then ask whether a character's action or plan directly contradicts or undermines that meaning.
evidencePoints: the last of its generation
why, if one climbed it at break of day, could not one see all the world, and easily discover whence the white heron flew, and mark the place, and find the hidden nest?
cards.question: The narrator describes the pine tree as 'the last of its generation,' the sole survivor after 'the woodchoppers who had felled its mates were dead and gone long ago.' Yet Sylvia's plan is to climb it 'at break of day' to 'discover whence the white heron flew, and mark the place, and find the hidden nest.' What irony does this contrast create?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The tree is described as towering above 'pines and oaks and maples' and serving as 'a landmark for sea and shore miles and miles away,' yet Sylvia has never thought to use it for navigation until now.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The tree survived the destruction of all its companion trees and stands as a solitary refuge, yet Sylvia intends to use it as a tool to help a hunter locate and expose another creature's hidden sanctuary.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The tree's 'dark boughs' are stirred by wind 'no matter how hot and still the air might be below,' yet Sylvia believes the climb will be calm and easy at break of day.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Sylvia has 'always believed' climbing the tree would reveal the ocean, yet her new plan focuses entirely on finding the heron's nest rather than seeing the sea.

cards.standardTitle: Key literary elements add layers of meaning
cards.excerpt:
No, she must keep silence! What is it that suddenly forbids her and makes her dumb? Has she been nine years growing, and now, when the great world for the first time puts out a hand to her, must she thrust it aside for a bird’s sake? The murmur of the pine’s green branches is in her ears, she remembers how the white heron came flying through the golden air and how they watched the sea and the morning together, and Sylvia cannot speak; she cannot tell the heron’s secret and give its life away.

Dear loyalty, that suffered a sharp pang as the guest went away disappointed later in the day, that could have served and followed him and loved him as a dog loves! Many a night Sylvia heard the echo of his whistle haunting the pasture path as she came home with the loitering cow. She forgot even her sorrow at the sharp report of his gun and the piteous sight of thrushes and sparrows dropping silent to the ground, their songs hushed and their pretty feathers stained and wet with blood. Were the birds better friends than their hunter might have been,—who can tell? Whatever treasures were lost to her, woodlands and summer-time, remember! Bring your gifts and graces and tell your secrets to this lonely country child!
cards.whyThisWorks: Sylvia's silence in the face of temptation, combined with the narrator's apostrophe to nature at the close, reveals her as a character whose loyalty to the natural world defines her moral identity and deepens the story's theme of innocence versus worldly desire.
cards.skillStrategy: When a character acts or refuses to act at a key moment, ask what that choice reveals about who they are and what the author wants readers to understand about them.
evidencePoints: Sylvia cannot speak; she cannot tell the heron's secret and give its life away.
Dear loyalty, that suffered a sharp pang as the guest went away disappointed later in the day, that could have served and followed him and loved him as a dog loves!
cards.question: In the first paragraph, Sylvia 'cannot speak' even though she understands the cost of her silence. What does this moment of speechlessness reveal about her character?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Sylvia is too frightened of the hunter to answer him, showing that her silence comes from fear rather than from any personal conviction.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Sylvia's inability to speak shows that her bond with the natural world is stronger than her desire for human connection or approval, revealing her as a character defined by deep, instinctive loyalty.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Sylvia stays silent because she has already forgotten the heron's location, so her speechlessness reflects confusion rather than a deliberate moral choice.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Sylvia refuses to speak in order to punish the hunter for shooting the thrushes and sparrows, showing that her silence is an act of anger directed at him personally.

cards.question: In the first paragraph, Sylvia refuses to reveal the heron's location, and in the second paragraph, she endures loneliness and longing after the hunter departs. How do these two moments work together to develop a theme?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Sylvia's silence proves she has always disliked human company, and her loneliness after the hunter leaves confirms she prefers animals to people in every situation.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Sylvia's choice to protect the heron and her painful awareness of what that choice costs her together show that true loyalty to nature requires giving up something deeply desired.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Sylvia's refusal to speak reveals her fear of the hunter, and her sorrow over the dead thrushes and sparrows shows that witnessing violence has left her unable to trust anyone.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Sylvia's silence in the first moment and her grief in the second moment show that children who grow up in isolation are unprepared to make meaningful connections with the outside world.

cards.standardTitle: Narrator perspective, irony, and satire
cards.excerpt:
The child gives a long sigh a minute later when a company of shouting cat-birds comes also to the tree, and vexed by their fluttering and lawlessness the solemn heron goes away. She knows his secret now, the wild, light, slender bird that floats and wavers, and goes back like an arrow presently to his home in the green world beneath. Then Sylvia, well satisfied, makes her perilous way down again, not daring to look far below the branch she stands on, ready to cry sometimes because her fingers ache and her lamed feet slip. Wondering over and over again what the stranger would say to her, and what he would think when she told him how to find his way straight to the heron’s nest.

“Sylvy, Sylvy!” called the busy old grandmother again and again, but nobody answered, and the small husk bed was empty, and Sylvia had disappeared.

The guest waked from a dream, and remembering his day’s pleasure hurried to dress himself that it might sooner begin. He was sure from the way the shy little girl looked once or twice yesterday that she had at least seen the white heron, and now she must really be persuaded to tell. Here she comes now, paler than ever, and her worn old frock is torn and tattered, and smeared with pine pitch. The grandmother and the sportsman stand in the door together and question her, and the splendid moment has come to speak of the dead hemlock-tree by the green marsh.
cards.whyThisWorks: The excerpt builds dramatic irony by showing Sylvia mentally rehearsing how to direct the stranger to the heron's nest, then abruptly reversing that expectation when 'the splendid moment has come to speak' and she remains silent — a textbook reversal of anticipated outcome.
cards.skillStrategy: When you spot irony through reversal, ask: what does the passage lead you to expect, and what actually happens instead? The gap between those two things is the irony.
evidencePoints: Wondering over and over again what the stranger would say to her, and what he would think when she told him how to find his way straight to the heron's nest
the splendid moment has come to speak of the dead hemlock-tree by the green marsh
cards.question: During her descent, Sylvia spends the climb 'wondering over and over again what the stranger would say to her, and what he would think when she told him how to find his way straight to the heron's nest.' Yet when 'the splendid moment has come to speak of the dead hemlock-tree by the green marsh,' the narrator reports no words from Sylvia. What is ironic about the contrast between these two moments?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Sylvia rehearses what she will say during the climb, and when the stranger and grandmother question her at the door, she confidently describes the path to the heron's nest — confirming that her dangerous climb was worthwhile.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Sylvia spends the entire climb home mentally preparing to reveal the heron's location to the stranger, yet when the narrator announces 'the splendid moment has come to speak,' Sylvia says nothing — reversing the outcome the passage had been building toward.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Sylvia is so exhausted from the climb — her fingers aching and her feet slipping — that she forgets the heron's location entirely by the time she reaches the grandmother and the stranger at the door.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The stranger wakes up certain that Sylvia 'had at least seen the white heron,' and his confidence proves correct because Sylvia's torn, pitch-smeared frock silently confirms she found the nest and will lead him there.

cards.question: At the end of the passage, Sylvia arrives home 'paler than ever' with a 'torn and tattered' frock 'smeared with pine pitch' just as 'the splendid moment has come to speak.' What does this description of Sylvia reveal about her character?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Her exhausted, disheveled appearance shows she is too physically weak from the climb to answer the grandmother and the sportsman's questions.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Her battered appearance marks the cost of what she has done, and her silence at the moment she could speak reveals that she has chosen the heron's world over the stranger's approval.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Her torn frock and pale face suggest she regrets climbing the tree and wishes she had never discovered the heron's secret.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Her ragged condition causes the grandmother and the sportsman to lose interest in questioning her about the heron's location.

cards.question: The narrator describes the stranger's ten-dollar offer as 'so lightly spoken of,' yet states that 'no amount of thought, that night, could decide how many wished-for treasures' that sum would buy for Sylvia. What irony does this contrast create?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The stranger spends his whole vacation hunting the heron, yet he admits it may have only been migrating, making his costly effort pointless from the start.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The stranger throws out ten dollars as a careless, almost desperate incentive, while for Sylvia the identical amount represents a wealth of possibilities she cannot even fully imagine.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Sylvia has already seen the white heron near the dangerous swamp her grandmother warned her about, yet she remains silent, making the stranger's generous offer go to waste.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Mrs. Tilley listens with amazement to the stranger's offer while Sylvia watches a toad, suggesting Sylvia is too young to understand the value of money the way her grandmother does.

cards.question: The narrator distinguishes between Sylvia's climb through the oak, where 'she had often climbed there,' and the moment when 'the dangerous pass from one tree to the other' must be made, calling it the point where 'the great enterprise would really begin.' What meaning does this contrast between the familiar oak and the dangerous crossing add to the passage?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The contrast shows that Sylvia's experience on the oak has fully prepared her for the pine, so the 'dangerous pass' signals confidence rather than risk and makes her mission seem certain to succeed.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The contrast marks the boundary between Sylvia's zone of comfort and the true test of her quest, suggesting that her mission to protect the heron requires her to move beyond safety and accept real personal risk.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The contrast emphasizes that the oak is dangerous and the pine is safe, so Sylvia's relief at reaching the pine trunk shows the hardest part of her climb is already behind her.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The contrast between the two trees reflects the scolding squirrel and the fluttering bird, both of which warn Sylvia that crossing to the pine is a mistake she will regret.

cards.standardTitle: Theme development across a literary text
cards.excerpt: All night the door of the little house stood open, and the whippoorwills came and sang upon the very step. The young sportsman and his old hostess were sound asleep, but Sylvia’s great design kept her broad awake and watching. She forgot to think of sleep. The short summer night seemed as long as the winter darkness, and at last when the whippoorwills ceased, and she was afraid the morning would after all come too soon, she stole out of the house and followed the pasture path through the woods, hastening toward the open ground beyond, listening with a sense of comfort and companionship to the drowsy twitter of a half-awakened bird, whose perch she had jarred in passing. Alas, if the great wave of human interest which flooded for the first time this dull little life should sweep away the satisfactions of an existence heart to heart with nature and the dumb life of the forest!
cards.whyThisWorks: The excerpt pairs Sylvia's sleepless, purposeful night vigil with the narrator's direct lament about human interest threatening her bond with nature, giving students two distinct moments that together develop the theme of nature's pull versus the cost of human connection.
cards.skillStrategy: Look for two separate moments in the passage—an action and a reflection—and ask what idea both moments are building toward together.
evidencePoints: she stole out of the house and followed the pasture path through the woods, hastening toward the open ground beyond, listening with a sense of comfort and companionship to the drowsy twitter of a half-awakened bird

if the great wave of human interest which flooded for the first time this dull little life should sweep away the satisfactions of an existence heart to heart with nature and the dumb life of the forest!
cards.question:
Read the two moments below from the excerpt and answer the question.

Moment 1: Sylvia slips out before dawn, finding "comfort and companionship" in the sound of a half-awakened bird.
Moment 2: The narrator warns that "the great wave of human interest" may "sweep away the satisfactions of an existence heart to heart with nature."

How do these two moments work together to develop a theme in the passage?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Sylvia's restlessness shows she is excited about the sportsman's visit, and the narrator's warning confirms that meeting new people always brings danger to those who live alone.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Sylvia's instinctive turn toward the forest for comfort, and the narrator's fear that human connection could destroy that comfort, together suggest that belonging to the natural world is a fragile but deeply sustaining bond.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Sylvia's decision to leave the house before dawn shows her courage, and the narrator's lament about human interest develops the idea that young people must choose adventure over safety.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The bird's drowsy twitter soothes Sylvia's fear of the dark, and the narrator's warning about human interest shows that nature is indifferent to human problems.

cards.question: The narrator asks, 'when the great world for the first time puts out a hand to her, must she thrust it aside for a bird's sake?' What is ironic about Sylvia's silence at this exact moment?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Sylvia refuses to speak because she has always distrusted strangers, so her silence is exactly what the reader would expect from a girl who 'loitered' alone with the cow.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The first time the wider world reaches toward Sylvia—the very connection she has been denied—is the moment she chooses to protect the heron and 'cannot speak,' so the opportunity for belonging becomes the thing she sacrifices.

choices.label: C

choices.label: D

Were the birds better friends than their hunter might have been,—who can tell? Whatever treasures were lost to her, woodlands and summer-time, remember! Bring your gifts and graces and tell your secrets to this lonely country child!

cards.skillStrategy: When a character makes a hard decision at a turning point, ask what that choice costs them and what it reveals about what they value most — that tension is where deeper meaning lives.

cards.question: Sylvia chooses silence rather than revealing the heron's location, even though the narrator acknowledges she 'could have served and followed him and loved him as a dog loves.' What deeper meaning does this decision add to the passage?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Sylvia's silence shows that she is too shy and fearful of the hunter to speak, suggesting that her isolation has left her unable to form any meaningful human bond.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Sylvia's refusal to betray the heron, despite the real cost of losing human love and companionship, reveals that her bond with the natural world defines her identity more deeply than any social belonging could.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Sylvia's choice to protect the heron demonstrates that she has already decided the hunter is cruel, since she cannot forget 'the piteous sight of thrushes and sparrows dropping silent to the ground.'

choices.label: D
choices.text: Sylvia's silence proves that children are naturally more connected to animals than to people, and the passage suggests this instinct fades as one grows older and enters 'the great world.'

cards.standardTitle: Theme development across a literary text
cards.excerpt: The next day the young sportsman hovered about the woods, and Sylvia kept him company, having lost her first fear of the friendly lad, who proved to be most kind and sympathetic. He told her many things about the birds and what they knew and where they lived and what they did with themselves. And he gave her a jack-knife, which she thought as great a treasure as if she were a desert-islander. All day long he did not once make her troubled or afraid except when he brought down some unsuspecting singing creature from its bough. Sylvia would have liked him vastly better without his gun; she could not understand why he killed the very birds he seemed to like so much. But as the day waned, Sylvia still watched the young man with loving admiration. She had never seen anybody so charming and delightful; the woman’s heart, asleep in the child, was vaguely thrilled by a dream of love. Some premonition of that great power stirred and swayed these young foresters who traversed the solemn woodlands with soft-footed silent care. They stopped to listen to a bird’s song; they pressed forward again eagerly, parting the branches,—speaking to each other rarely and in whispers; the young man going first and Sylvia following, fascinated, a few steps behind, with her gray eyes dark with excitement.
cards.whyThisWorks: The excerpt pairs Sylvia's explicit moral confusion—'she could not understand why he killed the very birds he seemed to like so much'—with her physical and emotional surrender—'fascinated, a few steps behind, with her gray eyes dark with excitement'—creating a single paragraph moment that dramatizes how awakening feeling can draw a person toward what endangers what she loves, directly illustrating theme developed through a specific passage moment.
cards.skillStrategy: To find a theme developed through a moment, identify two details in the same scene that pull in opposite directions, then ask what truth about human experience both details together reveal.
evidencePoints: she could not understand why he killed the very birds he seemed to like so much
fascinated, a few steps behind, with her gray eyes dark with excitement
cards.question: In this paragraph, Sylvia 'could not understand why he killed the very birds he seemed to like so much,' yet she moves through the solemn woodlands 'fascinated, a few steps behind, with her gray eyes dark with excitement.' How do these two contrasting details work together to develop a theme?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Sylvia's confusion about the sportsman's killing and her wide-eyed excitement as she trails him suggest that spending a full day in the woods with a knowledgeable companion is enough to make a person forget her own values.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Sylvia's inability to reconcile the sportsman's love of birds with his killing of them, set against her helpless fascination as she follows him through the solemn woodlands, develops the theme that the awakening of human feeling can pull a person toward what threatens what she most values.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Sylvia's distress when the sportsman shoots unsuspecting birds and her silent movement a few steps behind him together suggest that a generous gift like the jack-knife can overcome a young person's moral objections to someone's harmful behavior.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Sylvia's failure to understand why the sportsman kills the birds he admires and her cautious position a few steps behind him together suggest that inexperience keeps young people from challenging the harmful actions of those they look up to.

cards.standardTitle: Narrator perspective, irony, and satire
cards.excerpt:
It was a surprise to find so clean and comfortable a little dwelling in this New England wilderness. The young man had known the horrors of its most primitive housekeeping, and the dreary squalor of that level of society which does not rebel at the companionship of hens. This was the best thrift of an old-fashioned farmstead, though on such a small scale that it seemed like a hermitage. He listened eagerly to the old woman’s quaint talk, he watched Sylvia’s pale face and shining gray eyes with ever growing enthusiasm, and insisted that this was the best supper he had eaten for a month; then, afterward, the new-made friends sat down in the doorway together while the moon came up.

Soon it would be berry-time, and Sylvia was a great help at picking. The cow was a good milker, though a plaguy thing to keep track of, the hostess gossiped frankly, adding presently that she had buried four children, so that Sylvia’s mother, and a son (who might be dead) in California were all the children she had left. “Dan, my boy, was a great hand to go gunning,” she explained sadly. “I never wanted for pa’tridges or gray squer’ls while he was to home. He’s been a great wand’rer, I expect, and he’s no hand to write letters. There, I don’t blame him, I’d ha’ seen the world myself if it had been so I could.
cards.whyThisWorks: The narrator's subtle condescension toward the young man's perspective—revealed through phrases like 'horrors of its most primitive housekeeping' and 'dreary squalor of that level of society'—contrasts with the grandmother's dignified, unselfconscious voice, giving students clear textual evidence to analyze how perspective shapes the reader's understanding of class and character.
cards.skillStrategy: Find the exact words the narrator uses to describe a character's view or attitude, then ask yourself whether those words reveal admiration, judgment, irony, or sympathy—and which choice is proven by the text.
evidencePoints: the dreary squalor of that level of society which does not rebel at the companionship of hens
I never wanted for pa'tridges or gray squer'ls while he was to home
cards.question: Read this sentence from the passage: 'He had known the horrors of its most primitive housekeeping, and the dreary squalor of that level of society which does not rebel at the companionship of hens.' What does this wording reveal about the narrator's perspective toward the young man?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The narrator shares the young man's disgust, presenting the farmstead as genuinely filthy and unfit for a visitor.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The narrator filters the farmstead through the young man's class-based prejudices, subtly exposing his condescension toward rural poverty rather than endorsing it.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The narrator sympathizes with the young man's discomfort, suggesting that life on the farm is too harsh for an outsider to appreciate.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The narrator uses the young man's reaction to warn the reader that the grandmother's home is not as welcoming as it first appears.

cards.question: The grandmother mentions almost in passing that she has 'buried four children' and that her son Dan 'has been a great wand'rer' she never hears from. How does this revelation add a deeper layer of meaning to the scene?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The detail about Dan's love of hunting explains why the young man with a gun feels immediately welcome, suggesting the farm has always been open to strangers who share that interest.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The grandmother's quiet recounting of her losses reveals that the farm's warmth and 'best thrift' conceal a life shaped by grief and unfulfilled longing, making the arrival of the young man feel both hopeful and fragile.

cards.standardTitle: Theme development across a literary text
cards.excerpt: There was the huge tree asleep yet in the paling moonlight, and small and hopeful Sylvia began with utmost bravery to mount to the top of it, with tingling, eager blood coursing the channels of her whole frame, with her bare feet and fingers, that pinched and held like bird’s claws to the monstrous ladder reaching up, up, almost to the sky itself. First she must mount the white oak tree that grew alongside, where she was almost lost among the dark branches and the green leaves heavy and wet with dew; a bird fluttered off its nest, and a red squirrel ran to and fro and scolded pettishly at the harmless housebreaker. Sylvia felt her way easily. She had often climbed there, and knew that higher still one of the oak’s upper branches chafed against the pine trunk, just where its lower boughs were set close together. There, when she made the dangerous pass from one tree to the other, the great enterprise would really begin.
cards.whyThisWorks: Jewett layers two distinct moments—Sylvia's 'utmost bravery' and 'tingling, eager blood' on the familiar oak, followed by her calm, knowing recognition that 'the great enterprise would really begin' only at 'the dangerous pass' to the pine—to show that theme develops through the contrast between initial daring and conscious preparation for a harder test.
cards.skillStrategy: To find a theme developed through moments, identify two specific scenes or details in the passage and ask what idea about life they build together when you connect them.
