cards.question: Jewett first describes Sylvia climbing the oak with 'utmost bravery' and 'tingling, eager blood,' then notes that Sylvia knows 'the great enterprise would really begin' only when she makes 'the dangerous pass' from the oak to the pine. What theme about courage do these two moments develop together?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Sylvia's 'tingling, eager blood' on the familiar oak shows that bravery exists only in safe, well-known places, and her awareness that the real test begins at the pine reveals she is unprepared for genuine danger.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Sylvia's climb described as 'utmost bravery' with 'tingling, eager blood' and her deliberate recognition that the true test begins at 'the dangerous pass' to the pine together suggest that genuine courage combines a daring spirit with conscious readiness for a greater challenge ahead.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Sylvia's 'tingling, eager blood' while ascending the oak shows she acts impulsively, and her realization that 'the great enterprise would really begin' at the pine reveals that reckless enthusiasm causes her to underestimate the danger she faces.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Because Sylvia 'had often climbed' the oak and 'felt her way easily,' her courage is rooted entirely in habit, and her awareness of the dangerous transfer to the pine suggests that courage fades once a person moves beyond familiar, well-known ground.

cards.question: The narrator states that Sylvia 'watched the young man with loving admiration' yet 'could not understand why he killed the very birds he seemed to like so much.' What meaning does this specific conflict add to the passage?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Sylvia's confusion about the killing shows she is too naive to appreciate the sportsman's knowledge of birds, suggesting her admiration will fade once she learns more about hunting.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Sylvia's simultaneous admiration for the young man and grief over his killing of birds reveals that her loyalty to the natural world and her growing feelings for him may be irreconcilable, foreshadowing a painful choice ahead.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The sportsman's gift of a jack-knife outweighs Sylvia's unease about the birds, suggesting that his kindness has already resolved any tension between her love of nature and her attraction to him.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Sylvia's admiration despite the gun shows she has fully set aside her attachment to the woods, and the detail about the killed birds signals that she is ready to follow the young man away from the forest.

cards.standardTitle: Theme development across a literary text
cards.excerpt: Half a mile from home, at the farther edge of the woods, where the land was highest, a great pine-tree stood, the last of its generation. Whether it was left for a boundary mark, or for what reason, no one could say; the woodchoppers who had felled its mates were dead and gone long ago, and a whole forest of sturdy trees, pines and oaks and maples, had grown again. But the stately head of this old pine towered above them all and made a landmark for sea and shore miles and miles away. Sylvia knew it well. She had always believed that whoever climbed to the top of it could see the ocean; and the little girl had often laid her hand on the great rough trunk and looked up wistfully at those dark boughs that the wind always stirred, no matter how hot and still the air might be below. Now she thought of the tree with a new excitement, for why, if one climbed it at break of day, could not one see all the world, and easily discover whence the white heron flew, and mark the place, and find the hidden nest?
cards.whyThisWorks: The paragraph's shift from Sylvia 'laying her hand on the great rough trunk and looking up wistfully' to thinking of the tree 'with a new excitement' and imagining climbing it at 'break of day' to 'see all the world' gives students a concrete passage moment through which to trace how a theme about nature and purpose develops.
cards.skillStrategy: When tracking theme, find the moment a character's feeling or action changes, then ask what idea about life that shift reveals.
evidencePoints: had often laid her hand on the great rough trunk and looked up wistfully
now she thought of the tree with a new excitement, for why, if one climbed it at break of day, could not one see all the world
cards.question: In the excerpt, Sylvia 'had often laid her hand on the great rough trunk and looked up wistfully,' yet 'now she thought of the tree with a new excitement' and imagined climbing it at 'break of day' to 'see all the world.' Which theme does this shift from years of wistful longing to sudden purposeful excitement most clearly develop?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Sylvia's years of touching the pine's rough trunk were wasted longing until the stranger's quest gave the tree a purpose, suggesting that nature only gains meaning when it serves someone else's goal.

choices.label: B
choices.text: A deep, long-held bond with nature—built through years of wistfully touching the pine's rough trunk—can awaken into active purpose when a reason to finally climb toward 'all the world' appears.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The pine's survival as 'the last of its generation' and its role as 'a landmark for sea and shore miles and miles away' are the true source of Sylvia's excitement, suggesting that a place's history is what gives it power over people.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Sylvia's new excitement about climbing the pine at 'break of day' to find the heron's hidden nest shows that personal ambition replaces the reverence she once felt standing at the trunk's base, suggesting that desire erodes respect for nature.

cards.question: Which quotation from the excerpt most clearly reveals the narrator's perspective that Sylvia's admiration for the young man exists alongside an unresolved tension about his character?

choices.label: A

choices.label: B
choices.text: "Sylvia would have liked him vastly better without his gun; she could not understand why he killed the very birds he seemed to like so much" — the narrator voices Sylvia's genuine affection while exposing the contradiction that quietly undermines the sportsman's appeal.

cards.standardTitle: Key literary elements add layers of meaning
cards.excerpt:
She crept out along the swaying oak limb at last, and took the daring step across into the old pine-tree. The way was harder than she thought; she must reach far and hold fast, the sharp dry twigs caught and held her and scratched her like angry talons, the pitch made her thin little fingers clumsy and stiff as she went round and round the tree’s great stem, higher and higher upward. The sparrows and robins in the woods below were beginning to wake and twitter to the dawn, yet it seemed much lighter there aloft in the pine-tree, and the child knew that she must hurry if her project were to be of any use.

The tree seemed to lengthen itself out as she went up, and to reach farther and farther upward. It was like a great main-mast to the voyaging earth; it must truly have been amazed that morning through all its ponderous frame as it felt this determined spark of human spirit creeping and climbing from higher branch to branch. Who knows how steadily the least twigs held themselves to advantage this light, weak creature on her way! The old pine must have loved his new dependent. More than all the hawks, and bats, and moths, and even the sweet-voiced thrushes, was the brave, beating heart of the solitary gray-eyed child. And the tree stood still and held away the winds that June morning while the dawn grew bright in the east.
cards.whyThisWorks: Sylvia's physical struggle against 'sharp dry twigs' and 'clumsy and stiff' fingers, contrasted with the pine tree's apparent willingness to shelter her and 'hold away the winds,' uses plot conflict to develop the theme that determined human spirit can create a near-spiritual bond with nature.
cards.skillStrategy: When a character faces a physical conflict, ask what the struggle reveals about the character's inner qualities and what the resolution—or the world's response—suggests about the story's deeper meaning.
evidencePoints: the sharp dry twigs caught and held her and scratched her like angry talons, the pitch made her thin little fingers clumsy and stiff
the tree stood still and held away the winds that June morning while the dawn grew bright in the east
cards.question: In the first paragraph, the pine tree's 'sharp dry twigs' scratch Sylvia 'like angry talons' and the pitch leaves her fingers 'clumsy and stiff,' yet by the end of the second paragraph 'the tree stood still and held away the winds' for her. What meaning does this shift from obstacle to shelter add to the passage?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The twigs and pitch show that the pine tree is genuinely dangerous, and the tree's stillness at the end signals that Sylvia has finally stopped climbing and is resting before attempting to descend.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The painful obstacles Sylvia overcomes, met ultimately by the pine's apparent protection and love for 'this determined spark of human spirit,' suggest that fierce perseverance can transform a hostile natural force into a willing ally.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Because the sparrows and robins are waking as Sylvia struggles with the twigs and pitch, the passage emphasizes that she is racing daylight and that the tree's stillness simply means the wind has died at dawn.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The scratching twigs and sticky pitch reveal that Sylvia is physically weak and ill-suited for the climb, and the tree's stillness at the end shows that nature remains indifferent to human effort.

cards.standardTitle: Theme development across a literary text
cards.excerpt: The birds sang louder and louder. At last the sun came up bewilderingly bright. Sylvia could see the white sails of ships out at sea, and the clouds that were purple and rose-colored and yellow at first began to fade away. Where was the white heron’s nest in the sea of green branches, and was this wonderful sight and pageant of the world the only reward for having climbed to such a giddy height? Now look down again, Sylvia, where the green marsh is set among the shining birches and dark hemlocks; there where you saw the white heron once you will see him again; look, look! a white spot of him like a single floating feather comes up from the dead hemlock and grows larger, and rises, and comes close at last, and goes by the landmark pine with steady sweep of wing and outstretched slender neck and crested head. And wait! wait! do not move a foot or a finger, little girl, do not send an arrow of light and consciousness from your two eager eyes, for the heron has perched on a pine bough not far beyond yours, and cries back to his mate on the nest, and plumes his feathers for the new day!
cards.whyThisWorks: The excerpt pairs Sylvia's internal doubt—'was this wonderful sight and pageant of the world the only reward'—with her physical stillness as the heron perches nearby, showing how two linked moments build the theme that nature's deepest rewards come through patient, non-intrusive witnessing.
cards.skillStrategy: When tracking theme through moments, find the turning point where a character's doubt or question is answered by what happens next, then ask what truth both moments together reveal.
evidencePoints: was this wonderful sight and pageant of the world the only reward for having climbed to such a giddy height?
do not move a foot or a finger, little girl, do not send an arrow of light and consciousness from your two eager eyes, for the heron has perched on a pine bough not far beyond yours
cards.question: In the excerpt, Sylvia first wonders whether 'this wonderful sight and pageant of the world' is 'the only reward' for her climb, then the narrator urges her not to 'move a foot or a finger' or 'send an arrow of light and consciousness' from her eyes as the heron perches nearby. How do these two moments work together to develop a theme?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Both moments show that Sylvia's climb was a failure: the 'wonderful sight' of the sea disappoints her, and her frozen stillness prevents her from locating the heron's nest for the hunter.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Both moments show that the true reward of nature is not something taken or seized, but something witnessed through patience and stillness—the heron perching freely beside Sylvia answers her doubt about whether the climb was worth it.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Both moments show that Sylvia is overwhelmed by fear—first by the 'giddy height' of the tree, then by the heron's sudden appearance—so together they reveal that nature is a source of danger rather than wonder.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The first moment shows Sylvia admiring the purple and rose-colored clouds, and the second shows her spotting the heron's nest in the 'dead hemlock,' so together they reveal that her mission to guide the hunter is nearly complete.

cards.standardTitle: Theme development across a literary text
cards.excerpt:
The child gives a long sigh a minute later when a company of shouting cat-birds comes also to the tree, and vexed by their fluttering and lawlessness the solemn heron goes away. She knows his secret now, the wild, light, slender bird that floats and wavers, and goes back like an arrow presently to his home in the green world beneath. Then Sylvia, well satisfied, makes her perilous way down again, not daring to look far below the branch she stands on, ready to cry sometimes because her fingers ache and her lamed feet slip. Wondering over and over again what the stranger would say to her, and what he would think when she told him how to find his way straight to the heron’s nest.

“Sylvy, Sylvy!” called the busy old grandmother again and again, but nobody answered, and the small husk bed was empty, and Sylvia had disappeared.

The guest waked from a dream, and remembering his day’s pleasure hurried to dress himself that it might sooner begin. He was sure from the way the shy little girl looked once or twice yesterday that she had at least seen the white heron, and now she must really be persuaded to tell. Here she comes now, paler than ever, and her worn old frock is torn and tattered, and smeared with pine pitch. The grandmother and the sportsman stand in the door together and question her, and the splendid moment has come to speak of the dead hemlock-tree by the green marsh.
cards.whyThisWorks: The excerpt pairs Sylvia's physical suffering on the descent ('ready to cry sometimes because her fingers ache and her lamed feet slip') with her deliberate silence when 'the splendid moment has come to speak,' showing how a character's choices across two concrete moments build the theme that loyalty to the natural world requires personal sacrifice.

the splendid moment has come to speak of the dead hemlock-tree by the green marsh
cards.question: In the excerpt, Sylvia descends the tree 'ready to cry sometimes because her fingers ache and her lamed feet slip,' and then, when the grandmother and the sportsman question her, 'the splendid moment has come to speak of the dead hemlock-tree by the green marsh'—yet the narrator implies she stays silent. What theme do these two specific moments work together to develop?

choices.label: B
choices.text: Both moments show Sylvia enduring physical pain on the descent and then withholding the heron's location despite direct questioning, developing the theme that genuine devotion to the natural world demands personal cost and quiet courage.

choices.label: C

choices.label: D

cards.standardTitle: Key literary elements add layers of meaning
cards.excerpt: Half a mile from home, at the farther edge of the woods, where the land was highest, a great pine-tree stood, the last of its generation. Whether it was left for a boundary mark, or for what reason, no one could say; the woodchoppers who had felled its mates were dead and gone long ago, and a whole forest of sturdy trees, pines and oaks and maples, had grown again. But the stately head of this old pine towered above them all and made a landmark for sea and shore miles and miles away. Sylvia knew it well. She had always believed that whoever climbed to the top of it could see the ocean; and the little girl had often laid her hand on the great rough trunk and looked up wistfully at those dark boughs that the wind always stirred, no matter how hot and still the air might be below. Now she thought of the tree with a new excitement, for why, if one climbed it at break of day, could not one see all the world, and easily discover whence the white heron flew, and mark the place, and find the hidden nest?
cards.whyThisWorks: Sylvia's decision to climb the pine tree at break of day transforms a childhood wish ('had often laid her hand on the great rough trunk and looked up wistfully') into a purposeful plan, creating a conflict between her loyalty to the heron and her desire to help the stranger—demonstrating how a character decision adds a deeper layer of meaning.
cards.skillStrategy: When a character makes a decision, ask what that decision costs them or what it puts at risk—that tension is where the deeper meaning lives.

cards.standardTitle: Theme development across a literary text
cards.excerpt:
She crept out along the swaying oak limb at last, and took the daring step across into the old pine-tree. The way was harder than she thought; she must reach far and hold fast, the sharp dry twigs caught and held her and scratched her like angry talons, the pitch made her thin little fingers clumsy and stiff as she went round and round the tree’s great stem, higher and higher upward. The sparrows and robins in the woods below were beginning to wake and twitter to the dawn, yet it seemed much lighter there aloft in the pine-tree, and the child knew that she must hurry if her project were to be of any use.

The tree seemed to lengthen itself out as she went up, and to reach farther and farther upward. It was like a great main-mast to the voyaging earth; it must truly have been amazed that morning through all its ponderous frame as it felt this determined spark of human spirit creeping and climbing from higher branch to branch. Who knows how steadily the least twigs held themselves to advantage this light, weak creature on her way! The old pine must have loved his new dependent. More than all the hawks, and bats, and moths, and even the sweet-voiced thrushes, was the brave, beating heart of the solitary gray-eyed child. And the tree stood still and held away the winds that June morning while the dawn grew bright in the east.
cards.whyThisWorks: Two distinct moments—Sylvia's painful physical struggle through the sharp twigs and pitch, and the pine tree's personified sheltering of her—work together to develop the theme that determined spirit can forge an unexpected bond with the natural world.
cards.skillStrategy: Look for two separate moments in the passage and ask what idea both moments are pointing toward together.

cards.standardTitle: Theme development across a literary text
cards.excerpt: The next day the young sportsman hovered about the woods, and Sylvia kept him company, having lost her first fear of the friendly lad, who proved to be most kind and sympathetic. He told her many things about the birds and what they knew and where they lived and what they did with themselves. And he gave her a jack-knife, which she thought as great a treasure as if she were a desert-islander. All day long he did not once make her troubled or afraid except when he brought down some unsuspecting singing creature from its bough. Sylvia would have liked him vastly better without his gun; she could not understand why he killed the very birds he seemed to like so much. But as the day waned, Sylvia still watched the young man with loving admiration. She had never seen anybody so charming and delightful; the woman’s heart, asleep in the child, was vaguely thrilled by a dream of love. Some premonition of that great power stirred and swayed these young foresters who traversed the solemn woodlands with soft-footed silent care. They stopped to listen to a bird’s song; they pressed forward again eagerly, parting the branches,—speaking to each other rarely and in whispers; the young man going first and Sylvia following, fascinated, a few steps behind, with her gray eyes dark with excitement.
cards.whyThisWorks: The excerpt places Sylvia in direct tension between her 'loving admiration' for the young man and her distress that 'he killed the very birds he seemed to like so much,' making the internal conflict a clear vehicle for the theme that human connection and loyalty to nature can pull a character toward an unavoidable choice.
cards.skillStrategy: When tracking theme through conflict, identify what two forces are pulling the character in opposite directions and ask what the consequence of that pull reveals about a larger truth.

choices.label: B

choices.label: C

choices.label: D

cards.standardTitle: Narrator perspective, irony, and satire
cards.excerpt:
Sylvia’s heart gave a wild beat; she knew that strange white bird, and had once stolen softly near where it stood in some bright green swamp grass, away over at the other side of the woods. There was an open place where the sunshine always seemed strangely yellow and hot, where tall, nodding rushes grew, and her grandmother had warned her that she might sink in the soft black mud underneath and never be heard of more. Not far beyond were the salt marshes and beyond those was the sea, the sea which Sylvia wondered and dreamed about, but never had looked upon, though its great voice could often be heard above the noise of the woods on stormy nights.

“I can’t think of anything I should like so much as to find that heron’s nest,” the handsome stranger was saying. “I would give ten dollars to anybody who could show it to me,” he added desperately, “and I mean to spend my whole vacation hunting for it if need be. Perhaps it was only migrating, or had been chased out of its own region by some bird of prey.”

Mrs. Tilley gave amazed attention to all this, but Sylvia still watched the toad, not divining, as she might have done at some calmer time, that the creature wished to get to its hole under the doorstep, and was much hindered by the unusual spectators at that hour of the evening. No amount of thought, that night, could decide how many wished-for treasures the ten dollars, so lightly spoken of, would buy.
cards.whyThisWorks: The narrator's close third-person perspective reveals Sylvia's inner conflict through contrasting details—her wonder at the heron and the sea versus her silent calculation of what ten dollars could buy—allowing students to trace how specific word choices expose her divided loyalties.
cards.skillStrategy: Find the exact words the narrator uses to describe a character's inner thoughts or reactions, then ask yourself what attitude or tension those words reveal.

cards.excerpt:
No, she must keep silence! What is it that suddenly forbids her and makes her dumb? Has she been nine years growing, and now, when the great world for the first time puts out a hand to her, must she thrust it aside for a bird’s sake? The murmur of the pine’s green branches is in her ears, she remembers how the white heron came flying through the golden air and how they watched the sea and the morning together, and Sylvia cannot speak; she cannot tell the heron’s secret and give its life away.

Dear loyalty, that suffered a sharp pang as the guest went away disappointed later in the day, that could have served and followed him and loved him as a dog loves! Many a night Sylvia heard the echo of his whistle haunting the pasture path as she came home with the loitering cow. She forgot even her sorrow at the sharp report of his gun and the piteous sight of thrushes and sparrows dropping silent to the ground, their songs hushed and their pretty feathers stained and wet with blood. Were the birds better friends than their hunter might have been,—who can tell? Whatever treasures were lost to her, woodlands and summer-time, remember! Bring your gifts and graces and tell your secrets to this lonely country child!
cards.whyThisWorks: Sylvia's silence in the face of temptation and the narrator's closing lament about 'treasures lost' directly show how an internal conflict and its consequence develop the theme that loyalty to nature demands personal sacrifice.

The murmur of the pine’s green branches is in her ears, she remembers how the white heron came flying through the golden air and how they watched the sea and the morning together, and Sylvia cannot speak; she cannot tell the heron’s secret and give its life away.

Dear loyalty, that suffered a sharp pang as the guest went away disappointed later in the day, that could have served and followed him and loved him as a dog loves! Many a night Sylvia heard the echo of his whistle haunting the pasture path as she came home with the loitering cow. She forgot even her sorrow at the sharp report of his gun and the piteous sight of thrushes and sparrows dropping silent to the ground, their songs hushed and their pretty feathers stained and wet with blood. Were the birds better friends than their hunter might have been,—who can tell? Whatever treasures were lost to her, woodlands and summer-time, remember! Bring your gifts and graces and tell your secrets to this lonely country child!

cards.standardTitle: Theme development across a literary text
cards.excerpt:
She crept out along the swaying oak limb at last, and took the daring step across into the old pine-tree. The way was harder than she thought; she must reach far and hold fast, the sharp dry twigs caught and held her and scratched her like angry talons, the pitch made her thin little fingers clumsy and stiff as she went round and round the tree’s great stem, higher and higher upward. The sparrows and robins in the woods below were beginning to wake and twitter to the dawn, yet it seemed much lighter there aloft in the pine-tree, and the child knew that she must hurry if her project were to be of any use.

The tree seemed to lengthen itself out as she went up, and to reach farther and farther upward. It was like a great main-mast to the voyaging earth; it must truly have been amazed that morning through all its ponderous frame as it felt this determined spark of human spirit creeping and climbing from higher branch to branch. Who knows how steadily the least twigs held themselves to advantage this light, weak creature on her way! The old pine must have loved his new dependent. More than all the hawks, and bats, and moths, and even the sweet-voiced thrushes, was the brave, beating heart of the solitary gray-eyed child. And the tree stood still and held away the winds that June morning while the dawn grew bright in the east.
cards.whyThisWorks: Sylvia's physical suffering—sharp talons, clumsy stiff fingers, an endlessly lengthening tree—combined with the pine's protective response creates a clear conflict-and-consequence structure that reveals a theme about the cost and reward of devotion to nature.
cards.skillStrategy: When tracking theme through conflict, identify what the character suffers, what changes as a result, and what that change suggests about a larger idea.
evidencePoints: the sharp dry twigs caught and held her and scratched her like angry talons, the pitch made her thin little fingers clumsy and stiff
the tree stood still and held away the winds that June morning while the dawn grew bright in the east
cards.question: The narrator describes Sylvia's hands as 'clumsy and stiff' from the pitch and her skin scratched 'like angry talons,' yet ends by saying 'the tree stood still and held away the winds' for her. How does this shift from painful struggle to the tree's protection develop a theme?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The contrast shows that nature punishes intruders at first but forgives them once they prove they mean no harm, suggesting that apology is the key to belonging in the natural world.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The contrast shows that enduring the pain of the climb—clumsy fingers, scratching twigs—earns Sylvia the tree's shelter and stillness, developing the idea that true connection with nature demands and is won through personal sacrifice.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The contrast shows that the tree's hostility gives way to calm only because dawn arrives, suggesting that time, not Sylvia's effort, is what ultimately controls the natural world.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The contrast shows that small, weak creatures like Sylvia are naturally suited to climbing trees, suggesting that physical size determines who can form a bond with the wilderness.

cards.standardTitle: Narrator perspective, irony, and satire
cards.excerpt:
It was a surprise to find so clean and comfortable a little dwelling in this New England wilderness. The young man had known the horrors of its most primitive housekeeping, and the dreary squalor of that level of society which does not rebel at the companionship of hens. This was the best thrift of an old-fashioned farmstead, though on such a small scale that it seemed like a hermitage. He listened eagerly to the old woman’s quaint talk, he watched Sylvia’s pale face and shining gray eyes with ever growing enthusiasm, and insisted that this was the best supper he had eaten for a month; then, afterward, the new-made friends sat down in the doorway together while the moon came up.

Soon it would be berry-time, and Sylvia was a great help at picking. The cow was a good milker, though a plaguy thing to keep track of, the hostess gossiped frankly, adding presently that she had buried four children, so that Sylvia’s mother, and a son (who might be dead) in California were all the children she had left. “Dan, my boy, was a great hand to go gunning,” she explained sadly. “I never wanted for pa’tridges or gray squer’ls while he was to home. He’s been a great wand’rer, I expect, and he’s no hand to write letters. There, I don’t blame him, I’d ha’ seen the world myself if it had been so I could.
cards.whyThisWorks: The narrator's inflated, class-conscious language—'horrors,' 'dreary squalor,' and 'that level of society which does not rebel at the companionship of hens'—satirizes the young man's pompous attitude toward rural farm life, making his disdain sound absurdly overblown compared to the clean, comfortable dwelling he actually finds.
cards.skillStrategy: When you spot exaggerated or overly formal language describing something ordinary, ask yourself whether the narrator is mocking the character's attitude rather than describing reality—that gap is often where satire lives.
evidencePoints: the dreary squalor of that level of society which does not rebel at the companionship of hens

cards.question: The narrator describes the young man's past experiences as 'the horrors of its most primitive housekeeping' and 'the dreary squalor of that level of society which does not rebel at the companionship of hens,' yet immediately notes 'it was a surprise to find so clean and comfortable a little dwelling.' cards.standardTitle: Theme development across a literary text
cards.excerpt: The next day the young sportsman hovered about the woods, and Sylvia kept him company, having lost her first fear of the friendly lad, who proved to be most kind and sympathetic. He told her many things about the birds and what they knew and where they lived and what they did with themselves. And he gave her a jack-knife, which she thought as great a treasure as if she were a desert-islander. All day long he did not once make her troubled or afraid except when he brought down some unsuspecting singing creature from its bough. Sylvia would have liked him vastly better without his gun; she could not understand why he killed the very birds he seemed to like so much. But as the day waned, Sylvia still watched the young man with loving admiration. She had never seen anybody so charming and delightful; the woman’s heart, asleep in the child, was vaguely thrilled by a dream of love. Some premonition of that great power stirred and swayed these young foresters who traversed the solemn woodlands with soft-footed silent care. They stopped to listen to a bird’s song; they pressed forward again eagerly, parting the branches,—speaking to each other rarely and in whispers; the young man going first and Sylvia following, fascinated, a few steps behind, with her gray eyes dark with excitement.
cards.whyThisWorks: The excerpt shows Sylvia simultaneously troubled by the sportsman's killing of birds and 'fascinated' by him, letting students distinguish the topic of admiration from the theme that powerful attraction can pull a person toward someone whose actions contradict her own values.

choices.text: Because the narrator stays inside Sylvia's perception, the reader sees a contradiction she cannot fully name—her admiration blinds her to a danger the reader recognizes in the man who destroys what he claims to love.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Because the narrator describes both characters equally, the reader understands that Sylvia and the sportsman share the same feelings about the birds, making her confusion a minor detail rather than a meaningful tension.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Because the narrator presents Sylvia's admiration without any doubt, the reader is meant to accept that the sportsman's kindness outweighs his violence and that Sylvia's judgment about him is correct.

cards.standardTitle: Theme development across a literary text
cards.excerpt: All night the door of the little house stood open, and the whippoorwills came and sang upon the very step. The young sportsman and his old hostess were sound asleep, but Sylvia’s great design kept her broad awake and watching. She forgot to think of sleep. The short summer night seemed as long as the winter darkness, and at last when the whippoorwills ceased, and she was afraid the morning would after all come too soon, she stole out of the house and followed the pasture path through the woods, hastening toward the open ground beyond, listening with a sense of comfort and companionship to the drowsy twitter of a half-awakened bird, whose perch she had jarred in passing. Alas, if the great wave of human interest which flooded for the first time this dull little life should sweep away the satisfactions of an existence heart to heart with nature and the dumb life of the forest!
cards.whyThisWorks: The narrator's direct lament—'if the great wave of human interest…should sweep away the satisfactions of an existence heart to heart with nature'—makes the tension between human society and the natural world explicit, giving students a clear passage moment to identify a transferable theme about belonging and the cost of connection.
cards.skillStrategy: Look for a moment where the narrator steps back to comment on a character's situation—that commentary often signals the theme the author wants readers to carry beyond the story.
evidencePoints: the great wave of human interest which flooded for the first time this dull little life should sweep away the satisfactions of an existence heart to heart with nature and the dumb life of the forest
listening with a sense of comfort and companionship to the drowsy twitter of a half-awakened bird
cards.question: The narrator ends the paragraph with the warning that 'the great wave of human interest…should sweep away the satisfactions of an existence heart to heart with nature.' Which statement best expresses the universal theme this moment develops?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Young people who stay awake all night to pursue a goal will eventually lose the peace they once had.

choices.label: B
choices.text: When a person opens herself to the pull of society, she risks losing the deep belonging she found in the natural world.

choices.label: C
choices.text: A quiet life in the countryside is always more fulfilling than any connection a person can form with another human being.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Sylvia's loyalty to the forest birds will ultimately protect her from the influence of the young sportsman.

cards.standardTitle: Narrator perspective, irony, and satire
cards.excerpt:
It was a surprise to find so clean and comfortable a little dwelling in this New England wilderness. The young man had known the horrors of its most primitive housekeeping, and the dreary squalor of that level of society which does not rebel at the companionship of hens. This was the best thrift of an old-fashioned farmstead, though on such a small scale that it seemed like a hermitage. He listened eagerly to the old woman’s quaint talk, he watched Sylvia’s pale face and shining gray eyes with ever growing enthusiasm, and insisted that this was the best supper he had eaten for a month; then, afterward, the new-made friends sat down in the doorway together while the moon came up.

Soon it would be berry-time, and Sylvia was a great help at picking. The cow was a good milker, though a plaguy thing to keep track of, the hostess gossiped frankly, adding presently that she had buried four children, so that Sylvia’s mother, and a son (who might be dead) in California were all the children she had left. “Dan, my boy, was a great hand to go gunning,” she explained sadly. “I never wanted for pa’tridges or gray squer’ls while he was to home. He’s been a great wand’rer, I expect, and he’s no hand to write letters. There, I don’t blame him, I’d ha’ seen the world myself if it had been so I could.
cards.whyThisWorks: The grandmother's fond, forgiving account of Dan's wandering and silence reveals her blind affection, while the reader can infer that Dan has likely abandoned his family—creating a clear gap between the speaker's charitable view and the reader's more critical understanding.
cards.skillStrategy: When a speaker describes someone's behavior in a positive or excusing way, ask yourself whether the details actually support that positive spin or point to something the speaker is unwilling to admit.
evidencePoints: He's been a great wand'rer, I expect, and he's no hand to write letters.
There, I don't blame him, I'd ha' seen the world myself if it had been so I could.
cards.question: The grandmother says of Dan, 'There, I don't blame him, I'd ha' seen the world myself if it had been so I could.' What does the reader understand about Dan that the grandmother does not seem willing to acknowledge?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Dan left home because he shared his mother's deep love of nature and the outdoors, making his wandering a natural extension of the family's values.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Dan has almost certainly neglected his family by cutting off contact, but the grandmother excuses this abandonment by framing his silence and absence as admirable freedom.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Dan is likely dead in California, and the grandmother's forgiving words are her way of quietly grieving a loss she has already accepted.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Dan's skill at hunting made him so valuable to the household that the grandmother resents his departure more than her words suggest.

cards.standardTitle: Figurative language effect
cards.excerpt:
No, she must keep silence! What is it that suddenly forbids her and makes her dumb? Has she been nine years growing, and now, when the great world for the first time puts out a hand to her, must she thrust it aside for a bird’s sake? The murmur of the pine’s green branches is in her ears, she remembers how the white heron came flying through the golden air and how they watched the sea and the morning together, and Sylvia cannot speak; she cannot tell the heron’s secret and give its life away.

Dear loyalty, that suffered a sharp pang as the guest went away disappointed later in the day, that could have served and followed him and loved him as a dog loves! Many a night Sylvia heard the echo of his whistle haunting the pasture path as she came home with the loitering cow. She forgot even her sorrow at the sharp report of his gun and the piteous sight of thrushes and sparrows dropping silent to the ground, their songs hushed and their pretty feathers stained and wet with blood. Were the birds better friends than their hunter might have been,—who can tell? Whatever treasures were lost to her, woodlands and summer-time, remember! Bring your gifts and graces and tell your secrets to this lonely country child!
cards.whyThisWorks: The phrase 'loved him as a dog loves' is an explicit simile functioning as an idiom of unconditional devotion, and 'woodlands and summer-time' are invoked as symbolic forces that ultimately claim Sylvia's loyalty—both figurative elements are fully unlockable from the passage's context alone.
cards.skillStrategy: When you spot a comparison or a direct address to an abstract idea, ask what feeling or value the author is attaching to it, then check the surrounding sentences to confirm that meaning.
evidencePoints: that could have served and followed him and loved him as a dog loves
woodlands and summer-time, remember! Bring your gifts and graces and tell your secrets to this lonely country child!
cards.question: Read the sentence: 'that could have served and followed him and loved him as a dog loves!' What does this comparison reveal about Sylvia's feelings toward the hunter?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Sylvia views the hunter as cruel and unworthy of any affection because he shoots birds without remorse.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Sylvia felt a deep, instinctive devotion to the hunter—one that required no reason or reward—making her sacrifice of that bond all the more painful.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Sylvia admired the hunter the way a working animal admires its owner, meaning she respected his skill but felt no personal attachment.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Sylvia's loyalty to the hunter was simple and childlike, suggesting she did not fully understand the consequences of protecting the heron.

choices.label: B

choices.label: C

choices.label: D

cards.question: The narrator describes Sylvia's silence as 'dear loyalty, that suffered a sharp pang' and acknowledges that 'whatever treasures were lost to her.' Which statement best expresses a universal theme developed by Sylvia's choice in these paragraphs?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Children who grow up in rural isolation are unable to form meaningful bonds with people from the outside world.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Remaining true to one's deepest loyalties can require surrendering relationships and opportunities that matter deeply.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The natural world ultimately offers more beauty and wonder than human companionship ever could.

choices.label: D
choices.text: A person who protects animals will be rewarded by nature in ways that outweigh any human loss.

cards.standardTitle: Narrator perspective, irony, and satire
cards.excerpt: The next day the young sportsman hovered about the woods, and Sylvia kept him company, having lost her first fear of the friendly lad, who proved to be most kind and sympathetic. He told her many things about the birds and what they knew and where they lived and what they did with themselves. And he gave her a jack-knife, which she thought as great a treasure as if she were a desert-islander. All day long he did not once make her troubled or afraid except when he brought down some unsuspecting singing creature from its bough. Sylvia would have liked him vastly better without his gun; she could not understand why he killed the very birds he seemed to like so much. But as the day waned, Sylvia still watched the young man with loving admiration. She had never seen anybody so charming and delightful; the woman’s heart, asleep in the child, was vaguely thrilled by a dream of love. Some premonition of that great power stirred and swayed these young foresters who traversed the solemn woodlands with soft-footed silent care. They stopped to listen to a bird’s song; they pressed forward again eagerly, parting the branches,—speaking to each other rarely and in whispers; the young man going first and Sylvia following, fascinated, a few steps behind, with her gray eyes dark with excitement.
cards.whyThisWorks: The narrator presents Sylvia's 'loving admiration' for the sportsman while simultaneously revealing her unspoken contradiction—she 'could not understand why he killed the very birds he seemed to like so much'—creating a clear gap between Sylvia's enchanted view and the reader's understanding of the young man's destructive nature.
cards.skillStrategy: When a narrator describes a character's feelings, look for details in the same passage that contradict or complicate those feelings—that gap is where the real meaning lives.
evidencePoints: Sylvia still watched the young man with loving admiration. She had never seen anybody so charming and delightful
she could not understand why he killed the very birds he seemed to like so much
cards.question: Sylvia views the young sportsman with 'loving admiration' and finds him 'charming and delightful,' yet the narrator also reveals that 'she could not understand why he killed the very birds he seemed to like so much.' What does this gap between Sylvia's feelings and her observation suggest to the reader?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Sylvia's admiration is fully justified because the young man's kindness and knowledge of birds outweigh the harm caused by his hunting.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Sylvia is too captivated by her feelings to recognize that the young man's affection for birds is undermined by his willingness to destroy them, a contradiction the reader can see even though she cannot.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Sylvia understands the young man's true character but chooses to overlook his faults because she values the jack-knife he gave her.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The narrator suggests that killing birds was a normal and accepted practice, so Sylvia's confusion reflects only her inexperience with the outside world.

cards.question: In the second paragraph, the grandmother uses the idiom 'a great hand to go gunning' to describe her son Dan. She then adds, 'I never wanted for pa'tridges or gray squer'ls while he was to home.' What does this follow-up detail reveal about the meaning of the idiom 'a great hand'?

choices.label: A
choices.text: It shows that 'a great hand' means restless and eager to leave, because Dan's frequent trips away from the farm foreshadow the grandmother's later remark that 'he's been a great wand'rer.'

choices.label: B
choices.text: It confirms that 'a great hand' means especially skilled or capable, because Dan's hunting consistently kept the household supplied with partridges and squirrels.

choices.label: C
choices.text: It suggests that 'a great hand' means physically strong, because pursuing partridges and squirrels through the New England wilderness described earlier would demand great endurance.

choices.label: D
choices.text: It implies that 'a great hand' means devoted and generous, because Dan willingly shared his game so that the grandmother never had to rely on neighbors for food.

cards.standardTitle: Key literary elements add layers of meaning
cards.excerpt: There was the huge tree asleep yet in the paling moonlight, and small and hopeful Sylvia began with utmost bravery to mount to the top of it, with tingling, eager blood coursing the channels of her whole frame, with her bare feet and fingers, that pinched and held like bird’s claws to the monstrous ladder reaching up, up, almost to the sky itself. First she must mount the white oak tree that grew alongside, where she was almost lost among the dark branches and the green leaves heavy and wet with dew; a bird fluttered off its nest, and a red squirrel ran to and fro and scolded pettishly at the harmless housebreaker. Sylvia felt her way easily. She had often climbed there, and knew that higher still one of the oak’s upper branches chafed against the pine trunk, just where its lower boughs were set close together. There, when she made the dangerous pass from one tree to the other, the great enterprise would really begin.
cards.whyThisWorks: The close third-person narrator filters Sylvia's climb through her physical sensations and inner knowledge, allowing readers to feel her courage and determination while also sensing the narrator's admiring, almost reverent tone toward the child—demonstrating how point of view shapes both mood and meaning.
cards.skillStrategy: Ask yourself: whose feelings and knowledge does the narrator share, and how does that access change what the moment means to you as a reader?

cards.question: The narrator describes Sylvia as 'small and hopeful' and reveals that 'tingling, eager blood' courses through her as she climbs. How does the narrator's close access to Sylvia's physical and emotional experience shape the meaning of this moment?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Because the narrator stays outside Sylvia's thoughts and only describes what an observer could see, the climb feels distant and impersonal, emphasizing how alone she is in the dark forest.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Because the narrator moves inside Sylvia's body and feelings, readers experience her courage as something real and urgent, making the climb feel like a heroic act rather than a simple childhood adventure.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Because the narrator focuses on the animals—the fluttering bird and scolding squirrel—rather than Sylvia's feelings, the mood shifts away from Sylvia and toward the indifference of the natural world.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Because the narrator reveals that Sylvia has climbed the oak many times before, the point of view removes all tension from the moment and suggests the climb holds no real danger or significance for her.

cards.standardTitle: Theme development across a literary text
cards.excerpt:
She crept out along the swaying oak limb at last, and took the daring step across into the old pine-tree. The way was harder than she thought; she must reach far and hold fast, the sharp dry twigs caught and held her and scratched her like angry talons, the pitch made her thin little fingers clumsy and stiff as she went round and round the tree’s great stem, higher and higher upward. The sparrows and robins in the woods below were beginning to wake and twitter to the dawn, yet it seemed much lighter there aloft in the pine-tree, and the child knew that she must hurry if her project were to be of any use.

The tree seemed to lengthen itself out as she went up, and to reach farther and farther upward. It was like a great main-mast to the voyaging earth; it must truly have been amazed that morning through all its ponderous frame as it felt this determined spark of human spirit creeping and climbing from higher branch to branch. Who knows how steadily the least twigs held themselves to advantage this light, weak creature on her way! The old pine must have loved his new dependent. More than all the hawks, and bats, and moths, and even the sweet-voiced thrushes, was the brave, beating heart of the solitary gray-eyed child. And the tree stood still and held away the winds that June morning while the dawn grew bright in the east.
cards.whyThisWorks: The narrator's personification of the pine tree as a loving, protective force that 'held away the winds' for 'this determined spark of human spirit' directly illustrates the transferable theme that sincere determination can inspire support from unexpected sources.
cards.skillStrategy: Find the moment in the passage where the narrator makes a surprising claim about how the world responds to the character, then ask what that claim suggests about people or life in general.
evidencePoints: it must truly have been amazed that morning through all its ponderous frame as it felt this determined spark of human spirit creeping and climbing from higher branch to higher branch
the tree stood still and held away the winds that June morning while the dawn grew bright in the east
cards.question: The narrator claims the pine tree 'must truly have been amazed' by 'this determined spark of human spirit' and that it 'held away the winds' for the climbing child. What universal theme about human experience do these claims develop?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A child's small size and physical weakness make her uniquely suited to tasks that stronger, larger people cannot accomplish.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Genuine determination in pursuit of a goal can move even the indifferent forces of the world to offer shelter and support.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The natural world is dangerous and punishing, as shown by the talons and pitch that slow the child's progress upward.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Solitude is the only condition under which a person can find the courage to attempt something truly difficult.

cards.standardTitle: Narrator perspective, irony, and satire
cards.excerpt:
The child gives a long sigh a minute later when a company of shouting cat-birds comes also to the tree, and vexed by their fluttering and lawlessness the solemn heron goes away. She knows his secret now, the wild, light, slender bird that floats and wavers, and goes back like an arrow presently to his home in the green world beneath. Then Sylvia, well satisfied, makes her perilous way down again, not daring to look far below the branch she stands on, ready to cry sometimes because her fingers ache and her lamed feet slip. Wondering over and over again what the stranger would say to her, and what he would think when she told him how to find his way straight to the heron’s nest.

“Sylvy, Sylvy!” called the busy old grandmother again and again, but nobody answered, and the small husk bed was empty, and Sylvia had disappeared.

The guest waked from a dream, and remembering his day’s pleasure hurried to dress himself that it might sooner begin. He was sure from the way the shy little girl looked once or twice yesterday that she had at least seen the white heron, and now she must really be persuaded to tell. Here she comes now, paler than ever, and her worn old frock is torn and tattered, and smeared with pine pitch. The grandmother and the sportsman stand in the door together and question her, and the splendid moment has come to speak of the dead hemlock-tree by the green marsh.
cards.whyThisWorks: The excerpt creates a clear dramatic irony gap: Sylvia climbs down 'well satisfied' and wonders what the stranger will say when she tells him the heron's location, but the final paragraph's silence—she never speaks—reveals to the reader that she has chosen to protect the heron, a decision the narrator withholds from the sportsman and grandmother who question her.
cards.skillStrategy: When a narrator describes what a character plans or expects, pause and check whether the character actually follows through—the gap between the plan and the action is where the reader understands something the character or other people in the scene do not.
evidencePoints: Wondering over and over again what the stranger would say to her, and what he would think when she told him how to find his way straight to the heron's nest.

choices.label: D

cards.question: The grandmother says, 'I never wanted for pa'tridges or gray squer'ls while he was to home.' How does this understatement affect the reader's understanding of her feelings about Dan?

cards.standardTitle: Key literary elements add layers of meaning
cards.excerpt: Half a mile from home, at the farther edge of the woods, where the land was highest, a great pine-tree stood, the last of its generation. Whether it was left for a boundary mark, or for what reason, no one could say; the woodchoppers who had felled its mates were dead and gone long ago, and a whole forest of sturdy trees, pines and oaks and maples, had grown again. But the stately head of this old pine towered above them all and made a landmark for sea and shore miles and miles away. Sylvia knew it well. She had always believed that whoever climbed to the top of it could see the ocean; and the little girl had often laid her hand on the great rough trunk and looked up wistfully at those dark boughs that the wind always stirred, no matter how hot and still the air might be below. Now she thought of the tree with a new excitement, for why, if one climbed it at break of day, could not one see all the world, and easily discover whence the white heron flew, and mark the place, and find the hidden nest?
cards.whyThisWorks: The narrator's close third-person perspective blends Sylvia's private longing ('looked up wistfully') with her sudden purposeful excitement ('a new excitement'), showing how the point of view shapes the reader's understanding of Sylvia's emotional shift and deepens the tree's symbolic weight.
cards.skillStrategy: Ask yourself: whose eyes and feelings are filtering this moment, and how does that perspective change what the scene means to the reader?
evidencePoints: the little girl had often laid her hand on the great rough trunk and looked up wistfully at those dark boughs
Now she thought of the tree with a new excitement, for why, if one climbed it at break of day, could not one see all the world
cards.question: The narrator describes Sylvia as someone who 'had often laid her hand on the great rough trunk and looked up wistfully' and then shifts to 'Now she thought of the tree with a new excitement.' How does the narrator's close focus on Sylvia's perspective shape the meaning of this passage?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The narrator's focus on Sylvia's past visits to the tree establishes that she is reckless and impulsive, making her sudden plan to climb it feel dangerous rather than hopeful.

choices.label: B
choices.text: By filtering the tree through Sylvia's private longing and then her sudden sense of purpose, the narrator transforms the pine from a simple landmark into a symbol of Sylvia's awakening desire to act on her own.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The narrator's description of the tree's history—the dead woodchoppers and the regrown forest—is the central focus, making Sylvia's feelings secondary to the passage's meaning.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Because the narrator describes the tree as a 'landmark for sea and shore miles and miles away,' the passage emphasizes the tree's practical value rather than Sylvia's emotional connection to it.

cards.standardTitle: Theme development across a literary text
cards.excerpt:
It was a surprise to find so clean and comfortable a little dwelling in this New England wilderness. The young man had known the horrors of its most primitive housekeeping, and the dreary squalor of that level of society which does not rebel at the companionship of hens. This was the best thrift of an old-fashioned farmstead, though on such a small scale that it seemed like a hermitage. He listened eagerly to the old woman’s quaint talk, he watched Sylvia’s pale face and shining gray eyes with ever growing enthusiasm, and insisted that this was the best supper he had eaten for a month; then, afterward, the new-made friends sat down in the doorway together while the moon came up.

Soon it would be berry-time, and Sylvia was a great help at picking. The cow was a good milker, though a plaguy thing to keep track of, the hostess gossiped frankly, adding presently that she had buried four children, so that Sylvia’s mother, and a son (who might be dead) in California were all the children she had left. “Dan, my boy, was a great hand to go gunning,” she explained sadly. “I never wanted for pa’tridges or gray squer’ls while he was to home. He’s been a great wand’rer, I expect, and he’s no hand to write letters. There, I don’t blame him, I’d ha’ seen the world myself if it had been so I could.
cards.whyThisWorks: The grandmother's resigned acceptance of hardship and longing — 'I'd ha' seen the world myself if it had been so I could' — alongside her matter-of-fact account of loss and survival, allows students to identify a transferable theme about how circumstances limit human freedom and shape the choices people make.
cards.skillStrategy: Look for what a character accepts, regrets, or longs for, then ask what that reveals about a truth that applies to people beyond this story.
evidencePoints: 'I never wanted for pa'tridges or gray squer'ls while he was to home.'
'There, I don't blame him, I'd ha' seen the world myself if it had been so I could.'
cards.question: The grandmother describes burying four children, losing track of her wandering son, and wishing she had seen the world herself. What theme about human experience do these details develop?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Rural life in New England produces self-reliant people who feel no need for the outside world.

choices.label: B
choices.text: People often carry private longings for lives they were never free to live, yet find ways to endure their circumstances without bitterness.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Children who leave home eventually abandon their families and forget the bonds they once shared.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Poverty forces people to rely on strangers, making hospitality the foundation of survival in isolated communities.

cards.standardTitle: Narrator perspective, irony, and satire
cards.excerpt:
Sylvia’s heart gave a wild beat; she knew that strange white bird, and had once stolen softly near where it stood in some bright green swamp grass, away over at the other side of the woods. There was an open place where the sunshine always seemed strangely yellow and hot, where tall, nodding rushes grew, and her grandmother had warned her that she might sink in the soft black mud underneath and never be heard of more. Not far beyond were the salt marshes and beyond those was the sea, the sea which Sylvia wondered and dreamed about, but never had looked upon, though its great voice could often be heard above the noise of the woods on stormy nights.

“I can’t think of anything I should like so much as to find that heron’s nest,” the handsome stranger was saying. “I would give ten dollars to anybody who could show it to me,” he added desperately, “and I mean to spend my whole vacation hunting for it if need be. Perhaps it was only migrating, or had been chased out of its own region by some bird of prey.”

Mrs. Tilley gave amazed attention to all this, but Sylvia still watched the toad, not divining, as she might have done at some calmer time, that the creature wished to get to its hole under the doorstep, and was much hindered by the unusual spectators at that hour of the evening. No amount of thought, that night, could decide how many wished-for treasures the ten dollars, so lightly spoken of, would buy.
cards.whyThisWorks: Sylvia's distracted, calculating silence about the ten dollars reveals to the reader that she is seriously tempted by the stranger's offer, even as the narrator presents her as simply watching a toad — creating a clear gap between her outward detachment and her inner desire.
cards.skillStrategy: When a narrator describes a character's actions as ordinary or innocent, ask what the character's private thoughts reveal that the surface behavior hides.
evidencePoints: Sylvia still watched the toad, not divining, as she might have done at some calmer time, that the creature wished to get to its hole under the doorstep
No amount of thought, that night, could decide how many wished-for treasures the ten dollars, so lightly spoken of, would buy.
cards.question: The narrator says Sylvia 'still watched the toad' while the stranger described his offer, yet the passage ends by revealing that 'no amount of thought, that night, could decide how many wished-for treasures the ten dollars…would buy.' What gap between Sylvia's outward behavior and her inner state does the reader understand that Sylvia's surface actions conceal?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Sylvia is genuinely uninterested in the stranger's offer and is distracted only because she feels protective of the toad being blocked from its hole.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Although Sylvia appears detached and absorbed in watching the toad, she is privately consumed by the possibility that the ten dollars could transform her life, revealing a temptation she does not openly show.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Sylvia already knows where the heron's nest is and watches the toad as a deliberate act to avoid giving away her secret to the stranger.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Sylvia is too young to understand the value of money, so her thoughts about 'wished-for treasures' show only childlike fantasy rather than any real conflict about the stranger's offer.

cards.standardTitle: Figurative language effect
cards.excerpt:
No, she must keep silence! What is it that suddenly forbids her and makes her dumb? Has she been nine years growing, and now, when the great world for the first time puts out a hand to her, must she thrust it aside for a bird’s sake? The murmur of the pine’s green branches is in her ears, she remembers how the white heron came flying through the golden air and how they watched the sea and the morning together, and Sylvia cannot speak; she cannot tell the heron’s secret and give its life away.

Dear loyalty, that suffered a sharp pang as the guest went away disappointed later in the day, that could have served and followed him and loved him as a dog loves! Many a night Sylvia heard the echo of his whistle haunting the pasture path as she came home with the loitering cow. She forgot even her sorrow at the sharp report of his gun and the piteous sight of thrushes and sparrows dropping silent to the ground, their songs hushed and their pretty feathers stained and wet with blood. Were the birds better friends than their hunter might have been,—who can tell? Whatever treasures were lost to her, woodlands and summer-time, remember! Bring your gifts and graces and tell your secrets to this lonely country child!
cards.whyThisWorks: The excerpt's layered figurative language—'haunting the pasture path' and birds with 'songs hushed and their pretty feathers stained and wet with blood'—directly illustrates how word choice builds a mood of grief and irreversible loss, making it ideal for teaching mood effect with evidence.
cards.skillStrategy: When identifying mood, find the figurative language (personification, imagery) and ask what emotion those specific words create together in the passage.
evidencePoints: the echo of his whistle haunting the pasture path
their songs hushed and their pretty feathers stained and wet with blood
cards.question: Read these lines from the second paragraph: 'the echo of his whistle haunting the pasture path' and 'their songs hushed and their pretty feathers stained and wet with blood.' What mood do these two images create together?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A mood of excitement and hope, suggesting Sylvia looks forward to the hunter's return to the pasture path.

choices.label: B
choices.text: A mood of grief and irreversible loss, showing the hunter's presence left Sylvia's world permanently diminished.

choices.label: C
choices.text: A mood of peaceful acceptance, suggesting Sylvia has come to terms with the violence she witnessed.

choices.label: D
choices.text: A mood of fear and danger, implying Sylvia believes the hunter will return to threaten her directly.

choices.label: A
choices.text: It reassures the reader that Sylvia has made the right choice by protecting the heron, removing any doubt about her decision.

choices.label: B
choices.text: It forces the reader to feel the full cost of Sylvia's silence by framing her loyalty to the heron as a sacrifice of her only chance at connection with the wider world.

cards.standardTitle: Key literary elements add layers of meaning
cards.excerpt: The birds sang louder and louder. At last the sun came up bewilderingly bright. Sylvia could see the white sails of ships out at sea, and the clouds that were purple and rose-colored and yellow at first began to fade away. Where was the white heron’s nest in the sea of green branches, and was this wonderful sight and pageant of the world the only reward for having climbed to such a giddy height? Now look down again, Sylvia, where the green marsh is set among the shining birches and dark hemlocks; there where you saw the white heron once you will see him again; look, look! a white spot of him like a single floating feather comes up from the dead hemlock and grows larger, and rises, and comes close at last, and goes by the landmark pine with steady sweep of wing and outstretched slender neck and crested head. And wait! wait! do not move a foot or a finger, little girl, do not send an arrow of light and consciousness from your two eager eyes, for the heron has perched on a pine bough not far beyond yours, and cries back to his mate on the nest, and plumes his feathers for the new day!
cards.whyThisWorks: The narrator shifts from third-person observation of Sylvia to direct second-person address ('Now look down again, Sylvia,' 'do not move a foot or a finger, little girl'), creating an intimate, urgent tone that pulls readers into Sylvia's perspective and raises the emotional stakes of her choice.
cards.skillStrategy: When a narrator speaks directly to a character, ask yourself what that shift in voice reveals about the narrator's relationship to the moment and how it shapes the reader's feelings.
evidencePoints: Now look down again, Sylvia, where the green marsh is set among the shining birches and dark hemlocks
do not move a foot or a finger, little girl, do not send an arrow of light and consciousness from your two eager eyes
cards.question: In the excerpt, the narrator shifts from describing the scene to directly addressing Sylvia with commands such as 'Now look down again, Sylvia' and 'do not move a foot or a finger, little girl.' How does this shift in point of view shape the meaning of the moment?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The direct address signals that Sylvia has lost focus on her task, suggesting she is too distracted by the sunrise to remember why she climbed the tree.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The narrator's direct commands draw the reader into Sylvia's experience, creating urgency and protectiveness around the heron's appearance that heightens the emotional weight of what she is about to witness.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The shift to second person reveals that the narrator is a separate character within the story who has also climbed the tree and is guiding Sylvia from a nearby branch.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The commands directed at Sylvia show that the narrator disapproves of her reckless behavior in climbing so high, adding a tone of parental scolding to the scene.

cards.standardTitle: Theme development across a literary text
cards.excerpt: The next day the young sportsman hovered about the woods, and Sylvia kept him company, having lost her first fear of the friendly lad, who proved to be most kind and sympathetic. He told her many things about the birds and what they knew and where they lived and what they did with themselves. And he gave her a jack-knife, which she thought as great a treasure as if she were a desert-islander. All day long he did not once make her troubled or afraid except when he brought down some unsuspecting singing creature from its bough. Sylvia would have liked him vastly better without his gun; she could not understand why he killed the very birds he seemed to like so much. But as the day waned, Sylvia still watched the young man with loving admiration. She had never seen anybody so charming and delightful; the woman’s heart, asleep in the child, was vaguely thrilled by a dream of love. Some premonition of that great power stirred and swayed these young foresters who traversed the solemn woodlands with soft-footed silent care. They stopped to listen to a bird’s song; they pressed forward again eagerly, parting the branches,—speaking to each other rarely and in whispers; the young man going first and Sylvia following, fascinated, a few steps behind, with her gray eyes dark with excitement.
cards.whyThisWorks: The excerpt shows Sylvia simultaneously troubled by the sportsman's killing of birds and 'fascinated' by him, modeling the universal theme that admiration and longing can cause a person to overlook what disturbs their conscience.
cards.skillStrategy: Find the moment in the passage where a character feels two opposing things at once, then ask what that tension reveals about people or human experience in general.
evidencePoints: she could not understand why he killed the very birds he seemed to like so much
Sylvia still watched the young man with loving admiration... fascinated, a few steps behind, with her gray eyes dark with excitement
cards.question: The narrator states that Sylvia 'could not understand why he killed the very birds he seemed to like so much,' yet she follows him 'fascinated, a few steps behind.' What universal theme about human experience does this tension develop?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Spending time outdoors with a knowledgeable companion gradually replaces a person's fear with genuine curiosity about the natural world.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The force of admiration and longing can lead a person to set aside actions that trouble their conscience.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Gifts and acts of kindness, such as the jack-knife the sportsman gives Sylvia, are what ultimately earn another person's trust.

choices.label: D
choices.text: A person who destroys what they claim to love will eventually lose the admiration of those who witness their cruelty.

cards.standardTitle: Narrator perspective, irony, and satire
cards.excerpt: All night the door of the little house stood open, and the whippoorwills came and sang upon the very step. The young sportsman and his old hostess were sound asleep, but Sylvia’s great design kept her broad awake and watching. She forgot to think of sleep. The short summer night seemed as long as the winter darkness, and at last when the whippoorwills ceased, and she was afraid the morning would after all come too soon, she stole out of the house and followed the pasture path through the woods, hastening toward the open ground beyond, listening with a sense of comfort and companionship to the drowsy twitter of a half-awakened bird, whose perch she had jarred in passing. Alas, if the great wave of human interest which flooded for the first time this dull little life should sweep away the satisfactions of an existence heart to heart with nature and the dumb life of the forest!
cards.whyThisWorks: The narrator's aside — 'Alas, if the great wave of human interest…should sweep away the satisfactions of an existence heart to heart with nature' — signals a concern the reader grasps fully while Sylvia, consumed by her 'great design,' remains unaware of the danger her own excitement poses to her bond with the natural world.
cards.skillStrategy: When a narrator steps in with a warning or lament that the character never voices, ask yourself what the character believes versus what the narrator fears — that gap is the irony.
evidencePoints: Sylvia's great design kept her broad awake and watching

Alas, if the great wave of human interest which flooded for the first time this dull little life should sweep away the satisfactions of an existence heart to heart with nature and the dumb life of the forest!
cards.question: The narrator describes Sylvia as driven by her 'great design' and then immediately exclaims, 'Alas, if the great wave of human interest…should sweep away the satisfactions of an existence heart to heart with nature.' What gap between Sylvia's understanding and the reader's understanding does this create?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Sylvia knows her nighttime journey is dangerous, but the reader understands she will reach the heron safely by dawn.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Sylvia experiences her excitement as purely thrilling and purposeful, while the reader understands that this same excitement may cost her the peaceful life in nature she has always treasured.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Sylvia believes the sportsman is a threat to the forest, while the reader understands she secretly wants to leave her rural home behind.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Sylvia feels guilty for sneaking out at night, while the reader understands the narrator approves of her decision to help the young sportsman.
