cards.question: In the excerpt, Jewett uses the simile 'it seemed like a hermitage' to describe the farmstead, and the grandmother closes her speech about Dan by admitting, 'I'd ha' seen the world myself if it had been so I could.' How do these two details work together to establish the mood of the passage?

choices.label: A
choices.text: They create a mood of contentment: 'hermitage' suggests the farmstead is a peaceful refuge the grandmother has freely chosen, and her final words confirm she has fully accepted the quiet, self-sufficient life she built there.

choices.label: B
choices.text: They create a mood of quiet isolation and longing: 'hermitage' frames the home as cut off from the wider world, and the grandmother's admission that she herself wished she could have traveled reveals a sorrow she can barely voice.

choices.label: C
choices.text: They create a mood of suspense: 'hermitage' hints the farmstead conceals something from outsiders, and the grandmother's vague remark that Dan 'might be dead' suggests a troubling mystery surrounds his disappearance.

choices.label: D
choices.text: They create a mood of admiration: 'hermitage' portrays the home as a dignified, self-sufficient retreat, and the grandmother's words celebrate Dan as a bold wanderer whose freedom she openly applauds without regret.

cards.standardTitle: Rhetoric and reader effect
cards.excerpt:
She crept out along the swaying oak limb at last, and took the daring step across into the old pine-tree. The way was harder than she thought; she must reach far and hold fast, the sharp dry twigs caught and held her and scratched her like angry talons, the pitch made her thin little fingers clumsy and stiff as she went round and round the tree’s great stem, higher and higher upward. The sparrows and robins in the woods below were beginning to wake and twitter to the dawn, yet it seemed much lighter there aloft in the pine-tree, and the child knew that she must hurry if her project were to be of any use.

The tree seemed to lengthen itself out as she went up, and to reach farther and farther upward. It was like a great main-mast to the voyaging earth; it must truly have been amazed that morning through all its ponderous frame as it felt this determined spark of human spirit creeping and climbing from higher branch to branch. Who knows how steadily the least twigs held themselves to advantage this light, weak creature on her way! The old pine must have loved his new dependent. More than all the hawks, and bats, and moths, and even the sweet-voiced thrushes, was the brave, beating heart of the solitary gray-eyed child. And the tree stood still and held away the winds that June morning while the dawn grew bright in the east.
cards.whyThisWorks: The excerpt contains a clear rhetorical question ('Who knows how steadily the least twigs held themselves to advantage this light, weak creature on her way!') that invites the reader to marvel at the natural world's apparent cooperation with Sylvia, making it an ideal anchor for analyzing how a rhetorical device shapes emotional effect.
cards.skillStrategy: When you spot a rhetorical question, ask yourself: what feeling or idea does the author want the reader to sit with instead of answering the question directly?
evidencePoints: Who knows how steadily the least twigs held themselves to advantage this light, weak creature on her way!
The old pine must have loved his new dependent.
cards.question: Read the following sentence from the second paragraph: 'Who knows how steadily the least twigs held themselves to advantage this light, weak creature on her way!' How does this rhetorical question affect the reader?

choices.label: B

choices.label: D
choices.text: It emphasizes Sylvia's physical weakness by reminding the reader how fragile she is compared to the massive pine tree.

evidencePoints: No amount of thought, that night, could decide how many wished-for treasures the ten dollars, so lightly spoken of, would buy.
Sylvia's heart gave a wild beat; she knew that strange white bird, and had once stolen softly near where it stood in some bright green swamp grass
cards.question: Sylvia's heart 'gave a wild beat' when she recognized the rare white heron, yet she spent the night calculating 'how many wished-for treasures the ten dollars…would buy.' How do these two details work together to develop a universal theme?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Venturing into unfamiliar places, like the swamp where the heron stands, leads only to danger and loss rather than reward.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The promise of material gain can tempt a person to weigh something rare and personally precious against a monetary reward.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Strangers who offer money disrupt peaceful communities and force young people to make choices they are not ready to face.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Dreams of distant places, like the sea Sylvia has never seen, are more powerful than any reward the real world can offer.

cards.standardTitle: Narrator perspective, irony, and satire
cards.excerpt: There was the huge tree asleep yet in the paling moonlight, and small and hopeful Sylvia began with utmost bravery to mount to the top of it, with tingling, eager blood coursing the channels of her whole frame, with her bare feet and fingers, that pinched and held like bird’s claws to the monstrous ladder reaching up, up, almost to the sky itself. First she must mount the white oak tree that grew alongside, where she was almost lost among the dark branches and the green leaves heavy and wet with dew; a bird fluttered off its nest, and a red squirrel ran to and fro and scolded pettishly at the harmless housebreaker. Sylvia felt her way easily. She had often climbed there, and knew that higher still one of the oak’s upper branches chafed against the pine trunk, just where its lower boughs were set close together. There, when she made the dangerous pass from one tree to the other, the great enterprise would really begin.
cards.whyThisWorks: The narrator frames Sylvia's climb with heroic, adventure-story language ('utmost bravery,' 'great enterprise'), while the reader understands she is a small barefoot child clinging to a tree in the dark—creating an ironic gap between the narrator's elevated tone and the physical vulnerability the details reveal.
cards.skillStrategy: Notice when the narrator's words sound grand or heroic, then look at the actual details to see what the situation really shows about the character.
evidencePoints: small and hopeful Sylvia began with utmost bravery to mount to the top of it
her bare feet and fingers, that pinched and held like bird's claws to the monstrous ladder reaching up, up, almost to the sky itself
cards.question: The narrator describes Sylvia's climb as an act of 'utmost bravery' and calls it 'the great enterprise.' What does the reader understand about Sylvia's situation that the narrator's elevated language tends to obscure?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Sylvia is reckless and foolish because she ignores the warnings of the red squirrel and the fluttering bird, which signal that the climb is forbidden.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Beneath the heroic framing, Sylvia is a barefoot child clinging to a massive tree in fading moonlight, and the physical details of her 'bare feet and fingers' gripping 'like bird's claws' reveal how small and exposed she actually is.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Sylvia feels no real danger because she has climbed the oak many times before, so the narrator's language of bravery accurately matches her calm, confident experience.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The narrator's grand language shows that Sylvia has already reached the top of the pine and is looking out over the landscape, making the climb a completed triumph rather than a struggle.

cards.standardTitle: Figurative language effect
cards.excerpt:
She crept out along the swaying oak limb at last, and took the daring step across into the old pine-tree. The way was harder than she thought; she must reach far and hold fast, the sharp dry twigs caught and held her and scratched her like angry talons, the pitch made her thin little fingers clumsy and stiff as she went round and round the tree’s great stem, higher and higher upward. The sparrows and robins in the woods below were beginning to wake and twitter to the dawn, yet it seemed much lighter there aloft in the pine-tree, and the child knew that she must hurry if her project were to be of any use.

The tree seemed to lengthen itself out as she went up, and to reach farther and farther upward. It was like a great main-mast to the voyaging earth; it must truly have been amazed that morning through all its ponderous frame as it felt this determined spark of human spirit creeping and climbing from higher branch to branch. Who knows how steadily the least twigs held themselves to advantage this light, weak creature on her way! The old pine must have loved his new dependent. More than all the hawks, and bats, and moths, and even the sweet-voiced thrushes, was the brave, beating heart of the solitary gray-eyed child. And the tree stood still and held away the winds that June morning while the dawn grew bright in the east.
cards.whyThisWorks: The second paragraph stacks multiple personifications onto the pine tree—it 'must truly have been amazed,' the twigs 'held themselves to advantage' the child, and 'the old pine must have loved his new dependent'—giving teachers a rich, specific passage moment to test whether students can connect human feeling attributed to a nonhuman thing to the scene's mood of protective wonder.
cards.skillStrategy: When a nonhuman thing is given a human feeling or action, ask yourself: what emotion does that choice create in the reader, and how does it change the feeling of the scene?
evidencePoints: it must truly have been amazed that morning through all its ponderous frame as it felt this determined spark of human spirit creeping and climbing from higher branch to branch
The old pine must have loved his new dependent. … the tree stood still and held away the winds that June morning while the dawn grew bright in the east.
cards.question: In the second paragraph, the narrator says the old pine tree 'must truly have been amazed' and 'must have loved his new dependent.' How does giving the pine tree these human feelings shape the mood of the scene?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The tree's amazement and love highlight how dangerous and indifferent the natural world is, making the child's climb feel reckless and doomed.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The tree's amazement and love transform the pine into a guardian figure, creating a mood in which the natural world actively shelters and honors the child's determined spirit.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The tree's amazement and love suggest the child is imagining things out of exhaustion, creating a mood of confusion and unreliability.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The tree's amazement and love emphasize how unusual trees are compared to other animals in the forest, creating a mood of scientific curiosity about nature.

cards.standardTitle: Rhetoric and reader effect
cards.excerpt: The next day the young sportsman hovered about the woods, and Sylvia kept him company, having lost her first fear of the friendly lad, who proved to be most kind and sympathetic. He told her many things about the birds and what they knew and where they lived and what they did with themselves. And he gave her a jack-knife, which she thought as great a treasure as if she were a desert-islander. All day long he did not once make her troubled or afraid except when he brought down some unsuspecting singing creature from its bough. Sylvia would have liked him vastly better without his gun; she could not understand why he killed the very birds he seemed to like so much. But as the day waned, Sylvia still watched the young man with loving admiration. She had never seen anybody so charming and delightful; the woman’s heart, asleep in the child, was vaguely thrilled by a dream of love. Some premonition of that great power stirred and swayed these young foresters who traversed the solemn woodlands with soft-footed silent care. They stopped to listen to a bird’s song; they pressed forward again eagerly, parting the branches,—speaking to each other rarely and in whispers; the young man going first and Sylvia following, fascinated, a few steps behind, with her gray eyes dark with excitement.
cards.whyThisWorks: The excerpt uses juxtaposition between Sylvia's 'loving admiration' for the sportsman and her inability to understand 'why he killed the very birds he seemed to like so much' to create dramatic irony and reader unease, directly illustrating how rhetorical contrast shapes emotional effect.
cards.skillStrategy: When a passage places two opposing ideas side by side—like admiration and unease—ask yourself what feeling that tension creates in the reader and why the author chose to put those ideas together.
evidencePoints: she could not understand why he killed the very birds he seemed to like so much
Sylvia still watched the young man with loving admiration
cards.question: In the excerpt, Jewett places the detail that Sylvia 'could not understand why he killed the very birds he seemed to like so much' directly alongside the statement that 'Sylvia still watched the young man with loving admiration.' What effect does this juxtaposition most likely create for the reader?

choices.label: A
choices.text: It reassures the reader that Sylvia's admiration will eventually replace her concern for the birds, since she follows the young man 'fascinated, a few steps behind.'

choices.label: B
choices.text: It creates unease in the reader by showing that Sylvia's growing admiration for the young man directly conflicts with her instinct to protect the birds she loves.

choices.label: C
choices.text: It signals to the reader that the young man is deliberately cruel, since he brings down 'unsuspecting singing creatures' only to impress Sylvia with his skill.

choices.label: D
choices.text: It suggests to the reader that Sylvia values the jack-knife he gave her more than the birds' lives, revealing her willingness to overlook his faults for a gift.

cards.standardTitle: Key literary elements add layers of meaning
cards.excerpt:
No, she must keep silence! What is it that suddenly forbids her and makes her dumb? Has she been nine years growing, and now, when the great world for the first time puts out a hand to her, must she thrust it aside for a bird’s sake? The murmur of the pine’s green branches is in her ears, she remembers how the white heron came flying through the golden air and how they watched the sea and the morning together, and Sylvia cannot speak; she cannot tell the heron’s secret and give its life away.

Dear loyalty, that suffered a sharp pang as the guest went away disappointed later in the day, that could have served and followed him and loved him as a dog loves! Many a night Sylvia heard the echo of his whistle haunting the pasture path as she came home with the loitering cow. She forgot even her sorrow at the sharp report of his gun and the piteous sight of thrushes and sparrows dropping silent to the ground, their songs hushed and their pretty feathers stained and wet with blood. Were the birds better friends than their hunter might have been,—who can tell? Whatever treasures were lost to her, woodlands and summer-time, remember! Bring your gifts and graces and tell your secrets to this lonely country child!
cards.whyThisWorks: The natural setting—pine branches, golden air, sea, morning, pasture path, and woodland—functions as a living force that pulls Sylvia away from the human world and toward loyalty to the heron, making the setting central to the story's moral conflict and elegiac tone.
cards.skillStrategy: When setting appears at a turning-point moment, ask what the place or natural world is 'doing' to the character emotionally and what that reveals about the story's meaning.
evidencePoints: The murmur of the pine's green branches is in her ears, she remembers how the white heron came flying through the golden air and how they watched the sea and the morning together, and Sylvia cannot speak
woodlands and summer-time, remember! Bring your gifts and graces and tell your secrets to this lonely country child!
cards.question: In the excerpt, how does the natural setting shape the meaning of Sylvia's silence?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The pine branches and golden air remind Sylvia of the hunter's skill, making her admire him too much to betray his location to anyone.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The remembered sights and sounds of the woodland—pine branches, golden air, sea, and morning—bind Sylvia to the heron so completely that the natural world itself becomes the force that keeps her silent and loyal.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The pasture path and loitering cow show that Sylvia's rural life is so isolated that she simply lacks the courage to speak to a stranger from the outside world.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The image of thrushes and sparrows dropping to the ground frightens Sylvia into silence because she fears the hunter will shoot her if she reveals what she knows.

cards.question: The narrator describes Sylvia as 'small and hopeful' yet climbing 'with utmost bravery' toward a 'dangerous pass' between the trees. Which theme does this moment most clearly develop?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Nature rewards those who study it carefully and learn its patterns over many years.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Pursuing something that truly matters demands that a person summon courage in the face of real risk.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Children are naturally more fearless than adults because they do not yet understand danger.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Familiar surroundings give people a false sense of safety when they attempt something new.

cards.standardTitle: Narrator perspective, irony, and satire
cards.excerpt: Half a mile from home, at the farther edge of the woods, where the land was highest, a great pine-tree stood, the last of its generation. Whether it was left for a boundary mark, or for what reason, no one could say; the woodchoppers who had felled its mates were dead and gone long ago, and a whole forest of sturdy trees, pines and oaks and maples, had grown again. But the stately head of this old pine towered above them all and made a landmark for sea and shore miles and miles away. Sylvia knew it well. She had always believed that whoever climbed to the top of it could see the ocean; and the little girl had often laid her hand on the great rough trunk and looked up wistfully at those dark boughs that the wind always stirred, no matter how hot and still the air might be below. Now she thought of the tree with a new excitement, for why, if one climbed it at break of day, could not one see all the world, and easily discover whence the white heron flew, and mark the place, and find the hidden nest?
cards.whyThisWorks: Sylvia frames climbing the pine as a straightforward solution to finding the heron's nest, but the reader can sense the cost she has not yet considered—betraying the bird's location to the hunter—creating a gap between her innocent excitement and the reader's unease.
cards.skillStrategy: Ask yourself: what does the speaker believe is true or simple, and what does the reader already suspect or fear that the speaker does not?
evidencePoints: Now she thought of the tree with a new excitement, for why, if one climbed it at break of day, could not one see all the world
easily discover whence the white heron flew, and mark the place, and find the hidden nest?
cards.question: Sylvia thinks of climbing the pine tree 'with a new excitement' and believes she could 'easily discover whence the white heron flew, and mark the place, and find the hidden nest.' What does the reader understand about this plan that Sylvia does not seem to recognize?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Sylvia is unaware that the pine tree is too tall and dangerous for a young girl to climb safely at dawn.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Sylvia sees her plan as a simple, hopeful solution, while the reader understands that finding the nest means leading the hunter to the heron she admires.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Sylvia believes the pine tree is a reliable landmark, but the reader knows the tree is too far from the shore to reveal the heron's location.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Sylvia is excited to see the ocean from the treetop, while the reader understands she has already forgotten her original reason for climbing.

cards.standardTitle: Figurative language effect
cards.excerpt: All night the door of the little house stood open, and the whippoorwills came and sang upon the very step. The young sportsman and his old hostess were sound asleep, but Sylvia’s great design kept her broad awake and watching. She forgot to think of sleep. The short summer night seemed as long as the winter darkness, and at last when the whippoorwills ceased, and she was afraid the morning would after all come too soon, she stole out of the house and followed the pasture path through the woods, hastening toward the open ground beyond, listening with a sense of comfort and companionship to the drowsy twitter of a half-awakened bird, whose perch she had jarred in passing. Alas, if the great wave of human interest which flooded for the first time this dull little life should sweep away the satisfactions of an existence heart to heart with nature and the dumb life of the forest!
cards.whyThisWorks: Jewett personifies the bird as 'half-awakened' and capable of providing 'comfort and companionship,' giving it human qualities that reveal how Sylvia experiences the natural world as a nurturing, intimate companion rather than an indifferent wilderness.
cards.skillStrategy: When you spot personification, ask what human quality is being given to the non-human thing and how that quality changes the feeling or meaning of the moment for the character.
evidencePoints: listening with a sense of comfort and companionship to the drowsy twitter of a half-awakened bird
the great wave of human interest which flooded for the first time this dull little life should sweep away the satisfactions of an existence heart to heart with nature
cards.question: In the sentence 'listening with a sense of comfort and companionship to the drowsy twitter of a half-awakened bird, whose perch she had jarred in passing,' Jewett personifies the bird as half-awakened and capable of offering companionship. How does this personification shape the mood of Sylvia's nighttime journey?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The bird's startled twitter signals that Sylvia is trespassing in a hostile environment, creating a mood of unease that foreshadows the danger her 'great design' may bring.

choices.label: B
choices.text: By portraying the bird as drowsy and half-awakened—able to offer Sylvia comfort and companionship—Jewett creates a mood of quiet intimacy, suggesting the natural world gently embraces her as she moves through the dark woods.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The bird's sleepy state mirrors Sylvia's own sleeplessness, creating a mood of exhaustion that makes her 'great design' feel like an overwhelming burden she may not be able to complete.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The bird's twitter breaks the silence of the woods and reminds Sylvia that the young sportsman could wake at any moment, creating a mood of suspense that overshadows her sense of purpose.

cards.standardTitle: Rhetoric and reader effect
cards.excerpt:
The child gives a long sigh a minute later when a company of shouting cat-birds comes also to the tree, and vexed by their fluttering and lawlessness the solemn heron goes away. She knows his secret now, the wild, light, slender bird that floats and wavers, and goes back like an arrow presently to his home in the green world beneath. Then Sylvia, well satisfied, makes her perilous way down again, not daring to look far below the branch she stands on, ready to cry sometimes because her fingers ache and her lamed feet slip. Wondering over and over again what the stranger would say to her, and what he would think when she told him how to find his way straight to the heron’s nest.

“Sylvy, Sylvy!” called the busy old grandmother again and again, but nobody answered, and the small husk bed was empty, and Sylvia had disappeared.

The guest waked from a dream, and remembering his day’s pleasure hurried to dress himself that it might sooner begin. He was sure from the way the shy little girl looked once or twice yesterday that she had at least seen the white heron, and now she must really be persuaded to tell. Here she comes now, paler than ever, and her worn old frock is torn and tattered, and smeared with pine pitch. The grandmother and the sportsman stand in the door together and question her, and the splendid moment has come to speak of the dead hemlock-tree by the green marsh.
cards.whyThisWorks: The excerpt pairs the simile 'like an arrow' describing the heron's swift departure with the contrasting image of Sylvia's painful, struggling descent—'her fingers ache and her lamed feet slip'—making it an ideal anchor for analyzing how a specific rhetorical device shapes the reader's emotional response.
cards.skillStrategy: When analyzing a rhetorical device, identify the exact comparison or technique, then ask what feeling or idea it creates and how that effect connects to the surrounding passage details.
evidencePoints: goes back like an arrow presently to his home in the green world beneath
not daring to look far below the branch she stands on, ready to cry sometimes because her fingers ache and her lamed feet slip
cards.question: In the sentence 'the wild, light, slender bird that floats and wavers, and goes back like an arrow presently to his home in the green world beneath,' the simile 'like an arrow' is placed just before the description of Sylvia's painful descent—'her fingers ache and her lamed feet slip.' What effect does this placement create for the reader?

choices.label: A
choices.text: It suggests the heron is fleeing in fear from Sylvia's presence, making the reader feel that her long climb has permanently driven the bird from the marsh.

choices.label: B
choices.text: It emphasizes the heron's swift, effortless freedom, creating a sharp contrast with Sylvia's slow, aching struggle down the tree that makes the reader feel the cost of her loyalty to the bird.

choices.label: C
choices.text: It highlights the heron's precision in navigating the forest, reassuring the reader that the stranger will be able to follow the bird's path straight to the nest in the green marsh.

choices.label: D
choices.text: It portrays the heron as dangerous and unpredictable, warning the reader that Sylvia's decision to climb toward it was reckless and has put her in physical danger.

cards.excerpt: There was the huge tree asleep yet in the paling moonlight, and small and hopeful Sylvia began with utmost bravery to mount to the top of it, with tingling, eager blood coursing the channels of her whole frame, with her bare feet and fingers, that pinched and held like bird’s claws to the monstrous ladder reaching up, up, almost to the sky itself. First she must mount the white oak tree that grew alongside, where she was almost lost among the dark branches and the green leaves heavy and wet with dew; a bird fluttered off its nest, and a red squirrel ran to and fro and scolded pettishly at the harmless housebreaker. Sylvia felt her way easily. She had often climbed there, and knew that higher still one of the oak’s upper branches chafed against the pine trunk, just where its lower boughs were set close together. There, when she made the dangerous pass from one tree to the other, the great enterprise would really begin.
cards.whyThisWorks: The excerpt pairs the simile 'like bird's claws' with the repetition 'up, up, almost to the sky itself,' giving students a concrete opportunity to analyze how two rhetorical devices work together to shape the reader's experience of Sylvia's climb.
cards.skillStrategy: When a passage combines two devices in one sentence, ask what each device does on its own, then ask how they reinforce each other to create a single emotional effect on the reader.
evidencePoints: bare feet and fingers, that pinched and held like bird's claws to the monstrous ladder reaching up, up, almost to the sky itself
small and hopeful Sylvia began with utmost bravery to mount to the top of it, with tingling, eager blood coursing the channels of her whole frame
cards.question: In the sentence 'bare feet and fingers, that pinched and held like bird's claws to the monstrous ladder reaching up, up, almost to the sky itself,' Jewett combines the simile 'like bird's claws' with the repetition of 'up, up.' How do these two devices work together to affect the reader?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The simile suggests Sylvia is frightened of losing her grip, while the repetition of 'up, up' signals that she is climbing too recklessly to reach the top safely.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The simile makes Sylvia's grip feel instinctive and animal-like, while the repetition of 'up, up' builds a sense of the climb's dizzying, seemingly endless height.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The simile connects Sylvia to the white heron she is searching for, while the repetition of 'up, up' reflects her growing impatience to spot the bird from above.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The simile shows that Sylvia is more at ease in trees than on the ground, while the repetition of 'up, up' suggests she has made this exact climb on the pine many times before.

cards.standardTitle: Key literary elements add layers of meaning
cards.excerpt: Half a mile from home, at the farther edge of the woods, where the land was highest, a great pine-tree stood, the last of its generation. Whether it was left for a boundary mark, or for what reason, no one could say; the woodchoppers who had felled its mates were dead and gone long ago, and a whole forest of sturdy trees, pines and oaks and maples, had grown again. But the stately head of this old pine towered above them all and made a landmark for sea and shore miles and miles away. Sylvia knew it well. She had always believed that whoever climbed to the top of it could see the ocean; and the little girl had often laid her hand on the great rough trunk and looked up wistfully at those dark boughs that the wind always stirred, no matter how hot and still the air might be below. Now she thought of the tree with a new excitement, for why, if one climbed it at break of day, could not one see all the world, and easily discover whence the white heron flew, and mark the place, and find the hidden nest?
cards.whyThisWorks: The pine tree's physical isolation, ancient survival, and wind-stirred boughs at the edge of the woods create a layered atmosphere of longing and possibility that directly shapes Sylvia's emotional shift from wistful gazing to excited purpose.
cards.skillStrategy: When a setting detail appears more than once or is described with strong sensory or emotional language, ask what feeling that detail creates and how it connects to what a character wants or fears.
evidencePoints: the little girl had often laid her hand on the great rough trunk and looked up wistfully at those dark boughs that the wind always stirred, no matter how hot and still the air might be below
Now she thought of the tree with a new excitement, for why, if one climbed it at break of day, could not one see all the world
cards.question: In the excerpt, Sylvia is described as having 'often laid her hand on the great rough trunk and looked up wistfully,' and then the narrator says 'Now she thought of the tree with a new excitement.' How does the setting detail of the pine tree's height and isolation contribute to this shift in atmosphere?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The tree's position at 'the farther edge of the woods' signals that Sylvia has wandered into forbidden territory, so her excitement is shadowed by a growing sense of danger and transgression.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Because the tree towers above all others and promises a view of 'all the world,' its height transforms Sylvia's long-held wistful longing into a sudden, urgent sense that the impossible may now be within reach.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The fact that the tree is 'the last of its generation' and its companions were felled by woodchoppers who are 'dead and gone' shifts the atmosphere toward grief, making Sylvia's excitement feel misplaced.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The detail that the tree serves as 'a landmark for sea and shore miles and miles away' creates an atmosphere of communal pride, suggesting Sylvia's excitement comes from wanting to protect a resource valued by her whole community.

cards.standardTitle: Theme development across a literary text
cards.excerpt:
The child gives a long sigh a minute later when a company of shouting cat-birds comes also to the tree, and vexed by their fluttering and lawlessness the solemn heron goes away. She knows his secret now, the wild, light, slender bird that floats and wavers, and goes back like an arrow presently to his home in the green world beneath. Then Sylvia, well satisfied, makes her perilous way down again, not daring to look far below the branch she stands on, ready to cry sometimes because her fingers ache and her lamed feet slip. Wondering over and over again what the stranger would say to her, and what he would think when she told him how to find his way straight to the heron’s nest.

“Sylvy, Sylvy!” called the busy old grandmother again and again, but nobody answered, and the small husk bed was empty, and Sylvia had disappeared.

The guest waked from a dream, and remembering his day’s pleasure hurried to dress himself that it might sooner begin. He was sure from the way the shy little girl looked once or twice yesterday that she had at least seen the white heron, and now she must really be persuaded to tell. Here she comes now, paler than ever, and her worn old frock is torn and tattered, and smeared with pine pitch. The grandmother and the sportsman stand in the door together and question her, and the splendid moment has come to speak of the dead hemlock-tree by the green marsh.
cards.whyThisWorks: The excerpt captures the exact moment Sylvia—physically torn, aching, and exhausted from her climb—stands silent before the sportsman who expects her to reveal the heron's nest, allowing students to trace how the author develops a universal theme about personal integrity versus external pressure.
cards.skillStrategy: To find the universal theme, identify the central conflict in the passage—what the character is being pressured to do versus what she chooses—and ask what that tension says about human experience in general.
evidencePoints: the splendid moment has come to speak of the dead hemlock-tree by the green marsh
her worn old frock is torn and tattered, and smeared with pine pitch
cards.question: The narrator describes Sylvia arriving 'paler than ever,' with her frock 'torn and tattered, and smeared with pine pitch,' while 'the splendid moment has come to speak of the dead hemlock-tree by the green marsh.' The sportsman is certain she will reveal the heron's location. Which universal theme does this moment most clearly develop?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The grandmother and the sportsman standing together in the doorway shows that community pressure always overpowers an individual's private loyalties.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Honoring one's deepest loyalties may demand physical sacrifice and the courage to disappoint those whose approval one desires.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The sportsman's certainty that Sylvia 'must really be persuaded to tell' reveals that adults routinely exploit children's eagerness to please.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Sylvia's torn frock and pine-smeared hands show that venturing into the natural world inevitably leads to physical and social ruin.

cards.standardTitle: Figurative language effect
cards.excerpt:
It was a surprise to find so clean and comfortable a little dwelling in this New England wilderness. The young man had known the horrors of its most primitive housekeeping, and the dreary squalor of that level of society which does not rebel at the companionship of hens. This was the best thrift of an old-fashioned farmstead, though on such a small scale that it seemed like a hermitage. He listened eagerly to the old woman’s quaint talk, he watched Sylvia’s pale face and shining gray eyes with ever growing enthusiasm, and insisted that this was the best supper he had eaten for a month; then, afterward, the new-made friends sat down in the doorway together while the moon came up.

Soon it would be berry-time, and Sylvia was a great help at picking. The cow was a good milker, though a plaguy thing to keep track of, the hostess gossiped frankly, adding presently that she had buried four children, so that Sylvia’s mother, and a son (who might be dead) in California were all the children she had left. “Dan, my boy, was a great hand to go gunning,” she explained sadly. “I never wanted for pa’tridges or gray squer’ls while he was to home. He’s been a great wand’rer, I expect, and he’s no hand to write letters. There, I don’t blame him, I’d ha’ seen the world myself if it had been so I could.
cards.whyThisWorks: The phrase 'the moon came up' personifies the moon as an active participant arriving at the scene, subtly shifting the mood from the warmth of supper conversation to a quiet, intimate, almost magical evening atmosphere.
cards.skillStrategy: When a nonhuman thing performs a human-like action, ask yourself what feeling that action adds to the scene — is it welcoming, threatening, peaceful, or something else?
evidencePoints: the new-made friends sat down in the doorway together while the moon came up
He listened eagerly to the old woman's quaint talk, he watched Sylvia's pale face and shining gray eyes with ever growing enthusiasm
cards.question: Read this sentence from the passage: 'the new-made friends sat down in the doorway together while the moon came up.' The phrase 'the moon came up' gives the moon a human-like action. How does this personification shape the mood of the scene?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The moon's arrival signals danger approaching the farmstead, creating a sense of unease beneath the friendly conversation.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The moon rising like a quiet companion joining the group deepens the scene's mood of warmth and gentle intimacy between the new-made friends.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The moon coming up reminds the reader that time is passing quickly, making the mood feel rushed and anxious for the characters.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The moon's appearance highlights the isolation of the wilderness, reinforcing the cold and dreary atmosphere described earlier in the passage.

Whether it was left for a boundary mark, or for what reason, no one could say; the woodchoppers who had felled its mates were dead and gone long ago, and a whole forest of sturdy trees, pines and oaks and maples, had grown again. cards.whyThisWorks: The closing rhetorical question—'for why, if one climbed it at break of day, could not one see all the world, and easily discover whence the white heron flew, and mark the place, and find the hidden nest?'—draws readers into Sylvia's mounting excitement and makes her plan feel urgent and inevitable, offering a clear, textually grounded example of how a rhetorical question shapes reader effect.
cards.skillStrategy: When you spot a rhetorical question, ask yourself what emotion or idea the author wants you to feel or accept without argument—that effect is the answer.
evidencePoints: for why, if one climbed it at break of day, could not one see all the world, and easily discover whence the white heron flew, and mark the place, and find the hidden nest?
Now she thought of the tree with a new excitement
cards.question: Read the closing sentence of the paragraph: 'Now she thought of the tree with a new excitement, for why, if one climbed it at break of day, could not one see all the world, and easily discover whence the white heron flew, and mark the place, and find the hidden nest?' How does the rhetorical question at the end of this sentence affect the reader?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The question creates doubt in the reader's mind about whether Sylvia is physically capable of climbing the tall pine tree.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The question pulls the reader into Sylvia's certainty, making her plan to climb the tree feel logical and her goal of finding the heron's nest feel within reach.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The question signals to the reader that Sylvia is asking the woodchoppers for permission before she attempts the dangerous climb.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The question slows the reader down and creates a sense of dread about what Sylvia might discover at the top of the pine tree.

cards.standardTitle: Key literary elements add layers of meaning
cards.excerpt: The next day the young sportsman hovered about the woods, and Sylvia kept him company, having lost her first fear of the friendly lad, who proved to be most kind and sympathetic. He told her many things about the birds and what they knew and where they lived and what they did with themselves. And he gave her a jack-knife, which she thought as great a treasure as if she were a desert-islander. All day long he did not once make her troubled or afraid except when he brought down some unsuspecting singing creature from its bough. Sylvia would have liked him vastly better without his gun; she could not understand why he killed the very birds he seemed to like so much. But as the day waned, Sylvia still watched the young man with loving admiration. She had never seen anybody so charming and delightful; the woman’s heart, asleep in the child, was vaguely thrilled by a dream of love. Some premonition of that great power stirred and swayed these young foresters who traversed the solemn woodlands with soft-footed silent care. They stopped to listen to a bird’s song; they pressed forward again eagerly, parting the branches,—speaking to each other rarely and in whispers; the young man going first and Sylvia following, fascinated, a few steps behind, with her gray eyes dark with excitement.
cards.whyThisWorks: Jewett uses the 'solemn woodlands' setting—with its hushed movement, whispered speech, and soft-footed care—to externalize Sylvia's internal emotional awakening, making the natural environment a mirror for the 'premonition of that great power' stirring within her.
cards.skillStrategy: When a setting detail appears right next to an emotional moment, ask yourself: is the author using the place to show what the character feels inside?
evidencePoints: Some premonition of that great power stirred and swayed these young foresters who traversed the solemn woodlands with soft-footed silent care.
speaking to each other rarely and in whispers; the young man going first and Sylvia following, fascinated, a few steps behind, with her gray eyes dark with excitement.
cards.question: In the final sentences, Jewett places Sylvia and the young man in 'solemn woodlands' where they move 'with soft-footed silent care' and speak 'rarely and in whispers,' while Sylvia follows 'fascinated' with her 'gray eyes dark with excitement.' What meaning does this woodland setting add to the scene?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The hushed movement and whispered speech show that both characters are focused entirely on locating the white heron, so the setting reinforces the young man's purpose as a hunter rather than Sylvia's inner feelings.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The reverent stillness of the solemn woodlands gives the scene a ceremonial quality that mirrors the emotional awakening—the 'premonition of that great power'—stirring inside Sylvia as she follows the young man, fascinated.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The soft-footed silence of the woods signals that Sylvia is retreating into her familiar comfort with nature and pulling inward, even though she appears to follow the young man a few steps behind.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The solemn, isolated woodland setting emphasizes how far the two characters are from society, suggesting that Sylvia's admiration—described as 'loving'—is only possible because no one else is present to observe them.

cards.standardTitle: Rhetoric and reader effect
cards.excerpt: The birds sang louder and louder. At last the sun came up bewilderingly bright. Sylvia could see the white sails of ships out at sea, and the clouds that were purple and rose-colored and yellow at first began to fade away. Where was the white heron’s nest in the sea of green branches, and was this wonderful sight and pageant of the world the only reward for having climbed to such a giddy height? Now look down again, Sylvia, where the green marsh is set among the shining birches and dark hemlocks; there where you saw the white heron once you will see him again; look, look! a white spot of him like a single floating feather comes up from the dead hemlock and grows larger, and rises, and comes close at last, and goes by the landmark pine with steady sweep of wing and outstretched slender neck and crested head. And wait! wait! do not move a foot or a finger, little girl, do not send an arrow of light and consciousness from your two eager eyes, for the heron has perched on a pine bough not far beyond yours, and cries back to his mate on the nest, and plumes his feathers for the new day!
cards.whyThisWorks: The narrator's direct-address commands 'look, look!' and 'wait! wait!' are clear examples of rhetorical repetition (anaphora/epizeuxis) whose urgency and intimacy pull the reader into Sylvia's perspective at the climactic moment the heron appears, making this an ideal passage for teaching how a specific device shapes reader experience.
cards.skillStrategy: When you spot a repeated word or phrase, ask yourself: what emotion or tension does that repetition create in me as a reader, and how does it connect to what is happening in the scene at that exact moment?
evidencePoints: look, look! a white spot of him like a single floating feather comes up from the dead hemlock
wait! wait! do not move a foot or a finger, little girl, do not send an arrow of light and consciousness from your two eager eyes
cards.question: The narrator uses the repeated commands 'look, look!' and 'wait! wait!' at the moment the heron rises from the dead hemlock and perches on a nearby bough. How does this repetition most likely affect the reader?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The repeated commands signal that Sylvia has nearly fallen asleep after her exhausting climb and must force herself to stay alert as the heron approaches.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The repeated commands create breathless urgency, pulling the reader into the fragile, tense instant when the heron glides close and Sylvia must remain perfectly still.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The repeated commands slow the scene's pace so the reader can linger on the earlier image of purple and rose-colored clouds fading at sunrise.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The repeated commands suggest the narrator doubts Sylvia's ability to spot the white heron among the shining birches and dark hemlocks below.

cards.question: In the final paragraph, the narrator describes 'the splendid moment' when Sylvia faces the grandmother and the sportsman. What does the word 'splendid' connote in this context that its dictionary definition alone does not capture?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The moment is visually beautiful because Sylvia arrives covered in pine pitch and wearing a tattered frock, creating a striking image.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The moment carries a sense of quiet heroism and inner triumph, as Sylvia stands at the edge of a decision that will cost her something she desires.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The moment is grand because the grandmother and the sportsman are both present, making the gathering feel like an important social occasion.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The moment is impressive because the sportsman is finally about to learn the location of the heron's nest after a long search.

cards.standardTitle: Key literary elements add layers of meaning
cards.excerpt:
Sylvia’s heart gave a wild beat; she knew that strange white bird, and had once stolen softly near where it stood in some bright green swamp grass, away over at the other side of the woods. There was an open place where the sunshine always seemed strangely yellow and hot, where tall, nodding rushes grew, and her grandmother had warned her that she might sink in the soft black mud underneath and never be heard of more. Not far beyond were the salt marshes and beyond those was the sea, the sea which Sylvia wondered and dreamed about, but never had looked upon, though its great voice could often be heard above the noise of the woods on stormy nights.

“I can’t think of anything I should like so much as to find that heron’s nest,” the handsome stranger was saying. “I would give ten dollars to anybody who could show it to me,” he added desperately, “and I mean to spend my whole vacation hunting for it if need be. Perhaps it was only migrating, or had been chased out of its own region by some bird of prey.”

Mrs. Tilley gave amazed attention to all this, but Sylvia still watched the toad, not divining, as she might have done at some calmer time, that the creature wished to get to its hole under the doorstep, and was much hindered by the unusual spectators at that hour of the evening. No amount of thought, that night, could decide how many wished-for treasures the ten dollars, so lightly spoken of, would buy.
cards.whyThisWorks: The swamp's 'soft black mud' danger and the sea Sylvia 'wondered and dreamed about, but never had looked upon' work together to show how setting layers meaning onto Sylvia's inner conflict between safety and longing.
cards.skillStrategy: When analyzing setting, ask what the described place reveals about a character's emotions or situation—look for contrasts like danger vs. desire.
evidencePoints: her grandmother had warned her that she might sink in the soft black mud underneath and never be heard of more
the sea which Sylvia wondered and dreamed about, but never had looked upon
cards.question: In the first paragraph, the swamp's 'soft black mud' and the sea Sylvia 'wondered and dreamed about, but never had looked upon' are placed side by side. What meaning does this combination of setting details add to the passage?

choices.label: A
choices.text: They show that Sylvia is already familiar with both the swamp and the sea, making the stranger's offer feel unimportant to her.

choices.label: B
choices.text: They create an atmosphere of danger and unfulfilled longing that reflects the difficult choice Sylvia is beginning to face.

choices.label: C
choices.text: They establish that the swamp is the only barrier keeping Sylvia from reaching the heron's nest on her own.

choices.label: D
choices.text: They suggest that the grandmother's warning has made Sylvia too fearful to ever leave the woods near her home.

cards.skillStrategy: When a question asks how setting adds meaning, find the specific words describing place, time, or atmosphere and ask what feeling or idea those details create for the character or reader.

cards.question: The narrator describes the tree as 'asleep yet in the paling moonlight' and the leaves as 'heavy and wet with dew.' How do these details about the pre-dawn setting shape the meaning of Sylvia's climb?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The moonlight and dew show that Sylvia has chosen a careless moment to climb, since the wet branches and dim light make her footing dangerously unreliable.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The still, barely-lit world surrounding Sylvia emphasizes that she alone is awake and moving against a sleeping landscape, making her small act of bravery feel bold and solitary.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The fading moonlight signals that daybreak will arrive quickly, creating urgency that forces Sylvia to rush and skip the careful preparation her climb requires.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The soft moonlight and dew-covered leaves produce a calm, reassuring mood that erases any real sense of risk from Sylvia's ascent through the oak.

cards.question: In the second paragraph, the narrator says the stranger added his offer of ten dollars "desperately." What does the word "desperately" connote about the stranger in this moment, beyond its dictionary meaning of being in extreme need?

choices.text: The stranger is in genuine financial distress and cannot afford to offer more than ten dollars for the heron's location.

Where was the white heron’s nest in the sea of green branches, and was this wonderful sight and pageant of the world the only reward for having climbed to such a giddy height? Now look down again, Sylvia, where the green marsh is set among the shining birches and dark hemlocks; there where you saw the white heron once you will see him again; look, look! a white spot of him like a single floating feather comes up from the dead hemlock and grows larger, and rises, and comes close at last, and goes by the landmark pine with steady sweep of wing and outstretched slender neck and crested head. And wait! wait! do not move a foot or a finger, little girl, do not send an arrow of light and consciousness from your two eager eyes, for the heron has perched on a pine bough not far beyond yours, and cries back to his mate on the nest, and plumes his feathers for the new day!
cards.whyThisWorks: The passage's dawn imagery—'bewilderingly bright' sunrise, fading colored clouds, the heron rising from 'the dead hemlock'—creates a charged atmosphere that elevates Sylvia's perch into a moment of rare natural revelation, directly illustrating how setting adds meaning and mood.
cards.skillStrategy: When analyzing setting, find the specific words describing place, time, or atmosphere and ask what feeling or idea those details create for the reader.
evidencePoints: At last the sun came up bewilderingly bright.
a white spot of him like a single floating feather comes up from the dead hemlock and grows larger, and rises, and comes close at last
cards.question: The narrator describes the sun coming up 'bewilderingly bright' and the heron rising 'like a single floating feather' from 'the dead hemlock.' What mood do these details create at this moment in the passage?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A mood of exhaustion and disappointment, because the blinding sunrise and the heron's distant appearance suggest that Sylvia's long climb has produced little more than a fleeting glimpse of what she sought.

choices.label: B
choices.text: A mood of overwhelming wonder, because the dazzling sunrise and the heron's gradual, almost miraculous rise from the dead hemlock make Sylvia's high perch feel like the site of a rare and fragile discovery.

choices.label: C
choices.text: A mood of dread and danger, because the brightness of the sun and the heron emerging from a dead tree signal that the natural world is threatening to Sylvia rather than rewarding.

choices.label: D
choices.text: A mood of calm resolution, because the steady light of dawn and the heron's predictable return to its nest suggest that Sylvia has already made her decision and feels no further conflict.

cards.standardTitle: Paraphrase grade-level text
cards.excerpt:
She crept out along the swaying oak limb at last, and took the daring step across into the old pine-tree. The way was harder than she thought; she must reach far and hold fast, the sharp dry twigs caught and held her and scratched her like angry talons, the pitch made her thin little fingers clumsy and stiff as she went round and round the tree’s great stem, higher and higher upward. The sparrows and robins in the woods below were beginning to wake and twitter to the dawn, yet it seemed much lighter there aloft in the pine-tree, and the child knew that she must hurry if her project were to be of any use.

The tree seemed to lengthen itself out as she went up, and to reach farther and farther upward. It was like a great main-mast to the voyaging earth; it must truly have been amazed that morning through all its ponderous frame as it felt this determined spark of human spirit creeping and climbing from higher branch to branch. Who knows how steadily the least twigs held themselves to advantage this light, weak creature on her way! The old pine must have loved his new dependent. More than all the hawks, and bats, and moths, and even the sweet-voiced thrushes, was the brave, beating heart of the solitary gray-eyed child. And the tree stood still and held away the winds that June morning while the dawn grew bright in the east.
cards.whyThisWorks: The sentence 'It must truly have been amazed that morning through all its ponderous frame as it felt this determined spark of human spirit creeping and climbing from higher branch to branch' contains inverted, figurative syntax that requires students to untangle personification and abstract phrasing to restate the literal and implied meaning accurately.
cards.skillStrategy: Break the long sentence into smaller parts—identify who or what is doing what, then restate each part in plain language before putting the meaning back together.
evidencePoints: it must truly have been amazed that morning through all its ponderous frame as it felt this determined spark of human spirit creeping and climbing from higher branch to branch
The old pine must have loved his new dependent.
cards.question: Read this sentence from the passage: 'It must truly have been amazed that morning through all its ponderous frame as it felt this determined spark of human spirit creeping and climbing from higher branch to branch.' Which restatement most accurately captures the meaning of this sentence?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The pine tree was so enormous and heavy that the girl's small body could not move it, no matter how high she climbed.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The massive pine tree seemed to sense, throughout its entire body, the remarkable determination of the small girl making her way up through its branches.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The tree was startled by the morning light and shook its branches, making the girl's climb more dangerous with every step.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The girl was so amazed by the size of the pine tree that she paused on each branch to take in how far she had climbed.

cards.standardTitle: Paraphrase grade-level text
cards.excerpt:
No, she must keep silence! What is it that suddenly forbids her and makes her dumb? Has she been nine years growing, and now, when the great world for the first time puts out a hand to her, must she thrust it aside for a bird’s sake? The murmur of the pine’s green branches is in her ears, she remembers how the white heron came flying through the golden air and how they watched the sea and the morning together, and Sylvia cannot speak; she cannot tell the heron’s secret and give its life away.

Dear loyalty, that suffered a sharp pang as the guest went away disappointed later in the day, that could have served and followed him and loved him as a dog loves! Many a night Sylvia heard the echo of his whistle haunting the pasture path as she came home with the loitering cow. She forgot even her sorrow at the sharp report of his gun and the piteous sight of thrushes and sparrows dropping silent to the ground, their songs hushed and their pretty feathers stained and wet with blood. Were the birds better friends than their hunter might have been,—who can tell? Whatever treasures were lost to her, woodlands and summer-time, remember! Bring your gifts and graces and tell your secrets to this lonely country child!
cards.whyThisWorks: The excerpt contains a clear, paraphrasable claim in 'Sylvia cannot speak; she cannot tell the heron's secret and give its life away,' which tests whether students can restate a character's decisive moral choice without distorting, overstating, or omitting its meaning.
cards.skillStrategy: Read the sentence carefully, then ask yourself: what is the character choosing to do, and why — make sure your restatement keeps both parts.
evidencePoints: Sylvia cannot speak; she cannot tell the heron's secret and give its life away.
she remembers how the white heron came flying through the golden air and how they watched the sea and the morning together
cards.question: Read this sentence from the passage: 'Sylvia cannot speak; she cannot tell the heron's secret and give its life away.' Which of the following most accurately restates what this sentence means?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Sylvia is physically unable to speak because she is too frightened of the hunter to say anything at all.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Sylvia chooses to stay silent rather than reveal where the heron lives, because doing so would cost the bird its life.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Sylvia decides to protect the heron by warning it to fly away before the hunter can find it.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Sylvia refuses to speak because she has promised the hunter she will keep the heron's location a secret.

cards.standardTitle: Key literary elements add layers of meaning
cards.excerpt:
The only sure way to save himself would be to put the child to death before he was old enough to do any harm. But when he had taken the little Perseus and his mother out of the prison and had seen how helpless the child was, he could not bear the thought of having him killed outright. For the king, although a great coward, was really a kind-hearted man and did not like to see anything suffer pain. Yet something must be done.

So he bade his servants make a wooden chest that was roomy and watertight and strong; and when it was done, he put Danaë and the child into it and had it taken far out to sea and left there to be tossed about by the waves. He thought that in this way he would rid himself of both daughter and grandson without seeing them die; for surely the chest would sink after a while, or else the winds would cause it to drift to some strange shore so far away that they could never come back to Argos again.
cards.whyThisWorks: The king's decision to seal Danaë and Perseus in a chest rather than kill them outright reveals a contradictory character—simultaneously cowardly, kind-hearted, and self-deceiving—which adds thematic meaning about moral compromise and rationalization.
cards.skillStrategy: When a character makes a choice, ask yourself what that choice reveals about who they really are and what the author wants you to understand about human nature.
evidencePoints: the king, although a great coward, was really a kind-hearted man and did not like to see anything suffer pain
He thought that in this way he would rid himself of both daughter and grandson without seeing them die
cards.question: The king chooses to seal Danaë and Perseus in a wooden chest rather than order their deaths directly. What does this action reveal about his character?

choices.label: A
choices.text: He is a calculating ruler who believes the chest will guarantee their deaths more efficiently than an outright execution.

choices.label: B
choices.text: He deceives himself into believing a cruel act is merciful because he avoids witnessing the suffering he causes.

choices.label: C
choices.text: He genuinely hopes the chest will carry them to safety on a distant shore, showing that his kindness outweighs his fear.

choices.label: D
choices.text: He acts out of loyalty to Argos by choosing a method that keeps him free from public blame for their deaths.

cards.standardTitle: Key literary elements add layers of meaning
cards.excerpt:
One morning Europa went out into a field near the seashore to pick flowers. Her father's cattle were in the field, grazing among the sweet clover. They were all very tame, and Europa knew every one of them by name. The herdsman was lying in the shade under a tree, trying to make music on a little flute of straw. Europa had played in the field a thousand times before, and no one had ever thought of any harm befalling her.

That morning she noticed that there was a strange bull with the herd. He was very large and as white as snow; and he had soft brown eyes which somehow made him look very gentle and kind. At first he did not even look at Europa, but went here and there, eating the tender grass which grew among the clover. But when she had gathered her apron full of daisies and buttercups, he came slowly towards her. She was not at all afraid of him; and so she stopped to look at him, he was so handsome. He came close to her, and rubbed her arm with his nose to say "Good-morning!"
cards.whyThisWorks: Europa's calm, curious response to the strange bull—stopping to admire him and feeling 'not at all afraid'—reveals her trusting, innocent nature, which deepens the dramatic irony and foreshadows danger the reader senses but she does not.
cards.skillStrategy: When a character acts or reacts in a surprising way, ask what that behavior reveals about who they are and what meaning it adds to the story.
evidencePoints: She was not at all afraid of him; and so she stopped to look at him, he was so handsome.
He came close to her, and rubbed her arm with his nose to say 'Good-morning!'
cards.question: Read the sentence: 'She was not at all afraid of him; and so she stopped to look at him, he was so handsome.' What does Europa's reaction to the strange bull reveal about her character, and how does it add meaning to the passage?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Her fearlessness shows she is reckless and ignores the herdsman's warnings, suggesting she often disobeys the rules set for her safety.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Her calm admiration of the bull reveals an innocent trust in her familiar, safe world, which makes the reader sense a danger that Europa herself cannot see.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Her focus on the bull's appearance shows she is vain and easily distracted, caring more about beauty than about the responsibilities she has in the field.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Her lack of fear proves she is experienced with strange animals, suggesting she has handled unfamiliar cattle in the field many times before.

cards.standardTitle: Theme development across a literary text
cards.excerpt:
By and by she came to a narrow neck of the sea, and, since the land on the other side looked as though she might find rest there, she leaped into the waves and swam across; and that place has been called Bosphorus--a word which means the Sea of the Cow--from that time till now, and you will find it so marked on the maps which you use at school. Then she went on through a strange land on the other side, but, let her do what she would, she could not get rid of the gadfly.

After a time she came to a place where there were high mountains with snow-capped peaks which seemed to touch the sky. There she stopped to rest a while; and she looked up at the calm, cold cliffs above her and wished that she might die where all was so grand and still. But as she looked she saw a giant form stretched upon the rocks midway between earth and sky, and she knew at once that it was Prometheus, the young Titan, whom Jupiter had chained there because he had given fire to men.
cards.whyThisWorks: The excerpt shows Io unable to escape suffering despite crossing seas and reaching grand mountains, while Prometheus is chained for helping humanity—two details that together develop a theme about inescapable suffering endured by those connected to divine conflict, allowing students to distinguish theme-developing evidence from true-but-topical details.
cards.skillStrategy: Ask yourself: does this detail show the theme growing, or does it just describe what happens in the story's setting or plot?
evidencePoints: let her do what she would, she could not get rid of the gadfly
she looked up at the calm, cold cliffs above her and wished that she might die where all was so grand and still
cards.question: Which detail from the excerpt best develops the theme that suffering cannot be escaped through flight or endurance alone?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The narrow neck of sea Io crosses has been called Bosphorus, meaning 'the Sea of the Cow,' a name still found on school maps.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Despite crossing the sea and reaching the grand, still mountains, Io cannot rid herself of the gadfly and wishes she could die, showing that her torment follows her everywhere.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Prometheus is a young Titan whom Jupiter chained to the rocks because he gave fire to men, which explains why he is found in the mountains.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The snow-capped mountain peaks seem to touch the sky, and Io stops there to rest after her long journey across the strange land.

cards.standardTitle: Key literary elements add layers of meaning
cards.excerpt:
So Danaë was kept shut up in the prison of brass. She had no one to talk to but her old nurse; and she never saw the land or the sea, but only the blue sky above the open window and now and then a white cloud sailing across. Day after day she sat under the window and wondered why her father kept her in that lonely place, and whether he would ever come and take her out. I do not know how many years passed by, but Danaë grew fairer every day, and by and by she was no longer a child, but a tall and beautiful woman; and Jupiter amid the clouds looked down and saw her and loved her.

One day it seemed to her that the sky opened and a shower of gold fell through the window into the room; and when the blinding shower had ceased, a noble young man stood smiling before her. She did not know--nor do I--that it was mighty Jupiter who had thus come down in the rain; but she thought that he was a brave prince who had come from over the sea to take her out of her prison-house.
cards.whyThisWorks: Danaë's misidentification of Jupiter as 'a brave prince who had come from over the sea to take her out of her prison-house' reveals how her years of lonely imprisonment have shaped her deepest longing, making her characterization inseparable from her isolation.
cards.skillStrategy: When a character misreads a situation, ask what that mistake tells you about what she most wants or fears based on her experiences in the story.
evidencePoints: she thought that he was a brave prince who had come from over the sea to take her out of her prison-house
Day after day she sat under the window and wondered why her father kept her in that lonely place, and whether he would ever come and take her out
cards.question: The narrator states that Danaë 'thought that he was a brave prince who had come from over the sea to take her out of her prison-house.' What does this mistaken belief reveal about her character?

choices.label: A
choices.text: It shows she is foolish, unable to recognize a divine visitor even after a shower of gold fills the room.

choices.label: B
choices.text: It shows her years of wondering 'whether he would ever come and take her out' have made rescue her most desperate hope.

choices.label: C
choices.text: It shows she is proud, assuming only a prince from across the sea would be worthy of visiting her.

choices.label: D
choices.text: It shows she already suspects the visitor is powerful but chooses to pretend he is an ordinary prince.

cards.standardTitle: Theme development across a literary text
cards.excerpt:
From that day the town grew and spread, and soon there was not room on the hilltop for all the people. Then houses were built in the plain around the foot of the hill, and a great road was built to the sea, three miles away; and in all the world there was no city more fair than Athens.

In the old market place on the top of the hill the people built a temple to Athena, the ruins of which may still be seen. The olive tree grew and nourished; and, when you visit Athens, people will show you the very spot where it stood. Many other trees sprang from it, and in time became a blessing both to Greece and to all the other countries round the great sea. As for the horse, he wandered away across the plains towards the north and found a home at last in distant Thessaly beyond the River Peneus. And I have heard it said that all the horses in the world have descended from that one which Neptune brought out of the rock; but of the truth of this story there may be some doubts.
cards.whyThisWorks: The excerpt contrasts Athena's olive tree—which 'grew and nourished' and 'in time became a blessing both to Greece and to all the other countries'—with Neptune's horse, which simply 'wandered away,' allowing students to distinguish details that develop the theme of enduring gifts benefiting civilization from true-but-topical details about the horse's fate.
cards.skillStrategy: Ask yourself: does this detail show the theme growing across the passage, or does it just add a true fact about what happened?
evidencePoints: Many other trees sprang from it, and in time became a blessing both to Greece and to all the other countries round the great sea.
As for the horse, he wandered away across the plains towards the north and found a home at last in distant Thessaly beyond the River Peneus.
cards.question: Which detail from the excerpt best develops the theme that a gift of lasting value shapes the world beyond its origins?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The narrator notes that 'the ruins of which may still be seen,' showing that the temple Athena's people built has survived to the present day.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The olive tree produced many other trees that 'in time became a blessing both to Greece and to all the other countries round the great sea,' showing Athena's gift spreading far beyond Athens.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Neptune's horse 'wandered away across the plains towards the north and found a home at last in distant Thessaly,' showing that the horse also traveled to other lands.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Athens grew until 'a great road was built to the sea, three miles away,' showing that the city expanded its physical boundaries over time.

cards.standardTitle: Key literary elements add layers of meaning
cards.excerpt:
There was a king of Argos who had but one child, and that child was a girl. If he had had a son, he would have trained him up to be a brave man and great king; but he did not know what to do with this fair-haired daughter. When he saw her growing up to be tall and slender and wise, he wondered if, after all, he would have to die some time and leave his lands and his gold and his kingdom to her. So he sent to Delphi and asked the Pythia about it. The Pythia told him that he would not only have to die some time, but that the son of his daughter would cause his death.

This frightened the king very much, and he tried to think of some plan by which he could keep the Pythia's words from coming true. At last he made up his mind that he would build a prison for his daughter and keep her in it all her life. So he called his workmen and had them dig a deep round hole in the ground, and in this hole they built a house of brass which had but one room and no door at all, but only a small window at the top. When it was finished, the king put the maiden, whose name was Danaë, into it; and with her he put her nurse and her toys and her pretty dresses and everything that he thought she would need to make her happy.
cards.whyThisWorks: The king's decision to imprison Danaë rather than confront fate directly reveals a character defined by fear and control, and the detail of including 'toys and pretty dresses' alongside a sealed brass prison deepens the irony of his self-deception.
cards.skillStrategy: When analyzing characterization, look at what a character does AND the contradictions in how they do it — those contradictions often reveal the character's deeper meaning.
evidencePoints: he tried to think of some plan by which he could keep the Pythia's words from coming true
with her he put her nurse and her toys and her pretty dresses and everything that he thought she would need to make her happy
cards.question: The king imprisons Danaë in a sealed brass house yet fills it with 'her nurse and her toys and her pretty dresses and everything that he thought she would need to make her happy.' What does this contradiction reveal about the king's character?

choices.label: A
choices.text: He is a devoted father who genuinely believes his daughter's comfort matters more than her freedom.

choices.label: B
choices.text: He is a fearful man who deceives himself into believing that controlling Danaë's circumstances can also control fate.

choices.label: C
choices.text: He is a practical ruler who understands that a comfortable prisoner is less likely to attempt escape.

choices.label: D
choices.text: He is indifferent to Danaë's suffering and adds the comforts only to satisfy the expectations of his kingdom.

cards.standardTitle: Key literary elements add layers of meaning
cards.excerpt:
At last the morning of the third day came, and the chest was tossed upon the sandy shore of a strange island where there were green fields and, beyond them, a little town. A man who happened to be walking near the shore saw it and dragged it far up on the beach. Then he looked inside, and there he saw the beautiful lady and the little boy. He helped them out and led them just as they were to his own house, where he cared for them very kindly. And when Danaë had told him her story, he bade her feel no more fear; for they might have a home with him as long as they should choose to stay, and he would be a true friend to them both.

So Danaë and her son stayed in the house of the kind man who had saved them from the sea. Years passed by, and Perseus grew up to be a tall young man, handsome, and brave, and strong. The king of the island, when he saw Danaë, was so pleased with her beauty that he wanted her to become his wife. But he was a dark, cruel man, and she did not like him at all; so she told him that she would not marry him. The king thought that Perseus was to blame for this, and that if he could find some excuse to send the young man on a far journey, he might force Danaë to have him whether she wished or not.
cards.whyThisWorks: The king's calculated scheme to remove Perseus so he can force Danaë into marriage reveals his cruelty and manipulative nature, while Danaë's flat refusal reveals her courage, giving students two contrasting characterizations to analyze for deeper meaning.
cards.skillStrategy: When a character makes a plan or a choice, ask yourself what that decision tells you about who they really are beneath the surface.
evidencePoints: he was a dark, cruel man, and she did not like him at all; so she told him that she would not marry him
The king thought that Perseus was to blame for this, and that if he could find some excuse to send the young man on a far journey, he might force Danaë to have him whether she wished or not
cards.question: What does the king's plan to send Perseus away on a 'far journey' reveal about his character?

choices.label: A
choices.text: He respects Perseus's strength and fears a direct confrontation with him.

choices.label: B
