choices.text: He is willing to use deception and manipulation to overpower someone who cannot defend herself.

choices.label: C
choices.text: He blames Perseus fairly, since Perseus is the one who convinced Danaë to refuse the marriage.

choices.label: D
choices.text: He wants to give Perseus a chance to prove himself worthy of a place on the island.

cards.standardTitle: Key literary elements add layers of meaning
cards.excerpt:
There was but little that the stranger knew how to do, and so he was sent to the hills to take care of the king's sheep and goats. For a whole year he tended the flocks, finding the greenest pastures and the freshest water for them, and keeping the wolves away. Admetus was very kind to him, as he was to all his servants, and the food and clothing which he gave him were of the best in the land. But the stranger did not tell his name nor say anything about his kindred or his home.

When a year and a day had passed, it so happened that Admetus was walking out among the hills to see his sheep. All at once the sound of music fell upon his ear. It was no such music as shepherds play, but sweeter and richer than any he had ever heard before. He looked to see where the sound came from. Ah! who was that sitting on the hilltop, with the sheep around him listening to his music? Surely it was not his shepherd?
cards.whyThisWorks: The stranger's refusal to reveal his name or origins, combined with the supernatural quality of his music, creates a layered characterization that signals hidden identity and divine nature, giving students a clear moment to analyze how action and withholding speech add meaning.
cards.skillStrategy: When a character deliberately stays silent or hides something, ask yourself what that choice reveals about who they are and why the author wants you to notice it.
evidencePoints: the stranger did not tell his name nor say anything about his kindred or his home
It was no such music as shepherds play, but sweeter and richer than any he had ever heard before
cards.question: Read this sentence from the passage: 'the stranger did not tell his name nor say anything about his kindred or his home.' What does this detail, combined with the description of the stranger's music, reveal about the stranger's character?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The stranger is ashamed of his origins and hides them because he fears Admetus will dismiss him from service.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The stranger conceals his true identity while possessing abilities far beyond an ordinary shepherd, suggesting he is more than he appears.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The stranger is ungrateful toward Admetus and refuses to share personal information as a sign of disrespect.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The stranger is a skilled but shy shepherd whose talent for music developed naturally from a year of tending flocks in the hills.

cards.standardTitle: Key literary elements add layers of meaning
cards.excerpt:
Now, not very far from the land of Arcadia there was a little city named Calydon. It lay in the midst of rich wheat fields and fruitful vineyards; but beyond the vineyards there was a deep dense forest where many wild beasts lived. The king of Calydon was named OEneus, and he dwelt in a white palace with his wife Althea and his boys and girls. His kingdom was so small that it was not much trouble to govern it, and so he spent the most of his time in hunting or in plowing or in looking after his grape vines. He was said to be a very brave man, and he was the friend of all the great heroes of that heroic time.

The two daughters of OEneus and Althea were famed all over the world for their beauty; and one of them was the wife of the hero Hercules, who had freed Prometheus from his chains, and done many other mighty deeds. The six sons of OEneus and Althea were noble, handsome fellows; but the noblest and handsomest of them all was Meleager, the youngest.
cards.whyThisWorks: The narrator's description of OEneus—a king who governs a small kingdom with little trouble and fills his days with hunting, plowing, and tending vines—reveals a character defined by humble, hands-on simplicity rather than royal grandeur, which adds meaning to the heroic world being established around him.
cards.skillStrategy: When a character is described through specific actions or daily habits, ask what those details reveal about who that person is and what role they play in the larger story.
evidencePoints: His kingdom was so small that it was not much trouble to govern it, and so he spent the most of his time in hunting or in plowing or in looking after his grape vines.
He was said to be a very brave man, and he was the friend of all the great heroes of that heroic time.
cards.question: The narrator describes OEneus as spending most of his time 'in hunting or in plowing or in looking after his grape vines' because his kingdom required little governing. What does this characterization reveal about OEneus's role in the story?

choices.label: A
choices.text: He is a neglectful ruler whose laziness will eventually bring disaster to Calydon and its people.

choices.label: B
choices.text: He is a modest, grounded king whose ordinary daily life contrasts with the larger heroic world surrounding his family.

choices.label: C
choices.text: He is a powerful warrior whose farming and hunting activities demonstrate his physical dominance over the land.

choices.label: D
choices.text: He is an isolated ruler who has no connection to the great heroes and events of his time.

cards.standardTitle: Key literary elements add layers of meaning
cards.excerpt:
Then AEgeus kissed his wife and the babe, and went on board the ship; the sailors shouted; the oars were dipped into the waves; the white sail was spread to the breeze; and AEthra from her palace window saw the vessel speed away over the blue waters towards AEgina and the distant Attic shore.

Year after year went by, and yet no word reached AEthra from her husband on the other side of the sea. Often and often she would climb the mountain above Troezen, and sit there all day, looking out over the blue waters and the purple hills of AEgina to the dim, distant shore beyond. Now and then she could see a white-winged ship sailing in the offing; but men said that it was a Cretan vessel, and very likely was filled with fierce Cretan warriors, bound upon some cruel errand of war. Then it was rumored that King Minos had seized upon all the ships of Athens, and had burned a part of the city, and had forced the people to pay him a most grievous tribute. But further than this there was no news.
cards.whyThisWorks: Aethra's repeated act of climbing the mountain to watch the sea reveals her enduring grief and loyalty, giving students a concrete character action to analyze for deeper meaning about love, loss, and waiting.
cards.skillStrategy: When a character repeats an action, ask yourself what that habit reveals about who they are and what they feel inside.
evidencePoints: Often and often she would climb the mountain above Troezen, and sit there all day, looking out over the blue waters
Year after year went by, and yet no word reached AEthra from her husband on the other side of the sea.
cards.question: The narrator states that 'often and often' Aethra would climb the mountain and 'sit there all day, looking out over the blue waters.' What does this repeated action reveal about Aethra's character?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Aethra distrusts the sailors who carried Aegeus away and watches the sea to guard against their return.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Aethra's devotion to Aegeus remains unbroken across years of silence, showing that her longing defines her daily existence.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Aethra has accepted that Aegeus will never return and climbs the mountain simply to pass the long, empty hours.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Aethra fears the Cretan warriors and watches the sea to warn Troezen of any approaching threat.

cards.standardTitle: Key literary elements add layers of meaning
cards.excerpt:
The king sent out his fastest ship to try to overtake the bull. The sailors rowed far out to sea, much farther than any ship had ever gone before; but no trace of Europa could be found. When they came back, everybody felt that there was no more hope. All the women and children in the town wept for the lost Europa. The king shut himself up in his house, and did not eat nor drink for three days. Then he called his son Cadmus, and bade him take a ship and go in search of his sister; and he told him that, no matter what dangers might be in his way, he must not come back until she was found.

Cadmus was glad to go. He chose twenty brave young men to go with him, and set sail the very next day. It was a great undertaking; for they were to pass through an unknown sea, and they did not know what lands they would come to. Indeed, it was feared that they would never come to any land at all. Ships did not dare to go far from the shore in those days. But Cadmus and his friends were not afraid. They were ready to face any danger.
cards.whyThisWorks: The contrast between the king's paralyzed grief and Cadmus's eager willingness reveals how Cadmus's courage and loyalty define him as a hero-in-the-making, adding meaning to the theme of duty over fear.
cards.skillStrategy: When a character acts differently from those around them, ask what that contrast reveals about who they are and what the author wants you to understand about them.
evidencePoints: Cadmus was glad to go.
But Cadmus and his friends were not afraid. They were ready to face any danger.
cards.question: The narrator states that 'Cadmus was glad to go' into an 'unknown sea' that ships 'did not dare' to sail. What does this detail reveal about Cadmus's character?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Cadmus does not fully understand the danger of the voyage because he is too young and inexperienced to recognize what the sailors already know.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Cadmus's willingness—even eagerness—in the face of dangers that have already defeated the king's fastest ship shows that his courage and sense of duty define him as exceptional among those around him.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Cadmus is glad to go because he is indifferent to his sister's fate and sees the voyage as an opportunity to escape his father's grief-stricken household.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Cadmus's confidence comes from knowing the route to Europa, which makes the voyage less dangerous for him than it was for the sailors who returned empty-handed.

cards.standardTitle: Theme development across a literary text
cards.excerpt:
"Take this child," he said, "and teach him all the lore of the mountains, the woods, and the fields. Teach him those things which he most needs to know in order to do great good to his fellow-men."

And AEsculapius proved to be a wise child, gentle and sweet and teachable; and among all the pupils of Cheiron he was the best loved. He learned the lore of the mountains, the woods, and the fields. He found out what virtue there is in herbs and flowers and senseless stones; and he studied the habits of birds and beasts and men. But above all he became skillful in dressing wounds and healing diseases; and to this day physicians remember and honor him as the first and greatest of their craft. When he grew up to manhood his name was heard in every land, and people blessed him because he was the friend of life and the foe of death.

As time went by, AEsculapius cured so many people and saved so many lives that Pluto, the pale-faced king of the Lower World, became alarmed.

"I shall soon have nothing to do," he said, "if this physician does not stop keeping people away from my kingdom."

And he sent word to his brother Jupiter, and complained that AEsculapius was cheating him out of what was his due. Great Jupiter listened to his complaint, and stood up among the storm clouds, and hurled his thunderbolts at AEsculapius until the great physician was cruelly slain. Then all the world was filled with grief, and even the beasts and the trees and the stones wept because the friend of life was no more.
cards.whyThisWorks: The excerpt contains both true-but-topic-only details (Aesculapius studied herbs and birds) and theme-developing details (his death causing universal grief and Pluto's fear), allowing students to distinguish between details that merely match the topic of healing and those that actively build the theme that devoted service to humanity invites both reverence and destruction.
cards.skillStrategy: Ask yourself: does this detail just tell me what the story is about, or does it show me what the story is saying about life, sacrifice, or human nature?
evidencePoints: people blessed him because he was the friend of life and the foe of death
Then all the world was filled with grief, and even the beasts and the trees and the stones wept because the friend of life was no more
cards.question: Which detail from the passage best develops the theme that a life devoted to the good of others earns a grief that transcends ordinary loss?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Aesculapius learned the lore of mountains, woods, and fields and discovered the virtue in herbs, flowers, and stones.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Even the beasts, trees, and stones wept because 'the friend of life was no more,' showing that his loss was mourned by all of creation.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Pluto complained to Jupiter that Aesculapius was 'cheating him out of what was his due' by keeping people from the Lower World.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Among all the pupils of Cheiron, Aesculapius was the best loved and proved to be gentle, sweet, and teachable.

cards.standardTitle: Key literary elements add layers of meaning
cards.excerpt:
At last the famous Island of Crete was reached, and there Daedalus landed and made himself known; and the King of Crete, who had already heard of his wondrous skill, welcomed him to his kingdom, and gave him a home in his palace, and promised that he should be rewarded with great riches and honor if he would but stay and practice his craft there as he had done in Athens.

Now the name of the King of Crete was Minos. His grandfather, whose name was also Minos, was the son of Europa, a young princess whom a white bull, it was said, had brought on his back across the sea from distant Asia. This elder Minos had been accounted the wisest of men--so wise, indeed, that Jupiter chose him to be one of the judges of the Lower World. The younger Minos was almost as wise as his grandfather; and he was brave and far-seeing and skilled as a ruler of men. He had made all the islands subject to his kingdom, and his ships sailed into every part of the world and brought back to Crete the riches of foreign lands. So it was not hard for him to persuade Daedalus to make his home with him and be the chief of his artisans.
cards.whyThisWorks: The narrator's detailed portrait of Minos—his lineage, wisdom, military power, and wealth—reveals why Daedalus would willingly stay in Crete, showing how characterization drives plot and deepens meaning about the relationship between power and talent.
cards.skillStrategy: When a character is described in detail, ask yourself: what does this description reveal about who they are and why other characters respond to them the way they do?
evidencePoints: he was brave and far-seeing and skilled as a ruler of men
So it was not hard for him to persuade Daedalus to make his home with him and be the chief of his artisans
cards.question: The narrator describes Minos as 'brave and far-seeing and skilled as a ruler of men' who made 'all the islands subject to his kingdom' and whose ships 'brought back to Crete the riches of foreign lands.' What does this characterization reveal about why Daedalus agrees to stay in Crete?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Daedalus stays because he fears Minos will punish him if he refuses, since Minos has already conquered all the surrounding islands.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Minos's combination of power, wealth, and wisdom makes him the kind of ruler whose offer of riches and honor would be nearly impossible for a skilled craftsman to turn down.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Daedalus is persuaded mainly by his admiration for Minos's grandfather, whose legendary wisdom Daedalus had long respected.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Minos's divine ancestry, traced back to Europa and Jupiter, gives him an authority over Daedalus that no ordinary king could claim.

cards.standardTitle: Key literary elements add layers of meaning
cards.excerpt:
She stroked his head and neck, and he seemed much pleased. Then she made a wreath of daisies, and hung it round his neck. He looked at her with his soft kind eyes, and seemed to thank her; and in a little while, he lay down among the clover. Europa then made a smaller wreath, and climbed upon his back to twine it round his horns. But all at once he sprang up, and ran away so swiftly that Europa could not help herself. She did not dare to jump off while he was going so fast, and all that she could think to do was to hold fast to his neck and scream very loud.

The herdsman under the tree heard her scream, and jumped up to see what was the matter. He saw the bull running with her towards the shore. He ran after them as fast as he could, but it was of no use. The bull leaped into the sea, and swam swiftly away, with poor Europa on his back. Several other people had seen him, and now they ran to tell the king. Soon the whole town was alarmed. Everybody ran out to the shore and looked. All that could be seen was something white moving very fast over the calm, blue water; and soon it was out of sight.
cards.whyThisWorks: Europa's shift from gently decorating the bull to clinging to his neck and screaming reveals how her trusting, playful nature makes her vulnerability complete, showing that innocence itself becomes the mechanism of her capture.
cards.skillStrategy: Track what a character does and feels at a key turning point — the change in their actions often reveals what the author wants you to understand about them.
evidencePoints: She stroked his head and neck, and he seemed much pleased.
all that she could think to do was to hold fast to his neck and scream very loud
cards.question: In the first paragraph, Europa moves from stroking the bull and weaving him a wreath to clinging to his neck and screaming. What does this shift in her actions reveal about her character?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Her willingness to climb onto the bull's back shows she is reckless and has ignored obvious warning signs throughout the encounter.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Her gentle, trusting behavior toward the bull is precisely what leaves her helpless once he turns dangerous, showing that her innocence makes her an easy victim.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Her screaming reveals that she is more concerned with calling for help from the herdsman than with protecting herself from the bull.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Her actions show she quickly regains her composure and makes a rational decision to hold on rather than jump, proving she is calm under pressure.

cards.standardTitle: Text structure and feature purpose
cards.excerpt:
Now, not very far from the land of Arcadia there was a little city named Calydon. It lay in the midst of rich wheat fields and fruitful vineyards; but beyond the vineyards there was a deep dense forest where many wild beasts lived. The king of Calydon was named OEneus, and he dwelt in a white palace with his wife Althea and his boys and girls. His kingdom was so small that it was not much trouble to govern it, and so he spent the most of his time in hunting or in plowing or in looking after his grape vines. He was said to be a very brave man, and he was the friend of all the great heroes of that heroic time.

The two daughters of OEneus and Althea were famed all over the world for their beauty; and one of them was the wife of the hero Hercules, who had freed Prometheus from his chains, and done many other mighty deeds. The six sons of OEneus and Althea were noble, handsome fellows; but the noblest and handsomest of them all was Meleager, the youngest.
cards.whyThisWorks: The two paragraphs model a clear introduce-then-narrow structure: paragraph one establishes the kingdom and OEneus broadly, while paragraph two zooms from 'daughters' and 'six sons' down to the single sentence spotlighting Meleager, giving students a concrete textual moment to analyze for paragraph job.
cards.skillStrategy: Ask yourself: does this paragraph open a new idea, add to what came before, or zoom in on one part of what was already introduced?
evidencePoints: The six sons of OEneus and Althea were noble, handsome fellows; but the noblest and handsomest of them all was Meleager, the youngest.
The king of Calydon was named OEneus, and he dwelt in a white palace with his wife Althea and his boys and girls.
cards.question: The second paragraph ends with the sentence 'but the noblest and handsomest of them all was Meleager, the youngest.' What is the job of the second paragraph in relation to the first?

choices.label: A
choices.text: It contradicts the first paragraph by arguing that OEneus's children, not his kingdom, define his importance in the story.

choices.label: B
choices.text: It extends the first paragraph's introduction of OEneus's household by narrowing from the whole family down to the single figure of Meleager.

choices.label: C
choices.text: It concludes the description of Calydon by explaining why the city became famous throughout the world because of its royal family.

choices.label: D
choices.text: It shifts the focus away from OEneus entirely by making Hercules the central figure through his connection to OEneus's daughter.

cards.standardTitle: Key literary elements add layers of meaning
cards.excerpt:
King Pittheus of Troezen was right glad to see AEgeus, for they had been boys together, and he welcomed him to his city and did all that he could to make his visit a pleasant one. So, day after day, there was feasting and merriment and music in the marble halls of old Troezen, and the two kings spent many a happy hour in talking of the deeds of their youth and of the mighty heroes whom both had known. And when the time came for the ship to sail back to Athens, AEgeus was not ready to go. He said he would stay yet a little longer in Troezen, for that the elders of the city would manage things well at home; and so the ship returned without him.

But AEgeus tarried, not so much for the rest and enjoyment which he was having in the home of his old friend, as for the sake of AEthra, his old friend's daughter. For AEthra was as fair as a summer morning, and she was the joy and pride of Troezen; and AEgeus was never so happy as when in her presence. So it happened that some time after the ship had sailed, there was a wedding in the halls of King Pittheus; but it was kept a secret, for AEgeus feared that his nephews, if they heard of it, would be very angry and would send men to Troezen to do him harm.
cards.whyThisWorks: AEgeus's decision to stay in Troezen and keep his wedding secret reveals his conflicted nature—drawn by personal desire yet fearful of political consequences—giving students a clear moment of characterization to analyze for deeper meaning.
cards.skillStrategy: When a character's actions contradict what they say or do something in secret, ask yourself what that gap reveals about who they really are and what they fear.
evidencePoints: AEgeus was not ready to go... and so the ship returned without him
it was kept a secret, for AEgeus feared that his nephews, if they heard of it, would be very angry and would send men to Troezen to do him harm
cards.question: AEgeus allows the ship to return to Athens without him and later keeps his wedding a secret. What do these two actions together reveal about his character?

choices.label: A
choices.text: He is a careless ruler who has forgotten his responsibilities to Athens entirely because of his friendship with King Pittheus.

choices.label: B
choices.text: He is a man driven by personal desire yet aware of the dangers that desire creates, willing to act on his feelings while hiding them from those who could threaten him.

choices.label: C
choices.text: He is a cowardly king who refuses to return to Athens because he is afraid of the voyage by sea.

choices.label: D
choices.text: He is a loyal friend who stays in Troezen solely out of respect for King Pittheus and the hospitality he has been shown.

cards.standardTitle: Theme development across a literary text
cards.excerpt:
The only sure way to save himself would be to put the child to death before he was old enough to do any harm. But when he had taken the little Perseus and his mother out of the prison and had seen how helpless the child was, he could not bear the thought of having him killed outright. For the king, although a great coward, was really a kind-hearted man and did not like to see anything suffer pain. Yet something must be done.

So he bade his servants make a wooden chest that was roomy and watertight and strong; and when it was done, he put Danaë and the child into it and had it taken far out to sea and left there to be tossed about by the waves. He thought that in this way he would rid himself of both daughter and grandson without seeing them die; for surely the chest would sink after a while, or else the winds would cause it to drift to some strange shore so far away that they could never come back to Argos again.
cards.whyThisWorks: The king's deliberate plan to cast Danaë and Perseus to sea 'without seeing them die' directly illustrates how self-deception enables harm while evading moral responsibility, supporting theme development.
cards.skillStrategy: Find the character's actions and stated reasoning, then ask what truth about human behavior those details reveal together.
evidencePoints: rid himself of both daughter and grandson without seeing them die
the king, although a great coward, was really a kind-hearted man and did not like to see anything suffer pain
cards.question: The king calls himself 'kind-hearted' yet arranges for Danaë and Perseus to be cast to sea. Which detail best supports the theme that people deceive themselves to avoid moral responsibility?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The king takes Danaë and Perseus 'out of the prison,' suggesting he believes releasing them proves his mercy.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The king plans to 'rid himself of both daughter and grandson without seeing them die,' convincing himself he bears no guilt.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The king orders a chest that is 'roomy and watertight and strong,' showing he wants them to survive the voyage.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The king hopes 'the winds would cause it to drift to some strange shore,' believing distance alone solves the problem.

cards.standardTitle: Text structure and feature purpose
cards.excerpt:
So Cecrops--the serpent man, as they still called him--became the king of the poor people on the hill. He taught them how to make bows and arrows, and how to set nets for birds, and how to take fish with hooks. He led them against the savage wild men of the woods, and helped them kill the fierce beasts that had been so great a terror to them. He showed them how to build houses of wood and to thatch them with the reeds which grew in the marshes. He taught them how to live in families instead of herding together like senseless beasts as they had always done before. And he told them about great Jupiter and the Mighty Folk who lived amid the clouds on the mountain top.

By and by, instead of the wretched caves among the rocks, there was a little town on the top of the hill, with neat houses and a market place; and around it was a strong wall with a single narrow gate just where the footpath began to descend to the plain. But as yet the place had no name.
cards.whyThisWorks: The two paragraphs model a clear cause-to-effect structure: paragraph one catalogs Cecrops's specific teachings, and paragraph two shows the concrete result—'a little town on the top of the hill'—making the paragraph job (extending/proving an idea through outcome) directly teachable.
cards.skillStrategy: Ask yourself: does this paragraph introduce a new idea, or does it show what happened because of the idea in the paragraph before it?
evidencePoints: He taught them how to live in families instead of herding together like senseless beasts as they had always done before.
By and by, instead of the wretched caves among the rocks, there was a little town on the top of the hill, with neat houses and a market place
cards.question: The second paragraph opens with 'By and by, instead of the wretched caves among the rocks, there was a little town on the top of the hill.' What is the job of this second paragraph in relation to the first paragraph?

choices.label: A
choices.text: It shifts focus away from Cecrops entirely by describing the town's wall and gate without connecting those details to his earlier actions.

choices.label: B
choices.text: It shows the outcome of the actions described in the first paragraph, revealing that Cecrops's teachings transformed 'wretched caves' into 'neat houses and a market place.'

choices.label: C
choices.text: It contrasts the townspeople's new skills with Cecrops's own limitations as a leader by noting the town still had no name.

choices.label: D
choices.text: It introduces the central conflict of the passage by presenting the 'strong wall with a single narrow gate' as a new threat to the community.

cards.standardTitle: Key literary elements add layers of meaning
cards.excerpt: One day when the men were hunting in the woods, they found a strange youth whose face was so fair and who was dressed so beautifully that they could hardly believe him to be a man like themselves. His body was so slender and lithe, and he moved so nimbly among the trees, that they fancied him to be a serpent in the guise of a human being; and they stood still in wonder and alarm. The young man spoke to them, but they could not understand a word that he said; then he made signs to them that he was hungry, and they gave him something to eat and were no longer afraid. Had they been like the wild men of the woods, they might have killed him at once. But they wanted their women and children to see the serpent man, as they called him, and hear him talk; and so they took him home with them to the top of the hill. They thought that after they had made a show of him for a few days, they would kill him and offer his body as a sacrifice to the unknown being whom they dimly fancied to have some sort of control over their lives.
cards.whyThisWorks: The men's decision to feed the stranger rather than kill him, contrasted with the narrator's note that 'wild men of the woods' would have killed him at once, reveals the men's capacity for curiosity and restraint while also exposing their underlying cruelty in planning to sacrifice him—layering their characterization with moral complexity.
cards.skillStrategy: When a character acts in a surprising way, ask what that action reveals about who they are beneath the surface—look for contrasts or contradictions that add depth.
evidencePoints: Had they been like the wild men of the woods, they might have killed him at once.

They thought that after they had made a show of him for a few days, they would kill him and offer his body as a sacrifice to the unknown being whom they dimly fancied to have some sort of control over their lives.
cards.question: The narrator states that the men fed the stranger and chose not to kill him immediately, yet also reveals their plan to sacrifice him after a few days. What does this contrast reveal about the men's character?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The men are shown to be genuinely compassionate, since their first instinct was to feed the stranger rather than harm him.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The men's apparent kindness is undermined by their calculating cruelty, showing that their mercy was driven by curiosity and self-interest rather than true goodwill.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The men are portrayed as deeply religious, since their primary motivation throughout the encounter is to honor the unknown being they worship.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The men are shown to be cowardly, since their fear of the stranger is what prevents them from killing him on the spot.

cards.standardTitle: Theme development across a literary text
cards.excerpt:
So Cecrops--the serpent man, as they still called him--became the king of the poor people on the hill. He taught them how to make bows and arrows, and how to set nets for birds, and how to take fish with hooks. He led them against the savage wild men of the woods, and helped them kill the fierce beasts that had been so great a terror to them. He showed them how to build houses of wood and to thatch them with the reeds which grew in the marshes. He taught them how to live in families instead of herding together like senseless beasts as they had always done before. And he told them about great Jupiter and the Mighty Folk who lived amid the clouds on the mountain top.

By and by, instead of the wretched caves among the rocks, there was a little town on the top of the hill, with neat houses and a market place; and around it was a strong wall with a single narrow gate just where the footpath began to descend to the plain. But as yet the place had no name.
cards.whyThisWorks: The excerpt contrasts the people's former savage, beast-like existence with the ordered, civilized community Cecrops builds, giving students clear details to distinguish between those that merely describe the setting and those that actively develop the theme of leadership transforming a people.
cards.skillStrategy: Ask yourself: does this detail show the theme changing or growing, or does it just describe what is true about the story's topic?
evidencePoints: He taught them how to live in families instead of herding together like senseless beasts as they had always done before.
instead of the wretched caves among the rocks, there was a little town on the top of the hill, with neat houses and a market place
cards.question: Which detail from the passage most directly develops the theme that wise leadership can transform a people from disorder to civilization?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Cecrops taught the people to make bows and arrows and to set nets for birds, showing that he improved their ability to hunt.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Cecrops taught the people 'to live in families instead of herding together like senseless beasts,' replacing their animal-like existence with human social order.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The new town was surrounded by 'a strong wall with a single narrow gate just where the footpath began to descend to the plain,' showing the town's physical layout.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Cecrops told the people about 'great Jupiter and the Mighty Folk who lived amid the clouds on the mountain top,' introducing them to the gods.

cards.standardTitle: Text structure and feature purpose
cards.excerpt:
Then AEgeus kissed his wife and the babe, and went on board the ship; the sailors shouted; the oars were dipped into the waves; the white sail was spread to the breeze; and AEthra from her palace window saw the vessel speed away over the blue waters towards AEgina and the distant Attic shore.

Year after year went by, and yet no word reached AEthra from her husband on the other side of the sea. Often and often she would climb the mountain above Troezen, and sit there all day, looking out over the blue waters and the purple hills of AEgina to the dim, distant shore beyond. Now and then she could see a white-winged ship sailing in the offing; but men said that it was a Cretan vessel, and very likely was filled with fierce Cretan warriors, bound upon some cruel errand of war. Then it was rumored that King Minos had seized upon all the ships of Athens, and had burned a part of the city, and had forced the people to pay him a most grievous tribute. But further than this there was no news.
cards.whyThisWorks: The two paragraphs move from a hopeful farewell scene to years of silence and mounting threat, giving students a clear contrast in tone and purpose to analyze at the paragraph level.
cards.skillStrategy: Ask yourself: what idea does the first paragraph end on, and does the second paragraph continue, contradict, or change that idea?
evidencePoints: AEthra from her palace window saw the vessel speed away over the blue waters towards AEgina and the distant Attic shore.
Year after year went by, and yet no word reached AEthra from her husband on the other side of the sea.
cards.question: The first paragraph ends with Aethra watching Aegeus's ship 'speed away over the blue waters.' What is the job of the second paragraph in relation to that moment?

choices.label: A
choices.text: It concludes the story by revealing that Aegeus eventually sent word to Aethra from the Attic shore.

choices.label: B
choices.text: It shifts from that hopeful departure to years of silence and the growing threat of King Minos, replacing hope with dread.

choices.label: C
choices.text: It contrasts Aethra's sorrow with Aegeus's happiness by describing his safe arrival in Athens.

choices.label: D
choices.text: It extends the departure scene by adding details about the sailors and the route the ship traveled.

cards.standardTitle: Key literary elements add layers of meaning
cards.excerpt: Apollo did not care to live much of the time with his mighty kinsfolk on the mountain top. He liked better to go about from place to place and from land to land, seeing people at their work and making their lives happy. When men first saw his fair boyish face and his soft white hands, they sneered and said he was only an idle, good-for-nothing fellow. But when they heard him speak, they were so charmed that they stood, spellbound, to listen; and ever after that they made his words their law. They wondered how it was that he was so wise; for it seemed to them that he did nothing but stroll about, playing on his wonderful lyre and looking at the trees and blossoms and birds and bees. But when any of them were sick they came to him, and he told them what to find in plants or stones or brooks that would heal them and make them strong again. They noticed that he did not grow old, as others did, but that he was always young and fair; and, even after he had gone away,--they knew not how, nor whither,--it seemed as though the earth were a brighter and sweeter place to live in than it had been before his coming.
cards.whyThisWorks: The excerpt uses a clear before-and-after contrast in how people perceive Apollo—from sneering at his appearance to standing spellbound by his words—to reveal that true wisdom and power are not found in outward appearance but in what one offers to others.
cards.skillStrategy: When a character is described through contrast—how others first judge them versus how they later respond—ask yourself what that shift reveals about the character's deeper meaning or purpose.
evidencePoints: When men first saw his fair boyish face and his soft white hands, they sneered and said he was only an idle, good-for-nothing fellow.
But when they heard him speak, they were so charmed that they stood, spellbound, to listen; and ever after that they made his words their law.
cards.question: In the excerpt, the contrast between how people first judge Apollo and how they later respond to him reveals which idea about his character?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Apollo deliberately hides his power from strangers so that he can test whether they are worthy of his wisdom.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Apollo's true nature—his wisdom and healing gifts—cannot be seen in his appearance but is revealed through his words and actions.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Apollo earns people's respect only because he refuses to grow old, making him seem more powerful than ordinary men.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Apollo prefers wandering among people rather than living on the mountain because he wants to be admired for his youthful looks.

cards.standardTitle: Theme development across a literary text
cards.excerpt:
One morning Europa went out into a field near the seashore to pick flowers. Her father's cattle were in the field, grazing among the sweet clover. They were all very tame, and Europa knew every one of them by name. The herdsman was lying in the shade under a tree, trying to make music on a little flute of straw. Europa had played in the field a thousand times before, and no one had ever thought of any harm befalling her.

That morning she noticed that there was a strange bull with the herd. He was very large and as white as snow; and he had soft brown eyes which somehow made him look very gentle and kind. At first he did not even look at Europa, but went here and there, eating the tender grass which grew among the clover. But when she had gathered her apron full of daisies and buttercups, he came slowly towards her. She was not at all afraid of him; and so she stopped to look at him, he was so handsome. He came close to her, and rubbed her arm with his nose to say "Good-morning!"
cards.whyThisWorks: The excerpt contrasts the bull's deceptively gentle appearance ('soft brown eyes which somehow made him look very gentle and kind') with the reader's awareness that he is a supernatural threat, giving students a clear case where a true detail (Europa knowing the cattle by name) matches only the topic of familiarity, while the bull's described gentleness actually builds the theme that danger disguises itself as harmless.
cards.skillStrategy: Ask yourself: does this detail show the theme being built, or does it just mention something related to the topic?
evidencePoints: He was very large and as white as snow; and he had soft brown eyes which somehow made him look very gentle and kind.
She was not at all afraid of him; and so she stopped to look at him, he was so handsome.
cards.question: The narrator describes the strange bull as having 'soft brown eyes which somehow made him look very gentle and kind,' and later says Europa 'was not at all afraid of him.' Which statement best explains how these two details together develop the theme that danger can conceal itself beneath a gentle appearance?

choices.label: A
choices.text: They show that Europa is careless because she ignores the fact that the bull is a stranger to the herd.

choices.label: B
choices.text: They show that the bull's outward softness and beauty successfully removes Europa's instinct to be cautious, making the hidden threat more convincing.

choices.label: C
choices.text: They establish that Europa has a long history with tame animals, so her comfort around the bull is completely reasonable.

choices.label: D
choices.text: They contrast the bull's large size with Europa's small apron full of flowers to emphasize how physically vulnerable she is.

cards.standardTitle: Text structure and feature purpose
cards.excerpt:
By and by she came to a narrow neck of the sea, and, since the land on the other side looked as though she might find rest there, she leaped into the waves and swam across; and that place has been called Bosphorus--a word which means the Sea of the Cow--from that time till now, and you will find it so marked on the maps which you use at school. Then she went on through a strange land on the other side, but, let her do what she would, she could not get rid of the gadfly.

After a time she came to a place where there were high mountains with snow-capped peaks which seemed to touch the sky. There she stopped to rest a while; and she looked up at the calm, cold cliffs above her and wished that she might die where all was so grand and still. But as she looked she saw a giant form stretched upon the rocks midway between earth and sky, and she knew at once that it was Prometheus, the young Titan, whom Jupiter had chained there because he had given fire to men.
cards.whyThisWorks: The two paragraphs model a clear structural shift: the first ends with Io still tormented ('she could not get rid of the gadfly'), while the second opens with her stopping to rest and then encountering Prometheus, giving students a concrete before-and-after to analyze.
cards.skillStrategy: Find the last sentence of the first paragraph and the first sentence of the second paragraph, then ask: does the second paragraph keep going the same way, or does something change?
evidencePoints: let her do what she would, she could not get rid of the gadfly
There she stopped to rest a while; and she looked up at the calm, cold cliffs above her and wished that she might die where all was so grand and still
cards.question: The first paragraph ends with the line 'let her do what she would, she could not get rid of the gadfly.' What is the job of the second paragraph in relation to that ending?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The second paragraph extends the idea of relentless torment by showing that the gadfly continues to drive Io through the mountain landscape just as it drove her across the Bosphorus.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The second paragraph shifts away from Io's ceaseless, tormented movement by placing her in a moment of stillness at the snow-capped peaks, where she stops, wishes for death, and then encounters Prometheus.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The second paragraph concludes Io's suffering by showing that the grand, calm cliffs finally free her from the gadfly and bring her the rest she sought when she crossed the Bosphorus.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The second paragraph introduces a contrast between the Bosphorus and the mountains in order to prove that each new land Io enters is colder and more dangerous than the one before.

cards.standardTitle: Central idea and supporting evidence
cards.excerpt:
The only sure way to save himself would be to put the child to death before he was old enough to do any harm. But when he had taken the little Perseus and his mother out of the prison and had seen how helpless the child was, he could not bear the thought of having him killed outright. For the king, although a great coward, was really a kind-hearted man and did not like to see anything suffer pain. Yet something must be done.

So he bade his servants make a wooden chest that was roomy and watertight and strong; and when it was done, he put Danaë and the child into it and had it taken far out to sea and left there to be tossed about by the waves. He thought that in this way he would rid himself of both daughter and grandson without seeing them die; for surely the chest would sink after a while, or else the winds would cause it to drift to some strange shore so far away that they could never come back to Argos again.
cards.whyThisWorks: The excerpt explicitly names the king's conflicting motives—fear, cowardice, and kind-heartedness—and then shows the chest plan as their direct result, giving students a concrete passage moment to anchor a central idea rather than a topic or isolated detail.
cards.skillStrategy: Find the tension or problem the passage keeps returning to, then state in your own words what the whole passage is really saying about that tension—not just one event or one detail.
evidencePoints: the king, although a great coward, was really a kind-hearted man and did not like to see anything suffer pain
He thought that in this way he would rid himself of both daughter and grandson without seeing them die
cards.question: The narrator describes the king as 'a great coward' who was also 'a kind-hearted man.' What central idea do both paragraphs develop through that description and the chest plan that follows?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The king's cruelty toward Danaë and Perseus reveals that he cared only about protecting his own power, with no concern for their suffering.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The king's fear and his reluctance to cause direct suffering led him to a plan that let him remove Danaë and Perseus while avoiding the sight of their deaths.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The wooden chest was a reliable solution because the king knew the sea would carry Danaë and Perseus safely to a distant shore.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The king's kindness was stronger than his fear, so he ultimately chose a plan designed to keep Danaë and Perseus alive.

cards.standardTitle: Key literary elements add layers of meaning
cards.excerpt:
Atalanta gave him a good start, and then she followed after, as swift as an arrow shot from the bow. Meilanion was not a very fast runner, and it would not be hard for her to overtake him. She thought that she would let him get almost to the goal, for she really pitied him. He heard her coming close behind him; he heard her quick breath as she gained on him very fast. Then he threw one of the golden apples over his shoulder.

Now, if there was anything in the world that Atalanta admired, it was a bright stone or a pretty piece of yellow gold. As the apple fell to the ground she saw how beautiful it was, and she stopped to pick it up; and while she was doing this, Meilanion gained a good many paces. But what of that? In a minute she was as close behind him as ever. And yet, she really did pity him.

Just then Meilanion threw the second apple over his shoulder. It was handsomer and larger than the first, and Atalanta could not bear the thought of allowing some one else to get it. So she stopped to pick it up from among the long grass, where it had fallen. It took somewhat longer to find it than she had expected, and when she looked up again Meilanion was a hundred feet ahead of her. But that was no matter. She could easily overtake him. And yet, how she did pity the foolish young man!
cards.whyThisWorks: Atalanta's repeated pauses to collect the golden apples, paired with the narrator's refrain that 'she really did pity him,' reveals a character whose self-assurance blinds her to her own vulnerability, adding ironic meaning to her eventual defeat.
cards.skillStrategy: When a character's actions contradict what they say or think, ask what that gap reveals about who they really are.
evidencePoints: she really did pity him
she stopped to pick it up
cards.question: Each time Atalanta stops to pick up a golden apple, the narrator adds that 'she really did pity him.' What does this combination of action and thought reveal about Atalanta's character?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Her compassion for Meilanion is so strong that she deliberately slows down to give him a fair chance at winning the race.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Her confidence in her own speed makes her unaware that her desire for the apples is the very weakness that will cost her the race.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Her admiration for beautiful objects is a flaw she recognizes and struggles against, but ultimately cannot overcome through willpower.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Her repeated pauses show that she has already decided to let Meilanion win because she finds him worthy of her respect.

cards.standardTitle: Text structure and feature purpose
cards.excerpt:
One morning Europa went out into a field near the seashore to pick flowers. Her father's cattle were in the field, grazing among the sweet clover. They were all very tame, and Europa knew every one of them by name. The herdsman was lying in the shade under a tree, trying to make music on a little flute of straw. Europa had played in the field a thousand times before, and no one had ever thought of any harm befalling her.

That morning she noticed that there was a strange bull with the herd. He was very large and as white as snow; and he had soft brown eyes which somehow made him look very gentle and kind. At first he did not even look at Europa, but went here and there, eating the tender grass which grew among the clover. But when she had gathered her apron full of daisies and buttercups, he came slowly towards her. She was not at all afraid of him; and so she stopped to look at him, he was so handsome. He came close to her, and rubbed her arm with his nose to say "Good-morning!"
cards.whyThisWorks: The two-paragraph structure clearly demonstrates how an author uses a second paragraph to introduce narrative tension by disrupting the safety established in the first, making it an ideal model for teaching paragraph job within a text structure standard.
cards.skillStrategy: Ask yourself: what job does this paragraph do compared to the one before it — does it confirm, contrast, shift, or complicate what was already set up?
evidencePoints: no one had ever thought of any harm befalling her
she noticed that there was a strange bull with the herd
cards.question: The first paragraph establishes that Europa 'had played in the field a thousand times before, and no one had ever thought of any harm befalling her.' What is the primary job of the second paragraph in relation to this established sense of safety?

choices.label: A
choices.text: It confirms the familiar safety of the field by showing that Europa 'was not at all afraid' of the bull and that he 'rubbed her arm with his nose to say Good-morning,' suggesting the field remains as harmless as it has always been.

choices.label: B
choices.text: It quietly unsettles the assurance of the first paragraph by introducing 'a strange bull with the herd' — an unfamiliar presence in a place Europa has always known — signaling that her ordinary routine has been disrupted.

choices.label: C
choices.text: It reinforces the peaceful routine of the first paragraph by showing the bull 'eating the tender grass which grew among the clover,' just as the familiar cattle had always grazed peacefully alongside Europa.

choices.label: D
choices.text: It replaces the first paragraph's focus on Europa's safety with a detailed description of the bull — 'as white as snow' with 'soft brown eyes' — shifting the paragraph's purpose entirely to physical appearance.

cards.standardTitle: Central idea and supporting evidence
cards.excerpt:
It happened soon afterwards that the king of a certain country not far away was holding games and giving prizes to the best runners and leapers and quoit throwers. And Perseus went thither to try his strength with the other young men of the land; for if he should be able to gain a prize, his name would become known all over the world. No one in that country knew who he was, but all wondered at his noble stature and his strength and skill; and it was easy enough for him to win all the prizes.

One day, as he was showing what he could do, he threw a heavy quoit a great deal farther than any had been thrown before. It fell in the crowd of lookers-on, and struck a stranger who was standing there. The stranger threw up his hands and sank upon the ground; and when Perseus ran to help him, he saw that he was dead. Now this man was none other than Danaë's father, the old king of Argos. He had fled from his kingdom to save his life, and in doing so had only met his death.
cards.whyThisWorks: The excerpt pairs Perseus's deliberate pursuit of fame through athletic competition with the accidental, ironic death of the very king who once threatened him, giving students a clear contrast between intention and outcome to synthesize into a central idea.
cards.skillStrategy: Ask yourself: what do both paragraphs add up to together — not just what happens in one moment, but what the whole passage is really saying about Perseus, his actions, and their consequences.
evidencePoints: if he should be able to gain a prize, his name would become known all over the world
He had fled from his kingdom to save his life, and in doing so had only met his death
cards.question: The first paragraph states that Perseus entered the games so 'his name would become known all over the world,' and the second paragraph ends with the detail that the dead stranger 'had fled from his kingdom to save his life, and in doing so had only met his death.' What central idea do these two details together express across both paragraphs?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Perseus's superior athletic ability made him famous throughout the world, but that fame came at the cost of his reputation when he accidentally killed a bystander.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Perseus's pursuit of glory sets in motion an accidental death that fulfills the old king's unavoidable fate, showing that neither ambition nor flight can prevent what is destined to happen.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The old king of Argos brought about his own death by choosing to stand among the crowd of spectators at a competition where heavy objects were being thrown.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Perseus traveled to a foreign country where no one recognized him so that he could compete freely and win prizes without interference from his enemies.

cards.standardTitle: Key literary elements add layers of meaning
cards.excerpt: All this time Jupiter might have helped her had he not been so much afraid of Juno. But now it so chanced that when the poor cow lay down by the bank of the Nile, Queen Juno, in her high house in the clouds, also lay down to take a nap. As soon as she was sound asleep, Jupiter like a flash of light sped over the sea to Egypt. He killed the cruel gadfly and threw it into the river. Then he stroked the cow's head with his hand, and the cow was seen no more; but in her place stood the young girl Io, pale and frail, but fair and good as she had been in her old home in the town of Argos. Jupiter said not a word, nor even showed himself to the tired, trembling maiden. He hurried back with all speed to his high home in the clouds, for he feared that Juno might waken and find out what he had done.
cards.whyThisWorks: Jupiter's secretive actions—restoring Io without a word, then fleeing before Juno wakes—reveal a god who is powerful yet cowardly, showing that fear of consequences shapes his character more than compassion for Io.
cards.skillStrategy: Look at what a character does AND avoids doing, then ask what that combination reveals about who they really are.
evidencePoints: Jupiter said not a word, nor even showed himself to the tired, trembling maiden.
He hurried back with all speed to his high home in the clouds, for he feared that Juno might waken and find out what he had done.
cards.question: Jupiter restores Io but 'said not a word, nor even showed himself to the tired, trembling maiden,' then immediately flees. What does this combination of actions reveal about Jupiter's character?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Jupiter is indifferent to Io's suffering and acts only because Juno has ordered him to free her.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Jupiter is capable of mercy but is ultimately driven by self-preservation rather than genuine care for Io.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Jupiter stays silent and hidden because he wants Io to believe she was freed by her own strength.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Jupiter's swift departure shows he considers Io unworthy of his direct attention now that she is restored.

cards.standardTitle: Theme development across a literary text
cards.excerpt:
Very stealthily he went nearer and nearer, always with his back towards the monsters and always looking into his bright shield to see where to go. Then he drew his sharp sword and, dashing quickly downward, struck a back blow, so sure, so swift, that the head of Medusa was cut from her shoulders and the black blood gushed like a river from her neck. Quick as thought he thrust the terrible head into his magic pouch and leaped again into the air, and flew away with the speed of the wind.

Then the two older Gorgons awoke, and rose with dreadful screams, and spread their great wings, and dashed after him. They could not see him, for the Cap of Darkness hid him from even their eyes; but they scented the blood of the head which he carried in the pouch, and like hounds in the chase, they followed him, sniffing the air. And as he flew through the clouds he could hear their dreadful cries and the clatter of their golden wings and the snapping of their horrible jaws. But the Magic Slippers were faster than any wings, and in a little while the monsters were left far behind, and their cries were heard no more; and Perseus flew on alone.
cards.whyThisWorks: The excerpt contrasts true-but-topic-only details (the Gorgons' pursuit, the blood gushing) with details that directly develop the theme that cleverness and the right tools enable a hero to defeat overwhelming danger, making it ideal for teaching students to distinguish thematic evidence from mere topic details.
cards.skillStrategy: Ask yourself: does this detail show HOW the hero overcomes danger through cleverness or tools, or does it just describe the danger or the action without connecting to that idea?
evidencePoints: always with his back towards the monsters and always looking into his bright shield to see where to go
the Cap of Darkness hid him from even their eyes
cards.question: The narrator describes Perseus moving 'always with his back towards the monsters and always looking into his bright shield to see where to go,' and later notes that 'the Cap of Darkness hid him from even their eyes.' Which statement best explains how BOTH of these details develop the theme that cleverness and the right tools allow a hero to overcome overwhelming danger?

choices.label: A
choices.text: They show that Perseus was terrified of the Gorgons and relied entirely on magical objects because he lacked the strength to fight them directly.

choices.label: B
choices.text: They show that Perseus used strategic thinking alongside his magical tools — avoiding direct sight of Medusa and then concealing himself — to survive threats that raw courage alone could not defeat.

choices.label: C
choices.text: They show that the Gorgons were so powerful that even a hero with magical gifts could barely escape, making the danger the central focus of the passage.

choices.label: D
choices.text: They show that the magical objects Perseus carried were so powerful on their own that his personal choices and actions had little effect on the outcome.

cards.standardTitle: Text structure and feature purpose
cards.excerpt:
And Daedalus built for King Minos a most wonderful palace with floors of marble and pillars of granite; and in the palace he set up golden statues which had tongues and could talk; and for splendor and beauty there was no other building in all the wide earth that could be compared with it.

There lived in those days among the hills of Crete a terrible monster called the Minotaur, the like of which has never been seen from that time until now. This creature, it was said, had the body of a man, but the face and head of a wild bull and the fierce nature of a mountain lion. The people of Crete would not have killed him if they could; for they thought that the Mighty Folk who lived with Jupiter on the mountain top had sent him among them, and that these beings would be angry if any one should take his life. He was the pest and terror of all the land. Where he was least expected, there he was sure to be; and almost every day some man, woman, or child was caught and devoured by him.
cards.whyThisWorks: The two paragraphs create a sharp structural contrast—paragraph one celebrates the palace's splendor and Daedalus's genius, while paragraph two abruptly introduces the Minotaur as 'the pest and terror of all the land,' giving students a clear before-and-after shift to analyze.
cards.skillStrategy: Ask yourself: does the new paragraph keep building the same idea, or does it move to something different? Look for signal words and topic changes to name the paragraph's job.
evidencePoints: for splendor and beauty there was no other building in all the wide earth that could be compared with it
He was the pest and terror of all the land. Where he was least expected, there he was sure to be; and almost every day some man, woman, or child was caught and devoured by him.
cards.question: The first paragraph ends by saying the palace had no equal 'in all the wide earth' for 'splendor and beauty.' What is the job of the second paragraph in relation to that ending?

choices.label: A
choices.text: It extends the first paragraph's praise of Crete by showing that the island's wonders included not only the palace but also a creature unlike any other on earth.

choices.label: B
choices.text: It shifts away from the palace's splendor to introduce the Minotaur as a source of daily terror that threatened the very people living in that land.

choices.label: C
choices.text: It proves the first paragraph's claim about the palace's greatness by contrasting the building's beauty with the ugliness of the Minotaur's face and head.

choices.label: D
choices.text: It concludes the account of Daedalus's work by explaining that the Mighty Folk sent the Minotaur as a reward for the palace he built for King Minos.

cards.standardTitle: Central idea and supporting evidence
cards.excerpt:
In that forest there dwelt a robber giant, called Club-carrier, who was the terror of all the country. For oftentimes he would go down into the valleys where the shepherds fed their flocks, and would carry off not only sheep and lambs, but sometimes children and the men themselves. It was his custom to hide in the thickets of underbrush, close to a pathway, and, when a traveler passed that way, leap out upon him and beat him to death. When he saw Theseus coming through the woods, he thought that he would have a rich prize, for he knew from the youth's dress and manner that he must be a prince. He lay on the ground, where leaves of ivy and tall grass screened him from view, and held his great iron club ready to strike.

But Theseus had sharp eyes and quick ears, and neither beast nor robber giant could have taken him by surprise. When Club-carrier leaped out of his hiding place to strike him down, the young man dodged aside so quickly that the heavy club struck the ground behind him; and then, before the robber giant could raise it for a second stroke, Theseus seized the fellow's legs and tripped him up.
cards.whyThisWorks: The two paragraphs form a clear cause-and-effect arc—Club-carrier's ambush strategy versus Theseus's alertness—giving students concrete textual evidence to distinguish a central idea from an isolated detail or topic.
cards.skillStrategy: Ask yourself: what do BOTH paragraphs together show about the characters and what happens between them, not just what one sentence says?
evidencePoints: he would go down into the valleys where the shepherds fed their flocks, and would carry off not only sheep and lambs, but sometimes children and the men themselves
Theseus had sharp eyes and quick ears, and neither beast nor robber giant could have taken him by surprise
cards.question: The first paragraph describes Club-carrier as someone who relied on hiding and surprise to overpower victims. The second paragraph states that 'neither beast nor robber giant could have taken him by surprise.' What central idea do these two details together develop across both paragraphs?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Club-carrier was the most feared robber in the forest because he preyed on shepherds, children, and travelers alike.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Club-carrier's ambush tactics, which had terrorized the countryside, were defeated by Theseus's alertness and quick action.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Theseus was able to survive because Club-carrier mistakenly believed a prince would be an easy prize.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The forest was a dangerous place where travelers had no way to protect themselves from hidden attackers.

cards.standardTitle: Key literary elements add layers of meaning
cards.excerpt: Then Perseus slipped the Gorgon's head back into the pouch and hastened to speak with the young girl whom he had saved. She told him that her name was Andromeda, and that she was the daughter of the king of that land. She said that her mother, the queen, was very beautiful and very proud of her beauty; and every day she went down to the seashore to look at her face as it was pictured in the quiet water; and she had boasted that not even the nymphs who live in the sea were as handsome as she. When the sea nymphs heard about this, they were very angry and asked great Neptune, the king of the sea, to punish the queen for her pride. So Neptune sent a sea monster to crush the king's ships and kill the cattle along the shore and break down all the fishermen's huts. The people were so much distressed that they sent at last to ask the Pythia what they should do; and the Pythia said that there was only one way to save the land from destruction,--that they must give the king's daughter, Andromeda, to the monster to be devoured.
cards.whyThisWorks: The queen's boast and its chain of consequences—sea nymphs' anger, Neptune's monster, and Andromeda's condemnation—demonstrate how a single character's pride shapes plot and reveals that innocent characters bear the cost of another's flaw, directly illustrating how characterization adds layers of meaning.
cards.skillStrategy: Trace what a character's words or actions cause to happen, then ask what that chain of events reveals about who that character is and what their traits mean for others in the story.
evidencePoints: she had boasted that not even the nymphs who live in the sea were as handsome as she
they must give the king's daughter, Andromeda, to the monster to be devoured
cards.question: In the excerpt, Andromeda explains that her mother 'had boasted that not even the nymphs who live in the sea were as handsome as she,' which leads Neptune to send a sea monster and ultimately to the decree that Andromeda must be 'given to the monster to be devoured.' What does this chain of events reveal about the queen's character and its effect on others?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The queen's boast shows she is unaware of the sea nymphs' existence, so her punishment results from ignorance rather than from any prideful flaw in her character.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The queen's boast reveals that her unchecked pride brings destruction on innocent people, since it is Andromeda—not the queen herself—who is condemned to be devoured by the monster.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The queen's daily visits to the seashore to admire her reflection show that she is a devoted ruler focused on maintaining her appearance for the good of her kingdom.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The queen's boast demonstrates that she is the most powerful figure in the land, which is why Neptune targets her family specifically rather than punishing the sea nymphs for their anger.

cards.standardTitle: Theme development across a literary text
cards.excerpt:
By and by twin babes were born to Leto in Delos. One was a boy whom she called Apollo, the other a girl whom she named Artemis, or Diana. When the news of their birth was carried to Jupiter and the Mighty Folk on the mountain top, all the world was glad. The sun danced on the waters, and singing swans flew seven times round the island of Delos. The moon stooped to kiss the babes in their cradle; and Juno forgot her anger, and bade all things on the earth and in the sky be kind to Leto.

The two children grew very fast. Apollo became tall and strong and graceful; his face was as bright as the sunbeams; and he carried joy and gladness with him wherever he went. Jupiter gave him a pair of swans and a golden chariot, which bore him over sea and land wherever he wanted to go; and he gave him a lyre on which he played the sweetest music that was ever heard, and a silver bow with sharp arrows which never missed the mark. When Apollo went out into the world, and men came to know about him, he was called by some the Bringer of Light, by others the Master of Song, and by still others the Lord of the Silver Bow.
cards.whyThisWorks: The excerpt contrasts true-but-topic-only details (e.g., Apollo received swans and a chariot) with details that actively develop the theme that divine gifts bring light, joy, and order to the world, allowing students to practice distinguishing thematic evidence from mere topic details.
cards.skillStrategy: Ask yourself: does this detail show the theme being built, or does it just describe what happened? Only details that show how the idea grows across the passage count as thematic evidence.
evidencePoints: he carried joy and gladness with him wherever he went
all the world was glad. The sun danced on the waters, and singing swans flew seven times round the island of Delos
cards.question: Which detail from the passage best develops the theme that the arrival of divine gifts brings harmony and joy to the world?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Jupiter gave Apollo a pair of swans and a golden chariot that could carry him over sea and land.

choices.label: B
choices.text: When Apollo's birth was announced, the sun danced on the waters, swans circled the island, and Juno forgot her anger and bade all things be kind to Leto.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Apollo became tall, strong, and graceful, and his face was as bright as the sunbeams.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Apollo was called by some the Bringer of Light, by others the Master of Song, and by still others the Lord of the Silver Bow.

cards.standardTitle: Text structure and feature purpose
cards.excerpt:
It happened soon afterwards that the king of a certain country not far away was holding games and giving prizes to the best runners and leapers and quoit throwers. And Perseus went thither to try his strength with the other young men of the land; for if he should be able to gain a prize, his name would become known all over the world. No one in that country knew who he was, but all wondered at his noble stature and his strength and skill; and it was easy enough for him to win all the prizes.

One day, as he was showing what he could do, he threw a heavy quoit a great deal farther than any had been thrown before. It fell in the crowd of lookers-on, and struck a stranger who was standing there. The stranger threw up his hands and sank upon the ground; and when Perseus ran to help him, he saw that he was dead. Now this man was none other than Danaë's father, the old king of Argos. He had fled from his kingdom to save his life, and in doing so had only met his death.
cards.whyThisWorks: The two-paragraph structure clearly contrasts Perseus's celebrated triumph in paragraph one with the fatal accident in paragraph two, giving students a concrete example of how a second paragraph can reframe or complicate the meaning of the first.
cards.skillStrategy: Ask yourself: what job does this paragraph do for the one before it—does it continue, contrast, explain, or complicate the earlier details?
evidencePoints: it was easy enough for him to win all the prizes
He had fled from his kingdom to save his life, and in doing so had only met his death
cards.question: The first paragraph establishes that Perseus entered the games so 'his name would become known all over the world' and that 'it was easy enough for him to win all the prizes.' What is the primary job of the second paragraph in relation to those details?

choices.label: A
choices.text: It extends the celebration of Perseus's athletic success by describing how the quoit 'fell in the crowd of lookers-on,' confirming that his throw surpassed every competitor and secured his worldwide fame.

choices.label: B
choices.text: It shifts from Perseus's effortless victory to an accidental death—the quoit strikes a stranger revealed to be 'Danaë's father, the old king of Argos'—showing that his triumph carries a fateful and devastating consequence.

choices.label: C
choices.text: It explains why 'no one in that country knew who he was' by revealing that Danaë's father had secretly traveled ahead of Perseus to warn the crowd not to recognize him.

choices.label: D
choices.text: It introduces Danaë's father as a rival who came to the games to publicly challenge Perseus and reclaim his throne, providing the reason Perseus had competed anonymously in the first place.

cards.standardTitle: Central idea and supporting evidence
cards.excerpt:
In a little town north of Delphi, and not very far from the sea, there lived a young man named Admetus. He was the ruler of the town, and hence was called its king; but his kingdom was so small that he could walk all round it in half a day. He knew the name of every man and woman and child in the town, and everybody loved him because he was so gentle and kind and at the same time a king.

Late one day, when the rain was falling and the wind was blowing cold from the mountains, a beggar came to his door. The man was ragged and dirty and half starved, and Admetus knew that he must have come from some strange land, for in his own country no one ever went hungry. So the kind king took him into the house and fed him; and after the man had bathed he gave him his own warm cloak, and bade the servants make a place for him to sleep through the night.
cards.whyThisWorks: The two paragraphs each show a different dimension of Admetus's character—beloved ruler and generous host—allowing students to practice lifting a central idea that unifies both details rather than selecting a single isolated fact.
cards.skillStrategy: Ask yourself what the two paragraphs are both trying to show about Admetus, then put that idea into your own words instead of just naming a topic like 'kindness' or copying one detail.
evidencePoints: everybody loved him because he was so gentle and kind and at the same time a king
the kind king took him into the house and fed him; and after the man had bathed he gave him his own warm cloak
cards.question: The narrator describes Admetus as someone 'everybody loved' in the first paragraph and then shows him feeding, clothing, and sheltering a ragged stranger in the second paragraph. What central idea do both of these details work together to express?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Admetus's kingdom was unusually small, which made it easy for him to know every person who lived there.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Admetus demonstrated through his actions toward both his own people and a helpless stranger that his kindness was a defining part of who he was as a ruler.

choices.label: C
choices.text: A cold, rainy night brought an unexpected beggar to Admetus's door, changing the king's quiet evening.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Admetus was admired because no one in his country ever went hungry, unlike people in distant lands.

cards.standardTitle: Key literary elements add layers of meaning
cards.excerpt: Just before dark on the second evening, a she-bear came strolling down the mountain side from her den. She was out looking for her cubs, for some hunters had stolen them that very day while she was away from home. She heard the moans of the little babe, and wondered if it was not one of her lost cubs; and when she saw it lying so helpless on the moss she went to it and looked at it kindly. Was it possible that a little bear could be changed into a pretty babe with fat white hands and with a beautiful gold chain around its neck? The old bear did not know; and as the child looked at her with its bright black eyes, she growled softly and licked its face with her warm tongue and then lay down beside it, just as she would have done with her own little cubs. The babe was too young to feel afraid, and it cuddled close to the old bear and felt that it had found a friend.
