After a while it fell asleep; but the bear guarded it until morning and then went down the mountain side to look for food.
cards.whyThisWorks: The bear's actions—growling softly, licking the baby's face, lying beside it, and guarding it through the night—reveal a maternal instinct that transcends species, adding thematic meaning about the universality of nurturing and the innocence of the child.
cards.skillStrategy: When a character acts in an unexpected way, ask yourself what that action reveals about who they are and what larger idea the author might be expressing.
evidencePoints: she growled softly and licked its face with her warm tongue and then lay down beside it, just as she would have done with her own little cubs
the bear guarded it until morning and then went down the mountain side to look for food
cards.question: The she-bear 'growled softly and licked its face with her warm tongue and then lay down beside it, just as she would have done with her own little cubs.' What does this action reveal about the she-bear's character?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The bear is confused by the baby's gold chain and stays close to investigate the strange object.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The bear's grief over her stolen cubs drives her to extend the same protective tenderness to the helpless infant, showing that her maternal instinct overrides the boundary between wild animal and human child.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The bear recognizes the baby as a human and remains beside it out of fear that the hunters who stole her cubs are still nearby.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The bear stays with the baby only until it falls asleep, revealing that her concern for her own missing cubs is stronger than any care she feels for the infant.

cards.standardTitle: Theme development across a literary text
cards.excerpt:
In the evening, before dark, the bear came again and carried the child to her own den under the shelter of a rock where vines and wild flowers grew; and every day after that she came and gave the child food and played with it. And all the bears on the mountain learned about the wonderful cub that had been found, and came to see it; but not one of them offered to harm it. And the little girl grew fast and became strong, and after a while could walk and run among the trees and rocks and brambles on the round top of the mountain; but her bear mother would not allow her to wander far from the den beneath the rock where the vines and the wild flowers grew.

One day some hunters came up the mountain to look for game, and one of them pulled aside the vines which grew in front of the old bear's home. He was surprised to see the beautiful child lying on the grass and playing with the flowers which she had gathered. But at sight of him she leaped to her feet and bounded away like a frightened deer. She led the hunters a fine chase among the trees and rocks; but there were a dozen of them, and it was not long till they caught her.
cards.whyThisWorks: The excerpt shows a girl raised by a bear mother in the wild who flees hunters 'like a frightened deer' yet is ultimately caught by 'a dozen of them,' providing concrete evidence that the human world inevitably reclaims those raised outside it—directly supporting theme development through specific textual details.
cards.skillStrategy: To find evidence that proves a theme, locate two or more specific details that point in the same direction and ask what idea they together support about life or human nature.
evidencePoints: she leaped to her feet and bounded away like a frightened deer
there were a dozen of them, and it was not long till they caught her
cards.question: The narrator describes the girl bounding away 'like a frightened deer' yet notes that 'there were a dozen of them, and it was not long till they caught her.' How do these two details work together to develop a theme in the excerpt?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Her deer-like speed shows she has become fully wild, and the dozen hunters simply illustrate that group hunting is more efficient than hunting alone on a mountain.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Her wild speed—gained from years among the bears—cannot overcome the collective force of a dozen hunters, developing the theme that the human world will reclaim those raised apart from it.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Her flight proves the mountain is too dangerous for a child, and her capture shows that the bear mother's protection was never strong enough to keep her safe from human threats.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Her ability to lead the hunters on a long chase through trees and rocks proves that the bear mother's care made her stronger than any ordinary child, which is the excerpt's central idea.

cards.standardTitle: Text structure and feature purpose
cards.excerpt:
From that day the town grew and spread, and soon there was not room on the hilltop for all the people. Then houses were built in the plain around the foot of the hill, and a great road was built to the sea, three miles away; and in all the world there was no city more fair than Athens.

In the old market place on the top of the hill the people built a temple to Athena, the ruins of which may still be seen. The olive tree grew and nourished; and, when you visit Athens, people will show you the very spot where it stood. Many other trees sprang from it, and in time became a blessing both to Greece and to all the other countries round the great sea. As for the horse, he wandered away across the plains towards the north and found a home at last in distant Thessaly beyond the River Peneus. And I have heard it said that all the horses in the world have descended from that one which Neptune brought out of the rock; but of the truth of this story there may be some doubts.
cards.whyThisWorks: The two paragraphs have distinct structural jobs—the first concludes the city's founding, the second extends the myth by tracing what happened to the olive tree and the horse afterward—giving students a clear contrast in paragraph function to analyze.
cards.skillStrategy: Ask yourself: does this paragraph start something new, wrap something up, or follow up on what came before? Look for signal words and what the paragraph adds to the story.
evidencePoints: in all the world there was no city more fair than Athens
As for the horse, he wandered away across the plains towards the north and found a home at last in distant Thessaly beyond the River Peneus
cards.question: The first paragraph ends with the claim that 'in all the world there was no city more fair than Athens.' What is the job of the second paragraph in relation to that ending?

choices.label: A
choices.text: It restates the founding of Athens by repeating how Athena won the contest over Neptune.

choices.label: B
choices.text: It extends the story beyond Athens's founding by tracing the separate fates of the olive tree and the horse after the city was established.

choices.label: C
choices.text: It shifts the focus to prove that Neptune's horse was more valuable than Athena's olive tree by describing its journey to Thessaly.

choices.label: D
choices.text: It contrasts Athens's greatness with the poverty of the northern lands where the horse eventually wandered.

cards.standardTitle: Central idea and supporting evidence
cards.excerpt:
And Daedalus built for King Minos a most wonderful palace with floors of marble and pillars of granite; and in the palace he set up golden statues which had tongues and could talk; and for splendor and beauty there was no other building in all the wide earth that could be compared with it.

There lived in those days among the hills of Crete a terrible monster called the Minotaur, the like of which has never been seen from that time until now. This creature, it was said, had the body of a man, but the face and head of a wild bull and the fierce nature of a mountain lion. The people of Crete would not have killed him if they could; for they thought that the Mighty Folk who lived with Jupiter on the mountain top had sent him among them, and that these beings would be angry if any one should take his life. He was the pest and terror of all the land. Where he was least expected, there he was sure to be; and almost every day some man, woman, or child was caught and devoured by him.
cards.whyThisWorks: The two paragraphs place Daedalus's marvel of human achievement directly beside the Minotaur's reign of terror, forcing students to synthesize both details into a central idea rather than selecting an isolated topic or single fact.
cards.skillStrategy: Ask yourself: what do BOTH paragraphs together say about Crete — not just one detail from each — and state that in a plain sentence.
evidencePoints: for splendor and beauty there was no other building in all the wide earth that could be compared with it
He was the pest and terror of all the land. Where he was least expected, there he was sure to be; and almost every day some man, woman, or child was caught and devoured by him.
cards.question: The first paragraph ends by saying the palace had no equal 'in all the wide earth,' and the second paragraph ends by saying the Minotaur devoured 'almost every day some man, woman, or child.' What central idea do these two closing statements together develop about Crete?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Crete was home to the greatest builder who ever lived, and his creations brought lasting fame to King Minos.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Crete was a place where unmatched human wonder and unrelenting deadly terror existed at the same time.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The gods who lived with Jupiter on the mountain top controlled both the beauty and the danger found in Crete.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The Minotaur's daily attacks made the splendor of Daedalus's palace meaningless to the people of Crete.

cards.standardTitle: Key literary elements add layers of meaning
cards.excerpt:
As he spoke he threw his rope towards Theseus and tried to entangle him in its coils. But the young man leaped aside, and when the robber rushed upon him, he dodged beneath his hands and seized his legs, as he had seized Club-carrier's, and threw him heavily to the ground. Then the two wrestled together among the trees, but not long, for Sinis was no match for his lithe young foe; and Theseus knelt upon the robber's back as he lay prone among the leaves, and tied him with his own cord to the two pine trees which were already bent down. "As you would have done unto me, so will I do unto you," he said.

Then Pine-bender wept and prayed and made many a fair promise; but Theseus would not hear him. He turned away, the trees sprang up, and the robber's body was left dangling from their branches.

Now this old Pine-bender had a daughter named Perigune, who was no more like him than a fair and tender violet is like the gnarled old oak at whose feet it nestles; and it was she who cared for the flowers and the rare plants which grew in the garden by the robber's house. When she saw how Theseus had dealt with her father, she was afraid and ran to hide herself from him.
cards.whyThisWorks: Theseus's words 'As you would have done unto me, so will I do unto you' and his refusal to hear Pine-bender's pleas reveal a character defined by strict, unyielding justice rather than mercy, adding moral complexity to his heroism.
cards.skillStrategy: When a character speaks or acts at a key moment, ask what that choice reveals about who they are and what the author wants readers to think about them.
evidencePoints: "As you would have done unto me, so will I do unto you," he said.
Then Pine-bender wept and prayed and made many a fair promise; but Theseus would not hear him.
cards.question: Read the following lines from the passage: 'Then Pine-bender wept and prayed and made many a fair promise; but Theseus would not hear him.' What does Theseus's refusal to listen reveal about his character?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Theseus is reckless and acts without thinking about the consequences of punishing Sinis.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Theseus is governed by an uncompromising sense of justice, unwilling to grant mercy even when his enemy begs for it.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Theseus is motivated by personal hatred for Sinis and acts out of anger rather than any principle.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Theseus is distracted by thoughts of Perigune and turns away before he can consider Sinis's pleas.

cards.standardTitle: Theme development across a literary text
cards.excerpt:
So, all through the day he pretended to be planning some great work for the king, but every night he locked himself up in his chamber and wrought secretly by candle light. By and by he had made for himself a pair of strong wings, and for Icarus another pair of smaller ones; and then, one midnight, when everybody was asleep, the two went out to see if they could fly. They fastened the wings to their shoulders with wax, and then sprang up into the air. They could not fly very far at first, but they did so well that they felt sure of doing much better in time.

The next night Daedalus made some changes in the wings. He put on an extra strap or two; he took out a feather from one wing, and put a new feather into another; and then he and Icarus went out in the moonlight to try them again. They did finely this time. They flew up to the top of the king's palace, and then they sailed away over the walls of the city and alighted on the top of a hill. But they were not ready to undertake a long journey yet; and so, just before daybreak, they flew back home. Every fair night after that they practiced with their wings, and at the end of a month they felt as safe in the air as on the ground, and could skim over the hilltops like birds.
cards.whyThisWorks: The excerpt contains both true-but-topic-only details (wax fastening, palace flight) and genuine theme-developing details (nightly practice, month-long progression to confidence), forcing students to distinguish evidence that builds the theme of mastery through persistence from details that merely advance the plot.
cards.skillStrategy: Ask yourself: does this detail show the theme growing over time, or does it just describe what happened in the story?
evidencePoints: Every fair night after that they practiced with their wings, and at the end of a month they felt as safe in the air as on the ground
He put on an extra strap or two; he took out a feather from one wing, and put a new feather into another
cards.question: The narrator states that 'at the end of a month they felt as safe in the air as on the ground, and could skim over the hilltops like birds.' Which earlier detail from the excerpt most directly develops the theme that mastery requires persistent, incremental effort?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Daedalus and Icarus fastened their wings to their shoulders with wax and sprang into the air on their first midnight attempt.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Daedalus adjusted the wings before the second attempt by adding extra straps and swapping individual feathers, and then the two practiced every fair night that followed.

choices.label: C
choices.text: On their second attempt, Daedalus and Icarus flew to the top of the king's palace and then sailed over the walls of the city.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Daedalus worked secretly by candlelight each night while pretending to plan a great work for the king during the day.

cards.standardTitle: Text structure and feature purpose
cards.excerpt:
Day after day, while at his work, Daedalus pondered over this matter, and soon his heart was filled with hatred towards young Perdix. One morning when the two were putting up an ornament on the outer wall of Athena's temple, Daedalus bade his nephew go out on a narrow scaffold which hung high over the edge of the rocky cliff whereon the temple stood. Then, when the lad obeyed, it was easy enough, with a blow of a hammer, to knock the scaffold from its fastenings.

Poor Perdix fell headlong through the air, and he would have been dashed in pieces upon the stones at the foot of the cliff had not kind Athena seen him and taken pity upon him. While he was yet whirling through mid-air she changed him into a partridge, and he flitted away to the hills to live forever in the woods and fields which he loved so well. And to this day, when summer breezes blow and the wild flowers bloom in meadow and glade, the voice of Perdix may still sometimes be heard, calling to his mate from among the grass and reeds or amid the leafy underwoods.
cards.whyThisWorks: The two-paragraph structure clearly demonstrates how a second paragraph can shift function from action/conflict to mythological resolution and origin explanation, making the 'paragraph job' subskill directly teachable.
cards.skillStrategy: Ask yourself: what work is this paragraph doing that the previous one did not — is it continuing the same action, shifting focus, resolving conflict, or explaining a cause?
evidencePoints: kind Athena seen him and taken pity upon him…she changed him into a partridge
to this day, when summer breezes blow and the wild flowers bloom in meadow and glade, the voice of Perdix may still sometimes be heard
cards.question: The first paragraph ends with Perdix falling 'headlong through the air' after Daedalus knocks the scaffold loose. What is the primary job of the second paragraph in relation to the first?

choices.label: A
choices.text: It returns attention to Daedalus by describing how his 'hatred towards young Perdix' grew as he watched the boy fall from the cliff above Athena's temple.

choices.label: B
choices.text: It shifts away from Daedalus's violent act to resolve Perdix's fate through Athena's intervention, then extends the moment into a mythological origin story ending with Perdix's voice heard 'to this day' in meadow and glade.

choices.label: C
choices.text: It introduces a new conflict by showing that Athena punished Daedalus for committing his crime against Perdix on the outer wall of her own temple.

choices.label: D
choices.text: It resolves the danger by revealing that Perdix survived the fall, landed safely at the foot of the cliff, and returned to finish placing the ornament on Athena's temple.

cards.standardTitle: Central idea and supporting evidence
cards.excerpt:
When at last he was arrayed to their liking, they told him where he would find the Gorgons, and what he should do to obtain the terrible head and escape alive. Then they kissed him and wished him good luck, and bade him hasten to do the dangerous deed. And Perseus donned the Cap of Darkness, and sped away and away towards the farthermost edge of the earth; and the three Maidens went back to their tree to sing and to dance and to guard the golden apples until the old world should become young again.

With the sharp sword at his side and the bright shield upon his arm, Perseus flew bravely onward in search of the dreadful Gorgons; but he had the Cap of Darkness upon his head, and you could no more have seen him than you can see the wind. He flew so swiftly that it was not long until he had crossed the mighty ocean which encircles the earth, and had come to the sunless land which lies beyond; and then he knew, from what the Maidens had told him, that the lair of the Gorgons could not be far away.
cards.whyThisWorks: The two paragraphs together trace Perseus's departure from the Maidens through his arrival near the Gorgons' lair, requiring students to distinguish the central idea from isolated details like the Cap of Darkness or the Maidens' farewell.
cards.skillStrategy: Ask yourself what most of the sentences are working together to show, not just what one sentence says.
evidencePoints: Perseus donned the Cap of Darkness, and sped away and away towards the farthermost edge of the earth
With the sharp sword at his side and the bright shield upon his arm, Perseus flew bravely onward in search of the dreadful Gorgons
cards.question: The narrator describes Perseus as departing with the Maidens' instructions, donning the Cap of Darkness, crossing 'the mighty ocean which encircles the earth,' and arriving near the Gorgons' lair. What central idea do these details work together to express?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The three Maidens' farewell kiss and good wishes were the most important preparation Perseus received before his quest.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Equipped with the Maidens' guidance and magical gifts, Perseus boldly undertakes a perilous journey toward his deadly goal.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The Cap of Darkness, which made Perseus invisible like the wind, was the single reason he could survive the journey.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The sunless land beyond the ocean marks the boundary of the known world, which Perseus was the first to cross.

cards.standardTitle: Rhetorical appeals and author purpose
cards.excerpt:
In a few days they came to a large island called Cyprus. Cadmus went on shore, and tried to talk with the strange people who lived there. They were very kind to him, but they did not understand his language. At last he made out by signs to tell them who he was, and to ask them if they had seen his little sister Europa or the white bull that had carried her away. They shook their heads and pointed to the west.

Then the young men sailed on in their little ship. They came to many islands, and stopped at every one, to see if they could find any trace of Europa; but they heard no news of her at all. At last, they came to the country which we now call Greece. It was a new country then, and only a few people lived there, and Cadmus soon learned to speak their language well. For a long time he wandered from one little town to another, always telling the story of his lost sister.
cards.whyThisWorks: The phrase 'always telling the story of his lost sister' functions as a refrain-like image that conveys Cadmus's relentless devotion, allowing students to analyze how figurative compression of repeated action serves the author's explanatory purpose of portraying heroic loyalty.
cards.skillStrategy: When you spot figurative or compressed language, ask yourself: what feeling or idea does this create, and how does that help the author make a point or build understanding?
evidencePoints: always telling the story of his lost sister
For a long time he wandered from one little town to another
cards.question: Read this sentence from the passage: 'For a long time he wandered from one little town to another, always telling the story of his lost sister.' How does the phrase 'always telling the story of his lost sister' help Baldwin achieve his explanatory purpose?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The phrase shows that Cadmus had given up hope of finding Europa and was simply sharing a tale to entertain the people of Greece.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The phrase compresses Cadmus's endless repetition into a single image, conveying that his search was driven by unwavering devotion rather than mere duty.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The phrase explains that Cadmus needed to practice the Greek language by repeating the same words in every town he visited.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The phrase suggests that Cadmus was famous throughout Greece because so many people had already heard his sister's story.

cards.standardTitle: Key literary elements add layers of meaning
cards.excerpt:
Then Apollo with his silver bow in his hands went up towards the place where the Python lay. The monster had worn great paths through the grass and among the rocks, and his lair was not hard to find. When he caught sight of Apollo, he uncoiled himself, and came out to meet him. The bright prince saw the creature's glaring eyes and blood-red mouth, and heard the rush of his scaly body over the stones. He fitted an arrow to his bow, and stood still. The Python saw that his foe was no common man, and turned to flee. Then the arrow sped from the bow--and the monster was dead.

"Here I will build my house," said Apollo.

Close to the foot of the steep cliff, and beneath the spot where Jupiter's eagles had fallen, he laid the foundations; and soon where had been the lair of the Python, the white walls of Apollo's temple arose among the rocks. Then the poor people of the land came and built their houses near by; and Apollo lived among them many years, and taught them to be gentle and wise, and showed them how to be happy. The mountain was no longer savage and wild, but was a place of music and song; the valley was no longer dark and lonely, but was filled with beauty and light.
cards.whyThisWorks: Apollo's calm, deliberate stillness in the face of the Python—fitting an arrow and standing still while the monster charges—contrasts sharply with the Python's frantic retreat, revealing Apollo as a figure of composed, divine authority whose character transforms the landscape itself.
cards.skillStrategy: When a character acts in a surprising or deliberate way, ask what that action reveals about who they are and what the author wants you to understand about them.
evidencePoints: He fitted an arrow to his bow, and stood still.
Apollo lived among them many years, and taught them to be gentle and wise, and showed them how to be happy.
cards.question: Read this sentence from the passage: 'He fitted an arrow to his bow, and stood still.' What does Apollo's stillness in this moment reveal about his character?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Apollo is uncertain whether his arrow can defeat the Python, so he pauses to calculate the risk before acting.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Apollo's calm composure in the face of the charging monster establishes him as a figure of controlled, superior power rather than fearful reaction.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Apollo stands still because he recognizes the Python as a worthy opponent and wants to give the creature a fair chance to escape.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Apollo freezes out of surprise when the Python turns to flee, showing that he did not expect the monster to back down.

cards.standardTitle: Theme development across a literary text
cards.excerpt:
The beast sprang at Cadmus, and tried to seize him with its sharp claws. But Cadmus leaped quickly aside and struck it in the neck with his long sword. A great stream of black blood gushed out, and the dragon soon fell to the ground dead. Cadmus had seen many fearful sights, but never anything so dreadful as this beast. He had never been in so great danger before. He sat down on the ground and trembled; and, all the time, he was weeping for his two friends. How now was he to build a city, with no one to help him?

While Cadmus was still weeping he was surprised to hear some one calling him. He stood up and looked around. On the hillside before him was a tall woman who had a helmet on her head and a shield in her hand. Her eyes were gray, and her face, though not beautiful, was very noble. Cadmus knew at once that she was Athena, the queen of the air--she who gives wisdom to men.
cards.whyThisWorks: The excerpt shows Cadmus defeating the dragon through strength yet immediately collapsing in grief and helplessness, then receiving Athena—'she who gives wisdom to men'—demonstrating that physical victory alone is insufficient for the greater task of building a city.
cards.skillStrategy: Look for the moment in the passage where a character's action or feeling directly supports the central message the author is building.
evidencePoints: How now was he to build a city, with no one to help him?
she who gives wisdom to men
cards.question: After killing the dragon, Cadmus asks, 'How now was he to build a city, with no one to help him?' and Athena appears as 'she who gives wisdom to men.' Which detail most directly develops the theme that physical strength alone cannot complete a great undertaking?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The dragon's black blood gushed out and it fell dead, proving Cadmus won the fight.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Cadmus sat trembling and weeping after his victory, unable to see how to build a city without help.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Cadmus had never encountered anything as dreadful as the dragon before this moment.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Athena's face was described as noble, though not beautiful, as she stood on the hillside.

cards.standardTitle: Text structure and feature purpose
cards.excerpt:
When at last he was arrayed to their liking, they told him where he would find the Gorgons, and what he should do to obtain the terrible head and escape alive. Then they kissed him and wished him good luck, and bade him hasten to do the dangerous deed. And Perseus donned the Cap of Darkness, and sped away and away towards the farthermost edge of the earth; and the three Maidens went back to their tree to sing and to dance and to guard the golden apples until the old world should become young again.

With the sharp sword at his side and the bright shield upon his arm, Perseus flew bravely onward in search of the dreadful Gorgons; but he had the Cap of Darkness upon his head, and you could no more have seen him than you can see the wind. He flew so swiftly that it was not long until he had crossed the mighty ocean which encircles the earth, and had come to the sunless land which lies beyond; and then he knew, from what the Maidens had told him, that the lair of the Gorgons could not be far away.
cards.whyThisWorks: The two paragraphs have distinct structural jobs—the first closes the scene with the Maidens and launches Perseus, while the second extends that departure by tracking his flight across the ocean toward the Gorgons—giving students a clear contrast in paragraph function to analyze.
cards.skillStrategy: Ask yourself: does this paragraph wrap something up, or does it push the action forward by adding new details about what happens next?
evidencePoints: Perseus donned the Cap of Darkness, and sped away and away towards the farthermost edge of the earth; and the three Maidens went back to their tree to sing and to dance
he flew so swiftly that it was not long until he had crossed the mighty ocean which encircles the earth, and had come to the sunless land which lies beyond
cards.question: The first paragraph ends with Perseus speeding away and the Maidens returning to their tree. What is the job of the second paragraph in relation to that ending?

choices.label: A
choices.text: It concludes the quest by revealing that Perseus has finally located the Gorgons in their sunless lair.

choices.label: B
choices.text: It extends Perseus's departure by tracing his flight across the ocean and bringing him to the edge of the Gorgons' territory.

choices.label: C
choices.text: It contrasts Perseus's bravery with the Maidens' carefree return to singing and dancing at the golden apple tree.

choices.label: D
choices.text: It introduces the Cap of Darkness as a new obstacle Perseus must overcome before he can face the Gorgons.

cards.standardTitle: Central idea and supporting evidence
cards.excerpt:
He heard a sound as of some one breathing heavily, and he looked around sharply to see where it came from. Among the foul weeds which grew close to the bank of a muddy river there was something which glittered in the pale light. He flew a little nearer; but he did not dare to look straight forward, lest he should all at once meet the gaze of a Gorgon, and be changed into stone. So he turned around, and held the shining shield before him in such a way that by looking into it he could see objects behind him as in a mirror.

Ah, what a dreadful sight it was! Half hidden among the weeds lay the three monsters, fast asleep, with their golden wings folded about them. Their brazen claws were stretched out as though ready to seize their prey; and their shoulders were covered with sleeping snakes. The two largest of the Gorgons lay with their heads tucked under their wings as birds hide their heads when they go to sleep. But the third, who lay between them, slept with her face turned up towards the sky; and Perseus knew that she was Medusa.
cards.whyThisWorks: The excerpt shows Perseus using a shield as a mirror to avoid the Gorgons' gaze while locating Medusa, giving students a concrete passage moment to identify as the central idea rather than an isolated detail or broad topic.
cards.skillStrategy: Ask yourself: what is the most important idea that both paragraphs are working together to show — not just a detail from one sentence, but the point the whole passage is building?
evidencePoints: he turned around, and held the shining shield before him in such a way that by looking into it he could see objects behind him as in a mirror
Perseus knew that she was Medusa
cards.question: In these two paragraphs, Perseus turns his back and uses his shield as a mirror before he can identify Medusa among the sleeping Gorgons. What central idea do both paragraphs work together to express?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The three Gorgons are so physically fearsome — with brazen claws, golden wings, and snakes on their shoulders — that no hero could survive a direct encounter with them.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Perseus must use careful, indirect observation to locate and identify Medusa without risking being turned to stone by a direct look.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Medusa is more dangerous than the other two Gorgons because she alone sleeps with her face turned upward, making her the greatest threat.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The Gorgons are completely unaware of Perseus because they are fast asleep, giving him a safe and easy opportunity to find Medusa.

cards.standardTitle: Key literary elements add layers of meaning
cards.excerpt:
The hunters had never taken such game as that before, and they were so well satisfied that they did not care to hunt any more that day. The child struggled and fought as hard as she knew how, but it was of no use. The hunters carried her down the mountain, and took her to the house where they lived on the other side of the forest. At first she cried all the time, for she sadly missed the bear that had been a mother to her so long. But the hunters made a great pet of her, and gave her many pretty things to play with, and were very kind; and it was not long till she began to like her new home.

The hunters named her Atalanta, and when she grew older, they made her a bow and arrows, and taught her how to shoot; and they gave her a light spear, and showed her how to carry it and how to hurl it at the game or at an enemy. Then they took her with them when they went hunting, and there was nothing in the world that pleased her so much as roaming through the woods and running after the deer and other wild animals. Her feet became very swift, so that she could run faster than any of the men; and her arms were so strong and her eyes so sharp and true that with her arrow or her spear she never missed the mark. And she grew up to be very tall and graceful, and was known throughout all Arcadia as the fleet-footed huntress.
cards.whyThisWorks: Atalanta's swift adaptation from grief to belonging, followed by her physical and skill development, shows how a character's actions and growth reveal themes of resilience and identity shaped by environment.
cards.skillStrategy: When a character changes or develops, ask what that change reveals about who they are becoming and what the author wants you to understand about them.
evidencePoints: At first she cried all the time, for she sadly missed the bear that had been a mother to her so long.
there was nothing in the world that pleased her so much as roaming through the woods and running after the deer and other wild animals
cards.question: In the second paragraph, the narrator describes how Atalanta's 'feet became very swift' and her 'arms were so strong and her eyes so sharp and true that with her arrow or her spear she never missed the mark.' What does this description of Atalanta's physical development reveal about her character?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Her physical growth shows that the hunters trained her against her will, and she mastered their skills only to one day escape back to the mountain.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Her mastery of speed, strength, and aim reveals that her identity is fully shaped by the wild life she was raised in, making the forest her true home rather than a place of captivity.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Her exceptional abilities prove she was always superior to the hunters, suggesting she never truly needed their guidance to survive.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Her swiftness and accuracy show that she grieved the bear by channeling her sadness into physical training as a way to honor her lost mother.

cards.standardTitle: Theme development across a literary text
cards.excerpt:
In a few days they came to a large island called Cyprus. Cadmus went on shore, and tried to talk with the strange people who lived there. They were very kind to him, but they did not understand his language. At last he made out by signs to tell them who he was, and to ask them if they had seen his little sister Europa or the white bull that had carried her away. They shook their heads and pointed to the west.

Then the young men sailed on in their little ship. They came to many islands, and stopped at every one, to see if they could find any trace of Europa; but they heard no news of her at all. At last, they came to the country which we now call Greece. It was a new country then, and only a few people lived there, and Cadmus soon learned to speak their language well. For a long time he wandered from one little town to another, always telling the story of his lost sister.
cards.whyThisWorks: The excerpt contains both theme-developing details (Cadmus's relentless searching and storytelling about Europa) and true-but-topic-only details (Cyprus being a large island, Greece being a new country), giving students clear practice distinguishing evidence that proves theme from evidence that merely matches the topic.
cards.skillStrategy: Ask yourself: does this detail show the theme in action, or does it just describe the setting or situation without connecting to what the theme claims about people?
evidencePoints: For a long time he wandered from one little town to another, always telling the story of his lost sister.
They came to many islands, and stopped at every one, to see if they could find any trace of Europa; but they heard no news of her at all.
cards.question: The theme of this excerpt is that loyalty to family drives a person to persist through repeated failure. Which detail from the excerpt best develops that theme, rather than simply describing the topic of Cadmus's journey?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Cyprus is described as 'a large island' whose people 'did not understand his language,' showing that Cadmus faced communication barriers.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Cadmus 'wandered from one little town to another' in Greece 'for a long time,' continuing to tell the story of his lost sister even after finding no news of her at any island.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Greece 'was a new country then, and only a few people lived there,' explaining why Cadmus had to learn a new language.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The people of Cyprus 'pointed to the west,' giving Cadmus a direction to sail after he communicated through signs.

cards.standardTitle: Text structure and feature purpose
cards.excerpt:
He heard a sound as of some one breathing heavily, and he looked around sharply to see where it came from. Among the foul weeds which grew close to the bank of a muddy river there was something which glittered in the pale light. He flew a little nearer; but he did not dare to look straight forward, lest he should all at once meet the gaze of a Gorgon, and be changed into stone. So he turned around, and held the shining shield before him in such a way that by looking into it he could see objects behind him as in a mirror.

Ah, what a dreadful sight it was! Half hidden among the weeds lay the three monsters, fast asleep, with their golden wings folded about them. Their brazen claws were stretched out as though ready to seize their prey; and their shoulders were covered with sleeping snakes. The two largest of the Gorgons lay with their heads tucked under their wings as birds hide their heads when they go to sleep. But the third, who lay between them, slept with her face turned up towards the sky; and Perseus knew that she was Medusa.
cards.whyThisWorks: The two paragraphs model a clear structural relationship: the first ends with Perseus turning his shield to use it as a mirror, and the second opens with 'Ah, what a dreadful sight it was!'—making the second paragraph's job explicitly to deliver what the mirror-trick reveals.
cards.skillStrategy: Ask yourself: what job does this paragraph do for the idea that came before it—does it introduce, extend, contrast, prove, shift, or conclude?
evidencePoints: he turned around, and held the shining shield before him in such a way that by looking into it he could see objects behind him as in a mirror
Ah, what a dreadful sight it was! Half hidden among the weeds lay the three monsters, fast asleep
cards.question: In the second paragraph, the narrator opens with 'Ah, what a dreadful sight it was!' and then describes the sleeping Gorgons. What job does this second paragraph perform in relation to the first paragraph's ending, where Perseus 'held the shining shield before him' to see 'objects behind him as in a mirror'?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The second paragraph contrasts the calm scene Perseus expected with the violent behavior the Gorgons actually display when disturbed.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The second paragraph reveals the sight produced by the mirror-shield strategy Perseus adopted at the end of the first paragraph, extending the action by showing exactly what he sees reflected back at him.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The second paragraph shifts away from Perseus entirely and focuses on describing the Gorgons' appearance without connecting back to his actions in the first paragraph.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The second paragraph introduces a new problem for Perseus by explaining that the two largest Gorgons, not Medusa, are the true threat he must overcome.

cards.standardTitle: Central idea and supporting evidence
cards.excerpt:
The king sent out his fastest ship to try to overtake the bull. The sailors rowed far out to sea, much farther than any ship had ever gone before; but no trace of Europa could be found. When they came back, everybody felt that there was no more hope. All the women and children in the town wept for the lost Europa. The king shut himself up in his house, and did not eat nor drink for three days. Then he called his son Cadmus, and bade him take a ship and go in search of his sister; and he told him that, no matter what dangers might be in his way, he must not come back until she was found.

Cadmus was glad to go. He chose twenty brave young men to go with him, and set sail the very next day. It was a great undertaking; for they were to pass through an unknown sea, and they did not know what lands they would come to. Indeed, it was feared that they would never come to any land at all. Ships did not dare to go far from the shore in those days. But Cadmus and his friends were not afraid. They were ready to face any danger.
cards.whyThisWorks: The excerpt contrasts the kingdom's despair and failed search with Cadmus's willing, fearless departure into unknown danger, giving students clear evidence to distinguish a central idea from isolated details or topics.
cards.skillStrategy: Ask yourself what both paragraphs are mostly about together, not just one detail or one character's feeling, and state it as a complete idea.
evidencePoints: he must not come back until she was found
Cadmus and his friends were not afraid. They were ready to face any danger.
cards.question: The narrator states that Cadmus 'was glad to go' and that he and his friends 'were ready to face any danger.' What central idea do these details, along with the king's command that Cadmus 'must not come back until she was found,' develop across both paragraphs?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The king's refusal to eat or drink for three days shows how deeply the royal family suffered after Europa's disappearance.

choices.label: B
choices.text: When all other efforts to find Europa failed, Cadmus accepted a dangerous and uncertain mission and set out without hesitation.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Ancient sailors feared open water so much that no ship had ever successfully traveled far from shore before Cadmus's voyage.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The entire kingdom lost hope of finding Europa, leaving the king with no choice but to send his son on an impossible task.

cards.standardTitle: Key literary elements add layers of meaning
cards.excerpt:
And so, as the years went by, Meleager grew up to be a brave young man, so gentle and noble that his name became known in every land of Greece. He did many daring deeds and, with other heroes, went on a famous voyage across the seas in search of a marvelous fleece of gold; and when he returned to Calydon the people declared that he was the worthiest of the sons of OEneus to become their king.

Now it happened one summer that the vineyards of Calydon were fuller of grapes than they had ever been before, and there was so much wheat in the fields that the people did not know what to do with it.

"I will tell you what to do," said King OEneus. "We will have a thanksgiving day, and we will give some of the grain and some of the fruit to the Mighty Beings who sit among the clouds on the mountain top. For it is from them that the sunshine and the fair weather and the moist winds and the warm rains have come; and without their aid we could never have had so fine a harvest."

The very next day the king and the people of Calydon went out into the fields and vineyards to offer up their thank offerings. Here and there they built little altars of turf and stones and laid dry grass and twigs upon them; and then on top of the twigs they put some of the largest bunches of grapes and some of the finest heads of wheat, which they thought would please the Mighty Beings who had sent them so great plenty.
cards.whyThisWorks: OEneus's speech in paragraph three directly characterizes him as a humble, grateful leader who attributes the harvest's abundance to divine forces rather than his own rule, giving students a clear passage moment to analyze how word choice in dialogue reveals character.
cards.skillStrategy: When a character speaks, ask what their exact words show about their values or personality—look for what they credit, blame, or prioritize.
evidencePoints: without their aid we could never have had so fine a harvest
it is from them that the sunshine and the fair weather and the moist winds and the warm rains have come
cards.question: In paragraph three, King OEneus tells his people, 'it is from them that the sunshine and the fair weather and the moist winds and the warm rains have come; and without their aid we could never have had so fine a harvest.' What does this speech reveal about OEneus's character as a leader?

choices.label: A
choices.text: He is afraid the Mighty Beings will destroy the harvest if the people do not offer gifts, so he organizes the thanksgiving to protect Calydon from punishment.

choices.label: B
choices.text: He leads with humility and gratitude, crediting the Mighty Beings for the sunshine, fair weather, and rains rather than taking personal credit for Calydon's abundance.

choices.label: C
choices.text: He uses the thanksgiving celebration mainly to display his authority over the people of Calydon by directing where and how the offerings are built.

choices.label: D
choices.text: He doubts his own judgment as king and relies on the Mighty Beings to tell him what to do with the surplus grain and grapes.

cards.standardTitle: Theme development across a literary text
cards.excerpt:
"He is coming!" cried Theseus, and he ran forward to meet the beast. The seven maidens shrieked, but tried to stand up bravely and face their fate; and the six young men stood together with firm-set teeth and clinched fists, ready to fight to the last.

Soon the Minotaur came into view, rushing down the passage towards Theseus, and roaring most terribly. He was twice as tall as a man, and his head was like that of a bull with huge sharp horns and fiery eyes and a mouth as large as a lion's; but the young men could not see the lower part of his body for the cloud of dust which he raised in running. When he saw Theseus with the sword in his hand coming to meet him, he paused, for no one had ever faced him in that way before. Then he put his head down, and rushed forward, bellowing. But Theseus leaped quickly aside, and made a sharp thrust with his sword as he passed, and hewed off one of the monster's legs above the knee.
cards.whyThisWorks: The excerpt contrasts passive endurance (maidens shrieking, young men clenching fists) with Theseus's active advance, letting students distinguish details that develop a theme of bold action over mere endurance from true-but-topic-only details about the monster's appearance.
cards.skillStrategy: Ask yourself: does this detail show the theme in action, or does it just describe the setting or topic without pushing the theme forward?
evidencePoints: When he saw Theseus with the sword in his hand coming to meet him, he paused, for no one had ever faced him in that way before.
Theseus leaped quickly aside, and made a sharp thrust with his sword as he passed, and hewed off one of the monster's legs above the knee.
cards.question: The narrator states that the Minotaur 'paused, for no one had ever faced him in that way before.' Which detail from the excerpt best develops the theme that bold, active resistance is more powerful than waiting to endure danger?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The Minotaur is described as twice as tall as a man, with a bull's head, sharp horns, and a mouth as large as a lion's, establishing how overwhelming the threat inside the labyrinth is.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Theseus runs forward to meet the Minotaur and then leaps aside to thrust with his sword, hewing off the monster's leg—actions that directly cause the creature's defeat rather than simply enduring its attack.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The seven maidens shriek but try to stand bravely and face their fate, showing that even those who are frightened can hold their ground when danger arrives.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The six young men stand together with firm-set teeth and clenched fists, ready to fight to the last, showing that the group prepares itself to meet whatever the Minotaur brings.

cards.standardTitle: Text structure and feature purpose
cards.excerpt:
So Danaë was kept shut up in the prison of brass. She had no one to talk to but her old nurse; and she never saw the land or the sea, but only the blue sky above the open window and now and then a white cloud sailing across. Day after day she sat under the window and wondered why her father kept her in that lonely place, and whether he would ever come and take her out. I do not know how many years passed by, but Danaë grew fairer every day, and by and by she was no longer a child, but a tall and beautiful woman; and Jupiter amid the clouds looked down and saw her and loved her.

One day it seemed to her that the sky opened and a shower of gold fell through the window into the room; and when the blinding shower had ceased, a noble young man stood smiling before her. She did not know--nor do I--that it was mighty Jupiter who had thus come down in the rain; but she thought that he was a brave prince who had come from over the sea to take her out of her prison-house.
cards.whyThisWorks: The two-paragraph structure creates a clear contrast between static captivity ('Day after day') and sudden change ('One day'), giving students a concrete example of how a paragraph's job can be to introduce a turning point that disrupts the pattern established before it.
cards.skillStrategy: Ask yourself: what pattern does the first paragraph set up, and what does the second paragraph do to that pattern — continue it, break it, explain it, or resolve it?
evidencePoints: Day after day she sat under the window and wondered why her father kept her in that lonely place
One day it seemed to her that the sky opened and a shower of gold fell through the window into the room
cards.question: The first paragraph establishes a pattern of unchanging captivity through the phrase 'Day after day she sat under the window and wondered why her father kept her in that lonely place.' What is the job of the second paragraph, which opens with 'One day it seemed to her that the sky opened and a shower of gold fell through the window into the room'?

choices.label: A
choices.text: It extends the pattern of isolation from the first paragraph by describing more time passing as Danaë continues to sit beneath the window, seeing only the sky and an occasional white cloud.

choices.label: B
choices.text: It introduces a sudden turning point — the shower of gold and the appearance of 'a noble young man' — that breaks the 'Day after day' sameness of Danaë's captivity described in the first paragraph.

choices.label: C
choices.text: It shifts the central focus from Danaë's experience to Jupiter's perspective, explaining why 'mighty Jupiter' chose to descend through the clouds and making him the main subject of the passage.

choices.label: D
choices.text: It resolves the wondering Danaë felt in the first paragraph by revealing that the noble young man who appeared through the shower of gold is her father, who has finally come to free her from the prison of brass.

cards.standardTitle: Central idea and supporting evidence
cards.excerpt:
At last the famous Island of Crete was reached, and there Daedalus landed and made himself known; and the King of Crete, who had already heard of his wondrous skill, welcomed him to his kingdom, and gave him a home in his palace, and promised that he should be rewarded with great riches and honor if he would but stay and practice his craft there as he had done in Athens.

Now the name of the King of Crete was Minos. His grandfather, whose name was also Minos, was the son of Europa, a young princess whom a white bull, it was said, had brought on his back across the sea from distant Asia. This elder Minos had been accounted the wisest of men--so wise, indeed, that Jupiter chose him to be one of the judges of the Lower World. The younger Minos was almost as wise as his grandfather; and he was brave and far-seeing and skilled as a ruler of men. He had made all the islands subject to his kingdom, and his ships sailed into every part of the world and brought back to Crete the riches of foreign lands. So it was not hard for him to persuade Daedalus to make his home with him and be the chief of his artisans.
cards.whyThisWorks: The two paragraphs work together to show that Minos's power, wisdom, and wealth—not just Daedalus's skill—explain why Daedalus chose to stay in Crete, giving students a clear central idea to distinguish from isolated details like the elder Minos's judgeship or Daedalus's arrival.
cards.skillStrategy: Ask yourself: what do BOTH paragraphs add up to saying together? The central idea is not just one detail from one paragraph—it is the point the whole passage is building toward.
evidencePoints: the King of Crete…welcomed him to his kingdom, and gave him a home in his palace, and promised that he should be rewarded with great riches and honor

He had made all the islands subject to his kingdom, and his ships sailed into every part of the world and brought back to Crete the riches of foreign lands. So it was not hard for him to persuade Daedalus to make his home with him
cards.question: The first paragraph describes Minos offering Daedalus 'great riches and honor,' and the second paragraph ends with the statement that 'it was not hard for him to persuade Daedalus to make his home with him.' What central idea do these two moments together support?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Daedalus's reputation for 'wondrous skill' was so great that any king in the ancient world would have sought him out.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Minos's combination of wealth, power, and wisdom made Crete an offer Daedalus had every reason to accept.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The elder Minos's legendary wisdom was the main reason the younger Minos became a successful ruler.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Daedalus left Athens in search of riches and found them only after a long journey to the Island of Crete.

cards.standardTitle: Key literary elements add layers of meaning
cards.excerpt:
Mercury did as he wished, and played such strains of sweet music as no one in all the world has heard from that day to this. And as he played, queer old Argus lay down upon the grass and listened, and thought that he had not had so great a treat in all his life. But by and by those sweet sounds wrapped him in so strange a spell that all his eyes closed at once, and he fell into a deep sleep.

This was just what Mercury wished. It was not a brave thing to do, and yet he drew a long, sharp knife from his belt and cut off the head of poor Argus while he slept. Then he ran down the hill to loose the cow and lead her to the town.

But Juno had seen him kill her watchman, and she met him on the road. She cried out to him and told him to let the cow go; and her face was so full of wrath that, as soon as he saw her, he turned and fled, and left poor Io to her fate.

Juno was so much grieved when she saw Argus stretched dead in the grass on the hilltop, that she took his hundred eyes and set them in the tail of a peacock; and there you may still see them to this day.

Then she found a great gadfly, as big as a bat, and sent it to buzz in the white cow's ears, and to bite her and sting her so that she could have no rest all day long. Poor Io ran from place to place to get out of its way; but it buzzed and buzzed, and stung and stung, till she was wild with fright and pain, and wished that she were dead. Day after day she ran, now through the thick woods, now in the long grass that grew on the treeless plains, and now by the shore of the sea.
cards.whyThisWorks: Mercury's actions—lulling Argus to sleep with music and then killing him while he slept—directly reveal his cunning but morally compromised character, and the narrator's aside 'It was not a brave thing to do' layers authorial judgment onto the characterization, giving students a clear moment to analyze how action and commentary together build meaning.
cards.skillStrategy: When a character acts, ask what that action reveals about who they are—and notice whether the narrator comments on it, because that comment adds another layer of meaning.
evidencePoints: It was not a brave thing to do, and yet he drew a long, sharp knife from his belt and cut off the head of poor Argus while he slept.
he turned and fled, and left poor Io to her fate.
cards.question: The narrator states, 'It was not a brave thing to do, and yet he drew a long, sharp knife from his belt and cut off the head of poor Argus while he slept.' What does this moment reveal about Mercury's character?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Mercury is portrayed as a fearless hero who carries out his mission without hesitation or doubt.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Mercury is willing to act through deception and violence to accomplish his goal, even when the narrator signals that his method lacks honor.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Mercury feels deep regret for killing Argus, which is why he later abandons Io when Juno confronts him.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Mercury's skill with music shows he prefers peaceful solutions, and the killing is presented as a last resort forced on him by the gods.

cards.standardTitle: Theme development across a literary text
cards.excerpt:
There was but little that the stranger knew how to do, and so he was sent to the hills to take care of the king's sheep and goats. For a whole year he tended the flocks, finding the greenest pastures and the freshest water for them, and keeping the wolves away. Admetus was very kind to him, as he was to all his servants, and the food and clothing which he gave him were of the best in the land. But the stranger did not tell his name nor say anything about his kindred or his home.

When a year and a day had passed, it so happened that Admetus was walking out among the hills to see his sheep. All at once the sound of music fell upon his ear. It was no such music as shepherds play, but sweeter and richer than any he had ever heard before. He looked to see where the sound came from. Ah! who was that sitting on the hilltop, with the sheep around him listening to his music? Surely it was not his shepherd?
cards.whyThisWorks: The excerpt contrasts the stranger's hidden identity with the unmistakable quality of his music, letting students distinguish a detail that advances the theme of concealed greatness from true-but-off-theme details about Admetus's kindness or the stranger's duties.
cards.skillStrategy: Ask yourself: does this detail show the theme being built, or does it just describe what is happening in the story?
evidencePoints: It was no such music as shepherds play, but sweeter and richer than any he had ever heard before.
the stranger did not tell his name nor say anything about his kindred or his home
cards.question: The narrator describes the music Admetus hears as 'no such music as shepherds play, but sweeter and richer than any he had ever heard before.' Which statement best explains how this specific detail develops the theme that true greatness cannot remain hidden?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The detail shows that Admetus was a careful king who paid close attention to the sounds around him while walking among the hills.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The detail reveals that the stranger's extraordinary nature is breaking through his disguise as a common shepherd, making his hidden greatness impossible to conceal.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The detail establishes that the stranger was skilled at his duties, having spent a whole year finding the greenest pastures and freshest water for the flocks.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The detail confirms that Admetus treated the stranger generously, giving him food and clothing of the best in the land despite not knowing his identity.

cards.standardTitle: Text structure and feature purpose
cards.excerpt:
Month after month passed by, and still AEgeus lingered with his bride and trusted his elders to see to the affairs of Athens. Then one morning, when the gardens of Troezen were full of roses and the heather was green on the hills, a babe was born to AEthra--a boy with a fair face and strong arms and eyes as sharp and as bright as the mountain eagle's. And now AEgeus was more loth to return home than he had been before, and he went up on the mountain which overlooks Troezen, and prayed to Athena, the queen of the air, to give him wisdom and show him what to do. Even while he prayed there came a ship into the harbor, bringing a letter to AEgeus and alarming news from Athens.

"Come home without delay"--these were words of the letter which the elders had sent--"come home quickly, or Athens will be lost. A great king from beyond the sea, Minos of Crete, is on the way with ships and a host of fighting men; and he declares that he will carry sword and fire within our walls, and will slay our young men and make our children his slaves. Come and save us!"
cards.whyThisWorks: The second paragraph functions as a pivot that shifts the narrative from Aegeus's domestic contentment to urgent political crisis, making it a clear example of a paragraph that introduces a contrasting complication and drives the story forward.
cards.skillStrategy: Ask yourself: does this paragraph continue what came before, or does it change the direction of the story by introducing a new problem, conflict, or idea?
evidencePoints: AEgeus was more loth to return home than he had been before
Come home without delay...come home quickly, or Athens will be lost
cards.question: What is the primary job of the second paragraph, beginning with 'Come home without delay'?

choices.label: A
choices.text: It concludes the story of Aegeus's time in Troezen by showing that he has finally decided to leave his bride and return to Athens.

choices.label: B
choices.text: It shifts the narrative by introducing an urgent threat from Minos of Crete that forces Aegeus to confront a crisis he has been avoiding.

choices.label: C
choices.text: It extends the first paragraph's description of Aegeus's happiness in Troezen by adding details about the people who depend on him.

choices.label: D
choices.text: It contrasts Minos of Crete with Aegeus by proving that Minos is a more powerful and decisive ruler than Aegeus has been.

cards.standardTitle: Central idea and supporting evidence
cards.excerpt:
There was once a king of Athens whose name was AEgeus. He had no son; but he had fifty nephews, and they were waiting for him to die, so that one of them might be king in his stead. They were wild, worthless fellows, and the people of Athens looked forward with dread to the day when the city should be in their power. Yet so long as AEgeus lived they could not do much harm, but were content to spend their time in eating and drinking at the king's table and in quarreling among themselves.

It so happened one summer that AEgeus left his kingdom in the care of the elders of the city and went on a voyage across the Saronic Sea to the old and famous city of Troezen, which lay nestled at the foot of the mountains on the opposite shore. Troezen was not fifty miles by water from Athens, and the purple-peaked island of AEgina lay between them; but to the people of that early time the distance seemed very great, and it was not often that ships passed from one place to the other. And as for going by land round the great bend of the sea, that was a thing so fraught with danger that no man had ever dared try it.
cards.whyThisWorks: The two paragraphs together establish a central idea about instability and threat—the nephews' greed in paragraph one and AEgeus's risky absence in paragraph two—requiring students to synthesize rather than pick an isolated detail.
cards.skillStrategy: Ask yourself: what problem or situation do BOTH paragraphs keep returning to, and state that in a plain sentence instead of just naming a topic or one detail.
evidencePoints: they were waiting for him to die, so that one of them might be king in his stead
the people of Athens looked forward with dread to the day when the city should be in their power
cards.question: The narrator says the people of Athens 'looked forward with dread' to the nephews gaining power, and then describes AEgeus leaving his kingdom in the care of elders to make a dangerous voyage. What central idea do these two details together develop?

choices.label: A
choices.text: AEgeus was a weak ruler because he had no son and was forced to rely on untrustworthy elders to govern Athens.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Athens stood in a fragile and threatened position, endangered both by greedy nephews waiting for power and by the king's risky absence.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The greatest danger facing Athens was the treacherous sea voyage between Athens and Troezen, which no traveler had safely completed by land.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The fifty nephews were the sole source of trouble in Athens, spending their time quarreling and feasting at the king's expense.

cards.standardTitle: Key literary elements add layers of meaning
cards.excerpt:
"Take this child," he said, "and teach him all the lore of the mountains, the woods, and the fields. Teach him those things which he most needs to know in order to do great good to his fellow-men."

And AEsculapius proved to be a wise child, gentle and sweet and teachable; and among all the pupils of Cheiron he was the best loved. He learned the lore of the mountains, the woods, and the fields. He found out what virtue there is in herbs and flowers and senseless stones; and he studied the habits of birds and beasts and men. But above all he became skillful in dressing wounds and healing diseases; and to this day physicians remember and honor him as the first and greatest of their craft. When he grew up to manhood his name was heard in every land, and people blessed him because he was the friend of life and the foe of death.

As time went by, AEsculapius cured so many people and saved so many lives that Pluto, the pale-faced king of the Lower World, became alarmed.

"I shall soon have nothing to do," he said, "if this physician does not stop keeping people away from my kingdom."

And he sent word to his brother Jupiter, and complained that AEsculapius was cheating him out of what was his due. Great Jupiter listened to his complaint, and stood up among the storm clouds, and hurled his thunderbolts at AEsculapius until the great physician was cruelly slain. Then all the world was filled with grief, and even the beasts and the trees and the stones wept because the friend of life was no more.
cards.whyThisWorks: The excerpt characterizes AEsculapius through accumulated actions, titles, and the world's reaction to his death, allowing students to trace how specific details build meaning about his role as a force for life against death.
cards.skillStrategy: When analyzing characterization, look at what a character does, what others say about him, and how the world responds to him — these details together reveal the deeper meaning the author wants you to understand.
evidencePoints: people blessed him because he was the friend of life and the foe of death
Then all the world was filled with grief, and even the beasts and the trees and the stones wept because the friend of life was no more
cards.question: The narrator describes AEsculapius as 'the friend of life and the foe of death' and later states that 'even the beasts and the trees and the stones wept' at his death. What do these details reveal about AEsculapius's significance in the story?

choices.label: A
choices.text: He is portrayed as a man whose medical skill made him arrogant, which is why powerful gods like Jupiter and Pluto felt threatened by him.

choices.label: B
choices.text: He is portrayed as a force so aligned with life itself that even the natural world mourns his loss, making his death feel like a wound to all of creation.

choices.label: C
choices.text: He is portrayed as a student who surpassed Cheiron's teachings, suggesting that human learning is more powerful than divine instruction.

choices.label: D
choices.text: He is portrayed as a healer whose fame spread widely, but whose death ultimately proved that no mortal can challenge the authority of the gods.

cards.standardTitle: Theme development across a literary text
cards.excerpt:
Now, not very far from the land of Arcadia there was a little city named Calydon. It lay in the midst of rich wheat fields and fruitful vineyards; but beyond the vineyards there was a deep dense forest where many wild beasts lived. The king of Calydon was named OEneus, and he dwelt in a white palace with his wife Althea and his boys and girls. His kingdom was so small that it was not much trouble to govern it, and so he spent the most of his time in hunting or in plowing or in looking after his grape vines. He was said to be a very brave man, and he was the friend of all the great heroes of that heroic time.

The two daughters of OEneus and Althea were famed all over the world for their beauty; and one of them was the wife of the hero Hercules, who had freed Prometheus from his chains, and done many other mighty deeds. The six sons of OEneus and Althea were noble, handsome fellows; but the noblest and handsomest of them all was Meleager, the youngest.
cards.whyThisWorks: The excerpt establishes a clear hierarchy—noble family, noble sons, then Meleager singled out as 'the noblest and handsomest of them all'—giving students a true-but-off-topic detail (Hercules's deeds) to reject in favor of the detail that actually builds the theme of exceptional individuals rising above the already privileged.
cards.skillStrategy: Ask yourself: does this detail show the theme happening, or does it just add a true fact about the topic?
evidencePoints: The six sons of OEneus and Althea were noble, handsome fellows
but the noblest and handsomest of them all was Meleager, the youngest
cards.question: A reader proposes this theme for the excerpt: even among those already praised for greatness, one individual rises above the rest. The narrator states that the six sons of OEneus 'were noble, handsome fellows' and then immediately adds 'but the noblest and handsomest of them all was Meleager, the youngest.' Which explanation best shows how that contrast develops the proposed theme?

choices.label: A
choices.text: By naming Meleager the youngest son, the narrator suggests that birth order, not personal merit, determines who stands above others in a family.

choices.label: B
choices.text: By first granting all six sons the same high praise and then singling Meleager out with 'but the noblest and handsomest of them all,' the narrator shows one person surpassing a group that is already exceptional.

choices.label: C
choices.text: By describing OEneus as 'a very brave man' and the friend of great heroes, the narrator establishes that the father's reputation, not Meleager's own qualities, sets him apart from his brothers.

choices.label: D
choices.text: By noting that one of OEneus's daughters married Hercules, who 'had freed Prometheus from his chains,' the narrator shows that the family's greatness comes from its connections to legendary heroes rather than from within.

cards.standardTitle: Text structure and feature purpose
cards.excerpt:
In that forest there dwelt a robber giant, called Club-carrier, who was the terror of all the country. For oftentimes he would go down into the valleys where the shepherds fed their flocks, and would carry off not only sheep and lambs, but sometimes children and the men themselves. It was his custom to hide in the thickets of underbrush, close to a pathway, and, when a traveler passed that way, leap out upon him and beat him to death. When he saw Theseus coming through the woods, he thought that he would have a rich prize, for he knew from the youth's dress and manner that he must be a prince. He lay on the ground, where leaves of ivy and tall grass screened him from view, and held his great iron club ready to strike.

But Theseus had sharp eyes and quick ears, and neither beast nor robber giant could have taken him by surprise. When Club-carrier leaped out of his hiding place to strike him down, the young man dodged aside so quickly that the heavy club struck the ground behind him; and then, before the robber giant could raise it for a second stroke, Theseus seized the fellow's legs and tripped him up.
cards.whyThisWorks: The two-paragraph structure creates a clear tension-and-resolution pattern: the first paragraph builds the threat of Club-carrier's ambush, and the second paragraph shows exactly how Theseus's 'sharp eyes and quick ears' neutralize it, giving students a concrete example of how a paragraph's job relates to the one before it.
cards.skillStrategy: Ask yourself: what problem or situation does the first paragraph set up, and what does the second paragraph do with that setup—does it continue it, resolve it, shift away from it, or add background to it?
evidencePoints: held his great iron club ready to strike
Theseus had sharp eyes and quick ears, and neither beast nor robber giant could have taken him by surprise
cards.question: The first paragraph ends with Club-carrier hidden in the grass, 'held his great iron club ready to strike.' What is the main job of the second paragraph in relation to the first paragraph?

choices.label: A
choices.text: It extends the first paragraph's buildup of Club-carrier's power by showing that his iron club lands a blow and forces Theseus to retreat along the pathway.

choices.label: B
choices.text: It resolves the ambush set up in the first paragraph by showing how Theseus's 'sharp eyes and quick ears' let him dodge the club and trip Club-carrier before a second stroke can land.

choices.label: C
choices.text: It shifts focus away from the ambush to explain why Club-carrier chose to hide 'in the thickets of underbrush' rather than confront travelers openly on the pathway.

choices.label: D
choices.text: It adds background detail about Club-carrier carrying off 'sheep and lambs' and 'children and the men themselves' to explain what brought Theseus into the forest.

cards.standardTitle: Central idea and supporting evidence
cards.excerpt:
But the greatest thing that Cadmus did is yet to be told. He was the first schoolmaster of the Greeks, and taught them the letters which were used in his own country across the sea. They called the first of these letters _alpha_ and the second _beta_, and that is why men speak of the _alphabet_ to this day. And when the Greeks had learned the alphabet from Cadmus, they soon began to read and write, and to make beautiful and useful books.

As for the maiden Europa, she was carried safe over the sea to a distant shore. She may have been happy in the new, strange land to which she was taken--I cannot tell; but she never heard of friends or home again. Whether it was really Jupiter in the form of a bull that carried her away, nobody knows. It all happened so long ago that there may have been some mistake about the story; and I should not think it strange if it were a sea robber who stole her from her home, and a swift ship with white sails that bore her away. Of one thing I am very sure: she was loved so well by all who knew her that the great unknown country to which she was taken has been called after her name ever since--Europe.
cards.whyThisWorks: The excerpt presents two distinct episodes—Cadmus teaching the alphabet and Europa's fate—and students must synthesize both to identify the central idea rather than selecting an isolated detail from one paragraph.
cards.skillStrategy: Ask yourself: what idea do BOTH paragraphs keep coming back to? That idea—not just one detail—is the central idea.
evidencePoints: the greatest thing that Cadmus did is yet to be told... He was the first schoolmaster of the Greeks... and that is why men speak of the alphabet to this day
she was loved so well by all who knew her that the great unknown country to which she was taken has been called after her name ever since--Europe
cards.question: The narrator calls teaching the alphabet 'the greatest thing that Cadmus did' and ends by explaining that Europa's name lives on in the word 'Europe.' What central idea do these two claims together express?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Cadmus's invention of the alphabet was more important to civilization than anything Europa experienced.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The legacies of Cadmus and Europa shaped language and geography in ways that still exist today.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Ancient stories like those of Cadmus and Europa cannot be trusted because the facts have been confused over time.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Europa's suffering after being taken from her home was remembered and honored by the people who loved her.

cards.standardTitle: Key literary elements add layers of meaning
cards.excerpt:
