Then the two went out into the courtyard where many a young man had met his fate, and there they wrestled until the sun went down, and neither could gain aught of advantage over the other. But it was plain that the trained skill of Theseus would, in the end, win against the brute strength of Cercyon. Then the men of Eleusis who stood watching the contest, saw the youth lift the giant king bodily into the air and hurl him headlong over his shoulder to the hard pavement beyond.

"As you have done to others, so will I do unto you!" cried Theseus.

But grim old Cercyon neither moved nor spoke; and when the youth turned his body over and looked into his cruel face, he saw that the life had quite gone out of him.

Then the people of Eleusis came to Theseus and wanted to make him their king. "You have slain the tyrant who was the bane of Eleusis," they said, "and we have heard how you have also rid the world of the giant robbers who were the terror of the land. Come now and be our king; for we know that you will rule over us wisely and well."

"Some day," said Theseus, "I will be your king, but not now; for there are other deeds for me to do." And with that he donned his sword and his sandals and his princely cloak, and threw his great iron club upon his shoulder, and went out of Eleusis; and all the people ran after him for quite a little way, shouting, "May good fortune be with you, O king, and may Athena bless and guide you!"
cards.whyThisWorks: Theseus's refusal of the kingship and his immediate departure reveal that his identity is defined by heroic duty rather than personal ambition, giving students a clear character action to interpret for deeper meaning.
cards.skillStrategy: When a character makes a surprising choice, ask what that choice reveals about who they are and what they value.
evidencePoints: "Some day," said Theseus, "I will be your king, but not now; for there are other deeds for me to do."
he donned his sword and his sandals and his princely cloak, and threw his great iron club upon his shoulder, and went out of Eleusis
cards.question: When the people of Eleusis offer Theseus their kingship and he replies, "Some day I will be your king, but not now; for there are other deeds for me to do," what does this moment reveal about his character?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Theseus distrusts the people of Eleusis and doubts they are sincere in their offer, so he delays accepting until he can verify their loyalty.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Theseus is driven by a sense of ongoing heroic duty that he values above personal reward, showing that glory and power are secondary to his mission.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Theseus fears he is not yet strong enough to rule wisely, so he leaves to gain more experience before returning to claim the throne.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Theseus is indifferent to the suffering of the people of Eleusis and leaves because he feels no connection to them after defeating Cercyon.

cards.standardTitle: Theme development across a literary text
cards.excerpt:
A young man who did not like Meleager, had run on in front and had reached the city before the rest of the company had fairly started. Queen Althea was standing at the door of the palace, and when she saw him she asked what had happened in the forest He told her at once that Meleager had killed her brothers, for he knew that, with all their faults, she loved them very dearly. It was terrible to see her grief. She shrieked, and tore her hair, and rushed wildly about from room to room. Her senses left her, and she did not know what she was doing.

It was the custom at that time for people to avenge the death of their kindred, and her only thought was how to punish the murderer of her brothers. In her madness she forgot that Meleager was her son. Then she thought of the three Fates and of the unburned firebrand which she had locked up in her chest so many years before. She ran and got the stick and threw it into the fire that was burning on the hearth.
cards.whyThisWorks: The excerpt contains both true-but-topic-only details (Althea's grief, the custom of vengeance) and details that directly develop the theme that blind rage destroys what one loves most, allowing students to distinguish thematic evidence from mere topic-matching details.
cards.skillStrategy: Ask yourself: does this detail show how the theme is being built, or does it just describe what is happening in the story?
evidencePoints: In her madness she forgot that Meleager was her son.
She ran and got the stick and threw it into the fire that was burning on the hearth.
cards.question: Which detail from the excerpt most directly develops the theme that grief-driven rage causes a person to destroy what they love most?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Althea loved her brothers deeply despite all their faults, showing how strong her bond with them was.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Althea forgot that Meleager was her son and threw the firebrand into the fire, turning her love for her son into the instrument of his destruction.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The custom of the time required people to avenge the deaths of their kindred, explaining why Althea felt obligated to act.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Althea shrieked, tore her hair, and rushed wildly from room to room, showing the depth of her sorrow over her brothers' deaths.

cards.standardTitle: Text structure and feature purpose
cards.excerpt:
The king sent out his fastest ship to try to overtake the bull. The sailors rowed far out to sea, much farther than any ship had ever gone before; but no trace of Europa could be found. When they came back, everybody felt that there was no more hope. All the women and children in the town wept for the lost Europa. The king shut himself up in his house, and did not eat nor drink for three days. Then he called his son Cadmus, and bade him take a ship and go in search of his sister; and he told him that, no matter what dangers might be in his way, he must not come back until she was found.

Cadmus was glad to go. He chose twenty brave young men to go with him, and set sail the very next day. It was a great undertaking; for they were to pass through an unknown sea, and they did not know what lands they would come to. Indeed, it was feared that they would never come to any land at all. Ships did not dare to go far from the shore in those days. But Cadmus and his friends were not afraid. They were ready to face any danger.
cards.whyThisWorks: The two paragraphs model a clear structural shift: the first ends in failure and grief ('no more hope'), while the second opens with 'Cadmus was glad to go,' giving students a precise textual hinge to analyze paragraph job.
cards.skillStrategy: Find the last sentence of one paragraph and the first sentence of the next — if the mood or direction changes, the second paragraph is shifting the idea.
evidencePoints: everybody felt that there was no more hope
Cadmus was glad to go
cards.question: The first paragraph ends with the king commanding Cadmus to search for Europa 'no matter what dangers might be in his way.' What is the job of the second paragraph in relation to that ending?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The second paragraph extends the king's grief by showing that Cadmus also mourns Europa before agreeing to leave.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The second paragraph shifts from the despair and failure of the first paragraph to Cadmus's eagerness and courage, signaled by the words 'Cadmus was glad to go.'

choices.label: C
choices.text: The second paragraph contrasts the king's command with Cadmus's refusal, showing that Cadmus chooses his crew before accepting the mission.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The second paragraph concludes the search for Europa by revealing the unknown sea where the bull carried her.

cards.standardTitle: Central idea and supporting evidence
cards.excerpt:
At last the morning of the third day came, and the chest was tossed upon the sandy shore of a strange island where there were green fields and, beyond them, a little town. A man who happened to be walking near the shore saw it and dragged it far up on the beach. Then he looked inside, and there he saw the beautiful lady and the little boy. He helped them out and led them just as they were to his own house, where he cared for them very kindly. And when Danaë had told him her story, he bade her feel no more fear; for they might have a home with him as long as they should choose to stay, and he would be a true friend to them both.

So Danaë and her son stayed in the house of the kind man who had saved them from the sea. Years passed by, and Perseus grew up to be a tall young man, handsome, and brave, and strong. The king of the island, when he saw Danaë, was so pleased with her beauty that he wanted her to become his wife. But he was a dark, cruel man, and she did not like him at all; so she told him that she would not marry him. The king thought that Perseus was to blame for this, and that if he could find some excuse to send the young man on a far journey, he might force Danaë to have him whether she wished or not.
cards.whyThisWorks: The two paragraphs move from rescue and safety to a new threat, requiring students to synthesize both movements into a central idea rather than selecting an isolated detail or topic.
cards.skillStrategy: Ask yourself: what idea do BOTH paragraphs build together? The central idea must cover the whole excerpt, not just one event or one character.
evidencePoints: he bade her feel no more fear; for they might have a home with him as long as they should choose to stay
The king thought that Perseus was to blame for this, and that if he could find some excuse to send the young man on a far journey, he might force Danaë to have him whether she wished or not
cards.question: The first paragraph ends with the promise that Danaë and Perseus 'might have a home with him as long as they should choose to stay,' yet the second paragraph closes with the king scheming to 'send the young man on a far journey' so he could 'force Danaë to have him whether she wished or not.' What central idea do these two moments develop across both paragraphs?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Perseus's growth into a 'tall young man, handsome, and brave, and strong' is the main development the two paragraphs trace.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The safety and kindness Danaë and Perseus find on the island are quickly threatened by a powerful man who plans to use Perseus's absence to control Danaë against her will.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The kind stranger who dragged the chest from the shore is the most important figure because his rescue shapes everything that follows for Danaë and Perseus.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Danaë's refusal to marry the king, captured in the line 'she told him that she would not marry him,' is the single event both paragraphs are building toward.

cards.standardTitle: Key literary elements add layers of meaning
cards.excerpt:
The people of the island were glad when they learned what had happened, for no one loved the wicked king. They were glad, too, because Perseus had come home again, and had brought with him his beautiful wife, Andromeda. So, after they had talked the matter over among themselves, they went to him and asked him to be their king. But he thanked them, and said that he would rule over them for one day only, and that then he would give the kingdom to another, so that he might take his mother back to her home and her kindred in distant Argos.

On the morrow therefore, he gave the kingdom to the kind man who had saved his mother and himself from the sea; and then he went on board his ship, with Andromeda and Danaë, and sailed away across the sea towards Argos.

When Danaë's old father, the king of Argos, heard that a strange ship was coming over the sea with his daughter and her son on board, he was in great distress; for he remembered what the Pythia had foretold about his death. So, without waiting to see the vessel, he left his palace in great haste and fled out of the country.

"My daughter's son cannot kill me if I will keep out of his way," he said.

But Perseus had no wish to harm him; and he was very sad when he learned that his poor grandfather had gone away in fear and without telling any one where he was going. The people of Argos welcomed Danaë to her old home; and they were very proud of her handsome son, and begged that he would stay in their city, so that he might some time become their king.
cards.whyThisWorks: Perseus's decision to rule for only one day and then give the kingdom away, contrasted with his grandfather's fearful flight, reveals Perseus as selfless and honorable while deepening the theme that virtue matters more than power.
cards.skillStrategy: When a character makes a surprising choice or speaks in a revealing way, ask yourself what that moment shows about who they are and what the author wants you to understand about them.
evidencePoints: he thanked them, and said that he would rule over them for one day only, and that then he would give the kingdom to another, so that he might take his mother back to her home
But Perseus had no wish to harm him; and he was very sad when he learned that his poor grandfather had gone away in fear
cards.question: When Perseus declines the kingship, saying 'he would rule over them for one day only, and that then he would give the kingdom to another, so that he might take his mother back to her home,' what does this action reveal about his character?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Perseus distrusts the islanders and refuses their offer because he fears they will betray him as they once betrayed his mother.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Perseus places loyalty to his mother above personal ambition, showing that his devotion to family defines him more than any desire for power or status.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Perseus gives up the kingdom because he knows the people of Argos will offer him a greater throne once he returns with Danaë.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Perseus surrenders the kingdom out of guilt for killing the wicked king, believing he does not deserve to rule over people he has wronged.

cards.standardTitle: Theme development across a literary text
cards.excerpt:
Then AEgeus kissed his wife and the babe, and went on board the ship; the sailors shouted; the oars were dipped into the waves; the white sail was spread to the breeze; and AEthra from her palace window saw the vessel speed away over the blue waters towards AEgina and the distant Attic shore.

Year after year went by, and yet no word reached AEthra from her husband on the other side of the sea. Often and often she would climb the mountain above Troezen, and sit there all day, looking out over the blue waters and the purple hills of AEgina to the dim, distant shore beyond. Now and then she could see a white-winged ship sailing in the offing; but men said that it was a Cretan vessel, and very likely was filled with fierce Cretan warriors, bound upon some cruel errand of war. Then it was rumored that King Minos had seized upon all the ships of Athens, and had burned a part of the city, and had forced the people to pay him a most grievous tribute. But further than this there was no news.
cards.whyThisWorks: The excerpt contrasts Aegeus's departure with Aethra's years of unanswered waiting, letting students distinguish details that build the theme of enduring uncertainty from true-but-topic-only details about war and tribute.
cards.skillStrategy: Ask yourself: does this detail show a character experiencing the theme, or does it just describe events that fit the topic?
evidencePoints: Year after year went by, and yet no word reached AEthra from her husband on the other side of the sea.
Often and often she would climb the mountain above Troezen, and sit there all day, looking out over the blue waters
cards.question: The narrator states that 'year after year went by, and yet no word reached AEthra from her husband on the other side of the sea.' Which other detail from the excerpt most directly develops the same theme as that statement — that those left behind must endure longing without relief?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The white sail was spread to the breeze and the sailors shouted as Aegeus's ship departed, marking the moment AEthra lost sight of him.

choices.label: B
choices.text: AEthra climbed the mountain above Troezen again and again, sitting all day to watch the distant shore, yet received no answer to her waiting.

choices.label: C
choices.text: King Minos seized the ships of Athens, burned part of the city, and forced the people to pay a grievous tribute.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Men said the white-winged ship visible in the offing was a Cretan vessel likely filled with fierce warriors bound on an errand of war.

cards.standardTitle: Text structure and feature purpose
cards.excerpt:
Very stealthily he went nearer and nearer, always with his back towards the monsters and always looking into his bright shield to see where to go. Then he drew his sharp sword and, dashing quickly downward, struck a back blow, so sure, so swift, that the head of Medusa was cut from her shoulders and the black blood gushed like a river from her neck. Quick as thought he thrust the terrible head into his magic pouch and leaped again into the air, and flew away with the speed of the wind.

Then the two older Gorgons awoke, and rose with dreadful screams, and spread their great wings, and dashed after him. They could not see him, for the Cap of Darkness hid him from even their eyes; but they scented the blood of the head which he carried in the pouch, and like hounds in the chase, they followed him, sniffing the air. And as he flew through the clouds he could hear their dreadful cries and the clatter of their golden wings and the snapping of their horrible jaws. But the Magic Slippers were faster than any wings, and in a little while the monsters were left far behind, and their cries were heard no more; and Perseus flew on alone.
cards.whyThisWorks: The two paragraphs model a clear structural shift: the first closes the beheading action, and the second opens a new threat and then resolves it, giving students a concrete example of a paragraph that both extends conflict and shifts to resolution.
cards.skillStrategy: Ask yourself: does this paragraph start a new problem, continue the same one, or wrap things up — then find the exact words that signal that move.
evidencePoints: Then the two older Gorgons awoke, and rose with dreadful screams, and spread their great wings, and dashed after him.
But the Magic Slippers were faster than any wings, and in a little while the monsters were left far behind, and their cries were heard no more; and Perseus flew on alone.
cards.question: After Perseus severs Medusa's head and leaps away, the second paragraph begins with 'Then the two older Gorgons awoke.' What is the job of this second paragraph in relation to the first?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The second paragraph repeats the danger of Medusa by describing how the Gorgons use her scent to track Perseus, showing the beheading was not yet complete.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The second paragraph extends the conflict by introducing the awakened Gorgons as a new threat, then shifts to resolution when 'the monsters were left far behind, and their cries were heard no more.'

choices.label: C
choices.text: The second paragraph contrasts the Gorgons' power with Perseus's weakness, proving that the Cap of Darkness — not the Magic Slippers — was responsible for his survival.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The second paragraph concludes the story by returning to the moment Perseus 'drew his sharp sword,' framing the escape as a consequence of that single decisive action.

cards.standardTitle: Central idea and supporting evidence
cards.excerpt: Perseus soon crossed the ocean and came again to the Land of the West. Far below him he could see the three Maidens dancing around the golden tree; but he did not stop, for, now that he had the head of Medusa safe in the pouch at his side, he must hasten home. Straight east he flew over the great sea, and after a time he came to a country where there were palm trees and pyramids and a great river flowing from the south. Here, as he looked down, a strange sight met his eyes: he saw a beautiful girl chained to a rock by the seashore, and far away a huge sea beast swimming towards her to devour her. Quick as thought, he flew down and spoke to her; but, as she could not see him for the Cap of Darkness which he wore, his voice only frightened her.
cards.whyThisWorks: The paragraph contains multiple vivid details—Perseus's urgent eastward flight, the exotic landscape, and the chained girl—that students must weigh against each other to identify the one idea that unifies them all, making it a strong central-idea discrimination task.
cards.skillStrategy: Ask yourself: which idea connects every detail in the paragraph, rather than describing just one moment or place?
evidencePoints: now that he had the head of Medusa safe in the pouch at his side, he must hasten home
he saw a beautiful girl chained to a rock by the seashore, and far away a huge sea beast swimming towards her to devour her
cards.question: The paragraph describes Perseus flying 'straight east,' passing over 'palm trees and pyramids,' and then spotting 'a beautiful girl chained to a rock.' What central idea do these details together develop?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Perseus's journey home is defined by the exotic landscapes he observes, from the golden tree in the Land of the West to the pyramids and great river of the east.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Even while urgently racing home after completing his quest, Perseus encounters a new crisis—a girl about to be devoured—that demands his attention.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Perseus regrets flying past the three Maidens dancing around the golden tree and wishes he had stopped before continuing east.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The Cap of Darkness Perseus wears makes him invisible and prevents the chained girl from recognizing him as a hero who can save her.

cards.standardTitle: Rhetoric and reader effect
cards.excerpt:
The beast sprang at Cadmus, and tried to seize him with its sharp claws. But Cadmus leaped quickly aside and struck it in the neck with his long sword. A great stream of black blood gushed out, and the dragon soon fell to the ground dead. Cadmus had seen many fearful sights, but never anything so dreadful as this beast. He had never been in so great danger before. He sat down on the ground and trembled; and, all the time, he was weeping for his two friends. How now was he to build a city, with no one to help him?

While Cadmus was still weeping he was surprised to hear some one calling him. He stood up and looked around. On the hillside before him was a tall woman who had a helmet on her head and a shield in her hand. Her eyes were gray, and her face, though not beautiful, was very noble. Cadmus knew at once that she was Athena, the queen of the air--she who gives wisdom to men.
cards.whyThisWorks: The rhetorical question 'How now was he to build a city, with no one to help him?' placed directly after Cadmus trembles and weeps gives students a clear, passage-specific moment to analyze how a device shapes the reader's emotional experience.
cards.skillStrategy: When you spot a rhetorical question, ask what feeling it creates in the reader right at that moment in the text, using the surrounding details as clues.
evidencePoints: He sat down on the ground and trembled; and, all the time, he was weeping for his two friends.
How now was he to build a city, with no one to help him?
cards.question: After Cadmus 'sat down on the ground and trembled' and wept for his friends, the narrator asks, 'How now was he to build a city, with no one to help him?' What effect does this rhetorical question most likely have on the reader?

choices.label: A
choices.text: It shifts the reader's focus from Cadmus's grief to admiration for his courage in killing the dragon.

choices.label: B
choices.text: It deepens the reader's sense of Cadmus's helplessness by making his loss feel overwhelming and unresolved.

choices.label: C
choices.text: It signals that Cadmus is about to abandon his mission because no answer is possible after losing his companions.

choices.label: D
choices.text: It reminds the reader how deadly the dragon was by linking the beast's attack to the deaths of Cadmus's friends.

cards.standardTitle: Key literary elements add layers of meaning
cards.excerpt:
"I would free you from your bargain if I could, but that is a thing which no one can do. You must hold to your agreement never to touch loom or spindle again. And yet, since you will never be happy unless you can spin and weave, I will give you a new form so that you can carry on your work with neither spindle nor loom."

Then she touched Arachne with the tip of the spear which she sometimes carried; and the maiden was changed at once into a nimble spider, which ran into a shady place in the grass and began merrily to spin and weave a beautiful web.

I have heard it said that all the spiders which have been in the world since then are the children of Arachne; but I doubt whether this be true. Yet, for aught I know, Arachne still lives and spins and weaves; and the very next spider that you see may be she herself.

[Illustration]

Long before you or I or anybody else can remember, there lived with the Mighty Folk on the mountain top a fair and gentle lady named Leto. So fair and gentle was she that Jupiter loved her and made her his wife. But when Juno, the queen of earth and sky, heard of this, she was very angry; and she drove Leto down from the mountain and bade all things great and small refuse to help her. So Leto fled like a wild deer from land to land and could find no place in which to rest. She could not stop, for then the ground would quake under her feet, and the stones would cry out, "Go on! go on!" and birds and beasts and trees and men would join in the cry; and no one in all the wide land took pity on her.
cards.whyThisWorks: Athena's speech and action toward Arachne reveal a character who is bound by divine law yet chooses mercy, showing students how a character's words and deeds together create layered meaning about justice and compassion.
cards.skillStrategy: When a character speaks and then acts, ask yourself: do the words and actions match, and what does that combination reveal about who the character truly is?
evidencePoints: I would free you from your bargain if I could, but that is a thing which no one can do.
I will give you a new form so that you can carry on your work with neither spindle nor loom.
cards.question: Read the following lines from the passage: 'I would free you from your bargain if I could, but that is a thing which no one can do. You must hold to your agreement never to touch loom or spindle again. And yet, since you will never be happy unless you can spin and weave, I will give you a new form so that you can carry on your work with neither spindle nor loom.' What do Athena's words and the action that follows reveal about her character?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Athena is indifferent to Arachne's suffering and transforms her only to enforce the terms of the original bargain.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Athena is constrained by divine law yet still acts with compassion, finding a way to preserve Arachne's happiness within the limits of what she can do.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Athena regrets her power over mortals and transforms Arachne as an apology for having made the bargain in the first place.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Athena is primarily concerned with her own reputation and transforms Arachne to prevent her from weaving again and challenging the gods.

cards.standardTitle: Theme development across a literary text
cards.excerpt:
And Daedalus built for King Minos a most wonderful palace with floors of marble and pillars of granite; and in the palace he set up golden statues which had tongues and could talk; and for splendor and beauty there was no other building in all the wide earth that could be compared with it.

There lived in those days among the hills of Crete a terrible monster called the Minotaur, the like of which has never been seen from that time until now. This creature, it was said, had the body of a man, but the face and head of a wild bull and the fierce nature of a mountain lion. The people of Crete would not have killed him if they could; for they thought that the Mighty Folk who lived with Jupiter on the mountain top had sent him among them, and that these beings would be angry if any one should take his life. He was the pest and terror of all the land. Where he was least expected, there he was sure to be; and almost every day some man, woman, or child was caught and devoured by him.
cards.whyThisWorks: The excerpt contrasts Daedalus's magnificent creations with the Minotaur's unchecked terror, and the people's refusal to kill the monster 'because they thought the Mighty Folk...would be angry' directly develops the theme that fear of divine punishment allows suffering to continue—letting students distinguish a theme-developing detail from a true-but-topic-only detail.
cards.skillStrategy: Ask yourself: does this detail show WHY the suffering continues, or does it just describe what the monster looks like? Only the detail that explains the cause of the ongoing harm develops the theme.
evidencePoints: The people of Crete would not have killed him if they could; for they thought that the Mighty Folk who lived with Jupiter on the mountain top had sent him among them, and that these beings would be angry if any one should take his life.
almost every day some man, woman, or child was caught and devoured by him
cards.question: A reader identifies the theme of this excerpt as: fear of divine punishment allows suffering to continue unchecked. The narrator states that 'the people of Crete would not have killed him if they could' and gives a reason for their inaction. Which detail from the excerpt most directly develops that theme by explaining why the Minotaur's daily killing of Cretans was never stopped?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The Minotaur had the body of a man but the face and head of a wild bull, making him a creature unlike any seen before or since.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The Cretans believed the gods had sent the Minotaur and would punish anyone who killed him, so they let him devour their neighbors day after day rather than act.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Daedalus built a palace of marble and granite with golden statues that could speak, making it the most splendid building on earth.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The Minotaur appeared where he was least expected and possessed the fierce nature of a mountain lion, making him a dangerous and unpredictable creature.

cards.standardTitle: Text structure and feature purpose
cards.excerpt:
At last the famous Island of Crete was reached, and there Daedalus landed and made himself known; and the King of Crete, who had already heard of his wondrous skill, welcomed him to his kingdom, and gave him a home in his palace, and promised that he should be rewarded with great riches and honor if he would but stay and practice his craft there as he had done in Athens.

Now the name of the King of Crete was Minos. His grandfather, whose name was also Minos, was the son of Europa, a young princess whom a white bull, it was said, had brought on his back across the sea from distant Asia. This elder Minos had been accounted the wisest of men--so wise, indeed, that Jupiter chose him to be one of the judges of the Lower World. The younger Minos was almost as wise as his grandfather; and he was brave and far-seeing and skilled as a ruler of men. He had made all the islands subject to his kingdom, and his ships sailed into every part of the world and brought back to Crete the riches of foreign lands. So it was not hard for him to persuade Daedalus to make his home with him and be the chief of his artisans.
cards.whyThisWorks: The second paragraph builds Minos's credibility through his lineage, wisdom, and naval wealth, directly supporting why his promise of 'great riches and honor' to Daedalus is believable—a clear paragraph-job relationship students can trace.
cards.skillStrategy: Ask yourself: what work does this paragraph do for the one before it—does it explain, contrast, prove, or shift the focus?
evidencePoints: promised that he should be rewarded with great riches and honor
his ships sailed into every part of the world and brought back to Crete the riches of foreign lands
cards.question: The first paragraph states that Minos 'promised that he should be rewarded with great riches and honor.' What is the main job of the second paragraph in relation to that promise?

choices.label: A
choices.text: It shifts focus away from Daedalus entirely to tell the separate legend of Europa and the white bull.

choices.label: B
choices.text: It supports the promise by showing Minos had the wealth and power—'his ships sailed into every part of the world and brought back to Crete the riches'—to fulfill it.

choices.label: C
choices.text: It contrasts Minos's generosity with his grandfather's role as a strict judge, suggesting Minos could not be trusted.

choices.label: D
choices.text: It reveals that Daedalus was reluctant to accept the offer, creating tension between him and Minos.

cards.standardTitle: Central idea and supporting evidence
cards.excerpt: Then Perseus slipped the Gorgon's head back into the pouch and hastened to speak with the young girl whom he had saved. She told him that her name was Andromeda, and that she was the daughter of the king of that land. She said that her mother, the queen, was very beautiful and very proud of her beauty; and every day she went down to the seashore to look at her face as it was pictured in the quiet water; and she had boasted that not even the nymphs who live in the sea were as handsome as she. When the sea nymphs heard about this, they were very angry and asked great Neptune, the king of the sea, to punish the queen for her pride. So Neptune sent a sea monster to crush the king's ships and kill the cattle along the shore and break down all the fishermen's huts. The people were so much distressed that they sent at last to ask the Pythia what they should do; and the Pythia said that there was only one way to save the land from destruction,--that they must give the king's daughter, Andromeda, to the monster to be devoured.
cards.whyThisWorks: The paragraph builds a clear cause-and-effect chain from the queen's boast to Andromeda's sacrifice, giving students a concrete central idea to distinguish from isolated details like Neptune's power or the Pythia's oracle.
cards.skillStrategy: Ask yourself: what single idea connects every event in the paragraph from the queen's boast all the way to Andromeda being offered to the monster?
evidencePoints: she had boasted that not even the nymphs who live in the sea were as handsome as she
they must give the king's daughter, Andromeda, to the monster to be devoured
cards.question: Andromeda explains a series of events that begins with her mother's boast—'not even the nymphs who live in the sea were as handsome as she'—and ends with Andromeda herself being offered to the sea monster. Which statement expresses the central idea that connects all of those events?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Neptune punished the entire kingdom because he wanted to prove his authority over both land and sea.

choices.label: B
choices.text: A queen's boastful pride angered the sea nymphs, triggered Neptune's punishment, and ultimately put her innocent daughter's life at risk.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The Pythia's oracle was the most important event in the paragraph because it gave the people their only path to survival.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Andromeda suffered because she was the daughter of a king, making her the natural target whenever the kingdom faced divine punishment.

cards.standardTitle: Rhetoric and reader effect
cards.excerpt:
Years passed by. Every spring when the roses began to bloom seven youths and seven maidens were put on board of a black-sailed ship and sent to Crete to pay the tribute which King Minos required. In every house in Athens there was sorrow and dread, and the people lifted up their hands to Athena on the hilltop and cried out, "How long, O Queen of the Air, how long shall this thing be?"

In the meanwhile the little child at Troezen on the other side of the sea had grown to be a man. His name, Theseus, was in everybody's mouth, for he had done great deeds of daring; and at last he had come to Athens to find his father, King AEgeus, who had never heard whether he was alive or dead; and when the youth had made himself known, the king had welcomed him to his home and all the people were glad because so noble a prince had come to dwell among them and, in time, to rule over their city.
cards.whyThisWorks: The rhetorical question 'How long, O Queen of the Air, how long shall this thing be?' uses both repetition of 'how long' and direct address to a deity, giving teachers a clear anchor for discussing how rhetorical questions create emotional urgency and reader empathy.
cards.skillStrategy: When you spot a rhetorical question, ask yourself: what emotion does it stir in the reader, and how does the author's word choice inside the question deepen that feeling?
evidencePoints: "How long, O Queen of the Air, how long shall this thing be?"
"In every house in Athens there was sorrow and dread"
cards.question: Read the rhetorical question the Athenians cry out: 'How long, O Queen of the Air, how long shall this thing be?' How does the repetition of 'how long' within this question affect the reader?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The repeated phrase signals that the Athenians are uncertain whether Athena actually exists, making the reader doubt the gods' power.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The repeated phrase mirrors the exhausting, year-after-year suffering already described, making the reader feel the weight of the people's desperation.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The repeated phrase shows that the Athenians are angry at King Minos rather than sorrowful, shifting the reader's sympathy away from Athens.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The repeated phrase emphasizes that the tribute has been paid only once, making the reader understand the event is a single, isolated tragedy.

cards.standardTitle: Key literary elements add layers of meaning
cards.excerpt:
Club-carrier roared loudly, and tried to strike again; but Theseus wrenched the club out of his hands, and then dealt him such a blow on the head that he never again harmed travelers passing through the forest. Then the youth went on his way, carrying the huge club on his shoulder, and singing a song of victory, and looking sharply around him for any other foes that might be lurking among the trees.

Just over the ridge of the next mountain he met an old man who warned him not to go any farther. He said that close by a grove of pine trees, which he would soon pass on his way down the slope, there dwelt a robber named Sinis, who was very cruel to strangers.

"He is called Pine-bender," said the old man; "for when he has caught a traveler, he bends two tall, lithe pine trees to the ground and binds his captive to them--a hand and a foot to the top of one, and a hand and a foot to the top of the other. Then he lets the trees fly up, and he roars with laughter when he sees the traveler's body torn in sunder."

"It seems to me," said Theseus, "that it is full time to rid the world of such a monster;" and he thanked the kind man who had warned him, and hastened onward, whistling merrily as he went down towards the grove of pines.

Soon he came in sight of the robber's house, built near the foot of a jutting cliff. Behind it was a rocky gorge and a roaring mountain stream; and in front of it was a garden wherein grew all kinds of rare plants and beautiful flowers. But the tops of the pine trees below it were laden with the bones of unlucky travelers, which hung bleaching white in the sun and wind.
cards.whyThisWorks: Theseus's response to the old man's warning—thanking him calmly and then 'hastening onward, whistling merrily'—reveals a character who is fearless and eager for danger, adding meaning to his role as a heroic monster-slayer rather than a cautious traveler.
cards.skillStrategy: When a character reacts to frightening news, ask yourself what that reaction tells you about who they are and what they value.
evidencePoints: 'it is full time to rid the world of such a monster'
he thanked the kind man who had warned him, and hastened onward, whistling merrily as he went down towards the grove of pines
cards.question: After the old man describes Sinis's brutal method of killing travelers, Theseus thanks him and walks toward the grove 'whistling merrily.' What does this response reveal about Theseus's character?

choices.label: A
choices.text: He does not fully believe the old man's account of Sinis and assumes the danger has been exaggerated.

choices.label: B
choices.text: He feels no fear at the prospect of confronting a deadly robber and views the encounter as an opportunity to protect others.

choices.label: C
choices.text: He is too proud to admit that the warning has frightened him, so he hides his anxiety behind a cheerful manner.

choices.label: D
choices.text: He is relieved that the old man's directions will allow him to avoid the grove of pine trees entirely.

cards.standardTitle: Theme development across a literary text
cards.excerpt:
It happened soon afterwards that the king of a certain country not far away was holding games and giving prizes to the best runners and leapers and quoit throwers. And Perseus went thither to try his strength with the other young men of the land; for if he should be able to gain a prize, his name would become known all over the world. No one in that country knew who he was, but all wondered at his noble stature and his strength and skill; and it was easy enough for him to win all the prizes.

One day, as he was showing what he could do, he threw a heavy quoit a great deal farther than any had been thrown before. It fell in the crowd of lookers-on, and struck a stranger who was standing there. The stranger threw up his hands and sank upon the ground; and when Perseus ran to help him, he saw that he was dead. Now this man was none other than Danaë's father, the old king of Argos. He had fled from his kingdom to save his life, and in doing so had only met his death.
cards.whyThisWorks: The narrator's closing statement—'He had fled from his kingdom to save his life, and in doing so had only met his death'—gives students a precise textual moment to test against the theme of inescapable fate, while the detail about Perseus winning prizes is true but develops only his heroic reputation, not that theme.
cards.skillStrategy: Find the detail that does more than match the topic—ask yourself which detail shows the theme in action, not just what the passage is about.
evidencePoints: He had fled from his kingdom to save his life, and in doing so had only met his death.
if he should be able to gain a prize, his name would become known all over the world
cards.question: The narrator ends the passage by saying Danaë's father 'had fled from his kingdom to save his life, and in doing so had only met his death.' Which detail from the excerpt most directly works together with that closing statement to develop the theme that fate cannot be escaped through human effort?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Perseus traveled to the games hoping that winning a prize would make his name known all over the world.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The thrown quoit fell into the crowd and struck a stranger who turned out to be Danaë's father—the very man whose flight was meant to keep him safe.

choices.label: C
choices.text: No one in the country knew who Perseus was, yet all wondered at his noble stature, strength, and skill.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Perseus threw the heavy quoit farther than any had been thrown before, winning all the prizes at the games.

cards.standardTitle: Text structure and feature purpose
cards.excerpt:
There was once a king of Athens whose name was AEgeus. He had no son; but he had fifty nephews, and they were waiting for him to die, so that one of them might be king in his stead. They were wild, worthless fellows, and the people of Athens looked forward with dread to the day when the city should be in their power. Yet so long as AEgeus lived they could not do much harm, but were content to spend their time in eating and drinking at the king's table and in quarreling among themselves.

It so happened one summer that AEgeus left his kingdom in the care of the elders of the city and went on a voyage across the Saronic Sea to the old and famous city of Troezen, which lay nestled at the foot of the mountains on the opposite shore. Troezen was not fifty miles by water from Athens, and the purple-peaked island of AEgina lay between them; but to the people of that early time the distance seemed very great, and it was not often that ships passed from one place to the other. And as for going by land round the great bend of the sea, that was a thing so fraught with danger that no man had ever dared try it.
cards.whyThisWorks: The second paragraph shifts from the threat of the nephews in Athens to Aegeus sailing away, and students must recognize that this shift removes the protective presence described in 'yet so long as AEgeus lived they could not do much harm.'
cards.skillStrategy: Ask yourself: does this paragraph keep building the same idea, or does it move the story in a new direction by changing who or what the focus is on?
evidencePoints: yet so long as AEgeus lived they could not do much harm
AEgeus left his kingdom in the care of the elders of the city and went on a voyage across the Saronic Sea
cards.question: The first paragraph states that the nephews 'could not do much harm' as long as Aegeus lived in Athens. What is the job of the second paragraph in relation to that claim?

choices.label: A
choices.text: It concludes the threat from the nephews by showing that the elders of the city successfully replace Aegeus as a source of protection.

choices.label: B
choices.text: It shifts away from that reassurance by moving Aegeus out of Athens entirely, which undermines the condition that kept the nephews in check.

choices.label: C
choices.text: It extends the description of the nephews' wild behavior by showing how they react when Aegeus sails to Troezen.

choices.label: D
choices.text: It contrasts Athens and Troezen to prove that the danger the people of Athens feared was actually located across the Saronic Sea.

cards.standardTitle: Central idea and supporting evidence
cards.excerpt:
But Perseus had not forgotten his mother; and so, one fine summer day, he and Andromeda sailed in a beautiful ship to his own home; for the Magic Slippers could not carry both him and his bride through the air. The ship came to land at the very spot where the wooden chest had been cast so many years before; and Perseus and his bride walked through the fields towards the town.

Now, the wicked king of that land had never ceased trying to persuade Danaë to become his wife; but she would not listen to him, and the more he pleaded and threatened, the more she disliked him. At last when he found that she could not be made to have him, he declared that he would kill her; and on this very morning he had started out, sword in hand, to take her life.

So, as Perseus and Andromeda came into the town, whom should they meet but his mother fleeing to the altar of Jupiter, and the king following after, intent on killing her? Danaë was so frightened that she did not see Perseus, but ran right on towards the only place of safety. For it was a law of that land that not even the king should be allowed to harm any one who took refuge on the altar of Jupiter.
cards.whyThisWorks: The excerpt pairs Perseus's stated motivation ('he had not forgotten his mother') with the dramatic timing of his arrival ('fleeing to the altar of Jupiter…intent on killing her'), giving students clear textual evidence to synthesize into a central idea about loyalty and providential timing.
cards.skillStrategy: To find the central idea, look for the detail the author repeats or emphasizes most—here, Perseus's loyalty to his mother—and ask what point all the other details (the ship, the king's threat, the altar) support about that loyalty.
evidencePoints: Perseus had not forgotten his mother
whom should they meet but his mother fleeing to the altar of Jupiter, and the king following after, intent on killing her
cards.question: The narrator opens by stating that 'Perseus had not forgotten his mother,' and he arrives to find her 'fleeing to the altar of Jupiter' with the king 'intent on killing her.' What central idea do these two details together express about Perseus's return home?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Perseus's choice to sail by ship rather than use the Magic Slippers delays his arrival and nearly allows the king to kill Danaë before he can intervene.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Perseus's loyalty to his mother brings him home at the exact moment she faces mortal danger from the king she has long refused to marry.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Danaë's survival depends on the law protecting those who reach Jupiter's altar, making Perseus's timely return less important than the sanctuary it provides.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The king's years of threats against Danaë show that the kingdom has been without any protection for her long before Perseus decides to return.

cards.standardTitle: Rhetoric and reader effect
cards.excerpt:
In a little town north of Delphi, and not very far from the sea, there lived a young man named Admetus. He was the ruler of the town, and hence was called its king; but his kingdom was so small that he could walk all round it in half a day. He knew the name of every man and woman and child in the town, and everybody loved him because he was so gentle and kind and at the same time a king.

Late one day, when the rain was falling and the wind was blowing cold from the mountains, a beggar came to his door. The man was ragged and dirty and half starved, and Admetus knew that he must have come from some strange land, for in his own country no one ever went hungry. So the kind king took him into the house and fed him; and after the man had bathed he gave him his own warm cloak, and bade the servants make a place for him to sleep through the night.
cards.whyThisWorks: The sentence 'The man was ragged and dirty and half starved…for in his own country no one ever went hungry' uses direct contrast as a rhetorical device to simultaneously characterize the beggar's suffering and validate Admetus's rule, giving students a clear, passage-anchored example of how contrast shapes reader perception of a character.
cards.skillStrategy: When a sentence sets two opposite conditions side by side, ask yourself what feeling or judgment the author wants you to form about a character or situation because of that gap.
evidencePoints: The man was ragged and dirty and half starved
in his own country no one ever went hungry
cards.question: Read this sentence from the passage: 'The man was ragged and dirty and half starved, and Admetus knew that he must have come from some strange land, for in his own country no one ever went hungry.' The author contrasts the beggar's desperate condition with the well-being of Admetus's own people. How does this contrast most likely affect the reader's view of Admetus as a ruler?

choices.label: A
choices.text: It suggests that Admetus is indifferent to suffering beyond his borders, since he only recognizes the beggar's hunger as a sign that the man is foreign.

choices.label: B
choices.text: It reinforces admiration for Admetus by showing that his gentle rule has kept his own people fed, making his decision to help the starving stranger feel like a natural extension of his character.

choices.label: C
choices.text: It creates suspicion toward the beggar by implying that his ragged condition proves he comes from a lawless or dangerous land unlike Admetus's peaceful kingdom.

choices.label: D
choices.text: It makes Admetus seem guilty about his kingdom's prosperity, suggesting he helps the beggar to make up for the suffering that exists in other lands.

cards.standardTitle: Key literary elements add layers of meaning
cards.excerpt:
A young man who did not like Meleager, had run on in front and had reached the city before the rest of the company had fairly started. Queen Althea was standing at the door of the palace, and when she saw him she asked what had happened in the forest He told her at once that Meleager had killed her brothers, for he knew that, with all their faults, she loved them very dearly. It was terrible to see her grief. She shrieked, and tore her hair, and rushed wildly about from room to room. Her senses left her, and she did not know what she was doing.

It was the custom at that time for people to avenge the death of their kindred, and her only thought was how to punish the murderer of her brothers. In her madness she forgot that Meleager was her son. Then she thought of the three Fates and of the unburned firebrand which she had locked up in her chest so many years before. She ran and got the stick and threw it into the fire that was burning on the hearth.
cards.whyThisWorks: Althea's physical frenzy and the deliberate act of burning the firebrand reveal how grief and vengeance can override a mother's love, showing that characterization through action and internal conflict carries thematic weight about the destructive power of rage.
cards.skillStrategy: When a character does something extreme, ask what that action reveals about who they are and what the author wants you to understand about a larger idea.
evidencePoints: In her madness she forgot that Meleager was her son.
She ran and got the stick and threw it into the fire that was burning on the hearth.
cards.question: What does Althea's decision to throw the firebrand into the fire reveal about her character in this moment?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Her action shows that she has always resented Meleager and was waiting for a reason to destroy him.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Her action reveals that grief and the desire for vengeance have overwhelmed her maternal love, driving her to condemn her own son.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Her action demonstrates that she is following the custom of avenging kindred in a calm and deliberate way.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Her action suggests she does not fully understand the power of the firebrand or what burning it will cause.

cards.standardTitle: Theme development across a literary text
cards.excerpt:
When at last he was arrayed to their liking, they told him where he would find the Gorgons, and what he should do to obtain the terrible head and escape alive. Then they kissed him and wished him good luck, and bade him hasten to do the dangerous deed. And Perseus donned the Cap of Darkness, and sped away and away towards the farthermost edge of the earth; and the three Maidens went back to their tree to sing and to dance and to guard the golden apples until the old world should become young again.

With the sharp sword at his side and the bright shield upon his arm, Perseus flew bravely onward in search of the dreadful Gorgons; but he had the Cap of Darkness upon his head, and you could no more have seen him than you can see the wind. He flew so swiftly that it was not long until he had crossed the mighty ocean which encircles the earth, and had come to the sunless land which lies beyond; and then he knew, from what the Maidens had told him, that the lair of the Gorgons could not be far away.
cards.whyThisWorks: The excerpt contrasts Perseus's solitary, invisible advance into a 'sunless land' with the Maidens' return to safety, letting students distinguish details that develop a theme of solitary courage from true-but-topic-only details about preparation or distance.
cards.skillStrategy: Ask yourself: does this detail show the theme in action, or does it just describe what happened in the story?
evidencePoints: you could no more have seen him than you can see the wind
Perseus flew bravely onward in search of the dreadful Gorgons
cards.question: The narrator describes Perseus as flying 'bravely onward' while wearing the Cap of Darkness, so that 'you could no more have seen him than you can see the wind.' Which detail from the excerpt most directly develops the theme that courage requires pressing forward alone into danger?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The Maidens told Perseus where to find the Gorgons and what he should do to obtain the terrible head and escape alive, giving him a clear plan before he departed.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Perseus flew invisibly and alone toward the Gorgons' lair, described as moving like the unseen wind into a 'sunless land' where the danger awaited him.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Perseus crossed the mighty ocean that encircles the earth, showing how great a distance separated him from the place where the Gorgons lived.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The three Maidens kissed Perseus, wished him good luck, and then returned to their tree to sing, dance, and guard the golden apples.

cards.standardTitle: Text structure and feature purpose
cards.excerpt:
Swifter than an eagle, Perseus flew up towards the sky. Then he turned, and the Magic Slippers bore him over the sea straight towards the north. On and on he went, and soon the sea was passed; and he came to a famous land, where there were cities and towns and many people. And then he flew over a range of snowy mountains, beyond which were mighty forests and a vast plain where many rivers wandered, seeking for the sea. And farther on was another range of mountains; and then there were frozen marshes and a wilderness of snow, and after all the sea again,--but a sea of ice. On and on he winged his way, among toppling icebergs and over frozen billows and through air which the sun never warmed, and at last he came to the cavern where the three Gray Sisters dwelt.

These three creatures were so old that they had forgotten their own age, and nobody could count the years which they had lived. The long hair which covered their heads had been gray since they were born; and they had among them only a single eye and a single tooth which they passed back and forth from one to another. Perseus heard them mumbling and crooning in their dreary home, and he stood very still and listened.
cards.whyThisWorks: The second paragraph's opening phrase 'These three creatures were so old' signals a deliberate shift from Perseus's journey to a description of the Gray Sisters, giving students a clear structural pivot to analyze.
cards.skillStrategy: Ask yourself: does this paragraph keep going with the same idea, or does it stop and introduce something new? Look at the first sentence for a signal word or new subject.
evidencePoints: On and on he winged his way, among toppling icebergs and over frozen billows and through air which the sun never warmed, and at last he came to the cavern where the three Gray Sisters dwelt.
These three creatures were so old that they had forgotten their own age, and nobody could count the years which they had lived.
cards.question: The first paragraph ends with Perseus arriving at 'the cavern where the three Gray Sisters dwelt.' What is the job of the second paragraph, which opens with 'These three creatures were so old that they had forgotten their own age'?

choices.label: A
choices.text: It extends the journey by describing more frozen terrain Perseus must cross before he can reach the Gray Sisters.

choices.label: B
choices.text: It shifts focus from Perseus's flight to introduce the Gray Sisters, establishing their ancient and unsettling nature as he prepares to confront them.

choices.label: C
choices.text: It concludes the episode by explaining why Perseus chose to seek out the Gray Sisters in the frozen north.

choices.label: D
choices.text: It contrasts the warmth of the cities Perseus passed over with the cold misery the Gray Sisters have endured for centuries.

cards.standardTitle: Central idea and supporting evidence
cards.excerpt: One day she came to the sea, and as she fled along the beach she lifted up her hands and called aloud to great Neptune to help her. Neptune, the king of the sea, heard her and was kind to her. He sent a huge fish, called a dolphin, to bear her away from the cruel land; and the fish, with Leto sitting on his broad back, swam through the waves to Delos, a little island which lay floating on top of the water like a boat. There the gentle lady found rest and a home; for the place belonged to Neptune, and the words of cruel Juno were not obeyed there. Neptune put four marble pillars under the island so that it should rest firm upon them; and then he chained it fast, with great chains which reached to the bottom of the sea, so that the waves might never move it.
cards.whyThisWorks: The paragraph builds a single central idea through Neptune's sequential acts—sending the dolphin, providing Delos, adding pillars, and chaining the island—all showing that his power and kindness created a permanent safe haven for Leto beyond Juno's reach, giving students concrete evidence to distinguish central idea from isolated detail.
cards.skillStrategy: Ask yourself: what do ALL the details in the paragraph add up to? The central idea is the 'so what' that ties every sentence together, not just one fact.
evidencePoints: Neptune, the king of the sea, heard her and was kind to her.

Neptune put four marble pillars under the island so that it should rest firm upon them; and then he chained it fast, with great chains which reached to the bottom of the sea, so that the waves might never move it.
cards.question: The paragraph describes Neptune hearing Leto's cry, sending a dolphin to carry her, anchoring Delos with pillars and chains, and ensuring 'the words of cruel Juno were not obeyed there.' What central idea do all of these details together express?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Leto's suffering was caused entirely by Juno's cruelty, which followed her even to the sea.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Neptune's kindness and power gave Leto a permanent refuge that Juno's authority could not touch.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Delos was unique because it floated on the water like a boat before Neptune anchored it.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The dolphin Neptune sent was powerful enough to carry Leto safely through dangerous ocean waves.

cards.standardTitle: Rhetoric and reader effect
cards.excerpt:
In a few days they came to a large island called Cyprus. Cadmus went on shore, and tried to talk with the strange people who lived there. They were very kind to him, but they did not understand his language. At last he made out by signs to tell them who he was, and to ask them if they had seen his little sister Europa or the white bull that had carried her away. They shook their heads and pointed to the west.

Then the young men sailed on in their little ship. They came to many islands, and stopped at every one, to see if they could find any trace of Europa; but they heard no news of her at all. At last, they came to the country which we now call Greece. It was a new country then, and only a few people lived there, and Cadmus soon learned to speak their language well. For a long time he wandered from one little town to another, always telling the story of his lost sister.
cards.whyThisWorks: Baldwin uses anaphoric repetition of searching actions ('came to many islands,' 'stopped at every one,' 'wandered from one little town to another') alongside the refrain of 'always telling the story of his lost sister' to create a cumulative rhetorical effect of grief and devotion that directly teaches how repeated structure shapes reader response.
cards.skillStrategy: When you notice a writer repeating an action or phrase across a passage, ask yourself what emotion or idea that repetition builds in the reader—then find the exact words that create that effect.
evidencePoints: always telling the story of his lost sister
They came to many islands, and stopped at every one, to see if they could find any trace of Europa; but they heard no news of her at all.
cards.question: In both paragraphs, Baldwin repeats the pattern of Cadmus arriving at a new place, searching for Europa, and finding nothing—ending with 'always telling the story of his lost sister.' What effect does this repeated pattern most likely create for the reader?

choices.label: A
choices.text: It suggests that Cadmus is careless in his search because he moves on from each island and town without thoroughly questioning the people who live there.

choices.label: B
choices.text: It builds a sense of endless, sorrowful devotion by showing that each new place—Cyprus, the islands, the towns of Greece—brings no news of Europa, yet Cadmus keeps searching and retelling her story.

choices.label: C
choices.text: It shows that Cadmus is gradually losing hope because he stops mentioning the white bull and focuses only on telling Europa's story to the people of Greece.

choices.label: D
choices.text: It emphasizes Cadmus's growing confidence, since each stop allows him to learn new languages and communicate more easily, as when he 'soon learned to speak their language well.'

cards.standardTitle: Key literary elements add layers of meaning
cards.excerpt:
In that forest there dwelt a robber giant, called Club-carrier, who was the terror of all the country. For oftentimes he would go down into the valleys where the shepherds fed their flocks, and would carry off not only sheep and lambs, but sometimes children and the men themselves. It was his custom to hide in the thickets of underbrush, close to a pathway, and, when a traveler passed that way, leap out upon him and beat him to death. When he saw Theseus coming through the woods, he thought that he would have a rich prize, for he knew from the youth's dress and manner that he must be a prince. He lay on the ground, where leaves of ivy and tall grass screened him from view, and held his great iron club ready to strike.

But Theseus had sharp eyes and quick ears, and neither beast nor robber giant could have taken him by surprise. When Club-carrier leaped out of his hiding place to strike him down, the young man dodged aside so quickly that the heavy club struck the ground behind him; and then, before the robber giant could raise it for a second stroke, Theseus seized the fellow's legs and tripped him up.
cards.whyThisWorks: Theseus's quick dodge and immediate counterattack against Club-carrier reveal his courage and tactical intelligence, showing students how a character's actions under pressure communicate deeper meaning about heroic identity.
cards.skillStrategy: When a character acts in a dangerous moment, ask what that action shows about who they are and what the author wants you to understand about them.
evidencePoints: Theseus had sharp eyes and quick ears, and neither beast nor robber giant could have taken him by surprise

the young man dodged aside so quickly that the heavy club struck the ground behind him; and then, before the robber giant could raise it for a second stroke, Theseus seized the fellow's legs and tripped him up
cards.question: Read this sentence from the passage: 'But Theseus had sharp eyes and quick ears, and neither beast nor robber giant could have taken him by surprise.' What does this description, followed by Theseus's actions in the same paragraph, reveal about his character?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Theseus relies on his royal status to intimidate Club-carrier, since the giant already recognizes him as a prince and hesitates before striking.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Theseus possesses both physical alertness and quick thinking, qualities that allow him to turn a moment of ambush into a demonstration of heroic capability.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Theseus is reckless and lucky, since he wanders into a known danger zone without a plan and only survives because Club-carrier swings carelessly.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Theseus is more powerful than Club-carrier in size and strength, which is why the giant's heavy club fails to reach him.

cards.standardTitle: Theme development across a literary text
cards.excerpt:
So Danaë was kept shut up in the prison of brass. She had no one to talk to but her old nurse; and she never saw the land or the sea, but only the blue sky above the open window and now and then a white cloud sailing across. Day after day she sat under the window and wondered why her father kept her in that lonely place, and whether he would ever come and take her out. I do not know how many years passed by, but Danaë grew fairer every day, and by and by she was no longer a child, but a tall and beautiful woman; and Jupiter amid the clouds looked down and saw her and loved her.

One day it seemed to her that the sky opened and a shower of gold fell through the window into the room; and when the blinding shower had ceased, a noble young man stood smiling before her. She did not know--nor do I--that it was mighty Jupiter who had thus come down in the rain; but she thought that he was a brave prince who had come from over the sea to take her out of her prison-house.
cards.whyThisWorks: The excerpt contains true-but-topic-only details (the brass prison, the sky view) alongside details that actively develop a theme of hope persisting through isolation, letting students practice distinguishing thematic evidence from mere topic details.
cards.skillStrategy: Ask yourself: does this detail show the theme in action, or does it just describe the setting or situation without connecting to a deeper idea?
evidencePoints: Day after day she sat under the window and wondered why her father kept her in that lonely place, and whether he would ever come and take her out.
she thought that he was a brave prince who had come from over the sea to take her out of her prison-house
cards.question: The narrator twice describes what Danaë imagines or hopes for—first that her father might 'come and take her out,' and then that the stranger was 'a brave prince who had come from over the sea to take her out of her prison-house.' Which statement best explains how both of these moments develop the theme that hope for rescue persists even through years of isolation?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Both moments show that Danaë misunderstood her situation: she wrongly blamed her father and wrongly identified Jupiter, proving that isolation leads to confusion rather than hope.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Both moments show that across years of confinement Danaë's longing to be freed never faded—she kept imagining a rescuer, first her father and then the golden stranger, even when no rescue came.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Both moments establish that powerful figures—her father and Jupiter—controlled Danaë's fate, showing that individuals in isolation are helpless against authority.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Both moments confirm that Danaë had been imprisoned for many years, which is important background information about how long she was kept in the brass prison.

cards.standardTitle: Text structure and feature purpose
cards.excerpt:
But the greatest thing that Cadmus did is yet to be told. He was the first schoolmaster of the Greeks, and taught them the letters which were used in his own country across the sea. They called the first of these letters _alpha_ and the second _beta_, and that is why men speak of the _alphabet_ to this day. And when the Greeks had learned the alphabet from Cadmus, they soon began to read and write, and to make beautiful and useful books.

As for the maiden Europa, she was carried safe over the sea to a distant shore. She may have been happy in the new, strange land to which she was taken--I cannot tell; but she never heard of friends or home again. Whether it was really Jupiter in the form of a bull that carried her away, nobody knows. It all happened so long ago that there may have been some mistake about the story; and I should not think it strange if it were a sea robber who stole her from her home, and a swift ship with white sails that bore her away. Of one thing I am very sure: she was loved so well by all who knew her that the great unknown country to which she was taken has been called after her name ever since--Europe.
cards.whyThisWorks: The two paragraphs have clearly distinct jobs—paragraph one celebrates Cadmus as the Greeks' first schoolmaster and the origin of the alphabet, while paragraph two shifts to Europa's uncertain fate and the narrator's open doubt about whether Jupiter or a sea robber took her—making the contrast in paragraph purpose directly teachable.
cards.skillStrategy: Ask yourself: what task is each paragraph doing for the reader—is it proving a claim, introducing a new subject, casting doubt, or wrapping up a story?
evidencePoints: He was the first schoolmaster of the Greeks, and taught them the letters which were used in his own country across the sea.
Whether it was really Jupiter in the form of a bull that carried her away, nobody knows.
cards.question: The first paragraph ends by stating that Cadmus taught the Greeks the alphabet and that 'they soon began to read and write, and to make beautiful and useful books.' What is the job of the second paragraph in relation to this ending?

choices.label: A
choices.text: It extends the celebration of Cadmus by showing how the alphabet he introduced eventually reached Europa's distant shore.

choices.label: B
choices.text: It shifts focus from Cadmus's accomplishments to Europa's fate, introducing the narrator's uncertainty about whether Jupiter or 'a sea robber' was responsible for her disappearance.

choices.label: C
choices.text: It supports the claim that Cadmus was 'the greatest' Greek by contrasting his lasting legacy with Europa's forgotten story.

choices.label: D
choices.text: It resolves the story of Cadmus by explaining that his search for Europa ended when he learned she had been taken to the land now called Europe.

cards.standardTitle: Central idea and supporting evidence
cards.excerpt: Apollo, who had always been so wise, was now almost as foolish as his crow. He fancied that Coronis had really deserted him for another man, and his mind was filled with grief and rage. With his silver bow in his hands he started at once for his home. He did not stop to speak with any one; he had made up his mind to learn the truth for himself. His swan-team and his golden chariot were not at hand--for, now that he was living with men, he must travel like men. The journey had to be made on foot, and it was no short journey in those days when there were no roads. But after a time, he came to the village where he had lived happily for so many years, and soon he saw his own house half-hidden among the dark-leaved olive trees. In another minute he would know whether the crow had told him the truth.
cards.whyThisWorks: The paragraph's opening contrast — 'Apollo, who had always been so wise, was now almost as foolish as his crow' — gives students a clear anchor for identifying the central idea rather than an isolated detail or broad topic.
cards.skillStrategy: Find the sentence that frames everything else in the paragraph, then ask: what idea do all the other details support?
evidencePoints: Apollo, who had always been so wise, was now almost as foolish as his crow.
his mind was filled with grief and rage
cards.question: The paragraph opens with the statement 'Apollo, who had always been so wise, was now almost as foolish as his crow.' Which statement expresses the central idea that this opening line introduces and the rest of the paragraph develops?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Apollo's crow had always been untrustworthy, and Apollo finally realized he should not have listened to it.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Grief and rage overcame Apollo's wisdom, driving him to rush toward the truth without pausing to think or seek help.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Traveling on foot through a land with no roads was the greatest hardship Apollo faced on his journey to the village.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Apollo's loss of his golden chariot and swan-team left him powerless and unable to act like a god among men.

cards.standardTitle: Rhetoric and reader effect
cards.excerpt:
The only sure way to save himself would be to put the child to death before he was old enough to do any harm. But when he had taken the little Perseus and his mother out of the prison and had seen how helpless the child was, he could not bear the thought of having him killed outright. For the king, although a great coward, was really a kind-hearted man and did not like to see anything suffer pain. Yet something must be done.

So he bade his servants make a wooden chest that was roomy and watertight and strong; and when it was done, he put Danaë and the child into it and had it taken far out to sea and left there to be tossed about by the waves. He thought that in this way he would rid himself of both daughter and grandson without seeing them die; for surely the chest would sink after a while, or else the winds would cause it to drift to some strange shore so far away that they could never come back to Argos again.
cards.whyThisWorks: The narrator's juxtaposition of 'great coward' and 'kind-hearted man' in a single sentence, followed by the king's chest-at-sea scheme, gives students a clear rhetorical device to analyze for its effect on how readers judge the king's moral character.
cards.skillStrategy: When a narrator places two contradictory traits side by side, ask what the surrounding actions reveal about which trait is really in control — that gap between stated character and actual behavior is the rhetorical effect.
evidencePoints: the king, although a great coward, was really a kind-hearted man and did not like to see anything suffer pain
he would rid himself of both daughter and grandson without seeing them die
cards.question: The narrator describes the king as 'a great coward' and 'a kind-hearted man' in the same sentence, then reveals he sealed Danaë and Perseus in a chest so he could 'rid himself of both…without seeing them die.' What effect does this contrast between the king's stated kindness and his actual scheme create for the reader?

choices.label: A
choices.text: It convinces the reader that the king's kindness is genuine, because choosing the chest over outright execution shows he truly could not bear to cause suffering.

choices.label: B
choices.text: It exposes the king's 'kindness' as self-serving — he avoids witnessing death rather than preventing it — making him appear morally hollow despite the narrator's sympathetic label.

choices.label: C
choices.text: It leaves the reader uncertain about the king's final intentions, since the chest could either sink or drift to safety, suggesting his cowardice and kindness are equally balanced.

choices.label: D
