choices.text: It encourages the reader to admire the king for finding a bloodless solution, because the narrator's tone signals that avoiding direct violence is the most honorable choice available to him.

cards.standardTitle: Paraphrase grade-level text
cards.excerpt:
The beast sprang at Cadmus, and tried to seize him with its sharp claws. But Cadmus leaped quickly aside and struck it in the neck with his long sword. A great stream of black blood gushed out, and the dragon soon fell to the ground dead. Cadmus had seen many fearful sights, but never anything so dreadful as this beast. He had never been in so great danger before. He sat down on the ground and trembled; and, all the time, he was weeping for his two friends. How now was he to build a city, with no one to help him?

While Cadmus was still weeping he was surprised to hear some one calling him. He stood up and looked around. On the hillside before him was a tall woman who had a helmet on her head and a shield in her hand. Her eyes were gray, and her face, though not beautiful, was very noble. Cadmus knew at once that she was Athena, the queen of the air--she who gives wisdom to men.
cards.whyThisWorks: The sentence 'He sat down on the ground and trembled; and, all the time, he was weeping for his two friends' uses a semicolon to join two related but distinct emotional actions, requiring students to hold both parts in mind and restate the full meaning without dropping either clause.
cards.skillStrategy: When a sentence has two parts joined by a semicolon or 'and,' restate each part separately, then check that your paraphrase captures both ideas together.
evidencePoints: He sat down on the ground and trembled; and, all the time, he was weeping for his two friends.
How now was he to build a city, with no one to help him?
cards.question: Read this sentence from the passage: 'He sat down on the ground and trembled; and, all the time, he was weeping for his two friends.' Which of the following most accurately restates the meaning of this sentence?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Cadmus collapsed from exhaustion after the battle and cried out for his friends to come and rescue him.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Cadmus sank to the ground shaking with fear while continuously grieving the loss of his two companions.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Cadmus sat down to rest after the fight and briefly thought about the two friends he had lost.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Cadmus trembled because he was afraid his friends would not return to help him build the city.

cards.standardTitle: Paraphrase grade-level text
cards.excerpt:
Years passed by. Every spring when the roses began to bloom seven youths and seven maidens were put on board of a black-sailed ship and sent to Crete to pay the tribute which King Minos required. In every house in Athens there was sorrow and dread, and the people lifted up their hands to Athena on the hilltop and cried out, "How long, O Queen of the Air, how long shall this thing be?"

In the meanwhile the little child at Troezen on the other side of the sea had grown to be a man. His name, Theseus, was in everybody's mouth, for he had done great deeds of daring; and at last he had come to Athens to find his father, King AEgeus, who had never heard whether he was alive or dead; and when the youth had made himself known, the king had welcomed him to his home and all the people were glad because so noble a prince had come to dwell among them and, in time, to rule over their city.
cards.whyThisWorks: The second paragraph contains a long, multi-clause sentence with embedded relative clauses and inverted information about Theseus's backstory, requiring students to untangle the syntax and restate the full meaning accurately.
cards.skillStrategy: Break the long sentence into smaller parts by identifying who is being described, what happened to him, and how others responded — then restate each part in your own words.
evidencePoints: at last he had come to Athens to find his father, King AEgeus, who had never heard whether he was alive or dead
when the youth had made himself known, the king had welcomed him to his home and all the people were glad because so noble a prince had come to dwell among them and, in time, to rule over their city
cards.question: Read this sentence from the second paragraph: 'at last he had come to Athens to find his father, King AEgeus, who had never heard whether he was alive or dead; and when the youth had made himself known, the king had welcomed him to his home and all the people were glad because so noble a prince had come to dwell among them and, in time, to rule over their city.' Which restatement most accurately captures the full meaning of this sentence?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Theseus traveled to Athens, where his father King AEgeus had been searching for him for years and had already prepared the city to welcome him as its future ruler.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Theseus finally arrived in Athens to find his father, King AEgeus, who had not known if Theseus was living or dead; once Theseus revealed who he was, the king welcomed him, and the people rejoiced that such a worthy prince would one day govern their city.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Theseus came to Athens and revealed himself to King AEgeus, but the people were uncertain whether to accept him because no one could confirm he was truly the king's son.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Theseus arrived in Athens after his father sent for him, and the king welcomed him publicly so that the people would accept Theseus as the rightful heir to the throne.

cards.standardTitle: Paraphrase grade-level text
cards.excerpt:
In a few days they came to a large island called Cyprus. Cadmus went on shore, and tried to talk with the strange people who lived there. They were very kind to him, but they did not understand his language. At last he made out by signs to tell them who he was, and to ask them if they had seen his little sister Europa or the white bull that had carried her away. They shook their heads and pointed to the west.

Then the young men sailed on in their little ship. They came to many islands, and stopped at every one, to see if they could find any trace of Europa; but they heard no news of her at all. At last, they came to the country which we now call Greece. It was a new country then, and only a few people lived there, and Cadmus soon learned to speak their language well. For a long time he wandered from one little town to another, always telling the story of his lost sister.
cards.whyThisWorks: The sentence 'For a long time he wandered from one little town to another, always telling the story of his lost sister' contains an adverbial phrase, a complex verb phrase, and a participial modifier that students must untangle to restate the full meaning accurately.
cards.skillStrategy: Break the sentence into its parts — who is doing what, for how long, and why — then put those parts together in your own words.
evidencePoints: For a long time he wandered from one little town to another, always telling the story of his lost sister.
Cadmus soon learned to speak their language well.
cards.question: Read this sentence from the passage: 'For a long time he wandered from one little town to another, always telling the story of his lost sister.' Which of the following most accurately restates the meaning of this sentence?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Cadmus quickly traveled through every town in Greece, searching for Europa by asking people whether they had seen a white bull.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Over an extended period, Cadmus moved continuously between towns in Greece, and wherever he went he shared the account of Europa's disappearance.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Cadmus spent a long time in a single Greek town, repeatedly telling the townspeople the story of how Europa was taken away.

choices.label: D
choices.text: After wandering through many towns, Cadmus eventually stopped traveling and settled in Greece, where he told his sister's story one final time.

cards.standardTitle: Key literary elements add layers of meaning
cards.excerpt:
The others assented, so they went inside and laid their cloaks on the benches and seats. They sacrificed the sheep, goats, pigs, and the heifer, and when the inward meats were cooked they served them round. They mixed the wine in the mixing-bowls, and the swineherd gave every man his cup, while Philoetius handed round the bread in the bread baskets, and Melanthius poured them out their wine. Then they laid their hands upon the good things that were before them.

Telemachus purposely made Ulysses sit in the part of the cloister that was paved with stone;158 he gave him a shabby looking seat at a little table to himself, and had his portion of the inward meats brought to him, with his wine in a gold cup. “Sit there,” said he, “and drink your wine among the great people. I will put a stop to the gibes and blows of the suitors, for this is no public house, but belongs to Ulysses, and has passed from him to me. Therefore, suitors, keep your hands and your tongues to yourselves, or there will be mischief.”

The suitors bit their lips, and marvelled at the boldness of his speech; then Antinous said, “We do not like such language but we will put up with it, for Telemachus is threatening us in good earnest. If Jove had let us we should have put a stop to his brave talk ere now.”

Thus spoke Antinous, but Telemachus heeded him not. Meanwhile the heralds were bringing the holy hecatomb through the city, and the Achaeans gathered under the shady grove of Apollo.

Then they roasted the outer meat, drew it off the spits, gave every man his portion, and feasted to their heart’s content; those who waited at table gave Ulysses exactly the same portion as the others had, for Telemachus had told them to do so.
cards.whyThisWorks: Telemachus's deliberate seating of the disguised Ulysses in a place of stone with a shabby seat yet a gold cup, combined with his direct warning to the suitors, reveals a character who is both strategically protective and newly assertive—demonstrating how action and speech together build meaning about his growth.
cards.skillStrategy: When a character does something on purpose and then speaks, ask yourself what those choices together reveal about who that character is becoming.
evidencePoints: Telemachus purposely made Ulysses sit in the part of the cloister that was paved with stone; he gave him a shabby looking seat at a little table to himself, and had his portion of the inward meats brought to him, with his wine in a gold cup.
I will put a stop to the gibes and blows of the suitors, for this is no public house, but belongs to Ulysses, and has passed from him to me.
cards.question: Read the following passage from the excerpt: 'Telemachus purposely made Ulysses sit in the part of the cloister that was paved with stone; he gave him a shabby looking seat at a little table to himself, and had his portion of the inward meats brought to him, with his wine in a gold cup.' What does this combination of actions reveal about Telemachus's character?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Telemachus is careless about the comfort of his guests, seating the beggar poorly without thinking about how the suitors might react.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Telemachus is deliberately protecting the disguised Ulysses by keeping him apart from the suitors while still honoring him with equal food and a gold cup, showing calculated loyalty beneath a humble surface.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Telemachus is humiliating the beggar in front of the suitors to prove that he controls the household and has no sympathy for outsiders.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Telemachus is following the traditional customs of hospitality that require guests of low status to sit separately from the noble guests at every feast.

cards.standardTitle: Epic poetry: characters, structures, and themes
cards.excerpt: On this they hurried off on their several errands. The heifer was brought in from the plain, and Telemachus’s crew came from the ship; the goldsmith brought the anvil, hammer, and tongs, with which he worked his gold, and Minerva herself came to accept the sacrifice. Nestor gave out the gold, and the smith gilded the horns of the heifer that the goddess might have pleasure in their beauty. Then Stratius and Echephron brought her in by the horns; Aretus fetched water from the house in a ewer that had a flower pattern on it, and in his other hand he held a basket of barley meal; sturdy Thrasymedes stood by with a sharp axe, ready to strike the heifer, while Perseus held a bucket. Then Nestor began with washing his hands and sprinkling the barley meal, and he offered many a prayer to Minerva as he threw a lock from the heifer’s head upon the fire.
cards.whyThisWorks: The excerpt shows Minerva as the divine recipient whose expected presence directly shapes every ritual action—gilding the horns for her pleasure, assembling the household, and closing with prayers to her—making it a clear model of divine intervention structuring human ceremony in epic poetry.
cards.skillStrategy: When identifying divine intervention, trace how the god's presence or expectation changes what the human characters do and say, using specific details from the text as evidence.
evidencePoints: Minerva herself came to accept the sacrifice
the smith gilded the horns of the heifer that the goddess might have pleasure in their beauty
cards.question: The excerpt states that 'Minerva herself came to accept the sacrifice' and that the heifer's horns were gilded 'that the goddess might have pleasure in their beauty.' How do these two details together show Minerva's role as divine recipient shaping the ritual actions of Nestor and his household?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Minerva's arrival shifts control of the ritual away from Nestor, so Stratius, Echephron, and Aretus independently decide to bring in the heifer, fetch water, and carry barley meal without any direction from him.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Minerva's role as divine recipient shapes every detail of the ritual: the horns are gilded specifically for her pleasure, the entire household gathers the required objects in her honor, and Nestor closes by offering prayers directly to her at the fire.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Minerva arrives only after the preparations are already complete and has no influence on them, since the gilding of the horns, Aretus fetching water, and Nestor sprinkling barley meal were standard steps performed before any goddess was expected.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Minerva's physical presence guarantees her favor in advance, which means the gilding of the horns and Nestor's prayers at the fire are empty formalities rather than acts intended to earn or honor her approval.

cards.standardTitle: Key literary elements add layers of meaning
cards.excerpt:
On this the old woman150 went out of the room to bid the maids go to their mistress. In the meantime Minerva bethought her of another matter, and sent Penelope off into a sweet slumber; so she lay down on her couch and her limbs became heavy with sleep. Then the goddess shed grace and beauty over her that all the Achaeans might admire her. She washed her face with the ambrosial loveliness that Venus wears when she goes dancing with the Graces; she made her taller and of a more commanding figure, while as for her complexion it was whiter than sawn ivory. When Minerva had done all this she went away, whereon the maids came in from the women’s room and woke Penelope with the sound of their talking.

“What an exquisitely delicious sleep I have been having,” said she, as she passed her hands over her face, “in spite of all my misery. I wish Diana would let me die so sweetly now at this very moment, that I might no longer waste in despair for the loss of my dear husband, who possessed every kind of good quality and was the most distinguished man among the Achaeans.”

With these words she came down from her upper room, not alone but attended by two of her maidens, and when she reached the suitors she stood by one of the bearing-posts supporting the roof of the cloister, holding a veil before her face, and with a staid maid servant on either side of her. As they beheld her the suitors were so overpowered and became so desperately enamoured of her, that each one prayed he might win her for his own bed fellow.
cards.whyThisWorks: Penelope's speech wishing for death alongside Minerva's divine beautification creates a meaningful contrast between her inner despair and her outward effect on the suitors, revealing the complexity of her grief and her unwilling power.
cards.skillStrategy: When a character's words contradict what is happening around them, ask what that gap reveals about who they truly are.
evidencePoints: I wish Diana would let me die so sweetly now at this very moment, that I might no longer waste in despair for the loss of my dear husband
the suitors were so overpowered and became so desperately enamoured of her, that each one prayed he might win her for his own bed fellow
cards.question: Penelope descends to the suitors wishing aloud that Diana would grant her death, yet the suitors respond by becoming 'desperately enamoured of her.' What does this contrast between Penelope's speech and the suitors' reaction reveal about her character?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Her wish for death is a calculated performance designed to make herself appear more desirable to the suitors gathered below.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Her genuine grief over her husband's absence consumes her inwardly even as she unknowingly commands the admiration of every man in the room, showing the depth of her loyalty and sorrow.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Her descent from the upper room signals that she has accepted her husband's death and is now ready to consider the suitors' proposals.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Her words reveal that she blames the suitors for her suffering and uses the wish for death to shame them into leaving her household.

cards.standardTitle: Epic poetry: characters, structures, and themes
cards.excerpt:
So saying she lashed the mules with her whip and they left the river. The mules drew well, and their hoofs went up and down upon the road. She was careful not to go too fast for Ulysses and the maids who were following on foot along with the waggon, so she plied her whip with judgement. As the sun was going down they came to the sacred grove of Minerva, and there Ulysses sat down and prayed to the mighty daughter of Jove.

“Hear me,” he cried, “daughter of Aegis-bearing Jove, unweariable, hear me now, for you gave no heed to my prayers when Neptune was wrecking me. Now, therefore, have pity upon me and grant that I may find friends and be hospitably received by the Phaeacians.”

Thus did he pray, and Minerva heard his prayer, but she would not show herself to him openly, for she was afraid of her uncle Neptune, who was still furious in his endeavors to prevent Ulysses from getting home.

RECEPTION OF ULYSSES AT THE PALACE OF KING ALCINOUS.

Thus, then, did Ulysses wait and pray; but the girl drove on to the town. When she reached her father’s house she drew up at the gateway, and her brothers—comely as the gods—gathered round her, took the mules out of the waggon, and carried the clothes into the house, while she went to her own room, where an old servant, Eurymedusa of Apeira, lit the fire for her. This old woman had been brought by sea from Apeira, and had been chosen as a prize for Alcinous because he was king over the Phaeacians, and the people obeyed him as though he were a god.57 She had been nurse to Nausicaa, and had now lit the fire for her, and brought her supper for her into her own room.
cards.whyThisWorks: Minerva's decision to hear but not openly appear—explicitly because 'she was afraid of her uncle Neptune, who was still furious'—gives students a precise textual moment of restrained divine intervention to analyze for its effect on Ulysses' situation.
cards.skillStrategy: When analyzing divine intervention in epic poetry, identify exactly what the god does or withholds, then trace how that choice directly shapes what the hero must do next.
evidencePoints: Minerva heard his prayer, but she would not show herself to him openly, for she was afraid of her uncle Neptune, who was still furious in his endeavors to prevent Ulysses from getting home.
grant that I may find friends and be hospitably received by the Phaeacians
cards.question: In the excerpt, Ulysses prays for Minerva to 'grant that I may find friends and be hospitably received by the Phaeacians,' and the narrator states she 'heard his prayer, but she would not show herself to him openly.' Why does Minerva withhold direct intervention at this moment, and what does that force Ulysses to rely on instead?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Minerva withholds her presence because Ulysses prayed at the sacred grove rather than at the palace, so she redirects him to seek Alcinous directly before she will act on his behalf.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Minerva stays hidden because Neptune's ongoing fury still endangers Ulysses, leaving him dependent on mortal hospitality—the 'friends' he prayed for—rather than open divine rescue to reach safety.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Minerva refuses to appear because she ignored Ulysses when Neptune wrecked his ship and continues to punish him, showing the gods have fully withdrawn their favor from him on Phaeacian shores.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Minerva withholds her appearance in order to test whether Nausicaa's brothers, described as 'comely as the gods,' will welcome Ulysses at the palace gate without divine prompting.

cards.standardTitle: Key literary elements add layers of meaning
cards.excerpt: Thereon he floated about for two nights and two days in the water, with a heavy swell on the sea and death staring him in the face; but when the third day broke, the wind fell and there was a dead calm without so much as a breath of air stirring. As he rose on the swell he looked eagerly ahead, and could see land quite near. Then, as children rejoice when their dear father begins to get better after having for a long time borne sore affliction sent him by some angry spirit, but the gods deliver him from evil, so was Ulysses thankful when he again saw land and trees, and swam on with all his strength that he might once more set foot upon dry ground. When, however, he got within earshot, he began to hear the surf thundering up against the rocks, for the swell still broke against them with a terrific roar. Everything was enveloped in spray; there were no harbours where a ship might ride, nor shelter of any kind, but only headlands, low-lying rocks, and mountain tops.
cards.whyThisWorks: The simile comparing Ulysses to a child whose father recovers from illness, paired with his immediate shift from relief to terror at the crashing surf, reveals a character whose hope and vulnerability deepen the reader's understanding of his endurance and mortal fragility.
cards.skillStrategy: When a character's emotion is compared to someone else's experience through a simile, ask what that comparison reveals about who the character is and what the moment means.
evidencePoints: so was Ulysses thankful when he again saw land and trees, and swam on with all his strength that he might once more set foot upon dry ground
he began to hear the surf thundering up against the rocks, for the swell still broke against them with a terrific roar
cards.question: The simile comparing Ulysses to children rejoicing over a father's recovery, followed immediately by his discovery of crashing surf and rocky headlands, reveals which aspect of his character?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Ulysses is reckless and overconfident, assuming land will always offer safety after surviving two days at sea.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Ulysses is deeply human in his longing for survival, yet his relief is fragile—hope and danger arrive together, showing that his endurance is constantly tested rather than rewarded.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Ulysses feels the same helpless grief as a child watching a parent suffer, suggesting he has lost all will to fight for his own life.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Ulysses is indifferent to the danger of the rocks because his relief at seeing land overwhelms any fear he might otherwise feel.

cards.standardTitle: Epic poetry: characters, structures, and themes
cards.excerpt:
She went wondering back into the house, and laid her son’s saying in her heart. Then going upstairs with her handmaids into her room, she mourned her dear husband till Minerva sent sweet sleep over her eyelids.

The swineherd now took up the bow and was for taking it to Ulysses, but the suitors clamoured at him from all parts of the cloisters, and one of them said, “You idiot, where are you taking the bow to? Are you out of your wits? If Apollo and the other gods will grant our prayer, your own boarhounds shall get you into some quiet little place, and worry you to death.”

Eumaeus was frightened at the outcry they all raised, so he put the bow down then and there, but Telemachus shouted out at him from the other side of the cloisters, and threatened him saying, “Father Eumaeus, bring the bow on in spite of them, or young as I am I will pelt you with stones back to the country, for I am the better man of the two. I wish I was as much stronger than all the other suitors in the house as I am than you, I would soon send some of them off sick and sorry, for they mean mischief.”

Thus did he speak, and they all of them laughed heartily, which put them in a better humour with Telemachus; so Eumaeus brought the bow on and placed it in the hands of Ulysses. When he had done this, he called Euryclea apart and said to her, “Euryclea, Telemachus says you are to close the doors of the women’s apartments. If they hear any groaning or uproar as of men fighting about the house, they are not to come out, but are to keep quiet and stay where they are at their work.”

Euryclea did as she was told and closed the doors of the women’s apartments.
cards.whyThisWorks: The suitors invoke Apollo's name as a threat against Eumaeus, showing how divine authority is weaponized to control human action—a clear example of how supernatural force (even when invoked falsely) shapes the plot's tension and the characters' choices.
cards.skillStrategy: When a god or divine force appears in an epic, ask yourself: does it directly cause an action, or does a character use it to influence someone else's behavior?
evidencePoints: If Apollo and the other gods will grant our prayer, your own boarhounds shall get you into some quiet little place, and worry you to death.
Eumaeus was frightened at the outcry they all raised, so he put the bow down then and there
cards.question: In the second paragraph, the suitors warn Eumaeus that 'if Apollo and the other gods will grant our prayer, your own boarhounds shall get you into some quiet little place, and worry you to death.' How does this invocation of Apollo shape the action that immediately follows?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Apollo directly intervenes to stop Eumaeus, proving the gods favor the suitors over Ulysses in this moment.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The threat of divine punishment frightens Eumaeus into abandoning the bow, showing that invoking a god's name alone is enough to alter a character's actions.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The mention of Apollo signals to Eumaeus that Ulysses has lost the gods' favor, so Eumaeus chooses loyalty to the suitors instead.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Eumaeus sets the bow down because Telemachus has not yet given him permission to deliver it, and the suitors' prayer is simply background noise.

cards.standardTitle: Key literary elements add layers of meaning
cards.excerpt: And Ulysses answered, “It would be a long story Madam, were I to relate in full the tale of my misfortunes, for the hand of heaven has been laid heavy upon me; but as regards your question, there is an island far away in the sea which is called ‘the Ogygian.’ Here dwells the cunning and powerful goddess Calypso, daughter of Atlas. She lives by herself far from all neighbours human or divine. Fortune, however, brought me to her hearth all desolate and alone, for Jove struck my ship with his thunderbolts, and broke it up in mid-ocean. My brave comrades were drowned every man of them, but I stuck to the keel and was carried hither and thither for the space of nine days, till at last during the darkness of the tenth night the gods brought me to the Ogygian island where the great goddess Calypso lives. She took me in and treated me with the utmost kindness; indeed she wanted to make me immortal that I might never grow old, but she could not persuade me to let her do so.
cards.whyThisWorks: Ulysses' refusal of immortality from Calypso, despite his suffering and isolation, reveals his defining commitment to mortal life and identity over divine comfort, making characterization central to meaning.
cards.skillStrategy: When a character makes a surprising choice, ask what that choice reveals about who they are and what they value most.
evidencePoints: she wanted to make me immortal that I might never grow old, but she could not persuade me to let her do so
Fortune, however, brought me to her hearth all desolate and alone
cards.question: Ulysses reveals that Calypso 'wanted to make me immortal that I might never grow old, but she could not persuade me to let her do so.' What does this detail most clearly reveal about Ulysses' character?

choices.label: A
choices.text: He distrusts Calypso's power because he doubts a goddess could truly grant immortality.

choices.label: B
choices.text: His sense of identity is so rooted in his mortal life that even after devastating loss he refuses to abandon it for divine comfort.

choices.label: C
choices.text: He is too proud to accept help from anyone, whether human or divine, after surviving the shipwreck alone.

choices.label: D
choices.text: He rejects Calypso's offer because he believes Jove's punishment must be endured without divine interference.

cards.standardTitle: Theme development across a literary text
cards.excerpt: When the bright star that heralds the approach of dawn began to show, the ship drew near to land.112 Now there is in Ithaca a haven of the old merman Phorcys, which lies between two points that break the line of the sea and shut the harbour in. These shelter it from the storms of wind and sea that rage outside, so that, when once within it, a ship may lie without being even moored. At the head of this harbour there is a large olive tree, and at no great distance a fine overarching cavern sacred to the nymphs who are called Naiads.113 There are mixing bowls within it and wine-jars of stone, and the bees hive there. Moreover, there are great looms of stone on which the nymphs weave their robes of sea purple—very curious to see—and at all times there is water within it. It has two entrances, one facing North by which mortals can go down into the cave, while the other comes from the South and is more mysterious; mortals cannot possibly get in by it, it is the way taken by the gods.
cards.whyThisWorks: The excerpt describes a sacred cave with two entrances—one accessible to mortals and one reserved for gods—allowing students to distinguish between true-but-topical details (the stone looms, the bees) and details that actually develop a theme about the boundary between the mortal and divine worlds.
cards.skillStrategy: Ask yourself: does this detail show the theme in action, or does it just describe the setting without pushing the theme forward?
evidencePoints: It has two entrances, one facing North by which mortals can go down into the cave, while the other comes from the South and is more mysterious; mortals cannot possibly get in by it, it is the way taken by the gods.
These shelter it from the storms of wind and sea that rage outside, so that, when once within it, a ship may lie without being even moored.
cards.question: Which detail from the passage most directly develops the theme that a clear and uncrossable boundary exists between the mortal world and the divine?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The harbour is sheltered by two points of land so that ships can rest inside without being moored, showing that Ithaca offers sailors a place of safety after long voyages.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The cave has one entrance mortals may use and a second that is 'more mysterious' and reserved exclusively for the gods, marking a boundary that humans cannot cross.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The nymphs called Naiads weave robes of sea purple on great looms of stone inside the cavern, showing that divine beings engage in skilled labor similar to mortal craftwork.

choices.label: D
choices.text: A large olive tree stands at the head of the harbour near the cavern, establishing that the landscape of Ithaca is rich with natural landmarks that make it recognizable to returning travelers.

cards.standardTitle: Epic poetry: characters, structures, and themes
cards.excerpt:
Then Minerva bethought her of another matter. She took his shape, and went round the town to each one of the crew, telling them to meet at the ship by sundown. She went also to Noemon son of Phronius, and asked him to let her have a ship—which he was very ready to do. When the sun had set and darkness was over all the land, she got the ship into the water, put all the tackle on board her that ships generally carry, and stationed her at the end of the harbour. Presently the crew came up, and the goddess spoke encouragingly to each of them.

Furthermore she went to the house of Ulysses, and threw the suitors into a deep slumber. She caused their drink to fuddle them, and made them drop their cups from their hands, so that instead of sitting over their wine, they went back into the town to sleep, with their eyes heavy and full of drowsiness. Then she took the form and voice of Mentor, and called Telemachus to come outside.
cards.whyThisWorks: Minerva's disguises, manipulation of the suitors, and direct orchestration of the ship's departure show divine intervention actively driving the plot forward and reinforcing the theme that mortal action depends on divine will.
cards.skillStrategy: When a god or goddess acts in disguise or causes a supernatural event, ask yourself: what would NOT happen without this divine force, and what does that reveal about the epic's theme?
evidencePoints: She took his shape, and went round the town to each one of the crew, telling them to meet at the ship by sundown.
she got the ship into the water, put all the tackle on board her that ships generally carry, and stationed her at the end of the harbour.
cards.question: How does Minerva's intervention in these two paragraphs shape the action of the epic?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Minerva warns Telemachus that the suitors plan to stop his voyage, motivating him to act quickly before they can interfere.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Minerva disguises herself, assembles the crew, prepares the ship, and neutralizes the suitors, making Telemachus's departure entirely dependent on her hidden efforts.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Minerva persuades Noemon to donate a ship by revealing her divine identity, showing that mortals willingly serve the gods when approached directly.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Minerva puts the suitors to sleep so that Telemachus can confront them without danger, demonstrating that the gods protect heroes from physical harm.

cards.standardTitle: Key literary elements add layers of meaning
cards.excerpt:
This was how they talked, but they knew nothing about it; and Alcinous said, “I remember now the old prophecy of my father. He said that Neptune would be angry with us for taking every one so safely over the sea, and would one day wreck a Phaeacian ship as it was returning from an escort, and bury our city under a high mountain. This was what my old father used to say, and now it is all coming true.117 Now therefore let us all do as I say; in the first place we must leave off giving people escorts when they come here, and in the next let us sacrifice twelve picked bulls to Neptune that he may have mercy upon us, and not bury our city under the high mountain.” When the people heard this they were afraid and got ready the bulls.

Thus did the chiefs and rulers of the Phaeacians pray to king Neptune, standing round his altar; and at the same time118 Ulysses woke up once more upon his own soil. He had been so long away that he did not know it again; moreover, Jove’s daughter Minerva had made it a foggy day, so that people might not know of his having come, and that she might tell him everything without either his wife or his fellow citizens and friends recognising him119 until he had taken his revenge upon the wicked suitors. Everything, therefore, seemed quite different to him—the long straight tracks, the harbours, the precipices, and the goodly trees, appeared all changed as he started up and looked upon his native land. So he smote his thighs with the flat of his hands and cried aloud despairingly.
cards.whyThisWorks: Ulysses' physical action of smiting his thighs and crying out despairingly, combined with his failure to recognize his own homeland, reveals his profound disorientation and the emotional weight of his long absence, demonstrating how character action and description layer meaning onto the homecoming moment.
cards.skillStrategy: When a character does or says something unexpected, ask what that action reveals about their inner state and what larger idea the author is building through that moment.
evidencePoints: he smote his thighs with the flat of his hands and cried aloud despairingly
He had been so long away that he did not know it again
cards.question: When Ulysses wakes on Ithaca and 'smote his thighs with the flat of his hands and cried aloud despairingly,' what does this action reveal about his situation and its meaning?

choices.label: A
choices.text: His grief shows that he is angry at Minerva for hiding his arrival from his wife and fellow citizens without his consent.

choices.label: B
choices.text: His anguish reflects how completely his long absence has severed his connection to home—even his own land is unrecognizable to him.

choices.label: C
choices.text: His despair signals that he has already learned about the suitors and fears he cannot defeat them alone.

choices.label: D
choices.text: His outburst shows that he blames Neptune for the fog that prevents him from seeing the harbours and trees clearly.

cards.standardTitle: Theme development across a literary text
cards.excerpt: Outside the gate of the outer court there is a large garden of about four acres with a wall all round it. It is full of beautiful trees—pears, pomegranates, and the most delicious apples. There are luscious figs also, and olives in full growth. The fruits never rot nor fail all the year round, neither winter nor summer, for the air is so soft that a new crop ripens before the old has dropped. Pear grows on pear, apple on apple, and fig on fig, and so also with the grapes, for there is an excellent vineyard: on the level ground of a part of this, the grapes are being made into raisins; in another part they are being gathered; some are being trodden in the wine tubs, others further on have shed their blossom and are beginning to show fruit, others again are just changing colour. In the furthest part of the ground there are beautifully arranged beds of flowers that are in bloom all the year round. Two streams go through it, the one turned in ducts throughout the whole garden, while the other is carried under the ground of the outer court to the house itself, and the town’s people draw water from it. Such, then, were the splendours with which the gods had endowed the house of king Alcinous.
cards.whyThisWorks: The excerpt contains both true-but-topic-only details (e.g., the garden's size and layout) and details that actively develop the theme of divine abundance transcending mortal limits, requiring students to distinguish between details that merely describe the garden and those that prove a theme about gods granting endless, supernatural plenty.
cards.skillStrategy: Ask yourself: does this detail just tell me what the place looks like, or does it show me something about a bigger idea—like what the gods can give that humans cannot?
evidencePoints: The fruits never rot nor fail all the year round, neither winter nor summer, for the air is so soft that a new crop ripens before the old has dropped.
Such, then, were the splendours with which the gods had endowed the house of king Alcinous.
cards.question: Which detail from the description of Alcinous's garden best develops the theme that divine favor lifts mortals beyond the natural limits of the human world?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The garden covers about four acres and is enclosed by a wall all the way around it, showing the wealth and power of King Alcinous.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The fruits never rot nor fail all the year round because a new crop ripens before the old has dropped, revealing that the gods' gift suspends the ordinary cycle of decay and season.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The vineyard contains grapes at every stage—being dried into raisins, gathered, trodden, blossoming, and ripening—showing how productive the land is.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Two streams run through the property, one irrigating the garden and one supplying water to the house and the townspeople, demonstrating the garden's practical value.

cards.standardTitle: Key literary elements add layers of meaning
cards.excerpt:
So saying she lashed the mules with her whip and they left the river. The mules drew well, and their hoofs went up and down upon the road. She was careful not to go too fast for Ulysses and the maids who were following on foot along with the waggon, so she plied her whip with judgement. As the sun was going down they came to the sacred grove of Minerva, and there Ulysses sat down and prayed to the mighty daughter of Jove.

“Hear me,” he cried, “daughter of Aegis-bearing Jove, unweariable, hear me now, for you gave no heed to my prayers when Neptune was wrecking me. Now, therefore, have pity upon me and grant that I may find friends and be hospitably received by the Phaeacians.”

Thus did he pray, and Minerva heard his prayer, but she would not show herself to him openly, for she was afraid of her uncle Neptune, who was still furious in his endeavors to prevent Ulysses from getting home.

RECEPTION OF ULYSSES AT THE PALACE OF KING ALCINOUS.

Thus, then, did Ulysses wait and pray; but the girl drove on to the town. When she reached her father’s house she drew up at the gateway, and her brothers—comely as the gods—gathered round her, took the mules out of the waggon, and carried the clothes into the house, while she went to her own room, where an old servant, Eurymedusa of Apeira, lit the fire for her. This old woman had been brought by sea from Apeira, and had been chosen as a prize for Alcinous because he was king over the Phaeacians, and the people obeyed him as though he were a god.57 She had been nurse to Nausicaa, and had now lit the fire for her, and brought her supper for her into her own room.
cards.whyThisWorks: Nausicaa's deliberate pacing of the mules so Ulysses and the maids can keep up on foot reveals her thoughtful consideration for others, and contrasting this with Ulysses' solitary, desperate prayer shows how characterization builds meaning about power, vulnerability, and hospitality.
cards.skillStrategy: When a character makes a deliberate choice or takes a careful action, ask what that choice reveals about who they are and what the author wants you to understand about them.
evidencePoints: she was careful not to go too fast for Ulysses and the maids who were following on foot along with the waggon, so she plied her whip with judgement
thus did Ulysses wait and pray; but the girl drove on to the town
cards.question: The narrator states that Nausicaa 'was careful not to go too fast for Ulysses and the maids who were following on foot along with the waggon, so she plied her whip with judgement.' What does this detail reveal about Nausicaa's character?

choices.label: A
choices.text: She is impatient to return home and must restrain herself from driving the mules at full speed.

choices.label: B
choices.text: She is attentive to those in her care, exercising deliberate restraint to protect a vulnerable stranger and her servants.

choices.label: C
choices.text: She fears the mules will tire before reaching the sacred grove of Minerva if driven too hard.

choices.label: D
choices.text: She is obeying a command from her father Alcinous, who instructed her to escort Ulysses safely to the palace.

cards.standardTitle: Key literary elements add layers of meaning
cards.excerpt:
The others applauded what Antinous had said, and each one sent his servant to bring his present. Antinous’s man returned with a large and lovely dress most exquisitely embroidered. It had twelve beautifully made brooch pins of pure gold with which to fasten it. Eurymachus immediately brought her a magnificent chain of gold and amber beads that gleamed like sunlight. Eurydamas’s two men returned with some earrings fashioned into three brilliant pendants which glistened most beautifully; while king Pisander son of Polyctor gave her a necklace of the rarest workmanship, and every one else brought her a beautiful present of some kind.

Then the queen went back to her room upstairs, and her maids brought the presents after her. Meanwhile the suitors took to singing and dancing, and stayed till evening came. They danced and sang till it grew dark; they then brought in three braziers151 to give light, and piled them up with chopped firewood very old and dry, and they lit torches from them, which the maids held up turn and turn about. Then Ulysses said:

“Maids, servants of Ulysses who has so long been absent, go to the queen inside the house; sit with her and amuse her, or spin, and pick wool. I will hold the light for all these people. They may stay till morning, but shall not beat me, for I can stand a great deal.”

The maids looked at one another and laughed, while pretty Melantho began to gibe at him contemptuously. She was daughter to Dolius, but had been brought up by Penelope, who used to give her toys to play with, and looked after her when she was a child; but in spite of all this she showed no consideration for the sorrows of her mistress, and used to misconduct herself with Eurymachus, with whom she was in love.
cards.whyThisWorks: Melantho's backstory of being raised by Penelope contrasted with her contempt toward Ulysses and indifference to Penelope's suffering illustrates how characterization through ironic contrast deepens the passage's theme of loyalty and betrayal.
cards.skillStrategy: When a character's actions contradict their background or upbringing, ask what that contrast reveals about who they truly are and what the author wants you to understand.
evidencePoints: Penelope, who used to give her toys to play with, and looked after her when she was a child
she showed no consideration for the sorrows of her mistress, and used to misconduct herself with Eurymachus
cards.question: The narrator states that Penelope 'looked after her when she was a child' yet Melantho 'showed no consideration for the sorrows of her mistress' and 'began to gibe at him contemptuously.' What does this contrast most reveal about Melantho's character?

choices.label: A
choices.text: She mocks Ulysses because she fears the suitors and laughs along with them to avoid punishment.

choices.label: B
choices.text: She repays Penelope's past kindness with disloyalty, marking her as a figure of ingratitude and betrayal.

choices.label: C
choices.text: She follows the suitors' lead out of indifference, showing she has no strong feelings toward anyone in the household.

choices.label: D
choices.text: She feels entitled to mock a stranger because her privileged upbringing set her apart from the other servants.

cards.standardTitle: Epic poetry: characters, structures, and themes
cards.excerpt: Menelaus on hearing this was very much shocked. “So,” he exclaimed, “these cowards would usurp a brave man’s bed? A hind might as well lay her new born young in the lair of a lion, and then go off to feed in the forest or in some grassy dell: the lion when he comes back to his lair will make short work with the pair of them—and so will Ulysses with these suitors. By father Jove, Minerva, and Apollo, if Ulysses is still the man that he was when he wrestled with Philomeleides in Lesbos, and threw him so heavily that all the Achaeans cheered him—if he is still such and were to come near these suitors, they would have a short shrift and a sorry wedding. As regards your questions, however, I will not prevaricate nor deceive you, but will tell you without concealment all that the old man of the sea told me.
cards.whyThisWorks: Menelaus explicitly invokes three divine figures—Jove, Minerva, and Apollo—as guarantors of Ulysses' power, making the gods the force that shapes the anticipated action against the suitors and reinforcing the theme of divine justice.
cards.skillStrategy: When a character calls on gods by name to predict or justify an outcome, ask yourself: what do the gods make possible or certain that humans alone could not guarantee?
evidencePoints: By father Jove, Minerva, and Apollo, if Ulysses is still the man that he was
they would have a short shrift and a sorry wedding
cards.question: When Menelaus swears 'By father Jove, Minerva, and Apollo' before predicting the suitors' fate, what role do these divine figures play in his speech?

choices.label: A
choices.text: They remind Menelaus of past battles he and Ulysses fought together under divine protection, making him nostalgic rather than confident about the future.

choices.label: B
choices.text: They serve as the ultimate authority behind Menelaus's prediction, suggesting that the gods' power—not human strength alone—guarantees the suitors will be destroyed.

choices.label: C
choices.text: They are invoked to warn Telemachus that the gods may punish Ulysses if he acts violently against the suitors in his own home.

choices.label: D
choices.text: They establish that Menelaus himself has divine favor and is therefore the one who will avenge the wrongs done to Ulysses' household.

cards.standardTitle: Key literary elements add layers of meaning
cards.excerpt:
TELEMACHUS AND HIS MOTHER MEET—ULYSSES AND EUMAEUS COME DOWN TO THE TOWN, AND ULYSSES IS INSULTED BY MELANTHIUS—HE IS RECOGNISED BY THE DOG ARGOS—HE IS INSULTED AND PRESENTLY STRUCK BY ANTINOUS WITH A STOOL—PENELOPE DESIRES THAT HE SHALL BE SENT TO HER.

When the child of morning, rosy-fingered Dawn, appeared, Telemachus bound on his sandals and took a strong spear that suited his hands, for he wanted to go into the city. “Old friend,” said he to the swineherd, “I will now go to the town and show myself to my mother, for she will never leave off grieving till she has seen me. As for this unfortunate stranger, take him to the town and let him beg there of any one who will give him a drink and a piece of bread. I have trouble enough of my own, and cannot be burdened with other people. If this makes him angry so much the worse for him, but I like to say what I mean.”

Then Ulysses said, “Sir, I do not want to stay here; a beggar can always do better in town than country, for any one who likes can give him something. I am too old to care about remaining here at the beck and call of a master. Therefore let this man do as you have just told him, and take me to the town as soon as I have had a warm by the fire, and the day has got a little heat in it. My clothes are wretchedly thin, and this frosty morning I shall be perished with cold, for you say the city is some way off.”

On this Telemachus strode off through the yards, brooding his revenge upon the suitors. When he reached home he stood his spear against a bearing-post of the cloister, crossed the stone floor of the cloister itself, and went inside.
cards.whyThisWorks: Telemachus's blunt dismissal of the disguised Ulysses—'I cannot be burdened with other people'—contrasted with Ulysses's measured, dignified response reveals both characters' inner natures and adds meaning to their unrecognized father-son dynamic.
cards.skillStrategy: When a character speaks or acts, ask what that choice reveals about who they are inside—then check whether another character's response deepens or complicates that meaning.
evidencePoints: I have trouble enough of my own, and cannot be burdened with other people. If this makes him angry so much the worse for him, but I like to say what I mean.
I am too old to care about remaining here at the beck and call of a master.
cards.question: Read Telemachus's words: 'I have trouble enough of my own, and cannot be burdened with other people. If this makes him angry so much the worse for him, but I like to say what I mean.' What do these words reveal about Telemachus's character at this moment in the excerpt?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Telemachus is deeply compassionate toward the stranger but hides his feelings to appear strong in front of the swineherd.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Telemachus is self-focused and blunt, prioritizing his own burdens over the welfare of the disguised stranger, which shows his immaturity despite his outward readiness for action.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Telemachus recognizes that the stranger is Ulysses in disguise and speaks harshly to protect their secret from the swineherd.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Telemachus is indifferent to his mother's grief and uses concern for the stranger as an excuse to avoid returning home.

cards.standardTitle: Epic poetry: characters, structures, and themes
cards.excerpt: Thus did he pray, and Minerva heard his prayer. He then led the way to his own house, followed by his sons and sons in law. When they had got there and had taken their places on the benches and seats, he mixed them a bowl of sweet wine that was eleven years old when the housekeeper took the lid off the jar that held it. As he mixed the wine, he prayed much and made drink offerings to Minerva, daughter of Aegis-bearing Jove. Then, when they had made their drink offerings and had drunk each as much as he was minded, the others went home to bed each in his own abode; but Nestor put Telemachus to sleep in the room that was over the gateway along with Pisistratus, who was the only unmarried son now left him. As for himself, he slept in an inner room of the house, with the queen his wife by his side.
cards.whyThisWorks: The excerpt explicitly states 'Minerva heard his prayer' and shows Nestor making drink offerings 'to Minerva, daughter of Aegis-bearing Jove,' demonstrating how divine acknowledgment elevates a mortal act of hospitality into a divinely sanctioned event—a core feature of epic divine intervention.
cards.skillStrategy: When identifying divine intervention in epic poetry, look for moments where a god directly responds to a mortal's prayer or action, then ask how that response changes the meaning or importance of what the mortal is doing.
evidencePoints: Thus did he pray, and Minerva heard his prayer.
he prayed much and made drink offerings to Minerva, daughter of Aegis-bearing Jove
cards.question: The narrator states, 'Thus did he pray, and Minerva heard his prayer,' and later describes Nestor making 'drink offerings to Minerva, daughter of Aegis-bearing Jove.' What do these two details together suggest about the significance of Nestor's hospitality toward Telemachus?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Nestor's repeated prayers to Minerva reveal his anxiety that the eleven-year-old wine is not a worthy enough offering for such a distinguished guest.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Minerva's acknowledgment of Nestor's prayer and his drink offerings to her suggest that divine favor consecrates the hospitality shown to Telemachus, elevating it beyond ordinary social custom.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The two references to Minerva show that Nestor is performing a routine religious ritual that has no special connection to Telemachus's presence in his home.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Nestor's prayers to Minerva indicate that he fears conflict will break out among his sons and sons-in-law before Telemachus can be safely put to bed.

cards.standardTitle: Key literary elements add layers of meaning
cards.excerpt:
But she would not give him full victory as yet, for she wished still further to prove his own prowess and that of his brave son, so she flew up to one of the rafters in the roof of the cloister and sat upon it in the form of a swallow.

Meanwhile Agelaus son of Damastor, Eurynomus, Amphimedon, Demoptolemus, Pisander, and Polybus son of Polyctor bore the brunt of the fight upon the suitors’ side; of all those who were still fighting for their lives they were by far the most valiant, for the others had already fallen under the arrows of Ulysses. Agelaus shouted to them and said, “My friends, he will soon have to leave off, for Mentor has gone away after having done nothing for him but brag. They are standing at the doors unsupported. Do not aim at him all at once, but six of you throw your spears first, and see if you cannot cover yourselves with glory by killing him. When he has fallen we need not be uneasy about the others.”

They threw their spears as he bade them, but Minerva made them all of no effect. One hit the door post; another went against the door; the pointed shaft of another struck the wall; and as soon as they had avoided all the spears of the suitors Ulysses said to his own men, “My friends, I should say we too had better let drive into the middle of them, or they will crown all the harm they have done us by killing us outright.”

They therefore aimed straight in front of them and threw their spears. Ulysses killed Demoptolemus, Telemachus Euryades, Eumaeus Elatus, while the stockman killed Pisander. These all bit the dust, and as the others drew back into a corner Ulysses and his men rushed forward and regained their spears by drawing them from the bodies of the dead.
cards.whyThisWorks: Ulysses' calm, decisive command—'I should say we too had better let drive into the middle of them'—reveals a leader who remains composed and tactically clear even under lethal pressure, showing how speech characterizes heroic resolve.
cards.skillStrategy: When a character speaks under pressure, ask what their word choice and tone reveal about who they are and what they value.
evidencePoints: My friends, I should say we too had better let drive into the middle of them, or they will crown all the harm they have done us by killing us outright.
They therefore aimed straight in front of them and threw their spears. Ulysses killed Demoptolemus...
cards.question: After the suitors' spears miss, Ulysses says to his men, 'My friends, I should say we too had better let drive into the middle of them, or they will crown all the harm they have done us by killing us outright.' What does this speech reveal about Ulysses' character?

choices.label: A
choices.text: He is desperate and uncertain, relying on his companions to decide the next move because he fears the suitors' numbers.

choices.label: B
choices.text: He remains composed and strategically focused even in the middle of battle, taking command by turning a near-miss into an immediate counterattack.

choices.label: C
choices.text: He is reckless and driven by anger, ordering his men forward without considering that the suitors still outnumber them.

choices.label: D
choices.text: He depends entirely on Minerva's divine protection and speaks only to reassure his men that the gods will finish the fight for them.

cards.standardTitle: Key literary elements add layers of meaning
cards.excerpt:
This made Antinous very angry, and he scowled at him saying, “You shall pay for this before you get clear of the court.” With these words he threw a footstool at him, and hit him on the right shoulder blade near the top of his back. Ulysses stood firm as a rock and the blow did not even stagger him, but he shook his head in silence as he brooded on his revenge. Then he went back to the threshold and sat down there, laying his well filled wallet at his feet.

“Listen to me,” he cried, “you suitors of Queen Penelope, that I may speak even as I am minded. A man knows neither ache nor pain if he gets hit while fighting for his money, or for his sheep or his cattle; and even so Antinous has hit me while in the service of my miserable belly, which is always getting people into trouble. Still, if the poor have gods and avenging deities at all, I pray them that Antinous may come to a bad end before his marriage.”

“Sit where you are, and eat your victuals in silence, or be off elsewhere,” shouted Antinous. “If you say more I will have you dragged hand and foot through the courts, and the servants shall flay you alive.”

The other suitors were much displeased at this, and one of the young men said, “Antinous, you did ill in striking that poor wretch of a tramp: it will be worse for you if he should turn out to be some god—and we know the gods go about disguised in all sorts of ways as people from foreign countries, and travel about the world to see who do amiss and who righteously.”146

Thus said the suitors, but Antinous paid them no heed. Meanwhile Telemachus was furious about the blow that had been given to his father, and though no tear fell from him, he shook his head in silence and brooded on his revenge.
cards.whyThisWorks: Ulysses' silent head-shake and brooding after being struck by a footstool—mirrored almost exactly by Telemachus at the passage's close—reveals that both characters mask fury with outward restraint, showing how repeated characterization details deepen meaning about patience, disguise, and planned vengeance.
cards.skillStrategy: When a character's action or reaction appears more than once, ask what that repetition tells you about who the character is and what the author wants you to understand.
evidencePoints: Ulysses stood firm as a rock and the blow did not even stagger him, but he shook his head in silence as he brooded on his revenge.
he shook his head in silence and brooded on his revenge.
cards.question: Both Ulysses and Telemachus respond to Antinous's violence by shaking their heads in silence and brooding on revenge. What does this parallel characterization reveal about them?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Father and son are too frightened of Antinous to speak, so they suppress their anger out of cowardice rather than strategy.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Father and son share a disciplined restraint that conceals dangerous intent, suggesting their silence is a form of power rather than weakness.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Telemachus copies his father's gesture out of respect for custom, showing that mourning in silence is the proper response to insult in their culture.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Both characters are indifferent to the blow itself and focus only on the suitors' warning that Antinous may have struck a god in disguise.

cards.standardTitle: Epic poetry: characters, structures, and themes
cards.excerpt:
This was how they talked, but they knew nothing about it; and Alcinous said, “I remember now the old prophecy of my father. He said that Neptune would be angry with us for taking every one so safely over the sea, and would one day wreck a Phaeacian ship as it was returning from an escort, and bury our city under a high mountain. This was what my old father used to say, and now it is all coming true.117 Now therefore let us all do as I say; in the first place we must leave off giving people escorts when they come here, and in the next let us sacrifice twelve picked bulls to Neptune that he may have mercy upon us, and not bury our city under the high mountain.” When the people heard this they were afraid and got ready the bulls.

Thus did the chiefs and rulers of the Phaeacians pray to king Neptune, standing round his altar; and at the same time118 Ulysses woke up once more upon his own soil. He had been so long away that he did not know it again; moreover, Jove’s daughter Minerva had made it a foggy day, so that people might not know of his having come, and that she might tell him everything without either his wife or his fellow citizens and friends recognising him119 until he had taken his revenge upon the wicked suitors. Everything, therefore, seemed quite different to him—the long straight tracks, the harbours, the precipices, and the goodly trees, appeared all changed as he started up and looked upon his native land. So he smote his thighs with the flat of his hands and cried aloud despairingly.
cards.whyThisWorks: Minerva's deliberate use of fog to hide Ulysses' return and her plan to 'tell him everything' before he takes revenge on the suitors is a clear, textually grounded example of divine intervention shaping plot and character action in epic poetry.
cards.skillStrategy: When identifying divine intervention in an epic, locate the exact action a god takes, the stated reason for it, and the consequence it creates for the hero's next steps.
evidencePoints: Jove's daughter Minerva had made it a foggy day, so that people might not know of his having come
that she might tell him everything without either his wife or his fellow citizens and friends recognising him until he had taken his revenge upon the wicked suitors
cards.question: In the second paragraph, Minerva makes Ulysses' homeland appear 'quite different to him' by covering it in fog. According to the excerpt, what is Minerva's stated purpose for this divine intervention?

choices.label: A
choices.text: She creates the fog to punish Ulysses for being away so long, causing him to smite his thighs and cry out in despair upon seeing his changed homeland.

choices.label: B
choices.text: She hides his arrival in fog so she can inform him of what he needs to know and he can move against the suitors before his wife, citizens, or friends recognize him.

choices.label: C
choices.text: She disguises the landscape—the tracks, harbours, precipices, and trees—so that the suitors will not discover Ulysses has landed and will remain unprepared for his return.

choices.label: D
choices.text: She conceals his arrival so that the Phaeacians who escorted him can escape Neptune's wrath before anyone in Ithaca learns they provided him safe passage home.

cards.standardTitle: Key literary elements add layers of meaning
cards.excerpt:
Then Minerva bethought her of another matter. She took his shape, and went round the town to each one of the crew, telling them to meet at the ship by sundown. She went also to Noemon son of Phronius, and asked him to let her have a ship—which he was very ready to do. When the sun had set and darkness was over all the land, she got the ship into the water, put all the tackle on board her that ships generally carry, and stationed her at the end of the harbour. Presently the crew came up, and the goddess spoke encouragingly to each of them.

Furthermore she went to the house of Ulysses, and threw the suitors into a deep slumber. She caused their drink to fuddle them, and made them drop their cups from their hands, so that instead of sitting over their wine, they went back into the town to sleep, with their eyes heavy and full of drowsiness. Then she took the form and voice of Mentor, and called Telemachus to come outside.
cards.whyThisWorks: Minerva's sequence of disguises, logistical preparations, and manipulation of the suitors reveals a character who is a deliberate, all-controlling divine protector, showing how characterization through action adds meaning to Telemachus's situation.
cards.skillStrategy: To analyze how characterization adds meaning, track what a character does, says, and becomes across the passage, then ask what those specific actions reveal about who they are and why it matters to the story.
evidencePoints: She took his shape, and went round the town to each one of the crew, telling them to meet at the ship by sundown.
She caused their drink to fuddle them, and made them drop their cups from their hands, so that instead of sitting over their wine, they went back into the town to sleep.
cards.question: In the excerpt, Minerva takes the shape of a crew member to gather sailors, secures a ship from Noemon, causes the suitors' drink to 'fuddle them' so they drop their cups and leave, and then takes 'the form and voice of Mentor' to call Telemachus outside. What does this sequence of actions reveal about Minerva's character and the meaning it adds to the passage?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Minerva's repeated use of disguise shows she is deceptive by nature and acts primarily to confuse both the suitors and Telemachus rather than to help him.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Minerva is characterized as a careful, unseen protector who personally handles every step—gathering the crew, securing the ship, neutralizing the suitors, and summoning Telemachus—so that no human obstacle can block his departure.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Minerva's actions reveal that she doubts Telemachus's courage, and her manipulation of the suitors is meant to shame him into acting rather than to clear a path for his escape.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Minerva is characterized as impulsive, reacting to each problem as it appears rather than following a deliberate plan, which is shown by her switching between different disguises throughout the passage.

cards.standardTitle: Key literary elements add layers of meaning
cards.excerpt:
Now when the child of morning, rosy-fingered Dawn, appeared Telemachus rose and dressed himself. He bound his sandals on to his comely feet, girded his sword about his shoulder, and left his room looking like an immortal god. He at once sent the criers round to call the people in assembly, so they called them and the people gathered thereon; then, when they were got together, he went to the place of assembly spear in hand—not alone, for his two hounds went with him. Minerva endowed him with a presence of such divine comeliness that all marvelled at him as he went by, and when he took his place in his father’s seat even the oldest councillors made way for him.

Aegyptius, a man bent double with age, and of infinite experience, was the first to speak. His son Antiphus had gone with Ulysses to Ilius, land of noble steeds, but the savage Cyclops had killed him when they were all shut up in the cave, and had cooked his last dinner for him.17 He had three sons left, of whom two still worked on their father’s land, while the third, Eurynomus, was one of the suitors; nevertheless their father could not get over the loss of Antiphus, and was still weeping for him when he began his speech.
cards.whyThisWorks: The excerpt contrasts Telemachus's god-like appearance and commanding presence with Aegyptius's grief-bent, aged figure, allowing students to analyze how physical description and action reveal character meaning.
cards.skillStrategy: When a character's appearance or actions are described in detail, ask yourself what those details reveal about who that character is and what they represent in the story.

even the oldest councillors made way for him
cards.question: The description of Telemachus leaving his room 'looking like an immortal god' and the detail that 'even the oldest councillors made way for him' work together to reveal which meaning about his character?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Telemachus is reckless and overconfident, rushing into the assembly without understanding the gravity of his father's absence.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Telemachus has grown into a figure of authority and dignity, commanding respect that signals his readiness to step into his father's role.

choices.label: C

choices.label: D

cards.standardTitle: Theme development across a literary text
cards.excerpt:
But she would not give him full victory as yet, for she wished still further to prove his own prowess and that of his brave son, so she flew up to one of the rafters in the roof of the cloister and sat upon it in the form of a swallow.

Meanwhile Agelaus son of Damastor, Eurynomus, Amphimedon, Demoptolemus, Pisander, and Polybus son of Polyctor bore the brunt of the fight upon the suitors’ side; of all those who were still fighting for their lives they were by far the most valiant, for the others had already fallen under the arrows of Ulysses. Agelaus shouted to them and said, “My friends, he will soon have to leave off, for Mentor has gone away after having done nothing for him but brag. They are standing at the doors unsupported. Do not aim at him all at once, but six of you throw your spears first, and see if you cannot cover yourselves with glory by killing him. When he has fallen we need not be uneasy about the others.”

They threw their spears as he bade them, but Minerva made them all of no effect. One hit the door post; another went against the door; the pointed shaft of another struck the wall; and as soon as they had avoided all the spears of the suitors Ulysses said to his own men, “My friends, I should say we too had better let drive into the middle of them, or they will crown all the harm they have done us by killing us outright.”

They therefore aimed straight in front of them and threw their spears. Ulysses killed Demoptolemus, Telemachus Euryades, Eumaeus Elatus, while the stockman killed Pisander. These all bit the dust, and as the others drew back into a corner Ulysses and his men rushed forward and regained their spears by drawing them from the bodies of the dead.
cards.whyThisWorks: The excerpt contains a direct authorial statement of divine withholding ('she would not give him full victory as yet, for she wished still further to prove his own prowess') alongside action that forces Ulysses to fight on without divine rescue, giving students a true-detail distractor (Minerva's swallow form) to reject and a theme-developing detail to identify.
cards.skillStrategy: Ask yourself: does this detail show WHY the theme is true, or does it just describe something that happened in the story?

Minerva made them all of no effect... Ulysses said to his own men, 'My friends, I should say we too had better let drive into the middle of them'
cards.question: The narrator states that Minerva 'would not give him full victory as yet, for she wished still further to prove his own prowess and that of his brave son.' Which detail from the excerpt most directly develops the theme that genuine victory requires personal courage rather than divine rescue?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Minerva transforms into a swallow and perches on a rafter in the roof of the cloister, remaining physically present in the hall throughout the battle.

choices.label: B
choices.text: After Minerva deflects the suitors' spears, Ulysses rallies his men to throw their own spears into the suitors rather than waiting for further divine intervention, driving the fight forward through his own command.

choices.label: C

choices.label: D

cards.standardTitle: Epic poetry: characters, structures, and themes
cards.excerpt:
On this the old woman150 went out of the room to bid the maids go to their mistress. In the meantime Minerva bethought her of another matter, and sent Penelope off into a sweet slumber; so she lay down on her couch and her limbs became heavy with sleep. Then the goddess shed grace and beauty over her that all the Achaeans might admire her. She washed her face with the ambrosial loveliness that Venus wears when she goes dancing with the Graces; she made her taller and of a more commanding figure, while as for her complexion it was whiter than sawn ivory. When Minerva had done all this she went away, whereon the maids came in from the women’s room and woke Penelope with the sound of their talking.

“What an exquisitely delicious sleep I have been having,” said she, as she passed her hands over her face, “in spite of all my misery. I wish Diana would let me die so sweetly now at this very moment, that I might no longer waste in despair for the loss of my dear husband, who possessed every kind of good quality and was the most distinguished man among the Achaeans.”

With these words she came down from her upper room, not alone but attended by two of her maidens, and when she reached the suitors she stood by one of the bearing-posts supporting the roof of the cloister, holding a veil before her face, and with a staid maid servant on either side of her. As they beheld her the suitors were so overpowered and became so desperately enamoured of her, that each one prayed he might win her for his own bed fellow.
cards.whyThisWorks: Minerva's two-part divine intervention—sending Penelope to sleep and then enhancing her beauty with 'ambrosial loveliness'—directly causes the suitors to become 'so overpowered and became so desperately enamoured of her,' making the passage a clear model of how a goddess shapes both action and theme.
cards.skillStrategy: When you spot a god or goddess acting in the passage, trace exactly what they do and then find the sentence that shows the result—that cause-and-effect chain is the divine intervention.
evidencePoints: Minerva bethought her of another matter, and sent Penelope off into a sweet slumber
the goddess shed grace and beauty over her that all the Achaeans might admire her

cards.question: The narrator states that Minerva 'shed grace and beauty over' Penelope 'that all the Achaeans might admire her.' How does this act of divine intervention shape the action that follows in the passage?

choices.label: A

choices.label: B
choices.text: Because Minerva beautifies Penelope while she sleeps, Penelope descends to the suitors unknowingly transformed, and every suitor is so overwhelmed that each prays to claim her, heightening the competition over her.

choices.label: C

choices.label: D
