cards.excerpt:
To this Eurymachus son of Polybus answered, “Take heart, Queen Penelope daughter of Icarius, and do not trouble yourself about these matters. The man is not yet born, nor never will be, who shall lay hands upon your son Telemachus, while I yet live to look upon the face of the earth. I say—and it shall surely be—that my spear shall be reddened with his blood; for many a time has Ulysses taken me on his knees, held wine up to my lips to drink, and put pieces of meat into my hands. Therefore Telemachus is much the dearest friend I have, and has nothing to fear from the hands of us suitors. Of course, if death comes to him from the gods, he cannot escape it.” He said this to quiet her, but in reality he was plotting against Telemachus.

Then Penelope went upstairs again and mourned her husband till Minerva shed sleep over her eyes. In the evening Eumaeus got back to Ulysses and his son, who had just sacrificed a young pig of a year old and were helping one another to get supper ready; Minerva therefore came up to Ulysses, turned him into an old man with a stroke of her wand, and clad him in his old clothes again, for fear that the swineherd might recognise him and not keep the secret, but go and tell Penelope.
cards.whyThisWorks: Eurymachus's elaborate speech of loyalty to Penelope, immediately undercut by the narrator's revelation that 'he was plotting against Telemachus,' provides a textbook example of how the gap between a character's words and true intentions reveals hypocrisy and the theme of deception.
cards.skillStrategy: When a character says one thing but the narrator tells you something different, ask yourself what that gap reveals about who the character really is and what the author wants you to understand.
evidencePoints: He said this to quiet her, but in reality he was plotting against Telemachus.
my spear shall be reddened with his blood; for many a time has Ulysses taken me on his knees
cards.question: Read the following passage detail: 'He said this to quiet her, but in reality he was plotting against Telemachus.' What does this contrast between Eurymachus's speech and his true intentions reveal about his character?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Eurymachus genuinely cares for Telemachus because of his past bond with Ulysses, but fears the gods will intervene before he can protect him.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Eurymachus is a calculating deceiver who uses false loyalty and emotional appeals to manipulate Penelope while concealing his true threat to her son.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Eurymachus is torn between his affection for Telemachus and his duty to the other suitors, making him an uncertain and conflicted figure.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Eurymachus respects Penelope's grief and chooses his words carefully out of politeness, unaware that his plans will eventually harm Telemachus.

cards.standardTitle: Theme development across a literary text
cards.excerpt:
He led the way as he spoke, and Minerva followed him. When they were within he took her spear and set it in the spear-stand against a strong bearing-post along with the many other spears of his unhappy father, and he conducted her to a richly decorated seat under which he threw a cloth of damask. There was a footstool also for her feet,2 and he set another seat near her for himself, away from the suitors, that she might not be annoyed while eating by their noise and insolence, and that he might ask her more freely about his father.

A maid servant then brought them water in a beautiful golden ewer and poured it into a silver basin for them to wash their hands, and she drew a clean table beside them. An upper servant brought them bread, and offered them many good things of what there was in the house, the carver fetched them plates of all manner of meats and set cups of gold by their side, and a manservant brought them wine and poured it out for them.
cards.whyThisWorks: The excerpt contrasts Telemachus's deliberate, protective seating of Minerva 'away from the suitors' with the surrounding disorder, letting students distinguish a detail that builds the theme of hospitality as dignity-protection from true-but-topic-only details about household wealth or servant routines.
cards.skillStrategy: Ask yourself: does this detail show WHY the host acts—to protect the guest—or does it just describe what the house looks like or what servants do?
evidencePoints: he set another seat near her for himself, away from the suitors, that she might not be annoyed while eating by their noise and insolence
he conducted her to a richly decorated seat under which he threw a cloth of damask
cards.question: The narrator states that Telemachus 'set another seat near her for himself, away from the suitors, that she might not be annoyed while eating by their noise and insolence.' Which detail from the excerpt most directly develops the theme that true hospitality means shielding a guest from harm or dishonor?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A maid servant brought water in a beautiful golden ewer and poured it into a silver basin, showing that the household possesses costly objects used in welcoming guests.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Telemachus positions himself between Minerva and the suitors and explains his reason as preventing her from being annoyed by their noise and insolence, making her comfort and honor his stated purpose.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Telemachus places Minerva's spear in the spear-stand alongside the many spears of his unhappy father, indicating that weapons belonging to guests were stored with care inside the hall.

choices.label: D
choices.text: An upper servant brought bread and a carver fetched plates of all manner of meats, showing that multiple household staff members participated in serving the meal.

cards.standardTitle: Epic poetry: characters, structures, and themes
cards.excerpt:
When the pair had thus laid their plans they parted, and the goddess went straight to Lacedaemon to fetch Telemachus.

Ulysses now left the haven, and took the rough track up through the wooded country and over the crest of the mountain till he reached the place where Minerva had said that he would find the swineherd, who was the most thrifty servant he had. He found him sitting in front of his hut, which was by the yards that he had built on a site which could be seen from far. He had made them spacious126 and fair to see, with a free run for the pigs all round them; he had built them during his master’s absence, of stones which he had gathered out of the ground, without saying anything to Penelope or Laertes, and he had fenced them on top with thorn bushes. Outside the yard he had run a strong fence of oaken posts, split, and set pretty close together, while inside he had built twelve styes near one another for the sows to lie in. There were fifty pigs wallowing in each stye, all of them breeding sows; but the boars slept outside and were much fewer in number, for the suitors kept on eating them, and the swineherd had to send them the best he had continually. There were three hundred and sixty boar pigs, and the herdsman’s four hounds, which were as fierce as wolves, slept always with them. The swineherd was at that moment cutting out a pair of sandals127 from a good stout ox hide. Three of his men were out herding the pigs in one place or another, and he had sent the fourth to town with a boar that he had been forced to send the suitors that they might sacrifice it and have their fill of meat.
cards.whyThisWorks: The excerpt opens with Minerva departing to fetch Telemachus and then shows Ulysses following her prior directions to find the swineherd, illustrating how divine intervention steers a hero's path even after the god has left the scene.
cards.skillStrategy: When analyzing divine intervention in epic poetry, trace the god's specific instructions or actions and show exactly how they control what the hero does next.
evidencePoints: the goddess went straight to Lacedaemon to fetch Telemachus
Ulysses now left the haven, and took the rough track up through the wooded country and over the crest of the mountain till he reached the place where Minerva had said that he would find the swineherd
cards.question: The passage states that Ulysses traveled 'the rough track up through the wooded country and over the crest of the mountain till he reached the place where Minerva had said that he would find the swineherd.' What does this detail reveal about the role of Minerva's divine intervention in Ulysses' journey?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Minerva travels alongside Ulysses on the mountain track, personally guiding each step of his route to the swineherd's hut.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Minerva's prior instructions determine both the exact route Ulysses takes and the specific person he seeks, directing his movement before she departs for Lacedaemon.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Because Minerva has already left for Lacedaemon, Ulysses must rely entirely on his own knowledge of the land to locate the swineherd's yard.

choices.label: D

cards.standardTitle: Key literary elements add layers of meaning
cards.excerpt: The suitors then returned to their singing and dancing until the evening; but when night fell upon their pleasuring they went home to bed each in his own abode.12 Telemachus’s room was high up in a tower13 that looked on to the outer court; hither, then, he hied, brooding and full of thought. A good old woman, Euryclea, daughter of Ops, the son of Pisenor, went before him with a couple of blazing torches. Laertes had bought her with his own money when she was quite young; he gave the worth of twenty oxen for her, and shewed as much respect to her in his household as he did to his own wedded wife, but he did not take her to his bed for he feared his wife’s resentment.14 She it was who now lighted Telemachus to his room, and she loved him better than any of the other women in the house did, for she had nursed him when he was a baby. He opened the door of his bed room and sat down upon the bed; as he took off his shirt15 he gave it to the good old woman, who folded it tidily up, and hung it for him over a peg by his bed side, after which she went out, pulled the door to by a silver catch, and drew the bolt home by means of the strap.16 But Telemachus as he lay covered with a woollen fleece kept thinking all night through of his intended voyage and of the counsel that Minerva had given him.
cards.whyThisWorks: Telemachus's restless brooding while the suitors celebrate, combined with his sleepless night planning his voyage, reveals his inner conflict and growing resolve through contrasting actions and thoughts.
cards.skillStrategy: When a character's thoughts or actions contrast with the world around them, ask what that contrast reveals about who the character is becoming.
evidencePoints: hither, then, he hied, brooding and full of thought
Telemachus as he lay covered with a woollen fleece kept thinking all night through of his intended voyage and of the counsel that Minerva had given him
cards.question: The excerpt contrasts the suitors returning home after 'their singing and dancing' with Telemachus going to his room 'brooding and full of thought' and lying awake all night. What does this contrast reveal about Telemachus's character?

choices.label: A
choices.text: He resents the suitors for enjoying themselves while he is forced to remain isolated in his tower room.

choices.label: B
choices.text: While those around him are consumed by pleasure and ease, he is already separating himself from that world through serious purpose and private determination.

choices.label: C
choices.text: He is too young and inexperienced to join the suitors' celebration, so he retreats to his room out of embarrassment.

choices.label: D
choices.text: His sleeplessness shows that he is anxious and uncertain about Minerva's counsel, suggesting he lacks the confidence to act on her advice.

cards.standardTitle: Theme development across a literary text
cards.excerpt:
He counted his goodly coppers and cauldrons, his gold and all his clothes, but there was nothing missing; still he kept grieving about not being in his own country, and wandered up and down by the shore of the sounding sea bewailing his hard fate. Then Minerva came up to him disguised as a young shepherd of delicate and princely mien, with a good cloak folded double about her shoulders; she had sandals on her comely feet and held a javelin in her hand. Ulysses was glad when he saw her, and went straight up to her.

“My friend,” said he, “you are the first person whom I have met with in this country; I salute you, therefore, and beg you to be well disposed towards me. Protect these my goods, and myself too, for I embrace your knees and pray to you as though you were a god. Tell me, then, and tell me truly, what land and country is this? Who are its inhabitants? Am I on an island, or is this the sea board of some continent?”

Minerva answered, “Stranger, you must be very simple, or must have come from somewhere a long way off, not to know what country this is. It is a very celebrated place, and everybody knows it East and West. It is rugged and not a good driving country, but it is by no means a bad island for what there is of it. It grows any quantity of corn and also wine, for it is watered both by rain and dew; it breeds cattle also and goats; all kinds of timber grow here, and there are watering places where the water never runs dry; so, sir, the name of Ithaca is known even as far as Troy, which I understand to be a long way off from this Achaean country.”

Ulysses was glad at finding himself, as Minerva told him, in his own country, and he began to answer, but he did not speak the truth, and made up a lying story in the instinctive wiliness of his heart.
cards.whyThisWorks: The excerpt contrasts Ulysses' emotional longing for home with his immediate pivot to deception upon arriving there, giving students a true-but-off-topic detail (counting possessions) to reject and a theme-developing detail (lying 'in the instinctive wiliness of his heart') to select.
cards.skillStrategy: Ask yourself: does this detail show the theme in action, or does it just describe something true that happened in the passage?
evidencePoints: he did not speak the truth, and made up a lying story in the instinctive wiliness of his heart
still he kept grieving about not being in his own country, and wandered up and down by the shore of the sounding sea bewailing his hard fate
cards.question: The final sentence of the excerpt states that Ulysses 'did not speak the truth, and made up a lying story in the instinctive wiliness of his heart.' Which detail from the excerpt best develops the theme that cunning is an instinct Ulysses cannot set aside, even in moments of relief?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Ulysses counts his 'goodly coppers and cauldrons, his gold and all his clothes' and finds nothing missing, showing he arrived on Ithaca with his belongings safe.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Although Ulysses is 'glad' to learn he is in his own country, he immediately invents a false story, showing that deception is his reflex even at the moment of his greatest longing fulfilled.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Minerva describes Ithaca as 'a very celebrated place' known 'even as far as Troy,' establishing that Ulysses' homeland has a wide reputation throughout the ancient world.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Ulysses greets Minerva by embracing her knees and praying to her 'as though you were a god,' revealing that he is desperate for protection in an unfamiliar land.

cards.whyThisWorks: Minerva's disguised appearance as a shepherd who reveals 'the name of Ithaca' to a grieving Ulysses directly illustrates how divine intervention shifts a hero's emotional and strategic state, activating his 'instinctive wiliness' in the very next moment.
cards.skillStrategy: When analyzing divine intervention in epic poetry, trace what the god does, what the hero learns, and how the hero's behavior changes immediately after — the shift reveals the intervention's purpose.
evidencePoints: Minerva came up to him disguised as a young shepherd of delicate and princely mien
he did not speak the truth, and made up a lying story in the instinctive wiliness of his heart
cards.question: Minerva appears 'disguised as a young shepherd of delicate and princely mien' and tells Ulysses that the land is Ithaca. How does this act of divine intervention explain why Ulysses, who was 'bewailing his hard fate' at the opening, responds in the final sentence by making up 'a lying story in the instinctive wiliness of his heart'?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Because Ulysses prays to the disguised Minerva 'as though you were a god' without recognizing her divinity, she withholds the full name of the island, leaving him still uncertain whether he is on 'an island, or the sea board of some continent' and unable to stop grieving.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Minerva's disguised revelation that the land is Ithaca transforms Ulysses from a man 'bewailing his hard fate' into one who, now knowing he is home, immediately responds with cunning by making up 'a lying story in the instinctive wiliness of his heart,' showing how divine intervention activates his heroic resourcefulness.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Minerva appears as a shepherd primarily to warn Ulysses that his 'coppers and cauldrons, his gold and all his clothes' are at risk, so his lying response is simply an attempt to conceal his wealth from a stranger rather than a sign of heroic cunning restored by divine help.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Because Ulysses embraces Minerva's knees and begs her to 'protect these my goods,' she is moved to drop her shepherd's disguise, reveal herself as a goddess, and promise to guide him inland, and it is this promise — not the news of Ithaca — that ends his grief and prompts the lie.

cards.standardTitle: Key literary elements add layers of meaning
cards.excerpt: While he was thus in two minds, Neptune sent a terrible great wave that seemed to rear itself above his head till it broke right over the raft, which then went to pieces as though it were a heap of dry chaff tossed about by a whirlwind. Ulysses got astride of one plank and rode upon it as if he were on horseback; he then took off the clothes Calypso had given him, bound Ino’s veil under his arms, and plunged into the sea—meaning to swim on shore. King Neptune watched him as he did so, and wagged his head, muttering to himself and saying, “There now, swim up and down as you best can till you fall in with well-to-do people. I do not think you will be able to say that I have let you off too lightly.” On this he lashed his horses and drove to Aegae where his palace is.
cards.whyThisWorks: Neptune's mocking speech and head-wagging gesture directly contrast with Ulysses' desperate survival actions, allowing students to analyze how characterization through speech and behavior reveals Neptune's cruel indifference and Ulysses' determined resilience.
cards.skillStrategy: When a character speaks or acts in a moment of crisis, ask yourself what that behavior reveals about who they are and what they value.
evidencePoints: wagged his head, muttering to himself and saying, 'There now, swim up and down as you best can till you fall in with well-to-do people.'
Ulysses got astride of one plank and rode upon it as if he were on horseback; he then took off the clothes Calypso had given him, bound Ino's veil under his arms, and plunged into the sea
cards.question: Read Neptune's words: 'There now, swim up and down as you best can till you fall in with well-to-do people. I do not think you will be able to say that I have let you off too lightly.' What do Neptune's speech and the detail that he 'wagged his head' reveal about his character?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Neptune feels a grudging respect for Ulysses because he acknowledges that Ulysses has survived the destruction of the raft.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Neptune is contemptuous and self-satisfied, treating Ulysses' life-or-death struggle as a source of amusement rather than concern.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Neptune is uncertain whether his punishment has been severe enough, so he lingers to observe whether Ulysses will survive.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Neptune is indifferent to Ulysses because he has already moved on to other concerns before Ulysses even enters the water.

cards.standardTitle: Theme development across a literary text
cards.excerpt:
Then Minerva bethought her of another matter. She took his shape, and went round the town to each one of the crew, telling them to meet at the ship by sundown. She went also to Noemon son of Phronius, and asked him to let her have a ship—which he was very ready to do. When the sun had set and darkness was over all the land, she got the ship into the water, put all the tackle on board her that ships generally carry, and stationed her at the end of the harbour. Presently the crew came up, and the goddess spoke encouragingly to each of them.

Furthermore she went to the house of Ulysses, and threw the suitors into a deep slumber. She caused their drink to fuddle them, and made them drop their cups from their hands, so that instead of sitting over their wine, they went back into the town to sleep, with their eyes heavy and full of drowsiness. Then she took the form and voice of Mentor, and called Telemachus to come outside.
cards.whyThisWorks: Minerva's two-part intervention—disguising herself to assemble the crew and then fudding the suitors into sleep—provides concrete evidence that divine assistance removes obstacles mortals cannot clear alone, directly illustrating how theme is built through accumulated evidence.
cards.skillStrategy: To find evidence of theme, identify the specific actions a character takes and ask what those actions prove about a larger idea the author is developing.
evidencePoints: She caused their drink to fuddle them, and made them drop their cups from their hands, so that instead of sitting over their wine, they went back into the town to sleep
She took his shape, and went round the town to each one of the crew, telling them to meet at the ship by sundown
cards.question: Minerva 'caused their drink to fuddle them, and made them drop their cups from their hands, so that instead of sitting over their wine, they went back into the town to sleep.' Combined with her earlier act of taking Telemachus's shape to gather the crew, how do these two actions work together to develop the theme that divine power enables a mortal's journey when human effort alone is insufficient?

choices.label: A
choices.text: They show that Minerva's disguises—first as Telemachus and later as Mentor—are her most important tools, suggesting the theme is that deception is the only reliable path to success.

choices.label: B
choices.text: They remove the two obstacles Telemachus could not overcome alone—assembling a loyal crew and neutralizing the suitors' watchful presence—proving that supernatural intervention was necessary to open the way for his departure.

choices.label: C
choices.text: They suggest the suitors' own excessive drinking would have eventually caused them to sleep on their own, implying Telemachus could have departed without Minerva's help if he had simply waited.

choices.label: D
choices.text: They reveal that Minerva's goal is to punish the suitors by humiliating them with sleep, and that helping Telemachus reach the ship is only a secondary concern in her plan.

cards.standardTitle: Epic poetry: characters, structures, and themes
cards.excerpt:
Now when the child of morning, rosy-fingered Dawn, appeared Telemachus rose and dressed himself. He bound his sandals on to his comely feet, girded his sword about his shoulder, and left his room looking like an immortal god. He at once sent the criers round to call the people in assembly, so they called them and the people gathered thereon; then, when they were got together, he went to the place of assembly spear in hand—not alone, for his two hounds went with him. Minerva endowed him with a presence of such divine comeliness that all marvelled at him as he went by, and when he took his place in his father’s seat even the oldest councillors made way for him.

Aegyptius, a man bent double with age, and of infinite experience, was the first to speak. His son Antiphus had gone with Ulysses to Ilius, land of noble steeds, but the savage Cyclops had killed him when they were all shut up in the cave, and had cooked his last dinner for him.17 He had three sons left, of whom two still worked on their father’s land, while the third, Eurynomus, was one of the suitors; nevertheless their father could not get over the loss of Antiphus, and was still weeping for him when he began his speech.
cards.whyThisWorks: Minerva's direct endowment of divine comeliness on Telemachus and its immediate social effect—councillors yielding Odysseus's seat—gives students a clear, textually supported example of divine intervention shaping a mortal's status and actions in epic poetry.
cards.skillStrategy: When identifying divine intervention, trace the exact moment a god acts and then find the specific human reaction the text directly links to that action.
evidencePoints: Minerva endowed him with a presence of such divine comeliness that all marvelled at him as he went by
when he took his place in his father's seat even the oldest councillors made way for him
cards.question: The text states that 'Minerva endowed him with a presence of such divine comeliness that all marvelled at him as he went by.' Which two outcomes does the excerpt directly attribute to this divine intervention by Minerva?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The criers immediately obey Telemachus's command and the people gather in assembly before he arrives at the meeting place, showing Minerva's influence over the crowd.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The assembled people marvel at Telemachus as he passes, and even the oldest councillors yield his father's seat to him when he arrives.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Aegyptius rises to speak first and sets aside his grief over his son Antiphus, moved by the divine authority Minerva has placed on Telemachus.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Telemachus's two hounds and his spear signal Minerva's protection, causing the suitors among the councillors to remain silent rather than challenge him.

cards.standardTitle: Key literary elements add layers of meaning
cards.excerpt: As he said this he crept from under his bush, and broke off a bough covered with thick leaves to hide his nakedness. He looked like some lion of the wilderness that stalks about exulting in his strength and defying both wind and rain; his eyes glare as he prowls in quest of oxen, sheep, or deer, for he is famished, and will dare break even into a well fenced homestead, trying to get at the sheep—even such did Ulysses seem to the young women, as he drew near to them all naked as he was, for he was in great want. On seeing one so unkempt and so begrimed with salt water, the others scampered off along the spits that jutted out into the sea, but the daughter of Alcinous stood firm, for Minerva put courage into her heart and took away all fear from her. She stood right in front of Ulysses, and he doubted whether he should go up to her, throw himself at her feet, and embrace her knees as a suppliant, or stay where he was and entreat her to give him some clothes and show him the way to the town. In the end he deemed it best to entreat her from a distance in case the girl should take offence at his coming near enough to clasp her knees, so he addressed her in honeyed and persuasive language.
cards.whyThisWorks: Ulysses' deliberate choice to entreat Nausicaa from a distance rather than clasp her knees reveals a calculating, socially aware character even in desperate vulnerability, directly illustrating how characterization adds meaning.
cards.skillStrategy: When a character weighs two options and chooses one, ask what that choice reveals about who they are and what they value.
evidencePoints: he doubted whether he should go up to her, throw himself at her feet, and embrace her knees as a suppliant, or stay where he was and entreat her
In the end he deemed it best to entreat her from a distance in case the girl should take offence at his coming near enough to clasp her knees
cards.question: In the excerpt, Ulysses weighs whether to 'throw himself at her feet' or 'entreat her from a distance in case the girl should take offence.' What does this internal deliberation reveal about his character?

choices.label: A
choices.text: He is too ashamed of his nakedness to approach Nausicaa and chooses distance out of embarrassment rather than strategy.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Even desperate and 'in great want,' he carefully considers Nausicaa's reaction and chooses the approach most likely to gain her help.

choices.label: C
choices.text: He distrusts Nausicaa because the other women fled, so he keeps his distance to avoid being driven away as well.

choices.label: D
choices.text: He believes kneeling as a suppliant would make him appear weak, so he chooses words to project strength before her.

cards.standardTitle: Theme development across a literary text
cards.excerpt:
Then Mercury of Cyllene summoned the ghosts of the suitors, and in his hand he held the fair golden wand with which he seals men’s eyes in sleep or wakes them just as he pleases; with this he roused the ghosts and led them, while they followed whining and gibbering behind him. As bats fly squealing in the hollow of some great cave, when one of them has fallen out of the cluster in which they hang, even so did the ghosts whine and squeal as Mercury the healer of sorrow led them down into the dark abode of death. When they had passed the waters of Oceanus and the rock Leucas, they came to the gates of the sun and the land of dreams, whereon they reached the meadow of asphodel where dwell the souls and shadows of them that can labour no more.

Here they found the ghost of Achilles son of Peleus, with those of Patroclus, Antilochus, and Ajax, who was the finest and handsomest man of all the Danaans after the son of Peleus himself.
cards.whyThisWorks: The excerpt contrasts the suitors' undignified arrival—'whining and gibbering' like displaced bats—with the already-settled, named heroes in the meadow of asphodel, giving students concrete textual evidence that conduct in life shapes one's condition in death, directly supporting theme development.
cards.skillStrategy: To find evidence that proves theme, locate two contrasting images or descriptions in the passage and ask what idea about life or human behavior they both point toward.
evidencePoints: the ghosts whine and squeal as Mercury the healer of sorrow led them down into the dark abode of death
they reached the meadow of asphodel where dwell the souls and shadows of them that can labour no more
cards.question: The suitors arrive 'whining and gibbering' like bats shaken from a cave cluster, while Achilles, Patroclus, and Ajax are already present in the meadow of asphodel. How does this specific contrast most directly develop a theme about the consequences of one's conduct in life?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Mercury's act of guiding the suitors with 'the fair golden wand' to the same underworld destination as Achilles and Ajax suggests that divine power erases all distinctions between the honorable and the dishonorable after death.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The suitors' bat-like 'whining and gibbering' as they are herded into 'the dark abode of death' contrasts with Achilles and Ajax's settled presence in the meadow of asphodel, showing that how a person lives determines the dignity or shame they carry into death.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The shared journey through 'the waters of Oceanus and the rock Leucas' reduces the suitors and the heroes to the same diminished condition, suggesting that the hardships of death ultimately make all souls equal.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Ajax's description as 'the finest and handsomest man of all the Danaans after the son of Peleus himself' implies that physical excellence, rather than moral conduct, is what earns a warrior an honored place in the meadow of asphodel.

cards.standardTitle: Epic poetry: characters, structures, and themes
cards.excerpt:
To this Eurymachus son of Polybus answered, “Take heart, Queen Penelope daughter of Icarius, and do not trouble yourself about these matters. The man is not yet born, nor never will be, who shall lay hands upon your son Telemachus, while I yet live to look upon the face of the earth. I say—and it shall surely be—that my spear shall be reddened with his blood; for many a time has Ulysses taken me on his knees, held wine up to my lips to drink, and put pieces of meat into my hands. Therefore Telemachus is much the dearest friend I have, and has nothing to fear from the hands of us suitors. Of course, if death comes to him from the gods, he cannot escape it.” He said this to quiet her, but in reality he was plotting against Telemachus.

Then Penelope went upstairs again and mourned her husband till Minerva shed sleep over her eyes. In the evening Eumaeus got back to Ulysses and his son, who had just sacrificed a young pig of a year old and were helping one another to get supper ready; Minerva therefore came up to Ulysses, turned him into an old man with a stroke of her wand, and clad him in his old clothes again, for fear that the swineherd might recognise him and not keep the secret, but go and tell Penelope.
cards.whyThisWorks: Minerva's two direct interventions—sending sleep to Penelope and transforming Ulysses with her wand—demonstrate how divine action controls both characters' fates and advances the plot's secrecy, making the subskill of divine intervention concrete and analyzable.
cards.skillStrategy: When a god or goddess acts in an epic, ask what would happen without that action and how it changes what characters can do or know.
evidencePoints: Minerva shed sleep over her eyes

Minerva therefore came up to Ulysses, turned him into an old man with a stroke of her wand, and clad him in his old clothes again, for fear that the swineherd might recognise him and not keep the secret
cards.question: In the second paragraph, Minerva intervenes twice in quick succession. How do these two acts of divine intervention work together to shape the action?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Minerva puts Penelope to sleep to punish her for mourning Ulysses, and she disguises Ulysses to prepare him for a confrontation with the suitors that same night.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Minerva removes Penelope from the scene by sending her to sleep, and she conceals Ulysses' true identity from Eumaeus so that Ulysses' return remains secret and his plan can move forward.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Minerva comforts Penelope by granting her a vision of Ulysses in her sleep, and she transforms Ulysses so that Eumaeus will trust him more readily as a stranger.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Minerva causes Penelope to sleep so she will not interfere with the suitors, and she disguises Ulysses to protect him from Eurymachus, who has just threatened Telemachus.

cards.standardTitle: Key literary elements add layers of meaning
cards.excerpt: Then Ulysses in his turn melted, and wept as he clasped his dear and faithful wife to his bosom. As the sight of land is welcome to men who are swimming towards the shore, when Neptune has wrecked their ship with the fury of his winds and waves; a few alone reach the land, and these, covered with brine, are thankful when they find themselves on firm ground and out of danger—even so was her husband welcome to her as she looked upon him, and she could not tear her two fair arms from about his neck. Indeed they would have gone on indulging their sorrow till rosy-fingered morn appeared, had not Minerva determined otherwise, and held night back in the far west, while she would not suffer Dawn to leave Oceanus, nor to yoke the two steeds Lampus and Phaethon that bear her onward to break the day upon mankind.
cards.whyThisWorks: The extended simile comparing Penelope's welcome of Ulysses to shipwrecked sailors reaching land directly characterizes her inner state through vivid contrast and physical action, giving students a concrete passage moment to analyze for meaning.
cards.skillStrategy: When a character's feeling is shown through a comparison, ask what the comparison reveals about the depth or nature of that feeling—not just what the character does, but what it means.
evidencePoints: she could not tear her two fair arms from about his neck
even so was her husband welcome to her as she looked upon him
cards.question: In the excerpt, Homer writes that Penelope 'could not tear her two fair arms from about his neck' and then compares her welcome of Ulysses to the relief of shipwrecked sailors who finally reach firm ground. What does this combination of physical action and simile reveal about Penelope's character?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Her inability to release Ulysses shows she distrusts that he will stay, just as sailors cling to shore fearing the sea will pull them back.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Her clinging embrace and the simile together reveal that she has endured a desperate, survival-level ordeal, and Ulysses' return brings her the overwhelming relief of someone rescued from mortal danger.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Her physical grip on Ulysses suggests she is more focused on confirming he is real than on expressing genuine emotion, mirroring sailors who inspect the ground before trusting it.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Her refusal to let go reflects her anger at the gods for prolonging Ulysses' absence, just as the shipwrecked sailors resent Neptune for destroying their vessel.

cards.standardTitle: Theme development across a literary text
cards.excerpt:
So Eteoneus bustled back and bade the other servants come with him. They took their sweating steeds from under the yoke, made them fast to the mangers, and gave them a feed of oats and barley mixed. Then they leaned the chariot against the end wall of the courtyard, and led the way into the house. Telemachus and Pisistratus were astonished when they saw it, for its splendour was as that of the sun and moon; then, when they had admired everything to their heart’s content, they went into the bath room and washed themselves.

When the servants had washed them and anointed them with oil, they brought them woollen cloaks and shirts, and the two took their seats by the side of Menelaus. A maid-servant brought them water in a beautiful golden ewer, and poured it into a silver basin for them to wash their hands; and she drew a clean table beside them. An upper servant brought them bread, and offered them many good things of what there was in the house, while the carver fetched them plates of all manner of meats and set cups of gold by their side.
cards.whyThisWorks: The excerpt contrasts true-but-topic-only details (horses fed, chariot stored) with details that actively develop the theme of hospitality as a display of power and honor (golden ewer, silver basin, cups of gold, anointing with oil), giving students a clear test of whether a detail merely fits the topic or actually advances the theme.
cards.skillStrategy: Ask yourself: does this detail show what hospitality *means* or *costs* the host, or does it just confirm that guests arrived and were present?
evidencePoints: A maid-servant brought them water in a beautiful golden ewer, and poured it into a silver basin for them to wash their hands
the carver fetched them plates of all manner of meats and set cups of gold by their side
cards.question: The narrator describes a maid-servant bringing water 'in a beautiful golden ewer' poured 'into a silver basin' and a carver setting 'cups of gold' beside the guests. Which statement explains how these specific details develop the theme that a host's generosity reveals his status and honor?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The golden ewer and silver basin show that Menelaus's servants are highly trained, which proves that skilled labor, not costly objects, is the true mark of a noble household.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The repeated emphasis on precious materials—gold and silver vessels used for ordinary acts like hand-washing—signals that Menelaus honors guests by surrounding even routine hospitality with symbols of his wealth and rank.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The golden ewer and cups of gold confirm that Telemachus and Pisistratus are wealthy travelers who brought valuable goods with them, explaining why Menelaus treats them so lavishly.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The detail that a maid-servant, not Menelaus himself, carried the golden ewer shows that the host remains distant from his guests, which undermines any theme about personal generosity.

cards.standardTitle: Epic poetry: characters, structures, and themes
cards.excerpt: The bard inspired of heaven took up the story at the point where some of the Argives set fire to their tents and sailed away while others, hidden within the horse,73 were waiting with Ulysses in the Trojan place of assembly. For the Trojans themselves had drawn the horse into their fortress, and it stood there while they sat in council round it, and were in three minds as to what they should do. Some were for breaking it up then and there; others would have it dragged to the top of the rock on which the fortress stood, and then thrown down the precipice; while yet others were for letting it remain as an offering and propitiation for the gods. And this was how they settled it in the end, for the city was doomed when it took in that horse, within which were all the bravest of the Argives waiting to bring death and destruction on the Trojans. Anon he sang how the sons of the Achaeans issued from the horse, and sacked the town, breaking out from their ambuscade. He sang how they overran the city hither and thither and ravaged it, and how Ulysses went raging like Mars along with Menelaus to the house of Deiphobus. It was there that the fight raged most furiously, nevertheless by Minerva’s help he was victorious.
cards.whyThisWorks: The excerpt explicitly names Minerva as the divine force that enables Ulysses' victory at the house of Deiphobus 'where the fight raged most furiously,' making it a clear, textually grounded example of divine intervention shaping heroic outcome in epic poetry.
cards.skillStrategy: When identifying divine intervention in epic poetry, locate the exact moment a god acts, then ask: what would have happened to the hero without that help?
evidencePoints: It was there that the fight raged most furiously, nevertheless by Minerva's help he was victorious.
Ulysses went raging like Mars along with Menelaus to the house of Deiphobus.
cards.question: The excerpt states that at the house of Deiphobus 'the fight raged most furiously' and that Ulysses was victorious 'by Minerva's help.' What does this detail most clearly show about divine intervention in the epic?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Minerva directs Ulysses and Menelaus to the house of Deiphobus before the battle begins, ensuring they arrive before the other Argives can claim the victory.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Minerva's aid allows Ulysses to prevail at the single most intense point of fighting in the sack of Troy, suggesting his victory there depended on divine support rather than strength alone.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Minerva causes the Trojans to accept the horse as 'an offering and propitiation for the gods,' which is the divine act that ultimately dooms the city.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Minerva inspires the bard to sing the story of Troy, so her intervention shapes the telling of events rather than the events themselves.

cards.standardTitle: Key literary elements add layers of meaning
cards.excerpt: He found her at home. There was a large fire burning on the hearth, and one could smell from far the fragrant reek of burning cedar and sandal wood. As for herself, she was busy at her loom, shooting her golden shuttle through the warp and singing beautifully. Round her cave there was a thick wood of alder, poplar, and sweet smelling cypress trees, wherein all kinds of great birds had built their nests—owls, hawks, and chattering sea-crows that occupy their business in the waters. A vine loaded with grapes was trained and grew luxuriantly about the mouth of the cave; there were also four running rills of water in channels cut pretty close together, and turned hither and thither so as to irrigate the beds of violets and luscious herbage over which they flowed. 51 Even a god could not help being charmed with such a lovely spot, so Mercury stood still and looked at it; but when he had admired it sufficiently he went inside the cave.
cards.whyThisWorks: The description of Calypso weaving and singing while surrounded by an almost supernaturally beautiful environment characterizes her as an enchanting, powerful figure whose domestic actions and setting together reveal her ability to captivate even divine visitors.
cards.skillStrategy: When a character is described through both actions and surroundings, ask what those details together reveal about who that character is and what effect she has on others.
evidencePoints: she was busy at her loom, shooting her golden shuttle through the warp and singing beautifully
Even a god could not help being charmed with such a lovely spot, so Mercury stood still and looked at it
cards.question: In the excerpt, Calypso is shown 'busy at her loom, shooting her golden shuttle through the warp and singing beautifully' while Mercury is stopped in his tracks by her surroundings. What do these details together reveal about Calypso's character?

choices.label: A
choices.text: She is so absorbed in her weaving that she is unaware of Mercury's arrival, suggesting she is careless and inattentive to the world beyond her cave.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Her graceful domestic activity and the enchanting beauty of her domain together establish her as a figure of irresistible, almost supernatural allure—powerful enough to hold even a god spellbound.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Her focus on weaving and singing shows she is content with a simple, ordinary life, making her no different from mortal women described elsewhere in the epic.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The lush surroundings reflect Mercury's own divine power rather than anything about Calypso, since only a god's presence could make a place appear so beautiful.

cards.standardTitle: Theme development across a literary text
cards.excerpt:
Now when the child of morning, rosy-fingered Dawn, appeared Telemachus rose and dressed himself. He bound his sandals on to his comely feet, girded his sword about his shoulder, and left his room looking like an immortal god. He at once sent the criers round to call the people in assembly, so they called them and the people gathered thereon; then, when they were got together, he went to the place of assembly spear in hand—not alone, for his two hounds went with him. Minerva endowed him with a presence of such divine comeliness that all marvelled at him as he went by, and when he took his place in his father’s seat even the oldest councillors made way for him.

Aegyptius, a man bent double with age, and of infinite experience, was the first to speak. His son Antiphus had gone with Ulysses to Ilius, land of noble steeds, but the savage Cyclops had killed him when they were all shut up in the cave, and had cooked his last dinner for him.17 He had three sons left, of whom two still worked on their father’s land, while the third, Eurynomus, was one of the suitors; nevertheless their father could not get over the loss of Antiphus, and was still weeping for him when he began his speech.
cards.whyThisWorks: The excerpt contrasts Telemachus's emerging authority—marked by divine comeliness and elders yielding his father's seat—with Aegyptius's unresolved grief over a son lost to war, allowing students to distinguish details that develop a theme of duty and legacy from true-but-thematically-irrelevant details about the Cyclops.
cards.skillStrategy: Ask yourself: does this detail show the theme growing, or does it just add background information that fits the topic without pushing the theme forward?
evidencePoints: when he took his place in his father's seat even the oldest councillors made way for him
nevertheless their father could not get over the loss of Antiphus, and was still weeping for him when he began his speech
cards.question: Which detail from the excerpt most directly develops the theme that a son must step into his father's place and carry on his legacy?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Aegyptius had three sons remaining after Antiphus's death, two of whom still worked on their father's land while the third joined the suitors.

choices.label: B
choices.text: When Telemachus took his place in his father's seat, even the oldest councillors made way for him, signaling that he has assumed Odysseus's role in the community.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The savage Cyclops killed Antiphus when the men were shut up in the cave and cooked his last dinner for him.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Telemachus bound his sandals on his comely feet and girded his sword about his shoulder before leaving his room.

cards.standardTitle: Epic poetry: characters, structures, and themes
cards.excerpt:
The others assented, so they went inside and laid their cloaks on the benches and seats. They sacrificed the sheep, goats, pigs, and the heifer, and when the inward meats were cooked they served them round. They mixed the wine in the mixing-bowls, and the swineherd gave every man his cup, while Philoetius handed round the bread in the bread baskets, and Melanthius poured them out their wine. Then they laid their hands upon the good things that were before them.

Telemachus purposely made Ulysses sit in the part of the cloister that was paved with stone;158 he gave him a shabby looking seat at a little table to himself, and had his portion of the inward meats brought to him, with his wine in a gold cup. “Sit there,” said he, “and drink your wine among the great people. I will put a stop to the gibes and blows of the suitors, for this is no public house, but belongs to Ulysses, and has passed from him to me. Therefore, suitors, keep your hands and your tongues to yourselves, or there will be mischief.”

The suitors bit their lips, and marvelled at the boldness of his speech; then Antinous said, “We do not like such language but we will put up with it, for Telemachus is threatening us in good earnest. If Jove had let us we should have put a stop to his brave talk ere now.”

Thus spoke Antinous, but Telemachus heeded him not. Meanwhile the heralds were bringing the holy hecatomb through the city, and the Achaeans gathered under the shady grove of Apollo.

Then they roasted the outer meat, drew it off the spits, gave every man his portion, and feasted to their heart’s content; those who waited at table gave Ulysses exactly the same portion as the others had, for Telemachus had told them to do so.
cards.whyThisWorks: Antinous's line 'If Jove had let us we should have put a stop to his brave talk ere now' directly illustrates divine intervention as the force restraining the suitors, making this a clear teaching moment for how gods shape human action in epic poetry.
cards.skillStrategy: When a character credits a god for why something did or did not happen, ask yourself: who actually has the power in this moment—the human or the divine force?
evidencePoints: If Jove had let us we should have put a stop to his brave talk ere now
The suitors bit their lips, and marvelled at the boldness of his speech
cards.question: Antinous tells the suitors, 'If Jove had let us we should have put a stop to his brave talk ere now,' after they 'bit their lips' at Telemachus's bold warning. What does Antinous's reference to Jove reveal about the role of divine intervention in this moment?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Antinous is confessing that the suitors are outnumbered by Telemachus's allies at the feast and cannot act without risking open violence.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Jove's will, not the suitors' own restraint, is what has prevented them from silencing Telemachus, meaning divine authority is the true force protecting his boldness.

choices.label: C

choices.label: D

cards.standardTitle: Key literary elements add layers of meaning
cards.excerpt: Thus did they converse, and meanwhile the ship which had brought Telemachus and his crew from Pylos had reached the town of Ithaca. When they had come inside the harbour they drew the ship on to the land; their servants came and took their armour from them, and they left all the presents at the house of Clytius. Then they sent a servant to tell Penelope that Telemachus had gone into the country, but had sent the ship to the town to prevent her from being alarmed and made unhappy. This servant and Eumaeus happened to meet when they were both on the same errand of going to tell Penelope. When they reached the House, the servant stood up and said to the queen in the presence of the waiting women, “Your son, Madam, is now returned from Pylos”; but Eumaeus went close up to Penelope, and said privately all that her son had bidden him tell her. When he had given his message he left the house with its outbuildings and went back to his pigs again.

cards.skillStrategy: Compare how two characters handle the same situation — the difference in their actions reveals what each character values and who they truly are.

Eumaeus went close up to Penelope, and said privately all that her son had bidden him tell her

choices.label: B

choices.label: D

cards.standardTitle: Theme development across a literary text
cards.excerpt:
Tell me, O Muse, of that ingenious hero who travelled far and wide after he had sacked the famous town of Troy. Many cities did he visit, and many were the nations with whose manners and customs he was acquainted; moreover he suffered much by sea while trying to save his own life and bring his men safely home; but do what he might he could not save his men, for they perished through their own sheer folly in eating the cattle of the Sun-god Hyperion; so the god prevented them from ever reaching home. Tell me, too, about all these things, oh daughter of Jove, from whatsoever source you may know them.

So now all who escaped death in battle or by shipwreck had got safely home except Ulysses, and he, though he was longing to return to his wife and country, was detained by the goddess Calypso, who had got him into a large cave and wanted to marry him. But as years went by, there came a time when the gods settled that he should go back to Ithaca; even then, however, when he was among his own people, his troubles were not yet over; nevertheless all the gods had now begun to pity him except Neptune, who still persecuted him without ceasing and would not let him get home.

cards.skillStrategy: Ask yourself: does this detail show the theme in action, or does it just describe what the passage is about?
evidencePoints: he suffered much by sea while trying to save his own life and bring his men safely home
even then, however, when he was among his own people, his troubles were not yet over; nevertheless all the gods had now begun to pity him except Neptune, who still persecuted him without ceasing
cards.question: The narrator states that Ulysses suffered 'while trying to save his own life and bring his men safely home,' and that even after the gods agreed he should return, 'his troubles were not yet over.' Which detail from the excerpt most directly develops the theme that suffering follows a person even through sincere and persistent effort?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Ulysses visited many cities and became acquainted with the manners and customs of many nations during his travels.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Neptune continued to persecute Ulysses without ceasing even after all the other gods had begun to pity him and agreed he should go home.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The goddess Calypso detained Ulysses in a large cave because she wanted to marry him.

choices.label: D

cards.excerpt:
When the pair had thus laid their plans they parted, and the goddess went straight to Lacedaemon to fetch Telemachus.

Ulysses now left the haven, and took the rough track up through the wooded country and over the crest of the mountain till he reached the place where Minerva had said that he would find the swineherd, who was the most thrifty servant he had. He found him sitting in front of his hut, which was by the yards that he had built on a site which could be seen from far. He had made them spacious126 and fair to see, with a free run for the pigs all round them; he had built them during his master’s absence, of stones which he had gathered out of the ground, without saying anything to Penelope or Laertes, and he had fenced them on top with thorn bushes. Outside the yard he had run a strong fence of oaken posts, split, and set pretty close together, while inside he had built twelve styes near one another for the sows to lie in. There were fifty pigs wallowing in each stye, all of them breeding sows; but the boars slept outside and were much fewer in number, for the suitors kept on eating them, and the swineherd had to send them the best he had continually. There were three hundred and sixty boar pigs, and the herdsman’s four hounds, which were as fierce as wolves, slept always with them. The swineherd was at that moment cutting out a pair of sandals127 from a good stout ox hide. Three of his men were out herding the pigs in one place or another, and he had sent the fourth to town with a boar that he had been forced to send the suitors that they might sacrifice it and have their fill of meat.
cards.whyThisWorks: The swineherd's detailed, self-initiated labor—building styes from gathered stones, fencing the yard, cutting sandals—reveals a character whose loyalty and industriousness define his moral worth in contrast to the wasteful suitors.
cards.skillStrategy: When a character acts without being told, ask what that choice reveals about who they are and what they value.
evidencePoints: he had built them during his master's absence, of stones which he had gathered out of the ground, without saying anything to Penelope or Laertes
The swineherd was at that moment cutting out a pair of sandals from a good stout ox hide
cards.question: The narrator describes the swineherd building the yards 'during his master's absence, of stones which he had gathered out of the ground, without saying anything to Penelope or Laertes.' What does this action reveal about the swineherd's character?

choices.label: B

choices.label: C

choices.label: D
choices.text: He demonstrates ambition by expanding the estate beyond what Ulysses originally owned, hoping to earn a higher position.

cards.standardTitle: Epic poetry: characters, structures, and themes
cards.excerpt: When they reached the water side they went to the washing cisterns, through which there ran at all times enough pure water to wash any quantity of linen, no matter how dirty. Here they unharnessed the mules and turned them out to feed on the sweet juicy herbage that grew by the water side. They took the clothes out of the waggon, put them in the water, and vied with one another in treading them in the pits to get the dirt out. After they had washed them and got them quite clean, they laid them out by the sea side, where the waves had raised a high beach of shingle, and set about washing themselves and anointing themselves with olive oil. Then they got their dinner by the side of the stream, and waited for the sun to finish drying the clothes. When they had done dinner they threw off the veils that covered their heads and began to play at ball, while Nausicaa sang for them. As the huntress Diana goes forth upon the mountains of Taygetus or Erymanthus to hunt wild boars or deer, and the wood nymphs, daughters of Aegis-bearing Jove, take their sport along with her (then is Leto proud at seeing her daughter stand a full head taller than the others, and eclipse the loveliest amid a whole bevy of beauties), even so did the girl outshine her handmaids.
cards.whyThisWorks: The Diana simile is a classic example of divine intervention through comparison, elevating Nausicaa's status by linking her to a goddess who towers above her companions, which signals her epic importance.
cards.skillStrategy: When you spot a simile comparing a character to a god or goddess, ask what quality the comparison highlights and what it suggests about that character's role in the epic.
evidencePoints: even so did the girl outshine her handmaids
then is Leto proud at seeing her daughter stand a full head taller than the others, and eclipse the loveliest amid a whole bevy of beauties
cards.question: In the simile comparing Nausicaa to Diana, Leto is described as 'proud at seeing her daughter stand a full head taller than the others.' What does this detail most likely suggest about Nausicaa's role in the epic?

choices.label: A
choices.text: It shows that Nausicaa's own mother watches over her near the water, just as Leto watches Diana on the mountains.

choices.label: B
choices.text: It marks Nausicaa as a figure of divine-like distinction who stands above those around her, signaling her special importance.

choices.label: C
choices.text: It implies that Nausicaa has earned the gods' favor by completing the washing task more skillfully than her handmaids.

choices.label: D
choices.text: It suggests that Diana's hunting companions, like the handmaids, are jealous of Nausicaa's beauty near the sea.

cards.excerpt:
Tell me, O Muse, of that ingenious hero who travelled far and wide after he had sacked the famous town of Troy. Many cities did he visit, and many were the nations with whose manners and customs he was acquainted; moreover he suffered much by sea while trying to save his own life and bring his men safely home; but do what he might he could not save his men, for they perished through their own sheer folly in eating the cattle of the Sun-god Hyperion; so the god prevented them from ever reaching home. cards.whyThisWorks: The two paragraphs present back-to-back moments—the men's folly destroying them despite Ulysses' efforts, and Ulysses' own detention by Calypso followed by Neptune's continued persecution even after the gods agree he should go home—that together build the theme that the journey home demands enduring layered, unrelenting obstacles beyond any single cause.
cards.skillStrategy: Identify the specific moment in the passage where a character's situation changes or worsens, then ask what idea about life that moment, combined with another moment, keeps reinforcing.

even then, however, when he was among his own people, his troubles were not yet over; nevertheless all the gods had now begun to pity him except Neptune, who still persecuted him without ceasing and would not let him get home
cards.question: In the first paragraph, Ulysses cannot save his men because 'they perished through their own sheer folly,' and in the second paragraph, even after the gods agree he should return, Neptune 'still persecuted him without ceasing.' What theme do these two specific moments develop together?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The gods punish those who act with folly, as shown by the men's death, but ultimately reward patient heroes like Ulysses with a safe return.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The path home is blocked by unrelenting obstacles—human folly, divine detention, and a god's ongoing persecution—that no single act of effort or favor can fully overcome.

choices.label: C
choices.text: A hero's worth is proven by how many cities he visits and how well he learns the manners and customs of foreign nations.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Mortals who disobey the gods, like the men who ate Hyperion's cattle, are destroyed, while obedient heroes like Ulysses are protected and guided safely home.

cards.standardTitle: Epic poetry: characters, structures, and themes
cards.excerpt: As he said this he crept from under his bush, and broke off a bough covered with thick leaves to hide his nakedness. He looked like some lion of the wilderness that stalks about exulting in his strength and defying both wind and rain; his eyes glare as he prowls in quest of oxen, sheep, or deer, for he is famished, and will dare break even into a well fenced homestead, trying to get at the sheep—even such did Ulysses seem to the young women, as he drew near to them all naked as he was, for he was in great want. On seeing one so unkempt and so begrimed with salt water, the others scampered off along the spits that jutted out into the sea, but the daughter of Alcinous stood firm, for Minerva put courage into her heart and took away all fear from her. She stood right in front of Ulysses, and he doubted whether he should go up to her, throw himself at her feet, and embrace her knees as a suppliant, or stay where he was and entreat her to give him some clothes and show him the way to the town. In the end he deemed it best to entreat her from a distance in case the girl should take offence at his coming near enough to clasp her knees, so he addressed her in honeyed and persuasive language.
cards.whyThisWorks: The excerpt explicitly names Minerva as the force that puts courage into Nausicaa's heart and removes her fear, directly causing her to stand firm while the other women flee—a textbook example of divine intervention shaping action.
cards.skillStrategy: When identifying divine intervention, find the exact moment a god acts, then trace what changes in the scene because of that action.
evidencePoints: Minerva put courage into her heart and took away all fear from her
the others scampered off along the spits that jutted out into the sea, but the daughter of Alcinous stood firm
cards.question: The narrator states that 'Minerva put courage into her heart and took away all fear from her.' How does this moment of divine intervention shape the action that follows in the excerpt?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Nausicaa's courage, given by Minerva, causes her to chase the other women back so that Ulysses has a larger audience for his appeal.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Because Minerva removes Nausicaa's fear, she stands firm before Ulysses rather than fleeing as the other women do, making it possible for Ulysses to address her and seek help.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Minerva's gift of courage leads Nausicaa to invite Ulysses to clasp her knees as a suppliant, which is the approach Ulysses ultimately chooses.

choices.label: D

cards.standardTitle: Key literary elements add layers of meaning
cards.excerpt:
But Ulysses, when he had taken it up and examined it all over, strung it as easily as a skilled bard strings a new peg of his lyre and makes the twisted gut fast at both ends. Then he took it in his right hand to prove the string, and it sang sweetly under his touch like the twittering of a swallow. The suitors were dismayed, and turned colour as they heard it; at that moment, moreover, Jove thundered loudly as a sign, and the heart of Ulysses rejoiced as he heard the omen that the son of scheming Saturn had sent him.

He took an arrow that was lying upon the table165—for those which the Achaeans were so shortly about to taste were all inside the quiver—he laid it on the centre-piece of the bow, and drew the notch of the arrow and the string toward him, still seated on his seat. When he had taken aim he let fly, and his arrow pierced every one of the handle-holes of the axes from the first onwards till it had gone right through them, and into the outer courtyard. Then he said to Telemachus:

“Your guest has not disgraced you, Telemachus. I did not miss what I aimed at, and I was not long in stringing my bow. I am still strong, and not as the suitors twit me with being. Now, however, it is time for the Achaeans to prepare supper while there is still daylight, and then otherwise to disport themselves with song and dance which are the crowning ornaments of a banquet.”

As he spoke he made a sign with his eyebrows, and Telemachus girded on his sword, grasped his spear, and stood armed beside his father’s seat.
cards.whyThisWorks: Ulysses' calm, almost casual speech to Telemachus after the feat—downplaying his strength while subtly threatening the suitors—reveals a character who is controlled, strategic, and confident, adding meaning beyond the physical action.
cards.skillStrategy: When a character speaks after a major action, ask what the words reveal about who they are and what they want others to believe or feel.
evidencePoints: I am still strong, and not as the suitors twit me with being.

cards.question: After piercing all the axes with his arrow, Ulysses speaks to Telemachus in a measured, almost casual tone. What does this speech reveal about Ulysses' character?

choices.label: A
choices.text: He is unaware of the danger the suitors pose and genuinely wants the evening to end with a peaceful celebration.

choices.label: B
choices.text: He is deliberately composed and in control, using understated words to mask a calculated threat while keeping the suitors off guard.

choices.label: C
choices.text: He is primarily concerned with restoring his reputation as a warrior and cares little about what happens to Telemachus.

choices.label: D
choices.text: He is relieved that the contest is over and speaks freely because he no longer fears the suitors' reaction.

cards.excerpt:
Then Minerva bethought her of another matter. She took his shape, and went round the town to each one of the crew, telling them to meet at the ship by sundown. She went also to Noemon son of Phronius, and asked him to let her have a ship—which he was very ready to do. When the sun had set and darkness was over all the land, she got the ship into the water, put all the tackle on board her that ships generally carry, and stationed her at the end of the harbour. Presently the crew came up, and the goddess spoke encouragingly to each of them.

Furthermore she went to the house of Ulysses, and threw the suitors into a deep slumber. She caused their drink to fuddle them, and made them drop their cups from their hands, so that instead of sitting over their wine, they went back into the town to sleep, with their eyes heavy and full of drowsiness. Then she took the form and voice of Mentor, and called Telemachus to come outside.
cards.whyThisWorks: The two paragraphs each show Minerva taking a different disguise to clear obstacles for Telemachus—gathering the crew and neutralizing the suitors—so students must connect both moments to trace how divine intervention enabling a hero's journey develops as a theme across the excerpt.
cards.skillStrategy: Look at what happens in each paragraph separately, then ask what idea both moments are building together—that is the theme at work.
evidencePoints: She took his shape, and went round the town to each one of the crew, telling them to meet at the ship by sundown.
she went to the house of Ulysses, and threw the suitors into a deep slumber. She caused their drink to fuddle them, and made them drop their cups from their hands
cards.question: In the first paragraph, Minerva disguises herself to assemble Telemachus's crew, and in the second paragraph she puts the suitors into a stupor. How do both moments work together to develop a theme?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Both moments show that disguise is a dangerous tool, since Minerva risks being discovered each time she changes her form to help Telemachus.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Both moments show that a young person's path forward depends on powerful forces quietly removing the obstacles that stand in his way.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Both moments reveal that the suitors are the true source of Telemachus's problems, because Minerva focuses all of her effort on neutralizing them.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Both moments suggest that loyalty among a crew is more important than any single act of divine help, since the sailors arrive at the ship on their own.

cards.standardTitle: Epic poetry: characters, structures, and themes
cards.excerpt: The suitors then returned to their singing and dancing until the evening; but when night fell upon their pleasuring they went home to bed each in his own abode.12 Telemachus’s room was high up in a tower13 that looked on to the outer court; hither, then, he hied, brooding and full of thought. A good old woman, Euryclea, daughter of Ops, the son of Pisenor, went before him with a couple of blazing torches. Laertes had bought her with his own money when she was quite young; he gave the worth of twenty oxen for her, and shewed as much respect to her in his household as he did to his own wedded wife, but he did not take her to his bed for he feared his wife’s resentment.14 She it was who now lighted Telemachus to his room, and she loved him better than any of the other women in the house did, for she had nursed him when he was a baby. He opened the door of his bed room and sat down upon the bed; as he took off his shirt15 he gave it to the good old woman, who folded it tidily up, and hung it for him over a peg by his bed side, after which she went out, pulled the door to by a silver catch, and drew the bolt home by means of the strap.16 But Telemachus as he lay covered with a woollen fleece kept thinking all night through of his intended voyage and of the counsel that Minerva had given him.
cards.whyThisWorks: The closing line explicitly names Minerva's counsel as the force occupying Telemachus's mind all night, showing how divine guidance directly shapes his thoughts and motivates his upcoming voyage.

the counsel that Minerva had given him
