choices.text: Telemachus's thoughts about the voyage reflect his gratitude toward Euryclea, whose loyal care throughout the night inspires him to finally take charge of his household.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The detail emphasizes that Telemachus is an obedient son who spends the night planning how to honor his father Laertes rather than acting on any outside influence.

cards.standardTitle: Key literary elements add layers of meaning
cards.excerpt:
She went wondering back into the house, and laid her son’s saying in her heart. Then going upstairs with her handmaids into her room, she mourned her dear husband till Minerva sent sweet sleep over her eyelids.

The swineherd now took up the bow and was for taking it to Ulysses, but the suitors clamoured at him from all parts of the cloisters, and one of them said, “You idiot, where are you taking the bow to? Are you out of your wits? If Apollo and the other gods will grant our prayer, your own boarhounds shall get you into some quiet little place, and worry you to death.”

Eumaeus was frightened at the outcry they all raised, so he put the bow down then and there, but Telemachus shouted out at him from the other side of the cloisters, and threatened him saying, “Father Eumaeus, bring the bow on in spite of them, or young as I am I will pelt you with stones back to the country, for I am the better man of the two. I wish I was as much stronger than all the other suitors in the house as I am than you, I would soon send some of them off sick and sorry, for they mean mischief.”

Thus did he speak, and they all of them laughed heartily, which put them in a better humour with Telemachus; so Eumaeus brought the bow on and placed it in the hands of Ulysses. When he had done this, he called Euryclea apart and said to her, “Euryclea, Telemachus says you are to close the doors of the women’s apartments. If they hear any groaning or uproar as of men fighting about the house, they are not to come out, but are to keep quiet and stay where they are at their work.”

Euryclea did as she was told and closed the doors of the women’s apartments.
cards.whyThisWorks: Telemachus's threat to stone Eumaeus followed by his laughter-inducing speech reveals his calculated boldness and growing authority, showing how a character's speech can simultaneously demonstrate courage and political savvy.
cards.skillStrategy: When a character speaks, ask what the words reveal about who they are and what they want — look for contradictions or surprises that add deeper meaning.
evidencePoints: I will pelt you with stones back to the country, for I am the better man of the two
they all of them laughed heartily, which put them in a better humour with Telemachus
cards.question: Read the following passage from the excerpt: 'I will pelt you with stones back to the country, for I am the better man of the two. I wish I was as much stronger than all the other suitors in the house as I am than you, I would soon send some of them off sick and sorry.' What does Telemachus's speech to Eumaeus reveal about his character?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Telemachus is genuinely furious at Eumaeus for his cowardice and intends to punish him once the suitors are defeated.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Telemachus uses an exaggerated threat against a loyal servant to pressure him forward while signaling to the suitors that he is bold enough to challenge them, showing he is both strategic and assertive.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Telemachus reveals that he is reckless and immature, unable to control his anger in a dangerous situation, which causes the suitors to dismiss him as a serious threat.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Telemachus openly admits his physical weakness compared to the suitors, which earns their sympathy and causes them to allow Eumaeus to deliver the bow.

cards.standardTitle: Theme development across a literary text
cards.excerpt:
Then Mercury of Cyllene summoned the ghosts of the suitors, and in his hand he held the fair golden wand with which he seals men’s eyes in sleep or wakes them just as he pleases; with this he roused the ghosts and led them, while they followed whining and gibbering behind him. As bats fly squealing in the hollow of some great cave, when one of them has fallen out of the cluster in which they hang, even so did the ghosts whine and squeal as Mercury the healer of sorrow led them down into the dark abode of death. When they had passed the waters of Oceanus and the rock Leucas, they came to the gates of the sun and the land of dreams, whereon they reached the meadow of asphodel where dwell the souls and shadows of them that can labour no more.

Here they found the ghost of Achilles son of Peleus, with those of Patroclus, Antilochus, and Ajax, who was the finest and handsomest man of all the Danaans after the son of Peleus himself.
cards.whyThisWorks: The two paragraphs each contribute a distinct moment—the suitors' undignified descent as squealing bats and the arrival at the asphodel meadow where even great heroes like Achilles dwell—allowing students to track how both moments together build the theme that death is the great equalizer, reducing all souls, noble or disgraced, to the same shadowy existence.
cards.skillStrategy: Identify what each separate moment shows on its own, then ask what idea both moments share to find the theme they build together.
evidencePoints: even so did the ghosts whine and squeal as Mercury the healer of sorrow led them down into the dark abode of death
they reached the meadow of asphodel where dwell the souls and shadows of them that can labour no more
cards.question: Read the two paragraphs carefully. In the first paragraph, the suitors' ghosts are compared to squealing bats and led helplessly into death's realm. In the second paragraph, the great hero Achilles and his companions are found waiting in the same meadow of asphodel. What theme do these two moments develop together?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The suitors' shameful deaths mark them as permanently inferior to warriors like Achilles, even in the afterlife.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Death strips away all distinctions of honor and disgrace, gathering the disgraced suitors and the greatest of heroes into the same shadowy realm.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Mercury's power over the dead reveals that the gods, not human choices, determine a person's fate after death.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The journey through Oceanus and the land of dreams shows that the afterlife rewards those who endured great suffering in life.

cards.standardTitle: Epic poetry: characters, structures, and themes
cards.excerpt: Then Ulysses in his turn melted, and wept as he clasped his dear and faithful wife to his bosom. As the sight of land is welcome to men who are swimming towards the shore, when Neptune has wrecked their ship with the fury of his winds and waves; a few alone reach the land, and these, covered with brine, are thankful when they find themselves on firm ground and out of danger—even so was her husband welcome to her as she looked upon him, and she could not tear her two fair arms from about his neck. Indeed they would have gone on indulging their sorrow till rosy-fingered morn appeared, had not Minerva determined otherwise, and held night back in the far west, while she would not suffer Dawn to leave Oceanus, nor to yoke the two steeds Lampus and Phaethon that bear her onward to break the day upon mankind.
cards.whyThisWorks: Minerva's act of holding back night and preventing Dawn from yoking her steeds is a direct, named divine intervention that extends the reunion scene, making the supernatural force's role in shaping action unmistakable.
cards.skillStrategy: When you spot a god or goddess acting in the passage, ask: what would have happened without that action, and how does it change what the characters experience?
evidencePoints: had not Minerva determined otherwise, and held night back in the far west
she would not suffer Dawn to leave Oceanus, nor to yoke the two steeds Lampus and Phaethon that bear her onward to break the day upon mankind
cards.question: The narrator states that Ulysses and Penelope 'would have gone on indulging their sorrow till rosy-fingered morn appeared, had not Minerva determined otherwise.' What does Minerva's decision to hold back night and prevent Dawn from yoking her steeds reveal about the role of divine intervention in this moment?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Minerva intervenes to punish Dawn for abandoning Oceanus, which accidentally gives Ulysses and Penelope more time together.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Minerva deliberately suspends the natural order of day and night so that the reunion between Ulysses and Penelope can continue undisturbed.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Minerva restrains the steeds Lampus and Phaethon because she fears Neptune will use the coming dawn to renew his fury against Ulysses.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Minerva holds back the night because Ulysses and Penelope's grief has grown so overwhelming that morning light would cause them greater sorrow.

cards.standardTitle: Key literary elements add layers of meaning
cards.excerpt:
Pontonous mixed the wine and handed it to every one in turn; the others each from his own seat made a drink-offering to the blessed gods that live in heaven, but Ulysses rose and placed the double cup in the hands of queen Arete.

“Farewell, queen,” said he, “henceforward and for ever, till age and death, the common lot of mankind, lay their hands upon you. I now take my leave; be happy in this house with your children, your people, and with king Alcinous.”

As he spoke he crossed the threshold, and Alcinous sent a man to conduct him to his ship and to the sea shore. Arete also sent some maidservants with him—one with a clean shirt and cloak, another to carry his strong box, and a third with corn and wine. When they got to the water side the crew took these things and put them on board, with all the meat and drink; but for Ulysses they spread a rug and a linen sheet on deck that he might sleep soundly in the stern of the ship. Then he too went on board and lay down without a word, but the crew took every man his place and loosed the hawser from the pierced stone to which it had been bound. Thereon, when they began rowing out to sea, Ulysses fell into a deep, sweet, and almost deathlike slumber.111

The ship bounded forward on her way as a four in hand chariot flies over the course when the horses feel the whip. Her prow curvetted as it were the neck of a stallion, and a great wave of dark blue water seethed in her wake. She held steadily on her course, and even a falcon, swiftest of all birds, could not have kept pace with her. Thus, then, she cut her way through the water, carrying one who was as cunning as the gods, but who was now sleeping peacefully, forgetful of all that he had suffered both on the field of battle and by the waves of the weary sea.
cards.whyThisWorks: Ulysses' farewell speech to Arete, his silent boarding of the ship, and his 'deep, sweet, and almost deathlike slumber' together reveal a man who is dignified in departure yet utterly exhausted—showing that beneath his heroic composure lies profound weariness, adding layers of meaning to his character.
cards.skillStrategy: When a character's actions or words contrast with what we know about them, ask what that contrast reveals about who they really are beneath the surface.
evidencePoints: Ulysses rose and placed the double cup in the hands of queen Arete
he too went on board and lay down without a word, but the crew took every man his place
cards.question: In the final paragraph, Ulysses is described as 'one who was as cunning as the gods, but who was now sleeping peacefully, forgetful of all that he had suffered both on the field of battle and by the waves of the weary sea.' What does this description reveal about Ulysses as a character?

choices.label: A
choices.text: His sleep shows that he has abandoned his identity as a warrior and no longer cares about returning home.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The contrast between his legendary cunning and his exhausted, forgetful sleep reveals that even a hero of great endurance carries the weight of suffering and finally surrenders to it.

choices.label: C
choices.text: His peaceful sleep suggests he feels no gratitude toward the Phaeacians who helped him, since he boards the ship without speaking to the crew.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The description emphasizes that Ulysses is unaware of the ship's speed, showing he is no longer capable of the alertness that once made him a great leader.

cards.standardTitle: Theme development across a literary text
cards.excerpt:
He led the way as he spoke, and Minerva followed him. When they were within he took her spear and set it in the spear-stand against a strong bearing-post along with the many other spears of his unhappy father, and he conducted her to a richly decorated seat under which he threw a cloth of damask. There was a footstool also for her feet,2 and he set another seat near her for himself, away from the suitors, that she might not be annoyed while eating by their noise and insolence, and that he might ask her more freely about his father.

A maid servant then brought them water in a beautiful golden ewer and poured it into a silver basin for them to wash their hands, and she drew a clean table beside them. An upper servant brought them bread, and offered them many good things of what there was in the house, the carver fetched them plates of all manner of meats and set cups of gold by their side, and a manservant brought them wine and poured it out for them.
cards.whyThisWorks: Two distinct moments—Telemachus seating Minerva away from the suitors and the servants' careful presentation of food and wine—both develop the theme that true hospitality honors guests with protection and dignity, requiring students to track how separate story moments build the same idea rather than reading one detail in isolation.
cards.skillStrategy: Ask yourself: what idea do two different moments in the passage both point toward, and how does each moment add to that idea?
evidencePoints: he set another seat near her for himself, away from the suitors, that she might not be annoyed while eating by their noise and insolence
An upper servant brought them bread, and offered them many good things of what there was in the house, the carver fetched them plates of all manner of meats and set cups of gold by their side
cards.question: Read the two paragraphs from The Odyssey. How do Telemachus seating Minerva away from the suitors AND the servants' careful presentation of food and drink work together to develop a theme?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Both moments show that Telemachus is eager to impress a stranger so she will help him find his father, making self-interest the central idea of the passage.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Both moments show that a worthy host shields a guest from discomfort and provides abundantly for her needs, developing the theme that true hospitality demands active care for a guest's well-being.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The seating arrangement reveals the suitors' cruelty, while the servants' actions reveal the household's wealth, so the two moments develop separate ideas rather than a single theme.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Both moments highlight the contrast between the richly decorated house and Telemachus's unhappy situation, developing the theme that outward prosperity cannot mask inner grief.

cards.standardTitle: Epic poetry: characters, structures, and themes
cards.excerpt: Thus spoke the stockman, and Ulysses struck the son of Damastor with a spear in close fight, while Telemachus hit Leocritus son of Evenor in the belly, and the dart went clean through him, so that he fell forward full on his face upon the ground. Then Minerva from her seat on the rafter held up her deadly aegis, and the hearts of the suitors quailed. They fled to the other end of the court like a herd of cattle maddened by the gadfly in early summer when the days are at their longest. As eagle-beaked, crook-taloned vultures from the mountains swoop down on the smaller birds that cower in flocks upon the ground, and kill them, for they cannot either fight or fly, and lookers on enjoy the sport—even so did Ulysses and his men fall upon the suitors and smite them on every side. They made a horrible groaning as their brains were being battered in, and the ground seethed with their blood.
cards.whyThisWorks: Minerva's act of raising her aegis from the rafter directly causes the suitors' panic and flight, making this a clear, traceable example of divine intervention shaping the outcome of an epic battle.
cards.skillStrategy: When identifying divine intervention in epic poetry, trace the cause-and-effect chain: find the god's specific action, then follow how it changes what the human characters do next.
evidencePoints: Minerva from her seat on the rafter held up her deadly aegis, and the hearts of the suitors quailed
They fled to the other end of the court like a herd of cattle maddened by the gadfly
cards.question: In the excerpt, after 'Minerva from her seat on the rafter held up her deadly aegis,' the suitors flee 'like a herd of cattle maddened by the gadfly' and Ulysses and his men 'smite them on every side.' How does Minerva's act of raising the aegis determine the outcome of the battle?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Minerva's aegis signals to Ulysses and Telemachus that the gods approve of their cause, inspiring the two men to fight harder after Telemachus kills Leocritus son of Evenor in the belly.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Minerva's aegis fills the suitors with terror so that their hearts 'quailed' and they flee in panic, unable to 'either fight or fly,' leaving Ulysses and his men free to 'smite them on every side.'

choices.label: C
choices.text: Minerva's aegis physically shields Ulysses and Telemachus from the suitors' weapons, preventing any counterattack after Ulysses strikes the son of Damastor and before the remaining suitors can regroup.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Minerva raises the aegis to drive the suitors toward Ulysses and Telemachus in a concentrated charge, allowing the two men to strike each suitor individually rather than fighting them scattered across the court.

cards.standardTitle: Key literary elements add layers of meaning
cards.excerpt:
He counted his goodly coppers and cauldrons, his gold and all his clothes, but there was nothing missing; still he kept grieving about not being in his own country, and wandered up and down by the shore of the sounding sea bewailing his hard fate. Then Minerva came up to him disguised as a young shepherd of delicate and princely mien, with a good cloak folded double about her shoulders; she had sandals on her comely feet and held a javelin in her hand. Ulysses was glad when he saw her, and went straight up to her.

“My friend,” said he, “you are the first person whom I have met with in this country; I salute you, therefore, and beg you to be well disposed towards me. Protect these my goods, and myself too, for I embrace your knees and pray to you as though you were a god. Tell me, then, and tell me truly, what land and country is this? Who are its inhabitants? Am I on an island, or is this the sea board of some continent?”

Minerva answered, “Stranger, you must be very simple, or must have come from somewhere a long way off, not to know what country this is. It is a very celebrated place, and everybody knows it East and West. It is rugged and not a good driving country, but it is by no means a bad island for what there is of it. It grows any quantity of corn and also wine, for it is watered both by rain and dew; it breeds cattle also and goats; all kinds of timber grow here, and there are watering places where the water never runs dry; so, sir, the name of Ithaca is known even as far as Troy, which I understand to be a long way off from this Achaean country.”

Ulysses was glad at finding himself, as Minerva told him, in his own country, and he began to answer, but he did not speak the truth, and made up a lying story in the instinctive wiliness of his heart.
cards.whyThisWorks: Ulysses' decision to fabricate a 'lying story' despite his joy at learning he is home reveals that cunning self-concealment is his defining trait, showing students how a character's action in a single moment can communicate deeper meaning about identity and survival.
cards.skillStrategy: When a character acts in a surprising or contradictory way, ask what that action reveals about who they truly are beneath the surface.
evidencePoints: he did not speak the truth, and made up a lying story in the instinctive wiliness of his heart
Ulysses was glad at finding himself, as Minerva told him, in his own country
cards.question: At the end of the passage, Ulysses learns he has finally reached Ithaca, yet he immediately 'made up a lying story in the instinctive wiliness of his heart.' What does this action reveal about his character?

choices.label: A
choices.text: His relief at reaching home overwhelms his judgment, causing him to speak carelessly without thinking through what he says.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Deception is so deeply rooted in his nature that even genuine joy cannot stop him from concealing the truth as an instinct for self-protection.

choices.label: C
choices.text: He distrusts Minerva's information and lies because he suspects the shepherd has given him false directions about the island's true name.

choices.label: D
choices.text: He feels ashamed of how long he has been away from Ithaca and lies to hide his identity from someone who might judge him for his absence.

cards.standardTitle: Theme development across a literary text
cards.excerpt:
So Eteoneus bustled back and bade the other servants come with him. They took their sweating steeds from under the yoke, made them fast to the mangers, and gave them a feed of oats and barley mixed. Then they leaned the chariot against the end wall of the courtyard, and led the way into the house. Telemachus and Pisistratus were astonished when they saw it, for its splendour was as that of the sun and moon; then, when they had admired everything to their heart’s content, they went into the bath room and washed themselves.

When the servants had washed them and anointed them with oil, they brought them woollen cloaks and shirts, and the two took their seats by the side of Menelaus. A maid-servant brought them water in a beautiful golden ewer, and poured it into a silver basin for them to wash their hands; and she drew a clean table beside them. An upper servant brought them bread, and offered them many good things of what there was in the house, while the carver fetched them plates of all manner of meats and set cups of gold by their side.
cards.whyThisWorks: The two paragraphs each present a distinct moment—caring for the horses and then bathing and feasting the guests—that together build the theme of hospitality as a sacred, all-encompassing duty in the heroic world.
cards.skillStrategy: Look at what happens in each paragraph separately, then ask what idea both moments are working together to develop.
evidencePoints: They took their sweating steeds from under the yoke, made them fast to the mangers, and gave them a feed of oats and barley mixed.
A maid-servant brought them water in a beautiful golden ewer, and poured it into a silver basin for them to wash their hands; and she drew a clean table beside them.
cards.question: In the first paragraph, the servants tend carefully to the travelers' horses, and in the second paragraph, servants bathe, anoint, clothe, and feed the travelers themselves. How do these two moments work together to develop a theme?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Both moments show that Menelaus is wealthier than any other king, since his household can afford golden ewers and silver basins as well as stables full of feed.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Both moments show that true hospitality extends to every part of a guest's arrival—from the animals they ride to the bodies they inhabit—suggesting that welcoming strangers is a complete and honorable obligation.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The first moment shows that servants are obedient workers, while the second moment shows that Telemachus and Pisistratus are too proud to care for themselves, together suggesting that social rank determines who performs labor.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The first moment establishes that the journey was long and exhausting, and the second moment rewards the travelers for enduring it, together developing the theme that suffering is always followed by comfort.

cards.standardTitle: Epic poetry: characters, structures, and themes
cards.excerpt: He found her at home. There was a large fire burning on the hearth, and one could smell from far the fragrant reek of burning cedar and sandal wood. As for herself, she was busy at her loom, shooting her golden shuttle through the warp and singing beautifully. Round her cave there was a thick wood of alder, poplar, and sweet smelling cypress trees, wherein all kinds of great birds had built their nests—owls, hawks, and chattering sea-crows that occupy their business in the waters. A vine loaded with grapes was trained and grew luxuriantly about the mouth of the cave; there were also four running rills of water in channels cut pretty close together, and turned hither and thither so as to irrigate the beds of violets and luscious herbage over which they flowed. 51 Even a god could not help being charmed with such a lovely spot, so Mercury stood still and looked at it; but when he had admired it sufficiently he went inside the cave.
cards.whyThisWorks: Mercury's pause before Calypso's cave—where 'even a god could not help being charmed'—shows divine intervention shaped by supernatural enchantment, illustrating how a goddess's domain exerts power even over gods sent on a mission.
cards.skillStrategy: When a god pauses or changes behavior because of a supernatural force or setting, ask yourself how that moment shifts the action or reveals a theme about divine power.
evidencePoints: Even a god could not help being charmed with such a lovely spot, so Mercury stood still and looked at it
but when he had admired it sufficiently he went inside the cave
cards.question: The narrator states that 'even a god could not help being charmed with such a lovely spot, so Mercury stood still and looked at it.' What does this moment reveal about the supernatural power at work in the passage?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Calypso's singing and weaving demonstrate that her domestic skills are more impressive than Mercury's divine abilities, making him feel inferior before entering.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Calypso's enchanted domain holds such irresistible power that it momentarily delays even a god on a divine errand, suggesting her supernatural influence extends beyond mortals.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Mercury's pause shows that he is uncertain whether he has found the correct cave, so he stops to confirm the location before completing his mission.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The lush landscape of vines, birds, and flowing water signals that Calypso has no real power, since nature alone—not the goddess—creates the beauty Mercury admires.

cards.standardTitle: Key literary elements add layers of meaning
cards.excerpt: Menelaus on hearing this was very much shocked. “So,” he exclaimed, “these cowards would usurp a brave man’s bed? A hind might as well lay her new born young in the lair of a lion, and then go off to feed in the forest or in some grassy dell: the lion when he comes back to his lair will make short work with the pair of them—and so will Ulysses with these suitors. By father Jove, Minerva, and Apollo, if Ulysses is still the man that he was when he wrestled with Philomeleides in Lesbos, and threw him so heavily that all the Achaeans cheered him—if he is still such and were to come near these suitors, they would have a short shrift and a sorry wedding. As regards your questions, however, I will not prevaricate nor deceive you, but will tell you without concealment all that the old man of the sea told me.
cards.whyThisWorks: Menelaus's lion-and-hind comparison, paired with his invocation of Ulysses's wrestling victory at Lesbos, reveals fierce confidence and contempt for the suitors, making characterization through figurative language and allusion directly teachable here.
cards.skillStrategy: When a character uses a vivid comparison or recalls a past event, ask what that choice shows about the character's attitude or values.
evidencePoints: A hind might as well lay her new born young in the lair of a lion, and then go off to feed in the forest
if Ulysses is still the man that he was when he wrestled with Philomeleides in Lesbos, and threw him so heavily that all the Achaeans cheered him
cards.question: Read these lines from Menelaus's speech: 'A hind might as well lay her new born young in the lair of a lion' and 'if Ulysses is still the man that he was when he wrestled with Philomeleides in Lesbos.' What do these two details together reveal about Menelaus's character?

choices.label: A
choices.text: He doubts Ulysses can succeed, using the helpless hind to suggest the suitors may escape.

choices.label: B
choices.text: He is fiercely confident in Ulysses, casting the suitors as doomed prey and recalling Ulysses's proven strength.

choices.label: C
choices.text: He feels pity for the suitors, comparing them to vulnerable young animals unaware of danger.

choices.label: D
choices.text: He believes the gods, not Ulysses, will decide the suitors' fate, as shown by his call to Jove and Minerva.

cards.standardTitle: Theme development across a literary text
cards.excerpt:
Thus did they converse. Meanwhile Eurynome and the nurse took torches and made the bed ready with soft coverlets; as soon as they had laid them, the nurse went back into the house to go to her rest, leaving the bed chamber woman Eurynome183 to show Ulysses and Penelope to bed by torch light. When she had conducted them to their room she went back, and they then came joyfully to the rites of their own old bed. Telemachus, Philoetius, and the swineherd now left off dancing, and made the women leave off also. They then laid themselves down to sleep in the cloisters.

When Ulysses and Penelope had had their fill of love they fell talking with one another. She told him how much she had had to bear in seeing the house filled with a crowd of wicked suitors who had killed so many sheep and oxen on her account, and had drunk so many casks of wine. Ulysses in his turn told her what he had suffered, and how much trouble he had himself given to other people. He told her everything, and she was so delighted to listen that she never went to sleep till he had ended his whole story.
cards.whyThisWorks: The two paragraphs each present a distinct moment—physical reunion in bed and the exchange of spoken suffering—that together build a theme about what complete restoration of a relationship requires, giving students two trackable story moments to compare.
cards.skillStrategy: Find the specific action or event in each paragraph, then ask what idea both moments are pushing toward together.
evidencePoints: they then came joyfully to the rites of their own old bed
she told him how much she had had to bear…Ulysses in his turn told her what he had suffered…she was so delighted to listen that she never went to sleep till he had ended his whole story
cards.question: In the first paragraph, Ulysses and Penelope 'came joyfully to the rites of their own old bed.' In the second paragraph, they 'fell talking with one another,' each recounting years of suffering until Penelope 'never went to sleep till he had ended his whole story.' How do these two moments work together to develop a theme?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The first moment shows that physical closeness is enough to heal the years apart, and the second moment simply repeats that idea by showing Penelope's contentment as she listens.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The first moment restores the couple through physical closeness, and the second restores them through the full exchange of each other's suffering, together suggesting that a true reunion requires both bodily and emotional reconnection.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The first moment establishes Penelope's loyalty by showing her willingness to return to the marriage bed, and the second moment shifts focus entirely to Ulysses' heroic adventures, suggesting that his story is the real subject of the reunion.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The first moment shows the household servants restoring order, and the second moment shows Penelope learning the truth about the suitors' deaths, together suggesting that domestic peace depends on honest communication between masters and servants.

cards.standardTitle: Epic poetry: characters, structures, and themes
cards.excerpt: In the end he deemed it best to take to the woods, and he found one upon some high ground not far from the water. There he crept beneath two shoots of olive that grew from a single stock—the one an ungrafted sucker, while the other had been grafted. No wind, however squally, could break through the cover they afforded, nor could the sun’s rays pierce them, nor the rain get through them, so closely did they grow into one another. Ulysses crept under these and began to make himself a bed to lie on, for there was a great litter of dead leaves lying about—enough to make a covering for two or three men even in hard winter weather. He was glad enough to see this, so he laid himself down and heaped the leaves all round him. Then, as one who lives alone in the country, far from any neighbor, hides a brand as fire-seed in the ashes to save himself from having to get a light elsewhere, even so did Ulysses cover himself up with leaves; and Minerva shed a sweet sleep upon his eyes, closed his eyelids, and made him lose all memories of his sorrows.
cards.whyThisWorks: Minerva's closing act of granting sleep and erasing sorrow directly illustrates divine intervention as a structural and thematic force in epic poetry, showing how the gods sustain the hero at his lowest point.
cards.skillStrategy: When identifying divine intervention in an epic, ask what the god's action changes for the hero and what idea about heroism or fate that change supports.
evidencePoints: Minerva shed a sweet sleep upon his eyes, closed his eyelids, and made him lose all memories of his sorrows
even so did Ulysses cover himself up with leaves
cards.question: After Ulysses covers himself with leaves using his own resourcefulness, the narrator adds that 'Minerva shed a sweet sleep upon his eyes, closed his eyelids, and made him lose all memories of his sorrows.' How does this moment of divine intervention function alongside Ulysses' own actions to develop a theme in the passage?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Minerva's gift of sleep replaces Ulysses' own effort entirely, suggesting that the hero's decision to gather leaves and build a bed was unnecessary because the goddess would have protected him regardless.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Minerva's gift of sleep completes what Ulysses' resourcefulness began, reinforcing the theme that the hero's survival depends on both his own ingenuity and divine protection working together.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Minerva's gift of sleep signals her disapproval of Ulysses hiding in the woods rather than seeking human shelter, and she erases his sorrows so he will make a better choice when he wakes.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Minerva's gift of sleep shows that the olive tree's perfect shelter—blocking wind, sun, and rain—was a divine creation, making the leaves Ulysses gathered the only contribution he made to his own survival.

cards.standardTitle: Key literary elements add layers of meaning
cards.excerpt: As he spoke he threw his shabby old tattered wallet over his shoulders, by the cord from which it hung, and Eumaeus gave him a stick to his liking. The two then started, leaving the station in charge of the dogs and herdsmen who remained behind; the swineherd led the way and his master followed after, looking like some broken down old tramp as he leaned upon his staff, and his clothes were all in rags. When they had got over the rough steep ground and were nearing the city, they reached the fountain from which the citizens drew their water. This had been made by Ithacus, Neritus, and Polyctor. There was a grove of water-loving poplars planted in a circle all round it, and the clear cold water came down to it from a rock high up,143 while above the fountain there was an altar to the nymphs, at which all wayfarers used to sacrifice. Here Melanthius son of Dolius overtook them as he was driving down some goats, the best in his flock, for the suitors’ dinner, and there were two shepherds with him. When he saw Eumaeus and Ulysses he reviled them with outrageous and unseemly language, which made Ulysses very angry.
cards.whyThisWorks: Melanthius's unprovoked verbal attack on Ulysses and Eumaeus, contrasted with Ulysses's disguised but inwardly angry response, reveals how characterization through speech and reaction exposes social hierarchy, pride, and the tension beneath Ulysses's disguise.
cards.skillStrategy: When a character speaks or reacts in a surprising way, ask what that moment reveals about who they truly are beneath the surface.
evidencePoints: he reviled them with outrageous and unseemly language
which made Ulysses very angry
cards.question: When Melanthius 'reviled them with outrageous and unseemly language, which made Ulysses very angry,' what does this moment reveal about Ulysses's character?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Ulysses's anger shows he is quick-tempered and easily provoked by strangers he meets on the road.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Ulysses's anger beneath his beggar's disguise reveals that his sense of dignity and identity as a king remains intact despite his outward appearance of a broken-down tramp.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Ulysses's anger proves he has already abandoned his disguise and is ready to reveal himself to the citizens of Ithaca.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Ulysses's anger reflects his loyalty to Eumaeus, showing that he is more concerned with protecting the swineherd than with his own wounded pride.

cards.standardTitle: Theme development across a literary text
cards.excerpt:
Now when the child of morning, rosy-fingered Dawn, appeared Telemachus rose and dressed himself. He bound his sandals on to his comely feet, girded his sword about his shoulder, and left his room looking like an immortal god. He at once sent the criers round to call the people in assembly, so they called them and the people gathered thereon; then, when they were got together, he went to the place of assembly spear in hand—not alone, for his two hounds went with him. Minerva endowed him with a presence of such divine comeliness that all marvelled at him as he went by, and when he took his place in his father’s seat even the oldest councillors made way for him.

Aegyptius, a man bent double with age, and of infinite experience, was the first to speak. His son Antiphus had gone with Ulysses to Ilius, land of noble steeds, but the savage Cyclops had killed him when they were all shut up in the cave, and had cooked his last dinner for him.17 He had three sons left, of whom two still worked on their father’s land, while the third, Eurynomus, was one of the suitors; nevertheless their father could not get over the loss of Antiphus, and was still weeping for him when he began his speech.
cards.whyThisWorks: The two paragraphs place Telemachus in his absent father's seat while showing Aegyptius still weeping for his lost son, giving students two concrete moments to trace how absence shapes both duty and grief.
cards.skillStrategy: Find the key action or emotion in each paragraph, then ask what idea both moments point toward together.
evidencePoints: he took his place in his father's seat even the oldest councillors made way for him
their father could not get over the loss of Antiphus, and was still weeping for him when he began his speech
cards.question: Telemachus sits in 'his father's seat' while Aegyptius speaks 'still weeping' for his dead son. How do these two moments work together to develop a theme?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Both moments show that public assembly restores order, replacing grief with political purpose.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Both moments show that absent men leave voids others must fill with responsibility or grief.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Both moments show that Minerva's divine favor determines who earns respect in Ithaca.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Both moments show that youth and age are in conflict over who should lead the assembly.

cards.standardTitle: Epic poetry: characters, structures, and themes
cards.excerpt: On either side there stood gold and silver mastiffs which Vulcan, with his consummate skill, had fashioned expressly to keep watch over the palace of king Alcinous; so they were immortal and could never grow old. Seats were ranged all along the wall, here and there from one end to the other, with coverings of fine woven work which the women of the house had made. Here the chief persons of the Phaeacians used to sit and eat and drink, for there was abundance at all seasons; and there were golden figures of young men with lighted torches in their hands, raised on pedestals, to give light by night to those who were at table. There are60 fifty maid servants in the house, some of whom are always grinding rich yellow grain at the mill, while others work at the loom, or sit and spin, and their shuttles go backwards and forwards like the fluttering of aspen leaves, while the linen is so closely woven that it will turn oil. As the Phaeacians are the best sailors in the world, so their women excel all others in weaving, for Minerva has taught them all manner of useful arts, and they are very intelligent.
cards.whyThisWorks: The excerpt contains two distinct acts of divine intervention—Vulcan crafting immortal mastiffs and Minerva teaching the Phaeacian women to weave—allowing students to analyze how supernatural forces directly shape both the palace's protection and its household excellence.
cards.skillStrategy: When identifying divine intervention, locate the god's name, the action the god performs, and the result that would be impossible without that supernatural force.
evidencePoints: Vulcan, with his consummate skill, had fashioned expressly to keep watch over the palace of king Alcinous; so they were immortal and could never grow old
Minerva has taught them all manner of useful arts, and they are very intelligent
cards.question: The narrator states that 'Minerva has taught them all manner of useful arts' immediately after praising the Phaeacian women as the best weavers in the world. What does this placement reveal about the role of divine intervention in the excerpt?

choices.label: A
choices.text: It shows that the women's skill in weaving linen 'so closely woven that it will turn oil' comes entirely from decades of mortal practice rather than any outside force.

choices.label: B
choices.text: It establishes that the women's unmatched weaving ability is a direct result of a goddess's instruction, making divine favor the source of the household's greatest human achievement.

choices.label: C
choices.text: It suggests that Minerva intervenes only to keep the fifty maid servants occupied at the mill and loom so the palace maintains its abundance at all seasons.

choices.label: D
choices.text: It implies that Minerva's teaching is secondary to Vulcan's craftsmanship, since the immortal mastiffs Vulcan fashioned provide more lasting protection than any skill taught to mortals.

cards.standardTitle: Key literary elements add layers of meaning
cards.excerpt: Meanwhile the bard began to sing the loves of Mars and Venus, and how they first began their intrigue in the house of Vulcan. Mars made Venus many presents, and defiled King Vulcan’s marriage bed, so the sun, who saw what they were about, told Vulcan. Vulcan was very angry when he heard such dreadful news, so he went to his smithy brooding mischief, got his great anvil into its place, and began to forge some chains which none could either unloose or break, so that they might stay there in that place.69 When he had finished his snare he went into his bedroom and festooned the bed-posts all over with chains like cobwebs; he also let many hang down from the great beam of the ceiling. Not even a god could see them so fine and subtle were they. As soon as he had spread the chains all over the bed, he made as though he were setting out for the fair state of Lemnos, which of all places in the world was the one he was most fond of. But Mars kept no blind look out, and as soon as he saw him start, hurried off to his house, burning with love for Venus.
cards.whyThisWorks: Vulcan's deliberate, methodical actions—forging invisible chains, festooning the bed, then pretending to leave—reveal a character defined by calculated patience and wounded pride rather than open rage, showing students how action sequence builds characterization.
cards.skillStrategy: Track what a character does step by step and ask what those choices reveal about who they are on the inside.
evidencePoints: he went to his smithy brooding mischief, got his great anvil into its place, and began to forge some chains which none could either unloose or break
he made as though he were setting out for the fair state of Lemnos
cards.question: After learning of Venus and Mars's betrayal, Vulcan forges invisible chains, secretly covers the bed with them, and then pretends to leave for Lemnos. What do these actions reveal about Vulcan's character?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Vulcan is too cowardly to confront Mars directly, so he flees to Lemnos to avoid a fight with a more powerful god.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Vulcan channels his anger into careful, hidden planning, showing that he is a patient and cunning schemer rather than someone who acts on rage alone.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Vulcan's love for his craft at the smithy matters more to him than his marriage, which is why he returns to forging before addressing the betrayal.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Vulcan trusts that the other gods will intervene on his behalf, so his departure for Lemnos signals that he has already forgiven Venus and Mars.

cards.standardTitle: Theme development across a literary text
cards.excerpt: Outside the gate of the outer court there is a large garden of about four acres with a wall all round it. It is full of beautiful trees—pears, pomegranates, and the most delicious apples. There are luscious figs also, and olives in full growth. The fruits never rot nor fail all the year round, neither winter nor summer, for the air is so soft that a new crop ripens before the old has dropped. Pear grows on pear, apple on apple, and fig on fig, and so also with the grapes, for there is an excellent vineyard: on the level ground of a part of this, the grapes are being made into raisins; in another part they are being gathered; some are being trodden in the wine tubs, others further on have shed their blossom and are beginning to show fruit, others again are just changing colour. In the furthest part of the ground there are beautifully arranged beds of flowers that are in bloom all the year round. Two streams go through it, the one turned in ducts throughout the whole garden, while the other is carried under the ground of the outer court to the house itself, and the town’s people draw water from it. Such, then, were the splendours with which the gods had endowed the house of king Alcinous.
cards.whyThisWorks: The garden description accumulates specific details—fruit that never rots, crops ripening before old ones drop, flowers blooming all year, and two streams sustaining the land—that together build the theme of divine favor transcending natural limits, making this a strong moment for tracing theme development.
cards.skillStrategy: When tracking theme, look for repeated details that point to the same idea—ask yourself what the accumulation of those details says about life, people, or the world.
evidencePoints: The fruits never rot nor fail all the year round, neither winter nor summer, for the air is so soft that a new crop ripens before the old has dropped.
Such, then, were the splendours with which the gods had endowed the house of king Alcinous.
cards.question: The narrator states that 'the fruits never rot nor fail all the year round' and concludes that these are 'splendours with which the gods had endowed the house of king Alcinous.' How do these two details work together to develop a theme in the passage?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The staged labor in the vineyard—grapes being trodden, gathered, and left to ripen—shows that a kingdom's abundance depends on the disciplined work of its people, not on any outside force.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Divine favor lifts Alcinous's realm beyond the limits of ordinary nature, producing endless renewal—fruit that never fails, flowers that never fade—that no ungifted land could sustain.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The garden wall surrounding the four-acre estate shows that a ruler's greatest achievement is separating his cultivated civilization from the disorder of the natural world outside.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The two streams running through the garden and into the town reveal that a king earns his people's loyalty by sharing practical resources rather than by displaying ornamental beauty.

cards.standardTitle: Epic poetry: characters, structures, and themes
cards.excerpt: Meanwhile the bard began to sing the loves of Mars and Venus, and how they first began their intrigue in the house of Vulcan. Mars made Venus many presents, and defiled King Vulcan’s marriage bed, so the sun, who saw what they were about, told Vulcan. Vulcan was very angry when he heard such dreadful news, so he went to his smithy brooding mischief, got his great anvil into its place, and began to forge some chains which none could either unloose or break, so that they might stay there in that place.69 When he had finished his snare he went into his bedroom and festooned the bed-posts all over with chains like cobwebs; he also let many hang down from the great beam of the ceiling. Not even a god could see them so fine and subtle were they. As soon as he had spread the chains all over the bed, he made as though he were setting out for the fair state of Lemnos, which of all places in the world was the one he was most fond of. But Mars kept no blind look out, and as soon as he saw him start, hurried off to his house, burning with love for Venus.
cards.whyThisWorks: The Sun's act of informing Vulcan about Mars and Venus is a clear example of divine intervention that directly triggers the chain of events—Vulcan's trap-forging, the false departure to Lemnos, and Mars's rush to the house—making this excerpt ideal for teaching how divine intervention shapes epic structure.
cards.skillStrategy: When analyzing divine intervention in epic poetry, trace the exact moment a god acts and follow the chain of consequences it sets in motion to see how it drives the plot structure.
evidencePoints: the sun, who saw what they were about, told Vulcan
he made as though he were setting out for the fair state of Lemnos…But Mars kept no blind look out, and as soon as he saw him start, hurried off to his house, burning with love for Venus
cards.question: In the excerpt, 'the sun, who saw what they were about, told Vulcan' about Mars defiling his marriage bed. How does this single act of divine intervention by the Sun directly shape the sequence of events that follows?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The Sun's warning reaches Mars as well as Vulcan, so Mars 'kept no blind look out' to detect the hidden chains before entering the house, allowing him to avoid the trap Vulcan had festooned across the bed-posts.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The Sun's warning enrages Vulcan, who secretly forges chains 'none could either unloose or break,' hides them across the bed so finely 'not even a god could see them,' and then stages a false departure to Lemnos to lure the unsuspecting Mars into the trap.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The Sun's warning causes Vulcan to abandon his smithy and travel at once to Lemnos, 'which of all places in the world was the one he was most fond of,' leaving the marriage bed unguarded and giving Mars time to visit Venus freely.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The Sun's warning prompts Vulcan to confront Mars openly at his smithy rather than set a hidden trap, so Mars 'burning with love for Venus' persuades the other gods to intervene before Vulcan can finish forging the chains.

cards.standardTitle: Key literary elements add layers of meaning
cards.excerpt:
Tell me, O Muse, of that ingenious hero who travelled far and wide after he had sacked the famous town of Troy. Many cities did he visit, and many were the nations with whose manners and customs he was acquainted; moreover he suffered much by sea while trying to save his own life and bring his men safely home; but do what he might he could not save his men, for they perished through their own sheer folly in eating the cattle of the Sun-god Hyperion; so the god prevented them from ever reaching home. Tell me, too, about all these things, oh daughter of Jove, from whatsoever source you may know them.

So now all who escaped death in battle or by shipwreck had got safely home except Ulysses, and he, though he was longing to return to his wife and country, was detained by the goddess Calypso, who had got him into a large cave and wanted to marry him. But as years went by, there came a time when the gods settled that he should go back to Ithaca; even then, however, when he was among his own people, his troubles were not yet over; nevertheless all the gods had now begun to pity him except Neptune, who still persecuted him without ceasing and would not let him get home.
cards.whyThisWorks: The men's decision to eat the cattle of Hyperion and the consequence of their deaths—contrasted with Ulysses' ongoing suffering despite his survival—establishes that folly and divine punishment are central forces shaping the epic's conflict and its deeper meaning about human responsibility.
cards.skillStrategy: When a character's decision leads to a consequence, ask what that outcome reveals about a larger idea the author wants you to understand.
evidencePoints: they perished through their own sheer folly in eating the cattle of the Sun-god Hyperion; so the god prevented them from ever reaching home
even then, however, when he was among his own people, his troubles were not yet over
cards.question: The men's decision to eat the cattle of Hyperion results in their deaths and their failure to reach home. What deeper meaning does this consequence add to the opening of the epic?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The men's fate shows that the gods are indifferent to human suffering and punish mortals randomly, regardless of their choices.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The men's destruction through their own 'sheer folly' establishes that human choices carry fatal consequences, framing Ulysses' survival as a test of whether wisdom can outlast recklessness.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The men's deaths prove that Ulysses was a poor leader who failed to protect his crew, making his journey home a form of punishment for his own failures.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The men's fate reveals that the gods, not human decisions, control all outcomes in the epic, since Ulysses also cannot reach home despite making no similar mistake.

cards.standardTitle: Theme development across a literary text
cards.excerpt:
To this Eurymachus son of Polybus answered, “Take heart, Queen Penelope daughter of Icarius, and do not trouble yourself about these matters. The man is not yet born, nor never will be, who shall lay hands upon your son Telemachus, while I yet live to look upon the face of the earth. I say—and it shall surely be—that my spear shall be reddened with his blood; for many a time has Ulysses taken me on his knees, held wine up to my lips to drink, and put pieces of meat into my hands. Therefore Telemachus is much the dearest friend I have, and has nothing to fear from the hands of us suitors. Of course, if death comes to him from the gods, he cannot escape it.” He said this to quiet her, but in reality he was plotting against Telemachus.

Then Penelope went upstairs again and mourned her husband till Minerva shed sleep over her eyes. In the evening Eumaeus got back to Ulysses and his son, who had just sacrificed a young pig of a year old and were helping one another to get supper ready; Minerva therefore came up to Ulysses, turned him into an old man with a stroke of her wand, and clad him in his old clothes again, for fear that the swineherd might recognise him and not keep the secret, but go and tell Penelope.
cards.whyThisWorks: The excerpt pairs Eurymachus's false oath of protection—'in reality he was plotting against Telemachus'—with Minerva disguising Ulysses 'for fear that the swineherd might recognise him,' giving students two distinct passage moments where concealed intentions drive the action and develop a theme about deception as survival.
cards.skillStrategy: Find two moments in the passage where a character hides something important, then ask what idea both moments together are building across the text.
evidencePoints: He said this to quiet her, but in reality he was plotting against Telemachus.

Minerva therefore came up to Ulysses, turned him into an old man with a stroke of her wand, and clad him in his old clothes again, for fear that the swineherd might recognise him and not keep the secret.
cards.question: Eurymachus swears 'my spear shall be reddened with his blood' in defense of Telemachus, yet the narrator reveals 'he was plotting against Telemachus.' Minerva then disguises Ulysses 'for fear that the swineherd might recognise him.' What theme do these two moments develop together?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The gods hold final power over human affairs, as shown when Eurymachus concedes 'if death comes to him from the gods, he cannot escape it' and when Minerva transforms Ulysses with a stroke of her wand.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Survival in a dangerous world requires hiding one's true intentions, as Eurymachus conceals his plot behind a sworn oath of protection and Ulysses conceals his identity behind a divine disguise.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Loyalty forged in the past shapes present alliances, as Eurymachus recalls that Ulysses 'taken me on his knees' and Ulysses returns home to reunite with his son and trusted swineherd.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Grief leaves the innocent powerless, as Penelope mourns alone upstairs while Eurymachus plots against her son and Ulysses must hide even from those who might help him.

cards.standardTitle: Epic poetry: characters, structures, and themes
cards.excerpt:
But Ulysses, when he had taken it up and examined it all over, strung it as easily as a skilled bard strings a new peg of his lyre and makes the twisted gut fast at both ends. Then he took it in his right hand to prove the string, and it sang sweetly under his touch like the twittering of a swallow. The suitors were dismayed, and turned colour as they heard it; at that moment, moreover, Jove thundered loudly as a sign, and the heart of Ulysses rejoiced as he heard the omen that the son of scheming Saturn had sent him.

He took an arrow that was lying upon the table165—for those which the Achaeans were so shortly about to taste were all inside the quiver—he laid it on the centre-piece of the bow, and drew the notch of the arrow and the string toward him, still seated on his seat. When he had taken aim he let fly, and his arrow pierced every one of the handle-holes of the axes from the first onwards till it had gone right through them, and into the outer courtyard. Then he said to Telemachus:

“Your guest has not disgraced you, Telemachus. I did not miss what I aimed at, and I was not long in stringing my bow. I am still strong, and not as the suitors twit me with being. Now, however, it is time for the Achaeans to prepare supper while there is still daylight, and then otherwise to disport themselves with song and dance which are the crowning ornaments of a banquet.”

As he spoke he made a sign with his eyebrows, and Telemachus girded on his sword, grasped his spear, and stood armed beside his father’s seat.
cards.whyThisWorks: Jove's thunder arrives at the precise moment Ulysses strings the bow, functioning as a divine omen that confirms his identity and emboldens him to act, making the intervention directly traceable to a specific textual moment and its effect on the hero's resolve.
cards.skillStrategy: When a god acts in an epic, ask what the hero does immediately after and how the supernatural moment changes the direction of events.
evidencePoints: at that moment, moreover, Jove thundered loudly as a sign, and the heart of Ulysses rejoiced as he heard the omen that the son of scheming Saturn had sent him
he took an arrow that was lying upon the table…he laid it on the centre-piece of the bow, and drew the notch of the arrow and the string toward him
cards.question: In the first paragraph, Jove thunders 'as a sign' at the moment Ulysses strings the bow. How does this act of divine intervention shape the action that follows?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The thunder frightens the suitors into surrendering before Ulysses fires a single arrow, ending the contest without violence.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The thunder serves as a divine confirmation that emboldens Ulysses, and he immediately proceeds to shoot the arrow through the axes rather than hesitating or withdrawing.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The thunder signals to Telemachus alone that he must arm himself, and Ulysses remains unaware of any divine message during the contest.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The thunder warns Ulysses that the suitors are about to attack, causing him to abandon the bow contest and call for Telemachus to defend him.

cards.excerpt:

cards.whyThisWorks: Eurymachus's false vow of protection, immediately undercut by the narrator's revelation that 'he was plotting against Telemachus,' creates a dramatic irony that deepens the theme of deception threatening the household Odysseus has left behind.
cards.skillStrategy: When a character makes a promise or declaration, look for what the narrator or other details reveal about the character's true intentions—that gap adds a deeper layer of meaning to the conflict.

my spear shall be reddened with his blood; for many a time has Ulysses taken me on his knees
cards.question: Eurymachus swears that Telemachus 'has nothing to fear from the hands of us suitors,' yet the narrator immediately reveals 'he was plotting against Telemachus.' What deeper meaning does this contrast add to the conflict in the passage?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Eurymachus's fond memories of Ulysses placing meat in his hands show that the suitors once respected Ulysses, suggesting the conflict stems from grief over his long absence rather than from deliberate treachery.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The gap between Eurymachus's sworn protection and his secret plotting reveals that Penelope and Telemachus are surrounded by hidden enemies, deepening the danger of Odysseus's absence into a threat of betrayal from within.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Eurymachus's acknowledgment that 'if death comes to him from the gods, he cannot escape it' shows that the true conflict is between mortals and divine will, not between the suitors and Telemachus.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Penelope's decision to go upstairs and mourn rather than confront Eurymachus suggests the central conflict is her own inability to act, making Eurymachus's words irrelevant to the household's danger.

cards.standardTitle: Theme development across a literary text
cards.excerpt: When they reached the water side they went to the washing cisterns, through which there ran at all times enough pure water to wash any quantity of linen, no matter how dirty. Here they unharnessed the mules and turned them out to feed on the sweet juicy herbage that grew by the water side. They took the clothes out of the waggon, put them in the water, and vied with one another in treading them in the pits to get the dirt out. After they had washed them and got them quite clean, they laid them out by the sea side, where the waves had raised a high beach of shingle, and set about washing themselves and anointing themselves with olive oil. Then they got their dinner by the side of the stream, and waited for the sun to finish drying the clothes. When they had done dinner they threw off the veils that covered their heads and began to play at ball, while Nausicaa sang for them. As the huntress Diana goes forth upon the mountains of Taygetus or Erymanthus to hunt wild boars or deer, and the wood nymphs, daughters of Aegis-bearing Jove, take their sport along with her (then is Leto proud at seeing her daughter stand a full head taller than the others, and eclipse the loveliest amid a whole bevy of beauties), even so did the girl outshine her handmaids.
cards.whyThisWorks: The excerpt develops theme through two contrasting moments—Nausicaa 'vied with one another' in shared labor at the cisterns and then is set apart by the Diana simile declaring she 'outshine her handmaids'—showing that true distinction persists even within shared, ordinary circumstance.
cards.skillStrategy: To find theme developed through moments, identify two specific scenes that seem to contradict each other, then ask what idea both scenes together are building toward.
evidencePoints: vied with one another in treading them in the pits to get the dirt out
even so did the girl outshine her handmaids
cards.question: In the excerpt, Nausicaa 'vied with one another [with her handmaids] in treading them in the pits to get the dirt out,' participating as an equal in shared labor, yet the Diana simile concludes that 'even so did the girl outshine her handmaids.' What theme do these two contrasting moments work together to develop?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The shared labor at the cisterns and the shared play on the shore create such strong bonds among Nausicaa and her handmaids that the Diana simile's claim of her superiority is undermined by the equality the excerpt has already established.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Even though Nausicaa joins her handmaids as an equal in washing, anointing with olive oil, eating, and play, the Diana simile's declaration that she 'eclipse[s] the loveliest amid a whole bevy of beauties' suggests that true distinction cannot be hidden by shared circumstance.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Because the handmaids 'vied with one another' in the washing and later played ball together, the Diana simile rewards their collective effort by elevating all of them equally, suggesting that shared work produces shared glory.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The ordered sequence of washing, anointing with olive oil, eating dinner, and playing ball shows that Nausicaa's disciplined leadership over her handmaids is the quality the Diana simile ultimately celebrates as the source of her superiority.

cards.standardTitle: Epic poetry: characters, structures, and themes
cards.excerpt:
But she would not give him full victory as yet, for she wished still further to prove his own prowess and that of his brave son, so she flew up to one of the rafters in the roof of the cloister and sat upon it in the form of a swallow.

Meanwhile Agelaus son of Damastor, Eurynomus, Amphimedon, Demoptolemus, Pisander, and Polybus son of Polyctor bore the brunt of the fight upon the suitors’ side; of all those who were still fighting for their lives they were by far the most valiant, for the others had already fallen under the arrows of Ulysses. Agelaus shouted to them and said, “My friends, he will soon have to leave off, for Mentor has gone away after having done nothing for him but brag. They are standing at the doors unsupported. Do not aim at him all at once, but six of you throw your spears first, and see if you cannot cover yourselves with glory by killing him. When he has fallen we need not be uneasy about the others.”

They threw their spears as he bade them, but Minerva made them all of no effect. One hit the door post; another went against the door; the pointed shaft of another struck the wall; and as soon as they had avoided all the spears of the suitors Ulysses said to his own men, “My friends, I should say we too had better let drive into the middle of them, or they will crown all the harm they have done us by killing us outright.”

They therefore aimed straight in front of them and threw their spears. Ulysses killed Demoptolemus, Telemachus Euryades, Eumaeus Elatus, while the stockman killed Pisander. These all bit the dust, and as the others drew back into a corner Ulysses and his men rushed forward and regained their spears by drawing them from the bodies of the dead.
cards.whyThisWorks: Minerva's two distinct actions—withholding full victory and deflecting the suitors' spears—are explicitly stated in the excerpt, making divine intervention both visible and analyzable for students.
cards.skillStrategy: When a god acts in an epic, ask what the god does AND what the god holds back, then decide what that combination reveals about the theme.
evidencePoints: she would not give him full victory as yet, for she wished still further to prove his own prowess and that of his brave son
Minerva made them all of no effect. One hit the door post; another went against the door; the pointed shaft of another struck the wall
cards.question: The narrator states that Minerva 'would not give him full victory as yet' and then 'made them all of no effect' when the suitors threw their spears. What do these two actions together reveal about how divine intervention shapes the theme of this passage?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Minerva's decision to withhold victory shows she has abandoned Ulysses, while deflecting the spears proves the suitors are too weak to pose a real threat without her interference.

choices.label: B
choices.text: By deliberately delaying Ulysses' victory while still blocking the suitors' spears, Minerva controls the outcome of the battle to test Ulysses' worth, suggesting that a hero's glory must be earned under a god's watchful design.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Minerva deflects the suitors' spears to punish them for mocking Mentor, and her refusal to grant full victory is a warning to Ulysses that he has not yet honored the gods properly.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Minerva's two actions cancel each other out, showing that the gods are indifferent to the battle's outcome and that Ulysses' survival depends entirely on his own skill and his men's loyalty.

cards.standardTitle: Key literary elements add layers of meaning
cards.excerpt:
Then Mercury of Cyllene summoned the ghosts of the suitors, and in his hand he held the fair golden wand with which he seals men’s eyes in sleep or wakes them just as he pleases; with this he roused the ghosts and led them, while they followed whining and gibbering behind him. As bats fly squealing in the hollow of some great cave, when one of them has fallen out of the cluster in which they hang, even so did the ghosts whine and squeal as Mercury the healer of sorrow led them down into the dark abode of death. When they had passed the waters of Oceanus and the rock Leucas, they came to the gates of the sun and the land of dreams, whereon they reached the meadow of asphodel where dwell the souls and shadows of them that can labour no more.

Here they found the ghost of Achilles son of Peleus, with those of Patroclus, Antilochus, and Ajax, who was the finest and handsomest man of all the Danaans after the son of Peleus himself.
cards.whyThisWorks: The juxtaposition of the suitors' 'whining and gibbering' bat-like descent with the honored presence of Achilles, Patroclus, and Ajax in the meadow of asphodel creates a plot-driven contrast that deepens the meaning of how one's actions in life shape one's legacy in death.
cards.skillStrategy: When a plot sequence places two contrasting groups side by side, ask yourself what the author wants you to conclude about each group based on how they are described.
evidencePoints: the ghosts whine and squeal as Mercury the healer of sorrow led them down into the dark abode of death
Here they found the ghost of Achilles son of Peleus, with those of Patroclus, Antilochus, and Ajax, who was the finest and handsomest man of all the Danaans
cards.question: In the passage, the suitors arrive in the underworld 'whining and gibbering' like bats, and the very next paragraph introduces Achilles, described as 'the finest and handsomest man of all the Danaans.' What meaning does this sequence of events add to the passage?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The suitors' bat-like squealing during their descent shows that Mercury, 'the healer of sorrow,' treats every soul with the same gentleness, making their arrival no different from that of Achilles or Ajax.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The contrast between the suitors' undignified, squealing arrival and the honored presence of Achilles—'the finest and handsomest man of all the Danaans'—suggests that how one lives determines the legacy one carries even into death.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The suitors' passage through 'the gates of the sun and the land of dreams' before reaching the meadow of asphodel signals that, like Achilles, they will eventually be celebrated for their role in the events at Ithaca.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The appearance of Achilles, Patroclus, and Ajax in the same meadow of asphodel where the suitors arrive suggests that all souls in the underworld share an equal fate, regardless of how they behaved in life.

cards.standardTitle: Theme development across a literary text
cards.excerpt:
Alcinous then led the way, and the others followed after, while a servant went to fetch Demodocus. The fifty-two picked oarsmen went to the sea shore as they had been told, and when they got there they drew the ship into the water, got her mast and sails inside her, bound the oars to the thole-pins with twisted thongs of leather, all in due course, and spread the white sails aloft. They moored the vessel a little way out from land, and then came on shore and went to the house of King Alcinous. The out houses,66 yards, and all the precincts were filled with crowds of men in great multitudes both old and young; and Alcinous killed them a dozen sheep, eight full grown pigs, and two oxen. These they skinned and dressed so as to provide a magnificent banquet.

A servant presently led in the famous bard Demodocus, whom the muse had dearly loved, but to whom she had given both good and evil, for though she had endowed him with a divine gift of song, she had robbed him of his eyesight. Pontonous set a seat for him among the guests, leaning it up against a bearing-post. He hung the lyre for him on a peg over his head, and showed him where he was to feel for it with his hands. He also set a fair table with a basket of victuals by his side, and a cup of wine from which he might drink whenever he was so disposed.
cards.whyThisWorks: The two paragraphs each present a distinct moment—the oarsmen's disciplined preparation and the community's generous welcome of Demodocus—that together develop the theme that a community honors its roles and members through careful, devoted service.
cards.skillStrategy: Look at what happens in each paragraph separately, then ask what idea both moments are building together rather than picking just one detail as the whole message.
evidencePoints: bound the oars to the thole-pins with twisted thongs of leather, all in due course, and spread the white sails aloft
He hung the lyre for him on a peg over his head, and showed him where he was to feel for it with his hands. He also set a fair table with a basket of victuals by his side
cards.question: Both the oarsmen's preparations at the shore and the servants' care for Demodocus develop which theme across these two paragraphs?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Blindness and physical limitation prevent a person from fully participating in community celebrations.

choices.label: B
choices.text: A community fulfills its obligations by performing each duty with thoroughness and attentiveness toward others.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Feasting and entertainment are the primary ways a king demonstrates his power over his subjects.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The gods grant gifts to mortals only when those mortals have already proven their worth through labor.

cards.standardTitle: Epic poetry: characters, structures, and themes
cards.excerpt:
This made Antinous very angry, and he scowled at him saying, “You shall pay for this before you get clear of the court.” With these words he threw a footstool at him, and hit him on the right shoulder blade near the top of his back. Ulysses stood firm as a rock and the blow did not even stagger him, but he shook his head in silence as he brooded on his revenge. Then he went back to the threshold and sat down there, laying his well filled wallet at his feet.

“Listen to me,” he cried, “you suitors of Queen Penelope, that I may speak even as I am minded. A man knows neither ache nor pain if he gets hit while fighting for his money, or for his sheep or his cattle; and even so Antinous has hit me while in the service of my miserable belly, which is always getting people into trouble. Still, if the poor have gods and avenging deities at all, I pray them that Antinous may come to a bad end before his marriage.”

“Sit where you are, and eat your victuals in silence, or be off elsewhere,” shouted Antinous. “If you say more I will have you dragged hand and foot through the courts, and the servants shall flay you alive.”

The other suitors were much displeased at this, and one of the young men said, “Antinous, you did ill in striking that poor wretch of a tramp: it will be worse for you if he should turn out to be some god—and we know the gods go about disguised in all sorts of ways as people from foreign countries, and travel about the world to see who do amiss and who righteously.”146

Thus said the suitors, but Antinous paid them no heed. Meanwhile Telemachus was furious about the blow that had been given to his father, and though no tear fell from him, he shook his head in silence and brooded on his revenge.
cards.whyThisWorks: The excerpt pairs Ulysses' prayer that 'Antinous may come to a bad end' with the unnamed suitor's warning that 'the gods go about disguised in all sorts of ways,' creating a layered moment of dramatic irony that directly illustrates how divine intervention operates as both threat and theme in epic poetry.
cards.skillStrategy: When analyzing divine intervention in epic poetry, look for moments where a character's prayer or a warning about the gods connects to a specific act of cruelty—this pairing signals that the gods are watching and that consequences are coming.
