evidencePoints: I pray them that Antinous may come to a bad end before his marriage.
we know the gods go about disguised in all sorts of ways as people from foreign countries, and travel about the world to see who do amiss and who righteously.
cards.question: In the excerpt, Ulysses prays that 'Antinous may come to a bad end before his marriage,' and an unnamed suitor warns that 'the gods go about disguised in all sorts of ways as people from foreign countries.' How do these two specific moments work together to develop the theme of divine intervention?

choices.label: A
choices.text: They show that Antinous already suspects the beggar may be divine, which is why he threatens to have him 'dragged hand and foot through the courts' rather than striking him a second time.

choices.label: B
choices.text: They establish that cruelty toward a stranger invites punishment from the gods, suggesting that Antinous's violence against the beggar will bring consequences he cannot escape simply by ignoring the suitor's warning.

choices.label: C
choices.text: They reveal that the other suitors defend the beggar out of personal loyalty to him rather than any genuine belief that the gods monitor whether people 'do amiss and who righteously.'

choices.label: D
choices.text: They demonstrate that divine justice in the epic is immediate, as the gods visibly punish Antinous in the courtyard before he can carry out his threat to have the beggar 'flay[ed] alive.'

cards.standardTitle: Paraphrase grade-level text
cards.excerpt:
He led the way as he spoke, and Minerva followed him. When they were within he took her spear and set it in the spear-stand against a strong bearing-post along with the many other spears of his unhappy father, and he conducted her to a richly decorated seat under which he threw a cloth of damask. There was a footstool also for her feet,2 and he set another seat near her for himself, away from the suitors, that she might not be annoyed while eating by their noise and insolence, and that he might ask her more freely about his father.

A maid servant then brought them water in a beautiful golden ewer and poured it into a silver basin for them to wash their hands, and she drew a clean table beside them. An upper servant brought them bread, and offered them many good things of what there was in the house, the carver fetched them plates of all manner of meats and set cups of gold by their side, and a manservant brought them wine and poured it out for them.
cards.whyThisWorks: The sentence about Telemachus seating Minerva away from the suitors contains layered subordinate clauses with two distinct purposes ('that she might not be annoyed' and 'that he might ask her more freely'), requiring students to untangle parallel syntax and restate both reasons accurately.
cards.skillStrategy: When a sentence has multiple 'that' or 'so that' clauses, break each one into its own idea and check that your paraphrase captures all of them.
evidencePoints: he set another seat near her for himself, away from the suitors, that she might not be annoyed while eating by their noise and insolence
and that he might ask her more freely about his father
cards.question: Read this sentence from the passage: 'he set another seat near her for himself, away from the suitors, that she might not be annoyed while eating by their noise and insolence, and that he might ask her more freely about his father.' Which paraphrase most accurately restates the meaning of this sentence?

choices.label: A
choices.text: He sat beside her to protect her from the suitors, who had already begun to insult her during the meal.

choices.label: B
choices.text: He placed his seat close to hers and apart from the suitors so that their rude behavior would not disturb her meal and so that he could speak with her more openly about his father.

choices.label: C
choices.text: He moved his seat away from the suitors so that he could eat in peace, leaving her to sit alone near the noisy crowd.

choices.label: D
choices.text: He seated himself beside her and away from the suitors mainly because he was embarrassed by their insolence toward his guest.

cards.standardTitle: Paraphrase grade-level text
cards.excerpt:
Tell me, O Muse, of that ingenious hero who travelled far and wide after he had sacked the famous town of Troy. Many cities did he visit, and many were the nations with whose manners and customs he was acquainted; moreover he suffered much by sea while trying to save his own life and bring his men safely home; but do what he might he could not save his men, for they perished through their own sheer folly in eating the cattle of the Sun-god Hyperion; so the god prevented them from ever reaching home. Tell me, too, about all these things, oh daughter of Jove, from whatsoever source you may know them.

So now all who escaped death in battle or by shipwreck had got safely home except Ulysses, and he, though he was longing to return to his wife and country, was detained by the goddess Calypso, who had got him into a large cave and wanted to marry him. But as years went by, there came a time when the gods settled that he should go back to Ithaca; even then, however, when he was among his own people, his troubles were not yet over; nevertheless all the gods had now begun to pity him except Neptune, who still persecuted him without ceasing and would not let him get home.
cards.whyThisWorks: The sentence 'even then, however, when he was among his own people, his troubles were not yet over' contains an inverted, embedded clause structure that requires students to untangle the conditional timing and the continuation of hardship to restate the meaning accurately.
cards.skillStrategy: When a sentence has interrupting phrases like 'however' or 'even then,' break it into parts: identify what the condition is, what happened, and what the result was.
evidencePoints: even then, however, when he was among his own people, his troubles were not yet over
there came a time when the gods settled that he should go back to Ithaca
cards.question: Read this sentence from the passage: 'even then, however, when he was among his own people, his troubles were not yet over.' Which restatement most accurately captures the meaning of this sentence?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Once Ulysses finally returned to Ithaca, the gods immediately resolved all of his remaining difficulties.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Even after Ulysses reached his homeland and was back among his own people, his suffering had still not ended.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Ulysses was prevented from ever returning to his people because his troubles were too great to overcome.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Although Ulysses was reunited with his people, they were the ones who caused his continued hardships.

cards.standardTitle: Key literary elements add layers of meaning
cards.excerpt:
She said. With awe divine, the queen of love Obey’d the sister and the wife of Jove; And from her fragrant breast the zone embraced, With various skill and high embroidery graced. In this was every art, and every charm, To win the wisest, and the coldest warm: Fond love, the gentle vow, the gay desire, The kind deceit, the still-reviving fire, Persuasive speech, and the more persuasive sighs, Silence that spoke, and eloquence of eyes. This on her hand the Cyprian Goddess laid: “Take this, and with it all thy wish;” she said. With smiles she took the charm; and smiling press’d The powerful cestus to her snowy breast.

Then Venus to the courts of Jove withdrew; Whilst from Olympus pleased Saturnia flew. O’er high Pieria thence her course she bore, O’er fair Emathia’s ever-pleasing shore, O’er Hemus’ hills with snows eternal crown’d; Nor once her flying foot approach’d the ground. Then taking wing from Athos’ lofty steep, She speeds to Lemnos o’er the rolling deep, And seeks the cave of Death’s half-brother, Sleep.
cards.whyThisWorks: Juno's swift, purposeful flight across mountains and seas—combined with her pleased demeanor after obtaining the cestus—reveals her as a calculating, determined schemer whose actions carry the meaning that divine power is willingly bent toward personal manipulation.
cards.skillStrategy: When a character acts, ask what that action shows about who they are and what it means for the story—look at how Homer describes the action, not just what happens.
evidencePoints: O'er high Pieria thence her course she bore, O'er fair Emathia's ever-pleasing shore, O'er Hemus' hills with snows eternal crown'd; Nor once her flying foot approach'd the ground.
whilst from Olympus pleased Saturnia flew
cards.question: In the second paragraph, Homer describes Juno flying over mountains and seas without once touching the ground. What does this description of Juno's flight reveal about her character?

choices.label: A
choices.text: She is distracted by the beauty of the landscapes she passes over, suggesting she is easily swayed from her purpose.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Her swift, uninterrupted flight shows she is driven by urgent, single-minded determination to carry out her scheme.

choices.label: C
choices.text: She avoids the ground because she fears the mortal world below, revealing her as timid despite her divine status.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Her journey across so many lands shows she is lost and uncertain about where to find the cave of Sleep.

cards.standardTitle: Key literary elements add layers of meaning
cards.excerpt: The following observations of Coleridge furnish a most gallant and interesting view of Helen’s character— “Few things are more interesting than to observe how the same hand that has given us the fury and inconsistency of Achilles, gives us also the consummate elegance and tenderness of Helen. She is through the Iliad a genuine lady, graceful in motion and speech, noble in her associations, full of remorse for a fault for which higher powers seem responsible, yet grateful and affectionate towards those with whom that fault had committed her. I have always thought the following speech in which Helen laments Hector, and hints at her own invidious and unprotected situation in Troy, as almost the sweetest passage in the poem. It is another striking instance of that refinement of feeling and softness of tone which so generally distinguish the last book of the Iliad from the rest.”—Classic Poets, p. 198, seq.
cards.whyThisWorks: Coleridge's commentary explicitly traces how Helen's remorse, gratitude, and affection—despite her fault—reveal a character of moral complexity and refinement, giving students a clear model of how characterization layers meaning.
cards.skillStrategy: When analyzing characterization, look for contrasting traits or emotions in a character and ask what that tension reveals about who they are and what the author wants you to understand.
evidencePoints: full of remorse for a fault for which higher powers seem responsible, yet grateful and affectionate towards those with whom that fault had committed her
consummate elegance and tenderness of Helen
cards.question: According to Coleridge's observations, what does Helen's simultaneous remorse and affection reveal about her character in the Iliad?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Helen feels no genuine guilt because she blames the gods entirely for her situation in Troy.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Helen's ability to feel deep regret while remaining loyal and tender toward those around her shows her as morally complex rather than simply villainous.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Helen's elegance and grace in speech make her indifferent to the suffering her actions caused others.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Helen's remorse is directed only at Hector, which is why her lament for him stands apart from her behavior elsewhere in the poem.

cards.standardTitle: Epic poetry: characters, structures, and themes
cards.excerpt: Diomed, assisted by Pallas, performs wonders in this day’s battle. Pandarus wounds him with an arrow, but the goddess cures him, enables him to discern gods from mortals, and prohibits him from contending with any of the former, excepting Venus. Æneas joins Pandarus to oppose him; Pandarus is killed, and Æneas in great danger but for the assistance of Venus; who, as she is removing her son from the fight, is wounded on the hand by Diomed. Apollo seconds her in his rescue, and at length carries off Æneas to Troy, where he is healed in the temple of Pergamus. Mars rallies the Trojans, and assists Hector to make a stand. In the meantime Æneas is restored to the field, and they overthrow several of the Greeks; among the rest Tlepolemus is slain by Sarpedon. Juno and Minerva descend to resist Mars; the latter incites Diomed to go against that god; he wounds him, and sends him groaning to heaven. The first battle continues through this book. The scene is the same as in the former.
cards.whyThisWorks: The excerpt shows Pallas performing two linked acts—curing Diomed's wound and granting him divine sight while restricting him to fighting only Venus—demonstrating how divine intervention in epic poetry both empowers and constrains a hero, directly teaching the subskill of divine intervention within ELA.9.R.1.4.
cards.skillStrategy: When analyzing divine intervention in epic poetry, trace exactly what a god gives the hero AND what limits come with that gift, then check whether the story follows through on both.
evidencePoints: enables him to discern gods from mortals, and prohibits him from contending with any of the former, excepting Venus
as she is removing her son from the fight, is wounded on the hand by Diomed
cards.question: The excerpt states that Pallas 'enables him to discern gods from mortals, and prohibits him from contending with any of the former, excepting Venus.' How does this paired gift and restriction shape the specific moment when Diomed wounds Venus as she carries Æneas from the battlefield?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The gift of divine sight allows Diomed to avoid all gods entirely, so his wounding of Venus is an accident rather than a deliberate act permitted by Pallas's restriction.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The restriction channels Diomed's new divine awareness into one permitted target: because Venus enters the fight to rescue Æneas, Diomed can recognize her as a god and still strike her without violating Pallas's prohibition.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The prohibition against fighting gods overrides the gift of sight in this moment, meaning Diomed wounds Venus only after losing the divine awareness Pallas granted him earlier in the battle.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The gift of divine sight causes Diomed to pursue every god on the battlefield, and the exception for Venus is simply the first opportunity he finds, with no connection to her act of rescuing Æneas.

cards.standardTitle: Key literary elements add layers of meaning
cards.excerpt: He said: Patroclus o’er the blazing fire Heaps in a brazen vase three chines entire: The brazen vase Automedon sustains, Which flesh of porker, sheep, and goat contains. Achilles at the genial feast presides, The parts transfixes, and with skill divides. Meanwhile Patroclus sweats, the fire to raise; The tent is brighten’d with the rising blaze: Then, when the languid flames at length subside, He strows a bed of glowing embers wide, Above the coals the smoking fragments turns And sprinkles sacred salt from lifted urns; With bread the glittering canisters they load, Which round the board Menoetius’ son bestow’d; Himself, opposed to Ulysses full in sight, Each portion parts, and orders every rite. The first fat offering to the immortals due, Amidst the greedy flames Patroclus threw; Then each, indulging in the social feast, His thirst and hunger soberly repress’d. That done, to Phœnix Ajax gave the sign: Not unperceived; Ulysses crown’d with wine The foaming bowl, and instant thus began, His speech addressing to the godlike man.
cards.whyThisWorks: The excerpt contrasts Patroclus's exhausting physical labor—sweating over the fire, spreading embers, turning fragments, and casting the sacred offering—with Achilles's role presiding at the feast, revealing through action how Patroclus's selfless devotion defines his character.
cards.skillStrategy: When analyzing characterization, look at what a character does versus what others do in the same scene, and ask what those specific actions reveal about who that character is.
evidencePoints: Patroclus sweats, the fire to raise
The first fat offering to the immortals due, Amidst the greedy flames Patroclus threw
cards.question: The excerpt describes Patroclus sweating to raise the fire, spreading 'a bed of glowing embers wide,' turning the smoking fragments, and casting 'the first fat offering to the immortals' into the flames—while 'Achilles at the genial feast presides.' What does this pattern of actions reveal about Patroclus's character?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Patroclus performs every physical task—tending fire, turning meat, and casting the sacred offering—because he resents Achilles's idle presiding and wants the visiting ambassadors to recognize his own importance.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Patroclus's tireless labor—from sweating over the fire to personally casting the sacred offering into the flames—reveals a selfless devotion to Achilles that defines him even in a moment of honored hospitality.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Patroclus handles the fire, the embers, and the sacred offering because he is the most skilled cook among the warriors, making him the natural choice to manage the feast for guests like Ulysses and Ajax.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Patroclus sweats over the fire and performs the sacred offering to signal to Phoenix, Ajax, and Ulysses that the feast follows proper ritual, showing he is more concerned with impressing the ambassadors than serving Achilles.

cards.standardTitle: Key literary elements add layers of meaning
cards.excerpt:
Thus having said, the glorious chief resumes His towery helmet, black with shading plumes. His princess parts with a prophetic sigh, Unwilling parts, and oft reverts her eye That stream’d at every look; then, moving slow, Sought her own palace, and indulged her woe. There, while her tears deplored the godlike man, Through all her train the soft infection ran; The pious maids their mingled sorrows shed, And mourn the living Hector, as the dead.

But now, no longer deaf to honour’s call, Forth issues Paris from the palace wall. In brazen arms that cast a gleamy ray, Swift through the town the warrior bends his way. The wanton courser thus with reins unbound Breaks from his stall, and beats the trembling ground; Pamper’d and proud, he seeks the wonted tides, And laves, in height of blood his shining sides; His head now freed, he tosses to the skies; His mane dishevell’d o’er his shoulders flies; He snuffs the females in the distant plain, And springs, exulting, to his fields again. With equal triumph, sprightly, bold, and gay, In arms refulgent as the god of day, The son of Priam, glorying in his might, Rush’d forth with Hector to the fields of fight.
cards.whyThisWorks: The excerpt contrasts Andromache's grief-stricken farewell with Paris's carefree, triumphant departure, allowing students to analyze how the characterization of Paris through the wild-horse simile reveals his shallow vanity and indifference to the war's cost.
cards.skillStrategy: When a character is compared to something in a simile, ask what that comparison reveals about who the character truly is and what the author wants you to think of them.
evidencePoints: The wanton courser thus with reins unbound / Breaks from his stall, and beats the trembling ground; / Pamper'd and proud, he seeks the wonted tides
With equal triumph, sprightly, bold, and gay, / In arms refulgent as the god of day, / The son of Priam, glorying in his might, / Rush'd forth with Hector to the fields of fight.
cards.question: In the second paragraph, Paris is compared to a horse that is 'wanton,' 'pamper'd and proud,' and rushing toward 'the females in the distant plain.' What does this comparison reveal about Paris's character?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Paris is portrayed as a fearless and disciplined warrior whose eagerness to fight demonstrates his deep loyalty to Troy and to Hector.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Paris is portrayed as vain and driven by pleasure rather than duty, suggesting his rush to battle is motivated by self-glorification rather than genuine heroism.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Paris is portrayed as reckless but ultimately tragic, mirroring Andromache's sorrow and showing that he too fears the outcome of the coming battle.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Paris is portrayed as physically powerful and superior to Hector, with the horse simile emphasizing that he will be the more effective fighter on the battlefield.

cards.standardTitle: Key literary elements add layers of meaning
cards.excerpt: To him the Lycian: “Whom your eyes behold, If right I judge, is Diomed the bold: Such coursers whirl him o’er the dusty field, So towers his helmet, and so flames his shield. If ’tis a god, he wears that chief’s disguise: Or if that chief, some guardian of the skies, Involved in clouds, protects him in the fray, And turns unseen the frustrate dart away. I wing’d an arrow, which not idly fell, The stroke had fix’d him to the gates of hell; And, but some god, some angry god withstands, His fate was due to these unerring hands. Skill’d in the bow, on foot I sought the war, Nor join’d swift horses to the rapid car. Ten polish’d chariots I possess’d at home, And still they grace Lycaon’s princely dome: There veil’d in spacious coverlets they stand; And twice ten coursers wait their lord’s command. The good old warrior bade me trust to these, When first for Troy I sail’d the sacred seas; In fields, aloft, the whirling car to guide, And through the ranks of death triumphant ride. But vain with youth, and yet to thrift inclined, I heard his counsels with unheedful mind, And thought the steeds (your large supplies unknown) Might fail of forage in the straiten’d town; So took my bow and pointed darts in hand And left the chariots in my native land.
cards.whyThisWorks: The Lycian's admission that he ignored his father's wise counsel and left his chariots behind out of youthful overconfidence reveals a character whose pride and poor judgment have directly undermined his effectiveness in battle, adding meaning to his failure against Diomed.
cards.skillStrategy: When a character explains a past decision, ask what that choice reveals about who they are and how it connects to their current situation.
evidencePoints: But vain with youth, and yet to thrift inclined, I heard his counsels with unheedful mind
And thought the steeds (your large supplies unknown) Might fail of forage in the straiten'd town; So took my bow and pointed darts in hand And left the chariots in my native land.
cards.question: The Lycian reveals that he ignored his father's advice and left his chariots at home. What does this admission reveal about his character and its effect on his situation in battle?

choices.label: A
choices.text: His decision shows that he trusted his skill with a bow more than any chariot could provide, making him a deliberately unconventional warrior who fights on his own terms.

choices.label: B
choices.text: His admission that he acted with an 'unheedful mind' out of youthful vanity reveals a character whose overconfidence led to a strategic mistake, leaving him less equipped to defeat Diomed and forcing him to blame the gods for his failure.

choices.label: C
choices.text: His explanation that he feared the horses would lack food in Troy shows he is a practical and cautious thinker whose careful planning simply did not account for the length of the war.

choices.label: D
choices.text: His description of the ten chariots waiting at home establishes him as a wealthy and powerful warrior whose true strength has not yet been displayed on the battlefield.

cards.standardTitle: Key literary elements add layers of meaning
cards.excerpt: The giant spoke; and in a stupid gaze The host beheld him, silent with amaze! ’Twas thou, Euryalus! who durst aspire To meet his might, and emulate thy sire, The great Mecistheus; who in days of yore In Theban games the noblest trophy bore, (The games ordain’d dead OEdipus to grace,) And singly vanquish the Cadmean race. Him great Tydides urges to contend, Warm with the hopes of conquest for his friend; Officious with the cincture girds him round; And to his wrist the gloves of death are bound. Amid the circle now each champion stands, And poises high in air his iron hands; With clashing gauntlets now they fiercely close, Their crackling jaws re-echo to the blows, And painful sweat from all their members flows. At length Epeus dealt a weighty blow Full on the cheek of his unwary foe; Beneath that ponderous arm’s resistless sway Down dropp’d he, nerveless, and extended lay. As a large fish, when winds and waters roar, By some huge billow dash’d against the shore, Lies panting; not less batter’d with his wound, The bleeding hero pants upon the ground. To rear his fallen foe, the victor lends, Scornful, his hand; and gives him to his friends; Whose arms support him, reeling through the throng, And dragging his disabled legs along; Nodding, his head hangs down his shoulder o’er; His mouth and nostrils pour the clotted gore; Wrapp’d round in mists he lies, and lost to thought; His friends receive the bowl, too dearly bought.
cards.whyThisWorks: Epeus's gesture of scornfully lending his hand to his fallen opponent reveals a character whose pride and contempt undercut any apparent sportsmanship, adding meaning to the theme of glory and humiliation in combat.
cards.skillStrategy: When a character acts in a way that seems contradictory—like helping someone while showing contempt—ask what that tension reveals about who the character really is.
evidencePoints: To rear his fallen foe, the victor lends, / Scornful, his hand; and gives him to his friends
His mouth and nostrils pour the clotted gore; / Wrapp'd round in mists he lies, and lost to thought
cards.question: After defeating Euryalus, Epeus helps him up but does so 'Scornful.' What does this action reveal about Epeus's character?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Epeus feels genuine remorse for the severity of the wounds he has inflicted on Euryalus during the match.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Epeus's contempt in the moment of apparent mercy shows that his true motivation is dominance and public humiliation of his opponent, not honorable sportsmanship.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Epeus extends his hand because the rules of the games require the winner to assist the loser off the field.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Epeus respects Euryalus's lineage as the son of the great Mecistheus and helps him out of admiration for that noble heritage.

cards.standardTitle: Epic poetry: characters, structures, and themes
cards.excerpt: Jupiter, awaking, sees the Trojans repulsed from the trenches, Hector in a swoon, and Neptune at the head of the Greeks: he is highly incensed at the artifice of Juno, who appeases him by her submissions; she is then sent to Iris and Apollo. Juno, repairing to the assembly of the gods, attempts, with extraordinary address, to incense them against Jupiter; in particular she touches Mars with a violent resentment; he is ready to take arms, but is prevented by Minerva. Iris and Apollo obey the orders of Jupiter; Iris commands Neptune to leave the battle, to which, after much reluctance and passion, he consents. Apollo reinspires Hector with vigour, brings him back to the battle, marches before him with his ægis, and turns the fortune of the fight. He breaks down great part of the Grecian wall: the Trojans rush in, and attempt to fire the first line of the fleet, but are, as yet, repelled by the greater Ajax with a prodigious slaughter.
cards.whyThisWorks: This excerpt directly illustrates divine intervention shaping battle outcomes, showing how Apollo's two acts—reinspiring Hector and marching before him with the ægis—combine to reverse the Greeks' advantage and drive the Trojans to breach the Grecian wall and threaten the fleet.
cards.skillStrategy: When analyzing divine intervention in epic poetry, trace the specific actions a god takes and follow the chain of consequences those actions produce in the battle or plot.
evidencePoints: Apollo reinspires Hector with vigour, brings him back to the battle, marches before him with his ægis, and turns the fortune of the fight.
He breaks down great part of the Grecian wall: the Trojans rush in, and attempt to fire the first line of the fleet.
cards.question: According to the excerpt, Apollo 'reinspires Hector with vigour' and then 'marches before him with his ægis.' What is the combined effect of these two acts of divine intervention on the battle?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Apollo restores Hector's strength so that Hector can persuade Neptune to leave the battle willingly, removing the Greeks' divine protector before the Trojans advance.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Apollo revives Hector and shields his advance with the ægis, together turning the fortune of the fight so that the Trojans break down the Grecian wall and threaten to fire the fleet.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Apollo's ægis prevents Jupiter from intervening on behalf of the Greeks, while Hector's restored vigour allows him single-handedly to destroy the entire Grecian wall without Trojan support.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Apollo uses the ægis to drive Juno's allies from the battlefield, and his restoration of Hector convinces Jupiter to lift his anger so that the Trojans can advance unopposed.

cards.standardTitle: Key literary elements add layers of meaning
cards.excerpt: He said: and, seizing Thrasymedes’ shield, (His valiant offspring,) hasten’d to the field; (That day the son his father’s buckler bore;) Then snatch’d a lance, and issued from the door. Soon as the prospect open’d to his view, His wounded eyes the scene of sorrow knew; Dire disarray! the tumult of the fight, The wall in ruins, and the Greeks in flight. As when old ocean’s silent surface sleeps, The waves just heaving on the purple deeps: While yet the expected tempest hangs on high, Weighs down the cloud, and blackens in the sky, The mass of waters will no wind obey; Jove sends one gust, and bids them roll away. While wavering counsels thus his mind engage, Fluctuates in doubtful thought the Pylian sage, To join the host, or to the general haste; Debating long, he fixes on the last: Yet, as he moves, the sight his bosom warms, The field rings dreadful with the clang of arms, The gleaming falchions flash, the javelins fly; Blows echo blows, and all or kill or die.
cards.whyThisWorks: Nestor's internal wavering followed by his decisive move toward battle—despite his wounds and age—reveals a character defined by duty overcoming hesitation, giving students a clear action-plus-thought moment to analyze for meaning.
cards.skillStrategy: When a character hesitates and then acts anyway, ask yourself what that tension reveals about who they are and what they value.
evidencePoints: Fluctuates in doubtful thought the Pylian sage, / To join the host, or to the general haste; / Debating long, he fixes on the last
Yet, as he moves, the sight his bosom warms, / The field rings dreadful with the clang of arms
cards.question: Read the following lines: 'Fluctuates in doubtful thought the Pylian sage, / To join the host, or to the general haste; / Debating long, he fixes on the last: / Yet, as he moves, the sight his bosom warms.' What do Nestor's internal debate and final decision reveal about his character?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Nestor is paralyzed by fear of the battle's chaos and ultimately retreats to protect himself from further harm.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Nestor's prolonged hesitation followed by his choice to advance shows that his sense of duty to the fight overcomes his personal caution.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Nestor debates only because he is uncertain which weapon to carry into battle, not because he doubts whether to fight at all.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Nestor's wavering reveals that he is too old and wounded to make sound decisions, and the sight of battle only confuses him further.

cards.standardTitle: Key literary elements add layers of meaning
cards.excerpt: From ship to ship thus Ajax swiftly flew, No less the wonder of the warring crew. As furious, Hector thunder’d threats aloud, And rush’d enraged before the Trojan crowd; Then swift invades the ships, whose beaky prores Lay rank’d contiguous on the bending shores; So the strong eagle from his airy height, Who marks the swans’ or cranes’ embodied flight, Stoops down impetuous, while they light for food, And, stooping, darkens with his wings the flood. Jove leads him on with his almighty hand, And breathes fierce spirits in his following band. The warring nations meet, the battle roars, Thick beats the combat on the sounding prores. Thou wouldst have thought, so furious was their fire, No force could tame them, and no toil could tire; As if new vigour from new fights they won, And the long battle was but then begun. Greece, yet unconquer’d, kept alive the war, Secure of death, confiding in despair: Troy in proud hopes already view’d the main Bright with the blaze, and red with heroes slain: Like strength is felt from hope, and from despair, And each contends, as his were all the war.
cards.whyThisWorks: Hector's characterization through the eagle simile and the phrases 'thunder'd threats aloud' and 'rush'd enraged' reveals how his ferocity and divine backing create a sense of unstoppable menace, adding meaning to the battle's stakes.
cards.skillStrategy: When a character is described through a comparison or vivid action words, ask yourself what that description reveals about who they are and what their role means in the larger conflict.
evidencePoints: Hector thunder'd threats aloud, And rush'd enraged before the Trojan crowd
So the strong eagle from his airy height... Stoops down impetuous, while they light for food, And, stooping, darkens with his wings the flood
cards.question: Read the following lines: 'Hector thunder'd threats aloud, And rush'd enraged before the Trojan crowd; Then swift invades the ships... So the strong eagle from his airy height... Stoops down impetuous... And, stooping, darkens with his wings the flood.' What does this characterization of Hector reveal about his role in the battle?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Hector is reckless and undisciplined, charging forward without a plan and putting his own army at risk.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Hector is a predatory, overwhelming force whose rage and speed make him appear nearly impossible for the Greeks to resist.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Hector is driven by personal grief rather than military strategy, making his attack more emotional than effective.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Hector mirrors Ajax in courage and skill, suggesting the two warriors are equally matched in the coming fight.

cards.standardTitle: Epic poetry: characters, structures, and themes
cards.excerpt:
Fresh water fowl, especially swans, were found in great numbers about the Asian Marsh, a fenny tract of country in Lydia, formed by the river Cayster, near its mouth. See Virgil, “Georgics,” vol. i. 383, sq.

_Scamander_, or Scamandros, was a river of Troas, rising, according to Strabo, on the highest part of Mount Ida, in the same hill with the Granicus and the OEdipus, and falling into the sea at Sigaeum; everything tends to identify it with Mendere, as Wood, Rennell, and others maintain; the Mendere is 40 miles long, 300 feet broad, deep in the time of flood, nearly dry in the summer. Dr. Clarke successfully combats the opinion of those who make the Scamander to have arisen from the springs of Bounabarshy, and traces the source of the river to the highest mountain in the chain of Ida, now Kusdaghy; receives the Simois in its course; towards its mouth it is very muddy, and flows through marshes. Between the Scamander and Simois, Homer’s Troy is supposed to have stood: this river, according to Homer, was called Xanthus by the gods, Scamander by men. The waters of the Scamander had the singular property of giving a beautiful colour to the hair or wool of such animals as bathed in them; hence the three goddesses, Minerva, Juno, and Venus, bathed there before they appeared before Paris to obtain the golden apple: the name Xanthus, “yellow,” was given to the Scamander, from the peculiar colour of its waters, still applicable to the Mendere, the yellow colour of whose waters attracts the attention of travellers.

It should be “his _chest_ like Neptune.” The torso of Neptune, in the “Elgin Marbles,” No. 103, (vol. ii. p. 26,) is remarkable for its breadth and massiveness of development.
cards.whyThisWorks: The excerpt explicitly names Minerva, Juno, and Venus bathing in the Scamander before the Judgment of Paris, illustrating how divine intervention—gods acting in the human world—drives the epic's central conflict.
cards.skillStrategy: When identifying divine intervention, ask: what specific action do the gods take, and how does that action directly cause or shape a major event in the human story?
evidencePoints: the three goddesses, Minerva, Juno, and Venus, bathed there before they appeared before Paris to obtain the golden apple
this river, according to Homer, was called Xanthus by the gods, Scamander by men
cards.question: According to the excerpt, Minerva, Juno, and Venus bathed in the Scamander 'before they appeared before Paris to obtain the golden apple.' How does this act of divine preparation function as an example of divine intervention in the epic?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The goddesses bathe in the Scamander because its waters give 'a beautiful colour to the hair or wool,' and this physical transformation is the prize Paris awards rather than the golden apple itself.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The goddesses use the Scamander's color-giving waters to prepare themselves before competing for the golden apple before Paris, making their direct appearance in the human world the divine act that sets the epic's central rivalry in motion.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The goddesses bathe in the Scamander to honor the river god Xanthus, whose dual name—'Xanthus by the gods, Scamander by men'—signals that only a god-blessed mortal like Paris may judge between them.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The goddesses visit the Scamander because it flows between the Scamander and Simois rivers where 'Homer's Troy is supposed to have stood,' and their bathing there consecrates the site before the war begins.

cards.standardTitle: Key literary elements add layers of meaning
cards.excerpt: The hero said. His friend obey’d with haste, Through intermingled ships and tents he pass’d; The chiefs descending from their car he found: The panting steeds Eurymedon unbound. The warriors standing on the breezy shore, To dry their sweat, and wash away the gore, Here paused a moment, while the gentle gale Convey’d that freshness the cool seas exhale; Then to consult on farther methods went, And took their seats beneath the shady tent. The draught prescribed, fair Hecamede prepares, Arsinous’ daughter, graced with golden hairs: (Whom to his aged arms, a royal slave, Greece, as the prize of Nestor’s wisdom gave:) A table first with azure feet she placed; Whose ample orb a brazen charger graced; Honey new-press’d, the sacred flour of wheat, And wholesome garlic, crown’d the savoury treat, Next her white hand an antique goblet brings, A goblet sacred to the Pylian kings From eldest times: emboss’d with studs of gold, Two feet support it, and four handles hold; On each bright handle, bending o’er the brink, In sculptured gold, two turtles seem to drink: A massy weight, yet heaved with ease by him, When the brisk nectar overlook’d the brim. Temper’d in this, the nymph of form divine Pours a large portion of the Pramnian wine; With goat’s-milk cheese a flavourous taste bestows, And last with flour the smiling surface strows: This for the wounded prince the dame prepares: The cordial beverage reverend Nestor shares: Salubrious draughts the warriors’ thirst allay, And pleasing conference beguiles the day.
cards.whyThisWorks: Hecamede's precise, layered service—selecting the ancient sacred goblet, mixing Pramnian wine with cheese and flour, and preparing the drink specifically for the wounded prince—characterizes her as an embodiment of civilized order and care that persists even amid the chaos of war, adding meaning to the theme of hospitality.
cards.skillStrategy: When analyzing characterization, look at what a character does step by step and ask what those specific actions reveal about who they are and what they represent in the larger story.
evidencePoints: A goblet sacred to the Pylian kings / From eldest times: emboss'd with studs of gold
This for the wounded prince the dame prepares: The cordial beverage reverend Nestor shares
cards.question: In the excerpt, Hecamede selects 'A goblet sacred to the Pylian kings / From eldest times,' layers in Pramnian wine, goat's-milk cheese, and flour, and prepares the drink specifically 'for the wounded prince.' What does this step-by-step characterization of Hecamede reveal about her role in the passage?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Her careful handling of the ancient goblet and precise mixing of ingredients shows she resents her status as a war prize and uses the ritual to assert her own identity.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Her deliberate, skilled preparation—choosing the sacred goblet, blending the wine with cheese and flour, and serving the wounded prince—presents her as a figure of order and healing care that endures even on the battlefield.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Her exclusive control over the sacred goblet and the drink's ingredients suggests she holds greater authority than Nestor, who merely shares what she has prepared.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Her focus on the goblet's gold studs, two feet, and four handles suggests the warriors value the cup's ancient craftsmanship more than the healing properties of the drink she mixes.

cards.standardTitle: Epic poetry: characters, structures, and themes
cards.excerpt:
So looks the lion o’er a mangled boar, All grim with rage, and horrible with gore; High on the chariot at one bound he sprung, And o’er his seat the bloody trophies hung.

And now Minerva from the realms of air Descends impetuous, and renews the war; For, pleased at length the Grecian arms to aid, The lord of thunders sent the blue-eyed maid. As when high Jove denouncing future woe, O’er the dark clouds extends his purple bow, (In sign of tempests from the troubled air, Or from the rage of man, destructive war,) The drooping cattle dread the impending skies, And from his half-till’d field the labourer flies: In such a form the goddess round her drew A livid cloud, and to the battle flew. Assuming Phœnix’ shape on earth she falls, And in his well-known voice to Sparta calls: “And lies Achilles’ friend, beloved by all, A prey to dogs beneath the Trojan wall? What shame 'o Greece for future times to tell, To thee the greatest in whose cause he fell!” “O chief, O father! (Atreus’ son replies) O full of days! by long experience wise! What more desires my soul, than here unmoved To guard the body of the man I loved? Ah, would Minerva send me strength to rear This wearied arm, and ward the storm of war! But Hector, like the rage of fire, we dread, And Jove’s own glories blaze around his head!”

Pleased to be first of all the powers address’d, She breathes new vigour in her hero’s breast, And fills with keen revenge, with fell despite, Desire of blood, and rage, and lust of fight. So burns the vengeful hornet (soul all o’er), Repulsed in vain, and thirsty still of gore; (Bold son of air and heat) on angry wings Untamed, untired, he turns, attacks, and stings. Fired with like ardour fierce Atrides flew, And sent his soul with every lance he threw.
cards.whyThisWorks: Minerva's two-step intervention—disguising herself as Phoenix to shame Atrides and then secretly infusing him with 'keen revenge' and 'rage'—provides a clear, textually rich example of divine intervention shaping both character motivation and epic action.
cards.skillStrategy: When analyzing divine intervention in epic poetry, trace exactly what the god does in disguise or secret, what the mortal believes is happening, and how the god's action directly causes the mortal's next move.
evidencePoints: Assuming Phœnix' shape on earth she falls, And in his well-known voice to Sparta calls
She breathes new vigour in her hero's breast, And fills with keen revenge, with fell despite, Desire of blood, and rage, and lust of fight
cards.question: In the second paragraph, Minerva 'assum[es] Phœnix' shape' to shame Atrides, and in the third paragraph 'breathes new vigour in her hero's breast.' What do these two actions together reveal about how divine intervention functions in this passage?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Minerva reveals herself openly as a goddess, first rebuking Atrides for cowardice and then granting him a divine weapon, so that his courage comes from obedience to the gods rather than personal fury.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Minerva works through deception and hidden influence: she borrows Phoenix's voice to provoke Atrides' shame, then secretly fills him with rage and desire for blood, making his fierce assault the direct product of her unseen manipulation.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Minerva descends to inform Atrides that Jove has withdrawn his 'glories' from Hector's head, so Atrides fights boldly because he now knows the gods have already decided the battle in Greece's favor.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Minerva answers Atrides' spoken prayer for strength by lifting his 'wearied arm' and removing Hector's divine protection, allowing Atrides to wound Hector through his own restored physical power.

cards.standardTitle: Key literary elements add layers of meaning
cards.excerpt: This said, he seized (while yet the carcase heaved) The bloody armour, which his train received: Then sudden mix’d among the warring crew, And the bold son of Pylæmenes slew. Harpalion had through Asia travell’d far, Following his martial father to the war: Through filial love he left his native shore, Never, ah, never to behold it more! His unsuccessful spear he chanced to fling Against the target of the Spartan king; Thus of his lance disarm’d, from death he flies, And turns around his apprehensive eyes. Him, through the hip transpiercing as he fled, The shaft of Merion mingled with the dead. Beneath the bone the glancing point descends, And, driving down, the swelling bladder rends: Sunk in his sad companions’ arms he lay, And in short pantings sobb’d his soul away; (Like some vile worm extended on the ground;) While life’s red torrent gush’d from out the wound.
cards.whyThisWorks: Harpalion's characterization through his filial motivation, failed spear throw, fearful flight, and ignoble death creates a layered portrait of a young soldier whose love for his father leads only to a shameful, worm-like end, revealing the epic's brutal irony about war's promises.
cards.skillStrategy: When analyzing characterization, trace what a character does, why he does it, and how the narrator describes the outcome — the gap between intention and result often reveals the author's deeper meaning.
evidencePoints: Through filial love he left his native shore, Never, ah, never to behold it more!
Like some vile worm extended on the ground
cards.question: The narrator reveals that Harpalion followed his father to war 'through filial love' and then describes his death as resembling 'some vile worm extended on the ground.' What meaning does this contrast in characterization convey?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Harpalion's devotion to his father marks him as one of the war's most heroic figures, and his death is presented as a noble sacrifice worthy of an epic warrior.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The noble motive of filial love that brought Harpalion to war is rendered meaningless by his degrading death, suggesting that war destroys even the most honorable intentions.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Harpalion's failed spear throw against the Spartan king reveals his cowardice, and the narrator uses his death to warn soldiers against challenging more powerful opponents.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The description of Harpalion's wound and death is meant to honor Merion's skill as an archer rather than to say anything meaningful about Harpalion's character or fate.

cards.standardTitle: Theme development across a literary text
cards.excerpt:
From forth his open’d stores, this said, he drew Twelve costly carpets of refulgent hue, As many vests, as many mantles told, And twelve fair veils, and garments stiff with gold, Two tripods next, and twice two chargers shine, With ten pure talents from the richest mine; And last a large well-labour’d bowl had place, (The pledge of treaties once with friendly Thrace:) Seem’d all too mean the stores he could employ, For one last look to buy him back to Troy!

Lo! the sad father, frantic with his pain, Around him furious drives his menial train: In vain each slave with duteous care attends, Each office hurts him, and each face offends. “What make ye here, officious crowds! (he cries): Hence! nor obtrude your anguish on my eyes. Have ye no griefs at home, to fix ye there: Am I the only object of despair? Am I become my people’s common show, Set up by Jove your spectacle of woe? No, you must feel him too; yourselves must fall; The same stern god to ruin gives you all: Nor is great Hector lost by me alone; Your sole defence, your guardian power is gone! I see your blood the fields of Phrygia drown, I see the ruins of your smoking town! O send me, gods! ere that sad day shall come, A willing ghost to Pluto’s dreary dome!”

He said, and feebly drives his friends away: The sorrowing friends his frantic rage obey. Next on his sons his erring fury falls, Polites, Paris, Agathon, he calls; His threats Deiphobus and Dius hear, Hippothous, Pammon, Helenes the seer, And generous Antiphon: for yet these nine Survived, sad relics of his numerous line.
cards.whyThisWorks: The excerpt shows Priam's grief escalating from hoarding treasures for ransom, to lashing out at loyal servants, to finally turning his 'erring fury' on his own surviving sons—a clear progression that lets students distinguish details that develop the theme of grief corrupting love from details that merely establish the topic of loss.
cards.skillStrategy: Ask yourself: does this detail show grief actively changing how Priam treats the people he loves, or does it just tell me he is sad or that Troy is doomed?
evidencePoints: each office hurts him, and each face offends
Next on his sons his erring fury falls
cards.question: The narrator states that after driving away his servants, Priam's 'erring fury falls' on his surviving sons. Which detail from the excerpt most directly develops the theme that grief can turn a parent's love into a destructive force?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Priam draws twelve costly carpets, ten talents of gold, and a bowl once pledged in a treaty with Thrace, offering everything he owns for one last look at Hector.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Priam lashes out at the servants whose 'duteous care' he cannot bear, then turns that same uncontrolled rage on Polites, Paris, Agathon, and the six other sons still alive to him.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Priam names nine sons who survived the war, calling them 'sad relics of his numerous line,' showing how many children the war has already taken from him.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Priam declares that Hector was Troy's 'sole defence' and 'guardian power,' and that without him the city's fields will drown in blood and its towers will burn.

cards.standardTitle: Epic poetry: characters, structures, and themes
cards.excerpt:
The generous Greeks recede with tardy pace, Though Mars and Hector thunder in their face; None turn their backs to mean ignoble flight, Slow they retreat, and even retreating fight. Who first, who last, by Mars’ and Hector’s hand, Stretch’d in their blood, lay gasping on the sand? Tenthras the great, Orestes the renown’d For managed steeds, and Trechus press’d the ground; Next Œnomaus and OEnops’ offspring died; Oresbius last fell groaning at their side: Oresbius, in his painted mitre gay, In fat Bœotia held his wealthy sway, Where lakes surround low Hylè’s watery plain; A prince and people studious of their gain.

The carnage Juno from the skies survey’d, And touch’d with grief bespoke the blue-eyed maid: “Oh, sight accursed! Shall faithless Troy prevail, And shall our promise to our people fail? How vain the word to Menelaus given By Jove’s great daughter and the queen of heaven, Beneath his arms that Priam’s towers should fall, If warring gods for ever guard the wall! Mars, red with slaughter, aids our hated foes: Haste, let us arm, and force with force oppose!”

She spoke; Minerva burns to meet the war: And now heaven’s empress calls her blazing car. At her command rush forth the steeds divine; Rich with immortal gold their trappings shine. Bright Hebe waits; by Hebe, ever young, The whirling wheels are to the chariot hung. On the bright axle turns the bidden wheel Of sounding brass; the polished axle steel. Eight brazen spokes in radiant order flame; The circles gold, of uncorrupted frame, Such as the heavens produce: and round the gold Two brazen rings of work divine were roll’d. The bossy naves of sold silver shone; Braces of gold suspend the moving throne: The car, behind, an arching figure bore; The bending concave form’d an arch before. Silver the beam, the extended yoke was gold, And golden reins the immortal coursers hold. Herself, impatient, to the ready car, The coursers joins, and breathes revenge and war.
cards.whyThisWorks: Juno's speech in paragraph two explicitly names Mars as the divine force aiding Troy, voices her grievance that a promise from heaven is being broken, and directly triggers Minerva's preparation for war in paragraph three, making the mechanism of divine intervention traceable word by word.
cards.skillStrategy: When tracking divine intervention, find the exact moment a god speaks or acts, identify what problem they name, and trace what changes in the story because of that speech or action.
evidencePoints: Mars, red with slaughter, aids our hated foes: Haste, let us arm, and force with force oppose!
She spoke; Minerva burns to meet the war: And now heaven's empress calls her blazing car.
cards.question: In the second paragraph, Juno declares, 'Mars, red with slaughter, aids our hated foes: Haste, let us arm, and force with force oppose!' What effect does this declaration have on the action that follows in the third paragraph?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Juno's words cause Mars to abandon the Trojan side and join the Greeks on the battlefield.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Juno's declaration that Mars is aiding Troy and her call to oppose him with force moves Minerva to prepare for war, as shown when 'Minerva burns to meet the war' and heaven's empress summons her divine chariot.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Juno's accusation that the promise to Menelaus has been broken convinces Minerva to seek a truce rather than enter the fighting.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Juno's speech reminds Minerva of the prophecy that Priam's towers will fall, so Minerva chooses to wait and let the prophecy fulfill itself without divine interference.

cards.standardTitle: Key literary elements add layers of meaning
cards.excerpt: He said; and backward to the lines retired; Forth rush’d the youth with martial fury fired, Beyond the foremost ranks; his lance he threw, And round the black battalions cast his view. The troops of Troy recede with sudden fear, While the swift javelin hiss’d along in air. Advancing Melanippus met the dart With his bold breast, and felt it in his heart: Thundering he falls; his falling arms resound, And his broad buckler rings against the ground. The victor leaps upon his prostrate prize: Thus on a roe the well-breath’d beagle flies, And rends his side, fresh-bleeding with the dart The distant hunter sent into his heart. Observing Hector to the rescue flew; Bold as he was, Antilochus withdrew. So when a savage, ranging o’er the plain, Has torn the shepherd’s dog, or shepherd’s swain, While conscious of the deed, he glares around, And hears the gathering multitude resound, Timely he flies the yet-untasted food, And gains the friendly shelter of the wood: So fears the youth; all Troy with shouts pursue, While stones and darts in mingled tempest flew; But enter’d in the Grecian ranks, he turns His manly breast, and with new fury burns.
cards.whyThisWorks: Antilochus's retreat followed immediately by his turning to face Troy with 'new fury' creates a contrast that reveals a character who is tactically shrewd rather than recklessly brave, adding meaning to the epic's portrayal of heroic conduct.
cards.skillStrategy: When a character does two opposite things in quick succession, ask what that contrast reveals about who they really are beneath the surface action.
evidencePoints: Bold as he was, Antilochus withdrew.
But enter'd in the Grecian ranks, he turns / His manly breast, and with new fury burns.
cards.question: Read the following lines: 'Bold as he was, Antilochus withdrew… But enter'd in the Grecian ranks, he turns / His manly breast, and with new fury burns.' What does this contrast in Antilochus's behavior reveal about his character?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Antilochus retreats because he is overwhelmed by fear of Hector and never recovers his courage during the battle.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Antilochus combines boldness with strategic judgment, retreating from Hector's superior force only to regroup and fight again, showing that true heroism includes knowing when to withdraw.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Antilochus withdraws out of respect for Hector's rank, choosing to honor the Trojan champion rather than risk dishonoring himself in an unequal fight.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Antilochus flees because the Trojan troops' stones and darts wound him, and his renewed fury at the end is driven purely by physical pain rather than courage.

cards.standardTitle: Epic poetry: characters, structures, and themes
cards.excerpt:
She said. With awe divine, the queen of love Obey’d the sister and the wife of Jove; And from her fragrant breast the zone embraced, With various skill and high embroidery graced. In this was every art, and every charm, To win the wisest, and the coldest warm: Fond love, the gentle vow, the gay desire, The kind deceit, the still-reviving fire, Persuasive speech, and the more persuasive sighs, Silence that spoke, and eloquence of eyes. This on her hand the Cyprian Goddess laid: “Take this, and with it all thy wish;” she said. With smiles she took the charm; and smiling press’d The powerful cestus to her snowy breast.

Then Venus to the courts of Jove withdrew; Whilst from Olympus pleased Saturnia flew. O’er high Pieria thence her course she bore, O’er fair Emathia’s ever-pleasing shore, O’er Hemus’ hills with snows eternal crown’d; Nor once her flying foot approach’d the ground. Then taking wing from Athos’ lofty steep, She speeds to Lemnos o’er the rolling deep, And seeks the cave of Death’s half-brother, Sleep.
cards.whyThisWorks: Aphrodite's transfer of the cestus—described as holding powers of 'fond love,' 'persuasive speech,' and 'the more persuasive sighs'—directly enables Hera's flight toward Sleep, making divine intervention the engine of the plot in both paragraphs.
cards.skillStrategy: When a god gives a supernatural object or power to another character, trace what that character does immediately after to see how the divine gift drives the action forward.
evidencePoints: In this was every art, and every charm, To win the wisest, and the coldest warm
With smiles she took the charm; and smiling press'd / The powerful cestus to her snowy breast. / Then Venus to the courts of Jove withdrew; / Whilst from Olympus pleased Saturnia flew.
cards.question: The narrator describes the cestus as holding 'every art, and every charm, / To win the wisest, and the coldest warm.' How does Aphrodite placing this object in Hera's hands shape the action in the lines that immediately follow?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Hera is so overwhelmed by the cestus's power that she returns to Jove's courts alongside Aphrodite rather than pursuing her own plan.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Armed with the cestus's supernatural power to persuade and enchant, Hera departs Olympus at once and flies toward the cave of Sleep, setting her scheme in motion.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The cestus transfers Aphrodite's divine authority to Hera permanently, which is why the narrator calls her 'pleased Saturnia' as she leaves Olympus.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Hera presses the cestus to her breast as a sign of gratitude, but she waits at Olympus for Aphrodite to return before beginning her journey to Lemnos.

cards.standardTitle: Key literary elements add layers of meaning
cards.excerpt: She said: the cloud-compeller, overcome, Assents to fate, and ratifies the doom. Then touch’d with grief, the weeping heavens distill’d A shower of blood o’er all the fatal field: The god, his eyes averting from the plain, Laments his son, predestined to be slain, Far from the Lycian shores, his happy native reign. Now met in arms, the combatants appear; Each heaved the shield, and poised the lifted spear; From strong Patroclus’ hand the javelin fled, And pass’d the groin of valiant Thrasymed; The nerves unbraced no more his bulk sustain, He falls, and falling bites the bloody plain. Two sounding darts the Lycian leader threw: The first aloof with erring fury flew, The next transpierced Achilles’ mortal steed, The generous Pedasus of Theban breed: Fix’d in the shoulder’s joint, he reel’d around, Roll’d in the bloody dust, and paw’d the slippery ground. His sudden fall the entangled harness broke; Each axle crackled, and the chariot shook: When bold Automedon, to disengage The starting coursers, and restrain their rage, Divides the traces with his sword, and freed The encumbered chariot from the dying steed: The rest move on, obedient to the rein: The car rolls slowly o’er the dusty plain.
cards.whyThisWorks: Automedon's swift, decisive action of cutting the traces with his sword to free the dying horse reveals a character defined by cool-headed competence and loyalty under chaos, adding meaning to the broader theme of duty amid catastrophic loss.
cards.skillStrategy: When a character acts under pressure, ask what that action reveals about who they are and what the author wants readers to understand about them.
evidencePoints: bold Automedon, to disengage / The starting coursers, and restrain their rage, / Divides the traces with his sword
The rest move on, obedient to the rein: / The car rolls slowly o'er the dusty plain.
cards.question: Read the following lines from the excerpt: 'bold Automedon, to disengage / The starting coursers, and restrain their rage, / Divides the traces with his sword, and freed / The encumbered chariot from the dying steed.' What does Automedon's action in these lines reveal about his character?

choices.label: A
choices.text: He acts out of personal grief over the horse Pedasus, cutting the traces as an emotional response to watching the animal suffer in the dust.

choices.label: B
choices.text: He responds to sudden disaster with decisive, practical judgment, showing that his loyalty to the mission overrides the panic consuming the other horses.

choices.label: C
choices.text: He abandons the battle entirely by freeing the horses, revealing that he prioritizes his own survival over the outcome of the fight.

choices.label: D
choices.text: He acts on Zeus's divine command, showing that his courage comes from heavenly intervention rather than his own character.

cards.standardTitle: Theme development across a literary text
cards.excerpt: He spoke, and foremost to the combat flew: The bold example all his hosts pursue. Then, first, Leocritus beneath him bled, In vain beloved by valiant Lycomede; Who view’d his fall, and, grieving at the chance, Swift to revenge it sent his angry lance; The whirling lance, with vigorous force address’d, Descends, and pants in Apisaon’s breast; From rich Paeonia’s vales the warrior came, Next thee, Asteropeus! in place and fame. Asteropeus with grief beheld the slain, And rush’d to combat, but he rush’d in vain: Indissolubly firm, around the dead, Rank within rank, on buckler buckler spread, And hemm’d with bristled spears, the Grecians stood, A brazen bulwark, and an iron wood. Great Ajax eyes them with incessant care, And in an orb contracts the crowded war, Close in their ranks commands to fight or fall, And stands the centre and the soul of all: Fix’d on the spot they war, and wounded, wound; A sanguine torrent steeps the reeking ground: On heaps the Greeks, on heaps the Trojans bled, And, thickening round them, rise the hills of dead.
cards.whyThisWorks: The excerpt's closing parallel construction 'On heaps the Greeks, on heaps the Trojans bled' places both armies in identical grammatical and physical positions, providing direct textual evidence that war's destruction falls equally on all combatants—a central theme of The Iliad.
cards.skillStrategy: When identifying evidence for theme, look for repeated grammatical structures or mirrored images that place two groups in the same situation, then ask what idea that symmetry supports.
evidencePoints: On heaps the Greeks, on heaps the Trojans bled
thickening round them, rise the hills of dead
cards.question: The excerpt ends with 'On heaps the Greeks, on heaps the Trojans bled, / And, thickening round them, rise the hills of dead.' How does the parallel phrasing 'on heaps the Greeks, on heaps the Trojans' develop the theme that war brings equal destruction to both sides?

choices.label: A
choices.text: It contrasts the Greeks' disciplined 'brazen bulwark' formation with the Trojans' disorganized charge, showing that superior strategy reduces Greek losses.

choices.label: B
choices.text: It places both armies in identical grammatical and physical positions—heaped together beneath the same 'hills of dead'—making mounting loss the shared outcome for each side.

choices.label: C
choices.text: It highlights the Greeks' greater suffering because Ajax's role as 'the centre and the soul of all' draws the heaviest Trojan attacks onto the Greek ranks.

choices.label: D
choices.text: It emphasizes the Trojans' heavier burden by echoing Asteropeus, who 'rush'd in vain,' suggesting Trojan losses far outnumber Greek casualties by the passage's end.

cards.standardTitle: Epic poetry: characters, structures, and themes
cards.excerpt:
The gods deliberate in council concerning the Trojan war: they agree upon the continuation of it, and Jupiter sends down Minerva to break the truce. She persuades Pandarus to aim an arrow at Menelaus, who is wounded, but cured by Machaon. In the meantime some of the Trojan troops attack the Greeks. Agamemnon is distinguished in all the parts of a good general; he reviews the troops, and exhorts the leaders, some by praises and others by reproof. Nestor is particularly celebrated for his military discipline. The battle joins, and great numbers are slain on both sides. The same day continues through this as through the last book (as it does also through the two following, and almost to the end of the seventh book). The scene is wholly in the field before Troy.

And now Olympus’ shining gates unfold; The gods, with Jove, assume their thrones of gold: Immortal Hebe, fresh with bloom divine, The golden goblet crowns with purple wine: While the full bowls flow round, the powers employ Their careful eyes on long-contended Troy.
cards.whyThisWorks: The excerpt explicitly shows Jupiter ordering Minerva to break the truce, which causes Pandarus to wound Menelaus, demonstrating how divine will directly initiates and shapes mortal conflict in epic poetry.
cards.skillStrategy: When analyzing divine intervention, trace the chain from a god's decision to its effect on mortal characters, and ask: whose will is truly driving the action?
evidencePoints: Jupiter sends down Minerva to break the truce. She persuades Pandarus to aim an arrow at Menelaus
the powers employ / Their careful eyes on long-contended Troy
cards.question: The excerpt states that 'Jupiter sends down Minerva to break the truce' and that she 'persuades Pandarus to aim an arrow at Menelaus.' How does this chain of events—from Jupiter's council decision to Pandarus's shot—illustrate the role of divine intervention in the conflict?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The gods 'employ their careful eyes on long-contended Troy' but remain neutral, allowing Pandarus to wound Menelaus based on his own choice rather than any god's command.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Jupiter's council decision to break the truce sets the chain in motion: Minerva manipulates Pandarus into wounding Menelaus, making a god's will the true origin of the renewed fighting.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Minerva defies Jupiter's intention to continue the war by persuading Pandarus to wound Menelaus, hoping Machaon's cure will restore the truce and end the conflict.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Pandarus wounds Menelaus on his own initiative, and Jupiter sends Minerva only afterward to ensure Machaon can cure the wound and preserve the truce the gods agreed upon.

cards.standardTitle: Key literary elements add layers of meaning
cards.excerpt: Silent he heard the queen of woods upbraid: Not so Saturnia bore the vaunting maid: But furious thus: “What insolence has driven Thy pride to face the majesty of heaven? What though by Jove the female plague design’d, Fierce to the feeble race of womankind, The wretched matron feels thy piercing dart; Thy sex’s tyrant, with a tiger’s heart? What though tremendous in the woodland chase Thy certain arrows pierce the savage race? How dares thy rashness on the powers divine Employ those arms, or match thy force with mine? Learn hence, no more unequal war to wage—” She said, and seized her wrists with eager rage; These in her left hand lock’d, her right untied The bow, the quiver, and its plumy pride. About her temples flies the busy bow; Now here, now there, she winds her from the blow; The scattering arrows, rattling from the case, Drop round, and idly mark the dusty place. Swift from the field the baffled huntress flies, And scarce restrains the torrent in her eyes: So, when the falcon wings her way above, To the cleft cavern speeds the gentle dove; (Not fated yet to die;) there safe retreats, Yet still her heart against the marble beats.
cards.whyThisWorks: Saturnia's furious speech, physical domination of Artemis, and the simile of the fleeing dove together reveal a sharp contrast in power and character that layers meaning onto both figures.
cards.skillStrategy: When a character speaks or acts aggressively while another retreats, ask what that contrast reveals about each character's power, identity, or inner state.
evidencePoints: She said, and seized her wrists with eager rage; These in her left hand lock'd, her right untied / The bow, the quiver, and its plumy pride.
Swift from the field the baffled huntress flies, / And scarce restrains the torrent in her eyes
cards.question: Read the following lines: 'She said, and seized her wrists with eager rage; These in her left hand lock'd, her right untied / The bow, the quiver, and its plumy pride.' Then: 'Swift from the field the baffled huntress flies, / And scarce restrains the torrent in her eyes.' What do Saturnia's actions and Artemis's response together reveal about these two characters?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Saturnia regrets humiliating Artemis and acts out of wounded pride rather than genuine superiority, suggesting the two goddesses are more evenly matched than they appear.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Saturnia's physical seizure of Artemis's weapons strips the huntress of her defining identity, and Artemis's near-tears flight exposes her as powerful only within her own domain but helpless before a greater divine authority.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Artemis chooses to retreat strategically rather than fight, showing she is wiser than Saturnia, whose rage blinds her to the consequences of attacking a fellow goddess.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The removal of Artemis's bow and quiver signals that she has willingly surrendered her role as huntress, accepting Saturnia's authority over all divine females.

cards.standardTitle: Theme development across a literary text
cards.excerpt: This counsel pleased: the godlike Hector sprung Swift from his seat; his clanging armour rung. The chief’s example follow’d by his train, Each quits his car, and issues on the plain, By orders strict the charioteers enjoin’d Compel the coursers to their ranks behind. The forces part in five distinguish’d bands, And all obey their several chiefs’ commands. The best and bravest in the first conspire, Pant for the fight, and threat the fleet with fire: Great Hector glorious in the van of these, Polydamas, and brave Cebriones. Before the next the graceful Paris shines, And bold Alcathous, and Agenor joins. The sons of Priam with the third appear, Deiphobus, and Helenas the seer; In arms with these the mighty Asius stood, Who drew from Hyrtacus his noble blood, And whom Arisba’s yellow coursers bore, The coursers fed on Sellè’s winding shore. Antenor’s sons the fourth battalion guide, And great Æneas, born on fountful Ide. Divine Sarpedon the last band obey’d, Whom Glaucus and Asteropaeus aid. Next him, the bravest, at their army’s head, But he more brave than all the hosts he led.
cards.whyThisWorks: The narrator's closing declaration—'But he more brave than all the hosts he led'—singles out Sarpedon above every named warrior, giving students a precise textual moment to test whether a detail develops the theme of personal valor surpassing rank or merely adds true but thematic-topic-only information about military organization.
cards.skillStrategy: Ask yourself: does this detail show the theme in action, or does it just describe something true about the topic of battle?
evidencePoints: Divine Sarpedon the last band obey'd
But he more brave than all the hosts he led
cards.question: The narrator ends the passage by saying Sarpedon was 'more brave than all the hosts he led.' Which detail from the excerpt most directly develops the theme that a warrior's true worth comes from personal courage rather than rank or lineage?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Asius 'drew from Hyrtacus his noble blood' and was carried by 'Arisba's yellow coursers,' establishing his distinguished ancestry and regional origin.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Sarpedon commands the last of the five battalions, yet the narrator declares him 'more brave than all the hosts he led,' placing his personal valor above his position in the battle order.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The five forces are divided into 'distinguish'd bands' and each group obeys its own chief's commands, showing the army's carefully organized military structure.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Hector's 'clanging armour rung' as he sprang from his seat, and his chiefs followed his example by quitting their chariots to stand on the plain.

cards.standardTitle: Epic poetry: characters, structures, and themes
cards.excerpt:
Then died Hypsenor, generous and divine, Sprung from the brave Dolopion’s mighty line, Who near adored Scamander made abode, Priest of the stream, and honoured as a god. On him, amidst the flying numbers found, Eurypylus inflicts a deadly wound; On his broad shoulders fell the forceful brand, Thence glancing downwards, lopp’d his holy hand, Which stain’d with sacred blood the blushing sand. Down sunk the priest: the purple hand of death Closed his dim eye, and fate suppress’d his breath.

Thus toil’d the chiefs, in different parts engaged. In every quarter fierce Tydides raged; Amid the Greek, amid the Trojan train, Rapt through the ranks he thunders o’er the plain; Now here, now there, he darts from place to place, Pours on the rear, or lightens in their face. Thus from high hills the torrents swift and strong Deluge whole fields, and sweep the trees along, Through ruin’d moles the rushing wave resounds, O’erwhelm’s the bridge, and bursts the lofty bounds; The yellow harvests of the ripen’d year, And flatted vineyards, one sad waste appear! While Jove descends in sluicy sheets of rain, And all the labours of mankind are vain.
cards.whyThisWorks: The closing lines explicitly name Jove (Jupiter/Zeus) descending in rain to render 'all the labours of mankind vain,' directly modeling how divine intervention shapes the action and reinforces the epic theme of mortal helplessness before the gods.
cards.skillStrategy: When identifying divine intervention, locate the god's action and trace how it changes or overwhelms what mortals are doing in the same moment.
evidencePoints: While Jove descends in sluicy sheets of rain, And all the labours of mankind are vain.
Thus from high hills the torrents swift and strong Deluge whole fields, and sweep the trees along
cards.question: In the second paragraph, the simile comparing Tydides to a torrent ends with 'Jove descends in sluicy sheets of rain, / And all the labours of mankind are vain.' How does this reference to Jove shape the meaning of Tydides' rampage on the battlefield?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Jove's rain physically stops Tydides from fighting, forcing the Greeks and Trojans to retreat from the flooded plain.

choices.label: B
choices.text: By crediting Jove as the ultimate source of the flood-like destruction, the simile suggests that even Tydides' overwhelming power is an extension of divine will, making mortal effort secondary to the gods' control.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The mention of Jove signals that Tydides has received a prophecy granting him invincibility, which explains why no Trojan warrior can wound him during the battle.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Jove's descent in rain is meant to honor the slain priest Hypsenor, whose sacred blood stained the sand and provoked the god's mourning.

cards.standardTitle: Key literary elements add layers of meaning
cards.excerpt:
Soon as the Greeks the chief’s retreat beheld, With double fury each invades the field. Oilean Ajax first his javelin sped, Pierced by whose point the son of Enops bled; (Satnius the brave, whom beauteous Neis bore Amidst her flocks on Satnio’s silver shore;) Struck through the belly’s rim, the warrior lies Supine, and shades eternal veil his eyes. An arduous battle rose around the dead; By turns the Greeks, by turns the Trojans bled.

Fired with revenge, Polydamas drew near, And at Prothoënor shook the trembling spear; The driving javelin through his shoulder thrust, He sinks to earth, and grasps the bloody dust. “Lo thus (the victor cries) we rule the field, And thus their arms the race of Panthus wield: From this unerring hand there flies no dart But bathes its point within a Grecian heart.
