Propp’d on that spear to which thou owest thy fall, Go, guide thy darksome steps to Pluto’s dreary hall.”

He said, and sorrow touch’d each Argive breast: The soul of Ajax burn’d above the rest. As by his side the groaning warrior fell, At the fierce foe he launch’d his piercing steel; The foe, reclining, shunn’d the flying death; But fate, Archilochus, demands thy breath: Thy lofty birth no succour could impart, The wings of death o’ertook thee on the dart; Swift to perform heaven’s fatal will, it fled Full on the juncture of the neck and head, And took the joint, and cut the nerves in twain: The dropping head first tumbled on the plain. So just the stroke, that yet the body stood Erect, then roll’d along the sands in blood.
cards.whyThisWorks: Polydamas's taunting speech over the fallen Prothoënor reveals his arrogance and pride, while Ajax's immediate, grief-driven counterattack contrasts sharply, showing how characterization through speech and action deepens the meaning of battlefield honor and vengeance.
cards.skillStrategy: When a character speaks or acts in a charged moment, ask what that behavior reveals about who they are and what the author wants you to understand about them.
evidencePoints: Lo thus (the victor cries) we rule the field, / And thus their arms the race of Panthus wield: / From this unerring hand there flies no dart / But bathes its point within a Grecian heart.
The soul of Ajax burn'd above the rest. / As by his side the groaning warrior fell, / At the fierce foe he launch'd his piercing steel
cards.question: Read the following lines from the passage: "Lo thus (the victor cries) we rule the field, / And thus their arms the race of Panthus wield: / From this unerring hand there flies no dart / But bathes its point within a Grecian heart." What do Polydamas's words reveal about his character, and how does Ajax's immediate response deepen that meaning?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Polydamas's boast shows his loyalty to Troy, and Ajax's response confirms that the Greeks respect Trojan warriors as worthy opponents.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Polydamas's gloating over a dying enemy exposes his arrogance, and Ajax's rage-fueled counterattack shows that such pride on the battlefield provokes fierce, personal vengeance rather than cold strategy.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Polydamas's speech demonstrates his military skill, and Ajax's reaction shows that the Greeks are overwhelmed and unable to match Trojan strength.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Polydamas's words reveal his grief over fallen comrades, and Ajax's response suggests that both sides share a mutual sorrow that drives the fighting.

cards.standardTitle: Theme development across a literary text
cards.excerpt: Tydides thus. The goddess, seized with dread, Confused, distracted, from the conflict fled. To aid her, swift the winged Iris flew, Wrapt in a mist above the warring crew. The queen of love with faded charms she found. Pale was her cheek, and livid look’d the wound. To Mars, who sat remote, they bent their way: Far, on the left, with clouds involved he lay; Beside him stood his lance, distain’d with gore, And, rein’d with gold, his foaming steeds before. Low at his knee, she begg’d with streaming eyes Her brother’s car, to mount the distant skies, And show’d the wound by fierce Tydides given, A mortal man, who dares encounter heaven. Stern Mars attentive hears the queen complain, And to her hand commits the golden rein; She mounts the seat, oppress’d with silent woe, Driven by the goddess of the painted bow. The lash resounds, the rapid chariot flies, And in a moment scales the lofty skies: They stopp’d the car, and there the coursers stood, Fed by fair Iris with ambrosial food; Before her mother, love’s bright queen appears, O’erwhelmed with anguish, and dissolved in tears: She raised her in her arms, beheld her bleed, And ask’d what god had wrought this guilty deed?
cards.whyThisWorks: The excerpt shows a wounded goddess fleeing battle, begging for help, and weeping before her mother—details that either develop the theme of divine vulnerability or merely establish setting/power, letting students distinguish theme-building evidence from true-but-topic-only details.
cards.skillStrategy: Ask yourself: does this detail show the theme happening, or does it just describe the world of the story without pushing the theme forward?
evidencePoints: Pale was her cheek, and livid look'd the wound
Low at his knee, she begg'd with streaming eyes
cards.question: A student claims the passage develops the theme that even immortal beings are made helpless when a mortal dares to challenge the gods. Which detail from the excerpt most directly supports that claim?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Iris wraps herself in a mist above the warring crew while flying to Aphrodite's aid, showing that the gods move unseen among mortals.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Aphrodite's cheek is pale and her wound livid, and she must kneel before Mars with streaming eyes to beg for his chariot—reduced by a mortal's blow to a wounded supplicant who cannot escape without another god's help.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Mars sits remote from the battle with his gore-stained lance beside him and his foaming steeds reined in gold, establishing him as a formidable war god.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The chariot scales the lofty skies in a moment and the horses are fed ambrosial food by Iris, confirming that the gods possess resources and speed beyond human reach.

cards.standardTitle: Epic poetry: characters, structures, and themes
cards.excerpt:
Apollo thus from Ilion’s lofty towers, Array’d in terrors, roused the Trojan powers: While war’s fierce goddess fires the Grecian foe, And shouts and thunders in the fields below. Then great Diores fell, by doom divine, In vain his valour and illustrious line. A broken rock the force of Pyrus threw, (Who from cold Ænus led the Thracian crew,) Full on his ankle dropp’d the ponderous stone, Burst the strong nerves, and crash’d the solid bone. Supine he tumbles on the crimson sands, Before his helpless friends, and native bands, And spreads for aid his unavailing hands. The foe rush’d furious as he pants for breath, And through his navel drove the pointed death: His gushing entrails smoked upon the ground, And the warm life came issuing from the wound.

His lance bold Thoas at the conqueror sent, Deep in his breast above the pap it went, Amid the lungs was fix’d the winged wood, And quivering in his heaving bosom stood: Till from the dying chief, approaching near, The Ætolian warrior tugg’d his weighty spear: Then sudden waved his flaming falchion round, And gash’d his belly with a ghastly wound; The corpse now breathless on the bloody plain, To spoil his arms the victor strove in vain; The Thracian bands against the victor press’d, A grove of lances glitter’d at his breast. Stern Thoas, glaring with revengeful eyes, In sullen fury slowly quits the prize.
cards.whyThisWorks: The excerpt explicitly names Apollo and 'war's fierce goddess' as forces that rouse armies before battle, and then labels Diores's death 'by doom divine,' giving students a direct textual link between divine intervention and a warrior's fate.
cards.skillStrategy: When you see a god named or a phrase like 'doom divine,' ask yourself: what action or outcome does that supernatural force directly cause or explain in the passage?
evidencePoints: Apollo thus from Ilion's lofty towers, Array'd in terrors, roused the Trojan powers
Then great Diores fell, by doom divine, / In vain his valour and illustrious line.
cards.question: The narrator states that Diores fell 'by doom divine' immediately after describing his 'valour and illustrious line.' What does placing these details side by side reveal about the role of divine intervention in the passage?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Diores's noble lineage earned him a death that the gods considered honorable, so divine fate rewarded rather than punished him.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Supernatural fate overrides even a warrior's personal courage and high birth, making divine will the true force controlling who lives and dies.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Apollo directly guided Pyrus's throw so that the gods could punish Diores for abandoning the Trojan side before the battle.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The phrase signals that Diores's death was accidental rather than meaningful, since no warrior's skill could have changed the random outcome.

cards.standardTitle: Key literary elements add layers of meaning
cards.excerpt:
He said: and Merion to th’ appointed place, Fierce as the god of battles, urged his pace. Soon as the foe the shining chiefs beheld Rush like a fiery torrent o’er the field, Their force embodied in a tide they pour; The rising combat sounds along the shore. As warring winds, in Sirius’ sultry reign, From different quarters sweep the sandy plain; On every side the dusty whirlwinds rise, And the dry fields are lifted to the skies: Thus by despair, hope, rage, together driven, Met the black hosts, and, meeting, darken’d heaven. All dreadful glared the iron face of war, Bristled with upright spears, that flash’d afar; Dire was the gleam of breastplates, helms, and shields, And polish’d arms emblazed the flaming fields: Tremendous scene! that general horror gave, But touch’d with joy the bosoms of the brave.

Saturn’s great sons in fierce contention vied, And crowds of heroes in their anger died. The sire of earth and heaven, by Thetis won To crown with glory Peleus’ godlike son, Will’d not destruction to the Grecian powers, But spared awhile the destined Trojan towers; While Neptune, rising from his azure main, Warr’d on the king of heaven with stern disdain, And breathed revenge, and fired the Grecian train. Gods of one source, of one ethereal race, Alike divine, and heaven their native place; But Jove the greater; first-born of the skies, And more than men, or gods, supremely wise. For this, of Jove’s superior might afraid, Neptune in human form conceal’d his aid. These powers enfold the Greek and Trojan train In war and discord’s adamantine chain, Indissolubly strong: the fatal tie Is stretch’d on both, and close compell’d they die.
cards.whyThisWorks: Neptune's choice to conceal his divine identity while still intervening in battle reveals how even gods are shaped by fear and political hierarchy, adding meaning to the theme that power operates through deception as much as force.
cards.skillStrategy: When a character makes a deliberate choice—especially one that hides who they really are—ask what that choice reveals about their values, fears, or the world they live in.
evidencePoints: For this, of Jove's superior might afraid, Neptune in human form conceal'd his aid.
Gods of one source, of one ethereal race, Alike divine, and heaven their native place; But Jove the greater
cards.question: According to the second paragraph, Neptune chooses to disguise himself as a human while aiding the Greeks. What does this action reveal about Neptune's character and the world of the poem?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Neptune's disguise shows that he is indifferent to the outcome of the war and acts only out of obligation to the other gods rather than genuine anger toward Jove.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Neptune's disguise reveals that even a god of immense power is constrained by fear of a greater authority, suggesting that hierarchy and submission shape behavior even among divine beings.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Neptune's disguise demonstrates that he respects Jove's decision to protect the Trojans and conceals himself so as not to interfere with the fated outcome of the war.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Neptune's disguise proves that the gods are fundamentally deceptive by nature and that their involvement in human battles is always hidden from both sides of the conflict.

cards.standardTitle: Theme development across a literary text
cards.excerpt:
The prince replies: “Ah cease, divinely fair, Nor add reproaches to the wounds I bear; This day the foe prevail’d by Pallas’ power: We yet may vanquish in a happier hour: There want not gods to favour us above; But let the business of our life be love: These softer moments let delights employ, And kind embraces snatch the hasty joy. Not thus I loved thee, when from Sparta’s shore My forced, my willing heavenly prize I bore, When first entranced in Cranae’s isle I lay, Mix’d with thy soul, and all dissolved away!” Thus having spoke, the enamour’d Phrygian boy Rush’d to the bed, impatient for the joy. Him Helen follow’d slow with bashful charms, And clasp’d the blooming hero in her arms.

While these to love’s delicious rapture yield, The stern Atrides rages round the field: So some fell lion whom the woods obey, Roars through the desert, and demands his prey. Paris he seeks, impatient to destroy, But seeks in vain along the troops of Troy; Even those had yielded to a foe so brave The recreant warrior, hateful as the grave. Then speaking thus, the king of kings arose, “Ye Trojans, Dardans, all our generous foes! Hear and attest! from Heaven with conquest crown’d, Our brother’s arms the just success have found: Be therefore now the Spartan wealth restor’d, Let Argive Helen own her lawful lord; The appointed fine let Ilion justly pay, And age to age record this signal day.”

He ceased; his army’s loud applauses rise, And the long shout runs echoing through the skies.
cards.whyThisWorks: The excerpt directly contrasts Paris rushing to bed with Helen while Menelaus rages across the battlefield, providing concrete evidence that personal pleasure leads a warrior to abandon duty—the core of ELA.9.R.1.2 theme development.
cards.skillStrategy: Find the moment in the passage where a character's choice reveals the theme, then match it to the exact words the author uses to show that choice.
evidencePoints: But let the business of our life be love
the stern Atrides rages round the field
cards.question: Paris declares 'the business of our life be love' and rushes to bed with Helen while Menelaus 'rages round the field.' Which detail most directly develops the theme that personal pleasure causes a warrior to abandon duty?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Paris blames his defeat on Pallas' power, suggesting the gods, not his own choices, decided the duel's outcome.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Paris retreats to Helen's arms at the very moment Menelaus is still searching the battlefield to destroy him.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Menelaus publicly demands that Helen and the Spartan wealth be restored, claiming Heaven has granted him a just victory.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Paris recalls first lying with Helen on Cranae's isle after bringing her from Sparta, showing their love predates the war.

cards.standardTitle: Epic poetry: characters, structures, and themes
cards.excerpt:
Neptune and Pallas haste to his relief, And thus in human form address’d the chief: The power of ocean first: “Forbear thy fear, O son of Peleus! Lo, thy gods appear! Behold! from Jove descending to thy aid, Propitious Neptune, and the blue-eyed maid. Stay, and the furious flood shall cease to rave ’Tis not thy fate to glut his angry wave. But thou, the counsel heaven suggests, attend! Nor breathe from combat, nor thy sword suspend, Till Troy receive her flying sons, till all Her routed squadrons pant behind their wall: Hector alone shall stand his fatal chance, And Hector’s blood shall smoke upon thy lance. Thine is the glory doom’d.” Thus spake the gods: Then swift ascended to the bright abodes.

Stung with new ardour, thus by heaven impell’d, He springs impetuous, and invades the field: O’er all the expanded plain the waters spread; Heaved on the bounding billows danced the dead, Floating ’midst scatter’d arms; while casques of gold And turn’d-up bucklers glitter’d as they roll’d. High o’er the surging tide, by leaps and bounds, He wades, and mounts; the parted wave resounds. Not a whole river stops the hero’s course, While Pallas fills him with immortal force. With equal rage, indignant Xanthus roars, And lifts his billows, and o’erwhelms his shores.
cards.whyThisWorks: Neptune's prophecy assigns Achilles a fated destiny—slaying Hector and winning glory—and Pallas fills him with 'immortal force,' showing how divine intervention directly drives heroic action and the theme of fate over personal choice.
cards.skillStrategy: When identifying divine intervention, trace exactly what the god commands or grants and then find the hero's immediate response in the next paragraph.
evidencePoints: Thine is the glory doom'd.
Pallas fills him with immortal force.
cards.question: Neptune tells Achilles 'Thine is the glory doom'd,' and the next paragraph states 'Pallas fills him with immortal force.' How do these two moments of divine intervention shape the theme of the passage?

choices.label: A
choices.text: They show that Achilles fights only to escape the flood, not to pursue glory or obey the gods.

choices.label: B
choices.text: They show that fated destiny and divine power, not personal choice, drive Achilles into unstoppable heroic action.

choices.label: C
choices.text: They show that the gods intervene to protect Troy's walls rather than to guarantee Achilles any victory.

choices.label: D
choices.text: They show that Achilles distrusts the gods' prophecy and charges forward on his own desire for revenge.

cards.standardTitle: Key literary elements add layers of meaning
cards.excerpt:
Thus prayed the chief: his unavailing prayer Great Jove refused, and toss’d in empty air: The God averse, while yet the fumes arose, Prepared new toils, and doubled woes on woes. Their prayers perform’d the chiefs the rite pursue, The barley sprinkled, and the victim slew. The limbs they sever from the inclosing hide, The thighs, selected to the gods, divide. On these, in double cauls involved with art, The choicest morsels lie from every part, From the cleft wood the crackling flames aspire While the fat victims feed the sacred fire. The thighs thus sacrificed, and entrails dress’d The assistants part, transfix, and roast the rest; Then spread the tables, the repast prepare, Each takes his seat, and each receives his share. Soon as the rage of hunger was suppress’d, The generous Nestor thus the prince address’d.

“Now bid thy heralds sound the loud alarms, And call the squadrons sheathed in brazen arms; Now seize the occasion, now the troops survey, And lead to war when heaven directs the way.”

He said; the monarch issued his commands; Straight the loud heralds call the gathering bands; The chiefs inclose their king; the hosts divide, In tribes and nations rank’d on either side. High in the midst the blue-eyed virgin flies; From rank to rank she darts her ardent eyes; The dreadful ægis, Jove’s immortal shield, Blazed on her arm, and lighten’d all the field: Round the vast orb a hundred serpents roll’d, Form’d the bright fringe, and seem’d to burn in gold, With this each Grecian’s manly breast she warms, Swells their bold hearts, and strings their nervous arms, No more they sigh, inglorious, to return, But breathe revenge, and for the combat burn.
cards.whyThisWorks: The blue-eyed virgin's characterization through physical action ('darts her ardent eyes'), divine weaponry ('dreadful ægis...Blazed on her arm'), and measurable effect on the soldiers ('No more they sigh, inglorious, to return, / But breathe revenge, and for the combat burn') gives students a clear model of how divine characterization adds meaning by showing a god as the direct cause of human transformation.
cards.skillStrategy: When analyzing characterization, trace what a character does, what tools or traits they are given, and what changes because of them — the gap between before and after reveals their role and meaning.
evidencePoints: From rank to rank she darts her ardent eyes
No more they sigh, inglorious, to return, / But breathe revenge, and for the combat burn
cards.question: In the final paragraph, the blue-eyed virgin 'darts her ardent eyes' through the ranks, her 'dreadful ægis...Blazed on her arm, and lighten'd all the field,' and afterward the soldiers 'No more they sigh, inglorious, to return, / But breathe revenge, and for the combat burn.' What does this sequence of characterization reveal about her function in the passage?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Her darting eyes and blazing aegis show that she is fulfilling Nestor's earlier command to 'call the squadrons sheathed in brazen arms,' making her a messenger who carries out human orders rather than an independent force.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Her fierce gaze and blazing shield characterize her as a transformative divine force whose presence directly converts the soldiers' inglorious desire to return into a burning hunger for revenge and combat.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Her movement from rank to rank and her blazing aegis characterize her as an instrument of Jove's will, enforcing his earlier refusal of the chief's prayer by preventing the soldiers from retreating as the chief had hoped.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The description of her 'ardent eyes' and the aegis that 'lighten'd all the field' characterizes her primarily as a symbol of Greek military wealth and divine favor, signaling to the troops that the sacrifice and rite have been accepted.

cards.standardTitle: Epic poetry: characters, structures, and themes
cards.excerpt:
When now the Thunderer on the sea-beat coast Had fix’d great Hector and his conquering host, He left them to the fates, in bloody fray To toil and struggle through the well-fought day. Then turn’d to Thracia from the field of fight Those eyes that shed insufferable light, To where the Mysians prove their martial force, And hardy Thracians tame the savage horse; And where the far-famed Hippomolgian strays, Renown’d for justice and for length of days; Thrice happy race! that, innocent of blood, From milk, innoxious, seek their simple food: Jove sees delighted; and avoids the scene Of guilty Troy, of arms, and dying men: No aid, he deems, to either host is given, While his high law suspends the powers of Heaven.

Meantime the monarch of the watery main Observed the Thunderer, nor observed in vain. In Samothracia, on a mountain’s brow, Whose waving woods o’erhung the deeps below, He sat; and round him cast his azure eyes Where Ida’s misty tops confusedly rise; Below, fair Ilion’s glittering spires were seen; The crowded ships and sable seas between. There, from the crystal chambers of the main Emerged, he sat, and mourn’d his Argives slain. At Jove incensed, with grief and fury stung, Prone down the rocky steep he rush’d along; Fierce as he pass’d, the lofty mountains nod, The forest shakes; earth trembled as he trod, And felt the footsteps of the immortal god. From realm to realm three ample strides he took, And, at the fourth, the distant Ægae shook.
cards.whyThisWorks: The excerpt shows Zeus deliberately withdrawing his gaze and suspending divine aid, which directly triggers Poseidon's furious descent from Samothracia—making the cause-and-effect of divine intervention on plot action explicit and teachable.
cards.skillStrategy: When identifying divine intervention, trace what a god does (or stops doing) and then find the exact moment in the text where that action causes something else to happen.
evidencePoints: No aid, he deems, to either host is given, While his high law suspends the powers of Heaven.
At Jove incensed, with grief and fury stung, Prone down the rocky steep he rush'd along
cards.question: In the first paragraph, Zeus turns his gaze away from Troy and declares that 'his high law suspends the powers of Heaven.' How does this moment of divine withdrawal shape Poseidon's behavior in the second paragraph?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Poseidon interprets Zeus's suspension of divine aid as a direct command to remain seated on the mountain in Samothracia and continue mourning the slain Greeks.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Because Zeus has turned away and suspended divine oversight, Poseidon acts on his fury over the slain Greeks and rushes down from the mountain toward the battle, defying the law Zeus intended to enforce.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Zeus's withdrawal causes Poseidon to travel to Ægae to seek Zeus's permission before offering any assistance to the Greeks on the battlefield.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Poseidon descends from Samothracia in order to enforce Zeus's suspended law and prevent either army from receiving supernatural help during the battle.

cards.standardTitle: Key literary elements add layers of meaning
cards.excerpt:
The nations hear with rising hopes possess’d, And peaceful prospects dawn in every breast. Within the lines they drew their steeds around, And from their chariots issued on the ground; Next, all unbuckling the rich mail they wore, Laid their bright arms along the sable shore. On either side the meeting hosts are seen With lances fix’d, and close the space between. Two heralds now, despatch’d to Troy, invite The Phrygian monarch to the peaceful rite.

Talthybius hastens to the fleet, to bring The lamb for Jove, the inviolable king.

Meantime to beauteous Helen, from the skies The various goddess of the rainbow flies: (Like fair Laodice in form and face, The loveliest nymph of Priam’s royal race:) Her in the palace, at her loom she found; The golden web her own sad story crown’d, The Trojan wars she weaved (herself the prize) And the dire triumphs of her fatal eyes. To whom the goddess of the painted bow: “Approach, and view the wondrous scene below! Each hardy Greek, and valiant Trojan knight, So dreadful late, and furious for the fight, Now rest their spears, or lean upon their shields; Ceased is the war, and silent all the fields. Paris alone and Sparta’s king advance, In single fight to toss the beamy lance; Each met in arms, the fate of combat tries, Thy love the motive, and thy charms the prize.”

This said, the many-coloured maid inspires Her husband’s love, and wakes her former fires; Her country, parents, all that once were dear, Rush to her thought, and force a tender tear, O’er her fair face a snowy veil she threw, And, softly sighing, from the loom withdrew. Her handmaids, Clymene and Æthra, wait Her silent footsteps to the Scæan gate.
cards.whyThisWorks: Helen's actions—weaving her own story into a tapestry, then silently withdrawing with tears and a veil—reveal her complex inner life as both object of war and a woman of grief and longing, making her characterization central to the passage's meaning.
cards.skillStrategy: When a character's actions and thoughts appear together, ask what those details reveal about who the character truly is beneath the surface role they play in the story.
evidencePoints: The golden web her own sad story crown'd, / The Trojan wars she weaved (herself the prize) / And the dire triumphs of her fatal eyes.
Her country, parents, all that once were dear, / Rush to her thought, and force a tender tear, / O'er her fair face a snowy veil she threw, / And, softly sighing, from the loom withdrew.
cards.question: The narrator describes Helen weaving 'The Trojan wars she weaved (herself the prize) / And the dire triumphs of her fatal eyes,' and then shows her silently withdrawing with a veil and tears. What do these details reveal about Helen's character?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Helen is indifferent to the war because she continues weaving rather than rushing immediately to the gate when the goddess arrives.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Helen is both aware of her role as the cause of the war and burdened by grief and longing, making her a figure of sorrow rather than simply a passive prize.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Helen weaves the war into her tapestry to celebrate Paris's bravery and show her loyalty to Troy over her homeland.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Helen's tears and veil show that she is afraid of the goddess Iris and obeys her out of fear rather than genuine emotion.

cards.standardTitle: Theme development across a literary text
cards.excerpt:
Great Ajax first to conquest led the way, Broke the thick ranks, and turn’d the doubtful day. The Thracian Acamas his falchion found, And hew’d the enormous giant to the ground; His thundering arm a deadly stroke impress’d Where the black horse-hair nodded o’er his crest; Fix’d in his front the brazen weapon lies, And seals in endless shades his swimming eyes. Next Teuthras’ son distain’d the sands with blood, Axylus, hospitable, rich, and good: In fair Arisbe’s walls (his native place) He held his seat! a friend to human race. Fast by the road, his ever-open door Obliged the wealthy, and relieved the poor. To stern Tydides now he falls a prey, No friend to guard him in the dreadful day! Breathless the good man fell, and by his side His faithful servant, old Calesius died.

By great Euryalus was Dresus slain, And next he laid Opheltius on the plain. Two twins were near, bold, beautiful, and young, From a fair naiad and Bucolion sprung: (Laomedon’s white flocks Bucolion fed, That monarch’s first-born by a foreign bed; In secret woods he won the naiad’s grace, And two fair infants crown’d his strong embrace:) Here dead they lay in all their youthful charms; The ruthless victor stripp’d their shining arms.
cards.whyThisWorks: The excerpt contrasts Axylus's celebrated generosity ('ever-open door,' 'relieved the poor') with his death 'no friend to guard him,' and the twins' youth and beauty with being stripped of their arms, giving students true-but-topic-only details to reject and a theme-developing detail to identify.
cards.skillStrategy: Ask yourself: does this detail show how the theme is built, or does it just describe what happens in the battle?
evidencePoints: Fast by the road, his ever-open door / Obliged the wealthy, and relieved the poor. / To stern Tydides now he falls a prey, / No friend to guard him in the dreadful day!
Here dead they lay in all their youthful charms; / The ruthless victor stripp'd their shining arms.
cards.question: The narrator describes Axylus as a man whose 'ever-open door / Obliged the wealthy, and relieved the poor,' then immediately states he falls 'No friend to guard him in the dreadful day.' Which statement best explains how this contrast develops a theme in the excerpt?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Axylus's wealth and his home in 'fair Arisbe's walls' mark him as a man of high social standing, showing that war claims soldiers from every level of society.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The gap between Axylus's life of generosity toward all people and his death utterly unprotected develops the theme that war annihilates human goodness without offering any return.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Axylus is identified as 'hospitable, rich, and good,' confirming that Homer values characters who display traditional virtues alongside physical courage.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The detail that Axylus's servant Calesius dies beside him shows that loyalty between master and servant was a defining feature of Trojan War society.

cards.standardTitle: Epic poetry: characters, structures, and themes
cards.excerpt: Thus to bold Hector spoke the son of Jove, And breathed immortal ardour from above. As when the pamper’d steed, with reins unbound, Breaks from his stall, and pours along the ground; With ample strokes he rushes to the flood, To bathe his sides, and cool his fiery blood; His head, now freed, he tosses to the skies; His mane dishevell’d o’er his shoulders flies: He snuffs the females in the well-known plain, And springs, exulting, to his fields again: Urged by the voice divine, thus Hector flew, Full of the god; and all his hosts pursue. As when the force of men and dogs combined Invade the mountain goat, or branching hind; Far from the hunter’s rage secure they lie Close in the rock, (not fated yet to die) When lo! a lion shoots across the way! They fly: at once the chasers and the prey. So Greece, that late in conquering troops pursued, And mark’d their progress through the ranks in blood, Soon as they see the furious chief appear, Forget to vanquish, and consent to fear.
cards.whyThisWorks: The phrase 'Urged by the voice divine, thus Hector flew, / Full of the god' directly names divine intervention as the cause of Hector's charge and the Greeks' subsequent terror, making the supernatural force's effect on action unmistakable.
cards.skillStrategy: When you see a god act in an epic, trace the chain: what does the god do, and what changes in the human world right after?
evidencePoints: Urged by the voice divine, thus Hector flew, Full of the god; and all his hosts pursue.
So Greece, that late in conquering troops pursued, And mark'd their progress through the ranks in blood, Soon as they see the furious chief appear, Forget to vanquish, and consent to fear.
cards.question: The narrator states that Hector flew 'Urged by the voice divine' and was 'Full of the god.' How does this divine intervention directly shape the action described in the lines that follow?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Hector pauses to rally his troops with a speech, and the Greeks use the delay to regroup behind their defensive lines.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Hector charges with supernatural energy, and the Greek soldiers who had been advancing and drawing blood suddenly stop pursuing and give way to fear.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Hector's divine inspiration causes the Greek gods to intervene on the other side, balancing the battle and preventing a Greek retreat.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The god's voice reveals a prophecy to Hector that fate protects him, so Hector advances slowly and the Greeks hold their ground in confusion.

cards.standardTitle: Key literary elements add layers of meaning
cards.excerpt:
The effect succeeds the speech. Pelides cries, “Thy artful praise deserves a better prize. Nor Greece in vain shall hear thy friend extoll’d; Receive a talent of the purest gold.” The youth departs content. The host admire The son of Nestor, worthy of his sire.

Next these a buckler, spear, and helm, he brings; Cast on the plain, the brazen burden rings: Arms which of late divine Sarpedon wore, And great Patroclus in short triumph bore. “Stand forth the bravest of our host! (he cries) Whoever dares deserve so rich a prize, Now grace the lists before our army’s sight, And sheathed in steel, provoke his foe to fight. Who first the jointed armour shall explore, And stain his rival’s mail with issuing gore, The sword Asteropaeus possess’d of old, (A Thracian blade, distinct with studs of gold,) Shall pay the stroke, and grace the striker’s side: These arms in common let the chiefs divide: For each brave champion, when the combat ends, A sumptuous banquet at our tents attends.”

Fierce at the word uprose great Tydeus’ son, And the huge bulk of Ajax Telamon. Clad in refulgent steel, on either hand, The dreadful chiefs amid the circle stand; Louring they meet, tremendous to the sight; Each Argive bosom beats with fierce delight. Opposed in arms not long they idly stood, But thrice they closed, and thrice the charge renew’d. A furious pass the spear of Ajax made Through the broad shield, but at the corslet stay’d. Not thus the foe: his javelin aim’d above The buckler’s margin, at the neck he drove. But Greece, now trembling for her hero’s life, Bade share the honours, and surcease the strife. Yet still the victor’s due Tydides gains, With him the sword and studded belt remains.
cards.whyThisWorks: The contrasting combat actions of Ajax and Tydides—Ajax's spear stopped at the corslet versus Tydides' javelin aimed precisely at the neck above the buckler—characterize Tydides as the more dangerous and calculated warrior, adding meaning to his ultimate victory and the crowd's fear for their hero's life.
cards.skillStrategy: When analyzing characterization, look at what a character does in a key moment and compare it to another character's action to understand what the author wants you to think about each person.
evidencePoints: A furious pass the spear of Ajax made / Through the broad shield, but at the corslet stay'd.
his javelin aim'd above / The buckler's margin, at the neck he drove
cards.question: In the combat scene, Ajax's spear drives 'through the broad shield, but at the corslet stay'd,' while Tydides aims 'above / The buckler's margin, at the neck.' What does this contrast in their strikes reveal about Tydides' characterization as a warrior?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Tydides fights recklessly by targeting the neck, and Greece trembles because his wild strike endangers the entire contest rather than demonstrating superior skill.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Tydides is the more precise and dangerous fighter, whose calculated strike at the unguarded neck above the buckler surpasses Ajax's powerful but stopped blow, justifying his claim to the victor's prize.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Tydides wins only because Ajax deliberately holds back after his spear is stopped at the corslet, unwilling to risk killing a fellow Greek champion before the assembled army.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The contrast between Ajax's blocked spear and Tydides' neck strike shows both warriors are equally matched, which is why Greece intervenes and the arms are divided rather than awarded to one champion.

cards.standardTitle: Theme development across a literary text
cards.excerpt:
The son of Venus to the counsel yields; Then o’er their backs they spread their solid shields: With brass refulgent the broad surface shined, And thick bull-hides the spacious concave lined. Them Chromius follows, Aretus succeeds; Each hopes the conquest of the lofty steeds: In vain, brave youths, with glorious hopes ye burn, In vain advance! not fated to return.

Unmov’d, Automedon attends the fight, Implores the Eternal, and collects his might. Then turning to his friend, with dauntless mind: “Oh keep the foaming coursers close behind! Full on my shoulders let their nostrils blow, For hard the fight, determined is the foe; ’Tis Hector comes: and when he seeks the prize, War knows no mean; he wins it or he dies.”

Then through the field he sends his voice aloud, And calls the Ajaces from the warring crowd, With great Atrides. “Hither turn, (he said,) Turn where distress demands immediate aid; The dead, encircled by his friends, forego, And save the living from a fiercer foe. Unhelp’d we stand, unequal to engage The force of Hector, and Æneas’ rage: Yet mighty as they are, my force to prove Is only mine: the event belongs to Jove.”

He spoke, and high the sounding javelin flung, Which pass’d the shield of Aretus the young: It pierced his belt, emboss’d with curious art, Then in the lower belly struck the dart. As when a ponderous axe, descending full, Cleaves the broad forehead of some brawny bull: Struck ’twixt the horns, he springs with many a bound, Then tumbling rolls enormous on the ground: Thus fell the youth; the air his soul received, And the spear trembled as his entrails heaved.
cards.whyThisWorks: The excerpt explicitly contrasts human ambition with fate through the narrator's address to Chromius and Aretus ('not fated to return') and Automedon's declaration that 'the event belongs to Jove,' giving students two clear evidence points for how fate overrides warrior effort.
cards.skillStrategy: Find the moment where a character's words or the narrator's comment directly limits what a warrior can achieve, then ask which detail best proves the theme.
evidencePoints: In vain, brave youths, with glorious hopes ye burn, / In vain advance! not fated to return.
the event belongs to Jove
cards.question: The narrator tells Chromius and Aretus they advance 'not fated to return,' and Automedon states 'the event belongs to Jove.' Which detail from the excerpt most clearly develops the theme that human ambition cannot overcome fate?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Automedon calls the Ajaces and Atrides to help, admitting he stands 'unequal to engage / The force of Hector, and Æneas' rage.'

choices.label: B
choices.text: Automedon claims the effort is 'only mine' but immediately surrenders the outcome to Jove, showing warrior will is bound by a higher power.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Automedon's javelin pierces Aretus's belt and strikes his belly, proving skill alone decides the battle's outcome.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Chromius and Aretus spread brass-faced shields across their backs before advancing, showing warriors prepare carefully for combat.

cards.standardTitle: Epic poetry: characters, structures, and themes
cards.excerpt: Jupiter assembles a council of the deities, and threatens them with the pains of Tartarus if they assist either side: Minerva only obtains of him that she may direct the Greeks by her counsels. The armies join battle: Jupiter on Mount Ida weighs in his balances the fates of both, and affrights the Greeks with his thunders and lightnings. Nestor alone continues in the field in great danger: Diomed relieves him; whose exploits, and those of Hector, are excellently described. Juno endeavours to animate Neptune to the assistance of the Greeks, but in vain. The acts of Teucer, who is at length wounded by Hector, and carried off. Juno and Minerva prepare to aid the Grecians, but are restrained by Iris, sent from Jupiter. The night puts an end to the battle. Hector continues in the field, (the Greeks being driven to their fortifications before the ships,) and gives orders to keep the watch all night in the camp, to prevent the enemy from re-embarking and escaping by flight. They kindle fires through all the fields, and pass the night under arms. The time of seven and twenty days is employed from the opening of the poem to the end of this book. The scene here (except of the celestial machines) lies in the field towards the seashore.
cards.whyThisWorks: The excerpt shows Jupiter actively shaping the battle's outcome through two distinct acts—terrifying the Greeks with thunder and lightning, then sending Iris to block Juno and Minerva's aid—demonstrating how divine intervention in epic poetry controls mortal fate.
cards.skillStrategy: When analyzing divine intervention in epic poetry, trace each god's specific action and ask: what would have happened to the mortals without it?
evidencePoints: Jupiter on Mount Ida weighs in his balances the fates of both, and affrights the Greeks with his thunders and lightnings
Juno and Minerva prepare to aid the Grecians, but are restrained by Iris, sent from Jupiter
cards.question: The excerpt describes Jupiter weighing 'the fates of both' armies, then 'affrights the Greeks with his thunders and lightnings,' and later sending Iris to restrain Juno and Minerva from aiding the Greeks. How do these two acts of divine intervention work together to produce the outcome described at the end of the excerpt?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Jupiter's thunders cause both armies to halt, and restraining Juno and Minerva forces Diomed and Teucer to win the battle through heroic deeds alone, without any divine guidance.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Jupiter's thunders terrify the Greeks and weaken their resolve, and by sending Iris to block Juno and Minerva's aid, he ensures no divine help reaches the Greeks, driving them back to their fortifications by nightfall.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Jupiter's thunders signal Minerva to begin directing the Greeks with her counsels, and restraining Juno prevents a conflict among the gods that would have forced both armies to stop fighting before nightfall.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Jupiter's thunders inspire Hector to press his attack, and restraining Juno and Minerva frees Neptune to enter the battle on the Greeks' side, balancing the two armies evenly through the night.

cards.whyThisWorks: Automedon's calm commands, his prayer, and his decision to hurl the javelin alone against Hector reveal a character defined by disciplined courage and self-aware heroism, giving students a clear moment to trace how action and speech build meaning.
cards.skillStrategy: When a character speaks and acts under pressure, ask what those choices reveal about who they are and what the author wants readers to understand about them.
evidencePoints: 'Tis Hector comes: and when he seeks the prize, War knows no mean; he wins it or he dies.
Yet mighty as they are, my force to prove / Is only mine: the event belongs to Jove.
cards.question: In the second and third paragraphs, Automedon tells his companion to keep the horses close, calls for reinforcements, and then declares, 'my force to prove / Is only mine: the event belongs to Jove.' What do these actions and words together reveal about Automedon's character?

choices.label: A
choices.text: He is reckless and overconfident, charging into battle without any plan or awareness of the danger Hector poses.

choices.label: B
choices.text: He is clear-eyed about the odds against him yet chooses to act with full commitment, trusting his own effort while accepting that the outcome rests beyond his control.

choices.label: C
choices.text: He is primarily concerned with protecting the horses rather than engaging the enemy, using the call for reinforcements as a way to avoid direct combat.

choices.label: D
choices.text: He doubts his own ability and relies entirely on the Ajaces and Atrides to defeat Hector, stepping back from the fight once help is summoned.

cards.standardTitle: Theme development across a literary text
cards.excerpt:
Perhaps great Hector then had found his fate, But Jove and destiny prolong’d his date. Safe from the darts, the care of heaven he stood, Amidst alarms, and death, and dust, and blood.

Now past the tomb where ancient Ilus lay, Through the mid field the routed urge their way: Where the wild figs the adjoining summit crown, The path they take, and speed to reach the town. As swift, Atrides with loud shouts pursued, Hot with his toil, and bathed in hostile blood. Now near the beech-tree, and the Scæan gates, The hero halts, and his associates waits. Meanwhile on every side around the plain, Dispersed, disorder’d, fly the Trojan train. So flies a herd of beeves, that hear dismay’d The lion’s roaring through the midnight shade; On heaps they tumble with successless haste; The savage seizes, draws, and rends the last. Not with less fury stern Atrides flew, Still press’d the rout, and still the hindmost slew; Hurl’d from their cars the bravest chiefs are kill’d, And rage, and death, and carnage load the field.
cards.whyThisWorks: The excerpt contrasts Hector's divine protection with the Trojans' helpless rout and Atrides' unstoppable slaughter, giving students clear textual evidence to trace how fate—not human effort—governs survival.
cards.skillStrategy: Look for details that show characters succeeding or failing despite their own actions, then ask whether a divine or outside force—not the character—is controlling the outcome.
evidencePoints: Jove and destiny prolong'd his date
tumble with successless haste
cards.question: The narrator says 'Jove and destiny prolong'd his date' to explain Hector's survival. Which detail from the excerpt most directly supports the theme that divine will, not human effort, decides who lives in battle?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Atrides is 'hot with his toil, and bathed in hostile blood,' showing the physical cost of fighting.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The Trojans 'tumble with successless haste,' showing that their own speed and effort cannot save them from the fated outcome.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The Trojans pass 'the tomb where ancient Ilus lay' on their way back to the town gates.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Hector halts near 'the beech-tree, and the Scæan gates' to wait for his associates.

cards.standardTitle: Epic poetry: characters, structures, and themes
cards.excerpt: Dione then: “Thy wrongs with patience bear, And share those griefs inferior powers must share: Unnumber’d woes mankind from us sustain, And men with woes afflict the gods again. The mighty Mars in mortal fetters bound, And lodged in brazen dungeons underground, Full thirteen moons imprison’d roar’d in vain; Otus and Ephialtes held the chain: Perhaps had perish’d had not Hermes’ care Restored the groaning god to upper air. Great Juno’s self has borne her weight of pain, The imperial partner of the heavenly reign; Amphitryon’s son infix’d the deadly dart, And fill’d with anguish her immortal heart. E’en hell’s grim king Alcides’ power confess’d, The shaft found entrance in his iron breast; To Jove’s high palace for a cure he fled, Pierced in his own dominions of the dead; Where Paeon, sprinkling heavenly balm around, Assuaged the glowing pangs, and closed the wound. Rash, impious man! to stain the bless’d abodes, And drench his arrows in the blood of gods!
cards.whyThisWorks: Dione's speech uses paired examples—Hermes rescuing Mars from 'brazen dungeons underground' and Paeon healing Hades with 'heavenly balm'—to illustrate how divine intervention restores cosmic order after mortals temporarily overpower gods, directly teaching the subskill of divine intervention in epic poetry.
cards.skillStrategy: When analyzing divine intervention in epic poetry, identify who intervenes, what mortal action triggered the need, and what the intervention restores—then ask what that pattern reveals about the epic's view of divine order.
evidencePoints: Perhaps had perish'd had not Hermes' care / Restored the groaning god to upper air
Where Paeon, sprinkling heavenly balm around, / Assuaged the glowing pangs, and closed the wound
cards.question: In Dione's speech, Hermes rescues Mars after mortals lodge him in 'brazen dungeons underground,' and Paeon heals Hades by 'sprinkling heavenly balm around' after Alcides' arrow pierces him. How do these two acts of divine intervention function together in Dione's argument?

choices.label: A
choices.text: They prove that mortals hold lasting dominance over the gods, since Mars 'roar'd in vain' for thirteen moons and Hades was forced to flee 'his own dominions of the dead' with no guarantee of recovery.

choices.label: B
choices.text: They show that even when mortals wound or imprison gods, divine figures like Hermes and Paeon step in to restore the injured god, supporting Dione's claim that the gods' realm endures despite its vulnerability to mortal force.

choices.label: C
choices.text: They establish that Hermes and Paeon outrank all other gods, including Jove, because only they possess healing and rescue powers capable of undoing the suffering that Otus, Ephialtes, and Alcides inflicted.

choices.label: D
choices.text: They suggest that Dione is warning gods to avoid mortal conflicts entirely, since both Mars and Hades suffered for extended periods before receiving aid that arrived only by chance rather than by divine design.

cards.standardTitle: Rhetorical appeals and author purpose
cards.excerpt: The battle renewing with double ardour upon the return of Hector, Minerva is under apprehensions for the Greeks. Apollo, seeing her descend from Olympus, joins her near the Scæan gate. They agree to put off the general engagement for that day, and incite Hector to challenge the Greeks to a single combat. Nine of the princes accepting the challenge, the lot is cast and falls upon Ajax. These heroes, after several attacks, are parted by the night. The Trojans calling a council, Antenor purposes the delivery of Helen to the Greeks, to which Paris will not consent, but offers to restore them her riches. Priam sends a herald to make this offer, and to demand a truce for burning the dead, the last of which only is agreed to by Agamemnon. When the funerals are performed, the Greeks, pursuant to the advice of Nestor, erect a fortification to protect their fleet and camp, flanked with towers, and defended by a ditch and palisades. Neptune testifies his jealousy at this work, but is pacified by a promise from Jupiter. Both armies pass the night in feasting but Jupiter disheartens the Trojans with thunder, and other signs of his wrath. The three and twentieth day ends with the duel of Hector and Ajax, the next day the truce is agreed; another is taken up in the funeral rites of the slain and one more in building the fortification before the ships. So that somewhat about three days is employed in this book. The scene lies wholly in the field.
cards.whyThisWorks: The phrase 'double ardour' is a figurative intensifier that conveys the surge of renewed battle energy, allowing students to analyze how Homer uses figurative language to heighten the stakes and explain the momentum of the conflict to readers.
cards.skillStrategy: When you spot figurative language, ask yourself: what idea is the author trying to make clearer or more powerful, and how does that word choice serve that goal?
evidencePoints: The battle renewing with double ardour upon the return of Hector
Jupiter disheartens the Trojans with thunder, and other signs of his wrath
cards.question: Homer writes that 'the battle renewing with double ardour upon the return of Hector.' How does the figurative phrase 'double ardour' help Homer achieve his explanatory purpose in this passage?

choices.label: A
choices.text: It signals that exactly twice as many soldiers entered the battle when Hector returned, giving the reader a precise count of the forces involved.

choices.label: B
choices.text: It conveys that Hector's return dramatically intensified the fighting, helping readers understand why the gods felt compelled to intervene and redirect the conflict.

choices.label: C
choices.text: It suggests that Hector fought two separate duels that day, explaining why the passage later describes both Ajax and Agamemnon as his opponents.

choices.label: D
choices.text: It implies that the Greeks were twice as powerful as the Trojans, preparing the reader for the Greek victory described at the end of the passage.

cards.standardTitle: Key literary elements add layers of meaning
cards.excerpt:
He said: both javelins at an instant flew; Both struck, both wounded, but Sarpedon’s slew: Full in the boaster’s neck the weapon stood, Transfix’d his throat, and drank the vital blood; The soul disdainful seeks the caves of night, And his seal’d eyes for ever lose the light.

Yet not in vain, Tlepolemus, was thrown Thy angry lance; which piercing to the bone Sarpedon’s thigh, had robb’d the chief of breath; But Jove was present, and forbade the death. Borne from the conflict by his Lycian throng, The wounded hero dragg’d the lance along. (His friends, each busied in his several part, Through haste, or danger, had not drawn the dart.) The Greeks with slain Tlepolemus retired; Whose fall Ulysses view’d, with fury fired; Doubtful if Jove’s great son he should pursue, Or pour his vengeance on the Lycian crew. But heaven and fate the first design withstand, Nor this great death must grace Ulysses’ hand. Minerva drives him on the Lycian train; Alastor, Cronius, Halius, strew’d the plain, Alcander, Prytanis, Noëmon fell: And numbers more his sword had sent to hell, But Hector saw; and, furious at the sight, Rush’d terrible amidst the ranks of fight. With joy Sarpedon view’d the wish’d relief, And, faint, lamenting, thus implored the chief:

“O suffer not the foe to bear away My helpless corpse, an unassisted prey; If I, unbless’d, must see my son no more, My much-loved consort, and my native shore, Yet let me die in Ilion’s sacred wall; Troy, in whose cause I fell, shall mourn my fall.”

He said, nor Hector to the chief replies, But shakes his plume, and fierce to combat flies; Swift as a whirlwind, drives the scattering foes; And dyes the ground with purple as he goes.
cards.whyThisWorks: Sarpedon's wounded speech—asking Hector not to let his body be taken and accepting death as long as Troy mourns him—reveals a hero whose loyalty to Troy outweighs his fear of dying, adding meaning to the epic's themes of honor and sacrifice.
cards.skillStrategy: When a character speaks under pressure, ask what that speech reveals about their deepest values—not just what they want, but what they are willing to accept.
evidencePoints: Yet let me die in Ilion's sacred wall; Troy, in whose cause I fell, shall mourn my fall.
O suffer not the foe to bear away / My helpless corpse, an unassisted prey
cards.question: Read Sarpedon's speech beginning 'O suffer not the foe to bear away.' What does this speech reveal about Sarpedon's character?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Sarpedon is consumed by fear of death and begs Hector to save his life at any cost.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Sarpedon accepts that he may die but places his honor and Troy's recognition of his sacrifice above his own survival.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Sarpedon's primary concern is returning to his family and homeland rather than the outcome of the battle.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Sarpedon blames Hector for failing to protect him and demands that Hector personally avenge his wound.

cards.standardTitle: Theme development across a literary text
cards.excerpt:
She ceased, and Juno rein’d the steeds with care: (Heaven’s awful empress, Saturn’s other heir:) Pallas, meanwhile, her various veil unbound, With flowers adorn’d, with art immortal crown’d; The radiant robe her sacred fingers wove Floats in rich waves, and spreads the court of Jove. Her father’s arms her mighty limbs invest, His cuirass blazes on her ample breast. The vigorous power the trembling car ascends: Shook by her arm, the massy javelin bends: Huge, ponderous, strong! that when her fury burns Proud tyrants humbles, and whole hosts o’erturns.

Saturnia lends the lash; the coursers fly; Smooth glides the chariot through the liquid sky. Heaven’s gates spontaneous open to the powers, Heaven’s golden gates, kept by the winged Hours. Commission’d in alternate watch they stand, The sun’s bright portals and the skies command; Close, or unfold, the eternal gates of day Bar heaven with clouds, or roll those clouds away. The sounding hinges ring, the clouds divide. Prone down the steep of heaven their course they guide. But Jove, incensed, from Ida’s top survey’d, And thus enjoin’d the many-colour’d maid.
cards.whyThisWorks: The excerpt shows Pallas and Juno armed with divine power and moving freely through heaven's gates, yet the final image of 'Jove, incensed, from Ida's top survey'd' undercuts their apparent freedom, letting students distinguish a true-but-topic-only detail (the Hours guarding the gates) from a detail that actually develops the theme that power answers to higher authority.
cards.skillStrategy: Ask yourself: does this detail just describe what is happening, or does it show something about how power is limited or controlled by something greater?
evidencePoints: Huge, ponderous, strong! that when her fury burns / Proud tyrants humbles, and whole hosts o'erturns.
But Jove, incensed, from Ida's top survey'd
cards.question: The narrator describes Pallas's javelin as capable of overthrowing 'proud tyrants' and 'whole hosts,' yet the passage ends with 'Jove, incensed, from Ida's top survey'd.' Which detail from the excerpt most directly develops the theme that even the mightiest power remains subject to a greater authority?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The winged Hours stand guard at heaven's golden gates, opening and closing them to command 'the sun's bright portals and the skies,' showing that divine travel requires a formal system of passage.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Despite the goddesses descending fully armed through heaven's gates unopposed, Jove watches 'incensed' from Ida's top, making clear that their show of power has drawn the scrutiny and anger of a higher divine force.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Pallas dons her father's cuirass and wields a javelin so massive it 'bends' under her grip, establishing that she possesses the physical strength to challenge any opponent on the battlefield.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Saturnia lashes the coursers and 'smooth glides the chariot through the liquid sky,' demonstrating that the goddesses move through heaven without friction or delay on their journey.

cards.standardTitle: Epic poetry: characters, structures, and themes
cards.excerpt: Pallas disrobes; her radiant veil untied, With flowers adorn’d, with art diversified, (The laboured veil her heavenly fingers wove,) Flows on the pavement of the court of Jove. Now heaven’s dread arms her mighty limbs invest, Jove’s cuirass blazes on her ample breast; Deck’d in sad triumph for the mournful field, O’er her broad shoulders hangs his horrid shield, Dire, black, tremendous! Round the margin roll’d, A fringe of serpents hissing guards the gold: Here all the terrors of grim War appear, Here rages Force, here tremble Flight and Fear, Here storm’d Contention, and here Fury frown’d, And the dire orb portentous Gorgon crown’d. The massy golden helm she next assumes, That dreadful nods with four o’ershading plumes; So vast, the broad circumference contains A hundred armies on a hundred plains. The goddess thus the imperial car ascends; Shook by her arm the mighty javelin bends, Ponderous and huge; that when her fury burns, Proud tyrants humbles, and whole hosts o’erturns.
cards.whyThisWorks: The passage depicts Athena arming herself in Zeus's divine weapons—cuirass, Gorgon shield, helm, and javelin—making the supernatural preparation itself the mechanism of divine intervention that will shape the battle's outcome.
cards.skillStrategy: When identifying divine intervention, locate the exact moment a god acts or prepares to act, then trace how that action shapes what happens next in the story.
evidencePoints: Jove's cuirass blazes on her ample breast
that when her fury burns, Proud tyrants humbles, and whole hosts o'erturns
cards.question: The passage ends by describing Athena's javelin as one 'that when her fury burns, / Proud tyrants humbles, and whole hosts o'erturns.' How does this detail shape the theme of divine power over mortal warfare?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The javelin's description shows that Athena's power is limited to intimidating individual rulers rather than changing the outcome of large battles.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The javelin's capacity to humble tyrants and overturn whole armies reveals that Athena's divine fury—not human strategy or courage—is the force that decides the fate of armies on the battlefield.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The javelin's size and weight suggest that Athena must exert the same physical effort as a mortal warrior, making her intervention no more decisive than that of a skilled human soldier.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The javelin's description emphasizes Athena's personal anger at specific tyrants, indicating that her intervention is driven by private vengeance rather than any broader influence over war.

cards.standardTitle: Rhetorical appeals and author purpose
cards.excerpt:
Dryden.

In reference to the whole scene that follows, the remarks of Coleridge are well worth reading:— “By a close study of life, and by a true and natural mode of expressing everything, Homer was enabled to venture upon the most peculiar and difficult situations, and to extricate himself from them with the completest success. The whole scene between Achilles and Priam, when the latter comes to the Greek camp for the purpose of redeeming the body of Hector, is at once the most profoundly skilful, and yet the simplest and most affecting passage in the Iliad. Quinctilian has taken notice of the following speech of Priam, the rhetorical artifice of which is so transcendent, that if genius did not often, especially in oratory, unconsciously fulfil the most subtle precepts of criticism, we might be induced, on this account alone, to consider the last book of the Iliad as what is called spurious, in other words, of later date than the rest of the poem. Observe the exquisite taste of Priam in occupying the mind of Achilles, from the outset, with the image of his father; in gradually introducing the parallel of his own situation; and, lastly, mentioning Hector’s name when he perceives that the hero is softened, and then only in such a manner as to flatter the pride of the conqueror. The ego d’eleeinoteros per, and the apusato aecha geronta, are not exactly like the tone of the earlier parts of the Iliad. They are almost too fine and pathetic. The whole passage defies translation, for there is that about the Greek which has no name, but which is of so fine and ethereal a subtlety that it can only be felt in the original, and is lost in an attempt to transfuse it into another language.”—Coleridge, p. 195.
cards.whyThisWorks: Coleridge's description of Priam's speech uses figurative language—'so fine and ethereal a subtlety'—to explain why the rhetorical power of the original Greek cannot survive translation, giving students a clear example of figurative language serving an explanatory purpose about persuasion.
cards.skillStrategy: When you spot figurative language, ask yourself: what idea is the author trying to make clearer or more convincing, and how does that comparison or image do that work?
evidencePoints: there is that about the Greek which has no name, but which is of so fine and ethereal a subtlety that it can only be felt in the original
The whole passage defies translation
cards.question: Coleridge describes the quality of Priam's speech in the original Greek as 'so fine and ethereal a subtlety that it can only be felt in the original.' How does this figurative description help Coleridge achieve his explanatory purpose?

choices.label: A
choices.text: It emphasizes that Priam's speech is too long and complex for any translator to reproduce word for word.

choices.label: B
choices.text: By comparing the speech's power to something nearly invisible and atmospheric, Coleridge explains why the effect is impossible to capture in another language—it exists beyond what words alone can transfer.

choices.label: C
choices.text: By calling the speech 'ethereal,' Coleridge argues that Priam's words were divinely inspired and therefore beyond human critical analysis.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The description of subtlety suggests that Priam deliberately hid his true meaning from Achilles so that only a careful reader could detect the rhetorical trick.

cards.standardTitle: Key literary elements add layers of meaning
cards.excerpt:
Greece, in close order, and collected might, Yet suffers least, and sways the wavering fight; Fierce as conflicting fires the combat burns, And now it rises, now it sinks by turns. In one thick darkness all the fight was lost; The sun, the moon, and all the ethereal host Seem’d as extinct: day ravish’d from their eyes, And all heaven’s splendours blotted from the skies. Such o’er Patroclus’ body hung the night, The rest in sunshine fought, and open light; Unclouded there, the aerial azure spread, No vapour rested on the mountain’s head, The golden sun pour’d forth a stronger ray, And all the broad expansion flamed with day. Dispersed around the plain, by fits they fight, And here and there their scatter’d arrows light: But death and darkness o’er the carcase spread, There burn’d the war, and there the mighty bled.

Meanwhile the sons of Nestor, in the rear, (Their fellows routed,) toss the distant spear, And skirmish wide: so Nestor gave command, When from the ships he sent the Pylian band. The youthful brothers thus for fame contend, Nor knew the fortune of Achilles’ friend; In thought they view’d him still, with martial joy, Glorious in arms, and dealing death to Troy.
cards.whyThisWorks: The sons of Nestor imagining Patroclus 'Glorious in arms' while his body lies shrouded in darkness illustrates how characterization—their unknowing hope—deepens the tragedy and meaning of the passage.
cards.skillStrategy: When a character's belief or action contrasts with what the reader knows, ask what that gap reveals about the character and the passage's deeper meaning.
evidencePoints: In thought they view'd him still, with martial joy, / Glorious in arms, and dealing death to Troy
death and darkness o'er the carcase spread, / There burn'd the war, and there the mighty bled
cards.question: The sons of Nestor 'in thought they view'd him still, with martial joy, / Glorious in arms, and dealing death to Troy,' while 'death and darkness o'er the carcase spread.' What does this contrast reveal about the sons of Nestor?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Their distant skirmishing shows they are cowards who deliberately avoid the darkness surrounding Patroclus' body.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Their false belief that Patroclus still fights gloriously creates tragic irony, showing how war cuts soldiers off from the truth.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Their joyful image of Patroclus reveals they care more about personal fame than about the outcome of the battle.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Their vision of Patroclus reflects the confident mood shared by all Greek soldiers fighting in the open sunlight.

cards.standardTitle: Theme development across a literary text
cards.excerpt:
Then died Hypsenor, generous and divine, Sprung from the brave Dolopion’s mighty line, Who near adored Scamander made abode, Priest of the stream, and honoured as a god. On him, amidst the flying numbers found, Eurypylus inflicts a deadly wound; On his broad shoulders fell the forceful brand, Thence glancing downwards, lopp’d his holy hand, Which stain’d with sacred blood the blushing sand. Down sunk the priest: the purple hand of death Closed his dim eye, and fate suppress’d his breath.

Thus toil’d the chiefs, in different parts engaged. In every quarter fierce Tydides raged; Amid the Greek, amid the Trojan train, Rapt through the ranks he thunders o’er the plain; Now here, now there, he darts from place to place, Pours on the rear, or lightens in their face. Thus from high hills the torrents swift and strong Deluge whole fields, and sweep the trees along, Through ruin’d moles the rushing wave resounds, O’erwhelm’s the bridge, and bursts the lofty bounds; The yellow harvests of the ripen’d year, And flatted vineyards, one sad waste appear! While Jove descends in sluicy sheets of rain, And all the labours of mankind are vain.
cards.whyThisWorks: The excerpt pairs the death of a sacred priest with a simile declaring 'all the labours of mankind are vain,' giving students two concrete evidence points to trace how war destroys both sacred purpose and human effort.
cards.skillStrategy: To find evidence of theme, look for the moment in the passage where the author states or strongly implies the central message—often in a final line or a comparison.
evidencePoints: all the labours of mankind are vain
Priest of the stream, and honoured as a god
cards.question: The closing line of the excerpt states that 'all the labours of mankind are vain.' Which earlier detail from the excerpt most directly supports this as evidence of a theme about war?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Tydides rages 'amid the Greek, amid the Trojan train,' showing he fights on both sides of the battlefield.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Hypsenor, 'Priest of the stream, and honoured as a god,' is cut down mid-battle, showing war spares nothing—not even sacred roles.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Eurypylus inflicts a wound on Hypsenor's 'broad shoulders,' showing the physical force warriors use in combat.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The torrent sweeps 'trees along' and bursts 'the lofty bounds,' showing that nature, not war, is the true destructive force.

cards.standardTitle: Epic poetry: characters, structures, and themes
cards.excerpt: Then godlike Diomed preferr’d his prayer: “Daughter of Jove, unconquer’d Pallas! hear. Great queen of arms, whose favour Tydeus won, As thou defend’st the sire, defend the son. When on Æsopus’ banks the banded powers Of Greece he left, and sought the Theban towers, Peace was his charge; received with peaceful show, He went a legate, but return’d a foe: Then help’d by thee, and cover’d by thy shield, He fought with numbers, and made numbers yield. So now be present, O celestial maid! So still continue to the race thine aid! A youthful steer shall fall beneath the stroke, Untamed, unconscious of the galling yoke, With ample forehead, and with spreading horns, Whose taper tops refulgent gold adorns.” The heroes pray’d, and Pallas from the skies Accords their vow, succeeds their enterprise. Now, like two lions panting for the prey, With dreadful thoughts they trace the dreary way, Through the black horrors of the ensanguined plain, Through dust, through blood, o’er arms, and hills of slain.
cards.whyThisWorks: Diomed's prayer explicitly recalls Pallas's past aid to his father Tydeus and promises a sacrificial steer, and the narrator confirms 'Pallas from the skies / Accords their vow, succeeds their enterprise,' directly modeling how divine intervention propels heroic action in epic poetry.
cards.skillStrategy: When analyzing divine intervention in epic poetry, trace the cause-and-effect chain: identify the prayer or appeal, the god's response, and how that response changes what the hero does next.
evidencePoints: Pallas from the skies / Accords their vow, succeeds their enterprise
Now, like two lions panting for the prey, / With dreadful thoughts they trace the dreary way, / Through the black horrors of the ensanguined plain
cards.question: In the excerpt, after Pallas 'accords their vow' and 'succeeds their enterprise,' Diomed and his companion advance 'like two lions panting for the prey' through 'the black horrors of the ensanguined plain.' What does this sequence reveal about the role of divine intervention in shaping the heroes' action?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Pallas descends visibly onto the battlefield and clears a path through 'dust, through blood, o'er arms, and hills of slain' by fighting alongside the heroes herself.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Pallas's approval of the prayer transforms the heroes' resolve, enabling them to charge boldly through 'the black horrors of the ensanguined plain' in a way the prayer implies they could not have done without her favor.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Diomed's reminder that Pallas once shielded his father Tydeus at 'Æsopus' banks' obligates her to intervene, but the heroes' advance depends entirely on their own courage rather than any divine aid.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The promise of 'a youthful steer' with 'refulgent gold' on its horns is what moves Pallas to act, indicating that the goddess responds only to the richness of the offering rather than to the heroes' need.

cards.standardTitle: Key literary elements add layers of meaning
cards.excerpt:
To this, Idomeneus: “The fields of fight Have proved thy valour, and unconquer’d might: And were some ambush for the foes design’d, Even there thy courage would not lag behind: In that sharp service, singled from the rest, The fear of each, or valour, stands confess’d. No force, no firmness, the pale coward shows; He shifts his place: his colour comes and goes: A dropping sweat creeps cold on every part; Against his bosom beats his quivering heart; Terror and death in his wild eye-balls stare; With chattering teeth he stands, and stiffening hair, And looks a bloodless image of despair! Not so the brave—still dauntless, still the same, Unchanged his colour, and unmoved his frame: Composed his thought, determined is his eye, And fix’d his soul, to conquer or to die: If aught disturb the tenour of his breast, ’Tis but the wish to strike before the rest.

“In such assays thy blameless worth is known, And every art of dangerous war thy own. By chance of fight whatever wounds you bore, Those wounds were glorious all, and all before; Such as may teach, ’twas still thy brave delight T’oppose thy bosom where thy foremost fight. But why, like infants, cold to honour’s charms, Stand we to talk, when glory calls to arms? Go—from my conquer’d spears the choicest take, And to their owners send them nobly back.”

Swift at the word bold Merion snatch’d a spear And, breathing slaughter, follow’d to the war. So Mars armipotent invades the plain, (The wide destroyer of the race of man,) Terror, his best-beloved son, attends his course, Arm’d with stern boldness, and enormous force; The pride of haughty warriors to confound, And lay the strength of tyrants on the ground: From Thrace they fly, call’d to the dire alarms Of warring Phlegyans, and Ephyrian arms; Invoked by both, relentless they dispose, To these glad conquest, murderous rout to those. So march’d the leaders of the Cretan train, And their bright arms shot horror o’er the plain.
cards.whyThisWorks: Idomeneus's extended contrast between the coward's physical collapse and the brave warrior's composed stillness reveals character through vivid description and direct speech, making the subskill of characterization through contrast and description highly teachable.
cards.skillStrategy: When a character describes two opposing types of people in detail, ask what that contrast reveals about the speaker's values and what meaning it adds to the scene.
evidencePoints: He shifts his place: his colour comes and goes: A dropping sweat creeps cold on every part; Against his bosom beats his quivering heart
Not so the brave—still dauntless, still the same, Unchanged his colour, and unmoved his frame: Composed his thought, determined is his eye, And fix'd his soul, to conquer or to die
cards.question: In his speech, Idomeneus contrasts the coward's 'chattering teeth,' 'quivering heart,' and shifting color with the brave warrior's 'unchanged colour' and 'unmoved frame.' What does this contrast most reveal about Idomeneus as a character?

choices.label: A
choices.text: He is boasting about his own past victories in ambush to impress Merion and claim superiority over him.

choices.label: B
choices.text: He measures a man's worth by inner steadiness under pressure, showing that composure and resolve are the values he prizes most in a warrior.

choices.label: C
choices.text: He believes physical strength alone determines the outcome of battle, dismissing fear as a minor obstacle any soldier can overcome.

choices.label: D
choices.text: He is warning Merion that cowardice is spreading through the Cretan ranks and that the army is on the verge of collapse.

cards.standardTitle: Epic poetry: characters, structures, and themes
cards.excerpt: The Trojans being safe within the walls, Hector only stays to oppose Achilles. Priam is struck at his approach, and tries to persuade his son to re-enter the town. Hecuba joins her entreaties, but in vain. Hector consults within himself what measures to take; but at the advance of Achilles, his resolution fails him, and he flies. Achilles pursues him thrice round the walls of Troy. The gods debate concerning the fate of Hector; at length Minerva descends to the aid of Achilles. She deludes Hector in the shape of Deiphobus; he stands the combat, and is slain. Achilles drags the dead body at his chariot in the sight of Priam and Hecuba. Their lamentations, tears, and despair. Their cries reach the ears of Andromache, who, ignorant of this, was retired into the inner part of the palace: she mounts up to the walls, and beholds her dead husband. She swoons at the spectacle. Her excess of grief and lamentation. The thirtieth day still continues. The scene lies under the walls, and on the battlements of Troy.
