cards.skillStrategy: When a sentence has inverted or old-fashioned word order, reorder the parts into subject-verb-object and check that every detail from the original is still present in your restatement.
evidencePoints: High on the deck the king of men appears, / And his refulgent arms in triumph wears
Proud of his host, unrivall'd in his reign, / In silent pomp he moves along the main.
cards.question: Read the following lines from the passage: 'High on the deck the king of men appears, / And his refulgent arms in triumph wears; / Proud of his host, unrivall'd in his reign, / In silent pomp he moves along the main.' Which restatement most accurately captures the full meaning of these lines?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Agamemnon stands on the deck wearing his armor, but he is troubled by the size of his fleet and moves quietly to hide his uncertainty from his men.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Agamemnon stands visibly on the deck, displaying his gleaming armor proudly, and sails in quiet grandeur, unmatched as a ruler and confident in his vast army.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Agamemnon appears on the deck wearing his armor and commands his soldiers loudly, proving that no other king can rival his power on land or sea.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Agamemnon moves silently across the water because he is humbled by the greatness of his host and chooses not to display his armor in front of his men.

cards.standardTitle: Paraphrase grade-level text
cards.excerpt:
The gods deliberate in council concerning the Trojan war: they agree upon the continuation of it, and Jupiter sends down Minerva to break the truce. She persuades Pandarus to aim an arrow at Menelaus, who is wounded, but cured by Machaon. In the meantime some of the Trojan troops attack the Greeks. Agamemnon is distinguished in all the parts of a good general; he reviews the troops, and exhorts the leaders, some by praises and others by reproof. Nestor is particularly celebrated for his military discipline. The battle joins, and great numbers are slain on both sides. The same day continues through this as through the last book (as it does also through the two following, and almost to the end of the seventh book). The scene is wholly in the field before Troy.

And now Olympus’ shining gates unfold; The gods, with Jove, assume their thrones of gold: Immortal Hebe, fresh with bloom divine, The golden goblet crowns with purple wine: While the full bowls flow round, the powers employ Their careful eyes on long-contended Troy.
cards.whyThisWorks: The inverted, multi-clause poetic sentence 'While the full bowls flow round, the powers employ / Their careful eyes on long-contended Troy' requires students to untangle subordinate clauses and archaic diction to restate that the gods are watching Troy while drinking, making it an ideal chunk-complex-syntax task.
cards.skillStrategy: When a sentence has multiple clauses and old-fashioned word order, identify who is doing what, then restate each part in plain language before putting them together.
evidencePoints: While the full bowls flow round, the powers employ / Their careful eyes on long-contended Troy.
Immortal Hebe, fresh with bloom divine, / The golden goblet crowns with purple wine
cards.question: Read this sentence from the poem: 'While the full bowls flow round, the powers employ / Their careful eyes on long-contended Troy.' Which restatement most accurately captures the meaning of these lines?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The gods pour wine into golden bowls and send it down to the warriors fighting at Troy.

choices.label: B
choices.text: As the wine cups are passed around, the gods turn their close attention to Troy, the city that has been fought over for so long.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The gods grow careless and distracted by their feast, forgetting to watch over the long battle at Troy.

choices.label: D
choices.text: While the gods drink, the people of Troy raise their bowls in a prayer asking the gods to end the war.

cards.standardTitle: Narrator perspective, irony, and satire
cards.excerpt:
A prince, therefore, ought always to take counsel, but only when he wishes and not when others wish; he ought rather to discourage every one from offering advice unless he asks it; but, however, he ought to be a constant inquirer, and afterwards a patient listener concerning the things of which he inquired; also, on learning that any one, on any consideration, has not told him the truth, he should let his anger be felt.

And if there are some who think that a prince who conveys an impression of his wisdom is not so through his own ability, but through the good advisers that he has around him, beyond doubt they are deceived, because this is an axiom which never fails: that a prince who is not wise himself will never take good advice, unless by chance he has yielded his affairs entirely to one person who happens to be a very prudent man. In this case indeed he may be well governed, but it would not be for long, because such a governor would in a short time take away his state from him.
cards.whyThisWorks: Machiavelli creates situational irony by instructing a prince to discourage unsolicited advice while simultaneously commanding him to be 'a constant inquirer'—a direct contradiction that reveals the gap between the prince's projected authority and his actual dependence on others' counsel.
cards.skillStrategy: When you spot a contradiction between two instructions or outcomes in the same passage, ask yourself what the author expects you to notice about the gap—that gap is often the irony.
evidencePoints: he ought rather to discourage every one from offering advice unless he asks it; but, however, he ought to be a constant inquirer

a prince who is not wise himself will never take good advice, unless by chance he has yielded his affairs entirely to one person who happens to be a very prudent man. In this case indeed he may be well governed, but it would not be for long, because such a governor would in a short time take away his state from him.
cards.question: Read the following passage from paragraph one: 'he ought rather to discourage every one from offering advice unless he asks it; but, however, he ought to be a constant inquirer.' What contradiction in this instruction creates irony?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The prince is told to listen patiently to advisers, yet he is also told to feel anger when they lie, suggesting advisers are both trusted and suspected at the same time.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The prince is told to silence those who offer advice freely, yet he is also told to constantly seek out that same advice himself, making his authority over counsel depend entirely on the counsel he claims to control.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The prince is told to appear wise through his own ability, yet Machiavelli admits that surrounding oneself with good advisers is the true source of a prince's reputation.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The prince is told to take counsel only when he wishes, yet the passage ends by warning that a prudent governor will eventually seize the prince's state, showing that timing advice is impossible.

cards.standardTitle: Theme development across a literary text
cards.excerpt:
But the difficulties occur in a new principality. And firstly, if it be not entirely new, but is, as it were, a member of a state which, taken collectively, may be called composite, the changes arise chiefly from an inherent difficulty which there is in all new principalities; for men change their rulers willingly, hoping to better themselves, and this hope induces them to take up arms against him who rules: wherein they are deceived, because they afterwards find by experience they have gone from bad to worse. This follows also on another natural and common necessity, which always causes a new prince to burden those who have submitted to him with his soldiery and with infinite other hardships which he must put upon his new acquisition.

In this way you have enemies in all those whom you have injured in seizing that principality, and you are not able to keep those friends who put you there because of your not being able to satisfy them in the way they expected, and you cannot take strong measures against them, feeling bound to them. For, although one may be very strong in armed forces, yet in entering a province one has always need of the goodwill of the natives.
cards.whyThisWorks: The excerpt presents a clear theme—that acquiring power creates unavoidable enemies on all sides—and contains both details that directly develop that theme and true-but-tangential details about soldiers and hardships that students might confuse with thematic evidence.
cards.skillStrategy: Ask yourself: does this detail show WHY the theme is true, or does it just describe something that happens in the passage?
evidencePoints: you have enemies in all those whom you have injured in seizing that principality, and you are not able to keep those friends who put you there

men change their rulers willingly, hoping to better themselves, and this hope induces them to take up arms against him who rules: wherein they are deceived, because they afterwards find by experience they have gone from bad to worse
cards.question: Which detail from the excerpt most directly develops the theme that a ruler who gains power through conquest cannot escape becoming isolated by it?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A new prince must burden those who submitted to him with soldiers and hardships, which shows that military occupation is the primary cost of ruling a new territory.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The new prince has injured those he conquered and cannot satisfy those who helped him seize power, leaving him without reliable allies on either side.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Men willingly change rulers hoping to improve their condition, which shows that subjects are naturally disloyal and self-interested.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Even a prince with strong armed forces still needs the goodwill of the natives, which shows that military strength alone determines whether a ruler survives.

cards.standardTitle: Narrator perspective, irony, and satire
cards.excerpt:
Hence it is to be remarked that, in seizing a state, the usurper ought to examine closely into all those injuries which it is necessary for him to inflict, and to do them all at one stroke so as not to have to repeat them daily; and thus by not unsettling men he will be able to reassure them, and win them to himself by benefits. He who does otherwise, either from timidity or evil advice, is always compelled to keep the knife in his hand; neither can he rely on his subjects, nor can they attach themselves to him, owing to their continued and repeated wrongs. For injuries ought to be done all at one time, so that, being tasted less, they offend less; benefits ought to be given little by little, so that the flavour of them may last longer.

And above all things, a prince ought to live amongst his people in such a way that no unexpected circumstances, whether of good or evil, shall make him change; because if the necessity for this comes in troubled times, you are too late for harsh measures; and mild ones will not help you, for they will be considered as forced from you, and no one will be under any obligation to you for them.
cards.whyThisWorks: Machiavelli's advice that a ruler should concentrate injuries 'at one stroke' to 'reassure' subjects creates situational irony: the very act of cruelty is framed as the path to winning loyalty, reversing the expected relationship between harm and trust.
cards.skillStrategy: Look for moments where the outcome or advice contradicts what you would normally expect — that gap between expectation and reality is where irony lives.
evidencePoints: injuries ought to be done all at one time, so that, being tasted less, they offend less
by not unsettling men he will be able to reassure them, and win them to himself by benefits
cards.question: Read the following passage from The Prince: 'injuries ought to be done all at one time, so that, being tasted less, they offend less; benefits ought to be given little by little, so that the flavour of them may last longer.' What contrast in this passage creates irony?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Machiavelli contrasts timid rulers with bold ones, suggesting that only cowardly princes rely on repeated injuries rather than swift action.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Machiavelli advises that concentrated harm leads to reassurance and loyalty, reversing the expected idea that injuring subjects would destroy their trust in a ruler.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Machiavelli contrasts the prince's use of benefits with his use of injuries, showing that generosity is always more effective than cruelty in governing a state.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Machiavelli contrasts troubled times with stable times, warning that a prince who changes his behavior during a crisis will lose the respect of his subjects.

cards.standardTitle: Narrator perspective, irony, and satire
cards.excerpt:
But it is impossible to hold with such tranquillity states constituted like that of France. Hence arose those frequent rebellions against the Romans in Spain, France, and Greece, owing to the many principalities there were in these states, of which, as long as the memory of them endured, the Romans always held an insecure possession; but with the power and long continuance of the empire the memory of them passed away, and the Romans then became secure possessors. And when fighting afterwards amongst themselves, each one was able to attach to himself his own parts of the country, according to the authority he had assumed there; and the family of the former lord being exterminated, none other than the Romans were acknowledged.

When these things are remembered no one will marvel at the ease with which Alexander held the Empire of Asia, or at the difficulties which others have had to keep an acquisition, such as Pyrrhus and many more; this is not occasioned by the little or abundance of ability in the conqueror, but by the want of uniformity in the subject state.
cards.whyThisWorks: Machiavelli creates situational irony by arguing that Alexander's seemingly miraculous ease of conquest was not due to superior ability, directly contradicting the common assumption that great conquests reflect great conquerors, revealing instead that the subject state's uniformity—not the conqueror's genius—determined the outcome.
cards.skillStrategy: When you spot a reversal of what seems obvious or expected, ask yourself what assumption is being flipped and what the author says is the real cause instead.
evidencePoints: this is not occasioned by the little or abundance of ability in the conqueror, but by the want of uniformity in the subject state
no one will marvel at the ease with which Alexander held the Empire of Asia, or at the difficulties which others have had to keep an acquisition
cards.question: Read the following sentence from the passage: 'this is not occasioned by the little or abundance of ability in the conqueror, but by the want of uniformity in the subject state.' What irony does Machiavelli create with this statement?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Machiavelli suggests that Alexander's conquest of Asia was actually more difficult than historians have recorded, making his reputation for military genius undeserved.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Machiavelli reverses the expected logic that a conqueror's success reflects his personal ability, arguing instead that the conquered state's internal structure determined the outcome.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Machiavelli implies that Pyrrhus failed because he lacked the military skill Alexander possessed, confirming that a conqueror's ability is the most important factor in holding territory.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Machiavelli argues that the Romans succeeded in France and Spain because their generals were more capable than the local rulers whose families were exterminated.

cards.standardTitle: Theme development across a literary text
cards.excerpt: And although Swiss and Spanish infantry may be considered very formidable, nevertheless there is a defect in both, by reason of which a third order would not only be able to oppose them, but might be relied upon to overthrow them. For the Spaniards cannot resist cavalry, and the Switzers are afraid of infantry whenever they encounter them in close combat. Owing to this, as has been and may again be seen, the Spaniards are unable to resist French cavalry, and the Switzers are overthrown by Spanish infantry. And although a complete proof of this latter cannot be shown, nevertheless there was some evidence of it at the battle of Ravenna, when the Spanish infantry were confronted by German battalions, who follow the same tactics as the Swiss; when the Spaniards, by agility of body and with the aid of their shields, got in under the pikes of the Germans and stood out of danger, able to attack, while the Germans stood helpless, and, if the cavalry had not dashed up, all would have been over with them. It is possible, therefore, knowing the defects of both these infantries, to invent a new one, which will resist cavalry and not be afraid of infantry; this need not create a new order of arms, but a variation upon the old. And these are the kind of improvements which confer reputation and power upon a new prince.
cards.whyThisWorks: The excerpt explicitly builds toward a theme about how a leader gains power through identifying weaknesses and innovating—students must distinguish details that develop this theme from true details that merely describe military tactics without connecting to the prince's reputation and power.
cards.skillStrategy: Ask yourself: does this detail show how the theme grows, or does it just describe what happened in the passage?
evidencePoints: knowing the defects of both these infantries, to invent a new one, which will resist cavalry and not be afraid of infantry
these are the kind of improvements which confer reputation and power upon a new prince
cards.question: Which detail from the passage most directly develops the theme that a leader gains power by recognizing weakness and turning it into opportunity?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The Spaniards used their shields and agility to get beneath the German pikes at the battle of Ravenna, demonstrating superior individual fighting skill.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Machiavelli argues that identifying the specific failures of Spanish and Swiss infantry makes it possible to design a force that overcomes both, and that doing so earns a new prince reputation and power.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The Swiss infantry fear close combat with other infantry, while the Spanish infantry cannot withstand cavalry charges from the French.

choices.label: D
choices.text: German battalions follow the same tactics as the Swiss, which is why the Spanish infantry were able to exploit their weaknesses at Ravenna.

cards.standardTitle: Narrator perspective, irony, and satire
cards.excerpt:
Therefore it is unnecessary for a prince to have all the good qualities I have enumerated, but it is very necessary to appear to have them. And I shall dare to say this also, that to have them and always to observe them is injurious, and that to appear to have them is useful; to appear merciful, faithful, humane, religious, upright, and to be so, but with a mind so framed that should you require not to be so, you may be able and know how to change to the opposite.

And you have to understand this, that a prince, especially a new one, cannot observe all those things for which men are esteemed, being often forced, in order to maintain the state, to act contrary to fidelity, friendship, humanity, and religion. Therefore it is necessary for him to have a mind ready to turn itself accordingly as the winds and variations of fortune force it, yet, as I have said above, not to diverge from the good if he can avoid doing so, but, if compelled, then to know how to set about it.
cards.whyThisWorks: Machiavelli's advice that a prince must 'appear merciful, faithful, humane, religious, upright' while being ready to 'change to the opposite' creates a sharp verbal irony: the very virtues praised as necessary are simultaneously declared harmful to actually possess, reversing conventional moral wisdom.
cards.skillStrategy: When you spot a reversal—where something expected to be good is called harmful, or something deceptive is called useful—ask yourself what the author is contradicting to find the irony.
evidencePoints: to have them and always to observe them is injurious, and that to appear to have them is useful

a prince, especially a new one, cannot observe all those things for which men are esteemed, being often forced, in order to maintain the state, to act contrary to fidelity, friendship, humanity, and religion
cards.question: Read the following sentence from the passage: 'to have them and always to observe them is injurious, and that to appear to have them is useful.' What reversal in this sentence creates irony?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Machiavelli argues that princes who appear virtuous will eventually become truly virtuous, so the distinction between appearance and reality disappears over time.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Genuinely possessing virtues such as mercy and faithfulness is declared harmful, while merely pretending to have those same virtues is declared beneficial—the opposite of what moral tradition would expect.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Machiavelli warns that appearing virtuous is just as dangerous as being virtuous, because both expose a prince to the same political risks.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The prince is advised to abandon all appearance of virtue so that enemies cannot predict his behavior, making honesty the safest political strategy.

cards.standardTitle: Narrator perspective, irony, and satire
cards.excerpt:
And if those seigniors are considered who have lost their states in Italy in our times, such as the King of Naples, the Duke of Milan, and others, there will be found in them, firstly, one common defect in regard to arms from the causes which have been discussed at length; in the next place, some one of them will be seen, either to have had the people hostile, or if he has had the people friendly, he has not known how to secure the nobles. In the absence of these defects states that have power enough to keep an army in the field cannot be lost.

Philip of Macedon, not the father of Alexander the Great, but he who was conquered by Titus Quintius, had not much territory compared to the greatness of the Romans and of Greece who attacked him, yet being a warlike man who knew how to attract the people and secure the nobles, he sustained the war against his enemies for many years, and if in the end he lost the dominion of some cities, nevertheless he retained the kingdom.
cards.whyThisWorks: Machiavelli creates situational irony by contrasting Philip of Macedon's military disadvantage—far less territory than Rome and Greece—with his successful survival of the war, reversing the expected outcome that a weaker ruler would simply be defeated.
cards.skillStrategy: When you spot a reversal of what you'd expect—a weaker side outlasting a stronger one, or a 'loser' who actually wins something—ask what contradiction Machiavelli is building and what lesson it creates.
evidencePoints: had not much territory compared to the greatness of the Romans and of Greece who attacked him
if in the end he lost the dominion of some cities, nevertheless he retained the kingdom
cards.question: Read the following passage moment: Philip of Macedon 'had not much territory compared to the greatness of the Romans and of Greece who attacked him, yet . . . he sustained the war against his enemies for many years.' What contrast creates irony in Machiavelli's account of Philip?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Philip is introduced as a lesser-known ruler rather than Alexander's famous father, which makes his military record seem untrustworthy compared to the Italian seigniors Machiavelli praises.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Philip commanded far fewer resources than Rome and Greece, yet he preserved his kingdom—the opposite outcome readers would expect from such a mismatched conflict.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Philip lost several cities to his enemies, which confirms the same pattern of failure Machiavelli identified in the King of Naples and the Duke of Milan.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Philip's ability to attract the people contrasts with his failure to secure the nobles, placing him in the same category of rulers who lost their states through a single common defect.

cards.standardTitle: Narrator perspective, irony, and satire
cards.excerpt:
I was not intending to go beyond Italian and recent examples, but I am unwilling to leave out Hiero, the Syracusan, he being one of those I have named above. This man, as I have said, made head of the army by the Syracusans, soon found out that a mercenary soldiery, constituted like our Italian condottieri, was of no use; and it appearing to him that he could neither keep them nor let them go, he had them all cut to pieces, and afterwards made war with his own forces and not with aliens.

I wish also to recall to memory an instance from the Old Testament applicable to this subject. David offered himself to Saul to fight with Goliath, the Philistine champion, and, to give him courage, Saul armed him with his own weapons; which David rejected as soon as he had them on his back, saying he could make no use of them, and that he wished to meet the enemy with his sling and his knife. In conclusion, the arms of others either fall from your back, or they weigh you down, or they bind you fast.
cards.whyThisWorks: The David and Goliath anecdote creates situational irony through reversal: Saul's gift of royal armor—meant to give David courage and advantage—is immediately rejected as a burden, contradicting the expected logic that more protection equals greater strength.
cards.skillStrategy: When you spot a moment where something meant to help actually hinders, ask yourself what the reader expected versus what actually happened—that gap is the irony.
evidencePoints: to give him courage, Saul armed him with his own weapons; which David rejected as soon as he had them on his back
the arms of others either fall from your back, or they weigh you down, or they bind you fast
cards.question: Read the following passage from the excerpt: 'to give him courage, Saul armed him with his own weapons; which David rejected as soon as he had them on his back, saying he could make no use of them.' What reversal in this moment creates irony?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Saul, a king, chooses to arm a shepherd, showing that rank determines who receives the best weapons in battle.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The armor given to David to increase his strength instead immediately becomes something he must discard because it weakens his ability to fight.

choices.label: C
choices.text: David's decision to use a sling and knife proves that simple weapons are always superior to elaborate ones in any conflict.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Saul's willingness to share his own weapons with David shows that generous leaders are ultimately betrayed by those they try to help.

cards.standardTitle: Theme development across a literary text
cards.excerpt:
Upon this the duke, before his departure from Fano, which was to be on 30th December 1502, communicated his designs to eight of his most trusted followers, among whom were Don Michele and the Monsignor d’Euna, who was afterwards cardinal; and he ordered that, as soon as Vitellozzo, Pagolo Orsini, the Duke di Gravina, and Oliverotto should arrive, his followers in pairs should take them one by one, entrusting certain men to certain pairs, who should entertain them until they reached Sinigalia; nor should they be permitted to leave until they came to the duke’s quarters, where they should be seized.

The duke afterwards ordered all his horsemen and infantry, of which there were more than two thousand cavalry and ten thousand footmen, to assemble by daybreak at the Metauro, a river five miles distant from Fano, and await him there. He found himself, therefore, on the last day of December at the Metauro with his men, and having sent a cavalcade of about two hundred horsemen before him, he then moved forward the infantry, whom he accompanied with the rest of the men-at-arms.
cards.whyThisWorks: The excerpt shows Cesare Borgia's meticulous, layered deception—assigning trusted men to entertain targets and massing troops in secret—allowing students to distinguish details that develop the theme of calculated power from true-but-topic-only military logistics.
cards.skillStrategy: Ask yourself: does this detail show HOW the theme is built, or does it just describe what happened without connecting to the central idea?
evidencePoints: his followers in pairs should take them one by one, entrusting certain men to certain pairs, who should entertain them until they reached Sinigalia; nor should they be permitted to leave until they came to the duke's quarters, where they should be seized
communicated his designs to eight of his most trusted followers
cards.question: Which detail from the excerpt most directly develops the theme that effective power depends on concealing one's true intentions until the moment of action?

choices.label: A

choices.label: B
choices.text: The duke's followers were assigned to entertain Vitellozzo and the others as companions while secretly ensuring none could leave before reaching the duke's quarters to be seized.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The duke planned his departure from Fano for the 30th of December 1502, showing that the events described took place at the end of that year.

choices.label: D

cards.standardTitle: Narrator perspective, irony, and satire
cards.excerpt:
But to enable a prince to form an opinion of his servant there is one test which never fails; when you see the servant thinking more of his own interests than of yours, and seeking inwardly his own profit in everything, such a man will never make a good servant, nor will you ever be able to trust him; because he who has the state of another in his hands ought never to think of himself, but always of his prince, and never pay any attention to matters in which the prince is not concerned.

On the other hand, to keep his servant honest the prince ought to study him, honouring him, enriching him, doing him kindnesses, sharing with him the honours and cares; and at the same time let him see that he cannot stand alone, so that many honours may not make him desire more, many riches make him wish for more, and that many cares may make him dread chances. When, therefore, servants, and princes towards servants, are thus disposed, they can trust each other, but when it is otherwise, the end will always be disastrous for either one or the other.
cards.whyThisWorks: Machiavelli creates situational irony by advising the prince to keep his servant honest through lavish rewards and shared honors — the very conditions that could tempt a servant toward self-interest — directly contradicting his earlier warning that a servant who seeks his own profit cannot be trusted.
cards.skillStrategy: When you spot a contradiction between what a character warns against and what they then recommend, ask yourself: does the solution actually recreate the problem? That gap is the irony.
evidencePoints: when you see the servant thinking more of his own interests than of yours...such a man will never make a good servant
to keep his servant honest the prince ought to study him, honouring him, enriching him, doing him kindnesses, sharing with him the honours and cares
cards.question: Read the following passage from The Prince: 'when you see the servant thinking more of his own interests than of yours...such a man will never make a good servant' and 'to keep his servant honest the prince ought to...honouring him, enriching him, doing him kindnesses, sharing with him the honours and cares.' What irony is created by placing these two ideas together?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Machiavelli contradicts himself by first praising loyal servants and then arguing that no servant can ever truly be loyal to a prince.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The prince is told to prevent self-interested servants by showering them with wealth and honors — the very rewards that could fuel the self-interest he warned against.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Machiavelli warns that princes who share honors with servants will eventually lose power, reversing his earlier claim that trust between them is possible.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The servant is expected to think only of the prince, yet the prince is also expected to think only of the servant, making loyalty impossible for either party.

cards.standardTitle: Narrator perspective, irony, and satire
cards.excerpt:
I conclude, therefore that, fortune being changeful and mankind steadfast in their ways, so long as the two are in agreement men are successful, but unsuccessful when they fall out. For my part I consider that it is better to be adventurous than cautious, because fortune is a woman, and if you wish to keep her under it is necessary to beat and ill-use her; and it is seen that she allows herself to be mastered by the adventurous rather than by those who go to work more coldly. She is, therefore, always, woman-like, a lover of young men, because they are less cautious, more violent, and with more audacity command her.

Having carefully considered the subject of the above discourses, and wondering within myself whether the present times were propitious to a new prince, and whether there were elements that would give an opportunity to a wise and virtuous one to introduce a new order of things which would do honour to him and good to the people of this country, it appears to me that so many things concur to favour a new prince that I never knew a time more fit than the present.
cards.whyThisWorks: Machiavelli's claim that fortune must be 'beat and ill-used' to be mastered creates situational irony through reversal: the path to success with an unpredictable, powerful force is not careful reason but violent aggression, directly contradicting the expectation that wisdom and caution lead to control.
cards.skillStrategy: When you spot a reversal—where the expected path to a goal is replaced by its opposite—ask yourself what the reader would normally assume and how the text flips that assumption to create irony.
evidencePoints: it is better to be adventurous than cautious, because fortune is a woman, and if you wish to keep her under it is necessary to beat and ill-use her
she allows herself to be mastered by the adventurous rather than by those who go to work more coldly
cards.question: Read the following passage from the first paragraph: 'it is better to be adventurous than cautious, because fortune is a woman, and if you wish to keep her under it is necessary to beat and ill-use her.' What reversal in this passage creates irony?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Machiavelli praises fortune as a reliable guide, yet immediately warns that fortune is constantly changing, suggesting she cannot be trusted at all.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Machiavelli argues that mastering an unpredictable, powerful force requires not careful reasoning but aggression and violence, reversing the expectation that control comes through caution and wisdom.

choices.label: C

choices.label: D

cards.standardTitle: Theme development across a literary text
cards.excerpt:
A prince, therefore, ought always to take counsel, but only when he wishes and not when others wish; he ought rather to discourage every one from offering advice unless he asks it; but, however, he ought to be a constant inquirer, and afterwards a patient listener concerning the things of which he inquired; also, on learning that any one, on any consideration, has not told him the truth, he should let his anger be felt.

And if there are some who think that a prince who conveys an impression of his wisdom is not so through his own ability, but through the good advisers that he has around him, beyond doubt they are deceived, because this is an axiom which never fails: that a prince who is not wise himself will never take good advice, unless by chance he has yielded his affairs entirely to one person who happens to be a very prudent man. In this case indeed he may be well governed, but it would not be for long, because such a governor would in a short time take away his state from him.
cards.whyThisWorks: The excerpt explicitly develops the theme that true leadership depends on the ruler's own wisdom rather than borrowed counsel, and students must distinguish details that build this theme from true details that merely describe advisory behavior without advancing the central idea.
cards.skillStrategy: Ask yourself: does this detail show WHY the theme is true, or does it just describe something that happens in the passage without connecting to the central idea?

cards.excerpt:
But to enable a prince to form an opinion of his servant there is one test which never fails; when you see the servant thinking more of his own interests than of yours, and seeking inwardly his own profit in everything, such a man will never make a good servant, nor will you ever be able to trust him; because he who has the state of another in his hands ought never to think of himself, but always of his prince, and never pay any attention to matters in which the prince is not concerned.

On the other hand, to keep his servant honest the prince ought to study him, honouring him, enriching him, doing him kindnesses, sharing with him the honours and cares; and at the same time let him see that he cannot stand alone, so that many honours may not make him desire more, many riches make him wish for more, and that many cares may make him dread chances. When, therefore, servants, and princes towards servants, are thus disposed, they can trust each other, but when it is otherwise, the end will always be disastrous for either one or the other.
cards.whyThisWorks: The excerpt presents two contrasting portraits—the self-serving servant and the mutually invested servant—allowing students to distinguish details that develop the theme of loyalty requiring reciprocal obligation from true-but-topical details about wealth or honor.
cards.skillStrategy: Ask yourself: does this detail show WHY loyalty breaks down or holds together, or does it just describe what happens in the relationship without explaining the deeper truth?
evidencePoints: he who has the state of another in his hands ought never to think of himself, but always of his prince
they can trust each other, but when it is otherwise, the end will always be disastrous for either one or the other
cards.question: Which detail from the excerpt most directly develops the theme that genuine loyalty between a leader and a servant depends on mutual obligation rather than self-interest?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The prince enriches his servant and shares honors with him, showing that financial reward is the foundation of a trustworthy relationship.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The servant who thinks of his own profit in everything will never be trusted, while servants and princes who are mutually devoted can trust each other—revealing that loyalty collapses when either party pursues only personal gain.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The prince studies his servant carefully, which shows that a ruler's observational skill is the most important quality in managing those who serve him.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The servant is warned that he cannot stand alone, demonstrating that dependence on the prince is what prevents servants from becoming dangerous rivals.

cards.standardTitle: Narrator perspective, irony, and satire
cards.excerpt:
And as if it were not enough to have aggrandized the Church, and deprived himself of friends, he, wishing to have the kingdom of Naples, divided it with the King of Spain, and where he was the prime arbiter in Italy he takes an associate, so that the ambitious of that country and the malcontents of his own should have somewhere to shelter; and whereas he could have left in the kingdom his own pensioner as king, he drove him out, to put one there who was able to drive him, Louis, out in turn.

The wish to acquire is in truth very natural and common, and men always do so when they can, and for this they will be praised not blamed; but when they cannot do so, yet wish to do so by any means, then there is folly and blame. Therefore, if France could have attacked Naples with her own forces she ought to have done so; if she could not, then she ought not to have divided it. And if the partition which she made with the Venetians in Lombardy was justified by the excuse that by it she got a foothold in Italy, this other partition merited blame, for it had not the excuse of that necessity.
cards.whyThisWorks: Machiavelli's observation that Louis drove out a weak king only to install one 'able to drive him, Louis, out in turn' is a textbook situational irony through reversal: the action meant to secure power directly produces the opposite outcome.
cards.skillStrategy: When you spot a moment where a character's action produces the exact opposite of what they intended, that reversal is the engine of the irony — name what was wanted and what actually resulted.
evidencePoints: he drove him out, to put one there who was able to drive him, Louis, out in turn

the wish to acquire is in truth very natural and common, and men always do so when they can, and for this they will be praised not blamed; but when they cannot do so, yet wish to do so by any means, then there is folly and blame
cards.question: Read this sentence from the excerpt: 'he drove him out, to put one there who was able to drive him, Louis, out in turn.' What contrast or reversal in this sentence creates irony?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Louis removed a weak king to gain sole control of Naples, and the irony is that Spain, not the new king, ultimately claimed the territory.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Louis removed a king to strengthen his own hold on Naples, yet the replacement king was powerful enough to expel Louis himself, so the act of seizing power directly caused Louis to lose it.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Louis divided Naples with Spain to gain an ally, and the irony is that Machiavelli praises this decision while condemning the earlier partition of Lombardy.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Louis wished to acquire Naples because acquiring territory is natural and praiseworthy, yet he is blamed simply for wanting more than France already possessed.

cards.standardTitle: Theme development across a literary text
cards.excerpt:
I conclude, therefore that, fortune being changeful and mankind steadfast in their ways, so long as the two are in agreement men are successful, but unsuccessful when they fall out. For my part I consider that it is better to be adventurous than cautious, because fortune is a woman, and if you wish to keep her under it is necessary to beat and ill-use her; and it is seen that she allows herself to be mastered by the adventurous rather than by those who go to work more coldly. She is, therefore, always, woman-like, a lover of young men, because they are less cautious, more violent, and with more audacity command her.

Having carefully considered the subject of the above discourses, and wondering within myself whether the present times were propitious to a new prince, and whether there were elements that would give an opportunity to a wise and virtuous one to introduce a new order of things which would do honour to him and good to the people of this country, it appears to me that so many things concur to favour a new prince that I never knew a time more fit than the present.
cards.whyThisWorks: The excerpt explicitly develops the theme that bold, aggressive action—not caution—is the path to mastering fortune, allowing students to distinguish details that build this theme from true details that merely describe fortune or the political moment.
cards.skillStrategy: Ask yourself: does this detail show WHY boldness beats caution, or does it just describe something true about the passage without connecting to that argument?
evidencePoints: it is better to be adventurous than cautious, because fortune is a woman, and if you wish to keep her under it is necessary to beat and ill-use her
she allows herself to be mastered by the adventurous rather than by those who go to work more coldly
cards.question: Which detail from the excerpt most directly develops Machiavelli's theme that bold, forceful action is necessary to control fortune?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Machiavelli observes that fortune is changeful while mankind remains steadfast in their ways, showing that humans and fortune are fundamentally different in nature.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Machiavelli argues that fortune 'allows herself to be mastered by the adventurous rather than by those who go to work more coldly,' directly linking aggressive action to success over fortune.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Machiavelli wonders whether the present times were propitious to a new prince who could introduce a new order of things that would do honour to him.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Machiavelli concludes that men are successful when their personal ways are in agreement with fortune and unsuccessful when the two fall out.

cards.standardTitle: Theme development across a literary text
cards.excerpt:
I say at once there are fewer difficulties in holding hereditary states, and those long accustomed to the family of their prince, than new ones; for it is sufficient only not to transgress the customs of his ancestors, and to deal prudently with circumstances as they arise, for a prince of average powers to maintain himself in his state, unless he be deprived of it by some extraordinary and excessive force; and if he should be so deprived of it, whenever anything sinister happens to the usurper, he will regain it.

We have in Italy, for example, the Duke of Ferrara, who could not have withstood the attacks of the Venetians in ’84, nor those of Pope Julius in ’10, unless he had been long established in his dominions. For the hereditary prince has less cause and less necessity to offend; hence it happens that he will be more loved; and unless extraordinary vices cause him to be hated, it is reasonable to expect that his subjects will be naturally well disposed towards him; and in the antiquity and duration of his rule the memories and motives that make for change are lost, for one change always leaves the toothing for another.
cards.whyThisWorks: The excerpt contains both theme-developing details (the hereditary prince's continuity breeds love and erases motives for change) and true-but-topic-only details (the Duke of Ferrara example names a historical fact without advancing the theme of stability through continuity), giving students a clear test of whether they can distinguish evidence that proves the theme from evidence that merely illustrates the topic.
cards.skillStrategy: Ask yourself: does this detail show WHY continuity creates stability, or does it just mention a ruler or event connected to the topic?
evidencePoints: the hereditary prince has less cause and less necessity to offend; hence it happens that he will be more loved
in the antiquity and duration of his rule the memories and motives that make for change are lost, for one change always leaves the toothing for another
cards.question: Machiavelli states that 'one change always leaves the toothing for another.' Which detail from the excerpt most directly develops the theme that lasting political stability depends on continuity rather than change?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The Duke of Ferrara withstood attacks from the Venetians in '84 and from Pope Julius in '10 because he had long been established in his dominions.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Because the hereditary prince has less cause to offend his subjects, he is more loved, and over time 'the memories and motives that make for change are lost.'

choices.label: C
choices.text: A prince of average powers can maintain himself in his state as long as no 'extraordinary and excessive force' deprives him of it.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Whenever anything sinister happens to the usurper, the deprived hereditary prince will regain his state.

cards.standardTitle: Narrator perspective, irony, and satire
cards.excerpt:
But let us come to Alexander, who was a man of such great goodness, that among the other praises which are accorded him is this, that in the fourteen years he held the empire no one was ever put to death by him unjudged; nevertheless, being considered effeminate and a man who allowed himself to be governed by his mother, he became despised, the army conspired against him, and murdered him.

Turning now to the opposite characters of Commodus, Severus, Antoninus Caracalla, and Maximinus, you will find them all cruel and rapacious-men who, to satisfy their soldiers, did not hesitate to commit every kind of iniquity against the people; and all, except Severus, came to a bad end; but in Severus there was so much valour that, keeping the soldiers friendly, although the people were oppressed by him, he reigned successfully; for his valour made him so much admired in the sight of the soldiers and people that the latter were kept in a way astonished and awed and the former respectful and satisfied. And because the actions of this man, as a new prince, were great, I wish to show briefly that he knew well how to counterfeit the fox and the lion, which natures, as I said above, it is necessary for a prince to imitate.
cards.whyThisWorks: The excerpt explicitly contrasts Alexander's just rule ending in murder with Severus's oppressive rule ending in success, creating textbook situational irony through direct reversal of expected outcomes.
cards.skillStrategy: When you spot a 'nevertheless' or 'but,' ask yourself whether the outcome is the opposite of what the cause should logically produce — that reversal is the irony.
evidencePoints: no one was ever put to death by him unjudged; nevertheless...he became despised, the army conspired against him, and murdered him
the people were oppressed by him, he reigned successfully
cards.question: Machiavelli writes that Alexander ensured 'no one was ever put to death by him unjudged; nevertheless...he became despised, the army conspired against him, and murdered him.' What makes this statement ironic?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Alexander's fourteen-year reign was shorter than expected for a ruler praised for his goodness, suggesting his virtues were not genuine.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Alexander's strict commitment to justice — the very quality Machiavelli praises — produced the opposite of its expected reward: not security, but murder at the hands of his own army.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Alexander was considered effeminate because he obeyed his mother, which directly caused his soldiers to conspire against him rather than his judicial record.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Alexander's goodness earned him widespread praise from the people, yet Machiavelli argues that popular praise alone was never enough to protect any prince.

cards.standardTitle: Theme development across a literary text
cards.excerpt: Charles the Seventh, the father of King Louis the Eleventh, having by good fortune and valour liberated France from the English, recognized the necessity of being armed with forces of his own, and he established in his kingdom ordinances concerning men-at-arms and infantry. Afterwards his son, King Louis, abolished the infantry and began to enlist the Switzers, which mistake, followed by others, is, as is now seen, a source of peril to that kingdom; because, having raised the reputation of the Switzers, he has entirely diminished the value of his own arms, for he has destroyed the infantry altogether; and his men-at-arms he has subordinated to others, for, being as they are so accustomed to fight along with Switzers, it does not appear that they can now conquer without them. Hence it arises that the French cannot stand against the Switzers, and without the Switzers they do not come off well against others. The armies of the French have thus become mixed, partly mercenary and partly national, both of which arms together are much better than mercenaries alone or auxiliaries alone, but much inferior to one’s own forces. And this example proves it, for the kingdom of France would be unconquerable if the ordinance of Charles had been enlarged or maintained.
cards.whyThisWorks: The excerpt contrasts Charles VII's self-reliant military ordinances with Louis XI's dependence on Swiss mercenaries, giving students a clear thematic claim—that relying on one's own forces is essential to lasting power—and multiple details to evaluate as either developing that theme or merely matching the topic of military history.
cards.skillStrategy: Ask yourself: does this detail show WHY the theme is true, or does it just describe what happened without connecting to the central lesson?
evidencePoints: the kingdom of France would be unconquerable if the ordinance of Charles had been enlarged or maintained
having raised the reputation of the Switzers, he has entirely diminished the value of his own arms
cards.question: The passage develops the theme that a ruler's power depends on maintaining forces of his own. Which detail from the passage most directly develops this theme rather than simply describing the military situation in France?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Charles the Seventh liberated France from the English through good fortune and valour, making him a celebrated king in French history.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Louis's decision to abolish his own infantry and rely on the Switzers left France unable to conquer without them, proving that surrendering self-reliance destroys military strength.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The armies of France became mixed, consisting of both mercenary and national soldiers fighting alongside one another.

choices.label: D
choices.text: King Louis the Eleventh was the son of Charles the Seventh and succeeded him as ruler of the French kingdom.

cards.standardTitle: Narrator perspective, irony, and satire
cards.excerpt:
For this reason a prince ought to take care that he never lets anything slip from his lips that is not replete with the above-named five qualities, that he may appear to him who sees and hears him altogether merciful, faithful, humane, upright, and religious. There is nothing more necessary to appear to have than this last quality, inasmuch as men judge generally more by the eye than by the hand, because it belongs to everybody to see you, to few to come in touch with you. Every one sees what you appear to be, few really know what you are, and those few dare not oppose themselves to the opinion of the many, who have the majesty of the state to defend them; and in the actions of all men, and especially of princes, which it is not prudent to challenge, one judges by the result.

For that reason, let a prince have the credit of conquering and holding his state, the means will always be considered honest, and he will be praised by everybody; because the vulgar are always taken by what a thing seems to be and by what comes of it; and in the world there are only the vulgar, for the few find a place there only when the many have no ground to rest on.
cards.whyThisWorks: Machiavelli's advice that a prince need only 'appear' virtuous while the 'means will always be considered honest' as long as he wins creates sharp situational irony: the very qualities society prizes—mercy, faithfulness, uprightness—are reduced to performances, and dishonest means become 'honest' through success alone.
cards.skillStrategy: Look for a moment where what is said or praised directly contradicts what is actually true or happening—that gap between appearance and reality is where irony lives.
evidencePoints: he may appear to him who sees and hears him altogether merciful, faithful, humane, upright, and religious
let a prince have the credit of conquering and holding his state, the means will always be considered honest
cards.question: Read the following passage from The Prince: 'let a prince have the credit of conquering and holding his state, the means will always be considered honest, and he will be praised by everybody.' What contradiction in this statement creates irony?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Machiavelli praises the vulgar crowd for their wisdom, yet later admits they can only judge by appearances, suggesting he genuinely respects their judgment.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Machiavelli declares that dishonest means become 'honest' simply because a prince succeeds, reversing the ordinary understanding that honesty is a quality of the action itself, not its outcome.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Machiavelli argues that princes are judged by the eye rather than the hand, meaning that physical appearance matters more than a prince's military strength.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Machiavelli warns that the few who truly know a prince dare not speak, suggesting that silence among advisors is the greatest threat to a prince's rule.

cards.excerpt:

The wish to acquire is in truth very natural and common, and men always do so when they can, and for this they will be praised not blamed; but when they cannot do so, yet wish to do so by any means, then there is folly and blame. cards.question: Machiavelli states that Louis 'drove him out, to put one there who was able to drive him, Louis, out in turn.' Which of the following details from the excerpt most directly uses this moment to develop the theme that acting beyond one's actual power produces self-defeating consequences?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Louis divided the kingdom of Naples with the King of Spain, which gave Spain a permanent presence in Italian affairs.

choices.label: B
choices.text: By installing a ruler strong enough to expel him, Louis converted his own ambition into the direct cause of his removal from Italy.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The partition France made with the Venetians in Lombardy was justified because it gave France a necessary foothold in Italy.

choices.label: D
