cards.standardTitle: Narrator perspective, irony, and satire
cards.excerpt:
I compare her to one of those raging rivers, which when in flood overflows the plains, sweeping away trees and buildings, bearing away the soil from place to place; everything flies before it, all yield to its violence, without being able in any way to withstand it; and yet, though its nature be such, it does not follow therefore that men, when the weather becomes fair, shall not make provision, both with defences and barriers, in such a manner that, rising again, the waters may pass away by canal, and their force be neither so unrestrained nor so dangerous. So it happens with fortune, who shows her power where valour has not prepared to resist her, and thither she turns her forces where she knows that barriers and defences have not been raised to constrain her.

And if you will consider Italy, which is the seat of these changes, and which has given to them their impulse, you will see it to be an open country without barriers and without any defence. For if it had been defended by proper valour, as are Germany, Spain, and France, either this invasion would not have made the great changes it has made or it would not have come at all. And this I consider enough to say concerning resistance to fortune in general.
cards.whyThisWorks: Machiavelli's river metaphor creates situational irony by depicting fortune as an overwhelming, unstoppable force—yet immediately reversing that claim by arguing that human preparation (barriers and canals) can neutralize her power, contradicting the very helplessness he just described.
cards.skillStrategy: When you spot a reversal—where the text first says one thing is true, then shows the opposite is also true—ask yourself what contradiction the author is building and what point that tension makes.
evidencePoints: everything flies before it, all yield to its violence, without being able in any way to withstand it

it does not follow therefore that men, when the weather becomes fair, shall not make provision, both with defences and barriers, in such a manner that, rising again, the waters may pass away by canal, and their force be neither so unrestrained nor so dangerous
cards.question: Read the following passage from the excerpt: 'everything flies before it, all yield to its violence, without being able in any way to withstand it.' How does the rest of the paragraph create irony through contrast with this statement?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Machiavelli confirms that fortune is truly unstoppable by showing that Italy, Germany, Spain, and France have all failed to resist her invasions equally.

choices.label: B
choices.text: After declaring that nothing can withstand fortune's violence, Machiavelli immediately argues that human preparation—barriers, defences, and canals—can limit and redirect that same force, reversing the claim of total helplessness.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Machiavelli uses the river's destruction of trees and buildings to show that fortune punishes only nations that are already weak, so stronger nations never face her power at all.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The description of the raging river is meant to praise fortune's power as something men should admire rather than resist, which is why Machiavelli points to Italy as a model.

cards.standardTitle: Theme development across a literary text
cards.excerpt:
Considering the difficulties which men have had to hold to a newly acquired state, some might wonder how, seeing that Alexander the Great became the master of Asia in a few years, and died whilst it was scarcely settled (whence it might appear reasonable that the whole empire would have rebelled), nevertheless his successors maintained themselves, and had to meet no other difficulty than that which arose among themselves from their own ambitions.

I answer that the principalities of which one has record are found to be governed in two different ways; either by a prince, with a body of servants, who assist him to govern the kingdom as ministers by his favour and permission; or by a prince and barons, who hold that dignity by antiquity of blood and not by the grace of the prince. Such barons have states and their own subjects, who recognize them as lords and hold them in natural affection. Those states that are governed by a prince and his servants hold their prince in more consideration, because in all the country there is no one who is recognized as superior to him, and if they yield obedience to another they do it as to a minister and official, and they do not bear him any particular affection.
cards.whyThisWorks: The excerpt contrasts two governance structures and explicitly states that subjects in prince-and-servant states hold their prince 'in more consideration,' giving students a clear thematic claim to test against true-but-off-topic details.
cards.skillStrategy: Find the detail that directly explains WHY the theme is true, not just a detail that mentions the same topic.
evidencePoints: Those states that are governed by a prince and his servants hold their prince in more consideration, because in all the country there is no one who is recognized as superior to him
if they yield obedience to another they do it as to a minister and official, and they do not bear him any particular affection
cards.question: Machiavelli states that subjects in prince-and-servant states 'hold their prince in more consideration' than subjects in other states do. Which detail from the excerpt most directly develops the theme that centralized authority produces stronger, more durable loyalty?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Alexander the Great became master of Asia in a few years and died whilst it was scarcely settled, leaving his successors to face difficulties arising from their own ambitions.

choices.label: B
choices.text: In prince-and-servant states, no one in the country is recognized as superior to the prince, so when subjects obey anyone else, they do so only as to a minister and bear him no particular affection.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Barons hold their dignity by antiquity of blood and not by the grace of the prince, and their own subjects recognize them as lords and hold them in natural affection.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Alexander's successors maintained themselves after his death despite the empire being scarcely settled at the time he died.

cards.standardTitle: Narrator perspective, irony, and satire
cards.excerpt:
The contrary happens in kingdoms governed like that of France, because one can easily enter there by gaining over some baron of the kingdom, for one always finds malcontents and such as desire a change. Such men, for the reasons given, can open the way into the state and render the victory easy; but if you wish to hold it afterwards, you meet with infinite difficulties, both from those who have assisted you and from those you have crushed. Nor is it enough for you to have exterminated the family of the prince, because the lords that remain make themselves the heads of fresh movements against you, and as you are unable either to satisfy or exterminate them, that state is lost whenever time brings the opportunity.

Now if you will consider what was the nature of the government of Darius, you will find it similar to the kingdom of the Turk, and therefore it was only necessary for Alexander, first to overthrow him in the field, and then to take the country from him. After which victory, Darius being killed, the state remained secure to Alexander, for the above reasons. And if his successors had been united they would have enjoyed it securely and at their ease, for there were no tumults raised in the kingdom except those they provoked themselves.
cards.whyThisWorks: Machiavelli creates situational irony by showing that the very allies who make conquest easy become the source of 'infinite difficulties' afterward, reversing the expected benefit of having helpers into a liability.
cards.skillStrategy: When you spot a reversal—where something that should help actually hurts, or something that should be hard turns out easy—ask yourself what expectation is being flipped, because that contrast is the irony.
evidencePoints: such men, for the reasons given, can open the way into the state and render the victory easy
if you wish to hold it afterwards, you meet with infinite difficulties, both from those who have assisted you and from those you have crushed
cards.question: Read the following passage from the first paragraph: 'Such men, for the reasons given, can open the way into the state and render the victory easy; but if you wish to hold it afterwards, you meet with infinite difficulties, both from those who have assisted you and from those you have crushed.' What contrast in this passage creates irony?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The malcontents desire change before the conquest but become loyal supporters once the new ruler takes power.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The allies who make conquest easy become a source of the very difficulties that threaten the conqueror's hold on power.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The crushed enemies prove more dangerous than the assisting lords because they have stronger motivation for revenge.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Entering the kingdom requires gaining over barons, yet holding it requires exterminating the prince's entire family.

cards.standardTitle: Theme development across a literary text
cards.excerpt:
Hence it is to be remarked that, in seizing a state, the usurper ought to examine closely into all those injuries which it is necessary for him to inflict, and to do them all at one stroke so as not to have to repeat them daily; and thus by not unsettling men he will be able to reassure them, and win them to himself by benefits. He who does otherwise, either from timidity or evil advice, is always compelled to keep the knife in his hand; neither can he rely on his subjects, nor can they attach themselves to him, owing to their continued and repeated wrongs. For injuries ought to be done all at one time, so that, being tasted less, they offend less; benefits ought to be given little by little, so that the flavour of them may last longer.

And above all things, a prince ought to live amongst his people in such a way that no unexpected circumstances, whether of good or evil, shall make him change; because if the necessity for this comes in troubled times, you are too late for harsh measures; and mild ones will not help you, for they will be considered as forced from you, and no one will be under any obligation to you for them.
cards.whyThisWorks: The excerpt presents a clear theme about the strategic management of power through concentrated harm and gradual reward, allowing students to distinguish details that develop this theme from true details that merely relate to the topic of ruling.
cards.skillStrategy: Ask yourself: does this detail show HOW the theme is built, or does it just mention something true about the topic? Only details that directly support the central idea count as theme evidence.
evidencePoints: injuries ought to be done all at one time, so that, being tasted less, they offend less; benefits ought to be given little by little, so that the flavour of them may last longer.
a prince ought to live amongst his people in such a way that no unexpected circumstances, whether of good or evil, shall make him change
cards.question: Which detail from the excerpt most directly develops Machiavelli's theme that a ruler's long-term power depends on deliberate control over how subjects experience harm and reward?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Machiavelli notes that a prince who acts from timidity or evil advice is always compelled to keep the knife in his hand, showing that weak rulers exist and face consequences.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Machiavelli argues that injuries done all at once are 'tasted less' and 'offend less,' while benefits given gradually allow their 'flavour' to last longer, showing that timing shapes whether subjects submit or resist.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Machiavelli advises that a prince should examine closely all the injuries he must inflict before seizing a state, indicating that rulers must plan carefully before taking power.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Machiavelli warns that in troubled times mild measures will be considered forced and earn no obligation, showing that crises make governing more difficult.

cards.standardTitle: Narrator perspective, irony, and satire
cards.excerpt: Thus Castruccio passed from the house of Messer Antonio the priest to the house of Messer Francesco Guinigi the soldier, and it was astonishing to find that in a very short time he manifested all that virtue and bearing which we are accustomed to associate with a true gentleman. In the first place he became an accomplished horseman, and could manage with ease the most fiery charger, and in all jousts and tournaments, although still a youth, he was observed beyond all others, and he excelled in all exercises of strength and dexterity. But what enhanced so much the charm of these accomplishments, was the delightful modesty which enabled him to avoid offence in either act or word to others, for he was deferential to the great men, modest with his equals, and courteous to his inferiors. These gifts made him beloved, not only by all the Guinigi family, but by all Lucca. When Castruccio had reached his eighteenth year, the Ghibellines were driven from Pavia by the Guelphs, and Messer Francesco was sent by the Visconti to assist the Ghibellines, and with him went Castruccio, in charge of his forces. Castruccio gave ample proof of his prudence and courage in this expedition, acquiring greater reputation than any other captain, and his name and fame were known, not only in Pavia, but throughout all Lombardy.
cards.whyThisWorks: The passage creates situational irony through reversal: Castruccio moves from a priest's house to a soldier's house and immediately displays every virtue 'we are accustomed to associate with a true gentleman,' implying that the martial, worldly environment—not the religious one—produces moral and social excellence, which contradicts the expected association of virtue with the church.
cards.skillStrategy: When looking for irony, ask yourself: does the outcome contradict what you would normally expect given the setup? If so, that reversal is where the irony lives.
evidencePoints: Thus Castruccio passed from the house of Messer Antonio the priest to the house of Messer Francesco Guinigi the soldier
it was astonishing to find that in a very short time he manifested all that virtue and bearing which we are accustomed to associate with a true gentleman
cards.question: Read the following sentence from the passage: 'Thus Castruccio passed from the house of Messer Antonio the priest to the house of Messer Francesco Guinigi the soldier, and it was astonishing to find that in a very short time he manifested all that virtue and bearing which we are accustomed to associate with a true gentleman.' What contrast in this sentence creates irony?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Castruccio is described as both modest and courageous, two qualities that seem to contradict each other in a young soldier.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Castruccio leaves a priest's household—where virtue would conventionally be cultivated—and immediately develops the qualities of a true gentleman under a soldier's roof, reversing the expected source of moral refinement.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Castruccio is praised for his deferential treatment of great men, yet he also excels in tournaments, suggesting his gentleness conflicts with his physical dominance.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Castruccio earns fame throughout all Lombardy despite beginning his military career as a youth still under someone else's command.

cards.standardTitle: Theme development across a literary text
cards.excerpt:
But let us come to Alexander, who was a man of such great goodness, that among the other praises which are accorded him is this, that in the fourteen years he held the empire no one was ever put to death by him unjudged; nevertheless, being considered effeminate and a man who allowed himself to be governed by his mother, he became despised, the army conspired against him, and murdered him.

Turning now to the opposite characters of Commodus, Severus, Antoninus Caracalla, and Maximinus, you will find them all cruel and rapacious-men who, to satisfy their soldiers, did not hesitate to commit every kind of iniquity against the people; and all, except Severus, came to a bad end; but in Severus there was so much valour that, keeping the soldiers friendly, although the people were oppressed by him, he reigned successfully; for his valour made him so much admired in the sight of the soldiers and people that the latter were kept in a way astonished and awed and the former respectful and satisfied. And because the actions of this man, as a new prince, were great, I wish to show briefly that he knew well how to counterfeit the fox and the lion, which natures, as I said above, it is necessary for a prince to imitate.
cards.whyThisWorks: The excerpt contrasts Alexander's just but despised reign with Severus's cruel but successful one, giving students concrete evidence to distinguish details that develop the theme—that a prince's survival depends on commanding fear and admiration, not on moral virtue—from true details that merely describe the rulers.
cards.skillStrategy: Ask yourself: does this detail show WHY a ruler succeeded or failed, or does it just describe what he did without connecting to that outcome?
evidencePoints: being considered effeminate and a man who allowed himself to be governed by his mother, he became despised, the army conspired against him, and murdered him
his valour made him so much admired in the sight of the soldiers and people that the latter were kept in a way astonished and awed and the former respectful and satisfied
cards.question: Which detail from the excerpt most directly develops the theme that a prince's survival depends on commanding admiration and fear rather than practicing justice?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Alexander ruled for fourteen years and never put anyone to death without a proper judgment, demonstrating his commitment to lawful governance.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Severus kept his soldiers friendly and left the people 'astonished and awed,' and because of this he 'reigned successfully' despite oppressing the people.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Commodus, Antoninus Caracalla, and Maximinus are described as cruel and rapacious men who committed iniquities against the people to satisfy their soldiers.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Machiavelli identifies Severus as a 'new prince' whose actions were great and worthy of brief examination.

cards.standardTitle: Narrator perspective, irony, and satire
cards.excerpt:
From these causes it arose that Marcus, Pertinax, and Alexander, being all men of modest life, lovers of justice, enemies to cruelty, humane, and benignant, came to a sad end except Marcus; he alone lived and died honoured, because he had succeeded to the throne by hereditary title, and owed nothing either to the soldiers or the people; and afterwards, being possessed of many virtues which made him respected, he always kept both orders in their places whilst he lived, and was neither hated nor despised.

But Pertinax was created emperor against the wishes of the soldiers, who, being accustomed to live licentiously under Commodus, could not endure the honest life to which Pertinax wished to reduce them; thus, having given cause for hatred, to which hatred there was added contempt for his old age, he was overthrown at the very beginning of his administration. And here it should be noted that hatred is acquired as much by good works as by bad ones, therefore, as I said before, a prince wishing to keep his state is very often forced to do evil; for when that body is corrupt whom you think you have need of to maintain yourself—it may be either the people or the soldiers or the nobles—you have to submit to its humours and to gratify them, and then good works will do you harm.
cards.whyThisWorks: Machiavelli's claim that 'hatred is acquired as much by good works as by bad ones' directly reverses the expected moral logic that virtuous rulers earn loyalty, creating a sharp situational irony illustrated by Pertinax's downfall.
cards.skillStrategy: When you spot a reversal of what you'd normally expect—like good behavior causing harm instead of reward—ask yourself what the contrast reveals about the author's argument.
evidencePoints: hatred is acquired as much by good works as by bad ones

Pertinax was created emperor against the wishes of the soldiers, who, being accustomed to live licentiously under Commodus, could not endure the honest life to which Pertinax wished to reduce them; thus, having given cause for hatred
cards.question: Which statement best identifies the irony created by the contrast in the second paragraph?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Pertinax failed because he was too old to command the soldiers' respect, while younger rulers like Marcus succeeded through physical strength.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Pertinax's honest and virtuous conduct—the very qualities expected to earn loyalty—instead produced the hatred that destroyed his rule.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Marcus survived because he was more willing than Pertinax to use cruelty, proving that only ruthless rulers can hold power.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The soldiers' contempt for Pertinax arose from his failure to reward them financially, not from any moral difference between his reign and Commodus's.

cards.standardTitle: Central idea and supporting evidence
cards.excerpt:
A prince, therefore, ought always to take counsel, but only when he wishes and not when others wish; he ought rather to discourage every one from offering advice unless he asks it; but, however, he ought to be a constant inquirer, and afterwards a patient listener concerning the things of which he inquired; also, on learning that any one, on any consideration, has not told him the truth, he should let his anger be felt.

And if there are some who think that a prince who conveys an impression of his wisdom is not so through his own ability, but through the good advisers that he has around him, beyond doubt they are deceived, because this is an axiom which never fails: that a prince who is not wise himself will never take good advice, unless by chance he has yielded his affairs entirely to one person who happens to be a very prudent man. In this case indeed he may be well governed, but it would not be for long, because such a governor would in a short time take away his state from him.
cards.whyThisWorks: The two paragraphs build a single argument—that a prince's wisdom must be his own, not borrowed—making them ideal for distinguishing a central idea from isolated details or topic labels.
cards.skillStrategy: Ask yourself: what claim do BOTH paragraphs keep returning to? That claim, not a single detail from one paragraph, is the central idea.
evidencePoints: a prince who is not wise himself will never take good advice
he ought rather to discourage every one from offering advice unless he asks it
cards.question: Machiavelli states 'a prince who is not wise himself will never take good advice' and also insists a prince must control when and whether counsel is offered. What central idea do these two points together support?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A prince's greatest danger is an adviser who withholds the truth, so rulers must punish dishonesty to maintain good counsel.

choices.label: B
choices.text: A prince's ability to govern well depends on his own judgment, because neither the advice he receives nor the advisers around him can replace his personal wisdom.

choices.label: C
choices.text: A prince who relies entirely on one prudent governor can be well governed, making the selection of a single trusted adviser the key to stable rule.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Princes should seek counsel constantly and listen patiently, since gathering wide advice from many sources is what produces wise decisions.

cards.standardTitle: Theme development across a literary text
cards.excerpt:
For this reason a prince ought to take care that he never lets anything slip from his lips that is not replete with the above-named five qualities, that he may appear to him who sees and hears him altogether merciful, faithful, humane, upright, and religious. There is nothing more necessary to appear to have than this last quality, inasmuch as men judge generally more by the eye than by the hand, because it belongs to everybody to see you, to few to come in touch with you. Every one sees what you appear to be, few really know what you are, and those few dare not oppose themselves to the opinion of the many, who have the majesty of the state to defend them; and in the actions of all men, and especially of princes, which it is not prudent to challenge, one judges by the result.

For that reason, let a prince have the credit of conquering and holding his state, the means will always be considered honest, and he will be praised by everybody; because the vulgar are always taken by what a thing seems to be and by what comes of it; and in the world there are only the vulgar, for the few find a place there only when the many have no ground to rest on.
cards.whyThisWorks: The excerpt contains two competing types of details—those that merely describe political reality (e.g., few people know a prince personally) and those that directly build the theme that appearances and outcomes override truth—allowing students to practice rejecting true-but-topic-only details in favor of theme-developing evidence.
cards.skillStrategy: Ask yourself: does this detail show WHY appearances and results replace truth in politics, or does it just describe a fact about how princes operate?
evidencePoints: the vulgar are always taken by what a thing seems to be and by what comes of it
let a prince have the credit of conquering and holding his state, the means will always be considered honest, and he will be praised by everybody
cards.question: Machiavelli closes the passage with the claim that 'let a prince have the credit of conquering and holding his state, the means will always be considered honest.' Which earlier detail from the excerpt most directly develops the same theme as this claim?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Machiavelli lists five qualities—merciful, faithful, humane, upright, and religious—that a prince must appear to possess, cataloguing the specific virtues rulers are expected to perform.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Machiavelli states that 'the vulgar are always taken by what a thing seems to be and by what comes of it,' showing that the majority of people judge rulers by surface impressions and results rather than by actual character or methods.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Machiavelli observes that 'it belongs to everybody to see you, to few to come in touch with you,' establishing that a prince's personal contact with subjects is limited by the nature of political life.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Machiavelli notes that 'men judge generally more by the eye than by the hand,' explaining that sight is a more common human faculty than touch when evaluating others.

cards.standardTitle: Narrator perspective, irony, and satire
cards.excerpt:
And the duke succeeded so well in this that they sent Signor Pagolo to him to negotiate for a reconciliation, and they brought their army to a standstill. But the duke did not stop his preparations, and took every care to provide himself with cavalry and infantry, and that such preparations might not be apparent to the others, he sent his troops in separate parties to every part of the Romagna. In the meanwhile there came also to him five hundred French lancers, and although he found himself sufficiently strong to take vengeance on his enemies in open war, he considered that it would be safer and more advantageous to outwit them, and for this reason he did not stop the work of reconciliation.

And that this might be effected the duke concluded a peace with them in which he confirmed their former covenants; he gave them four thousand ducats at once; he promised not to injure the Bentivogli; and he formed an alliance with Giovanni; and moreover he would not force them to come personally into his presence unless it pleased them to do so. On the other hand, they promised to restore to him the duchy of Urbino and other places seized by them, to serve him in all his expeditions, and not to make war against or ally themselves with any one without his permission.
cards.whyThisWorks: The excerpt creates situational irony through a clear reversal: the duke publicly pursues peace and reconciliation while secretly and continuously preparing for war, making his stated intentions the opposite of his actual actions.
cards.skillStrategy: When you spot a character saying one thing while doing the opposite, ask yourself what the contrast reveals — that gap between appearance and reality is where irony lives.
evidencePoints: he did not stop the work of reconciliation
he considered that it would be safer and more advantageous to outwit them
cards.question: Read the following passage detail: 'he considered that it would be safer and more advantageous to outwit them, and for this reason he did not stop the work of reconciliation.' What irony is created by this statement?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The duke's enemies believe he is weak, yet he openly declares his military strength to intimidate them into surrendering.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The duke pursues peace negotiations precisely because he intends to deceive his enemies, making reconciliation itself the instrument of betrayal.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The duke's enemies send Signor Pagolo to negotiate, not realizing the duke has already decided to abandon the Romagna entirely.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The duke promises not to injure the Bentivogli, yet he immediately breaks this promise by launching an open military attack.

cards.standardTitle: Central idea and supporting evidence
cards.excerpt:
I say at once there are fewer difficulties in holding hereditary states, and those long accustomed to the family of their prince, than new ones; for it is sufficient only not to transgress the customs of his ancestors, and to deal prudently with circumstances as they arise, for a prince of average powers to maintain himself in his state, unless he be deprived of it by some extraordinary and excessive force; and if he should be so deprived of it, whenever anything sinister happens to the usurper, he will regain it.

We have in Italy, for example, the Duke of Ferrara, who could not have withstood the attacks of the Venetians in ’84, nor those of Pope Julius in ’10, unless he had been long established in his dominions. For the hereditary prince has less cause and less necessity to offend; hence it happens that he will be more loved; and unless extraordinary vices cause him to be hated, it is reasonable to expect that his subjects will be naturally well disposed towards him; and in the antiquity and duration of his rule the memories and motives that make for change are lost, for one change always leaves the toothing for another.
cards.whyThisWorks: The excerpt opens with a direct claim ('I say at once there are fewer difficulties in holding hereditary states') and then supports it with the Duke of Ferrara example and the reasoning about loyalty, giving students a clear central idea to distinguish from isolated details or topic labels.
cards.skillStrategy: Find the author's opening claim, then check whether each answer choice restates that claim as a complete idea—not just a topic word or a single supporting detail.
evidencePoints: I say at once there are fewer difficulties in holding hereditary states, and those long accustomed to the family of their prince, than new ones
the hereditary prince has less cause and less necessity to offend; hence it happens that he will be more loved
cards.question: Machiavelli opens with the claim 'I say at once there are fewer difficulties in holding hereditary states.' Which statement most accurately expresses the central idea that both paragraphs develop from that opening claim?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The Duke of Ferrara's survival against Venice and Pope Julius proves that military strength is the most important quality a hereditary prince can possess.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Hereditary rulers face fewer threats to their power because long-established rule naturally produces loyalty among subjects and removes the need for actions that cause resentment.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Any prince, whether hereditary or new, will lose his state if he is confronted by an extraordinary and excessive force from a foreign power.

choices.label: D
choices.text: A hereditary prince must actively follow his ancestors' customs and suppress change, or his subjects will eventually turn against him.

cards.standardTitle: Theme development across a literary text
cards.excerpt:
I compare her to one of those raging rivers, which when in flood overflows the plains, sweeping away trees and buildings, bearing away the soil from place to place; everything flies before it, all yield to its violence, without being able in any way to withstand it; and yet, though its nature be such, it does not follow therefore that men, when the weather becomes fair, shall not make provision, both with defences and barriers, in such a manner that, rising again, the waters may pass away by canal, and their force be neither so unrestrained nor so dangerous. So it happens with fortune, who shows her power where valour has not prepared to resist her, and thither she turns her forces where she knows that barriers and defences have not been raised to constrain her.

And if you will consider Italy, which is the seat of these changes, and which has given to them their impulse, you will see it to be an open country without barriers and without any defence. For if it had been defended by proper valour, as are Germany, Spain, and France, either this invasion would not have made the great changes it has made or it would not have come at all. And this I consider enough to say concerning resistance to fortune in general.
cards.whyThisWorks: The excerpt explicitly develops the theme that human preparation and valor can limit fortune's destructive power, while also offering true-but-topic-only details (like Italy's geography) that students must distinguish from theme-developing evidence.
cards.skillStrategy: Ask yourself: does this detail show how the theme is built, or does it just describe what the passage is about?
evidencePoints: it does not follow therefore that men, when the weather becomes fair, shall not make provision, both with defences and barriers, in such a manner that, rising again, the waters may pass away by canal, and their force be neither so unrestrained nor so dangerous
fortune, who shows her power where valour has not prepared to resist her, and thither she turns her forces where she knows that barriers and defences have not been raised to constrain her
cards.question: Which detail from the excerpt most directly develops the theme that human preparation can reduce the destructive power of fortune?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Machiavelli compares fortune to a raging river that overflows plains, sweeps away trees and buildings, and bears away soil, showing that fortune is a natural and unstoppable force.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Machiavelli argues that fortune turns her force where 'barriers and defences have not been raised to constrain her,' meaning that nations which build such defenses through valor can limit fortune's damage.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Machiavelli identifies Italy as 'an open country without barriers and without any defence,' establishing that Italy is the geographic center of political change in Europe.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Machiavelli notes that Germany, Spain, and France were defended by proper valor, showing that those nations were historically more powerful than Italy.

cards.standardTitle: Narrator perspective, irony, and satire
cards.excerpt:
But the Florentines, from hatred, for sundry reasons, of the Vitelli and Orsini, not only would not ally themselves, but sent Nicolo Machiavelli, their secretary, to offer shelter and assistance to the duke against his enemies. The duke was found full of fear at Imola, because, against everybody’s expectation, his soldiers had at once gone over to the enemy and he found himself disarmed and war at his door. But recovering courage from the offers of the Florentines, he decided to temporize before fighting with the few soldiers that remained to him, and to negotiate for a reconciliation, and also to get assistance. This latter he obtained in two ways, by sending to the King of France for men and by enlisting men-at-arms and others whom he turned into cavalry of a sort: to all he gave money.

Notwithstanding this, his enemies drew near to him, and approached Fossombrone, where they encountered some men of the duke and, with the aid of the Orsini and Vitelli, routed them. When this happened, the duke resolved at once to see if he could not close the trouble with offers of reconciliation, and being a most perfect dissembler he did not fail in any practices to make the insurgents understand that he wished every man who had acquired anything to keep it, as it was enough for him to have the title of prince, whilst others might have the principality.
cards.whyThisWorks: The passage creates situational irony through the duke's reversal: a ruler so powerful he commands princes now claims he is satisfied with only a title while others hold actual power, a statement his identity as 'a most perfect dissembler' immediately exposes as false.
cards.skillStrategy: When a character's words directly contradict what the narrator tells you about that character, look for the gap between the claim and the truth — that gap is the irony.
evidencePoints: being a most perfect dissembler he did not fail in any practices to make the insurgents understand that he wished every man who had acquired anything to keep it
as it was enough for him to have the title of prince, whilst others might have the principality
cards.question: Read the following passage from the second paragraph: 'being a most perfect dissembler he did not fail in any practices to make the insurgents understand that he wished every man who had acquired anything to keep it, as it was enough for him to have the title of prince, whilst others might have the principality.' What contradiction in this passage creates irony?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The duke claims he wants reconciliation, yet he had already sent to the King of France for military reinforcements, showing he was preparing for war at the same time.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The narrator identifies the duke as 'a most perfect dissembler' immediately before describing the duke's offer to surrender real power, exposing the offer as deliberate deception rather than genuine surrender.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The duke's enemies routed his men at Fossombrone, yet the duke still believed he held enough military strength to defeat the Orsini and Vitelli without negotiating.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The Florentines offered the duke shelter and assistance even though they had previously refused to ally with the Vitelli and Orsini, revealing their inconsistent loyalties.

cards.standardTitle: Central idea and supporting evidence
cards.excerpt:
The contrary happens in kingdoms governed like that of France, because one can easily enter there by gaining over some baron of the kingdom, for one always finds malcontents and such as desire a change. Such men, for the reasons given, can open the way into the state and render the victory easy; but if you wish to hold it afterwards, you meet with infinite difficulties, both from those who have assisted you and from those you have crushed. Nor is it enough for you to have exterminated the family of the prince, because the lords that remain make themselves the heads of fresh movements against you, and as you are unable either to satisfy or exterminate them, that state is lost whenever time brings the opportunity.

Now if you will consider what was the nature of the government of Darius, you will find it similar to the kingdom of the Turk, and therefore it was only necessary for Alexander, first to overthrow him in the field, and then to take the country from him. After which victory, Darius being killed, the state remained secure to Alexander, for the above reasons. And if his successors had been united they would have enjoyed it securely and at their ease, for there were no tumults raised in the kingdom except those they provoked themselves.
cards.whyThisWorks: The two paragraphs present a direct contrast—France-style kingdoms are easy to enter but hard to hold, while Darius-style kingdoms are hard to enter but secure once taken—giving students a clear structural argument to identify as the central idea rather than a topic or isolated detail.
cards.skillStrategy: Ask yourself what claim the author is making across both paragraphs, not just what topic they mention or what one example shows.
evidencePoints: one can easily enter there by gaining over some baron of the kingdom…but if you wish to hold it afterwards, you meet with infinite difficulties
it was only necessary for Alexander, first to overthrow him in the field, and then to take the country from him…the state remained secure to Alexander
cards.question: Machiavelli opens the first paragraph by saying a kingdom like France is easy to enter but then adds 'if you wish to hold it afterwards, you meet with infinite difficulties,' and he closes the second paragraph by noting that after Alexander's victory 'the state remained secure.' What central idea do these two contrasting outcomes develop?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Barons and lords who help a conqueror enter a kingdom will always betray him once he has taken power.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Whether a conqueror can keep control of a defeated state is determined by how power was distributed in that state before the conquest.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Alexander the Great was a more skilled military commander than Darius because he won his battles in open fields.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Conquering a kingdom is always the hardest part of gaining power, and holding it is relatively simple once the ruling family is removed.

cards.question: Machiavelli argues that gaining entry into a kingdom like France is far easier than holding it. Which detail from the excerpt most directly develops this claim?

cards.standardTitle: Narrator perspective, irony, and satire
cards.excerpt: These principalities are liable to danger when they are passing from the civil to the absolute order of government, for such princes either rule personally or through magistrates. In the latter case their government is weaker and more insecure, because it rests entirely on the goodwill of those citizens who are raised to the magistracy, and who, especially in troubled times, can destroy the government with great ease, either by intrigue or open defiance; and the prince has not the chance amid tumults to exercise absolute authority, because the citizens and subjects, accustomed to receive orders from magistrates, are not of a mind to obey him amid these confusions, and there will always be in doubtful times a scarcity of men whom he can trust. For such a prince cannot rely upon what he observes in quiet times, when citizens have need of the state, because then every one agrees with him; they all promise, and when death is far distant they all wish to die for him; but in troubled times, when the state has need of its citizens, then he finds but few. And so much the more is this experiment dangerous, inasmuch as it can only be tried once. Therefore a wise prince ought to adopt such a course that his citizens will always in every sort and kind of circumstance have need of the state and of him, and then he will always find them faithful.
cards.whyThisWorks: Machiavelli's observation that citizens 'all promise, and when death is far distant they all wish to die for him; but in troubled times, when the state has need of its citizens, then he finds but few' creates a sharp situational irony: the moments of greatest declared loyalty are precisely the moments of least actual danger, while the moments of real need expose the loyalty as hollow.
cards.skillStrategy: Look for a moment where what people say or appear to do is the opposite of what actually happens when circumstances change — that gap between appearance and reality is the irony.
evidencePoints: they all promise, and when death is far distant they all wish to die for him
but in troubled times, when the state has need of its citizens, then he finds but few
cards.question: Read the following passage from the excerpt: 'they all promise, and when death is far distant they all wish to die for him; but in troubled times, when the state has need of its citizens, then he finds but few.' What irony does Machiavelli create through this contrast?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Citizens who swear loyalty in peaceful times are simply too cowardly to act when danger arrives, revealing a personal moral failing rather than a political contradiction.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Citizens declare their willingness to die for the prince precisely when dying is not required, yet disappear when the prince actually needs them — making their loudest pledges of loyalty the least reliable measure of true support.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The prince's authority is strongest during troubled times because citizens rally around a leader who exercises absolute power, which contradicts Machiavelli's earlier warning about instability.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Citizens who promise loyalty in quiet times are sincere, but external enemies during troubled times prevent them from fulfilling those promises to the prince.

cards.standardTitle: Central idea and supporting evidence
cards.excerpt:
And if, as I said, it was necessary that the people of Israel should be captive so as to make manifest the ability of Moses; that the Persians should be oppressed by the Medes so as to discover the greatness of the soul of Cyrus; and that the Athenians should be dispersed to illustrate the capabilities of Theseus: then at the present time, in order to discover the virtue of an Italian spirit, it was necessary that Italy should be reduced to the extremity that she is now in, that she should be more enslaved than the Hebrews, more oppressed than the Persians, more scattered than the Athenians; without head, without order, beaten, despoiled, torn, overrun; and to have endured every kind of desolation.

Although lately some spark may have been shown by one, which made us think he was ordained by God for our redemption, nevertheless it was afterwards seen, in the height of his career, that fortune rejected him; so that Italy, left as without life, waits for him who shall yet heal her wounds and put an end to the ravaging and plundering of Lombardy, to the swindling and taxing of the kingdom and of Tuscany, and cleanse those sores that for long have festered. It is seen how she entreats God to send someone who shall deliver her from these wrongs and barbarous insolencies. It is seen also that she is ready and willing to follow a banner if only someone will raise it.
cards.whyThisWorks: The excerpt explicitly parallels ancient peoples' suffering with Italy's current desolation and closes with Italy waiting for a deliverer, giving students a clear two-part structure from which to distinguish central idea from supporting detail or isolated claim.
cards.skillStrategy: Ask yourself what the whole passage is arguing, not just what one sentence says — the central idea must account for both the historical comparisons AND the final plea.
evidencePoints: it was necessary that Italy should be reduced to the extremity that she is now in…that she should be more enslaved than the Hebrews, more oppressed than the Persians, more scattered than the Athenians
Italy, left as without life, waits for him who shall yet heal her wounds…she is ready and willing to follow a banner if only someone will raise it
cards.question: In the first paragraph, Machiavelli argues that Israel, Persia, and Athens each had to suffer before a great leader could arise. He then states that Italy is 'more enslaved than the Hebrews, more oppressed than the Persians, more scattered than the Athenians.' What central idea do both paragraphs together develop through this comparison and the closing image of Italy waiting 'for him who shall yet heal her wounds'?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The suffering of Israel, Persia, and Athens proves that ancient civilizations endured greater hardships than any modern nation.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Italy's unmatched suffering and disorder have made her ripe for a great leader to emerge and deliver her, just as ancient peoples' oppression made their heroes possible.

choices.label: C
choices.text: A leader once appeared capable of redeeming Italy, but fortune's rejection of him left the country permanently without hope of rescue.

choices.label: D
choices.text: God has ordained a specific Italian leader to heal Italy's wounds, and the people must identify and support that divinely chosen figure.

cards.standardTitle: Theme development across a literary text
cards.excerpt:
From these causes it arose that Marcus, Pertinax, and Alexander, being all men of modest life, lovers of justice, enemies to cruelty, humane, and benignant, came to a sad end except Marcus; he alone lived and died honoured, because he had succeeded to the throne by hereditary title, and owed nothing either to the soldiers or the people; and afterwards, being possessed of many virtues which made him respected, he always kept both orders in their places whilst he lived, and was neither hated nor despised.

But Pertinax was created emperor against the wishes of the soldiers, who, being accustomed to live licentiously under Commodus, could not endure the honest life to which Pertinax wished to reduce them; thus, having given cause for hatred, to which hatred there was added contempt for his old age, he was overthrown at the very beginning of his administration. And here it should be noted that hatred is acquired as much by good works as by bad ones, therefore, as I said before, a prince wishing to keep his state is very often forced to do evil; for when that body is corrupt whom you think you have need of to maintain yourself—it may be either the people or the soldiers or the nobles—you have to submit to its humours and to gratify them, and then good works will do you harm.
cards.whyThisWorks: The excerpt explicitly contrasts Marcus's survival with Pertinax's downfall despite both being virtuous, and then states the named claim 'hatred is acquired as much by good works as by bad ones'—forcing students to distinguish the detail that develops the theme of virtue's insufficiency from true-but-topic-only details about Roman corruption.
cards.skillStrategy: Ask yourself: does this detail show WHY the theme is true, or does it just describe the situation without connecting to the central idea?
evidencePoints: hatred is acquired as much by good works as by bad ones, therefore, as I said before, a prince wishing to keep his state is very often forced to do evil
Pertinax wished to reduce them; thus, having given cause for hatred, to which hatred there was added contempt for his old age, he was overthrown at the very beginning of his administration
cards.question: Machiavelli writes that Pertinax 'having given cause for hatred, to which hatred there was added contempt for his old age, he was overthrown at the very beginning of his administration.' Which detail from the excerpt most directly develops the theme that virtuous conduct alone cannot secure a ruler's power?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Marcus, Pertinax, and Alexander are all described as 'lovers of justice, enemies to cruelty, humane, and benignant,' confirming that virtuous rulers were present in Rome during this period.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Machiavelli's claim that 'hatred is acquired as much by good works as by bad ones' directly explains why Pertinax's honest reforms destroyed him just as surely as corrupt behavior would have.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The soldiers under Commodus were 'accustomed to live licentiously,' showing that widespread corruption in the army made discipline difficult for any new emperor to impose.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Marcus 'had succeeded to the throne by hereditary title, and owed nothing either to the soldiers or the people,' establishing that his path to power differed from Pertinax's.

cards.standardTitle: Narrator perspective, irony, and satire
cards.excerpt:
And if, as I said, it was necessary that the people of Israel should be captive so as to make manifest the ability of Moses; that the Persians should be oppressed by the Medes so as to discover the greatness of the soul of Cyrus; and that the Athenians should be dispersed to illustrate the capabilities of Theseus: then at the present time, in order to discover the virtue of an Italian spirit, it was necessary that Italy should be reduced to the extremity that she is now in, that she should be more enslaved than the Hebrews, more oppressed than the Persians, more scattered than the Athenians; without head, without order, beaten, despoiled, torn, overrun; and to have endured every kind of desolation.

Although lately some spark may have been shown by one, which made us think he was ordained by God for our redemption, nevertheless it was afterwards seen, in the height of his career, that fortune rejected him; so that Italy, left as without life, waits for him who shall yet heal her wounds and put an end to the ravaging and plundering of Lombardy, to the swindling and taxing of the kingdom and of Tuscany, and cleanse those sores that for long have festered. It is seen how she entreats God to send someone who shall deliver her from these wrongs and barbarous insolencies. It is seen also that she is ready and willing to follow a banner if only someone will raise it.
cards.whyThisWorks: Machiavelli's argument that Italy's extreme suffering is a necessary precondition for the emergence of a great leader creates situational irony: the worse the devastation, the more it signals Italy's readiness for redemption, reversing the expected relationship between destruction and hope.
cards.skillStrategy: When you spot a reversal—where something bad is treated as proof of something good—ask yourself what the expected relationship would be and how the text flips it.
evidencePoints: it was necessary that Italy should be reduced to the extremity that she is now in, that she should be more enslaved than the Hebrews, more oppressed than the Persians, more scattered than the Athenians
Italy, left as without life, waits for him who shall yet heal her wounds
cards.question: Read the following passage from The Prince: 'it was necessary that Italy should be reduced to the extremity that she is now in, that she should be more enslaved than the Hebrews, more oppressed than the Persians, more scattered than the Athenians.' What irony is created by this claim?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Machiavelli contradicts himself by first praising Moses, Cyrus, and Theseus and then suggesting Italy's leader will surpass all three of them.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Italy's total ruin—being more enslaved, oppressed, and scattered than any historical example—is presented as the very condition that makes a great leader's rise possible, reversing the expectation that devastation signals hopelessness.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Machiavelli compares Italy to Israel, Persia, and Athens to show that Italian suffering is less severe than what those peoples endured, which understates the crisis.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The reference to a leader who 'fortune rejected' reveals that Machiavelli believes no Italian ruler can ever succeed, contradicting his call for someone to raise a banner.

cards.standardTitle: Central idea and supporting evidence
cards.excerpt: For these reasons Louis the Twelfth, King of France, quickly occupied Milan, and as quickly lost it; and to turn him out the first time it only needed Lodovico’s own forces; because those who had opened the gates to him, finding themselves deceived in their hopes of future benefit, would not endure the ill-treatment of the new prince. It is very true that, after acquiring rebellious provinces a second time, they are not so lightly lost afterwards, because the prince, with little reluctance, takes the opportunity of the rebellion to punish the delinquents, to clear out the suspects, and to strengthen himself in the weakest places. Thus to cause France to lose Milan the first time it was enough for the Duke Lodovico to raise insurrections on the borders; but to cause him to lose it a second time it was necessary to bring the whole world against him, and that his armies should be defeated and driven out of Italy; which followed from the causes above mentioned.
cards.whyThisWorks: The paragraph explicitly contrasts why Milan was easy to lose the first time versus why it required 'the whole world against him' the second time, giving students a clear structural anchor to identify the central idea rather than a topic or isolated detail.
cards.skillStrategy: Find the idea that the paragraph keeps returning to and ask: what does every sentence in this paragraph work together to prove?
evidencePoints: after acquiring rebellious provinces a second time, they are not so lightly lost afterwards, because the prince, with little reluctance, takes the opportunity of the rebellion to punish the delinquents, to clear out the suspects, and to strengthen himself in the weakest places

to cause France to lose Milan the first time it was enough for the Duke Lodovico to raise insurrections on the borders; but to cause him to lose it a second time it was necessary to bring the whole world against him
cards.question: Machiavelli contrasts what 'was enough' to drive France from Milan the first time with what 'was necessary' to drive France out the second time. What central idea does this contrast develop across the paragraph?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Louis XII lost Milan both times because he failed to win the loyalty of the people who originally opened the gates to him.

choices.label: B
choices.text: A prince who retakes a rebellious territory becomes far harder to remove because he uses the revolt to punish enemies, eliminate suspects, and repair his weaknesses.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Duke Lodovico proved to be a superior military strategist who understood how to exploit France's dependence on unreliable allies.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Foreign rulers like Louis XII can never hold Italian territories because local populations will always eventually rise against outside control.

cards.standardTitle: Rhetorical appeals and author purpose
cards.excerpt: Agathocles, the Sicilian, became King of Syracuse not only from a private but from a low and abject position. This man, the son of a potter, through all the changes in his fortunes always led an infamous life. Nevertheless, he accompanied his infamies with so much ability of mind and body that, having devoted himself to the military profession, he rose through its ranks to be Praetor of Syracuse. Being established in that position, and having deliberately resolved to make himself prince and to seize by violence, without obligation to others, that which had been conceded to him by assent, he came to an understanding for this purpose with Amilcar, the Carthaginian, who, with his army, was fighting in Sicily. One morning he assembled the people and the senate of Syracuse, as if he had to discuss with them things relating to the Republic, and at a given signal the soldiers killed all the senators and the richest of the people; these dead, he seized and held the princedom of that city without any civil commotion. And although he was twice routed by the Carthaginians, and ultimately besieged, yet not only was he able to defend his city, but leaving part of his men for its defence, with the others he attacked Africa, and in a short time raised the siege of Syracuse. The Carthaginians, reduced to extreme necessity, were compelled to come to terms with Agathocles, and, leaving Sicily to him, had to be content with the possession of Africa.
cards.whyThisWorks: Machiavelli's phrase 'low and abject position' combined with 'son of a potter' functions as a figurative contrast that anchors his explanatory purpose: to argue that virtue and ability, not noble birth, determine a ruler's rise to power.
cards.skillStrategy: When you spot figurative or loaded language, ask yourself: what idea is the author trying to prove or explain, and how does this specific word choice push that idea forward?
evidencePoints: became King of Syracuse not only from a private but from a low and abject position
he accompanied his infamies with so much ability of mind and body
cards.question: Read this phrase from the passage: 'became King of Syracuse not only from a private but from a low and abject position.' How does Machiavelli's use of 'low and abject' serve his explanatory purpose in this paragraph?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The phrase condemns Agathocles morally, signaling that Machiavelli disapproves of rulers who come from common origins.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The phrase establishes the extreme depth of Agathocles' origins so that his rise to king becomes evidence that personal ability, not social rank, drives political success.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The phrase emphasizes Agathocles' poverty to explain why he was forced to rely on Amilcar and the Carthaginian army rather than his own resources.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The phrase highlights the disgrace of Agathocles' character to warn readers that rulers who rise through violence will ultimately be defeated.

cards.standardTitle: Theme development across a literary text
cards.excerpt: These principalities are liable to danger when they are passing from the civil to the absolute order of government, for such princes either rule personally or through magistrates. In the latter case their government is weaker and more insecure, because it rests entirely on the goodwill of those citizens who are raised to the magistracy, and who, especially in troubled times, can destroy the government with great ease, either by intrigue or open defiance; and the prince has not the chance amid tumults to exercise absolute authority, because the citizens and subjects, accustomed to receive orders from magistrates, are not of a mind to obey him amid these confusions, and there will always be in doubtful times a scarcity of men whom he can trust. For such a prince cannot rely upon what he observes in quiet times, when citizens have need of the state, because then every one agrees with him; they all promise, and when death is far distant they all wish to die for him; but in troubled times, when the state has need of its citizens, then he finds but few. And so much the more is this experiment dangerous, inasmuch as it can only be tried once. Therefore a wise prince ought to adopt such a course that his citizens will always in every sort and kind of circumstance have need of the state and of him, and then he will always find them faithful.
cards.whyThisWorks: The excerpt explicitly contrasts citizens' behavior in 'quiet times' versus 'troubled times,' giving students a concrete textual moment to test whether a detail develops the theme of manufactured necessity versus voluntary loyalty or merely describes a related topic.
cards.skillStrategy: Ask yourself: does this detail show WHY the theme is true, or does it just describe something that happens in the passage?
evidencePoints: they all promise, and when death is far distant they all wish to die for him; but in troubled times, when the state has need of its citizens, then he finds but few
a wise prince ought to adopt such a course that his citizens will always in every sort and kind of circumstance have need of the state and of him, and then he will always find them faithful
cards.question: Machiavelli contrasts what citizens do 'when death is far distant' with what they do 'in troubled times, when the state has need of its citizens.' Which statement explains how this contrast develops the theme that a ruler's security depends on creating necessity rather than trusting voluntary loyalty?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The contrast shows that citizens are naturally cowardly, which is why princes should rule personally rather than through magistrates.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The contrast reveals that citizens' promises of loyalty are meaningless without pressure, so a prince must structure the state so that citizens always depend on him rather than rely on their goodwill.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The contrast demonstrates that troubled times are more dangerous than quiet times, proving that a prince should avoid political instability at all costs.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The contrast illustrates that citizens who serve under magistrates are less loyal than those who serve the prince directly, making personal rule the safer choice.

cards.standardTitle: Narrator perspective, irony, and satire
cards.excerpt: Agathocles, the Sicilian, became King of Syracuse not only from a private but from a low and abject position. This man, the son of a potter, through all the changes in his fortunes always led an infamous life. Nevertheless, he accompanied his infamies with so much ability of mind and body that, having devoted himself to the military profession, he rose through its ranks to be Praetor of Syracuse. Being established in that position, and having deliberately resolved to make himself prince and to seize by violence, without obligation to others, that which had been conceded to him by assent, he came to an understanding for this purpose with Amilcar, the Carthaginian, who, with his army, was fighting in Sicily. One morning he assembled the people and the senate of Syracuse, as if he had to discuss with them things relating to the Republic, and at a given signal the soldiers killed all the senators and the richest of the people; these dead, he seized and held the princedom of that city without any civil commotion.
