cards.whyThisWorks: Machiavelli's account of Agathocles creates situational irony through a sharp reversal: a man described as living an 'infamous life' from a 'low and abject position' ultimately forces the powerful Carthaginians to surrender Sicily to him, inverting expected outcomes of virtue and success.
cards.skillStrategy: When looking for irony, find the moment where the outcome is the opposite of what the setup leads you to expect — ask yourself what 'should' happen based on the details given, then notice what actually happens instead.
evidencePoints: This man, the son of a potter, through all the changes in his fortunes always led an infamous life.
the Carthaginians, reduced to extreme necessity, were compelled to come to terms with Agathocles, and, leaving Sicily to him, had to be content with the possession of Africa.
cards.question: Read the following sentences from the passage: 'This man, the son of a potter, through all the changes in his fortunes always led an infamous life' and 'the Carthaginians…were compelled to come to terms with Agathocles, and, leaving Sicily to him, had to be content with the possession of Africa.' What contrast between these two moments creates irony in the passage?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Agathocles rises from a low birth to military rank, which confirms that honorable conduct is the surest path to power in Syracuse.

choices.label: B
choices.text: A man introduced as infamous and low-born, expected to fail, ends up forcing a dominant military empire to surrender territory to him.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Agathocles is twice defeated by the Carthaginians, and this repeated failure ultimately prevents him from holding power in Syracuse.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The senators and wealthy citizens of Syracuse are killed, which causes the Carthaginians to intervene and strip Agathocles of his princedom.

cards.standardTitle: Central idea and supporting evidence
cards.excerpt:
Upon this the duke, before his departure from Fano, which was to be on 30th December 1502, communicated his designs to eight of his most trusted followers, among whom were Don Michele and the Monsignor d’Euna, who was afterwards cardinal; and he ordered that, as soon as Vitellozzo, Pagolo Orsini, the Duke di Gravina, and Oliverotto should arrive, his followers in pairs should take them one by one, entrusting certain men to certain pairs, who should entertain them until they reached Sinigalia; nor should they be permitted to leave until they came to the duke’s quarters, where they should be seized.

The duke afterwards ordered all his horsemen and infantry, of which there were more than two thousand cavalry and ten thousand footmen, to assemble by daybreak at the Metauro, a river five miles distant from Fano, and await him there. He found himself, therefore, on the last day of December at the Metauro with his men, and having sent a cavalcade of about two hundred horsemen before him, he then moved forward the infantry, whom he accompanied with the rest of the men-at-arms.
cards.whyThisWorks: The two paragraphs together show the duke executing a coordinated trap—assigning trusted men to detain specific enemies and massing his army at the Metauro—so students must synthesize both paragraphs to distinguish the central idea from isolated details like troop numbers or the departure date.
cards.skillStrategy: Ask yourself: what is the duke actually doing across both paragraphs, not just one detail he orders—then put that action in your own words.
evidencePoints: he ordered that, as soon as Vitellozzo, Pagolo Orsini, the Duke di Gravina, and Oliverotto should arrive, his followers in pairs should take them one by one
he then moved forward the infantry, whom he accompanied with the rest of the men-at-arms
cards.question: The first paragraph describes the duke assigning paired followers to detain specific enemies, and the second describes him positioning thousands of soldiers at the Metauro by daybreak. What central idea do both paragraphs together develop?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The duke's eight trusted followers, including Don Michele and the Monsignor d'Euna, were the most important figures in the operation against Vitellozzo and the Orsini.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The duke executed a carefully coordinated plan, using trusted insiders to detain his enemies while simultaneously moving a large armed force into position.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The duke's army of more than two thousand cavalry and ten thousand infantry was the decisive factor that made his operation at Sinigalia possible.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The duke's departure from Fano on December 30th set a strict deadline that forced him to rely on a small group of trusted men rather than his full army.

cards.standardTitle: Rhetorical appeals and author purpose
cards.excerpt:
It is necessary, therefore, if we desire to discuss this matter thoroughly, to inquire whether these innovators can rely on themselves or have to depend on others: that is to say, whether, to consummate their enterprise, have they to use prayers or can they use force? In the first instance they always succeed badly, and never compass anything; but when they can rely on themselves and use force, then they are rarely endangered. Hence it is that all armed prophets have conquered, and the unarmed ones have been destroyed. Besides the reasons mentioned, the nature of the people is variable, and whilst it is easy to persuade them, it is difficult to fix them in that persuasion. And thus it is necessary to take such measures that, when they believe no longer, it may be possible to make them believe by force.

If Moses, Cyrus, Theseus, and Romulus had been unarmed they could not have enforced their constitutions for long—as happened in our time to Fra Girolamo Savonarola, who was ruined with his new order of things immediately the multitude believed in him no longer, and he had no means of keeping steadfast those who believed or of making the unbelievers to believe. Therefore such as these have great difficulties in consummating their enterprise, for all their dangers are in the ascent, yet with ability they will overcome them; but when these are overcome, and those who envied them their success are exterminated, they will begin to be respected, and they will continue afterwards powerful, secure, honoured, and happy.
cards.whyThisWorks: Machiavelli's metaphor of 'armed prophets' versus 'unarmed ones' is a concrete figurative comparison that directly advances his persuasive argument that force, not persuasion alone, is necessary for political success.
cards.skillStrategy: When you spot figurative language, ask yourself: what idea is the author trying to prove or explain, and how does this comparison make that argument stronger or clearer?
evidencePoints: all armed prophets have conquered, and the unarmed ones have been destroyed
If Moses, Cyrus, Theseus, and Romulus had been unarmed they could not have enforced their constitutions for long
cards.question: Machiavelli writes that 'all armed prophets have conquered, and the unarmed ones have been destroyed.' How does this figurative contrast help him achieve his persuasive purpose in these paragraphs?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The contrast between armed and unarmed prophets shows that religious leaders are more trustworthy than military commanders, supporting Machiavelli's call for moral leadership.

choices.label: B
choices.text: By casting political innovators as 'prophets' who are either armed or unarmed, Machiavelli frames force as the decisive factor in whether a leader's reforms survive, making his argument that persuasion alone cannot hold power feel like a universal law rather than mere opinion.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The image of prophets being destroyed warns readers that religious figures should avoid politics entirely, which is the central lesson Machiavelli wants his audience to accept.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The contrast between armed and unarmed prophets appeals to the reader's emotions by creating sympathy for leaders like Savonarola, persuading the audience to admire those who fail without violence.

cards.standardTitle: Theme development across a literary text
cards.excerpt: Before Charles, King of France, passed into Italy, this country was under the dominion of the Pope, the Venetians, the King of Naples, the Duke of Milan, and the Florentines. These potentates had two principal anxieties: the one, that no foreigner should enter Italy under arms; the other, that none of themselves should seize more territory. Those about whom there was the most anxiety were the Pope and the Venetians. To restrain the Venetians the union of all the others was necessary, as it was for the defence of Ferrara; and to keep down the Pope they made use of the barons of Rome, who, being divided into two factions, Orsini and Colonnesi, had always a pretext for disorder, and, standing with arms in their hands under the eyes of the Pontiff, kept the pontificate weak and powerless. And although there might arise sometimes a courageous pope, such as Sixtus, yet neither fortune nor wisdom could rid him of these annoyances. And the short life of a pope is also a cause of weakness; for in the ten years, which is the average life of a pope, he can with difficulty lower one of the factions; and if, so to speak, one people should almost destroy the Colonnesi, another would arise hostile to the Orsini, who would support their opponents, and yet would not have time to ruin the Orsini. This was the reason why the temporal powers of the pope were little esteemed in Italy.
cards.whyThisWorks: The excerpt contains both true-but-topic-only details (e.g., the names of the factions) and details that directly develop the theme that fragmented, short-lived power cannot sustain lasting authority, giving students clear practice distinguishing thematic evidence from mere topical facts.
cards.skillStrategy: Ask yourself: does this detail show WHY power fails or just describe WHO was involved — only the 'why' details build the theme.
evidencePoints: the short life of a pope is also a cause of weakness; for in the ten years, which is the average life of a pope, he can with difficulty lower one of the factions
standing with arms in their hands under the eyes of the Pontiff, kept the pontificate weak and powerless
cards.question: Which detail from the passage most directly develops the theme that divided and unstable power prevents any ruler from achieving lasting authority?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The Roman barons were split into two factions called the Orsini and the Colonnesi, each with its own name and history in Rome.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Even a courageous pope like Sixtus could not escape these annoyances, because a pope's short reign left him unable to destroy one faction before another rose to replace it.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Before Charles of France entered Italy, the country was governed by five major powers, including the Pope, the Venetians, and the King of Naples.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The other Italian potentates united specifically to restrain the Venetians and to defend the territory of Ferrara from outside threats.

cards.standardTitle: Narrator perspective, irony, and satire
cards.excerpt:
With us there is great justice, because that war is just which is necessary, and arms are hallowed when there is no other hope but in them. Here there is the greatest willingness, and where the willingness is great the difficulties cannot be great if you will only follow those men to whom I have directed your attention. Further than this, how extraordinarily the ways of God have been manifested beyond example: the sea is divided, a cloud has led the way, the rock has poured forth water, it has rained manna, everything has contributed to your greatness; you ought to do the rest. God is not willing to do everything, and thus take away our free will and that share of glory which belongs to us.

And it is not to be wondered at if none of the above-named Italians have been able to accomplish all that is expected from your illustrious house; and if in so many revolutions in Italy, and in so many campaigns, it has always appeared as if military virtue were exhausted, this has happened because the old order of things was not good, and none of us have known how to find a new one. And nothing honours a man more than to establish new laws and new ordinances when he himself was newly risen. Such things when they are well founded and dignified will make him revered and admired, and in Italy there are not wanting opportunities to bring such into use in every form.
cards.whyThisWorks: Machiavelli creates situational irony by invoking divine miracles as proof of God's favor while immediately declaring 'God is not willing to do everything,' reversing the expectation that divine intervention alone will secure Italy's liberation and placing the burden back on human action.
cards.skillStrategy: When you spot a reversal—where a statement builds up one expectation and then contradicts it—ask yourself what the reader expected to happen and what actually happens instead; that gap is the irony.
evidencePoints: how extraordinarily the ways of God have been manifested beyond example: the sea is divided, a cloud has led the way, the rock has poured forth water, it has rained manna, everything has contributed to your greatness
God is not willing to do everything, and thus take away our free will and that share of glory which belongs to us
cards.question: Read the following passage from the excerpt: 'how extraordinarily the ways of God have been manifested beyond example: the sea is divided, a cloud has led the way, the rock has poured forth water, it has rained manna, everything has contributed to your greatness' followed immediately by 'God is not willing to do everything.' What irony is created by this contrast?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Machiavelli argues that biblical miracles are unreliable, so Italy's leaders should abandon faith and rely solely on military strategy.

choices.label: B
choices.text: After citing miraculous divine intervention as evidence of God's extraordinary support, Machiavelli reverses course by declaring that God will not complete the work, making human effort—not divine power—the deciding force.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Machiavelli praises God's miracles to show that Italy has already achieved greatness and no further action from its leaders is required.

choices.label: D
choices.text: By listing miracles from scripture, Machiavelli implies that Italy's current rulers are as powerful as the biblical figures who performed those miracles.

cards.standardTitle: Central idea and supporting evidence
cards.excerpt:
Therefore it is unnecessary for a prince to have all the good qualities I have enumerated, but it is very necessary to appear to have them. And I shall dare to say this also, that to have them and always to observe them is injurious, and that to appear to have them is useful; to appear merciful, faithful, humane, religious, upright, and to be so, but with a mind so framed that should you require not to be so, you may be able and know how to change to the opposite.

And you have to understand this, that a prince, especially a new one, cannot observe all those things for which men are esteemed, being often forced, in order to maintain the state, to act contrary to fidelity, friendship, humanity, and religion. Therefore it is necessary for him to have a mind ready to turn itself accordingly as the winds and variations of fortune force it, yet, as I have said above, not to diverge from the good if he can avoid doing so, but, if compelled, then to know how to set about it.
cards.whyThisWorks: The excerpt explicitly states two contrasting claims—that possessing virtues is 'injurious' while appearing to have them is 'useful'—giving students a concrete textual anchor for identifying the central idea rather than a topic or isolated detail.
cards.skillStrategy: Find the sentence where the author states his main claim directly, then ask: what idea do all the other sentences in the passage support or explain?
evidencePoints: to have them and always to observe them is injurious, and that to appear to have them is useful

it is necessary for him to have a mind ready to turn itself accordingly as the winds and variations of fortune force it, yet, as I have said above, not to diverge from the good if he can avoid doing so, but, if compelled, then to know how to set about it
cards.question: Machiavelli states that 'to have them and always to observe them is injurious, and that to appear to have them is useful.' Which statement expresses the central idea that this claim introduces and both paragraphs develop?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A prince who genuinely practices mercy, faithfulness, and religion will earn the loyalty needed to maintain his state.

choices.label: B
choices.text: A prince must project the appearance of virtue while remaining ready to abandon virtuous conduct whenever holding power demands it.

choices.label: C
choices.text: A new prince faces unique dangers because he has not yet established a reputation for the good qualities his subjects expect.

choices.label: D

cards.standardTitle: Theme development across a literary text
cards.excerpt: When the duke occupied the Romagna he found it under the rule of weak masters, who rather plundered their subjects than ruled them, and gave them more cause for disunion than for union, so that the country was full of robbery, quarrels, and every kind of violence; and so, wishing to bring back peace and obedience to authority, he considered it necessary to give it a good governor. Thereupon he promoted Messer Ramiro d’Orco, a swift and cruel man, to whom he gave the fullest power. This man in a short time restored peace and unity with the greatest success. Afterwards the duke considered that it was not advisable to confer such excessive authority, for he had no doubt but that he would become odious, so he set up a court of judgment in the country, under a most excellent president, wherein all cities had their advocates. And because he knew that the past severity had caused some hatred against himself, so, to clear himself in the minds of the people, and gain them entirely to himself, he desired to show that, if any cruelty had been practised, it had not originated with him, but in the natural sternness of the minister. Under this pretence he took Ramiro, and one morning caused him to be executed and left on the piazza at Cesena with the block and a bloody knife at his side. The barbarity of this spectacle caused the people to be at once satisfied and dismayed.
cards.whyThisWorks: The excerpt contains a true-but-topic-only detail (Ramiro restored peace) alongside a theme-developing detail (the duke staged the execution to transfer blame), forcing students to distinguish between details that merely match the topic of rulership and details that actually develop the theme of controlling perception to maintain authority.
cards.skillStrategy: Ask yourself: does this detail just describe what happened, or does it show HOW the ruler's calculated action builds the theme about power and perception?
evidencePoints: he desired to show that, if any cruelty had been practised, it had not originated with him, but in the natural sternness of the minister
The barbarity of this spectacle caused the people to be at once satisfied and dismayed.
cards.question: The passage describes the duke's decision to have Ramiro publicly executed and left 'on the piazza at Cesena with the block and a bloody knife at his side.' Which statement explains how this specific moment develops the theme that a ruler must shape public perception to hold onto power?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Ramiro's execution proves the duke was willing to punish officials who abused their authority, showing that just governance requires holding subordinates accountable.

choices.label: B
choices.text: By staging the spectacle so the people would believe cruelty 'had not originated with him, but in the natural sternness of the minister,' the duke used Ramiro's death as a calculated performance to redirect blame and secure loyalty.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The duke's removal of Ramiro after he 'restored peace and unity' shows that rulers must eliminate officials once their usefulness has ended, regardless of their success.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The fact that the spectacle left the people 'satisfied and dismayed' confirms that the Romagna had suffered under cruel rule before the duke's arrival and welcomed the change.

cards.standardTitle: Narrator perspective, irony, and satire
cards.excerpt:
But the duke noticing that Oliverotto, who had remained with his band in Sinigalia, was missing—for Oliverotto was waiting in the square before his quarters near the river, keeping his men in order and drilling them—signalled with his eye to Don Michelle, to whom the care of Oliverotto had been committed, that he should take measures that Oliverotto should not escape. Therefore Don Michele rode off and joined Oliverotto, telling him that it was not right to keep his men out of their quarters, because these might be taken up by the men of the duke; and he advised him to send them at once to their quarters and to come himself to meet the duke. And Oliverotto, having taken this advice, came before the duke, who, when he saw him, called to him; and Oliverotto, having made his obeisance, joined the others.

So the whole party entered Sinigalia, dismounted at the duke’s quarters, and went with him into a secret chamber, where the duke made them prisoners; he then mounted on horseback, and issued orders that the men of Oliverotto and the Orsini should be stripped of their arms. Those of Oliverotto, being at hand, were quickly settled, but those of the Orsini and Vitelli, being at a distance, and having a presentiment of the destruction of their masters, had time to prepare themselves, and bearing in mind the valour and discipline of the Orsinian and Vitellian houses, they stood together against the hostile forces of the country and saved themselves.

cards.skillStrategy: When a character's action or advice seems helpful but produces the opposite result for the recipient, look for the gap between what appears to be happening and what is actually happening — that gap is the irony.
evidencePoints: he advised him to send them at once to their quarters and to come himself to meet the duke
Oliverotto, having taken this advice, came before the duke, who, when he saw him, called to him; and Oliverotto, having made his obeisance, joined the others
cards.question: Read this passage from the excerpt: 'he advised him to send them at once to their quarters and to come himself to meet the duke. And Oliverotto, having taken this advice, came before the duke.' What is ironic about Don Michele's advice to Oliverotto?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Don Michele warns Oliverotto that his men are in danger, and the men are indeed attacked while Oliverotto escapes safely.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Don Michele frames his words as a helpful precaution for Oliverotto's benefit, yet following that advice strips Oliverotto of his armed protection and leads directly to his capture.

choices.label: C

choices.label: D

cards.standardTitle: Central idea and supporting evidence
cards.excerpt:
But to enable a prince to form an opinion of his servant there is one test which never fails; when you see the servant thinking more of his own interests than of yours, and seeking inwardly his own profit in everything, such a man will never make a good servant, nor will you ever be able to trust him; because he who has the state of another in his hands ought never to think of himself, but always of his prince, and never pay any attention to matters in which the prince is not concerned.

On the other hand, to keep his servant honest the prince ought to study him, honouring him, enriching him, doing him kindnesses, sharing with him the honours and cares; and at the same time let him see that he cannot stand alone, so that many honours may not make him desire more, many riches make him wish for more, and that many cares may make him dread chances. When, therefore, servants, and princes towards servants, are thus disposed, they can trust each other, but when it is otherwise, the end will always be disastrous for either one or the other.
cards.whyThisWorks: The excerpt explicitly states a two-part argument—what makes a servant untrustworthy and what a prince must do to keep a servant honest—giving students a clear central idea to synthesize rather than a topic or isolated detail.
cards.skillStrategy: Ask yourself: what is the one main point both paragraphs are building toward together? The last sentence often signals it—look for where Machiavelli states the outcome of following or ignoring his advice.
evidencePoints: he who has the state of another in his hands ought never to think of himself, but always of his prince

cards.question: Machiavelli closes the passage by stating that when servants and princes are not 'thus disposed,' the outcome 'will always be disastrous for either one or the other.' What central idea do both paragraphs develop to support that conclusion?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A prince's greatest danger comes from servants who openly seek personal profit rather than hiding their ambitions.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Mutual trust between a prince and servant depends on the servant placing the prince's interests above his own and the prince actively investing in the servant's loyalty.

choices.label: C
choices.text: A prince should shower servants with honors and riches so that no servant ever feels the need to seek outside profit.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The only reliable way for a prince to govern is to test every servant's loyalty before granting any trust or responsibility.

cards.standardTitle: Theme development across a literary text
cards.excerpt:
With us there is great justice, because that war is just which is necessary, and arms are hallowed when there is no other hope but in them. Here there is the greatest willingness, and where the willingness is great the difficulties cannot be great if you will only follow those men to whom I have directed your attention. Further than this, how extraordinarily the ways of God have been manifested beyond example: the sea is divided, a cloud has led the way, the rock has poured forth water, it has rained manna, everything has contributed to your greatness; you ought to do the rest. God is not willing to do everything, and thus take away our free will and that share of glory which belongs to us.

And it is not to be wondered at if none of the above-named Italians have been able to accomplish all that is expected from your illustrious house; and if in so many revolutions in Italy, and in so many campaigns, it has always appeared as if military virtue were exhausted, this has happened because the old order of things was not good, and none of us have known how to find a new one. And nothing honours a man more than to establish new laws and new ordinances when he himself was newly risen. Such things when they are well founded and dignified will make him revered and admired, and in Italy there are not wanting opportunities to bring such into use in every form.
cards.whyThisWorks: The excerpt contains both thematic evidence (human agency paired with divine favor, the call to establish new laws) and true-but-topical details (biblical allusions, Italian military failures) that students must distinguish when identifying what actually develops the theme of human responsibility in achieving greatness.
cards.skillStrategy: Ask yourself: does this detail show the theme being built, or does it just describe what the passage is about without pushing the central idea forward?
evidencePoints: God is not willing to do everything, and thus take away our free will and that share of glory which belongs to us.
nothing honours a man more than to establish new laws and new ordinances when he himself was newly risen.
cards.question: Which detail from the excerpt most directly develops the theme that human beings must take responsibility for achieving their own greatness?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The references to the sea dividing, the cloud leading the way, and manna raining down show that divine intervention has historically guided chosen people toward victory.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The claim that 'God is not willing to do everything' so that free will and glory remain ours establishes that people cannot rely on providence alone but must act to earn their own greatness.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The observation that Italian military virtue appeared exhausted through 'so many revolutions in Italy' explains why past leaders repeatedly failed to unify the peninsula.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The assertion that 'that war is just which is necessary' provides a moral justification for armed conflict when no other option remains available.

cards.standardTitle: Narrator perspective, irony, and satire
cards.excerpt: Pope Julius came afterwards and found the Church strong, possessing all the Romagna, the barons of Rome reduced to impotence, and, through the chastisements of Alexander, the factions wiped out; he also found the way open to accumulate money in a manner such as had never been practised before Alexander’s time. Such things Julius not only followed, but improved upon, and he intended to gain Bologna, to ruin the Venetians, and to drive the French out of Italy. All of these enterprises prospered with him, and so much the more to his credit, inasmuch as he did everything to strengthen the Church and not any private person. He kept also the Orsini and Colonnesi factions within the bounds in which he found them; and although there was among them some mind to make disturbance, nevertheless he held two things firm: the one, the greatness of the Church, with which he terrified them; and the other, not allowing them to have their own cardinals, who caused the disorders among them. For whenever these factions have their cardinals they do not remain quiet for long, because cardinals foster the factions in Rome and out of it, and the barons are compelled to support them, and thus from the ambitions of prelates arise disorders and tumults among the barons. For these reasons his Holiness Pope Leo found the pontificate most powerful, and it is to be hoped that, if others made it great in arms, he will make it still greater and more venerated by his goodness and infinite other virtues.
cards.whyThisWorks: Machiavelli praises Julius II for strengthening the Church through military conquest and political suppression, then closes with ironic hope that Leo X will make the Church 'greater and more venerated by his goodness and infinite other virtues'—a reversal that contrasts ruthless power-building with the sudden invocation of moral virtue.
cards.skillStrategy: When you spot a sharp contrast between what has been described and what is suddenly claimed or hoped for, ask yourself whether the two ideas contradict each other in a way that creates irony.
evidencePoints: if others made it great in arms, he will make it still greater and more venerated by his goodness and infinite other virtues
he did everything to strengthen the Church and not any private person
cards.question: Machiavelli spends most of the passage describing how popes like Alexander and Julius built the Church's power through military force, political suppression, and the elimination of rival factions. What irony is created by the final sentence, which expresses hope that Pope Leo will make the Church 'still greater and more venerated by his goodness and infinite other virtues'?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The passage reveals that Leo had already surpassed Julius in military achievement, making the praise of his virtues a straightforward compliment rather than a contrast.

choices.label: B
choices.text: After detailing a legacy of conquest, intimidation, and factional control as the foundation of Church power, Machiavelli suddenly attributes the Church's future greatness to moral virtue, contradicting the ruthless methods he just praised.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Machiavelli implies that Leo's goodness will fail because the Church was built on violence, so the final sentence functions as a direct warning rather than a hopeful contrast.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The reference to Leo's 'infinite other virtues' echoes the earlier praise of Julius for acting on behalf of the Church rather than himself, so the two leaders are presented as equally admirable without contradiction.

cards.standardTitle: Central idea and supporting evidence
cards.excerpt:
I conclude, therefore that, fortune being changeful and mankind steadfast in their ways, so long as the two are in agreement men are successful, but unsuccessful when they fall out. For my part I consider that it is better to be adventurous than cautious, because fortune is a woman, and if you wish to keep her under it is necessary to beat and ill-use her; and it is seen that she allows herself to be mastered by the adventurous rather than by those who go to work more coldly. She is, therefore, always, woman-like, a lover of young men, because they are less cautious, more violent, and with more audacity command her.

Having carefully considered the subject of the above discourses, and wondering within myself whether the present times were propitious to a new prince, and whether there were elements that would give an opportunity to a wise and virtuous one to introduce a new order of things which would do honour to him and good to the people of this country, it appears to me that so many things concur to favour a new prince that I never knew a time more fit than the present.
cards.whyThisWorks: The excerpt makes two explicit, connected claims—that boldness masters fortune and that the present moment favors a new prince—forcing students to distinguish the overarching central idea from an isolated supporting detail or topic.
cards.skillStrategy: Ask yourself: which idea do both paragraphs keep returning to, rather than just mentioning once?
evidencePoints: it is better to be adventurous than cautious, because fortune is a woman, and if you wish to keep her under it is necessary to beat and ill-use her
so many things concur to favour a new prince that I never knew a time more fit than the present
cards.question: Machiavelli opens by declaring 'it is better to be adventurous than cautious' and closes by stating he 'never knew a time more fit than the present.' What central idea do both of these claims work together to express?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Fortune punishes cautious rulers and rewards those who study political conditions before acting.

choices.label: B
choices.text: A prince who acts boldly can seize control of fortune, and the current moment makes that bold action especially possible.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Young men are naturally suited to rule because their violence and audacity make them superior to older, colder leaders.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The present political conditions are so favorable that even a cautious prince could successfully establish a new order.

cards.question: Machiavelli states that Julius's enterprises 'prospered with him, and so much the more to his credit.' Which detail from the passage best develops the theme that lasting institutional power requires subordinating personal ambition to the strength of the institution itself?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Julius intended to gain Bologna, ruin the Venetians, and drive the French out of Italy, demonstrating that military ambition on a grand scale was the primary source of the Church's growing dominance.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Julius did everything to strengthen the Church and not any private person, meaning his success was credited to serving the institution rather than advancing individual gain.

cards.standardTitle: Narrator perspective, irony, and satire
cards.excerpt:
It is necessary, therefore, if we desire to discuss this matter thoroughly, to inquire whether these innovators can rely on themselves or have to depend on others: that is to say, whether, to consummate their enterprise, have they to use prayers or can they use force? In the first instance they always succeed badly, and never compass anything; but when they can rely on themselves and use force, then they are rarely endangered. Hence it is that all armed prophets have conquered, and the unarmed ones have been destroyed. Besides the reasons mentioned, the nature of the people is variable, and whilst it is easy to persuade them, it is difficult to fix them in that persuasion. And thus it is necessary to take such measures that, when they believe no longer, it may be possible to make them believe by force.

If Moses, Cyrus, Theseus, and Romulus had been unarmed they could not have enforced their constitutions for long—as happened in our time to Fra Girolamo Savonarola, who was ruined with his new order of things immediately the multitude believed in him no longer, and he had no means of keeping steadfast those who believed or of making the unbelievers to believe. Therefore such as these have great difficulties in consummating their enterprise, for all their dangers are in the ascent, yet with ability they will overcome them; but when these are overcome, and those who envied them their success are exterminated, they will begin to be respected, and they will continue afterwards powerful, secure, honoured, and happy.
cards.whyThisWorks: Machiavelli's claim that 'all armed prophets have conquered, and the unarmed ones have been destroyed' sets up a stark reversal that is then illustrated ironically by Savonarola, whose power to persuade people to believe in him became the very source of his ruin once that belief collapsed—demonstrating irony through structural contrast between the basis of power and the cause of destruction.
cards.skillStrategy: When you spot a reversal—where the thing that should help actually causes harm—ask yourself what the author expected versus what actually happened, and that gap is the irony.
evidencePoints: all armed prophets have conquered, and the unarmed ones have been destroyed
who was ruined with his new order of things immediately the multitude believed in him no longer, and he had no means of keeping steadfast those who believed or of making the unbelievers to believe
cards.question: Machiavelli states that 'all armed prophets have conquered, and the unarmed ones have been destroyed,' then describes Savonarola as someone 'ruined with his new order of things immediately the multitude believed in him no longer.' What irony does this contrast create?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Savonarola is presented as more virtuous than Moses, Cyrus, Theseus, and Romulus, yet his greater virtue made him less capable of holding power than those ancient rulers.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Savonarola's entire power rested on persuading people to believe in him, yet that dependence on belief—rather than force—meant the moment belief faded, the very foundation of his authority became the instrument of his destruction.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Savonarola attempted to use force against his followers after they stopped believing in him, which turned a loyal population into enemies and guaranteed his ruin.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Savonarola succeeded in persuading the multitude to believe in him, but his failure to expand that belief to neighboring states left him without the military alliances needed to survive.

cards.standardTitle: Central idea and supporting evidence
cards.excerpt:
But the difficulties occur in a new principality. And firstly, if it be not entirely new, but is, as it were, a member of a state which, taken collectively, may be called composite, the changes arise chiefly from an inherent difficulty which there is in all new principalities; for men change their rulers willingly, hoping to better themselves, and this hope induces them to take up arms against him who rules: wherein they are deceived, because they afterwards find by experience they have gone from bad to worse. This follows also on another natural and common necessity, which always causes a new prince to burden those who have submitted to him with his soldiery and with infinite other hardships which he must put upon his new acquisition.

In this way you have enemies in all those whom you have injured in seizing that principality, and you are not able to keep those friends who put you there because of your not being able to satisfy them in the way they expected, and you cannot take strong measures against them, feeling bound to them. For, although one may be very strong in armed forces, yet in entering a province one has always need of the goodwill of the natives.
cards.whyThisWorks: The two paragraphs build a single argument about why new rulers inevitably face opposition, giving students a clear central idea to distinguish from isolated details like rebellion outcomes or military strength.
cards.skillStrategy: Ask yourself: what one problem do BOTH paragraphs keep returning to, and state it as a complete idea, not just a topic word like 'power' or 'enemies'.
evidencePoints: you have enemies in all those whom you have injured in seizing that principality, and you are not able to keep those friends who put you there

men change their rulers willingly, hoping to better themselves, and this hope induces them to take up arms against him who rules: wherein they are deceived, because they afterwards find by experience they have gone from bad to worse
cards.question: Machiavelli states that a new prince gains 'enemies in all those whom you have injured in seizing that principality' and also cannot satisfy 'those friends who put you there.' What central idea do both paragraphs develop through these two claims?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Subjects who rebel against a new ruler always suffer worse conditions than they endured before, making armed resistance a self-defeating choice.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Seizing a new principality forces a ruler into unavoidable opposition on both sides—those he harmed to gain power and those he cannot reward for helping him gain it.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Armed force alone determines whether a new prince can hold a principality, because goodwill from natives is impossible to earn after conquest.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Composite states present greater governing challenges than entirely new principalities because their populations already have divided loyalties.

cards.question: Machiavelli develops the theme that lasting power requires the ability to compel, not merely persuade. Which detail from the excerpt most directly supports this theme?
