cards.standardTitle: Narrator perspective, irony, and satire
cards.excerpt: Therefore, one who becomes a prince through the favour of the people ought to keep them friendly, and this he can easily do seeing they only ask not to be oppressed by him. But one who, in opposition to the people, becomes a prince by the favour of the nobles, ought, above everything, to seek to win the people over to himself, and this he may easily do if he takes them under his protection. Because men, when they receive good from him of whom they were expecting evil, are bound more closely to their benefactor; thus the people quickly become more devoted to him than if he had been raised to the principality by their favours; and the prince can win their affections in many ways, but as these vary according to the circumstances one cannot give fixed rules, so I omit them; but, I repeat, it is necessary for a prince to have the people friendly, otherwise he has no security in adversity.
cards.whyThisWorks: Machiavelli's observation that a prince who rose against the people's will can earn deeper loyalty than one the people originally supported creates a clear situational irony through reversal—the expected outcome (hostility from those who were wronged) is contradicted by the actual outcome (stronger devotion).
cards.skillStrategy: When you spot a reversal—where the outcome is the opposite of what logic or expectation would predict—ask yourself what the reader would normally expect and how the text flips that expectation to create irony.
evidencePoints: men, when they receive good from him of whom they were expecting evil, are bound more closely to their benefactor
the people quickly become more devoted to him than if he had been raised to the principality by their favours
cards.question: Read the following passage from The Prince: 'men, when they receive good from him of whom they were expecting evil, are bound more closely to their benefactor; thus the people quickly become more devoted to him than if he had been raised to the principality by their favours.' What reversal in this passage creates irony?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A prince who already has the people's support must work harder to keep it than a prince who never had it.

choices.label: B
choices.text: A prince who originally rose to power against the people's will can end up commanding stronger loyalty from them than a prince the people willingly supported from the start.

choices.label: C
choices.text: A prince who relies on the nobles for power is ultimately more secure than one who relies on the people, because nobles are easier to satisfy.

choices.label: D
choices.text: A prince who protects the people from oppression is rewarded with their devotion only when he follows fixed rules of governance.

cards.standardTitle: Central idea and supporting evidence
cards.excerpt:
Thus it arose that, men’s minds being thus unsettled, it was decided by certain men of Urbino to seize the fortress of San Leo, which was held for the duke, and which they captured by the following means. The castellan was fortifying the rock and causing timber to be taken there; so the conspirators watched, and when certain beams which were being carried to the rock were upon the bridge, so that it was prevented from being drawn up by those inside, they took the opportunity of leaping upon the bridge and thence into the fortress. Upon this capture being effected, the whole state rebelled and recalled the old duke, being encouraged in this, not so much by the capture of the fort, as by the Diet at Magione, from whom they expected to get assistance.

Those who heard of the rebellion at Urbino thought they would not lose the opportunity, and at once assembled their men so as to take any town, should any remain in the hands of the duke in that state; and they sent again to Florence to beg that republic to join with them in destroying the common firebrand, showing that the risk was lessened and that they ought not to wait for another opportunity.
cards.whyThisWorks: The two paragraphs move from a single tactical event (the bridge/beams capture) to a region-wide political consequence, requiring students to distinguish the central idea from the isolated detail of the fortress seizure.
cards.skillStrategy: Ask yourself: what do both paragraphs together add up to — not just what happens in one moment, but what that moment causes across the whole passage?
evidencePoints: encouraged in this, not so much by the capture of the fort, as by the Diet at Magione, from whom they expected to get assistance
Those who heard of the rebellion at Urbino thought they would not lose the opportunity, and at once assembled their men
cards.question: The narrator states that the people were encouraged 'not so much by the capture of the fort' as by outside support, and then describes others assembling men after 'hearing of the rebellion at Urbino.' What central idea do these two details together develop across both paragraphs?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The conspirators' clever use of the beams on the bridge was the decisive factor that brought down the duke's control of the region.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The fall of a single fortress set off a spreading rebellion, as the act of resistance gave others across the region the confidence and occasion to move against the duke.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Florence held the power to determine the outcome of the conflict, and the rebels' repeated appeals to that republic were the true engine of the uprising.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The Diet of Magione was the primary cause of the rebellion, and the capture of San Leo was merely a minor event that the narrator uses to introduce it.

cards.standardTitle: Theme development across a literary text
cards.excerpt: The cities of Germany are absolutely free, they own but little country around them, and they yield obedience to the emperor when it suits them, nor do they fear this or any other power they may have near them, because they are fortified in such a way that every one thinks the taking of them by assault would be tedious and difficult, seeing they have proper ditches and walls, they have sufficient artillery, and they always keep in public depots enough for one year’s eating, drinking, and firing. And beyond this, to keep the people quiet and without loss to the state, they always have the means of giving work to the community in those labours that are the life and strength of the city, and on the pursuit of which the people are supported; they also hold military exercises in repute, and moreover have many ordinances to uphold them.
cards.whyThisWorks: The excerpt presents multiple true details about German cities—artillery, food stores, employment, military exercises—but only the details about keeping citizens employed and engaged in city labor directly develop Machiavelli's theme that a ruler's security depends on maintaining the loyalty and stability of the people, not just on physical fortifications.
cards.skillStrategy: Ask yourself: does this detail show WHY the city stays strong and free, or does it just describe what the city has? Only details that connect to the central idea about power and loyalty develop the theme.
evidencePoints: they always have the means of giving work to the community in those labours that are the life and strength of the city
they are fortified in such a way that every one thinks the taking of them by assault would be tedious and difficult
cards.question: Machiavelli develops the theme that a ruler's true security comes from keeping the people content and unified. Which detail from the excerpt best develops this theme?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The German cities keep public depots stocked with enough food, drink, and fuel to last one year, showing their careful preparation for siege.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The German cities always have the means of giving work to the community in labours described as 'the life and strength of the city,' showing that the people's engagement sustains the city's power.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The German cities yield obedience to the emperor only when it suits them, showing that they are largely independent from outside authority.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The German cities have proper ditches, walls, and sufficient artillery, making any assault on them appear tedious and difficult to enemies.

cards.standardTitle: Narrator perspective, irony, and satire
cards.excerpt: But to come to those who, by their own ability and not through fortune, have risen to be princes, I say that Moses, Cyrus, Romulus, Theseus, and such like are the most excellent examples. And although one may not discuss Moses, he having been a mere executor of the will of God, yet he ought to be admired, if only for that favour which made him worthy to speak with God. But in considering Cyrus and others who have acquired or founded kingdoms, all will be found admirable; and if their particular deeds and conduct shall be considered, they will not be found inferior to those of Moses, although he had so great a preceptor. And in examining their actions and lives one cannot see that they owed anything to fortune beyond opportunity, which brought them the material to mould into the form which seemed best to them. Without that opportunity their powers of mind would have been extinguished, and without those powers the opportunity would have come in vain.
cards.whyThisWorks: Machiavelli creates situational irony by praising Moses as a supreme example of a prince who rose through his own ability, then immediately qualifying that Moses was 'a mere executor of the will of God'—a direct contradiction that undercuts the very claim of self-made greatness.
cards.skillStrategy: When a writer makes a strong claim and then says something that contradicts or reverses it, look for the gap between what is stated and what is actually implied—that gap is the irony.
evidencePoints: those who, by their own ability and not through fortune, have risen to be princes
although one may not discuss Moses, he having been a mere executor of the will of God
cards.question: Read the following sentences from the passage: 'But to come to those who, by their own ability and not through fortune, have risen to be princes, I say that Moses, Cyrus, Romulus, Theseus, and such like are the most excellent examples. And although one may not discuss Moses, he having been a mere executor of the will of God…' What contradiction in these sentences creates irony?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Moses is praised alongside Cyrus and Romulus, yet the passage later admits that Cyrus owed his success entirely to fortune rather than personal ability.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Moses is introduced as a prime example of someone who rose through his own ability, yet he is immediately described as merely carrying out God's will, which undermines the claim of self-made greatness.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The passage argues that opportunity alone is sufficient for greatness, yet Moses is presented as proof that divine favor matters more than any personal opportunity.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Moses is called admirable for speaking with God, yet the passage suggests that this divine connection made him inferior to leaders like Cyrus who acted without any outside guidance.

cards.standardTitle: Central idea and supporting evidence
cards.excerpt: But when states are acquired in a country differing in language, customs, or laws, there are difficulties, and good fortune and great energy are needed to hold them, and one of the greatest and most real helps would be that he who has acquired them should go and reside there. This would make his position more secure and durable, as it has made that of the Turk in Greece, who, notwithstanding all the other measures taken by him for holding that state, if he had not settled there, would not have been able to keep it. Because, if one is on the spot, disorders are seen as they spring up, and one can quickly remedy them; but if one is not at hand, they are heard of only when they are great, and then one can no longer remedy them. Besides this, the country is not pillaged by your officials; the subjects are satisfied by prompt recourse to the prince; thus, wishing to be good, they have more cause to love him, and wishing to be otherwise, to fear him. He who would attack that state from the outside must have the utmost caution; as long as the prince resides there it can only be wrested from him with the greatest difficulty.
cards.whyThisWorks: The excerpt builds a single, traceable argument—illustrated by the Turk-in-Greece example and the list of practical benefits—that a prince must physically reside in a conquered foreign state to keep it, giving students concrete evidence to distinguish the central idea from supporting details or the opening topic statement.
cards.skillStrategy: Ask yourself: what claim does every sentence in the paragraph keep coming back to? That recurring claim—not the opening problem or one supporting reason—is the central idea.
evidencePoints: one of the greatest and most real helps would be that he who has acquired them should go and reside there
as long as the prince resides there it can only be wrested from him with the greatest difficulty
cards.question: Machiavelli opens by naming several difficulties of holding a foreign state, then states that 'one of the greatest and most real helps would be that he who has acquired them should go and reside there,' and closes by saying the state 'can only be wrested from him with the greatest difficulty' as long as the prince stays. What central idea do these framing statements, along with the Turk-in-Greece example in between, work together to express?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Acquiring a state that differs in language, customs, or laws requires both good fortune and great energy, making such conquests far riskier than conquering similar states.

choices.label: B
choices.text: A prince who personally lives in a newly acquired foreign state gains decisive advantages in security and control that a distant ruler cannot achieve.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The Turkish ruler's success in Greece proves that taking many different measures together is the only reliable way to hold a foreign state.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Subjects in a foreign state remain loyal because prompt access to the prince gives those who wish to be good more reason to love him and those who do not more reason to fear him.

cards.standardTitle: Theme development across a literary text
cards.excerpt: Therefore, a prince who has a strong city, and had not made himself odious, will not be attacked, or if any one should attack he will only be driven off with disgrace; again, because that the affairs of this world are so changeable, it is almost impossible to keep an army a whole year in the field without being interfered with. And whoever should reply: If the people have property outside the city, and see it burnt, they will not remain patient, and the long siege and self-interest will make them forget their prince; to this I answer that a powerful and courageous prince will overcome all such difficulties by giving at one time hope to his subjects that the evil will not be for long, at another time fear of the cruelty of the enemy, then preserving himself adroitly from those subjects who seem to him to be too bold.
cards.whyThisWorks: The excerpt forces students to distinguish between details that merely describe siege conditions (true but topical) and the specific psychological strategy—alternating hope and fear—that develops the theme of deliberate leadership.
cards.skillStrategy: Ask yourself: does this detail show HOW the prince keeps power, or does it just describe what happens during a siege? Only the 'how' details develop the theme.
evidencePoints: giving at one time hope to his subjects that the evil will not be for long, at another time fear of the cruelty of the enemy
a powerful and courageous prince will overcome all such difficulties
cards.question: Machiavelli claims that 'a powerful and courageous prince will overcome all such difficulties' by alternating between giving subjects 'hope' and instilling 'fear of the cruelty of the enemy.' Which answer choice explains how this specific claim develops the theme that effective leadership requires deliberate control over subjects' emotions?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The claim shows that a prince's physical courage on the battlefield is what ultimately prevents subjects from abandoning him during a prolonged siege.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The claim shows that a prince sustains loyalty not through force alone but through a calculated strategy of managing what subjects feel—cycling between reassurance and dread—to keep them from turning against him.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The claim confirms that the unpredictability of worldly affairs, not the prince's actions, is the primary reason an attacking army cannot maintain a siege for a full year.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The claim establishes that avoiding hatred before a conflict begins is the prince's most important tool, making psychological management during a siege unnecessary.

cards.standardTitle: Narrator perspective, irony, and satire
cards.excerpt: Therefore, to make this point clearer, I say that the nobles ought to be looked at mainly in two ways: that is to say, they either shape their course in such a way as binds them entirely to your fortune, or they do not. Those who so bind themselves, and are not rapacious, ought to be honoured and loved; those who do not bind themselves may be dealt with in two ways; they may fail to do this through pusillanimity and a natural want of courage, in which case you ought to make use of them, especially of those who are of good counsel; and thus, whilst in prosperity you honour them, in adversity you do not have to fear them. But when for their own ambitious ends they shun binding themselves, it is a token that they are giving more thought to themselves than to you, and a prince ought to guard against such, and to fear them as if they were open enemies, because in adversity they always help to ruin him.
cards.whyThisWorks: Machiavelli creates situational irony by advising the prince to 'honour' nobles in prosperity who lack the courage to commit to him—the very people whose weakness makes them useless allies—while reserving fear for the bold, ambitious nobles whose strength would seem to make them more valuable.
cards.skillStrategy: Look for a moment where the expected outcome is flipped: ask yourself whether the group being rewarded or trusted is the one you would logically expect to receive that treatment.
evidencePoints: whilst in prosperity you honour them, in adversity you do not have to fear them
when for their own ambitious ends they shun binding themselves… a prince ought to guard against such, and to fear them as if they were open enemies
cards.question: Read the following passage from The Prince: 'whilst in prosperity you honour them, in adversity you do not have to fear them' and 'when for their own ambitious ends they shun binding themselves… a prince ought to fear them as if they were open enemies.' What irony is created by the contrast between these two statements?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Nobles who openly declare loyalty to the prince are ultimately the ones who betray him in times of crisis, making public pledges worthless.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The nobles who are too cowardly to fully commit to the prince—and therefore seem least worthy of reward—are honored and considered safe, while the bold, self-interested nobles who appear stronger are treated as the greater threat.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Nobles who offer good counsel during prosperity become dangerous advisors in adversity because their knowledge of the prince's affairs gives them power over him.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The prince's decision to honor nobles in prosperity backfires because those same nobles grow greedy and rapacious once they feel secure in his favor.

cards.standardTitle: Central idea and supporting evidence
cards.excerpt:
And as if it were not enough to have aggrandized the Church, and deprived himself of friends, he, wishing to have the kingdom of Naples, divided it with the King of Spain, and where he was the prime arbiter in Italy he takes an associate, so that the ambitious of that country and the malcontents of his own should have somewhere to shelter; and whereas he could have left in the kingdom his own pensioner as king, he drove him out, to put one there who was able to drive him, Louis, out in turn.

The wish to acquire is in truth very natural and common, and men always do so when they can, and for this they will be praised not blamed; but when they cannot do so, yet wish to do so by any means, then there is folly and blame. Therefore, if France could have attacked Naples with her own forces she ought to have done so; if she could not, then she ought not to have divided it. And if the partition which she made with the Venetians in Lombardy was justified by the excuse that by it she got a foothold in Italy, this other partition merited blame, for it had not the excuse of that necessity.
cards.whyThisWorks: The second paragraph opens with an explicit general claim about acquiring territory and then applies it directly to France's actions in Naples, giving students a clear central idea to identify rather than a topic or isolated detail.
cards.skillStrategy: Find the sentence where the author states a rule or judgment in plain terms, then check whether the rest of the passage supports that rule — that sentence is likely the central idea.
evidencePoints: when they cannot do so, yet wish to do so by any means, then there is folly and blame
this other partition merited blame, for it had not the excuse of that necessity
cards.question: Machiavelli writes, 'when they cannot do so, yet wish to do so by any means, then there is folly and blame.' Which statement expresses the central idea that this claim, together with the example of France and Naples, is meant to support?

choices.label: A
choices.text: France's greatest mistake was strengthening the Church and losing its allies in Italy before attempting to take Naples.

choices.label: B
choices.text: A ruler who pursues territorial gain beyond his actual capacity to secure it acts foolishly and earns blame rather than praise.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Dividing conquered territory with any partner is inherently dangerous because it always produces a rival capable of expelling the original conqueror.

choices.label: D
choices.text: France deserved blame specifically because it drove out a loyal king in Naples and replaced him with an enemy.

cards.standardTitle: Theme development across a literary text
cards.excerpt: For these reasons Louis the Twelfth, King of France, quickly occupied Milan, and as quickly lost it; and to turn him out the first time it only needed Lodovico’s own forces; because those who had opened the gates to him, finding themselves deceived in their hopes of future benefit, would not endure the ill-treatment of the new prince. It is very true that, after acquiring rebellious provinces a second time, they are not so lightly lost afterwards, because the prince, with little reluctance, takes the opportunity of the rebellion to punish the delinquents, to clear out the suspects, and to strengthen himself in the weakest places. Thus to cause France to lose Milan the first time it was enough for the Duke Lodovico to raise insurrections on the borders; but to cause him to lose it a second time it was necessary to bring the whole world against him, and that his armies should be defeated and driven out of Italy; which followed from the causes above mentioned.
cards.whyThisWorks: The excerpt contrasts two losses of Milan—one caused by broken promises to subjects, one requiring full military defeat—letting students distinguish a detail that develops the theme of expectation-based loyalty from true-but-off-theme military details.
cards.skillStrategy: Ask yourself: does this detail show WHY the ruler lost power, or does it just describe WHAT happened militarily? Only the detail that explains the cause connects to the theme.
evidencePoints: finding themselves deceived in their hopes of future benefit, would not endure the ill-treatment of the new prince
to cause France to lose Milan the first time it was enough for the Duke Lodovico to raise insurrections on the borders
cards.question: Machiavelli states that Louis lost Milan the first time because those who 'opened the gates to him, finding themselves deceived in their hopes of future benefit, would not endure the ill-treatment of the new prince.' Which detail from the excerpt most directly uses this moment to develop the theme that a ruler cannot hold power when he fails to meet his subjects' expectations?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Louis 'quickly occupied Milan, and as quickly lost it,' showing that the speed of his conquest made his hold on the territory fragile from the start.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The people who opened the gates to Louis refused to endure his ill-treatment once they realized the promised benefits would not come, and their rebellion—not an outside army—was enough to remove him, proving that a ruler's broken promises directly destroy his hold on power.

choices.label: C
choices.text: To lose Milan a second time 'it was necessary to bring the whole world against him, and that his armies should be defeated and driven out of Italy,' showing that military force is the true measure of a ruler's power.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Duke Lodovico needed only his own forces to drive Louis out the first time, demonstrating that Lodovico was a more capable and better-prepared military commander than Louis.

cards.standardTitle: Narrator perspective, irony, and satire
cards.excerpt: These matters coming to the knowledge of the Vitelli and Orsini and their following, it appeared to them that the duke would become too powerful, and it was feared that, having seized Bologna, he would seek to destroy them in order that he might become supreme in Italy. Upon this a meeting was called at Magione in the district of Perugia, to which came the cardinal, Pagolo, and the Duke di Gravina Orsini, Vitellozzo Vitelli, Oliverotto da Fermo, Gianpagolo Baglioni, the tyrant of Perugia, and Messer Antonio da Venafro, sent by Pandolfo Petrucci, the Prince of Siena. Here were discussed the power and courage of the duke and the necessity of curbing his ambitions, which might otherwise bring danger to the rest of being ruined. And they decided not to abandon the Bentivogli, but to strive to win over the Florentines; and they sent their men to one place and another, promising to one party assistance and to another encouragement to unite with them against the common enemy. This meeting was at once reported throughout all Italy, and those who were discontented under the duke, among whom were the people of Urbino, took hope of effecting a revolution.
cards.whyThisWorks: The excerpt creates situational irony through a clear reversal: the very lords who conspired with Cesare Borgia (the duke) to destroy others now fear being destroyed by him, turning their former alliance into the source of their danger.
cards.skillStrategy: Look for a moment where the outcome or situation is the opposite of what the characters expected or caused — that reversal is the irony.
evidencePoints: it was feared that, having seized Bologna, he would seek to destroy them in order that he might become supreme in Italy
the necessity of curbing his ambitions, which might otherwise bring danger to the rest of being ruined
cards.question: Read the following passage detail: 'it was feared that, having seized Bologna, he would seek to destroy them in order that he might become supreme in Italy.' What is ironic about the situation described in this excerpt?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The lords gathered at Magione are afraid of the duke even though they outnumber him, which shows their fear is irrational.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The lords who helped the duke gain power by eliminating rivals now find themselves threatened with destruction by the very power they helped him build.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The people of Urbino take hope in a revolution, even though the meeting at Magione was reported throughout all of Italy, making secrecy impossible.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The duke's ambitions are described as dangerous, yet the lords at Magione make promises to multiple parties, showing they share his methods.

cards.standardTitle: Central idea and supporting evidence
cards.excerpt:
I compare her to one of those raging rivers, which when in flood overflows the plains, sweeping away trees and buildings, bearing away the soil from place to place; everything flies before it, all yield to its violence, without being able in any way to withstand it; and yet, though its nature be such, it does not follow therefore that men, when the weather becomes fair, shall not make provision, both with defences and barriers, in such a manner that, rising again, the waters may pass away by canal, and their force be neither so unrestrained nor so dangerous. So it happens with fortune, who shows her power where valour has not prepared to resist her, and thither she turns her forces where she knows that barriers and defences have not been raised to constrain her.

And if you will consider Italy, which is the seat of these changes, and which has given to them their impulse, you will see it to be an open country without barriers and without any defence. For if it had been defended by proper valour, as are Germany, Spain, and France, either this invasion would not have made the great changes it has made or it would not have come at all. And this I consider enough to say concerning resistance to fortune in general.
cards.whyThisWorks: Machiavelli's river metaphor and the Italy example together force students to distinguish the central claim—preparation limits fortune's power—from the isolated detail about Italy or the distractor that fortune is wholly unstoppable.
cards.skillStrategy: Ask yourself what the author wants you to believe after reading both paragraphs, not just what one sentence says or what topic is mentioned.
evidencePoints: it does not follow therefore that men, when the weather becomes fair, shall not make provision, both with defences and barriers, in such a manner that, rising again, the waters may pass away by canal, and their force be neither so unrestrained nor so dangerous
fortune, who shows her power where valour has not prepared to resist her, and thither she turns her forces where she knows that barriers and defences have not been raised to constrain her
cards.question: Machiavelli writes that fortune 'shows her power where valour has not prepared to resist her.' What central idea do both paragraphs develop through this claim and the river comparison that precedes it?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Fortune is an overwhelming force, like a flooding river, that destroys everything in its path and cannot be slowed by any human action.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Although fortune can be as destructive as a raging flood, people who build defenses in advance can limit how much damage fortune does.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Italy's open geography made it uniquely unable to resist foreign invasion, unlike the naturally protected nations of Germany, Spain, and France.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Rulers who study the behavior of rivers will understand fortune well enough to prevent any harm it might cause their nations.

cards.standardTitle: Theme development across a literary text
cards.excerpt: But when states are acquired in a country differing in language, customs, or laws, there are difficulties, and good fortune and great energy are needed to hold them, and one of the greatest and most real helps would be that he who has acquired them should go and reside there. This would make his position more secure and durable, as it has made that of the Turk in Greece, who, notwithstanding all the other measures taken by him for holding that state, if he had not settled there, would not have been able to keep it. Because, if one is on the spot, disorders are seen as they spring up, and one can quickly remedy them; but if one is not at hand, they are heard of only when they are great, and then one can no longer remedy them. Besides this, the country is not pillaged by your officials; the subjects are satisfied by prompt recourse to the prince; thus, wishing to be good, they have more cause to love him, and wishing to be otherwise, to fear him. He who would attack that state from the outside must have the utmost caution; as long as the prince resides there it can only be wrested from him with the greatest difficulty.
cards.whyThisWorks: The excerpt presents multiple true details about a prince residing in a conquered state, but only the contrast between seeing 'disorders as they spring up' versus hearing of them 'only when they are great' directly develops the theme that physical presence is the foundation of lasting control—forcing students to distinguish theme-developing evidence from topic-matching details.
cards.skillStrategy: Ask yourself: does this detail show WHY the theme is true, or does it just relate to the same topic? Only details that prove the central claim develop the theme.
evidencePoints: if one is on the spot, disorders are seen as they spring up, and one can quickly remedy them; but if one is not at hand, they are heard of only when they are great, and then one can no longer remedy them
one of the greatest and most real helps would be that he who has acquired them should go and reside there
cards.question: Machiavelli states that 'if one is on the spot, disorders are seen as they spring up, and one can quickly remedy them; but if one is not at hand, they are heard of only when they are great, and then one can no longer remedy them.' Which statement best explains how this contrast develops the theme that a ruler's physical presence is the foundation of lasting control?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The contrast shows that conquered territories with different languages and customs produce more frequent disorders, making cultural difference the true threat to a prince's power.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The contrast proves that presence gives a prince the ability to intervene before problems become unmanageable, making residence the practical source of his control rather than military strength or good fortune.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The contrast illustrates that outside attackers are deterred when they know a prince is nearby, showing that the prince's location matters mainly as a military deterrent.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The contrast demonstrates that subjects who fear their prince report disorders more quickly, meaning fear—not physical presence—is what allows a ruler to maintain lasting control.

cards.standardTitle: Narrator perspective, irony, and satire
cards.excerpt: This reconciliation being completed, Guido Ubaldo, the Duke of Urbino, again fled to Venice, having first destroyed all the fortresses in his state; because, trusting in the people, he did not wish that the fortresses, which he did not think he could defend, should be held by the enemy, since by these means a check would be kept upon his friends. But the Duke Valentino, having completed this convention, and dispersed his men throughout the Romagna, set out for Imola at the end of November together with his French men-at-arms: thence he went to Cesena, where he stayed some time to negotiate with the envoys of the Vitelli and Orsini, who had assembled with their men in the duchy of Urbino, as to the enterprise in which they should now take part; but nothing being concluded, Oliverotto da Fermo was sent to propose that if the duke wished to undertake an expedition against Tuscany they were ready; if he did not wish it, then they would besiege Sinigalia. To this the duke replied that he did not wish to enter into war with Tuscany, and thus become hostile to the Florentines, but that he was very willing to proceed against Sinigalia.
cards.whyThisWorks: Guido Ubaldo destroys his own fortresses to protect his people from the enemy, yet this act of apparent loyalty leaves his state defenseless—a situational irony created by the reversal between his protective intention and the self-defeating outcome.
cards.skillStrategy: When you spot a character's stated reason for an action that produces the opposite of the intended result, you have found situational irony through reversal.
evidencePoints: trusting in the people, he did not wish that the fortresses, which he did not think he could defend, should be held by the enemy
having first destroyed all the fortresses in his state
cards.question: Read the following passage detail: 'Guido Ubaldo, the Duke of Urbino, again fled to Venice, having first destroyed all the fortresses in his state; because, trusting in the people, he did not wish that the fortresses, which he did not think he could defend, should be held by the enemy.' What is ironic about the Duke of Urbino's decision to destroy his own fortresses?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The duke destroys the fortresses out of cowardice, yet his flight to Venice proves he never trusted his people at all.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The duke demolishes his own defenses in order to protect his people, yet this act of loyalty leaves his state completely vulnerable to the very enemy he feared.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The duke trusts his people to rebuild the fortresses, yet Duke Valentino's army arrives before any reconstruction can begin.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The duke destroys the fortresses to prevent the enemy from using them, and this strategy successfully keeps Duke Valentino's forces out of Urbino.

cards.standardTitle: Central idea and supporting evidence
cards.excerpt: The other and better course is to send colonies to one or two places, which may be as keys to that state, for it is necessary either to do this or else to keep there a great number of cavalry and infantry. A prince does not spend much on colonies, for with little or no expense he can send them out and keep them there, and he offends a minority only of the citizens from whom he takes lands and houses to give them to the new inhabitants; and those whom he offends, remaining poor and scattered, are never able to injure him; whilst the rest being uninjured are easily kept quiet, and at the same time are anxious not to err for fear it should happen to them as it has to those who have been despoiled. In conclusion, I say that these colonies are not costly, they are more faithful, they injure less, and the injured, as has been said, being poor and scattered, cannot hurt. Upon this, one has to remark that men ought either to be well treated or crushed, because they can avenge themselves of lighter injuries, of more serious ones they cannot; therefore the injury that is to be done to a man ought to be of such a kind that one does not stand in fear of revenge.
cards.whyThisWorks: The paragraph opens with a policy recommendation, develops it with cost and control reasoning, and closes with a blunt maxim—giving students a clear arc from claim to evidence to central idea.
cards.skillStrategy: Find the sentence where the author sums up his argument, then ask what idea all the supporting details are building toward.
evidencePoints: these colonies are not costly, they are more faithful, they injure less, and the injured, as has been said, being poor and scattered, cannot hurt
the injury that is to be done to a man ought to be of such a kind that one does not stand in fear of revenge
cards.question: Near the end of the passage, Machiavelli writes, 'these colonies are not costly, they are more faithful, they injure less, and the injured, as has been said, being poor and scattered, cannot hurt.' What central idea does this summary statement, together with the rest of the passage, express?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A prince who takes land from citizens to give to colonists will always create enemies who eventually unite against him.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Colonies are the shrewdest method for a prince to hold conquered territory because they cost little, keep most subjects compliant, and reduce any opposition to a scattered, powerless minority.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The only real danger a prince faces in a new territory comes from citizens who lose their homes, so he must compensate them generously to prevent rebellion.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Maintaining a large force of cavalry and infantry is ultimately more reliable than sending colonies because it leaves no citizens with a grievance.

cards.standardTitle: Paraphrase grade-level text
cards.excerpt:
A prince, therefore, ought always to take counsel, but only when he wishes and not when others wish; he ought rather to discourage every one from offering advice unless he asks it; but, however, he ought to be a constant inquirer, and afterwards a patient listener concerning the things of which he inquired; also, on learning that any one, on any consideration, has not told him the truth, he should let his anger be felt.

And if there are some who think that a prince who conveys an impression of his wisdom is not so through his own ability, but through the good advisers that he has around him, beyond doubt they are deceived, because this is an axiom which never fails: that a prince who is not wise himself will never take good advice, unless by chance he has yielded his affairs entirely to one person who happens to be a very prudent man. In this case indeed he may be well governed, but it would not be for long, because such a governor would in a short time take away his state from him.
cards.whyThisWorks: The second paragraph contains a long, syntactically complex sentence with an embedded conditional clause ('unless by chance he has yielded his affairs entirely to one person') followed by a consequence clause, requiring students to untangle the nested logic to restate the full meaning accurately.
cards.skillStrategy: Break the sentence into its main claim, its exception, and the result of that exception — then check that your restatement keeps all three parts.
evidencePoints: a prince who is not wise himself will never take good advice, unless by chance he has yielded his affairs entirely to one person who happens to be a very prudent man
such a governor would in a short time take away his state from him
cards.question: Read the following sentence from the second paragraph: 'a prince who is not wise himself will never take good advice, unless by chance he has yielded his affairs entirely to one person who happens to be a very prudent man. In this case indeed he may be well governed, but it would not be for long, because such a governor would in a short time take away his state from him.' Which restatement most accurately captures the full meaning of these sentences?

choices.label: A
choices.text: An unwise prince can always find good advice if he surrounds himself with many prudent advisers, and by doing so he will remain well governed indefinitely.

choices.label: B
choices.text: An unwise prince cannot receive good counsel on his own; if he happens to hand all control to one truly wise man, he might be governed well for a time, but that adviser would eventually seize power from him.

choices.label: C
choices.text: An unwise prince will never be well governed under any circumstances, because no single adviser, however prudent, can compensate for a ruler's lack of wisdom.

choices.label: D
choices.text: An unwise prince who relies on one prudent adviser will receive good counsel, and as long as he trusts that adviser completely, his rule will remain secure.

cards.standardTitle: Key literary elements add layers of meaning
cards.excerpt: CLY. (_to an attendant_). Then lift for me those fruitful offerings, While to Apollo, before whom we stand, I raise my supplication for release From doubts and fears that shake my bosom now. And, O defender of our house! attend My secret utterance. No friendly ear Is that which hearkens for my voice. My thought Must not be blazoned with her standing by, Lest through her envious and wide-babbling tongue She fill the city full of wild surmise. List, then, as I shall speak: and grant the dreams Whose two-fold apparition I to-night Have seen, if good their bodement, be fulfilled: If hostile, turn their influence on my foes. And yield not them their wish that would by guile Thrust me from this high fortune, but vouchsafe That ever thus exempt from harms I rule The Atridae's home and kingdom, in full life, Partaking with the friends I live with now All fair prosperity, and with my children, Save those who hate and vex me bitterly. Lykeian Phoebus, favourably hear My prayer, and grant to all of us our need! More is there, which, though I be silent here, A God should understand. No secret thing Is hidden from the all-seeing sons of Heaven.
cards.whyThisWorks: Clytemnestra's demand for secrecy, her fear of Electra's 'wide-babbling tongue,' and her prayer to keep her 'high fortune' reveal a ruler whose piety masks political self-interest, making this a rich characterization moment.
cards.skillStrategy: When a character's words and actions contradict what we expect, ask what that gap reveals about who they really are.
evidencePoints: Lest through her envious and wide-babbling tongue She fill the city full of wild surmise.
yield not them their wish that would by guile Thrust me from this high fortune
cards.question: Clytemnestra prays in secret so Electra's 'wide-babbling tongue' cannot 'fill the city full of wild surmise,' and asks Apollo to protect her 'high fortune.' What do these details reveal about her character?

choices.label: A
choices.text: She is a devoted worshipper who fears Electra will disrupt the sacred ritual itself.

choices.label: B
choices.text: She is a calculating ruler who hides her fear of losing power behind a show of piety.

choices.label: C
choices.text: She is a grieving mother who prays for peace with her children and protection from outside enemies.

choices.label: D
choices.text: She is a humble queen who confesses her sins and asks Apollo for honest guidance.

cards.standardTitle: Text structure and feature purpose
cards.excerpt:
CHORUS. An erring seer am I, I 1 Of sense and wisdom lorn, If this prophetic Power of right, O'ertaking the offender, come not nigh Ere many an hour be born. Yon vision of the night, That lately breathed into my listening ear, Hath freed me, O my daughter, from all fear. Sweet was that bodement. He doth not forget, The Achaean lord that gave thee being, nor yet The bronzen-griding axe, edged like a spear, Hungry and keen, though dark with stains of time, That in the hour of hideous crime Quelled him with cruel butchery: That, too, remembers, and shall testify.

From ambush deep and dread I 2 With power of many a hand And many hastening feet shall spring The Fury of the adamantine tread, Visiting Argive land Swift recompense to bring For eager dalliance of a blood-stained pair Unhallowed, foul, forbidden. No omen fair,-- Their impious course hath fixed this in my soul,-- Nought but black portents full of blame shall roll Before their eyes that wrought or aided there. Small force of divination would there seem In prophecy or solemn dream, Should not this vision of the night Reach harbour in reality aright.
cards.whyThisWorks: The two-paragraph structure clearly shows the Chorus moving from a past crime (the axe that 'quelled' Agamemnon) to a promised future punishment ('swift recompense'), giving students a concrete example of how a second paragraph extends and shifts the focus of the first.
cards.skillStrategy: Ask yourself: what job does this paragraph do that the previous one did not—does it add new information, shift time, contradict, or summarize?
evidencePoints: Hath freed me, O my daughter, from all fear
With power of many a hand / And many hastening feet shall spring / The Fury of the adamantine tread, / Visiting Argive land / Swift recompense to bring
cards.question: In the first paragraph, the Chorus says the dream 'hath freed me…from all fear' and recalls the 'bronzen-griding axe' that killed Agamemnon. What is the job of the second paragraph ('From ambush deep and dread…') in relation to the first?

choices.label: A
choices.text: It undermines the Chorus's confidence from the first paragraph by warning that 'small force of divination' means the dream about the axe may not come true.

choices.label: B
choices.text: It extends the Chorus's certainty established in the first paragraph by shifting from the past crime of the 'bronzen-griding axe' to the future punishment the Fury will bring as 'swift recompense' to the guilty pair.

choices.label: C
choices.text: It summarizes the first paragraph by restating the details of Agamemnon's murder—the axe, the 'hideous crime,' and the 'cruel butchery'—without adding new information.

choices.label: D
choices.text: It introduces the 'blood-stained pair' as an entirely new subject unconnected to the dream or the fear the Chorus described in the first paragraph.

cards.standardTitle: Key literary elements add layers of meaning
cards.excerpt: CHR. True, noble women, and before she spake Sound thought should have prevented the rash talk That now hath proved her reckless. What wild aim Beckons thee forth in arming this design Whereto thou wouldst demand my ministry? Dost not perceive, thou art not man but woman, Of strength inferior to thine enemies,-- Their Genius daily prospering more and more, Whilst ours is dwindling into nothingness? Who then that plots against a life so strong Shall quit him of the danger without harm? Take heed we do not add to our distress Should some one hear of this our colloquy. Small help and poor advantage 'twere for us To win brief praise and then inglorious die. Nay, death is not so hateful as when one Desiring death is balked of that desire. And I beseech thee, ere in utter ruin We perish and make desolate our race, Refrain thy rage. And I will guard for thee In silence these thy words unrealized; If thou wilt learn this wisdom from long time, Having no strength, to bend before the strong.
cards.whyThisWorks: Chrysothemis's speech reveals her character through cautious, pragmatic reasoning—urging submission to power rather than reckless action—which contrasts sharply with Electra's defiance and adds meaning about survival versus honor.
cards.skillStrategy: When a character speaks at length, ask what their words reveal about their values and how those values create contrast or tension with another character's choices.
evidencePoints: Dost not perceive, thou art not man but woman, Of strength inferior to thine enemies
Having no strength, to bend before the strong
cards.question: In her speech, Chrysothemis urges Electra to 'bend before the strong.' What does this counsel reveal about Chrysothemis's character?

choices.label: A
choices.text: She is indifferent to Electra's suffering and refuses to acknowledge the injustice their family has endured.

choices.label: B
choices.text: She values self-preservation and practical caution over honor, prioritizing survival above the glory of resistance.

choices.label: C
choices.text: She secretly admires their enemies and wishes to align herself with those in power for personal gain.

choices.label: D
choices.text: She believes Electra's plan will succeed but fears punishment if she is discovered helping her sister.

cards.skillStrategy: When analyzing characterization, track how a character's own words about themselves change within a passage and ask what that shift reveals about their role or the text's larger meaning.

Hath freed me, O my daughter, from all fear
cards.question: In the first paragraph, the Chorus describes itself as 'An erring seer… of sense and wisdom lorn,' but then declares that the night vision 'hath freed me, O my daughter, from all fear.' What does this shift in the Chorus's self-characterization reveal about its role in the passage?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The Chorus presents itself as permanently unreliable, admitting that neither the night vision nor the 'bronzen-griding axe' can confirm whether divine justice will arrive.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The Chorus moves from doubting its own prophetic power to renewed certainty, showing that the night vision has restored its confidence that divine justice will overtake the offender.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The Chorus shifts from mourning Electra's suffering to celebrating the 'blood-stained pair,' suggesting its fear was rooted in sympathy for the guilty rather than concern for justice.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The Chorus reveals that it initially doubted Electra's grief but is reassured by the vision, showing that its characterization centers on personal loyalty to Electra rather than prophecy.

cards.excerpt:

Yon vision of the night, That lately breathed into my listening ear, Hath freed me, O my daughter, from all fear. Sweet was that bodement. He doth not forget, The Achaean lord that gave thee being, nor yet The bronzen-griding axe, edged like a spear, Hungry and keen, though dark with stains of time, That in the hour of hideous crime Quelled him with cruel butchery: That, too, remembers, and shall testify.

cards.whyThisWorks: The excerpt contains both theme-developing details (the Fury's promised vengeance, the axe that 'remembers,' the 'blood-stained pair' facing retribution) and true-but-topic-only details (the dream's sweetness, the chorus's fear being lifted), allowing students to distinguish evidence that actually builds the theme of divine justice from details that merely establish mood or setting.
cards.skillStrategy: Ask yourself: does this detail show the theme in action, or does it just describe what is happening in the scene without pushing the central idea forward?
evidencePoints: The bronzen-griding axe, edged like a spear, Hungry and keen, though dark with stains of time, That in the hour of hideous crime Quelled him with cruel butchery: That, too, remembers, and shall testify.

With power of many a hand And many hastening feet shall spring The Fury of the adamantine tread, Visiting Argive land Swift recompense to bring For eager dalliance of a blood-stained pair Unhallowed, foul, forbidden.
cards.question: Which detail from the Chorus's speech most directly develops the theme that violent crimes against the innocent will ultimately be punished by a force greater than human will?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The Chorus describes the night vision as 'sweet' and says it has freed them 'from all fear,' showing that the dream brought comfort to those who mourned.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The axe that killed Electra's father is said to 'remember' and 'testify,' and the Fury is described as already moving toward Argos to deliver 'swift recompense' to the 'blood-stained pair,' showing that the crime itself demands retribution.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The Chorus admits it would be an 'erring seer' lacking 'sense and wisdom' if the prophetic power of right did not arrive, revealing the Chorus's own uncertainty about its role.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The Chorus warns that 'black portents full of blame shall roll before their eyes,' which describes the guilty pair's awareness of omens but focuses on their psychological dread rather than on justice itself.

cards.standardTitle: Text structure and feature purpose
cards.excerpt: CHR. Well, I will tell thee all I saw:--I came Unto the ancient tomb that holds our sire; And from the topmost mound I marked a stream Of milk fresh-flowing, and his resting place Ringed round with garlands of all flowers that blow. I marvelled at the sight, and peered about, Lest some one might be nearer than we knew. But finding all was quiet in the spot, I ventured closer to the tomb, and there, Hard by the limit, I beheld a curl Of hair new shorn, with all the gloss of youth And straight it struck my heart, as with a sense Of something seen, ah me! long, long ago, And told me that my sight encountered here The token of Orestes, dearest soul Then, clasping it, I did not cry aloud, But straight mine eyes were filled with tears of joy. And now as much as then I feel assured He and none else bestowed this ornament. To whom beyond thyself and me belongs Such consecration? And I know this well, I did it not,--nor thou. Impossible! Thou canst not worship even the blessed Gods Forth of this roof, unpunished. And, most sure, Our mother is not minded so to act, Nor, had she done it, could we fail to know. This offering comes then of Orestes' hand. Take courage, dear one. Not one fate pursues One house perpetually, but changeth still. Ours was a sullen Genius, but perchance This day begins the assurance of much good.
cards.whyThisWorks: Chrysothemis's speech moves from describing physical evidence at the tomb to drawing a firm conclusion about Orestes' return, making the paragraph's job—to build from observation to reasoned proof—clearly identifiable and teachable.
cards.skillStrategy: Ask yourself: what is this paragraph doing to the overall argument—is it introducing a new idea, backing up a claim with evidence, or shifting the direction of thought?
evidencePoints: I beheld a curl / Of hair new shorn, with all the gloss of youth / And straight it struck my heart
This offering comes then of Orestes' hand. / Take courage, dear one.
cards.question: In this speech, Chrysothemis moves from describing what she found at the tomb to declaring 'This offering comes then of Orestes' hand.' What is the primary job of this paragraph in the speech as a whole?

choices.label: A
choices.text: To introduce the idea that Orestes has already returned home and is hiding nearby

choices.label: B
choices.text: To use physical evidence at the tomb—the milk, garlands, and shorn hair—to prove that Orestes is alive and has returned, then shift toward urging Electra to have hope

choices.label: C
choices.text: To contrast Chrysothemis's cautious nature with Electra's reckless grief by showing that Chrysothemis alone visits their father's tomb

choices.label: D
choices.text: To conclude that their mother placed the offerings at the tomb as a sign of hidden remorse for her crimes

cards.standardTitle: Key literary elements add layers of meaning
cards.excerpt: EL. 'Tis strange and pitiful, thy father's child Can leave him in oblivion and subserve The mother. All thy schooling of me springs From her suggestion, not of thine own wit. Sure, either thou art senseless, or thy sense Deserts thy friends. Treason or dulness then? Choose!--You declared but now, if you had strength, You would display your hatred of this pair. Yet, when I plan full vengeance for my sire, You aid me not, but turn me from the attempt. What's this but adding cowardice to evil? For tell me, or be patient till I show, What should I gain by ceasing this my moan? I live to vex them:--though my life be poor, Yet that suffices, for I honour him, My father,--if affection touch the dead. You say you hate them, but belie your word, Consorting with our father's murderers. I then, were all the gifts in which you glory Laid at my feet, will never more obey This tyrant power. I leave you your rich board And life of luxury. Ne'er be it mine to feed On dainties that would poison my heart's peace! I care not for such honour as thou hast. Nor wouldst thou care if thou wert wise. But now, Having the noblest of all men for sire, Be called thy mother's offspring; so shall most Discern thine infamy and traitorous mind To thy dead father and thy dearest kin.
cards.whyThisWorks: Electra's speech reveals her character through direct accusation, moral contrast, and self-definition against her sister's compliance, making her values and motivations unmistakably clear.
cards.skillStrategy: When a character speaks directly to another, notice what they accuse, what they refuse, and what they claim to value — these choices reveal who they truly are.
evidencePoints: I live to vex them:--though my life be poor, Yet that suffices, for I honour him, My father
were all the gifts in which you glory Laid at my feet, will never more obey This tyrant power
cards.question: In this passage, Electra declares, 'I live to vex them:--though my life be poor, Yet that suffices, for I honour him, My father.' What does this statement reveal about Electra's character?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Electra acknowledges that her poverty has weakened her resolve and that she may eventually accept her sister's more comfortable way of life.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Electra defines her purpose through loyalty to her dead father, showing that she values moral duty over personal comfort or survival.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Electra admits that her grief has made her irrational and that her continued mourning serves no real purpose beyond personal suffering.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Electra reveals that her primary motivation is jealousy of her sister's wealth and the luxuries their mother's household provides.

cards.standardTitle: Text structure and feature purpose
cards.excerpt: EL. Dear brother, wheresoe'er thy pleasure leads, My will shall follow, since the joys I know, Not from myself I took them, but from thee. And ne'er would I consent thy slightest grief Should win for me great gain. Ill should I then Serve the divinity of this high hour! Thou knowest how matters in the palace stand. Thou hast surely heard, Aegisthus is from home, And she, our mother, is within. Nor fear She should behold me with a smiling face. Mine ancient hate of her hath sunk too deep. And from the time I saw thee, tears of joy Will cease not. Wherefore should I stint their flow? I, who in this thy coming have beheld Thee dead and living? Strangely hast thou wrought On me;--that should my father come alive, I would not think the sight were miracle, But sober truth. Since such thy presence, then, Lead as thy spirit prompts. For I alone Of two things surely had achieved one, Noble deliverance or a noble death.
cards.whyThisWorks: Electra's speech moves from subordinating her will to Orestes, to delivering urgent tactical information about Aegisthus and their mother, to a passionate declaration of joy and resolve—making the paragraph's structural shift from deference to strategic briefing to personal commitment clearly teachable.
cards.skillStrategy: Ask yourself: what job does each part of the paragraph do—does it introduce, contrast, extend, prove, shift, or conclude the central idea?
evidencePoints: Thou hast surely heard, Aegisthus is from home, / And she, our mother, is within.
Lead as thy spirit prompts. For I alone / Of two things surely had achieved one, / Noble deliverance or a noble death.
cards.question: In Electra's speech, the lines 'Thou hast surely heard, Aegisthus is from home, / And she, our mother, is within' serve which purpose within the paragraph?

choices.label: A
choices.text: They conclude Electra's argument that her hatred of her mother has grown too deep to conceal any longer.

choices.label: B
choices.text: They shift the paragraph from Electra's personal declaration of loyalty to practical information Orestes needs to act.

choices.label: C
choices.text: They extend Electra's earlier claim that her joys come entirely from Orestes rather than from herself.

choices.label: D
choices.text: They contrast Orestes' freedom outside the palace with Electra's suffering inside it.

cards.standardTitle: Key literary elements add layers of meaning
cards.excerpt:
EL. Now, dear Chrysothemis, of what thou bearest Let nothing touch his tomb. 'Tis impious And criminal to offer to thy sire Rites and libations from a hateful wife. Then cast them to the winds, or deep in dust Conceal them, where no particle may reach His resting-place: but lie in store for her When she goes underground. Sure, were she not Most hardened of all women that have been, She ne'er had sent those loveless offerings To grace the sepulchre of him she slew. For think how likely is the buried king To take such present kindly from her hand, Who slew him like an alien enemy, Dishonoured even in death, and mangled him, And wiped the death-stain with his flowing locks-- Sinful purgation! Think you that you bear In those cold gifts atonement for her guilt? It is not possible. Wherefore let be. But take a ringlet from thy comely head, And this from mine, that lingers on my brow Longing to shade his tomb. Ah, give it to him, All I can give, and this my maiden-zone, Not daintily adorned, as once erewhile. Then, humbly kneeling, pray that from the ground He would arise to help us 'gainst his foes, And grant his son Orestes with high hand Strongly to trample on his enemies; That in our time to come from ampler stores We may endow him, than are ours to-day. I cannot but imagine that his will Hath part in visiting her sleep with fears. But howsoe'er, I pray thee, sister mine, Do me this service, and thyself, and him, Dearest of all the world to me and thee, The father of us both, who rests below.

CH. She counsels piously; and thou, dear maid, If thou art wise, wilt do her bidding here.
cards.whyThisWorks: Electra's decision to offer her own hair and girdle in place of Clytemnestra's 'loveless offerings' reveals her fierce devotion to her father and her moral conviction, demonstrating how a character's actions and speech deepen meaning about grief, justice, and loyalty.
cards.skillStrategy: When a character makes a deliberate choice and explains it in their own words, ask yourself what that choice reveals about who they are and what they value.
evidencePoints: take a ringlet from thy comely head, / And this from mine, that lingers on my brow / Longing to shade his tomb. Ah, give it to him, / All I can give, and this my maiden-zone
'Tis impious / And criminal to offer to thy sire / Rites and libations from a hateful wife
cards.question: Electra instructs Chrysothemis to discard Clytemnestra's offerings and replace them with locks of their own hair and Electra's girdle. What does this action reveal about Electra's character?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Electra is primarily concerned with following the proper religious customs of her society, regardless of who performs them.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Electra's willingness to give the only things she possesses shows that her devotion to her father is inseparable from her sense of justice and personal sacrifice.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Electra acts out of jealousy toward Clytemnestra, wanting to claim the ritual for herself rather than out of genuine love for her father.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Electra doubts that any offering can reach her father, so she substitutes her own gifts only to comfort Chrysothemis.

cards.standardTitle: Theme development across a literary text
cards.excerpt:
CHORUS. An erring seer am I, I 1 Of sense and wisdom lorn, If this prophetic Power of right, O'ertaking the offender, come not nigh Ere many an hour be born. Yon vision of the night, That lately breathed into my listening ear, Hath freed me, O my daughter, from all fear. Sweet was that bodement. He doth not forget, The Achaean lord that gave thee being, nor yet The bronzen-griding axe, edged like a spear, Hungry and keen, though dark with stains of time, That in the hour of hideous crime Quelled him with cruel butchery: That, too, remembers, and shall testify.

From ambush deep and dread I 2 With power of many a hand And many hastening feet shall spring The Fury of the adamantine tread, Visiting Argive land Swift recompense to bring For eager dalliance of a blood-stained pair Unhallowed, foul, forbidden. No omen fair,-- Their impious course hath fixed this in my soul,-- Nought but black portents full of blame shall roll Before their eyes that wrought or aided there. Small force of divination would there seem In prophecy or solemn dream, Should not this vision of the night Reach harbour in reality aright.
cards.whyThisWorks: The two stanzas each present a distinct moment—the prophetic dream of the axe and the Fury's promised vengeance—that together build the theme that divine justice inevitably overtakes those who commit violent crimes, requiring students to track how both moments reinforce the same message rather than treating either alone as the full theme.
cards.skillStrategy: Find two separate moments in the passage and ask what idea they both point toward—that shared idea is the theme.
evidencePoints: The bronzen-griding axe, edged like a spear, Hungry and keen, though dark with stains of time, That in the hour of hideous crime Quelled him with cruel butchery: That, too, remembers, and shall testify.
With power of many a hand And many hastening feet shall spring The Fury of the adamantine tread, Visiting Argive land Swift recompense to bring For eager dalliance of a blood-stained pair
cards.question: In the first stanza, the Chorus describes the axe that killed Electra's father as something that 'remembers, and shall testify.' In the second stanza, the Chorus declares that the Fury will bring 'swift recompense' to the 'blood-stained pair.' How do these two moments work together to develop a theme?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Both moments suggest that prophetic dreams are unreliable unless confirmed by physical signs, since the axe is a real object while the Fury is only a vision.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Both moments develop the idea that violent crimes cannot escape punishment—the memory of the murder weapon and the Fury's approaching vengeance each show that justice will eventually reach those who committed the killing.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Both moments focus on the Chorus's personal fear, showing that witnesses to violence are permanently haunted by what they have seen and cannot find peace.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The first moment establishes that the father's death was unjust, while the second moment shifts the theme to warn that all bloodshed, even righteous revenge, brings further suffering.

cards.standardTitle: Theme development across a literary text
cards.excerpt: CLY. (_to an attendant_). Then lift for me those fruitful offerings, While to Apollo, before whom we stand, I raise my supplication for release From doubts and fears that shake my bosom now. And, O defender of our house! attend My secret utterance. No friendly ear Is that which hearkens for my voice. My thought Must not be blazoned with her standing by, Lest through her envious and wide-babbling tongue She fill the city full of wild surmise. List, then, as I shall speak: and grant the dreams Whose two-fold apparition I to-night Have seen, if good their bodement, be fulfilled: If hostile, turn their influence on my foes. And yield not them their wish that would by guile Thrust me from this high fortune, but vouchsafe That ever thus exempt from harms I rule The Atridae's home and kingdom, in full life, Partaking with the friends I live with now All fair prosperity, and with my children, Save those who hate and vex me bitterly. Lykeian Phoebus, favourably hear My prayer, and grant to all of us our need! More is there, which, though I be silent here, A God should understand. No secret thing Is hidden from the all-seeing sons of Heaven.
cards.whyThisWorks: Clytemnestra's prayer reveals theme through two distinct moments: her demand that Electra not overhear her 'secret utterance' because of her 'envious and wide-babbling tongue,' and her plea that those who would 'by guile thrust me from this high fortune' be denied their wish—together these moments show that power depends on concealing weakness from those closest to the throne.
cards.skillStrategy: To find theme developed through moments, identify two specific actions or statements in the passage and ask what truth about human experience both moments point toward.
evidencePoints: My thought Must not be blazoned with her standing by, Lest through her envious and wide-babbling tongue She fill the city full of wild surmise.
yield not them their wish that would by guile Thrust me from this high fortune
cards.question: In her prayer, Clytemnestra first demands that Electra not overhear her words because her 'envious and wide-babbling tongue' could 'fill the city full of wild surmise,' and then pleads that those who would 'by guile thrust me from this high fortune' be denied their wish. How do these two specific moments work together to develop a theme in this passage?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Clytemnestra's worry about Electra spreading 'wild surmise' and her prayer for continued rule over 'the Atridae's home and kingdom' show that a ruler's primary concern is controlling the public narrative to maintain popularity.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Clytemnestra's insistence on keeping her prayer secret from Electra and her plea against those who scheme 'by guile' to remove her both reveal that maintaining power requires concealing one's fears and vulnerabilities from enemies close at hand.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Clytemnestra's appeal to Apollo as 'defender of our house' and her acknowledgment that 'no secret thing is hidden from the all-seeing sons of Heaven' show that she trusts divine judgment more than human loyalty to secure her reign.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Clytemnestra's request that her dreams' 'good bodement be fulfilled' and her prayer for 'fair prosperity' with her children suggest that a ruler's deepest wish is to secure peace for her family rather than to guard against political rivals.

cards.excerpt: CLY. (_to an attendant_).
