cards.whyThisWorks: The paragraph demonstrates a clear two-part structure: a public ceremonial opening ('lift for me those fruitful offerings') that pivots into a guarded private petition ('No friendly ear / Is that which hearkens for my voice'), making it ideal for teaching how a section's job shifts within a single unit of text.
cards.skillStrategy: To identify a paragraph's job, track what the speaker or narrator is doing at the start versus the end, and name the shift using specific words from the text.
evidencePoints: No friendly ear / Is that which hearkens for my voice
grant the dreams / Whose two-fold apparition I to-night / Have seen, if good their bodement, be fulfilled
cards.question: In this paragraph, Clytemnestra opens with a public ceremonial act—directing an attendant to 'lift for me those fruitful offerings' before Apollo. What is the primary job of the rest of the paragraph after that opening moment?

choices.label: A
choices.text: To show Clytemnestra shifting her address from Apollo to Electra, warning Electra that her 'envious and wide-babbling tongue' will be punished if she repeats what she hears.

choices.label: B
choices.text: To reveal Clytemnestra's hidden fears by moving into a guarded private petition in which she asks Apollo to fulfill her dreams, protect her rule, and silence enemies she refuses to name openly.

choices.label: C
choices.text: To establish that Clytemnestra's prayer is meant for the entire city, as she asks Apollo to prevent 'wild surmise' from spreading and to grant prosperity to all of the Atridae's household equally.

choices.label: D
choices.text: To show Clytemnestra confessing a past wrong to Apollo, ending with the admission that 'no secret thing is hidden' and asking the god to pardon the harm she has already done to her children.

cards.standardTitle: Key literary elements add layers of meaning
cards.excerpt: CHR. True, noble women, and before she spake Sound thought should have prevented the rash talk That now hath proved her reckless. What wild aim Beckons thee forth in arming this design Whereto thou wouldst demand my ministry? Dost not perceive, thou art not man but woman, Of strength inferior to thine enemies,-- Their Genius daily prospering more and more, Whilst ours is dwindling into nothingness? Who then that plots against a life so strong Shall quit him of the danger without harm? Take heed we do not add to our distress Should some one hear of this our colloquy. Small help and poor advantage 'twere for us To win brief praise and then inglorious die. Nay, death is not so hateful as when one Desiring death is balked of that desire. And I beseech thee, ere in utter ruin We perish and make desolate our race, Refrain thy rage. And I will guard for thee In silence these thy words unrealized; If thou wilt learn this wisdom from long time, Having no strength, to bend before the strong.
cards.whyThisWorks: Chrysothemis's warning that Electra, 'not man but woman, of strength inferior to thine enemies,' risks dying 'inglorious' rather than achieving justice illustrates how the sisters' conflict deepens the theme that noble intentions without power lead to destruction rather than redemption.
cards.skillStrategy: When a conflict adds meaning, ask what the disagreement reveals about a larger truth—look at what each character stands to gain or lose and what the author seems to be saying about the human condition through their clash.
evidencePoints: thou art not man but woman, Of strength inferior to thine enemies
Small help and poor advantage 'twere for us To win brief praise and then inglorious die
cards.question: Chrysothemis tells Electra, 'thou art not man but woman, Of strength inferior to thine enemies,' and warns that their plot would win only 'brief praise and then inglorious die.' What meaning does this conflict between the two sisters add to the passage?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The conflict reveals that Chrysothemis resents Electra's boldness and is motivated by jealousy, suggesting that rivalry between sisters is more destructive than any outside enemy.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The conflict reveals that courage without sufficient power leads to ruin rather than justice, suggesting that noble rage alone cannot overcome an enemy whose 'Genius daily' grows stronger.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The conflict shows that Electra's plan is sound but poorly timed, and that Chrysothemis would support it if Electra waited until their enemies' strength began 'dwindling into nothingness.'

choices.label: D
choices.text: The conflict demonstrates that both women ultimately agree revenge is impossible, and that Chrysothemis speaks only to protect Electra from the shame of being overheard in their 'colloquy.'

cards.standardTitle: Text structure and feature purpose
cards.excerpt:
EL. Now, dear Chrysothemis, of what thou bearest Let nothing touch his tomb. 'Tis impious And criminal to offer to thy sire Rites and libations from a hateful wife. Then cast them to the winds, or deep in dust Conceal them, where no particle may reach His resting-place: but lie in store for her When she goes underground. Sure, were she not Most hardened of all women that have been, She ne'er had sent those loveless offerings To grace the sepulchre of him she slew. For think how likely is the buried king To take such present kindly from her hand, Who slew him like an alien enemy, Dishonoured even in death, and mangled him, And wiped the death-stain with his flowing locks-- Sinful purgation! Think you that you bear In those cold gifts atonement for her guilt? It is not possible. Wherefore let be. But take a ringlet from thy comely head, And this from mine, that lingers on my brow Longing to shade his tomb. Ah, give it to him, All I can give, and this my maiden-zone, Not daintily adorned, as once erewhile. Then, humbly kneeling, pray that from the ground He would arise to help us 'gainst his foes, And grant his son Orestes with high hand Strongly to trample on his enemies; That in our time to come from ampler stores We may endow him, than are ours to-day. I cannot but imagine that his will Hath part in visiting her sleep with fears. But howsoe'er, I pray thee, sister mine, Do me this service, and thyself, and him, Dearest of all the world to me and thee, The father of us both, who rests below.

CH. She counsels piously; and thou, dear maid, If thou art wise, wilt do her bidding here.
cards.whyThisWorks: The Chorus's two-line closing section performs a distinct paragraph job—it concludes and validates Electra's argument—giving students a clear opportunity to identify how a brief section functions to affirm and seal the preceding speech.
cards.skillStrategy: Ask yourself what work the paragraph is doing for the ideas around it: is it starting something new, pushing back, adding on, proving a point, or wrapping things up?
evidencePoints: She counsels piously; and thou, dear maid, If thou art wise, wilt do her bidding here.
But take a ringlet from thy comely head, And this from mine...Then, humbly kneeling, pray that from the ground He would arise to help us
cards.question: What is the primary job of the Chorus's final two lines—'She counsels piously; and thou, dear maid, / If thou art wise, wilt do her bidding here'—in relation to Electra's speech?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The lines introduce a new concern about whether Chrysothemis has the courage to defy Clytemnestra's orders.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The lines conclude Electra's argument by confirming that her reasoning is righteous and that Chrysothemis should follow it.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The lines contrast with Electra's position by suggesting that honoring the dead with any offering is acceptable.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The lines extend Electra's prayer by adding the Chorus's own requests for Orestes to return from exile.

cards.standardTitle: Key literary elements add layers of meaning
cards.excerpt: EL. Dear brother, wheresoe'er thy pleasure leads, My will shall follow, since the joys I know, Not from myself I took them, but from thee. And ne'er would I consent thy slightest grief Should win for me great gain. Ill should I then Serve the divinity of this high hour! Thou knowest how matters in the palace stand. Thou hast surely heard, Aegisthus is from home, And she, our mother, is within. Nor fear She should behold me with a smiling face. Mine ancient hate of her hath sunk too deep. And from the time I saw thee, tears of joy Will cease not. Wherefore should I stint their flow? I, who in this thy coming have beheld Thee dead and living? Strangely hast thou wrought On me;--that should my father come alive, I would not think the sight were miracle, But sober truth. Since such thy presence, then, Lead as thy spirit prompts. For I alone Of two things surely had achieved one, Noble deliverance or a noble death.
cards.whyThisWorks: Electra's declaration that she would have achieved 'Noble deliverance or a noble death' shows how the prolonged conflict with Aegisthus and Clytemnestra has stripped away her fear of death and replaced it with a demand for honorable action, directly illustrating how plot and conflict add meaning to character.
cards.skillStrategy: When a character states what they were willing to do or die for, ask how the conflict they have lived through pushed them to that point.
evidencePoints: Noble deliverance or a noble death
Mine ancient hate of her hath sunk too deep
cards.question: Electra says her 'ancient hate' has 'sunk too deep' and that she alone would have achieved 'Noble deliverance or a noble death.' What do these two statements together reveal about how the conflict has shaped her?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The conflict has made her reckless, so she acts without thinking about consequences.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The conflict has hardened her to the point where honorable action matters more to her than survival.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The conflict has weakened her resolve, leaving her dependent on Orestes to act in her place.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The conflict has faded now that Orestes has returned, replacing her hatred with relief.

cards.standardTitle: Theme development across a literary text
cards.excerpt: CHR. Well, I will tell thee all I saw:--I came Unto the ancient tomb that holds our sire; And from the topmost mound I marked a stream Of milk fresh-flowing, and his resting place Ringed round with garlands of all flowers that blow. I marvelled at the sight, and peered about, Lest some one might be nearer than we knew. But finding all was quiet in the spot, I ventured closer to the tomb, and there, Hard by the limit, I beheld a curl Of hair new shorn, with all the gloss of youth And straight it struck my heart, as with a sense Of something seen, ah me! long, long ago, And told me that my sight encountered here The token of Orestes, dearest soul Then, clasping it, I did not cry aloud, But straight mine eyes were filled with tears of joy. And now as much as then I feel assured He and none else bestowed this ornament. To whom beyond thyself and me belongs Such consecration? And I know this well, I did it not,--nor thou. Impossible! Thou canst not worship even the blessed Gods Forth of this roof, unpunished. And, most sure, Our mother is not minded so to act, Nor, had she done it, could we fail to know. This offering comes then of Orestes' hand. Take courage, dear one. Not one fate pursues One house perpetually, but changeth still. Ours was a sullen Genius, but perchance This day begins the assurance of much good.
cards.whyThisWorks: Chrysothemis's sequential discoveries—first the milk and garlands, then the shorn curl that 'struck my heart' and filled her eyes 'with tears of joy'—build toward her declaration 'This day begins the assurance of much good,' making this passage a clear example of theme developed through specific moments.
cards.skillStrategy: Track how each moment in the passage shifts a character's emotion or belief, then ask what idea about life those shifts add up to.
evidencePoints: straight it struck my heart, as with a sense / Of something seen, ah me! long, long ago
Not one fate pursues / One house perpetually, but changeth still. Ours was a sullen Genius, but perchance / This day begins the assurance of much good.
cards.question: When Chrysothemis sees the milk and garlands at the tomb, she 'marvelled at the sight'; when she finds the shorn curl of hair, it 'struck my heart' and filled her eyes 'with tears of joy,' leading her to declare, 'This day begins the assurance of much good.' How do these two moments work together to develop a theme in the passage?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The milk and garlands show that the gods have accepted the family's offerings, while the curl of hair proves Orestes has already taken revenge, together suggesting that divine favor rewards patient worship.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Each discovery deepens Chrysothemis's certainty that Orestes is near—moving her from wonder at the offerings to joyful recognition of the curl—developing the theme that small, hidden signs of loyalty can restore hope after long suffering.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The sight of the milk and garlands fills Chrysothemis with grief for her father, and the curl of hair intensifies that grief, together developing the theme that mourning the dead is a duty that can never truly be completed.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The offerings at the tomb reveal Chrysothemis's own careful piety, and the curl of hair confirms her suspicion that Electra has been secretly visiting the tomb, developing the theme that sisters must rely on each other to survive.

evidencePoints: 'take a ringlet from thy comely head, / And this from mine, that lingers on my brow / Longing to shade his tomb'
'think how likely is the buried king / To take such present kindly from her hand, / Who slew him like an alien enemy'
cards.question: Electra instructs Chrysothemis to discard Clytemnestra's offerings and instead bring 'a ringlet from thy comely head' and Electra's own 'maiden-zone' to their father's tomb. How does this conflict over the offerings add meaning to the passage?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The conflict shows that Electra distrusts Chrysothemis's loyalty and uses the substitute offerings as a test to see whether her sister will obey Clytemnestra or side with the daughters.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The conflict reveals that sincere mourning demands personal sacrifice—the sisters' humble locks and girdle—while Clytemnestra's gifts are 'loveless offerings' from the hand that 'slew him like an alien enemy,' exposing her guilt rather than honoring the dead.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The conflict demonstrates that Electra believes elaborate ritual objects are unnecessary because her father's spirit is too weakened in death to receive any offering, whether from Clytemnestra or from the daughters.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The conflict suggests that Electra is primarily concerned with protecting the tomb's physical purity from contamination, and that the substitute offerings are meant to satisfy religious law rather than express personal grief.

cards.standardTitle: Theme development across a literary text
cards.excerpt: EL. Dear brother, wheresoe'er thy pleasure leads, My will shall follow, since the joys I know, Not from myself I took them, but from thee. And ne'er would I consent thy slightest grief Should win for me great gain. Ill should I then Serve the divinity of this high hour! Thou knowest how matters in the palace stand. Thou hast surely heard, Aegisthus is from home, And she, our mother, is within. Nor fear She should behold me with a smiling face. Mine ancient hate of her hath sunk too deep. cards.whyThisWorks: Electra's refusal of personal gain at her brother's expense and her acceptance of 'Noble deliverance or a noble death' as equal outcomes show how two specific speech moments build the theme that honor and loyalty outweigh self-preservation.
cards.skillStrategy: Find two moments in the passage and ask what value or belief both moments point to—that shared idea is the theme.
evidencePoints: ne'er would I consent thy slightest grief Should win for me great gain
I alone Of two things surely had achieved one, Noble deliverance or a noble death
cards.question: Electra says she would never let her brother's grief bring her 'great gain,' and she later declares she would have achieved either 'Noble deliverance or a noble death.' What theme do these two moments develop together?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Personal survival matters less than acting with honor, whether that means refusing gain at a loved one's expense or accepting death as equal to victory.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Hatred of her mother drives every choice Electra makes, turning both her loyalty to Orestes and her readiness to die into acts of revenge.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Joy at her brother's return temporarily replaces Electra's grief, but her willingness to die shows that sorrow still controls her.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Electra doubts her own emotions, first questioning whether her brother's return is real and then unsure whether deliverance or death is the better outcome.

cards.question: The Chorus declares that the 'vision of the night' has 'freed me, O my daughter, from all fear' and foretells that the Fury will spring 'with power of many a hand' to bring 'swift recompense' to the 'blood-stained pair.' How does this prophetic vision deepen the meaning of the conflict between the killers and those seeking justice?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The vision deepens the conflict by revealing that the Chorus witnessed the murder firsthand and now believes the 'blood-stained pair' will escape because no mortal in Argos has moved against them.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The vision deepens the conflict by shifting it from human helplessness to divine certainty, suggesting that the 'bronzen-griding axe' and the 'blood-stained pair's' crimes have set in motion a retribution that no mortal power can prevent.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The vision deepens the conflict by warning that the 'blood-stained pair' will silence Electra before the Fury can reach Argos, making the outcome of the revenge plot uncertain.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The vision deepens the conflict by showing that the Chorus has lost faith in prophecy and 'solemn dream,' and now depends entirely on Electra's grief to drive any action against the killers.

cards.whyThisWorks: Chrysothemis's speech contains two distinct moments—warning Electra that their enemies grow stronger while they weaken, and urging her to 'bend before the strong'—that together develop the theme that survival under oppression requires submission over defiance.
cards.skillStrategy: Find two separate moments in the passage where a character's words or actions push the same idea forward, then ask what message both moments are building together.
evidencePoints: Their Genius daily prospering more and more, Whilst ours is dwindling into nothingness?
Having no strength, to bend before the strong.
cards.question: Read the following two moments from Chrysothemis's speech: first, her warning that their enemies' power grows 'daily prospering more and more, Whilst ours is dwindling into nothingness,' and second, her final plea that Electra learn 'Having no strength, to bend before the strong.' Together, how do these two moments develop a theme in the passage?

choices.label: A
choices.text: They show that Chrysothemis is a coward who refuses to act because she fears personal punishment, suggesting that self-preservation always outweighs loyalty to family.

choices.label: B
choices.text: They develop the idea that when one side holds overwhelming power and the other is weakening, survival depends on yielding rather than resisting.

choices.label: C
choices.text: They argue that Electra's plan will succeed only if she waits for the right moment, suggesting that patience eventually rewards those who seek justice.

choices.label: D
choices.text: They reveal that Chrysothemis secretly supports Electra's goal but fears public disgrace, suggesting that reputation matters more than action.

cards.standardTitle: Text structure and feature purpose
cards.excerpt: EL. 'Tis strange and pitiful, thy father's child Can leave him in oblivion and subserve The mother. All thy schooling of me springs From her suggestion, not of thine own wit. Sure, either thou art senseless, or thy sense Deserts thy friends. Treason or dulness then? Choose!--You declared but now, if you had strength, You would display your hatred of this pair. Yet, when I plan full vengeance for my sire, You aid me not, but turn me from the attempt. What's this but adding cowardice to evil? For tell me, or be patient till I show, What should I gain by ceasing this my moan? I live to vex them:--though my life be poor, Yet that suffices, for I honour him, My father,--if affection touch the dead. You say you hate them, but belie your word, Consorting with our father's murderers. I then, were all the gifts in which you glory Laid at my feet, will never more obey This tyrant power. I leave you your rich board And life of luxury. Ne'er be it mine to feed On dainties that would poison my heart's peace! I care not for such honour as thou hast. Nor wouldst thou care if thou wert wise. But now, Having the noblest of all men for sire, Be called thy mother's offspring; so shall most Discern thine infamy and traitorous mind To thy dead father and thy dearest kin.
cards.whyThisWorks: Electra's speech builds through a series of accusations, a forced choice ('Treason or dulness then? Choose!'), and a final renunciation, allowing students to trace how the escalating structure reinforces her purpose of shaming her sister into action or condemning her as a traitor.
cards.skillStrategy: Notice how the author arranges the argument—accusation, forced choice, personal vow—and ask what that order is meant to make the reader (or the other character) feel or understand.
evidencePoints: Treason or dulness then? Choose!
Having the noblest of all men for sire, Be called thy mother's offspring; so shall most Discern thine infamy and traitorous mind To thy dead father and thy dearest kin.
cards.question: Electra's speech moves from accusing her sister of senselessness, to demanding she choose between 'Treason or dulness,' to finally declaring she will never obey and calling her sister her 'mother's offspring.' What does this escalating structure reveal about Electra's purpose in the speech?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Electra gradually softens her anger toward her sister by acknowledging that their different choices come from different kinds of grief over their father.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Electra builds from questioning her sister's loyalty to publicly shaming her identity, making clear that her sister's inaction is not merely weakness but a betrayal that defines who she truly is.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Electra shifts her focus away from her sister and toward condemning their mother, using the forced choice only to remind the audience of the original crime against their father.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Electra's escalating accusations show that she is primarily concerned with securing her sister's material wealth and luxury for herself rather than avenging their father.

cards.excerpt:
EL. Now, dear Chrysothemis, of what thou bearest Let nothing touch his tomb. 'Tis impious And criminal to offer to thy sire Rites and libations from a hateful wife. Then cast them to the winds, or deep in dust Conceal them, where no particle may reach His resting-place: but lie in store for her When she goes underground. Sure, were she not Most hardened of all women that have been, She ne'er had sent those loveless offerings To grace the sepulchre of him she slew. For think how likely is the buried king To take such present kindly from her hand, Who slew him like an alien enemy, Dishonoured even in death, and mangled him, And wiped the death-stain with his flowing locks-- Sinful purgation! Think you that you bear In those cold gifts atonement for her guilt? It is not possible. Wherefore let be. But take a ringlet from thy comely head, And this from mine, that lingers on my brow Longing to shade his tomb. Ah, give it to him, All I can give, and this my maiden-zone, Not daintily adorned, as once erewhile. Then, humbly kneeling, pray that from the ground He would arise to help us 'gainst his foes, And grant his son Orestes with high hand Strongly to trample on his enemies; That in our time to come from ampler stores We may endow him, than are ours to-day. I cannot but imagine that his will Hath part in visiting her sleep with fears. But howsoe'er, I pray thee, sister mine, Do me this service, and thyself, and him, Dearest of all the world to me and thee, The father of us both, who rests below.

CH. She counsels piously; and thou, dear maid, If thou art wise, wilt do her bidding here.
cards.whyThisWorks: The excerpt contains two distinct moments—Electra rejecting Clytemnestra's offerings as hollow and then offering her own hair and girdle with genuine grief—that together develop the theme that authentic devotion requires personal sacrifice, not empty ritual.
cards.skillStrategy: Look for two separate actions or speeches in the passage and ask what idea both moments are building toward together.

take a ringlet from thy comely head, / And this from mine...and this my maiden-zone, / Not daintily adorned, as once erewhile. / Then, humbly kneeling, pray that from the ground / He would arise to help us
cards.question: Read the two moments in the excerpt: Electra's command to discard Clytemnestra's offerings and her instruction to replace them with locks of hair and a girdle. How do both moments work together to develop a theme?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Both moments show that Electra distrusts Chrysothemis and fears her sister will side with Clytemnestra rather than honor their father.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Both moments develop the idea that true devotion to the dead demands personal sacrifice rather than hollow gestures made out of guilt or obligation.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Both moments reveal that Electra's primary concern is securing Orestes' return so he can take revenge, making grief secondary to political strategy.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Both moments suggest that funeral rites are meaningless unless performed by a priest, so Electra substitutes her own objects only as a temporary measure.

cards.standardTitle: Key literary elements add layers of meaning
cards.excerpt: CHR. Well, I will tell thee all I saw:--I came Unto the ancient tomb that holds our sire; And from the topmost mound I marked a stream Of milk fresh-flowing, and his resting place Ringed round with garlands of all flowers that blow. I marvelled at the sight, and peered about, Lest some one might be nearer than we knew. But finding all was quiet in the spot, I ventured closer to the tomb, and there, Hard by the limit, I beheld a curl Of hair new shorn, with all the gloss of youth And straight it struck my heart, as with a sense Of something seen, ah me! long, long ago, And told me that my sight encountered here The token of Orestes, dearest soul Then, clasping it, I did not cry aloud, But straight mine eyes were filled with tears of joy. And now as much as then I feel assured He and none else bestowed this ornament. To whom beyond thyself and me belongs Such consecration? And I know this well, I did it not,--nor thou. Impossible! Thou canst not worship even the blessed Gods Forth of this roof, unpunished. And, most sure, Our mother is not minded so to act, Nor, had she done it, could we fail to know. This offering comes then of Orestes' hand. Take courage, dear one. Not one fate pursues One house perpetually, but changeth still. Ours was a sullen Genius, but perchance This day begins the assurance of much good.
cards.whyThisWorks: Chrysothemis's logical elimination of every possible giver of the offerings—herself, Electra, their mother—until only Orestes remains creates a plot reversal that transforms the sisters' despair into hope, directly illustrating how a discovery adds a deeper layer of meaning to the conflict.
cards.skillStrategy: When a character reasons through who could or could not have done something, trace that logic to see what the conclusion reveals about the larger conflict.
evidencePoints: I did it not,--nor thou. Impossible! Thou canst not worship even the blessed Gods Forth of this roof, unpunished.
Ours was a sullen Genius, but perchance This day begins the assurance of much good.
cards.question: In the excerpt, Chrysothemis rules out herself, Electra, and their mother as the source of the offerings at the tomb, then declares, 'This offering comes then of Orestes' hand. Take courage, dear one.' What deeper meaning does this moment of reasoning and conclusion add to the sisters' conflict with their oppressors?

choices.label: A
choices.text: By eliminating their mother as a possible giver of the offerings, Chrysothemis confirms that their mother feels no remorse, showing the sisters' suffering will never end and deepening their sense of hopelessness.

choices.label: B
choices.text: By systematically ruling out every other possible giver and naming Orestes, Chrysothemis transforms the sisters' long endurance under oppression into the threshold of potential justice, suggesting that years of powerlessness may be about to reverse.

choices.label: C
choices.text: By noting that Electra cannot leave the house to worship the gods without punishment, Chrysothemis shifts the conflict away from Orestes and focuses it entirely on Electra's personal imprisonment.

choices.label: D
choices.text: By concluding that Orestes left the curl of hair, Chrysothemis reveals that Orestes has been secretly communicating with the sisters all along, proving the conflict with their oppressors was never as dangerous as the sisters believed.

cards.standardTitle: Theme development across a literary text
cards.excerpt:
EL. O gladsome day! Dear only saviour of our father's house, How earnest thou hither? Art thou he indeed, That didst preserve Orestes and myself From many sorrows? O dear hands, kind feet, Swift in our service,--how couldst thou so long Be near, nor show one gleam, but didst destroy My heart with words, hiding the loveliest deeds? Father!--in thee methinks I see my father. O welcome! thou of all the world to me Most hated and most loved in one short hour.

OLD M. Enough, dear maiden! Many nights and days Are circling hitherward, that shall reveal In clear recountment all that came between. But to you two that stand beside I tell, Now is your moment, with the Queen alone, And none of men within; but if you pause, Know that with others of profounder skill You'll have to strive, more than your present foes.

OR. Then, Pylades, we need no more to dwell On words, but enter on this act with speed, First worshipping the holy shrines o' the Gods That were my father's, harboured at the gate. [_They pass within_. ELECTRA _remains in an attitude of prayer_

EL. O King Apollo! hear them graciously, And hear me too, that with incessant hand Honoured thee richly from my former store! And now, fierce slayer, I importune thee, And woo thee with such gifts as I can give, Be kindly aidant to this enterprise, And make the world take note, what meed of bane Heaven still bestows on man's iniquity. [ELECTRA _goes within_

CH. Lo, where the War-god moves 1 With soft, sure footstep, on to his design, Breathing hot slaughter of an evil feud! Even now the inevitable hounds that track Dark deeds of hideous crime Are gone beneath the covert of the domes. Not long in wavering suspense shall hang The dreaming presage of my wistful soul.
cards.whyThisWorks: Two distinct moments—Electra's emotional reunion with the Old Man and her prayer to Apollo before Orestes enters the palace—both develop the theme that justice requires both personal sacrifice and divine sanction, allowing students to track theme across multiple story moments rather than a single detail.
cards.skillStrategy: Find two separate moments in the passage and ask what idea both moments are pushing toward together.
evidencePoints: O dear hands, kind feet, Swift in our service,--how couldst thou so long / Be near, nor show one gleam, but didst destroy / My heart with words, hiding the loveliest deeds?

And now, fierce slayer, I importune thee, / And woo thee with such gifts as I can give, / Be kindly aidant to this enterprise, / And make the world take note, what meed of bane / Heaven still bestows on man's iniquity.
cards.question:
Read the two moments below from the excerpt and answer the question.

Moment 1: Electra cries to the Old Man, 'how couldst thou so long / Be near, nor show one gleam, but didst destroy / My heart with words, hiding the loveliest deeds?'

Moment 2: Electra prays to Apollo, 'Be kindly aidant to this enterprise, / And make the world take note, what meed of bane / Heaven still bestows on man's iniquity.'

How do both moments work together to develop a theme in this passage?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Both moments show that Electra resents the people around her and refuses to forgive those who have caused her suffering, suggesting that personal grudges drive all action in the play.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Both moments show that justice demands enduring hidden pain and then calling on a higher power to sanction the act of revenge, suggesting that righteous vengeance requires both human suffering and divine approval.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Both moments reveal that Electra doubts whether Orestes is capable of carrying out the plan, suggesting that the theme is the danger of relying on others to act on one's behalf.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Both moments focus on Electra's grief over her father's death, suggesting that the passage's central theme is that mourning never truly ends for those who have lost a parent.

cards.standardTitle: Text structure and feature purpose
cards.excerpt: CLY. (_to an attendant_). Then lift for me those fruitful offerings, While to Apollo, before whom we stand, I raise my supplication for release From doubts and fears that shake my bosom now. And, O defender of our house! attend My secret utterance. No friendly ear Is that which hearkens for my voice. My thought Must not be blazoned with her standing by, Lest through her envious and wide-babbling tongue She fill the city full of wild surmise. List, then, as I shall speak: and grant the dreams Whose two-fold apparition I to-night Have seen, if good their bodement, be fulfilled: If hostile, turn their influence on my foes. And yield not them their wish that would by guile Thrust me from this high fortune, but vouchsafe That ever thus exempt from harms I rule The Atridae's home and kingdom, in full life, Partaking with the friends I live with now All fair prosperity, and with my children, Save those who hate and vex me bitterly. Lykeian Phoebus, favourably hear My prayer, and grant to all of us our need! More is there, which, though I be silent here, A God should understand. No secret thing Is hidden from the all-seeing sons of Heaven.
cards.whyThisWorks: Clytemnestra's prayer is structured as a private appeal to Apollo that she explicitly hides from Electra, and this dramatic aside structure reveals her fear and guilt while showing the audience her true motives—making it a strong vehicle for connecting structural choice to authorial purpose.
cards.skillStrategy: Ask yourself: why does the author arrange this moment the way he does, and what does that arrangement force the reader to notice about the character or situation?
evidencePoints: No friendly ear / Is that which hearkens for my voice.
Lest through her envious and wide-babbling tongue / She fill the city full of wild surmise.
cards.question: Clytemnestra structures her prayer to Apollo as a secret utterance, explicitly noting that Electra must not overhear it. What does this structural choice reveal about Clytemnestra that Sophocles wants the audience to notice?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Clytemnestra is devoted to Apollo above all other gods and believes only he can protect her household from outside enemies.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Clytemnestra's need to hide her true fears and wishes from Electra exposes that her power is built on concealment rather than rightful authority.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Clytemnestra distrusts Electra only because Electra has previously spread false rumors about her throughout the city.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Clytemnestra's prayer shows she is a generous ruler who wants prosperity for all members of her household equally.

cards.question: Which statement best expresses the central idea of Clytemnestra's speech to Apollo?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Clytemnestra is troubled by two disturbing dreams and asks Apollo to explain their meaning before she takes any action.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Clytemnestra secretly prays for protection of her power and safety, fearing both enemies who would overthrow her and Electra's ability to expose her hidden anxieties.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Clytemnestra wishes to offer gifts to Apollo so that her entire household, including Electra, will share in prosperity and peace.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Clytemnestra believes Apollo already knows all secrets, so she chooses to remain silent rather than speak her true desires aloud.

cards.standardTitle: Theme development across a literary text
cards.excerpt:
CHORUS. An erring seer am I, I 1 Of sense and wisdom lorn, If this prophetic Power of right, O'ertaking the offender, come not nigh Ere many an hour be born. Yon vision of the night, That lately breathed into my listening ear, Hath freed me, O my daughter, from all fear. Sweet was that bodement. He doth not forget, The Achaean lord that gave thee being, nor yet The bronzen-griding axe, edged like a spear, Hungry and keen, though dark with stains of time, That in the hour of hideous crime Quelled him with cruel butchery: That, too, remembers, and shall testify.

From ambush deep and dread I 2 With power of many a hand And many hastening feet shall spring The Fury of the adamantine tread, Visiting Argive land Swift recompense to bring For eager dalliance of a blood-stained pair Unhallowed, foul, forbidden. No omen fair,-- Their impious course hath fixed this in my soul,-- Nought but black portents full of blame shall roll Before their eyes that wrought or aided there. Small force of divination would there seem In prophecy or solemn dream, Should not this vision of the night Reach harbour in reality aright.
cards.whyThisWorks: The Chorus's prophecy directly links the consequence of murder—divine retribution through the Furies—to the theme that violent crime against kin cannot escape justice, making conflict and consequence the engine of theme development.
cards.skillStrategy: When tracking theme through consequence, ask: what wrong was committed, what punishment is promised, and what truth about human life does that promise reveal?
evidencePoints: The bronzen-griding axe, edged like a spear, Hungry and keen, though dark with stains of time, That in the hour of hideous crime Quelled him with cruel butchery: That, too, remembers, and shall testify.

cards.question: In both stanzas, the Chorus describes the murder of Electra's father and then prophesies the coming of the Furies. How does this sequence of crime and promised consequence develop a theme in the passage?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Because the Chorus admits it may be wrong about the vision, the passage suggests that divine prophecy is unreliable and mortals must act without expecting justice.

choices.label: B
choices.text: By presenting the axe that killed Electra's father as something that 'remembers' and by promising the Furies will deliver 'swift recompense,' the passage develops the theme that violent crimes against family carry consequences that time and power cannot erase.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Because the Chorus focuses on the dream that freed it from fear, the passage develops the theme that personal comfort and relief matter more than the pursuit of justice for past wrongs.

choices.label: D
choices.text: By describing the Furies as arriving with 'many a hand' and 'many hastening feet,' the passage develops the theme that collective human action, rather than divine will, is the true source of justice.

cards.question: The Chorus speaks after Orestes, Pylades, and Electra have all gone within. How does placing the Chorus's speech at the end of this passage connect to what Sophocles wants the reader to understand?

choices.text: The Chorus's speech reassures the reader that the gods have already guaranteed Orestes will succeed, removing any remaining tension from the scene.

choices.label: B
choices.text: By closing with the Chorus describing vengeance as an unstoppable force moving 'with soft, sure footstep,' Sophocles signals that the moment of action is now beyond hesitation or reversal.

You say you hate them, but belie your word, Consorting with our father's murderers. I then, were all the gifts in which you glory Laid at my feet, will never more obey This tyrant power. I leave you your rich board And life of luxury. Ne'er be it mine to feed On dainties that would poison my heart's peace! I care not for such honour as thou hast. Ne'er be it mine to feed On dainties that would poison my heart's peace!
cards.question: Read the following lines from Electra's speech: 'I live to vex them:--though my life be poor, Yet that suffices, for I honour him, My father' and 'Ne'er be it mine to feed On dainties that would poison my heart's peace!' How do these two moments work together to develop the central idea of the passage?

choices.label: A
choices.text: They show that Electra is resigned to suffering because she believes her father cannot be avenged, shifting the passage toward hopelessness.

choices.label: B
choices.text: They reinforce that honoring her father requires rejecting material comfort, proving that loyalty demands personal sacrifice rather than silent compliance.

choices.label: C
choices.text: They reveal that Electra's primary concern is escaping poverty, and her grief for her father is a secondary motivation she uses to justify her complaints.

choices.label: D
choices.text: They demonstrate that Electra envies her sister's wealth and uses her father's memory as an excuse to criticize a lifestyle she secretly desires.

cards.standardTitle: Key literary elements add layers of meaning
cards.excerpt:
EL. O gladsome day! Dear only saviour of our father's house, How earnest thou hither? Art thou he indeed, That didst preserve Orestes and myself From many sorrows? O dear hands, kind feet, Swift in our service,--how couldst thou so long Be near, nor show one gleam, but didst destroy My heart with words, hiding the loveliest deeds? Father!--in thee methinks I see my father. O welcome! thou of all the world to me Most hated and most loved in one short hour.

OLD M. Enough, dear maiden! Many nights and days Are circling hitherward, that shall reveal In clear recountment all that came between. But to you two that stand beside I tell, Now is your moment, with the Queen alone, And none of men within; but if you pause, Know that with others of profounder skill You'll have to strive, more than your present foes.

OR. Then, Pylades, we need no more to dwell On words, but enter on this act with speed, First worshipping the holy shrines o' the Gods That were my father's, harboured at the gate. [_They pass within_. ELECTRA _remains in an attitude of prayer_

EL. O King Apollo! hear them graciously, And hear me too, that with incessant hand Honoured thee richly from my former store! And now, fierce slayer, I importune thee, And woo thee with such gifts as I can give, Be kindly aidant to this enterprise, And make the world take note, what meed of bane Heaven still bestows on man's iniquity. [ELECTRA _goes within_

CH. Lo, where the War-god moves 1 With soft, sure footstep, on to his design, Breathing hot slaughter of an evil feud! Even now the inevitable hounds that track Dark deeds of hideous crime Are gone beneath the covert of the domes. Not long in wavering suspense shall hang The dreaming presage of my wistful soul.
cards.whyThisWorks: Orestes' decision to enter the palace immediately after the Old Man's warning—rather than delay—marks a decisive turning point that signals the revenge plot is irreversible and underscores the play's theme that justice, once set in motion, cannot be stopped.
cards.skillStrategy: When a character makes a decision at a critical moment, ask what that choice reveals about the story's deeper meaning beyond just what happens next.
evidencePoints: Then, Pylades, we need no more to dwell / On words, but enter on this act with speed
Lo, where the War-god moves / With soft, sure footstep, on to his design, / Breathing hot slaughter of an evil feud!
cards.question: When Orestes declares, 'we need no more to dwell / On words, but enter on this act with speed,' and immediately passes within the palace, what deeper meaning does this decision add to the conflict?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Orestes' haste shows he is reckless and unprepared, suggesting the revenge plot will fail because he ignores the Old Man's counsel about more skilled opponents.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Orestes' swift, wordless action signals that the moment of reckoning has become unstoppable, reinforcing the idea that divine justice—not human hesitation—now drives events toward their inevitable end.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Orestes moves quickly because he distrusts Pylades and wants to act before Pylades can interfere, revealing a conflict of loyalty within the group of avengers.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Orestes' decision to enter the palace first demonstrates his respect for his father's household gods, and the scene's meaning is primarily about proper religious ritual before battle.

cards.standardTitle: Theme development across a literary text
cards.excerpt: EL. Dear brother, wheresoe'er thy pleasure leads, My will shall follow, since the joys I know, Not from myself I took them, but from thee. And ne'er would I consent thy slightest grief Should win for me great gain. Ill should I then Serve the divinity of this high hour! Thou knowest how matters in the palace stand. Thou hast surely heard, Aegisthus is from home, And she, our mother, is within. Nor fear She should behold me with a smiling face. Mine ancient hate of her hath sunk too deep. And from the time I saw thee, tears of joy Will cease not. Wherefore should I stint their flow? I, who in this thy coming have beheld Thee dead and living? Strangely hast thou wrought On me;--that should my father come alive, I would not think the sight were miracle, But sober truth. Since such thy presence, then, Lead as thy spirit prompts. For I alone Of two things surely had achieved one, Noble deliverance or a noble death.
cards.whyThisWorks: Electra's declaration that she would accept 'noble deliverance or a noble death' reveals how the consequence of years of hatred and grief has hardened her resolve, directly developing the theme that suffering under injustice compels a person toward extreme, irreversible action.
cards.skillStrategy: When tracking theme through conflict or consequence, find the moment a character states what they are willing to do or sacrifice—that declaration usually names the theme directly.
evidencePoints: Mine ancient hate of her hath sunk too deep.
For I alone / Of two things surely had achieved one, / Noble deliverance or a noble death.
cards.question: How does Electra's declaration that she would have achieved 'Noble deliverance or a noble death' develop a theme in this passage?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Her words show that reuniting with Orestes has erased her suffering, suggesting that family loyalty alone is enough to restore peace.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Her words reveal that years of hatred and grief have driven her to accept death as willingly as rescue, suggesting that prolonged injustice pushes a person toward absolute, irreversible commitment.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Her words demonstrate that she fears Aegisthus's return above all else, suggesting that political danger is the central force shaping her choices.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Her words indicate that she defers entirely to Orestes's judgment, suggesting that obedience to a stronger sibling is the passage's central idea.

cards.question: Read the stage direction: '[They pass within. ELECTRA remains in an attitude of prayer].' What does this stage direction convey that Electra's spoken words in the excerpt do not fully communicate on their own?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Electra has decided to abandon the plan and stay behind out of fear rather than devotion.

choices.label: B
choices.text: While Orestes and Pylades move immediately to action, Electra pauses in a posture of reverence, showing that her prayer to Apollo is a physical act of faith, not merely spoken words.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Orestes and Pylades enter the palace without Electra's knowledge, leaving her confused about what to do next.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Electra's prayer is directed at the Chorus rather than at Apollo, signaling that she wants the Chorus to intervene on her behalf.

cards.whyThisWorks: The excerpt provides layered support for the central idea that divine retribution is imminent and unstoppable, with Electra's prayer, the Old Man's urgency, and the Chorus's closing imagery each adding a distinct layer of development that students can trace.
cards.skillStrategy: Identify the central idea first, then ask how each specific detail, example, or description in the passage adds to or strengthens that idea.
evidencePoints: Lo, where the War-god moves / With soft, sure footstep, on to his design, / Breathing hot slaughter of an evil feud!
Even now the inevitable hounds that track / Dark deeds of hideous crime / Are gone beneath the covert of the domes.
cards.question: The central idea of this passage is that divine retribution against those who committed 'dark deeds of hideous crime' is now unstoppable. In the Chorus's final speech, the lines 'Even now the inevitable hounds that track / Dark deeds of hideous crime / Are gone beneath the covert of the domes' develop this idea by doing which of the following?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The image of hounds going 'beneath the covert of the domes' suggests that Orestes and Pylades have lost their way inside the palace and face an uncertain outcome.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The word 'inevitable' paired with hounds already inside the palace presents retribution as a force that has already been set in motion and cannot be stopped, reinforcing that justice will be carried out.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The reference to 'dark deeds of hideous crime' shifts the central idea away from retribution and toward mourning the original crimes committed against Agamemnon.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The Chorus's description of hounds tracking crime introduces doubt about whether the gods truly support Orestes, since hounds can fail to catch their prey.

cards.standardTitle: Key literary elements add layers of meaning
cards.excerpt:
CHORUS. An erring seer am I, I 1 Of sense and wisdom lorn, If this prophetic Power of right, O'ertaking the offender, come not nigh Ere many an hour be born. Yon vision of the night, That lately breathed into my listening ear, Hath freed me, O my daughter, from all fear. Sweet was that bodement. He doth not forget, The Achaean lord that gave thee being, nor yet The bronzen-griding axe, edged like a spear, Hungry and keen, though dark with stains of time, That in the hour of hideous crime Quelled him with cruel butchery: That, too, remembers, and shall testify.

From ambush deep and dread I 2 With power of many a hand And many hastening feet shall spring The Fury of the adamantine tread, Visiting Argive land Swift recompense to bring For eager dalliance of a blood-stained pair Unhallowed, foul, forbidden. No omen fair,-- Their impious course hath fixed this in my soul,-- Nought but black portents full of blame shall roll Before their eyes that wrought or aided there. Small force of divination would there seem In prophecy or solemn dream, Should not this vision of the night Reach harbour in reality aright.
cards.whyThisWorks: The Chorus speaks as a collective prophetic voice, and its first-person declarations ('An erring seer am I,' 'Hath freed me from all fear') shape the reader's understanding of the coming vengeance as divinely certain rather than merely hoped for, demonstrating how point of view controls tone and meaning.
cards.skillStrategy: Ask yourself: who is speaking, what do they claim to know, and how does their position make the reader feel about what will happen next?
evidencePoints: An erring seer am I, I Of sense and wisdom lorn, If this prophetic Power of right, O'ertaking the offender, come not nigh
Hath freed me, O my daughter, from all fear.
cards.question: The Chorus opens by saying, 'An erring seer am I, I / Of sense and wisdom lorn, / If this prophetic Power of right, / O'ertaking the offender, come not nigh.' How does the Chorus's point of view as a collective prophetic voice shape the meaning of this passage?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The Chorus expresses personal grief over the murder of Electra's father, making the reader sympathize with the Chorus rather than with Electra.

choices.label: B
choices.text: By speaking as prophetic witnesses who claim to be freed from fear by a divine vision, the Chorus frames the coming vengeance as inevitable, creating a tone of dark certainty rather than doubt.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Because the Chorus admits it could be wrong about its prophecy, the passage creates a tone of uncertainty that leaves the reader unsure whether justice will arrive.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The Chorus speaks as an outside observer with no stake in the outcome, which distances the reader from the events and reduces the emotional weight of the prophecy.

cards.standardTitle: Theme development across a literary text
cards.excerpt: CHR. True, noble women, and before she spake Sound thought should have prevented the rash talk That now hath proved her reckless. What wild aim Beckons thee forth in arming this design Whereto thou wouldst demand my ministry? Dost not perceive, thou art not man but woman, Of strength inferior to thine enemies,-- Their Genius daily prospering more and more, Whilst ours is dwindling into nothingness? Who then that plots against a life so strong Shall quit him of the danger without harm? Take heed we do not add to our distress Should some one hear of this our colloquy. Small help and poor advantage 'twere for us To win brief praise and then inglorious die. Nay, death is not so hateful as when one Desiring death is balked of that desire. And I beseech thee, ere in utter ruin We perish and make desolate our race, Refrain thy rage. And I will guard for thee In silence these thy words unrealized; If thou wilt learn this wisdom from long time, Having no strength, to bend before the strong.
cards.whyThisWorks: Chrysothemis's speech directly dramatizes the conflict between defiant action and pragmatic submission, and her warning that 'death is not so hateful as when one / Desiring death is balked of that desire' captures the consequence of reckless courage, making the theme of powerlessness versus rash action traceable through specific lines.
cards.skillStrategy: Find the exact moment of conflict or consequence in the passage, then ask what truth about human experience that moment reveals.
evidencePoints: Who then that plots against a life so strong / Shall quit him of the danger without harm?
death is not so hateful as when one / Desiring death is balked of that desire
cards.question: Chrysothemis asks, 'Who then that plots against a life so strong / Shall quit him of the danger without harm?' and later warns that 'death is not so hateful as when one / Desiring death is balked of that desire.' How do these two moments work together to develop a theme?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Both lines show that Chrysothemis resents Electra's bravery, suggesting that the theme is the rivalry between sisters who want different kinds of glory.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The first line establishes that acting against superior power invites destruction, and the second deepens the consequence by showing that reckless defiance can produce an outcome worse than death itself, together developing the theme that powerless rage leads to ruin rather than redemption.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The first line questions whether any plan can succeed, and the second line argues that dying honorably is preferable to living in submission, together suggesting that the theme is the nobility of sacrifice in the face of oppression.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Both lines warn against speaking openly about dangerous plans, suggesting that the theme is the importance of secrecy and silence when living under a powerful enemy.

cards.whyThisWorks: Chrysothemis's speech contains multiple true details—some central to her argument that Electra should submit to the stronger enemy, and others that are tangential (e.g., the risk of being overheard), allowing students to distinguish strong from weak supporting evidence.
cards.skillStrategy: Ask yourself which piece of evidence directly proves the speaker's main claim, not just a side worry or extra detail.

cards.question: Chrysothemis's central argument is that Electra should abandon her plan because acting against a more powerful enemy will lead to destruction rather than victory. Which detail from the speech most directly supports this central argument?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Chrysothemis warns that someone nearby might overhear their conversation and report it, adding to their current troubles.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Chrysothemis points out that their enemies grow stronger every day while their own power shrinks, making resistance futile.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Chrysothemis reminds Electra that she spoke without thinking first, making her words reckless and her plan poorly formed.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Chrysothemis promises to keep Electra's words secret and guard them in silence so no harm will come from this conversation.

cards.standardTitle: Key literary elements add layers of meaning
cards.excerpt: EL. 'Tis strange and pitiful, thy father's child Can leave him in oblivion and subserve The mother. All thy schooling of me springs From her suggestion, not of thine own wit. Sure, either thou art senseless, or thy sense Deserts thy friends. Treason or dulness then? Choose!--You declared but now, if you had strength, You would display your hatred of this pair. Yet, when I plan full vengeance for my sire, You aid me not, but turn me from the attempt. What's this but adding cowardice to evil? For tell me, or be patient till I show, What should I gain by ceasing this my moan? I live to vex them:--though my life be poor, Yet that suffices, for I honour him, My father,--if affection touch the dead. You say you hate them, but belie your word, Consorting with our father's murderers. I then, were all the gifts in which you glory Laid at my feet, will never more obey This tyrant power. I leave you your rich board And life of luxury. Ne'er be it mine to feed On dainties that would poison my heart's peace! I care not for such honour as thou hast. Nor wouldst thou care if thou wert wise. But now, Having the noblest of all men for sire, Be called thy mother's offspring; so shall most Discern thine infamy and traitorous mind To thy dead father and thy dearest kin.
cards.whyThisWorks: Electra's first-person accusatory voice transforms her sister's caution into moral cowardice, showing students how point of view controls tone and shapes the reader's sympathies.
cards.skillStrategy: When a character speaks in first person, ask: what does this speaker's position—her grief, loyalty, or anger—make the reader feel about the other characters in the scene?
evidencePoints: I live to vex them:--though my life be poor, Yet that suffices, for I honour him, My father
Having the noblest of all men for sire, Be called thy mother's offspring; so shall most Discern thine infamy and traitorous mind To thy dead father and thy dearest kin.
cards.question: Electra declares, 'I live to vex them:--though my life be poor, Yet that suffices, for I honour him, My father,' and later calls her sister's conduct 'traitorous mind / To thy dead father.' How does Electra's point of view in these moments shape the reader's understanding of her sister's choice to comply with their mother?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Because Electra openly admits her life is poor and difficult, the reader sees her as reckless and concludes that her sister's compliance with their mother is the more reasonable and admirable path.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Because Electra frames her own poverty and suffering as proof of loyalty to her father, her point of view casts her sister's comfortable compliance not as caution but as a shameful betrayal of family duty.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Because Electra speaks with intense emotion, the reader recognizes that her accusations are exaggerated and that her sister has done nothing genuinely wrong in accepting their mother's guidance.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Because Electra addresses her sister in the second person throughout, the reader gains a balanced view of both sisters and cannot determine which one is more loyal to their father.

cards.standardTitle: Theme development across a literary text
cards.excerpt: CHR. Well, I will tell thee all I saw:--I came Unto the ancient tomb that holds our sire; And from the topmost mound I marked a stream Of milk fresh-flowing, and his resting place Ringed round with garlands of all flowers that blow. I marvelled at the sight, and peered about, Lest some one might be nearer than we knew. But finding all was quiet in the spot, I ventured closer to the tomb, and there, Hard by the limit, I beheld a curl Of hair new shorn, with all the gloss of youth And straight it struck my heart, as with a sense Of something seen, ah me! long, long ago, And told me that my sight encountered here The token of Orestes, dearest soul Then, clasping it, I did not cry aloud, But straight mine eyes were filled with tears of joy. And now as much as then I feel assured He and none else bestowed this ornament. To whom beyond thyself and me belongs Such consecration? And I know this well, I did it not,--nor thou. Impossible! Thou canst not worship even the blessed Gods Forth of this roof, unpunished. And, most sure, Our mother is not minded so to act, Nor, had she done it, could we fail to know. This offering comes then of Orestes' hand. Take courage, dear one. Not one fate pursues One house perpetually, but changeth still. Ours was a sullen Genius, but perchance This day begins the assurance of much good.
cards.whyThisWorks: Chrysothemis's shift from fearful inspection to tearful joy upon recognizing Orestes' curl of hair enacts a consequence-driven realization that directly develops the theme of hope emerging from prolonged suffering.
cards.skillStrategy: Find the moment a character's feelings or situation change, then ask what idea about life that change reveals.
evidencePoints: straight it struck my heart, as with a sense / Of something seen, ah me! long, long ago
Ours was a sullen Genius, but perchance / This day begins the assurance of much good.
cards.question: When Chrysothemis says 'Ours was a sullen Genius, but perchance / This day begins the assurance of much good,' how does this conclusion develop a theme in the passage?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Her conclusion that the offering could only have come from Orestes proves that careful reasoning is more powerful than emotion, developing the theme that logic alone can restore a family's honor.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Her shift from years of oppression under a 'sullen Genius' to the belief that one sign of Orestes' return signals coming relief develops the theme that prolonged suffering can be broken by an unexpected moment of hope.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Her certainty that their mother did not leave the offerings at the tomb reveals that the household's deception is total, developing the theme that enemies within the family can never be trusted or defeated.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Her silent weeping rather than crying aloud when she finds the curl of hair shows that grief must be hidden from those in power, developing the theme that survival requires concealing one's true feelings.

cards.skillStrategy: When a character narrates in first person, ask how their personal stake in what they see changes the meaning of what they describe — does their closeness make the moment feel more urgent, more doubtful, or more emotionally loaded?
