But straight mine eyes were filled with tears of joy. / And now as much as then I feel assured / He and none else bestowed this ornament.
cards.question: Chrysothemis says the curl of hair 'struck my heart' and that 'mine eyes were filled with tears of joy' before she has confirmed Orestes left the offering. How does her first-person point of view at this moment shape the meaning of her conclusion that 'He and none else bestowed this ornament'?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Her emotional reaction before she has proof shows she is too distressed to reason clearly, so her conclusion that Orestes left the offering feels uncertain and unconvincing to the reader.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Because the reader experiences her grief and longing from inside her perspective, her tears and her certainty merge, making her logical conclusion feel like an emotionally earned truth rather than a cold deduction.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Her focus on her own feelings causes her to overlook the physical evidence — the milk and garlands — so the reader understands the hair curl as the only meaningful detail at the tomb.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Her first-person account distances the reader from the tomb scene because she describes her emotions rather than the objects themselves, making the discovery feel less vivid than if another character had reported it.

cards.standardTitle: Theme development across a literary text
cards.excerpt:
EL. Now, dear Chrysothemis, of what thou bearest Let nothing touch his tomb. 'Tis impious And criminal to offer to thy sire Rites and libations from a hateful wife. Then cast them to the winds, or deep in dust Conceal them, where no particle may reach His resting-place: but lie in store for her When she goes underground. Sure, were she not Most hardened of all women that have been, She ne'er had sent those loveless offerings To grace the sepulchre of him she slew. For think how likely is the buried king To take such present kindly from her hand, Who slew him like an alien enemy, Dishonoured even in death, and mangled him, And wiped the death-stain with his flowing locks-- Sinful purgation! Think you that you bear In those cold gifts atonement for her guilt? It is not possible. Wherefore let be. But take a ringlet from thy comely head, And this from mine, that lingers on my brow Longing to shade his tomb. Ah, give it to him, All I can give, and this my maiden-zone, Not daintily adorned, as once erewhile. Then, humbly kneeling, pray that from the ground He would arise to help us 'gainst his foes, And grant his son Orestes with high hand Strongly to trample on his enemies; That in our time to come from ampler stores We may endow him, than are ours to-day. I cannot but imagine that his will Hath part in visiting her sleep with fears. But howsoe'er, I pray thee, sister mine, Do me this service, and thyself, and him, Dearest of all the world to me and thee, The father of us both, who rests below.

CH. She counsels piously; and thou, dear maid, If thou art wise, wilt do her bidding here.
cards.whyThisWorks: Electra's explicit rejection of Clytemnestra's offerings as incapable of atonement—'It is not possible'—and her substitution of her own hair and girdle as acts of personal sacrifice directly illustrate how conflict and consequence build the theme that genuine devotion requires real cost, not hollow gesture.
cards.skillStrategy: When a character faces a conflict and makes a choice with consequences, ask what that choice reveals about what the author believes is true about life—that belief is the theme.
evidencePoints: 'Think you that you bear / In those cold gifts atonement for her guilt? / It is not possible.'
'But take a ringlet from thy comely head, / And this from mine... And this my maiden-zone, / Not daintily adorned, as once erewhile.'
cards.question: Electra declares that Clytemnestra's offerings cannot provide 'atonement for her guilt' and then instructs Chrysothemis to replace them with locks of hair and a plain girdle. How does this specific contrast develop a theme in the passage?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The contrast shows that Electra doubts Chrysothemis will carry out the task faithfully, developing the theme that loyalty between sisters collapses under family tragedy.

choices.label: B
choices.text: By declaring the murderer's gifts incapable of atonement and substituting tokens stripped from her own body, Electra's actions develop the theme that true devotion requires personal sacrifice, while guilt cannot be erased by outward ceremony.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The contrast between rich offerings and plain tokens develops the theme that the gods favor the poor over the powerful, rewarding poverty rather than wealth.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Electra's rejection of the offerings develops the theme that the dead retain authority over the living and will punish anyone who approaches their tomb with impure motives.

cards.standardTitle: Key literary elements add layers of meaning
cards.excerpt: EL. Dear brother, wheresoe'er thy pleasure leads, My will shall follow, since the joys I know, Not from myself I took them, but from thee. And ne'er would I consent thy slightest grief Should win for me great gain. Ill should I then Serve the divinity of this high hour! Thou knowest how matters in the palace stand. Thou hast surely heard, Aegisthus is from home, And she, our mother, is within. Nor fear She should behold me with a smiling face. Mine ancient hate of her hath sunk too deep. And from the time I saw thee, tears of joy Will cease not. Wherefore should I stint their flow? I, who in this thy coming have beheld Thee dead and living? Strangely hast thou wrought On me;--that should my father come alive, I would not think the sight were miracle, But sober truth. Since such thy presence, then, Lead as thy spirit prompts. For I alone Of two things surely had achieved one, Noble deliverance or a noble death.
cards.whyThisWorks: Electra speaks in first person throughout this monologue, and her direct address to Orestes reveals how her subjective perspective—shaped by years of hatred, grief, and isolation—transforms his return into something more miraculous than even a father's resurrection, giving the moment an intensity only she could convey.
cards.skillStrategy: Ask yourself: because THIS character is speaking, what do I understand about the moment that I would not understand if someone else were telling it?
evidencePoints: I, who in this thy coming have beheld Thee dead and living? Strangely hast thou wrought On me
that should my father come alive, I would not think the sight were miracle, But sober truth.
cards.question: Electra says that if her father came back to life, she 'would not think the sight were miracle, / But sober truth.' What does Electra's first-person perspective reveal through this comparison?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Electra doubts that Orestes has truly returned and suspects she may be imagining him, just as she might imagine her father alive.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Orestes' return has so overwhelmed Electra's emotions that she measures it as more astonishing than even her father's resurrection would be, showing how her years of grief and isolation have made this moment feel beyond ordinary miracle.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Electra believes her father's death was less significant than Orestes' absence, revealing that she cares more for her brother than she ever did for Agamemnon.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Electra is warning Orestes that the palace holds dangers as real as death, using their father's fate as a reminder of what Aegisthus is capable of doing.

cards.standardTitle: Theme development across a literary text
cards.excerpt:
CHORUS. An erring seer am I, I 1 Of sense and wisdom lorn, If this prophetic Power of right, O'ertaking the offender, come not nigh Ere many an hour be born. Yon vision of the night, That lately breathed into my listening ear, Hath freed me, O my daughter, from all fear. Sweet was that bodement. He doth not forget, The Achaean lord that gave thee being, nor yet The bronzen-griding axe, edged like a spear, Hungry and keen, though dark with stains of time, That in the hour of hideous crime Quelled him with cruel butchery: That, too, remembers, and shall testify.

From ambush deep and dread I 2 With power of many a hand And many hastening feet shall spring The Fury of the adamantine tread, Visiting Argive land Swift recompense to bring For eager dalliance of a blood-stained pair Unhallowed, foul, forbidden. No omen fair,-- Their impious course hath fixed this in my soul,-- Nought but black portents full of blame shall roll Before their eyes that wrought or aided there. Small force of divination would there seem In prophecy or solemn dream, Should not this vision of the night Reach harbour in reality aright.
cards.whyThisWorks: The Chorus's speech moves from the topic of justice to a universal claim that wrongdoers cannot escape divine retribution, giving students a clear model for distinguishing a subject word from a full thematic statement.
cards.skillStrategy: Ask yourself: can I turn the topic into a sentence that says something true about all people or life? That sentence is the theme.
evidencePoints: If this prophetic Power of right, O'ertaking the offender, come not nigh Ere many an hour be born
Nought but black portents full of blame shall roll Before their eyes that wrought or aided there
cards.question: The Chorus speaks of 'the Fury of the adamantine tread' bringing 'swift recompense' to those who committed 'hideous crime.' Which statement best expresses the theme developed across both paragraphs, rather than simply naming the topic?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The passage is about justice and divine punishment in ancient Argos.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Those who commit violent crimes against their own kin cannot escape the retribution that divine forces will inevitably deliver.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Prophetic dreams are a reliable source of comfort for those who grieve a murdered loved one.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The Chorus warns that prophecy and solemn dreams lose their power when they fail to come true.

cards.standardTitle: Key literary elements add layers of meaning
cards.excerpt: CHR. True, noble women, and before she spake Sound thought should have prevented the rash talk That now hath proved her reckless. What wild aim Beckons thee forth in arming this design Whereto thou wouldst demand my ministry? Dost not perceive, thou art not man but woman, Of strength inferior to thine enemies,-- Their Genius daily prospering more and more, Whilst ours is dwindling into nothingness? Who then that plots against a life so strong Shall quit him of the danger without harm? Take heed we do not add to our distress Should some one hear of this our colloquy. Small help and poor advantage 'twere for us To win brief praise and then inglorious die. Nay, death is not so hateful as when one Desiring death is balked of that desire. And I beseech thee, ere in utter ruin We perish and make desolate our race, Refrain thy rage. And I will guard for thee In silence these thy words unrealized; If thou wilt learn this wisdom from long time, Having no strength, to bend before the strong.
cards.whyThisWorks: Chrysothemis speaks as a cautious insider who frames Electra's defiance through the lens of gendered weakness and political powerlessness, making her point of view directly shape whether the reader reads Electra's plan as courageous or reckless.
cards.skillStrategy: Ask yourself: who is speaking, what is their position, and how does that position change what the words mean — would the same warning feel different coming from someone else?
evidencePoints: Dost not perceive, thou art not man but woman, Of strength inferior to thine enemies
If thou wilt learn this wisdom from long time, Having no strength, to bend before the strong
cards.question: Chrysothemis tells Electra, 'Dost not perceive, thou art not man but woman, / Of strength inferior to thine enemies.' How does Chrysothemis's point of view as someone who accepts their powerlessness shape the meaning of this claim?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Because Chrysothemis shares Electra's suffering, her reminder that Electra is a woman reads as solidarity, suggesting both sisters should unite and resist their enemies together.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Because Chrysothemis has already surrendered to their enemies' dominance, her appeal to Electra's weakness frames bold resistance not as courage but as self-destructive pride that will only deepen their ruin.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Because Chrysothemis speaks as someone who once attempted rebellion herself, her warning about being a woman carries regret, giving the passage a tone of personal shame rather than practical caution.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Because Chrysothemis admires Electra's determination, her reference to Electra's inferior strength is meant to challenge Electra to prove her enemies wrong rather than to discourage her plan.

cards.standardTitle: Theme development across a literary text
cards.excerpt: EL. 'Tis strange and pitiful, thy father's child Can leave him in oblivion and subserve The mother. All thy schooling of me springs From her suggestion, not of thine own wit. Sure, either thou art senseless, or thy sense Deserts thy friends. Treason or dulness then? Choose!--You declared but now, if you had strength, You would display your hatred of this pair. Yet, when I plan full vengeance for my sire, You aid me not, but turn me from the attempt. What's this but adding cowardice to evil? For tell me, or be patient till I show, What should I gain by ceasing this my moan? I live to vex them:--though my life be poor, Yet that suffices, for I honour him, My father,--if affection touch the dead. You say you hate them, but belie your word, Consorting with our father's murderers. I then, were all the gifts in which you glory Laid at my feet, will never more obey This tyrant power. I leave you your rich board And life of luxury. Ne'er be it mine to feed On dainties that would poison my heart's peace! I care not for such honour as thou hast. Nor wouldst thou care if thou wert wise. But now, Having the noblest of all men for sire, Be called thy mother's offspring; so shall most Discern thine infamy and traitorous mind To thy dead father and thy dearest kin.
cards.whyThisWorks: Electra's speech contrasts the topic of loyalty with a universal claim—that true loyalty demands personal sacrifice over comfort—allowing students to practice distinguishing a subject from a thematic statement.
cards.skillStrategy: Ask yourself: does this statement just name what the passage is about, or does it make a claim about people and choices that the passage proves through specific details?
evidencePoints: Ne'er be it mine to feed On dainties that would poison my heart's peace!
I live to vex them:--though my life be poor, Yet that suffices, for I honour him, My father
cards.question: When Electra declares 'Ne'er be it mine to feed on dainties that would poison my heart's peace' and 'though my life be poor, yet that suffices, for I honour him,' she is building a case for which universal statement about loyalty?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Loyalty between siblings is the most powerful bond a person can have.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Remaining loyal to those we love demands choosing hardship over the comfort that silence and betrayal can buy.

choices.label: C
choices.text: A life of poverty is always more virtuous than a life of wealth, regardless of the choices that produced it.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Chrysothemis is too cowardly to ever act on her stated hatred of their mother.

cards.standardTitle: Key literary elements add layers of meaning
cards.excerpt: CLY. (_to an attendant_). Then lift for me those fruitful offerings, While to Apollo, before whom we stand, I raise my supplication for release From doubts and fears that shake my bosom now. And, O defender of our house! attend My secret utterance. No friendly ear Is that which hearkens for my voice. My thought Must not be blazoned with her standing by, Lest through her envious and wide-babbling tongue She fill the city full of wild surmise. List, then, as I shall speak: and grant the dreams Whose two-fold apparition I to-night Have seen, if good their bodement, be fulfilled: If hostile, turn their influence on my foes. And yield not them their wish that would by guile Thrust me from this high fortune, but vouchsafe That ever thus exempt from harms I rule The Atridae's home and kingdom, in full life, Partaking with the friends I live with now All fair prosperity, and with my children, Save those who hate and vex me bitterly. Lykeian Phoebus, favourably hear My prayer, and grant to all of us our need! More is there, which, though I be silent here, A God should understand. No secret thing Is hidden from the all-seeing sons of Heaven.
cards.whyThisWorks: Clytemnestra's aside to Apollo—delivered while Electra stands nearby—reveals her private fears and manipulative intent in a way that would be impossible if Electra were the narrator, showing students how the speaker's perspective shapes tone, dramatic irony, and reader understanding.
cards.skillStrategy: Ask yourself: because THIS character is speaking, what do I know that other characters don't, and how does that change what the moment feels like?
evidencePoints: No friendly ear / Is that which hearkens for my voice.
Lest through her envious and wide-babbling tongue / She fill the city full of wild surmise.
cards.question: Clytemnestra addresses Apollo directly while Electra stands nearby, saying 'No friendly ear / Is that which hearkens for my voice' and warning against Electra's 'wide-babbling tongue.' How does Clytemnestra's point of view as the speaker shape the reader's understanding of this moment?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Because Clytemnestra speaks openly to the crowd, the reader understands she is confident her prayer will be answered and has no reason to fear Electra's reaction.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Because Clytemnestra speaks her fears aloud while Electra is present but unaware of the prayer's content, the reader gains access to her hidden guilt and paranoia, creating dramatic irony that would be lost if Electra narrated the scene.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Because Clytemnestra prays to Apollo on behalf of her household, the reader understands she is a devoted mother whose only concern is protecting her children from outside enemies.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Because Clytemnestra speaks in the presence of an attendant, the reader understands the attendant is the true threat she fears, not Electra, whose presence is incidental to the prayer.

cards.standardTitle: Theme development across a literary text
cards.excerpt: CHR. Well, I will tell thee all I saw:--I came Unto the ancient tomb that holds our sire; And from the topmost mound I marked a stream Of milk fresh-flowing, and his resting place Ringed round with garlands of all flowers that blow. I marvelled at the sight, and peered about, Lest some one might be nearer than we knew. But finding all was quiet in the spot, I ventured closer to the tomb, and there, Hard by the limit, I beheld a curl Of hair new shorn, with all the gloss of youth And straight it struck my heart, as with a sense Of something seen, ah me! long, long ago, And told me that my sight encountered here The token of Orestes, dearest soul Then, clasping it, I did not cry aloud, But straight mine eyes were filled with tears of joy. And now as much as then I feel assured He and none else bestowed this ornament. To whom beyond thyself and me belongs Such consecration? And I know this well, I did it not,--nor thou. Impossible! Thou canst not worship even the blessed Gods Forth of this roof, unpunished. And, most sure, Our mother is not minded so to act, Nor, had she done it, could we fail to know. This offering comes then of Orestes' hand. Take courage, dear one. Not one fate pursues One house perpetually, but changeth still. Ours was a sullen Genius, but perchance This day begins the assurance of much good.
cards.whyThisWorks: Chrysothemis's speech moves from the topic of hope to a universal claim—'Not one fate pursues / One house perpetually, but changeth still'—giving students a clear contrast between the subject (hope or fate) and a fully developed thematic statement about how suffering does not last forever.
cards.skillStrategy: Ask yourself: is this just a subject word like 'hope,' or does the passage make a complete claim about what hope or fate means for people's lives?
evidencePoints: Not one fate pursues / One house perpetually, but changeth still.
Ours was a sullen Genius, but perchance / This day begins the assurance of much good.
cards.question: Chrysothemis ends her speech with the lines 'Not one fate pursues / One house perpetually, but changeth still.' Which statement best expresses the theme developed by these lines?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The central idea of the passage is the topic of fate, because Chrysothemis discovers signs at their father's tomb.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Suffering does not define a family's destiny forever, because circumstances and fortune are always subject to change.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Loyalty to family is rewarded, because Orestes secretly returns to honor his father's grave with offerings.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Hope is dangerous, because Chrysothemis may be wrong that the offerings truly came from Orestes.

cards.standardTitle: Key literary elements add layers of meaning
cards.excerpt:
EL. Now, dear Chrysothemis, of what thou bearest Let nothing touch his tomb. 'Tis impious And criminal to offer to thy sire Rites and libations from a hateful wife. Then cast them to the winds, or deep in dust Conceal them, where no particle may reach His resting-place: but lie in store for her When she goes underground. Sure, were she not Most hardened of all women that have been, She ne'er had sent those loveless offerings To grace the sepulchre of him she slew. For think how likely is the buried king To take such present kindly from her hand, Who slew him like an alien enemy, Dishonoured even in death, and mangled him, And wiped the death-stain with his flowing locks-- Sinful purgation! Think you that you bear In those cold gifts atonement for her guilt? It is not possible. Wherefore let be. But take a ringlet from thy comely head, And this from mine, that lingers on my brow Longing to shade his tomb. Ah, give it to him, All I can give, and this my maiden-zone, Not daintily adorned, as once erewhile. Then, humbly kneeling, pray that from the ground He would arise to help us 'gainst his foes, And grant his son Orestes with high hand Strongly to trample on his enemies; That in our time to come from ampler stores We may endow him, than are ours to-day. I cannot but imagine that his will Hath part in visiting her sleep with fears. But howsoe'er, I pray thee, sister mine, Do me this service, and thyself, and him, Dearest of all the world to me and thee, The father of us both, who rests below.

CH. She counsels piously; and thou, dear maid, If thou art wise, wilt do her bidding here.
cards.whyThisWorks: Electra's first-person commands and self-offered gifts ('take a ringlet from thy comely head, / And this from mine') reveal how her personal grief and hatred shape the moral weight of the scene, making point of view inseparable from meaning.
cards.skillStrategy: When a character speaks in first person, ask yourself: what does this speaker's relationship to the events make them see, feel, or judge differently than an outsider would?
evidencePoints: 'Tis impious / And criminal to offer to thy sire / Rites and libations from a hateful wife.
take a ringlet from thy comely head, / And this from mine, that lingers on my brow / Longing to shade his tomb.
cards.question: In the excerpt, Electra calls Clytemnestra's offerings 'impious and criminal' and then instructs Chrysothemis to replace them with a lock of hair from each sister's head. How does Electra's point of view as a grieving, vengeful daughter shape the meaning of this contrast between the two sets of offerings?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Because Electra is an impartial observer of burial customs, her judgment that Clytemnestra's gifts are 'impious' reflects a shared community standard, and the hair offerings simply follow the same religious tradition Clytemnestra was attempting.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Because Electra speaks as a daughter consumed by grief and hatred for her mother, her condemnation of Clytemnestra's gifts as pollution and her substitution of her own hair transform the offerings into a moral contest—one set represents the guilt of a murderer, the other the devotion of a wronged child—making the reader feel the injustice of her father's death through her eyes.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Because Electra is focused entirely on securing Orestes' return to power, her rejection of Clytemnestra's offerings reveals that honoring her father is secondary to political strategy, which causes the reader to question whether her grief is genuine.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Because Electra speaks as an older sister correcting Chrysothemis's ignorance, her instructions create a tone of calm religious authority, and the reader understands the hair offerings as a standard substitute when proper grave goods are unavailable.

cards.standardTitle: Theme development across a literary text
cards.excerpt: EL. Dear brother, wheresoe'er thy pleasure leads, My will shall follow, since the joys I know, Not from myself I took them, but from thee. And ne'er would I consent thy slightest grief Should win for me great gain. Ill should I then Serve the divinity of this high hour! Thou knowest how matters in the palace stand. Thou hast surely heard, Aegisthus is from home, And she, our mother, is within. Nor fear She should behold me with a smiling face. Mine ancient hate of her hath sunk too deep. And from the time I saw thee, tears of joy Will cease not. Wherefore should I stint their flow? I, who in this thy coming have beheld Thee dead and living? Strangely hast thou wrought On me;--that should my father come alive, I would not think the sight were miracle, But sober truth. Since such thy presence, then, Lead as thy spirit prompts. For I alone Of two things surely had achieved one, Noble deliverance or a noble death.
cards.whyThisWorks: Electra's declaration 'ne'er would I consent thy slightest grief / Should win for me great gain' moves beyond the topic of sibling loyalty to a universal claim about self-sacrifice, giving students a concrete textual moment to distinguish topic from theme.
cards.skillStrategy: Find the moment where a character makes a claim about what people should do or feel—that claim is closer to a theme than a one-word topic label.
evidencePoints: ne'er would I consent thy slightest grief / Should win for me great gain
For I alone / Of two things surely had achieved one, / Noble deliverance or a noble death.
cards.question: When Electra says she would 'ne'er consent' that her brother's 'slightest grief / Should win for me great gain,' and later declares she sought either 'Noble deliverance or a noble death,' which statement expresses a theme those lines develop rather than simply naming their topic?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The passage is about the loyalty Electra feels toward Orestes.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Genuine devotion requires refusing personal benefit at the cost of a loved one's suffering.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The passage is about Electra's deep hatred for her mother, Clytemnestra.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Electra believes that seeing Orestes alive is as miraculous as their father returning from the dead.

cards.standardTitle: Key literary elements add layers of meaning
cards.excerpt:
EL. O gladsome day! Dear only saviour of our father's house, How earnest thou hither? Art thou he indeed, That didst preserve Orestes and myself From many sorrows? O dear hands, kind feet, Swift in our service,--how couldst thou so long Be near, nor show one gleam, but didst destroy My heart with words, hiding the loveliest deeds? Father!--in thee methinks I see my father. O welcome! thou of all the world to me Most hated and most loved in one short hour.

OLD M. Enough, dear maiden! Many nights and days Are circling hitherward, that shall reveal In clear recountment all that came between. But to you two that stand beside I tell, Now is your moment, with the Queen alone, And none of men within; but if you pause, Know that with others of profounder skill You'll have to strive, more than your present foes.

OR. Then, Pylades, we need no more to dwell On words, but enter on this act with speed, First worshipping the holy shrines o' the Gods That were my father's, harboured at the gate. [_They pass within_. ELECTRA _remains in an attitude of prayer_

EL. O King Apollo! hear them graciously, And hear me too, that with incessant hand Honoured thee richly from my former store! And now, fierce slayer, I importune thee, And woo thee with such gifts as I can give, Be kindly aidant to this enterprise, And make the world take note, what meed of bane Heaven still bestows on man's iniquity. [ELECTRA _goes within_

CH. Lo, where the War-god moves 1 With soft, sure footstep, on to his design, Breathing hot slaughter of an evil feud! Even now the inevitable hounds that track Dark deeds of hideous crime Are gone beneath the covert of the domes. Not long in wavering suspense shall hang The dreaming presage of my wistful soul.
cards.whyThisWorks: The excerpt contrasts Electra's first-person grief and prayer with the Chorus's detached, cosmic description of the War-god's 'soft, sure footstep,' showing students how point of view shapes whether revenge feels personal or inevitable.
cards.skillStrategy: Ask yourself: who is speaking, what do they know or feel, and how does that position change what the moment means to the reader?
evidencePoints: O King Apollo! hear them graciously, And hear me too, that with incessant hand Honoured thee richly from my former store!
Lo, where the War-god moves With soft, sure footstep, on to his design, Breathing hot slaughter of an evil feud!
cards.question: In the excerpt, Electra prays, 'O King Apollo! hear them graciously, And hear me too,' while the Chorus later declares, 'Lo, where the War-god moves / With soft, sure footstep, on to his design.' How does this difference in who is speaking shape the meaning of the revenge plot at this moment?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Electra's prayer shows she is confident the gods will act, and the Chorus confirms that confidence by celebrating the revenge as already finished.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Electra's prayer places the revenge in the realm of personal longing and uncertain petition, while the Chorus's detached observation reframes it as an unstoppable, impersonal force already in motion.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Electra's prayer reveals her doubt that Orestes will succeed, and the Chorus echoes that doubt by describing the War-god's footstep as hesitant and wavering.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Electra's prayer shifts blame for the revenge onto the gods, and the Chorus agrees by naming Apollo rather than Orestes as the true agent of the plan.

cards.question: The Chorus declares that a 'prophetic Power of right' will overtake the offenders and that 'swift recompense' will come to 'a blood-stained pair.' Which statement best expresses the universal theme developed across both paragraphs?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Dreams and visions are unreliable guides that lead people to false hope in times of grief.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Those who commit acts of violence and betrayal cannot ultimately escape the punishment their deeds demand.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Loyalty to a murdered father is the highest obligation a person can fulfill in a time of injustice.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Divine forces intervene in human affairs only when mortal courage has already been exhausted.

CHORUS. An erring seer am I, I 1 Of sense and wisdom lorn, If this prophetic Power of right, O'ertaking the offender, come not nigh Ere many an hour be born. Yon vision of the night, That lately breathed into my listening ear, Hath freed me, O my daughter, from all fear. Sweet was that bodement. He doth not forget, The Achaean lord that gave thee being, nor yet The bronzen-griding axe, edged like a spear, Hungry and keen, though dark with stains of time, That in the hour of hideous crime Quelled him with cruel butchery: That, too, remembers, and shall testify.

From ambush deep and dread I 2 With power of many a hand And many hastening feet shall spring The Fury of the adamantine tread, Visiting Argive land Swift recompense to bring For eager dalliance of a blood-stained pair Unhallowed, foul, forbidden. No omen fair,-- Their impious course hath fixed this in my soul,-- Nought but black portents full of blame shall roll Before their eyes that wrought or aided there. Small force of divination would there seem In prophecy or solemn dream, Should not this vision of the night Reach harbour in reality aright.
cards.whyThisWorks: The Chorus's references to 'vision of the night,' 'ambush deep and dread,' and 'black portents' establish a dark, foreboding atmosphere tied to Argos that directly shapes the mood of inevitable divine retribution.
cards.skillStrategy: When analyzing setting, look for words describing time, place, or atmosphere and ask what feeling or meaning those details create for the reader.
evidencePoints: From ambush deep and dread / With power of many a hand / And many hastening feet shall spring / The Fury of the adamantine tread, / Visiting Argive land
Nought but black portents full of blame shall roll / Before their eyes that wrought or aided there.
cards.question: In the second stanza, the Chorus describes the Fury emerging from 'ambush deep and dread' to visit 'Argive land.' How does this depiction of place and atmosphere contribute to the meaning of the passage?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The reference to Argive land suggests the Chorus feels pride in the city's history, creating a tone of patriotic celebration.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The image of a hidden, threatening force descending upon Argos creates an atmosphere of inescapable doom, reinforcing the idea that divine punishment will inevitably reach the guilty.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The darkness of the setting signals that the Chorus is uncertain whether justice will arrive, leaving the outcome of the prophecy in doubt.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The Argive land is portrayed as a place of refuge where the Fury offers protection to the innocent rather than punishment to the guilty.

cards.standardTitle: Theme development across a literary text
cards.excerpt: EL. 'Tis strange and pitiful, thy father's child Can leave him in oblivion and subserve The mother. All thy schooling of me springs From her suggestion, not of thine own wit. Sure, either thou art senseless, or thy sense Deserts thy friends. Treason or dulness then? Choose!--You declared but now, if you had strength, You would display your hatred of this pair. Yet, when I plan full vengeance for my sire, You aid me not, but turn me from the attempt. What's this but adding cowardice to evil? For tell me, or be patient till I show, What should I gain by ceasing this my moan? I live to vex them:--though my life be poor, Yet that suffices, for I honour him, My father,--if affection touch the dead. You say you hate them, but belie your word, Consorting with our father's murderers. I then, were all the gifts in which you glory Laid at my feet, will never more obey This tyrant power. I leave you your rich board And life of luxury. Ne'er be it mine to feed On dainties that would poison my heart's peace! I care not for such honour as thou hast. Nor wouldst thou care if thou wert wise. But now, Having the noblest of all men for sire, Be called thy mother's offspring; so shall most Discern thine infamy and traitorous mind To thy dead father and thy dearest kin.

cards.skillStrategy: Ask yourself: what does the character's conflict teach about all people, not just this one person in this one story?

Ne'er be it mine to feed On dainties that would poison my heart's peace!
cards.question: Electra declares, 'Ne'er be it mine to feed / On dainties that would poison my heart's peace!' and 'though my life be poor, / Yet that suffices.' Which theme is most clearly developed through these statements?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Grief over a parent's death eventually fades when a person accepts the comforts offered by those in power.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Maintaining one's moral convictions matters more than accepting comfort or security that requires betraying what one holds sacred.

choices.label: C
choices.text: A person who openly expresses hatred toward family members will ultimately destroy any chance of reconciliation.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Loyalty to the dead is a form of weakness that prevents the living from moving forward and building a better life.

cards.standardTitle: Key literary elements add layers of meaning
cards.excerpt:
EL. Now, dear Chrysothemis, of what thou bearest Let nothing touch his tomb. 'Tis impious And criminal to offer to thy sire Rites and libations from a hateful wife. Then cast them to the winds, or deep in dust Conceal them, where no particle may reach His resting-place: but lie in store for her When she goes underground. Sure, were she not Most hardened of all women that have been, She ne'er had sent those loveless offerings To grace the sepulchre of him she slew. For think how likely is the buried king To take such present kindly from her hand, Who slew him like an alien enemy, Dishonoured even in death, and mangled him, And wiped the death-stain with his flowing locks-- Sinful purgation! Think you that you bear In those cold gifts atonement for her guilt? It is not possible. Wherefore let be. But take a ringlet from thy comely head, And this from mine, that lingers on my brow Longing to shade his tomb. Ah, give it to him, All I can give, and this my maiden-zone, Not daintily adorned, as once erewhile. Then, humbly kneeling, pray that from the ground He would arise to help us 'gainst his foes, And grant his son Orestes with high hand Strongly to trample on his enemies; That in our time to come from ampler stores We may endow him, than are ours to-day. I cannot but imagine that his will Hath part in visiting her sleep with fears. But howsoe'er, I pray thee, sister mine, Do me this service, and thyself, and him, Dearest of all the world to me and thee, The father of us both, who rests below.

CH. She counsels piously; and thou, dear maid, If thou art wise, wilt do her bidding here.
cards.whyThisWorks: The tomb setting is not merely backdrop but a moral arena: Electra's commands about what may or may not 'reach his resting-place' and her substitution of her own hair and girdle for Clytemnestra's offerings show how the physical place of burial generates the scene's ethical and emotional stakes.
cards.skillStrategy: When a setting detail appears in a character's direct speech, ask what that place makes possible or impossible for the characters—that reveals how setting adds meaning.
evidencePoints: 'Tis impious / And criminal to offer to thy sire / Rites and libations from a hateful wife. Then cast them to the winds, or deep in dust / Conceal them, where no particle may reach / His resting-place
take a ringlet from thy comely head, / And this from mine, that lingers on my brow / Longing to shade his tomb. Ah, give it to him, / All I can give, and this my maiden-zone
cards.question: Electra commands Chrysothemis to ensure that 'no particle may reach his resting-place' from Clytemnestra, then offers her own hair and girdle instead. What does the tomb's physical presence contribute to the meaning of this moment?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The tomb's distance from the palace shows that Electra and Chrysothemis are isolated from power, suggesting their offerings are futile gestures that cannot change their situation.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The tomb functions as a boundary that separates worthy devotion from corrupt guilt: what crosses into the resting-place either honors or defiles the king, making the burial ground itself the measure of loyalty and moral standing.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The tomb setting reveals that Electra's primary concern is preventing Chrysothemis from obeying Clytemnestra, so the place matters only as a location where the sisters' conflict over obedience plays out.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The tomb reminds both sisters that their father is beyond help, creating an atmosphere of hopelessness that undercuts Electra's prayer for Orestes to 'trample on his enemies.'

cards.standardTitle: Theme development across a literary text
cards.excerpt: CHR. True, noble women, and before she spake Sound thought should have prevented the rash talk That now hath proved her reckless. What wild aim Beckons thee forth in arming this design Whereto thou wouldst demand my ministry? Dost not perceive, thou art not man but woman, Of strength inferior to thine enemies,-- Their Genius daily prospering more and more, Whilst ours is dwindling into nothingness? Who then that plots against a life so strong Shall quit him of the danger without harm? Take heed we do not add to our distress Should some one hear of this our colloquy. Small help and poor advantage 'twere for us To win brief praise and then inglorious die. Nay, death is not so hateful as when one Desiring death is balked of that desire. And I beseech thee, ere in utter ruin We perish and make desolate our race, Refrain thy rage. And I will guard for thee In silence these thy words unrealized; If thou wilt learn this wisdom from long time, Having no strength, to bend before the strong.
cards.whyThisWorks: Chrysothemis's speech directly articulates a transferable theme about the tension between righteous anger and pragmatic survival, urging submission to power as wisdom—a universal human dilemma about when to fight and when to yield.
cards.skillStrategy: Ask yourself: what does this character's argument reveal about a truth that applies to all people, not just these characters in this moment?
evidencePoints: Having no strength, to bend before the strong.
Small help and poor advantage 'twere for us To win brief praise and then inglorious die.
cards.question: Chrysothemis warns Electra that acting against their powerful enemies will bring ruin rather than glory, concluding that those without strength must 'bend before the strong.' Which universal theme does this argument most clearly develop?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Loyalty to family demands that individuals sacrifice their own safety to defend those they love, no matter the cost.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Survival sometimes requires people to suppress righteous anger and accept the limits of their own power.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Silence is always the most honorable response when a person faces an unjust and overwhelming authority.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Women who challenge those in power are destined to fail because society will never recognize their courage.

cards.standardTitle: Key literary elements add layers of meaning
cards.excerpt: CLY. (_to an attendant_). Then lift for me those fruitful offerings, While to Apollo, before whom we stand, I raise my supplication for release From doubts and fears that shake my bosom now. And, O defender of our house! attend My secret utterance. No friendly ear Is that which hearkens for my voice. My thought Must not be blazoned with her standing by, Lest through her envious and wide-babbling tongue She fill the city full of wild surmise. List, then, as I shall speak: and grant the dreams Whose two-fold apparition I to-night Have seen, if good their bodement, be fulfilled: If hostile, turn their influence on my foes. And yield not them their wish that would by guile Thrust me from this high fortune, but vouchsafe That ever thus exempt from harms I rule The Atridae's home and kingdom, in full life, Partaking with the friends I live with now All fair prosperity, and with my children, Save those who hate and vex me bitterly. Lykeian Phoebus, favourably hear My prayer, and grant to all of us our need! More is there, which, though I be silent here, A God should understand. No secret thing Is hidden from the all-seeing sons of Heaven.
cards.whyThisWorks: The scene is set at Apollo's temple, a sacred public space where Clytemnestra must whisper her darkest fears aloud, and that religious-political setting creates dramatic irony, tension, and reveals her vulnerability and guilt.
cards.skillStrategy: Ask yourself: where and when does this moment take place, and how does that location force the character to behave in a way that reveals something deeper about the conflict or mood?
evidencePoints: And, O defender of our house! attend / My secret utterance. No friendly ear / Is that which hearkens for my voice.
Lest through her envious and wide-babbling tongue / She fill the city full of wild surmise.
cards.question: Clytemnestra delivers her prayer at Apollo's temple while Electra stands nearby. How does this setting shape the mood and meaning of her speech?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The sacred temple setting reassures Clytemnestra that her prayer will be answered, creating a mood of confidence and divine favor.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Being forced to pray in a public sacred space while an enemy listens creates a mood of paranoia and secrecy, revealing that Clytemnestra's power is shadowed by fear and guilt.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The temple setting signals that Clytemnestra is a devoted worshipper, establishing a tone of religious sincerity and moral authority.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Standing before Apollo's altar while Electra is present shows that Clytemnestra wants to humiliate her daughter publicly, creating a tone of open hostility.

cards.question: Clytemnestra prays in secret, asks the gods to silence her enemies, and begs to remain 'exempt from harms' while ruling. Which universal theme does her prayer most clearly develop?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Faith in the gods brings peace of mind to those who are troubled by guilt.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Those who hold power often rely on secrecy and self-interest to protect their position rather than on justice.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Dreams are powerful warnings that force rulers to change their behavior before it is too late.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Family loyalty ultimately matters more to a ruler than personal ambition or political survival.

cards.question: Read the lines: 'Small force of divination would there seem / In prophecy or solemn dream, / Should not this vision of the night / Reach harbour in reality aright.' How does this rhetorical question affect the reader at the close of the passage?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The question invites the reader to doubt whether the Chorus has any real knowledge of the future, leaving the outcome of vengeance genuinely uncertain.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The question reinforces the Chorus's certainty by implying that prophecy would be worthless if this vision did not come true, making the punishment of the guilty feel unavoidable.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The question shifts the reader's focus away from vengeance and toward sympathy for the 'blood-stained pair,' suggesting the Chorus is reconsidering its harsh judgment.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The question signals the Chorus's fear that the dream may be false, creating suspense about whether divine justice will fail Electra entirely.

cards.standardTitle: Key literary elements add layers of meaning
cards.excerpt:
EL. O gladsome day! Dear only saviour of our father's house, How earnest thou hither? Art thou he indeed, That didst preserve Orestes and myself From many sorrows? O dear hands, kind feet, Swift in our service,--how couldst thou so long Be near, nor show one gleam, but didst destroy My heart with words, hiding the loveliest deeds? Father!--in thee methinks I see my father. O welcome! thou of all the world to me Most hated and most loved in one short hour.

OLD M. Enough, dear maiden! Many nights and days Are circling hitherward, that shall reveal In clear recountment all that came between. But to you two that stand beside I tell, Now is your moment, with the Queen alone, And none of men within; but if you pause, Know that with others of profounder skill You'll have to strive, more than your present foes.

OR. Then, Pylades, we need no more to dwell On words, but enter on this act with speed, First worshipping the holy shrines o' the Gods That were my father's, harboured at the gate. [_They pass within_. ELECTRA _remains in an attitude of prayer_

EL. O King Apollo! hear them graciously, And hear me too, that with incessant hand Honoured thee richly from my former store! And now, fierce slayer, I importune thee, And woo thee with such gifts as I can give, Be kindly aidant to this enterprise, And make the world take note, what meed of bane Heaven still bestows on man's iniquity. [ELECTRA _goes within_

CH. Lo, where the War-god moves 1 With soft, sure footstep, on to his design, Breathing hot slaughter of an evil feud! Even now the inevitable hounds that track Dark deeds of hideous crime Are gone beneath the covert of the domes. Not long in wavering suspense shall hang The dreaming presage of my wistful soul.
cards.whyThisWorks: The Chorus's closing description of the palace interior as a shadowed, predatory space—'gone beneath the covert of the domes'—creates an atmosphere of lurking doom that deepens the mood of inevitable, violent justice.
cards.skillStrategy: When a setting detail appears, ask yourself: what feeling does this place or moment create, and how does that feeling connect to what the characters are about to do or suffer?
evidencePoints: Even now the inevitable hounds that track / Dark deeds of hideous crime / Are gone beneath the covert of the domes.
Lo, where the War-god moves / With soft, sure footstep, on to his design, / Breathing hot slaughter of an evil feud!
cards.question: In the Chorus's final speech, the palace interior is described as a place where 'the inevitable hounds' have gone 'beneath the covert of the domes.' How does this depiction of the setting contribute to the mood of the passage?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The palace is portrayed as a sacred refuge, suggesting that Orestes and Pylades are protected by divine favor once they cross the threshold.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The palace is portrayed as a dark, enclosed trap, creating an atmosphere of inescapable doom in which violent retribution is already in motion.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The palace is portrayed as a place of mourning and grief, reflecting Electra's long suffering rather than any approaching danger.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The palace is portrayed as a site of political power, emphasizing that the Queen's authority makes Orestes' mission likely to fail.

cards.standardTitle: Theme development across a literary text
cards.excerpt: EL. Dear brother, wheresoe'er thy pleasure leads, My will shall follow, since the joys I know, Not from myself I took them, but from thee. And ne'er would I consent thy slightest grief Should win for me great gain. Ill should I then Serve the divinity of this high hour! Thou knowest how matters in the palace stand. Thou hast surely heard, Aegisthus is from home, And she, our mother, is within. Nor fear She should behold me with a smiling face. Mine ancient hate of her hath sunk too deep. And from the time I saw thee, tears of joy Will cease not. Wherefore should I stint their flow? I, who in this thy coming have beheld Thee dead and living? Strangely hast thou wrought On me;--that should my father come alive, I would not think the sight were miracle, But sober truth. Since such thy presence, then, Lead as thy spirit prompts. For I alone Of two things surely had achieved one, Noble deliverance or a noble death.
cards.whyThisWorks: Electra's declaration that she would accept 'noble deliverance or a noble death' rather than compromise her loyalty illustrates the transferable theme that true devotion demands personal sacrifice, making it ideal for teaching universal theme development.
cards.skillStrategy: Look for a statement a character makes about what they value or would sacrifice, then ask yourself what that reveals about people or choices in general—not just in this story.
evidencePoints: ne'er would I consent thy slightest grief / Should win for me great gain
I alone / Of two things surely had achieved one, / Noble deliverance or a noble death
cards.question: Electra tells her brother, 'ne'er would I consent thy slightest grief / Should win for me great gain' and declares she would have sought 'Noble deliverance or a noble death.' Which universal theme do these statements develop?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Reunions with lost family members bring overwhelming joy that erases years of suffering.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Genuine loyalty requires a person to place another's well-being above personal advantage, even at the cost of one's own life.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Hatred toward an enemy grows stronger over time and ultimately destroys the person who holds it.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Those who have suffered the longest are rewarded when justice finally arrives.

cards.question: Read the following lines from Electra's speech: 'What's this but adding cowardice to evil?' and 'What should I gain by ceasing this my moan?' How do these rhetorical questions affect the reader?

choices.label: A
choices.text: They reveal that Electra is genuinely uncertain about her plan and is asking Chrysothemis for practical guidance on how to proceed.

choices.label: B
choices.text: They pressure the reader to accept Electra's moral judgments as self-evident, making Chrysothemis's silence seem like an admission of guilt rather than a reasonable choice.

choices.label: C
choices.text: They slow the speech's momentum by introducing doubt, causing the reader to question whether Electra's grief is justified.

choices.label: D
choices.text: They shift the reader's sympathy toward Chrysothemis by showing that Electra cannot defend her own position without asking for help.

cards.standardTitle: Key literary elements add layers of meaning
cards.excerpt: CHR. Well, I will tell thee all I saw:--I came Unto the ancient tomb that holds our sire; And from the topmost mound I marked a stream Of milk fresh-flowing, and his resting place Ringed round with garlands of all flowers that blow. I marvelled at the sight, and peered about, Lest some one might be nearer than we knew. But finding all was quiet in the spot, I ventured closer to the tomb, and there, Hard by the limit, I beheld a curl Of hair new shorn, with all the gloss of youth And straight it struck my heart, as with a sense Of something seen, ah me! long, long ago, And told me that my sight encountered here The token of Orestes, dearest soul Then, clasping it, I did not cry aloud, But straight mine eyes were filled with tears of joy. And now as much as then I feel assured He and none else bestowed this ornament. To whom beyond thyself and me belongs Such consecration? And I know this well, I did it not,--nor thou. Impossible! Thou canst not worship even the blessed Gods Forth of this roof, unpunished. And, most sure, Our mother is not minded so to act, Nor, had she done it, could we fail to know. This offering comes then of Orestes' hand. Take courage, dear one. Not one fate pursues One house perpetually, but changeth still. Ours was a sullen Genius, but perchance This day begins the assurance of much good.
cards.whyThisWorks: The tomb setting—marked by fresh milk, garlands, and a shorn curl of hair—functions as a charged atmosphere of grief, hope, and ancestral reverence that drives the emotional and thematic meaning of the scene.
cards.skillStrategy: When a setting detail appears more than once or triggers a character's emotional reaction, ask yourself what feeling or idea that detail creates and why the author placed it there.
evidencePoints: I came Unto the ancient tomb that holds our sire; And from the topmost mound I marked a stream Of milk fresh-flowing, and his resting place Ringed round with garlands of all flowers that blow.
Ours was a sullen Genius, but perchance This day begins the assurance of much good.
cards.question: In the excerpt, Chrysothemis describes the tomb of their father adorned with fresh milk, garlands, and a shorn curl of hair. How does this setting contribute to the meaning of the passage?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The tomb's remote and quiet location emphasizes that the sisters are completely isolated from any allies, deepening the hopelessness of their situation.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The tomb decorated with fresh offerings transforms a place of death into a site of renewed hope, signaling that the family's long suffering may be approaching a turning point.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The presence of garlands and milk at the tomb suggests their mother has secretly begun to mourn their father, hinting at her hidden guilt.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The ancient tomb setting establishes that the family's grief is so old it has become routine, showing that Chrysothemis feels little emotion when she arrives there.

Thou canst not worship even the blessed Gods Forth of this roof, unpunished. And, most sure, Our mother is not minded so to act, Nor, had she done it, could we fail to know. This offering comes then of Orestes' hand. Take courage, dear one. Not one fate pursues One house perpetually, but changeth still. Ours was a sullen Genius, but perchance This day begins the assurance of much good.
cards.whyThisWorks: Chrysothemis closes her speech with a direct contrast between past suffering and present hope—'Ours was a sullen Genius, but perchance / This day begins the assurance of much good'—giving teachers a clear anchor for discussing how contrast shapes the reader's emotional shift from dread to anticipation.
cards.skillStrategy: When you spot a contrast, ask yourself: what feeling does the first part create, and how does the second part change or challenge that feeling for the reader?
evidencePoints: Ours was a sullen Genius, but perchance / This day begins the assurance of much good.
straight it struck my heart, as with a sense / Of something seen, ah me! long, long ago
cards.question: Read the following lines from Chrysothemis's speech: 'Ours was a sullen Genius, but perchance / This day begins the assurance of much good.' How does the contrast in these lines affect the reader?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The contrast reinforces that the house of Agamemnon has always been cursed and that no relief is possible, deepening the reader's sense of hopelessness.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The contrast shifts the reader from a feeling of prolonged suffering toward cautious hope, suggesting that the discovery at the tomb may mark a turning point for the family.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The contrast highlights Chrysothemis's doubt about whether Orestes truly left the offering, leaving the reader uncertain about the evidence she has described.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The contrast between the sullen past and the present day emphasizes that Chrysothemis blames their mother for all the family's misfortune.

cards.standardTitle: Key literary elements add layers of meaning
cards.excerpt: CHR. True, noble women, and before she spake Sound thought should have prevented the rash talk That now hath proved her reckless. What wild aim Beckons thee forth in arming this design Whereto thou wouldst demand my ministry? Dost not perceive, thou art not man but woman, Of strength inferior to thine enemies,-- Their Genius daily prospering more and more, Whilst ours is dwindling into nothingness? Who then that plots against a life so strong Shall quit him of the danger without harm? Take heed we do not add to our distress Should some one hear of this our colloquy. Small help and poor advantage 'twere for us To win brief praise and then inglorious die. Nay, death is not so hateful as when one Desiring death is balked of that desire. And I beseech thee, ere in utter ruin We perish and make desolate our race, Refrain thy rage. And I will guard for thee In silence these thy words unrealized; If thou wilt learn this wisdom from long time, Having no strength, to bend before the strong.
cards.whyThisWorks: Chrysothemis's warnings about being overheard, the sisters' inferior strength, and the enemies' daily-growing power establish a social and atmospheric setting of danger and powerlessness that directly shapes the scene's meaning.
cards.skillStrategy: When a character describes the world around them—who holds power, what dangers exist, what could happen if they are caught—ask how those conditions shape the mood and meaning of the scene.
evidencePoints: Their Genius daily prospering more and more, Whilst ours is dwindling into nothingness?
Take heed we do not add to our distress Should some one hear of this our colloquy.
cards.question: Chrysothemis warns Electra that 'Their Genius daily prospering more and more, Whilst ours is dwindling into nothingness' and that someone might overhear 'this our colloquy.' How do these two conditions work together to shape the atmosphere of the scene?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The enemies' growing power suggests Electra's plan could succeed if kept secret, creating a mood of guarded hope that Chrysothemis is trying to channel into careful action.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The sisters' shrinking power combined with the danger of being overheard creates an atmosphere of suffocating entrapment, in which even speaking against their oppressors carries the threat of destruction.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The reference to the enemies' prosperity establishes a tone of admiration, while the fear of being overheard adds excitement, together suggesting the sisters are on the edge of a daring and winnable revolt.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The warning about being overheard shifts the atmosphere away from danger toward secrecy and strategy, implying that Chrysothemis believes the plan will work as long as it remains hidden.

cards.standardTitle: Rhetoric and reader effect
cards.excerpt: EL. Dear brother, wheresoe'er thy pleasure leads, My will shall follow, since the joys I know, Not from myself I took them, but from thee. And ne'er would I consent thy slightest grief Should win for me great gain. Ill should I then Serve the divinity of this high hour! Thou knowest how matters in the palace stand. Thou hast surely heard, Aegisthus is from home, And she, our mother, is within. Nor fear She should behold me with a smiling face. Mine ancient hate of her hath sunk too deep. And from the time I saw thee, tears of joy Will cease not. Wherefore should I stint their flow? I, who in this thy coming have beheld Thee dead and living? Strangely hast thou wrought On me;--that should my father come alive, I would not think the sight were miracle, But sober truth. Since such thy presence, then, Lead as thy spirit prompts. For I alone Of two things surely had achieved one, Noble deliverance or a noble death.
cards.whyThisWorks: Electra's rhetorical question 'Wherefore should I stint their flow?' combined with the hyperbolic analogy comparing Orestes' return to a dead father coming back to life creates a measurable emotional effect that students can analyze for how rhetoric shapes reader response.
cards.skillStrategy: When you spot a rhetorical question or analogy, ask yourself: what feeling or idea is the speaker pushing the reader toward, and how does that device create that push?
evidencePoints: Wherefore should I stint their flow? I, who in this thy coming have beheld Thee dead and living?
should my father come alive, I would not think the sight were miracle, But sober truth.
cards.question: Read the following lines from Electra's speech: 'Wherefore should I stint their flow? I, who in this thy coming have beheld Thee dead and living?' How does this rhetorical question affect the reader?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The question signals Electra's uncertainty about whether her tears are appropriate, making the reader doubt her emotional sincerity.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The question challenges any expectation that Electra should restrain her grief, drawing the reader into the overwhelming force of her joy at Orestes' return.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The question shifts the reader's focus away from Electra's emotions and toward the practical danger posed by Aegisthus and their mother inside the palace.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The question reminds the reader that Electra has been weeping for a long time, emphasizing her exhaustion rather than her happiness.

cards.standardTitle: Key literary elements add layers of meaning
cards.excerpt:
CHORUS. An erring seer am I, I 1 Of sense and wisdom lorn, If this prophetic Power of right, O'ertaking the offender, come not nigh Ere many an hour be born. Yon vision of the night, That lately breathed into my listening ear, Hath freed me, O my daughter, from all fear. Sweet was that bodement. He doth not forget, The Achaean lord that gave thee being, nor yet The bronzen-griding axe, edged like a spear, Hungry and keen, though dark with stains of time, That in the hour of hideous crime Quelled him with cruel butchery: That, too, remembers, and shall testify.

From ambush deep and dread I 2 With power of many a hand And many hastening feet shall spring The Fury of the adamantine tread, Visiting Argive land Swift recompense to bring For eager dalliance of a blood-stained pair Unhallowed, foul, forbidden. No omen fair,-- Their impious course hath fixed this in my soul,-- Nought but black portents full of blame shall roll Before their eyes that wrought or aided there. Small force of divination would there seem In prophecy or solemn dream, Should not this vision of the night Reach harbour in reality aright.
cards.whyThisWorks: Sophocles layers dense, archaic diction ('adamantine tread,' 'bronzen-griding axe,' 'black portents') with inverted syntax and personified abstractions to create a voice of prophetic dread, giving students rich material to connect specific language choices to the Chorus's tone of inevitable divine vengeance.
cards.skillStrategy: When analyzing style, ask yourself: what specific word choices or sentence structures create the speaker's tone, and what idea does that tone reinforce?
evidencePoints: The Fury of the adamantine tread, Visiting Argive land Swift recompense to bring
Nought but black portents full of blame shall roll Before their eyes that wrought or aided there
cards.question: Read the following lines from the second paragraph: 'The Fury of the adamantine tread, / Visiting Argive land / Swift recompense to bring.' How does the diction in these lines contribute to the Chorus's voice?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The word 'visiting' softens the Chorus's warning by suggesting the Fury arrives as a peaceful guest rather than a punishing force.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The phrase 'adamantine tread' — evoking an unyielding, stone-hard force — gives the Chorus a voice of absolute certainty that divine punishment cannot be stopped or delayed.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The reference to 'Argive land' shifts the Chorus's focus from vengeance to a celebration of the region's power and history.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The word 'recompense' signals that the Chorus believes the guilty pair will eventually be forgiven once they make amends.

cards.question: Read the rhetorical questions in Chrysothemis's speech, including 'Who then that plots against a life so strong / Shall quit him of the danger without harm?' What effect do these questions have on the reader?

choices.label: A
choices.text: They show that Chrysothemis genuinely does not know the answer and is asking Electra for guidance on how to resist their enemies.

choices.label: B
choices.text: They force the reader to confront the hopelessness of Electra's plan by implying that no one can challenge such power and survive, making Chrysothemis's warning feel inevitable rather than cowardly.

choices.label: C
choices.text: They reveal that Chrysothemis secretly admires Electra's courage and is using questions to encourage her to reconsider only the timing of her plan.

choices.label: D
choices.text: They suggest that Chrysothemis believes the enemies can be defeated if Electra waits, since the questions imply a future moment when their strength will be equal.

cards.standardTitle: Key literary elements add layers of meaning
cards.excerpt: CLY. (_to an attendant_). Then lift for me those fruitful offerings, While to Apollo, before whom we stand, I raise my supplication for release From doubts and fears that shake my bosom now. And, O defender of our house! attend My secret utterance. No friendly ear Is that which hearkens for my voice. My thought Must not be blazoned with her standing by, Lest through her envious and wide-babbling tongue She fill the city full of wild surmise. List, then, as I shall speak: and grant the dreams Whose two-fold apparition I to-night Have seen, if good their bodement, be fulfilled: If hostile, turn their influence on my foes. And yield not them their wish that would by guile Thrust me from this high fortune, but vouchsafe That ever thus exempt from harms I rule The Atridae's home and kingdom, in full life, Partaking with the friends I live with now All fair prosperity, and with my children, Save those who hate and vex me bitterly. Lykeian Phoebus, favourably hear My prayer, and grant to all of us our need! More is there, which, though I be silent here, A God should understand. No secret thing Is hidden from the all-seeing sons of Heaven.
cards.whyThisWorks: Clytemnestra's prayer uses elevated diction, euphemism, and syntactic indirection ('More is there, which, though I be silent here, / A God should understand') to reveal a calculating, self-concealing voice that layers dramatic irony over her apparent piety.
cards.skillStrategy: When analyzing style, ask what the speaker's word choices and sentence structures reveal about their true motives or character beyond what they openly state.
evidencePoints: No friendly ear / Is that which hearkens for my voice.
More is there, which, though I be silent here, / A God should understand.
cards.question: Read the lines: 'More is there, which, though I be silent here, / A God should understand. No secret thing / Is hidden from the all-seeing sons of Heaven.' What does Clytemnestra's choice to leave her full meaning unspoken reveal about her character in this moment?

choices.label: A
choices.text: She is overcome by genuine religious devotion and trusts that Apollo will interpret her grief without further words.

choices.label: B
choices.text: She deliberately withholds her darkest wishes from open speech, exposing a calculating nature that hides its true intentions even within a prayer.

choices.label: C
choices.text: She doubts Apollo's power to hear her and therefore chooses silence rather than risk an unanswered petition.

choices.label: D
choices.text: She fears Electra will overhear the end of the prayer, so she stops speaking before she can reveal anything meaningful.
