cards.question: In her prayer, Clytemnestra repeatedly contrasts 'friends' and prosperity with 'foes' and those who 'hate and vex' her. How does this contrast affect the reader?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The contrast reassures the reader that Clytemnestra is a devoted ruler who genuinely seeks peace for her household and kingdom.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The contrast exposes Clytemnestra's self-interest, making the reader suspicious of a prayer that asks the gods to bless her allies and punish her enemies rather than seek justice.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The contrast emphasizes Clytemnestra's fear of Apollo, suggesting she prays out of religious duty rather than personal desire.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The contrast shows that Clytemnestra is uncertain about who her true enemies are, leaving the reader sympathetic toward her confusion.

cards.standardTitle: Key literary elements add layers of meaning
cards.excerpt: EL. 'Tis strange and pitiful, thy father's child Can leave him in oblivion and subserve The mother. All thy schooling of me springs From her suggestion, not of thine own wit. Sure, either thou art senseless, or thy sense Deserts thy friends. Treason or dulness then? Choose!--You declared but now, if you had strength, You would display your hatred of this pair. Yet, when I plan full vengeance for my sire, You aid me not, but turn me from the attempt. What's this but adding cowardice to evil? For tell me, or be patient till I show, What should I gain by ceasing this my moan? I live to vex them:--though my life be poor, Yet that suffices, for I honour him, My father,--if affection touch the dead. You say you hate them, but belie your word, Consorting with our father's murderers. I then, were all the gifts in which you glory Laid at my feet, will never more obey This tyrant power. I leave you your rich board And life of luxury. Ne'er be it mine to feed On dainties that would poison my heart's peace! I care not for such honour as thou hast. Nor wouldst thou care if thou wert wise. But now, Having the noblest of all men for sire, Be called thy mother's offspring; so shall most Discern thine infamy and traitorous mind To thy dead father and thy dearest kin.
cards.whyThisWorks: Electra's speech is rich with rhetorical questions, sharp commands, and loaded diction ('cowardice,' 'treason,' 'infamy') that together create a voice of fierce moral accusation, giving students clear evidence to connect style choices to characterization and emotional effect.
cards.skillStrategy: When analyzing style, ask yourself: what specific word choices or sentence structures reveal how the speaker feels and what effect they create on the listener?
evidencePoints: What's this but adding cowardice to evil?
Having the noblest of all men for sire, Be called thy mother's offspring; so shall most Discern thine infamy and traitorous mind
cards.question: Read the following lines from Electra's speech: 'Treason or dulness then? Choose!' and 'What's this but adding cowardice to evil?' What effect do these rhetorical questions and sharp commands create in Electra's voice?

choices.label: A
choices.text: They reveal Electra's uncertainty about whether her sister is truly guilty, suggesting she is open to hearing Chrysothemis defend herself.

choices.label: B
choices.text: They force Chrysothemis into a moral corner, making Electra sound like a relentless judge who refuses to accept compromise or excuse.

choices.label: C
choices.text: They show Electra admitting that her own plan for vengeance may be flawed, and she is asking her sister to help her correct it.

choices.label: D
choices.text: They demonstrate that Electra respects her sister's intelligence and is appealing to Chrysothemis as an equal in deciding their next action.

cards.standardTitle: Rhetoric and reader effect
cards.excerpt:
EL. Now, dear Chrysothemis, of what thou bearest Let nothing touch his tomb. 'Tis impious And criminal to offer to thy sire Rites and libations from a hateful wife. Then cast them to the winds, or deep in dust Conceal them, where no particle may reach His resting-place: but lie in store for her When she goes underground. Sure, were she not Most hardened of all women that have been, She ne'er had sent those loveless offerings To grace the sepulchre of him she slew. For think how likely is the buried king To take such present kindly from her hand, Who slew him like an alien enemy, Dishonoured even in death, and mangled him, And wiped the death-stain with his flowing locks-- Sinful purgation! Think you that you bear In those cold gifts atonement for her guilt? It is not possible. Wherefore let be. But take a ringlet from thy comely head, And this from mine, that lingers on my brow Longing to shade his tomb. Ah, give it to him, All I can give, and this my maiden-zone, Not daintily adorned, as once erewhile. Then, humbly kneeling, pray that from the ground He would arise to help us 'gainst his foes, And grant his son Orestes with high hand Strongly to trample on his enemies; That in our time to come from ampler stores We may endow him, than are ours to-day. I cannot but imagine that his will Hath part in visiting her sleep with fears. But howsoe'er, I pray thee, sister mine, Do me this service, and thyself, and him, Dearest of all the world to me and thee, The father of us both, who rests below.

CH. She counsels piously; and thou, dear maid, If thou art wise, wilt do her bidding here.
cards.whyThisWorks: Electra's repeated use of the rhetorical question—'For think how likely is the buried king / To take such present kindly from her hand' and 'Think you that you bear / In those cold gifts atonement for her guilt?'—gives teachers a clear, textually grounded opportunity to ask students how this device shapes the reader's judgment of Clytemnestra's hypocrisy.
cards.skillStrategy: When you spot a rhetorical question, ask yourself: what answer does the speaker assume, and how does forcing that assumption on the reader change how we feel about the subject?
evidencePoints: For think how likely is the buried king / To take such present kindly from her hand, / Who slew him like an alien enemy
Think you that you bear / In those cold gifts atonement for her guilt? / It is not possible.
cards.question:
Read the following lines from Electra's speech:

'For think how likely is the buried king / To take such present kindly from her hand, / Who slew him like an alien enemy' and 'Think you that you bear / In those cold gifts atonement for her guilt? / It is not possible.'

How do these rhetorical questions affect the reader?

choices.label: A
choices.text: They reveal Electra's uncertainty about whether the burial offerings will reach her father, making the reader sympathize with her confusion about funeral customs.

choices.label: B
choices.text: They force the reader to arrive at Electra's conclusion—that Clytemnestra's offerings are a hollow, even offensive gesture—by making the answer seem self-evident before Electra states it outright.

choices.label: C
choices.text: They shift the reader's focus away from Clytemnestra's guilt and toward Chrysothemis, pressuring her to refuse the errand on moral grounds.

choices.label: D
choices.text: They create suspense about whether the dead king can truly communicate with the living, leaving the reader uncertain about the power of the burial rites.

cards.standardTitle: Key literary elements add layers of meaning
cards.excerpt: CHR. Well, I will tell thee all I saw:--I came Unto the ancient tomb that holds our sire; And from the topmost mound I marked a stream Of milk fresh-flowing, and his resting place Ringed round with garlands of all flowers that blow. I marvelled at the sight, and peered about, Lest some one might be nearer than we knew. But finding all was quiet in the spot, I ventured closer to the tomb, and there, Hard by the limit, I beheld a curl Of hair new shorn, with all the gloss of youth And straight it struck my heart, as with a sense Of something seen, ah me! long, long ago, And told me that my sight encountered here The token of Orestes, dearest soul Then, clasping it, I did not cry aloud, But straight mine eyes were filled with tears of joy. And now as much as then I feel assured He and none else bestowed this ornament. To whom beyond thyself and me belongs Such consecration? And I know this well, I did it not,--nor thou. Impossible! Thou canst not worship even the blessed Gods Forth of this roof, unpunished. And, most sure, Our mother is not minded so to act, Nor, had she done it, could we fail to know. This offering comes then of Orestes' hand. Take courage, dear one. Not one fate pursues One house perpetually, but changeth still. Ours was a sullen Genius, but perchance This day begins the assurance of much good.
cards.whyThisWorks: Chrysothemis's shift from careful, observational diction ('I marvelled,' 'I ventured closer,' 'I beheld') to emotionally charged figurative language ('straight it struck my heart, as with a sense / Of something seen, ah me! long, long ago') demonstrates how Sophocles uses syntax and figurative language to move the speech from report to revelation, layering grief, recognition, and hope.
cards.skillStrategy: Notice how the writer's word choices and sentence rhythms shift at a key moment — that shift often signals a change in emotion or meaning that reveals the speaker's deeper state.
evidencePoints: straight it struck my heart, as with a sense / Of something seen, ah me! long, long ago
Ours was a sullen Genius, but perchance / This day begins the assurance of much good.
cards.question: Read the following lines from Chrysothemis's speech: 'And straight it struck my heart, as with a sense / Of something seen, ah me! long, long ago.' What effect does this figurative language create at this moment in the speech?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The phrase signals that Chrysothemis doubts the curl of hair belongs to Orestes, since the memory feels too distant to trust.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The phrase transforms a physical discovery into an emotional awakening, conveying that the sight of the hair instantly floods Chrysothemis with buried grief and longing for her lost brother.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The phrase emphasizes Chrysothemis's fear that someone was watching her at the tomb, which is why she peered around before approaching.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The phrase shows that Chrysothemis recognizes the curl of hair only because she has seen Orestes recently and remembers his appearance clearly.

cards.standardTitle: Key literary elements add layers of meaning
cards.excerpt:
Praskovya Fyodorovna’s external attitude to her husband’s illness, openly expressed to others and to himself, was that Ivan llyitch was to blame in the matter of his illness, and that the whole illness was another injury he was doing to his wife Ivan Ilyitch felt that the expression of this dropped from her unconsciously, but that made it no easier for him.

In his official life, too, Ivan Ilyitch noticed, or fancied he noticed, a strange attitude to him At one time it seemed to him that people were looking inquisitively at him, as a man who would shortly have to vacate his position, at another time his friends would suddenly begin chaffing him m a friendly way over his nervous fears, as though that awful and horrible, unheard-of thing that was going on within him, incessantly gnawing at him, and irresistibly dragging him away somewhere, were the most agreeable subject for joking. Shvarts especially, with his jocoseness, his liveliness, and his camme-il-faut tone, exasperated Ivan Ilyitch by reminding him of himself ten years ago.
cards.whyThisWorks: The excerpt uses Praskovya's unconscious blame and Shvarts's joking liveliness as contrasting characterization techniques that reveal Ivan Ilyitch's profound isolation and the gap between his inner suffering and others' indifference.
cards.skillStrategy: When a character reacts to another character's behavior, ask what that reaction reveals about the character's inner state and the meaning of their situation.

Shvarts especially, with his jocoseness, his liveliness, and his comme-il-faut tone, exasperated Ivan Ilyitch by reminding him of himself ten years ago
cards.question: How does Tolstoy's description of Shvarts's 'jocoseness, his liveliness, and his comme-il-faut tone' contribute to the meaning of Ivan Ilyitch's situation?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Shvarts's cheerfulness signals that Ivan Ilyitch's colleagues genuinely believe his illness is minor and will soon pass, which gives Ivan Ilyitch a brief sense of hope.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Shvarts's carefree manner mirrors the person Ivan Ilyitch once was, deepening Ivan Ilyitch's anguish by showing how completely his dying self has been cut off from the world of the living.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Shvarts's behavior reveals that he is deliberately cruel toward Ivan Ilyitch and wants to hasten Ivan Ilyitch's removal from his official position.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Shvarts's liveliness embarrasses Ivan Ilyitch because Ivan Ilyitch recognizes that his own nervous fears have made him behave inappropriately at work.

cards.excerpt: Ivan Ilyitch went out slowly and dejectedly, got into his sledge, and drove home. All the way home he was incessantly going over all the doctor had said, trying to translate all these complicated, obscure, scientific phrases into simple language, and to read in them an answer to the question. It ’s bad — is it very bad, or nothing much as yet ? And it seemed to him that the upshot of all the doctor had said was that it was very bad. Everything seemed dismal to Ivan Ilyitch in the streets The sledge-drivers were dismal, the houses were dismal, the people passing, and the shops were dismal. This ache, this dull gnawing ache, that never ceased for a second, seemed, when connected with the doctor’s obscure utterances, to have gained a new, more serious significance. With a new sense of misery Ivan Ilyitch kept watch on it now.

cards.excerpt: The young lady, Praskovya Fyodorovna, was of good family, nice>looking. There was a little bit of property. To say that Ivan Ilyitch got married because he fell in love with his wife and found in her sympathy wdth his views of life, would be as untrue as to say that he got married because the people of his world approved of the match. cards.standardTitle: Key literary elements add layers of meaning
cards.excerpt:
With the birth of the baby, the attempts at nursing it, and the various unsuccessful experiments with foods, with the illnesses, real and imaginary, of the infant and its mother, in which Ivan Ilyitch was expected to sympathise, though he never had the slightest idea about them, the need for him to fence off a world apart for himself outside his family life became still more imperative. h.s his wife grew more irritable and exacting, so did Ivan Ilyitch more and more transfer the centre of gravity of his life to his official work. He became fonder and fonder of official life, and more ambitious than he had been.

Very quickly, not more than a year after his wedding, Ivan Ilyitch had become aware that conjugal life, though providing certain comforts, was in reality a very intricate and difficult business towards which one must, if one is to do one's duty, that is, lead the decorous life approved by society, work out for oneself a definite line, just as in the government service.

And such a line Ivan Ilyitch did work out for himself in his married life. He expected from his home life only those comforts — of dinner at home, of housekeeper and bed which it could give him, and, above all, that perfect propriety in external observances required by public opinion. For the rest, he looked for good-humoured pleasantness, and if he found it he was very thankful. If he met with antagonism and querulousness, he promptly retreated into the separate world he had shut off for himself in his official life, and there he found solace.
cards.whyThisWorks: Tolstoy reveals Ivan Ilyich's emotional detachment and self-protective ambition through his deliberate retreat into official work whenever domestic life becomes demanding, showing how a character's repeated action exposes his core values and inner emptiness.
cards.skillStrategy: When a character repeatedly chooses the same action in response to conflict, ask what that pattern reveals about what the character truly values or fears.

And in his relations with Gerasim there was something approaching to that And that was why being with Gerasim was a comfort to him. cards.standardTitle: Key literary elements add layers of meaning
cards.excerpt: Ivan Ilyitch went out slowly and dejectedly, got into his sledge, and drove home. All the way home he was incessantly going over all the doctor had said, trying to translate all these complicated, obscure, scientific phrases into simple language, and to read in them an answer to the question. It ’s bad — is it very bad, or nothing much as yet ? And it seemed to him that the upshot of all the doctor had said was that it was very bad. Everything seemed dismal to Ivan Ilyitch in the streets The sledge-drivers were dismal, the houses were dismal, the people passing, and the shops were dismal. This ache, this dull gnawing ache, that never ceased for a second, seemed, when connected with the doctor’s obscure utterances, to have gained a new, more serious significance. With a new sense of misery Ivan Ilyitch kept watch on it now.
cards.whyThisWorks: The close third-person narration filters the entire world through Ivan Ilyitch's dread, making external details like sledge-drivers and shops feel dismal—demonstrating how point of view shapes mood and reader understanding.

cards.standardTitle: Theme development across a literary text
cards.excerpt:
With the birth of the baby, the attempts at nursing it, and the various unsuccessful experiments with foods, with the illnesses, real and imaginary, of the infant and its mother, in which Ivan Ilyitch was expected to sympathise, though he never had the slightest idea about them, the need for him to fence off a world apart for himself outside his family life became still more imperative. h.s his wife grew more irritable and exacting, so did Ivan Ilyitch more and more transfer the centre of gravity of his life to his official work. He became fonder and fonder of official life, and more ambitious than he had been.

Very quickly, not more than a year after his wedding, Ivan Ilyitch had become aware that conjugal life, though providing certain comforts, was in reality a very intricate and difficult business towards which one must, if one is to do one's duty, that is, lead the decorous life approved by society, work out for oneself a definite line, just as in the government service.

And such a line Ivan Ilyitch did work out for himself in his married life. He expected from his home life only those comforts — of dinner at home, of housekeeper and bed which it could give him, and, above all, that perfect propriety in external observances required by public opinion. For the rest, he looked for good-humoured pleasantness, and if he found it he was very thankful. If he met with antagonism and querulousness, he promptly retreated into the separate world he had shut off for himself in his official life, and there he found solace.
cards.whyThisWorks: The excerpt shows Ivan Ilyich deliberately constructing a separate inner world of official work to escape marital friction, which illustrates the transferable theme that people retreat into public roles and social performance when intimate relationships feel threatening.

cards.question: The narrator explains that Ivan Ilyitch married neither purely for love nor purely for social approval, but for both reasons at once. What universal theme about human behavior does this moment most clearly develop?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Marrying someone from a good family is the surest path to personal happiness, because shared social standing creates lasting harmony between partners.

choices.label: B
choices.text: People frequently make significant life choices by blending self-interest with the desire to conform to what their society considers acceptable, rather than acting on deeply held personal values.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Love is ultimately impossible between people of different social classes, because practical concerns will always override genuine emotional connection.

choices.label: D
choices.text: When individuals ignore the expectations of those around them, they risk making choices they will later regret, as Ivan's indifference to his wife's feelings shows.

cards.standardTitle: Narrator perspective, irony, and satire
cards.excerpt:
Praskovya Fyodorovna’s external attitude to her husband’s illness, openly expressed to others and to himself, was that Ivan llyitch was to blame in the matter of his illness, and that the whole illness was another injury he was doing to his wife Ivan Ilyitch felt that the expression of this dropped from her unconsciously, but that made it no easier for him.

In his official life, too, Ivan Ilyitch noticed, or fancied he noticed, a strange attitude to him At one time it seemed to him that people were looking inquisitively at him, as a man who would shortly have to vacate his position, at another time his friends would suddenly begin chaffing him m a friendly way over his nervous fears, as though that awful and horrible, unheard-of thing that was going on within him, incessantly gnawing at him, and irresistibly dragging him away somewhere, were the most agreeable subject for joking. Shvarts especially, with his jocoseness, his liveliness, and his camme-il-faut tone, exasperated Ivan Ilyitch by reminding him of himself ten years ago.
cards.whyThisWorks: The excerpt shows Ivan Ilyitch experiencing others' casual or self-serving responses to his dying—his wife treating his illness as a personal offense, his colleagues joking about it—while the reader understands the profound isolation and cruelty of these reactions, creating a clear gap between the characters' surface behavior and the reader's moral understanding.
cards.skillStrategy: Ask yourself: what does the narrator report characters doing or saying, and what does the reader recognize that those characters fail to see?
evidencePoints: Praskovya Fyodorovna's external attitude to her husband's illness…was that Ivan Ilyitch was to blame in the matter of his illness, and that the whole illness was another injury he was doing to his wife

his friends would suddenly begin chaffing him in a friendly way over his nervous fears, as though that awful and horrible, unheard-of thing that was going on within him…were the most agreeable subject for joking
cards.question: The narrator describes Ivan Ilyitch's wife believing 'the whole illness was another injury he was doing to his wife,' and his colleagues treating his suffering as 'the most agreeable subject for joking.' What gap does the reader recognize that the people around Ivan Ilyitch do not?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Ivan Ilyitch is exaggerating his suffering to gain sympathy from his wife and coworkers, so their dismissive responses are actually reasonable.

choices.label: B
choices.text: While those around Ivan Ilyitch reframe his dying as an inconvenience or a joke, the reader understands he is facing a genuine, consuming terror that his companions are unwilling or unable to acknowledge.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Ivan Ilyitch secretly agrees with his wife that he is responsible for his illness, which is why he does not correct her attitude or challenge his colleagues' jokes.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The people around Ivan Ilyitch are aware of how serious his illness is but pretend otherwise because they are afraid of confronting their own mortality.

cards.standardTitle: Key literary elements add layers of meaning
cards.excerpt: The young lady, Praskovya Fyodorovna, was of good family, nice>looking. There was a little bit of property. Ivan Ilyitch might have reckoned on a more brilliant match, but this was a good match. Ivan Ilyitch had his salary ; she, he hoped, would have as much of her own. It was a good family ; she was a sweet, pretty, and perfectly comme U faut young woman. To say that Ivan Ilyitch got married because he fell in love with his wife and found in her sympathy wdth his views of life, would be as untrue as to say that he got married because the people of his world approved of the match. Ivan Ilyitch was influenced by both considerations, he was doing what was agreeable to himself in securing such a wife, and at the same time doing what persons of higher standing looked upon as the correct thing.
cards.whyThisWorks: The third-person omniscient narrator directly contradicts romantic explanations for Ivan's marriage and instead exposes his calculating motivations, showing how the narrator's detached, ironic perspective shapes the reader's understanding of Ivan's character and creates a tone of quiet condemnation.
cards.skillStrategy: Ask yourself: who is telling this moment, and what does that narrator reveal or withhold that a character telling his own story would hide?
evidencePoints: To say that Ivan Ilyitch got married because he fell in love with his wife and found in her sympathy with his views of life, would be as untrue as to say that he got married because the people of his world approved of the match.

Ivan Ilyitch was influenced by both considerations, he was doing what was agreeable to himself in securing such a wife, and at the same time doing what persons of higher standing looked upon as the correct thing.
cards.question: The narrator states that it would be 'as untrue' to say Ivan married for love as to say he married purely for social approval. How does this narrative choice shape the reader's understanding of Ivan?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The narrator's balanced phrasing suggests Ivan was a thoughtful man who carefully weighed his emotions against the expectations of his social circle before committing to marriage.

choices.label: B
choices.text: By dismissing both the romantic and the purely social explanations before offering a third, the narrator exposes Ivan's self-interest as the true motive, creating a tone of ironic detachment that undermines any sympathy the reader might feel for him.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Because the narrator presents both love and social approval as false reasons, the reader is left uncertain about why Ivan married at all, which creates a mood of mystery surrounding his character.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The narrator's refusal to confirm that Ivan married for love reveals that Praskovya Fyodorovna was the one who pursued the match, shifting the reader's judgment away from Ivan.

cards.standardTitle: Theme development across a literary text
cards.excerpt: Apart from this deception, or in consequence of it, what made the ^eatest misery for Ivan Ilyitch was that no one felt for him as he would have liked them to feel for him. At ceiliam moments, after prolonged suffering, Ivan Ilyitch, ashamed as he would have been to own it, longed more than anything for some one to feel sorry for him, as for a sick child. He longed to be petted, kissed, and wept over, as children are petted and comforted. He knew that he was an important member of the law-courts, that he had a beard turning grey, and that therefore it was impossible But still he longed for it. And in his relations with Gerasim there was something approaching to that And that was why being with Gerasim was a comfort to him. Ivan Ilyitch longs to weep, longs to be petted and wept over, and then there comes in a colleague, Sliebek ; and instead of weeping and being petted, Ivan Ilyitch puts on his serious, seveie, earnest face, and from mere inertia gives his views on the effect of the last decision in the Court of Appeal, and obstinately insists upon them. This falsity around him and within him did more than anything to poison Ivan Ilyitch’s last days.
cards.whyThisWorks: The excerpt shows Ivan Ilyitch suppressing his genuine need for compassion behind a mask of professional seriousness, illustrating the universal theme that social roles and pride can isolate people from the human connection they most desperately need.

cards.question: The narrator describes Ivan Ilyitch longing to be comforted 'as for a sick child' yet performing a 'serious, severe, earnest face' for his colleague Shebek. What universal theme about human experience does this contrast develop?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Professional success in law and society ultimately brings a person lasting satisfaction and a sense of purpose, even in times of personal suffering.

choices.label: B
choices.text: People often deny themselves the emotional connection they crave most because they feel pressured to maintain the identity that society expects of them.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Childhood experiences of being comforted shape a person's ability to form meaningful relationships with others later in life.

choices.label: D
choices.text: When people face death, they come to resent colleagues and acquaintances who are unable to understand the seriousness of their condition.

cards.standardTitle: Narrator perspective, irony, and satire
cards.excerpt: Ivan Ilyitch went out slowly and dejectedly, got into his sledge, and drove home. All the way home he was incessantly going over all the doctor had said, trying to translate all these complicated, obscure, scientific phrases into simple language, and to read in them an answer to the question. It ’s bad — is it very bad, or nothing much as yet ? And it seemed to him that the upshot of all the doctor had said was that it was very bad. Everything seemed dismal to Ivan Ilyitch in the streets The sledge-drivers were dismal, the houses were dismal, the people passing, and the shops were dismal. This ache, this dull gnawing ache, that never ceased for a second, seemed, when connected with the doctor’s obscure utterances, to have gained a new, more serious significance. With a new sense of misery Ivan Ilyitch kept watch on it now.
cards.whyThisWorks: Ivan's frantic effort to 'translate' the doctor's words into a hopeful answer contrasts sharply with the reader's recognition that his dread is already the answer, creating a clear gap between the narrator's reported self-deception and the reader's understanding of his terminal situation.
cards.skillStrategy: Ask yourself: what does the narrator or character believe is still uncertain, and what does the reader already know for certain based on the details provided?
evidencePoints: trying to translate all these complicated, obscure, scientific phrases into simple language, and to read in them an answer to the question
it seemed to him that the upshot of all the doctor had said was that it was very bad
cards.question: Ivan Ilyitch spends the ride home 'trying to translate all these complicated, obscure, scientific phrases into simple language, and to read in them an answer to the question.' What does the reader understand that Ivan Ilyitch does not yet fully accept?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Ivan is confused because the doctor deliberately withheld all information, so no conclusion about his condition can be drawn from the visit.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The answer Ivan is searching for has already revealed itself through his physical pain and his own dread, making his effort to find certainty in the doctor's words a way of avoiding what he already knows.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Ivan's gloomy perception of the streets and shops shows that his illness has caused a physical change in his eyesight rather than a shift in his emotional state.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Ivan understands his condition completely but is translating the doctor's words so he can explain his diagnosis accurately to his family when he arrives home.

cards.standardTitle: Key literary elements add layers of meaning
cards.excerpt:
They all see that he’s in pain, and say to him, ‘We can stop if you ’re tired. You go and lie down.’ Lie down ? No, he ’s not in the least tired , they will play the rubber. All are gloomy and silent. Ivan Ilyitch feels that it is he who has brought this gloom upon them, and he cannot disperse it. They have supper, and the party breaks up, and Ivan Ilyitch is left alone with the consciousness that his life is poisoned for him and poisons the life of others, and that this poison is not losing its force, but is continually penetrating more and more deeply into his whole existence.

And with the consciousness of this, and with the physical pain in addition, and the terror in addition to that, he must he in his bed, often not able to sleep for pain the greater part of the night , and in the morning he must get up again, dress, go to the law-court, speak, write, or, if he does not go out, stay at home for all the four-and-twenty hours of the day and night, of which each one is a torture. And he had to live thus on the edge of the precipice alone, without one man who would understand and feel for him.
cards.whyThisWorks: The social setting of the card party and the domestic routine of bed and law-court together show how Ivan Ilyich's illness transforms familiar, ordinary spaces into sites of isolation and torment, making setting central to the passage's meaning.
cards.skillStrategy: When a passage names a specific place or social situation, ask what feeling or idea that setting creates and how it changes the character's experience.
evidencePoints: Ivan Ilyitch feels that it is he who has brought this gloom upon them, and he cannot disperse it
he had to live thus on the edge of the precipice alone, without one man who would understand and feel for him
cards.question: In the first paragraph, Ivan Ilyich observes that 'it is he who has brought this gloom upon them, and he cannot disperse it.' What does the setting of the card party among silent companions reveal about Ivan Ilyich's situation?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The card party exposes Ivan Ilyich's friends as indifferent people who attend social gatherings only out of obligation, not genuine affection.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The social gathering, a space once meant for companionship, has become a place where Ivan Ilyich's illness cuts him off from others even while he sits among them, showing that his suffering cannot be shared.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The card party setting suggests that Ivan Ilyich's refusal to lie down is an act of pride that prevents his friends from offering him real comfort.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The gloomy atmosphere at the card party reflects the friends' fear that Ivan Ilyich's illness is contagious, causing them to keep their distance.

cards.question: After Ivan leaves the doctor's office, the narrator states that 'the sledge-drivers were dismal, the houses were dismal, the people passing, and the shops were dismal.' What universal theme does this repeated observation develop?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Urban environments are indifferent to the suffering of any single person who moves through them.

choices.label: B
choices.text: When a person confronts the possibility of serious illness or death, that fear transforms the way ordinary life appears to them.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Doctors who speak in complicated language cause more harm to patients than the illnesses they treat.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Physical pain becomes unbearable only when a person is forced to travel alone without comfort or companionship.

cards.standardTitle: Narrator perspective, irony, and satire
cards.excerpt: In reality, it was all just what is commonly seen in the houses of people who aie not exactly wealthy but want to look like wealthy people, and so succeed only in being like one another — hangings, dark wood, flowers, rugs and bronzes, everything dark and highly polished, everything that all people of a certain class have so as to be like all people of a certain class. And in his case it was all so like that it made no impression at ajl ; but it all seemed to him somehow special. When he met his family at the railway station and brought them to his newly furnished rooms, all lighted up in readiness, and a footman in a white tie opened the door into an entry decorated with flowers, and then they walked into the drawing-room and the study, uttering cries of delight, he was very happy, conducted them everywhere, eagerly drinking in their praises, and beaming with satisfaction. The same evening, while they talked about various things at tea, Praskovya Fyodorovna inquired about his fall, and he laughed and showed them how he had gone flying, and how he had frightened the upholsterer.
cards.whyThisWorks: The narrator explicitly tells the reader that Ivan's apartment is generic and unremarkable while Ivan himself believes it is 'somehow special,' creating a clear ironic gap between Ivan's self-satisfied pride and the reader's understanding that he has achieved nothing distinctive.
cards.skillStrategy: When a narrator describes a character's feelings about something, ask whether the narrator's own words contradict or undercut what the character believes — that gap is where irony lives.

he was very happy, conducted them everywhere, eagerly drinking in their praises, and beaming with satisfaction
cards.question: The narrator states that Ivan's apartment 'made no impression at all' yet Ivan considers it 'somehow special' and is 'beaming with satisfaction' as his family praises it. What does this gap between Ivan's view and the narrator's description reveal to the reader?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Ivan's family genuinely admires the apartment, which proves the narrator's harsh judgment of it is unfair and overstated.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Ivan's pride in his home is self-deception — he has achieved only bland conformity, yet he mistakes the approval of others for evidence that he is truly distinguished.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Ivan is aware that his apartment is ordinary but performs enthusiasm to spare his family's feelings after a difficult journey.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The narrator admires Ivan's ability to create a welcoming home and uses the family's cries of delight to confirm that the apartment is a genuine success.

cards.question: How does the description of Ivan's newly furnished rooms contribute to the meaning of the passage?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The elegant décor of the rooms signals that Ivan has genuinely achieved a higher social rank than his peers, earning the admiration his family expresses.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The rooms' generic, imitative atmosphere creates an ironic contrast with Ivan's pride, suggesting that his sense of distinction is an illusion shaped by social conformity.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The darkness and polish of the furnishings foreshadow a coming tragedy by establishing a gloomy, threatening mood that Ivan's family senses but ignores.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The lighted rooms and decorated entry reflect Ivan's genuine warmth as a host, showing that his domestic life is a source of authentic happiness.

choices.label: A
choices.text: Wealth and fine possessions bring lasting happiness to those who work hard to acquire them.

choices.label: B
choices.text: People often blind themselves to their own conformity because they need to believe their choices reflect a unique and meaningful identity.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Family approval is the most reliable measure of whether a person has made good decisions in life.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The desire to impress others eventually forces people to abandon the social class into which they were born.

cards.question: Read the following sentence from the second paragraph: 'as though that awful and horrible, unheard-of thing that was going on within him, incessantly gnawing at him, and irresistibly dragging him away somewhere, were the most agreeable subject for joking.' He became fonder and fonder of official life, and more ambitious than he had been.

Very quickly, not more than a year after his wedding, Ivan Ilyitch had become aware that conjugal life, though providing certain comforts, was in reality a very intricate and difficult business towards which one must, if one is to do one's duty, that is, lead the decorous life approved by society, work out for oneself a definite line, just as in the government service.

And such a line Ivan Ilyitch did work out for himself in his married life. He expected from his home life only those comforts — of dinner at home, of housekeeper and bed which it could give him, and, above all, that perfect propriety in external observances required by public opinion. For the rest, he looked for good-humoured pleasantness, and if he found it he was very thankful. cards.standardTitle: Key literary elements add layers of meaning
cards.excerpt: That Enkidu originally played the part of the slayer is also shown by the statement that it is he who insults Ishtar by throwing a piece of the carcass into the goddess' face, adding also an insulting speech; and this despite the fact that Ishtar in her rage accuses Gilgamesh of killing the bull. It is thus evident that the Epic alters the original character of the episodes in order to find a place for Gilgamesh, with the further desire to assign to the latter the _chief_ rôle. Be it noted also that Enkidu, not Gilgamesh, is punished for the insult to Ishtar. Enkidu must therefore in the original form of the episode have been the guilty party, who is stricken with mortal disease as a punishment to which after twelve days he succumbs. In view of this, we may supply the name of Enkidu in the little song introduced at the close of the encounter with the bull, and not Gilgamesh as has hitherto been done.

cards.standardTitle: Theme development across a literary text
cards.excerpt:
He prays to Sin and Ishtar to protect and save him. When, therefore, in another passage some one celebrates Gilgamesh as the one who overcame the "guardian," who dispatched Hu(m)baba in the cedar forest, who killed lions and overthrew the bull, we have the completion of the process which transferred to Gilgamesh exploits and powers which originally belonged to Enkidu, though ordinarily the process stops short at making Gilgamesh a _sharer_ in the exploits; with the natural tendency, to be sure, to enlarge the share of the favorite.

We can now understand why the two heroes are described in the Pennsylvania tablet as alike, as born in the same place, aye, as brothers. Gilgamesh in the Epic is merely a reflex of Enkidu. The latter is the real hero and presumably, therefore, the older figure. Gilgamesh resembles Enkidu, because he _is_ originally Enkidu. The "resemblance" _motif_ is merely the manner in which in the course of the partly popular, partly literary transfer, the recollection is preserved that Enkidu is the original, and Gilgamesh the copy.

On the basis of our investigations, we are now in a position to reconstruct in part the cycle of episodes that once formed part of an Enkidu Epic. The fight between Enkidu and Gilgamesh, in which the former is the victor, is typical of the kind of tales told of Enkidu. He is the real prototype of the Greek Hercules. cards.standardTitle: Key literary elements add layers of meaning
cards.excerpt: Next to the new light thrown upon the names and original character of the two main figures of the Epic, one of the chief points of interest in the Pennsylvania fragment is the proof that it furnishes for a striking resemblance of the two heroes, Gish and Enkidu, to one another. In interpreting the dream of Gish, his mother. Ninsun, lays stress upon the fact that the dream portends the coming of someone who is like Gish, "born in the field and reared in the mountain" (lines 18-19). Both, therefore, are shown by this description to have come to Babylonia from a mountainous region, i.e., they are foreigners; and in the case of Enkidu we have seen that the mountain in all probability refers to a region in the West, while the same may also be the case with Gish. The resemblance of the two heroes to one another extends to their personal appearance. When Enkidu appears on the streets of Erech, the people are struck by this resemblance. They remark that he is "like Gish," though "shorter in stature" (lines 179-180). Enkidu is described as a rival or counterpart.

cards.standardTitle: Epic poetry: characters, structures, and themes
cards.excerpt: The description of Enkidu in the Pennsylvania tablet as a parallel figure to Gilgamesh leads us to a consideration of the relationship of the two figures to one another. Many years ago it was pointed out that the Gilgamesh Epic was a composite tale in which various stories of an independent origin had been combined and brought into more or less artificial connection with the _heros eponymos_ of southern Babylonia. We may now go a step further and point out that not only is Enkidu originally an entirely independent figure, having no connection with Gish or Gilgamesh, but that the latter is really depicted in the Epic as the counterpart of Enkidu, a reflection who has been given the traits of extraordinary physical power that belong to Enkidu. This is shown in the first place by the fact that in the encounter it is Enkidu who triumphs over Gilgamesh. The entire analysis of the episode of the meeting between the two heroes as given by Gressmann must be revised. It is not Enkidu who is terrified and who is warned against the encounter. It is Gilgamesh who, during the night on his way from the house in which the goddess Ishhara lies, encounters Enkidu on the highway. Enkidu "blocks the path" of Gilgamesh. He prevents Gilgamesh from re-entering the house, and the two attack each other "like oxen." They grapple with each other, and Enkidu forces Gilgamesh to the ground. Enkidu is, therefore, the real hero whose traits of physical prowess are afterwards transferred to Gilgamesh.
cards.whyThisWorks: The excerpt explicitly names the goddess Ishhara and places Gilgamesh in relation to her house at the moment of the fateful encounter, making divine presence a direct trigger for the conflict between the two heroes.

cards.standardTitle: Epic poetry: characters, structures, and themes
cards.excerpt: Now with the tendency to attach to popular tales and nature myths lessons illustrative of current beliefs and aspirations, Gilgamesh's search for renewal of life is viewed as man's longing for eternal life. The sun-god's waning power after midsummer is past suggests man's growing weakness after the meridian of life has been left behind. Winter is death, and man longs to escape it. Gilgamesh's wanderings are used as illustration of this longing, and accordingly the search for life becomes also the quest for immortality. Can the precious boon of eternal life be achieved? Popular fancy created the figure of a favorite of the gods who had escaped a destructive deluge in which all mankind had perished. Gilgamesh hears of this favorite and determines to seek him out and learn from him the secret of eternal life. The deluge story, again a pure nature myth, symbolical of the rainy season which destroys all life in nature, is thus attached to the Epic. Gilgamesh after many adventures finds himself in the presence of the survivor of the Deluge who, although human, enjoys immortal life among the gods. He asks the survivor how he came to escape the common fate of mankind, and in reply Utnapishtim tells the story of the catastrophe that brought about universal destruction. The moral of the tale is obvious. Only those singled out by the special favor of the gods can hope to be removed to the distant "source of the streams" and live forever. The rest of mankind must face death as the end of life.
cards.whyThisWorks: The excerpt explicitly states that only those granted 'special favor of the gods' can achieve immortality, making divine intervention the direct force that shapes both Gilgamesh's quest and the epic's central theme about mortality.

cards.standardTitle: Epic poetry: characters, structures, and themes
cards.excerpt: That Enkidu originally played the part of the slayer is also shown by the statement that it is he who insults Ishtar by throwing a piece of the carcass into the goddess' face, adding also an insulting speech; and this despite the fact that Ishtar in her rage accuses Gilgamesh of killing the bull. It is thus evident that the Epic alters the original character of the episodes in order to find a place for Gilgamesh, with the further desire to assign to the latter the _chief_ rôle. Be it noted also that Enkidu, not Gilgamesh, is punished for the insult to Ishtar. Enkidu must therefore in the original form of the episode have been the guilty party, who is stricken with mortal disease as a punishment to which after twelve days he succumbs. In view of this, we may supply the name of Enkidu in the little song introduced at the close of the encounter with the bull, and not Gilgamesh as has hitherto been done.

cards.excerpt: But after all, the parallels are of too general a character to be of much moment; and moreover the parallels stop short at the critical point, for Gilgamesh though worsted is _not_ killed by Enkidu, whereas one of the "Heavenly Twins" is always killed by the brother, as Abel is by Cain, and Iphikles by his twin brother Herakles. cards.excerpt: Gilgamesh now begins a series of wanderings in search of the restoration of his vigor, and this _motif_ is evidently a continuation of the nature myth to symbolize the sun's wanderings during the dark winter in the hope of renewed vigor with the coming of the spring. cards.standardTitle: Key literary elements add layers of meaning
cards.excerpt: The description of Enkidu in the Pennsylvania tablet as a parallel figure to Gilgamesh leads us to a consideration of the relationship of the two figures to one another. Many years ago it was pointed out that the Gilgamesh Epic was a composite tale in which various stories of an independent origin had been combined and brought into more or less artificial connection with the _heros eponymos_ of southern Babylonia. We may now go a step further and point out that not only is Enkidu originally an entirely independent figure, having no connection with Gish or Gilgamesh, but that the latter is really depicted in the Epic as the counterpart of Enkidu, a reflection who has been given the traits of extraordinary physical power that belong to Enkidu. This is shown in the first place by the fact that in the encounter it is Enkidu who triumphs over Gilgamesh. The entire analysis of the episode of the meeting between the two heroes as given by Gressmann must be revised. It is not Enkidu who is terrified and who is warned against the encounter. It is Gilgamesh who, during the night on his way from the house in which the goddess Ishhara lies, encounters Enkidu on the highway. Enkidu "blocks the path" of Gilgamesh. He prevents Gilgamesh from re-entering the house, and the two attack each other "like oxen." They grapple with each other, and Enkidu forces Gilgamesh to the ground. Enkidu is, therefore, the real hero whose traits of physical prowess are afterwards transferred to Gilgamesh.
cards.whyThisWorks: The reversal in the encounter—where Enkidu, not Gilgamesh, triumphs and 'forces Gilgamesh to the ground'—adds the deeper meaning that Gilgamesh's celebrated heroic identity was originally borrowed from Enkidu, challenging assumptions about who the true hero is.

cards.standardTitle: Theme development across a literary text
cards.excerpt: Now with the tendency to attach to popular tales and nature myths lessons illustrative of current beliefs and aspirations, Gilgamesh's search for renewal of life is viewed as man's longing for eternal life. The sun-god's waning power after midsummer is past suggests man's growing weakness after the meridian of life has been left behind. Winter is death, and man longs to escape it. Gilgamesh's wanderings are used as illustration of this longing, and accordingly the search for life becomes also the quest for immortality. Can the precious boon of eternal life be achieved? Popular fancy created the figure of a favorite of the gods who had escaped a destructive deluge in which all mankind had perished. Gilgamesh hears of this favorite and determines to seek him out and learn from him the secret of eternal life. The deluge story, again a pure nature myth, symbolical of the rainy season which destroys all life in nature, is thus attached to the Epic. Gilgamesh after many adventures finds himself in the presence of the survivor of the Deluge who, although human, enjoys immortal life among the gods. He asks the survivor how he came to escape the common fate of mankind, and in reply Utnapishtim tells the story of the catastrophe that brought about universal destruction. The moral of the tale is obvious. Only those singled out by the special favor of the gods can hope to be removed to the distant "source of the streams" and live forever. The rest of mankind must face death as the end of life.
cards.whyThisWorks: The excerpt explicitly states a moral ('The rest of mankind must face death as the end of life') while also containing true but theme-neutral details (e.g., the deluge story's origin as a nature myth), forcing students to distinguish details that develop the theme of mortality's inevitability from details that merely describe the epic's mythological sources.

When, therefore, in another passage some one celebrates Gilgamesh as the one who overcame the "guardian," who dispatched Hu(m)baba in the cedar forest, who killed lions and overthrew the bull, we have the completion of the process which transferred to Gilgamesh exploits and powers which originally belonged to Enkidu, though ordinarily the process stops short at making Gilgamesh a _sharer_ in the exploits; with the natural tendency, to be sure, to enlarge the share of the favorite.

We can now understand why the two heroes are described in the Pennsylvania tablet as alike, as born in the same place, aye, as brothers. Gilgamesh in the Epic is merely a reflex of Enkidu. The latter is the real hero and presumably, therefore, the older figure. Gilgamesh resembles Enkidu, because he _is_ originally Enkidu. cards.excerpt: But after all, the parallels are of too general a character to be of much moment; and moreover the parallels stop short at the critical point, for Gilgamesh though worsted is _not_ killed by Enkidu, whereas one of the "Heavenly Twins" is always killed by the brother, as Abel is by Cain, and Iphikles by his twin brother Herakles. The two will become one, like man and wife.

On the basis of our investigations, we are now in a position to reconstruct in part the cycle of episodes that once formed part of an Enkidu Epic. The fight between Enkidu and Gilgamesh, in which the former is the victor, is typical of the kind of tales told of Enkidu. He is the real prototype of the Greek Hercules. He slays lions, he overcomes a powerful opponent dwelling in the forests of Lebanon, he kills the bull, and he finally succumbs to disease sent as a punishment by an angry goddess. cards.excerpt: That the story of the Deluge is told in the eleventh tablet of the series, corresponding to the eleventh month, known as the month of "rain curse" and marking the height of the rainy season, may be intentional, just as it may not be accidental that Gilgamesh's rejection of Ishtar is recounted in the sixth tablet, corresponding to the sixth month, which marks the end of the summer season. cards.standardTitle: Theme development across a literary text
cards.excerpt: That Enkidu originally played the part of the slayer is also shown by the statement that it is he who insults Ishtar by throwing a piece of the carcass into the goddess' face, adding also an insulting speech; and this despite the fact that Ishtar in her rage accuses Gilgamesh of killing the bull. cards.standardTitle: Epic poetry: characters, structures, and themes
cards.excerpt: The description of Enkidu in the Pennsylvania tablet as a parallel figure to Gilgamesh leads us to a consideration of the relationship of the two figures to one another. Many years ago it was pointed out that the Gilgamesh Epic was a composite tale in which various stories of an independent origin had been combined and brought into more or less artificial connection with the _heros eponymos_ of southern Babylonia. We may now go a step further and point out that not only is Enkidu originally an entirely independent figure, having no connection with Gish or Gilgamesh, but that the latter is really depicted in the Epic as the counterpart of Enkidu, a reflection who has been given the traits of extraordinary physical power that belong to Enkidu. This is shown in the first place by the fact that in the encounter it is Enkidu who triumphs over Gilgamesh. The entire analysis of the episode of the meeting between the two heroes as given by Gressmann must be revised. It is not Enkidu who is terrified and who is warned against the encounter. It is Gilgamesh who, during the night on his way from the house in which the goddess Ishhara lies, encounters Enkidu on the highway. Enkidu "blocks the path" of Gilgamesh. He prevents Gilgamesh from re-entering the house, and the two attack each other "like oxen." They grapple with each other, and Enkidu forces Gilgamesh to the ground. Enkidu is, therefore, the real hero whose traits of physical prowess are afterwards transferred to Gilgamesh.

cards.standardTitle: Theme development across a literary text
cards.excerpt: The description of Enkidu in the Pennsylvania tablet as a parallel figure to Gilgamesh leads us to a consideration of the relationship of the two figures to one another. Many years ago it was pointed out that the Gilgamesh Epic was a composite tale in which various stories of an independent origin had been combined and brought into more or less artificial connection with the _heros eponymos_ of southern Babylonia. We may now go a step further and point out that not only is Enkidu originally an entirely independent figure, having no connection with Gish or Gilgamesh, but that the latter is really depicted in the Epic as the counterpart of Enkidu, a reflection who has been given the traits of extraordinary physical power that belong to Enkidu. This is shown in the first place by the fact that in the encounter it is Enkidu who triumphs over Gilgamesh. The entire analysis of the episode of the meeting between the two heroes as given by Gressmann must be revised. It is not Enkidu who is terrified and who is warned against the encounter. It is Gilgamesh who, during the night on his way from the house in which the goddess Ishhara lies, encounters Enkidu on the highway. Enkidu "blocks the path" of Gilgamesh. He prevents Gilgamesh from re-entering the house, and the two attack each other "like oxen." They grapple with each other, and Enkidu forces Gilgamesh to the ground. Enkidu is, therefore, the real hero whose traits of physical prowess are afterwards transferred to Gilgamesh.

cards.standardTitle: Key literary elements add layers of meaning
cards.excerpt:
To sum up, there are four main currents that flow together in the Gilgamesh Epic even in its old Babylonian form: (1) the adventures of a mighty warrior Enkidu, resting perhaps on a faint tradition of the conquest of Amurru by the hero; (2) the more definite recollection of the exploits of a foreign invader of Babylonia by the name of Gilgamesh, whose home appears likewise to have been in the West; (3) nature myths and didactic tales transferred to Enkidu and Gilgamesh as popular figures; and (4) the process of weaving the traditions, exploits, myths and didactic tales together, in the course of which process Gilgamesh becomes the main hero, and Enkidu his companion.

Furthermore, our investigation has shown that to Enkidu belongs the episode with the woman, used to illustrate the evolution of primitive man to the ways and conditions of civilized life, the conquest of Huwawa in the land of Amurru, the killing of lions and also of the bull, while Gilgamesh is the hero who conquers Erech. Identified with the sun-god, the nature myth of the union of the sun with the earth and the subsequent separation of the two is also transferred to him. The wanderings of the hero, smitten with disease, are a continuation of the nature myth, symbolizing the waning vigor of the sun with the approach of the wintry season.
cards.whyThisWorks: The excerpt explicitly connects Enkidu's encounter with the woman to the theme of civilization's emergence from primitive life, making it a clear example of how a single plot event carries deeper thematic meaning about human development.

cards.standardTitle: Theme development across a literary text
cards.excerpt: Now with the tendency to attach to popular tales and nature myths lessons illustrative of current beliefs and aspirations, Gilgamesh's search for renewal of life is viewed as man's longing for eternal life. The sun-god's waning power after midsummer is past suggests man's growing weakness after the meridian of life has been left behind. Winter is death, and man longs to escape it. Gilgamesh's wanderings are used as illustration of this longing, and accordingly the search for life becomes also the quest for immortality. Can the precious boon of eternal life be achieved? Popular fancy created the figure of a favorite of the gods who had escaped a destructive deluge in which all mankind had perished. Gilgamesh hears of this favorite and determines to seek him out and learn from him the secret of eternal life. The deluge story, again a pure nature myth, symbolical of the rainy season which destroys all life in nature, is thus attached to the Epic. Gilgamesh after many adventures finds himself in the presence of the survivor of the Deluge who, although human, enjoys immortal life among the gods. He asks the survivor how he came to escape the common fate of mankind, and in reply Utnapishtim tells the story of the catastrophe that brought about universal destruction. The moral of the tale is obvious. Only those singled out by the special favor of the gods can hope to be removed to the distant "source of the streams" and live forever. The rest of mankind must face death as the end of life.
cards.whyThisWorks: The excerpt presents two distinct story moments—Gilgamesh's wandering search for renewal and his encounter with Utnapishtim after the Deluge—that together build the theme that immortality is reserved only for those chosen by the gods, requiring students to track how both moments contribute rather than treating either alone as the full message.
cards.skillStrategy: When tracking theme, ask yourself how each story moment adds a new layer to the same idea, rather than letting one scene carry the whole message.

cards.standardTitle: Key literary elements add layers of meaning
cards.excerpt: That Enkidu originally played the part of the slayer is also shown by the statement that it is he who insults Ishtar by throwing a piece of the carcass into the goddess' face, adding also an insulting speech; and this despite the fact that Ishtar in her rage accuses Gilgamesh of killing the bull. It is thus evident that the Epic alters the original character of the episodes in order to find a place for Gilgamesh, with the further desire to assign to the latter the _chief_ rôle. Be it noted also that Enkidu, not Gilgamesh, is punished for the insult to Ishtar. Enkidu must therefore in the original form of the episode have been the guilty party, who is stricken with mortal disease as a punishment to which after twelve days he succumbs. In view of this, we may supply the name of Enkidu in the little song introduced at the close of the encounter with the bull, and not Gilgamesh as has hitherto been done.

cards.standardTitle: Key literary elements add layers of meaning
cards.excerpt: But after all, the parallels are of too general a character to be of much moment; and moreover the parallels stop short at the critical point, for Gilgamesh though worsted is _not_ killed by Enkidu, whereas one of the "Heavenly Twins" is always killed by the brother, as Abel is by Cain, and Iphikles by his twin brother Herakles. Even the trait which is frequent in the earliest forms of the "Heavenly Twins," according to which one is immortal and the other is mortal, though applying in a measure to Enkidu who is killed by Ishtar, while Gilgamesh the offspring of a divine pair is only smitten with disease, is too unsubstantial to warrant more than a general comparison between the Enkidu-Gilgamesh pair and the various forms of the "twin" _motif_ found throughout the ancient world. For all that, the point is of some interest that in the Gilgamesh Epic we should encounter two figures who are portrayed as possessing the same traits and accomplishing feats in common, which suggest a partial parallel to the various forms in which the twin-_motif_ appears in the mythologies, folk-lore and legends of many nations; and it may be that in some of these instances the duplication is due, as in the case of Enkidu and Gilgamesh, to an actual transfer of the traits of one figure to another who usurped his place.
cards.whyThisWorks: The excerpt is narrated by a scholarly, analytical third-person voice that distances itself from the myth and qualifies every claim, which shapes the reader's understanding of Gilgamesh and Enkidu as subjects of academic debate rather than heroic figures—demonstrating how point of view controls tone and meaning.

cards.standardTitle: Theme development across a literary text
cards.excerpt:
The artificiality of the process which brings the two heroes together is apparent in the dreams of Gilgamesh which are interpreted by his mother as portending the coming of Enkidu. Not the conflict is foreseen, but the subsequent close association, naïvely described as due to the personal charm which Enkidu exercises, which will lead Gilgamesh to fall in love with the one whom he is to meet. The two will become one, like man and wife.

On the basis of our investigations, we are now in a position to reconstruct in part the cycle of episodes that once formed part of an Enkidu Epic. The fight between Enkidu and Gilgamesh, in which the former is the victor, is typical of the kind of tales told of Enkidu. He is the real prototype of the Greek Hercules. He slays lions, he overcomes a powerful opponent dwelling in the forests of Lebanon, he kills the bull, and he finally succumbs to disease sent as a punishment by an angry goddess. The death of Enkidu naturally formed the close of the Enkidu Epic, which in its original form may, of course, have included other exploits besides those taken over into the Gilgamesh Epic.
cards.whyThisWorks: The excerpt explicitly traces how conflict between Enkidu and Gilgamesh transforms into deep companionship, and how Enkidu's death as divine punishment closes his arc—both moments illustrating how conflict and consequence drive the theme of mortality and human connection.

cards.standardTitle: Epic poetry: characters, structures, and themes
cards.excerpt: Gilgamesh now begins a series of wanderings in search of the restoration of his vigor, and this _motif_ is evidently a continuation of the nature myth to symbolize the sun's wanderings during the dark winter in the hope of renewed vigor with the coming of the spring. Professor Haupt's view is that the disease from which Gilgamesh is supposed to be suffering is of a venereal character, affecting the organs of reproduction. This would confirm the position here taken that the myth symbolizes the loss of the sun's vigor. The sun's rays are no longer strong enough to fertilize the earth. In accord with this, Gilgamesh's search for healing leads him to the dark regions in which the scorpion-men dwell. The terrors of the region symbolize the gloom of the winter season. At last Gilgamesh reaches a region of light again, described as a landscape situated at the sea. The maiden in control of this region bolts the gate against Gilgamesh's approach, but the latter forces his entrance. It is the picture of the sun-god bursting through the darkness, to emerge as the youthful reinvigorated sun-god of the spring.

cards.standardTitle: Key literary elements add layers of meaning
cards.excerpt:
He prays to Sin and Ishtar to protect and save him. When, therefore, in another passage some one celebrates Gilgamesh as the one who overcame the "guardian," who dispatched Hu(m)baba in the cedar forest, who killed lions and overthrew the bull, we have the completion of the process which transferred to Gilgamesh exploits and powers which originally belonged to Enkidu, though ordinarily the process stops short at making Gilgamesh a _sharer_ in the exploits; with the natural tendency, to be sure, to enlarge the share of the favorite.

We can now understand why the two heroes are described in the Pennsylvania tablet as alike, as born in the same place, aye, as brothers. Gilgamesh in the Epic is merely a reflex of Enkidu. The latter is the real hero and presumably, therefore, the older figure. Gilgamesh resembles Enkidu, because he _is_ originally Enkidu. The "resemblance" _motif_ is merely the manner in which in the course of the partly popular, partly literary transfer, the recollection is preserved that Enkidu is the original, and Gilgamesh the copy.

cards.standardTitle: Theme development across a literary text
cards.excerpt: Now with the tendency to attach to popular tales and nature myths lessons illustrative of current beliefs and aspirations, Gilgamesh's search for renewal of life is viewed as man's longing for eternal life. The sun-god's waning power after midsummer is past suggests man's growing weakness after the meridian of life has been left behind. Winter is death, and man longs to escape it. Gilgamesh's wanderings are used as illustration of this longing, and accordingly the search for life becomes also the quest for immortality. Can the precious boon of eternal life be achieved? Popular fancy created the figure of a favorite of the gods who had escaped a destructive deluge in which all mankind had perished. Gilgamesh hears of this favorite and determines to seek him out and learn from him the secret of eternal life. The deluge story, again a pure nature myth, symbolical of the rainy season which destroys all life in nature, is thus attached to the Epic. Gilgamesh after many adventures finds himself in the presence of the survivor of the Deluge who, although human, enjoys immortal life among the gods. He asks the survivor how he came to escape the common fate of mankind, and in reply Utnapishtim tells the story of the catastrophe that brought about universal destruction. The moral of the tale is obvious. Only those singled out by the special favor of the gods can hope to be removed to the distant "source of the streams" and live forever. The rest of mankind must face death as the end of life.
cards.whyThisWorks: The excerpt explicitly traces how Gilgamesh's conflict with mortality and his quest for immortality leads to a consequence—learning from Utnapishtim—that reveals the theme: only those chosen by the gods escape death, while all others must accept it.

cards.standardTitle: Epic poetry: characters, structures, and themes
cards.excerpt:
To sum up, there are four main currents that flow together in the Gilgamesh Epic even in its old Babylonian form: (1) the adventures of a mighty warrior Enkidu, resting perhaps on a faint tradition of the conquest of Amurru by the hero; (2) the more definite recollection of the exploits of a foreign invader of Babylonia by the name of Gilgamesh, whose home appears likewise to have been in the West; (3) nature myths and didactic tales transferred to Enkidu and Gilgamesh as popular figures; and (4) the process of weaving the traditions, exploits, myths and didactic tales together, in the course of which process Gilgamesh becomes the main hero, and Enkidu his companion.

Furthermore, our investigation has shown that to Enkidu belongs the episode with the woman, used to illustrate the evolution of primitive man to the ways and conditions of civilized life, the conquest of Huwawa in the land of Amurru, the killing of lions and also of the bull, while Gilgamesh is the hero who conquers Erech. Identified with the sun-god, the nature myth of the union of the sun with the earth and the subsequent separation of the two is also transferred to him. The wanderings of the hero, smitten with disease, are a continuation of the nature myth, symbolizing the waning vigor of the sun with the approach of the wintry season.

cards.excerpt: Next to the new light thrown upon the names and original character of the two main figures of the Epic, one of the chief points of interest in the Pennsylvania fragment is the proof that it furnishes for a striking resemblance of the two heroes, Gish and Enkidu, to one another. In interpreting the dream of Gish, his mother. Ninsun, lays stress upon the fact that the dream portends the coming of someone who is like Gish, "born in the field and reared in the mountain" (lines 18-19). Both, therefore, are shown by this description to have come to Babylonia from a mountainous region, i.e., they are foreigners; and in the case of Enkidu we have seen that the mountain in all probability refers to a region in the West, while the same may also be the case with Gish. The resemblance of the two heroes to one another extends to their personal appearance. When Enkidu appears on the streets of Erech, the people are struck by this resemblance. They remark that he is "like Gish," though "shorter in stature" (lines 179-180). Enkidu is described as a rival or counterpart.

cards.standardTitle: Epic poetry: characters, structures, and themes
cards.excerpt: The description of Enkidu in the Pennsylvania tablet as a parallel figure to Gilgamesh leads us to a consideration of the relationship of the two figures to one another. Many years ago it was pointed out that the Gilgamesh Epic was a composite tale in which various stories of an independent origin had been combined and brought into more or less artificial connection with the _heros eponymos_ of southern Babylonia. We may now go a step further and point out that not only is Enkidu originally an entirely independent figure, having no connection with Gish or Gilgamesh, but that the latter is really depicted in the Epic as the counterpart of Enkidu, a reflection who has been given the traits of extraordinary physical power that belong to Enkidu. This is shown in the first place by the fact that in the encounter it is Enkidu who triumphs over Gilgamesh. The entire analysis of the episode of the meeting between the two heroes as given by Gressmann must be revised. It is not Enkidu who is terrified and who is warned against the encounter. It is Gilgamesh who, during the night on his way from the house in which the goddess Ishhara lies, encounters Enkidu on the highway. Enkidu "blocks the path" of Gilgamesh. He prevents Gilgamesh from re-entering the house, and the two attack each other "like oxen." They grapple with each other, and Enkidu forces Gilgamesh to the ground. Enkidu is, therefore, the real hero whose traits of physical prowess are afterwards transferred to Gilgamesh.
cards.whyThisWorks: The excerpt explicitly attributes physical prowess and dominance in combat to Enkidu, allowing students to identify and support an epic hero trait—physical courage and strength—with direct textual evidence.
cards.skillStrategy: When identifying an epic hero trait, find the exact moment in the text where a character's action or quality is described, then ask yourself what that action proves about who the real hero is.

cards.standardTitle: Key literary elements add layers of meaning
cards.excerpt: That the story of the Deluge is told in the eleventh tablet of the series, corresponding to the eleventh month, known as the month of "rain curse" and marking the height of the rainy season, may be intentional, just as it may not be accidental that Gilgamesh's rejection of Ishtar is recounted in the sixth tablet, corresponding to the sixth month, which marks the end of the summer season. The two tales may have formed part of a cycle of myths, distributed among the months of the year. The Gilgamesh Epic, however, does not form such a cycle. Both myths have been artificially attached to the adventures of the hero. For the deluge story we now have the definite proof for its independent existence, through Dr. Poebel's publication of a Sumerian text which embodies the tale, and without any reference to Gilgamesh. Similarly, Scheil and Hilprecht have published fragments of deluge stories written in Akkadian and likewise without any connection with the Gilgamesh Epic.

cards.standardTitle: Theme development across a literary text
cards.excerpt: The description of Enkidu in the Pennsylvania tablet as a parallel figure to Gilgamesh leads us to a consideration of the relationship of the two figures to one another. Many years ago it was pointed out that the Gilgamesh Epic was a composite tale in which various stories of an independent origin had been combined and brought into more or less artificial connection with the _heros eponymos_ of southern Babylonia. We may now go a step further and point out that not only is Enkidu originally an entirely independent figure, having no connection with Gish or Gilgamesh, but that the latter is really depicted in the Epic as the counterpart of Enkidu, a reflection who has been given the traits of extraordinary physical power that belong to Enkidu. This is shown in the first place by the fact that in the encounter it is Enkidu who triumphs over Gilgamesh. The entire analysis of the episode of the meeting between the two heroes as given by Gressmann must be revised. It is not Enkidu who is terrified and who is warned against the encounter. It is Gilgamesh who, during the night on his way from the house in which the goddess Ishhara lies, encounters Enkidu on the highway. Enkidu "blocks the path" of Gilgamesh. He prevents Gilgamesh from re-entering the house, and the two attack each other "like oxen." They grapple with each other, and Enkidu forces Gilgamesh to the ground. Enkidu is, therefore, the real hero whose traits of physical prowess are afterwards transferred to Gilgamesh.
cards.whyThisWorks: The excerpt centers on the relationship between Gilgamesh and Enkidu, allowing students to practice distinguishing the broad topic of heroism or rivalry from a specific universal theme statement about how power and identity can be transferred or redefined through conflict.
cards.skillStrategy: A topic is just a word or phrase like 'rivalry'; a theme is a full sentence claim about what the text says about people or life — look for what the details add up to mean.
