cards.question: Friar Lawrence argues that Juliet's death is actually her 'advancement' rather than a loss. What deeper meaning does this reversal add to the scene?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The reversal shows that Friar Lawrence is indifferent to Juliet's fate and uses religious language only to silence the mourners quickly so the funeral can proceed.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The reversal exposes a painful gap between religious consolation and human grief, suggesting that the parents' love for Juliet was ultimately self-serving because it was rooted in earthly ambition rather than her true well-being.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The reversal reveals that Friar Lawrence secretly blames the parents for Juliet's death and uses the argument about heaven to punish them for their role in the feud.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The reversal demonstrates that dying young is universally accepted in the play's world as a blessing, and the mourners immediately find comfort in Friar Lawrence's words.

cards.standardTitle: Theme development across a literary text
cards.excerpt: CAPULET. God’s bread, it makes me mad! Day, night, hour, ride, time, work, play, Alone, in company, still my care hath been To have her match’d, and having now provided A gentleman of noble parentage, Of fair demesnes, youthful, and nobly allied, Stuff’d, as they say, with honourable parts, Proportion’d as one’s thought would wish a man, And then to have a wretched puling fool, A whining mammet, in her fortune’s tender, To answer, ‘I’ll not wed, I cannot love, I am too young, I pray you pardon me.’ But, and you will not wed, I’ll pardon you. Graze where you will, you shall not house with me. Look to’t, think on’t, I do not use to jest. Thursday is near; lay hand on heart, advise. And you be mine, I’ll give you to my friend; And you be not, hang, beg, starve, die in the streets, For by my soul, I’ll ne’er acknowledge thee, Nor what is mine shall never do thee good. Trust to’t, bethink you, I’ll not be forsworn.
cards.whyThisWorks: Capulet's speech contains two distinct moments—his boast of tireless devotion to arranging Juliet's match and his brutal threat to disown her—that together develop the theme that parental authority, when unchecked, becomes a form of cruelty rather than care.
cards.skillStrategy: Find two separate moments in the passage and ask what idea both moments are pushing toward together, not just what one moment shows on its own.
evidencePoints: Day, night, hour, ride, time, work, play, Alone, in company, still my care hath been To have her match'd
hang, beg, starve, die in the streets, For by my soul, I'll ne'er acknowledge thee
cards.question:
Read the two moments below from Capulet's speech.

First: 'Day, night, hour, ride, time, work, play, / Alone, in company, still my care hath been / To have her match'd'

Second: 'hang, beg, starve, die in the streets, / For by my soul, I'll ne'er acknowledge thee'

How do these two moments work together to develop a theme in this passage?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Capulet's exhaustive list of his efforts shows he is a devoted father, and his final threat reveals he has simply run out of patience after years of sacrifice.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Capulet's claim of constant devotion to Juliet's future and his willingness to let her 'hang, beg, starve' together reveal that his so-called care was always about control, not Juliet's well-being.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Capulet's pride in the match he arranged and his anger at Juliet's refusal develop the theme that young people are ungrateful for the advantages their parents provide.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Capulet's detailed description of Paris's qualities and his threat to disown Juliet develop the theme that wealth and noble status are the only measures of a worthy marriage.

cards.standardTitle: Key literary elements add layers of meaning
cards.excerpt:
JULIET. Wilt thou be gone? It is not yet near day. It was the nightingale, and not the lark, That pierc’d the fearful hollow of thine ear; Nightly she sings on yond pomegranate tree. Believe me, love, it was the nightingale.

ROMEO. It was the lark, the herald of the morn, No nightingale. Look, love, what envious streaks Do lace the severing clouds in yonder east. Night’s candles are burnt out, and jocund day Stands tiptoe on the misty mountain tops. I must be gone and live, or stay and die.

JULIET. Yond light is not daylight, I know it, I. It is some meteor that the sun exhales To be to thee this night a torchbearer And light thee on thy way to Mantua. Therefore stay yet, thou need’st not to be gone.

ROMEO. Let me be ta’en, let me be put to death, I am content, so thou wilt have it so. I’ll say yon grey is not the morning’s eye, ’Tis but the pale reflex of Cynthia’s brow. Nor that is not the lark whose notes do beat The vaulty heaven so high above our heads. I have more care to stay than will to go. Come, death, and welcome. Juliet wills it so. How is’t, my soul? Let’s talk. It is not day.

JULIET. It is, it is! Hie hence, be gone, away. It is the lark that sings so out of tune, Straining harsh discords and unpleasing sharps. Some say the lark makes sweet division; This doth not so, for she divideth us. Some say the lark and loathed toad change eyes. O, now I would they had chang’d voices too, Since arm from arm that voice doth us affray, Hunting thee hence with hunt’s-up to the day. O now be gone, more light and light it grows.
cards.whyThisWorks: Juliet's reversal—shifting from denying daylight to urgently commanding Romeo to flee—deepens the meaning of their separation by showing that love itself must become the force that drives them apart, adding tragic irony to the conflict.
cards.skillStrategy: When a character reverses a position or decision, ask what that reversal reveals about the deeper stakes of the conflict.
evidencePoints: Therefore stay yet, thou need'st not to be gone.
It is, it is! Hie hence, be gone, away.
cards.question: In the final speech, Juliet reverses her earlier insistence that Romeo stay. What deeper meaning does this reversal add to the conflict between the lovers?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Juliet's change of heart shows she has grown indifferent to Romeo and is willing to end their relationship without grief.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Juliet's reversal reveals that her love for Romeo is so consuming that she must become the very force separating them, making their bond the source of their tragedy.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Juliet's sudden urgency proves she was never truly convinced it was night and had been testing Romeo's willingness to risk death for her.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Juliet's command for Romeo to leave shows that she fears the lark's song as a supernatural omen rather than as a sign of ordinary daybreak.

cards.standardTitle: Key literary elements add layers of meaning
cards.excerpt:
FRIAR LAWRENCE. O Juliet, I already know thy grief; It strains me past the compass of my wits. I hear thou must, and nothing may prorogue it, On Thursday next be married to this County.

JULIET. Tell me not, Friar, that thou hear’st of this, Unless thou tell me how I may prevent it. If in thy wisdom, thou canst give no help, Do thou but call my resolution wise, And with this knife I’ll help it presently. God join’d my heart and Romeo’s, thou our hands; And ere this hand, by thee to Romeo’s seal’d, Shall be the label to another deed, Or my true heart with treacherous revolt Turn to another, this shall slay them both. Therefore, out of thy long-experienc’d time, Give me some present counsel, or behold ’Twixt my extremes and me this bloody knife Shall play the empire, arbitrating that Which the commission of thy years and art Could to no issue of true honour bring. Be not so long to speak. I long to die, If what thou speak’st speak not of remedy.
cards.whyThisWorks: Juliet's ultimatum—threatening suicide with the knife unless Friar Lawrence offers a remedy—creates a crisis-point conflict that deepens the play's meaning by showing how the forced marriage traps her between loyalty to Romeo and social obligation, raising the stakes of honor, agency, and fate.
cards.skillStrategy: When a character faces a conflict or makes a desperate decision, ask what that moment reveals about the deeper forces—social, moral, or personal—that are driving the story.
evidencePoints: 'Twixt my extremes and me this bloody knife / Shall play the empire, arbitrating that / Which the commission of thy years and art / Could to no issue of true honour bring.

God join'd my heart and Romeo's, thou our hands; / And ere this hand, by thee to Romeo's seal'd, / Shall be the label to another deed, / Or my true heart with treacherous revolt / Turn to another, this shall slay them both.
cards.question: Juliet threatens to use the knife rather than marry County Paris. What deeper meaning does this conflict add to the scene?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Juliet's threat reveals that she blames Friar Lawrence for performing her marriage to Romeo and now expects him to undo it by any means necessary.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Juliet's willingness to die rather than betray her vow to Romeo shows that the forced marriage has made personal honor and loyalty more powerful than the authority of family, church, or law.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Juliet's desperation proves she is too impulsive to think clearly, suggesting that youthful emotion, not social pressure, is the true source of the tragedy.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Juliet's ultimatum demonstrates that she trusts Friar Lawrence's wisdom completely and is certain he will produce a remedy before she is forced to act.

cards.question: Read the following lines from the passage: 'O mischief thou art swift / To enter in the thoughts of desperate men' and 'And if a man did need a poison now, / Whose sale is present death in Mantua, / Here lives a caitiff wretch would sell it him.' How do these two moments work together to develop a theme?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Both moments show that poverty forces ordinary people to break the law, suggesting society is to blame for crime.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The first moment names desperation as the force that opens the mind to wrongdoing, and the second shows Romeo already acting on that desperation by planning to buy illegal poison, together developing the theme that grief drives people to dangerous and irreversible choices.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The first moment establishes that Romeo is impulsive by nature, and the second reveals that the apothecary is a criminal, together suggesting that bad people attract each other.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Both moments focus on the apothecary's miserable condition, developing the theme that extreme poverty destroys a person's sense of right and wrong.

cards.standardTitle: Key literary elements add layers of meaning
cards.excerpt:
JULIET. O God! O Nurse, how shall this be prevented? My husband is on earth, my faith in heaven. How shall that faith return again to earth, Unless that husband send it me from heaven By leaving earth? Comfort me, counsel me. Alack, alack, that heaven should practise stratagems Upon so soft a subject as myself. What say’st thou? Hast thou not a word of joy? Some comfort, Nurse.

NURSE. Faith, here it is. Romeo is banished; and all the world to nothing That he dares ne’er come back to challenge you. Or if he do, it needs must be by stealth. Then, since the case so stands as now it doth, I think it best you married with the County. O, he’s a lovely gentleman. Romeo’s a dishclout to him. An eagle, madam, Hath not so green, so quick, so fair an eye As Paris hath. Beshrew my very heart, I think you are happy in this second match, For it excels your first: or if it did not, Your first is dead, or ’twere as good he were, As living here and you no use of him.
cards.whyThisWorks: The Nurse's advice that Juliet marry Paris—delivered immediately after Juliet's desperate plea for comfort—creates a pivotal conflict between loyalty and self-interest that deepens the theme of isolation: the one person Juliet trusted most has abandoned her at her greatest need.
cards.skillStrategy: When a character makes a surprising decision or gives unexpected advice, ask what that choice reveals about the deeper conflict and what it means for the story's themes.
evidencePoints: Hast thou not a word of joy? Some comfort, Nurse.
I think it best you married with the County. O, he's a lovely gentleman. Romeo's a dishclout to him.
cards.question: Juliet begs the Nurse for 'a word of joy' and 'some comfort,' but the Nurse responds by urging Juliet to marry Paris and calling Romeo 'a dishclout' compared to him. What deeper meaning does this moment add to the play?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The Nurse's praise of Paris shows that she has always preferred him over Romeo and has been secretly working to arrange a second marriage for Juliet.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The Nurse's betrayal of Juliet's confidence at her most desperate moment deepens the theme that Juliet is utterly alone, with no trustworthy ally left to help her navigate her impossible situation.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The Nurse's practical advice reveals that she is the wisest character in the scene because she correctly understands that Romeo's banishment makes the marriage effectively over.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The contrast between Juliet's grief and the Nurse's cheerfulness shows that the Nurse does not yet know how serious Romeo's banishment truly is.

cards.standardTitle: Theme development across a literary text
cards.excerpt: JULIET. Thou knowest the mask of night is on my face, Else would a maiden blush bepaint my cheek For that which thou hast heard me speak tonight. Fain would I dwell on form, fain, fain deny What I have spoke; but farewell compliment. Dost thou love me? I know thou wilt say Ay, And I will take thy word. Yet, if thou swear’st, Thou mayst prove false. At lovers’ perjuries, They say Jove laughs. O gentle Romeo, If thou dost love, pronounce it faithfully. Or if thou thinkest I am too quickly won, I’ll frown and be perverse, and say thee nay, So thou wilt woo. But else, not for the world. In truth, fair Montague, I am too fond; And therefore thou mayst think my ’haviour light: But trust me, gentleman, I’ll prove more true Than those that have more cunning to be strange. I should have been more strange, I must confess, But that thou overheard’st, ere I was ’ware, My true-love passion; therefore pardon me, And not impute this yielding to light love, Which the dark night hath so discovered.
cards.whyThisWorks: Juliet's speech contains two distinct moments—her admission that she is 'too fond' and her vow to 'prove more true'—that together develop the theme that authentic love requires vulnerability and honesty rather than performance, allowing students to track theme across multiple story moments rather than reducing it to a single line.
cards.skillStrategy: Find two separate moments in the passage where a character's words or actions point to the same big idea, then name the theme both moments share.
evidencePoints: In truth, fair Montague, I am too fond; And therefore thou mayst think my 'haviour light
trust me, gentleman, I'll prove more true Than those that have more cunning to be strange
cards.question:
Read the two moments below from Juliet's speech.

First: 'In truth, fair Montague, I am too fond; And therefore thou mayst think my 'haviour light.'

Second: 'trust me, gentleman, I'll prove more true / Than those that have more cunning to be strange.'

How do these two moments work together to develop a theme in the passage?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Juliet's fear of seeming too eager in the first moment is resolved when she decides to pretend indifference in the second, developing a theme that playing hard to get protects a person from heartbreak.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Juliet's admission that openness may make her look reckless in the first moment, paired with her pledge that this same openness will make her more faithful in the second, develops a theme that genuine love demands honesty even at the cost of appearing vulnerable.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Juliet's worry about Romeo's loyalty in the first moment and her promise to watch his behavior in the second develop a theme that love cannot survive without constant proof of commitment from both partners.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Juliet's embarrassment at being overheard in the first moment and her request for pardon in the second develop a theme that social rules of courtship must be followed to earn lasting respect.

cards.standardTitle: Key literary elements add layers of meaning
cards.excerpt:
ROMEO. Then plainly know my heart’s dear love is set On the fair daughter of rich Capulet. As mine on hers, so hers is set on mine; And all combin’d, save what thou must combine By holy marriage. When, and where, and how We met, we woo’d, and made exchange of vow, I’ll tell thee as we pass; but this I pray, That thou consent to marry us today.

FRIAR LAWRENCE. Holy Saint Francis! What a change is here! Is Rosaline, that thou didst love so dear, So soon forsaken? Young men’s love then lies Not truly in their hearts, but in their eyes. Jesu Maria, what a deal of brine Hath wash’d thy sallow cheeks for Rosaline! How much salt water thrown away in waste, To season love, that of it doth not taste. The sun not yet thy sighs from heaven clears, Thy old groans yet ring in mine ancient ears. Lo here upon thy cheek the stain doth sit Of an old tear that is not wash’d off yet. If ere thou wast thyself, and these woes thine, Thou and these woes were all for Rosaline, And art thou chang’d? Pronounce this sentence then, Women may fall, when there’s no strength in men.
cards.whyThisWorks: Friar Lawrence's challenge to Romeo's sudden shift from Rosaline to Juliet creates a conflict of credibility that deepens the play's meaning by questioning whether Romeo's love is genuine devotion or impulsive infatuation.
cards.skillStrategy: When a character's decision or reversal is challenged by another character, ask what that conflict reveals about a deeper theme or truth the author wants readers to consider.
evidencePoints: Young men's love then lies / Not truly in their hearts, but in their eyes.
Lo here upon thy cheek the stain doth sit / Of an old tear that is not wash'd off yet.
cards.question: Friar Lawrence points out that Romeo's tears for Rosaline have not yet dried when Romeo asks him to perform a new marriage. What deeper meaning does this moment add to the scene?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Romeo's request reveals that he has matured since loving Rosaline, and Friar Lawrence's reminder of past tears confirms that Romeo has learned from his earlier heartbreak.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The speed of Romeo's reversal from Rosaline to Juliet raises doubt about whether his love is rooted in genuine feeling or in fleeting desire, suggesting that impulsive passion can be mistaken for true devotion.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Friar Lawrence's reference to Rosaline shows that he disapproves of Juliet specifically because she is a Capulet, and his concern is primarily about the danger of the feud rather than Romeo's character.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Romeo's decision to pursue marriage so quickly demonstrates his confidence that Juliet's love is more reliable than Rosaline's was, and Friar Lawrence ultimately accepts this reasoning.

cards.standardTitle: Theme development across a literary text
cards.excerpt: BENVOLIO. Tybalt, here slain, whom Romeo’s hand did slay; Romeo, that spoke him fair, bid him bethink How nice the quarrel was, and urg’d withal Your high displeasure. All this uttered With gentle breath, calm look, knees humbly bow’d Could not take truce with the unruly spleen Of Tybalt, deaf to peace, but that he tilts With piercing steel at bold Mercutio’s breast, Who, all as hot, turns deadly point to point, And, with a martial scorn, with one hand beats Cold death aside, and with the other sends It back to Tybalt, whose dexterity Retorts it. Romeo he cries aloud, ‘Hold, friends! Friends, part!’ and swifter than his tongue, His agile arm beats down their fatal points, And ’twixt them rushes; underneath whose arm An envious thrust from Tybalt hit the life Of stout Mercutio, and then Tybalt fled. But by and by comes back to Romeo, Who had but newly entertain’d revenge, And to’t they go like lightning; for, ere I Could draw to part them was stout Tybalt slain; And as he fell did Romeo turn and fly. This is the truth, or let Benvolio die.
cards.whyThisWorks: The excerpt contains two distinct story moments—Romeo's failed attempt at peaceful intervention and his eventual surrender to revenge—that together develop the theme that good intentions cannot prevent violence when hatred and passion override reason.
cards.skillStrategy: Find at least two separate moments in the passage and ask what idea both moments are building toward together.
evidencePoints: Romeo, that spoke him fair, bid him bethink / How nice the quarrel was, and urg'd withal / Your high displeasure. All this uttered / With gentle breath, calm look, knees humbly bow'd / Could not take truce with the unruly spleen / Of Tybalt
Who had but newly entertain'd revenge, / And to't they go like lightning
cards.question:
Read the two moments below from Benvolio's account and consider what theme they develop together.

Moment 1: Romeo speaks calmly, bows his knees, and urges peace, yet Tybalt still attacks Mercutio.
Moment 2: After Mercutio dies, Romeo 'had but newly entertain'd revenge' and rushes into a fatal duel with Tybalt.

What theme do both moments develop?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Tybalt's cruelty alone is responsible for every death, because he refuses Romeo's peace and strikes Mercutio first.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Even a person who genuinely seeks peace can be overtaken by violence, because hatred and passion ultimately overwhelm reason and good intentions.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Loyalty to friends is the highest virtue, because Romeo's devotion to Mercutio drives every decision he makes in this scene.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Words are always powerless in conflict, because no one in Verona ever listens to reason or calm speech.

cards.standardTitle: Key literary elements add layers of meaning
cards.excerpt: MERCUTIO. Nay, an there were two such, we should have none shortly, for one would kill the other. Thou? Why, thou wilt quarrel with a man that hath a hair more or a hair less in his beard than thou hast. Thou wilt quarrel with a man for cracking nuts, having no other reason but because thou hast hazel eyes. What eye but such an eye would spy out such a quarrel? Thy head is as full of quarrels as an egg is full of meat, and yet thy head hath been beaten as addle as an egg for quarrelling. Thou hast quarrelled with a man for coughing in the street, because he hath wakened thy dog that hath lain asleep in the sun. Didst thou not fall out with a tailor for wearing his new doublet before Easter? with another for tying his new shoes with an old riband? And yet thou wilt tutor me from quarrelling!
cards.whyThisWorks: Mercutio's catalog of Benvolio's petty quarrels creates an ironic conflict that deepens the play's theme about how pride and hair-trigger aggression make violence inevitable, even among friends.
cards.skillStrategy: When a character's behavior is exposed through a list of past conflicts, ask what that pattern reveals about the deeper forces driving the story's danger.
evidencePoints: Thy head is as full of quarrels as an egg is full of meat, and yet thy head hath been beaten as addle as an egg for quarrelling.
And yet thou wilt tutor me from quarrelling!
cards.question: Mercutio ends his speech by saying, 'And yet thou wilt tutor me from quarrelling!' How does this moment deepen the meaning of the conflict Mercutio has just described?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Mercutio's final line shows he genuinely respects Benvolio's experience with conflict and is asking him for advice on how to avoid fights in the future.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The reversal in Mercutio's final line exposes that neither man can honestly claim to stand above quarreling, suggesting that the characters' pride blinds them to their own role in the violence surrounding them.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Mercutio's accusation proves that Benvolio is the most dangerous character in the play and that his quarrels will directly cause the tragedy that follows.

choices.label: D
choices.text: By listing Benvolio's trivial disputes, Mercutio argues that small quarrels are harmless and that only serious provocations, like those involving weapons, carry real consequences.

cards.standardTitle: Figurative language effect
cards.excerpt:
FRIAR LAWRENCE. O Juliet, I already know thy grief; It strains me past the compass of my wits. I hear thou must, and nothing may prorogue it, On Thursday next be married to this County.

JULIET. Tell me not, Friar, that thou hear’st of this, Unless thou tell me how I may prevent it. If in thy wisdom, thou canst give no help, Do thou but call my resolution wise, And with this knife I’ll help it presently. God join’d my heart and Romeo’s, thou our hands; And ere this hand, by thee to Romeo’s seal’d, Shall be the label to another deed, Or my true heart with treacherous revolt Turn to another, this shall slay them both. Therefore, out of thy long-experienc’d time, Give me some present counsel, or behold ’Twixt my extremes and me this bloody knife Shall play the empire, arbitrating that Which the commission of thy years and art Could to no issue of true honour bring. Be not so long to speak. I long to die, If what thou speak’st speak not of remedy.
cards.whyThisWorks: Juliet's extended metaphor of the knife as 'empire' and 'arbitrating' force, combined with the symbolic sealing of hands, gives students rich figurative language to interpret using only the passage's context clues.
cards.skillStrategy: When you spot a figurative phrase, ask yourself: what two things are being compared or represented here, and what does that reveal about the character's situation or feelings?
evidencePoints: 'Twixt my extremes and me this bloody knife / Shall play the empire, arbitrating that / Which the commission of thy years and art / Could to no issue of true honour bring.
And ere this hand, by thee to Romeo's seal'd, / Shall be the label to another deed
cards.question: Read the following lines from Juliet's speech: "'Twixt my extremes and me this bloody knife / Shall play the empire, arbitrating that / Which the commission of thy years and art / Could to no issue of true honour bring." What does Juliet mean by calling the knife an "empire" that will "arbitrate"?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The knife represents Juliet's anger toward the Friar for failing to use his authority to stop the marriage.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The knife holds the final power to resolve her impossible situation if the Friar's wisdom and experience cannot offer her an honorable way out.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The knife symbolizes the political power of the County Paris, whose rank forces Juliet into a marriage she cannot escape.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The knife stands for the Friar's long years of experience, which Juliet believes should be enough to settle the conflict between her and her family.

cards.standardTitle: Key literary elements add layers of meaning
cards.excerpt: CAPULET. God’s bread, it makes me mad! Day, night, hour, ride, time, work, play, Alone, in company, still my care hath been To have her match’d, and having now provided A gentleman of noble parentage, Of fair demesnes, youthful, and nobly allied, Stuff’d, as they say, with honourable parts, Proportion’d as one’s thought would wish a man, And then to have a wretched puling fool, A whining mammet, in her fortune’s tender, To answer, ‘I’ll not wed, I cannot love, I am too young, I pray you pardon me.’ But, and you will not wed, I’ll pardon you. Graze where you will, you shall not house with me. Look to’t, think on’t, I do not use to jest. Thursday is near; lay hand on heart, advise. And you be mine, I’ll give you to my friend; And you be not, hang, beg, starve, die in the streets, For by my soul, I’ll ne’er acknowledge thee, Nor what is mine shall never do thee good. Trust to’t, bethink you, I’ll not be forsworn.
cards.whyThisWorks: Capulet's ultimatum—disown Juliet if she refuses Paris—creates a conflict that strips Juliet of family protection and forces her toward desperate action, adding a layer of meaning about patriarchal power and its consequences for young women.
cards.skillStrategy: When a character makes a decision or delivers an ultimatum, ask what it forces the other character to do and what that reveals about the deeper theme.
evidencePoints: 'hang, beg, starve, die in the streets, / For by my soul, I'll ne'er acknowledge thee'
'And you be mine, I'll give you to my friend; / And you be not, hang, beg, starve, die in the streets'
cards.question: Capulet tells Juliet, 'And you be not, hang, beg, starve, die in the streets, / For by my soul, I'll ne'er acknowledge thee.' How does this ultimatum add a deeper layer of meaning to the play's conflict?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Capulet's anger reveals that he has always resented Juliet's ingratitude, suggesting the father-daughter relationship was never loving.

choices.label: B
choices.text: By threatening to cast Juliet out with nothing, Capulet transforms a private family disagreement into a life-or-death crisis, showing that parental authority—not just the feud—traps Juliet with no safe path forward.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Capulet's ultimatum demonstrates that he values Paris's noble rank above his own daughter's happiness, making his character purely villainous from this point on.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The threat of poverty and homelessness shows that Juliet's real conflict is financial, since losing her father's wealth is what ultimately drives her decisions.

cards.standardTitle: Figurative language effect
cards.excerpt:
JULIET. O God! O Nurse, how shall this be prevented? My husband is on earth, my faith in heaven. How shall that faith return again to earth, Unless that husband send it me from heaven By leaving earth? Comfort me, counsel me. Alack, alack, that heaven should practise stratagems Upon so soft a subject as myself. What say’st thou? Hast thou not a word of joy? Some comfort, Nurse.

NURSE. Faith, here it is. Romeo is banished; and all the world to nothing That he dares ne’er come back to challenge you. Or if he do, it needs must be by stealth. Then, since the case so stands as now it doth, I think it best you married with the County. O, he’s a lovely gentleman. Romeo’s a dishclout to him. An eagle, madam, Hath not so green, so quick, so fair an eye As Paris hath. Beshrew my very heart, I think you are happy in this second match, For it excels your first: or if it did not, Your first is dead, or ’twere as good he were, As living here and you no use of him.
cards.whyThisWorks: The Nurse's comparison 'Romeo's a dishclout to him' alongside the eagle simile provides a clear, context-supported figurative expression students can analyze for meaning and effect without outside knowledge.
cards.skillStrategy: When you spot a comparison or symbol, ask what quality the writer is emphasizing and what attitude that reveals about the speaker.
evidencePoints: Romeo's a dishclout to him.
An eagle, madam, Hath not so green, so quick, so fair an eye As Paris hath.
cards.question: Read the Nurse's lines: 'Romeo's a dishclout to him. An eagle, madam, Hath not so green, so quick, so fair an eye As Paris hath.' What do these two figurative comparisons together reveal about the Nurse's view of Romeo?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Romeo is dangerous and unpredictable, like a soiled cloth that could spread disease, while Paris is noble and restrained like a caged eagle.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Romeo is dull and worthless compared to Paris, who possesses a sharpness and vitality that Romeo entirely lacks.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Romeo was once admirable but has been ruined by banishment, just as a clean cloth becomes a dishclout through hard use.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Romeo and Paris are equally matched in worth, but Paris has the advantage of being present while Romeo is absent.

cards.standardTitle: Key literary elements add layers of meaning
cards.excerpt: FRIAR LAWRENCE. The grey-ey’d morn smiles on the frowning night, Chequering the eastern clouds with streaks of light; And fleckled darkness like a drunkard reels From forth day’s pathway, made by Titan’s fiery wheels Now, ere the sun advance his burning eye, The day to cheer, and night’s dank dew to dry, I must upfill this osier cage of ours With baleful weeds and precious-juiced flowers. The earth that’s nature’s mother, is her tomb; What is her burying grave, that is her womb: And from her womb children of divers kind We sucking on her natural bosom find. Many for many virtues excellent, None but for some, and yet all different. O, mickle is the powerful grace that lies In plants, herbs, stones, and their true qualities. For naught so vile that on the earth doth live But to the earth some special good doth give; Nor aught so good but, strain’d from that fair use, Revolts from true birth, stumbling on abuse. Virtue itself turns vice being misapplied, And vice sometime’s by action dignified.
cards.whyThisWorks: Friar Lawrence's speech about plants that can heal or poison depending on their use foreshadows the play's central conflict—that the same love potion scheme meant to unite Romeo and Juliet will ultimately destroy them—making his philosophical observation a structural turning point that deepens the tragedy's meaning.
cards.skillStrategy: When a character makes a decision or states a belief, ask yourself: how does this moment connect to what goes wrong later, and what deeper idea does that connection reveal?
evidencePoints: Virtue itself turns vice being misapplied
Nor aught so good but, strain'd from that fair use, Revolts from true birth, stumbling on abuse
cards.question: Friar Lawrence observes that 'Virtue itself turns vice being misapplied, / And vice sometime's by action dignified.' How does this statement add a deeper layer of meaning to the play's central conflict?

choices.label: A
choices.text: It establishes that Friar Lawrence is a skilled herbalist whose knowledge of plants makes him a trustworthy advisor to Romeo, justifying Romeo's decision to seek his help.

choices.label: B
choices.text: It foreshadows that Friar Lawrence's well-intentioned plan to help Romeo and Juliet will cause destruction precisely because a good purpose, misapplied, becomes the source of tragedy.

choices.label: C
choices.text: It suggests that the feud between the Montagues and Capulets began as something virtuous but was corrupted over time by the families' refusal to seek peace.

choices.label: D
choices.text: It reveals that Friar Lawrence secretly doubts whether Romeo's love for Juliet is genuine, and he gathers herbs as a way to test Romeo's true intentions before agreeing to help.

If in thy wisdom, thou canst give no help, Do thou but call my resolution wise, And with this knife I’ll help it presently. God join’d my heart and Romeo’s, thou our hands; And ere this hand, by thee to Romeo’s seal’d, Shall be the label to another deed, Or my true heart with treacherous revolt Turn to another, this shall slay them both. Therefore, out of thy long-experienc’d time, Give me some present counsel, or behold ’Twixt my extremes and me this bloody knife Shall play the empire, arbitrating that Which the commission of thy years and art Could to no issue of true honour bring. Be not so long to speak. I long to die, If what thou speak’st speak not of remedy.
cards.whyThisWorks: Juliet's extended metaphor of the knife as an 'empire' and 'arbitrating' force, combined with her direct threat of self-destruction, gives students clear figurative language tied to a measurable mood of desperate urgency.
cards.skillStrategy: Find the figurative language, name the feeling it creates, then check which answer choice pairs the correct mood word with a direct quote from the passage.

Be not so long to speak. I long to die, / If what thou speak'st speak not of remedy.
cards.question: Read Juliet's lines: "'Twixt my extremes and me this bloody knife / Shall play the empire, arbitrating that / Which the commission of thy years and art / Could to no issue of true honour bring." How does this figurative language contribute to the mood of the scene?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Describing the knife as a ruler who settles disputes creates a mood of calm resignation, suggesting Juliet has already accepted that death is her only dignified option.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Personifying the knife as an empire and judge creates a mood of desperate urgency, framing Juliet's threatened suicide as the only authority powerful enough to resolve what the Friar's wisdom cannot.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Comparing the knife to a governing empire creates a mood of bitter anger directed at the Friar, blaming his failure of wisdom for forcing Juliet into an impossible situation.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Elevating the knife to the role of an empire creates a mood of solemn reverence, honoring the sacred bond between Juliet and Romeo that the Friar himself sealed.

cards.standardTitle: Key literary elements add layers of meaning
cards.excerpt: But soft, what light through yonder window breaks? It is the east, and Juliet is the sun! Arise fair sun and kill the envious moon, Who is already sick and pale with grief, That thou her maid art far more fair than she. Be not her maid since she is envious; Her vestal livery is but sick and green, And none but fools do wear it; cast it off. It is my lady, O it is my love! O, that she knew she were! She speaks, yet she says nothing. What of that? Her eye discourses, I will answer it. I am too bold, ’tis not to me she speaks. Two of the fairest stars in all the heaven, Having some business, do entreat her eyes To twinkle in their spheres till they return. What if her eyes were there, they in her head? The brightness of her cheek would shame those stars, As daylight doth a lamp; her eyes in heaven Would through the airy region stream so bright That birds would sing and think it were not night. See how she leans her cheek upon her hand. O that I were a glove upon that hand, That I might touch that cheek.
cards.whyThisWorks: Romeo's internal conflict between bold desire and fearful restraint—captured in 'I am too bold, 'tis not to me she speaks'—adds a layer of meaning about the danger of loving someone who does not yet know you love them, deepening the tragedy of the play's central relationship.
cards.skillStrategy: When a character makes a decision or holds back from one, ask what that moment reveals about the deeper stakes or meaning of the conflict.
evidencePoints: I am too bold, 'tis not to me she speaks.
O that I were a glove upon that hand, That I might touch that cheek.
cards.question: Romeo says, 'I am too bold, 'tis not to me she speaks,' and then retreats into silent longing rather than calling out to Juliet. What deeper meaning does this moment of restraint add to the scene?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Romeo's silence shows he has decided Juliet is unworthy of his attention, which foreshadows his eventual rejection of her.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Romeo's inability to act on his feelings reveals that his love exists in a space of longing and distance, suggesting the relationship is built on desire for something just out of reach rather than mutual connection.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Romeo holds back because he is distracted by the beauty of the stars and the moon, showing that nature matters more to him than Juliet does.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Romeo's restraint proves he is a cautious and practical person who carefully weighs consequences before speaking.

cards.standardTitle: Theme development across a literary text
cards.excerpt:
MERCUTIO. Nay, I’ll conjure too. Romeo! Humours! Madman! Passion! Lover! Appear thou in the likeness of a sigh, Speak but one rhyme, and I am satisfied; Cry but ‘Ah me!’ Pronounce but Love and dove; Speak to my gossip Venus one fair word, One nickname for her purblind son and heir, Young Abraham Cupid, he that shot so trim When King Cophetua lov’d the beggar-maid. He heareth not, he stirreth not, he moveth not; The ape is dead, and I must conjure him. I conjure thee by Rosaline’s bright eyes, By her high forehead and her scarlet lip, By her fine foot, straight leg, and quivering thigh, And the demesnes that there adjacent lie, That in thy likeness thou appear to us.

BENVOLIO. An if he hear thee, thou wilt anger him.

MERCUTIO. This cannot anger him. ’Twould anger him To raise a spirit in his mistress’ circle, Of some strange nature, letting it there stand Till she had laid it, and conjur’d it down; That were some spite. My invocation Is fair and honest, and, in his mistress’ name, I conjure only but to raise up him.

BENVOLIO. Come, he hath hid himself among these trees To be consorted with the humorous night. Blind is his love, and best befits the dark.

MERCUTIO. If love be blind, love cannot hit the mark. Now will he sit under a medlar tree, And wish his mistress were that kind of fruit As maids call medlars when they laugh alone. O Romeo, that she were, O that she were An open-arse and thou a poperin pear! Romeo, good night. I’ll to my truckle-bed. This field-bed is too cold for me to sleep. Come, shall we go?
cards.whyThisWorks: Two distinct moments—Mercutio's mock-conjuring of Romeo by Rosaline's physical features and Benvolio's observation that 'blind is his love'—both develop the theme that romantic infatuation distorts reason and perception, giving students two trackable passage moments rather than a single detail.
cards.skillStrategy: Find two separate moments in the passage that point to the same big idea, then ask yourself what both moments are really saying together.
evidencePoints: I conjure thee by Rosaline's bright eyes, / By her high forehead and her scarlet lip, / By her fine foot, straight leg, and quivering thigh
Blind is his love, and best befits the dark.
cards.question: Both Mercutio's conjuring of Romeo by Rosaline's physical features and Benvolio's remark that 'Blind is his love, and best befits the dark' develop which theme about romantic love?

choices.label: A
choices.text: True love requires secrecy and must be hidden from friends who cannot understand it.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Romantic infatuation reduces a person to obsession with physical appearance and clouds clear judgment.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Friendship is ultimately more reliable than romantic love when a person is in distress.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Love poetry and flattery are the only tools available to someone who wants to win another person's affection.

cards.standardTitle: Figurative language effect
cards.excerpt:
JULIET. O God! O Nurse, how shall this be prevented? My husband is on earth, my faith in heaven. How shall that faith return again to earth, Unless that husband send it me from heaven By leaving earth? Comfort me, counsel me. Alack, alack, that heaven should practise stratagems Upon so soft a subject as myself. What say’st thou? Hast thou not a word of joy? Some comfort, Nurse.

NURSE. Faith, here it is. Romeo is banished; and all the world to nothing That he dares ne’er come back to challenge you. Or if he do, it needs must be by stealth. Then, since the case so stands as now it doth, I think it best you married with the County. O, he’s a lovely gentleman. Romeo’s a dishclout to him. An eagle, madam, Hath not so green, so quick, so fair an eye As Paris hath. Beshrew my very heart, I think you are happy in this second match, For it excels your first: or if it did not, Your first is dead, or ’twere as good he were, As living here and you no use of him.
cards.whyThisWorks: The Nurse's comparison of Paris to 'an eagle' with a 'green, so quick, so fair an eye' while calling Romeo 'a dishclout' creates a dismissive, almost callous mood that contrasts sharply with Juliet's desperate grief, giving students a clear figurative language moment tied to a specific emotional effect.
cards.skillStrategy: Find the figurative language, name the feeling it creates, then check which answer choice pairs the correct quote with the correct mood.
evidencePoints: Romeo's a dishclout to him.
An eagle, madam, Hath not so green, so quick, so fair an eye As Paris hath.
cards.question: Read the Nurse's lines: 'Romeo's a dishclout to him. An eagle, madam, / Hath not so green, so quick, so fair an eye / As Paris hath.' How does this figurative language shape the mood of the Nurse's speech?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Comparing Paris to an eagle creates a hopeful mood, suggesting the Nurse genuinely believes Juliet's future with Paris will bring her the same deep love she found with Romeo.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Reducing Romeo to a 'dishclout' while elevating Paris to an eagle creates a coldly pragmatic mood, showing the Nurse's indifference to Juliet's grief as she casually discards the marriage Juliet holds sacred.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Calling Romeo a 'dishclout' creates a sorrowful mood, as the Nurse mourns the loss of Romeo alongside Juliet and uses the comparison to express shared heartbreak.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The eagle comparison creates a tense, fearful mood by warning Juliet that Paris is a powerful figure who could punish her if she refuses to comply with the proposed marriage.

cards.standardTitle: Key literary elements add layers of meaning
cards.excerpt:
Enter Juliet.

JULIET. Gallop apace, you fiery-footed steeds, Towards Phoebus’ lodging. Such a waggoner As Phaeton would whip you to the west And bring in cloudy night immediately. Spread thy close curtain, love-performing night, That runaway’s eyes may wink, and Romeo Leap to these arms, untalk’d of and unseen. Lovers can see to do their amorous rites By their own beauties: or, if love be blind, It best agrees with night. Come, civil night, Thou sober-suited matron, all in black, And learn me how to lose a winning match, Play’d for a pair of stainless maidenhoods. Hood my unmann’d blood, bating in my cheeks, With thy black mantle, till strange love, grow bold, Think true love acted simple modesty. Come, night, come Romeo; come, thou day in night; For thou wilt lie upon the wings of night Whiter than new snow upon a raven’s back. Come gentle night, come loving black-brow’d night, Give me my Romeo, and when I shall die, Take him and cut him out in little stars, And he will make the face of heaven so fine That all the world will be in love with night, And pay no worship to the garish sun. O, I have bought the mansion of a love, But not possess’d it; and though I am sold, Not yet enjoy’d. So tedious is this day As is the night before some festival To an impatient child that hath new robes And may not wear them. O, here comes my Nurse, And she brings news, and every tongue that speaks But Romeo’s name speaks heavenly eloquence.
cards.whyThisWorks: Juliet's anguished waiting—captured in her comparison of the day to 'the night before some festival / To an impatient child'—is a plot moment of suspended anticipation that deepens the tragedy by showing how her joy is already shadowed by urgency and vulnerability before Romeo even arrives.
cards.skillStrategy: When a character is caught between wanting something and not yet having it, ask what that gap reveals about the deeper stakes of the story.
evidencePoints: I have bought the mansion of a love, But not possess'd it; and though I am sold, Not yet enjoy'd.
So tedious is this day As is the night before some festival To an impatient child that hath new robes And may not wear them.
cards.question: Juliet compares herself to 'an impatient child that hath new robes / And may not wear them' while waiting for Romeo. What deeper meaning does this moment of suspended anticipation add to the scene?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Juliet's childlike excitement shows she is too immature to understand the seriousness of her secret marriage, suggesting the union is built on naivety rather than genuine love.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The gap between Juliet's complete emotional commitment—'bought' and 'sold'—and her inability to possess that love yet reveals how fragile and exposed her happiness is, deepening the sense that joy in this play is always on the edge of being lost.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Juliet's frustration with the slow passage of time shows that her primary concern is physical desire rather than any lasting emotional bond with Romeo.

choices.label: D
choices.text: By comparing the day to a festival eve, Juliet signals that her marriage to Romeo will ultimately be a public celebration, contrasting with the secrecy she calls for earlier in the speech.

cards.standardTitle: Theme development across a literary text
cards.excerpt:
JULIET. Wilt thou be gone? It is not yet near day. It was the nightingale, and not the lark, That pierc’d the fearful hollow of thine ear; Nightly she sings on yond pomegranate tree. Believe me, love, it was the nightingale.

ROMEO. It was the lark, the herald of the morn, No nightingale. Look, love, what envious streaks Do lace the severing clouds in yonder east. Night’s candles are burnt out, and jocund day Stands tiptoe on the misty mountain tops. I must be gone and live, or stay and die.

JULIET. Yond light is not daylight, I know it, I. It is some meteor that the sun exhales To be to thee this night a torchbearer And light thee on thy way to Mantua. Therefore stay yet, thou need’st not to be gone.

ROMEO. Let me be ta’en, let me be put to death, I am content, so thou wilt have it so. I’ll say yon grey is not the morning’s eye, ’Tis but the pale reflex of Cynthia’s brow. Nor that is not the lark whose notes do beat The vaulty heaven so high above our heads. I have more care to stay than will to go. Come, death, and welcome. Juliet wills it so. How is’t, my soul? Let’s talk. It is not day.

JULIET. It is, it is! Hie hence, be gone, away. It is the lark that sings so out of tune, Straining harsh discords and unpleasing sharps. Some say the lark makes sweet division; This doth not so, for she divideth us. Some say the lark and loathed toad change eyes. O, now I would they had chang’d voices too, Since arm from arm that voice doth us affray, Hunting thee hence with hunt’s-up to the day. O now be gone, more light and light it grows.
cards.whyThisWorks: The scene contains two distinct moments—Juliet calling daylight 'some meteor' to keep Romeo, then calling the lark's song 'harsh discords' that 'divideth us' to send him away—that together show love cannot override reality, requiring students to track theme across moments rather than reading one speech in isolation.
cards.skillStrategy: Find two separate moments in the passage where a character's words or actions point to the same idea, then ask what message both moments together are building.
evidencePoints: Yond light is not daylight, I know it, I. / It is some meteor that the sun exhales / To be to thee this night a torchbearer
It is the lark that sings so out of tune, / Straining harsh discords and unpleasing sharps. / This doth not so, for she divideth us.
cards.question: In the third paragraph, Juliet claims the light is 'some meteor' so Romeo will stay, but in the fifth paragraph she calls the lark's song 'harsh discords' that 'divideth us' and commands Romeo to 'be gone.' How do these two moments work together to develop a theme?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Juliet's attempt to rename the meteor and her curse on the lark's voice both show that she is more emotionally unstable than Romeo, developing the theme that grief destroys clear thinking.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Juliet's reinterpretation of daylight as a meteor and her later admission that the lark 'divideth us' together show that desire can only briefly delay the truth—love cannot stop reality from forcing the lovers apart.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Juliet's claim about the meteor and her complaint about the lark both develop the theme that nature is a cruel force that deliberately targets those who love each other.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Juliet's willingness to deceive Romeo about the light and her sudden reversal in the fifth paragraph develop the theme that loyalty in love requires sacrifice, since she ultimately puts Romeo's survival above her own wishes.

cards.standardTitle: Figurative language effect
cards.excerpt:
JULIET. O God! O Nurse, how shall this be prevented? My husband is on earth, my faith in heaven. How shall that faith return again to earth, Unless that husband send it me from heaven By leaving earth? Comfort me, counsel me. Alack, alack, that heaven should practise stratagems Upon so soft a subject as myself. What say’st thou? Hast thou not a word of joy? Some comfort, Nurse.

NURSE. Faith, here it is. Romeo is banished; and all the world to nothing That he dares ne’er come back to challenge you. Or if he do, it needs must be by stealth. Then, since the case so stands as now it doth, I think it best you married with the County. O, he’s a lovely gentleman. Romeo’s a dishclout to him. An eagle, madam, Hath not so green, so quick, so fair an eye As Paris hath. Beshrew my very heart, I think you are happy in this second match, For it excels your first: or if it did not, Your first is dead, or ’twere as good he were, As living here and you no use of him.
cards.whyThisWorks: Juliet's line 'that heaven should practise stratagems / Upon so soft a subject as myself' personifies heaven as a scheming, calculating force, which deepens the mood of helplessness and betrayal central to the scene.
cards.skillStrategy: When a nonhuman thing is given a human action or feeling, ask yourself what emotion that action creates and how it changes the way the scene feels.
evidencePoints: that heaven should practise stratagems / Upon so soft a subject as myself
My husband is on earth, my faith in heaven
cards.question: Read Juliet's lines: 'Alack, alack, that heaven should practise stratagems / Upon so soft a subject as myself.' How does giving heaven the human action of plotting stratagems shape the mood of this moment?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Heaven is portrayed as a distant, indifferent place, creating a mood of cold emptiness because Juliet feels Romeo has abandoned her there.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Heaven is portrayed as a scheming, deliberate force working against Juliet, creating a mood of helpless victimization in which even the divine seems to conspire against her.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Heaven is portrayed as a protective guardian that Juliet trusts, creating a hopeful mood because she believes her faith will eventually guide Romeo back to her.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Heaven is portrayed as a judge weighing Juliet's choices, creating a mood of guilt because she fears punishment for her secret marriage to Romeo.

cards.standardTitle: Key literary elements add layers of meaning
cards.excerpt: JULIET. Thou knowest the mask of night is on my face, Else would a maiden blush bepaint my cheek For that which thou hast heard me speak tonight. Fain would I dwell on form, fain, fain deny What I have spoke; but farewell compliment. Dost thou love me? I know thou wilt say Ay, And I will take thy word. Yet, if thou swear’st, Thou mayst prove false. At lovers’ perjuries, They say Jove laughs. O gentle Romeo, If thou dost love, pronounce it faithfully. Or if thou thinkest I am too quickly won, I’ll frown and be perverse, and say thee nay, So thou wilt woo. But else, not for the world. In truth, fair Montague, I am too fond; And therefore thou mayst think my ’haviour light: But trust me, gentleman, I’ll prove more true Than those that have more cunning to be strange. I should have been more strange, I must confess, But that thou overheard’st, ere I was ’ware, My true-love passion; therefore pardon me, And not impute this yielding to light love, Which the dark night hath so discovered.
cards.whyThisWorks: Juliet's conflict between social convention ('fain would I dwell on form') and her already-revealed true feelings creates a dramatic reversal that deepens the theme of authenticity versus performance in love.
cards.skillStrategy: When a character faces a conflict between what they feel and what they think they should do, ask what that tension reveals about a larger idea in the text.
evidencePoints: Fain would I dwell on form, fain, fain deny / What I have spoke; but farewell compliment.
I should have been more strange, I must confess, / But that thou overheard'st, ere I was 'ware, / My true-love passion
cards.question: Juliet admits she would have 'been more strange' but instead abandons social form and openly declares her love. How does this decision deepen the meaning of the scene?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Her decision shows she is reckless and does not consider the consequences of confessing love to a Montague, suggesting she is too young to understand the danger.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Her decision reveals that genuine feeling, once exposed by accident, cannot be hidden behind social performance, suggesting that authentic love demands honesty even at personal risk.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Her decision proves she trusts Romeo completely because she has known him long enough to be certain he will not betray her confession.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Her decision demonstrates that she is testing Romeo by pretending to be open so she can later judge whether his love is sincere.

cards.standardTitle: Theme development across a literary text
cards.excerpt:
ROMEO. In bed asleep, while they do dream things true.

MERCUTIO. O, then, I see Queen Mab hath been with you. She is the fairies’ midwife, and she comes In shape no bigger than an agate-stone On the fore-finger of an alderman, Drawn with a team of little atomies Over men’s noses as they lie asleep: Her waggon-spokes made of long spinners’ legs; The cover, of the wings of grasshoppers; Her traces, of the smallest spider’s web; The collars, of the moonshine’s watery beams; Her whip of cricket’s bone; the lash, of film; Her waggoner, a small grey-coated gnat, Not half so big as a round little worm Prick’d from the lazy finger of a maid: Her chariot is an empty hazelnut, Made by the joiner squirrel or old grub, Time out o’ mind the fairies’ coachmakers. And in this state she gallops night by night Through lovers’ brains, and then they dream of love; O’er courtiers’ knees, that dream on curtsies straight; O’er lawyers’ fingers, who straight dream on fees; O’er ladies’ lips, who straight on kisses dream, Which oft the angry Mab with blisters plagues, Because their breaths with sweetmeats tainted are: Sometime she gallops o’er a courtier’s nose, And then dreams he of smelling out a suit; And sometime comes she with a tithe-pig’s tail, Tickling a parson’s nose as a lies asleep, Then dreams he of another benefice: Sometime she driveth o’er a soldier’s neck, And then dreams he of cutting foreign throats, Of breaches, ambuscados, Spanish blades, Of healths five fathom deep; and then anon Drums in his ear, at which he starts and wakes; And, being thus frighted, swears a prayer or two, And sleeps again. This is that very Mab That plats the manes of horses in the night; And bakes the elf-locks in foul sluttish hairs, Which, once untangled, much misfortune bodes: This is the hag, when maids lie on their backs, That presses them, and learns them first to bear, Making them women of good carriage: This is she,—

ROMEO. Peace, peace, Mercutio, peace, Thou talk’st of nothing.
cards.whyThisWorks: Mercutio's Queen Mab speech and Romeo's dismissal ('Thou talk'st of nothing') together develop the theme that dreams and imagination are illusions disconnected from reality, requiring students to track two distinct moments rather than reading either line in isolation.
cards.skillStrategy: When tracking theme, find at least two moments in the passage that point to the same idea, then ask what both moments together are saying about life or human nature.
evidencePoints: She is the fairies' midwife...Through lovers' brains, and then they dream of love; O'er courtiers' knees, that dream on curtsies straight; O'er lawyers' fingers, who straight dream on fees
Thou talk'st of nothing.
cards.question: Read the following two moments from the passage: Mercutio describes Queen Mab riding through the brains of lovers, courtiers, lawyers, and soldiers, causing each to dream of his own desires; then Romeo interrupts with 'Thou talk'st of nothing.' How do these two moments work together to develop a theme?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Each person's dream reflects a unique truth about his character, suggesting that the inner self is revealed most honestly during sleep.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Dreams appear to feel meaningful to the dreamers, yet Romeo's dismissal frames them as empty fantasies, developing the idea that human desires are illusions people mistake for reality.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Mercutio's detailed description of Queen Mab's tiny chariot shows that imagination is a powerful creative force, while Romeo's interruption proves he lacks that same imaginative gift.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The soldier who wakes in fright and the lovers who dream of kisses both show that dreams bring more harm than comfort, warning that sleep itself is dangerous.

cards.standardTitle: Figurative language effect
cards.excerpt:
FRIAR LAWRENCE. O Juliet, I already know thy grief; It strains me past the compass of my wits. I hear thou must, and nothing may prorogue it, On Thursday next be married to this County.

JULIET. Tell me not, Friar, that thou hear’st of this, Unless thou tell me how I may prevent it. If in thy wisdom, thou canst give no help, Do thou but call my resolution wise, And with this knife I’ll help it presently. God join’d my heart and Romeo’s, thou our hands; And ere this hand, by thee to Romeo’s seal’d, Shall be the label to another deed, Or my true heart with treacherous revolt Turn to another, this shall slay them both. Therefore, out of thy long-experienc’d time, Give me some present counsel, or behold ’Twixt my extremes and me this bloody knife Shall play the empire, arbitrating that Which the commission of thy years and art Could to no issue of true honour bring. Be not so long to speak. I long to die, If what thou speak’st speak not of remedy.
cards.whyThisWorks: Juliet personifies the knife as 'the empire' that will 'play the arbitrator' between her and her extremes, giving a weapon the human role of a judge or ruler, which sharpens the scene's mood of desperate, cornered resolve.
cards.skillStrategy: When a nonhuman thing is given a human role or action, ask what that role suggests about the character's emotional state and the scene's overall feeling.
evidencePoints: 'Twixt my extremes and me this bloody knife / Shall play the empire, arbitrating that / Which the commission of thy years and art / Could to no issue of true honour bring.
If what thou speak'st speak not of remedy.
cards.question:
Read the following lines from Juliet's speech:

"'Twixt my extremes and me this bloody knife / Shall play the empire, arbitrating that / Which the commission of thy years and art / Could to no issue of true honour bring."

How does giving the knife the human role of an empire and arbitrator shape the mood of this moment?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The knife is cast as a wise counselor, creating a mood of calm deliberation as Juliet waits patiently for the Friar's guidance.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The knife is cast as a sovereign judge with final authority over Juliet's fate, creating a mood of desperate urgency in which death feels like the only power left to her.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The knife is cast as a loyal companion, creating a mood of comfort as Juliet feels supported in her decision to accept the marriage.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The knife is cast as a symbol of the Friar's failure, creating a mood of bitter accusation directed entirely at him rather than at Juliet's own circumstances.

cards.excerpt:

cards.skillStrategy: When you spot repeated words or contrasting ideas close together, ask yourself: what emotion or pressure does this create for the reader, and how does it shape your understanding of the speaker's situation?

Give me some present counsel, or behold / 'Twixt my extremes and me this bloody knife / Shall play the empire
cards.question: Read these lines from Juliet's speech: 'Be not so long to speak. I long to die.' How does the repetition of the word 'long' in these consecutive lines affect the reader?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The repeated word 'long' emphasizes how much time Friar Lawrence has wasted in his life, making the reader lose trust in his ability to help Juliet.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The shift from 'long' meaning delay to 'long' meaning desire creates a jarring contrast that intensifies the reader's sense of Juliet's desperation and the knife-edge urgency of her ultimatum.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The repeated word 'long' slows the pace of Juliet's speech, signaling to the reader that she is uncertain about whether she truly wants to die.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The repetition of 'long' mirrors Friar Lawrence's earlier hesitation, showing the reader that Juliet has adopted his cautious way of speaking.

cards.standardTitle: Key literary elements add layers of meaning
cards.excerpt:
MERCUTIO. Nay, I’ll conjure too. Romeo! Humours! Madman! Passion! Lover! Appear thou in the likeness of a sigh, Speak but one rhyme, and I am satisfied; Cry but ‘Ah me!’ Pronounce but Love and dove; Speak to my gossip Venus one fair word, One nickname for her purblind son and heir, Young Abraham Cupid, he that shot so trim When King Cophetua lov’d the beggar-maid. He heareth not, he stirreth not, he moveth not; The ape is dead, and I must conjure him. I conjure thee by Rosaline’s bright eyes, By her high forehead and her scarlet lip, By her fine foot, straight leg, and quivering thigh, And the demesnes that there adjacent lie, That in thy likeness thou appear to us.

BENVOLIO. An if he hear thee, thou wilt anger him.

MERCUTIO. This cannot anger him. ’Twould anger him To raise a spirit in his mistress’ circle, Of some strange nature, letting it there stand Till she had laid it, and conjur’d it down; That were some spite. My invocation Is fair and honest, and, in his mistress’ name, I conjure only but to raise up him.

BENVOLIO. Come, he hath hid himself among these trees To be consorted with the humorous night. Blind is his love, and best befits the dark.

MERCUTIO. If love be blind, love cannot hit the mark. Now will he sit under a medlar tree, And wish his mistress were that kind of fruit As maids call medlars when they laugh alone. O Romeo, that she were, O that she were An open-arse and thou a poperin pear! Romeo, good night. I’ll to my truckle-bed. This field-bed is too cold for me to sleep. Come, shall we go?
cards.whyThisWorks: Mercutio's failed attempt to conjure Romeo back—mocking his lovesickness for Rosaline while Romeo has already fallen for Juliet—creates dramatic irony and deepens the theme that blind, obsessive love isolates people from their closest bonds.
cards.skillStrategy: When a character's action fails or goes unanswered, ask what that failure reveals about the deeper conflict or theme the author is building.
evidencePoints: He heareth not, he stirreth not, he moveth not; The ape is dead, and I must conjure him.
Blind is his love, and best befits the dark.
cards.question: Mercutio calls out to Romeo repeatedly, yet Romeo neither answers nor returns. What does Romeo's silence and absence add to the meaning of this scene?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Romeo's refusal to respond shows that he is angry with Mercutio for mocking Rosaline, suggesting their friendship has already broken down beyond repair.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Romeo's silence reveals that love has pulled him away from his companions into isolation, suggesting that passionate love separates a person from reason and community.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Romeo's absence proves he has already forgotten Rosaline entirely, showing that his love was never serious and that Mercutio's mockery is fully justified.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Romeo's failure to answer Mercutio demonstrates that he fears being teased, implying that shame, not love, is the central conflict driving his behavior in this scene.

cards.question: In the final speech, Juliet reverses her earlier argument and urges Romeo to leave. How does this reversal develop a theme about love?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Juliet's sudden change shows that her love for Romeo was never strong enough to make her risk the consequences of keeping him near.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Juliet's acceptance that the lark 'divideth us' reveals that love, no matter how powerful, cannot protect the people who share it from forces that threaten to destroy them.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Juliet's willingness to send Romeo away proves that she values his safety more than her own feelings, suggesting that true love requires one partner to sacrifice everything.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Juliet's anger at the lark's 'harsh discords' shows that nature itself is indifferent to human suffering, which is the scene's central theme.

cards.skillStrategy: When you spot a comparison or analogy, ask yourself what feeling or idea the author wants you to walk away with — and whether that feeling matches or clashes with the character's situation.

cards.question: In her speech, the Nurse compares Romeo to a 'dishclout' and Paris to an eagle with a 'green, so quick, so fair an eye.' How does this analogy affect the reader?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The analogy reassures the reader that the Nurse has carefully weighed both men's characters and arrived at a wise, trustworthy conclusion about Juliet's future.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The analogy reveals the Nurse's shallow judgment and creates a sense of betrayal, as she reduces Juliet's devoted husband to a dirty rag while praising Paris based only on his appearance.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The analogy shows that the Nurse genuinely grieves Romeo's banishment but feels obligated to encourage Juliet to move forward for practical reasons.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The analogy emphasizes that Paris is a dangerous rival who threatens Romeo's claim to Juliet, building suspense about whether Romeo will return to challenge him.
