cards.question: At the start of the excerpt Romeo says he dreams 'things true,' but at the end he tells Mercutio, 'Thou talk'st of nothing.' What deeper meaning does this conflict between the two characters add to the scene?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Romeo's dismissal proves he has stopped believing in dreams entirely, suggesting he is a purely rational character who will make careful decisions throughout the play.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Romeo's insistence that dreams reveal truth, set against Mercutio's portrait of dreams as meaningless fairy tricks, exposes Romeo's dangerous tendency to trust illusions—a flaw that will drive his later tragic choices.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Mercutio's long speech about Queen Mab shows that he, not Romeo, is the more superstitious character, so Romeo's interruption simply corrects a factual misunderstanding about how dreams work.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The conflict reveals that both characters agree dreams are unimportant, and their brief exchange is meant only to introduce the fairy world as a lighthearted contrast to the feud between their families.

cards.standardTitle: Theme development across a literary text
cards.excerpt: FRIAR LAWRENCE. Hold then. Go home, be merry, give consent To marry Paris. Wednesday is tomorrow; Tomorrow night look that thou lie alone, Let not thy Nurse lie with thee in thy chamber. Take thou this vial, being then in bed, And this distilled liquor drink thou off, When presently through all thy veins shall run A cold and drowsy humour; for no pulse Shall keep his native progress, but surcease. No warmth, no breath shall testify thou livest, The roses in thy lips and cheeks shall fade To paly ashes; thy eyes’ windows fall, Like death when he shuts up the day of life. Each part depriv’d of supple government, Shall stiff and stark and cold appear like death. And in this borrow’d likeness of shrunk death Thou shalt continue two and forty hours, And then awake as from a pleasant sleep. Now when the bridegroom in the morning comes To rouse thee from thy bed, there art thou dead. Then as the manner of our country is, In thy best robes, uncover’d, on the bier, Thou shalt be borne to that same ancient vault Where all the kindred of the Capulets lie. In the meantime, against thou shalt awake, Shall Romeo by my letters know our drift, And hither shall he come, and he and I Will watch thy waking, and that very night Shall Romeo bear thee hence to Mantua. And this shall free thee from this present shame, If no inconstant toy nor womanish fear Abate thy valour in the acting it.
cards.whyThisWorks: Friar Lawrence's plan introduces a high-stakes conflict between Juliet's desperate situation and the dangerous consequences of a deceptive scheme, directly developing the theme that desperate measures taken to escape social pressure carry grave and uncontrollable risks.
cards.skillStrategy: When identifying theme through conflict or consequence, ask yourself: what does a character risk or lose because of the choice made here, and what idea about life does that risk reveal?
evidencePoints: And this shall free thee from this present shame, If no inconstant toy nor womanish fear Abate thy valour in the acting it.
In the meantime, against thou shalt awake, Shall Romeo by my letters know our drift
cards.question: Friar Lawrence's plan depends on a chain of events working perfectly, yet he warns Juliet that 'no inconstant toy nor womanish fear' must interfere. How does this conflict between the plan's fragility and the pressure placed on Juliet develop a theme in the play?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Because Friar Lawrence reassures Juliet that the potion is completely safe, the scene suggests that trust in authority figures always leads to positive outcomes.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Because the plan requires flawless execution yet rests on Juliet suppressing her fear and on Romeo receiving a letter in time, the scene develops the theme that desperate attempts to escape social pressure create consequences that quickly exceed anyone's control.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Because Friar Lawrence instructs Juliet to 'be merry, give consent to marry Paris,' the scene suggests that deception practiced for a good cause is morally justified and free of serious consequence.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Because Juliet will awaken in the Capulet vault surrounded by her kindred, the scene develops the theme that family loyalty ultimately overcomes the conflicts created by young love.

cards.standardTitle: Rhetoric and reader effect
cards.excerpt:
ROMEO. Then plainly know my heart’s dear love is set On the fair daughter of rich Capulet. As mine on hers, so hers is set on mine; And all combin’d, save what thou must combine By holy marriage. When, and where, and how We met, we woo’d, and made exchange of vow, I’ll tell thee as we pass; but this I pray, That thou consent to marry us today.

FRIAR LAWRENCE. Holy Saint Francis! What a change is here! Is Rosaline, that thou didst love so dear, So soon forsaken? Young men’s love then lies Not truly in their hearts, but in their eyes. Jesu Maria, what a deal of brine Hath wash’d thy sallow cheeks for Rosaline! How much salt water thrown away in waste, To season love, that of it doth not taste. The sun not yet thy sighs from heaven clears, Thy old groans yet ring in mine ancient ears. Lo here upon thy cheek the stain doth sit Of an old tear that is not wash’d off yet. If ere thou wast thyself, and these woes thine, Thou and these woes were all for Rosaline, And art thou chang’d? Pronounce this sentence then, Women may fall, when there’s no strength in men.
cards.whyThisWorks: Friar Lawrence's repeated references to Rosaline—'So soon forsaken,' 'all for Rosaline,' 'And art thou chang'd?'—demonstrate how repetition and rhetorical questions work together to challenge Romeo's sincerity and create a tone of skeptical rebuke that students can trace directly to the text.
cards.skillStrategy: When you spot a repeated name, word, or question in a speech, ask yourself: what feeling or idea does the speaker keep hammering, and how does that repetition shape what the reader thinks about the speaker or the target?
evidencePoints: Is Rosaline, that thou didst love so dear, / So soon forsaken?
And art thou chang'd? Pronounce this sentence then, / Women may fall, when there's no strength in men.
cards.question: In Friar Lawrence's speech, he repeatedly names Rosaline and ends with the rhetorical question 'And art thou chang'd?' How do these rhetorical devices affect the reader?

choices.label: A
choices.text: They show that Friar Lawrence has already forgiven Romeo and is simply reminding him of his past so that Romeo can move forward without guilt.

choices.label: B
choices.text: They build a tone of sharp skepticism, making the reader question whether Romeo's love for Juliet is genuine or just another fleeting infatuation like his feeling for Rosaline.

choices.label: C
choices.text: They reveal that Friar Lawrence secretly admires Rosaline and is personally hurt that Romeo has abandoned her so quickly.

choices.label: D
choices.text: They suggest that Friar Lawrence agrees Romeo should marry Juliet, and the repeated name is meant to help Romeo feel confident about his decision.

cards.standardTitle: Key literary elements add layers of meaning
cards.excerpt:
FRIAR LAWRENCE. O Juliet, I already know thy grief; It strains me past the compass of my wits. I hear thou must, and nothing may prorogue it, On Thursday next be married to this County.

JULIET. Tell me not, Friar, that thou hear’st of this, Unless thou tell me how I may prevent it. If in thy wisdom, thou canst give no help, Do thou but call my resolution wise, And with this knife I’ll help it presently. God join’d my heart and Romeo’s, thou our hands; And ere this hand, by thee to Romeo’s seal’d, Shall be the label to another deed, Or my true heart with treacherous revolt Turn to another, this shall slay them both. Therefore, out of thy long-experienc’d time, Give me some present counsel, or behold ’Twixt my extremes and me this bloody knife Shall play the empire, arbitrating that Which the commission of thy years and art Could to no issue of true honour bring. Be not so long to speak. I long to die, If what thou speak’st speak not of remedy.
cards.whyThisWorks: Juliet's first-person voice transforms what could be a plot summary into an urgent, desperate ultimatum, showing students how point of view shapes tone and the reader's emotional stakes.
cards.skillStrategy: Ask yourself: because THIS character is speaking, what do I feel and understand that I would not feel or understand if someone else told this moment?
evidencePoints: Tell me not, Friar, that thou hear'st of this, Unless thou tell me how I may prevent it.
Be not so long to speak. I long to die, If what thou speak'st speak not of remedy.
cards.question: Juliet, not the Friar, speaks the majority of this scene. How does Juliet's point of view shape the reader's understanding of her situation?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Because Juliet addresses the Friar directly, the reader understands that she trusts his judgment completely and expects him to solve her problem without her involvement.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Because Juliet speaks in her own voice, the reader experiences her desperation as an immediate, personal ultimatum rather than as a distant report of her suffering.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Because Juliet controls the conversation, the reader sees her as calm and strategic, carefully planning her next steps rather than acting out of emotion.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Because Juliet speaks before the Friar can respond, the reader understands that she has already accepted the marriage and is simply performing grief for his benefit.

cards.skillStrategy: When tracking theme through conflict, find the moment a character challenges another's choice and ask what truth that challenge reveals about human behavior.

And art thou chang'd? Pronounce this sentence then, / Women may fall, when there's no strength in men.
cards.question: Friar Lawrence responds to Romeo's request by saying, 'Young men's love then lies / Not truly in their hearts, but in their eyes.' How does this conflict between Romeo's urgency and Friar Lawrence's skepticism develop a theme in the passage?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Romeo's willingness to abandon Rosaline so quickly shows that loyalty between friends is more powerful than romantic love.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The clash between Romeo's certainty that his love is real and Friar Lawrence's observation that it is driven by sight rather than the heart develops the theme that unchecked passion can be mistaken for genuine love, with dangerous consequences.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Friar Lawrence's reference to Romeo's tears for Rosaline suggests that Romeo has already suffered enough consequences and deserves happiness with Juliet.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Romeo's request to marry Juliet immediately reveals that the theme of the passage is the importance of religious guidance in making life decisions.

cards.standardTitle: Rhetoric and reader effect
cards.excerpt: JULIET. Shall I speak ill of him that is my husband? Ah, poor my lord, what tongue shall smooth thy name, When I thy three-hours’ wife have mangled it? But wherefore, villain, didst thou kill my cousin? That villain cousin would have kill’d my husband. Back, foolish tears, back to your native spring, Your tributary drops belong to woe, Which you mistaking offer up to joy. My husband lives, that Tybalt would have slain, And Tybalt’s dead, that would have slain my husband. All this is comfort; wherefore weep I then? Some word there was, worser than Tybalt’s death, That murder’d me. I would forget it fain, But O, it presses to my memory Like damned guilty deeds to sinners’ minds. Tybalt is dead, and Romeo banished. That ‘banished,’ that one word ‘banished,’ Hath slain ten thousand Tybalts. Tybalt’s death Was woe enough, if it had ended there. Or if sour woe delights in fellowship, And needly will be rank’d with other griefs, Why follow’d not, when she said Tybalt’s dead, Thy father or thy mother, nay or both, Which modern lamentation might have mov’d? But with a rear-ward following Tybalt’s death, ‘Romeo is banished’—to speak that word Is father, mother, Tybalt, Romeo, Juliet, All slain, all dead. Romeo is banished, There is no end, no limit, measure, bound, In that word’s death, no words can that woe sound. Where is my father and my mother, Nurse?
cards.whyThisWorks: Juliet's repeated return to the word 'banished' — culminating in 'That one word banished / Hath slain ten thousand Tybalts' — gives students a clear, textually grounded example of how repetition and hyperbole combine to convey overwhelming emotional devastation.
cards.skillStrategy: When you spot a word or phrase repeated with growing intensity, ask yourself: what feeling does that repetition build in the reader, and how does it mirror what the speaker is experiencing?
evidencePoints: That 'banished,' that one word 'banished,' / Hath slain ten thousand Tybalts.
Romeo is banished, / There is no end, no limit, measure, bound, / In that word's death, no words can that woe sound.
cards.question: Read the following lines from Juliet's speech: 'That "banished," that one word "banished," / Hath slain ten thousand Tybalts.' How does Juliet's repetition of the word 'banished' combined with the hyperbole 'ten thousand Tybalts' affect the reader?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The repetition signals that Juliet has accepted Tybalt's death and is now shifting her grief entirely toward Romeo's departure, showing her loyalty to her husband over her family.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The repetition hammers the word into the reader's mind as an unbearable blow, while the exaggerated scale of 'ten thousand Tybalts' makes the reader feel that Romeo's banishment is a loss far greater than any single death.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The repetition creates a sense of confusion in the reader, suggesting that Juliet cannot decide whether Tybalt's death or Romeo's banishment is the worse news.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The hyperbole distances the reader from Juliet's grief by making her reaction seem so extreme that it becomes difficult to take her sorrow seriously.

cards.whyThisWorks: Juliet's sentence beginning 'And ere this hand, by thee to Romeo's seal'd, / Shall be the label to another deed' uses inverted syntax and archaic diction that requires students to untangle clause order and identify the conditional threat embedded in the structure.
cards.skillStrategy: When a sentence feels twisted or backward, identify the subject, verb, and condition separately, then restate each part in plain language before putting the meaning back together.
evidencePoints: And ere this hand, by thee to Romeo's seal'd, Shall be the label to another deed
Or my true heart with treacherous revolt Turn to another, this shall slay them both.
cards.question: Read Juliet's lines: 'And ere this hand, by thee to Romeo's seal'd, / Shall be the label to another deed, / Or my true heart with treacherous revolt / Turn to another, this shall slay them both.' Which restatement most accurately captures the meaning of these lines?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Juliet warns the Friar that her hand and heart have already betrayed Romeo, so she must die to restore her honor.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Before this hand—joined to Romeo's by the Friar—signs a marriage to another man, or before her heart turns unfaithfully away from Romeo, she will kill herself.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Juliet asks the Friar to seal a new agreement between her and Romeo before Thursday so that neither of them will have to die.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Juliet declares that because the Friar married her to Romeo, he alone is responsible if she and Romeo both die.

cards.skillStrategy: Flip the sentence into normal word order and ask: who is doing what, and what does it mean?

Is Rosaline, that thou didst love so dear, / So soon forsaken?
cards.question: Read Friar Lawrence's lines: 'Young men's love then lies / Not truly in their hearts, but in their eyes.' Which restatement most accurately captures the meaning of these lines?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Young men are dishonest about love because they hide their true feelings in their hearts rather than showing them.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Young men's love is not based on deep feeling; it is driven by physical appearance rather than genuine emotion.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Young men fall in love quickly because their hearts and eyes both respond to beauty at the same time.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Young men cannot be trusted in love because they lie to the women they pursue rather than speaking from the heart.

cards.standardTitle: Key literary elements add layers of meaning
cards.excerpt: Oft have I seen, in other days than these, How a dark temper maketh maladies No friend can heal. 'Twas easy to have kept Both land and home. It needed but to accept Unstrivingly the pleasure of our lords. But thou, for mere delight in stormy words, Wilt lose all! . . . Now thy speech provokes not me. Rail on. Of all mankind let Jason be Most evil; none shall check thee. But for these Dark threats cast out against the majesties Of Corinth, count as veriest gain thy path Of exile. I myself, when princely wrath Was hot against thee, strove with all good will To appease the wrath, and wished to keep thee still Beside me. But thy mouth would never stay From vanity, blaspheming night and day Our masters. Therefore thou shalt fly the land. Yet, even so, I will not hold my hand From succouring mine own people. Here am I To help thee, woman, pondering heedfully Thy new state. For I would not have thee flung Provisionless away--aye, and the young Children as well; nor lacking aught that will Of mine can bring thee. Many a lesser ill Hangs on the heels of exile. . . . Aye, and though Thou hate me, dream not that my heart can know Or fashion aught of angry will to thee.
cards.whyThisWorks: Jason's speech reveals his self-serving character through the contradiction between his claim of goodwill toward Medea and his repeated emphasis on her own fault for the exile, showing students how speech can expose a character's true motivations beneath a surface of generosity.
cards.skillStrategy: When a character speaks, ask yourself: does what they say match what they actually do or admit, and what does that gap tell you about who they really are?
evidencePoints: I myself, when princely wrath / Was hot against thee, strove with all good will / To appease the wrath
But thy mouth would never stay / From vanity, blaspheming night and day / Our masters. Therefore thou shalt fly the land.
cards.question: In this passage, Jason claims he 'strove with all good will' to protect Medea, yet repeatedly blames her speech for causing her own exile. What does this contradiction in Jason's words reveal about his character?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Jason is genuinely remorseful about Medea's exile and offers her provisions as proof that he still loves her.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Jason presents himself as a generous protector while shifting all blame onto Medea, exposing his self-justifying nature beneath a show of concern.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Jason is primarily motivated by fear of Corinth's rulers and speaks only to warn Medea about the danger of defying them.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Jason's offer of provisions shows he has fully accepted responsibility for the hardship Medea and her children will face in exile.

cards.standardTitle: Key literary elements add layers of meaning
cards.excerpt:
Ah, Ah, thou Wrath within me! Do not thou, Do not. . . . Down, down, thou tortured thing, and spare My children! They will dwell with us, aye, there Far off, and give thee peace. Too late, too late! By all Hell's living agonies of hate, They shall not take my little ones alive To make their mock with! Howsoe'er I strive The thing is doomed; it shall not escape now From being. Aye, the crown is on the brow, And the robe girt, and in the robe that high Queen dying. I know all. Yet . . . seeing that I Must go so long a journey, and these twain A longer yet and darker, I would fain Speak with them, ere I go.

[_A handmaid brings the_ CHILDREN _out again_.

Come, children; stand A little from me. There. Reach out your hand, Your right hand--so--to mother: and good-bye!

[_She has kept them hitherto at arm's length: but at the touch of their hands, her resolution breaks down, and she gathers them passionately into her arms._

Oh, darling hand! Oh, darling mouth, and eye, And royal mien, and bright brave faces clear, May you be blessed, but not here! What here Was yours, your father stole. . . . Ah God, the glow Of cheek on cheek, the tender touch; and Oh, Sweet scent of childhood. . . . Go! Go! . . . Am I blind? . . . Mine eyes can see not, when I look to find Their places. I am broken by the wings Of evil. . . . Yea, I know to what bad things I go, but louder than all thought doth cry Anger, which maketh man's worst misery.
cards.whyThisWorks: Medea's physical collapse from keeping her children 'at arm's length' to gathering them 'passionately into her arms,' combined with her admission that 'Anger, which maketh man's worst misery' overrides her love, reveals a character torn between maternal tenderness and destructive rage—making characterization the engine of the excerpt's tragic meaning.
cards.skillStrategy: When a character's actions contradict their words or shift suddenly, ask what that contradiction reveals about who they truly are and what the author wants you to understand.
evidencePoints: She has kept them hitherto at arm's length: but at the touch of their hands, her resolution breaks down, and she gathers them passionately into her arms.
Yea, I know to what bad things I go, but louder than all thought doth cry Anger, which maketh man's worst misery.
cards.question: Read the stage direction and Medea's final lines: she keeps her children 'at arm's length,' then 'gathers them passionately into her arms,' and finally declares that Anger cries 'louder than all thought.' What does this sequence of action and speech reveal about Medea?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Medea's physical distance from her children shows she has already hardened her heart and feels no genuine love for them.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Medea's shift from deliberate distance to an embrace, followed by her admission that Anger overpowers thought, reveals a character whose love and destructive rage exist simultaneously—and that rage ultimately dominates her will.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Medea embraces her children because she has changed her mind about harming them and intends to take them with her on her journey.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Medea's breakdown at her children's touch reveals that she is too emotionally weak to carry out any deliberate plan, making her actions unpredictable rather than purposeful.

cards.standardTitle: Text structure and feature purpose
cards.excerpt:
O miserable maiden, all my heart Is torn for thee, so sudden to depart From thy king's chambers and the light above To darkness, all for sake of Jason's love!

Women, my mind is clear. I go to slay My children with all speed, and then, away From hence; not wait yet longer till they stand Beneath another and an angrier hand To die. Yea, howsoe'er I shield them, die They must. And, seeing that they must, 'tis I Shall slay them, I their mother, touched of none Beside. Oh, up and get thine armour on, My heart! Why longer tarry we to win Our crown of dire inevitable sin? Take up thy sword, O poor right hand of mine, Thy sword: then onward to the thin-drawn line Where life turns agony. Let there be naught Of softness now: and keep thee from that thought, 'Born of thy flesh,' 'thine own beloved.' Now, For one brief day, forget thy children: thou Shalt weep hereafter. Though thou slay them, yet Sweet were they. . . . I am sore unfortunate.
cards.whyThisWorks: The second paragraph marks a clear internal shift from Medea's stated resolve to slay her children toward a moment of anguished hesitation, making it a strong model for identifying how a paragraph can both extend and complicate a central idea.
cards.skillStrategy: Ask yourself: does this paragraph keep moving the same idea forward, or does it pull in a new or opposing direction partway through?
evidencePoints: 'Women, my mind is clear. I go to slay / My children with all speed'
'Though thou slay them, yet / Sweet were they. . . . I am sore unfortunate.'
cards.question: What is the primary job of the second paragraph, beginning 'Women, my mind is clear'?

choices.label: A
choices.text: It introduces Medea's hatred of Jason as the reason she has decided to leave the king's chambers.

choices.label: B
choices.text: It opens with Medea's firm declaration to kill her children, then shifts toward grief and doubt as she commands herself to suppress her love for them.

choices.label: C
choices.text: It concludes the conflict by showing that Medea has fully overcome her maternal feelings and is ready to act without regret.

choices.label: D
choices.text: It contrasts Medea's plan with the first paragraph's warning that another, angrier hand will punish her children instead.

cards.question: In the second paragraph, Medea commands her own heart to 'get thine armour on' and orders herself to 'forget thy children.' What do these self-directed commands reveal about her character?

choices.label: A
choices.text: She has already hardened herself completely against her children and feels no grief over her decision.

choices.label: B
choices.text: She is deeply divided, forcing herself toward a violent act she recognizes as sinful while still acknowledging her children's sweetness, showing that her resolve is won through anguish rather than indifference.

choices.label: C
choices.text: She blames Jason entirely for the deaths of her children and sees herself as merely carrying out a punishment he has made unavoidable.

choices.label: D
choices.text: She is uncertain whether to kill her children at all and is still searching for an alternative that would spare them from harm.

cards.standardTitle: Text structure and feature purpose
cards.excerpt:
For one day only leave me in thy land At peace, to find some counsel, ere the strain Of exile fall, some comfort for these twain, Mine innocents; since others take no thought, It seems, to save the babes that they begot. Ah! Thou wilt pity them! Thou also art A father: thou hast somewhere still a heart That feels. . . . I reck not of myself: 'tis they That break me, fallen upon so dire a day.

Mine is no tyrant's mood. Aye, many a time Ere this my tenderness hath marred the chime Of wisest counsels. And I know that now I do mere folly. But so be it! Thou Shalt have this grace . . . But this I warn thee clear, If once the morrow's sunlight find thee here Within my borders, thee or child of thine, Thou diest! . . . Of this judgment not a line Shall waver nor abate. So linger on, If thou needs must, till the next risen sun; No further. . . . In one day there scarce can be Those perils wrought whose dread yet haunteth me.
cards.whyThisWorks: The second paragraph shifts from Medea's emotional plea to Creon's grudging, conditional grant of one day—allowing students to identify how a paragraph can pivot from one speaker's appeal to another character's contrasting response that both concedes and threatens.
cards.skillStrategy: Ask yourself: does this paragraph continue the same idea, or does it turn in a new direction by introducing a different voice, condition, or consequence?
evidencePoints: Mine is no tyrant's mood. Aye, many a time / Ere this my tenderness hath marred the chime / Of wisest counsels.

choices.label: D

cards.standardTitle: Text structure and feature purpose
cards.excerpt:
He loveth to bear bravely ills like these! But, Aegeus, by thy beard, oh, by thy knees, I pray thee, and I give me for thine own, Thy suppliant, pity me! Oh, pity one So miserable. Thou never wilt stand there And see me cast out friendless to despair. Give me a home in Athens . . . by the fire Of thine own hearth! Oh, so may thy desire Of children be fulfilled of God, and thou Die happy! . . . Thou canst know not; even now Thy prize is won! I, I will make of thee A childless man no more. The seed shall be, I swear it, sown. Such magic herbs I know.

Woman, indeed my heart goes forth to show This help to thee, first for religion's sake, Then for thy promised hope, to heal my ache Of childlessness. 'Tis this hath made mine whole Life as a shadow, and starved out my soul. But thus it stands with me. Once make thy way To Attic earth, I, as in law I may, Will keep thee and befriend. But in this land, Where Creon rules, I may not raise my hand To shelter thee. Move of thine own essay To seek my house, there thou shalt alway stay, Inviolate, never to be seized again. But come thyself from Corinth. I would fain Even in foreign eyes be alway just.
cards.whyThisWorks: The second paragraph clearly shifts from Medea's desperate pleading to Aegeus's conditional response, allowing students to identify how a paragraph can pivot from one speaker's emotional appeal to another character's reasoned, qualified agreement.
cards.skillStrategy: Ask yourself: does this paragraph continue the same idea, or does it change direction by introducing a new speaker, condition, or complication?

cards.standardTitle: Text structure and feature purpose
cards.excerpt: Oft have I seen, in other days than these, How a dark temper maketh maladies No friend can heal. 'Twas easy to have kept Both land and home. It needed but to accept Unstrivingly the pleasure of our lords. But thou, for mere delight in stormy words, Wilt lose all! . . . Now thy speech provokes not me. Rail on. Of all mankind let Jason be Most evil; none shall check thee. But for these Dark threats cast out against the majesties Of Corinth, count as veriest gain thy path Of exile. I myself, when princely wrath Was hot against thee, strove with all good will To appease the wrath, and wished to keep thee still Beside me. But thy mouth would never stay From vanity, blaspheming night and day Our masters. Therefore thou shalt fly the land. Yet, even so, I will not hold my hand From succouring mine own people. Here am I To help thee, woman, pondering heedfully Thy new state. For I would not have thee flung Provisionless away--aye, and the young Children as well; nor lacking aught that will Of mine can bring thee. Many a lesser ill Hangs on the heels of exile. . . . Aye, and though Thou hate me, dream not that my heart can know Or fashion aught of angry will to thee.
cards.whyThisWorks: Jason's speech moves through a clear structural arc—opening with blame, shifting to a declaration of non-retaliation, and closing with an offer of material aid—giving students a rich single-paragraph model for identifying how a speaker's purpose pivots mid-speech.
cards.skillStrategy: Track the speaker's tone and purpose sentence by sentence; when the subject or attitude changes, ask yourself whether the new section introduces, contrasts, extends, proves, shifts, or concludes the idea before it.
evidencePoints: Rail on. Of all mankind let Jason be Most evil; none shall check thee.
Yet, even so, I will not hold my hand From succouring mine own people.
cards.question: In this speech, Jason first dismisses Medea's anger by saying 'Rail on. Of all mankind let Jason be Most evil; none shall check thee.' What is the primary job of the lines that follow, beginning with 'Yet, even so, I will not hold my hand'?

choices.label: A
choices.text: They extend Jason's accusation that Medea's 'stormy words' caused her own exile, reinforcing his earlier blame.

choices.label: B
choices.text: They shift Jason's focus from dismissing Medea's rage to presenting himself as a generous provider who will still supply her and the children with material support.

choices.label: C
choices.text: They conclude Jason's argument by proving that Medea's blasphemy against Corinth's rulers was the sole reason for her banishment.

choices.label: D

cards.excerpt:
The sons of Erechtheus, the olden, Whom high gods planted of yore In an old land of heaven upholden, A proud land untrodden of war: They are hungered, and, lo, their desire With wisdom is fed as with meat: In their skies is a shining of fire, A joy in the fall of their feet: And thither, with manifold dowers, From the North, from the hills, from the morn, The Muses did gather their powers, That a child of the Nine should be born; And Harmony, sown as the flowers, Grew gold in the acres of corn.

And Cephisus, the fair-flowing river-- The Cyprian dipping her hand Hath drawn of his dew, and the shiver Of her touch is as joy in the land. For her breathing in fragrance is written, And in music her path as she goes, And the cloud of her hair, it is litten With stars of the wind-woven rose. So fareth she ever and ever, And forth of her bosom is blown, As dews on the winds of the river, An hunger of passions unknown. Strong Loves of all godlike endeavour, Whom Wisdom shall throne on her throne.
cards.whyThisWorks: The Cyprian (Aphrodite) is characterized through sensory description and divine action—dipping her hand in the river, breathing fragrance, scattering rose-stars—which reveals her as a force that transforms earthly desire into wisdom-guided love, adding thematic meaning about the relationship between passion and reason.

choices.label: A

choices.label: B

choices.label: C

choices.label: D

cards.standardTitle: Text structure and feature purpose
cards.excerpt: 'Tis not the first nor second time, O King, That fame hath hurt me, and come nigh to bring My ruin. . . . How can any man, whose eyes Are wholesome, seek to rear his children wise Beyond men's wont? Much helplessness in arts Of common life, and in their townsmen's hearts Envy deep-set . . . so much their learning brings! Come unto fools with knowledge of new things, They deem it vanity, not knowledge. Aye, And men that erst for wisdom were held high, Feel thee a thorn to fret them, privily Held higher than they. So hath it been with me. A wise-woman I am; and for that sin To divers ill names men would pen me in; A seed of strife; an eastern dreamer; one Of brand not theirs; one hard to play upon . . . Ah, I am not so wondrous wise!--And now, To thee, I am terrible! What fearest thou? What dire deed? Do I tread so proud a path-- Fear me not thou!--that I should brave the wrath Of princes? Thou: what has thou ever done To wrong me? Granted thine own child to one Whom thy soul chose.--Ah, _him_ out of my heart I hate; but thou, meseems, hast done thy part Not ill. And for thine houses' happiness I hold no grudge. Go: marry, and God bless Your issues. Only suffer me to rest Somewhere within this land. Though sore oppressed, I will be still, knowing mine own defeat.
cards.whyThisWorks: Medea's speech moves through a clear structural shift—from defending her reputation as a wise woman to directly addressing Creon's fear of her—making it an ideal passage for students to identify how a paragraph transitions from one argumentative purpose to another.
cards.skillStrategy: Ask yourself: does the paragraph stay on one idea the whole time, or does it pivot? Look for signal words or a change in who or what is being addressed.
evidencePoints: A wise-woman I am; and for that sin / To divers ill names men would pen me in
Ah, I am not so wondrous wise!--And now, / To thee, I am terrible! What fearest thou?

cards.question: In her speech to Creon, Medea first declares 'A wise-woman I am; and for that sin / To divers ill names men would pen me in,' then immediately says 'Ah, I am not so wondrous wise!' What does this shift reveal about Medea's character?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Medea genuinely doubts her own intelligence after years of being mocked by townspeople and dismissed as an outsider.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Medea is strategically downplaying her power to reduce Creon's fear of her, even as her earlier words confirm she understands exactly why she is perceived as a threat.

cards.standardTitle: Key literary elements add layers of meaning
cards.excerpt: Woman, indeed I praise thee now, nor say Ill of thine other hour. 'Tis nature's way, A woman needs must stir herself to wrath, When work of marriage by so strange a path Crosseth her lord. But thou, thine heart doth wend The happier road. Thou hast seen, ere quite the end, What choice must needs be stronger: which to do Shows a wise-minded woman. . . . And for you, Children; your father never has forgot Your needs. If God but help him, he hath wrought A strong deliverance for your weakness. Yea, I think you, with your brethren, yet one day Shall be the mightiest voices in this land. Do you grow tall and strong. Your father's hand Guideth all else, and whatso power divine Hath alway helped him. . . . Ah, may it be mine To see you yet in manhood, stern of brow, Strong-armed, set high o'er those that hate me. . . . How? Woman, thy face is turned. Thy cheek is swept With pallor of strange tears. Dost not accept Gladly and of good will my benisons?
cards.whyThisWorks: Jason's speech praises Medea for accepting his remarriage while simultaneously ignoring her visible grief, revealing his self-serving blindness and Medea's silent, suppressed anguish through the contrast between his words and her physical reaction.
cards.skillStrategy: When a character's words contradict what another character is physically showing, ask what that gap reveals about both characters' inner states and motivations.
evidencePoints: Woman, thy face is turned. Thy cheek is swept / With pallor of strange tears. Dost not accept / Gladly and of good will my benisons?

cards.question: Read the following lines from the excerpt: 'Woman, thy face is turned. Thy cheek is swept / With pallor of strange tears. Dost not accept / Gladly and of good will my benisons?' What do Jason's words in this moment reveal about his character?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Jason recognizes that Medea is deeply wounded by his remarriage and feels genuine guilt for causing her suffering.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Jason notices Medea's visible grief but immediately reframes it as ingratitude, exposing his inability to see beyond his own self-congratulation.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Jason is confused by Medea's tears because he believes she has already forgiven him and moved past her anger.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Jason questions Medea's emotional reaction in order to warn her that displaying sorrow in public will harm their children's future.

cards.standardTitle: Text structure and feature purpose
cards.excerpt:
Thou woman sullen-eyed and hot with hate Against thy lord, Medea, I here command That thou and thy two children from this land Go forth to banishment. Make no delay: Seeing ourselves, the King, are come this day To see our charge fulfilled; nor shall again Look homeward ere we have led thy children twain And thee beyond our realm's last boundary.

Lost! Lost! Mine haters at the helm with sail flung free Pursuing; and for us no beach nor shore In the endless waters! . . . Yet, though stricken sore, I still will ask thee, for what crime, what thing Unlawful, wilt thou cast me out, O King?

What crime? I fear thee, woman--little need To cloak my reasons--lest thou work some deed Of darkness on my child. And in that fear Reasons enough have part. Thou comest here A wise-woman confessed, and full of lore In unknown ways of evil. Thou art sore In heart, being parted from thy lover's arms. And more, thou hast made menace . . . so the alarms But now have reached mine ear . . . on bride and groom, And him who gave the bride, to work thy doom Of vengeance. Which, ere yet it be too late, I sweep aside. I choose to earn thine hate Of set will now, not palter with the mood Of mercy, and hereafter weep in blood.
cards.whyThisWorks: The three paragraphs have distinct structural jobs—issuing a command, expressing despair and questioning, and justifying the decision—allowing students to analyze how the King's final paragraph proves and extends his earlier decree by supplying explicit reasoning.
cards.skillStrategy: Ask yourself: does this paragraph introduce a new idea, push back on one, or back up something already said? Look for words that signal explanation or proof, like 'because,' 'lest,' or 'reasons.'
evidencePoints: What crime? I fear thee, woman--little need / To cloak my reasons--lest thou work some deed / Of darkness on my child.
I choose to earn thine hate / Of set will now, not palter with the mood / Of mercy, and hereafter weep in blood.
cards.question: What is the primary job of the King's final paragraph, beginning 'What crime? I fear thee, woman'?

choices.label: A
choices.text: It shifts the King's position by showing he now doubts whether banishing Medea is the right choice.

choices.label: B
choices.text: It proves the decree issued in the first paragraph by supplying the King's specific fears and deliberate reasoning for the banishment.

choices.label: C
choices.text: It introduces an entirely new conflict between the King and his daughter's bridegroom that was not present in the earlier paragraphs.

choices.label: D
choices.text: It contrasts the King's public authority with Medea's private grief, suggesting the two characters share equal power in the scene.

choices.label: B

cards.standardTitle: Text structure and feature purpose
cards.excerpt:
Poor, poor right hand of mine, whom he Did cling to, and these knees, so cravingly, We are unclean, thou and I; we have caught the stain Of bad men's flesh . . . and dreamed our dreams in vain. Thou comest to befriend me? Give me, then, Thy counsel. 'Tis not that I dream again For good from thee: but, questioned, thou wilt show The viler. Say: now whither shall I go? Back to my father? Him I did betray, And all his land, when we two fled away. To those poor Peliad maids? For them 'twere good To take me in, who spilled their father's blood. . . . Aye, so my whole life stands! There were at home Who loved me well: to them I am become A curse. And the first friends who sheltered me, Whom most I should have spared, to pleasure thee I have turned to foes. Oh, therefore hast thou laid My crown upon me, blest of many a maid In Hellas, now I have won what all did crave, Thee, the world-wondered lover and the brave; Who this day looks and sees me banished, thrown Away with these two babes, all, all, alone . . . Oh, merry mocking when the lamps are red: "Where go the bridegroom's babes to beg their bread In exile, and the woman who gave all To save him?" O great God, shall gold withal Bear thy clear mark, to sift the base and fine, And o'er man's living visage runs no sign To show the lie within, ere all too late?

Dire and beyond all healing is the hate When hearts that loved are turned to enmity.
cards.whyThisWorks: The final two-line paragraph ('Dire and beyond all healing is the hate / When hearts that loved are turned to enmity') functions as a concluding generalization that distills Medea's personal anguish into a universal truth, making the paragraph's job—to conclude and crystallize—clearly distinguishable from the extended lament that precedes it.
cards.skillStrategy: Ask yourself: does this paragraph start something new, keep building the same idea, or wrap up and leave you with a final thought? Look at how its tone and scope differ from what came before.
evidencePoints: Dire and beyond all healing is the hate / When hearts that loved are turned to enmity.
Oh, therefore hast thou laid / My crown upon me, blest of many a maid / In Hellas . . . Who this day looks and sees me banished, thrown / Away with these two babes, all, all, alone
cards.question: What is the primary job of the final two lines—'Dire and beyond all healing is the hate / When hearts that loved are turned to enmity'—in relation to the long speech that precedes them?

choices.label: A
choices.text: They introduce a new grievance against Jason that Medea has not yet expressed in the speech.

choices.label: B
choices.text: They distill Medea's specific suffering into a universal statement that concludes the emotional argument of the speech.

choices.label: C
choices.text: They shift the focus away from Medea's pain toward a warning directed at Jason about future consequences.

choices.label: D
choices.text: They contrast Medea's current bitterness with an earlier moment in the speech when she still hoped for reconciliation.

cards.standardTitle: Key literary elements add layers of meaning
cards.excerpt:
Poor, poor right hand of mine, whom he Did cling to, and these knees, so cravingly, We are unclean, thou and I; we have caught the stain Of bad men's flesh . . . and dreamed our dreams in vain. Thou comest to befriend me? Give me, then, Thy counsel. 'Tis not that I dream again For good from thee: but, questioned, thou wilt show The viler. Say: now whither shall I go? Back to my father? Him I did betray, And all his land, when we two fled away. To those poor Peliad maids? For them 'twere good To take me in, who spilled their father's blood. . . . Aye, so my whole life stands! There were at home Who loved me well: to them I am become A curse. And the first friends who sheltered me, Whom most I should have spared, to pleasure thee I have turned to foes. Oh, therefore hast thou laid My crown upon me, blest of many a maid In Hellas, now I have won what all did crave, Thee, the world-wondered lover and the brave; Who this day looks and sees me banished, thrown Away with these two babes, all, all, alone . . . Oh, merry mocking when the lamps are red: "Where go the bridegroom's babes to beg their bread In exile, and the woman who gave all To save him?" O great God, shall gold withal Bear thy clear mark, to sift the base and fine, And o'er man's living visage runs no sign To show the lie within, ere all too late?

Dire and beyond all healing is the hate When hearts that loved are turned to enmity.
cards.whyThisWorks: Medea's cataloguing of every person she betrayed or lost—father, the Peliad maids, former friends—reveals a character whose self-awareness deepens her tragedy and shows that her suffering is inseparable from her own choices, adding moral complexity beyond simple victimhood.
cards.skillStrategy: When a character lists their own past actions and their consequences, ask what those actions together reveal about who that character is and what the author wants you to understand about them.
evidencePoints: Him I did betray, And all his land, when we two fled away.
the first friends who sheltered me, Whom most I should have spared, to pleasure thee I have turned to foes.
cards.question: In the excerpt, Medea recounts betraying her father, causing the deaths of the Peliad maids' father, and turning her earliest protectors into enemies. What does this accumulation of self-indictments reveal about her character?

choices.label: A
choices.text: She is unaware of the harm she has caused and blames Jason entirely for the destruction of every relationship she once valued.

choices.label: B
choices.text: She is fully conscious that her own choices dismantled every bond that once protected her, making her isolation a consequence she cannot escape or deny.

choices.label: C
choices.text: She regrets only the loss of social status in Hellas and views her betrayals as minor sacrifices that Jason should have honored.

choices.label: D
choices.text: She catalogues her past to persuade Jason to reconsider the exile, hoping the reminder of her sacrifices will restore his loyalty.

cards.standardTitle: Key literary elements add layers of meaning
cards.excerpt: Woman, indeed I praise thee now, nor say Ill of thine other hour. 'Tis nature's way, A woman needs must stir herself to wrath, When work of marriage by so strange a path Crosseth her lord. But thou, thine heart doth wend The happier road. Thou hast seen, ere quite the end, What choice must needs be stronger: which to do Shows a wise-minded woman. . . . And for you, Children; your father never has forgot Your needs. If God but help him, he hath wrought A strong deliverance for your weakness. Yea, I think you, with your brethren, yet one day Shall be the mightiest voices in this land. Do you grow tall and strong. Your father's hand Guideth all else, and whatso power divine Hath alway helped him. . . . Ah, may it be mine To see you yet in manhood, stern of brow, Strong-armed, set high o'er those that hate me. . . . How? Woman, thy face is turned. Thy cheek is swept With pallor of strange tears. Dost not accept Gladly and of good will my benisons?
cards.whyThisWorks: Jason's oblivious praise of Medea's 'wise' acceptance, followed by his blessing of the children and his sudden notice of her tears and pallor, creates a dramatic reversal that deepens the conflict between his self-serving blindness and Medea's hidden, devastating intentions.
cards.skillStrategy: When a character's words or actions seem to go one way but the passage hints at something darker underneath, ask yourself what that gap reveals about the deeper conflict.
evidencePoints: Thou hast seen, ere quite the end, What choice must needs be stronger: which to do Shows a wise-minded woman.
Woman, thy face is turned. Thy cheek is swept With pallor of strange tears. Dost not accept Gladly and of good will my benisons?
cards.question: Jason praises Medea for accepting his remarriage as 'a wise-minded woman' and then blesses the children, yet the speech ends with his startled observation that Medea's face is pale and wet with tears. What deeper meaning does this moment add to the conflict between Jason and Medea?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Jason's blessing of the children reveals that he genuinely loves them and has no awareness of any danger, which suggests the conflict between him and Medea has already been resolved.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Jason's confident praise of Medea's 'wise' submission, shattered by the sudden sight of her silent tears, exposes how completely he misreads her true state, deepening the conflict by showing that his blindness makes the coming tragedy inevitable.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Medea's tears show that she is moved by Jason's kind words about the children and is beginning to forgive him, so the conflict is shifting toward reconciliation rather than revenge.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Jason's speech focuses on the children's future greatness, which means the central conflict is really about the children's social standing rather than the broken marriage between Jason and Medea.

cards.standardTitle: Key literary elements add layers of meaning
cards.excerpt: Oft have I seen, in other days than these, How a dark temper maketh maladies No friend can heal. 'Twas easy to have kept Both land and home. It needed but to accept Unstrivingly the pleasure of our lords. But thou, for mere delight in stormy words, Wilt lose all! . . . Now thy speech provokes not me. Rail on. Of all mankind let Jason be Most evil; none shall check thee. But for these Dark threats cast out against the majesties Of Corinth, count as veriest gain thy path Of exile. I myself, when princely wrath Was hot against thee, strove with all good will To appease the wrath, and wished to keep thee still Beside me. But thy mouth would never stay From vanity, blaspheming night and day Our masters. Therefore thou shalt fly the land. Yet, even so, I will not hold my hand From succouring mine own people. Here am I To help thee, woman, pondering heedfully Thy new state. For I would not have thee flung Provisionless away--aye, and the young Children as well; nor lacking aught that will Of mine can bring thee. Many a lesser ill Hangs on the heels of exile. . . . Aye, and though Thou hate me, dream not that my heart can know Or fashion aught of angry will to thee.
cards.whyThisWorks: Jason's decision to offer Medea provisions despite her exile—while simultaneously blaming her for bringing it on herself—creates a conflict between self-justification and obligation that reveals his character and deepens the theme of power and betrayal.
cards.skillStrategy: When a character makes a decision during a conflict, ask what that choice reveals about who they are and what the author wants you to understand about a larger idea.
evidencePoints: Yet, even so, I will not hold my hand From succouring mine own people.
thou, for mere delight in stormy words, Wilt lose all!
cards.question: Jason blames Medea for causing her own exile, yet still offers her financial support and provisions for the children. What does this contradiction in Jason's behavior reveal about the deeper conflict in this passage?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Jason's generosity proves he has forgiven Medea and no longer holds her responsible for the tension between them.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Jason uses the appearance of charity to maintain moral superiority while avoiding responsibility for the role his choices played in Medea's ruin.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Jason's offer of provisions shows that he fears Medea's threats and is trying to prevent her from acting against him.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Jason's willingness to help Medea suggests that the conflict between them has been resolved and exile is simply a political necessity.

cards.standardTitle: Text structure and feature purpose
cards.excerpt:
Ah, Ah, thou Wrath within me! Do not thou, Do not. . . . Down, down, thou tortured thing, and spare My children! They will dwell with us, aye, there Far off, and give thee peace. Too late, too late! By all Hell's living agonies of hate, They shall not take my little ones alive To make their mock with! Howsoe'er I strive The thing is doomed; it shall not escape now From being. Aye, the crown is on the brow, And the robe girt, and in the robe that high Queen dying. I know all. Yet . . . seeing that I Must go so long a journey, and these twain A longer yet and darker, I would fain Speak with them, ere I go.

[_A handmaid brings the_ CHILDREN _out again_.

Come, children; stand A little from me. There. Reach out your hand, Your right hand--so--to mother: and good-bye!

[_She has kept them hitherto at arm's length: but at the touch of their hands, her resolution breaks down, and she gathers them passionately into her arms._

Oh, darling hand! Oh, darling mouth, and eye, And royal mien, and bright brave faces clear, May you be blessed, but not here! What here Was yours, your father stole. . . . Ah God, the glow Of cheek on cheek, the tender touch; and Oh, Sweet scent of childhood. . . . Go! Go! . . . Am I blind? . . . Mine eyes can see not, when I look to find Their places. I am broken by the wings Of evil. . . . Yea, I know to what bad things I go, but louder than all thought doth cry Anger, which maketh man's worst misery.
cards.whyThisWorks: The second paragraph—beginning with 'Oh, darling hand!'—shifts from Medea's murderous resolve to an anguished outpouring of maternal love, giving students a clear structural pivot to identify and explain.
cards.skillStrategy: Ask yourself: does this paragraph continue the same idea, or does it turn in a new emotional or logical direction? Look for signal words and changes in tone.
evidencePoints: Oh, darling hand! Oh, darling mouth, and eye, / And royal mien, and bright brave faces clear, / May you be blessed, but not here!
Yea, I know to what bad things / I go, but louder than all thought doth cry / Anger, which maketh man's worst misery.
cards.question: What is the primary job of the paragraph beginning 'Oh, darling hand! Oh, darling mouth, and eye'?

choices.label: A
choices.text: It concludes Medea's internal conflict by showing she has fully accepted her plan and feels no further doubt about harming her children.

choices.label: B
choices.text: It shifts from Medea's hardened resolve to an uncontrollable surge of maternal tenderness, revealing that her love and her rage exist simultaneously and neither fully defeats the other.

choices.label: C
choices.text: It introduces the idea that Medea blames her children's father for all of her suffering and directs her anger entirely outward rather than inward.

choices.label: D
choices.text: It extends Medea's earlier certainty that the crown and robe have already killed the queen, proving her revenge plot is already complete.

cards.standardTitle: Key literary elements add layers of meaning
cards.excerpt:
Thou woman sullen-eyed and hot with hate Against thy lord, Medea, I here command That thou and thy two children from this land Go forth to banishment. Make no delay: Seeing ourselves, the King, are come this day To see our charge fulfilled; nor shall again Look homeward ere we have led thy children twain And thee beyond our realm's last boundary.

Lost! Lost! Mine haters at the helm with sail flung free Pursuing; and for us no beach nor shore In the endless waters! . . . Yet, though stricken sore, I still will ask thee, for what crime, what thing Unlawful, wilt thou cast me out, O King?

What crime? I fear thee, woman--little need To cloak my reasons--lest thou work some deed Of darkness on my child. And in that fear Reasons enough have part. Thou comest here A wise-woman confessed, and full of lore In unknown ways of evil. Thou art sore In heart, being parted from thy lover's arms. And more, thou hast made menace . . . so the alarms But now have reached mine ear . . . on bride and groom, And him who gave the bride, to work thy doom Of vengeance. Which, ere yet it be too late, I sweep aside. I choose to earn thine hate Of set will now, not palter with the mood Of mercy, and hereafter weep in blood.
cards.whyThisWorks: Creon's decision to banish Medea out of preemptive fear—rather than proven wrongdoing—creates a conflict that reveals how power, suspicion, and self-interest drive injustice, adding a deeper layer of meaning about the vulnerability of those without protection.
cards.skillStrategy: When a character makes a decision or takes an action, ask yourself: what does this choice reveal about the deeper ideas the author is exploring beyond the surface event?
evidencePoints: I fear thee, woman--little need / To cloak my reasons--lest thou work some deed / Of darkness on my child.
I choose to earn thine hate / Of set will now, not palter with the mood / Of mercy, and hereafter weep in blood.
cards.question: Creon admits he is banishing Medea not for a proven crime but because 'I fear thee, woman.' What deeper meaning does this decision add to the conflict between Medea and Creon?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Creon's admission of fear shows he respects Medea's power and hopes she will leave peacefully without causing further trouble for his kingdom.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Creon's willingness to punish Medea based on suspicion rather than evidence reveals that the powerful can use fear to justify injustice against those who are already vulnerable.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Creon's decision to banish Medea demonstrates that he is a cautious ruler who carefully weighs all evidence before acting to protect his family.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Creon's fear of Medea proves that her reputation as a wise-woman has made her genuinely dangerous, and his banishment is a reasonable response to a known threat.

cards.standardTitle: Text structure and feature purpose
cards.excerpt:
He loveth to bear bravely ills like these! But, Aegeus, by thy beard, oh, by thy knees, I pray thee, and I give me for thine own, Thy suppliant, pity me! Oh, pity one So miserable. Thou never wilt stand there And see me cast out friendless to despair. Give me a home in Athens . . . by the fire Of thine own hearth! Oh, so may thy desire Of children be fulfilled of God, and thou Die happy! . . . Thou canst know not; even now Thy prize is won! I, I will make of thee A childless man no more. The seed shall be, I swear it, sown. Such magic herbs I know.

Woman, indeed my heart goes forth to show This help to thee, first for religion's sake, Then for thy promised hope, to heal my ache Of childlessness. 'Tis this hath made mine whole Life as a shadow, and starved out my soul. But thus it stands with me. Once make thy way To Attic earth, I, as in law I may, Will keep thee and befriend. But in this land, Where Creon rules, I may not raise my hand To shelter thee. Move of thine own essay To seek my house, there thou shalt alway stay, Inviolate, never to be seized again. But come thyself from Corinth. I would fain Even in foreign eyes be alway just.
cards.whyThisWorks: The excerpt shows a clear problem/solution structure: Medea names her crisis ('cast out friendless to despair') and offers a cure for Aegeus's childlessness, while Aegeus names his own problem ('ache of childlessness') and offers Athens as the solution to her exile—making the structural pattern traceable to exact lines.
cards.skillStrategy: When you see a character name a problem and another character offer a fix, ask yourself whether the whole passage is built around that problem-then-solution pattern.
evidencePoints: Give me a home in Athens . . . by the fire / Of thine own hearth! Oh, so may thy desire / Of children be fulfilled of God
But thus it stands with me. Once make thy way / To Attic earth, I, as in law I may, / Will keep thee and befriend.
cards.question: Medea says 'Give me a home in Athens' and promises 'thy desire of children be fulfilled,' while Aegeus replies 'Once make thy way to Attic earth, I . . . will keep thee and befriend.' What structure do these paired moments create across the exchange?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Medea and Aegeus each describe their suffering in the order events happened, moving from past misfortune to present despair.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Medea names her exile as a crisis and offers her magic as the trade that earns refuge, and Aegeus names his childlessness as a crisis and offers Athens as the trade that earns her cure—each problem paired with its solution.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Medea contrasts life under Creon's rule with life in Athens, and Aegeus contrasts his own happiness with Medea's misery, so the passage is built on paired opposites.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Aegeus lists the qualities of Attic law that make Athens a just city, and Medea responds by listing the herbs and magic she commands, so the passage is organized as two parallel descriptions.

cards.standardTitle: Central idea and supporting evidence
cards.excerpt:
For one day only leave me in thy land At peace, to find some counsel, ere the strain Of exile fall, some comfort for these twain, Mine innocents; since others take no thought, It seems, to save the babes that they begot. Ah! Thou wilt pity them! Thou also art A father: thou hast somewhere still a heart That feels. . . . I reck not of myself: 'tis they That break me, fallen upon so dire a day.

Mine is no tyrant's mood. Aye, many a time Ere this my tenderness hath marred the chime Of wisest counsels. And I know that now I do mere folly. But so be it! Thou Shalt have this grace . . . But this I warn thee clear, If once the morrow's sunlight find thee here Within my borders, thee or child of thine, Thou diest! . . . Of this judgment not a line Shall waver nor abate. So linger on, If thou needs must, till the next risen sun; No further. . . . In one day there scarce can be Those perils wrought whose dread yet haunteth me.
cards.whyThisWorks: The two speakers' contrasting speeches—Medea's appeal to paternal pity and the king's self-aware concession paired with a death threat—give students a clear two-part central idea to synthesize rather than simply identify a topic or isolated detail.
cards.skillStrategy: Ask yourself what the passage is mostly saying by combining what Medea wants and what the king actually decides, then check that your answer covers both paragraphs, not just one moment.
evidencePoints: Thou wilt pity them! Thou also art / A father: thou hast somewhere still a heart / That feels.
Thou Shalt have this grace . . . But this I warn thee clear, / If once the morrow's sunlight find thee here / Within my borders, thee or child of thine, / Thou diest!
cards.question: Medea appeals to the king by saying 'Thou also art / A father: thou hast somewhere still a heart / That feels,' and the king responds by granting 'this grace' while warning 'Thou diest!' if she remains past one day. What central idea do these two moments together express?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Medea's children are the true focus of both speakers, and the king's one-day grace period is granted entirely for the children's sake rather than for Medea's.

choices.label: B
choices.text: A plea to shared parental feeling wins Medea a brief act of mercy, but that mercy comes with an unmistakable and final deadline.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The king admits his past kindness has repeatedly ruined wise decisions, and he now resolves to let no future appeal change his judgment again.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Medea argues that exile is unjust punishment for innocent children, and the king ultimately agrees that she and her children should remain in his land.

cards.standardTitle: Key literary elements add layers of meaning
cards.excerpt:
O miserable maiden, all my heart Is torn for thee, so sudden to depart From thy king's chambers and the light above To darkness, all for sake of Jason's love!

Women, my mind is clear. I go to slay My children with all speed, and then, away From hence; not wait yet longer till they stand Beneath another and an angrier hand To die. Yea, howsoe'er I shield them, die They must. And, seeing that they must, 'tis I Shall slay them, I their mother, touched of none Beside. Oh, up and get thine armour on, My heart! Why longer tarry we to win Our crown of dire inevitable sin? Take up thy sword, O poor right hand of mine, Thy sword: then onward to the thin-drawn line Where life turns agony. Let there be naught Of softness now: and keep thee from that thought, 'Born of thy flesh,' 'thine own beloved.' Now, For one brief day, forget thy children: thou Shalt weep hereafter. Though thou slay them, yet Sweet were they. . . . I am sore unfortunate.

cards.skillStrategy: When a character makes a shocking decision, ask what that choice reveals about the forces—internal or external—that drove them there, and what larger truth the author is exploring.

'Though thou slay them, yet / Sweet were they. . . . I am sore unfortunate.'
cards.question: Medea decides to kill her children herself rather than allow them to die at another's hand. What deeper meaning does this decision add to the passage?

choices.label: B

choices.label: C
choices.text: Medea's decision demonstrates that she believes her children will be better off dead than raised without her, reflecting a practical rather than emotional choice.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Medea's decision suggests she is mentally unstable and cannot be held responsible for her actions, which the passage frames as a moment of temporary madness.

cards.question: Which structure best describes how Jason organizes his speech in this passage?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Chronological order, tracing the events of Medea's life in Corinth from her arrival to her banishment in the sequence they occurred.

choices.label: B

choices.label: C
choices.text: Compare/contrast, measuring Medea's reckless speech against Jason's calm reasoning to show that his character is superior to hers.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Cause/effect, explaining that Medea's blasphemy caused the exile and then tracing how that exile will permanently destroy her children's futures.

cards.question: When Medea declares, 'seeing that they must, 'tis I / Shall slay them, I their mother, touched of none / Beside,' and then commands her own heart to 'take up thy sword,' what central idea do these moments together express?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Medea is paralyzed by grief over leaving the king's chambers and cannot bring herself to act against Jason.

choices.label: B

choices.label: C
choices.text: Medea believes her children have betrayed her and deserve to suffer the consequences of Jason's choices.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Medea's primary concern is escaping quickly before anyone can stop her, and the fate of her children is secondary to her own survival.
