cards.question: In the second paragraph, Creon says 'I know that now I do mere folly' and then immediately grants Medea one day's grace. What deeper meaning does this sequence of admission followed by action add to the passage?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Creon's acknowledgment of folly before granting the day reveals that his threat—'Thou diest!'—is an empty performance, since a king who admits weakness cannot be taken seriously as an enforcer of exile.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Creon's choice to act against his own judgment the moment he names it foolish suggests that pity, not power, governs the decision that may doom him, giving the conflict a tragic irony in which mercy itself becomes the source of danger.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Creon's self-described folly signals that he has been persuaded by Medea's argument about her innocent children, so the deeper meaning is that a just ruler must always yield to the needs of the powerless.

choices.label: D
choices.text: By calling his own decision folly before carrying it out, Creon shows that he is distracted by his role as a father, and the passage suggests his personal feelings for his own children—not Medea's—are what drive him to extend her stay.

cards.standardTitle: Text structure and feature purpose
cards.excerpt: 'Tis not the first nor second time, O King, That fame hath hurt me, and come nigh to bring My ruin. . . . How can any man, whose eyes Are wholesome, seek to rear his children wise Beyond men's wont? Much helplessness in arts Of common life, and in their townsmen's hearts Envy deep-set . . . so much their learning brings! Come unto fools with knowledge of new things, They deem it vanity, not knowledge. Aye, And men that erst for wisdom were held high, Feel thee a thorn to fret them, privily Held higher than they. So hath it been with me. A wise-woman I am; and for that sin To divers ill names men would pen me in; A seed of strife; an eastern dreamer; one Of brand not theirs; one hard to play upon . . . Ah, I am not so wondrous wise!--And now, To thee, I am terrible! What fearest thou? What dire deed? Do I tread so proud a path-- Fear me not thou!--that I should brave the wrath Of princes? Thou: what has thou ever done To wrong me? Granted thine own child to one Whom thy soul chose.--Ah, _him_ out of my heart I hate; but thou, meseems, hast done thy part Not ill. And for thine houses' happiness I hold no grudge. Go: marry, and God bless Your issues. Only suffer me to rest Somewhere within this land. Though sore oppressed, I will be still, knowing mine own defeat.
cards.whyThisWorks: Medea's speech moves from naming a specific harm ('fame hath hurt me') to requesting a specific remedy ('suffer me to rest / Somewhere within this land'), making problem/solution structure visible and teachable.
cards.skillStrategy: When identifying text structure, look for a named problem stated early and a direct request or solution stated near the end — that pattern signals problem/solution organization.
evidencePoints: 'Tis not the first nor second time, O King, That fame hath hurt me, and come nigh to bring My ruin.
Only suffer me to rest / Somewhere within this land. Though sore oppressed, / I will be still, knowing mine own defeat.
cards.question: Medea opens by declaring that 'fame hath hurt me, and come nigh to bring my ruin' and closes by asking Creon to 'suffer me to rest somewhere within this land.' How does this movement from opening to closing organize the speech?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Medea traces the events of her conflict with Jason in the order they occurred, ending with her arrival before Creon.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Medea names the harm her reputation for wisdom has repeatedly caused her and then asks Creon for a specific remedy — permission to remain in the land undisturbed.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Medea contrasts the injustice Jason has done her with the fairness Creon has shown her, using that contrast to argue she deserves to stay.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Medea describes the general suffering that wise people endure from envious townsmen and then applies those observations to explain why she is not truly dangerous.

cards.standardTitle: Central idea and supporting evidence
cards.excerpt:
The sons of Erechtheus, the olden, Whom high gods planted of yore In an old land of heaven upholden, A proud land untrodden of war: They are hungered, and, lo, their desire With wisdom is fed as with meat: In their skies is a shining of fire, A joy in the fall of their feet: And thither, with manifold dowers, From the North, from the hills, from the morn, The Muses did gather their powers, That a child of the Nine should be born; And Harmony, sown as the flowers, Grew gold in the acres of corn.

And Cephisus, the fair-flowing river-- The Cyprian dipping her hand Hath drawn of his dew, and the shiver Of her touch is as joy in the land. For her breathing in fragrance is written, And in music her path as she goes, And the cloud of her hair, it is litten With stars of the wind-woven rose. So fareth she ever and ever, And forth of her bosom is blown, As dews on the winds of the river, An hunger of passions unknown. Strong Loves of all godlike endeavour, Whom Wisdom shall throne on her throne.
cards.whyThisWorks: The two stanzas each develop a distinct divine gift to Athens—wisdom from the Muses and passionate love from Aphrodite—yet both conclude by linking those gifts to a unified ideal, requiring students to synthesize rather than select an isolated detail.
cards.skillStrategy: Ask yourself what the passage keeps returning to across both stanzas, not just what one line says, to find the central idea.
evidencePoints: They are hungered, and, lo, their desire / With wisdom is fed as with meat
Strong Loves of all godlike endeavour, / Whom Wisdom shall throne on her throne
cards.question: In the first stanza the speaker says the Athenians' desire is 'fed' with wisdom, and in the second stanza the speaker ends by declaring that 'Strong Loves of all godlike endeavour' are ones 'Whom Wisdom shall throne on her throne.' What central idea do these two moments together express about Athens?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Athens is celebrated because the river Cephisus and the goddess Aphrodite have made its land physically fertile and beautiful above all other places.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Athens is a place where passionate desire and divine wisdom are not opposites but are united, each strengthening the other.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Athens earned its greatness because the Nine Muses chose it as the birthplace of Harmony, giving its people unmatched artistic power.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Athens is threatened by the overwhelming force of Aphrodite's passions, which risk displacing the wisdom the city once prized.

cards.standardTitle: Key literary elements add layers of meaning
cards.excerpt:
He loveth to bear bravely ills like these! But, Aegeus, by thy beard, oh, by thy knees, I pray thee, and I give me for thine own, Thy suppliant, pity me! Oh, pity one So miserable. Thou never wilt stand there And see me cast out friendless to despair. Give me a home in Athens . . . by the fire Of thine own hearth! Oh, so may thy desire Of children be fulfilled of God, and thou Die happy! . . . Thou canst know not; even now Thy prize is won! I, I will make of thee A childless man no more. The seed shall be, I swear it, sown. Such magic herbs I know.

Woman, indeed my heart goes forth to show This help to thee, first for religion's sake, Then for thy promised hope, to heal my ache Of childlessness. 'Tis this hath made mine whole Life as a shadow, and starved out my soul. But thus it stands with me. Once make thy way To Attic earth, I, as in law I may, Will keep thee and befriend. But in this land, Where Creon rules, I may not raise my hand To shelter thee. Move of thine own essay To seek my house, there thou shalt alway stay, Inviolate, never to be seized again. But come thyself from Corinth. I would fain Even in foreign eyes be alway just.
cards.whyThisWorks: Medea's decision to offer Aegeus a cure for his childlessness in exchange for shelter creates a transactional conflict that reveals how desperation drives manipulation, adding meaning about the lengths to which the powerless will go to survive.
cards.skillStrategy: When a character makes a deal or decision under pressure, ask what that choice reveals about their situation and what deeper idea the author is developing.
evidencePoints: I, I will make of thee A childless man no more. The seed shall be, I swear it, sown. Such magic herbs I know.
Woman, indeed my heart goes forth to show This help to thee, first for religion's sake, Then for thy promised hope, to heal my ache Of childlessness.
cards.question: Medea offers Aegeus a cure for his childlessness in exchange for shelter in Athens. What deeper meaning does this exchange add to the passage?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Medea's offer shows that she is a generous healer who uses her knowledge of herbs to help those who are suffering, regardless of what she receives in return.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Medea's willingness to trade her magical knowledge for survival reveals that the powerless must exploit others' vulnerabilities to escape their own desperate circumstances.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Aegeus's acceptance of Medea's offer proves that rulers in this world are easily deceived and cannot distinguish between genuine friendship and self-interested bargaining.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The exchange between Medea and Aegeus demonstrates that religious duty, not personal gain, is the true force that drives people to help one another in times of crisis.

cards.standardTitle: Text structure and feature purpose
cards.excerpt:
Poor, poor right hand of mine, whom he Did cling to, and these knees, so cravingly, We are unclean, thou and I; we have caught the stain Of bad men's flesh . . . and dreamed our dreams in vain. Thou comest to befriend me? Give me, then, Thy counsel. 'Tis not that I dream again For good from thee: but, questioned, thou wilt show The viler. Say: now whither shall I go? Back to my father? Him I did betray, And all his land, when we two fled away. To those poor Peliad maids? For them 'twere good To take me in, who spilled their father's blood. . . . Aye, so my whole life stands! There were at home Who loved me well: to them I am become A curse. And the first friends who sheltered me, Whom most I should have spared, to pleasure thee I have turned to foes. Oh, therefore hast thou laid My crown upon me, blest of many a maid In Hellas, now I have won what all did crave, Thee, the world-wondered lover and the brave; Who this day looks and sees me banished, thrown Away with these two babes, all, all, alone . . . Oh, merry mocking when the lamps are red: "Where go the bridegroom's babes to beg their bread In exile, and the woman who gave all To save him?" O great God, shall gold withal Bear thy clear mark, to sift the base and fine, And o'er man's living visage runs no sign To show the lie within, ere all too late?

Dire and beyond all healing is the hate When hearts that loved are turned to enmity.
cards.whyThisWorks: Medea's speech moves through a cause-and-effect chain—each betrayal she committed for Jason is directly linked to a consequence that now leaves her with nowhere to go—making this a strong model for teaching cause-and-effect structure doing real work.
cards.skillStrategy: When you see a speaker listing actions and then naming what those actions cost them, ask yourself: is each action paired with a result? If so, the structure is cause-and-effect.
evidencePoints: Back to my father? Him I did betray, And all his land, when we two fled away.
the first friends who sheltered me, Whom most I should have spared, to pleasure thee I have turned to foes.
cards.question: In lines beginning 'Back to my father? Him I did betray' through 'I have turned to foes,' how does Medea organize her situation?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Medea compares her father's betrayal to the Peliad maids' betrayal to show that both losses hurt her equally.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Medea pairs each person she wronged for Jason's sake with the consequence that she now has no refuge among them.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Medea lists the people she wronged in the chronological order in which she wronged them, ending with Jason himself.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Medea describes a problem—having no home—and then proposes returning to her father as the most likely solution.

cards.question: Medea opens by saying her fame 'hath hurt me, and come nigh to bring / My ruin' and closes by asking only to 'rest / Somewhere within this land.' What central idea do these two moments, taken together, express across the whole speech?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Medea's primary concern is punishing Jason, whom she says 'out of my heart I hate,' for abandoning her and marrying the king's daughter.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Her reputation as a wise woman has repeatedly made her a target of fear and resentment, and she asks only to be left in peace rather than driven out for that reputation.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Medea argues that the king has wronged her by granting his daughter to Jason, and she demands he correct that injustice before she will accept exile.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Educated people everywhere are envied by fools, and Medea presents her own suffering as proof of that universal pattern.

cards.skillStrategy: When a character explains a conflict they face, ask what deeper truth about the world the conflict exposes beyond the character's personal situation.
evidencePoints: A wise-woman I am; and for that sin / To divers ill names men would pen me in
Come unto fools with knowledge of new things, / They deem it vanity, not knowledge.
cards.question: In the excerpt, Medea describes how her reputation for wisdom has repeatedly brought her 'nigh to bring / My ruin.' What deeper meaning does this conflict add to the passage?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Medea's conflict with Creon shows that kings are naturally suspicious of foreigners, suggesting that political power depends on excluding outsiders.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Medea's suffering because she is called a 'wise-woman' reveals that society punishes women who possess knowledge by casting them as dangerous, making her personal exile a consequence of a broader injustice.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Medea's admission that she is 'not so wondrous wise' shows that her reputation was always exaggerated, and her conflict stems from her own failure to manage how others perceive her.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Medea's conflict with the king is rooted in her hatred of Jason, and her speech about wisdom is a strategy to distract Creon from her true intentions of revenge.

cards.standardTitle: Text structure and feature purpose
cards.excerpt:
For one day only leave me in thy land At peace, to find some counsel, ere the strain Of exile fall, some comfort for these twain, Mine innocents; since others take no thought, It seems, to save the babes that they begot. Ah! Thou wilt pity them! Thou also art A father: thou hast somewhere still a heart That feels. . . . I reck not of myself: 'tis they That break me, fallen upon so dire a day.

Mine is no tyrant's mood. Aye, many a time Ere this my tenderness hath marred the chime Of wisest counsels. And I know that now I do mere folly. But so be it! Thou Shalt have this grace . . . But this I warn thee clear, If once the morrow's sunlight find thee here Within my borders, thee or child of thine, Thou diest! . . . Of this judgment not a line Shall waver nor abate. So linger on, If thou needs must, till the next risen sun; No further. . . . In one day there scarce can be Those perils wrought whose dread yet haunteth me.
cards.whyThisWorks: The excerpt's two-paragraph structure mirrors a rhetorical turn: Medea's appeal to Creon's fatherhood produces a concession immediately undercut by a death threat, making the structural shift visible and purposeful for students.
cards.skillStrategy: When a passage shifts tone or speaker mid-way, ask what the author wants you to notice about the relationship between the two halves.
evidencePoints: Thou also art / A father: thou hast somewhere still a heart / That feels
If once the morrow's sunlight find thee here / Within my borders, thee or child of thine, / Thou diest!
cards.question: In the first paragraph, Medea tells Creon, 'Thou also art / A father: thou hast somewhere still a heart / That feels.' In the second paragraph, Creon responds by granting one day but then declares, 'thee or child of thine, / Thou diest!' What does placing these two moments back-to-back help the reader understand?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Creon's fatherly feelings are entirely false, and his death threat reveals he never considered Medea's children at all.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Creon's compassion as a father is real enough to move him to grant the one day Medea requests, but his fear of her ultimately forces him to reassert his authority with a death threat in the same breath.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Medea's appeal to Creon's fatherhood succeeds so fully that his death threat is merely a formality he does not intend to carry out.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The two paragraphs show that Creon and Medea share equal power, since her words force him to abandon his original judgment completely.

cards.standardTitle: Central idea and supporting evidence
cards.excerpt: Oft have I seen, in other days than these, How a dark temper maketh maladies No friend can heal. 'Twas easy to have kept Both land and home. It needed but to accept Unstrivingly the pleasure of our lords. But thou, for mere delight in stormy words, Wilt lose all! . . . Now thy speech provokes not me. Rail on. Of all mankind let Jason be Most evil; none shall check thee. But for these Dark threats cast out against the majesties Of Corinth, count as veriest gain thy path Of exile. I myself, when princely wrath Was hot against thee, strove with all good will To appease the wrath, and wished to keep thee still Beside me. But thy mouth would never stay From vanity, blaspheming night and day Our masters. Therefore thou shalt fly the land. Yet, even so, I will not hold my hand From succouring mine own people. Here am I To help thee, woman, pondering heedfully Thy new state. For I would not have thee flung Provisionless away--aye, and the young Children as well; nor lacking aught that will Of mine can bring thee. Many a lesser ill Hangs on the heels of exile. . . . Aye, and though Thou hate me, dream not that my heart can know Or fashion aught of angry will to thee.
cards.whyThisWorks: The speaker's repeated pivot from blaming Medea ('thy mouth would never stay / From vanity') to pledging practical help ('I will not hold my hand / From succouring mine own people') forces students to distinguish the central idea from isolated details or topic labels.
cards.skillStrategy: Ask yourself what the speaker is ultimately claiming across the whole passage, not just what one sentence says or what the general topic is.
evidencePoints: I myself, when princely wrath / Was hot against thee, strove with all good will / To appease the wrath
I will not hold my hand / From succouring mine own people. Here am I / To help thee, woman, pondering heedfully / Thy new state.
cards.question: The speaker tells Medea, 'I will not hold my hand / From succouring mine own people,' after spending several lines explaining why her own conduct caused her exile. What central idea does this shift in the speaker's words convey across the passage as a whole?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Medea's 'blaspheming night and day' against Corinth's rulers is the event the speaker most wants her to understand, because it alone determined the outcome of her exile.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Although the speaker holds Medea responsible for provoking her own exile, he insists that he has worked on her behalf in the past and will continue to provide for her practical needs now.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The speaker's primary concern is warning Medea that a 'dark temper' destroys friendships, leaving exiles without anyone willing to help them survive.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The speaker argues that accepting 'the pleasure of our lords' without resistance is the only lesson Medea needed to learn in order to keep her home and avoid hardship.

cards.question: Medea recounts betraying her father, causing the deaths of the Peliad maids' father, and turning her earliest protectors into enemies. What deeper meaning does this accumulation of consequences add to her conflict with Jason?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Her conflict with Jason is primarily about wounded pride, since she focuses on the public mockery of being called a beggar in exile rather than on any lasting harm she has caused others.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Her conflict with Jason exposes that every sacrifice she made to secure his love has destroyed every possible source of refuge, leaving her trapped by her own past choices with nowhere to turn.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Her conflict with Jason reveals that she regrets leaving her homeland above all else, and that her anger at him is really displaced guilt over abandoning her father.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Her conflict with Jason shows that she blames the gods for her suffering, since she calls on 'great God' to mark dishonest men and implies divine forces are responsible for her fate.

cards.question: Euripides structures the passage so that Medea's desperate appeals — 'by thy beard, oh, by thy knees, I pray thee' — are immediately followed by Aegeus's conditional promises. What does this arrangement help the reader understand?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Aegeus is moved purely by compassion for Medea's suffering and offers her unconditional protection in Athens.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Medea's vulnerability gives her a kind of bargaining power, because her promise of an heir is what ultimately shapes the terms Aegeus sets.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Medea's pleas reveal that she has already lost all hope and expects Aegeus to refuse her request.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Aegeus's response shows that he fears Creon more than he values Medea's friendship, so he refuses to help her at all.

O great God, shall gold withal Bear thy clear mark, to sift the base and fine, And o'er man's living visage runs no sign To show the lie within, ere all too late?

Dire and beyond all healing is the hate When hearts that loved are turned to enmity.
cards.whyThisWorks: The closing couplet 'Dire and beyond all healing is the hate / When hearts that loved are turned to enmity' states the central idea explicitly, giving students a concrete anchor to test against the full monologue's evidence of Medea's self-inflicted isolation.
cards.skillStrategy: Find the sentence or lines that make a broad claim about the whole situation, then check whether the rest of the passage supports that claim rather than just one detail.
evidencePoints: Dire and beyond all healing is the hate / When hearts that loved are turned to enmity.
There were at home / Who loved me well: to them I am become / A curse. And the first friends who sheltered me, / Whom most I should have spared, to pleasure thee / I have turned to foes.
cards.question: In the final couplet, Medea declares that hate between former lovers is 'dire and beyond all healing.' Which statement expresses the central idea that this closing claim and the rest of the monologue together develop?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Medea's greatest regret is betraying her father and his land, a wrong she knows can never be forgiven.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Choosing to destroy every bond of love and loyalty for Jason's sake has left Medea with nothing but irreversible hatred and ruin.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Jason's public humiliation of Medea before the women of Hellas is the source of the hatred she can no longer control.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Medea warns that men who appear brave and admirable, like Jason, always conceal a corrupt nature beneath the surface.

cards.standardTitle: Key literary elements add layers of meaning
cards.excerpt:
Alas, the Love that falleth like a flood, Strong-winged and transitory: Why praise ye him? What beareth he of good To man, or glory? Yet Love there is that moves in gentleness, Heart-filling, sweetest of all powers that bless. Loose not on me, O Holder of man's heart, Thy golden quiver, Nor steep in poison of desire the dart That heals not ever.

The pent hate of the word that cavilleth, The strife that hath no fill, Where once was fondness; and the mad heart's breath For strange love panting still: O Cyprian, cast me not on these; but sift, Keen-eyed, of love the good and evil gift. Make Innocence my friend, God's fairest star, Yea, and abate not The rare sweet beat of bosoms without war, That love, and hate not.

_Others._

Home of my heart, land of my own, Cast me not, nay, for pity, Out on my ways, helpless, alone, Where the feet fail in the mire and stone, A woman without a city. Ah, not that! Better the end: The green grave cover me rather, If a break must come in the days I know, And the skies be changed and the earth below; For the weariest road that man may wend Is forth from the home of his father.

Lo, we have seen: 'tis not a song Sung, nor learned of another. For whom hast thou in thy direst wrong For comfort? Never a city strong To hide thee, never a brother. Ah, but the man--cursed be he, Cursed beyond recover, Who openeth, shattering, seal by seal, A friend's clean heart, then turns his heel, Deaf unto love: never in me Friend shall he know nor lover.
cards.whyThisWorks: The Chorus's curse on the man who 'shatters seal by seal a friend's clean heart' then turns away functions as a consequence that deepens the meaning of betrayal as a violation of sacred trust, not merely a personal wound.
cards.skillStrategy: When a character faces a consequence or a curse is pronounced, ask what larger truth about human relationships or values that moment reveals beyond the surface event.
evidencePoints: Cursed be he, Cursed beyond recover, Who openeth, shattering, seal by seal, A friend's clean heart, then turns his heel, Deaf unto love
never in me Friend shall he know nor lover
cards.question: In the final stanza, the Chorus pronounces a curse on the man who breaks 'a friend's clean heart' and turns away 'deaf unto love.' What deeper meaning does this conflict between betrayer and betrayed add to the passage?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The curse reveals that the Chorus blames Medea for her own suffering because she chose to love someone unworthy of her trust.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The curse suggests that betraying intimate trust is not merely a personal injury but a moral violation so severe it permanently destroys the betrayer's capacity for human connection.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The curse shows that the Chorus values loyalty to one's city above loyalty to any individual, since the earlier stanza mourns exile more than lost love.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The curse indicates that the Chorus believes love itself is dangerous and that all romantic bonds inevitably end in the kind of destruction described in the first stanza.

cards.standardTitle: Text structure and feature purpose
cards.excerpt:
Poor, poor right hand of mine, whom he Did cling to, and these knees, so cravingly, We are unclean, thou and I; we have caught the stain Of bad men's flesh . . . and dreamed our dreams in vain. Thou comest to befriend me? Give me, then, Thy counsel. 'Tis not that I dream again For good from thee: but, questioned, thou wilt show The viler. Say: now whither shall I go? Back to my father? Him I did betray, And all his land, when we two fled away. To those poor Peliad maids? For them 'twere good To take me in, who spilled their father's blood. . . . Aye, so my whole life stands! There were at home Who loved me well: to them I am become A curse. And the first friends who sheltered me, Whom most I should have spared, to pleasure thee I have turned to foes. Oh, therefore hast thou laid My crown upon me, blest of many a maid In Hellas, now I have won what all did crave, Thee, the world-wondered lover and the brave; Who this day looks and sees me banished, thrown Away with these two babes, all, all, alone . . . Oh, merry mocking when the lamps are red: "Where go the bridegroom's babes to beg their bread In exile, and the woman who gave all To save him?" O great God, shall gold withal Bear thy clear mark, to sift the base and fine, And o'er man's living visage runs no sign To show the lie within, ere all too late?

Dire and beyond all healing is the hate When hearts that loved are turned to enmity.
cards.whyThisWorks: Euripides structures Medea's speech as a series of rhetorical questions that catalog every door closed to her, culminating in a final couplet that shifts to a declarative statement, allowing students to trace how the accumulation of unanswerable questions builds toward the author's purpose of showing that betrayal makes return impossible and hatred inevitable.
cards.skillStrategy: Ask yourself: why does the author arrange the text this way—what does this structure push the reader to feel or understand that a different arrangement would not?
evidencePoints: Back to my father? Him I did betray, / And all his land, when we two fled away. / To those poor Peliad maids? For them 'twere good / To take me in, who spilled their father's blood.
Dire and beyond all healing is the hate / When hearts that loved are turned to enmity.
cards.question: Euripides structures Medea's speech as a series of rhetorical questions before ending with the couplet 'Dire and beyond all healing is the hate / When hearts that loved are turned to enmity.' What does this shift in structure help the reader understand?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Medea is uncertain about her own guilt and uses the questions to invite Jason to defend himself before she reaches any conclusion.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The unanswerable questions show that every refuge Medea destroyed for Jason's sake is now gone, so the closing couplet lands as an unavoidable truth: her love has nowhere to go but into hatred.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The questions reveal that Medea still hopes one of the people she wronged—her father or the Peliad maids—will forgive her, and the couplet expresses relief that reconciliation is possible.

choices.label: D
choices.text: By listing her past crimes through questions, Medea shifts blame onto Jason so that the final couplet reads as a warning directed at him rather than a reflection on her own situation.

cards.standardTitle: Central idea and supporting evidence
cards.excerpt: Woman, indeed I praise thee now, nor say Ill of thine other hour. 'Tis nature's way, A woman needs must stir herself to wrath, When work of marriage by so strange a path Crosseth her lord. But thou, thine heart doth wend The happier road. Thou hast seen, ere quite the end, What choice must needs be stronger: which to do Shows a wise-minded woman. . . . And for you, Children; your father never has forgot Your needs. If God but help him, he hath wrought A strong deliverance for your weakness. Yea, I think you, with your brethren, yet one day Shall be the mightiest voices in this land. Do you grow tall and strong. Your father's hand Guideth all else, and whatso power divine Hath alway helped him. . . . Ah, may it be mine To see you yet in manhood, stern of brow, Strong-armed, set high o'er those that hate me. . . . How? Woman, thy face is turned. Thy cheek is swept With pallor of strange tears. Dost not accept Gladly and of good will my benisons?
cards.whyThisWorks: Jason's speech moves from praising Medea's acceptance, to promising the children greatness, to noticing her tears—giving students a clear arc to synthesize into a central idea rather than picking an isolated detail.
cards.skillStrategy: Ask yourself: what is the speaker trying to prove across the whole passage, not just in one line?
evidencePoints: Thou hast seen, ere quite the end, What choice must needs be stronger: which to do Shows a wise-minded woman.
How? Woman, thy face is turned. Thy cheek is swept With pallor of strange tears. Dost not accept Gladly and of good will my benisons?
cards.question: Jason opens by calling Medea 'wise-minded' for accepting his choices and closes by asking why her 'cheek is swept with pallor of strange tears.' What central idea does this movement from praise to puzzled questioning develop across the passage?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Jason believes the children's future greatness—'the mightiest voices in this land'—is the only thing that truly matters to Medea, and her tears prove she agrees.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Jason presents his remarriage and ambitions as reasonable and even beneficial, yet Medea's silent tears expose that his self-justifying claims have not actually won her acceptance.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Jason's praise of Medea as 'wise-minded' is sincere, and her tears are simply a natural reaction that he expects will pass once she fully understands his good intentions.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The passage argues that a woman's anger at her husband's remarriage is natural and justified, and Jason's words confirm that Medea has every right to feel betrayed.

cards.standardTitle: Key literary elements add layers of meaning
cards.excerpt:
Ah, Ah, thou Wrath within me! Do not thou, Do not. . . . Down, down, thou tortured thing, and spare My children! They will dwell with us, aye, there Far off, and give thee peace. Too late, too late! By all Hell's living agonies of hate, They shall not take my little ones alive To make their mock with! Howsoe'er I strive The thing is doomed; it shall not escape now From being. Aye, the crown is on the brow, And the robe girt, and in the robe that high Queen dying. I know all. Yet . . . seeing that I Must go so long a journey, and these twain A longer yet and darker, I would fain Speak with them, ere I go.

[_A handmaid brings the_ CHILDREN _out again_.

Come, children; stand A little from me. There. Reach out your hand, Your right hand--so--to mother: and good-bye!

[_She has kept them hitherto at arm's length: but at the touch of their hands, her resolution breaks down, and she gathers them passionately into her arms._

Oh, darling hand! Oh, darling mouth, and eye, And royal mien, and bright brave faces clear, May you be blessed, but not here! What here Was yours, your father stole. . . . Ah God, the glow Of cheek on cheek, the tender touch; and Oh, Sweet scent of childhood. . . . Go! Go! . . . Am I blind? . . . Mine eyes can see not, when I look to find Their places. I am broken by the wings Of evil. . . . Yea, I know to what bad things I go, but louder than all thought doth cry Anger, which maketh man's worst misery.
cards.whyThisWorks: Medea's physical contact with her children's hands shatters her murderous resolve momentarily, showing how a single reversal—the touch that breaks her down—deepens the tragedy by revealing that love and rage are inseparable forces driving her toward destruction.
cards.skillStrategy: When a character makes a decision or experiences a reversal, ask what that moment reveals about the conflict beneath the surface and what larger truth it adds to the story.
evidencePoints: at the touch of their hands, her resolution breaks down, and she gathers them passionately into her arms
Yea, I know to what bad things I go, but louder than all thought doth cry Anger, which maketh man's worst misery
cards.question: When Medea's resolve breaks down at the touch of her children's hands, only to be overtaken again by her anger, what deeper meaning does this reversal add to the conflict?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The moment shows that Medea has changed her mind and will ultimately choose to protect her children from harm, making her earlier threats an empty expression of grief.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The reversal reveals that Medea's destruction of her children is not born of indifference but of a love consumed by rage, suggesting that the deepest human suffering arises when powerful love and uncontrollable anger occupy the same heart.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The moment demonstrates that Medea blames her children for her misery, and her brief tenderness is a performance meant to justify the revenge she has already planned against Jason.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The reversal shows that Medea is too emotionally unstable to carry out any deliberate action, and her conflict is driven entirely by grief over the dying queen rather than by her relationship with her children.

cards.whyThisWorks: Medea's closing lines—'I know to what bad things I go, but louder than all thought doth cry / Anger, which maketh man's worst misery'—state the central tension explicitly, requiring students to distinguish the central idea from isolated details like the farewell or the stolen happiness.
cards.skillStrategy: Find the sentence or lines where the speaker steps back and names what the whole moment is really about—that is usually where the central idea lives.
evidencePoints: I know to what bad things I go, but louder than all thought doth cry / Anger, which maketh man's worst misery.
Down, down, thou tortured thing, and spare / My children! . . . Too late, too late!
cards.question: In the final lines of the passage, Medea says, 'I know to what bad things I go, but louder than all thought doth cry / Anger, which maketh man's worst misery.' What central idea do these lines, together with the rest of the passage, express?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A mother's farewell to her children is the most painful moment a person can endure.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Medea's rage overpowers her love and her own judgment, driving her toward destruction she fully recognizes but cannot stop.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Jason's betrayal is the true cause of every misfortune Medea and her children suffer.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Medea's tenderness for her children, shown when she gathers them into her arms, ultimately outweighs her anger.

cards.standardTitle: Key literary elements add layers of meaning
cards.excerpt:
The sons of Erechtheus, the olden, Whom high gods planted of yore In an old land of heaven upholden, A proud land untrodden of war: They are hungered, and, lo, their desire With wisdom is fed as with meat: In their skies is a shining of fire, A joy in the fall of their feet: And thither, with manifold dowers, From the North, from the hills, from the morn, The Muses did gather their powers, That a child of the Nine should be born; And Harmony, sown as the flowers, Grew gold in the acres of corn.

And Cephisus, the fair-flowing river-- The Cyprian dipping her hand Hath drawn of his dew, and the shiver Of her touch is as joy in the land. For her breathing in fragrance is written, And in music her path as she goes, And the cloud of her hair, it is litten With stars of the wind-woven rose. So fareth she ever and ever, And forth of her bosom is blown, As dews on the winds of the river, An hunger of passions unknown. Strong Loves of all godlike endeavour, Whom Wisdom shall throne on her throne.
cards.whyThisWorks: The chorus's idealized portrait of Athens—fed by wisdom, blessed by the Muses, and touched by Aphrodite—functions as a foil to Medea's situation, deepening the conflict by contrasting a land of divine harmony with the passion-driven destruction Medea is about to unleash.
cards.skillStrategy: When a passage describes an ideal world or place, ask yourself what that ideal reveals about the conflict or tension the characters face—the contrast itself adds a layer of meaning.
evidencePoints: They are hungered, and, lo, their desire / With wisdom is fed as with meat
Strong Loves of all godlike endeavour, / Whom Wisdom shall throne on her throne
cards.question: In these stanzas, the chorus describes Athens as a place where desire is 'fed' by wisdom and where 'Strong Loves' are ultimately ruled by wisdom. What layer of meaning does this description add to the conflict surrounding Medea?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Athens is presented as a refuge Medea has already reached, suggesting her suffering is now behind her and the conflict has been resolved.

choices.label: B
choices.text: By portraying Athens as a place where passion is governed by wisdom, the chorus deepens the tragedy of Medea's situation—she is driven by ungoverned passion toward destruction in a world that prizes the very restraint she cannot achieve.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The description of the Muses gathering in Athens shows that the conflict is primarily about artistic rivalry between cultures rather than personal betrayal.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The chorus praises Athens to suggest that Medea's enemies will be punished there, implying justice will ultimately favor her cause.

cards.standardTitle: Central idea and supporting evidence
cards.excerpt:
Alas, the Love that falleth like a flood, Strong-winged and transitory: Why praise ye him? What beareth he of good To man, or glory? Yet Love there is that moves in gentleness, Heart-filling, sweetest of all powers that bless. Loose not on me, O Holder of man's heart, Thy golden quiver, Nor steep in poison of desire the dart That heals not ever.

The pent hate of the word that cavilleth, The strife that hath no fill, Where once was fondness; and the mad heart's breath For strange love panting still: O Cyprian, cast me not on these; but sift, Keen-eyed, of love the good and evil gift. Make Innocence my friend, God's fairest star, Yea, and abate not The rare sweet beat of bosoms without war, That love, and hate not.

Home of my heart, land of my own, Cast me not, nay, for pity, Out on my ways, helpless, alone, Where the feet fail in the mire and stone, A woman without a city. Ah, not that! Better the end: The green grave cover me rather, If a break must come in the days I know, And the skies be changed and the earth below; For the weariest road that man may wend Is forth from the home of his father.

Lo, we have seen: 'tis not a song Sung, nor learned of another. For whom hast thou in thy direst wrong For comfort? Never a city strong To hide thee, never a brother. Ah, but the man--cursed be he, Cursed beyond recover, Who openeth, shattering, seal by seal, A friend's clean heart, then turns his heel, Deaf unto love: never in me Friend shall he know nor lover.
cards.whyThisWorks: The chorus explicitly contrasts 'Love that falleth like a flood' with love that 'moves in gentleness,' giving students a clear textual anchor to distinguish topic (love) from central idea (gentle love is preferable to violent desire).
cards.skillStrategy: Ask yourself: what point does the passage keep returning to across all the stanzas, not just what it is about?
evidencePoints: Yet Love there is that moves in gentleness, Heart-filling, sweetest of all powers that bless.
O Cyprian, cast me not on these; but sift, Keen-eyed, of love the good and evil gift.
cards.question: The chorus opens by asking 'Why praise ye him?' about the 'Love that falleth like a flood' and then prays to be spared from 'the dart / That heals not ever.' What central idea do these lines introduce and the remaining stanzas develop?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The god of love is powerless to help mortals and should be abandoned in favor of reason and self-control.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Overwhelming, destructive desire causes suffering, whereas love that is gentle and peaceful is the only kind worth having.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Exile from one's homeland is a punishment more painful than any wound that love can inflict on a person.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Men who betray those who love them are the true source of suffering, not love itself.

cards.standardTitle: Key literary elements add layers of meaning
cards.excerpt:
O miserable maiden, all my heart Is torn for thee, so sudden to depart From thy king's chambers and the light above To darkness, all for sake of Jason's love!

Women, my mind is clear. I go to slay My children with all speed, and then, away From hence; not wait yet longer till they stand Beneath another and an angrier hand To die. Yea, howsoe'er I shield them, die They must. And, seeing that they must, 'tis I Shall slay them, I their mother, touched of none Beside. Oh, up and get thine armour on, My heart! Why longer tarry we to win Our crown of dire inevitable sin? Take up thy sword, O poor right hand of mine, Thy sword: then onward to the thin-drawn line Where life turns agony. Let there be naught Of softness now: and keep thee from that thought, 'Born of thy flesh,' 'thine own beloved.' Now, For one brief day, forget thy children: thou Shalt weep hereafter. Though thou slay them, yet Sweet were they. . . . I am sore unfortunate.
cards.whyThisWorks: The excerpt shifts from an outside voice lamenting Medea's fate to Medea's own first-person interior monologue, allowing students to see how point of view shapes the reader's understanding of her as both victim and agent of violence.
cards.skillStrategy: Ask yourself: who is speaking or observing this moment, and how does that perspective change what you feel or understand about the situation?
evidencePoints: O miserable maiden, all my heart Is torn for thee, so sudden to depart From thy king's chambers and the light above To darkness, all for sake of Jason's love!
Women, my mind is clear. I go to slay My children with all speed
cards.question: The excerpt opens with an outside voice calling Medea a 'miserable maiden' whose heart is torn, then shifts to Medea declaring, 'my mind is clear.' How does this shift in point of view shape the reader's understanding of Medea?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The outside voice's pity is confirmed by Medea's own words, showing that she is overwhelmed by grief and unable to act with any real resolve.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The outside voice frames Medea as a passive victim of Jason's betrayal, but her own first-person voice reveals a woman in deliberate, terrifying control of her choices, creating a more complex and unsettling portrait.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Medea's first-person voice contradicts the outside voice entirely, suggesting the outside speaker does not know Medea and therefore cannot be trusted as a reliable narrator.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The shift from the outside voice to Medea's voice shows that Medea has changed her mind about leaving, replacing her earlier sorrow with a plan to seek forgiveness from Jason.

cards.standardTitle: Central idea and supporting evidence
cards.excerpt:
He loveth to bear bravely ills like these! But, Aegeus, by thy beard, oh, by thy knees, I pray thee, and I give me for thine own, Thy suppliant, pity me! Oh, pity one So miserable. Thou never wilt stand there And see me cast out friendless to despair. Give me a home in Athens . . . by the fire Of thine own hearth! Oh, so may thy desire Of children be fulfilled of God, and thou Die happy! . . . Thou canst know not; even now Thy prize is won! I, I will make of thee A childless man no more. The seed shall be, I swear it, sown. Such magic herbs I know.

Woman, indeed my heart goes forth to show This help to thee, first for religion's sake, Then for thy promised hope, to heal my ache Of childlessness. 'Tis this hath made mine whole Life as a shadow, and starved out my soul. But thus it stands with me. Once make thy way To Attic earth, I, as in law I may, Will keep thee and befriend. But in this land, Where Creon rules, I may not raise my hand To shelter thee. Move of thine own essay To seek my house, there thou shalt alway stay, Inviolate, never to be seized again. But come thyself from Corinth. I would fain Even in foreign eyes be alway just.
cards.whyThisWorks: The excerpt shows how Medea's appeal to Aegeus builds the central idea that desperation drives people to offer and accept bargains, with her promise of magical fertility serving as the key piece of evidence that shifts Aegeus from sympathy to committed action.
cards.skillStrategy: Track how each new detail or reason in the passage adds a layer to the central idea — ask yourself what each piece of evidence makes the reader understand that the previous one did not.
evidencePoints: I, I will make of thee A childless man no more. The seed shall be, I swear it, sown. Such magic herbs I know.
'Tis this hath made mine whole Life as a shadow, and starved out my soul.
cards.question: In the excerpt, Aegeus explains that childlessness has made his 'whole Life as a shadow, and starved out my soul.' How does this detail develop the central idea that Medea's promise of magical fertility is the decisive reason Aegeus agrees to shelter her?

choices.label: A
choices.text: It shows that Aegeus is moved purely by religious duty, making Medea's offer of herbs irrelevant to his decision.

choices.label: B
choices.text: It reveals the depth of Aegeus's suffering, which makes Medea's offer to end his childlessness the specific need her promise directly answers, turning his sympathy into a firm commitment.

choices.label: C
choices.text: It establishes that Aegeus pities Medea's friendlessness above all else, so his agreement is based on her exile rather than anything she can offer him.

choices.label: D
choices.text: It suggests Aegeus doubts Medea's magical abilities, so he agrees to shelter her only because he fears breaking the laws of hospitality.

cards.standardTitle: Key literary elements add layers of meaning
cards.excerpt:
For one day only leave me in thy land At peace, to find some counsel, ere the strain Of exile fall, some comfort for these twain, Mine innocents; since others take no thought, It seems, to save the babes that they begot. Ah! Thou wilt pity them! Thou also art A father: thou hast somewhere still a heart That feels. . . . I reck not of myself: 'tis they That break me, fallen upon so dire a day.

Mine is no tyrant's mood. Aye, many a time Ere this my tenderness hath marred the chime Of wisest counsels. And I know that now I do mere folly. But so be it! Thou Shalt have this grace . . . But this I warn thee clear, If once the morrow's sunlight find thee here Within my borders, thee or child of thine, Thou diest! . . . Of this judgment not a line Shall waver nor abate. So linger on, If thou needs must, till the next risen sun; No further. . . . In one day there scarce can be Those perils wrought whose dread yet haunteth me.
cards.whyThisWorks: The excerpt places two speakers' perspectives in direct contrast—Medea's calculated appeal to Creon's fatherhood and Creon's self-aware admission of weakness—allowing students to trace how each character's first-person voice shapes the reader's understanding of power, vulnerability, and dramatic irony.
cards.skillStrategy: When a character speaks in first person, ask yourself: what does this speaker reveal about themselves that another narrator would hide, and how does that revelation change what the moment means?
evidencePoints: 'Thou also art / A father: thou hast somewhere still a heart / That feels.'
'I know that now / I do mere folly. But so be it!'
cards.question: In the first paragraph, Medea addresses Creon directly, saying 'Thou also art / A father: thou hast somewhere still a heart / That feels.' In the second paragraph, Creon responds in his own voice, 'I know that now / I do mere folly. But so be it!' What does the shift from Medea's appeal to Creon's self-admission reveal about the effect of point of view on the reader's understanding of this moment?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Medea's direct address to Creon as a father exposes her manipulation, and Creon's refusal to name her argument shows he sees through her appeal and grants the day out of political calculation rather than genuine feeling.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Medea's appeal frames Creon's fatherhood as his vulnerability, and Creon's own admission that he 'do mere folly' confirms that her framing worked—creating dramatic irony because the reader sees the danger Creon acknowledges but cannot resist.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Because both characters speak in first person throughout the scene, the reader cannot determine whose account of events is more trustworthy, leaving the meaning of Creon's decision deliberately ambiguous.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Creon's first-person admission that he acts from tenderness shifts the reader's sympathy entirely away from Medea, making her earlier claim that 'others take no thought' for her children seem dishonest and self-serving.

cards.standardTitle: Central idea and supporting evidence
cards.excerpt: Oft have I seen, in other days than these, How a dark temper maketh maladies No friend can heal. 'Twas easy to have kept Both land and home. It needed but to accept Unstrivingly the pleasure of our lords. But thou, for mere delight in stormy words, Wilt lose all! . . . Now thy speech provokes not me. Rail on. Of all mankind let Jason be Most evil; none shall check thee. But for these Dark threats cast out against the majesties Of Corinth, count as veriest gain thy path Of exile. I myself, when princely wrath Was hot against thee, strove with all good will To appease the wrath, and wished to keep thee still Beside me. But thy mouth would never stay From vanity, blaspheming night and day Our masters. Therefore thou shalt fly the land. Yet, even so, I will not hold my hand From succouring mine own people. Here am I To help thee, woman, pondering heedfully Thy new state. For I would not have thee flung Provisionless away--aye, and the young Children as well; nor lacking aught that will Of mine can bring thee. Many a lesser ill Hangs on the heels of exile. . . . Aye, and though Thou hate me, dream not that my heart can know Or fashion aught of angry will to thee.
cards.whyThisWorks: Jason's speech layers specific examples—his past attempts to calm Corinthian wrath, his offer of provisions, and his claim of harboring no anger—to develop the central idea that he presents himself as a reasonable benefactor despite Medea's exile, allowing students to trace how each detail advances that self-justifying claim.
cards.skillStrategy: Identify the central idea the speaker is pushing, then ask how each specific example or reason he gives is meant to prove that idea to the listener.
evidencePoints: I myself, when princely wrath / Was hot against thee, strove with all good will / To appease the wrath, and wished to keep thee still / Beside me.
I will not hold my hand / From succouring mine own people. Here am I / To help thee, woman, pondering heedfully / Thy new state.
cards.question: In this passage, Jason develops the central idea that he is acting as Medea's protector rather than her enemy. How do his references to appeasing 'princely wrath' and offering provisions for exile work together to support that idea?

choices.label: A
choices.text: They show that Jason regrets banishing Medea and hopes she will forgive him for siding with the Corinthian rulers.

choices.label: B
choices.text: They present Jason as someone who has already acted on Medea's behalf in the past and continues to do so now, building a portrait of himself as a generous protector despite her hostility.

choices.label: C
choices.text: They reveal that Jason blames Medea entirely for her exile and offers help only to silence her public accusations against him.

choices.label: D
choices.text: They demonstrate that Jason fears the Corinthian rulers and provides aid to Medea mainly to avoid being punished for his association with her.

cards.standardTitle: Key literary elements add layers of meaning
cards.excerpt:
He loveth to bear bravely ills like these! But, Aegeus, by thy beard, oh, by thy knees, I pray thee, and I give me for thine own, Thy suppliant, pity me! Oh, pity one So miserable. Thou never wilt stand there And see me cast out friendless to despair. Give me a home in Athens . . . by the fire Of thine own hearth! Oh, so may thy desire Of children be fulfilled of God, and thou Die happy! . . . Thou canst know not; even now Thy prize is won! I, I will make of thee A childless man no more. The seed shall be, I swear it, sown. Such magic herbs I know.

Woman, indeed my heart goes forth to show This help to thee, first for religion's sake, Then for thy promised hope, to heal my ache Of childlessness. 'Tis this hath made mine whole Life as a shadow, and starved out my soul. But thus it stands with me. Once make thy way To Attic earth, I, as in law I may, Will keep thee and befriend. But in this land, Where Creon rules, I may not raise my hand To shelter thee. Move of thine own essay To seek my house, there thou shalt alway stay, Inviolate, never to be seized again. But come thyself from Corinth. I would fain Even in foreign eyes be alway just.
cards.whyThisWorks: The excerpt shifts between Medea's desperate first-person pleading and Aegeus's measured first-person response, allowing students to see how each speaker's point of view shapes the tone—Medea's as urgent and manipulative, Aegeus's as cautious and self-interested—adding layers of meaning to the power dynamic between them.
cards.skillStrategy: Ask yourself: whose voice am I hearing right now, what does that speaker want, and how does hearing it from their perspective change what I understand or feel about the situation?
evidencePoints: by thy beard, oh, by thy knees, I pray thee, and I give me for thine own, Thy suppliant, pity me!
Woman, indeed my heart goes forth to show This help to thee, first for religion's sake, Then for thy promised hope, to heal my ache Of childlessness.
cards.question: The excerpt shifts between Medea's voice and Aegeus's voice. How does hearing Aegeus speak in his own words, rather than through Medea's description of him, affect the reader's understanding of his decision to help her?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Aegeus's own words confirm that he is moved purely by compassion for Medea's suffering, making him appear selflessly heroic.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Aegeus's own words reveal that his willingness to help is driven largely by his personal desperation over childlessness, showing his decision as self-interested rather than purely generous.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Aegeus's own words show that he distrusts Medea's promises and agrees to help only because he fears the gods will punish him if he refuses.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Aegeus's own words demonstrate that he is unaware of Medea's dangerous nature, making the reader feel sympathy for his ignorance.

cards.standardTitle: Central idea and supporting evidence
cards.excerpt:
Poor, poor right hand of mine, whom he Did cling to, and these knees, so cravingly, We are unclean, thou and I; we have caught the stain Of bad men's flesh . . . and dreamed our dreams in vain. Thou comest to befriend me? Give me, then, Thy counsel. 'Tis not that I dream again For good from thee: but, questioned, thou wilt show The viler. Say: now whither shall I go? Back to my father? Him I did betray, And all his land, when we two fled away. To those poor Peliad maids? For them 'twere good To take me in, who spilled their father's blood. . . . Aye, so my whole life stands! There were at home Who loved me well: to them I am become A curse. And the first friends who sheltered me, Whom most I should have spared, to pleasure thee I have turned to foes. Oh, therefore hast thou laid My crown upon me, blest of many a maid In Hellas, now I have won what all did crave, Thee, the world-wondered lover and the brave; Who this day looks and sees me banished, thrown Away with these two babes, all, all, alone . . . Oh, merry mocking when the lamps are red: "Where go the bridegroom's babes to beg their bread In exile, and the woman who gave all To save him?" O great God, shall gold withal Bear thy clear mark, to sift the base and fine, And o'er man's living visage runs no sign To show the lie within, ere all too late?

Dire and beyond all healing is the hate When hearts that loved are turned to enmity.
cards.whyThisWorks: Medea's catalog of specific betrayals and losses—her father, the Peliad maids, her homeland, her friends—each functions as a concrete example that builds toward the central idea that her devotion to Jason has left her utterly isolated and cursed, making the subskill of tracing how examples develop a central idea directly teachable.
cards.skillStrategy: Ask yourself: what specific examples or reasons does the speaker give, and how does each one add another layer to the main point she is making about her situation?
evidencePoints: Back to my father? Him I did betray, And all his land, when we two fled away.
the first friends who sheltered me, Whom most I should have spared, to pleasure thee I have turned to foes.
cards.question: In the excerpt, Medea references her father, the Peliad maids, and her earliest friends. How do these specific references develop the central idea of the passage?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Each reference shows that Medea regrets leaving her homeland and wishes to return to the life she had before meeting Jason.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Each reference adds another person Medea has lost or wronged for Jason's sake, building the case that her loyalty to him has destroyed every bond she once had.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Each reference demonstrates that the people in Medea's past were unworthy of her loyalty and therefore deserved to be abandoned.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Each reference establishes that Medea's suffering is caused by the cruelty of those around her rather than by any choice she made herself.

cards.standardTitle: Key literary elements add layers of meaning
cards.excerpt: 'Tis not the first nor second time, O King, That fame hath hurt me, and come nigh to bring My ruin. . . . How can any man, whose eyes Are wholesome, seek to rear his children wise Beyond men's wont? Much helplessness in arts Of common life, and in their townsmen's hearts Envy deep-set . . . so much their learning brings! Come unto fools with knowledge of new things, They deem it vanity, not knowledge. Aye, And men that erst for wisdom were held high, Feel thee a thorn to fret them, privily Held higher than they. So hath it been with me. A wise-woman I am; and for that sin To divers ill names men would pen me in; A seed of strife; an eastern dreamer; one Of brand not theirs; one hard to play upon . . . Ah, I am not so wondrous wise!--And now, To thee, I am terrible! What fearest thou? What dire deed? Do I tread so proud a path-- Fear me not thou!--that I should brave the wrath Of princes? Thou: what has thou ever done To wrong me? Granted thine own child to one Whom thy soul chose.--Ah, _him_ out of my heart I hate; but thou, meseems, hast done thy part Not ill. And for thine houses' happiness I hold no grudge. Go: marry, and God bless Your issues. Only suffer me to rest Somewhere within this land. Though sore oppressed, I will be still, knowing mine own defeat.
cards.whyThisWorks: Medea's first-person self-defense—'A wise-woman I am; and for that sin / To divers ill names men would pen me in'—lets readers hear her own framing of persecution, creating sympathy that a third-person or Creon's account would deny.
cards.skillStrategy: Ask yourself: because THIS speaker tells this moment in her own words, what do I believe or feel that I would not believe if someone else described her?
evidencePoints: A wise-woman I am; and for that sin / To divers ill names men would pen me in
Ah, I am not so wondrous wise!--And now, / To thee, I am terrible! What fearest thou?
cards.question: In the excerpt, Medea says, 'A wise-woman I am; and for that sin / To divers ill names men would pen me in.' Because Medea speaks these words in her own voice rather than being described by an outside narrator, how does this first-person point of view shape the reader's understanding of her situation?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The reader accepts Creon's fear as justified, because hearing Medea boast about her wisdom in her own words confirms that she is as dangerous as he believes.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The reader understands the 'ill names' as labels imposed on Medea by others rather than as accurate descriptions, making her seem a victim of prejudice against her intelligence rather than a genuine threat.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The reader sees Medea as fully accepting the reputation men have given her, since she names herself a 'wise-woman' without any protest or qualification.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The reader concludes that Medea is indifferent to Creon's judgment, because her direct address to him focuses entirely on her hatred for the man she calls 'him out of my heart I hate.'

cards.standardTitle: Central idea and supporting evidence
cards.excerpt: Woman, indeed I praise thee now, nor say Ill of thine other hour. 'Tis nature's way, A woman needs must stir herself to wrath, When work of marriage by so strange a path Crosseth her lord. But thou, thine heart doth wend The happier road. Thou hast seen, ere quite the end, What choice must needs be stronger: which to do Shows a wise-minded woman. . . . And for you, Children; your father never has forgot Your needs. If God but help him, he hath wrought A strong deliverance for your weakness. Yea, I think you, with your brethren, yet one day Shall be the mightiest voices in this land. Do you grow tall and strong. Your father's hand Guideth all else, and whatso power divine Hath alway helped him. . . . Ah, may it be mine To see you yet in manhood, stern of brow, Strong-armed, set high o'er those that hate me. . . . How? Woman, thy face is turned. Thy cheek is swept With pallor of strange tears. Dost not accept Gladly and of good will my benisons?
cards.whyThisWorks: Jason's speech contains both strong evidence of his self-serving rationalization (framing his remarriage as beneficial to Medea and the children) and weaker true details (generic praise of Medea, blessings for the boys' height and strength), allowing students to distinguish which evidence best supports the central idea that Jason manipulates Medea by recasting his betrayal as her good fortune.
cards.skillStrategy: Ask yourself which piece of evidence directly connects to the central idea—not just a true detail from the passage, but the one that most clearly proves the main point.
evidencePoints: Thou hast seen, ere quite the end, What choice must needs be stronger: which to do Shows a wise-minded woman.
your father never has forgot Your needs. If God but help him, he hath wrought A strong deliverance for your weakness.
cards.question: The central idea of this passage is that Jason reframes his betrayal of Medea as an act that benefits her and their children. Which quotation from the passage best supports this central idea?

choices.label: A
choices.text: "Woman, indeed I praise thee now, nor say Ill of thine other hour"—Jason opens by complimenting Medea's current behavior, showing he acknowledges her past suffering.

choices.label: B
choices.text: "If God but help him, he hath wrought A strong deliverance for your weakness"—Jason presents his own remarriage as a rescue of the children, casting his self-interest as their salvation.

choices.label: C
choices.text: "Do you grow tall and strong"—Jason urges the children to become powerful, showing he has affection for them.

choices.label: D
choices.text: "Woman, thy face is turned. Thy cheek is swept With pallor of strange tears"—Jason notices Medea's emotional reaction, revealing he is observant of her distress.

cards.question: The speech is delivered entirely from Jason's point of view. How does this perspective shape the reader's understanding of Jason's character?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Because Jason speaks directly to Medea, the reader sympathizes with his frustration and accepts his claim that her 'stormy words' alone caused her exile.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Because Jason narrates his own actions as selfless and reasonable, the reader can see the gap between his self-portrait as a generous protector and the dismissive, self-justifying tone his words actually reveal.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Because Jason controls the speech, the reader learns that Medea's blasphemy against Corinth's rulers was the sole cause of her punishment, making Jason a neutral witness to events.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Because Jason speaks in first person, the reader understands that his offer to provide for Medea and the children proves he still loves her and regrets the divorce.

cards.standardTitle: Central idea and supporting evidence
cards.excerpt:
The sons of Erechtheus, the olden, Whom high gods planted of yore In an old land of heaven upholden, A proud land untrodden of war: They are hungered, and, lo, their desire With wisdom is fed as with meat: In their skies is a shining of fire, A joy in the fall of their feet: And thither, with manifold dowers, From the North, from the hills, from the morn, The Muses did gather their powers, That a child of the Nine should be born; And Harmony, sown as the flowers, Grew gold in the acres of corn.

And Cephisus, the fair-flowing river-- The Cyprian dipping her hand Hath drawn of his dew, and the shiver Of her touch is as joy in the land. For her breathing in fragrance is written, And in music her path as she goes, And the cloud of her hair, it is litten With stars of the wind-woven rose. So fareth she ever and ever, And forth of her bosom is blown, As dews on the winds of the river, An hunger of passions unknown. Strong Loves of all godlike endeavour, Whom Wisdom shall throne on her throne.
cards.whyThisWorks: The choral ode presents a central idea that Athens is a divinely blessed land where wisdom and passion unite, and students must distinguish between details that directly support this claim versus true but peripheral details about geography or mythology.
cards.skillStrategy: Ask yourself: which detail directly proves the central idea, not just adds color or background to the scene?
evidencePoints: They are hungered, and, lo, their desire / With wisdom is fed as with meat
Strong Loves of all godlike endeavour, / Whom Wisdom shall throne on her throne
cards.question: The central idea of this choral ode is that Athens is a land where divine blessing joins wisdom with passionate desire. Which detail from the excerpt most directly supports this central idea?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The Muses gathered their powers from 'the North, from the hills, from the morn' to be born in Athens, showing the city draws from many directions.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The ode closes by describing 'Strong Loves of all godlike endeavour, / Whom Wisdom shall throne on her throne,' directly linking passionate striving to wisdom as Athens's defining quality.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Cephisus is described as a 'fair-flowing river' touched by the Cyprian, establishing that Athens has beautiful and sacred waterways.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The sons of Erechtheus inhabit 'an old land of heaven upholden, / A proud land untrodden of war,' showing Athens has long been protected from invasion.

cards.question: Jason opens by declaring 'Woman, indeed I praise thee now' and closes by asking 'Dost not accept / Gladly and of good will my benisons?' How does Jason's point of view in these lines shape the reader's understanding of the scene?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Jason's opening praise and closing question together confirm that Medea has genuinely accepted his remarriage, and her tears signal relief rather than grief.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Jason's certainty that he is offering praise and blessing blinds him to what his own closing question reveals—that Medea's pale face and tears contradict the willing acceptance he assumes, exposing his inability to read the moment the reader can clearly see.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Jason's focus on blessing the children in the middle of the speech overshadows his opening praise of Medea, so his closing question about her tears feels disconnected from the rest of his argument.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Jason's point of view as a father concerned with his children's future greatness earns the reader's sympathy, making his final question about Medea's tears seem like a reasonable expression of confusion.

cards.standardTitle: Key literary elements add layers of meaning
cards.excerpt:
Thou woman sullen-eyed and hot with hate Against thy lord, Medea, I here command That thou and thy two children from this land Go forth to banishment. Make no delay: Seeing ourselves, the King, are come this day To see our charge fulfilled; nor shall again Look homeward ere we have led thy children twain And thee beyond our realm's last boundary.

Lost! Lost! Mine haters at the helm with sail flung free Pursuing; and for us no beach nor shore In the endless waters! . . . Yet, though stricken sore, I still will ask thee, for what crime, what thing Unlawful, wilt thou cast me out, O King?

What crime? I fear thee, woman--little need To cloak my reasons--lest thou work some deed Of darkness on my child. And in that fear Reasons enough have part. Thou comest here A wise-woman confessed, and full of lore In unknown ways of evil. Thou art sore In heart, being parted from thy lover's arms. And more, thou hast made menace . . . so the alarms But now have reached mine ear . . . on bride and groom, And him who gave the bride, to work thy doom Of vengeance. Which, ere yet it be too late, I sweep aside. I choose to earn thine hate Of set will now, not palter with the mood Of mercy, and hereafter weep in blood.
cards.whyThisWorks: The excerpt shifts among three distinct speakers—Creon, Medea, and Creon again—each revealing a different perspective on the same banishment, so students must track how point of view shapes the reader's sympathy, tone, and understanding of power.
cards.skillStrategy: Ask yourself: whose voice am I hearing right now, what do they want me to believe, and how does hearing multiple sides change what I think about the situation?
evidencePoints: Lost! Lost! Mine haters at the helm with sail flung free / Pursuing; and for us no beach nor shore / In the endless waters!
I fear thee, woman--little need / To cloak my reasons--lest thou work some deed / Of darkness on my child.
cards.question: When Medea cries 'Lost! Lost! Mine haters at the helm with sail flung free / Pursuing; and for us no beach nor shore / In the endless waters!' between Creon's two speeches, what effect does placing her voice at that moment create for the reader?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Her outburst confirms Creon's suspicion that she is dangerous, making the reader agree that banishment is the only reasonable choice.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Her anguished perspective interrupts Creon's authority and forces the reader to feel the human cost of the decree before hearing Creon justify it as self-protection.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Her words reveal that she has already accepted the banishment, shifting the reader's focus away from Creon's power and toward her plans for escape.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Her grief shows she is too overwhelmed to argue logically, which causes the reader to view her later question to Creon as insincere.
