cards.question: In the opening lines, Medea addresses her own hand directly, saying 'Poor, poor right hand of mine, whom he / Did cling to . . . We are unclean, thou and I.' What does this first-person address to her own body reveal that a third-person narrator describing the same moment could not?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Medea's guilt is hidden from the reader because she speaks only to her hand rather than confessing her crimes to another character.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Medea experiences her betrayal as something that has contaminated her physically and morally from within, a feeling of shared 'unclean' stain that only her own voice can make the reader feel alongside her.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The address to her hand shows that Medea refuses to accept responsibility for her actions, since she blames the hand rather than herself for what happened.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Speaking to her hand allows Medea to present Jason's point of view objectively, so the reader understands why he chose to abandon her.

cards.standardTitle: Key literary elements add layers of meaning
cards.excerpt:
Alas, the Love that falleth like a flood, Strong-winged and transitory: Why praise ye him? What beareth he of good To man, or glory? Yet Love there is that moves in gentleness, Heart-filling, sweetest of all powers that bless. Loose not on me, O Holder of man's heart, Thy golden quiver, Nor steep in poison of desire the dart That heals not ever.

The pent hate of the word that cavilleth, The strife that hath no fill, Where once was fondness; and the mad heart's breath For strange love panting still: O Cyprian, cast me not on these; but sift, Keen-eyed, of love the good and evil gift. Make Innocence my friend, God's fairest star, Yea, and abate not The rare sweet beat of bosoms without war, That love, and hate not.

_Others._

Home of my heart, land of my own, Cast me not, nay, for pity, Out on my ways, helpless, alone, Where the feet fail in the mire and stone, A woman without a city. Ah, not that! Better the end: The green grave cover me rather, If a break must come in the days I know, And the skies be changed and the earth below; For the weariest road that man may wend Is forth from the home of his father.

Lo, we have seen: 'tis not a song Sung, nor learned of another. For whom hast thou in thy direst wrong For comfort? Never a city strong To hide thee, never a brother. Ah, but the man--cursed be he, Cursed beyond recover, Who openeth, shattering, seal by seal, A friend's clean heart, then turns his heel, Deaf unto love: never in me Friend shall he know nor lover.
cards.whyThisWorks: The Chorus speaks collectively in first-person plural ('we have seen') and shifts to direct address of Medea, making point of view central to how readers understand the emotional stakes of exile, betrayal, and the curse on Jason.
cards.skillStrategy: Ask yourself: Who is speaking, who are they speaking to, and how does that relationship shape what the words feel like — warning, comfort, accusation, or prayer?
evidencePoints: Lo, we have seen: 'tis not a song / Sung, nor learned of another.
Ah, but the man--cursed be he, / Cursed beyond recover, / Who openeth, shattering, seal by seal, / A friend's clean heart, then turns his heel
cards.question: In the final stanza, the Chorus shifts from addressing Medea's suffering to cursing the man who betrayed her. How does the Chorus's point of view as witness — stated in the line 'Lo, we have seen: 'tis not a song / Sung, nor learned of another' — shape the meaning of the curse that follows?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The Chorus distances itself from Medea's pain by speaking as outside observers, making the curse feel impersonal and detached from her situation.

choices.label: B
choices.text: By claiming direct witness to Medea's suffering rather than secondhand knowledge, the Chorus gives its curse moral authority, making the condemnation of the betrayer feel earned and just.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The Chorus speaks as witnesses to warn Medea that her own actions will bring the curse upon herself rather than upon the man who wronged her.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The Chorus uses the first-person plural to suggest that all of society, not just Medea, has been harmed by the betrayal, shifting blame away from any single person.

cards.standardTitle: Key literary elements add layers of meaning
cards.excerpt:
Ah, Ah, thou Wrath within me! Do not thou, Do not. . . . Down, down, thou tortured thing, and spare My children! They will dwell with us, aye, there Far off, and give thee peace. Too late, too late! By all Hell's living agonies of hate, They shall not take my little ones alive To make their mock with! Howsoe'er I strive The thing is doomed; it shall not escape now From being. Aye, the crown is on the brow, And the robe girt, and in the robe that high Queen dying. I know all. Yet . . . seeing that I Must go so long a journey, and these twain A longer yet and darker, I would fain Speak with them, ere I go.

[_A handmaid brings the_ CHILDREN _out again_.

Come, children; stand A little from me. There. Reach out your hand, Your right hand--so--to mother: and good-bye!

[_She has kept them hitherto at arm's length: but at the touch of their hands, her resolution breaks down, and she gathers them passionately into her arms._

Oh, darling hand! Oh, darling mouth, and eye, And royal mien, and bright brave faces clear, May you be blessed, but not here! What here Was yours, your father stole. . . . Ah God, the glow Of cheek on cheek, the tender touch; and Oh, Sweet scent of childhood. . . . Go! Go! . . . Am I blind? . . . Mine eyes can see not, when I look to find Their places. I am broken by the wings Of evil. . . . Yea, I know to what bad things I go, but louder than all thought doth cry Anger, which maketh man's worst misery.
cards.whyThisWorks: Medea's first-person soliloquy forces readers inside her fractured consciousness, so the point of view directly controls whether she reads as monster or tragic mother—a clear demonstration that who speaks shapes meaning and tone.
cards.skillStrategy: When a character speaks in first person, ask: what do I know because I am inside this mind that I could not know from the outside, and how does that change what I feel about the character?
evidencePoints: Oh, darling hand! Oh, darling mouth, and eye, / And royal mien, and bright brave faces clear, / May you be blessed, but not here!
Yea, I know to what bad things I go, but louder than all thought doth cry / Anger, which maketh man's worst misery.
cards.question: In the lines 'Oh, darling hand! Oh, darling mouth, and eye' and 'Yea, I know to what bad things I go, but louder than all thought doth cry / Anger,' readers hear both Medea's tenderness and her self-awareness in the same voice. How does this first-person point of view shape the reader's understanding of Medea in this moment?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Hearing Medea address her children's hands and faces directly proves she has changed her mind and will not harm them, so the point of view creates a hopeful tone that overrides the earlier threats.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Because readers receive Medea's grief over her children's 'darling hand' and 'sweet scent of childhood' at the same moment she confesses that anger overrides thought, the first-person voice makes her simultaneously pitiable and terrifying, producing a tragic rather than simply villainous portrait.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The first-person voice keeps readers focused on the children's physical features—hand, mouth, eye, cheek—rather than on Medea's emotions, so the point of view distances readers from her inner conflict.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Medea's admission that she knows 'to what bad things I go' shows she is fully in control of her choices, so the first-person point of view removes any sense of tragedy and instead creates a tone of cold calculation.

cards.standardTitle: Key literary elements add layers of meaning
cards.excerpt: Oft have I seen, in other days than these, How a dark temper maketh maladies No friend can heal. 'Twas easy to have kept Both land and home. It needed but to accept Unstrivingly the pleasure of our lords. But thou, for mere delight in stormy words, Wilt lose all! . . . Now thy speech provokes not me. Rail on. Of all mankind let Jason be Most evil; none shall check thee. But for these Dark threats cast out against the majesties Of Corinth, count as veriest gain thy path Of exile. I myself, when princely wrath Was hot against thee, strove with all good will To appease the wrath, and wished to keep thee still Beside me. But thy mouth would never stay From vanity, blaspheming night and day Our masters. Therefore thou shalt fly the land. Yet, even so, I will not hold my hand From succouring mine own people. Here am I To help thee, woman, pondering heedfully Thy new state. For I would not have thee flung Provisionless away--aye, and the young Children as well; nor lacking aught that will Of mine can bring thee. Many a lesser ill Hangs on the heels of exile. . . . Aye, and though Thou hate me, dream not that my heart can know Or fashion aught of angry will to thee.
cards.whyThisWorks: The social conditions of Corinth—where Medea is subject to 'princely wrath' and the 'pleasure of our lords'—create an atmosphere of political powerlessness that deepens the meaning of her exile and Jason's self-justifying speech.
cards.skillStrategy: When analyzing setting, ask how the social conditions or power structures of a place shape what characters can and cannot do, and what that reveals about mood or meaning.
evidencePoints: 'It needed but to accept / Unstrivingly the pleasure of our lords.'
'when princely wrath / Was hot against thee, strove with all good will / To appease the wrath'
cards.question: In this passage, Jason refers to 'the pleasure of our lords' and 'princely wrath' as forces Medea failed to navigate. How do these references to Corinth's social conditions add meaning to the passage?

choices.label: A
choices.text: They show that Corinth is a peaceful kingdom where Medea could have lived comfortably if she had simply remained silent about personal grievances.

choices.label: B
choices.text: They establish Corinth as a place where submission to ruling power is required for survival, making Medea's exile feel like an inevitable consequence of a society that punishes defiance rather than wrongdoing.

choices.label: C
choices.text: They reveal that Jason holds genuine political authority in Corinth and used that authority to protect Medea from punishment she deserved.

choices.label: D
choices.text: They suggest that Medea's exile results entirely from her own violent actions against the royal family rather than from the political atmosphere of Corinth.

cards.standardTitle: Paraphrase grade-level text
cards.excerpt:
O miserable maiden, all my heart Is torn for thee, so sudden to depart From thy king's chambers and the light above To darkness, all for sake of Jason's love!

Women, my mind is clear. I go to slay My children with all speed, and then, away From hence; not wait yet longer till they stand Beneath another and an angrier hand To die. Yea, howsoe'er I shield them, die They must. And, seeing that they must, 'tis I Shall slay them, I their mother, touched of none Beside. Oh, up and get thine armour on, My heart! Why longer tarry we to win Our crown of dire inevitable sin? Take up thy sword, O poor right hand of mine, Thy sword: then onward to the thin-drawn line Where life turns agony. Let there be naught Of softness now: and keep thee from that thought, 'Born of thy flesh,' 'thine own beloved.' Now, For one brief day, forget thy children: thou Shalt weep hereafter. Though thou slay them, yet Sweet were they. . . . I am sore unfortunate.
cards.whyThisWorks: Medea's inverted, clause-heavy sentence 'not wait yet longer till they stand / Beneath another and an angrier hand / To die' requires students to untangle subordinate clauses and archaic syntax to recover the core meaning.
cards.skillStrategy: When a sentence has multiple clauses and old-fashioned word order, identify the subject, the main verb, and what each clause adds, then restate the whole idea in plain language.
evidencePoints: not wait yet longer till they stand / Beneath another and an angrier hand / To die
seeing that they must, 'tis I / Shall slay them, I their mother, touched of none / Beside
cards.question: Read the following lines from Medea's speech: 'not wait yet longer till they stand / Beneath another and an angrier hand / To die.' Which restatement most accurately captures the meaning of these lines?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Medea refuses to wait because she fears her children will escape to another kingdom before she can reach them.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Medea will not delay, because if she does, someone else — a harsher person — will be the one to kill her children.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Medea decides to wait until a more powerful enemy arrives so that her children will be protected by a stronger hand.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Medea worries that her children will grow angry with her if she waits any longer to make a decision.

Forth against foemen. cards.skillStrategy: When a character takes a specific action—like giving a gift—ask what that action reveals about who they are and what they value.

cards.question: Read the following lines: 'the mighty-famed chieftain, / Hoard-ward of heroes, with horses and jewels / War-storms requited, that none e'er condemneth / Who willeth to tell truth with full justice.' What does the chieftain's act of rewarding Beowulf with horses and jewels reveal about his character?

choices.label: A
choices.text: He rewards Beowulf primarily to display his own wealth and intimidate rival kings who might challenge his rule.

choices.label: B
choices.text: He embodies the ideal of a just and honorable lord whose generosity in repaying Beowulf's courage earns him a reputation no truthful person could fault.

choices.label: C
choices.text: He gives the gifts reluctantly, parting with his prized war-steeds only because custom demands he acknowledge Beowulf's deeds publicly.

choices.label: D
choices.text: He demonstrates that he values material possessions above loyalty, using treasure to bind Beowulf to his service rather than to honor him.

cards.standardTitle: Epic poetry: characters, structures, and themes
cards.excerpt: That in it did perish. He early swam off then 60 Who had bided in combat the carnage of haters, Went up through the ocean; the eddies were cleansèd, The spacious expanses, when the spirit from farland His life put aside and this short-lived existence. The seamen's defender came swimming to land then 65 Doughty of spirit, rejoiced in his sea-gift, The bulky burden which he bore in his keeping. The excellent vassals advanced then to meet him, To God they were grateful, were glad in their chieftain, That to see him safe and sound was granted them. 70 From the high-minded hero, then, helmet and burnie Were speedily loosened: the ocean was putrid, The water 'neath welkin weltered with gore. Forth did they fare, then, their footsteps retracing, Merry and mirthful, measured the earth-way, 75 The highway familiar: men very daring Bare then the head from the sea-cliff, burdening Each of the earlmen, excellent-valiant.
cards.whyThisWorks: The vassals' gratitude directed explicitly 'To God' after Beowulf's survival demonstrates divine intervention shaping both the action of the return and the theme that heroic victory is granted by a higher power.
cards.skillStrategy: When you spot a prayer, a moment of gratitude toward a god, or a supernatural force changing what happens, ask yourself: what would have been different without that divine presence?

the spirit from farland / His life put aside and this short-lived existence
cards.question: In the excerpt, the vassals declare 'To God they were grateful' that Beowulf returned safely. How does this moment of gratitude shape the meaning of Beowulf's victory over Grendel's mother?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The vassals' gratitude shows that the warriors doubted Beowulf's strength and expected him to fail in the underwater battle.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The vassals' gratitude toward God frames Beowulf's survival as divinely permitted, suggesting that heroic triumph in the epic depends on a higher power's will rather than human strength alone.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The vassals' gratitude reflects their relief that the ocean was cleansed of gore, which was the true sign that the battle had ended.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The vassals' gratitude emphasizes Beowulf's physical endurance, proving that his 'doughty spirit' was the sole reason he survived the depths.

Sundered Hæthcyn the Hrethling from life-joys, When for pride overweening the War-Scylfings first did Seek the Geatmen with savage intentions. 35 Early did Ohthere's age-laden father, Old and terrible, give blow in requital, Killing the sea-king, the queen-mother rescued, The old one his consort deprived of her gold, Onela's mother and Ohthere's also, 40 And then followed the feud-nursing foemen till hardly, Reaved of their ruler, they Ravenswood entered. Then with vast-numbered forces he assaulted the remnant, Weary with wounds, woe often promised The livelong night to the sad-hearted war-troop: 45 Said he at morning would kill them with edges of weapons, Some on the gallows for glee to the fowls. Aid came after to the anxious-in-spirit At dawn of the day, after Higelac's bugle And trumpet-sound heard they, when the good one proceeded 50 And faring followed the flower of the troopers.

'Hige-méðum' (2910) is glossed by H. as dat. plu. (= for the dead). cards.whyThisWorks: The old king's actions—striking in requital, killing the sea-king, rescuing the queen, and threatening the trapped war-troop with death and gallows—reveal a ruthless, domineering character whose violence defines the feud's escalation and adds meaning to the cycle of vengeance in the poem.
cards.skillStrategy: When analyzing characterization, look at what a character does and says, then ask what those actions reveal about who they are and what the author wants you to understand about them.

cards.question: Read the following lines from the excerpt: 'Old and terrible, give blow in requital' and 'Said he at morning would kill them with edges of weapons, / Some on the gallows for glee to the fowls.' What do these actions and words reveal about Ohthere's father as a character?

choices.label: A
choices.text: He is a cautious leader who strikes only to protect his people from an unprovoked attack, showing restraint in the face of war.

choices.label: B
choices.text: He is a merciless and domineering force whose retaliatory violence and threats of public execution reveal that vengeance, not justice, drives his power.

choices.label: C
choices.text: He is a grieving father whose sorrow over the death of Hæthcyn motivates him to seek a fair resolution to the conflict between the Geatmen and the War-Scylfings.

choices.label: D
choices.text: He is a loyal ally who rescues the queen-mother and promises mercy to the wounded war-troop at dawn in exchange for their surrender.

cards.standardTitle: Epic poetry: characters, structures, and themes
cards.excerpt: Mighty achievements, many things hidden, 40 The strife of the Wælsing, the wide-going ventures The children of men knew of but little, The feud and the fury, but Fitela with him, When suchlike matters he minded to speak of, Uncle to nephew, as in every contention 45 Each to other was ever devoted: A numerous host of the race of the scathers They had slain with the sword-edge. To Sigmund accrued then No little of glory, when his life-days were over, Since he sturdy in struggle had destroyed the great dragon, 50 The hoard-treasure's keeper; 'neath the hoar-grayish stone he, The son of the atheling, unaided adventured The perilous project; not present was Fitela, Yet the fortune befell him of forcing his weapon Through the marvellous dragon, that it stood in the wall, 55 Well-honored weapon; the worm was slaughtered. The great one had gained then by his glorious achievement To reap from the ring-hoard richest enjoyment, As best it did please him: his vessel he loaded, Shining ornaments on the ship's bosom carried, 60 Kinsman of Wæls: the drake in heat melted.
cards.whyThisWorks: The Sigmund passage demonstrates elevated epic style through formal diction ('atheling,' 'scathers,' 'hoar-grayish'), alliterative phrasing, and an extended comparison of heroic deeds that builds Sigmund's glory as a parallel to Beowulf's own legend.
cards.skillStrategy: When analyzing epic style, look for formal or archaic word choices, repeated sound patterns, and extended descriptions of a single heroic act that stretch across multiple lines to magnify the hero's achievement.
evidencePoints: 'neath the hoar-grayish stone he, / The son of the atheling, unaided adventured / The perilous project
No little of glory, when his life-days were over, / Since he sturdy in struggle had destroyed the great dragon
cards.question: Read the following lines from the passage: "'neath the hoar-grayish stone he, / The son of the atheling, unaided adventured / The perilous project; not present was Fitela." How does the language in these lines contribute to the elevated style of the epic?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The reference to Fitela's absence shifts the focus away from Sigmund, suggesting that the poet doubts whether Sigmund truly deserves credit for slaying the dragon.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Archaic, formal diction such as 'atheling' and 'hoar-grayish,' combined with the drawn-out description of Sigmund acting alone, magnifies the hero's deed and creates a tone of solemn grandeur.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The phrase 'unaided adventured / The perilous project' uses simple, direct language to contrast with the more ornate descriptions elsewhere in the passage, creating a moment of plain speech.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The repeated mention of Fitela throughout the passage functions as an invocation, calling on a companion figure the way an epic poet would call on a Muse for inspiration.

cards.skillStrategy: When a character is described through repeated titles and a dramatic action, ask what those details reveal about who that character is and what they mean to others in the story.

cards.question: Read the following description of Beowulf entering the hall: 'Deed-valiant man, adorned with distinction, / Doughty shield-warrior, to address King Hrothgar.' What does the accumulation of these epithets, combined with the act of presenting Grendel's head, reveal about Beowulf's role in the community?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Beowulf is portrayed as a reluctant warrior who must prove himself to Hrothgar by displaying the head as evidence of a battle others doubted he fought.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Beowulf is established as a celebrated champion whose identity is defined by martial achievement and whose deeds demand public acknowledgment from the entire hall.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Beowulf is shown to be a boastful leader who carries Grendel's head primarily to humiliate the earlmen who failed to defeat the monster themselves.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Beowulf is depicted as a loyal servant of Hrothgar who presents the head as a formal tribute owed to the king rather than as proof of his own valor.

cards.question: Read the following lines from the excerpt: 'Weary with wounds, woe often promised / The livelong night to the sad-hearted war-troop' and 'Aid came after to the anxious-in-spirit / At dawn of the day, after Higelac's bugle.' cards.question:
Read the two moments below from the excerpt and answer the question.

Moment 1: Hrothgar commands eight gold-plated steeds and a jeweled saddle to be brought to Beowulf, granting him 'power over both, / O'er war-steeds and weapons.'

Moment 2: The narrator states that Hrothgar requited 'War-storms' with 'horses and jewels' in so worthy a manner 'that none e'er condemneth / Who willeth to tell truth with full justice.'

What theme do both moments work together to develop?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A king's greatest duty is to accumulate wealth in gold and horses so that his hall remains the most powerful in the land.

choices.label: B
choices.text: A leader who repays valor with generous, public reward earns a reputation that no honest person can dispute.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Beowulf's courage in battle is so extraordinary that no gift from any king could ever match what he truly deserves.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The splendor of decorated weapons and jeweled saddles reflects the glory of war itself rather than the character of the giver.

cards.standardTitle: Key literary elements add layers of meaning
cards.excerpt:
Four of them had to carry with labor The head of Grendel to the high towering gold-hall 80 Upstuck on the spear, till fourteen most-valiant And battle-brave Geatmen came there going Straight to the palace: the prince of the people Measured the mead-ways, their mood-brave companion. The atheling of earlmen entered the building, 85 Deed-valiant man, adorned with distinction, Doughty shield-warrior, to address King Hrothgar: Then hung by the hair, the head of Grendel Was borne to the building, where beer-thanes were drinking, Loth before earlmen and eke 'fore the lady: 90 The warriors beheld then a wonderful sight.

'Þæs monige gewearð' (1599) and 'hafað þæs geworden' (2027).--In a paper published some years ago in one of the Johns Hopkins University circulars, I tried to throw upon these two long-doubtful passages some light derived from a study of like passages in Alfred's prose.--The impersonal verb 'geweorðan,' with an accus. of the person, and a þæt-clause is used several times with the meaning 'agree.' See Orosius (Sweet's ed.) 178_7; 204_34; 208_28; 210_15; 280_20. In the two Beowulf passages, the þæt-clause is anticipated by 'þæs,' which is clearly a gen. of the thing agreed on.
cards.whyThisWorks: The public display of Grendel's severed head in Hrothgar's mead-hall is a plot event that carries deeper meaning about honor, victory, and the social rituals of warrior culture, making it ideal for teaching how a specific narrative moment adds layers of meaning beyond surface action.
cards.skillStrategy: Ask yourself: why does this event matter beyond what literally happens — what does it reveal about the characters, their world, or the story's deeper ideas?
evidencePoints: Then hung by the hair, the head of Grendel / Was borne to the building, where beer-thanes were drinking, / Loth before earlmen and eke 'fore the lady
Four of them had to carry with labor / The head of Grendel to the high towering gold-hall
cards.question: In the excerpt, Grendel's severed head is carried by four warriors and displayed before Hrothgar's court, including the lady and the earlmen. What deeper meaning does this event add to the narrative?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The difficulty of carrying the head shows that Grendel was physically enormous, which explains why no single warrior could have defeated him alone.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The public presentation of Grendel's head before the king, his warriors, and the lady transforms a battlefield victory into a communal act of restoration, showing that the hero's deed belongs to the entire society he has protected.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Displaying the head in the mead-hall where beer-thanes are drinking suggests that the warriors are celebrating carelessly, unaware of future dangers that still threaten the hall.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The detail that the head is described as 'loth before earlmen' reveals that the court is disgusted by Beowulf's brutal methods, even as they accept his protection.

cards.standardTitle: Key literary elements add layers of meaning
cards.excerpt:
Forth against foemen. The defender of earls then Commanded that eight steeds with bridles 45 Gold-plated, gleaming, be guided to hallward, Inside the building; on one of them stood then An art-broidered saddle embellished with jewels; 'Twas the sovereign's seat, when the son of King Healfdene Was pleased to take part in the play of the edges; 50 The famous one's valor ne'er failed at the front when Slain ones were bowing. And to Beowulf granted The prince of the Ingwins, power over both, O'er war-steeds and weapons; bade him well to enjoy them. In so manly a manner the mighty-famed chieftain, 55 Hoard-ward of heroes, with horses and jewels War-storms requited, that none e'er condemneth Who willeth to tell truth with full justice.

Kl. suggests 'hroden' for 'háten,' and renders: _Then quickly was Heorot adorned within, with hands bedecked_.--B. suggests 'gefrætwon' instead of 'gefrætwod,' and renders: _Then was it commanded to adorn Heorot within quickly with hands_.--The former has the advantage of affording a parallel to 'gefrætwod': both have the disadvantage of altering the text.
cards.whyThisWorks: Hrothgar's decision to reward Beowulf with eight gold-bridled horses and the king's own jeweled saddle is a plot event that carries deeper meaning about the heroic code of reciprocity, loyalty, and the weight of kingship being symbolically transferred through gift-giving.
cards.skillStrategy: When a character makes a decision or takes an action, ask yourself what that moment reveals about values, relationships, or themes beyond the surface event.
evidencePoints: 'Twas the sovereign's seat, when the son of King Healfdene / Was pleased to take part in the play of the edges
the mighty-famed chieftain, / Hoard-ward of heroes, with horses and jewels / War-storms requited, that none e'er condemneth / Who willeth to tell truth with full justice
cards.question: Hrothgar gives Beowulf eight gold-bridled horses along with the king's own jeweled battle saddle. What deeper meaning does this decision add to the passage?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The gift of horses reveals that Hrothgar is trying to bribe Beowulf into remaining at Heorot as a permanent warrior rather than returning to his homeland.

choices.label: B
choices.text: By surrendering his personal battle saddle—the seat reserved for the king himself in combat—Hrothgar signals that Beowulf's valor has earned a status equal to royalty, deepening the theme that heroic deeds carry the power to reshape social bonds.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The elaborate description of the jeweled saddle and gold bridles shows that Hrothgar values material wealth above all other forms of honor in his kingdom.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Hrothgar's generosity with horses and weapons suggests he fears Beowulf will leave without proper payment, so the gifts are meant to settle a debt rather than honor a hero.

cards.question: Read the following lines from the passage: 'Deed-valiant man, adorned with distinction, / Doughty shield-warrior, to address King Hrothgar.' How do these phrases contribute to the elevated style of the epic?

choices.label: A
choices.text: They slow the action to show that Beowulf is nervous about presenting Grendel's head to Hrothgar.

choices.label: B
choices.text: They stack formal compound descriptors to magnify Beowulf's heroic identity before he enters the king's presence.

choices.label: C
choices.text: They contrast Beowulf's humble character with the grandeur of the gold-hall he is entering.

choices.label: D
choices.text: They shift the focus from Grendel's severed head to the reactions of the beer-thanes watching in the hall.

cards.question: Read the following lines from the excerpt: 'In so manly a manner the mighty-famed chieftain, / Hoard-ward of heroes, with horses and jewels / War-storms requited, that none e'er condemneth / Who willeth to tell truth with full justice.' How does the phrase 'Hoard-ward of heroes' contribute to the elevated style of the poem?

choices.label: A
choices.text: It names the king plainly so the audience can identify him without confusion during the gift-giving scene.

choices.label: B
choices.text: It replaces the king's proper name with a compound title that glorifies his role as protector and treasure-giver, raising the dignity of the moment beyond ordinary speech.

choices.label: C
choices.text: It signals that the king is reluctant to part with his treasure, creating tension between the king and Beowulf.

choices.label: D
choices.text: It compares the king's generosity to a guardian standing watch, functioning as an extended simile that spans the entire passage.

cards.standardTitle: Theme development across a literary text
cards.excerpt: Mighty achievements, many things hidden, 40 The strife of the Wælsing, the wide-going ventures The children of men knew of but little, The feud and the fury, but Fitela with him, When suchlike matters he minded to speak of, Uncle to nephew, as in every contention 45 Each to other was ever devoted: A numerous host of the race of the scathers They had slain with the sword-edge. To Sigmund accrued then No little of glory, when his life-days were over, Since he sturdy in struggle had destroyed the great dragon, 50 The hoard-treasure's keeper; 'neath the hoar-grayish stone he, The son of the atheling, unaided adventured The perilous project; not present was Fitela, Yet the fortune befell him of forcing his weapon Through the marvellous dragon, that it stood in the wall, 55 Well-honored weapon; the worm was slaughtered. The great one had gained then by his glorious achievement To reap from the ring-hoard richest enjoyment, As best it did please him: his vessel he loaded, Shining ornaments on the ship's bosom carried, 60 Kinsman of Wæls: the drake in heat melted.
cards.whyThisWorks: The excerpt presents two distinct story moments—Sigmund and Fitela's joint battles against the scathers, and Sigmund's solitary slaying of the dragon—that together develop the theme that true glory is earned through both loyal partnership and individual courage tested alone.
cards.skillStrategy: When tracking theme, identify at least two separate moments in the passage and ask what idea both moments point toward together.
evidencePoints: Uncle to nephew, as in every contention / Each to other was ever devoted: / A numerous host of the race of the scathers / They had slain with the sword-edge.
not present was Fitela, / Yet the fortune befell him of forcing his weapon / Through the marvellous dragon... To Sigmund accrued then / No little of glory, when his life-days were over
cards.question: In the excerpt, the poet first describes Sigmund and Fitela slaying 'a numerous host of the race of the scathers' together, and then describes Sigmund destroying the dragon 'unaided' while 'not present was Fitela.' How do these two moments work together to develop a theme?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Both moments show that Sigmund's fame depended entirely on Fitela's loyalty, since their shared devotion in battle is what the poet emphasizes most.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Together the moments suggest that a hero's glory grows from both the bonds forged in shared struggle and the courage to face the greatest dangers alone.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Both moments reveal that wealth and treasure, not personal valor, are the true measure of a warrior's worth, since Sigmund loads his ship with the ring-hoard after the dragon fight.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The two moments contrast loyalty and betrayal, implying that Fitela's absence during the dragon fight was a deliberate abandonment that Sigmund had to overcome.

cards.standardTitle: Epic poetry: characters, structures, and themes
cards.excerpt: Then 'twas seen that the journey prospered him little Who wrongly within had the ornaments hidden Down 'neath the wall. The warden erst slaughtered Some few of the folk-troop: the feud then thereafter 5 Was hotly avengèd. 'Tis a wonder where, When the strength-famous trooper has attained to the end of Life-days allotted, then no longer the man may Remain with his kinsmen where mead-cups are flowing. So to Beowulf happened when the ward of the barrow, 10 Assaults, he sought for: himself had no knowledge How his leaving this life was likely to happen. So to doomsday, famous folk-leaders down did Call it with curses--who 'complished it there-- That that man should be ever of ill-deeds convicted, 15 Confined in foul-places, fastened in hell-bonds, Punished with plagues, who this place should e'er ravage. He cared not for gold: rather the Wielder's Favor preferred he first to get sight of.
cards.whyThisWorks: The excerpt contains a clear epic simile structure in lines 6–9 ('Tis a wonder where... So to Beowulf happened') that extends a general reflection on mortality into a specific application to Beowulf, demonstrating the formal, elevated style and extended comparison central to the subskill.
cards.skillStrategy: When you spot a general statement followed by 'So to [hero] happened,' trace how the comparison stretches across multiple lines to elevate the hero's fate to a universal truth.
evidencePoints: 'Tis a wonder where, / When the strength-famous trooper has attained to the end of / Life-days allotted, then no longer the man may / Remain with his kinsmen where mead-cups are flowing.
So to Beowulf happened when the ward of the barrow, / Assaults, he sought for: himself had no knowledge / How his leaving this life was likely to happen.
cards.question: Read the following lines from the excerpt: "'Tis a wonder where, / When the strength-famous trooper has attained to the end of / Life-days allotted, then no longer the man may / Remain with his kinsmen where mead-cups are flowing. / So to Beowulf happened..." How does this extended comparison contribute to the epic style of the passage?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The comparison focuses on the mead-hall as a symbol of Beowulf's personal failure, showing that he valued feasting over his duty to fight the dragon.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The passage first states a broad, formal reflection on the fate of all warriors whose allotted days end, then applies that universal truth directly to Beowulf, elevating his death to the level of an inevitable, timeless law of heroic life.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The lines contrast Beowulf's ignorance of his fate with the dragon's awareness, suggesting the dragon is the more powerful figure in the poem.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The repeated phrase 'So to Beowulf happened' functions as an invocation, calling on divine forces to witness Beowulf's final battle with the dragon.

cards.standardTitle: Key literary elements add layers of meaning
cards.excerpt:
Sundered Hæthcyn the Hrethling from life-joys, When for pride overweening the War-Scylfings first did Seek the Geatmen with savage intentions. 35 Early did Ohthere's age-laden father, Old and terrible, give blow in requital, Killing the sea-king, the queen-mother rescued, The old one his consort deprived of her gold, Onela's mother and Ohthere's also, 40 And then followed the feud-nursing foemen till hardly, Reaved of their ruler, they Ravenswood entered. Then with vast-numbered forces he assaulted the remnant, Weary with wounds, woe often promised The livelong night to the sad-hearted war-troop: 45 Said he at morning would kill them with edges of weapons, Some on the gallows for glee to the fowls. Aid came after to the anxious-in-spirit At dawn of the day, after Higelac's bugle And trumpet-sound heard they, when the good one proceeded 50 And faring followed the flower of the troopers.

'Hige-méðum' (2910) is glossed by H. as dat. plu. (= for the dead). S. proposes 'hige-méðe,' nom. sing. limiting Wigláf; i.e. _W., mood-weary, holds head-watch o'er friend and foe_.--B. suggests taking the word as dat. inst. plu. of an abstract noun in -'u.' The translation would be substantially the same as S.'s.
cards.whyThisWorks: The sudden arrival of Higelac's forces at dawn directly reverses the war-troop's desperate, promised doom, showing how a plot reversal conveys the theme that loyalty and timely aid can snatch survival from certain destruction.
cards.skillStrategy: When a reversal changes a character's fate, ask what the shift from doom to rescue reveals about the poem's deeper values or themes.
evidencePoints: Said he at morning would kill them with edges of weapons, Some on the gallows for glee to the fowls.
Aid came after to the anxious-in-spirit At dawn of the day, after Higelac's bugle And trumpet-sound heard they
cards.question: The enemy commander promises the trapped war-troop death by morning, yet Higelac's forces arrive at dawn and rescue them. What deeper meaning does this reversal add to the passage?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The reversal shows that the War-Scylfings were overconfident and therefore deserved to lose the battle they had started with the Geatmen.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The reversal reveals that loyalty to one's lord carries life-or-death power, transforming a night of promised slaughter into survival the moment Higelac answers his people's need.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The reversal demonstrates that the war-troop's wounds were not as severe as the enemy believed, allowing the Geatmen to hold out until morning on their own strength.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The reversal suggests that the enemy commander's threat was an empty boast, since he never truly intended to execute the prisoners at dawn.

cards.question: Read the following two moments from the excerpt: the thief whose 'journey prospered him little' after wrongly hiding the ornaments, and Beowulf, who 'cared not for gold' and 'the Wielder's Favor preferred he first to get sight of.' How do these two moments work together to develop a theme?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Both moments show that warriors who enter cursed places are doomed to die, regardless of their intentions or moral character.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The thief's ruin from wrongly seizing treasure and Beowulf's choice to value divine favor over gold together develop the idea that greed brings destruction while honorable devotion earns lasting worth.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The thief's punishment and Beowulf's death both show that no mortal can escape fate once the end of 'life-days allotted' has been determined by outside forces.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Both moments focus on the power of ancient curses to punish anyone who enters the barrow, suggesting that sacred places must never be disturbed by any person.

cards.whyThisWorks: Beowulf's fatal encounter with the barrow-warden—combined with the curse on any who would plunder the hoard and his own indifference to gold—creates a layered conflict between earthly treasure and divine favor that deepens the poem's theme of mortality and spiritual loyalty.
cards.skillStrategy: When a character faces a conflict or consequence, ask what the outcome reveals about a larger truth the author wants readers to understand beyond the surface event.
evidencePoints: himself had no knowledge / How his leaving this life was likely to happen

cards.question: The passage describes Beowulf seeking out the barrow-warden without knowing 'how his leaving this life was likely to happen,' and then concludes that 'He cared not for gold: rather the Wielder's Favor preferred he first to get sight of.' How does this sequence of events add a deeper layer of meaning to Beowulf's conflict?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Beowulf's ignorance of his fate shows that even the greatest warriors are undone by greed, since his decision to seek the barrow proves he valued treasure above all else.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Beowulf's unknowing approach to death, followed by the revelation that he sought divine favor over gold, suggests that his true conflict was never with the barrow-warden but with the mortal limits no warrior—however famous—can escape.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The curse placed on anyone who ravages the barrow is the central conflict, and Beowulf's death is simply the curse's punishment for his decision to plunder the hoard.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The passage shows that Beowulf's conflict with the barrow-warden is a straightforward battle, and the mention of the Wielder's Favor is a reminder that God rewards warriors who fight bravely in combat.

cards.question: Read the lines: 'the prince of the people / Measured the mead-ways, their mood-brave companion. / The atheling of earlmen entered the building, / Deed-valiant man, adorned with distinction.' What do these details reveal about Beowulf as an epic hero?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Beowulf's pride in his own glory causes him to enter the hall alone, separating himself from his warriors to claim sole credit for defeating Grendel.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Beowulf leads his men back to Hrothgar's hall and enters as their courageous and honored leader, demonstrating both his bravery and his role guiding his companions.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Beowulf is reluctant to present Grendel's head to Hrothgar and must be encouraged by his fourteen warriors to enter the gold-hall.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Beowulf's endurance is shown by the physical difficulty he personally experiences carrying Grendel's head on a spear to the mead-hall.

cards.question: The narrator emphasizes that Sigmund faced the dragon 'unaided' and that 'not present was Fitela.' How does this detail about Sigmund's solitary conflict deepen the meaning of the passage?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Fitela's absence shows that the bond between uncle and nephew had weakened by the time of the dragon fight, suggesting their earlier loyalty was temporary.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Sigmund's choice to face the dragon alone, unlike his earlier shared battles with Fitela, signals that the highest form of heroic glory belongs to the warrior who conquers the greatest danger without any companion's aid.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The dragon fight is presented as less important than Sigmund's earlier ventures with Fitela because the narrator spends more lines describing their shared feud and fury.

choices.label: D

choices.label: B
choices.text: Because Sigmund chooses to face the dragon alone and succeeds, the passage develops the idea that individual courage in the face of mortal danger is what earns a warrior enduring glory.

choices.label: D

choices.label: B

The atheling of earlmen entered the building, 85 Deed-valiant man, adorned with distinction, Doughty shield-warrior, to address King Hrothgar: Then hung by the hair, the head of Grendel Was borne to the building, where beer-thanes were drinking, Loth before earlmen and eke 'fore the lady: 90 The warriors beheld then a wonderful sight.

'Þæs monige gewearð' (1599) and 'hafað þæs geworden' (2027).--In a paper published some years ago in one of the Johns Hopkins University circulars, I tried to throw upon these two long-doubtful passages some light derived from a study of like passages in Alfred's prose.--The impersonal verb 'geweorðan,' with an accus. of the person, and a þæt-clause is used several times with the meaning 'agree.' choices.label: B

choices.label: D

cards.question: The passage begins by referencing 'mighty achievements' and 'things hidden' that 'the children of men knew of but little.' How does this opening affect the reader's understanding of Sigmund's story?

Four of them had to carry with labor The head of Grendel to the high towering gold-hall 80 Upstuck on the spear, till fourteen most-valiant And battle-brave Geatmen came there going Straight to the palace: the prince of the people Measured the mead-ways, their mood-brave companion. 'Þæs monige gewearð' (1599) and 'hafað þæs geworden' (2027).--In a paper published some years ago in one of the Johns Hopkins University circulars, I tried to throw upon these two long-doubtful passages some light derived from a study of like passages in Alfred's prose.--The impersonal verb 'geweorðan,' with an accus. of the person, and a þæt-clause is used several times with the meaning 'agree.' See Orosius (Sweet's ed.) 178_7; 204_34; 208_28; 210_15; 280_20. In the two Beowulf passages, the þæt-clause is anticipated by 'þæs,' which is clearly a gen. of the thing agreed on.

cards.excerpt: This is perhaps the least understood sentence in the poem, almost every word being open to dispute. (1) The 'nó' of our text is an emendation, and is rejected by many scholars. (2) 'Seldan' is by some taken as an adv. (= _seldom_), and by others as a noun (= _page_, _companion_). (3) 'Léod-hryre,' some render '_fall of the people_'; others, '_fall of the prince_.' (4) 'Búgeð,' most scholars regard as the intrans. verb meaning '_bend_,' '_rest_'; but one great scholar has translated it '_shall kill_.' (5) 'Hwær,' Very recently, has been attacked, 'wære' being suggested. (6) As a corollary to the above, the same critic proposes to drop 'oft' out of the text.--t.B. suggests: Oft seldan wære after léodhryre: lýtle hwíle bongár búgeð, þéah séo brýd duge = _often has a treaty been (thus) struck, after a prince had fallen: (but only) a short time is the spear (then) wont to rest, however excellent the bride may be_.
cards.whyThisWorks: The excerpt's dense accumulation of competing scholarly translations—each introduced by 'some,' 'others,' 'most,' or 'one great scholar'—demonstrates how the author's diction and syntax build a tone of scholarly uncertainty and intellectual humility, giving students a clear stylistic feature to analyze for effect.

cards.question: Read the following lines from the excerpt: 'Weary with wounds, woe often promised / The livelong night to the sad-hearted war-troop.' What effect does the poet's diction in these lines create?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The repeated references to wounds and night establish that the warriors have been fighting for many years without rest or reinforcement.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The compressed, heavy phrasing—'weary with wounds,' 'woe often promised,' 'sad-hearted'—piles suffering onto the warriors so that their endurance through the night feels both desperate and heroic.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The phrase 'the livelong night' signals that the poet is criticizing the war-troop for failing to escape when they had the opportunity to do so.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The diction shifts the focus away from the enemy's cruelty and onto the landscape of Ravenswood, making the setting the true source of the warriors' suffering.

cards.excerpt: That in it did perish. The seamen's defender came swimming to land then 65 Doughty of spirit, rejoiced in his sea-gift, The bulky burden which he bore in his keeping. The excellent vassals advanced then to meet him, To God they were grateful, were glad in their chieftain, That to see him safe and sound was granted them. 70 From the high-minded hero, then, helmet and burnie Were speedily loosened: the ocean was putrid, The water 'neath welkin weltered with gore. cards.question: The passage describes Beowulf as 'the seamen's defender' who 'came swimming to land' carrying 'the bulky burden' while his vassals 'were glad in their chieftain' and 'to see him safe and sound was granted them.' What role does this moment play in the epic's quest structure?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Beowulf's return to land with 'the bulky burden' signals the start of a new underwater obstacle, because the vassals' advance suggests they must re-enter the sea to assist him.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Beowulf surfaces carrying physical proof of his victory and is met by his men's grateful recognition, marking the completion of the underwater combat stage and the hero's return to his community.

choices.label: C

choices.label: D

To Sigmund accrued then No little of glory, when his life-days were over, Since he sturdy in struggle had destroyed the great dragon, 50 The hoard-treasure's keeper; 'neath the hoar-grayish stone he, The son of the atheling, unaided adventured The perilous project; not present was Fitela, Yet the fortune befell him of forcing his weapon Through the marvellous dragon, that it stood in the wall, 55 Well-honored weapon; the worm was slaughtered. The great one had gained then by his glorious achievement To reap from the ring-hoard richest enjoyment, As best it did please him: his vessel he loaded, Shining ornaments on the ship's bosom carried, 60 Kinsman of Wæls: the drake in heat melted.
cards.whyThisWorks: Sigmund's solitary slaying of the dragon—'unaided adventured / The perilous project'—directly develops the theme of honor earned through heroic action, showing how individual courage in the face of mortal danger brings lasting glory.
cards.skillStrategy: When identifying theme through heroic action, locate the specific deed a hero performs, then ask what value or idea the poet says that deed proves or earns for the hero.
evidencePoints: 'unaided adventured / The perilous project; not present was Fitela'
'To Sigmund accrued then / No little of glory, when his life-days were over, / Since he sturdy in struggle had destroyed the great dragon'
cards.question: In the passage, Sigmund slays the dragon alone, without Fitela. How does this detail develop a theme in the excerpt?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Sigmund's solitary act shows that loyalty between companions is the only path to lasting fame, since the poet emphasizes how uncle and nephew were 'ever devoted' in every other battle.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Sigmund's solitary act develops a theme of honor earned through individual courage, because the poet directly connects his unaided struggle against the dragon to the glory that outlasted his life.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Sigmund's solitary act develops a theme of fate's cruelty, because fighting without Fitela leads to Sigmund's death and proves that no warrior can survive without a trusted companion.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Sigmund's solitary act reveals a theme of greed, since the poet focuses most on the ring-hoard Sigmund claims and the shining ornaments he loads onto his vessel after the dragon melts.

cards.question: In the excerpt, the poet moves from 'woe often promised / The livelong night to the sad-hearted war-troop' to 'Aid came after to the anxious-in-spirit / At dawn of the day.' How does this contrast in the passage contribute to the poem's tone and theme?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The contrast between night and dawn shows that the war-troop's suffering was caused by their own cowardice, suggesting a theme of deserved punishment for those who flee into Ravenswood.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The shift from a night of promised death to dawn rescue creates a tone of hard-won relief, reinforcing a theme that loyal leadership—embodied by Higelac's timely arrival—can redeem even the most desperate suffering.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The movement from night to dawn establishes a tone of bitter irony, suggesting that the war-troop's rescue came too late to matter and that the theme is the futility of military alliances.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The contrast between the night threats and the morning bugle creates a tone of celebration focused on Higelac's personal glory, pointing toward a theme that individual fame is the highest reward a warrior can earn.

'Þæs monige gewearð' (1599) and 'hafað þæs geworden' (2027).--In a paper published some years ago in one of the Johns Hopkins University circulars, I tried to throw upon these two long-doubtful passages some light derived from a study of like passages in Alfred's prose.--The impersonal verb 'geweorðan,' with an accus. of the person, and a þæt-clause is used several times with the meaning 'agree.' See Orosius (Sweet's ed.) 178_7; 204_34; 208_28; 210_15; 280_20. In the two Beowulf passages, the þæt-clause is anticipated by 'þæs,' which is clearly a gen. of the thing agreed on.

Which restatement most accurately captures the meaning of this sentence?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Fourteen Geatmen struggled to lift Grendel's head onto a spear and then carried it alone to the gold-hall without any help.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Four men strained to carry Grendel's head, mounted on a spear, to the great hall, and they continued until all fourteen brave Geatmen arrived at the palace together.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Four warriors carried Grendel's entire body to the gold-hall on a spear, where fourteen Geatmen were already waiting inside.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Fourteen Geatmen took turns carrying Grendel's head to the palace because the task was too difficult for only four men to complete.

cards.question: Read this sentence from the passage: 'Furthermore, to call the Geats 'brave' might, at this point, seem like an implied thrust at the Danes, so long helpless; while to call his own men 'timid' would be befouling his own nest.' Which restatement most accurately captures the meaning of this sentence?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Describing the Geats as brave is the correct reading because it highlights the contrast between the Geats and the Danes, who are portrayed as cowardly throughout the poem.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Labeling the Geats as brave could come across as an indirect insult to the long-suffering Danes, and labeling his own men as timid would damage the speaker's own reputation.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Calling the Geats brave is a direct attack on the Danes, and calling his own men timid is the only honest description available to the speaker at this point in the text.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The speaker argues that neither 'brave' nor 'timid' is a meaningful description of the Geats, since both words create the same problem of offending the Danish audience.

cards.standardTitle: Narrator perspective, irony, and satire
cards.excerpt: The hallway smelt of boiled cabbage and old rag mats. At one end of it a colored poster, too large for indoor display, had been tacked to the wall. It depicted simply an enormous face, more than a meter wide: the face of a man of about forty-five, with a heavy black mustache and ruggedly handsome features. Winston made for the stairs. It was no use trying the lift. Even at the best of times it was seldom working, and at present the electric current was cut off during daylight hours. It was part of the economy drive in preparation for Hate Week. The flat was seven flights up, and Winston, who was thirty-nine, and had a varicose ulcer above his right ankle, went slowly, resting several times on the way. On each landing, opposite the lift ^ shaft, the poster with the enormous face gazed from the wall. K It was one of those pictures which are so contrived that the eyes follow you about when you move. Big Brother Is Watching You, the caption beneath it ran.
cards.whyThisWorks: The phrase 'Big Brother Is Watching You' paired with a broken lift, cut electricity, and a physically struggling Winston creates sharp irony: the regime projects total surveillance and power while its citizens live in obvious decay and neglect.
cards.skillStrategy: Look for a contradiction between what the government claims or displays and what the details of daily life actually reveal — that gap is where the irony lives.
evidencePoints: Big Brother Is Watching You, the caption beneath it ran.
Even at the best of times it was seldom working, and at present the electric current was cut off during daylight hours.
cards.question: Read the following sentences from the passage: 'Even at the best of times it was seldom working, and at present the electric current was cut off during daylight hours' and 'Big Brother Is Watching You, the caption beneath it ran.' What contradiction between these details creates irony?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The poster is too large for indoor display, yet it appears on every landing, suggesting the government wastes resources on decoration while ignoring citizens' needs.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The caption declares that Big Brother watches over everyone, yet the government cannot keep the electricity or the lift running for the very citizens it claims to oversee.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Winston climbs seven flights of stairs despite his varicose ulcer, showing that citizens are forced to work harder because of Hate Week preparations.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The enormous face on the poster appears ruggedly handsome and powerful, while Winston is described as aging and physically weakened, highlighting a contrast in appearance.

cards.standardTitle: Key literary elements add layers of meaning
cards.excerpt: Winston sat back against the window sill. It was no usgoing on. He was about to buy some more beer when the old man suddenly got up and shuffled rapidly into the stinking urinal at the side of the room. The extra half-liter was already working on him. Winston sat for a minute or two gazing at his empty glass, and hardly noticed when his feet carried him out into the street again. Within twenty years at the most, he reflected, the huge and simple question, "Was life better before the Revolution than it is now?" would have ceased once and for all to be answerable. But in effect it was unanswerable even now. since the few scattered survivors from the ancient world were incapable of comparing one age with another. They remembered a million useless things, a quarrel with a workmate, a hunt for a lost bicycle pump, the expression on a lone-dead sister’s face, the swirls of dust on a windy morning seventy years ago; but all the relevant facts were outside the range ot their vision. They were like the ant, which can see small objects but not large ones. And when memory failed and written records were falsified—when that happened, the claim of the Party to have improved the conditions of human, life had got to be accepted, because there did not exist, aa never again could exist, any standard against which it cou be tested.
cards.whyThisWorks: Winston's failed attempt to gather historical truth from the old man—ending when the man shuffles away to the urinal—functions as a plot reversal that deepens the novel's central conflict: the Party's erasure of the past makes objective truth permanently unverifiable.
cards.skillStrategy: When a scene ends without resolution, ask what the character loses because of that outcome and what larger idea that loss represents.
evidencePoints: It was no use going on.

when memory failed and written records were falsified—when that happened, the claim of the Party to have improved the conditions of human life had got to be accepted, because there did not exist, and never again could exist, any standard against which it could be tested.
cards.question: Winston's conversation with the old man ends abruptly when the man 'shuffled rapidly into the stinking urinal.' What deeper meaning does this moment add to the passage?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The old man's departure shows that ordinary citizens are too self-absorbed to care about Winston's political concerns, suggesting that apathy, not the Party, is the true enemy of truth.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The old man's exit cuts off Winston's last chance to recover a reliable memory of the past, reinforcing that once living witnesses are gone, the Party's version of history becomes the only version that can exist.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The old man's sudden departure reveals that he is afraid of Winston and suspects him of being a Party informant, which explains why he refuses to answer questions about life before the Revolution.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The interruption proves that the old man's memories are too fragmented to be useful, implying that Winston should seek written records rather than personal testimony to learn the truth about the past.

cards.standardTitle: Theme development across a literary text
cards.excerpt: The Hate rose to its climax. The voice of Goldstein had become an actual sheep's bleat, and for an instant the face ♦ changed into that of a sheep. Then the sheep-face melted into the figure of a Eurasian soldier who seemed to be advancing, huge and terrible, his submachine gun roaring, and seeming to spring out of the surface of the screen, so that some of the people in the front row actually flinched backwards in their seats. But in the same moment, drawing a deep sigh of relief from everybody, the hostile figure melted into the face of Big Brother, black-haired, black mustachio’d, full of power and mysterious calm, and so vast that it almost filled up the screen. Nobody heard what Big Brother was saying. It was merely a few words of encouragement, the sort of words that are uttered in the din of battle, not distinguishable individually but restoring confidence by the fact of being spoken.
cards.whyThisWorks: The excerpt dramatizes how manufactured fear and its sudden relief condition citizens to transfer hatred onto an enemy and devotion onto Big Brother, making the emotional sequence a direct vehicle for the theme that totalitarian power is sustained through psychological manipulation rather than truth.
cards.skillStrategy: Track what characters feel, then ask what consequence or change that feeling produces — the theme lives in that cause-and-effect chain.
evidencePoints: the hostile figure melted into the face of Big Brother, black-haired, black mustachio'd, full of power and mysterious calm, and so vast that it almost filled up the screen
drawing a deep sigh of relief from everybody
cards.question: In the excerpt, the crowd's shift from flinching terror at the Eurasian soldier to a 'deep sigh of relief' when Big Brother's face appears develops which theme?

choices.label: A
choices.text: War demands personal sacrifice, and citizens who witness combat footage naturally feel gratitude toward the leaders who protect them.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Totalitarian power is maintained by engineering fear and then replacing it with manufactured comfort, leaving citizens emotionally dependent on the state rather than capable of independent thought.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Propaganda loses its effectiveness over time because audiences eventually recognize that threatening images are exaggerated, as shown when the soldier's face dissolves.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Individuals are powerless against violence, and the crowd's flinching reveals that physical danger, not political loyalty, is the true force shaping human behavior.

cards.question: Winston concludes that the question of whether life was better before the Revolution 'was unanswerable even now' and compares the old survivors to ants that 'can see small objects but not large ones.' What does the reader understand about this situation that Winston's resigned reflection does not fully acknowledge?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The old man's inability to answer Winston's questions proves that ordinary citizens never cared about life before the Revolution.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The unanswerable quality of the question is not simply a natural failure of aging memory but the direct result of the Party deliberately falsifying written records to eliminate any standard of comparison.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Winston's comparison of survivors to ants shows he respects their limited perspective and believes their small memories are more trustworthy than official records.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The survivors' scattered memories of quarrels and lost bicycle pumps suggest that life before the Revolution was too trivial to be worth comparing to the present.

cards.question: Read the following sentence from the passage: 'They were like the ant, which can see small objects but not large ones.' Which of the following most accurately restates what this sentence means in context?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The survivors paid close attention to minor details of the past while deliberately ignoring the larger political changes the Party had made.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The survivors could recall specific personal memories but were unable to grasp the broader picture of how life had changed across time.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The survivors were physically weakened by age and could only manage small, simple tasks rather than the larger responsibilities of earlier life.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The survivors remembered only the smallest and least important events from before the Revolution, proving that those events never really mattered.

cards.standardTitle: Key literary elements add layers of meaning
cards.excerpt: It was even possible, at moments, to switch one's hatred this way or that by a voluntary act. Suddenly, by the sort of violent effort with which one wrenches one’s head away from the pillow in a nightmare, Winston succeeded in transferring his hatred from the face on the screen to the dark-haired girl behind him. Vivid, beautiful hallucinations flashed through his mind. He would flog her to death with a rubber truncheon. He would tie her naked to a stake and shoot her full of arrows like Saint Sebastian. He would ravish her and cut her throat at the moment of climax. Better than before, moreover, he realized why it was that he hated her. He hated her because she was young and pretty and sexless, because he wanted to go to bed with her and would never do so, because round her sweet supple waist, which seemed to ask you to encircle it with your arm, there was only the odious scarlet sash, aggressive symbol of chastity.
cards.whyThisWorks: Winston's deliberate redirection of hatred from the screen to the girl—and his sudden clarity about why he hates her—reveals how inner conflict driven by repressed desire and Party-enforced chastity adds a deeper layer of meaning about the psychological cost of totalitarian control.
cards.skillStrategy: When a character makes a decision or experiences a sudden realization, ask what that moment reveals about a larger truth the author is building.
evidencePoints: he realized why it was that he hated her. He hated her because she was young and pretty and sexless, because he wanted to go to bed with her and would never do so
round her sweet supple waist, which seemed to ask you to encircle it with your arm, there was only the odious scarlet sash, aggressive symbol of chastity
cards.question: Winston's sudden transfer of hatred from the screen to the dark-haired girl, followed by his realization of why he hates her, adds a deeper layer of meaning to the passage. What does this internal conflict most clearly reveal?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Winston's violent fantasies show that he is naturally cruel and that the Party has done nothing to change his character.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Winston's hatred is rooted in desire that the Party's rules have made impossible to act on, suggesting that totalitarian control distorts human emotion by turning longing into rage.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Winston redirects his hatred because he genuinely despises the girl's personality, and the scarlet sash is simply a detail he notices about her appearance.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Winston's ability to shift his hatred voluntarily proves he has mastered the Party's techniques and is becoming a loyal follower of its ideology.

The young, strong body, now helpless in sleep, awoke in him a pitying, protecting feeling. But the mindless tenderness ^^iat he had felt under the hazel tree, while the thrush was singing, had not quite come back. He pulled the overalls aside and studied her smooth white flank. In the old days, he thought, a man looked at a girl’s body and saw that it was desirable, and that was the end of the story. But you could not have pure love or pure lust nowadays. No emotion was pure, because everything was mixed up with fear and hatred. Their embrace had been a battle, the climax a victory. It was a blow struck against the Party. It was a political act.

‘‘We can come here once again,” said Julia. ‘‘It’s generally safe to use any hide-out twice. But not for another month or two, of course.”

As soon as she woke up her demeanor had changed. She became alert and businesslike, put her clothes on, knotted the scarlet sash about her waist, and began arranging the details of the journey home. It seemed natural to leave this to her. She obviously had a practical cunning which Winston lacked, and she seemed also to have an exhaustive knowledge of the countryside round London, stored away from innumerable community hikes. The route she gave him was quite different from the one by which he had come, and brought him out at a different railway station. “Never go home the same way as you went out,” she said, as though enunciating an important general principle. She would leave first, and Winston was to wait half an hour before following her.
cards.whyThisWorks: Winston's realization that 'their embrace had been a battle' and 'a political act' shows how the consequence of living under the Party corrupts even intimate human connection, directly developing a theme about totalitarianism's destruction of authentic emotion.
cards.skillStrategy: When a character has a realization or names a consequence, ask yourself: what does this moment reveal about a larger truth the author is building throughout the text?

cards.question: Winston reflects that 'their embrace had been a battle' and 'a political act' rather than an expression of genuine feeling. How does this realization develop a theme in the passage?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Winston's inability to feel tenderness toward Julia shows that he is personally incapable of love, suggesting that some individuals are emotionally damaged beyond repair.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Because the Party's control has made fear and hatred inseparable from every emotion, even an intimate act becomes a form of resistance rather than genuine human connection, suggesting that totalitarian power corrupts the most private aspects of life.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Winston's framing of the embrace as a victory reveals that he values defeating the Party more than he values Julia herself, suggesting that political ambition destroys personal relationships.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Julia's calm, businesslike behavior after waking contrasts with Winston's emotional turmoil, suggesting that practical people survive oppression better than those who dwell on their feelings.

Yet the cage with the rats was not two meters away from him. They were enormous rats. They were at the age when a rat s muzzle grows blunt and fierce and his fur brown instead of gray.

“The rat,” said O’Brien, still addressing his invisible audience, “although a rodent, is carnivorous. You are aware of that. You will have heard of the things that happen in the poor quarters of this town. In some streets a woman dare not leave her baby alone in the house, even for five minutes. The rats are certain to attack it. Within quite a small time they will strip it to the bones. They also attack sick or dying people. They show astonishing intelligence in knowing when a human being is helpless."

There was an outburst of squeals from the cage. It seemed to reach Winston from far away. The rats were fighting: they V^re trying to get at each other through the partition. He b *ard also a deep groan of despair. That, too, seemed to come from outside himself.

cards.standardTitle: Theme development across a literary text
cards.excerpt: Winston sat back against the window sill. It was no usgoing on. He was about to buy some more beer when the old man suddenly got up and shuffled rapidly into the stinking urinal at the side of the room. The extra half-liter was already working on him. Winston sat for a minute or two gazing at his empty glass, and hardly noticed when his feet carried him out into the street again. Within twenty years at the most, he reflected, the huge and simple question, "Was life better before the Revolution than it is now?" would have ceased once and for all to be answerable. But in effect it was unanswerable even now. since the few scattered survivors from the ancient world were incapable of comparing one age with another. They remembered a million useless things, a quarrel with a workmate, a hunt for a lost bicycle pump, the expression on a lone-dead sister’s face, the swirls of dust on a windy morning seventy years ago; but all the relevant facts were outside the range ot their vision. They were like the ant, which can see small objects but not large ones. And when memory failed and written records were falsified—when that happened, the claim of the Party to have improved the conditions of human, life had got to be accepted, because there did not exist, aa never again could exist, any standard against which it cou be tested.

cards.standardTitle: Narrator perspective, irony, and satire
cards.excerpt: Something in the tone of his voice seemed to add, “that bloody fool.” Parsons, Winston's fellow tenant at Victory Mansions, was in fact threading his way across the room—a tubby, middle-sized man with fair hair and a froglike face. At thirty-five he was already putting on rolls of fat at neck and waistline, but his movements were brisk and boyish. His whole appearance was that of a little boy grown large, so much so that although he was wearing the regulation overalls, it was almost impossible not to think of him as being dressed in the blue shorts, gray shirt, and red neckerchief of the Spies. In visualizing him one saw always a picture of dimpled knees and sleeves rolled back from pudgy forearms. Parsons did, indeed, invariably revert to shorts when a community hike or any other physical activity gave him an excuse for doing so. The young, strong body, now helpless in sleep, awoke in him a pitying, protecting feeling. In the old days, he thought, a man looked at a girl’s body and saw that it was desirable, and that was the end of the story. But you could not have pure love or pure lust nowadays. ‘‘We can come here once again,” said Julia. ‘‘It’s generally safe to use any hide-out twice. But not for another month or two, of course.”

As soon as she woke up her demeanor had changed. She became alert and businesslike, put her clothes on, knotted the scarlet sash about her waist, and began arranging the details of the journey home. It seemed natural to leave this to her. She obviously had a practical cunning which Winston lacked, and she seemed also to have an exhaustive knowledge of the countryside round London, stored away from innumerable community hikes. The route she gave him was quite different from the one by which he had come, and brought him out at a different railway station. “Never go home the same way as you went out,” she said, as though enunciating an important general principle. choices.label: D
