cards.excerpt: Something in the tone of his voice seemed to add, “that bloody fool.” Parsons, Winston's fellow tenant at Victory Mansions, was in fact threading his way across the room—a tubby, middle-sized man with fair hair and a froglike face. At thirty-five he was already putting on rolls of fat at neck and waistline, but his movements were brisk and boyish. His whole appearance was that of a little boy grown large, so much so that although he was wearing the regulation overalls, it was almost impossible not to think of him as being dressed in the blue shorts, gray shirt, and red neckerchief of the Spies. In visualizing him one saw always a picture of dimpled knees and sleeves rolled back from pudgy forearms. Parsons did, indeed, invariably revert to shorts when a community hike or any other physical activity gave him an excuse for doing so. He greeted them both with a cheery “Hullo, hullo!” and sat down at the table, giving off an intense smell of sweat. Beads of moisture stood out all over his pink face. His powers of sweating were extraordinary. At the Community Center you could always tell when he had been playing table tennis by the dampness of the bat handle. cards.excerpt: For the rest of the morning it was very difficult to work. What was even worse than having to focus his mind on a series of niggling jobs was the need to conceal his agitation from the telescreen. He felt as though a fire were burning in his belly. He had hoped to be alone for a little while during ^ the lunch hour, but as bad luck would have it the jmbecile Parsons flopped down beside him, the tang of his sweat almost defeating the tinny smell of stew, and kept up a stream of talk about the preparations for Hate Week. He was particularly enthusiastic about a papier-mache model of Big Brother’s head, two meters wide, which was being made for the occasion by his daughter’s troop of Spies. The irritating thing was that in the racket of voices Winston could hardly hear what Parsons was saying, and was constantly having to ask for some fatuous remark to be repeated. cards.excerpt: The Hate rose to its climax. The voice of Goldstein had become an actual sheep's bleat, and for an instant the face ♦ changed into that of a sheep. Then the sheep-face melted into the figure of a Eurasian soldier who seemed to be advancing, huge and terrible, his submachine gun roaring, and seeming to spring out of the surface of the screen, so that some of the people in the front row actually flinched backwards in their seats. cards.standardTitle: Key literary elements add layers of meaning
cards.excerpt: Winston sat back against the window sill. It was no usgoing on. He was about to buy some more beer when the old man suddenly got up and shuffled rapidly into the stinking urinal at the side of the room. The extra half-liter was already working on him. Winston sat for a minute or two gazing at his empty glass, and hardly noticed when his feet carried him out into the street again. Within twenty years at the most, he reflected, the huge and simple question, "Was life better before the Revolution than it is now?" would have ceased once and for all to be answerable. But in effect it was unanswerable even now. since the few scattered survivors from the ancient world were incapable of comparing one age with another. They remembered a million useless things, a quarrel with a workmate, a hunt for a lost bicycle pump, the expression on a lone-dead sister’s face, the swirls of dust on a windy morning seventy years ago; but all the relevant facts were outside the range ot their vision. They were like the ant, which can see small objects but not large ones. And when memory failed and written records were falsified—when that happened, the claim of the Party to have improved the conditions of human, life had got to be accepted, because there did not exist, aa never again could exist, any standard against which it cou be tested.

cards.excerpt: It was even possible, at moments, to switch one's hatred this way or that by a voluntary act. Suddenly, by the sort of violent effort with which one wrenches one’s head away from the pillow in a nightmare, Winston succeeded in transferring his hatred from the face on the screen to the dark-haired girl behind him. Vivid, beautiful hallucinations flashed through his mind. He would flog her to death with a rubber truncheon. He would tie her naked to a stake and shoot her full of arrows like Saint Sebastian. The young, strong body, now helpless in sleep, awoke in him a pitying, protecting feeling. ‘‘We can come here once again,” said Julia. ‘‘It’s generally safe to use any hide-out twice. But not for another month or two, of course.”

As soon as she woke up her demeanor had changed. She became alert and businesslike, put her clothes on, knotted the scarlet sash about her waist, and began arranging the details of the journey home. It seemed natural to leave this to her. She obviously had a practical cunning which Winston lacked, and she seemed also to have an exhaustive knowledge of the countryside round London, stored away from innumerable community hikes. cards.excerpt:
The little sandy-haired woman had flung herself forward over ^ the back of the chair in front of her. With a tremulous murmur that sounded like “My Savior!” she extended her arms toward the screen. Then she buried her face in her hands. It was apparent that she was uttering a prayer.

At this moment the entire group of people broke into a deep, slow, rhythmical chant of “B-B! . . . B-B! . . . B-B!” over i and over again, very slowly, with a long pause between the first “B” and the second—a heavy, murmurous sound, somehow curiously savage, in the background of which one seemed to hear the stamp of naked feet and the throbbing of tom-toms.

For perhaps as much as thirty seconds they kept it up. It was a refrain that was often heard in moments of overwhelming emotion. Partly it was a sort of hymn to the wisdom and majesty of Big Brother, but still more it was an act of selfhypnosis, a deliberate drowning of consciousness by means of rhythmic noise. Winston’s entrails seemed to grow cold. In the Two Minutes Hate he could not help sharing in the general delirium, but this subhuman chanting of “B-B! . . . B-B!" always filled him with horror. Of course he chanted with the rest: it was impossible to do otherwise. To dissemble your feelings, to control your face, to do what everyone else was doing, was an instinctive reaction. But there was a space of a couple of seconds during which the expression in his eyes might con-£* ceivably have betrayed him. And it was exactly at this moment that the significant thing happened—if, indeed, it did happen.

Momentarily he caught O'Brien’s eye. O'Brien had stood up.

cards.skillStrategy: When a character does one thing but thinks or feels the opposite, ask what that gap reveals about who they are and the world they live in.

choices.label: B

The man was led out, walking unsteadily, with head sunken, nursing his crushed hand, all the fight gone out of him.

A long time passed. If it had been midnight when the skull-faced man was taken away, it was morning; if morning, it was afternoon. Winston was alone, and had been alone for hours. The pain of sitting on the narrow bench was such that often he got up and walked about, unreproved by the telescreen. The piece of bread still lay where the chinlcss man had dropped it. At the beginning it needed a hard effort not to look at it, but presently hunger gave way to thirst. His mouth was sticky and evil-tasting. The humming sound and the unvarying white light induced a sort of faintness, an empty feeling inside his head. He would get up because the ache in his bones was no longer bearable, and then would sit down again almost at once because he was too dizzy to make sure of staying on his feet. Whenever his physical sensations were a little under control the terror returned. Sometimes with a fading hope he thought of O'Brien and the razor blade. It was thinkable that the razor blade might arrive concealed in his food, if he were ever fed. More dimly he thought of Julia. Somewhere or other she was suffering, perhaps far worse than he. She might be screaming with pain at this moment. He thought: “If I could save Julia by doubling my own pain, would I do it? Yes, I would.” But that was merely an intellectual decision, taken because he knew that he ought to take it. He did not feel it. In this place you could not feel

anything, except pain and the foreknowledge of pain. Besides, was it possible, when you were actually suffering it, to p wish for any reason whatever that your own pain should increase? But that question was not answerable yet.

The boots were approaching again. The door opened.

At thirty-five he was already putting on rolls of fat at neck and waistline, but his movements were brisk and boyish. His whole appearance was that of a little boy grown large, so much so that although he was wearing the regulation overalls, it was almost impossible not to think of him as being dressed in the blue shorts, gray shirt, and red neckerchief of the Spies. In visualizing him one saw always a picture of dimpled knees and sleeves rolled back from pudgy forearms. He greeted them both with a cheery “Hullo, hullo!” and sat down at the table, giving off an intense smell of sweat. Beads of moisture stood out all over his pink face. choices.text: The white light and humming sound contrast with the darkness Winston associates with Julia, suggesting the cell forces him to confront how little his emotional bonds matter under pressure.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The unvarying conditions of the cell give Winston a stable environment in which his mind, freed from distraction, can turn inward and honestly examine his loyalty to O'Brien.

cards.standardTitle: Key literary elements add layers of meaning
cards.excerpt: It was even possible, at moments, to switch one's hatred this way or that by a voluntary act. Suddenly, by the sort of violent effort with which one wrenches one’s head away from the pillow in a nightmare, Winston succeeded in transferring his hatred from the face on the screen to the dark-haired girl behind him. Vivid, beautiful hallucinations flashed through his mind. He would flog her to death with a rubber truncheon. He would tie her naked to a stake and shoot her full of arrows like Saint Sebastian. He would ravish her and cut her throat at the moment of climax. Better than before, moreover, he realized why it was that he hated her. He hated her because she was young and pretty and sexless, because he wanted to go to bed with her and would never do so, because round her sweet supple waist, which seemed to ask you to encircle it with your arm, there was only the odious scarlet sash, aggressive symbol of chastity.
cards.whyThisWorks: Orwell's shift from the nightmare simile to a rapid series of violent present-tense constructions ('He would flog…He would tie…He would ravish') demonstrates how syntax and diction together reveal the dehumanizing psychological distortion the Party produces in Winston.
cards.skillStrategy: When analyzing style, ask how the author's word choices and sentence patterns work together to create a specific emotional or thematic effect on the reader.
evidencePoints: by the sort of violent effort with which one wrenches one's head away from the pillow in a nightmare

What effect does Orwell create by repeating the construction 'He would' across these three sentences?

choices.label: B

choices.label: C

choices.label: D

cards.standardTitle: Key literary elements add layers of meaning
cards.excerpt: The Hate rose to its climax. The voice of Goldstein had become an actual sheep's bleat, and for an instant the face ♦ changed into that of a sheep. Then the sheep-face melted into the figure of a Eurasian soldier who seemed to be advancing, huge and terrible, his submachine gun roaring, and seeming to spring out of the surface of the screen, so that some of the people in the front row actually flinched backwards in their seats. But in the same moment, drawing a deep sigh of relief from everybody, the hostile figure melted into the face of Big Brother, black-haired, black mustachio’d, full of power and mysterious calm, and so vast that it almost filled up the screen. Nobody heard what Big Brother was saying. It was merely a few words of encouragement, the sort of words that are uttered in the din of battle, not distinguishable individually but restoring confidence by the fact of being spoken.
cards.whyThisWorks: The rapid visual transformation from Goldstein's sheep-face to a threatening soldier to Big Brother's 'mysterious calm' enacts the Party's psychological manipulation, allowing students to trace how imagery and sequence build a tone of manufactured fear and engineered relief that points toward a theme of totalitarian control over emotion.
cards.skillStrategy: Track how the order of images or events shifts the mood, then ask what idea about power or human nature that shift is pushing the reader toward.
evidencePoints: the hostile figure melted into the face of Big Brother, black-haired, black mustachio'd, full of power and mysterious calm
drawing a deep sigh of relief from everybody
cards.question: In the excerpt, Goldstein's face transforms into a sheep, then into a threatening soldier, and finally into Big Brother's 'full of power and mysterious calm' face. How does this sequence of transformations contribute to the tone and develop a theme?

choices.label: A

choices.label: B
choices.text: The sequence creates a tone of engineered dread followed by manufactured relief, suggesting that those in power deliberately manipulate fear to make submission feel like rescue.

choices.label: C

choices.label: D
choices.text: The sequence creates a tone of absurdity, suggesting that the crowd recognizes the sheep imagery as ridiculous and therefore loses faith in the Hate session's purpose.

cards.excerpt:
O’Brien picked up the cage and brought it across to the nearer table. He set it down carefully on the baize cloth. Winston could hear the blood singing in his ears. He had the feeling of sitting in utter loneliness. He was in the middle of a great empty plain, a flat desert drenched with sunlight, across which all sounds came to him out of immense distances. Yet the cage with the rats was not two meters away from him. They were enormous rats. They were at the age when a rat s muzzle grows blunt and fierce and his fur brown instead of gray.

“The rat,” said O’Brien, still addressing his invisible audience, “although a rodent, is carnivorous. You are aware of that. You will have heard of the things that happen in the poor quarters of this town. In some streets a woman dare not leave her baby alone in the house, even for five minutes. The rats are certain to attack it. Within quite a small time they will strip it to the bones. They also attack sick or dying people. They show astonishing intelligence in knowing when a human being is helpless."

There was an outburst of squeals from the cage. It seemed to reach Winston from far away. The rats were fighting: they V^re trying to get at each other through the partition. He b *ard also a deep groan of despair. That, too, seemed to come from outside himself.

cards.standardTitle: Key literary elements add layers of meaning
cards.excerpt: Behind Winston’s back the voice from the telescreen was still babbling away about pig iron and the overfulfillment of the Ninth Three-Year Plan. The telescreen received and transmitted simultaneously. Any sound that Winston made, above the level of a very low whisper, would be picked up by it; moreover, so long as he remained within the field of vision which the metal plaque commanded, he could be seen as well as heard. There was of course no way of knowing whether you were being watched at any given moment. How often, or on what system, the Thought Police plugged in on any individual wire was guesswork. It was even conceivable that they watched everybody all the time. But at any rate they could plug in your wire whenever they wanted to. You had to live—did live, from habit that became instinct—in the assumption that every sound you made was overheard, and, except in darkness, every move-^, ment scrutinized.
cards.whyThisWorks: The narrator's shift from 'Winston' to 'you' mid-paragraph forces the reader into Winston's psychological condition, demonstrating how point of view shapes tone and meaning.
cards.skillStrategy: When a narrator shifts from describing a character by name to using 'you,' ask yourself: who is now experiencing the situation, and how does that change what the moment feels like?

cards.standardTitle: Key literary elements add layers of meaning
cards.excerpt: For the rest of the morning it was very difficult to work. What was even worse than having to focus his mind on a series of niggling jobs was the need to conceal his agitation from the telescreen. He felt as though a fire were burning in his belly. Lunch in the hot, crowded, noise-filled canteen was torment. He had hoped to be alone for a little while during ^ the lunch hour, but as bad luck would have it the jmbecile Parsons flopped down beside him, the tang of his sweat almost defeating the tinny smell of stew, and kept up a stream of talk about the preparations for Hate Week. He was particularly enthusiastic about a papier-mache model of Big Brother’s head, two meters wide, which was being made for the occasion by his daughter’s troop of Spies. The irritating thing was that in the racket of voices Winston could hardly hear what Parsons was saying, and was constantly having to ask for some fatuous remark to be repeated. Just once he caught a glimpse of the girl, at a table with two other girls at the far end of the room. She appeared not to have seen him, and he did not look in that direction again.
cards.whyThisWorks: The close third-person limited narration filters every detail—Parsons's sweat, the noise, the girl's distant table—through Winston's agitated consciousness, showing students how point of view shapes tone and reader sympathy.

The young, strong body, now helpless in sleep, awoke in him a pitying, protecting feeling. But the mindless tenderness ^^iat he had felt under the hazel tree, while the thrush was singing, had not quite come back. He pulled the overalls aside and studied her smooth white flank. ‘‘We can come here once again,” said Julia. ‘‘It’s generally safe to use any hide-out twice. But not for another month or two, of course.”

As soon as she woke up her demeanor had changed. She became alert and businesslike, put her clothes on, knotted the scarlet sash about her waist, and began arranging the details of the journey home. It seemed natural to leave this to her. She obviously had a practical cunning which Winston lacked, and she seemed also to have an exhaustive knowledge of the countryside round London, stored away from innumerable community hikes. The route she gave him was quite different from the one by which he had come, and brought him out at a different railway station. “Never go home the same way as you went out,” she said, as though enunciating an important general principle. texts.title: Letter to the Grand Duchess Christina of Tuscany
texts.author: Galileo Galilei

cards.textTitle: Letter to the Grand Duchess Christina of Tuscany
cards.standardTitle: Text structure and feature purpose
cards.excerpt:
Oh! my dear mother, we are all here full of anxiety; Charles, who went very early this morning on horseback, with one of the servants, to pay Mr. Friendly a visit, and promised to return early, is not yet come home; and it is past nine o’clock. He was always punctual—some misfortune must have befallen him.—I do not know what to think, or fear. The night is very dark, and the weather stormy. Sir Charles has just sent off a servant to obtain some information:—how we all long for his return!

Eleven o’clock. The servant is come back; but no intelligence of Charles. He left Mr. Friendly’s soon after dinner, about four o’clock. Dear mother, where can he be? Drowned, I fear:—perhaps—perhaps what? I am afraid even to write the strange thoughts and conjectures which come into my head—I never seemed so much alive before, my soul feels as if it would fly out of my body to search for Charles—dear Charles! Lady Grandison sits silent; Emilia does nothing but cry; and Edward runs through the house quite frantic: Sir Charles endeavours to comfort his Lady, and has need of comfort himself. He has sent several servants different ways, and waits impatiently for day-break, when he intends going himself.—O that he would take me with him!
cards.whyThisWorks: The second paragraph clearly extends and intensifies the anxiety introduced in the first by adding new time, new failed information, and escalating emotional reactions from multiple characters, making the paragraph's job—to deepen rather than resolve the crisis—directly teachable.
cards.skillStrategy: Ask yourself: does this paragraph introduce a new idea, push the same idea further, or shift direction? Then find the specific words that show which job it is doing.
evidencePoints: The servant is come back; but no intelligence of Charles.
I never seemed so much alive before, my soul feels as if it would fly out of my body to search for Charles
cards.question: What is the primary job of the second paragraph, beginning with 'Eleven o'clock'?

choices.label: A
choices.text: It shifts the narrator's focus away from Charles and toward the distress of Lady Grandison and Emilia.

choices.label: B
choices.text: It extends the crisis introduced in the first paragraph by adding a later time, a failed search, and intensifying fear across the entire household.

choices.label: C
choices.text: It concludes the narrator's worry by revealing that Charles left Mr. Friendly's safely at four o'clock.

choices.label: D
choices.text: It introduces a new conflict between Sir Charles and the narrator over who should lead the search for Charles.

cards.textTitle: Letter to the Grand Duchess Christina of Tuscany
cards.standardTitle: Text structure and feature purpose
cards.excerpt:
Charles has played Emilia and me a fine trick this morning, dear mother. Dr. Bartlett generally rises with the sun to take a walk before breakfast; Charles, who was this morning just awake, heard him. He rose softly out of bed, hurried on his clothes, and ran down to ask him, in both our names, if we might go with him; to which he consented. It was hardly light. Charles knocked at his sister’s chamber door, Emilia, Emilia! are you still asleep, you little think it is almost ten o’clock. Oh! cried Emilia, what shall I do? I am afraid my mama will be angry with me. Come dress yourself quickly, said Charles, I will speak a good word for you. Emilia was quickly dressed; she was ashamed of being so lazy.

In the mean while he came to me, and told me the same story. Eleven o’clock—is it possible? But why did you not call me when you got up? And how comes it to be so dark? Does it rain? That signifies nothing, he replied, it will soon clear up. Come, make haste, I want to go to Dr. Bartlett. Well, you would have laughed to have seen our astonishment, when Emilia and I found it was but five o’clock. And we were very glad we had a pleasant walk, and the following conversation.
cards.whyThisWorks: The second paragraph extends Charles's trick to a second victim (the narrator), then resolves the anecdote with the reveal 'it was but five o'clock,' making the paragraph's structural job—extend then conclude—clearly traceable to specific lines.
cards.skillStrategy: Ask yourself: what idea from the first paragraph does this paragraph pick up, and does it add to it, flip it, or wrap it up?
evidencePoints: In the mean while he came to me, and told me the same story.
you would have laughed to have seen our astonishment, when Emilia and I found it was but five o'clock
cards.question: In the second paragraph, the narrator says Charles 'came to me, and told me the same story' and later reveals 'it was but five o'clock.' What is the job of the second paragraph in relation to the first?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The second paragraph introduces a new conflict between the narrator and Dr. Bartlett that the first paragraph never mentions.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The second paragraph extends Charles's trick to the narrator and then concludes the anecdote by exposing the deception and its cheerful outcome.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The second paragraph contrasts the narrator's calm response to being woken with Emilia's panicked reaction described in the first paragraph.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The second paragraph shifts the focus away from Charles's trick and proves that the narrator, not Charles, was responsible for waking everyone early.

cards.textTitle: Letter to the Grand Duchess Christina of Tuscany
cards.standardTitle: Central idea and supporting evidence
cards.excerpt:
You will still have a good mother, and you have a Father in heaven, who will never leave you nor forsake you; reconcile your mind to the event: if I die, recollect that I am only gone a little while before you; be virtuous, remember your Creator, fulfil all your duties to your fellow-creatures, and you will without fear wait for the last solemn hour, and the moment when we shall meet again.—But I have said sufficient, submit yourself to the Ruler of the universe, who loves you even better than I do.

My friend Charles rose up, and retired from the bed, without being able to speak, his heart was full, he threw himself into a chair. My father, said he, has commanded me to submit to the will of heaven; this affecting command is, perhaps, the last I shall ever receive from his dear mouth.—Well then, I must, I will be resigned. I will suppress my grief as well as I can, and wait the event with fortitude; my father has taught me how to live, and I shall now learn of him how to die; by imitating his virtues, I may be thought worthy to dwell with him in heaven, to meet him never to part again.
cards.whyThisWorks: The two paragraphs together show a dying father urging submission to God and virtuous living, and a son restating that lesson in his own words, giving students a clear central idea to identify rather than a topic or isolated detail.
cards.skillStrategy: Ask yourself what point both speakers keep returning to — not just what happens, but what idea the passage keeps building toward.
evidencePoints: submit yourself to the Ruler of the universe, who loves you even better than I do
my father has taught me how to live, and I shall now learn of him how to die; by imitating his virtues, I may be thought worthy to dwell with him in heaven
cards.question: The dying father tells his son to 'submit yourself to the Ruler of the universe,' and Charles responds that his father 'has taught me how to live, and I shall now learn of him how to die.' What central idea do both of these moments develop across the two paragraphs?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A father's final words leave his son Charles so overcome with grief that he cannot speak or control his emotions.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Accepting God's will and living virtuously prepares a person to face death with courage and the hope of reunion.

choices.label: C
choices.text: A dying father gives his son a specific list of duties he must fulfill toward other people after his death.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Charles decides to honor his father's memory by hiding his sorrow rather than expressing it openly.

cards.textTitle: Letter to the Grand Duchess Christina of Tuscany
cards.standardTitle: Text structure and feature purpose
cards.excerpt:
You are a comfort to me, my son, and Annette deserves my tender affection, she is so tractable and good. Your letters improve and please her; she requests me to read them twenty times over, that she may remember them. The tears were in her eyes when I read what you had written concerning the canary-bird. Poor Emilia, said she, how I do pity her. It gives me pleasure, replied I, that you participate in your friend’s grief; it is a sign that you have a good heart, and deserve the sympathy of others: mutual affection is necessary, it softens affliction. Indeed I have experienced it, mamma, answered she, that is, I have never been so much vexed at any thing, when I saw somebody pitied me, as when they laughed at me.—And I love those people who have compassion, they look so good-natured.

But, William, I must give you a caution. The beginning of your letter was too alarming, it startled me; I thought at least that Emilia had been dreadfully hurt; if she had lost an eye or a limb it could not have shocked me more. You might have expressed your pity, as she was grieved, but not in such terms; what other words could you have used, had she lost her mother? Learn in future, when a thing of the same kind occurs, to be more cautious how you write, and do not confound proper feelings; nor even the expressions, which should convey to others a notion of what passes in your mind.
cards.whyThisWorks: The two paragraphs model a clear structural shift—paragraph one praises William's letters and their effect on Annette, while paragraph two pivots with 'But, William, I must give you a caution,' correcting his alarming tone—making the paragraph job contrast explicit and teachable.
cards.skillStrategy: Find the signal word or phrase that marks a turn in the writing, then ask what job that new paragraph is doing compared to the one before it.
evidencePoints: Your letters improve and please her; she requests me to read them twenty times over
But, William, I must give you a caution. The beginning of your letter was too alarming, it startled me
cards.question: In the second paragraph, the writer opens with 'But, William, I must give you a caution.' What is the job of this second paragraph in relation to the first?

choices.label: A
choices.text: It extends the first paragraph's approval of William's letters by offering a second example of how his writing moved Annette to tears over Emilia's canary-bird.

choices.label: B
choices.text: It shifts from praising William's letters for pleasing Annette to correcting the alarming language he used when describing Emilia's grief over the canary-bird.

choices.label: C
choices.text: It concludes the writer's thoughts by restating that mutual affection softens affliction, connecting Annette's sympathy to William's own emotional growth.

choices.label: D
choices.text: It introduces a contrast between Emilia's serious injury and Annette's happiness, proving that William's concern for Emilia was justified.

cards.textTitle: Letter to the Grand Duchess Christina of Tuscany
cards.standardTitle: Central idea and supporting evidence
cards.excerpt:
We related the whole affair when we were at breakfast, and after Sir Charles had commended his son, he added, This may teach you all not to be terrified, but to enquire into things; and believe me, many causes, which at first appeared very alarming, will vanish, or only resemble the white cat. While God, the great Spirit, takes care of us, can phantoms harm us? He will support all those who trust in him—fear him—and you may banish every other fear. You may be certain, all the stories you have heard, took their rise from terror; a timid disturbed imagination created the spectre, or swelled some slight reality into one: none had the courage to search for the truth, or it eluded the search.

I shall never forget this incident, dear mother; I recollect what Charles said, a spirit cannot make a noise. The stories I have been told in Holland, I now think foolish; the tall woman, who walked in the grove at night, and the white monster, almost as high as the steeple, and many others of the same kind, I am sure would be found, on enquiry, to resemble the tale of the white cat, which Edward would have told, if Charles had not dragged the supposed spirit from its hiding place.
cards.whyThisWorks: Sir Charles's direct speech and the narrator's closing reflection both explicitly state that fearful imagination—not real danger—produces ghost stories, giving students two anchored moments to identify the central idea rather than a topic or isolated detail.
cards.skillStrategy: Find the claim a speaker or narrator repeats or returns to—that repeated claim is usually the central idea, not just a topic or a single detail.
evidencePoints: a timid disturbed imagination created the spectre, or swelled some slight reality into one: none had the courage to search for the truth
I am sure would be found, on enquiry, to resemble the tale of the white cat, which Edward would have told, if Charles had not dragged the supposed spirit from its hiding place
cards.question: Sir Charles tells his children that 'a timid disturbed imagination created the spectre,' and the narrator closes by saying the Holland stories 'would be found, on enquiry, to resemble the tale of the white cat.' What central idea do these two moments together develop?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Children who trust in God have no reason to fear the supernatural stories they hear from adults.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Ghost stories and frightening apparitions are products of fearful imagination, and honest investigation exposes them as harmless.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The tale of the white cat is the most memorable ghost story the narrator encountered during childhood.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Edward's failure to investigate the noise in the hiding place shows that children are more timid than adults.

cards.textTitle: Letter to the Grand Duchess Christina of Tuscany
cards.standardTitle: Text structure and feature purpose
cards.excerpt:
I mentioned to you that I expected to see some manufactories; yesterday Dr. Bartlett conducted us all, except Edward, who is gone for a short time to visit a relation, to several; and our curiosity was fully satisfied. I had seen some formerly, but without taking much notice of them: I viewed them all as something very common and rather mean; the case is altered now, I am taught to reason about them, and to admire the goodness of God displayed in the ingenuity of man. O, my dear mother, how wonderful are the ways of Providence! I must repeat an observation of Dr. Bartlett’s before I relate a conversation which passed between Emilia, Charles, and I, after we returned home.

The poor, said he, whilst they are earning their own bread, provide necessaries and superfluities for the rich; who, in return, often to aggrandize themselves, fight their battles, plan their laws, and enable the mechanics to send their work to foreign markets. The labourer also, who tills the ground, and anxiously turns the produce to a good account, that he may be able to pay his rent, is protected by the rich, and may reasonably expect to solace himself after his toil, under the shade of the trees his fathers have planted, or those he himself has reared. Thus does heaven bind us all together, and make our mutual wants the strong cement of society; and even the follies of individuals are so overruled as to produce good to the whole. Well, now for our conversation.
cards.whyThisWorks: The second paragraph delivers Dr. Bartlett's quoted observation about mutual dependence between rich and poor, which extends the first paragraph's claim that the narrator was 'taught to reason about them, and to admire the goodness of God displayed in the ingenuity of man,' making the paragraph's job as an extension clearly traceable.
cards.skillStrategy: Ask yourself: does this paragraph start something new, push an earlier idea further, or wrap things up? Then find the exact words that show which job it is doing.
evidencePoints: I am taught to reason about them, and to admire the goodness of God displayed in the ingenuity of man.
Thus does heaven bind us all together, and make our mutual wants the strong cement of society
cards.question: In the first paragraph, the narrator says she is now 'taught to reason about them, and to admire the goodness of God displayed in the ingenuity of man.' What is the job of the second paragraph in relation to that claim?

choices.label: A
choices.text: It contradicts the narrator's admiration by showing that the poor earn bread only so the rich can 'aggrandize themselves,' suggesting exploitation rather than divine order.

choices.label: B
choices.text: It extends the narrator's claim about God's goodness in human ingenuity by presenting Dr. Bartlett's observation that the rich and poor are bound through mutual need, concluding that 'heaven bind us all together' in society.

choices.label: C
choices.text: It shifts away from the manufactories entirely by introducing the unrelated figure of the labourer who 'tills the ground' and pays rent, beginning a new argument about agricultural life.

choices.label: D
choices.text: It concludes the narrator's account of the visit by summarizing the conversation between Emilia, Charles, and the narrator that Dr. Bartlett's observation was meant to introduce.

cards.textTitle: Letter to the Grand Duchess Christina of Tuscany
cards.standardTitle: Text structure and feature purpose
cards.excerpt: The whole family congratulated me, and indeed paid me many compliments, which I think I do not merit. If I have spent my time in useful exercises, did not my father render those exercises pleasant? And if I have endeavoured to be good, I only followed an example I admired. Believe me, William, all this deserves no reward, I think I merely do my duty: and if I did not I should be unhappy. My pleasure in the pursuit of science is necessary to keep me from the listlessness of an idle life. Yes, should some one say, Charles Grandison does his duty, he is studious, he honours his parents, he loves his fellow-creatures: I should answer, I do not know how all this has happened, and why you wonder at it; I must do so or lose the favour of God,—lose the esteem of my parents, whom I love so dearly; and as to my fellow-creatures, I cannot help loving them, and doing them good; it is not only the employment, but the pleasure of my life.
cards.whyThisWorks: The paragraph shifts from receiving praise to deflecting credit, then extends into a personal philosophy about duty and love of fellow-creatures, giving students a clear structural move to identify and explain.
cards.skillStrategy: Ask yourself: does this paragraph start a new idea, push an existing idea further, or turn in a new direction? Look for signal words and changes in the speaker's focus.
evidencePoints: all this deserves no reward, I think I merely do my duty: and if I did not I should be unhappy
I must do so or lose the favour of God,—lose the esteem of my parents, whom I love so dearly
cards.question: What is the primary job of this paragraph in relation to the speaker's opening statement that 'all this deserves no reward'?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The paragraph introduces the speaker's family for the first time and establishes that they are the source of his scientific ambitions.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The paragraph extends the speaker's rejection of praise by proving that his virtuous behavior is driven by inner necessity—duty, faith, and love—rather than by any desire for recognition.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The paragraph contrasts the speaker's humble character with William's prideful expectations, showing that the two men hold opposing views on reward.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The paragraph concludes the speaker's argument by admitting that he does, in fact, deserve the compliments his family has given him.

cards.textTitle: Letter to the Grand Duchess Christina of Tuscany
cards.standardTitle: Central idea and supporting evidence
cards.excerpt:
Oh! my dear mother, we are all here full of anxiety; Charles, who went very early this morning on horseback, with one of the servants, to pay Mr. Friendly a visit, and promised to return early, is not yet come home; and it is past nine o’clock. He was always punctual—some misfortune must have befallen him.—I do not know what to think, or fear. The night is very dark, and the weather stormy. Sir Charles has just sent off a servant to obtain some information:—how we all long for his return!

Eleven o’clock. The servant is come back; but no intelligence of Charles. He left Mr. Friendly’s soon after dinner, about four o’clock. Dear mother, where can he be? Drowned, I fear:—perhaps—perhaps what? I am afraid even to write the strange thoughts and conjectures which come into my head—I never seemed so much alive before, my soul feels as if it would fly out of my body to search for Charles—dear Charles! Lady Grandison sits silent; Emilia does nothing but cry; and Edward runs through the house quite frantic: Sir Charles endeavours to comfort his Lady, and has need of comfort himself. He has sent several servants different ways, and waits impatiently for day-break, when he intends going himself.—O that he would take me with him!
cards.whyThisWorks: The narrator's escalating statements—from 'some misfortune must have befallen him' to 'I never seemed so much alive before, my soul feels as if it would fly out of my body'—give students concrete language to distinguish the central idea of collective dread from isolated details like the storm or Sir Charles's actions.
cards.skillStrategy: Ask yourself: what feeling or situation do MOST of the details in both paragraphs keep returning to, rather than just one sentence mentioning?
evidencePoints: some misfortune must have befallen him.—I do not know what to think, or fear.
I never seemed so much alive before, my soul feels as if it would fly out of my body to search for Charles
cards.question: The narrator says, 'I never seemed so much alive before, my soul feels as if it would fly out of my body to search for Charles,' and earlier admits, 'I do not know what to think, or fear.' What central idea do these two statements, taken together with the rest of both paragraphs, develop?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A violent storm and late hour make it impossible for the family to search for Charles themselves.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The family is overwhelmed by mounting fear and helplessness as every attempt to locate Charles fails to bring news.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Sir Charles proves himself the most capable member of the household by organizing the search and comforting his wife.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Charles's unexplained absence reveals that his reputation for punctuality was mistaken.

cards.textTitle: Letter to the Grand Duchess Christina of Tuscany
cards.standardTitle: Text structure and feature purpose
cards.excerpt: Sir Charles and Lady Grandison have been for some days from home; but Dr. Bartlett is with us. The house-keeper, and all the servants, consult Emilia, and she, in the most modest manner, tells them what she knows her mother wishes them to do. She is not allowed to command any of them; the house-keeper in particular, a respectable woman, Lady Grandison said, ought not to receive orders from a child; but she behaves with such propriety, they are all eager to oblige her; indeed she follows her brother’s example. Edward, on the contrary, does nothing but romp and wrestle, and afterwards quarrel with them. He hates all employment; I should imagine, those who do not learn when they are young, must appear very foolish when they are old. You shall hear what Charles said to him yesterday. Charles, Emilia, and I sat on one side of the room, drawing; while Edward tied a thread to a beetle—and often he would jump, as if by accident, against our chairs, to disturb us and make us leave our employment. Charles spoke to him.
cards.whyThisWorks: The paragraph's final section—beginning with 'Edward, on the contrary'—performs a clear contrasting job against the preceding portrait of Emilia, making the structural shift visible and arguable for students.
cards.skillStrategy: Ask yourself: does this part of the paragraph introduce a new idea, extend the same one, or pivot to show an opposite—then find the exact words that signal that move.
evidencePoints: Edward, on the contrary, does nothing but romp and wrestle, and afterwards quarrel with them.
She is not allowed to command any of them… but she behaves with such propriety, they are all eager to oblige her
cards.question: What is the primary job of the sentences beginning with 'Edward, on the contrary, does nothing but romp and wrestle' within this paragraph?

choices.label: A
choices.text: They conclude the paragraph by summarizing how all three children—Emilia, Edward, and Charles—behave toward the household servants.

choices.label: B
choices.text: They contrast Edward's disruptive, idle behavior with the respectful, industrious conduct the narrator has just described in Emilia.

choices.label: C
choices.text: They introduce the paragraph's central idea that children who are left unsupervised will inevitably misbehave.

choices.label: D
choices.text: They extend the narrator's praise of Emilia by showing that even Edward occasionally follows her example of propriety.

cards.textTitle: Letter to the Grand Duchess Christina of Tuscany
cards.standardTitle: Central idea and supporting evidence
cards.excerpt: Well, now for a full and true account of all our disasters. When we came to the second stage, we could not get fresh horses; and those we had were scarcely able to drag the chaise. One lagged, and the other very unwillingly tried to get into its old pace; yet, though any human creature, I should have thought, would have pitied them, the postilion gave them lash after lash, till my patience was quite exhausted, and I remonstrated with him: indeed the strokes went to my heart; and I felt as if I had rather have called the horse my brother, than the wretch who treated him with such barbarity, who, whistling, turned his unmoved face to me, while he smacked his whip. I soon perceived that the harness had galled one of the horses; well might it winch, poor wretch!—at last it tottered, and fell. The postilion again began to use his whip; but we interposed; I could not help asking him if he had any bowels? He stared at me, and said, fine talking, it is only rust, it must be beat out of him. Ah! my dear friend, of what use is a good education? this man seemed so thoughtless, as not even to know he was cruel: my anger was turned into compassion.
cards.whyThisWorks: The narrator's closing shift—'my anger was turned into compassion'—gives students a precise textual moment to anchor the central idea rather than a vague topic or isolated detail.
cards.skillStrategy: Find the sentence where the narrator states what the whole experience taught or revealed, then ask what idea that sentence captures about the entire passage.
evidencePoints: my anger was turned into compassion
this man seemed so thoughtless, as not even to know he was cruel
cards.question: The narrator ends the passage by saying 'my anger was turned into compassion.' Which statement most accurately expresses the central idea that this closing line reveals about the passage as a whole?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The narrator's journey is ruined by exhausted horses and a postilion who refuses to stop whipping them despite repeated protests.

choices.label: B
choices.text: A person who inflicts suffering without recognizing it as cruelty deserves pity rather than rage, because ignorance is its own kind of poverty.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The narrator's education and sensitivity make it impossible to travel comfortably alongside people of a lower social class.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The fallen horse's suffering proves that the postilion's claim—'it is only rust, it must be beat out of him'—is both false and dangerous.

cards.textTitle: Letter to the Grand Duchess Christina of Tuscany
cards.standardTitle: Rhetorical appeals and author purpose
cards.excerpt: Oh! my dear mother, my friend Charles has scalded his leg, and cannot walk. Edward, who always does things rashly, was the occasion of it, by throwing down a kettle of boiling water. But I never saw such patience, such goodness as Charles possesses. Instead of being angry, he, on the contrary, concealed the pain he felt. It is nothing, said he, it has not hurt me much, do not make yourself uneasy Edward. But we soon perceived how it was, for his leg swelled so suddenly, they were obliged to cut his stocking, before they could get it off. Emilia began to cry, and upbraid Edward for his carelessness; and thoughtlessly wished he had scalded himself. Charles interrupted her; I do not wish any one to suffer, said he; be composed, dear sister, my leg will not, I hope, be much the worse. Edward did not do it on purpose, it was an accident; reproaches cannot mend the matter; and if it was worse we ought rather to encourage each other. He then sent for the house-keeper, and requested her to dress it—and hearing Dr. Bartlett’s foot-step, entreated his sister not to mention Edward as the cause of the accident; your anger, he added, gives me more pain than the scald.
cards.whyThisWorks: Charles's declaration 'your anger gives me more pain than the scald' is a clear example of figurative hyperbole/comparison that the author uses to characterize Charles as selflessly virtuous, advancing the explanatory purpose of modeling moral patience and forgiveness.
cards.skillStrategy: When you spot figurative language, ask yourself: what idea is the author trying to make the reader feel or believe, and how does this comparison or exaggeration push that idea forward?
evidencePoints: your anger, he added, gives me more pain than the scald
reproaches cannot mend the matter; and if it was worse we ought rather to encourage each other
cards.question: Read the following sentence from the passage: 'your anger, he added, gives me more pain than the scald.' How does this figurative comparison help the author achieve a purpose in the passage?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The comparison shows that Charles is exaggerating his physical injury to gain sympathy from his sister Emilia and avoid further conflict with Edward.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The comparison illustrates that Charles values emotional harmony over his own physical suffering, reinforcing the author's purpose of presenting Charles as a model of selfless patience and forgiveness.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The comparison reveals that Charles secretly blames Emilia for making the situation worse and uses figurative language to scold her indirectly.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The comparison emphasizes how severe the scald truly is by measuring physical pain against emotional distress, persuading the reader that Edward's carelessness caused lasting harm.

cards.textTitle: Letter to the Grand Duchess Christina of Tuscany
cards.standardTitle: Text structure and feature purpose
cards.excerpt: I could not guess the reason why my uncle sent in such a hurry for me. Now you shall hear, and certainly I am very fortunate. The day after I arrived, he took hold of my hand, we were alone, and pressing it, he said, I have observed with pleasure your improvement, Charles; you are the worthy son of a good father, and I doubt not will render his latter days happy—he deserves it, for he has made mine comfortable, I blush not to tell you, by teaching me to conquer myself and practise virtue. You have from your infancy been taught more by example than precept, and have not any inveterate bad habits to combat with.—Happy youth! shew your gratitude to heaven for this inestimable blessing; to you much has been given, and much indeed is required. He then presented me with a paper, and added, I now give you my estate in Hampshire, it is let out in small farms, and produces about one thousand pounds clear yearly rent; my life draws nigh to a close, and I wished to give you myself this testimony of my esteem.
cards.whyThisWorks: The paragraph moves from the uncle's spoken praise of Charles's character to the physical act of presenting a paper and gifting the Hampshire estate, giving students a clear structural shift from moral commendation to concrete reward that demonstrates the 'extends then concludes' paragraph job.
cards.skillStrategy: Track what the paragraph is doing at each moment: ask yourself whether each sentence is opening a new idea, building on the last one, or wrapping everything up with a final action or statement.
evidencePoints: you are the worthy son of a good father, and I doubt not will render his latter days happy
He then presented me with a paper, and added, I now give you my estate in Hampshire
cards.question: The uncle first praises Charles by saying 'you are the worthy son of a good father,' then closes by presenting a paper and declaring 'I now give you my estate in Hampshire.' What job do these two moments together perform in the paragraph?

choices.label: A
choices.text: They contrast the uncle's low opinion of Charles's father with his high opinion of Charles himself, setting up a rivalry between the two generations.

choices.label: B
choices.text: They extend the uncle's verbal praise of Charles's character and then conclude that praise with a material gift that proves the depth of his esteem.

choices.label: C
choices.text: They introduce Charles as a character who is meeting his uncle for the first time and learning about the uncle's past struggles with virtue.

choices.label: D
choices.text: They shift the paragraph's focus away from Charles's moral qualities entirely, replacing that subject with a legal explanation of how the Hampshire estate is managed.

cards.textTitle: Letter to the Grand Duchess Christina of Tuscany
cards.standardTitle: Central idea and supporting evidence
cards.excerpt: We have been greatly alarmed, dear mother. Mr. Wilson’s house was last night burned to the ground. Oh what frightful flames! The air was as red as blood; my heart beat very strong, I trembled lest the family should be destroyed in their beds.—It was dreadful to see such devastation by fire; how careful we ought to be to avoid the sudden horror of so terrible a calamity. If they had been careful, this misfortune would not have happened; the two Miss Wilsons were the occasion of it. They had in the evening, without its being observed, lighted a fire in their play-room; and spread the coals on the hearth to bake privately some cakes. The fire must certainly have caught the boards; but they did not perceive it; as they were interrupted before the cakes were half baked, and obliged to go to their mother, who called for them. They swallowed hastily the unwholesome, and even unpalatable cakes, and shut the door without thinking any more about it. The flames did not burst out till the whole family had been some time fast asleep. There is not any thing saved. All the furniture, clothes, and the stock of the farm were reduced to ashes. The poor girls escaped with only a single petticoat on; and Mrs. Wilson was with difficulty rescued from the devouring flames, which consumed all her substance.
cards.whyThisWorks: The narrator explicitly states a moral lesson ('how careful we ought to be to avoid the sudden horror of so terrible a calamity') and then narrates the girls' specific careless actions, giving students a clear central idea to distinguish from isolated details or topic labels.
cards.skillStrategy: Find the sentence where the narrator steps back and tells you what the story means — that is usually the central idea, not just a detail about what happened.
evidencePoints: how careful we ought to be to avoid the sudden horror of so terrible a calamity
If they had been careful, this misfortune would not have happened
cards.question: The narrator states, 'how careful we ought to be to avoid the sudden horror of so terrible a calamity' and follows with 'If they had been careful, this misfortune would not have happened.' What central idea do these two statements together express about the events described in the passage?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The Wilson family suffered because the fire spread while everyone was asleep and no one could raise an alarm in time.

choices.label: B
choices.text: A single act of carelessness can set off a chain of events that destroys everything a family has.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Children who disobey household rules by cooking secretly are responsible for any harm that results.

choices.label: D
choices.text: House fires are especially devastating when they consume furniture, clothing, and farm stock all at once.

cards.textTitle: Letter to the Grand Duchess Christina of Tuscany
cards.standardTitle: Rhetorical appeals and author purpose
cards.excerpt: But speaking of the ants brings to my remembrance some other creatures, that are still more skilful, I mean the beavers. How would you both be astonished, could I show you the habitations these wonderful creatures make! No experienced builder could form them better. They first choose a very healthful situation, and where there is plenty of provision, near a fresh stream of water; and then raise an eminence with great labour and dispatch. For this purpose they dig out the earth and clay with their fore feet, and carry their burdens on their tails (which nature has made a little hollow like a shovel) to the place they have chosen for their abode. With their teeth they cut with great expedition through trees as thick as my arm; and these piles they work into the ground to form a firm foundation. Then they begin to build a house, which consists of three stories, one above another; the walls are perpendicular, and more than a foot thick. It is within very neat, of a round form, and has an arched roof. The size in proportion to the number of the family that is to reside in it: for example, they allow fourteen or fifteen feet for twelve beavers. What think you of such creatures?
cards.whyThisWorks: The author uses the extended personification of beavers as skilled architects—complete with foundations, perpendicular walls, and proportioned living spaces—to persuade readers that nature produces intelligence rivaling human craftsmanship, making the figurative elevation of animals central to his argumentative purpose.
cards.skillStrategy: When you spot figurative language, ask yourself: what idea is the author trying to prove or explain, and how does this comparison or description push that idea forward?
evidencePoints: No experienced builder could form them better.
nature has made a little hollow like a shovel
cards.question: In the excerpt, the author describes beavers building a house with 'perpendicular' walls, 'a firm foundation,' and rooms 'in proportion to the number of the family.' How does this figurative elevation of beaver construction help the author achieve his purpose?

choices.label: A
choices.text: By comparing beavers to ants earlier in the passage, the author suggests that small creatures are more industrious than large ones, shifting focus away from human achievement.

choices.label: B
choices.text: By describing beaver construction in the language of skilled human architecture, the author persuades readers that nature produces a form of intelligence and design that rivals—or surpasses—human craftsmanship.

choices.label: C
choices.text: By detailing the exact measurements of beaver homes, such as 'fourteen or fifteen feet for twelve beavers,' the author provides scientific data to prove that beavers are the most advanced animals in nature.

choices.label: D
choices.text: By noting that beavers choose 'a very healthful situation' near fresh water, the author implies that animals follow instinct alone and cannot be compared to deliberate human planning.

cards.textTitle: Letter to the Grand Duchess Christina of Tuscany
cards.standardTitle: Text structure and feature purpose
cards.excerpt: Oh! my dear mother, my friend Charles has scalded his leg, and cannot walk. Edward, who always does things rashly, was the occasion of it, by throwing down a kettle of boiling water. But I never saw such patience, such goodness as Charles possesses. Instead of being angry, he, on the contrary, concealed the pain he felt. It is nothing, said he, it has not hurt me much, do not make yourself uneasy Edward. But we soon perceived how it was, for his leg swelled so suddenly, they were obliged to cut his stocking, before they could get it off. Emilia began to cry, and upbraid Edward for his carelessness; and thoughtlessly wished he had scalded himself. Charles interrupted her; I do not wish any one to suffer, said he; be composed, dear sister, my leg will not, I hope, be much the worse. Edward did not do it on purpose, it was an accident; reproaches cannot mend the matter; and if it was worse we ought rather to encourage each other. He then sent for the house-keeper, and requested her to dress it—and hearing Dr. Bartlett’s foot-step, entreated his sister not to mention Edward as the cause of the accident; your anger, he added, gives me more pain than the scald.
cards.whyThisWorks: The paragraph opens with the accident and then accumulates Charles's spoken responses—'It is nothing,' 'I do not wish any one to suffer,' 'Edward did not do it on purpose'—making it a clear case of a paragraph that introduces a situation and then extends a claim about character through layered evidence.
cards.skillStrategy: Ask yourself: does this paragraph start a new idea, add proof to one already started, or wrap something up? Then find the exact words that show the paragraph's job.
evidencePoints: Instead of being angry, he, on the contrary, concealed the pain he felt.
Edward did not do it on purpose, it was an accident; reproaches cannot mend the matter; and if it was worse we ought rather to encourage each other.
cards.question: After introducing Charles's scalded leg, the paragraph continues with Charles saying 'It is nothing,' 'I do not wish any one to suffer,' and 'Edward did not do it on purpose.' What is the job of these accumulated statements within the paragraph?

choices.label: A
choices.text: They shift the paragraph's focus from Charles's physical suffering to Emilia's guilt, making her the central concern by the end.

choices.label: B
choices.text: They extend the opening claim of Charles's patience by piling up separate moments that each prove his forgiveness and self-control under pain.

choices.label: C
choices.text: They contrast Charles's words with his private feelings in order to show that his calm is dishonest and performed for Edward's benefit.

choices.label: D
choices.text: They conclude the conflict entirely, signaling that once Charles speaks, no tension between Edward and Emilia remains.

cards.textTitle: Letter to the Grand Duchess Christina of Tuscany
cards.standardTitle: Central idea and supporting evidence
cards.excerpt: At this moment we came to a small cottage, where an old woman sat at a spinning-wheel, she seemed to be very poor. Let us go in and see her spin, said Charles; and we entered, begging the woman not to take it amiss, as we did not wish to interrupt her, but to see her spin. She began to talk to us, still turning her wheel. You are very diligent, said Charles. I must be so, replied the old woman, for it is my only support, except a trifle the gentry give me, in the winter, to buy coals, for they are very dear, and my hands are sometimes so cold, I cannot turn my wheel. Charles then asked, if her daily labour was sufficient to procure her bread. She answered yes, but it sometimes happens in the winter, when I have fewel to buy, that I have not money to purchase flax, and then I must sit in the cold idle and hungry. And is there nobody that will lend you a trifle, cried Charles, when you are in such extreme distress? Good lack, said the old woman, I dare say there are many good hearts in the world; but the rich, who are tender-hearted, sit in their warm parlours, and do not see the hardships we poor folk undergo. Charles then gave her a guinea and we hurried out of the cottage, to avoid her thanks; but her blessings followed us.
cards.whyThisWorks: The old woman's direct speech — 'the rich, who are tender-hearted, sit in their warm parlours, and do not see the hardships we poor folk undergo' — gives students a precise textual anchor for distinguishing the central idea from isolated details or topics.
cards.skillStrategy: Find the sentence in the passage that explains WHY the situation exists or matters, not just WHAT is happening — that explanation usually carries the central idea.
evidencePoints: the rich, who are tender-hearted, sit in their warm parlours, and do not see the hardships we poor folk undergo
when I have fewel to buy, that I have not money to purchase flax, and then I must sit in the cold idle and hungry
cards.question: When the old woman tells Charles, 'the rich, who are tender-hearted, sit in their warm parlours, and do not see the hardships we poor folk undergo,' she is expressing a claim that points to the central idea of the passage. Which statement most accurately captures that central idea?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Spinning flax is an unreliable trade because cold weather makes it impossible for elderly workers to keep their hands warm enough to work.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The poor endure serious hardship that goes unnoticed by those with the wealth and comfort to help them.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Wealthy people are selfish and refuse to give money to the poor even when they witness suffering directly.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Charles and his companion learn that visiting the poor is an uncomfortable experience best avoided.

cards.textTitle: Letter to the Grand Duchess Christina of Tuscany
cards.standardTitle: Rhetorical appeals and author purpose
cards.excerpt:
You are a comfort to me, my son, and Annette deserves my tender affection, she is so tractable and good. Your letters improve and please her; she requests me to read them twenty times over, that she may remember them. The tears were in her eyes when I read what you had written concerning the canary-bird. Poor Emilia, said she, how I do pity her. It gives me pleasure, replied I, that you participate in your friend’s grief; it is a sign that you have a good heart, and deserve the sympathy of others: mutual affection is necessary, it softens affliction. Indeed I have experienced it, mamma, answered she, that is, I have never been so much vexed at any thing, when I saw somebody pitied me, as when they laughed at me.—And I love those people who have compassion, they look so good-natured.

But, William, I must give you a caution. The beginning of your letter was too alarming, it startled me; I thought at least that Emilia had been dreadfully hurt; if she had lost an eye or a limb it could not have shocked me more. You might have expressed your pity, as she was grieved, but not in such terms; what other words could you have used, had she lost her mother? Learn in future, when a thing of the same kind occurs, to be more cautious how you write, and do not confound proper feelings; nor even the expressions, which should convey to others a notion of what passes in your mind.
cards.whyThisWorks: The narrator uses pathos deliberately — first modeling emotional sympathy through Annette's tears and the canary-bird story, then critiquing William's overwrought emotional language as disproportionate — giving students a clear contrast between appropriate and excessive emotional appeals.
cards.skillStrategy: When identifying pathos, ask whether the emotion fits the situation and whether the author approves or corrects the emotional response being described.
evidencePoints: It gives me pleasure, replied I, that you participate in your friend's grief; it is a sign that you have a good heart
what other words could you have used, had she lost her mother? Learn in future, when a thing of the same kind occurs, to be more cautious how you write, and do not confound proper feelings
cards.question: In the second paragraph, the narrator tells William that his letter was 'too alarming' and asks, 'what other words could you have used, had she lost her mother?' What is the narrator's primary purpose in using this appeal, and what type of appeal is it?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The narrator uses a logical appeal to argue that William's grammar and word choice were technically incorrect and needed to be corrected for clarity.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The narrator uses an emotional appeal to show William that his exaggerated language wasted the power of grief-filled words, leaving no stronger expression available for a truly devastating loss.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The narrator uses a credibility appeal to establish herself as a more experienced letter-writer whose own correspondence with William serves as the proper model to follow.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The narrator uses an emotional appeal to express her own personal hurt that William's alarming opening caused her unnecessary fear about Emilia's physical safety.

cards.textTitle: Letter to the Grand Duchess Christina of Tuscany
cards.standardTitle: Text structure and feature purpose
cards.excerpt: Well, now for a full and true account of all our disasters. When we came to the second stage, we could not get fresh horses; and those we had were scarcely able to drag the chaise. One lagged, and the other very unwillingly tried to get into its old pace; yet, though any human creature, I should have thought, would have pitied them, the postilion gave them lash after lash, till my patience was quite exhausted, and I remonstrated with him: indeed the strokes went to my heart; and I felt as if I had rather have called the horse my brother, than the wretch who treated him with such barbarity, who, whistling, turned his unmoved face to me, while he smacked his whip. I soon perceived that the harness had galled one of the horses; well might it winch, poor wretch!—at last it tottered, and fell. The postilion again began to use his whip; but we interposed; I could not help asking him if he had any bowels? He stared at me, and said, fine talking, it is only rust, it must be beat out of him. Ah! my dear friend, of what use is a good education? this man seemed so thoughtless, as not even to know he was cruel: my anger was turned into compassion.
cards.whyThisWorks: The paragraph moves through a clear emotional arc—from outrage at the postilion's cruelty to a final shift toward compassion—giving students a concrete moment of tonal and thematic transition to analyze as a structural 'shift' paragraph.
cards.skillStrategy: Track how the narrator's feelings change across the paragraph and ask yourself: does the ending emotion match the beginning, or does the paragraph pivot to a new idea?
evidencePoints: my patience was quite exhausted, and I remonstrated with him
my anger was turned into compassion
cards.question: What is the primary job of the final sentence, 'my anger was turned into compassion,' within this paragraph?

choices.label: A
choices.text: It extends the narrator's earlier outrage by providing one more example of the postilion's cruelty toward the fallen horse.

choices.label: B
choices.text: It marks a shift in the narrator's emotional stance, moving from moral indignation toward pity for the postilion's ignorance.

choices.label: C
choices.text: It introduces a new argument about the value of formal education that the narrator will develop in the paragraphs that follow.

choices.label: D
choices.text: It proves that the narrator's earlier decision to intervene successfully changed the postilion's behavior toward the horse.

cards.textTitle: Letter to the Grand Duchess Christina of Tuscany
cards.standardTitle: Central idea and supporting evidence
cards.excerpt: Harry would fain have persuaded us to go to bed; but Charles resolutely refused, and it was very happy we did not, for the poor man was delirious, and tried to get out of bed. And I believe he would have torn the bandage off his leg, if Charles, who was the only person he recollected, had not entreated him to let it alone. He obeyed him—did I not say truly, it was happy we were there? I could not help observing, that while Charles was busy about him, he did not seem to be afraid of any accident which might have happened to himself. When Harry became composed, I mentioned to him the remark I had made, and owned I should have been afraid to have held Harry, when he looked so frantic. Hear his answer. When I am doing what I think right, I never feel any thing like fear—should I be killed assisting a fellow-creature, would it not be a glorious death? But I will tell you when I have felt fear. Once or twice I have been in danger in a crowd, into which I entered to procure amusement or gratify idle curiosity; then, indeed, I was afraid, and I thought, if I now lose my life, how can I answer to my Creator for risking it. This single thought deprived me of the courage you admire: nothing terrifies me, when I can pray to God, and am conscious I am obeying his holy will.
cards.whyThisWorks: Charles's direct speech contrasting fearlessness when 'doing what I think right' with fear when entering a crowd for 'idle curiosity' gives students a concrete, quotable moment to identify the central idea rather than a topic or isolated detail.
cards.skillStrategy: Find the moment in the passage where a character or narrator makes a broad claim about life, then ask: what does the whole passage keep coming back to?
evidencePoints: When I am doing what I think right, I never feel any thing like fear
Once or twice I have been in danger in a crowd, into which I entered to procure amusement or gratify idle curiosity; then, indeed, I was afraid
cards.question: When Charles says 'When I am doing what I think right, I never feel any thing like fear' and then contrasts that with the fear he felt entering a crowd for 'idle curiosity,' what central idea do these two moments together express?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Crowds and public spaces are far more dangerous than caring for a delirious patient, so Charles learned to avoid them.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Courage depends not on the level of physical danger but on whether one's actions are guided by conscience and duty to God.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Charles is naturally braver than most people, which is why he alone could calm Harry while others wanted to go to bed.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Fear is unavoidable in any dangerous situation, but prayer can reduce its effects enough to allow a person to act.

cards.textTitle: Letter to the Grand Duchess Christina of Tuscany
cards.standardTitle: Text structure and feature purpose
cards.excerpt: We have been greatly alarmed, dear mother. Mr. Wilson’s house was last night burned to the ground. Oh what frightful flames! The air was as red as blood; my heart beat very strong, I trembled lest the family should be destroyed in their beds.—It was dreadful to see such devastation by fire; how careful we ought to be to avoid the sudden horror of so terrible a calamity. If they had been careful, this misfortune would not have happened; the two Miss Wilsons were the occasion of it. They had in the evening, without its being observed, lighted a fire in their play-room; and spread the coals on the hearth to bake privately some cakes. The fire must certainly have caught the boards; but they did not perceive it; as they were interrupted before the cakes were half baked, and obliged to go to their mother, who called for them. They swallowed hastily the unwholesome, and even unpalatable cakes, and shut the door without thinking any more about it. The flames did not burst out till the whole family had been some time fast asleep. There is not any thing saved. All the furniture, clothes, and the stock of the farm were reduced to ashes. The poor girls escaped with only a single petticoat on; and Mrs. Wilson was with difficulty rescued from the devouring flames, which consumed all her substance.
cards.whyThisWorks: The paragraph moves from emotional alarm to a stated moral claim ('how careful we ought to be') and then supplies a detailed causal narrative of the girls' actions, giving students a clear example of a paragraph that proves a claim through specific evidence.
cards.skillStrategy: Find the claim the writer makes, then ask whether the sentences that follow introduce, extend, contrast, or prove that claim using specific details.
evidencePoints: If they had been careful, this misfortune would not have happened; the two Miss Wilsons were the occasion of it.
They had in the evening, without its being observed, lighted a fire in their play-room; and spread the coals on the hearth to bake privately some cakes.
cards.question: The narrator states, 'If they had been careful, this misfortune would not have happened.' What job do the sentences that follow this statement perform in the paragraph?

choices.label: A
choices.text: They shift the narrator's focus from the fire's destruction to sympathy for Mrs. Wilson, who lost all her possessions.

choices.label: B
choices.text: They prove the claim of carelessness by tracing the exact sequence of the girls' actions that allowed the fire to spread unnoticed.

choices.label: C
choices.text: They introduce the Wilson family for the first time and establish what their household was like before the disaster.

choices.label: D
choices.text: They contrast the girls' reckless behavior with the responsible habits of the rest of the Wilson family.

cards.standardTitle: Central idea and supporting evidence

cards.skillStrategy: Ask yourself what the narrator is teaching across both paragraphs — not just what happens, but what lesson the narrator wants the reader to take away.
evidencePoints: mutual affection is necessary, it softens affliction
do not confound proper feelings; nor even the expressions, which should convey to others a notion of what passes in your mind
cards.question: In paragraph one the narrator praises Annette for sharing 'your friend's grief,' and in paragraph two the narrator scolds William for writing in terms so alarming they 'startled' her over a lost canary-bird. What central idea do these two moments together express?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Annette's compassion for Emilia proves she has a better character than William, who cares more about dramatic language than genuine feeling.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Sympathy for others is admirable, but the way grief is expressed must match the seriousness of the situation that caused it.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Writing letters is a skill that requires practice, and William must study Annette's example before he can communicate his emotions clearly.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The loss of a canary-bird is a trivial matter, and neither Emilia nor William should have treated it as a cause for deep sorrow.

cards.standardTitle: Text structure and feature purpose
