cards.whyThisWorks: The paragraph moves from introducing the old woman's poverty, through her explanation of winter hardship, to Charles's gift and the narrator's observation that 'her blessings followed us,' giving students a clear arc to analyze in terms of paragraph job.
cards.skillStrategy: Track what the paragraph is doing at each stage: ask yourself whether each new sentence introduces, extends, proves, or wraps up the central idea.
evidencePoints: the rich, who are tender-hearted, sit in their warm parlours, and do not see the hardships we poor folk undergo
Charles then gave her a guinea and we hurried out of the cottage, to avoid her thanks; but her blessings followed us
cards.question: The old woman tells Charles, 'the rich, who are tender-hearted, sit in their warm parlours, and do not see the hardships we poor folk undergo,' and the paragraph ends with Charles giving her a guinea and the narrator noting 'her blessings followed us.' What job do these two moments together perform in the paragraph?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The old woman's words introduce a new conflict between Charles and the narrator, and the guinea resolves that conflict before the paragraph ends.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The old woman's words prove the gap between wealth and visible suffering, and Charles's gift concludes the paragraph by showing one person acting on what he has just witnessed.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The old woman's words shift the paragraph's focus away from her poverty toward a general criticism of society, leaving Charles's response as an unrelated detail.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The old woman's words contrast her gratitude with Charles's discomfort, and the guinea signals that Charles wants to escape rather than help.

cards.textTitle: Letter to the Grand Duchess Christina of Tuscany
cards.standardTitle: Central idea and supporting evidence
cards.excerpt:
I mentioned to you that I expected to see some manufactories; yesterday Dr. Bartlett conducted us all, except Edward, who is gone for a short time to visit a relation, to several; and our curiosity was fully satisfied. I had seen some formerly, but without taking much notice of them: I viewed them all as something very common and rather mean; the case is altered now, I am taught to reason about them, and to admire the goodness of God displayed in the ingenuity of man. O, my dear mother, how wonderful are the ways of Providence! I must repeat an observation of Dr. Bartlett’s before I relate a conversation which passed between Emilia, Charles, and I, after we returned home.

The poor, said he, whilst they are earning their own bread, provide necessaries and superfluities for the rich; who, in return, often to aggrandize themselves, fight their battles, plan their laws, and enable the mechanics to send their work to foreign markets. The labourer also, who tills the ground, and anxiously turns the produce to a good account, that he may be able to pay his rent, is protected by the rich, and may reasonably expect to solace himself after his toil, under the shade of the trees his fathers have planted, or those he himself has reared. Thus does heaven bind us all together, and make our mutual wants the strong cement of society; and even the follies of individuals are so overruled as to produce good to the whole. Well, now for our conversation.
cards.whyThisWorks: The second paragraph's closing line—'Thus does heaven bind us all together, and make our mutual wants the strong cement of society'—states the central idea explicitly, giving students a precise textual anchor to distinguish the central idea from isolated details or topic labels.
cards.skillStrategy: Find the sentence that pulls the whole passage together—not just one example or topic word—and ask what point the writer is making across everything said.
evidencePoints: Thus does heaven bind us all together, and make our mutual wants the strong cement of society
even the follies of individuals are so overruled as to produce good to the whole
cards.question: Dr. Bartlett's observation ends with the claim that 'our mutual wants' are 'the strong cement of society.' Which statement most accurately expresses the central idea that this claim, and the examples before it, work together to develop?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Visiting manufactories changed the narrator's view of common laborers from contempt to admiration.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The poor, the laborer, and the rich each depend on what the others provide, and that web of mutual need is what holds society together.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Providence punishes the rich for their follies by forcing them to serve the needs of the poor.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The rich protect laborers and mechanics so that foreign markets remain open to British goods.

cards.whyThisWorks: Charles's speech beginning 'When I am doing what I think right' functions as a proof paragraph, providing direct evidence for the narrator's earlier observation about Charles's fearlessness, making the paragraph's job clearly identifiable as supporting a claim already introduced.
cards.skillStrategy: Ask yourself: does this paragraph introduce a new idea, or does it support, extend, or prove something already stated? Look for signal moments where evidence is offered in response to a question or observation.

cards.question: The narrator says 'Hear his answer' before quoting Charles at length. What is the primary job of Charles's quoted speech in the paragraph?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Charles's words shift the focus away from Harry's illness toward a new conflict between Charles and the narrator over the meaning of courage.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Charles's words prove the narrator's earlier observation that Charles showed no fear while caring for Harry, by explaining the moral reasoning behind his fearlessness.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Charles's words introduce the idea that religious faith is the only source of courage, a theme not previously suggested anywhere in the paragraph.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Charles's words conclude the narrator's account of Harry's illness by confirming that Harry recovered because of Charles's calm presence.

cards.textTitle: Letter to the Grand Duchess Christina of Tuscany
cards.standardTitle: Central idea and supporting evidence
cards.excerpt: The whole family congratulated me, and indeed paid me many compliments, which I think I do not merit. If I have spent my time in useful exercises, did not my father render those exercises pleasant? And if I have endeavoured to be good, I only followed an example I admired. Believe me, William, all this deserves no reward, I think I merely do my duty: and if I did not I should be unhappy. My pleasure in the pursuit of science is necessary to keep me from the listlessness of an idle life. Yes, should some one say, Charles Grandison does his duty, he is studious, he honours his parents, he loves his fellow-creatures: I should answer, I do not know how all this has happened, and why you wonder at it; I must do so or lose the favour of God,—lose the esteem of my parents, whom I love so dearly; and as to my fellow-creatures, I cannot help loving them, and doing them good; it is not only the employment, but the pleasure of my life.
cards.whyThisWorks: The speaker explicitly states 'all this deserves no reward, I think I merely do my duty' and then explains that duty, love of family, and love of fellow-creatures are not burdens but 'the pleasure of my life,' giving students a clear central idea to distinguish from isolated details like science or his father's example.
cards.skillStrategy: Find the sentence where the speaker directly states what he believes about himself, then ask: does the rest of the paragraph support that one idea, or is it just a detail?
evidencePoints: all this deserves no reward, I think I merely do my duty: and if I did not I should be unhappy
it is not only the employment, but the pleasure of my life
cards.question: When the speaker says 'all this deserves no reward, I think I merely do my duty: and if I did not I should be unhappy,' and then ends by calling virtue 'not only the employment, but the pleasure of my life,' what central idea do these two statements together express?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The speaker's family has praised him so generously that he now feels pressure to continue earning their admiration.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The speaker fulfills his duties to God, family, and others not for reward or recognition, but because doing so is the source of his own happiness.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The speaker pursues science above all else because it alone saves him from the listlessness of an idle life.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The speaker attributes his virtuous character entirely to the example set by his father, without whom he would have no direction.

cards.textTitle: Letter to the Grand Duchess Christina of Tuscany
cards.standardTitle: Text structure and feature purpose
cards.excerpt: You were right, my dear Emilia, when you imagined I could not be angry with you for following the humane dictates of your heart. As a proof of my approbation of your conduct, and to reward you for it, I will give you another opportunity of experiencing the pleasure which arises from benevolence. You will find in my drawers a piece of calico; send for the mantua-maker, and desire her to make Mrs. and Miss Wilson a dress immediately. I know this commission will afford you more pleasure, than if I gave it you for yourself. But, my Emilia, why did you mention their faults, when you related the circumstances which made them truly objects to excite my commiseration. You might silently have determined to behave properly to your inferiors, without exhibiting the disagreeable picture of their haughtiness, when it was receiving a severe chastisement. Never, my child, add to the miseries of others, even though the sufferers should be unworthy.—Be tender-hearted in every sense of the word. I do not mean to chide you, when I point out an error; you are a good girl.—You were judicious in not sending your best clothes; you considered the wants of the person you wished to assist, and your generosity had not that tincture of vanity which very frequently degrades it. Always, my child, define rather to do good, than to display your goodness: remember that the best of Beings notes your secret thoughts; and that it is truly noble to have sometimes his approbation singly in view.
cards.whyThisWorks: The paragraph opens with praise for Emilia's charitable act, then pivots with 'But, my Emilia, why did you mention their faults'—a clear structural shift that students can trace through exact words.
cards.skillStrategy: Find the turning-point word or phrase in the paragraph and ask what job the writing is doing before and after that pivot.
evidencePoints: As a proof of my approbation of your conduct, and to reward you for it, I will give you another opportunity of experiencing the pleasure which arises from benevolence.
But, my Emilia, why did you mention their faults, when you related the circumstances which made them truly objects to excite my commiseration.
cards.question: The writer opens by praising Emilia's conduct and promising a reward, then uses the word 'But' to introduce a new concern. What job does the section beginning with 'But, my Emilia, why did you mention their faults' perform in relation to the opening lines?

choices.label: A
choices.text: It concludes the paragraph by restating the praise already given for Emilia's decision not to send her best clothes.

choices.label: B
choices.text: It shifts from affirming Emilia's generosity to correcting her for pointing out the Wilsons' haughtiness while describing their misfortune.

choices.label: C
choices.text: It introduces the Wilson family for the first time in order to contrast their faults with Emilia's charitable character.

choices.label: D
choices.text: It extends the writer's approval of Emilia by proving that mentioning the Wilsons' faults was itself an act of benevolence.

cards.textTitle: Letter to the Grand Duchess Christina of Tuscany
cards.standardTitle: Central idea and supporting evidence
cards.excerpt: Immediately Charles mounted the tree, and caught the bird, whose feet were entangled in the branches. He then sent it by a servant to Falkland—and returned to us with a smiling face; I hardly ever saw so much satisfaction in his countenance: and when Edward still continued to laugh at him, he replied, I felt pleasure in returning good for evil, my pride impelled me to act thus, as well as a sense of duty; I do not pretend to any great merit in conquering one feeling to gratify another, but I should have been inexcusable if I had tormented an innocent helpless bird, merely to vex a being I despise. Nay, my anger would have been mean and selfish; I should only resent the loss of my dog, and not feel indignation on account of the vices this loss has forced me to discover in a character I was partial to. I shall forget my dog, long before I shall be able to drive from my remembrance a cruel action done by a fellow-creature. Charles looked teased, and Edward ceased to blame him,—and I tried to amuse him.
cards.whyThisWorks: Charles's extended speech distinguishes between venting anger on an innocent bird versus feeling genuine moral indignation, giving students a clear central claim to identify rather than a topic or isolated detail.
cards.skillStrategy: Find the speaker's main point by locating the sentence where he explains WHY he acted as he did, then ask what that reason reveals about his values overall.
evidencePoints: I should have been inexcusable if I had tormented an innocent helpless bird, merely to vex a being I despise.
my anger would have been mean and selfish; I should only resent the loss of my dog, and not feel indignation on account of the vices this loss has forced me to discover
cards.question: In his speech, Charles says he 'should have been inexcusable' if he had tormented the bird 'merely to vex a being I despise.' What central idea does this reasoning, along with the rest of his speech, express?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Charles rescued the bird primarily because his pride demanded he appear generous in front of Edward and the narrator.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Directing anger at an innocent creature to punish an enemy is a moral failure, because true indignation must be aimed at wrongdoing, not taken out on the helpless.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Charles believes forgiving the person who wronged him is the only way he will ever stop grieving the loss of his dog.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Edward's continued laughter proves that people who lack compassion cannot understand the satisfaction that comes from performing a kind act.

cards.textTitle: Letter to the Grand Duchess Christina of Tuscany
cards.standardTitle: Text structure and feature purpose
cards.excerpt: The conversation was interrupted, but I must tell you Emilia had tears in her eyes, when she told us about poor Mr. Beverley’s children. I remember now I used to be vexed when young Dulis laughed at me, and called me a coward, when I refused to do mischief; and mean, when I saved my money, though I intended to give it to a poor blind man; but he did not know that. I do not like to tell any one but yourself that I give most part of my allowance to the poor; it would look as if I wanted to be praised, and that the love of praise was my motive; but indeed it is not, the pleasure I feel at the moment, is a sufficient reward. Besides, I think I resemble my dear mother, and I am happy.—I am sure you will love me, if I practise virtue.
cards.whyThisWorks: The paragraph shifts from recounting an interrupted conversation to a personal confession about charitable giving, allowing students to identify how the writer pivots from external events to an internal moral defense.
cards.skillStrategy: Ask yourself: does this paragraph continue the same idea, or does it turn toward a new purpose—like defending a belief or revealing a private feeling?
evidencePoints: I do not like to tell any one but yourself that I give most part of my allowance to the poor; it would look as if I wanted to be praised
but indeed it is not, the pleasure I feel at the moment, is a sufficient reward
cards.question: The writer moves from mentioning Emilia's tears and young Dulis's mockery to the confession about giving away her allowance. What is the primary job of this shift within the paragraph?

choices.label: A
choices.text: To contrast the writer's generosity with Emilia's grief over Mr. Beverley's children, showing that charity takes different forms.

choices.label: B
choices.text: To defend the writer's private motivation for charitable acts by distinguishing genuine inner satisfaction from the desire for praise.

choices.label: C
choices.text: To conclude that young Dulis was ultimately correct in calling the writer a coward and a miser.

choices.label: D
choices.text: To introduce a new argument that imitating one's mother is the highest form of virtue a person can practice.

cards.textTitle: Letter to the Grand Duchess Christina of Tuscany
cards.standardTitle: Central idea and supporting evidence
cards.excerpt: I shall not soon forget this night, dear mother; the stillness of it, and the sight of Harry, who was perhaps on his deathbed, made me think very seriously, and I could not help praying to God, to enable me so to live, that I might not fear death. I used often to wish to be rich, but in this sick chamber, these wishes appeared foolish, I only desired to be good. I felt the truth of Sir Charles’s observation, that this was the solid distinction between man and man; I wondered I had not thought so before, the virtuous only appeared great in my eyes, because they can conquer death, and do not dread the end of life. And Charles agreed with me, that those who overcome the sorest earthly evil, must certainly be the truly great. We talked of all the heroes we had read an account of in history, and observed that few died happily whose chief aim had not been to benefit mankind, rather than obtain a great name for themselves. But I should tire you if I was to relate the whole of our conversation, on subjects we seldom talked of before.
cards.whyThisWorks: The excerpt explicitly contrasts the narrator's former wish to be rich with the new conviction that virtue and benefiting mankind define true greatness, giving students a clear central idea to distinguish from isolated details or topic labels.
cards.skillStrategy: Ask yourself: what single idea does the narrator keep returning to across the whole paragraph, not just in one sentence?
evidencePoints: I only desired to be good. I felt the truth of Sir Charles's observation, that this was the solid distinction between man and man
few died happily whose chief aim had not been to benefit mankind, rather than obtain a great name for themselves
cards.question: The narrator says she 'used often to wish to be rich' but that in the sick chamber 'these wishes appeared foolish.' What central idea does the rest of the paragraph develop from that shift?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Spending a night beside a dying friend is the most reliable way to overcome the fear of death.

choices.label: B
choices.text: True greatness belongs to those who live virtuously and aim to benefit others rather than pursue wealth or personal fame.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Reading about historical heroes teaches people how to face illness and suffering with courage.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Prayer is the only comfort available to people who are confronted with the possibility of death.

cards.textTitle: Letter to the Grand Duchess Christina of Tuscany
cards.standardTitle: Text structure and feature purpose
cards.excerpt: You have learned of me, you say, to be compassionate. It has ever been my wish and endeavour, to make your heart feel the miseries of your fellow-creatures; and I have laboured to inculcate the virtue, which next to the love, the goodness of God ought to inspire, is the noblest ornament of our nature. The request you make is a proof of the warm generosity of your heart: and so praise worthy a desire merits a reward. The fresh discovery I have made of your benevolent disposition, is of more value, in my estimation, than the two hundred pounds, which you will find enclosed. Go, my Charles, make glad poor Wilson’s heart, and taste the delight, which flows from benevolence. But let me tell you, the legacy must not be touched before you are of age: it was entrusted to my care as a guardian, and not as a father.
cards.whyThisWorks: The paragraph's closing sentence ('But let me tell you, the legacy must not be touched before you are of age') performs a clear structural shift from praise and reward to a firm legal constraint, giving students a precise moment to identify a paragraph's job as introducing a contrasting condition.
cards.skillStrategy: Ask yourself: does this sentence continue the same idea as what came before, or does it turn in a new direction? Signal words like 'But' often mark a shift in a paragraph's job.
evidencePoints: Go, my Charles, make glad poor Wilson's heart, and taste the delight, which flows from benevolence.
But let me tell you, the legacy must not be touched before you are of age: it was entrusted to my care as a guardian, and not as a father.
cards.question: Read the final two sentences of the paragraph, beginning with 'Go, my Charles' and ending with 'not as a father.' What is the job of the sentence beginning with 'But let me tell you'?

choices.label: A
choices.text: It extends the speaker's praise of Charles's generous character by adding another example of his virtue.

choices.label: B
choices.text: It shifts from encouraging Charles to act on his generosity to imposing a legal condition that limits his access to the money.

choices.label: C
choices.text: It concludes the paragraph by summarizing the speaker's overall lesson about the virtue of compassion.

choices.label: D
choices.text: It introduces the speaker's central argument that a guardian's duty is more important than a father's love.

cards.textTitle: Letter to the Grand Duchess Christina of Tuscany
cards.standardTitle: Central idea and supporting evidence
cards.excerpt: You have well observed, Emilia. We are very unreasonable when we are proud of dress. Where should we get the finery, if the hard hands of the diligent labourer did not provide the materials? A diamond is dug out of the earth without our assistance. Silk stuff, prepared by the industry of a worm, and in which we pride ourselves, is worked for us without our knowing how.—Yet, we are delighted with the praise we receive, as much as we could be had we invented the arts, or manufactured the product of the earth. We only wear what the skill and industry of others have procured for us.—What are we, when we recollect such foolish pride?—We who presume to arrogate merit to ourselves, which belongs to others; to the weavers and taylors—and even to the worms that contribute to adorn us. But you may say, such habits are a proof that we are rich, or born in a distinguished rank.—It is nothing!—We are, as I have just proved, indebted for the gold and silver to the poor miners, who, at the expence of health, dig it out of the mine—and we possess it by mere chance.—And our birth, of which we are apt to boast so much, is equally accidental.
cards.whyThisWorks: The excerpt explicitly names pride in dress, wealth, and birth as targets of critique, giving students concrete passage moments to anchor a central idea rather than a vague topic.
cards.skillStrategy: Ask yourself: what is the speaker arguing about across the whole passage, not just one example like silk or diamonds?
evidencePoints: We who presume to arrogate merit to ourselves, which belongs to others; to the weavers and taylors—and even to the worms that contribute to adorn us.
And our birth, of which we are apt to boast so much, is equally accidental.
cards.question: The speaker asks, 'What are we, when we recollect such foolish pride?' and then addresses pride in dress, wealth, and birth. Which statement expresses the central idea that this question introduces and the rest of the passage supports?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Weavers, tailors, and miners perform the most essential labor in society and deserve direct credit for the goods the wealthy enjoy.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Taking personal pride in fine clothing, riches, or noble birth is unjustified because all three depend on others' work or mere chance rather than one's own merit.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Wearing silk and owning diamonds is morally wrong because those materials are produced through the suffering of laborers and animals.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Wealth and distinguished rank can be defended as proof of a person's position in society, even if the goods themselves come from others' labor.

cards.textTitle: Letter to the Grand Duchess Christina of Tuscany
cards.standardTitle: Text structure and feature purpose
cards.excerpt: If William and I set the butterflies on a needle, only for our amusement, it would be wrong; but we do it to instruct ourselves—yet, though we seek instruction, I could not bear to torture them; the sight of their agonies would engross my whole attention. Dr. Bartlett has taught me to kill them expeditiously without injuring their appearance. I then gratify my curiosity without hardening my heart, for that tender-hearted man, our dear tutor, often says, that even the attainment of knowledge cannot compensate for a quick emotion of benevolence, banished by a habit of thoughtless cruelty. He wishes to make me wise; but still more ardently to incite me to practise goodness, to shew kindness to the insects who crawl under my feet; and to let my love mount up from them to the beings, who, while they enjoy the blessings of heaven, can recognize the hand which bestows them.
cards.whyThisWorks: The paragraph moves from a personal conflict (curiosity vs. cruelty) to Dr. Bartlett's solution and then extends into his broader moral philosophy, giving students a clear structure to trace how the paragraph shifts from a problem to an expanded ethical principle.
cards.skillStrategy: Ask yourself: does this paragraph stay on one idea, or does it start somewhere and move to a bigger or different point by the end?
evidencePoints: I then gratify my curiosity without hardening my heart

He wishes to make me wise; but still more ardently to incite me to practise goodness, to shew kindness to the insects who crawl under my feet; and to let my love mount up from them to the beings, who, while they enjoy the blessings of heaven, can recognize the hand which bestows them.
cards.question: The paragraph begins with the narrator's discomfort about harming butterflies and ends with Dr. Bartlett's wish that her love 'mount up from them to the beings, who…can recognize the hand which bestows them.' What is the job of this movement within the paragraph?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The paragraph concludes the narrator's moral education by showing she has fully resolved her conflict and no longer needs Dr. Bartlett's guidance.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The paragraph extends a personal problem—how to study insects without cruelty—into a broader moral principle about cultivating kindness toward all living things.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The paragraph contrasts the narrator's selfish curiosity with William's more compassionate approach to collecting butterflies.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The paragraph introduces Dr. Bartlett as a new character in order to prove that scientific knowledge is more valuable than emotional sensitivity.

cards.textTitle: Letter to the Grand Duchess Christina of Tuscany
cards.standardTitle: Central idea and supporting evidence
cards.excerpt:
Dear mother, how happy I am to learn all this. I already feel more love and reverence for God, the cause of all these wonders, than I had before. If I grew ever so tall, I should not think myself a man, till I knew something of the works of God.—Can a man be wise who sees him not in every surrounding object? Charles and I intend to make all the enquiries we possibly can—we will try to be good and wise.

LETTER XVII. WILLIAM _to his_ MOTHER.

We were this morning, mama, at half past two, in the fields, to see the beautiful scene of the sun rising. Edward would not go with us, he rather chose to sleep. He is very lazy, and ignorant of course, Dr. Bartlett says. Yet, though he plays much more than we do, he is not so happy; he often seems not to know what to do with himself, idleness making the hours so heavy. He wishes for his meals long before the time, and torments insects and animals wantonly to shorten the tedious interval. I heard Sir Charles say, the other day, he feared he would never be a man in understanding. That instead of rising gradually to a man, he was sinking into a brute. But I must relate our conversation. The stars were yet visible when we went out.
cards.whyThisWorks: The excerpt contrasts William's active pursuit of knowledge and reverence with Edward's idleness and cruelty, giving students clear textual evidence to distinguish a central idea from isolated details or topics.
cards.skillStrategy: Ask yourself: what single idea do ALL the details in the passage keep pointing back to? That recurring point — not just one example — is the central idea.
evidencePoints: he was sinking into a brute
I already feel more love and reverence for God, the cause of all these wonders, than I had before
cards.question: In Letter XVII, William describes Edward as someone who 'instead of rising gradually to a man, was sinking into a brute,' while William himself rose at half past two to observe the sunrise and pursue knowledge. What central idea do these contrasting details develop across both letters?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Waking early to watch the sunrise is the defining mark of a disciplined young person, as shown by William and Charles going to the fields at half past two.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Actively seeking knowledge and engaging with the world builds wisdom and true happiness, while idleness degrades a person's character and understanding.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Edward's habit of tormenting animals and wishing for meals early shows that he is disliked by the adults around him, including Sir Charles and Dr. Bartlett.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Reverence for God is the only path to wisdom, and anyone who fails to see God in surrounding objects, as the first letter warns, cannot grow into a man.

cards.textTitle: Letter to the Grand Duchess Christina of Tuscany
cards.standardTitle: Rhetoric and reader effect
cards.excerpt:
You are a comfort to me, my son, and Annette deserves my tender affection, she is so tractable and good. Your letters improve and please her; she requests me to read them twenty times over, that she may remember them. The tears were in her eyes when I read what you had written concerning the canary-bird. Poor Emilia, said she, how I do pity her. It gives me pleasure, replied I, that you participate in your friend’s grief; it is a sign that you have a good heart, and deserve the sympathy of others: mutual affection is necessary, it softens affliction. Indeed I have experienced it, mamma, answered she, that is, I have never been so much vexed at any thing, when I saw somebody pitied me, as when they laughed at me.—And I love those people who have compassion, they look so good-natured.

But, William, I must give you a caution. The beginning of your letter was too alarming, it startled me; I thought at least that Emilia had been dreadfully hurt; if she had lost an eye or a limb it could not have shocked me more. You might have expressed your pity, as she was grieved, but not in such terms; what other words could you have used, had she lost her mother? Learn in future, when a thing of the same kind occurs, to be more cautious how you write, and do not confound proper feelings; nor even the expressions, which should convey to others a notion of what passes in your mind.
cards.whyThisWorks: The mother's direct caution to William—warning him that his alarming opening made her fear Emilia had 'lost an eye or a limb'—gives students a clear rhetorical moment where exaggerated language is critiqued, allowing them to identify the feeling of unnecessary alarm the rhetoric produces in the reader.
cards.skillStrategy: When a writer or character reacts strongly to language choices, ask yourself: what emotion or belief did those words create, and is that the intended effect?
evidencePoints: The beginning of your letter was too alarming, it startled me; I thought at least that Emilia had been dreadfully hurt
if she had lost an eye or a limb it could not have shocked me more
cards.question: The mother describes how William's opening lines affected her by saying, 'I thought at least that Emilia had been dreadfully hurt; if she had lost an eye or a limb it could not have shocked me more.' What does this rhetoric make the reader understand about William's letter?

choices.label: A
choices.text: William's letter successfully conveyed the depth of Emilia's grief, and his mother admires his ability to express strong emotion.

choices.label: B
choices.text: William's exaggerated language created a sense of dread far greater than the situation warranted, misleading his mother about the seriousness of the event.

choices.label: C
choices.text: William's mother was already anxious about Emilia before reading the letter, so any mention of her friend would have caused alarm.

choices.label: D
choices.text: William's letter showed that he lacked compassion for Emilia, which is why his mother felt startled and disappointed in him.

cards.textTitle: Letter to the Grand Duchess Christina of Tuscany
cards.standardTitle: Text structure and feature purpose
cards.excerpt: When they are together, they are as one family. They build themselves a city, which is divided into several streets. They have each of them separate employments; one digs a hole in the earth, another sweeps the earth away, and a third brings grass or stubble to make the hole warm and dry, that they may preserve their eggs and their young from the cold and damp. Their labour to provide themselves food is wonderful: they are so industrious they will go to a great distance for it, and returning, always keep in a direct road, seldom mistaking it, though far from their own habitation. They take great care not to run in each others way; and are so very sagacious, that when they are obliged to carry any thing very heavy, from an eminence, they let it fall with deliberation, and take it up again when they arrive at the bottom.
cards.whyThisWorks: The paragraph opens with community life ('as one family,' 'divided into several streets') and then stacks increasingly specific examples of labor, navigation, and problem-solving, giving students a clear model of a paragraph that extends and proves a central claim rather than introducing, contrasting, or concluding.
cards.skillStrategy: Ask yourself: does this paragraph open a new idea, push an existing idea further with evidence, or wrap something up? Then match the paragraph's moves to one of those jobs.
evidencePoints: Their labour to provide themselves food is wonderful: they are so industrious they will go to a great distance for it
they are so very sagacious, that when they are obliged to carry any thing very heavy, from an eminence, they let it fall with deliberation, and take it up again when they arrive at the bottom
cards.question: The paragraph opens by calling the ants 'as one family' and closes with the detail about letting heavy objects fall 'with deliberation' before retrieving them. What job does this progression perform within the paragraph?

choices.label: A
choices.text: It introduces ants to a reader who has no prior knowledge of them, establishing only the basic facts that they live in groups and divide tasks among workers.

choices.label: B
choices.text: It builds a case for the claim that ants possess remarkable intelligence and industry by stacking specific examples — organized labor, long-distance navigation, and deliberate problem-solving — that grow more impressive as the paragraph continues.

choices.label: C
choices.text: It shifts away from the ants' community structure described in 'as one family' in order to contrast their behavior with the careless habits of other creatures.

choices.label: D
choices.text: It concludes a longer argument about ant society by restating points about their city, streets, and separate employments that were already proven in earlier sections of the text.

cards.textTitle: Letter to the Grand Duchess Christina of Tuscany
cards.standardTitle: Central idea and supporting evidence
cards.excerpt:
How much I was affected yesterday afternoon. I went, after I had done writing, to Sir Charles’s chamber, I opened the door softly, but instead of Charles, saw Lady Grandison and Emilia, both kneeling at the bed-side; I stole away unperceived to seek for Charles, I could not find him in any of the chambers, no one knew where he was. Oh! said I to myself, where is my dear Charles? I ran into the garden, and there I found him in the summer-house; he was kneeling down, his hands and eyes were lifted up to heaven, and big tears rolled down his cheeks; I heard him pray with earnestness, but could only distinguish a few words.

_Preserve, oh! my God, my dear, my affectionate father—grant him longer life, Thou knowest best, Thou art infinitely merciful, oh! pardon me, I wish to die to save him, to save my mother from the anguish she must endure if deprived of him._

He seemed in an agony, and at length arose with more apparent firmness; I could no longer be silent, I caught his hand, God will preserve your father, I exclaimed; I hope so, answered he, but let us walk round the garden, that my mother may not see that I have been crying, it would add to her sorrows. We walked backwards and forwards, when Charles resumed the discourse; You heard me pray then?
cards.whyThisWorks: The excerpt contrasts Charles's private, tearful prayer with his composed request to walk the garden so his mother won't see he has been crying, giving students a concrete passage moment to distinguish central idea from isolated detail.
cards.skillStrategy: Ask yourself what the whole passage is really about by connecting the opening scene, the prayer, and Charles's final words — not just one moment.
evidencePoints: I wish to die to save him, to save my mother from the anguish she must endure if deprived of him.
let us walk round the garden, that my mother may not see that I have been crying, it would add to her sorrows.
cards.question: The narrator discovers Charles alone in the garden, overhears his prayer, and then hears him say, 'let us walk round the garden, that my mother may not see that I have been crying, it would add to her sorrows.' What central idea do these connected moments express?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Charles has gone to the garden to be alone because he cannot bear to watch others pray at his father's bedside.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Charles's devotion to his family is so profound that he prays privately for his father's survival and then conceals his own grief to spare his mother additional pain.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The narrator feels guilty for intruding on Charles's private prayer and tries to comfort him by promising that God will save his father.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Charles struggles to accept his father's illness and believes that dying in his father's place would be the only way to truly help his family.

cards.textTitle: Letter to the Grand Duchess Christina of Tuscany
cards.standardTitle: Rhetoric and reader effect
cards.excerpt: Oh! my dear mother, my friend Charles has scalded his leg, and cannot walk. Edward, who always does things rashly, was the occasion of it, by throwing down a kettle of boiling water. But I never saw such patience, such goodness as Charles possesses. Instead of being angry, he, on the contrary, concealed the pain he felt. It is nothing, said he, it has not hurt me much, do not make yourself uneasy Edward. But we soon perceived how it was, for his leg swelled so suddenly, they were obliged to cut his stocking, before they could get it off. Emilia began to cry, and upbraid Edward for his carelessness; and thoughtlessly wished he had scalded himself. Charles interrupted her; I do not wish any one to suffer, said he; be composed, dear sister, my leg will not, I hope, be much the worse. Edward did not do it on purpose, it was an accident; reproaches cannot mend the matter; and if it was worse we ought rather to encourage each other. He then sent for the house-keeper, and requested her to dress it—and hearing Dr. Bartlett’s foot-step, entreated his sister not to mention Edward as the cause of the accident; your anger, he added, gives me more pain than the scald.
cards.whyThisWorks: Charles's repeated acts of restraint—concealing pain, defending Edward, and silencing Emilia—form a cumulative rhetorical pattern that reveals the author's purpose: to model moral virtue through contrast with impulsive behavior.
cards.skillStrategy: Ask yourself: why does the author include this specific moment or detail—what idea or value is being advanced by the choice?
evidencePoints: he, on the contrary, concealed the pain he felt. It is nothing, said he, it has not hurt me much, do not make yourself uneasy Edward.
your anger, he added, gives me more pain than the scald.
cards.question: When Charles tells his sister 'your anger gives me more pain than the scald,' what purpose does this rhetorical move serve in the passage as a whole?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Charles shifts blame away from himself by redirecting attention to Emilia's emotional reaction rather than his own injury.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Charles's words reinforce the author's purpose of demonstrating that moral self-control and concern for others are more admirable than physical endurance alone.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Charles reveals that he is more upset about Emilia's behavior than about Edward's carelessness, showing his preference for one sibling over the other.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Charles uses exaggeration to minimize the seriousness of his injury so that the household will not send for Dr. Bartlett.

cards.textTitle: Letter to the Grand Duchess Christina of Tuscany
cards.standardTitle: Text structure and feature purpose
cards.excerpt: That is, because we involuntarily pay respect to an improved mind. Dr. Bartlett has taught me to make distinctions. Those employments, in which the mind is exercised more than the body, tend to cultivate the understanding, the noblest kind of superiority. Those artists afford food for the mind; pleasures that the man has not any conception of who is occupied in manual labour. We may choose our companions and friends; but all the labourers in the great field of life, are our brothers; and equally deserve the rights of humanity. And they are superior to their fellow men who are most extensively useful, not those who, in false state, exhibit diamonds and gold on their body, whilst their minds are, perhaps, inferior to those of the poor creatures, who, by a weak taper’s light, dug them out of their hidden place, to decorate folly, not ornament virtue; for virtue has inherent splendor.
cards.whyThisWorks: The paragraph opens by praising mental cultivation as 'the noblest kind of superiority' and then pivots to contrast that true superiority against those who 'exhibit diamonds and gold on their body' while mentally inferior, giving students a clear extend-then-contrast structure to analyze.
cards.skillStrategy: Ask yourself: does this paragraph stay on one idea the whole time, or does it build on an idea and then turn against something? Track the shift word or moment.
evidencePoints: Those employments, in which the mind is exercised more than the body, tend to cultivate the understanding, the noblest kind of superiority.

they are superior to their fellow men who are most extensively useful, not those who, in false state, exhibit diamonds and gold on their body, whilst their minds are, perhaps, inferior to those of the poor creatures
cards.question: The paragraph first states that mental employment cultivates 'the noblest kind of superiority' and then describes those who 'exhibit diamonds and gold on their body, whilst their minds are, perhaps, inferior.' What is the job of that second move in the paragraph?

choices.label: A
choices.text: It concludes the paragraph's argument by proving that physical laborers who dig diamonds are the most virtuous group described.

choices.label: B
choices.text: It contrasts the genuine mental superiority established earlier against the false superiority of those who display wealth while remaining mentally inferior.

choices.label: C
choices.text: It shifts the paragraph's focus away from mental cultivation entirely in order to argue that all laborers deserve equal legal rights.

choices.label: D
choices.text: It introduces for the first time the idea that companions and friends should be chosen based on the wealth they display.

cards.textTitle: Letter to the Grand Duchess Christina of Tuscany
cards.standardTitle: Central idea and supporting evidence
cards.excerpt: You were right, my dear Emilia, when you imagined I could not be angry with you for following the humane dictates of your heart. As a proof of my approbation of your conduct, and to reward you for it, I will give you another opportunity of experiencing the pleasure which arises from benevolence. You will find in my drawers a piece of calico; send for the mantua-maker, and desire her to make Mrs. and Miss Wilson a dress immediately. I know this commission will afford you more pleasure, than if I gave it you for yourself. But, my Emilia, why did you mention their faults, when you related the circumstances which made them truly objects to excite my commiseration. You might silently have determined to behave properly to your inferiors, without exhibiting the disagreeable picture of their haughtiness, when it was receiving a severe chastisement. Never, my child, add to the miseries of others, even though the sufferers should be unworthy.—Be tender-hearted in every sense of the word. I do not mean to chide you, when I point out an error; you are a good girl.—You were judicious in not sending your best clothes; you considered the wants of the person you wished to assist, and your generosity had not that tincture of vanity which very frequently degrades it. Always, my child, define rather to do good, than to display your goodness: remember that the best of Beings notes your secret thoughts; and that it is truly noble to have sometimes his approbation singly in view.
cards.whyThisWorks: The letter's closing lines—'define rather to do good, than to display your goodness' and 'it is truly noble to have sometimes his approbation singly in view'—give students a precise textual anchor for distinguishing the central idea from isolated details or topic labels.
cards.skillStrategy: Find the idea the writer keeps returning to across the whole passage, not just one detail or the topic itself—ask yourself what lesson the writer wants Emilia to carry away from everything said here.
evidencePoints: Always, my child, define rather to do good, than to display your goodness
Never, my child, add to the miseries of others, even though the sufferers should be unworthy.—Be tender-hearted in every sense of the word.
cards.question: The writer closes by telling Emilia to 'define rather to do good, than to display your goodness.' Which statement expresses the central idea that this line, along with the rest of the letter, develops?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Emilia's decision to send calico fabric instead of her best clothes shows she already possesses the generosity her mother hopes to teach her.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Genuine compassion requires acting with humility and pure motives rather than seeking praise or drawing attention to one's own virtue.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Children should never mention the faults of people who are suffering, because pointing out those faults makes their misery worse.

choices.label: D
choices.text: A parent's role is to reward a child's good behavior by giving her opportunities to experience the pleasure that comes from helping others.

cards.textTitle: Letter to the Grand Duchess Christina of Tuscany
cards.standardTitle: Rhetoric and reader effect
cards.excerpt: But speaking of the ants brings to my remembrance some other creatures, that are still more skilful, I mean the beavers. How would you both be astonished, could I show you the habitations these wonderful creatures make! No experienced builder could form them better. They first choose a very healthful situation, and where there is plenty of provision, near a fresh stream of water; and then raise an eminence with great labour and dispatch. For this purpose they dig out the earth and clay with their fore feet, and carry their burdens on their tails (which nature has made a little hollow like a shovel) to the place they have chosen for their abode. With their teeth they cut with great expedition through trees as thick as my arm; and these piles they work into the ground to form a firm foundation. Then they begin to build a house, which consists of three stories, one above another; the walls are perpendicular, and more than a foot thick. It is within very neat, of a round form, and has an arched roof. The size in proportion to the number of the family that is to reside in it: for example, they allow fourteen or fifteen feet for twelve beavers. What think you of such creatures?
cards.whyThisWorks: The author's detailed, almost architectural description of beaver construction—complete with measurements, materials, and structural features—functions rhetorically to build credibility for natural intelligence, connecting the rhetorical move of precise enumeration to the purpose of persuading readers that animals possess remarkable, reasoned capabilities.
cards.skillStrategy: Ask yourself: why does the author include this specific detail or description right here—what is he trying to make the reader believe or feel?
evidencePoints: No experienced builder could form them better.
The size in proportion to the number of the family that is to reside in it: for example, they allow fourteen or fifteen feet for twelve beavers.
cards.question: The author describes the beavers' construction in precise detail, including measurements such as 'fourteen or fifteen feet for twelve beavers' and structural features like 'perpendicular' walls and an 'arched roof.' What is the author's primary purpose in accumulating these specific details?

choices.label: A
choices.text: To entertain the reader with an amusing comparison between animal homes and human architecture, making the letter more enjoyable to read.

choices.label: B
choices.text: To persuade the reader that animals demonstrate a form of reasoned intelligence by showing that their construction rivals the deliberate planning of skilled human builders.

choices.label: C
choices.text: To warn the reader that human builders are inferior to animals and should study nature more carefully before constructing homes.

choices.label: D
choices.text: To shift the reader's attention away from ants toward beavers simply because beavers are a more impressive example of animal size and strength.

cards.textTitle: Letter to the Grand Duchess Christina of Tuscany
cards.standardTitle: Text structure and feature purpose
cards.excerpt: It is indeed a very perverse pride, for with all their riches, they could not do without those useful men. O, thought I, when I saw the weaver, who sat sweating before his loom, this man exhausts his vigour to procure me a great comfort, linen. Without him, the flax, that valuable plant, which the earth produces for this purpose, would be useless. Every one will allow, that shoe-makers and taylors are necessary; in short, since I find that laborious people are so essential to the well-being of the world, I cannot imagine how men can treat them with so much contempt. As to myself I shall guard against such behaviour; in the use of those things, I shall endeavour always to remember the men who are the instruments to convey the blessings of heaven to me: and these considerations will make me esteem my fellow-members of society; and try to fulfil my part of the sociable compact.
cards.whyThisWorks: The paragraph moves from observing laborers' hardship to a personal resolution, making it a clear example of a paragraph that shifts from social critique to a personal moral commitment—ideal for teaching paragraph job identification.
cards.skillStrategy: Ask yourself: does this paragraph introduce a new idea, push an existing idea further, or turn in a new direction? Look for signal words like 'As to myself' that mark a shift in focus.
evidencePoints: I cannot imagine how men can treat them with so much contempt.
As to myself I shall guard against such behaviour; in the use of those things, I shall endeavour always to remember the men who are the instruments to convey the blessings of heaven to me
cards.question: What is the primary job of the final portion of the paragraph, beginning with 'As to myself I shall guard against such behaviour'?

choices.label: A
choices.text: It extends the narrator's argument that weavers and shoemakers are more skilled than other workers.

choices.label: B
choices.text: It shifts from criticizing how society treats laborers to stating the narrator's personal commitment to respect them.

choices.label: C
choices.text: It introduces the idea that laborers are essential to society for the first time in the paragraph.

choices.label: D
choices.text: It contrasts the narrator's wealth with the poverty experienced by weavers and tailors.

cards.textTitle: Letter to the Grand Duchess Christina of Tuscany
cards.standardTitle: Central idea and supporting evidence
cards.excerpt:
LETTER XX. WILLIAM _to his_ MOTHER.

One of the servants has been very ill. You cannot think how compassionately Emilia attended her. She rose very early this morning to carry her some refreshment, and tried to amuse her. She requested Dr. Bartlett to send for a physician; and she took as much care of her as if the poor girl had been her own sister. Edward reproached her. It well becomes you, said he, to be sure, to wait on the maid. And why not, answered she; you play with the servant to amuse yourself (and such a degree of familiarity is indeed improper) and I take care of the maid, through pity. A servant is a human being; we are differently educated, I cannot make them my companions, but I will ever try to treat them humanely—and remember that they are my fellow-creatures, when they are in distress. Edward was ashamed and ran out of the room. My mother, I thought, always acted in the same manner. I remember well, when our Hannah had the fever, that you took care of her yourself. But it brings to my remembrance something, which makes me sorrowful. How unfortunate you are! Here are so many servants, and you, my poor mother, have only a little girl to assist; you yourself are obliged to do many things—a colonel’s widow should have servants to wait on her; it is mean to work, and do not people despise you for being reduced to such a condition? When I am a man, and have increased my fortune, you shall have servants, and live as a gentlewoman ought to live.
cards.whyThisWorks: The letter presents a clear central idea—that servants deserve humane treatment as fellow human beings—supported by Emilia's actions, her direct speech, and William's reflection on his mother's similar behavior, giving students multiple evidence points to distinguish the central idea from isolated details or topics.
cards.skillStrategy: Ask yourself what the whole passage is really arguing or showing, not just what one moment describes—the central idea must be supported by most of the passage, not just one sentence.
evidencePoints: A servant is a human being; we are differently educated, I cannot make them my companions, but I will ever try to treat them humanely—and remember that they are my fellow-creatures, when they are in distress.
My mother, I thought, always acted in the same manner. I remember well, when our Hannah had the fever, that you took care of her yourself.
cards.question: Which statement best expresses the central idea of William's letter?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Edward's mockery of Emilia reveals that wealthy young men are generally selfish and unkind toward those around them.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Regardless of social rank, servants deserve compassionate treatment because they share a common humanity with those they serve.

choices.label: C
choices.text: William's mother has suffered financial hardship since becoming a colonel's widow and must work without adequate help.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Emilia's care for a sick servant demonstrates that women in this household are more virtuous than the men.

cards.textTitle: Letter to the Grand Duchess Christina of Tuscany
cards.standardTitle: Rhetoric and reader effect
cards.excerpt:
It is necessary; and they do not foresee, or taste the bitterness of death, if they are killed instantly.—Cruel, indeed, are those, who torment them—they sin against their own souls—and they will be judged without mercy who have not shewn any. He who is guilty of a cruel action has sapped the foundation of content; and the monster, no longer humane, enjoys not human comforts. Nor is he thoughtless, like the beasts of prey; conscience haunts him—he cannot hide himself, nor find darkness thick enough to conceal his crimes.

We now returned home, and found Sir Charles and his Lady already in the breakfast parlour. We mentioned the trick Charles had played us, they both laughed; but Sir Charles turned to him, I mean not gravely to reprove you, my son, only to point out to you, that truth is so sacred a thing it ought not to be jested with; lest a reverence for it should imperceptibly wear away, and leave the mind, stripped of its most beautiful ornament, to deck itself in gaudy rags.
cards.whyThisWorks: The excerpt contains a vivid analogy comparing truth to a 'most beautiful ornament' stripped away, alongside contrast between the cruel person's outward actions and inward torment, giving students concrete rhetorical devices to analyze for reader effect.
cards.skillStrategy: When you spot a comparison or contrast, ask yourself: what feeling or idea does the author want the reader to walk away with, and how does that device create that effect?
evidencePoints: leave the mind, stripped of its most beautiful ornament, to deck itself in gaudy rags
conscience haunts him—he cannot hide himself, nor find darkness thick enough to conceal his crimes
cards.question: Sir Charles tells his son that dishonesty leaves the mind 'stripped of its most beautiful ornament, to deck itself in gaudy rags.' How does this analogy affect the reader?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The analogy suggests that dishonesty is a minor social mistake, one that can be corrected simply by choosing better clothing or appearance.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The analogy frames the loss of truthfulness as a degrading exchange—trading something genuinely valuable for something hollow and false—making the moral cost of dishonesty feel vivid and personal.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The analogy emphasizes that wealthy people like Sir Charles place too much importance on fine clothing and outward appearances rather than inner character.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The analogy reassures the reader that a person who has been dishonest can restore their reputation by adorning themselves with new virtues over time.

cards.textTitle: Letter to the Grand Duchess Christina of Tuscany
cards.standardTitle: Central idea and supporting evidence
cards.excerpt: The conversation was interrupted, but I must tell you Emilia had tears in her eyes, when she told us about poor Mr. Beverley’s children. I remember now I used to be vexed when young Dulis laughed at me, and called me a coward, when I refused to do mischief; and mean, when I saved my money, though I intended to give it to a poor blind man; but he did not know that. I do not like to tell any one but yourself that I give most part of my allowance to the poor; it would look as if I wanted to be praised, and that the love of praise was my motive; but indeed it is not, the pleasure I feel at the moment, is a sufficient reward. Besides, I think I resemble my dear mother, and I am happy.—I am sure you will love me, if I practise virtue.
cards.whyThisWorks: The narrator explicitly states a motive ('the pleasure I feel at the moment, is a sufficient reward') and denies another ('that the love of praise was my motive; but indeed it is not'), giving students a clear central claim to distinguish from surrounding details like Emilia's tears or Dulis's mockery.
cards.skillStrategy: Find the sentence where the narrator makes a direct claim about why they act a certain way—that claim is likely the central idea, not the surrounding story details.
evidencePoints: the pleasure I feel at the moment, is a sufficient reward

I do not like to tell any one but yourself that I give most part of my allowance to the poor; it would look as if I wanted to be praised, and that the love of praise was my motive; but indeed it is not
cards.question: The narrator states, 'the love of praise was my motive; but indeed it is not, the pleasure I feel at the moment, is a sufficient reward.' What central idea does this claim, together with the rest of the passage, develop?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The narrator's generosity toward the poor is motivated by a desire to honor a beloved mother and carry on her memory.

choices.label: B
choices.text: True virtue brings its own inner reward, and the narrator acts rightly without needing recognition from others.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Being mocked by Dulis for refusing to do mischief taught the narrator the importance of keeping good deeds secret.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Emilia's grief over Mr. Beverley's children moves the narrator to reflect on the suffering caused by a lack of generosity.

cards.textTitle: Letter to the Grand Duchess Christina of Tuscany
cards.standardTitle: Paraphrase grade-level text
cards.excerpt:
It is necessary; and they do not foresee, or taste the bitterness of death, if they are killed instantly.—Cruel, indeed, are those, who torment them—they sin against their own souls—and they will be judged without mercy who have not shewn any. He who is guilty of a cruel action has sapped the foundation of content; and the monster, no longer humane, enjoys not human comforts. Nor is he thoughtless, like the beasts of prey; conscience haunts him—he cannot hide himself, nor find darkness thick enough to conceal his crimes.

We now returned home, and found Sir Charles and his Lady already in the breakfast parlour. We mentioned the trick Charles had played us, they both laughed; but Sir Charles turned to him, I mean not gravely to reprove you, my son, only to point out to you, that truth is so sacred a thing it ought not to be jested with; lest a reverence for it should imperceptibly wear away, and leave the mind, stripped of its most beautiful ornament, to deck itself in gaudy rags.
cards.whyThisWorks: Sir Charles's speech contains a long, syntactically complex sentence with an embedded conditional clause and figurative language ('lest a reverence for it should imperceptibly wear away, and leave the mind, stripped of its most beautiful ornament, to deck itself in gaudy rags'), requiring students to untangle subordinate clauses and restate the core warning accurately.
cards.skillStrategy: Break the long sentence into its main idea and its 'what happens if' part, then restate each piece in your own words before putting them back together.
evidencePoints: truth is so sacred a thing it ought not to be jested with
lest a reverence for it should imperceptibly wear away, and leave the mind, stripped of its most beautiful ornament, to deck itself in gaudy rags
cards.question: Read Sir Charles's words to his son: 'truth is so sacred a thing it ought not to be jested with; lest a reverence for it should imperceptibly wear away, and leave the mind, stripped of its most beautiful ornament, to deck itself in gaudy rags.' Which restatement most accurately captures the meaning of this sentence?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Truth is so powerful that joking about it actually strengthens a person's respect for honesty over time, decorating the mind with genuine virtue.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Truth is too important to treat as a joke, because repeatedly doing so can gradually erode one's respect for it, leaving the mind without its finest quality.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Truth should never be spoken aloud in casual settings, because the mind is too fragile to distinguish between serious statements and playful ones.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Joking about truth is harmless as long as the speaker eventually corrects himself, since the mind can recover its respect for honesty on its own.

cards.textTitle: Letter to the Grand Duchess Christina of Tuscany
cards.standardTitle: Paraphrase grade-level text
cards.excerpt:
Next Thursday is fixed for my departure, so that this is my last letter. I did wish to have remained here till after Emilia’s birth-day, but one of Sir Charles’s friends intends setting off next week for Holland, and he wishes me to go with him, as another opportunity may not soon occur.

How happens it, dear mother, that I am so low-spirited when I am returning to you whom I have so continually longed to see? I love Sir Charles and his Lady, and I love my friend as myself, yet, I love you better than all the world. I know not well what I feel, I would willingly return, and still wish to remain where I am. Sir Charles has given me reason to hope that I shall see my friend in Holland much sooner than I expected, and that we shall correspond constantly during our separation; he then gave me some books and mathematical instruments. How much I shall have to read to you, and how many things to tell you, when I am once more returned home!
cards.whyThisWorks: The sentence 'How happens it, dear mother, that I am so low-spirited when I am returning to you whom I have so continually longed to see?' uses inverted syntax and an embedded relative clause that students must untangle to grasp the speaker's paradox of feeling sad despite returning to someone deeply missed.
cards.skillStrategy: When a sentence has an unusual word order or a clause tucked inside it, break it into smaller pieces—identify who, what feeling, and what situation—then put the meaning back together in plain language.
evidencePoints: How happens it, dear mother, that I am so low-spirited when I am returning to you whom I have so continually longed to see?
I know not well what I feel, I would willingly return, and still wish to remain where I am.
cards.question: Read this sentence from the letter: 'How happens it, dear mother, that I am so low-spirited when I am returning to you whom I have so continually longed to see?' Which restatement most accurately captures the meaning of this sentence?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The writer wonders why her mother has not written, since she has been eagerly waiting to hear news from home before she departs.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The writer is puzzled by her own sadness, because she is on her way back to her mother—someone she has deeply missed the entire time she has been away.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The writer feels sad because she has not been able to see her mother in a very long time and fears she may not return home at all.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The writer questions whether her mother will be happy to see her, since she has been away so long and is now returning later than planned.

cards.textTitle: Letter to the Grand Duchess Christina of Tuscany
cards.standardTitle: Paraphrase grade-level text
cards.excerpt:
I thank you, dear mother, for your kind letter; it is so long since you wrote to me, I was almost afraid you were displeased with me. Hear what I do, I always carry your last letter in my bosom, then I can read it often, and remember the lessons you give me. I love dearly my little sister Annette, she is so good, and so dutiful to you. Miss Emilia sends her a fine doll, I am sure it will please her.

Yesterday was the birth-day of Lady Grandison. Charles was up an hour earlier than usual, and when I awoke I found him, for we sleep together, busy, praying to God for his dear mother; we read some chapters in the New Testament, and then Charles dressed himself in his new clothes. You perhaps may wonder at this; but I will tell you how it was. About a month ago Charles and Edward had each a new summer suit, and were allowed to choose the colour themselves. Edward wore his as soon as it came home; but Charles said that he would keep his till some holiday, and this was the holiday he fixed on. He was soon dressed, and we joined Emilia, who stood ready at our chamber door waiting for us.
cards.whyThisWorks: The sentence 'About a month ago Charles and Edward had each a new summer suit, and were allowed to choose the colour themselves' contains embedded clauses and compound structure that requires students to untangle who did what and under what conditions.
cards.skillStrategy: Break the sentence into smaller parts by asking: Who is involved? What happened? What were they allowed to do? Then restate each part in your own words.
evidencePoints: About a month ago Charles and Edward had each a new summer suit, and were allowed to choose the colour themselves.
Edward wore his as soon as it came home; but Charles said that he would keep his till some holiday, and this was the holiday he fixed on.
cards.question: Read the following sentence from the passage: 'About a month ago Charles and Edward had each a new summer suit, and were allowed to choose the colour themselves.' Which of the following most accurately restates the meaning of this sentence?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A month ago, Charles and Edward were each given identical summer suits in colors that had already been chosen for them.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Roughly a month earlier, both Charles and Edward received their own new summer suits and were each permitted to pick the color they wanted.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Charles and Edward shared a single new summer suit and took turns deciding what color it should be.

choices.label: D
choices.text: About a month ago, Charles and Edward were told they could have new suits only if they agreed on the same color.

cards.standardTitle: Narrator perspective, irony, and satire
cards.excerpt:
Infant’s flesh will be in season throughout the year, but more plentiful in March, and a little before and after; for we are told by a grave author, an eminent French physician, that fish being a prolifick dyet, there are more children born in Roman Catholick countries about nine months after Lent, than at any other season; therefore, reckoning a year after Lent, the markets will be more glutted than usual, because the number of Popish infants, is at least three to one in this kingdom, and therefore it will have one other collateral advantage, by lessening the number of Papists among us.

I have already computed the charge of nursing a beggar’s child (in which list I reckon all cottagers, labourers, and four-fifths of the farmers) to be about two shillings per annum, rags included; and I believe no gentleman would repine to give ten shillings for the carcass of a good fat child, which, as I have said, will make four dishes of excellent nutritive meat, when he hath only some particular friend, or his own family to dine with him. Thus the squire will learn to be a good landlord, and grow popular among his tenants, the mother will have eight shillings neat profit, and be fit for work till she produces another child.
cards.whyThisWorks: Swift's deadpan claim that selling children's flesh will teach landlords to 'be a good landlord' and make mothers 'fit for work' directly reverses the moral expectations of charity and human dignity, making the irony concrete and textually grounded.
cards.skillStrategy: When you spot a reversal—where the stated outcome is the opposite of what a reasonable person would expect—that gap between expectation and statement is the irony.
evidencePoints: Thus the squire will learn to be a good landlord, and grow popular among his tenants
the mother will have eight shillings neat profit, and be fit for work till she produces another child
cards.question: Read the following passage from the second paragraph: 'Thus the squire will learn to be a good landlord, and grow popular among his tenants, the mother will have eight shillings neat profit, and be fit for work till she produces another child.' What reversal creates irony in these lines?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The squire is portrayed as greedy, which confirms that landlords in Ireland were widely known to be corrupt and uncaring toward tenants.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Selling a child's body is presented as the path to becoming a good landlord and a productive mother, reversing the expectation that human decency—not cannibalism—defines those virtues.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The mother earns only eight shillings while the squire pays ten, showing that the economic system unfairly favors the wealthy over the poor.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The narrator praises the nutritional value of the meat, which contradicts his earlier claim that the proposal is meant to benefit the children of Ireland.

cards.standardTitle: Narrator perspective, irony, and satire
cards.excerpt:
Some persons of a desponding spirit are in great concern about that vast number of poor people, who are aged, diseased, or maimed; and I have been desired to employ my thoughts what course may be taken, to ease the nation of so grievous an incumbrance. But I am not in the least pain upon that matter, because it is very well known, that they are every day dying, and rotting, by cold and famine, and filth, and vermin, as fast as can be reasonably expected. And as to the young labourers, they are now in almost as hopeful a condition. They cannot get work, and consequently pine away from want of nourishment, to a degree, that if at any time they are accidentally hired to common labour, they have not strength to perform it, and thus the country and themselves are happily delivered from the evils to come.

I have too long digressed, and therefore shall return to my subject. I think the advantages by the proposal which I have made are obvious and many, as well as of the highest importance.
cards.whyThisWorks: Swift's cheerful language about the poor dying of cold, famine, and filth—framed as a relief from 'evils to come'—creates sharp situational irony through the reversal of suffering presented as a social benefit, making this a model example of irony through contrast.
cards.skillStrategy: When a narrator describes something horrifying in calm or positive language, ask yourself: what does the narrator claim is happening versus what is actually happening? That gap is the irony.
evidencePoints: they are every day dying, and rotting, by cold and famine, and filth, and vermin, as fast as can be reasonably expected
the country and themselves are happily delivered from the evils to come
cards.question: Read this sentence from the passage: 'the country and themselves are happily delivered from the evils to come.' What contrast creates irony in this statement?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The narrator claims to feel concern for the poor while admitting he has never personally witnessed their suffering.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The narrator describes the deaths of starving laborers as a happy deliverance, treating mass suffering as though it were a fortunate solution rather than a tragedy.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The narrator argues that young laborers are stronger than aged workers, yet admits neither group can find employment.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The narrator praises his own proposal as obvious and important while acknowledging he has digressed from his main argument.

cards.standardTitle: Text structure and feature purpose
cards.excerpt:
Fifthly, This food would likewise bring great custom to taverns, where the vintners will certainly be so prudent as to procure the best receipts for dressing it to perfection; and consequently have their houses frequented by all the fine gentlemen, who justly value themselves upon their knowledge in good eating; and a skilful cook, who understands how to oblige his guests, will contrive to make it as expensive as they please.

Sixthly, This would be a great inducement to marriage, which all wise nations have either encouraged by rewards, or enforced by laws and penalties. It would encrease the care and tenderness of mothers towards their children, when they were sure of a settlement for life to the poor babes, provided in some sort by the publick, to their annual profit instead of expence. We should soon see an honest emulation among the married women, which of them could bring the fattest child to the market. Men would become as fond of their wives, during the time of their pregnancy, as they are now of their mares in foal, their cows in calf, or sows when they are ready to farrow; nor offer to beat or kick them (as is too frequent a practice) for fear of a miscarriage.

cards.question: What is the primary job of the 'Sixthly' paragraph in relation to the 'Fifthly' paragraph?

choices.label: A
choices.text: It contradicts the economic reasoning of the previous paragraph by arguing that social benefits matter more than financial ones.

choices.label: B
choices.text: It extends the proposal's list of advantages by adding social benefits—stronger marriages and maternal care—to the economic benefits already described.

choices.label: C
choices.text: It concludes the proposal by summarizing all the advantages Swift has presented across both paragraphs.

choices.label: D
choices.text: It introduces an entirely new proposal, replacing the food-based scheme with a plan to reform marriage laws through government penalties.
