cards.question: Read the following claim from the passage: 'It would encrease the care and tenderness of mothers towards their children.' How does the rest of the paragraph create irony through this claim?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The paragraph confirms the claim by showing that mothers in poverty genuinely struggle to provide for their children and need government support.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The paragraph contradicts the claim by defining 'care and tenderness' as fattening children for sale at market and comparing wives to pregnant livestock, revealing that the 'tenderness' is purely financial and animal in nature.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The paragraph undermines the claim only by mentioning that husbands beat their wives, which is a separate social problem unrelated to the proposal's logic.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The paragraph extends the claim sincerely by arguing that marriage laws and public settlements would naturally produce more loving families across all social classes.

cards.standardTitle: Narrator perspective, irony, and satire
cards.excerpt: A very worthy person, a true lover of his country, and whose virtues I highly esteem, was lately pleased in discoursing on this matter, to offer a refinement upon my scheme. He said, that many gentlemen of this kingdom, having of late destroyed their deer, he conceived that the want of venison might be well supplied by the bodies of young lads and maidens, not exceeding fourteen years of age, nor under twelve; so great a number of both sexes in every county being now ready to starve for want of work and service: and these to be disposed of by their parents if alive, or otherwise by their nearest relations. But with due deference to so excellent a friend, and so deserving a patriot, I cannot be altogether in his sentiments; for as to the males, my American acquaintance assured me from frequent experience, that their flesh was generally tough and lean, like that of our schoolboys, by continual exercise, and their taste disagreeable, and to fatten them would not answer the charge. Then as to the females, it would, I think, with humble submission, be a loss to the publick, because they soon would become breeders themselves: and besides, it is not improbable that some scrupulous people might be apt to censure such a practice, (although indeed very unjustly) as a little bordering upon cruelty, which, I confess, hath always been with me the strongest objection against any project, how well soever intended.

cards.skillStrategy: When you spot a character saying one thing while doing the opposite, ask yourself: what does the gap between their stated values and their actual reasoning reveal?
evidencePoints: it is not improbable that some scrupulous people might be apt to censure such a practice, (although indeed very unjustly) as a little bordering upon cruelty
cruelty, which, I confess, hath always been with me the strongest objection against any project, how well soever intended
cards.question: Read the following passage from the excerpt: 'it is not improbable that some scrupulous people might be apt to censure such a practice, (although indeed very unjustly) as a little bordering upon cruelty, which, I confess, hath always been with me the strongest objection against any project.' What irony is created by the narrator's claim that cruelty is his 'strongest objection'?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The narrator genuinely opposes his friend's proposal because he believes young girls deserve legal protection under Irish law.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The narrator declares cruelty his greatest concern while rejecting the proposal for purely economic reasons—the girls are more profitable alive as future mothers—revealing that his stated moral principle is hollow.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The narrator's objection to cruelty shows that he is slowly recognizing the inhumanity of his own original proposal and beginning to abandon it.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The narrator dismisses his friend's refinement because eating young people of any age conflicts with the religious values he has upheld throughout the proposal.

cards.standardTitle: Theme development across a literary text
cards.excerpt:
Infant’s flesh will be in season throughout the year, but more plentiful in March, and a little before and after; for we are told by a grave author, an eminent French physician, that fish being a prolifick dyet, there are more children born in Roman Catholick countries about nine months after Lent, than at any other season; therefore, reckoning a year after Lent, the markets will be more glutted than usual, because the number of Popish infants, is at least three to one in this kingdom, and therefore it will have one other collateral advantage, by lessening the number of Papists among us.

I have already computed the charge of nursing a beggar’s child (in which list I reckon all cottagers, labourers, and four-fifths of the farmers) to be about two shillings per annum, rags included; and I believe no gentleman would repine to give ten shillings for the carcass of a good fat child, which, as I have said, will make four dishes of excellent nutritive meat, when he hath only some particular friend, or his own family to dine with him. Thus the squire will learn to be a good landlord, and grow popular among his tenants, the mother will have eight shillings neat profit, and be fit for work till she produces another child.

choices.label: A

choices.label: B
choices.text: The ruling class reduces the poor to economic units whose bodies and children exist only to generate profit and convenience for the wealthy.

choices.label: C

choices.label: D

cards.standardTitle: Narrator perspective, irony, and satire
cards.excerpt: But in order to justify my friend, he confessed, that this expedient was put into his head by the famous Psalmanaazor, a native of the island Formosa, who came from thence to London, above twenty years ago, and in conversation told my friend, that in his country, when any young person happened to be put to death, the executioner sold the carcass to persons of quality, as a prime dainty; and that, in his time, the body of a plump girl of fifteen, who was crucified for an attempt to poison the Emperor, was sold to his imperial majesty’s prime minister of state, and other great mandarins of the court in joints from the gibbet, at four hundred crowns. choices.label: A
choices.text: The narrator praises Psalmanaazor as a trustworthy source, yet Psalmanaazor is a foreigner whose customs are presented as barbaric, making the narrator's admiration seem misplaced.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The narrator uses the calm, measured language of civic improvement to suggest that consuming young women would benefit the kingdom, treating an act of horror as a reasonable policy solution.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The narrator criticizes young women for attending playhouses in foreign fineries, revealing a genuine moral concern that contradicts the proposal's otherwise indifferent tone.

choices.label: D

cards.standardTitle: Theme development across a literary text
cards.excerpt:
Some persons of a desponding spirit are in great concern about that vast number of poor people, who are aged, diseased, or maimed; and I have been desired to employ my thoughts what course may be taken, to ease the nation of so grievous an incumbrance. But I am not in the least pain upon that matter, because it is very well known, that they are every day dying, and rotting, by cold and famine, and filth, and vermin, as fast as can be reasonably expected. And as to the young labourers, they are now in almost as hopeful a condition. They cannot get work, and consequently pine away from want of nourishment, to a degree, that if at any time they are accidentally hired to common labour, they have not strength to perform it, and thus the country and themselves are happily delivered from the evils to come.

I have too long digressed, and therefore shall return to my subject. I think the advantages by the proposal which I have made are obvious and many, as well as of the highest importance.
cards.whyThisWorks: The excerpt presents two distinct moments—the dismissal of the aged and diseased dying in filth, and the dismissal of young laborers wasting away from hunger—that together build Swift's satirical theme that society treats the poor as burdens to be eliminated rather than people to be helped.
cards.skillStrategy: When tracking theme, find two separate moments in the text and ask what idea both moments are pushing toward together.
evidencePoints: they are every day dying, and rotting, by cold and famine, and filth, and vermin, as fast as can be reasonably expected
they have not strength to perform it, and thus the country and themselves are happily delivered from the evils to come
cards.question: The narrator dismisses the suffering of the aged poor as no cause for 'pain' and then describes young laborers too weak from hunger to work as 'happily delivered from the evils to come.' How do these two moments work together to develop a theme?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Both moments show that Ireland's poor have brought their suffering on themselves by refusing available work and ignoring charitable assistance.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Both moments reveal that those in power view the deaths and deterioration of the poor as convenient solutions rather than as crises demanding action.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The first moment establishes that disease is the primary cause of poverty, while the second moment shifts blame to a lack of individual ambition among young workers.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Both moments suggest that the narrator genuinely believes Ireland lacks the resources to support its poor and is honestly calculating who can still contribute to the economy.

cards.question: Which phrase most clearly reveals the narrator's satirical perspective toward the landlord class and their treatment of the Irish poor?

choices.label: B

choices.label: C
choices.text: 'I have already computed the charge of nursing a beggar's child' — the narrator's careful arithmetic shows sincere sympathy for the financial hardships faced by poor Irish families.

choices.label: D
choices.text: 'the squire will learn to be a good landlord, and grow popular among his tenants' — the narrator sincerely praises landlords for the economic benefits they provide to their communities.

What does this wording reveal about the narrator's perspective?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The narrator sincerely opposes the proposal because he believes cruelty toward children is morally wrong and wants readers to share his outrage.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The narrator dismisses concern about cruelty as an unjust criticism while simultaneously claiming cruelty is his greatest objection, exposing a perspective that treats moral feeling as a technicality rather than a genuine barrier.

choices.label: D

cards.standardTitle: Theme development across a literary text
cards.excerpt: I do therefore humbly offer it to publick consideration, that of the hundred and twenty thousand children, already computed, twenty thousand may be reserved for breed, whereof only one fourth part to be males; which is more than we allow to sheep, black cattle, or swine, and my reason is, that these children are seldom the fruits of marriage, a circumstance not much regarded by our savages, therefore, one male will be sufficient to serve four females. That the remaining hundred thousand may, at a year old, be offered in sale to the persons of quality and fortune, through the kingdom, always advising the mother to let them suck plentifully in the last month, so as to render them plump, and fat for a good table. A child will make two dishes at an entertainment for friends, and when the family dines alone, the fore or hind quarter will make a reasonable dish, and seasoned with a little pepper or salt, will be very good boiled on the fourth day, especially in winter.
cards.whyThisWorks: Two distinct moments in the excerpt—the livestock-like breeding calculation and the cooking instructions—both develop the satirical theme that dehumanization of the poor is the logical endpoint of treating human beings as economic commodities.

cards.question:

choices.label: A
choices.text: Poverty forces desperate people to make unthinkable sacrifices for the sake of their families' survival.

choices.label: B
choices.text: When a society reduces human beings to their economic value, it becomes capable of treating people with the same indifference shown to livestock.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The wealthy classes of Ireland are morally superior to the poor because they can afford to feed and clothe themselves properly.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Overpopulation is the root cause of Ireland's suffering, and controlling birth rates among the poor is the most practical solution.

Some persons of a desponding spirit are in great concern about that vast number of poor people, who are aged, diseased, or maimed; and I have been desired to employ my thoughts what course may be taken, to ease the nation of so grievous an incumbrance. But I am not in the least pain upon that matter, because it is very well known, that they are every day dying, and rotting, by cold and famine, and filth, and vermin, as fast as can be reasonably expected. And as to the young labourers, they are now in almost as hopeful a condition. They cannot get work, and consequently pine away from want of nourishment, to a degree, that if at any time they are accidentally hired to common labour, they have not strength to perform it, and thus the country and themselves are happily delivered from the evils to come.

I have too long digressed, and therefore shall return to my subject. I think the advantages by the proposal which I have made are obvious and many, as well as of the highest importance.

cards.standardTitle: Narrator perspective, irony, and satire
cards.excerpt: I do therefore humbly offer it to publick consideration, that of the hundred and twenty thousand children, already computed, twenty thousand may be reserved for breed, whereof only one fourth part to be males; which is more than we allow to sheep, black cattle, or swine, and my reason is, that these children are seldom the fruits of marriage, a circumstance not much regarded by our savages, therefore, one male will be sufficient to serve four females. That the remaining hundred thousand may, at a year old, be offered in sale to the persons of quality and fortune, through the kingdom, always advising the mother to let them suck plentifully in the last month, so as to render them plump, and fat for a good table. cards.skillStrategy: When you spot absurd comparisons or shockingly calm language about something horrifying, ask what real-world attitude or behavior the author is mocking through that exaggeration.

How do these details work together as satire?

choices.label: B

choices.label: C

choices.label: D

cards.standardTitle: Central idea and supporting evidence
cards.excerpt: A very worthy person, a true lover of his country, and whose virtues I highly esteem, was lately pleased in discoursing on this matter, to offer a refinement upon my scheme. He said, that many gentlemen of this kingdom, having of late destroyed their deer, he conceived that the want of venison might be well supplied by the bodies of young lads and maidens, not exceeding fourteen years of age, nor under twelve; so great a number of both sexes in every county being now ready to starve for want of work and service: and these to be disposed of by their parents if alive, or otherwise by their nearest relations. But with due deference to so excellent a friend, and so deserving a patriot, I cannot be altogether in his sentiments; for as to the males, my American acquaintance assured me from frequent experience, that their flesh was generally tough and lean, like that of our schoolboys, by continual exercise, and their taste disagreeable, and to fatten them would not answer the charge. Then as to the females, it would, I think, with humble submission, be a loss to the publick, because they soon would become breeders themselves: and besides, it is not improbable that some scrupulous people might be apt to censure such a practice, (although indeed very unjustly) as a little bordering upon cruelty, which, I confess, hath always been with me the strongest objection against any project, how well soever intended.

cards.excerpt:
Some persons of a desponding spirit are in great concern about that vast number of poor people, who are aged, diseased, or maimed; and I have been desired to employ my thoughts what course may be taken, to ease the nation of so grievous an incumbrance. But I am not in the least pain upon that matter, because it is very well known, that they are every day dying, and rotting, by cold and famine, and filth, and vermin, as fast as can be reasonably expected. And as to the young labourers, they are now in almost as hopeful a condition. They cannot get work, and consequently pine away from want of nourishment, to a degree, that if at any time they are accidentally hired to common labour, they have not strength to perform it, and thus the country and themselves are happily delivered from the evils to come.

I have too long digressed, and therefore shall return to my subject. I think the advantages by the proposal which I have made are obvious and many, as well as of the highest importance.
cards.whyThisWorks: Swift's narrator openly celebrates the deaths of the poor as a convenient solution, creating a sharp gap between the speaker's cheerful indifference and the reader's horror at his callousness.
cards.skillStrategy: When a narrator says something shocking without alarm, ask yourself: does the speaker seem to think this is good news, and do I agree? That gap is where irony lives.
evidencePoints: I am not in the least pain upon that matter, because it is very well known, that they are every day dying, and rotting, by cold and famine, and filth, and vermin, as fast as can be reasonably expected.
the country and themselves are happily delivered from the evils to come
cards.question: The narrator states he is 'not in the least pain' about the poor dying from 'cold and famine, and filth, and vermin,' and that the country is 'happily delivered' when laborers waste away. What does the reader understand that the narrator does not seem to recognize?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The narrator is genuinely relieved because the deaths of the poor reduce the financial burden on the nation without requiring any policy changes.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The narrator's calm satisfaction reveals a moral blindness: what he frames as a convenient resolution is actually a preventable human catastrophe that should provoke outrage, not comfort.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The narrator understands the suffering of the poor but chooses to focus on economic solutions rather than emotional responses to their deaths.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The narrator is criticizing 'persons of a desponding spirit' for worrying too much, suggesting that public concern about poverty is itself the real problem.

cards.standardTitle: Central idea and supporting evidence
cards.excerpt: A very worthy person, a true lover of his country, and whose virtues I highly esteem, was lately pleased in discoursing on this matter, to offer a refinement upon my scheme. He said, that many gentlemen of this kingdom, having of late destroyed their deer, he conceived that the want of venison might be well supplied by the bodies of young lads and maidens, not exceeding fourteen years of age, nor under twelve; so great a number of both sexes in every county being now ready to starve for want of work and service: and these to be disposed of by their parents if alive, or otherwise by their nearest relations. But with due deference to so excellent a friend, and so deserving a patriot, I cannot be altogether in his sentiments; for as to the males, my American acquaintance assured me from frequent experience, that their flesh was generally tough and lean, like that of our schoolboys, by continual exercise, and their taste disagreeable, and to fatten them would not answer the charge. Then as to the females, it would, I think, with humble submission, be a loss to the publick, because they soon would become breeders themselves: and besides, it is not improbable that some scrupulous people might be apt to censure such a practice, (although indeed very unjustly) as a little bordering upon cruelty, which, I confess, hath always been with me the strongest objection against any project, how well soever intended.
cards.whyThisWorks: The excerpt forces students to distinguish between details that merely confirm the proposal's context (poverty, public opinion) and the detail that most directly exposes the narrator's reduction of human beings to economic commodities—his rejection of males because 'to fatten them would not answer the charge.'
cards.skillStrategy: Ask yourself: which detail does more than confirm a fact—which one directly proves the central idea by showing the narrator's reasoning in his own words?
evidencePoints: their flesh was generally tough and lean, like that of our schoolboys, by continual exercise, and their taste disagreeable, and to fatten them would not answer the charge
it would, I think, with humble submission, be a loss to the publick, because they soon would become breeders themselves
cards.question: Read the following claim about the passage: The narrator evaluates human beings using purely economic and practical criteria, revealing the moral bankruptcy of his worldview. The narrator gives two reasons for rejecting the friend's extension of the scheme—one about males and one about females. Which reason most directly supports this claim?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The narrator dismisses the friend's proposal by noting that young people between twelve and fourteen are 'ready to starve for want of work and service,' showing that poverty, not practicality, drives his objection.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The narrator rejects using males because 'their flesh was generally tough and lean' and 'to fatten them would not answer the charge,' measuring human lives entirely by edibility and cost-efficiency.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The narrator concedes that 'some scrupulous people might be apt to censure such a practice as a little bordering upon cruelty,' revealing that fear of public criticism, not economics, shapes his objection.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The narrator praises his friend as 'a true lover of his country' and 'so deserving a patriot,' suggesting that patriotic concern for Ireland, not economic logic, motivates the proposal he is evaluating.

Fifthly, This food would likewise bring great custom to taverns, where the vintners will certainly be so prudent as to procure the best receipts for dressing it to perfection; and consequently have their houses frequented by all the fine gentlemen, who justly value themselves upon their knowledge in good eating; and a skilful cook, who understands how to oblige his guests, will contrive to make it as expensive as they please.

Sixthly, This would be a great inducement to marriage, which all wise nations have either encouraged by rewards, or enforced by laws and penalties. It would encrease the care and tenderness of mothers towards their children, when they were sure of a settlement for life to the poor babes, provided in some sort by the publick, to their annual profit instead of expence. We should soon see an honest emulation among the married women, which of them could bring the fattest child to the market. Men would become as fond of their wives, during the time of their pregnancy, as they are now of their mares in foal, their cows in calf, or sows when they are ready to farrow; nor offer to beat or kick them (as is too frequent a practice) for fear of a miscarriage.
cards.whyThisWorks: Swift's satirical 'benefits' of commodifying children expose how economic greed can corrupt human relationships and moral values, making the theme transferable to any society that reduces people to their monetary worth.

cards.question: In these two paragraphs, Swift describes a society that values children as a source of profit and praises mothers for raising the 'fattest child to the market.' Which statement best expresses a universal theme developed through these details?

choices.label: B
choices.text: When a society measures human beings by their economic value, it destroys the bonds of love and care that make us human.

choices.label: C

choices.label: D

cards.standardTitle: Narrator perspective, irony, and satire
cards.excerpt: But in order to justify my friend, he confessed, that this expedient was put into his head by the famous Psalmanaazor, a native of the island Formosa, who came from thence to London, above twenty years ago, and in conversation told my friend, that in his country, when any young person happened to be put to death, the executioner sold the carcass to persons of quality, as a prime dainty; and that, in his time, the body of a plump girl of fifteen, who was crucified for an attempt to poison the Emperor, was sold to his imperial majesty’s prime minister of state, and other great mandarins of the court in joints from the gibbet, at four hundred crowns. Neither indeed can I deny, that if the same use were made of several plump young girls in this town, who without one single groat to their fortunes, cannot stir abroad without a chair, and appear at a playhouse and assemblies in foreign fineries which they never will pay for, the kingdom would not be the worse.
cards.whyThisWorks: Swift's narrator calmly cites a foreign precedent for selling human flesh as a 'prime dainty' and then casually extends the logic to London girls, creating a sharp gap between the narrator's matter-of-fact tone and the reader's horror at the moral depravity being normalized.
cards.skillStrategy: Notice when a narrator's calm, reasonable tone clashes with the disturbing reality of what is actually being proposed — that gap is where irony lives.

the kingdom would not be the worse

choices.label: D

Infant’s flesh will be in season throughout the year, but more plentiful in March, and a little before and after; for we are told by a grave author, an eminent French physician, that fish being a prolifick dyet, there are more children born in Roman Catholick countries about nine months after Lent, than at any other season; therefore, reckoning a year after Lent, the markets will be more glutted than usual, because the number of Popish infants, is at least three to one in this kingdom, and therefore it will have one other collateral advantage, by lessening the number of Papists among us.

I have already computed the charge of nursing a beggar’s child (in which list I reckon all cottagers, labourers, and four-fifths of the farmers) to be about two shillings per annum, rags included; and I believe no gentleman would repine to give ten shillings for the carcass of a good fat child, which, as I have said, will make four dishes of excellent nutritive meat, when he hath only some particular friend, or his own family to dine with him. Thus the squire will learn to be a good landlord, and grow popular among his tenants, the mother will have eight shillings neat profit, and be fit for work till she produces another child.
cards.whyThisWorks: Swift's cold arithmetic—assigning shilling values to children's bodies while praising the 'profit' for mothers and landlords—makes visible the universal theme that reducing people to economic units enables exploitation of the powerless by the powerful.
cards.skillStrategy: Look past the surface argument and ask: what does the speaker's logic reveal about how society treats certain people—and what does that say about human nature or power?

the mother will have eight shillings neat profit, and be fit for work till she produces another child

cards.excerpt:
Fifthly, This food would likewise bring great custom to taverns, where the vintners will certainly be so prudent as to procure the best receipts for dressing it to perfection; and consequently have their houses frequented by all the fine gentlemen, who justly value themselves upon their knowledge in good eating; and a skilful cook, who understands how to oblige his guests, will contrive to make it as expensive as they please.

Sixthly, This would be a great inducement to marriage, which all wise nations have either encouraged by rewards, or enforced by laws and penalties. It would encrease the care and tenderness of mothers towards their children, when they were sure of a settlement for life to the poor babes, provided in some sort by the publick, to their annual profit instead of expence. We should soon see an honest emulation among the married women, which of them could bring the fattest child to the market. Men would become as fond of their wives, during the time of their pregnancy, as they are now of their mares in foal, their cows in calf, or sows when they are ready to farrow; nor offer to beat or kick them (as is too frequent a practice) for fear of a miscarriage.
cards.whyThisWorks: Swift's analogy comparing pregnant wives to livestock ('mares in foal, their cows in calf, or sows when they are ready to farrow') creates a jarring dehumanization effect that forces readers to confront the horror beneath the proposal's polite, rational surface.
cards.skillStrategy: When you spot an analogy, ask yourself: what two things are being compared, and what feeling does that comparison create in you as a reader?
evidencePoints: Men would become as fond of their wives, during the time of their pregnancy, as they are now of their mares in foal, their cows in calf, or sows when they are ready to farrow
We should soon see an honest emulation among the married women, which of them could bring the fattest child to the market.
cards.question: In the sixth point, Swift compares husbands caring for pregnant wives to farmers tending 'their mares in foal, their cows in calf, or sows when they are ready to farrow.' How does this analogy affect the reader?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The comparison flatters husbands by suggesting they are as responsible and hardworking as farmers who carefully tend their animals.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The comparison reduces women to the status of livestock valued only for what they produce, making the horror of the proposal impossible to ignore beneath its calm, logical tone.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The comparison highlights the genuine tenderness husbands feel toward their wives, reinforcing Swift's argument that the proposal would strengthen family bonds.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The comparison emphasizes how poorly Irish farmers treat their animals, shifting the reader's sympathy toward the livestock rather than toward the women.

cards.standardTitle: Rhetoric and reader effect
cards.excerpt:
Infant’s flesh will be in season throughout the year, but more plentiful in March, and a little before and after; for we are told by a grave author, an eminent French physician, that fish being a prolifick dyet, there are more children born in Roman Catholick countries about nine months after Lent, than at any other season; therefore, reckoning a year after Lent, the markets will be more glutted than usual, because the number of Popish infants, is at least three to one in this kingdom, and therefore it will have one other collateral advantage, by lessening the number of Papists among us.

I have already computed the charge of nursing a beggar’s child (in which list I reckon all cottagers, labourers, and four-fifths of the farmers) to be about two shillings per annum, rags included; and I believe no gentleman would repine to give ten shillings for the carcass of a good fat child, which, as I have said, will make four dishes of excellent nutritive meat, when he hath only some particular friend, or his own family to dine with him. Thus the squire will learn to be a good landlord, and grow popular among his tenants, the mother will have eight shillings neat profit, and be fit for work till she produces another child.
cards.whyThisWorks: Swift's clinical economic language — 'charge of nursing,' 'two shillings per annum,' 'eight shillings neat profit' — applied to human infants creates a sustained contrast between cold financial calculation and the horror of the subject, making the satirical critique of English exploitation viscerally clear.
cards.skillStrategy: When you spot a rhetorical device, ask yourself: what emotion or idea does this create in the reader, and why did the author choose this device here?
evidencePoints: I believe no gentleman would repine to give ten shillings for the carcass of a good fat child
the mother will have eight shillings neat profit, and be fit for work till she produces another child
cards.question: In the second paragraph, Swift describes a mother receiving 'eight shillings neat profit' and being 'fit for work till she produces another child.' How does this language affect the reader?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The precise monetary figures reassure the reader that Swift has carefully researched a practical solution to poverty in Ireland.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Framing a mother's child and future pregnancies in the language of business transactions forces the reader to feel the horror of reducing human life to commodity, sharpening Swift's critique of how the poor are treated.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The financial details create sympathy for landlords by showing how little profit they actually gain from purchasing children.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The accounting language signals that Swift admires the efficiency of the economic system he is describing and wants readers to adopt it.

cards.standardTitle: Rhetoric and reader effect
cards.excerpt: A very worthy person, a true lover of his country, and whose virtues I highly esteem, was lately pleased in discoursing on this matter, to offer a refinement upon my scheme. He said, that many gentlemen of this kingdom, having of late destroyed their deer, he conceived that the want of venison might be well supplied by the bodies of young lads and maidens, not exceeding fourteen years of age, nor under twelve; so great a number of both sexes in every county being now ready to starve for want of work and service: and these to be disposed of by their parents if alive, or otherwise by their nearest relations. But with due deference to so excellent a friend, and so deserving a patriot, I cannot be altogether in his sentiments; for as to the males, my American acquaintance assured me from frequent experience, that their flesh was generally tough and lean, like that of our schoolboys, by continual exercise, and their taste disagreeable, and to fatten them would not answer the charge. Then as to the females, it would, I think, with humble submission, be a loss to the publick, because they soon would become breeders themselves: and besides, it is not improbable that some scrupulous people might be apt to censure such a practice, (although indeed very unjustly) as a little bordering upon cruelty, which, I confess, hath always been with me the strongest objection against any project, how well soever intended.
cards.whyThisWorks: Swift's parenthetical aside '(although indeed very unjustly)' and his dismissal of 'cruelty' as merely a 'scrupulous' concern demonstrate irony and understatement working together, giving students a precise rhetorical moment to analyze for reader effect.
cards.skillStrategy: When you spot a word or phrase that seems shockingly mild or out of place given the subject, ask yourself what emotional effect that understatement creates in the reader and what Swift wants you to feel about the speaker.
evidencePoints: some scrupulous people might be apt to censure such a practice, (although indeed very unjustly) as a little bordering upon cruelty
cruelty, which, I confess, hath always been with me the strongest objection against any project, how well soever intended
cards.question: Read the following passage moment: 'some scrupulous people might be apt to censure such a practice, (although indeed very unjustly) as a little bordering upon cruelty.' How does Swift's use of understatement in this sentence affect the reader?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The phrase 'a little bordering upon cruelty' reassures the reader that the narrator genuinely believes the proposal is humane and well-reasoned, building trust in his judgment.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Describing the consumption of children as only 'a little bordering upon cruelty' creates a jarring gap between the horror of the act and the narrator's casual tone, exposing the narrator's moral blindness and provoking the reader's outrage.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The parenthetical '(although indeed very unjustly)' signals that Swift himself agrees with the critics who call the proposal cruel, revealing his true opposition to the scheme.

choices.label: D
choices.text: By calling critics 'scrupulous,' Swift flatters those who object to the proposal, encouraging the reader to side with them rather than with the narrator.

cards.standardTitle: Rhetoric and reader effect
cards.excerpt: I do therefore humbly offer it to publick consideration, that of the hundred and twenty thousand children, already computed, twenty thousand may be reserved for breed, whereof only one fourth part to be males; which is more than we allow to sheep, black cattle, or swine, and my reason is, that these children are seldom the fruits of marriage, a circumstance not much regarded by our savages, therefore, one male will be sufficient to serve four females. That the remaining hundred thousand may, at a year old, be offered in sale to the persons of quality and fortune, through the kingdom, always advising the mother to let them suck plentifully in the last month, so as to render them plump, and fat for a good table. A child will make two dishes at an entertainment for friends, and when the family dines alone, the fore or hind quarter will make a reasonable dish, and seasoned with a little pepper or salt, will be very good boiled on the fourth day, especially in winter.
cards.whyThisWorks: Swift's extended analogy comparing children to livestock ('sheep, black cattle, or swine') and his clinical culinary language ('plump, and fat for a good table,' 'two dishes at an entertainment') create a chilling satirical effect that forces readers to confront the dehumanization of the Irish poor.
cards.skillStrategy: When you spot an analogy or figurative comparison, ask yourself: what two things are being compared, and how does that comparison make you feel or think differently about the subject?
evidencePoints: which is more than we allow to sheep, black cattle, or swine
always advising the mother to let them suck plentifully in the last month, so as to render them plump, and fat for a good table
cards.question: In the excerpt, Swift compares the management of children to the management of 'sheep, black cattle, or swine' and then describes children as needing to be 'plump, and fat for a good table.' How does this extended analogy affect the reader?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The analogy reassures the reader that Swift's proposal is grounded in practical farming knowledge familiar to Irish landowners.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The analogy forces the reader to recognize the horror of treating human children as livestock, exposing how completely the poor have been stripped of their humanity by those in power.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The analogy highlights Swift's genuine concern for efficient breeding practices that could improve Ireland's agricultural economy.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The analogy creates sympathy for the landowners by showing how difficult it is to manage large populations of people and animals alike.

cards.standardTitle: Paraphrase grade-level text
cards.excerpt:
Some persons of a desponding spirit are in great concern about that vast number of poor people, who are aged, diseased, or maimed; and I have been desired to employ my thoughts what course may be taken, to ease the nation of so grievous an incumbrance. But I am not in the least pain upon that matter, because it is very well known, that they are every day dying, and rotting, by cold and famine, and filth, and vermin, as fast as can be reasonably expected. And as to the young labourers, they are now in almost as hopeful a condition. They cannot get work, and consequently pine away from want of nourishment, to a degree, that if at any time they are accidentally hired to common labour, they have not strength to perform it, and thus the country and themselves are happily delivered from the evils to come.

I have too long digressed, and therefore shall return to my subject. I think the advantages by the proposal which I have made are obvious and many, as well as of the highest importance.
cards.whyThisWorks: Swift's sentence about young labourers contains inverted logic, embedded clauses, and ironic understatement that require students to untangle syntax and restate the actual meaning accurately.
cards.skillStrategy: Break the long sentence into smaller parts—who is being described, what is happening to them, and what result Swift claims—then restate each part in plain language.
evidencePoints: They cannot get work, and consequently pine away from want of nourishment, to a degree, that if at any time they are accidentally hired to common labour, they have not strength to perform it
and thus the country and themselves are happily delivered from the evils to come
cards.question: Read this sentence from the passage: 'They cannot get work, and consequently pine away from want of nourishment, to a degree, that if at any time they are accidentally hired to common labour, they have not strength to perform it, and thus the country and themselves are happily delivered from the evils to come.' Which restatement most accurately captures the meaning of this sentence?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Young labourers refuse available work because they are too weak from hunger, and their laziness ultimately spares the country from future problems.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Young labourers are so weakened by starvation from unemployment that even on the rare occasion they find work they cannot do it, and Swift claims this somehow benefits both them and the country.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Young labourers occasionally find common work but choose to quit, leaving the country free from the burden of supporting an idle workforce.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Young labourers are starving because the country has failed to provide nourishment, and the nation will eventually face serious consequences as a result.

cards.standardTitle: Theme development across a literary text
cards.excerpt:
Mr. Brooks, of South Carolina, in one of his speeches, when they were presenting him canes, silver plate, gold pitchers, and the like, for assaulting Senator Sumner, distinctly affirmed his opinion that when this Constitution was formed it was the belief of no man that slavery would last to the present day. He said, what I think, that the framers of our Constitution placed the institution of slavery where the public mind rested in the hope that it was in the course of ultimate extinction. But he went on to say that the men of the present age, by their experience, have become wiser than the framers of the Constitution, and the invention of the cotton gin had made the perpetuity of slavery a necessity in this country.

As another piece of evidence tending to this same point: Quite recently in Virginia, a man--the owner of slaves--made a will providing that after his death certain of his slaves should have their freedom if they should so choose, and go to Liberia, rather than remain in slavery. They chose to be liberated. But the persons to whom they would descend as property claimed them as slaves. A suit was instituted, which finally came to the Supreme Court of Virginia, and was therein decided against the slaves upon the ground that a negro cannot make a choice; that they had no legal power to choose, could not perform the condition upon which their freedom depended.
cards.whyThisWorks: The excerpt contains two distinct anecdotes—Brooks's speech and the Virginia court case—that both develop the theme that slavery's defenders actively worked to make it permanent, allowing students to distinguish theme-developing evidence from true-but-topic-only details.
cards.skillStrategy: Ask yourself: does this detail show how the theme is being built, or does it just mention something related to the topic without pushing the central idea forward?
evidencePoints: the men of the present age, by their experience, have become wiser than the framers of the Constitution, and the invention of the cotton gin had made the perpetuity of slavery a necessity in this country

the Supreme Court of Virginia...decided against the slaves upon the ground that a negro cannot make a choice; that they had no legal power to choose, could not perform the condition upon which their freedom depended
cards.question: Lincoln includes the Virginia court case in which slaves were denied freedom on the grounds that 'a negro cannot make a choice.' Which statement best explains how this detail develops the theme that the institution of slavery was being deliberately secured rather than allowed to fade?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The case shows that Virginia's legal system was separate from the federal government, illustrating that states had independent authority over property disputes.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The court's ruling stripped enslaved people of the legal capacity to act on their own freedom, demonstrating that the law itself was being used as a tool to make slavery permanent.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The case proves that slave owners sometimes wrote wills offering freedom, which shows that some individuals in the South personally opposed slavery.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The detail about Liberia reveals that formerly enslaved people had limited options even after being freed, which is a true hardship of the era.

cards.standardTitle: Theme development across a literary text
cards.excerpt: I remember Judge Douglas once said that he saw the evidences on the statute books of Congress of a policy in the origin of government to divide slavery and freedom by a geographical line; that he saw an indisposition to maintain that policy, and therefore he set about studying up a way to settle the institution on the right basis,--the basis which he thought it ought to have been placed upon at first; and in that speech he confesses that he seeks to place it, not upon the basis that the fathers placed it upon, but upon one gotten up on "original principles." When he asks me why we cannot get along with it in the attitude where our fathers placed it, he had better clear up the evidences that he has himself changed it from that basis, that he has himself been chiefly instrumental in changing the policy of the fathers. Any one who will read his speech of the 22d of last March will see that he there makes an open confession, showing that he set about fixing the institution upon an altogether different set of principles. I think I have fully answered him when he asks me why we cannot let it alone upon the basis where our fathers left it, by showing that he has himself changed the whole policy of the government in that regard.
cards.whyThisWorks: Lincoln's accusation that Douglas 'changed the whole policy of the government' while claiming to restore original principles directly develops a theme about political hypocrisy and the betrayal of founding ideals, allowing students to distinguish theme-developing evidence from mere topical details about slavery policy.
cards.skillStrategy: Ask yourself: does this detail show WHY the theme is true, or does it just mention what the passage is about?
evidencePoints: he seeks to place it, not upon the basis that the fathers placed it upon, but upon one gotten up on 'original principles'
he has himself been chiefly instrumental in changing the policy of the fathers
cards.question: Which detail from the excerpt best develops the theme that political leaders who claim to honor founding principles may actually be the ones dismantling them?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Lincoln recalls that Douglas once observed a geographical line dividing slavery and freedom on the statute books of Congress.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Lincoln argues that Douglas cannot demand the nation leave slavery where the founders placed it, because Douglas himself 'changed the whole policy of the government in that regard.'

choices.label: C
choices.text: Lincoln references Douglas's speech of the 22nd of last March as a source that readers can consult.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Lincoln notes that Douglas expressed an indisposition to maintain the original geographical policy on slavery.

cards.standardTitle: Theme development across a literary text
cards.excerpt:
I do not mention this with any purpose of criticizing it, but to connect it with the arguments as affording additional evidence of the change of sentiment upon this question of slavery in the direction of making it perpetual and national. I argue now as I did before, that there is such a tendency; and I am backed, not merely by the facts, but by the open confession in the slave States.

And now as to the Judge's inference that because I wish to see slavery placed in the course of ultimate extinction,--placed where our fathers originally placed it,--I wish to annihilate the State Legislatures, to force cotton to grow upon the tops of the Green Mountains, to freeze ice in Florida, to cut lumber on the broad Illinois prairie,--that I am in favor of all these ridiculous and impossible things.

It seems to me it is a complete answer to all this to ask if, when Congress did have the fashion of restricting slavery from free territory; when courts did have the fashion of deciding that taking a slave into a free country made him free,--I say it is a sufficient answer to ask if any of this ridiculous nonsense about consolidation and uniformity did actually follow. Who heard of any such thing because of the Ordinance of '87? because of the Missouri restriction? because of the numerous court decisions of that character?
cards.whyThisWorks: Lincoln's rhetorical move of pointing to historical precedents—the Ordinance of '87, the Missouri restriction, and court decisions—as proof that restricting slavery never caused the catastrophic consequences Douglas predicts directly develops the theme that fear-based arguments for slavery's expansion are unsupported by evidence.
cards.skillStrategy: Ask yourself: does this detail show the theme being built, or does it just mention a topic from the passage without pushing the central idea forward?
evidencePoints: Who heard of any such thing because of the Ordinance of '87? because of the Missouri restriction? because of the numerous court decisions of that character?
there is such a tendency; and I am backed, not merely by the facts, but by the open confession in the slave States
cards.question: Which detail from the excerpt most directly develops Lincoln's theme that arguments defending the spread of slavery rely on exaggeration rather than historical truth?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Lincoln acknowledges that he is not criticizing the change of sentiment on slavery, only connecting it to a broader argument about its national expansion.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Lincoln points out that past restrictions on slavery—the Ordinance of '87, the Missouri restriction, and court decisions—never produced the chaos Douglas now predicts, exposing Douglas's warnings as baseless.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Lincoln states that he wishes to see slavery placed in the course of ultimate extinction, exactly where the nation's founders originally placed it.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Lincoln notes that slave States have openly confessed to a tendency toward making slavery perpetual and national, which backs his argument with additional evidence.

cards.standardTitle: Theme development across a literary text
cards.excerpt:
In complaining of what I said in my speech at Springfield, in which he says I accepted my nomination for the senatorship (where, by the way, he is at fault, for if he will examine it, he will find no acceptance in it), he again quotes that portion in which I said that "a house divided against itself cannot stand." Let me say a word in regard to that matter.

He tries to persuade us that there must be a variety in the different institutions of the States of the Union; that that variety necessarily proceeds from the variety of soil, climate, of the face of the country, and the difference in the natural features of the States. I agree to all that. Have these very matters ever produced any difficulty amongst us? Not at all. Have we ever had any quarrel over the fact that they have laws in Louisiana designed to regulate the commerce that springs from the production of sugar? Or because we have a different class relative to the production of flour in this State? Have they produced any differences? Not at all. They are the very cements of this Union. They don't make the house a house divided against itself. They are the props that hold up the house and sustain the Union.
cards.whyThisWorks: Douglas's distinction between natural regional differences ('the very cements of this Union') and the slavery dispute ('a house divided against itself') forces students to identify which details actually develop the theme of what threatens national unity versus what merely relates to the topic of regional differences.
cards.skillStrategy: Ask yourself: does this detail show WHY the house is divided, or does it just describe something different about the states? Only details that reveal the source of real division develop the theme.
evidencePoints: They are the very cements of this Union. They don't make the house a house divided against itself.
Have these very matters ever produced any difficulty amongst us? Not at all.
cards.question: Douglas argues that a central theme of his speech is that not all differences among states threaten the Union. Which detail from the excerpt best develops that theme rather than simply relating to the topic of regional variety?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Douglas notes that Louisiana has laws designed to regulate commerce from sugar production, showing that states have distinct economic industries.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Douglas argues that differences in soil, climate, and natural features have never caused quarrels among the states and instead act as 'the very cements of this Union,' proving that natural variety strengthens rather than divides the nation.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Douglas points out that Lincoln quoted the phrase 'a house divided against itself cannot stand' from Douglas's Springfield speech.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Douglas clarifies that his Springfield speech contained no formal acceptance of his nomination for the senatorship, correcting Lincoln's characterization of the speech.

cards.standardTitle: Theme development across a literary text
cards.excerpt: As introductory to these interrogatories which Judge Douglas propounded to me at Ottawa, he read a set of resolutions which he said Judge Trumbull and myself had participated in adopting, in the first Republican State Convention, held at Springfield in October, 1854. He insisted that I and Judge Trumbull, and perhaps the entire Republican party, were responsible for the doctrines contained in the set of resolutions which he read, and I understand that it was from that set of resolutions that he deduced the interrogatories which he propounded to me, using these resolutions as a sort of authority for propounding those questions to me. Now, I say here to-day that I do not answer his interrogatories because of their springing at all from that set of resolutions which he read. I answered them because Judge Douglas thought fit to ask them. I do not now, nor ever did, recognize any responsibility upon myself in that set of resolutions. When I replied to him on that occasion, I assured him that I never had anything to do with them. I repeat here to today that I never in any possible form had anything to do with that set of resolutions It turns out, I believe, that those resolutions were never passed in any convention held in Springfield.
cards.whyThisWorks: Lincoln's repeated insistence that he never participated in the resolutions and that they may never have existed at all develops the theme that political accountability requires honest attribution of responsibility — students must distinguish details that build this theme from true-but-topic-only details about the debate format.
cards.skillStrategy: Ask yourself: does this detail show the theme growing stronger, or does it just mention something that happened in the passage?
evidencePoints: I do not now, nor ever did, recognize any responsibility upon myself in that set of resolutions.
It turns out, I believe, that those resolutions were never passed in any convention held in Springfield.
cards.question: Which detail from the excerpt best develops the theme that political integrity depends on refusing to accept false accusations of responsibility?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Lincoln explains that Judge Douglas read the resolutions as an introduction to his interrogatories at Ottawa, establishing the sequence of events in the debate.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Lincoln declares he never recognized any responsibility for the resolutions and then reveals the resolutions may never have been passed at all, showing that accepting a false charge would have undermined his integrity.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Lincoln notes that the first Republican State Convention was held in Springfield in October 1854, providing historical context for the political moment.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Lincoln states that he answered Douglas's interrogatories because Douglas chose to ask them, confirming that the debate exchange actually took place.

cards.standardTitle: Theme development across a literary text
cards.excerpt: Now, about this story that Judge Douglas tells of Trumbull bargaining to sell out the old Democratic party, and Lincoln agreeing to sell out the old Whig party, I have the means of knowing about that: Judge Douglas cannot have; and I know there is no substance to it whatever. Yet I have no doubt he is "conscientious" about it. I know that after Mr. Lovejoy got into the Legislature that winter, he complained of me that I had told all the old Whigs of his district that the old Whig party was good enough for them, and some of them voted against him because I told them so. Now, I have no means of totally disproving such charges as this which the Judge makes. A man cannot prove a negative; but he has a right to claim that when a man makes an affirmative charge, he must offer some proof to show the truth of what he says. I certainly cannot introduce testimony to show the negative about things, but I have a right to claim that if a man says he knows a thing, then he must show how he knows it. I always have a right to claim this, and it is not satisfactory to me that he may be "conscientious" on the subject.
cards.whyThisWorks: Lincoln's repeated insistence that accusers must provide proof—not just claim 'conscientiousness'—develops the theme that truth requires evidence, not assertion, allowing students to distinguish details that build this theme from true-but-off-topic details about Lovejoy or Trumbull.
cards.skillStrategy: Ask yourself: does this detail show the theme growing, or does it just describe what happened in the passage?
evidencePoints: A man cannot prove a negative; but he has a right to claim that when a man makes an affirmative charge, he must offer some proof to show the truth of what he says.
I always have a right to claim this, and it is not satisfactory to me that he may be 'conscientious' on the subject.
cards.question: Which detail from the passage best develops the theme that sincerity alone does not substitute for proof?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Lincoln mentions that Lovejoy complained Lincoln had told old Whigs their party was good enough for them, causing some to vote against Lovejoy.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Lincoln argues that Douglas's personal certainty—his being 'conscientious'—is not satisfying because Douglas has not shown how he knows his charge to be true.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Lincoln states that he has the means of knowing about the bargaining story, while Judge Douglas cannot have such means.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Lincoln acknowledges that he has no means of totally disproving the charges Douglas makes against him.

cards.standardTitle: Theme development across a literary text
cards.excerpt: Let us go a little further. You remember we once had a National Bank. Some one owed the bank a debt; he was sued, and sought to avoid payment on the ground that the bank was unconstitutional. The case went to the Supreme Court, and therein it was decided that the bank was constitutional. The whole Democratic party revolted against that decision. General Jackson himself asserted that he, as President, would not be bound to hold a National Bank to be constitutional, even though the court had decided it to be so. He fell in precisely with the view of Mr. Jefferson, and acted upon it under his official oath, in vetoing a charter for a National Bank. The declaration that Congress does not possess this constitutional power to charter a bank has gone into the Democratic platform, at their National Conventions, and was brought forward and reaffirmed in their last Convention at Cincinnati. They have contended for that declaration, in the very teeth of the Supreme Court, for more than a quarter of a century. In fact, they have reduced the decision to an absolute nullity. That decision, I repeat, is repudiated in the Cincinnati platform; and still, as if to show that effrontery can go no further, Judge Douglas vaunts in the very speeches in which he denounces me for opposing the Dred Scott decision that he stands on the Cincinnati platform.
cards.whyThisWorks: Lincoln's paragraph layers specific historical examples—Jackson's veto, the Democratic platform, and Douglas's contradiction—to build the theme that political convenience, not principle, drives opposition to Supreme Court authority, giving students practice distinguishing theme-developing evidence from mere topical detail.
cards.skillStrategy: Ask yourself: does this detail show WHY the theme is true, or does it just mention the same topic? Only details that prove the central idea develop the theme.
evidencePoints: They have contended for that declaration, in the very teeth of the Supreme Court, for more than a quarter of a century.
Judge Douglas vaunts in the very speeches in which he denounces me for opposing the Dred Scott decision that he stands on the Cincinnati platform.
cards.question: Lincoln develops the theme that political leaders selectively respect the Supreme Court's authority when it serves their interests. Which detail from the paragraph most directly develops this theme?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The Supreme Court once ruled that a National Bank was constitutional, settling a legal dispute over an unpaid debt.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Douglas publicly condemns Lincoln for opposing the Dred Scott decision while simultaneously standing on the Cincinnati platform, which has repudiated a Supreme Court ruling for over twenty-five years.

choices.label: C
choices.text: General Jackson believed that as President he was not personally bound by the Supreme Court's ruling on the National Bank.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The Democratic party included a declaration against a National Bank in its platform at the Cincinnati Convention.

cards.standardTitle: Theme development across a literary text
cards.excerpt: Judge Douglas says he does not think differently. I am glad of it. Then can he tell me why he is looking up resolutions of five or six years ago, and insisting that they were my platform, notwithstanding my protest that they are not, and never were my platform, and my pointing out the platform of the State Convention which he delights to say nominated me for the Senate? I cannot see what he means by parading these resolutions, if it is not to hold me responsible for them in some way. If he says to me here that he does not hold the rule to be good, one way or the other, I do not comprehend how he could answer me more fully if he answered me at greater length. I will therefore put in as my answer to the resolutions that he has hunted up against me, what I, as a lawyer, would call a good plea to a bad declaration. I understand that it is an axiom of law that a poor plea may be a good plea to a bad declaration. I think that the opinions the Judge brings from those who support me, yet differ from me, is a bad declaration against me; but if I can bring the same things against him, I am putting in a good plea to that kind of declaration, and now I propose to try it.
cards.whyThisWorks: Lincoln's legal analogy — 'a good plea to a bad declaration' — directly develops the theme that fair argument requires equal standards, letting students distinguish a thematically loaded detail from true-but-topically-adjacent ones.
cards.skillStrategy: Ask yourself: does this detail show the theme being built, or does it just describe what is happening in the passage?
evidencePoints: I will therefore put in as my answer to the resolutions that he has hunted up against me, what I, as a lawyer, would call a good plea to a bad declaration.
if I can bring the same things against him, I am putting in a good plea to that kind of declaration, and now I propose to try it.
cards.question: Lincoln says he will answer Douglas's resolutions with 'a good plea to a bad declaration' and then states, 'if I can bring the same things against him, I am putting in a good plea to that kind of declaration.' Which detail from the passage best develops the theme that a fair argument requires holding both sides to the same standard?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Lincoln points out that Douglas has been searching for resolutions from five or six years ago, which shows that Douglas is willing to dig deep into political history to find material for the debate.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Lincoln invokes the legal principle that 'a poor plea may be a good plea to a bad declaration' to argue that because Douglas used Lincoln's own supporters' opinions against him, Lincoln is equally entitled to use the same kind of evidence against Douglas.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Lincoln reminds the audience that he was nominated by a State Convention and that Douglas 'delights to say' so, establishing that Lincoln had an official platform separate from the resolutions Douglas cited.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Lincoln opens by noting that Judge Douglas 'does not think differently' from him, which shows that the two men agree on at least one point before Lincoln raises his legal objection.

cards.standardTitle: Theme development across a literary text
cards.excerpt: Why did he oppose it? Partly, as he declares, because the members of the convention who framed it were not fairly elected by the people; that the people were not allowed to vote unless they had been registered; and that the people of whole counties, some instances, were not registered. For these reasons he declares the Constitution was not an emanation, in any true sense, from the people. He also has an additional objection as to the mode of submitting the Constitution back to the people. But bearing on the question of whether the delegates were fairly elected, a speech of his, made something more than twelve months ago, from this stand, becomes important. It was made a little while before the election of the delegates who made Lecompton. In that speech he declared there was every reason to hope and believe the election would be fair; and if any one failed to vote, it would be his own culpable fault.
cards.whyThisWorks: The excerpt shows Douglas using Lincoln's own earlier speech—where Lincoln said the election 'would be fair'—to undermine Lincoln's later objections about unfair delegate elections, giving students a concrete moment where a specific detail (the prior speech) develops the theme of political inconsistency rather than merely naming the topic.
cards.skillStrategy: Ask yourself: does this detail actually show the theme being built, or does it just mention something related to the topic? A detail that develops theme changes how we understand a character's argument or contradiction.
evidencePoints: In that speech he declared there was every reason to hope and believe the election would be fair
if any one failed to vote, it would be his own culpable fault
cards.question: Douglas references a speech Lincoln made 'something more than twelve months ago' in which Lincoln said 'there was every reason to hope and believe the election would be fair.' Which statement best explains how this detail develops the theme that political opponents can be exposed by their own prior words?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Lincoln's earlier speech proves that the Lecompton delegates were, in fact, fairly elected, which settles the constitutional dispute entirely.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Lincoln's earlier confidence that the election would be fair directly contradicts his later claim that unfair registration procedures made the Constitution illegitimate, weakening his credibility.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The reference to Lincoln's prior speech shows that Douglas agreed with Lincoln's objections about voter registration before changing his position.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Lincoln's statement that non-voters were at 'culpable fault' reveals that Lincoln personally opposed expanding voting rights to unregistered citizens.

cards.standardTitle: Theme development across a literary text
cards.excerpt: Lastly, I would ask: Is not Congress itself under obligation to give legislative support to any right that is established under the United States Constitution? I repeat the question: Is not Congress itself bound to give legislative support to any right that is established in the United States Constitution? A member of Congress swears to support the Constitution of the United States: and if he sees a right established by that Constitution which needs specific legislative protection, can he clear his oath without giving that protection? Let me ask you why many of us who are opposed to slavery upon principle give our acquiescence to a Fugitive Slave law? Why do we hold ourselves under obligations to pass such a law, and abide by it when it is passed? Because the Constitution makes provision that the owners of slaves shall have the right to reclaim them. It gives the right to reclaim slaves; and that right is, as Judge Douglas says, a barren right, unless there is legislation that will enforce it.
cards.whyThisWorks: Lincoln's admission that opponents of slavery 'upon principle' still feel bound to enforce the Fugitive Slave Law directly illustrates the theme that constitutional duty overrides personal moral belief, giving students a concrete detail to distinguish from true-but-topic-only details.
cards.skillStrategy: Find the detail that shows the theme in action — not just a detail that is true or related to the topic.
evidencePoints: many of us who are opposed to slavery upon principle give our acquiescence to a Fugitive Slave law
the Constitution makes provision that the owners of slaves shall have the right to reclaim them
cards.question: Lincoln states that 'many of us who are opposed to slavery upon principle give our acquiescence to a Fugitive Slave law.' Which detail from the excerpt most directly develops the theme that constitutional obligation can override personal moral belief?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Lincoln repeats the question 'Is not Congress itself bound to give legislative support to any right that is established in the United States Constitution?' twice, showing that he wants to emphasize the importance of the question.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Lincoln explains that those who oppose slavery on principle still feel bound to pass and abide by the Fugitive Slave Law because the Constitution grants slaveholders the right to reclaim their slaves.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Lincoln notes that Judge Douglas described a constitutional right as 'a barren right' without legislation to enforce it, showing that Douglas and Lincoln agreed on the limits of unenforced rights.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Lincoln points out that a member of Congress swears an oath to support the Constitution, establishing that lawmakers in this debate had taken a formal pledge before taking office.

cards.standardTitle: Theme development across a literary text
cards.excerpt: He says if I should vote for the admission of a slave State I would be voting for a dissolution of the Union, because I hold that the Union cannot permanently exist half slave and half free. I repeat that I do not believe this government can endure permanently half slave and half free; yet I do not admit, nor does it at all follow, that the admission of a single slave State will permanently fix the character and establish this as a universal slave nation. The Judge is very happy indeed at working up these quibbles. Before leaving the subject of answering questions, I aver as my confident belief, when you come to see our speeches in print, that you will find every question which he has asked me more fairly and boldly and fully answered than he has answered those which I put to him. Is not that so? The two speeches may be placed side by side, and I will venture to leave it to impartial judges whether his questions have not been more directly and circumstantially answered than mine.
cards.whyThisWorks: The excerpt lets students distinguish between details that develop Lincoln's theme—that a divided nation cannot endure—and true but off-topic details about debate tactics, forcing them to apply the subskill of separating thematic evidence from mere topic-matching details.
cards.skillStrategy: Ask yourself: does this detail show the theme growing or changing, or does it just mention something related to the topic without pushing the central idea forward?
evidencePoints: I do not believe this government can endure permanently half slave and half free
the admission of a single slave State will permanently fix the character and establish this as a universal slave nation
cards.question: Lincoln's central theme in this passage is that a nation permanently divided between slavery and freedom cannot survive. Which detail from the passage most directly develops that theme?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Lincoln challenges Douglas to place their two speeches side by side so impartial judges can compare how fully each man answered the other's questions.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Lincoln insists that while the government cannot endure permanently half slave and half free, admitting one slave State does not by itself make the entire nation a 'universal slave nation.'

choices.label: C
choices.text: Lincoln accuses Douglas of being 'very happy indeed at working up these quibbles,' suggesting Douglas is more interested in rhetorical tricks than honest debate.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Lincoln expresses confidence that when the speeches appear in print, readers will see that he answered Douglas's questions more 'fairly and boldly and fully' than Douglas answered his.

cards.standardTitle: Theme development across a literary text
cards.excerpt: One more thing. Last night Judge Douglas tormented himself with horrors about my disposition to make negroes perfectly equal with white men in social and political relations. He did not stop to show that I have said any such thing, or that it legitimately follows from anything I have said, but he rushes on with his assertions. I adhere to the Declaration of Independence. If Judge Douglas and his friends are not willing to stand by it, let them come up and amend it. Let them make it read that all men are created equal except negroes. Let us have it decided whether the Declaration of Independence, in this blessed year of 1858, shall be thus amended. In his construction of the Declaration last year, he said it only meant that Americans in America were equal to Englishmen in England. Then, when I pointed out to him that by that rule he excludes the Germans, the Irish, the Portuguese, and all the other people who have come among us since the revolution, he reconstructs his construction. In his last speech he tells us it meant Europeans.
cards.whyThisWorks: Douglas's shifting definitions—from 'Americans equal to Englishmen' to 'Europeans'—give students a concrete textual moment to distinguish a detail that actively develops the theme of equality's shrinking scope from true-but-topic-only details about the debate's emotional tone or historical setting.
cards.skillStrategy: Ask yourself: does this detail show the theme being built step by step, or does it just confirm what the passage is about?
evidencePoints: he said it only meant that Americans in America were equal to Englishmen in England
In his last speech he tells us it meant Europeans
cards.question: Lincoln traces two specific moments when Douglas revised his interpretation of the Declaration of Independence—first limiting it to Americans equal to Englishmen, then expanding it to Europeans. Which statement best explains how those two moments together develop the theme that opponents of universal equality are forced to continuously narrow its meaning?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The two revisions show that Douglas was willing to include Germans, Irish, and Portuguese under the Declaration, proving he did not actually oppose equality for immigrant groups.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Each time Douglas's definition was challenged—first by excluding non-English immigrants, then by Lincoln naming specific groups—Douglas shifted the boundary rather than accepting a universal standard, demonstrating that resisting equality requires constant redefinition.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Douglas's two different definitions reveal that he was confused about American history, which Lincoln uses to question whether Douglas is qualified to interpret the Declaration at all.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The shift from 'Englishmen' to 'Europeans' shows that Douglas gradually moved closer to Lincoln's position, suggesting the two men were actually narrowing their disagreement over the course of the debates.

cards.standardTitle: Theme development across a literary text
cards.excerpt: MY FELLOW-CITIZENS:--When a man hears himself somewhat misrepresented, it provokes him, at least, I find it so with myself; but when misrepresentation becomes very gross and palpable, it is more apt to amuse him.
