The first thing I see fit to notice is the fact that Judge Douglas alleges, after running through the history of the old Democratic and the old Whig parties, that Judge Trumbull and myself made an arrangement in 1854, by which I was to have the place of General Shields in the United States Senate, and Judge Trumbull was to have the place of Judge Douglas. Now, all I have to say upon that subject is that I think no man not even Judge Douglas can prove it, because it is not true. I have no doubt he is "conscientious" in saying it. As to those resolutions that he took such a length of time to read, as being the platform of the Republican party in 1854, I say I never had anything to do with them, and I think Trumbull never had. Judge Douglas cannot show that either of us ever did have anything to do with them.
cards.whyThisWorks: Lincoln's shift from acknowledging provocation to expressing amusement at 'gross and palpable' misrepresentation, paired with his calm insistence that the arrangement 'is not true' and 'cannot be proved,' lets students distinguish details that develop a theme of reasoned truth over emotional reaction from true-but-topic-only details about the political dispute.
cards.skillStrategy: Ask yourself: does this detail show HOW the theme is built, or does it just describe what the passage is about?
evidencePoints: when misrepresentation becomes very gross and palpable, it is more apt to amuse him
I think no man not even Judge Douglas can prove it, because it is not true
cards.question: Lincoln says that when misrepresentation becomes 'very gross and palpable, it is more apt to amuse him,' and then immediately states that Douglas's allegation about the 1854 arrangement 'cannot be proved, because it is not true.' Which detail from the excerpt most directly develops the theme that calm reliance on truth is a stronger response to dishonesty than anger?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Lincoln names General Shields and Judge Douglas as the two Senate figures involved in the alleged 1854 arrangement, establishing the specific political stakes of the accusation.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Lincoln moves from admitting the accusation 'provokes him' to saying gross misrepresentation is 'more apt to amuse him,' then anchors his response entirely in the factual claim that the arrangement is 'not true' and unprovable—showing composure and evidence replace outrage.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Lincoln notes that Judge Douglas spent 'such a length of time' reading resolutions he claimed were the 1854 Republican party platform, revealing that Douglas relied on lengthy recitation during the debate.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Lincoln states that he and Trumbull 'never had anything to do' with the 1854 resolutions, which confirms that both men denied involvement in the Republican platform Douglas described.

cards.standardTitle: Theme development across a literary text
cards.excerpt: Again: There is in that same quotation from the Nebraska Bill this clause: "It being the true intent and meaning of this bill not to legislate slavery into any Territory or State." I have always been puzzled to know what business the word "State" had in that connection. Judge Douglas knows. He put it there. He knows what he put it there for. We outsiders cannot say what he put it there for. The law they were passing was not about States, and was not making provisions for States. What was it placed there for? After seeing the Dred Scott decision, which holds that the people cannot exclude slavery from a Territory, if another Dred Scott decision shall come, holding that they cannot exclude it from a State, we shall discover that when the word was originally put there, it was in view of something which was to come in due time, we shall see that it was the other half of something. I now say again, if there is any different reason for putting it there, Judge Douglas, in a good-humored way, without calling anybody a liar, can tell what the reason was.
cards.whyThisWorks: Lincoln's argument that the word 'State' was planted in the Nebraska Bill as preparation for a future Dred Scott-style ruling develops the theme that political language can be deliberately crafted to expand the reach of slavery, requiring students to distinguish this structural evidence from true-but-topical details about the Dred Scott decision itself.
cards.skillStrategy: Ask yourself: does this detail show how the theme is being built, or does it just mention something related to the topic?
evidencePoints: He put it there. He knows what he put it there for.
it was in view of something which was to come in due time, we shall see that it was the other half of something
cards.question: Lincoln argues that the word 'State' was deliberately inserted into the Nebraska Bill. Which detail from the passage most directly develops the theme that political power can be quietly arranged in advance to expand slavery's reach?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Lincoln acknowledges that 'outsiders cannot say' why Douglas placed the word 'State' in the bill, which shows that Lincoln admits he lacks enough evidence to accuse Douglas of wrongdoing.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Lincoln reasons that the word 'State' was placed in the bill 'in view of something which was to come in due time,' suggesting it was the hidden groundwork for a future ruling that would prevent states from excluding slavery.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Lincoln notes that the Dred Scott decision 'holds that the people cannot exclude slavery from a Territory,' which is a true legal outcome described in the passage.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Lincoln invites Douglas to explain 'in a good-humored way, without calling anybody a liar' what the reason was, showing that Lincoln values civil debate over personal accusation.

cards.standardTitle: Theme development across a literary text
cards.excerpt: We were often,--more than once, at least,--in the course of Judge Douglas's speech last night, reminded that this government was made for white men; that he believed it was made for white men. Well, that is putting it into a shape in which no one wants to deny it; but the Judge then goes into his passion for drawing inferences that are not warranted. I protest, now and forever, against that counterfeit logic which presumes that because I did not want a negro woman for a slave, I do necessarily want her for a wife. My understanding is that I need not have her for either, but, as God made us separate, we can leave one another alone, and do one another much good thereby. There are white men enough to marry all the white women, and enough black men to marry all the black women; and in God's name let them be so married. The Judge regales us with the terrible enormities that take place by the mixture of races; that the inferior race bears the superior down. Why, Judge, if we do not let them get together in the Territories, they won't mix there.
cards.whyThisWorks: Lincoln's rebuttal of Douglas's 'counterfeit logic' directly develops the theme that opposing slavery does not require social equality, forcing students to distinguish details that build that argument from true-but-off-topic details about race and marriage.
cards.skillStrategy: Ask yourself: does this detail show the theme growing, or does it just mention something true about the topic?
evidencePoints: I protest, now and forever, against that counterfeit logic which presumes that because I did not want a negro woman for a slave, I do necessarily want her for a wife.
My understanding is that I need not have her for either, but, as God made us separate, we can leave one another alone, and do one another much good thereby.
cards.question: Lincoln's argument develops the theme that opposing slavery does not require accepting social equality between races. Which detail from the passage best develops that theme?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Lincoln notes that Douglas reminded the audience 'more than once' that the government was made for white men, showing that Douglas repeated this claim throughout his speech.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Lincoln argues that rejecting slavery and rejecting intermarriage are not logically connected, because a person 'need not have her for either' — neither as a slave nor as a wife — dismantling the idea that one position forces the other.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Lincoln observes that Douglas warned about 'the terrible enormities that take place by the mixture of races,' confirming that racial mixing was a genuine concern in the debate.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Lincoln points out that if the races are kept separate in the Territories, they will not mix there, which shows Lincoln agreed with Douglas's goal of keeping the Territories racially separate.

cards.standardTitle: Theme development across a literary text
cards.excerpt: I do not wish to dwell at great length on this branch of the subject at this time, but allow me to repeat one thing that I have stated before. Brooks--the man who assaulted Senator Sumner on the floor of the Senate, and who was complimented with dinners, and silver pitchers, and gold-headed canes, and a good many other things for that feat--in one of his speeches declared that when this government was originally established, nobody expected that the institution of slavery would last until this day. That was but the opinion of one man, but it was such an opinion as we can never get from Judge Douglas or anybody in favor of slavery, in the North, at all. You can sometimes get it from a Southern man. He said at the same time that the framers of our government did not have the knowledge that experience has taught us; that experience and the invention of the cotton-gin have taught us that the perpetuation of slavery is a necessity. He insisted, therefore, upon its being changed from the basis upon which the fathers of the government left it to the basis of its perpetuation and nationalization.
cards.whyThisWorks: The excerpt contains both true-but-topical details (Brooks's assault, the cotton-gin) and a detail that directly develops Lincoln's theme that slavery was always expected to be temporary—requiring students to distinguish evidence that proves the theme from details that merely relate to the topic of slavery.
cards.skillStrategy: Ask yourself: does this detail show the theme growing or changing, or does it just mention something connected to the topic?
evidencePoints: nobody expected that the institution of slavery would last until this day
the framers of our government did not have the knowledge that experience has taught us
cards.question: Lincoln's central theme in this passage is that slavery was never meant to be a permanent national institution. Which detail from the passage most directly develops that theme?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Brooks was celebrated with dinners, silver pitchers, and gold-headed canes after assaulting Senator Sumner on the Senate floor.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Brooks stated that when the government was originally established, nobody expected slavery would last until this day, an admission Lincoln notes can never be drawn from Northern slavery supporters.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The invention of the cotton-gin taught Americans that the perpetuation of slavery was a necessity.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Judge Douglas and others in favor of slavery in the North refuse to speak openly about the origins of the institution.

cards.standardTitle: Opposing arguments, claims, evidence, and validity
cards.excerpt:
Mr. Brooks, of South Carolina, in one of his speeches, when they were presenting him canes, silver plate, gold pitchers, and the like, for assaulting Senator Sumner, distinctly affirmed his opinion that when this Constitution was formed it was the belief of no man that slavery would last to the present day. He said, what I think, that the framers of our Constitution placed the institution of slavery where the public mind rested in the hope that it was in the course of ultimate extinction. But he went on to say that the men of the present age, by their experience, have become wiser than the framers of the Constitution, and the invention of the cotton gin had made the perpetuity of slavery a necessity in this country.

As another piece of evidence tending to this same point: Quite recently in Virginia, a man--the owner of slaves--made a will providing that after his death certain of his slaves should have their freedom if they should so choose, and go to Liberia, rather than remain in slavery. They chose to be liberated. But the persons to whom they would descend as property claimed them as slaves. A suit was instituted, which finally came to the Supreme Court of Virginia, and was therein decided against the slaves upon the ground that a negro cannot make a choice; that they had no legal power to choose, could not perform the condition upon which their freedom depended.
cards.whyThisWorks: Lincoln develops his claim about slavery's intended extinction through two distinct types of evidence—a political opponent's own admission and a legal case outcome—allowing students to compare how each piece functions differently in building the argument.
cards.skillStrategy: Ask yourself: what kind of evidence is each example (testimony, data, anecdote, legal ruling), and how does each one push the claim forward in a different way?
evidencePoints: the framers of our Constitution placed the institution of slavery where the public mind rested in the hope that it was in the course of ultimate extinction
a negro cannot make a choice; that they had no legal power to choose, could not perform the condition upon which their freedom depended
cards.question: Lincoln uses two pieces of evidence in these paragraphs to support his argument about slavery. How do the two pieces of evidence differ in the way they develop his claim?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The first piece of evidence shows that Southerners always supported slavery, while the second shows that Northern courts eventually overturned those views.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The first piece of evidence uses a political opponent's own words to show that even slavery's defenders once acknowledged its intended end, while the second uses a legal ruling to show how current law actively denies enslaved people the rights the founders assumed would fade.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The first piece of evidence relies on the invention of the cotton gin to explain slavery's growth, while the second relies on the personal choice of enslaved people to argue for abolition.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Both pieces of evidence draw on court decisions to demonstrate that slavery was never intended to be permanent under the original Constitution.

cards.standardTitle: Theme development across a literary text
cards.excerpt: I believe I have the amendment here before me, which was offered, and under which the people of the Territory, through their representatives, might, if they saw fit, prohibit the existence of slavery therein. And now I state it as a fact, to be taken back if there is any mistake about it, that Judge Douglas and those acting with him voted that amendment down. I now think that those men who voted it down had a real reason for doing so. They know what that reason was. It looks to us, since we have seen the Dred Scott decision pronounced, holding that "under the Constitution" the people cannot exclude slavery, I say it looks to outsiders, poor, simple, "amiable, intelligent gentlemen," as though the niche was left as a place to put that Dred Scott decision in,--a niche which would have been spoiled by adopting the amendment. And now, I say again, if this was not the reason, it will avail the Judge much more to calmly and good-humoredly point out to these people what that other reason was for voting the amendment down, than, swelling himself up, to vociferate that he may be provoked to call somebody a liar.
cards.whyThisWorks: Lincoln's argument that the amendment was deliberately voted down to preserve a 'niche' for the Dred Scott decision develops the theme that political power is manipulated to entrench injustice, requiring students to distinguish this structural evidence from true-but-thematic-neutral details like the amendment's procedural description.
cards.skillStrategy: Ask yourself: does this detail show how the theme is being built, or does it just describe what happened without connecting to the larger idea?
evidencePoints: the niche was left as a place to put that Dred Scott decision in,--a niche which would have been spoiled by adopting the amendment
Judge Douglas and those acting with him voted that amendment down
cards.question: Lincoln argues a theme about the deliberate manipulation of political processes to protect the institution of slavery. Which detail from the passage most directly develops that theme?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Lincoln acknowledges that the amendment would have allowed the people of the Territory, through their representatives, to prohibit slavery if they chose to do so.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Lincoln contends that the amendment was voted down specifically to preserve a legal opening for the Dred Scott decision, suggesting the outcome was engineered rather than accidental.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Lincoln notes that the Dred Scott decision held that under the Constitution the people cannot exclude slavery from a territory.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Lincoln challenges Judge Douglas to calmly explain his reason for voting the amendment down rather than threatening to call someone a liar.

cards.standardTitle: Opposing arguments, claims, evidence, and validity
cards.excerpt: I remember Judge Douglas once said that he saw the evidences on the statute books of Congress of a policy in the origin of government to divide slavery and freedom by a geographical line; that he saw an indisposition to maintain that policy, and therefore he set about studying up a way to settle the institution on the right basis,--the basis which he thought it ought to have been placed upon at first; and in that speech he confesses that he seeks to place it, not upon the basis that the fathers placed it upon, but upon one gotten up on "original principles." When he asks me why we cannot get along with it in the attitude where our fathers placed it, he had better clear up the evidences that he has himself changed it from that basis, that he has himself been chiefly instrumental in changing the policy of the fathers. Any one who will read his speech of the 22d of last March will see that he there makes an open confession, showing that he set about fixing the institution upon an altogether different set of principles. I think I have fully answered him when he asks me why we cannot let it alone upon the basis where our fathers left it, by showing that he has himself changed the whole policy of the government in that regard.
cards.whyThisWorks: Lincoln builds his counter-claim by turning Douglas's own prior speech and 'original principles' language against him, demonstrating how each debater develops evidence differently—Douglas through abstract principle, Lincoln through specific textual citation and logical reversal.
cards.skillStrategy: When comparing how authors develop claims, track what kind of evidence each one uses—direct quotation, personal testimony, historical record, or logical reasoning—and ask what that choice does for their argument.
evidencePoints: he confesses that he seeks to place it, not upon the basis that the fathers placed it upon, but upon one gotten up on 'original principles'

Any one who will read his speech of the 22d of last March will see that he there makes an open confession, showing that he set about fixing the institution upon an altogether different set of principles
cards.question: Lincoln references Douglas's 'speech of the 22d of last March' and Douglas's own phrase 'original principles' to develop his claim. How does this approach to evidence differ from the way Douglas originally developed his position, as Lincoln describes it?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Douglas relied on a specific congressional record to prove the founders intended a geographical division, while Lincoln relies on personal memory of conversations with Douglas.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Douglas appealed to abstract reasoning about what the founders should have done, while Lincoln cites Douglas's own recorded words to show Douglas himself abandoned the founders' framework.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Douglas built his claim by quoting the statute books of Congress directly, while Lincoln dismisses those statutes as irrelevant to the debate over slavery's expansion.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Douglas developed his claim by acknowledging the fathers' policy was flawed, while Lincoln argues the fathers' policy was never actually applied to the question of slavery.

cards.standardTitle: Theme development across a literary text
cards.excerpt: I hold that the proposition that slavery cannot enter a new country without police regulations is historically false. It is not true at all. I hold that the history of this country shows that the institution of slavery was originally planted upon this continent without these "police regulations," which the Judge now thinks necessary for the actual establishment of it. Not only so, but is there not another fact: how came this Dred Scott decision to be made? It was made upon the case of a negro being taken and actually held in slavery in Minnesota Territory, claiming his freedom because the Act of Congress prohibited his being so held there. Will the Judge pretend that Dred Scott was not held there without police regulations? There is at least one matter of record as to his having been held in slavery in the Territory, not only without police regulations, but in the teeth of Congressional legislation supposed to be valid at the time. This shows that there is vigor enough in slavery to plant itself in a new country even against unfriendly legislation. It takes not only law, but the enforcement of law to keep it out. That is the history of this country upon the subject.
cards.whyThisWorks: The excerpt contains a true-but-topic-only detail (slavery's long history on the continent) alongside a theme-developing detail (slavery sustained itself 'in the teeth of Congressional legislation'), giving students a clear opportunity to distinguish topic from theme.
cards.skillStrategy: Ask yourself: does this detail just tell me what the passage is about, or does it show me what the author wants me to understand about human institutions and power?
evidencePoints: there is vigor enough in slavery to plant itself in a new country even against unfriendly legislation
It takes not only law, but the enforcement of law to keep it out
cards.question: Lincoln closes the paragraph with the claim: 'It takes not only law, but the enforcement of law to keep it out. That is the history of this country upon the subject.' Which detail from the passage most directly develops the theme that oppressive institutions can sustain themselves even when the law formally opposes them?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Lincoln states that 'the history of this country shows that the institution of slavery was originally planted upon this continent without these police regulations,' establishing that slavery has existed in America for a long time.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Lincoln argues that Dred Scott was held in slavery 'in the teeth of Congressional legislation supposed to be valid at the time,' demonstrating that slavery maintained itself even where federal law formally prohibited it.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Lincoln explains that the Dred Scott decision arose from 'a negro being taken and actually held in slavery in Minnesota Territory, claiming his freedom because the Act of Congress prohibited his being so held there,' identifying the legal origin of the case.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Lincoln challenges Douglas by asking whether Douglas will 'pretend that Dred Scott was not held there without police regulations,' exposing an inconsistency in Douglas's argument about the necessity of local laws.

cards.standardTitle: Opposing arguments, claims, evidence, and validity
cards.excerpt:
When he spoke at Chicago, on Friday evening of last week, he made this same point upon me. On Saturday evening I replied, and reminded him of a Supreme Court decision which he opposed for at least several years. Last night, at Bloomington, he took some notice of that reply, but entirely forgot to remember that part of it.

He renews his onslaught upon me, forgetting to remember that I have turned the tables against himself on that very point. I renew the effort to draw his attention to it. I wish to stand erect before the country, as well as Judge Douglas, on this question of judicial authority; and therefore I add something to the authority in favor of my own position. I wish to show that I am sustained by authority, in addition to that heretofore presented. I do not expect to convince the Judge. It is part of the plan of his campaign, and he will cling to it with a desperate grip. Even turn it upon him,--the sharp point against him, and gaff him through,--he will still cling to it till he can invent some new dodge to take the place of it.
cards.whyThisWorks: Lincoln explicitly contrasts his own evidence-building strategy ('I add something to the authority in favor of my own position') with Douglas's pattern of repeating a charge while ignoring Lincoln's rebuttal, giving students a direct textual comparison of how each debater develops his claim.
cards.skillStrategy: When comparing how two authors develop claims, find the exact words each author uses to describe their own evidence or their opponent's evidence, then ask what those words reveal about each author's method.
evidencePoints: I wish to show that I am sustained by authority, in addition to that heretofore presented.
He renews his onslaught upon me, forgetting to remember that I have turned the tables against himself on that very point.
cards.question: Lincoln says he will 'add something to the authority in favor of my own position' and also accuses Douglas of 'forgetting to remember' Lincoln's rebuttal. What do these two statements reveal about how each debater develops his claim in this exchange?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Lincoln builds his claim by appealing to the crowd's sympathy, while Douglas develops his claim by introducing a new Supreme Court decision Lincoln cannot refute.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Lincoln develops his claim by layering additional judicial authority onto his existing argument, while Douglas repeats his original charge without addressing the rebuttal Lincoln has already made.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Lincoln abandons his earlier judicial evidence and replaces it with a personal challenge to Douglas's honesty, while Douglas develops his claim by acknowledging Lincoln's point and offering a counter-explanation.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Lincoln develops his claim by admitting the Supreme Court decision weakens his position, while Douglas develops his claim by pressing the same judicial authority Lincoln originally cited.

cards.standardTitle: Theme development across a literary text
cards.excerpt: After Senator Douglas left Washington, as his movements were made known by the public prints, he tarried a considerable time in the city of New York; and it was heralded that, like another Napoleon, he was lying by and framing the plan of his campaign. It was telegraphed to Washington City, and published in the Union, that he was framing his plan for the purpose of going to Illinois to pounce upon and annihilate the treasonable and disunion speech which Lincoln had made here on the 16th of June. Now, I do suppose that the Judge really spent some time in New York maturing the plan of the campaign, as his friends heralded for him. I have been able, by noting his movements since his arrival in Illinois, to discover evidences confirmatory of that allegation. I think I have been able to see what are the material points of that plan. I will, for a little while, ask your attention to some of them. What I shall point out, though not showing the whole plan, are, nevertheless, the main points, as I suppose.
cards.whyThisWorks: Lincoln's deliberate framing of Douglas as a calculating strategist—using the Napoleon comparison and the word 'pounce'—develops the theme that political power depends on controlling public perception, allowing students to distinguish theme-developing details from mere topical facts.
cards.skillStrategy: Ask yourself: does this detail show something about a bigger idea the author is building, or does it just tell me what happened? Only theme-developing details reveal a truth about human behavior or conflict.
evidencePoints: like another Napoleon, he was lying by and framing the plan of his campaign
going to Illinois to pounce upon and annihilate the treasonable and disunion speech which Lincoln had made
cards.question: Lincoln compares Douglas to 'another Napoleon' who was 'lying by and framing the plan of his campaign.' Which detail from the paragraph most directly develops the theme that political rivals use calculated strategy to shape how the public sees their opponents?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Douglas traveled from Washington to New York before returning to Illinois, which shows the geographic scope of his political activities.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Douglas's plan was reportedly designed to 'pounce upon and annihilate' Lincoln's speech, revealing that his public campaign was a deliberate act of political destruction rather than honest debate.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Lincoln's speech was delivered on June 16th in Illinois, which establishes the specific event that prompted Douglas to respond.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The Union newspaper published reports about Douglas's movements, which shows that the press followed political figures closely during this period.

cards.standardTitle: Opposing arguments, claims, evidence, and validity
cards.excerpt:
In complaining of what I said in my speech at Springfield, in which he says I accepted my nomination for the senatorship (where, by the way, he is at fault, for if he will examine it, he will find no acceptance in it), he again quotes that portion in which I said that "a house divided against itself cannot stand." Let me say a word in regard to that matter.

He tries to persuade us that there must be a variety in the different institutions of the States of the Union; that that variety necessarily proceeds from the variety of soil, climate, of the face of the country, and the difference in the natural features of the States. I agree to all that. Have these very matters ever produced any difficulty amongst us? Not at all. Have we ever had any quarrel over the fact that they have laws in Louisiana designed to regulate the commerce that springs from the production of sugar? Or because we have a different class relative to the production of flour in this State? Have they produced any differences? Not at all. They are the very cements of this Union. They don't make the house a house divided against itself. They are the props that hold up the house and sustain the Union.
cards.whyThisWorks: Douglas develops his counter-claim by conceding Lincoln's point about regional variety and then redirecting with rhetorical questions and the 'cements' metaphor to argue that variety strengthens rather than divides the Union, giving students a clear example of evidence-through-reasoning to compare against Lincoln's approach.
cards.skillStrategy: When comparing how authors develop claims, track what kind of evidence each uses—examples, reasoning, concessions, or analogies—and ask what work that evidence does for the argument.
evidencePoints: I agree to all that. Have these very matters ever produced any difficulty amongst us? Not at all.
They are the very cements of this Union. They don't make the house a house divided against itself. They are the props that hold up the house and sustain the Union.
cards.question: Douglas develops his counter-argument against Lincoln's 'house divided' claim primarily by doing which of the following?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Citing specific historical conflicts over Louisiana sugar laws and Illinois flour production as proof that regional differences have caused serious national harm.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Conceding that regional differences exist, then using rhetorical questions and an extended metaphor to argue those differences actually hold the Union together rather than divide it.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Challenging Lincoln's credentials as a senator by pointing out that Lincoln never formally accepted his nomination in the Springfield speech.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Arguing that soil, climate, and geography are irrelevant to the question of national unity and should not be used as evidence in a political debate.

cards.standardTitle: Theme development across a literary text
cards.excerpt:
My answer as to whether I desire that slavery should be prohibited in all the Territories of the United States is full and explicit within itself, and cannot be made clearer by any comments of mine. So I suppose in regard to the question whether I am opposed to the acquisition of any more territory unless slavery is first prohibited therein, my answer is such that I could add nothing by way of illustration, or making myself better understood, than the answer which I have placed in writing.

Now in all this the Judge has me, and he has me on the record. I suppose he had flattered himself that I was really entertaining one set of opinions for one place, and another set for another place; that I was afraid to say at one place what I uttered at another. What I am saying here I suppose I say to a vast audience as strongly tending to Abolitionism as any audience in the State of Illinois, and I believe I am saying that which, if it would be offensive to any persons and render them enemies to myself, would be offensive to persons in this audience.
cards.whyThisWorks: Lincoln's insistence on saying the same thing to every audience—even one 'tending to Abolitionism'—develops the theme that moral consistency, not political calculation, defines true integrity, allowing students to distinguish theme-developing evidence from mere topic details about slavery or debates.
cards.skillStrategy: Ask yourself: does this detail show WHY the theme is true, or does it just mention what the passage is about?
evidencePoints: I suppose he had flattered himself that I was really entertaining one set of opinions for one place, and another set for another place
What I am saying here I suppose I say to a vast audience as strongly tending to Abolitionism as any audience in the State of Illinois
cards.question: Which detail from the excerpt best develops the theme that a person of integrity maintains consistent convictions regardless of audience?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Lincoln states that his written answer on the prohibition of slavery in the Territories is 'full and explicit within itself,' showing that the debate centered on the expansion of slavery.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Lincoln declares he is saying the same thing to an audience 'strongly tending to Abolitionism' that he would say anywhere, directly countering Douglas's assumption that Lincoln changed his positions to suit different crowds.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Lincoln acknowledges that his words 'would be offensive to persons in this audience,' confirming that the debate took place before a large Illinois crowd with strong opinions.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Lincoln notes that Douglas 'has me on the record,' indicating that written records of the debates were available to the public during the campaign.

cards.standardTitle: Opposing arguments, claims, evidence, and validity
cards.excerpt: Judge Douglas says he does not think differently. I am glad of it. Then can he tell me why he is looking up resolutions of five or six years ago, and insisting that they were my platform, notwithstanding my protest that they are not, and never were my platform, and my pointing out the platform of the State Convention which he delights to say nominated me for the Senate? I cannot see what he means by parading these resolutions, if it is not to hold me responsible for them in some way. If he says to me here that he does not hold the rule to be good, one way or the other, I do not comprehend how he could answer me more fully if he answered me at greater length. I will therefore put in as my answer to the resolutions that he has hunted up against me, what I, as a lawyer, would call a good plea to a bad declaration. I understand that it is an axiom of law that a poor plea may be a good plea to a bad declaration. I think that the opinions the Judge brings from those who support me, yet differ from me, is a bad declaration against me; but if I can bring the same things against him, I am putting in a good plea to that kind of declaration, and now I propose to try it.
cards.whyThisWorks: Lincoln explicitly models how he counters Douglas's evidence strategy by reframing it through a legal analogy, allowing students to analyze how a speaker develops a claim by challenging the validity of an opponent's evidence rather than directly refuting its content.
cards.skillStrategy: When comparing how authors develop claims, ask yourself: does each author use direct evidence, reasoning, examples, or does one challenge the other's evidence as invalid before presenting a counter-claim?
evidencePoints: I will therefore put in as my answer to the resolutions that he has hunted up against me, what I, as a lawyer, would call a good plea to a bad declaration.

I think that the opinions the Judge brings from those who support me, yet differ from me, is a bad declaration against me; but if I can bring the same things against him, I am putting in a good plea to that kind of declaration
cards.question: In this passage, how does Lincoln develop his claim that Douglas's evidence against him is invalid?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Lincoln concedes that the resolutions Douglas found are accurate but argues they no longer reflect his current beliefs.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Lincoln argues that Douglas's evidence is flawed on its own terms by using a legal analogy — a 'good plea to a bad declaration' — and then proposes to turn the same type of evidence against Douglas.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Lincoln develops his claim by citing the State Convention platform as direct proof that Douglas's resolutions are fabricated.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Lincoln dismisses Douglas's evidence entirely without offering any reasoning, stating only that the resolutions were never his platform.

cards.standardTitle: Theme development across a literary text
cards.excerpt:
Q. 7.--"I desire him to answer whether he is opposed to the acquisition of any new territory unless slavery is first prohibited therein?" Answer:--I am not generally opposed to honest acquisition of territory; and, in any given case, I would or would not oppose such acquisition, accordingly as I might think such acquisition would or would not aggravate the slavery question among ourselves.

Now, my friends, it will be perceived, upon an examination of these questions and answers, that so far I have only answered that I was not pledged to this, that, or the other. The Judge has not framed his interrogatories to ask me anything more than this, and I have answered in strict accordance with the interrogatories, and have answered truly, that I am not pledged at all upon any of the points to which I have answered. But I am not disposed to hang upon the exact form of his interrogatory. I am rather disposed to take up at least some of these questions, and state what I really think upon them.
cards.whyThisWorks: Lincoln's explicit pivot from 'I have only answered that I was not pledged' to 'I am rather disposed to state what I really think' lets students distinguish a detail that drives the theme of authentic candor from true-but-topic-only details about slavery or debate format.
cards.skillStrategy: Ask yourself: does this detail show the theme being built, or does it just belong to the same topic? Only one detail shows Lincoln choosing a higher standard than the question required.
evidencePoints: I have only answered that I was not pledged to this, that, or the other.
I am rather disposed to take up at least some of these questions, and state what I really think upon them.
cards.question: Lincoln says, 'I have only answered that I was not pledged to this, that, or the other,' and then immediately adds that he is 'rather disposed to…state what I really think upon them.' Which detail from the excerpt best develops the theme that true integrity requires going beyond the minimum a question demands?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Lincoln says he is 'not generally opposed to honest acquisition of territory,' which shows his openness to expanding the nation's borders.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Lincoln acknowledges he answered Douglas's questions truthfully and within their exact form, yet declares he is 'not disposed to hang upon the exact form of his interrogatory' and will state what he 'really think[s],' showing that satisfying the letter of a question is not enough for genuine candor.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Lincoln notes that Douglas 'has not framed his interrogatories to ask me anything more' than whether Lincoln was pledged on certain points, revealing that Douglas shaped the debate to limit Lincoln's responses.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Lincoln explains that his stance on acquiring new territory would depend on whether it would 'aggravate the slavery question among ourselves,' showing his awareness of sectional tensions.

cards.standardTitle: Opposing arguments, claims, evidence, and validity
cards.excerpt:
Mr. Brooks, of South Carolina, in one of his speeches, when they were presenting him canes, silver plate, gold pitchers, and the like, for assaulting Senator Sumner, distinctly affirmed his opinion that when this Constitution was formed it was the belief of no man that slavery would last to the present day. He said, what I think, that the framers of our Constitution placed the institution of slavery where the public mind rested in the hope that it was in the course of ultimate extinction. But he went on to say that the men of the present age, by their experience, have become wiser than the framers of the Constitution, and the invention of the cotton gin had made the perpetuity of slavery a necessity in this country.

As another piece of evidence tending to this same point: Quite recently in Virginia, a man--the owner of slaves--made a will providing that after his death certain of his slaves should have their freedom if they should so choose, and go to Liberia, rather than remain in slavery. They chose to be liberated. But the persons to whom they would descend as property claimed them as slaves. A suit was instituted, which finally came to the Supreme Court of Virginia, and was therein decided against the slaves upon the ground that a negro cannot make a choice; that they had no legal power to choose, could not perform the condition upon which their freedom depended.
cards.whyThisWorks: The excerpt presents two distinct claims about slavery's future—Brooks argues that modern experience and the cotton gin made slavery's permanence a necessity, while Lincoln's evidence (the Virginia court case) argues that slavery actively denies enslaved people basic legal personhood—allowing students to practice keeping each speaker's position separate.
cards.skillStrategy: When two sources address the same topic, pause at each speaker's name or signal phrase and ask: what exact position does THIS person defend, in their own words?
evidencePoints: the men of the present age, by their experience, have become wiser than the framers of the Constitution, and the invention of the cotton gin had made the perpetuity of slavery a necessity in this country
the Supreme Court of Virginia...decided against the slaves upon the ground that a negro cannot make a choice; that they had no legal power to choose
cards.question: According to the excerpt, how does Brooks's claim about slavery differ from the claim Lincoln supports through the Virginia court case?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Brooks argues that the framers of the Constitution intended slavery to end, while Lincoln argues that the framers always intended slavery to be permanent.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Brooks argues that modern circumstances such as the cotton gin made slavery's continuation a necessity, while Lincoln's evidence shows that slavery required denying enslaved people any legal capacity to choose freedom.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Brooks argues that enslaved people should be sent to Liberia, while Lincoln argues that enslaved people should remain in the United States under existing law.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Brooks argues that the Supreme Court of Virginia was wrong to rule against the slaves, while Lincoln argues that the ruling correctly reflected the original intent of the Constitution.

cards.standardTitle: Theme development across a literary text
cards.excerpt:
A little now on the other point,--the Dred Scott decision. Another of the issues he says that is to be made with me is upon his devotion to the Dred Scott decision, and my opposition to it.

I have expressed heretofore, and I now repeat, my opposition to the Dred Scott decision; but I should be allowed to state the nature of that opposition, and I ask your indulgence while I do so. What is fairly implied by the term Judge Douglas has used, "resistance to the decision"? I do not resist it. If I wanted to take Dred Scott from his master, I would be interfering with property, and that terrible difficulty that Judge Douglas speaks of, of interfering with property, would arise. But I am doing no such thing as that, but all that I am doing is refusing to obey it as a political rule. If I were in Congress, and a vote should come up on a question whether slavery should be prohibited in a new Territory, in spite of the Dred Scott decision, I would vote that it should.
cards.whyThisWorks: Lincoln's careful distinction between refusing to obey the Dred Scott decision as a 'political rule' versus physically 'resisting' it develops the theme that principled opposition to unjust authority can be exercised through lawful means, allowing students to separate true-but-topical details from details that actually build that theme.
cards.skillStrategy: Ask yourself: does this detail show HOW the theme is built, or does it just mention a topic from the passage? Only details that reveal Lincoln's reasoning about lawful versus unlawful opposition actually develop the theme.
evidencePoints: all that I am doing is refusing to obey it as a political rule
If I were in Congress, and a vote should come up on a question whether slavery should be prohibited in a new Territory, in spite of the Dred Scott decision, I would vote that it should.
cards.question: Which detail from the excerpt best develops the theme that principled opposition to unjust authority can be expressed through lawful action rather than direct defiance?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Lincoln acknowledges that Judge Douglas has accused him of 'resistance to the decision,' showing that the two men disagree about the Dred Scott ruling.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Lincoln draws a line between physically taking Dred Scott from his master—which he refuses to do—and voting in Congress against the expansion of slavery, which he says he would do, showing that opposition can work within legal boundaries.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Lincoln states that he has expressed his opposition to the Dred Scott decision before and repeats that opposition in this speech, confirming his long-held position on the ruling.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Lincoln mentions that interfering with property is the 'terrible difficulty' Judge Douglas warns about, indicating that property rights were a central concern in the debate over the decision.

cards.standardTitle: Opposing arguments, claims, evidence, and validity
cards.excerpt:
There is one other point. Judge Douglas has a very affectionate leaning toward the Americans and Old Whigs. Last evening, in a sort of weeping tone, he described to us a death-bed scene. He had been called to the side of Mr. Clay, in his last moments, in order that the genius of "popular sovereignty" might duly descend from the dying man and settle upon him, the living and most worthy successor. He could do no less than promise that he would devote the remainder of his life to "popular sovereignty"; and then the great statesman departs in peace. By this part of the "plan of the campaign" the Judge has evidently promised himself that tears shall be drawn down the cheeks of all Old Whigs, as large as half-grown apples.

Mr. Webster, too, was mentioned; but it did not quite come to a death-bed scene as to him. It would be amusing, if it were not disgusting, to see how quick these compromise-breakers administer on the political effects of their dead adversaries, trumping up claims never before heard of, and dividing the assets among themselves. If I should be found dead to-morrow morning, nothing but my insignificance could prevent a speech being made on my authority, before the end of next week. It so happens that in that "popular sovereignty" with which Mr. Clay was identified, the Missouri Compromise was expressly reversed; and it was a little singular if Mr. Clay cast his mantle upon Judge Douglas on purpose to have that compromise repealed.
cards.whyThisWorks: Lincoln's speech directly challenges Douglas's claim that he is the rightful heir to Clay's 'popular sovereignty,' allowing students to distinguish Lincoln's opposing claim—that Douglas actually betrayed Clay's legacy by repealing the Missouri Compromise—from Douglas's original assertion.
cards.skillStrategy: When two speakers address the same topic, ask yourself: what does each side say this evidence proves? Their answers will be opposite claims.
evidencePoints: the genius of 'popular sovereignty' might duly descend from the dying man and settle upon him, the living and most worthy successor
it was a little singular if Mr. Clay cast his mantle upon Judge Douglas on purpose to have that compromise repealed
cards.question: According to Lincoln, Douglas claims that Henry Clay passed the legacy of 'popular sovereignty' to him. What is Lincoln's opposing claim about that same legacy?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Douglas genuinely mourned Clay's death and honored his memory by continuing to defend the Missouri Compromise.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Douglas could not be Clay's true successor because Douglas repealed the Missouri Compromise that Clay's 'popular sovereignty' had expressly protected.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Clay never supported popular sovereignty and therefore had no political legacy that Douglas could rightfully inherit.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Douglas invented the death-bed scene entirely and Clay never spoke with him in his final moments.

cards.standardTitle: Theme development across a literary text
cards.excerpt:
I have said a hundred times, and I have now no inclination to take it back, that I believe there is no right, and ought to be no inclination, in the people of the free States to enter into the slave States and interfere with the question of slavery at all. I have said that always; Judge Douglas has heard me say it, if not quite a hundred times, at least as good as a hundred times; and when it is said that I am in favor of interfering with slavery where it exists, I know it is unwarranted by anything I have ever intended, and, as I believe, by anything I have ever said. If, by any means, I have ever used language which could fairly be so construed (as, however, I believe I never have), I now correct it.

So much, then, for the inference that Judge Douglas draws, that I am in favor of setting the sections at war with one another. I know that I never meant any such thing, and I believe that no fair mind can infer any such thing from anything I have ever said.
cards.whyThisWorks: Lincoln's repeated denial of interference paired with his offer to correct any misread language gives students a true-but-topic-only detail (the hundred-times repetition) to reject and a theme-developing detail (the correction offer proving false inference can distort a consistent record) to select.
cards.skillStrategy: Ask yourself: does this detail just match the topic of the speech, or does it actually show how the theme is built — look for the moment where Lincoln's action or word choice pushes the idea forward.
evidencePoints: I know it is unwarranted by anything I have ever intended, and, as I believe, by anything I have ever said.
If, by any means, I have ever used language which could fairly be so construed (as, however, I believe I never have), I now correct it.
cards.question: Lincoln says, 'I know it is unwarranted by anything I have ever intended' and then adds, 'I now correct it.' Which detail from the excerpt best develops the theme that a speaker's true position can be buried under false political inference?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Lincoln notes that he has stated his position 'a hundred times' and that Judge Douglas has heard him say it 'as good as a hundred times,' showing the debate has gone on for a long time.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Lincoln declares the charge 'unwarranted by anything I have ever intended' and then offers to correct any language that could be misread, revealing that even a consistent, repeated record cannot fully protect a speaker from a distorting inference.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Lincoln confirms that people in the free States have no right to enter the slave States and interfere with the question of slavery, establishing his actual policy position.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Lincoln states that 'no fair mind can infer any such thing' from anything he has said, indicating that he believes most listeners will judge him honestly.

cards.standardTitle: Opposing arguments, claims, evidence, and validity
cards.excerpt: Does Judge Douglas, when he says that several of the past years of his life have been devoted to the question of "popular sovereignty," and that all the remainder of his life shall be devoted to it, does he mean to say that he has been devoting his life to securing to the people of the Territories the right to exclude slavery from the Territories? If he means so to say he means to deceive; because he and every one knows that the decision of the Supreme Court, which he approves and makes especial ground of attack upon me for disapproving, forbids the people of a Territory to exclude slavery. This covers the whole ground, from the settlement of a Territory till it reaches the degree of maturity entitling it to form a State Constitution. So far as all that ground is concerned, the Judge is not sustaining popular sovereignty, but absolutely opposing it. He sustains the decision which declares that the popular will of the Territory has no constitutional power to exclude slavery during their territorial existence. This being so, the period of time from the first settlement of a Territory till it reaches the point of forming a State Constitution is not the thing that the Judge has fought for or is fighting for, but, on the contrary, he has fought for, and is fighting for, the thing that annihilates and crushes out that same popular sovereignty.
cards.whyThisWorks: Lincoln directly names and then dismantles Douglas's claim about 'popular sovereignty,' giving students a clear example of two opposing positions on the same concept that must be kept distinct.
cards.skillStrategy: When two speakers address the same topic, track what each one says that concept means—their definitions and conclusions will likely contradict each other.
evidencePoints: he means to deceive; because he and every one knows that the decision of the Supreme Court, which he approves and makes especial ground of attack upon me for disapproving, forbids the people of a Territory to exclude slavery
the Judge is not sustaining popular sovereignty, but absolutely opposing it
cards.question: According to Lincoln, how does Douglas's position on popular sovereignty differ from what Douglas claims it to be?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Douglas claims popular sovereignty gives territories the right to form state constitutions, and Lincoln agrees that this limited right is genuine.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Douglas claims to champion the people's right to exclude slavery from territories, but Lincoln argues Douglas actually supports a Supreme Court decision that destroys that very right.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Douglas claims the Supreme Court decision is unconstitutional, while Lincoln argues the Court's ruling correctly protects territorial self-governance.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Douglas claims popular sovereignty applies only after a territory becomes a state, and Lincoln argues it should apply during the territorial period as well.

cards.standardTitle: Theme development across a literary text
cards.excerpt: My friend has said to me that I am a poor hand to quote Scripture. I will try it again, however. It is said in one of the admonitions of our Lord, "As your Father in heaven is perfect, be ye also perfect." The Savior, I suppose, did not expect that any human creature could be perfect as the Father in heaven; but he said, "As your Father in heaven is perfect, be ye also perfect." He set that up as a standard; and he who did most towards reaching that standard attained the highest degree of moral perfection. So I say in relation to the principle that all men are created equal, let it be as nearly reached as we can. If we cannot give freedom to every creature, let us do nothing that will impose slavery upon any other creature. Let us then turn this government back into the channel in which the framers of the Constitution originally placed it. Let us stand firmly by each other. If we do not do so, we are turning in the contrary direction, that our friend Judge Douglas proposes--not intentionally--as working in the traces tends to make this one universal slave nation. He is one that runs in that direction, and as such I resist him.
cards.whyThisWorks: Lincoln's biblical analogy and the call to 'do nothing that will impose slavery upon any other creature' give students a clear thematic claim about moral striving toward equality, while the historical reference to the framers and the attack on Douglas are true details that only match the topic of slavery without developing the theme.
cards.skillStrategy: Ask yourself: does this detail show WHY the theme matters or HOW it develops, or does it just mention a topic from the passage?
evidencePoints: he who did most towards reaching that standard attained the highest degree of moral perfection
let it be as nearly reached as we can. If we cannot give freedom to every creature, let us do nothing that will impose slavery upon any other creature
cards.question: Lincoln uses the biblical standard of perfection to develop a theme about striving toward equality. Which detail from the excerpt most directly develops that theme?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Lincoln acknowledges that Judge Douglas does not act intentionally to make the nation a 'universal slave nation,' showing that political opponents can have good motives.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Lincoln argues that just as no human can be perfectly like God yet must still strive toward that standard, Americans cannot fully achieve equality but must refuse to move further from it by imposing slavery on anyone.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Lincoln calls for returning the government to 'the channel in which the framers of the Constitution originally placed it,' showing his respect for the founding generation.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Lincoln admits he is 'a poor hand to quote Scripture,' revealing his humility about his own religious knowledge compared to his opponents.

cards.standardTitle: Opposing arguments, claims, evidence, and validity
cards.excerpt: Let us see. Lecompton in the raw was defeated. It afterward took a sort of cooked-up shape, and was passed in the English bill. It is said by the Judge that the defeat was a good and proper thing. If it was a good thing, why is he entitled to more credit than others for the performance of that good act, unless there was something in the antecedents of the Republicans that might induce every one to expect them to join in that good work, and at the same time something leading them to doubt that he would? Does he place his superior claim to credit on the ground that he performed a good act which was never expected of him? He says I have a proneness for quoting Scripture. If I should do so now, it occurs that perhaps he places himself somewhat upon the ground of the parable of the lost sheep which went astray upon the mountains, and when the owner of the hundred sheep found the one that was lost, and threw it upon his shoulders and came home rejoicing, it was said that there was more rejoicing over the one sheep that was lost and had been found than over the ninety and nine in the fold. The application is made by the Saviour in this parable, thus: "Verily, I say unto you, there is more rejoicing in heaven over one sinner that repenteth, than over ninety and nine just persons that need no repentance."
cards.whyThisWorks: Lincoln's paragraph directly engages Douglas's claim that defeating Lecompton was 'a good and proper thing,' then turns that claim against Douglas by arguing that credit belongs to those (Republicans) who were always expected to oppose it—allowing students to distinguish Douglas's position from Lincoln's rebuttal.
cards.skillStrategy: When two speakers address the same event, ask: what does each one claim about it, and how does the second speaker use the first speaker's own words to challenge that claim?
evidencePoints: It is said by the Judge that the defeat was a good and proper thing.
Does he place his superior claim to credit on the ground that he performed a good act which was never expected of him?
cards.question: According to this passage, how does Lincoln's claim about the defeat of Lecompton differ from Douglas's claim about it?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Douglas argues the defeat of Lecompton was harmful to the nation, while Lincoln argues it was a necessary step toward justice.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Douglas claims credit for the defeat as a good act, while Lincoln argues that credit belongs to Republicans who were always expected to oppose Lecompton.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Douglas claims the English bill was a fair compromise, while Lincoln argues the bill should have been rejected entirely.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Douglas argues that Republicans blocked the defeat of Lecompton, while Lincoln argues that Douglas acted alone in opposing it.

cards.standardTitle: Theme development across a literary text
cards.excerpt: I allude to this extraordinary matter in this canvass for some further purpose than anything yet advanced. Judge Douglas did not make his statement upon that occasion as matters that he believed to be true, but he stated them roundly as being true, in such form as to pledge his veracity for their truth. When the whole matter turns out as it does, and when we consider who Judge Douglas is, that he is a distinguished Senator of the United States; that he has served nearly twelve years as such; that his character is not at all limited as an ordinary Senator of the United States, but that his name has become of world-wide renown,--it is most extraordinary that he should so far forget all the suggestions of justice to an adversary, or of prudence to himself, as to venture upon the assertion of that which the slightest investigation would have shown him to be wholly false. I can only account for his having done so upon the supposition that that evil genius which has attended him through his life, giving to him an apparent astonishing prosperity, such as to lead very many good men to doubt there being any advantage in virtue over vice,--I say I can only account for it on the supposition that that evil genius has as last made up its mind to forsake him.
cards.whyThisWorks: Lincoln's closing image of Douglas's 'evil genius' forsaking him transforms a factual accusation into a moral claim about the consequences of dishonesty, letting students distinguish theme-developing details from true-but-topical ones.
cards.skillStrategy: Ask yourself: does this detail show what the passage is arguing about human behavior or morality, or does it just describe what happened?
evidencePoints: that evil genius which has attended him through his life, giving to him an apparent astonishing prosperity, such as to lead very many good men to doubt there being any advantage in virtue over vice
I can only account for it on the supposition that that evil genius has at last made up its mind to forsake him
cards.question: Lincoln ends the passage by suggesting that Douglas's 'evil genius has at last made up its mind to forsake him.' Which detail from the passage most directly develops the theme that dishonesty ultimately undermines even the most powerful figures?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Lincoln notes that Douglas 'has served nearly twelve years' as a Senator, establishing how long Douglas has held public office.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Lincoln argues that Douglas's prosperity led 'very many good men to doubt there being any advantage in virtue over vice,' framing Douglas's false assertion as proof that unchecked dishonesty eventually collapses on itself.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Lincoln states that Douglas made his false claims 'in such form as to pledge his veracity for their truth,' showing that Douglas spoke with confidence.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Lincoln observes that Douglas's 'name has become of world-wide renown,' confirming that Douglas was a nationally recognized political figure.

cards.standardTitle: Opposing arguments, claims, evidence, and validity
cards.excerpt:
When he spoke at Chicago, on Friday evening of last week, he made this same point upon me. On Saturday evening I replied, and reminded him of a Supreme Court decision which he opposed for at least several years. Last night, at Bloomington, he took some notice of that reply, but entirely forgot to remember that part of it.

He renews his onslaught upon me, forgetting to remember that I have turned the tables against himself on that very point. I renew the effort to draw his attention to it. I wish to stand erect before the country, as well as Judge Douglas, on this question of judicial authority; and therefore I add something to the authority in favor of my own position. I wish to show that I am sustained by authority, in addition to that heretofore presented. I do not expect to convince the Judge. It is part of the plan of his campaign, and he will cling to it with a desperate grip. Even turn it upon him,--the sharp point against him, and gaff him through,--he will still cling to it till he can invent some new dodge to take the place of it.
cards.whyThisWorks: Lincoln's paragraph explicitly contrasts his own position—that he is 'sustained by authority'—against Douglas's position of clinging to a point despite being refuted, giving students a clear two-claim structure to separate.
cards.skillStrategy: When two speakers address the same topic, track what each person claims by asking: what does Speaker 1 say he is doing, and what does Speaker 2 say he is doing?
evidencePoints: I wish to stand erect before the country, as well as Judge Douglas, on this question of judicial authority
It is part of the plan of his campaign, and he will cling to it with a desperate grip.
cards.question: According to Lincoln, how does his own position on judicial authority differ from Douglas's position?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Lincoln admits he has no Supreme Court precedent to support him, while Douglas relies entirely on established court decisions.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Lincoln claims he is adding new authority to support his stance, while Douglas clings to a point even after Lincoln has turned it against him.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Lincoln argues that Douglas has already conceded the debate at Bloomington, while Douglas insists the original point still stands unchallenged.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Lincoln believes the Supreme Court should be ignored on this issue, while Douglas wants the court's ruling to settle the dispute permanently.

cards.standardTitle: Theme development across a literary text
cards.excerpt:
That is what I should do. Judge Douglas said last night that before the decision he might advance his opinion, and it might be contrary to the decision when it was made; but after it was made he would abide by it until it was reversed. Just so! We let this property abide by the decision, but we will try to reverse that decision. We will try to put it where Judge Douglas would not object, for he says he will obey it until it is reversed. Somebody has to reverse that decision, since it is made, and we mean to reverse it, and we mean to do it peaceably.

What are the uses of decisions of courts? They have two uses. As rules of property they have two uses. First, they decide upon the question before the court. They decide in this case that Dred Scott is a slave. Nobody resists that, not only that, but they say to everybody else that persons standing just as Dred Scott stands are as he is. That is, they say that when a question comes up upon another person, it will be so decided again, unless the court decides in another way, unless the court overrules its decision. Well, we mean to do what we can to have the court decide the other way. That is one thing we mean to try to do.
cards.whyThisWorks: Lincoln's repeated phrase 'we mean to reverse it' paired with 'peaceably' gives students a concrete textual anchor to distinguish a detail that develops the theme of lawful civic resistance from true-but-thematically-weaker details about court procedure.
cards.skillStrategy: Ask yourself: does this detail show the theme in action, or does it just describe what is happening in the passage?
evidencePoints: we mean to reverse it, and we mean to do it peaceably
We will try to put it where Judge Douglas would not object, for he says he will obey it until it is reversed
cards.question: Lincoln closes the first paragraph by saying, 'we mean to reverse it, and we mean to do it peaceably.' Which choice explains how this specific statement develops the theme that unjust legal decisions must be challenged through lawful, persistent civic effort?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The statement shows that Lincoln and his allies refuse to follow the Dred Scott ruling at all, proving that citizens are not bound by court decisions they consider unjust.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The statement pairs a commitment to overturning the ruling with a commitment to doing so through peaceful means, showing that opposition to injustice must work within lawful boundaries.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The statement reveals that Lincoln agrees with Judge Douglas's position, since both men accept the ruling while waiting for the court to change its mind on its own.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The statement explains the two uses of court decisions as rules of property, establishing that legal rulings apply to all persons in the same situation as Dred Scott.

cards.standardTitle: Opposing arguments, claims, evidence, and validity
cards.excerpt: Now, about this story that Judge Douglas tells of Trumbull bargaining to sell out the old Democratic party, and Lincoln agreeing to sell out the old Whig party, I have the means of knowing about that: Judge Douglas cannot have; and I know there is no substance to it whatever. Yet I have no doubt he is "conscientious" about it. I know that after Mr. Lovejoy got into the Legislature that winter, he complained of me that I had told all the old Whigs of his district that the old Whig party was good enough for them, and some of them voted against him because I told them so. Now, I have no means of totally disproving such charges as this which the Judge makes. A man cannot prove a negative; but he has a right to claim that when a man makes an affirmative charge, he must offer some proof to show the truth of what he says. I certainly cannot introduce testimony to show the negative about things, but I have a right to claim that if a man says he knows a thing, then he must show how he knows it. I always have a right to claim this, and it is not satisfactory to me that he may be "conscientious" on the subject.
cards.whyThisWorks: Lincoln directly names and responds to Douglas's specific charge about a bargain, allowing students to distinguish Douglas's affirmative claim from Lincoln's counter-claim about the burden of proof.
cards.skillStrategy: When two speakers address the same topic, track who is making each claim and what evidence—or lack of evidence—each speaker offers to support it.
evidencePoints: Judge Douglas tells of Trumbull bargaining to sell out the old Democratic party, and Lincoln agreeing to sell out the old Whig party
when a man makes an affirmative charge, he must offer some proof to show the truth of what he says
cards.question: Which statement accurately keeps Douglas's claim separate from Lincoln's claim in this passage?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Douglas argues that Lincoln has no right to demand proof, while Lincoln argues that Trumbull was the one who arranged the bargain.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Douglas charges that Lincoln agreed to sell out the old Whig party, while Lincoln argues that Douglas has offered no proof to support that affirmative charge.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Douglas claims that Lovejoy complained about Lincoln's conduct, while Lincoln claims that Douglas invented the story about Lovejoy entirely.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Both Douglas and Lincoln agree that a bargain occurred but disagree only about whether Trumbull or Lincoln was responsible for arranging it.

cards.standardTitle: Paraphrase grade-level text
cards.excerpt:
Mr. Brooks, of South Carolina, in one of his speeches, when they were presenting him canes, silver plate, gold pitchers, and the like, for assaulting Senator Sumner, distinctly affirmed his opinion that when this Constitution was formed it was the belief of no man that slavery would last to the present day. He said, what I think, that the framers of our Constitution placed the institution of slavery where the public mind rested in the hope that it was in the course of ultimate extinction. But he went on to say that the men of the present age, by their experience, have become wiser than the framers of the Constitution, and the invention of the cotton gin had made the perpetuity of slavery a necessity in this country.

As another piece of evidence tending to this same point: Quite recently in Virginia, a man--the owner of slaves--made a will providing that after his death certain of his slaves should have their freedom if they should so choose, and go to Liberia, rather than remain in slavery. They chose to be liberated. But the persons to whom they would descend as property claimed them as slaves. A suit was instituted, which finally came to the Supreme Court of Virginia, and was therein decided against the slaves upon the ground that a negro cannot make a choice; that they had no legal power to choose, could not perform the condition upon which their freedom depended.
cards.whyThisWorks: The excerpt contains a precise, paraphraseable claim attributed to Mr. Brooks—that the framers placed slavery where the public mind rested in the hope of its ultimate extinction—which students must restate accurately while distractors distort, overstate, or omit key parts of that meaning.
cards.skillStrategy: When paraphrasing a specific claim, keep all parts of the original meaning intact—who said it, what they believed, and why—without adding, removing, or twisting any piece.
evidencePoints: the framers of our Constitution placed the institution of slavery where the public mind rested in the hope that it was in the course of ultimate extinction
Mr. Brooks...distinctly affirmed his opinion that when this Constitution was formed it was the belief of no man that slavery would last to the present day
cards.question: In the first paragraph, Lincoln quotes Mr. Brooks as saying that 'the framers of our Constitution placed the institution of slavery where the public mind rested in the hope that it was in the course of ultimate extinction.' Which of the following most accurately restates what that sentence means?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The framers of the Constitution deliberately protected slavery in the document because they believed it was necessary for the nation's economic survival.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The people who wrote the Constitution handled slavery in a way that matched the public's expectation that slavery would gradually come to an end.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The framers of the Constitution placed slavery at the center of public debate, hoping citizens would vote to abolish it immediately after ratification.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The framers of the Constitution ignored public opinion about slavery and privately hoped the issue would disappear without any action.

cards.standardTitle: Text structure and feature purpose
cards.excerpt:
Can the masses of the Negro people be in any possible way more quickly raised than by the effort and example of this aristocracy of talent and character? Was there ever a nation on God's fair earth civilized from the bottom upward? Never; it is, ever was and ever will be from the top downward that culture filters. The Talented Tenth rises and pulls all that are worth the saving up to their vantage ground. This is the history of human progress; and the two historic mistakes which have hindered that progress were the thinking first that no more could ever rise save the few already risen; or second, that it would better the unrisen to pull the risen down.

How then shall the leaders of a struggling people be trained and the hands of the risen few strengthened? There can be but one answer: The best and most capable of their youth must be schooled in the colleges and universities of the land. We will not quarrel as to just what the university of the Negro should teach or how it should teach it--I willingly admit that each soul and each race-soul needs its own peculiar curriculum. But this is true: A university is a human invention for the transmission of knowledge and culture from generation to generation, through the training of quick minds and pure hearts, and for this work no other human invention will suffice, not even trade and industrial schools.
