cards.whyThisWorks: The second paragraph shifts from Du Bois's abstract historical argument about top-down progress to a concrete, actionable answer about how leaders must be trained, making the paragraph's job—extending and applying the first paragraph's claim—clearly identifiable from the text.
cards.skillStrategy: Ask yourself: does this paragraph introduce a new idea, prove the previous one, or move the argument forward by answering a question the first paragraph raised?
evidencePoints: How then shall the leaders of a struggling people be trained and the hands of the risen few strengthened? There can be but one answer
A university is a human invention for the transmission of knowledge and culture from generation to generation, through the training of quick minds and pure hearts
cards.question: What is the primary job of the second paragraph in relation to the first?

choices.label: A
choices.text: It contradicts the first paragraph by arguing that industrial schools, not the Talented Tenth, are the true source of progress.

choices.label: B
choices.text: It extends the first paragraph's claim about top-down progress by answering how the risen few should be prepared to lead.

choices.label: C
choices.text: It restates the first paragraph's two historic mistakes using the example of university education.

choices.label: D
choices.text: It shifts away from the Talented Tenth argument entirely to introduce a debate about curriculum design.

cards.standardTitle: Text structure and feature purpose
cards.excerpt: Thus, again, in the manning of trade schools and manual training schools we are thrown back upon the higher training as its source and chief support. There was a time when any aged and wornout carpenter could teach in a trade school. But not so to-day. Indeed the demand for college-bred men by a school like Tuskegee, ought to make Mr. Booker T. Washington the firmest friend of higher training. Here he has as helpers the son of a Negro senator, trained in Greek and the humanities, and graduated at Harvard; the son of a Negro congressman and lawyer, trained in Latin and mathematics, and graduated at Oberlin; he has as his wife, a woman who read Virgil and Homer in the same class room with me; he has as college chaplain, a classical graduate of Atlanta University; as teacher of science, a graduate of Fisk; as teacher of history, a graduate of Smith,--indeed some thirty of his chief teachers are college graduates, and instead of studying French grammars in the midst of weeds, or buying pianos for dirty cabins, they are at Mr. Washington's right hand helping him in a noble work. And yet one of the effects of Mr. Washington's propaganda has been to throw doubt upon the expediency of such training for Negroes, as these persons have had.
cards.whyThisWorks: The paragraph's final sentence performs a clear structural shift—after spending most of the paragraph proving that Washington's own Tuskegee depends on college-trained teachers, Du Bois pivots to expose the contradiction in Washington's propaganda against higher training, making the paragraph's job (extend-then-shift) directly teachable.
cards.skillStrategy: Ask yourself: does the paragraph keep building one idea the whole way through, or does it turn at some point—and what does that turn do to the argument?
evidencePoints: indeed some thirty of his chief teachers are college graduates, and instead of studying French grammars in the midst of weeds, or buying pianos for dirty cabins, they are at Mr. Washington's right hand helping him in a noble work
And yet one of the effects of Mr. Washington's propaganda has been to throw doubt upon the expediency of such training for Negroes, as these persons have had
cards.question: What is the primary job of the final sentence, beginning 'And yet one of the effects of Mr. Washington's propaganda…,' in relation to the rest of the paragraph?

choices.label: A
choices.text: It concludes the paragraph by summarizing the names and credentials of Washington's college-trained staff at Tuskegee.

choices.label: B
choices.text: It shifts the paragraph's direction by exposing a contradiction: Washington relies on college-trained teachers yet his public campaign casts doubt on that very training for Black Americans.

choices.label: C
choices.text: It extends Du Bois's earlier claim that trade schools are superior to colleges by showing Washington agrees with that position.

choices.label: D
choices.text: It introduces a new argument about the low quality of instruction at Tuskegee that Du Bois will develop in the paragraphs that follow.

cards.standardTitle: Text structure and feature purpose
cards.excerpt: After emancipation came a new group of educated and gifted leaders: Langston, Bruce and Elliot, Greener, Williams and Payne. Through political organization, historical and polemic writing and moral regeneration, these men strove to uplift their people. It is the fashion of to-day to sneer at them and to say that with freedom Negro leadership should have begun at the plow and not in the Senate--a foolish and mischievous lie; two hundred and fifty years that black serf toiled at the plow and yet that toiling was in vain till the Senate passed the war amendments; and two hundred and fifty years more the half-free serf of to-day may toil at his plow, but unless he have political rights and righteously guarded civic status, he will still remain the poverty-stricken and ignorant plaything of rascals, that he now is. This all sane men know even if they dare not say it.
cards.whyThisWorks: The paragraph visibly shifts from naming post-emancipation leaders and their work to directly attacking 'the fashion of to-day to sneer at them,' giving students a clear structural pivot to identify and explain.
cards.skillStrategy: Find the moment in the paragraph where the topic or tone changes, then ask what job that shift does for the author's argument.
evidencePoints: It is the fashion of to-day to sneer at them and to say that with freedom Negro leadership should have begun at the plow and not in the Senate--a foolish and mischievous lie
two hundred and fifty years that black serf toiled at the plow and yet that toiling was in vain till the Senate passed the war amendments
cards.question: Du Bois opens by naming leaders such as 'Langston, Bruce and Elliot' and their work, then pivots to 'the fashion of to-day to sneer at them.' What is the job of everything that follows that pivot in the paragraph?

choices.label: A
choices.text: To extend the praise of post-emancipation leaders by listing additional accomplishments they achieved through political organization and moral regeneration.

choices.label: B
choices.text: To refute the sneering claim that Black leadership 'should have begun at the plow and not in the Senate' by using two hundred and fifty years of history as counter-evidence.

choices.label: C
choices.text: To contrast the political leaders named at the opening with a separate group of agricultural workers who chose a different path after emancipation.

choices.label: D
choices.text: To concede that beginning 'at the plow' had some merit before concluding that political rights are now no longer necessary.

cards.standardTitle: Text structure and feature purpose
cards.excerpt: These figures illustrate vividly the function of the college-bred Negro. He is, as he ought to be, the group leader, the man who sets the ideals of the community where he lives, directs its thoughts and heads its social movements. It need hardly be argued that the Negro people need social leadership more than most groups; that they have no traditions to fall back upon, no long established customs, no strong family ties, no well defined social classes. All these things must be slowly and painfully evolved. The preacher was, even before the war, the group leader of the Negroes, and the church their greatest social institution. Naturally this preacher was ignorant and often immoral, and the problem of replacing the older type by better educated men has been a difficult one. Both by direct work and by direct influence on other preachers, and on congregations, the college-bred preacher has an opportunity for reformatory work and moral inspiration, the value of which cannot be overestimated.
cards.whyThisWorks: The paragraph opens by referencing prior 'figures,' proves the leadership claim with social-need evidence, then pivots to the preacher's specific reform opportunity—giving students a clear introduce-prove-extend structure to analyze.
cards.skillStrategy: Ask yourself: what job does each sentence do—does it open a new idea, back up a claim already made, or push the argument into new territory?
evidencePoints: These figures illustrate vividly the function of the college-bred Negro.
the college-bred preacher has an opportunity for reformatory work and moral inspiration, the value of which cannot be overestimated.
cards.question: Du Bois opens this paragraph with 'These figures illustrate vividly the function of the college-bred Negro' and closes with the college-bred preacher's 'opportunity for reformatory work and moral inspiration.' What does this movement from 'figures' to 'opportunity' reveal about the paragraph's job in his argument?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The paragraph introduces the concept of the college-bred Negro for the first time, defining his role before any evidence has been offered.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The paragraph uses data already presented to confirm the college-bred Negro's leadership role, then extends that claim by identifying the college-bred preacher as a specific agent of reform.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The paragraph shifts Du Bois's focus away from leadership entirely, replacing it with a critique of the ignorant and immoral preachers who led Black communities before the Civil War.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The paragraph concludes Du Bois's argument by restating that Black communities lack traditions and social classes, leaving the reader with those limitations as the final point.

cards.standardTitle: Text structure and feature purpose
cards.excerpt: It has, however, been in the furnishing of teachers that the Negro college has found its peculiar function. Few persons realize how vast a work, how mighty a revolution has been thus accomplished. To furnish five millions and more of ignorant people with teachers of their own race and blood, in one generation, was not only a very difficult undertaking, but a very important one, in that, it placed before the eyes of almost every Negro child an attainable ideal. It brought the masses of the blacks in contact with modern civilization, made black men the leaders of their communities and trainers of the new generation. In this work college-bred Negroes were first teachers, and then teachers of teachers. And here it is that the broad culture of college work has been of peculiar value. Knowledge of life and its wider meaning, has been the point of the Negro's deepest ignorance, and the sending out of teachers whose training has not been simply for bread winning, but also for human culture, has been of inestimable value in the training of these men.
cards.whyThisWorks: The paragraph opens with a named claim ('peculiar function'), then spends every remaining sentence extending and proving that claim with specific effects—making it a clear model of a paragraph that introduces and then develops a central idea.
cards.skillStrategy: Find the sentence that states the main claim, then ask whether the rest of the paragraph introduces, contrasts, extends, proves, shifts, or concludes that claim.
evidencePoints: It has, however, been in the furnishing of teachers that the Negro college has found its peculiar function.
In this work college-bred Negroes were first teachers, and then teachers of teachers.
cards.question: Du Bois opens the paragraph by stating that 'the Negro college has found its peculiar function' in furnishing teachers. What job do the sentences that follow perform in relation to that opening claim?

choices.label: A
choices.text: They contradict the opening claim by showing that most Black children never encountered a college-trained teacher.

choices.label: B
choices.text: They extend and prove the opening claim by detailing how those teachers transformed Black communities, spread modern civilization, and provided cultural training beyond bread winning.

choices.label: C
choices.text: They shift away from the opening claim to introduce a separate argument about why Black men should lead their communities politically.

choices.label: D
choices.text: They concede that furnishing teachers was difficult before concluding that the Negro college ultimately failed to reach the masses of Black people.

cards.standardTitle: Text structure and feature purpose
cards.excerpt: I am an earnest advocate of manual training and trade teaching for black boys, and for white boys, too. I believe that next to the founding of Negro colleges the most valuable addition to Negro education since the war, has been industrial training for black boys. Nevertheless, I insist that the object of all true education is not to make men carpenters, it is to make carpenters men; there are two means of making the carpenter a man, each equally important: the first is to give the group and community in which he works, liberally trained teachers and leaders to teach him and his family what life means; the second is to give him sufficient intelligence and technical skill to make him an efficient workman; the first object demands the Negro college and college-bred men--not a quantity of such colleges, but a few of excellent quality; not too many college-bred men, but enough to leaven the lump, to inspire the masses, to raise the Talented Tenth to leadership; the second object demands a good system of common schools, well-taught, conveniently located and properly equipped.
cards.whyThisWorks: The paragraph's pivot sentence — 'the object of all true education is not to make men carpenters, it is to make carpenters men' — signals a clear structural shift from concession to central argument, giving students a precise textual moment to analyze for paragraph job.
cards.skillStrategy: Find the sentence where the writer changes direction — a word like 'nevertheless' or a contrast statement — and ask what job that turn does for the whole paragraph.
evidencePoints: Nevertheless, I insist that the object of all true education is not to make men carpenters, it is to make carpenters men

the first object demands the Negro college and college-bred men--not a quantity of such colleges, but a few of excellent quality; not too many college-bred men, but enough to leaven the lump, to inspire the masses, to raise the Talented Tenth to leadership
cards.question: Du Bois opens by calling industrial training 'the most valuable addition to Negro education since the war,' then writes, 'Nevertheless, I insist that the object of all true education is not to make men carpenters, it is to make carpenters men.' What job does this shift perform in the paragraph?

choices.label: A
choices.text: It concludes the paragraph by restating that industrial training and college education deserve equal funding and equal numbers of institutions.

choices.label: B
choices.text: It concedes the value of industrial training and then pivots to argue that college-educated leaders are what give that training its full human meaning.

choices.label: C
choices.text: It introduces Du Bois's rejection of manual training by claiming that teaching carpentry has actively harmed Black communities since the war.

choices.label: D
choices.text: It extends Du Bois's praise of industrial training by proving that trade schools already produce the liberally trained teachers Black families need.

cards.standardTitle: Text structure and feature purpose
cards.excerpt: Three of these were established in border States before the War; thirteen were planted by the Freedmen's Bureau in the years 1864-1869; nine were established between 1870 and 1880 by various church bodies; five were established after 1881 by Negro churches, and four are state institutions supported by United States' agricultural funds. In most cases the college departments are small adjuncts to high and common school work. As a matter of fact six institutions--Atlanta, Fisk, Howard, Shaw, Wilberforce and Leland, are the important Negro colleges so far as actual work and number of students are concerned. In all these institutions, seven hundred and fifty Negro college students are enrolled. In grade the best of these colleges are about a year behind the smaller New England colleges and a typical curriculum is that of Atlanta University. Here students from the grammar grades, after a three years' high school course, take a college course of 136 weeks. One-fourth of this time is given to Latin and Greek; one-fifth, to English and modern languages; one-sixth, to history and social science; one-seventh, to natural science; one-eighth to mathematics, and one-eighth to philosophy and pedagogy.
cards.whyThisWorks: The paragraph moves from broad historical categorization of Negro colleges to a narrowing focus on six key institutions and then to the specific curriculum of Atlanta University, giving students a clear example of a paragraph that extends and proves a claim through increasingly specific evidence.
cards.skillStrategy: Ask yourself: does this paragraph introduce a new idea, or does it keep building on one idea by adding more specific proof? Trace how the details get more and more focused.
evidencePoints: In most cases the college departments are small adjuncts to high and common school work.
a typical curriculum is that of Atlanta University. Here students from the grammar grades, after a three years' high school course, take a college course of 136 weeks.
cards.question: What is the primary job of this paragraph in Du Bois's argument about Negro colleges?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The paragraph shifts away from the topic of Negro colleges to argue that New England colleges are superior models of education.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The paragraph proves the limited but real scope of Negro higher education by moving from a broad historical count of institutions down to the specific curriculum of one college.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The paragraph introduces the idea that church bodies were the most important founders of Negro colleges during Reconstruction.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The paragraph concludes Du Bois's case by showing that Negro colleges have fully matched the standards of Northern institutions.

cards.standardTitle: Text structure and feature purpose
cards.excerpt:
Of these graduates 2,079 were men and 252 were women; 50 per cent. of Northern-born college men come South to work among the masses of their people, at a sacrifice which few people realize; nearly 90 per cent. of the Southern-born graduates instead of seeking that personal freedom and broader intellectual atmosphere which their training has led them, in some degree, to conceive, stay and labor and wait in the midst of their black neighbors and relatives.

The most interesting question, and in many respects the crucial question, to be asked concerning college-bred Negroes, is: Do they earn a living? It has been intimated more than once that the higher training of Negroes has resulted in sending into the world of work, men who could find nothing to do suitable to their talents. Now and then there comes a rumor of a colored college man working at menial service, etc. Fortunately, returns as to occupations of college-bred Negroes, gathered by the Atlanta conference, are quite full--nearly sixty per cent. of the total number of graduates.
cards.whyThisWorks: The second paragraph opens with a stated 'crucial question' about earning a living, then introduces a counter-claim ('it has been intimated') and resolves it with Atlanta conference data, giving students a clear problem/solution structure to identify and trace.
cards.skillStrategy: When a paragraph names a problem or doubt and then points to evidence that addresses it, that is a problem/solution structure—look for signal words like 'fortunately' that mark the shift to the solution.
evidencePoints: It has been intimated more than once that the higher training of Negroes has resulted in sending into the world of work, men who could find nothing to do suitable to their talents.
Fortunately, returns as to occupations of college-bred Negroes, gathered by the Atlanta conference, are quite full
cards.question: In the second paragraph, Du Bois writes that 'it has been intimated more than once' that college-trained Black men 'could find nothing to do suitable to their talents,' and then states 'Fortunately, returns as to occupations...gathered by the Atlanta conference, are quite full.' What structure does this movement from intimation to Atlanta conference data create?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A chronological sequence that traces college-bred Black men from their graduation through their search for employment to their eventual placement in occupations.

choices.label: B
choices.text: A problem/solution structure in which the doubt that college training leaves Black men unemployable is the problem and the Atlanta conference occupational data is the countering evidence.

choices.label: C
choices.text: A compare/contrast structure that sets the experiences of college-bred Black men against those of men without higher training to measure which group finds more suitable work.

choices.label: D
choices.text: A cause/effect structure in which higher training is presented as the direct cause of Black college men being forced into menial service.

cards.standardTitle: Central idea and supporting evidence
cards.excerpt:
The truth of this has been strikingly shown in the marked improvement of white teachers in the South. Twenty years ago the rank and file of white public school teachers were not as good as the Negro teachers. But they, by scholarships and good salaries, have been encouraged to thorough normal and collegiate preparation, while the Negro teachers have been discouraged by starvation wages and the idea that any training will do for a black teacher. If carpenters are needed it is well and good to train men as carpenters. But to train men as carpenters, and then set them to teaching is wasteful and criminal; and to train men as teachers and then refuse them living wages, unless they become carpenters, is rank nonsense.

The United States Commissioner of Education says in his report for 1900: "For comparison between the white and colored enrollment in secondary and higher education, I have added together the enrollment in high schools and secondary schools, with the attendance on colleges and universities, not being sure of the actual grade of work done in the colleges and universities. The work done in the secondary schools is reported in such detail in this office, that there can be no doubt of its grade."
cards.whyThisWorks: The first paragraph's closing sentence—'to train men as teachers and then refuse them living wages, unless they become carpenters, is rank nonsense'—forces students to distinguish the central idea from the supporting detail about white teachers and the distractor about carpentry training.
cards.skillStrategy: Ask yourself: what point is the whole paragraph building toward, not just what one sentence says?
evidencePoints: to train men as teachers and then refuse them living wages, unless they become carpenters, is rank nonsense
the Negro teachers have been discouraged by starvation wages and the idea that any training will do for a black teacher
cards.question: Du Bois ends the first paragraph by calling it 'rank nonsense' to train men as teachers and then deny them living wages unless they become carpenters. What central idea does this conclusion, along with the rest of the paragraph, support?

choices.label: A
choices.text: White teachers in the South became more qualified than Black teachers because they received scholarships and competitive salaries over twenty years.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Withholding fair wages and proper preparation from Black teachers while pushing them into trades wastes their abilities and damages education.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Training men as carpenters is a reasonable goal only when society has a genuine and immediate need for skilled tradespeople.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The Commissioner of Education's enrollment data proves that Black students are being shut out of secondary and higher education entirely.

cards.standardTitle: Text structure and feature purpose
cards.excerpt: Thus, again, in the manning of trade schools and manual training schools we are thrown back upon the higher training as its source and chief support. There was a time when any aged and wornout carpenter could teach in a trade school. But not so to-day. Indeed the demand for college-bred men by a school like Tuskegee, ought to make Mr. Booker T. Washington the firmest friend of higher training. Here he has as helpers the son of a Negro senator, trained in Greek and the humanities, and graduated at Harvard; the son of a Negro congressman and lawyer, trained in Latin and mathematics, and graduated at Oberlin; he has as his wife, a woman who read Virgil and Homer in the same class room with me; he has as college chaplain, a classical graduate of Atlanta University; as teacher of science, a graduate of Fisk; as teacher of history, a graduate of Smith,--indeed some thirty of his chief teachers are college graduates, and instead of studying French grammars in the midst of weeds, or buying pianos for dirty cabins, they are at Mr. Washington's right hand helping him in a noble work. And yet one of the effects of Mr. Washington's propaganda has been to throw doubt upon the expediency of such training for Negroes, as these persons have had.
cards.whyThisWorks: The paragraph lists college-trained teachers at Tuskegee and then pivots to show that Washington's own propaganda undermines the very training those teachers received, making cause-and-effect the dominant structure doing real argumentative work.
cards.skillStrategy: When identifying structure, ask what relationship the author is building between ideas — here, ask why Du Bois lists all those college graduates right before the sentence beginning 'And yet one of the effects of Mr. Washington's propaganda has been...'
evidencePoints: Indeed the demand for college-bred men by a school like Tuskegee, ought to make Mr. Booker T. Washington the firmest friend of higher training.
And yet one of the effects of Mr. Washington's propaganda has been to throw doubt upon the expediency of such training for Negroes, as these persons have had.
cards.question: Du Bois opens by stating that Tuskegee's demand for college-trained teachers 'ought to make Mr. Booker T. Washington the firmest friend of higher training,' then closes with 'one of the effects of Mr. Washington's propaganda has been to throw doubt upon the expediency of such training.' What structure do these two moments create across the paragraph?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Chronological order — Du Bois moves from an earlier era when 'any aged and worn-out carpenter could teach' to the present day at Tuskegee, arranging events by time.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Cause and effect — the documented reliance on college graduates at Tuskegee becomes the evidence that Washington's campaign against higher training contradicts and damages his own school.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Compare and contrast — Du Bois measures the credentials of Tuskegee's teachers against those of graduates from Harvard, Oberlin, and Smith to rank the schools by academic prestige.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Problem and solution — Du Bois identifies the shortage of qualified trade school instructors and proposes that Washington personally recruit more classical graduates to fill those positions.

cards.standardTitle: Central idea and supporting evidence
cards.excerpt: It has, however, been in the furnishing of teachers that the Negro college has found its peculiar function. Few persons realize how vast a work, how mighty a revolution has been thus accomplished. To furnish five millions and more of ignorant people with teachers of their own race and blood, in one generation, was not only a very difficult undertaking, but a very important one, in that, it placed before the eyes of almost every Negro child an attainable ideal. It brought the masses of the blacks in contact with modern civilization, made black men the leaders of their communities and trainers of the new generation. In this work college-bred Negroes were first teachers, and then teachers of teachers. And here it is that the broad culture of college work has been of peculiar value. Knowledge of life and its wider meaning, has been the point of the Negro's deepest ignorance, and the sending out of teachers whose training has not been simply for bread winning, but also for human culture, has been of inestimable value in the training of these men.
cards.whyThisWorks: The excerpt builds a central idea through a chain of specific claims—teachers placed 'an attainable ideal' before children, brought 'modern civilization' to Black communities, and trained leaders—allowing students to practice distinguishing the overarching central idea from isolated supporting details or topic labels.
cards.skillStrategy: Ask yourself: which statement ties together ALL the evidence in the paragraph, not just one detail? The central idea must account for the 'attainable ideal,' the 'modern civilization,' and the 'broad culture' claims together.
evidencePoints: it placed before the eyes of almost every Negro child an attainable ideal
the sending out of teachers whose training has not been simply for bread winning, but also for human culture, has been of inestimable value in the training of these men
cards.question: Du Bois writes that Negro college-trained teachers placed 'an attainable ideal' before Black children and sent out educators trained 'not simply for bread winning, but also for human culture.' What central idea do these two claims work together to express?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Negro colleges faced an enormous challenge because five million people needed teachers within a single generation.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The Negro college's greatest contribution was producing teachers who gave Black communities both visible leadership and a broad human education, not merely job training.

choices.label: C
choices.text: College-bred Negroes became teachers first and then teachers of teachers because no other profession was open to educated Black men.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Placing Black role models in front of Black children was the only way to connect African Americans to modern civilization.

cards.standardTitle: Text structure and feature purpose
cards.excerpt:
Can the masses of the Negro people be in any possible way more quickly raised than by the effort and example of this aristocracy of talent and character? Was there ever a nation on God's fair earth civilized from the bottom upward? Never; it is, ever was and ever will be from the top downward that culture filters. The Talented Tenth rises and pulls all that are worth the saving up to their vantage ground. This is the history of human progress; and the two historic mistakes which have hindered that progress were the thinking first that no more could ever rise save the few already risen; or second, that it would better the unrisen to pull the risen down.

How then shall the leaders of a struggling people be trained and the hands of the risen few strengthened? There can be but one answer: The best and most capable of their youth must be schooled in the colleges and universities of the land. We will not quarrel as to just what the university of the Negro should teach or how it should teach it--I willingly admit that each soul and each race-soul needs its own peculiar curriculum. But this is true: A university is a human invention for the transmission of knowledge and culture from generation to generation, through the training of quick minds and pure hearts, and for this work no other human invention will suffice, not even trade and industrial schools.
cards.whyThisWorks: Du Bois explicitly names a problem ('How then shall the leaders of a struggling people be trained') and then declares 'There can be but one answer,' making the problem/solution structure visible and teachable at the sentence level.
cards.skillStrategy: When an author names a challenge and then signals a direct answer with a phrase like 'There can be but one answer,' look for a problem/solution structure doing real work in the passage.
evidencePoints: How then shall the leaders of a struggling people be trained and the hands of the risen few strengthened? There can be but one answer
The best and most capable of their youth must be schooled in the colleges and universities of the land.
cards.question: Du Bois opens the second paragraph with the question 'How then shall the leaders of a struggling people be trained and the hands of the risen few strengthened?' and immediately follows with 'There can be but one answer.' What structure do these two sentences signal for the paragraph that follows?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A chronological sequence, because Du Bois traces the training of leaders from ancient civilizations through the present generation.

choices.label: B
choices.text: A problem/solution structure, because Du Bois names the challenge of training leaders and then declares that university education is the necessary remedy.

choices.label: C
choices.text: A compare/contrast structure, because Du Bois weighs the value of 'trade and industrial schools' against the value of colleges to determine which is superior.

choices.label: D
choices.text: A cause/effect structure, because Du Bois explains that the failure to train leaders has directly produced the two historic mistakes he described in the first paragraph.

cards.standardTitle: Central idea and supporting evidence
cards.excerpt: But I have already said that human education is not simply a matter of schools; it is much more a matter of family and group life--the training of one's home, of one's daily companions, of one's social class. Now the black boy of the South moves in a black world--a world with its own leaders, its own thoughts, its own ideals. In this world he gets by far the larger part of his life training, and through the eyes of this dark world he peers into the veiled world beyond. Who guides and determines the education which he receives in his world? His teachers here are the group-leaders of the Negro people--the physicians and clergymen, the trained fathers and mothers, the influential and forceful men about him of all kinds; here it is, if at all, that the culture of the surrounding world trickles through and is handed on by the graduates of the higher schools. Can such culture training of group leaders be neglected? Can we afford to ignore it? Do you think that if the leaders of thought among Negroes are not trained and educated thinkers, that they will have no leaders? On the contrary a hundred half-trained demagogues will still hold the places they so largely occupy now, and hundreds of vociferous busy-bodies will multiply. You have no choice; either you must help furnish this race from within its own ranks with thoughtful men of trained leadership, or you must suffer the evil consequences of a headless misguided rabble.
cards.whyThisWorks: The paragraph builds to an explicit either/or conclusion—'either you must help furnish this race from within its own ranks with thoughtful men of trained leadership, or you must suffer the evil consequences of a headless misguided rabble'—giving students a precise textual anchor from which to derive the central idea rather than a topic or isolated detail.
cards.skillStrategy: Find the sentence where the author states the stakes or the 'so what,' then ask yourself what the whole paragraph is arguing—that is the central idea.
evidencePoints: either you must help furnish this race from within its own ranks with thoughtful men of trained leadership, or you must suffer the evil consequences of a headless misguided rabble
Can such culture training of group leaders be neglected? Can we afford to ignore it?
cards.question: Du Bois ends the paragraph with the warning: 'either you must help furnish this race from within its own ranks with thoughtful men of trained leadership, or you must suffer the evil consequences of a headless misguided rabble.' What central idea does this either/or statement bring into focus for the entire paragraph?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Black Americans receive most of their education not in formal schools but through family, daily companions, and the leaders within their own community.

choices.label: B
choices.text: A community that does not develop educated leaders from within its own ranks will be left in the hands of demagogues and will face destructive consequences.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Physicians, clergymen, and trained parents are already passing culture on to the next generation, so formal higher education is less urgent than Du Bois implies.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Half-trained demagogues currently hold positions of influence among Negro communities, and removing them is the most pressing problem Du Bois addresses.

cards.standardTitle: Text structure and feature purpose
cards.excerpt: Even at this point, however, the difficulties were not surmounted. In the first place modern industry has taken great strides since the war, and the teaching of trades is no longer a simple matter. Machinery and long processes of work have greatly changed the work of the carpenter, the ironworker and the shoemaker. A really efficient workman must be to-day an intelligent man who has had good technical training in addition to thorough common school, and perhaps even higher training. To meet this situation the industrial schools began a further development; they established distinct Trade Schools for the thorough training of better class artisans, and at the same time they sought to preserve for the purposes of general education, such of the simpler processes of elementary trade learning as were best suited therefor. In this differentiation of the Trade School and manual training, the best of the industrial schools simply followed the plain trend of the present educational epoch. A prominent educator tells us that, in Sweden, "In the beginning the economic conception was generally adopted, and everywhere manual training was looked upon as a means of preparing the children of the common people to earn their living. But gradually it came to be recognized that manual training has a more elevated purpose, and one, indeed, more useful in the deeper meaning of the term. It came to be considered as an educative process for the complete moral, physical and intellectual development of the child."
cards.whyThisWorks: The paragraph explicitly names a problem ('the difficulties were not surmounted'), then details a two-part institutional response (Trade Schools plus preserved elementary manual training), making problem/solution structure visible and teachable through direct textual evidence.
cards.skillStrategy: When identifying structure, look for signal phrases like 'to meet this situation' that announce a response to a stated difficulty — those phrases are the skeleton of a problem/solution structure.
evidencePoints: the difficulties were not surmounted
To meet this situation the industrial schools began a further development; they established distinct Trade Schools
cards.question: Du Bois opens the paragraph by stating 'the difficulties were not surmounted' and later writes 'To meet this situation the industrial schools began a further development.' Which structure do these two moments reveal?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Chronological order, because the paragraph moves from the post-war period forward in time to Sweden's educational practices

choices.label: B
choices.text: Problem/solution, because 'the difficulties were not surmounted' names an obstacle and 'to meet this situation' introduces the institutional response of Trade Schools and redefined manual training

choices.label: C
choices.text: Compare/contrast, because Du Bois places American industrial schools alongside Sweden's manual training system to highlight their opposing economic and moral goals

choices.label: D
choices.text: Cause/effect, because the moral and intellectual development described at the paragraph's end is presented as the cause that forced industrial schools to abandon simple trade teaching

cards.standardTitle: Central idea and supporting evidence
cards.excerpt: These figures illustrate vividly the function of the college-bred Negro. He is, as he ought to be, the group leader, the man who sets the ideals of the community where he lives, directs its thoughts and heads its social movements. It need hardly be argued that the Negro people need social leadership more than most groups; that they have no traditions to fall back upon, no long established customs, no strong family ties, no well defined social classes. All these things must be slowly and painfully evolved. The preacher was, even before the war, the group leader of the Negroes, and the church their greatest social institution. Naturally this preacher was ignorant and often immoral, and the problem of replacing the older type by better educated men has been a difficult one. Both by direct work and by direct influence on other preachers, and on congregations, the college-bred preacher has an opportunity for reformatory work and moral inspiration, the value of which cannot be overestimated.
cards.whyThisWorks: The excerpt opens with a direct thesis statement—'the function of the college-bred Negro'—and then builds supporting evidence around it, giving students a clear anchor to distinguish the central idea from surrounding details about the church, traditions, and preachers.
cards.skillStrategy: Find the sentence that makes the biggest claim the whole paragraph keeps returning to, then check whether the other sentences support it rather than replace it.
evidencePoints: He is, as he ought to be, the group leader, the man who sets the ideals of the community where he lives, directs its thoughts and heads its social movements.
the college-bred preacher has an opportunity for reformatory work and moral inspiration, the value of which cannot be overestimated.
cards.question: Du Bois opens the paragraph by stating that 'these figures illustrate vividly the function of the college-bred Negro.' Which statement most accurately expresses the central idea that the rest of the paragraph develops from that claim?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Black communities before the Civil War depended entirely on the church because they lacked traditions, strong family ties, and defined social classes.

choices.label: B
choices.text: College-educated Black men fulfill a necessary leadership role by shaping the moral ideals and social direction of their communities.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Replacing ignorant and immoral preachers with educated ministers has been the single most difficult problem facing Black communities.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The Black preacher held authority over his congregation before the war, making the church the foundation of all community progress.

He is, as he ought to be, the group leader, the man who sets the ideals of the community where he lives, directs its thoughts and heads its social movements. cards.skillStrategy: When a passage names a gap or difficulty and then introduces a figure or action that addresses it, look for problem/solution structure at work.

the college-bred preacher has an opportunity for reformatory work and moral inspiration, the value of which cannot be overestimated
cards.question: Du Bois states that Negro communities have 'no traditions to fall back upon, no long established customs, no strong family ties, no well defined social classes.' How does the rest of the paragraph respond to that statement?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Du Bois lists those deficiencies in the order they developed historically, ending with the rise of the college-bred preacher as the most recent stage.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Du Bois presents those deficiencies as the central difficulty facing Negro communities and then identifies the college-bred Negro—especially the college-bred preacher—as the means of overcoming them.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Du Bois contrasts those deficiencies with the strengths of other groups in order to argue that Negro communities are uniquely disadvantaged compared to everyone else.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Du Bois describes those deficiencies in detail but does not connect them to the role of the college-bred Negro introduced earlier in the paragraph.

cards.excerpt:

How then shall the leaders of a struggling people be trained and the hands of the risen few strengthened? We will not quarrel as to just what the university of the Negro should teach or how it should teach it--I willingly admit that each soul and each race-soul needs its own peculiar curriculum. cards.question: Du Bois opens by asking whether the Negro people can be 'more quickly raised' by 'this aristocracy of talent and character,' then closes by declaring that 'the best and most capable of their youth must be schooled in the colleges and universities of the land.' What central idea do these two moments together express?

choices.label: A

choices.label: B
choices.text: Uplifting Black Americans requires university-educated leaders whose talent and training draw the broader community forward.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Trade and industrial schools are inadequate replacements for the moral character that only an aristocracy of talent can provide.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Every nation in history has depended on a talented few, proving that Black Americans are no different from any other people.

cards.standardTitle: Opposing arguments, claims, evidence, and validity
cards.excerpt:
The truth of this has been strikingly shown in the marked improvement of white teachers in the South. Twenty years ago the rank and file of white public school teachers were not as good as the Negro teachers. But they, by scholarships and good salaries, have been encouraged to thorough normal and collegiate preparation, while the Negro teachers have been discouraged by starvation wages and the idea that any training will do for a black teacher. If carpenters are needed it is well and good to train men as carpenters. The work done in the secondary schools is reported in such detail in this office, that there can be no doubt of its grade."

cards.skillStrategy: When comparing evidence, ask yourself: does this piece show a pattern over time, a specific case, or outside authority—and how does each type strengthen or limit the author's claim?

But they, by scholarships and good salaries, have been encouraged to thorough normal and collegiate preparation, while the Negro teachers have been discouraged by starvation wages
The United States Commissioner of Education says in his report for 1900: 'For comparison between the white and colored enrollment in secondary and higher education...'
cards.question: How does Du Bois's use of the historical comparison in the first paragraph differ from his use of the Commissioner of Education's report in the second paragraph?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The historical comparison focuses on salary differences, while the Commissioner's report focuses on the quality of instruction in Black schools.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The historical comparison uses a cause-and-effect pattern to show how policy choices produced unequal outcomes, while the Commissioner's report supplies official enrollment data to ground the argument in documented fact.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The historical comparison acknowledges a limitation in Du Bois's argument, while the Commissioner's report restates the same limitation using government language.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The historical comparison draws on Du Bois's personal experience as a teacher, while the Commissioner's report provides a counterargument that Du Bois then refutes.

It brought the masses of the blacks in contact with modern civilization, made black men the leaders of their communities and trainers of the new generation. In this work college-bred Negroes were first teachers, and then teachers of teachers. And here it is that the broad culture of college work has been of peculiar value. Knowledge of life and its wider meaning, has been the point of the Negro's deepest ignorance, and the sending out of teachers whose training has not been simply for bread winning, but also for human culture, has been of inestimable value in the training of these men.
cards.whyThisWorks: The paragraph's chain of outcomes—teachers produced, masses reached, leaders formed, teachers of teachers trained—makes cause-and-effect the dominant structure, giving students a clear text to analyze for structural purpose rather than just topic identification.
cards.skillStrategy: When a paragraph shows one thing leading to another (look for words like 'placed before,' 'brought,' 'made'), ask yourself whether the author is showing causes producing effects rather than simply describing or comparing.
evidencePoints: it placed before the eyes of almost every Negro child an attainable ideal
It brought the masses of the blacks in contact with modern civilization, made black men the leaders of their communities and trainers of the new generation
cards.question: Du Bois writes that furnishing Black communities with college-trained teachers 'placed before the eyes of almost every Negro child an attainable ideal' and 'brought the masses of the blacks in contact with modern civilization.' How does this sequence of statements organize the paragraph?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The paragraph contrasts the limited training of teachers focused on 'bread winning' with the broader training focused on 'human culture' to show two competing educational philosophies.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The paragraph traces a chain in which Negro colleges training teachers produced a series of outcomes—ideals for children, community contact with civilization, Black leadership, and ultimately teachers training more teachers.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The paragraph describes the daily experiences of college-bred Negroes in chronological order, moving from their student years through their careers as community leaders.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The paragraph identifies the problem of 'five millions and more of ignorant people' and then proposes a step-by-step solution that Du Bois argues Negro colleges should adopt.

cards.standardTitle: Central idea and supporting evidence
cards.excerpt: Even at this point, however, the difficulties were not surmounted. In the first place modern industry has taken great strides since the war, and the teaching of trades is no longer a simple matter. Machinery and long processes of work have greatly changed the work of the carpenter, the ironworker and the shoemaker. A really efficient workman must be to-day an intelligent man who has had good technical training in addition to thorough common school, and perhaps even higher training. To meet this situation the industrial schools began a further development; they established distinct Trade Schools for the thorough training of better class artisans, and at the same time they sought to preserve for the purposes of general education, such of the simpler processes of elementary trade learning as were best suited therefor. In this differentiation of the Trade School and manual training, the best of the industrial schools simply followed the plain trend of the present educational epoch. A prominent educator tells us that, in Sweden, "In the beginning the economic conception was generally adopted, and everywhere manual training was looked upon as a means of preparing the children of the common people to earn their living. But gradually it came to be recognized that manual training has a more elevated purpose, and one, indeed, more useful in the deeper meaning of the term. It came to be considered as an educative process for the complete moral, physical and intellectual development of the child."
cards.whyThisWorks: The paragraph moves from a narrow problem (outdated trade teaching) to a broader claim about education's purpose, requiring students to distinguish the central idea from supporting details like the Swedish example or the Trade School solution.
cards.skillStrategy: Ask yourself: what does the whole paragraph add up to — not just one detail or example, but the main point the author is building toward by the final sentence?
evidencePoints: manual training has a more elevated purpose, and one, indeed, more useful in the deeper meaning of the term
It came to be considered as an educative process for the complete moral, physical and intellectual development of the child
cards.question: The paragraph opens by describing problems with teaching trades and ends with a Swedish educator's observation that manual training 'came to be considered as an educative process for the complete moral, physical and intellectual development of the child.' What central idea does Du Bois build across the entire paragraph?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Modern machinery permanently damaged the ability of industrial schools to train carpenters, ironworkers, and shoemakers for real employment.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Industrial education must move beyond preparing students to earn wages and instead develop their full moral, physical, and intellectual potential.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Sweden's approach to manual training became the model that American industrial schools copied when they created separate Trade Schools.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Separating Trade Schools from general manual training programs was the most important reform industrial schools made after the war.

cards.question: Du Bois uses two distinct pieces of evidence in this paragraph to support his claim that industrial education must go beyond simple trade training. How do these two pieces of evidence function differently in developing that claim?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The observation about machinery establishes that trade schools have already solved the problem, while the Swedish example shows that other countries have not yet caught up.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The observation about machinery and changed trades identifies the specific problem that makes higher training necessary, while the Swedish example provides outside authority showing that other educators reached the same conclusion through their own experience.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The observation about machinery argues that physical labor is no longer valuable, while the Swedish example argues that moral development should replace all technical instruction.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Both pieces of evidence serve the same function by describing historical changes in labor, with the Swedish example simply repeating Du Bois's point in a different national context.

cards.standardTitle: Text structure and feature purpose
cards.excerpt: I am an earnest advocate of manual training and trade teaching for black boys, and for white boys, too. I believe that next to the founding of Negro colleges the most valuable addition to Negro education since the war, has been industrial training for black boys. Nevertheless, I insist that the object of all true education is not to make men carpenters, it is to make carpenters men; there are two means of making the carpenter a man, each equally important: the first is to give the group and community in which he works, liberally trained teachers and leaders to teach him and his family what life means; the second is to give him sufficient intelligence and technical skill to make him an efficient workman; the first object demands the Negro college and college-bred men--not a quantity of such colleges, but a few of excellent quality; not too many college-bred men, but enough to leaven the lump, to inspire the masses, to raise the Talented Tenth to leadership; the second object demands a good system of common schools, well-taught, conveniently located and properly equipped.
cards.whyThisWorks: Du Bois explicitly labels 'the first object' and 'the second object' and pairs each with a distinct institution, making the compare/contrast and parallel structure visible and teachable at the sentence level.
cards.skillStrategy: When a writer numbers or labels parts of an argument ('the first,' 'the second'), look at what each part does — if each names a problem and matches it to a solution, the structure is problem/solution; if each sets up a side-by-side pairing, the structure is compare/contrast.
evidencePoints: the first object demands the Negro college and college-bred men
the second object demands a good system of common schools, well-taught, conveniently located and properly equipped
cards.question: Du Bois writes, 'there are two means of making the carpenter a man, each equally important: the first is to give the group and community in which he works, liberally trained teachers and leaders… the second is to give him sufficient intelligence and technical skill.' How does this 'first… second' structure organize the paragraph's argument?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Du Bois arranges events in the order they occurred, showing how industrial training came before college education in the history of Black schooling.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Du Bois sets up two parallel goals for Black education and then matches each goal to a specific type of institution — the Negro college for the first, common schools for the second.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Du Bois presents the problem of inadequate trade schools and proposes replacing them with Negro colleges as the single solution.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Du Bois contrasts the educational needs of Black carpenters with those of white carpenters to argue that their required institutions are fundamentally different.

cards.standardTitle: Central idea and supporting evidence
cards.excerpt: After emancipation came a new group of educated and gifted leaders: Langston, Bruce and Elliot, Greener, Williams and Payne. Through political organization, historical and polemic writing and moral regeneration, these men strove to uplift their people. It is the fashion of to-day to sneer at them and to say that with freedom Negro leadership should have begun at the plow and not in the Senate--a foolish and mischievous lie; two hundred and fifty years that black serf toiled at the plow and yet that toiling was in vain till the Senate passed the war amendments; and two hundred and fifty years more the half-free serf of to-day may toil at his plow, but unless he have political rights and righteously guarded civic status, he will still remain the poverty-stricken and ignorant plaything of rascals, that he now is. This all sane men know even if they dare not say it.
cards.whyThisWorks: Du Bois explicitly labels a popular belief a 'foolish and mischievous lie' and then counters it with historical evidence, giving students a clear central claim to identify rather than a topic or isolated detail.
cards.skillStrategy: Find the sentence where the author takes a direct stand, then ask what that stand is really arguing—that is the central idea.
evidencePoints: a foolish and mischievous lie; two hundred and fifty years that black serf toiled at the plow and yet that toiling was in vain till the Senate passed the war amendments
unless he have political rights and righteously guarded civic status, he will still remain the poverty-stricken and ignorant plaything of rascals
cards.question: Du Bois calls the idea that 'Negro leadership should have begun at the plow and not in the Senate' a 'foolish and mischievous lie.' What central idea does the rest of the paragraph develop to support that label?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The post-emancipation leaders—Langston, Bruce, Elliot, and others—were more talented than any leaders who could have come from agricultural work.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Labor alone cannot free Black Americans; without political rights and protected civic status, centuries of toil will continue to leave them powerless and exploited.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The war amendments passed by the Senate were the single greatest achievement in American history and ended all hardship for Black Americans after emancipation.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Most Americans after emancipation secretly agreed that political leadership was necessary but were too afraid of public opinion to say so openly.

cards.question: Du Bois ends the paragraph with a quotation from a Swedish educator describing manual training as 'an educative process for the complete moral, physical and intellectual development of the child.' How does placing this quotation at the end of the paragraph connect to Du Bois's larger purpose?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The quotation shows that Sweden solved the problem of industrial training before American schools did, suggesting American educators should look abroad for all their solutions.

choices.label: B
choices.text: After tracing how industrial schools evolved from simple trade preparation to something broader, Du Bois uses the quotation to argue that the true purpose of manual training is the full development of the person, not merely economic usefulness.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The quotation interrupts Du Bois's argument to introduce a competing view that manual training should remain focused on preparing working-class children for specific trades.

choices.label: D
choices.text: By ending with a foreign example, Du Bois concedes that American industrial schools have failed to keep pace with modern industry and must adopt the Swedish model entirely.

cards.question: Du Bois writes, 'the object of all true education is not to make men carpenters, it is to make carpenters men.' Which statement most accurately expresses the central idea that this claim introduces for the rest of the paragraph?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Industrial training for Black boys is the most valuable educational development since the Civil War, surpassing even the founding of Negro colleges.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Developing the full humanity of workers requires both college-trained leaders to guide communities and strong common schools to build workers' skills.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Negro colleges should be few in number but excellent in quality so that college-bred men can inspire the masses.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Du Bois supports manual training and trade teaching equally for Black and white boys throughout the United States.

cards.standardTitle: Central idea and supporting evidence
cards.excerpt: Three of these were established in border States before the War; thirteen were planted by the Freedmen's Bureau in the years 1864-1869; nine were established between 1870 and 1880 by various church bodies; five were established after 1881 by Negro churches, and four are state institutions supported by United States' agricultural funds. In most cases the college departments are small adjuncts to high and common school work. As a matter of fact six institutions--Atlanta, Fisk, Howard, Shaw, Wilberforce and Leland, are the important Negro colleges so far as actual work and number of students are concerned. In all these institutions, seven hundred and fifty Negro college students are enrolled. In grade the best of these colleges are about a year behind the smaller New England colleges and a typical curriculum is that of Atlanta University. Here students from the grammar grades, after a three years' high school course, take a college course of 136 weeks. One-fourth of this time is given to Latin and Greek; one-fifth, to English and modern languages; one-sixth, to history and social science; one-seventh, to natural science; one-eighth to mathematics, and one-eighth to philosophy and pedagogy.
cards.whyThisWorks: The paragraph opens with a list of founding facts but then pivots to the claim that only six institutions do 'actual work' with a small enrolled population, forcing students to distinguish a founding-history topic from the central limiting claim.
cards.skillStrategy: Ask yourself: what is the paragraph ultimately arguing about Negro higher education, not just listing or describing?
evidencePoints: six institutions--Atlanta, Fisk, Howard, Shaw, Wilberforce and Leland, are the important Negro colleges so far as actual work and number of students are concerned
seven hundred and fifty Negro college students are enrolled
cards.question: Du Bois states that 'six institutions…are the important Negro colleges so far as actual work and number of students are concerned' and that only 'seven hundred and fifty Negro college students are enrolled.' What central idea do these details together support?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Negro colleges were created by many different organizations—the Freedmen's Bureau, church bodies, and state governments—over several decades.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Despite the existence of numerous Negro colleges, genuine college-level education reaches only a small number of students through a very limited set of institutions.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Atlanta University's curriculum, which devotes one-fourth of its time to Latin and Greek, sets the standard that all other Negro colleges should follow.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Negro colleges fall roughly one year behind New England colleges because their students must complete high school coursework before entering college study.

cards.standardTitle: Central idea and supporting evidence
cards.excerpt: Thus, again, in the manning of trade schools and manual training schools we are thrown back upon the higher training as its source and chief support. There was a time when any aged and wornout carpenter could teach in a trade school. But not so to-day. Indeed the demand for college-bred men by a school like Tuskegee, ought to make Mr. Booker T. Washington the firmest friend of higher training. Here he has as helpers the son of a Negro senator, trained in Greek and the humanities, and graduated at Harvard; the son of a Negro congressman and lawyer, trained in Latin and mathematics, and graduated at Oberlin; he has as his wife, a woman who read Virgil and Homer in the same class room with me; he has as college chaplain, a classical graduate of Atlanta University; as teacher of science, a graduate of Fisk; as teacher of history, a graduate of Smith,--indeed some thirty of his chief teachers are college graduates, and instead of studying French grammars in the midst of weeds, or buying pianos for dirty cabins, they are at Mr. Washington's right hand helping him in a noble work. And yet one of the effects of Mr. Washington's propaganda has been to throw doubt upon the expediency of such training for Negroes, as these persons have had.
cards.whyThisWorks: Du Bois builds his central idea—that higher education is essential even for trade schools—by cataloguing the specific college-trained teachers at Tuskegee, which gives students a clear model of how concrete examples accumulate to support a claim.
cards.skillStrategy: When a writer lines up specific examples one after another, ask yourself: what single idea do all these examples prove together?
evidencePoints: the demand for college-bred men by a school like Tuskegee, ought to make Mr. Booker T. Washington the firmest friend of higher training
some thirty of his chief teachers are college graduates
cards.question: Du Bois lists the educational backgrounds of multiple Tuskegee teachers—graduates of Harvard, Oberlin, Atlanta University, Fisk, and Smith. How does this accumulation of examples develop the central idea of the paragraph?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The examples show that Tuskegee's teachers were personally loyal to Washington, which explains why the school succeeded despite limited resources.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The examples demonstrate that even a school devoted to practical training depends on college-educated instructors, contradicting Washington's skepticism toward higher education.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The examples prove that Black graduates of elite Northern universities were superior to graduates of Southern institutions like Atlanta University.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The examples suggest that Washington privately supported classical education but was forced by public pressure to argue against it.

evidencePoints: seven hundred and fifty Negro college students are enrolled

cards.question: Du Bois includes the enrollment figure of 'seven hundred and fifty Negro college students' and the comparison to 'smaller New England colleges' in the same paragraph. How do these two details work together to develop his central idea?

choices.label: A
choices.text: They show that Negro colleges were founded by many different organizations, proving that no single group took responsibility for Black education.

choices.label: B
choices.text: They establish that Black higher education, though present, was severely limited in both the number of students it reached and the academic level it had achieved.

choices.label: C
choices.text: They demonstrate that Atlanta University's curriculum was superior to other Negro colleges because it devoted the most time to Latin and Greek.

choices.label: D
choices.text: They suggest that the Freedmen's Bureau was the most important force in building Negro colleges because it founded the greatest number of institutions.

cards.standardTitle: Central idea and supporting evidence
cards.excerpt:
Can the masses of the Negro people be in any possible way more quickly raised than by the effort and example of this aristocracy of talent and character? Was there ever a nation on God's fair earth civilized from the bottom upward? Never; it is, ever was and ever will be from the top downward that culture filters. The Talented Tenth rises and pulls all that are worth the saving up to their vantage ground. This is the history of human progress; and the two historic mistakes which have hindered that progress were the thinking first that no more could ever rise save the few already risen; or second, that it would better the unrisen to pull the risen down.

How then shall the leaders of a struggling people be trained and the hands of the risen few strengthened? There can be but one answer: The best and most capable of their youth must be schooled in the colleges and universities of the land. We will not quarrel as to just what the university of the Negro should teach or how it should teach it--I willingly admit that each soul and each race-soul needs its own peculiar curriculum. But this is true: A university is a human invention for the transmission of knowledge and culture from generation to generation, through the training of quick minds and pure hearts, and for this work no other human invention will suffice, not even trade and industrial schools.
cards.whyThisWorks: The excerpt gives students two clearly sequenced moves—a historical claim about top-down progress in paragraph one and a prescription for university training in paragraph two—so they can trace exactly how each piece of evidence builds the central idea that a trained Talented Tenth is the engine of collective advancement.
cards.skillStrategy: Find the central idea, then ask: what does each specific detail, example, or reason add to prove it?
evidencePoints: Was there ever a nation on God's fair earth civilized from the bottom upward? Never; it is, ever was and ever will be from the top downward that culture filters.
The best and most capable of their youth must be schooled in the colleges and universities of the land.
cards.question: In paragraph one, Du Bois states, 'it is, ever was and ever will be from the top downward that culture filters.' In paragraph two, he concludes that 'the best and most capable of their youth must be schooled in the colleges and universities of the land.' How does the second statement develop the central idea established by the first?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The first statement argues that only a fixed few can ever rise, and the second statement narrows that claim by limiting university education to those who have already proven their talent.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The first statement establishes that progress has always depended on a capable few leading others upward, and the second statement identifies university training as the specific means of producing those capable leaders.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The first statement blames historical leaders for blocking progress, and the second statement proposes that universities correct that injustice by offering a curriculum identical to that of any other race.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The first statement concedes that bottom-up progress is possible under certain conditions, and the second statement argues that trade and industrial schools can fulfill that role as well as universities.

cards.standardTitle: Central idea and supporting evidence
cards.excerpt: These figures illustrate vividly the function of the college-bred Negro. He is, as he ought to be, the group leader, the man who sets the ideals of the community where he lives, directs its thoughts and heads its social movements. It need hardly be argued that the Negro people need social leadership more than most groups; that they have no traditions to fall back upon, no long established customs, no strong family ties, no well defined social classes. All these things must be slowly and painfully evolved. The preacher was, even before the war, the group leader of the Negroes, and the church their greatest social institution. Naturally this preacher was ignorant and often immoral, and the problem of replacing the older type by better educated men has been a difficult one. Both by direct work and by direct influence on other preachers, and on congregations, the college-bred preacher has an opportunity for reformatory work and moral inspiration, the value of which cannot be overestimated.
cards.whyThisWorks: Du Bois builds his central idea—that college-educated Black leaders are essential—by layering specific evidence: the absence of established traditions, the historical role of the ignorant preacher, and the reformatory potential of the college-bred preacher, giving students a clear model of how examples and reasons accumulate to support one claim.
cards.skillStrategy: Track how each new detail or example adds a specific reason why the central idea is true, rather than just repeating it.
evidencePoints: they have no traditions to fall back upon, no long established customs, no strong family ties, no well defined social classes
the college-bred preacher has an opportunity for reformatory work and moral inspiration, the value of which cannot be overestimated
cards.question: Du Bois states that the Negro people 'have no traditions to fall back upon, no long established customs, no strong family ties, no well defined social classes.' How does this detail develop the central idea of the paragraph?

choices.label: A
choices.text: It shows that the church was historically the most powerful institution in Black communities, making religious leadership the only viable path forward.

choices.label: B
choices.text: It establishes the depth of the community's need for leadership, strengthening the claim that college-educated men must fill the role of guiding social ideals and movements.

choices.label: C
choices.text: It argues that Black communities are fundamentally different from all other groups and therefore cannot benefit from the same educational institutions.

choices.label: D
choices.text: It concedes a weakness in Du Bois's argument by admitting that no form of leadership, educated or otherwise, can overcome the absence of established traditions.

cards.standardTitle: Central idea and supporting evidence
cards.excerpt:
The truth of this has been strikingly shown in the marked improvement of white teachers in the South. Twenty years ago the rank and file of white public school teachers were not as good as the Negro teachers. But they, by scholarships and good salaries, have been encouraged to thorough normal and collegiate preparation, while the Negro teachers have been discouraged by starvation wages and the idea that any training will do for a black teacher. If carpenters are needed it is well and good to train men as carpenters. But to train men as carpenters, and then set them to teaching is wasteful and criminal; and to train men as teachers and then refuse them living wages, unless they become carpenters, is rank nonsense.

The United States Commissioner of Education says in his report for 1900: "For comparison between the white and colored enrollment in secondary and higher education, I have added together the enrollment in high schools and secondary schools, with the attendance on colleges and universities, not being sure of the actual grade of work done in the colleges and universities. The work done in the secondary schools is reported in such detail in this office, that there can be no doubt of its grade."
cards.whyThisWorks: Du Bois builds his central idea—that denying Black teachers proper training and wages is both wasteful and unjust—through a concrete comparison, a cause-and-effect chain, and a logical analogy, giving students clear examples of how evidence accumulates to develop a central idea.
cards.skillStrategy: Track how each example or reason the author gives connects back to the main claim, asking yourself: what does this detail prove about the central idea?
evidencePoints: they, by scholarships and good salaries, have been encouraged to thorough normal and collegiate preparation, while the Negro teachers have been discouraged by starvation wages
