cards.question: How does the comparison between white teachers and Negro teachers in the first paragraph develop Du Bois's central idea?

choices.label: A
choices.text: It shows that white teachers were always more qualified than Negro teachers, proving that investment in education produces natural differences in ability.

choices.label: B
choices.text: It demonstrates that unequal investment—scholarships and good salaries for white teachers versus starvation wages for Negro teachers—produces unequal outcomes, supporting the idea that denying proper support to Black educators is both wasteful and unjust.

choices.label: C
choices.text: It argues that carpentry training is a reasonable substitute for teacher preparation, as long as workers are eventually given the opportunity to teach.

choices.label: D
choices.text: It establishes that the quality of public schools in the South declined over twenty years because neither white nor Negro teachers received adequate preparation.

cards.standardTitle: Central idea and supporting evidence
cards.excerpt:
The truth of this has been strikingly shown in the marked improvement of white teachers in the South. Twenty years ago the rank and file of white public school teachers were not as good as the Negro teachers. But they, by scholarships and good salaries, have been encouraged to thorough normal and collegiate preparation, while the Negro teachers have been discouraged by starvation wages and the idea that any training will do for a black teacher. If carpenters are needed it is well and good to train men as carpenters. But to train men as carpenters, and then set them to teaching is wasteful and criminal; and to train men as teachers and then refuse them living wages, unless they become carpenters, is rank nonsense.

The United States Commissioner of Education says in his report for 1900: "For comparison between the white and colored enrollment in secondary and higher education, I have added together the enrollment in high schools and secondary schools, with the attendance on colleges and universities, not being sure of the actual grade of work done in the colleges and universities. The work done in the secondary schools is reported in such detail in this office, that there can be no doubt of its grade."
cards.whyThisWorks: The excerpt contains both a strong causal claim about unequal teacher preparation and a statistical enrollment report, allowing students to distinguish between direct, reasoning-based evidence and a tangential data point that does not directly support Du Bois's central argument about the consequences of denying Black teachers proper training and wages.
cards.skillStrategy: Ask yourself which piece of evidence directly proves the central idea — not just a related fact, but the one that shows the cause-and-effect relationship the author is building.
evidencePoints: they, by scholarships and good salaries, have been encouraged to thorough normal and collegiate preparation, while the Negro teachers have been discouraged by starvation wages and the idea that any training will do for a black teacher
to train men as teachers and then refuse them living wages, unless they become carpenters, is rank nonsense
cards.question: Du Bois's central idea in the first paragraph is that denying Black teachers proper preparation and fair wages is both wasteful and unjust. Which piece of evidence from the excerpt most directly supports this central idea?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The U.S. Commissioner of Education's 1900 report combined high school and college enrollment figures because the grade of work in colleges and universities was uncertain.

choices.label: B
choices.text: White teachers were encouraged toward thorough collegiate preparation through scholarships and good salaries, while Black teachers were discouraged by starvation wages and the assumption that any training would suffice.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Twenty years ago, white public school teachers were not as good as Negro teachers in the South.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Training men as carpenters when carpenters are needed is described as well and good.

cards.standardTitle: Paraphrase grade-level text
cards.excerpt: Even at this point, however, the difficulties were not surmounted. In the first place modern industry has taken great strides since the war, and the teaching of trades is no longer a simple matter. Machinery and long processes of work have greatly changed the work of the carpenter, the ironworker and the shoemaker. A really efficient workman must be to-day an intelligent man who has had good technical training in addition to thorough common school, and perhaps even higher training. To meet this situation the industrial schools began a further development; they established distinct Trade Schools for the thorough training of better class artisans, and at the same time they sought to preserve for the purposes of general education, such of the simpler processes of elementary trade learning as were best suited therefor. In this differentiation of the Trade School and manual training, the best of the industrial schools simply followed the plain trend of the present educational epoch. A prominent educator tells us that, in Sweden, "In the beginning the economic conception was generally adopted, and everywhere manual training was looked upon as a means of preparing the children of the common people to earn their living. But gradually it came to be recognized that manual training has a more elevated purpose, and one, indeed, more useful in the deeper meaning of the term. It came to be considered as an educative process for the complete moral, physical and intellectual development of the child."
cards.whyThisWorks: The Swedish educator's quoted claim moves through two distinct stages of thinking about manual training, giving students a clear sentence to paraphrase while testing whether they preserve both the shift and the final elevated purpose.
cards.skillStrategy: When paraphrasing, ask yourself: does my restatement keep every part of the original idea—including any change in thinking or two-part claim—without adding new ideas or dropping key details?
evidencePoints: In the beginning the economic conception was generally adopted, and everywhere manual training was looked upon as a means of preparing the children of the common people to earn their living.
But gradually it came to be recognized that manual training has a more elevated purpose, and one, indeed, more useful in the deeper meaning of the term.
cards.question: Read the following sentence from the excerpt: 'But gradually it came to be recognized that manual training has a more elevated purpose, and one, indeed, more useful in the deeper meaning of the term.' Which of the following most accurately restates this sentence?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Manual training was eventually abandoned in Sweden because educators decided it served no practical economic purpose for working-class children.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Over time, people came to understand that manual training served a higher and more genuinely meaningful purpose than simply preparing poor children to earn a wage.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Manual training was always understood to be the most important form of education, valued above all other subjects in Swedish schools.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Educators slowly realized that manual training was useful only for the moral development of children, not for any intellectual or economic goals.

texts.title: Choice: A Tribute to Dr. Martin Luther King, Jr.
texts.author: Alice Walker

cards.textTitle: Choice: A Tribute to Dr. Martin Luther King, Jr.
cards.standardTitle: Text structure and feature purpose
cards.excerpt: They are visible all around you. His voice you would recognize sooner than any other voice you have heard in this century—this in spite of the fact that certain municipal libraries, like the one in downtown Jackson, do not carry recordings of his speeches, and the librarians chuckle cruelly when asked why they do not. You know, if you have read his books, that his is a complex and revolutionary philosophy that few people are capable of understanding fully or have the patience to embody in themselves. Which is our weakness, which is our loss. And if you know anything about good Baptist preaching, you can imagine what you missed if you never had a chance to hear Martin Luther King, Jr., preach at Ebenezer Baptist Church.
cards.whyThisWorks: The paragraph both deepens admiration for King's legacy and pivots sharply to critique institutional suppression ('librarians chuckle cruelly'), giving students a clear contrast-within-extension structure to analyze.
cards.skillStrategy: Ask yourself: does this paragraph start a new idea, build on one already in motion, or pull in an opposing detail—and what does that move do for the reader?
evidencePoints: His voice you would recognize sooner than any other voice you have heard in this century
certain municipal libraries, like the one in downtown Jackson, do not carry recordings of his speeches, and the librarians chuckle cruelly when asked why they do not
cards.question: Walker writes that King's voice is one 'you would recognize sooner than any other voice you have heard in this century,' then immediately notes that the Jackson library does not carry recordings of his speeches and that librarians 'chuckle cruelly' when asked why. What job does this move perform in the paragraph?

choices.label: A
choices.text: It concludes the paragraph's praise of King by shifting entirely to a criticism of Southern libraries, leaving the tribute behind.

choices.label: B
choices.text: It extends the paragraph's celebration of King's enduring presence while sharpening it with a contrast that exposes deliberate efforts to erase that presence.

choices.label: C
choices.text: It introduces King to an audience assumed to be unfamiliar with him, using the library detail to establish why his name is not widely known.

choices.label: D
choices.text: It proves that King's philosophy was too complex for most institutions to understand, using the library's refusal as evidence of that complexity.

cards.question: Read the following sentence from the passage: 'Which is our weakness, which is our loss.' What rhetorical appeal does Walker primarily use in this sentence, and how does it serve her purpose?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Walker uses logos by presenting a logical argument that King's philosophy is too difficult for most people to understand, supporting her claim with evidence about his books.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Walker uses pathos by turning a description of King's complex philosophy into a shared indictment of the audience, making readers feel the weight of their own failure to fully embrace his ideas.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Walker uses ethos by positioning herself as a credible judge of King's philosophy, establishing that she has read his books and therefore earned the authority to evaluate his legacy.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Walker uses logos by contrasting King's revolutionary philosophy with the librarians' refusal to carry his recordings, building a reasoned case for institutional injustice.

cards.textTitle: Choice: A Tribute to Dr. Martin Luther King, Jr.
cards.standardTitle: Paraphrase grade-level text
cards.excerpt: In 1960, my mother bought a television set, and each day after school I watched Hamilton Holmes and Charlayne Hunter as they struggled to integrate—fair-skinned as they were—the University of Georgia. And then, one day, there appeared the face of Dr. Martin Luther King, Jr. What a funny name, I thought. At the moment I first saw him, he was being handcuffed and shoved into a police truck. He had dared to claim his rights as a native son and had been arrested. He displayed no fear, but seemed calm and serene, unaware of his own extraordinary courage. His whole body, like his conscience, was at peace. At the moment I saw his resistance I knew I would never be able to live in this country without resisting everything that sought to disinherit me, and I would never be forced away from the land of my birth without a fight.
cards.whyThisWorks: The sentence 'At the moment I saw his resistance I knew I would never be able to live in this country without resisting everything that sought to disinherit me' presents a clear, testable claim about how witnessing King's courage transformed the narrator's personal resolve, making it ideal for a paraphrase item.
cards.skillStrategy: Read the target sentence carefully, then ask yourself: which answer keeps the same meaning without adding, removing, or twisting any part of it?
evidencePoints: At the moment I saw his resistance I knew I would never be able to live in this country without resisting everything that sought to disinherit me
I would never be forced away from the land of my birth without a fight
cards.question: Read the following sentence from the passage: 'At the moment I saw his resistance I knew I would never be able to live in this country without resisting everything that sought to disinherit me, and I would never be forced away from the land of my birth without a fight.' Which of the following most accurately restates the meaning of this sentence?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Watching Dr. King on television inspired the narrator to leave the country and find a place where she would not face injustice.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Seeing Dr. King resist arrest made the narrator realize she would spend her life fighting against anything that tried to strip her of her place and rights in her own country.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The narrator decided that, like Dr. King, she would remain calm and show no fear whenever she was treated unjustly by authorities.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Witnessing Dr. King's arrest convinced the narrator that resisting the law was the only way to bring about change in the United States.

cards.textTitle: Choice: A Tribute to Dr. Martin Luther King, Jr.
cards.standardTitle: Rhetoric and reader effect
cards.excerpt: And I knew it for sure when my mother added his name to the list of people she prayed for every night. I sometimes think that it was literally the prayers of people like my mother and father, who had bowed down in the struggle for such a long time, that kept Dr. King alive until five years ago. For years we went to bed praying for his life and awoke with the question “Is the ‘Lord’ still here?” The public acts of Dr. King you know. They are visible all around you. His voice you would recognize sooner than any other voice you have heard in this century—this in spite of the fact that certain municipal libraries, like the one in downtown Jackson, do not carry recordings of his speeches, and the librarians chuckle cruelly when asked why they do not.
cards.whyThisWorks: Walker's rhetorical question 'Is the Lord still here?' and the contrast between King's universal recognition and the library's deliberate erasure of his voice give students two clear rhetorical moves to analyze for emotional and persuasive effect.
cards.skillStrategy: When you spot a rhetorical question or a sharp contrast in a passage, ask yourself: what feeling or idea does the author want the reader to carry away from that moment?
evidencePoints: awoke with the question 'Is the "Lord" still here?'

His voice you would recognize sooner than any other voice you have heard in this century—this in spite of the fact that certain municipal libraries, like the one in downtown Jackson, do not carry recordings of his speeches, and the librarians chuckle cruelly when asked why they do not.
cards.question: Walker writes that people 'awoke with the question "Is the "Lord" still here?"' and then immediately states, 'The public acts of Dr. King you know. They are visible all around you.' How does this contrast affect the reader?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The contrast reassures the reader that the community's fears about Dr. King were never truly serious, since his legacy was always publicly celebrated.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The contrast deepens the sense of loss and injustice: the daily terror of fearing King's death makes the later suppression of his recorded voice feel like a continuation of that same threat.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The contrast shifts the reader's focus away from Dr. King's personal danger and toward the political achievements he accomplished during his lifetime.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The contrast suggests that Walker's community eventually stopped worrying about Dr. King once his acts became widely visible to the public.

cards.textTitle: Choice: A Tribute to Dr. Martin Luther King, Jr.
cards.standardTitle: Text structure and feature purpose
cards.excerpt: And you know of his concern for the disinherited—the American Indian, the Mexican American, and the poor American white—for whom he cared much. You know that this very room, in this very restaurant, was closed to people of color not more than five years ago. And that we eat here together tonight largely through his efforts and his blood. We accept the common pleasures of life, assuredly, in his name. 11. What does Alice Walker mean in the above highlighted statement? But add to all of these things the one thing that seems to me second to none in importance: He gave us back our heritage. He gave us back our homeland; the bones and dust of our ancestors, who may now sleep within our caring and our hearing.
cards.whyThisWorks: The paragraph shifts from cataloguing King's known achievements to introducing what Walker considers his most important contribution—restoring cultural heritage—making it a clear pivot that students can identify and explain.
cards.skillStrategy: Ask yourself: does this paragraph keep building the same idea, or does it turn a corner and introduce something new? Look for signal phrases like 'But add to all of these things' to spot the shift.
evidencePoints: But add to all of these things the one thing that seems to me second to none in importance
He gave us back our heritage. He gave us back our homeland; the bones and dust of our ancestors
cards.question: In this paragraph, Walker first acknowledges King's well-known contributions, then writes, 'But add to all of these things the one thing that seems to me second to none in importance.' What is the primary job of this shift in the paragraph?

choices.label: A
choices.text: To conclude Walker's tribute by summarizing all of King's contributions that were mentioned earlier in the speech.

choices.label: B
choices.text: To move beyond King's recognized civil rights work and introduce what Walker argues is his most significant—yet overlooked—achievement: restoring a cultural and ancestral heritage.

choices.label: C
choices.text: To contrast King's concern for the disinherited with his failure to address the needs of African Americans specifically.

choices.label: D
choices.text: To prove that the integration of the restaurant where the audience is gathered was King's greatest single accomplishment.

choices.text: The paragraph concludes Walker's argument by restating that King's philosophy was too complex for ordinary people to understand or embody.

cards.textTitle: Choice: A Tribute to Dr. Martin Luther King, Jr.
cards.standardTitle: Central idea and supporting evidence
cards.excerpt: And I knew it for sure when my mother added his name to the list of people she prayed for every night. I sometimes think that it was literally the prayers of people like my mother and father, who had bowed down in the struggle for such a long time, that kept Dr. King alive until five years ago. For years we went to bed praying for his life and awoke with the question “Is the ‘Lord’ still here?” The public acts of Dr. King you know. They are visible all around you. His voice you would recognize sooner than any other voice you have heard in this century—this in spite of the fact that certain municipal libraries, like the one in downtown Jackson, do not carry recordings of his speeches, and the librarians chuckle cruelly when asked why they do not.
cards.whyThisWorks: The excerpt layers personal testimony (the mother's prayers, the family's nightly fear) alongside a public injustice (libraries suppressing King's speeches) to show how private devotion and institutional resistance together develop the central idea that King's significance was both deeply felt and deliberately suppressed.
cards.skillStrategy: Ask yourself: what specific examples or details does the author include, and how does each one push the central idea forward rather than just repeat it?
evidencePoints: I sometimes think that it was literally the prayers of people like my mother and father, who had bowed down in the struggle for such a long time, that kept Dr. King alive until five years ago.
certain municipal libraries, like the one in downtown Jackson, do not carry recordings of his speeches, and the librarians chuckle cruelly when asked why they do not.
cards.question: How do the detail about Walker's mother's prayers and the detail about municipal libraries work together to develop the central idea of this passage?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Both details show that ordinary people misunderstood Dr. King's public work and needed guidance to appreciate his speeches.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The prayers reveal how profoundly ordinary people valued Dr. King's survival, while the library detail reveals that institutions actively worked to erase his voice, together showing that his significance was both deeply felt and deliberately suppressed.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The prayers suggest that Dr. King's influence was limited to religious communities, and the library detail confirms that his speeches were too controversial for public audiences.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Both details focus on the private sphere of Walker's family life and are meant to contrast with the public acts of Dr. King mentioned earlier in the passage.

cards.textTitle: Choice: A Tribute to Dr. Martin Luther King, Jr.
cards.standardTitle: Rhetorical appeals and author purpose
cards.excerpt: In the same cemetery are most of my mother’s people, who have lived in Georgia for so long nobody even remembers when they came. And all of my great-aunts and - uncles are there, and my grandfather and grandmother, and very recently, my own father. If it is true that land does not belong to anyone until they have buried a body in it, then the land of my birthplace belongs to me, dozens of times over. Yet the history of my family, like that of all black Southerners, is a history of dispossession. We loved the land and worked the land, but we never owned it; and even if we bought land, as my great-grandfather did after the Civil War, it was always in danger of being taken away, as his was, during the period following Reconstruction.
cards.whyThisWorks: Walker layers personal family history with a logical claim about land ownership and then pivots to the painful contradiction of dispossession, giving students a clear example of pathos built through specific emotional detail rather than abstract argument.
cards.skillStrategy: Ask yourself: is the author trying to prove something with facts and reasoning, build trust through expertise, or make you feel something through personal experience and loss — then find the exact words that create that effect.
evidencePoints: the history of my family, like that of all black Southerners, is a history of dispossession
We loved the land and worked the land, but we never owned it
cards.question: In the sentence 'We loved the land and worked the land, but we never owned it,' Walker primarily uses which rhetorical appeal, and what purpose does it serve?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Logos, because Walker presents a logical sequence showing that labor should legally result in ownership under property law.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Pathos, because the contrast between deep personal devotion to the land and the denial of ownership evokes grief and injustice in the reader.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Ethos, because Walker establishes her credibility as a reliable historian of black Southern land ownership after the Civil War.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Logos, because Walker uses her great-grandfather's purchase of land as documented evidence that black Southerners could legally own property.

cards.textTitle: Choice: A Tribute to Dr. Martin Luther King, Jr.
cards.standardTitle: Rhetoric and reader effect
cards.excerpt: It is a part of the black Southern sensibility that we treasure memories; for such a long time, that is all of our homeland those of us who at one time or another were forced away from it have been allowed to have. I watched my brothers, one by one, leave our home and leave the South. I watched my sisters do the same. This was not unusual; abandonment, except for memories, was the common thing, except for those who “could not do any better” or those whose strength or stubbornness was so colossal they took the risk that others could not bear. In 1960, my mother bought a television set, and each day after school I watched Hamilton Holmes and Charlayne Hunter as they struggled to integrate—fair-skinned as they were—the University of Georgia.
cards.whyThisWorks: Walker's deliberate repetition of 'I watched' creates an anaphoric rhythm that builds cumulative emotional weight, giving teachers a clear textual anchor for discussing how repetition shapes the reader's sense of loss and inevitability.
cards.skillStrategy: When you spot a phrase repeated at the start of sentences, ask yourself what feeling builds with each repetition and how that feeling changes your understanding of the writer's message.
evidencePoints: I watched my brothers, one by one, leave our home and leave the South.
I watched my sisters do the same.
cards.question: Read the following sentences from the passage: 'I watched my brothers, one by one, leave our home and leave the South. I watched my sisters do the same.' How does the repetition of 'I watched' affect the reader?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The repeated phrase signals that Walker was a passive, uninvolved observer who felt no personal connection to her family's departures.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The repeated phrase accumulates a sense of helpless witness, making the reader feel the steady, unavoidable loss Walker experienced as family member after family member left the South.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The repeated phrase emphasizes Walker's pride in her siblings for having the courage to leave, suggesting she admired their decision to abandon the South.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The repeated phrase creates confusion about the timeline of events, leaving the reader uncertain whether the brothers or the sisters left first.

cards.textTitle: Choice: A Tribute to Dr. Martin Luther King, Jr.
cards.standardTitle: Text structure and feature purpose
cards.excerpt: It is a part of the black Southern sensibility that we treasure memories; for such a long time, that is all of our homeland those of us who at one time or another were forced away from it have been allowed to have. I watched my brothers, one by one, leave our home and leave the South. I watched my sisters do the same. This was not unusual; abandonment, except for memories, was the common thing, except for those who “could not do any better” or those whose strength or stubbornness was so colossal they took the risk that others could not bear. In 1960, my mother bought a television set, and each day after school I watched Hamilton Holmes and Charlayne Hunter as they struggled to integrate—fair-skinned as they were—the University of Georgia.
cards.whyThisWorks: The paragraph opens with a stated claim about memory as homeland, then moves through personal observation of family departure, and closes with a specific historical moment — giving students a clear structure to trace from introduction of idea to grounding evidence.
cards.skillStrategy: Ask yourself: what idea does the first sentence announce, and does the rest of the paragraph prove it, shift away from it, or extend it with examples?
evidencePoints: we treasure memories; for such a long time, that is all of our homeland those of us who at one time or another were forced away from it have been allowed to have
I watched my brothers, one by one, leave our home and leave the South. I watched my sisters do the same.
cards.question: Walker opens the paragraph by stating that memory is 'all of our homeland' Black Southerners 'have been allowed to have.' What job do the sentences that follow — about her brothers, her sisters, and Hamilton Holmes and Charlayne Hunter — perform in relation to that opening claim?

choices.label: A
choices.text: They contradict the opening claim by showing that Black Southerners who stayed behind, like Walker's family, actually retained full access to their homeland.

choices.label: B
choices.text: They extend and ground the opening claim by offering Walker's personal witness of departure and a televised civil rights struggle as evidence that memory replaced physical belonging.

choices.label: C
choices.text: They shift the paragraph's focus away from memory entirely, replacing it with a new argument about the courage required to integrate Southern universities.

choices.label: D
choices.text: They qualify the opening claim by suggesting that only fair-skinned Black Southerners like Holmes and Hunter were truly forced to rely on memory as homeland.

cards.textTitle: Choice: A Tribute to Dr. Martin Luther King, Jr.
cards.standardTitle: Central idea and supporting evidence
cards.excerpt: In 1960, my mother bought a television set, and each day after school I watched Hamilton Holmes and Charlayne Hunter as they struggled to integrate—fair-skinned as they were—the University of Georgia. And then, one day, there appeared the face of Dr. Martin Luther King, Jr. What a funny name, I thought. At the moment I first saw him, he was being handcuffed and shoved into a police truck. He had dared to claim his rights as a native son and had been arrested. He displayed no fear, but seemed calm and serene, unaware of his own extraordinary courage. His whole body, like his conscience, was at peace. At the moment I saw his resistance I knew I would never be able to live in this country without resisting everything that sought to disinherit me, and I would never be forced away from the land of my birth without a fight.
cards.whyThisWorks: The paragraph builds from a specific scene—King being handcuffed and shoved into a police truck—to the narrator's declaration that she 'would never be able to live in this country without resisting everything that sought to disinherit me,' giving students a concrete anchor for distinguishing the central idea from isolated details.
cards.skillStrategy: Ask yourself: what does the narrator say she learned or decided because of what she witnessed? That conclusion is the central idea, not just a description of what happened.
evidencePoints: At the moment I saw his resistance I knew I would never be able to live in this country without resisting everything that sought to disinherit me
He displayed no fear, but seemed calm and serene, unaware of his own extraordinary courage.
cards.question: The narrator ends the paragraph by stating she 'would never be able to live in this country without resisting everything that sought to disinherit me.' What central idea does this declaration, together with the scene of King's arrest, express?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Watching Hamilton Holmes and Charlayne Hunter integrate the University of Georgia on television first introduced the narrator to the civil rights movement.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Seeing King remain calm and courageous while being arrested transformed the narrator's understanding of herself and produced a lifelong personal commitment to resist injustice in her own country.

choices.label: C
choices.text: King's arrest proved that even peaceful civil rights leaders were treated as criminals by authorities in the 1960s.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The narrator was struck by King's unusual name and his physical composure at the moment she first saw him on television.

cards.textTitle: Choice: A Tribute to Dr. Martin Luther King, Jr.
cards.standardTitle: Rhetorical appeals and author purpose
cards.excerpt: If it is true that land does not belong to anyone until they have buried a body in it, then the land of my birthplace belongs to me, dozens of times over. Yet the history of my family, like that of all black Southerners, is a history of dispossession. We loved the land and worked the land, but we never owned it; and even if we bought land, as my great-grandfather did after the Civil War, it was always in danger of being taken away, as his was, during the period following Reconstruction. My father inherited nothing of material value from his father, and when I came of age in the early sixties I awoke to the bitter knowledge that in order just to continue to love the land of my birth, I was expected to leave it.
cards.whyThisWorks: Walker's closing line — 'in order just to continue to love the land of my birth, I was expected to leave it' — is a clear pathos-driven moment where painful irony invites readers to feel the emotional cost of racial dispossession, making the appeal and its purpose directly identifiable from the text.
cards.skillStrategy: When identifying a rhetorical appeal, find the exact words the author uses and ask: is the author giving evidence and reasoning (logos), establishing trust and authority (ethos), or triggering an emotional response (pathos)?
evidencePoints: in order just to continue to love the land of my birth, I was expected to leave it
We loved the land and worked the land, but we never owned it
cards.question: Walker ends the paragraph with the statement that 'in order just to continue to love the land of my birth, I was expected to leave it.' Which rhetorical appeal does this statement primarily represent, and why does Walker use it here?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Logos, because the statement completes a cause-and-effect argument Walker has built across the paragraph to prove that Black Southerners were legally barred from land ownership after Reconstruction.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Pathos, because the painful irony of being forced to abandon the land she loved — simply to survive — is meant to make readers feel the personal and emotional weight of racial injustice.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Ethos, because Walker positions herself as a credible witness to Southern history by connecting her own experience to her great-grandfather's documented land loss after the Civil War.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Pathos, because Walker uses the word 'love' to appeal to readers' feelings about family loyalty, shifting the paragraph's focus away from racial injustice toward a universal theme of belonging.

cards.textTitle: Choice: A Tribute to Dr. Martin Luther King, Jr.
cards.standardTitle: Rhetoric and reader effect
cards.excerpt: You know that this very room, in this very restaurant, was closed to people of color not more than five years ago. And that we eat here together tonight largely through his efforts and his blood. We accept the common pleasures of life, assuredly, in his name. 11. What does Alice Walker mean in the above highlighted statement? But add to all of these things the one thing that seems to me second to none in importance: He gave us back our heritage. He gave us back our homeland; the bones and dust of our ancestors, who may now sleep within our caring and our hearing. He gave us the blueness of the Georgia sky, in autumn as in summer; the colors of the Southern winter as well as glimpses of the green of vacation-time spring.
cards.whyThisWorks: Walker's anaphoric repetition of 'He gave us back' builds emotional momentum and reinforces the magnitude of King's legacy, making it an ideal example for analyzing how repetition affects the reader.
cards.skillStrategy: When you spot repeated phrases, ask yourself: what feeling does this pattern build, and why might the writer choose to hammer that idea more than once?
evidencePoints: He gave us back our heritage. He gave us back our homeland; the bones and dust of our ancestors
He gave us the blueness of the Georgia sky, in autumn as in summer; the colors of the Southern winter as well as glimpses of the green of vacation-time spring.
cards.question: Read the following sentences from the passage: 'He gave us back our heritage. He gave us back our homeland; the bones and dust of our ancestors, who may now sleep within our caring and our hearing. He gave us the blueness of the Georgia sky.' How does Walker's repetition of 'He gave us' affect the reader?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The repeated phrase signals that Walker is listing King's political achievements in order of importance, from greatest to least.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The repeated phrase creates a cumulative sense of gratitude and reverence, making King's contributions feel vast and deeply personal to Black Americans.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The repeated phrase suggests that Walker doubts whether King alone deserves credit, implying others also contributed to these gains.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The repeated phrase slows the reader down to emphasize that the restaurant described earlier was the most important symbol of King's work.

cards.textTitle: Choice: A Tribute to Dr. Martin Luther King, Jr.
cards.standardTitle: Paraphrase grade-level text
cards.excerpt: What a funny name, I thought. At the moment I first saw him, he was being handcuffed and shoved into a police truck. He had dared to claim his rights as a native son and had been arrested. He displayed no fear, but seemed calm and serene, unaware of his own extraordinary courage. His whole body, like his conscience, was at peace. At the moment I saw his resistance I knew I would never be able to live in this country without resisting everything that sought to disinherit me, and I would never be forced away from the land of my birth without a fight. He was The One, The Hero, The One Fearless Person for whom we had waited.
cards.whyThisWorks: The sentence 'At the moment I saw his resistance I knew I would never be able to live in this country without resisting everything that sought to disinherit me' presents a clear, testable claim about how witnessing King's courage transformed the narrator's personal resolve, making it ideal for a paraphrase item.

evidencePoints: At the moment I saw his resistance I knew I would never be able to live in this country without resisting everything that sought to disinherit me
I would never be forced away from the land of my birth without a fight
cards.question: Read the following sentence from the passage: 'At the moment I saw his resistance I knew I would never be able to live in this country without resisting everything that sought to disinherit me.' Which of the following most accurately restates the meaning of this sentence?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Watching King be arrested made the narrator feel hopeless about ever belonging in America.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Seeing King resist inspired the narrator to commit to fighting back against anything that tried to strip away her rightful place in her own country.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The narrator decided to follow King's example by getting arrested alongside him to protest injustice.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Witnessing King's calm demeanor convinced the narrator that peaceful acceptance was the only way to survive in America.

cards.question: Read the following sentence from the passage: 'At the moment I saw his resistance I knew I would never be able to live in this country without resisting everything that sought to disinherit me, and I would never be forced away from the land of my birth without a fight.' Which of the following most accurately restates the meaning of this sentence?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Watching King be arrested made the narrator realize she needed to leave the country in order to protect herself from those who wanted to take away her rights.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Seeing King resist injustice inspired the narrator to commit to standing up against anything that tried to strip her of her place and rights in her own country.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The narrator decided that King's courage proved no one could ever truly be forced from their homeland, because resistance always leads to victory.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Witnessing King's arrest caused the narrator to feel afraid that she, too, would one day be handcuffed and removed from the country she was born in.

cards.standardTitle: Paraphrase grade-level text
cards.excerpt: If we pay proper attention, we shall find that whenever it is said that a State cannot act because it has no central point, it is the centralization of the government in which it is deficient. It is frequently asserted, and we are prepared to assent to the proposition, that the German empire was never able to bring all its powers into action. But the reason was, that the State was never able to enforce obedience to its general laws, because the several members of that great body always claimed the right, or found the means, of refusing their co-operation to the representatives of the common authority, even in the affairs which concerned the mass of the people; in other words, because there was no centralization of government. The same remark is applicable to the Middle Ages; the cause of all the confusion of feudal society was that the control, not only of local but of general interests, was divided amongst a thousand hands, and broken up in a thousand different ways; the absence of a central government prevented the nations of Europe from advancing with energy in any straightforward course.
cards.whyThisWorks: Tocqueville makes a clear, arguable claim about why the German empire failed—that it could not enforce obedience to its general laws because members refused to cooperate with central authority—giving students a specific sentence to paraphrase and test for meaning preservation versus distortion.
cards.skillStrategy: When paraphrasing a claim, keep the cause-and-effect relationship intact and make sure your restatement includes both what happened and why, without adding or removing key ideas.
evidencePoints: the State was never able to enforce obedience to its general laws
the several members of that great body always claimed the right, or found the means, of refusing their co-operation to the representatives of the common authority
cards.question: Read the following sentence from the passage: 'the State was never able to enforce obedience to its general laws, because the several members of that great body always claimed the right, or found the means, of refusing their co-operation to the representatives of the common authority.' Which of the following most accurately restates this claim about the German empire?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The German empire's central government was too weak to create general laws, so its member states were forced to govern themselves without any common authority.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The German empire could not make its general laws obeyed because its member states consistently withheld their cooperation from the central authority.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The German empire failed because its representatives refused to enforce the laws passed by the member states, leaving the common authority powerless.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The German empire's member states eventually claimed full independence from the central authority, making it impossible to pass any general laws at all.

cards.standardTitle: Paraphrase grade-level text
cards.excerpt: The citizen of the United States is taught from his earliest infancy to rely upon his own exertions in order to resist the evils and the difficulties of life; he looks upon social authority with an eye of mistrust and anxiety, and he only claims its assistance when he is quite unable to shift without it. This habit may even be traced in the schools of the rising generation, where the children in their games are wont to submit to rules which they have themselves established, and to punish misdemeanors which they have themselves defined. The same spirit pervades every act of social life. If a stoppage occurs in a thoroughfare, and the circulation of the public is hindered, the neighbors immediately constitute a deliberative body; and this extemporaneous assembly gives rise to an executive power which remedies the inconvenience before anybody has thought of recurring to an authority superior to that of the persons immediately concerned. If the public pleasures are concerned, an association is formed to provide for the splendor and the regularity of the entertainment. Societies are formed to resist enemies which are exclusively of a moral nature, and to diminish the vice of intemperance: in the United States associations are established to promote public order, commerce, industry, morality, and religion; for there is no end which the human will, seconded by the collective exertions of individuals, despairs of attaining.
cards.whyThisWorks: The final sentence of the excerpt states a clear, paraphraseable claim about the power of collective human effort, making it ideal for testing whether students can accurately restate a complex idea in simpler terms without distorting its meaning.
cards.skillStrategy: Read the target sentence carefully, identify its core claim, then check each answer choice to see which one keeps the same meaning without adding, removing, or twisting any part of it.
evidencePoints: for there is no end which the human will, seconded by the collective exertions of individuals, despairs of attaining
associations are established to promote public order, commerce, industry, morality, and religion
cards.question: Read the following sentence from the passage: 'for there is no end which the human will, seconded by the collective exertions of individuals, despairs of attaining.' Which of the following most accurately restates the meaning of this sentence?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Human willpower alone is strong enough to accomplish any goal, regardless of outside help.

choices.label: B
choices.text: When individual determination is supported by people working together, there is no goal that seems impossible to reach.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Americans have given up hope of achieving goals that require the combined efforts of many people.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Collective effort in society is only useful when individuals have already exhausted their personal resources.

cards.standardTitle: Paraphrase grade-level text
cards.excerpt:
It may be conceived that, in the case under consideration, the Union might have used the State before a Federal court, which would have annulled the act, and by this means it would have adopted a natural course of proceeding; but the judicial power would have been placed in open hostility to the State, and it was desirable to avoid this predicament as much as possible. The Americans hold that it is nearly impossible that a new law should not impair the interests of some private individual by its provisions: these private interests are assumed by the American legislators as the ground of attack against such measures as may be prejudicial to the Union, and it is to these cases that the protection of the Supreme Court is extended.

Suppose a State vends a certain portion of its territory to a company, and that a year afterwards it passes a law by which the territory is otherwise disposed of, and that clause of the Constitution which prohibits laws impairing the obligation of contracts violated. When the purchaser under the second act appears to take possession, the possessor under the first act brings his action before the tribunals of the Union, and causes the title of the claimant to be pronounced null and void. *l Thus, in point of fact, the judicial power of the Union is contesting the claims of the sovereignty of a State; but it only acts indirectly and upon a special application of detail: it attacks the law in its consequences, not in its principle, and it rather weakens than destroys it.
cards.whyThisWorks: Tocqueville's closing sentence makes a precise, paraphraseable claim about how federal judicial power challenges state authority indirectly—by targeting a law's effects rather than its existence—giving students a rich, nuanced statement to restate accurately.
cards.skillStrategy: Read the sentence carefully, identify its main claim, then check which answer keeps all parts of that meaning without adding, removing, or twisting anything.
evidencePoints: it only acts indirectly and upon a special application of detail: it attacks the law in its consequences, not in its principle
it rather weakens than destroys it
cards.question: Read this sentence from the second paragraph: 'Thus, in point of fact, the judicial power of the Union is contesting the claims of the sovereignty of a State; but it only acts indirectly and upon a special application of detail: it attacks the law in its consequences, not in its principle, and it rather weakens than destroys it.' Which of the following most accurately restates the meaning of this sentence?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The federal courts openly challenge state sovereignty by striking down state laws entirely, which destroys the authority of states to govern themselves.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Federal judicial power does oppose state authority, but it does so in a roundabout way—targeting the harmful effects of a specific law rather than the law itself—so the law is damaged but not eliminated.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The Union avoids any conflict with state sovereignty by refusing to rule on the principles behind state laws, leaving those laws fully intact and in force.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Federal courts contest state laws only when private individuals bring cases, and in doing so they completely abolish whichever state law violated the Constitution.

cards.standardTitle: Paraphrase grade-level text
cards.excerpt:
Every Federal system contains defects which baffle the efforts of the legislator—The Federal system is complex—It demands a daily exercise of discretion on the part of the citizens—Practical knowledge of government common amongst the Americans—Relative weakness of the Government of the Union, another defect inherent in the Federal system—The Americans have diminished without remedying it—The sovereignty of the separate States apparently weaker, but really stronger, than that of the Union—Why?—Natural causes of union must exist between confederate peoples besides the laws—What these causes are amongst the Anglo-Americans—Maine and Georgia, separated by a distance of a thousand miles, more naturally united than Normandy and Brittany—War, the main peril of confederations—This proved even by the example of the United States—The Union has no great wars to fear—Why?—Dangers to which Europeans would be exposed if they adopted the Federal system of the Americans.

When a legislator succeeds, after persevering efforts, in exercising an indirect influence upon the destiny of nations, his genius is lauded by mankind, whilst, in point of fact, the geographical position of the country which he is unable to change, a social condition which arose without his co-operation, manners and opinions which he cannot trace to their source, and an origin with which he is unacquainted, exercise so irresistible an influence over the courses of society that he is himself borne away by the current, after an ineffectual resistance. Like the navigator, he may direct the vessel which bears him along, but he can neither change its structure, nor raise the winds, nor lull the waters which swell beneath him.
cards.whyThisWorks: The final sentence of the second paragraph contains a complex extended metaphor with multiple embedded clauses that students must untangle to accurately restate Tocqueville's claim about the legislator's limited power.
cards.skillStrategy: Break the long sentence into its core subject, verb, and key comparisons, then check that your restatement keeps all the limits the author places on the navigator/legislator.
evidencePoints: Like the navigator, he may direct the vessel which bears him along, but he can neither change its structure, nor raise the winds, nor lull the waters which swell beneath him.
he is himself borne away by the current, after an ineffectual resistance
cards.question: Read the following sentence from the passage: 'Like the navigator, he may direct the vessel which bears him along, but he can neither change its structure, nor raise the winds, nor lull the waters which swell beneath him.' Which restatement most accurately captures the meaning of this sentence?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A legislator, like a navigator, has complete control over the direction of society as long as he steers carefully and avoids dangerous conditions.

choices.label: B
choices.text: A legislator can guide the course of society to some degree, but he cannot alter the deeper forces—such as geography, social conditions, and manners—that ultimately carry him along.

choices.label: C
choices.text: A legislator is entirely powerless, unable even to steer society, because the forces of geography and opinion overwhelm any action he attempts.

choices.label: D
choices.text: A legislator resembles a navigator who must abandon the vessel when the winds and waters become too strong to manage.

cards.standardTitle: Paraphrase grade-level text
cards.excerpt:
These topics are collaterally connected with my subject without forming a part of it; they are American without being democratic; and to portray democracy has been my principal aim. It was therefore necessary to postpone these questions, which I now take up as the proper termination of my work.

The territory now occupied or claimed by the American Union spreads from the shores of the Atlantic to those of the Pacific Ocean. On the east and west its limits are those of the continent itself. On the south it advances nearly to the tropic, and it extends upwards to the icy regions of the North. The human beings who are scattered over this space do not form, as in Europe, so many branches of the same stock. Three races, naturally distinct, and, I might almost say, hostile to each other, are discoverable amongst them at the first glance. Almost insurmountable barriers had been raised between them by education and by law, as well as by their origin and outward characteristics; but fortune has brought them together on the same soil, where, although they are mixed, they do not amalgamate, and each race fulfils its destiny apart.
cards.whyThisWorks: The sentence about three races being brought together yet remaining separate offers a precise, complex claim that students must paraphrase without overstating the conflict, understating the separation, or confusing cause and effect.
cards.skillStrategy: Read the original sentence carefully, then ask yourself: does my paraphrase keep every part of the author's idea — no more, no less?
evidencePoints: Almost insurmountable barriers had been raised between them by education and by law, as well as by their origin and outward characteristics
fortune has brought them together on the same soil, where, although they are mixed, they do not amalgamate, and each race fulfils its destiny apart
cards.question: Read this sentence from the excerpt: 'fortune has brought them together on the same soil, where, although they are mixed, they do not amalgamate, and each race fulfils its destiny apart.' Which of the following most accurately restates the meaning of this sentence?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Chance placed the three races on the same land, and over time they gradually merged into a single unified people with a shared future.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Circumstance placed the three races on the same land, but despite living alongside one another, they did not blend together and each followed its own separate path.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The three races were forcibly relocated to the same territory, where constant hostility prevented any form of coexistence or shared society.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The three races happened to occupy the same land, and while they interacted frequently, their differences were minor and easily overcome with time.

cards.standardTitle: Paraphrase grade-level text
cards.excerpt: And indeed the lawyer-like character which I am endeavoring to depict is most distinctly to be met with in England: there laws are esteemed not so much because they are good as because they are old; and if it be necessary to modify them in any respect, or to adapt them the changes which time operates in society, recourse is had to the most inconceivable contrivances in order to uphold the traditionary fabric, and to maintain that nothing has been done which does not square with the intentions and complete the labors of former generations. The very individuals who conduct these changes disclaim all intention of innovation, and they had rather resort to absurd expedients than plead guilty to so great a crime. This spirit appertains more especially to the English lawyers; they seem indifferent to the real meaning of what they treat, and they direct all their attention to the letter, seeming inclined to infringe the rules of common sense and of humanity rather than to swerve one title from the law. The English legislation may be compared to the stock of an old tree, upon which lawyers have engrafted the most various shoots, with the hope that, although their fruits may differ, their foliage at least will be confounded with the venerable trunk which supports them all.
cards.whyThisWorks: The sentence about English lawyers directing 'all their attention to the letter' rather than 'the real meaning' offers a precise, paraphraseable claim with multiple distortion opportunities—overstating, understating, or reversing the lawyer-letter/meaning contrast.
cards.skillStrategy: Restate the author's exact idea in your own words, making sure you keep both parts of any contrast the author makes—don't drop one side or flip the meaning.
evidencePoints: they seem indifferent to the real meaning of what they treat, and they direct all their attention to the letter
seeming inclined to infringe the rules of common sense and of humanity rather than to swerve one title from the law
cards.question: Read this sentence from the passage: 'They seem indifferent to the real meaning of what they treat, and they direct all their attention to the letter, seeming inclined to infringe the rules of common sense and of humanity rather than to swerve one title from the law.' Which of the following most accurately restates this sentence?

choices.label: A
choices.text: English lawyers care deeply about the spirit of the law and will bend its exact wording whenever common sense demands it.

choices.label: B
choices.text: English lawyers show little concern for what the law actually means and focus instead on its precise wording, even when doing so conflicts with common sense or human welfare.

choices.label: C
choices.text: English lawyers ignore both the meaning and the wording of the law, preferring to follow their own judgment about what is humane.

choices.label: D
choices.text: English lawyers value the real meaning of the law above all else, refusing to let technical wording override justice.

cards.standardTitle: Paraphrase grade-level text
cards.excerpt:
Men who have more especially devoted themselves to legal pursuits derive from those occupations certain habits of order, a taste for formalities, and a kind of instinctive regard for the regular connection of ideas, which naturally render them very hostile to the revolutionary spirit and the unreflecting passions of the multitude.

The special information which lawyers derive from their studies ensures them a separate station in society, and they constitute a sort of privileged body in the scale of intelligence. This notion of their superiority perpetually recurs to them in the practice of their profession: they are the masters of a science which is necessary, but which is not very generally known; they serve as arbiters between the citizens; and the habit of directing the blind passions of parties in litigation to their purpose inspires them with a certain contempt for the judgment of the multitude. To this it may be added that they naturally constitute a body, not by any previous understanding, or by an agreement which directs them to a common end; but the analogy of their studies and the uniformity of their proceedings connect their minds together, as much as a common interest could combine their endeavors.
cards.whyThisWorks: Tocqueville's formal 18th-century prose—phrases like 'instinctive regard for the regular connection of ideas' and 'directing the blind passions of parties in litigation'—requires students to translate elevated, archaic diction into plain modern meaning, making it ideal for the paraphrase/translation subskill.
cards.skillStrategy: When you hit formal or old-fashioned wording, break the sentence into smaller pieces and swap each difficult phrase for a simpler everyday equivalent, then check that your restatement keeps the same idea.
evidencePoints: the habit of directing the blind passions of parties in litigation to their purpose inspires them with a certain contempt for the judgment of the multitude

they naturally constitute a body, not by any previous understanding, or by an agreement which directs them to a common end; but the analogy of their studies and the uniformity of their proceedings connect their minds together
cards.question: Read this sentence from the passage: 'the habit of directing the blind passions of parties in litigation to their purpose inspires them with a certain contempt for the judgment of the multitude.' Which restatement most accurately captures the meaning of this sentence in plain language?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Because lawyers must control their own emotions during trials, they eventually lose respect for the legal system and its procedures.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Regularly steering the uncontrolled emotions of people involved in lawsuits leads lawyers to look down on the reasoning of ordinary people.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Lawyers develop contempt for their clients because those clients refuse to follow legal advice during court proceedings.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Managing the strong feelings of people in court cases teaches lawyers to distrust other lawyers who lack courtroom experience.

cards.standardTitle: Paraphrase grade-level text
cards.excerpt:
A portion of the tastes and of the habits of the aristocracy may consequently be discovered in the characters of men in the profession of the law. They participate in the same instinctive love of order and of formalities; and they entertain the same repugnance to the actions of the multitude, and the same secret contempt of the government of the people. I do not mean to say that the natural propensities of lawyers are sufficiently strong to sway them irresistibly; for they, like most other men, are governed by their private interests and the advantages of the moment.

In a state of society in which the members of the legal profession are prevented from holding that rank in the political world which they enjoy in private life, we may rest assured that they will be the foremost agents of revolution. But it must then be inquired whether the cause which induces them to innovate and to destroy is accidental, or whether it belongs to some lasting purpose which they entertain. It is true that lawyers mainly contributed to the overthrow of the French monarchy in 1789; but it remains to be seen whether they acted thus because they had studied the laws, or because they were prohibited from co-operating in the work of legislation.
cards.whyThisWorks: Tocqueville's formal, archaic phrasing—'repugnance to the actions of the multitude' and 'secret contempt of the government of the people'—requires students to translate elevated 19th-century diction into plain modern meaning without distorting his claim about lawyers.
cards.skillStrategy: When you encounter formal or old-fashioned language, break the sentence into parts and swap each difficult phrase for a plain modern word or phrase, then check that the overall meaning still matches.
evidencePoints: they entertain the same repugnance to the actions of the multitude, and the same secret contempt of the government of the people
A portion of the tastes and of the habits of the aristocracy may consequently be discovered in the characters of men in the profession of the law

Which restatement most accurately captures the meaning of this sentence in plain language?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Lawyers openly oppose all forms of government and publicly declare their hatred of ordinary citizens.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Lawyers share the aristocracy's natural preference for order and rules, along with a hidden dislike of mass popular action and democratic rule.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Lawyers enjoy the same social privileges as aristocrats and therefore support the rights of common people over formal institutions.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Lawyers are drawn to order and formality, but they ultimately respect the will of the majority more than aristocratic traditions.

cards.standardTitle: Paraphrase grade-level text
cards.excerpt: The main object of the political jurisdiction which obtains in the United States is, therefore, to deprive the ill-disposed citizen of an authority which he has used amiss, and to prevent him from ever acquiring it again. This is evidently an administrative measure sanctioned by the formalities of a judicial decision. In this matter the Americans have created a mixed system; they have surrounded the act which removes a public functionary with the securities of a political trial; and they have deprived all political condemnations of their severest penalties. Every link of the system may easily be traced from this point; we at once perceive why the American constitutions subject all the civil functionaries to the jurisdiction of the Senate, whilst the military, whose crimes are nevertheless more formidable, are exempted from that tribunal. In the civil service none of the American functionaries can be said to be removable; the places which some of them occupy are inalienable, and the others are chosen for a term which cannot be shortened. It is therefore necessary to try them all in order to deprive them of their authority. But military officers are dependent on the chief magistrate of the State, who is himself a civil functionary, and the decision which condemns him is a blow upon them all.
cards.whyThisWorks: Tocqueville's formal 18th-century political prose—phrases like 'ill-disposed citizen,' 'authority which he has used amiss,' and 'administrative measure sanctioned by the formalities of a judicial decision'—requires students to translate dense, archaic diction into plain modern meaning.
cards.skillStrategy: When you encounter formal or archaic language, break the sentence into parts and ask what each phrase means in everyday terms, then combine those meanings into a plain restatement.
evidencePoints: The main object of the political jurisdiction which obtains in the United States is, therefore, to deprive the ill-disposed citizen of an authority which he has used amiss, and to prevent him from ever acquiring it again.
This is evidently an administrative measure sanctioned by the formalities of a judicial decision.
cards.question: Read this sentence from the passage: 'The main object of the political jurisdiction which obtains in the United States is, therefore, to deprive the ill-disposed citizen of an authority which he has used amiss, and to prevent him from ever acquiring it again.' Which of the following most accurately restates what this sentence means?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The American legal system punishes all citizens equally by permanently removing their political rights after any wrongdoing.

choices.label: B

choices.label: C

choices.label: D

cards.standardTitle: Paraphrase grade-level text
cards.excerpt:
Hitherto, wherever the whites have been the most powerful, they have maintained the blacks in a subordinate or a servile position; wherever the negroes have been strongest they have destroyed the whites; such has been the only retribution which has ever taken place between the two races.

I see that in a certain portion of the territory of the United States at the present day, the legal barrier which separated the two races is tending to fall away, but not that which exists in the manners of the country; slavery recedes, but the prejudice to which it has given birth remains stationary. Whosoever has inhabited the United States must have perceived that in those parts of the Union in which the negroes are no longer slaves, they have in no wise drawn nearer to the whites. On the contrary, the prejudice of the race appears to be stronger in the States which have abolished slavery, than in those where it still exists; and nowhere is it so intolerant as in those States where servitude has never been known.
cards.whyThisWorks: The sentence 'slavery recedes, but the prejudice to which it has given birth remains stationary' uses inverted and compressed syntax that requires students to unpack the causal relationship between slavery's decline and the persistence of racial prejudice.
cards.skillStrategy: Break the sentence into its two parts—what is changing and what is not—then restate each part in plain language before combining them.
evidencePoints: slavery recedes, but the prejudice to which it has given birth remains stationary
the prejudice of the race appears to be stronger in the States which have abolished slavery, than in those where it still exists
cards.question: Read this sentence from the passage: 'slavery recedes, but the prejudice to which it has given birth remains stationary.' Which restatement most accurately captures the meaning of this sentence?

choices.label: A
choices.text: As slavery slowly disappears, racial prejudice disappears along with it, leaving both institutions weakened at the same pace.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Although slavery is declining, the racial prejudice that slavery created has not diminished and stays fixed in place.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Slavery has already been fully abolished, and the prejudice it once produced has been replaced by new legal barriers between the races.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Racial prejudice existed before slavery and continues to grow stronger precisely because slavery is retreating from society.

cards.standardTitle: Paraphrase grade-level text
cards.excerpt:
I am no longer comparing the Anglo-American States to foreign nations; but I am contrasting them with each other, and endeavoring to discover why they are so unlike. The arguments which are derived from the nature of the country and the difference of legislation are here all set aside. Recourse must be had to some other cause; and what other cause can there be except the manners of the people?

It is in the Eastern States that the Anglo-Americans have been longest accustomed to the government of democracy, and that they have adopted the habits and conceived the notions most favorable to its maintenance. Democracy has gradually penetrated into their customs, their opinions, and the forms of social intercourse; it is to be found in all the details of daily life equally as in the laws. In the Eastern States the instruction and practical education of the people have been most perfected, and religion has been most thoroughly amalgamated with liberty. Now these habits, opinions, customs, and convictions are precisely the constituent elements of that which I have denominated manners.
cards.whyThisWorks: The sentence 'Now these habits, opinions, customs, and convictions are precisely the constituent elements of that which I have denominated manners' uses formal, inverted syntax and abstract vocabulary that requires students to break it into parts and restate its core claim accurately.
cards.skillStrategy: When a sentence stacks abstract nouns and uses formal phrasing like 'that which I have denominated,' break it into two parts: what things are being listed, and what those things add up to.
evidencePoints: Now these habits, opinions, customs, and convictions are precisely the constituent elements of that which I have denominated manners.
Democracy has gradually penetrated into their customs, their opinions, and the forms of social intercourse; it is to be found in all the details of daily life equally as in the laws.
cards.question: Read this sentence from the passage: 'Now these habits, opinions, customs, and convictions are precisely the constituent elements of that which I have denominated manners.' Which of the following most accurately restates the meaning of this sentence?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Habits, opinions, customs, and convictions are qualities that democracy gradually introduces into a society over time.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The habits, opinions, customs, and convictions Tocqueville has described are exactly what he means when he uses the word 'manners.'

choices.label: C
choices.text: Manners are one of several elements that shape habits, opinions, customs, and convictions in a democratic society.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The Eastern States developed strong manners because their habits and convictions were shaped by religious and democratic instruction.

cards.standardTitle: Paraphrase grade-level text
cards.excerpt:
But sometimes the sovereign authority is composed of preorganized political bodies, by virtue of circumstances anterior to their union; and in this case the provincial governments assume the control, not only of those affairs which more peculiarly belong to their province, but of all, or of a part of the mixed affairs to which allusion has been made. For the confederate nations which were independent sovereign States before their union, and which still represent a very considerable share of the sovereign power, have only consented to cede to the general Government the exercise of those rights which are indispensable to the Union.

When the national Government, independently of the prerogatives inherent in its nature, is invested with the right of regulating the affairs which relate partly to the general and partly to the local interests, it possesses a preponderating influence. Not only are its own rights extensive, but all the rights which it does not possess exist by its sufferance, and it may be apprehended that the provincial governments may be deprived of their natural and necessary prerogatives by its influence.
cards.whyThisWorks: The sentence beginning 'Not only are its own rights extensive…' uses inverted syntax and abstract legal vocabulary that requires students to untangle a two-part claim about the national government's power and its relationship to provincial rights.
cards.skillStrategy: Break the sentence into its two main parts—what the national government has directly, and what it controls indirectly—then restate each part in plain language.
evidencePoints: Not only are its own rights extensive, but all the rights which it does not possess exist by its sufferance
it may be apprehended that the provincial governments may be deprived of their natural and necessary prerogatives by its influence
cards.question: Read this sentence from the second paragraph: 'Not only are its own rights extensive, but all the rights which it does not possess exist by its sufferance, and it may be apprehended that the provincial governments may be deprived of their natural and necessary prerogatives by its influence.' Which of the following most accurately restates the meaning of this sentence?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The national government holds unlimited rights, and provincial governments have already lost all of their authority to the national government's direct commands.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The national government not only holds broad rights of its own, but even the rights it does not directly hold exist only because the national government allows them to, putting provincial governments at risk of losing their essential powers.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The national government's rights are extensive, but provincial governments retain full control over their own affairs because the national government cannot interfere with local prerogatives.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Because the national government tolerates the rights of provincial governments, those provincial governments have gained more influence than the national government originally intended.

cards.standardTitle: Paraphrase grade-level text
cards.excerpt:
Lastly, when we arrive at the new South-western States, in which the constitution of society dates but from yesterday, and presents an agglomeration of adventurers and speculators, we are amazed at the persons who are invested with public authority, and we are led to ask by what force, independent of the legislation and of the men who direct it, the State can be protected, and society be made to flourish.

There are certain laws of a democratic nature which contribute, nevertheless, to correct, in some measure, the dangerous tendencies of democracy. On entering the House of Representatives of Washington one is struck by the vulgar demeanor of that great assembly. The eye frequently does not discover a man of celebrity within its walls. Its members are almost all obscure individuals whose names present no associations to the mind: they are mostly village lawyers, men in trade, or even persons belonging to the lower classes of society. In a country in which education is very general, it is said that the representatives of the people do not always know how to write correctly.
cards.whyThisWorks: The sentence 'In a country in which education is very general, it is said that the representatives of the people do not always know how to write correctly' uses an inverted conditional structure and embedded irony that requires students to untangle the relationship between widespread education and the surprising inadequacy of elected officials.
cards.skillStrategy: Break the sentence into its two parts — what is true about the country and what is surprisingly true about its representatives — then restate both parts together in plain language.
evidencePoints: In a country in which education is very general, it is said that the representatives of the people do not always know how to write correctly.

Its members are almost all obscure individuals whose names present no associations to the mind: they are mostly village lawyers, men in trade, or even persons belonging to the lower classes of society.
