cards.question: What is the primary job of the paragraph beginning 'For I have known them all already, known them all'?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The paragraph introduces Prufrock's fear of social judgment for the first time by describing the voices he hears around him.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The paragraph extends and deepens Prufrock's paralysis by replacing his hypothetical future deferrals with evidence of a lifetime already spent in passive routine, ending in the same unanswered question.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The paragraph contrasts Prufrock's past confidence with his present hesitation, showing that he once acted boldly before age diminished him.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The paragraph concludes Prufrock's self-examination by resolving his indecision and preparing him to speak to the women in the room.

choices.label: A

choices.label: B

cards.standardTitle: Rhetoric and reader effect
cards.excerpt: And if America is to be a great nation, this must become true. And so let freedom ring from the prodigious hilltops of New Hampshire. Let freedom ring from the mighty mountains of New York. Let freedom ring from the heightening Alleghenies of Pennsylvania. Let freedom ring from the snow‐capped Rockies of Colorado. Let freedom ring from the curvaceous slopes of California. But not only that: Let freedom ring from Stone Mountain of Georgia. Let freedom ring from Lookout Mountain of Tennessee. Let freedom ring from every hill and molehill of Mississippi. From every mountainside, let freedom ring. And when this happens, when we allow freedom ring, when we let it ring from every village and every hamlet, from every state and every city, we will be able to speed up that day when all of God's children, black men and white men, Jews and Gentiles, Protestants and Catholics, will be able to join hands and sing in the words of the old Negro spiritual: Free at last! Free at last! Thank God Almighty, we are free at last!
cards.whyThisWorks: The excerpt's anaphoric repetition of 'Let freedom ring' across a geographic sweep, culminating in the exclamatory 'Free at last! Free at last!', gives students a clear, traceable rhetorical structure whose emotional effect can be analyzed and debated.
cards.skillStrategy: When you see a phrase repeated multiple times in a row, ask yourself: what feeling does that build up in me, and how does the moment right after the repetition land differently because of it?
evidencePoints: Let freedom ring from the prodigious hilltops of New Hampshire. Let freedom ring from the mighty mountains of New York. Let freedom ring from the heightening Alleghenies of Pennsylvania.
Free at last! Free at last! Thank God Almighty, we are free at last!
cards.question: In the excerpt, King repeats the phrase 'Let freedom ring' eight times across locations ranging from 'the prodigious hilltops of New Hampshire' to 'every hill and molehill of Mississippi,' then closes with 'Free at last! Free at last!' What effect does this shift from repeated demand to exclamation produce in the reader?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The geographic list of locations distracts the reader from King's argument, so the final cry of 'Free at last!' feels abrupt and disconnected from the rest of the passage.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Each repetition of 'Let freedom ring' accumulates urgency and longing, so that when 'Free at last!' arrives, the reader experiences it as the release of that built tension—a collective triumph rather than a distant hope.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The repeated phrase 'Let freedom ring' signals that freedom already exists in each named location, making 'Free at last!' a simple confirmation of a fact the reader already accepted.

choices.label: D
choices.text: By naming only specific mountains and states, King limits the reader's sense of who freedom applies to, so 'Free at last!' reads as a celebration for those regions alone rather than for all people.

texts.title: Speech to the Troops at Tilbury
texts.author: Queen Elizabeth I

cards.textTitle: Speech to the Troops at Tilbury
cards.standardTitle: Central idea and supporting evidence
cards.excerpt:
I know I have the body of a weak and feeble woman; but I have the heart and stomach of a king, and of a king of England too, and think foul scorn that Parma or Spain, or any prince of Europe, should dare to invade the borders of my realm: to which rather than any dishonour shall grow by me, I myself will take up arms, I myself will be your general, judge, and rewarder of every one of your virtues in the field.

I know already, for your forwardness you have deserved rewards and crowns; and We do assure you on a word of a prince, they shall be duly paid. In the mean time, my lieutenant general shall be in my stead, than whom never prince commanded a more noble or worthy subject; not doubting but by your obedience to my general, by your concord in the camp, and your valour in the field, we shall shortly have a famous victory over these enemies of my God, of my kingdom, and of my people.
cards.whyThisWorks: Elizabeth's explicit contrast between 'the body of a weak and feeble woman' and 'the heart and stomach of a king' gives students a concrete textual anchor for distinguishing a central claim from isolated details or topic labels.
cards.skillStrategy: Find the sentence where the speaker makes her biggest claim about herself or her purpose, then ask: does this idea connect everything else in the passage, or is it just one detail?

cards.question: When Elizabeth says, 'I know I have the body of a weak and feeble woman; but I have the heart and stomach of a king,' she is establishing a contrast that drives the rest of the speech. Which statement most accurately expresses the central idea that this contrast introduces and the rest of the passage supports?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Elizabeth admits that her physical weakness as a woman makes her unfit to lead in battle, so she must rely entirely on her lieutenant general to command the troops.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Despite her physical limitations as a woman, Elizabeth's royal courage and personal commitment to her troops and kingdom make her a capable leader who will secure victory against foreign invaders.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Elizabeth's primary concern in the speech is ensuring that her soldiers receive the financial rewards and crowns they have already earned through their bravery.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Elizabeth warns her troops that Spain and Parma are the most dangerous military threats England has ever faced and that defeat would bring dishonor to her reign.

cards.textTitle: Speech to the Troops at Tilbury
cards.standardTitle: Central idea and supporting evidence
cards.excerpt:
I know I have the body of a weak and feeble woman; but I have the heart and stomach of a king, and of a king of England too, and think foul scorn that Parma or Spain, or any prince of Europe, should dare to invade the borders of my realm: to which rather than any dishonour shall grow by me, I myself will take up arms, I myself will be your general, judge, and rewarder of every one of your virtues in the field.

I know already, for your forwardness you have deserved rewards and crowns; and We do assure you on a word of a prince, they shall be duly paid. In the mean time, my lieutenant general shall be in my stead, than whom never prince commanded a more noble or worthy subject; not doubting but by your obedience to my general, by your concord in the camp, and your valour in the field, we shall shortly have a famous victory over these enemies of my God, of my kingdom, and of my people.
cards.whyThisWorks: The excerpt contains both a central idea—Elizabeth's personal commitment to defend England regardless of her physical limitations—and a mix of strong evidence (her vow to take up arms herself) and weaker true details (promises of pay), allowing students to distinguish which evidence most directly supports that central idea.
cards.skillStrategy: Ask yourself: which piece of evidence directly proves the central idea, not just a related or supporting fact about the situation?
evidencePoints: I have the heart and stomach of a king, and of a king of England too
I myself will take up arms, I myself will be your general, judge, and rewarder of every one of your virtues in the field
cards.question: The central idea of Elizabeth's speech is that she is fully committed to defending England and leading her troops despite being a woman. Which evidence from the speech most directly supports this central idea?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Elizabeth promises that rewards and crowns already deserved by the troops 'shall be duly paid,' showing she values their service.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Elizabeth declares she has 'the heart and stomach of a king' and will personally 'take up arms' and serve as the troops' 'general, judge, and rewarder,' directly countering any doubt about her leadership.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Elizabeth names her lieutenant general as a 'noble or worthy subject' who will command in her stead, proving the army is well organized.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Elizabeth acknowledges she has 'the body of a weak and feeble woman,' which shows she is honest about the challenges she faces as a ruler.

cards.question: Read the following lines from the speech: 'I know I have the body of a weak and feeble woman; but I have the heart and stomach of a king.' How does this contrast affect the reader?

choices.label: A
choices.text: It causes the reader to doubt Elizabeth's fitness to lead because she openly admits physical weakness before her troops.

choices.label: B
choices.text: It shifts the reader's focus from Elizabeth's physical limitations to her inner strength and royal authority, making her claim to lead the army more convincing.

choices.label: C
choices.text: It reminds the reader that Elizabeth is asking her troops to overlook her gender out of loyalty rather than genuine confidence in her leadership.

choices.label: D
choices.text: It suggests that Elizabeth views the king's qualities as separate from her own identity, distancing herself from personal responsibility for the battle.

cards.question: The first paragraph ends with Elizabeth declaring, 'I myself will take up arms, I myself will be your general.' What is the job of the second paragraph in relation to that declaration?

choices.label: A
choices.text: It contradicts the declaration by revealing that Elizabeth will not personally lead, replacing her vow with a promise that her lieutenant general will command in her place.

choices.label: B
choices.text: It extends the declaration by shifting from Elizabeth's personal resolve to concrete promises of reward, delegated command, and a confident prediction of 'a famous victory.'

choices.label: C
choices.text: It restates the declaration by repeating Elizabeth's claim to have 'the heart and stomach of a king' as the basis for the soldiers' obedience.

choices.label: D
choices.text: It introduces the threat of Parma and Spain as a new argument that the declaration in the first paragraph does not yet address.

texts.title: The Danger of a Single Story
texts.author: Chimamanda Ngozi Adichie

cards.textTitle: The Danger of a Single Story
cards.standardTitle: Rhetoric and reader effect
cards.excerpt: I teach writing workshops in Lagos every summer, and it is amazing to me how many people apply, how many people are eager to write, to tell stories. My Nigerian publisher and I have just started a non-profit called Farafina Trust, and we have big dreams of building libraries and refurbishing libraries that already exist and providing books for state schools that don't have anything in their libraries, and also of organizing lots and lots of workshops, in reading and writing, for all the people who are eager to tell our many stories. Many stories matter. Stories have been used to dispossess and to malign, but stories can also be used to empower and to humanize. Stories can break the dignity of a people, but stories can also repair that broken dignity. The American writer Alice Walker wrote this about her Southern relatives who had moved to the North. She introduced them to a book about the Southern life that they had left behind: "They sat around, reading the book themselves, listening to me read the book, and a kind of paradise was regained." I would like to end with this thought: That when we reject the single story, when we realize that there is never a single story about any place, we regain a kind of paradise.
cards.whyThisWorks: Adichie's parallel contrasting structure — 'Stories have been used to dispossess and to malign, but stories can also be used to empower and to humanize' — gives students a clear, analyzable example of contrast as a rhetorical device with a measurable effect on the reader's understanding of storytelling's dual power.
cards.skillStrategy: When you spot a 'but' that flips an idea, ask yourself: what does the contrast force the reader to feel or believe that a single statement could not?
evidencePoints: Stories have been used to dispossess and to malign, but stories can also be used to empower and to humanize.
Stories can break the dignity of a people, but stories can also repair that broken dignity.
cards.question: Read the following sentences from the passage: 'Stories have been used to dispossess and to malign, but stories can also be used to empower and to humanize. Stories can break the dignity of a people, but stories can also repair that broken dignity.' How does Adichie's use of contrast in these sentences affect the reader?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The contrast between 'dispossess' and 'malign' shows that harmful stories are more dangerous than readers might expect, leaving the reader feeling alarmed about storytelling.

choices.label: B
choices.text: By pairing destructive uses of stories against restorative ones, Adichie pushes the reader to see storytelling not as inherently harmful but as a force whose direction depends on whose stories are told.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The repeated use of 'but' signals that Adichie is uncertain about her argument, causing the reader to question whether stories are truly powerful at all.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The contrast between breaking and repairing dignity focuses the reader's attention on physical harm rather than on the broader social role of storytelling.

cards.skillStrategy: Ask yourself: who is the audience, what does the author want them to feel or believe, and why does this specific appeal—emotional, logical, or ethical—fit that goal better than another approach would?

cards.question: Adichie ends her speech by quoting Alice Walker's phrase 'a kind of paradise was regained' and then applying that same phrase to her own conclusion. Why is this emotional appeal appropriate for her audience and purpose?

choices.label: A
choices.text: It establishes Adichie's credibility by showing she has read widely, which persuades her audience to trust her claims about Nigerian publishing.

choices.label: B
choices.text: It invites the audience to feel the personal restoration that comes from embracing multiple stories, making the abstract argument about dignity concrete and emotionally resonant.

choices.label: C
choices.text: It shifts responsibility onto Alice Walker so that Adichie avoids making a direct claim about the power of storytelling herself.

choices.label: D
choices.text: It appeals to the audience's sense of logic by providing a documented historical example that proves stories have always repaired broken communities.

cards.skillStrategy: Ask yourself: Is the author building trust (ethos), using logic or evidence (logos), or stirring emotion (pathos)—then find the exact words that create that effect.

cards.question: Adichie closes her speech by quoting Alice Walker's description of her Southern relatives—'a kind of paradise was regained'—and then echoing that phrase in her own final sentence. What rhetorical appeal does this strategy primarily create, and why does it fit Adichie's purpose?

choices.label: A
choices.text: It establishes ethos by citing a respected American author, which proves Adichie has researched the topic thoroughly enough to be trusted.

choices.label: B
choices.text: It creates pathos by connecting the image of 'paradise regained' to a feeling of wholeness and belonging, moving the audience to feel the personal cost of a single story and the hope of rejecting it.

choices.label: C
choices.text: It builds a logos-based argument by presenting Walker's relatives as statistical evidence that reading diverse stories produces measurable improvements in communities.

choices.label: D
choices.text: It shifts the appeal to ethos by showing that Adichie's non-profit, Farafina Trust, shares the same goals as Walker's work with Southern relatives.
